## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning to bench press, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set.
    2. When aiming to touch the bar to your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    3. To touch your lower chest, you will have to keep your elbows tucked to a degree instead of being fully flared out, and the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar to your lower chest. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Once the bar contacts your chest, pause in that bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds) while staying tight.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest.
    3. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
6. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
7. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
8. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
This time-tested exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

## Setting up
1. If you are using an adjustable incline bench, position it in the fully upright setting. Otherwise, proceed to the next step.
    1. You can interchangeably use an adjustable bench that is positioned fully upright or a seated bench that is permanently fixed in an upright position.
    2. Alternatively, you can use a bench that is permanently fixed in a flat position. This will preclude you from resting your back against the bench, but otherwise allow you to use the same technique that the exercise involves when using back support.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and hold them with your palms facing in toward your sides.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
3. Sit down on a seated bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your lower thighs without leaning back onto the back rest.
    1. To move the dumbbells into the proper position, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up against the end of the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
    2. When seated, your elbows should be tucked by your sides with your palms facing in toward each other.
4. March your thighs up one at a time as you lift the dumbbells up near your shoulders with your elbows bent. Simultaneously lean back to situate your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench.
    1. After doing so, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your shoulders with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
5. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling, and maintain this posture throughout your set.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
6. In the starting position, your palms should be facing in toward each other as your upper arms are close to being parallel to each other in front of your body (as opposed to being flared out away from your sides).
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. While keeping your palms facing in toward each other, press the dumbbells upward by driving your elbows upward as you progressively straighten them until your elbows are fully straightened with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your forearms should be in a vertical position throughout the press as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your feet flat on the floor along with your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. Since they will naturally arc back toward your shoulders as you press up, your elbows and dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders at the end of the lifting phase.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner as your elbows progressively bend while simultaneously moving downward until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbells in front of your shoulders.
    1. Lower the dumbbells as far as you can while keeping your wrists in a straight position stacked over your elbows as your forearms remain vertical, which should result in your elbows being lower than your shoulders.
    2. Avoid descending beyond the point at which you can keep your forearms vertical.
    3. If you are using heavy, bulky dumbbells, the dumbbells contacting your shoulders may also determine your end range of the lowering phase.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your dumbbells are by your shoulders following the lowering phase of the last rep, march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to situate the dumbbells on your thighs before standing up with them.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [upper pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a moderate incline near 45 degrees.
    1. Alternatively, you can also use a fixed moderate incline bench for this exercise.
    2. Any bench angle that is greater than 30 degrees but less than 60 degrees can be considered a moderate incline. 
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on the incline bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your lower thighs near your abdomen with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    2. To move the dumbbells into the proper position, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up against the end of the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
3. While marching your thighs up one at a time in quick succession to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench.
    1. Once you are inclined, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
4. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    3. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
5. Flare your elbows moderately out to your sides such that your upper arms form approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    1. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable on your shoulders, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbows out within this range.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Press the dumbbells up by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten them until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press, as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, keep your feet flat on the floor and your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner toward the sides of your chest through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Let your elbows moderately flare out to your sides as they descend and bend enough to keep your wrists stacked above them with vertical forearms. Lifters often find that at least a mild degree of elbow tuck makes this exercise feel most comfortable for the shoulders compared to fully flaring the elbows straight out to the sides.
    2. How far you can lower the dumbbells with vertical forearms will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hands are at least level with their chest.
    3. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom.
    4. There is no need to lower the dumbbells extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.
4. Once you have fully lowered the dumbbells, pause in this bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., about two seconds).
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your dumbbells are by your chest following the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arms in line with your sides to tuck your elbows and position the dumbbells closer to your thighs.
    2. Then march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs before standing up with them.
## Description
With an emphasis on your [upper pec](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), this exercise primarily trains your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) and [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), which are assisted by your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that situates the handles level with your middle-to-upper chest once you are seated.
    1. This is an appropriate starting point for most people, and it can result in somewhat of a range of viable seat heights. Feel free to try out different settings to determine what personally feels best to your body.
    2. The seat height that is ideal for you as an individual should allow your shoulders to feel comfortable throughout the exercise while simultaneously allowing you to feel meaningful tension in your chest.
    3. If the seat is excessively low or high, the exercise may feel awkward and uncomfortable.
2. If your machine allows you to do so, adjust the stoppers (that are positioned under the arms) to a height that allows you to press through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Ideally, position the stoppers as low as you can while being able to grip the handles comfortably with elbows stacked under your wrists in the starting position.
    2. Finding the optimal height may require some trial and error, but you can initially position the stoppers to the bottom setting before performing a couple of warm-up reps without any additional load on the machine. If you experience shoulder discomfort getting into the starting position or are unable to grasp the handles with proper positioning, the stoppers are likely too low, and you should try raising them. Otherwise, the stopper height is appropriate, and you can proceed to add weight to the machine.
    3. Various machine models do not allow you to adjust the stoppers.
3. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
4. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against the back pad.
    1. Your feet should be flat on the ground under your bent knees.
    2. If the back pad is sufficiently tall, rest your head against it. Otherwise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
5. Firmly grasp the horizontally directed handles with an overhand grip. Stack your elbows with your wrists such that your forearms align with the incline angle at which you will press.
    1. In contrast to a purely horizontal seated chest press, where you would position your elbows at the height of your wrists, your elbows should be lower than your wrists during this incline variation. Specifically how much lower you should position your elbows will be affected by the machine model you are using, but machines commonly allow you to press at an angle that is 30-45 degrees beyond horizontal. Consequently, you can initially position your elbows so that your forearms form approximately 30-45 degree angles with the ground. After starting your set, you can allow this forearm angle based on what feels most natural and comfortable with the machine you are using.
    2. Aligning your forearms with the incline angle at which you will press will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare during this exercise, provided that you selected a proper seat height.
    3. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    4. If your machine has sufficiently long handles, you may be able to adjust your grip width with different hand placements. Placing your hands moderately outside shoulder width can work well for many people, but you can try out different grip widths to determine where you personally feel best.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. While keeping your forearms aligned with the angle at which you are pressing, press the handles forward and upward until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows diagonally forward and upward while they progressively straighten.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together, back snugly against the back pad, and feet planted on the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by allowing the handles to move downward and backward in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. Continue keeping your forearms aligned with the angle of your press.
    2. At the end range, you can lightly tap the machine’s arms against the stoppers behind them or stop just before that point.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s weight swing your arms abruptly back in an uncontrolled fashion.
    4. If your machine allows you to train through the full range of motion that your mobility enables, it is normal to feel a painless stretching sensation in your chest and/or the front of your shoulders at the end range. Some machines will limit the range of motion before reaching this point, even when set up ideally.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on a flat exercise bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your upper thighs near your abdomen, with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Position yourself so that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    2. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    3. To move heavy dumbbells efficiently into the proper position, you can initially situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up. Then you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
2. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
4. Flare your elbows moderately out to your sides such that your upper arms form approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    1. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable for your shoulders, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbows out within this range.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbells up by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten them until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press, as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, keep your feet flat on the floor and your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner toward the sides of your chest through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Let your elbows moderately flare out to your sides as they descend and bend enough to keep your wrists stacked above them with vertical forearms. Lifters often find that at least a mild degree of elbow tuck makes this exercise feel most comfortable for the shoulders compared to fully flaring the elbows straight out to the sides.
    2. How far you can lower the dumbbells with vertical forearms will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hands are at least level with their chest.
    3. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom.
    4. There is no need to lower the dumbbells extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.
4. Once you have fully lowered the dumbbells, pause in this bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., about two seconds).
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way you initially set up.
    1. After your dumbbells are by your chest following the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arms in line with your sides to tuck your elbows and position the dumbbells closer to your thighs.
    2. Then march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs before standing up with them.

While not loading your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) as effectively as a barbell bench press, this exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also meaningfully training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md).

## Setting up
You have the option of performing this exercise within a specific incline press station (in which the bench is fused to the rack) or within an adjustable power rack using a mobile incline bench. Specifically how you will set up will differ depending on which equipment you use, so the setup for each approach is described separately. However, the exercise technique is the same for either option. A power rack normally takes longer to prepare than an incline press station, but power racks typically have safety pins in contrast to incline press stations. It is recommended to have a spotter behind you if you will incline press without safety pins.

### Setting up in a power rack

1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a moderate incline near 45 degrees.
    1. Any bench angle that is greater than 30 degrees but less than 60 degrees can be considered a moderate incline.
2. Center the bench within a power rack with the head of the bench in between the posts, where you will adjust the J-hooks.
    1. You should position the bench in a spot that allows your shoulders to be a little in front of the J-hooks’ front edges after setting up the rack and lying down on the bench. After initially estimating which bench placement allows this to occur, you may have to move the bench a bit forward or backward during later steps if you notice that you are not positioned appropriately.
3. Position the J-hooks at a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the incline bench.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking. This can place you in a less stable position to start your set since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
4. After placing the bar on top of the J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of incline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section. Use these reps to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your incline press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins.
    2. Certain power rack models have fairly wide spaces between safety pinholes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your incline press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. It is not ideal if this applies to your rack, but the safety pins can still enhance safety if they are high enough to receive the bar if you dump it forward in the event that you become completely pinned without anyone to assist you.
6. After loading the bar with your intended weight, lie down with your back and head on the incline bench. Firmly place your feet flat on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart with your knees bent and buttocks resting on the seat of the bench.
    1. With the appropriate bench placement, your shoulders should now be a little in front of the front edge of the J-hooks. If your shoulders are under the J-hooks from the bench being situated too far back, you may bump the J-hooks with the bar when pressing the bar up. If the J-hooks are excessively behind your shoulders from the bench being situated too far forward, it can be difficult to unrack the bar.
    2. Based on what feels most stable, you can position your heels directly under your knees with vertical shins, or you can bend your knees a bit beyond this point to position your heels slightly behind your knees with slightly angled shins.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
7. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for bench press variations is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
8. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development.

## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform for pressing.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your upper chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other. Descend until you are able to tap your upper chest lightly with the bar or until you have fully moved through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom, but certain individuals with limited shoulder mobility may not be able to touch their upper chest with the bar without discomfort. If this applies to you, lower the bar as far as you can without discomfort.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath (when viewed from the side) your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set.
    3. Avoid fully flaring your elbows out away from your sides or completely tucking them. The appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on the higher end of the bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your upper thighs near your abdomen. Tuck your elbows close to your sides.
    1. Your palms should be facing inward with the dumbbells as their handles are vertical.
    2. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. 3. Snugly position the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
4. Lean back in a controlled manner to lie down while keeping your elbows tucked by your sides and the dumbbells close to your chest.
    1. Move your torso and arms together as one unit to minimize any shoulder stress when lying down.
    2. Your head and upper back should now be in contact with the bench, along with your buttocks and feet (which remain hooked under the pad). Maintain this body position until you have finished your set.
    3. Strive to have the dumbbells be vertically stacked over your elbows once you are lying down, resulting in your forearms being in a vertical position.

5. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
6. Flare your elbows moderately out to your sides such that your upper arms form approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso.
    1. Keep your forearms vertical while doing so.
    2. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable for your shoulders, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbows out within this range.
    3. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbows are completely tucked by your sides, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your upper arms would form a “T-shape” with your torso.

1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.

2. Press the dumbbells up by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten them until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your wrists stacked over your elbows, which will keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press.

6. If you are able to do so, rock forward in a sit-up motion until you are sitting upright and can place the dumbbells on top of your thighs before unhooking your feet and stepping down with the dumbbells by your sides.

1. At a dual cable station, adjust each cable to be between knee and hip height, connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.

    1. You want to be sufficiently positioned in front of the cables that the cables exert resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.     2. If your shoulder mobility comfortably allows your arms to move further behind your torso than they initially are, you can take another step forward to be able to train through a full range of motion.
    3. In line with the resistance from the cables, your upper arms should form approximately 45-60-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your arms are straight by your sides, and 90 degrees means your arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
4. While mildly bending your knees, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other.
    1. In this position, you should feel stable and balanced.
5. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.

1. While keeping your elbows mildly bent, pull your hands in toward each other as they move diagonally forward and upward until they are close to touching with your arms out in front of your torso.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, your hands should be fairly close to shoulder height.
    2. Keep your chest up throughout the set as you avoid hunching over with your shoulders slouched forward.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your hands to spread apart from each other in a controlled manner as they move diagonally backward and downward in line with the resistance from the cables until you have returned to the starting position with your arms fully spread apart.
    1. At the end of this movement, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulders, but the end range should not be painful.
    2. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to allow their arms to pull back until their elbows are slightly behind the torso, but your shoulder mobility will determine what your individual end range is.

3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and place them on the ground far enough apart that you can sit in between them while being able to reach them.
2. Sit down with your buttocks and the back of your heels on the ground in between the dumbbells with your knees straight and your torso upright.
    1. Based on your preference, you can situate your feet hip-width apart from each other, or you can spread your legs further apart from each other to widen your base of support.
3. Firmly grasp the dumbbells and lift them up near your shoulders with your elbows bent, forearms in a vertical position, and wrists stacked over your elbows while keeping your torso upright.
    1. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
    2. If the dumbbells are light enough to do so, you can lift the dumbbells toward your shoulders by curling them up as you swing your elbows forward.
    3. With heavier dumbbells, you can initially place their handles across your lower thighs near your knees with your palms facing your thighs. Then you can bend your knees and march your thighs up one at a time to help lift the dumbbells up toward your shoulders.
    4. At a certain weight, moving the dumbbells into the starting position can be the limiting factor rather than pressing them up during this variation, so you are not alone if you find it awkward and difficult to use at least moderately heavy loads for this exercise. If you wish to train a dumbbell Z press with heavier loads than you can move into position with this variation, you can select the [single arm dumbbell Z press](Single%20arm%20dumbbell%20Z%20press%202265c6f170d8801388daf25ba257a0c3.md), which allows you to use your free arm to assist with setting up.
4. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, pull your shoulder blades back together to adopt a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
5. Flare your elbows at least moderately out to your sides to a degree that feels comfortable for your shoulders.
    1. When 0 degrees of elbow flare means that your wrists are directly in front of your shoulders with your palms facing each other, and 90 degrees of elbow flare means that your wrists are fully out to your sides with your palms facing straight forward, using about 60-75 degrees of elbow flare is commonly appropriate. In this position, your elbows will point more out to the side than forward, but they will not be fully flared out.
    2. If your shoulders feel comfortable when pressing with a greater degree of elbow flare, you can certainly flare your elbows beyond that point, but some people find that utilizing a closer to moderate degree of elbow flare feels most comfortable.
    3. The handles of the dumbbells should be parallel to your upper arms.

1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.

    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your forearms should be in a vertical position throughout the press as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.

## Setting up
1. Position the J-hooks of a rack to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are lying on the ground with your mouth under the bar.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
2. Load the bar with your intended weight, and have your spotter stand behind the bar if you are using a spotter (which is recommended).
    1. For comfort, you can optionally place a yoga mat on the floor where you will lie.
    2. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, it will be safer and easier to bail if you have at least one pair of full-diameter weight plates (e.g., 45lb (20kg) plates or bumper plates) loaded on the bar.
3. Lie down with your back on the ground, with your legs out in front of you and your knees straight. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell
    1. The back of your heels should be on the ground, about hip-width to shoulder-width apart.
    2. The back of your head and buttocks should be resting on the ground.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
5. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your middle chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other while descending.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists (when viewed from the side). This will keep your forearms close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set.
    2. When bringing the bar toward your middle, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    3. Avoid fully flaring your elbows out away from your sides or completely tucking them. The appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar toward your middle chest.
4. Continue lowering the bar toward your middle chest until the back of your upper arms and elbows contact the ground in a controlled manner.
    1. While you do not have to finish the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you certainly should avoid slamming your arms onto the ground.
    2. You will not be bouncing your arms off the ground.
5. Pause with your upper arms on the ground for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds) while staying tight.
    1. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back, glutes squeezed, and core braced.
    2. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability since this is not a touch-and-go press.
6. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up with explosive intent. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your chest.
    3. Continue keeping your buttocks and the back of your heels firmly planted on the ground.
7. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
8. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
9. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. Lift the dumbbells up near the front of your shoulders with your elbows bent by curling the weights and using momentum from your lower body as needed.
    1. You can perform a cheat curl-like motion to move the dumbbells into position if they are too heavy to lift without momentum. To do so, first sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and simultaneously rocking the dumbbells mildly backward. Then drive your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body while bending your elbows to curl the weights upward while swinging your elbows forward. The hip drive motion, which is similar to the lockout of a deadlift, will bring your torso into a vertical position with your knees straightened.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your shoulders with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, pull your shoulder blades back together, and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    3. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back along with your neck, like when you are normally standing upright.
4. Flare your elbows at least moderately out to your sides to a degree that feels comfortable for your shoulders.
    1. When 0 degrees of elbow flare means that your wrists are directly in front of your shoulders with your palms facing each other, and 90 degrees of elbow flare means that your wrists are fully out to your sides with your palms facing straight forward, using about 60-75 degrees of elbow flare is commonly appropriate. In this position, your elbows will point more out to the side than forward, but they will not be fully flared out.
    2. If your shoulders feel comfortable when pressing with a greater degree of elbow flare, you can certainly flare your elbows beyond that point, but some people find that utilizing a closer to moderate degree of elbow flare feels most comfortable.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes like you are trying to crush a walnut, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core and tightening your glutes throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbells upward by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten your elbows until they are fully straightened with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your forearms should be in a vertical position throughout the press as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your knees and hips straightened as you avoid using your legs to help lift the weights or leaning your torso back via lower back arching.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner as your elbows progressively bend while simultaneously moving outward and downward until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbells by the sides of your shoulders.
    1. Lower the dumbbells as far as you can while keeping your wrists in a straight position stacked over your elbows as your forearms remain vertical, which should result in your elbows being lower than your shoulders.
    2. Avoid descending beyond the point at which you can keep your forearms vertical.
    3. If you are using heavy, bulky dumbbells, the dumbbells contacting your shoulders may also determine your end range of the lowering phase.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your dumbbells are by your shoulders following the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arms in line with your sides to point the backside of your elbows forward, which will result in your palms facing in toward each other.
    2. Then lower the dumbbells to your sides as you straighten your elbows and swing your elbows back by your sides.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
As an alternative to setting up with the bar starting from a rack, you may begin with the bar on the floor and perform a [clean](Clean%201a45c6f170d880bd9cd4e075a346c3ce.md) or [power clean](Power%20clean%201a45c6f170d8804a9e47ea9bf9442850.md) to move the bar into the starting position for your push press. Either option is viable, but cleans and power cleans are distinct exercises described in detail by their own exercise pages.

1. Adjust the J-hooks of a power rack or squat stand to a height that allows you to position the bar on the front of your shoulders and walk out the weight comfortably.
    1. As an initial approximation, you can position the J-hooks a couple of finger widths below the height of your collarbone.
    2. If you find that the J-hook increments available to you are further apart than ideal, it is better to place the J-hooks lower than what is optimal, compared to higher than optimal.
    3. If you are unsure whether you initially positioned the J-hooks to an appropriate height, you can finish setting up without adding plates to the bar, unrack the empty bar, walk it out, and then rerack it. This can allow you to confirm that the J-hooks are appropriate before adding plates to the bar.
    4. If you need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks excessively high.
    5. If you find that a greater than a mild knee bend (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) is required to position the bar on your shoulders, you initially positioned the J-hooks excessively low.
2. Place the barbell on top of the J-hooks, and add weight plates of your desired load to it.
3. Face the center of the bar with approximately a hip-width stance, and grasp the bar with your palms facing down as your hands are mildly outside shoulder width.
    1. For the full clean grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your 2nd-5th fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. Starting with a mildly outside shoulder-width grip is appropriate for many lifters, but you can try out different grip widths over time to determine where you personally feel the best. A proportion of lifters feel strongest with a moderately outside shoulder-width grip.
4. While simultaneously bending your elbows, shallowly bend at your knees and hips with an upright torso to walk under the bar and situate the bar on the front of your shoulders just in front of the base of your neck.
    1. The bar should be resting on your front delts (which are the muscles on the front of your shoulders that attach to the outer aspects of your collarbones) and the outer portions of your collarbones, which together form a shelf with the base of your neck to cradle the bar.
    2. While the bar should be directly in front of your neck, it should not be pressing into your neck to the extent that it feels like it is choking you.
    3. With the appropriate bar positioning, you should feel that the bar is stable on the front of your shoulders if you were to un-rack the bar and walk out without even having your hands around the bar.
    4. If you are not accustomed to push presses or front squats, it is normal to experience discomfort from the pressure the bar places on the front of your shoulders (which may cause some form of skin bruising), but it should not be painful with the correct bar placement.
5. With the bar now on the front of your shoulders, lift your elbows up until your upper arms are parallel to the ground while keeping your fingers wrapped around the bar.
    1. You can perform steps 3 and 4 simultaneously with each other.
    2. The bony prominence on the back of each elbow should now be pointing straight forward as your palms are facing backward.
    3. Your hands can assist in keeping the bar balanced, but the bar should first and foremost be resting on the front of your shoulders without necessarily needing your hands to hold it there.
    4. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your wrists and/or forearm muscles in this position. However, if you find this position to be painful or lack the mobility to achieve it, you can lift your elbows as high as is comfortable to you rather than trying to force yourself into an aggravating position.
    5. You will maintain this arm position and bar position until you start driving the bar up during your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Stand up in a quarter squat-like manner by extending (straightening) your knees and hips.
3. Take a couple of steps backward, and position your feet near hip width apart from each other as your toes are pointing slightly out to the sides (rather than pointing straight ahead).
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to push press effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on hip structure.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling strong and stable when push pressing, which may involve trying out mildly different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
4. Tuck your chin back to move your head behind the bar.
    1. The goal is to move your head out of the bar’s way so that you can press straight upward without hitting your face with the bar.
    2. You can perform this step simultaneously when dipping during the next step.
5. Mildly bend your knees to dip down while maintaining an upright torso position and keeping your chest and elbows up.
    1. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground during this dip phase.
    2. Your knees should track straight forward toward your toes rather than caving inward.
    3. The dip should resemble a quarter squat but without any of the forward trunk lean that occurs when squatting. Your shoulders should remain vertically stacked above your hips by keeping your torso fully upright.
6. Directly after reaching the bottom of your dip, forcibly push through your feet as you rapidly extend (straighten) your knees and hips to generate upward momentum.
    1. The intent of this leg drive phase should be akin to a jump without lifting your feet fully off the ground.
    2. At the end of this drive, you can allow your heels to lift up slightly off the ground while keeping the front of your feet firmly in contact with the ground if a slight heel lift feels natural to you. However, you do not need to think about lifting your heels up intentionally, and you can keep your heels down when learning how to push press if doing so allows you to feel more stable and balanced.
7. Directly after you have finished extending your legs, explosively press the bar upward by forcibly driving your elbows upward. Immediately after the bar clears the top of your head, mildly push your head forward until your ears are close to being under the bar.
    1. To the best of your ability, avoid pushing the bar forward out in front of your shoulders. This can be challenging if you are new to this exercise, since you want to avoid hitting your face with the bar, but initially tucking your chin back appropriately can provide sufficient clearance.
    2. Rather than pushing your head excessively forward during this step, you primarily should be reversing the backward chin tuck/tilt you previously performed.
8. Continue explosively pressing the bar upward until you have fully straightened your elbows with the bar overhead.
    1. At the top, you ideally should be able to draw a straight line down from the bar that passes through your shoulders, hips, knees, and the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    2. Regardless of whether you lifted your heels up off the ground after extending your legs during the leg drive phase, your heels should be flat on the ground with the rest of your feet at the end of the pressing phase.
    3. Throughout the exercise, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back. Your torso should remain vertical rather than leaning back.
    4. While they are presented as different steps for clarity, you should fluidly perform steps 6-8 as a continuous movement.
9. Reverse the movement by tucking your chin back and lowering the bar toward your shoulders in a controlled manner.
    1. If you are using a load that meaningfully exceeds what you can overhead press without leg drive, you may have to lower the bar fairly quickly, even when controlling it to the best of your ability, since your legs cannot assist you until the end.
10. Shallowly bend your knees as you did during step 5 (the dip phase) to help control the weight once the bar reaches your shoulders at the end of the lowering phase.
11. Stand upright with the bar on your shoulders by fully straightening your knees to return to the starting position.
12. Alternate between steps 4-11 until you have completed your set.
13. Following completion of your final rep, walk forward until the bar contacts the back of both J-hooks before bending your knees to lower the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
While developing explosive overhead pressing strength and engaging the [quads](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md) to generate leg drive, this exercise can train  your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md),  and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).
