## Setting up
1. Pick up a long looped elastic band with both hands inside its ends and your thumbs outside.
    1. The band should be situated between the bases of your palms and the bases of your fingers, with one side of the band contacting your palms and the other side of the band contacting the backside of your hands.
    2. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
2. Loop the band around the lower aspect of your upper back (i.e., near the bottom of your shoulder blades) by lifting your arms up and back before making sure the band is resting flat on your back without being twisted.
    1. After doing so, your palms should be facing forward, and the band should be taut in a stable position against your back, where it will not excessively roll up or down.
3. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.
    1. In this “on all fours” position, your elbows should be stacked underneath your shoulders with your arms pointing straight down toward the ground.
    2. As you are setting up, it is common for the band to slide a bit up or down, but the band should remain on your upper back or just below your upper back. At no point should the band slide up to your neck.
4. With your fingers spread somewhat apart from each other, situate your hands mildly outside shoulder width apart from each other.
    1. Your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
    2. You will now be feeling peak resistance from the band.
5. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you, and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest in a controlled manner until it lightly touches the ground.
    1. Let your elbows flare out moderately away from your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you. This commonly results in the upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with the torso (when viewed from above) at the bottom of the push-up. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbows are fully tucked to your sides, remaining shoulder-width the whole rep, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows point straight out to your sides, letting your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ground instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    5. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
    6. Resistance from the band will progressively decrease as you descend.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ground to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
    4. Resistance from the band will progressively increase as you push up.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a moderate incline near 45 degrees.
    1. Alternatively, you can also use a fixed moderate incline bench for this exercise.
    2. Any bench angle that is greater than 30 degrees but less than 60 degrees can be considered a moderate incline. 
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on the incline bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your lower thighs near your abdomen with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    2. To move the dumbbells into the proper position, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up against the end of the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
3. While marching your thighs up one at a time in quick succession to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench.
    1. Once you are inclined, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
4. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    3. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
5. In the starting position, your palms should face each other, and your elbows should be tucked fairly close to your sides.
    1. Keeping your elbows tucked to the extent that your upper arms form near 30-degree angles with your torso (when viewed from above) is generally appropriate.
    2. If you completely tuck your elbows, you will likely reduce how effectively this exercise can train your chest compared to using a mild degree of elbow flare.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbells upward by driving your elbows upward as you progressively straighten them until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your palms facing each other as you avoid notably flaring your elbows out away from your sides, like you otherwise do with a standard dumbbell bench press.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press, as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    3. Keep your feet flat on the floor and your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench throughout the exercise. 
    4. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
3. While keeping your elbows tucked fairly close to your sides, reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. While they descend, let your elbows bend enough to keep your wrists stacked above them with vertical forearms.
    2. Strive to finish with your upper arms forming close to 30-degree angles with your torso.
    3. How far you can lower the dumbbells with vertical forearms will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hands are at least level with their chest.
    4. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders at the bottom.
    5. There is no need to lower the dumbbells extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your dumbbells are by your chest following the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arms in line with your sides to tuck your elbows and position the dumbbells closer to your thighs.
    2. Then march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs before standing up with them.

## Setting up
In addition to situating a mobile seated or adjustable bench within a power rack or squat stand, you have the option of setting up this exercise within a seated overhead press station in which a seated bench is fused to a rack. The exercise technique is the same for either option, but the set-up details differ depending on which equipment you use, so each set-up is described separately.

### **Setting up a power rack or squat stand**

1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a 90-degree angle, or approach a mobile exercise bench that is permanently fixed with an upright backrest.
    1. If you have access to one, a seated bench with a backrest that does not reach your head is ideal because it can allow you to move your head back away from the bar during the exercise.
2. Place the bench centered within a power rack or squat stand with the backrest in between the uprights, where you will adjust the J-hooks.
    1. The proper placement of the bench should allow you to unrack the bar comfortably without bumping the J-hooks with the bar during your set. This may require some trial and error.
    2. If the backrest is situated in front of where the bar will start, you will have to reach back behind your head to unrack the bar, which requires greater than typical shoulder mobility.
    3. If the backrest is situated too far behind where the bar will start, you may bump the J-hooks with the bar when pressing the bar up.
3. Position the J-hooks at a height that will allow you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are seated on the bench.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks without having to shrug your shoulders up.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the top of the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If neither of the two J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little lower than optimal, since it may not be feasible to unrack the bar with proper positioning if the J-hooks are excessively high.
    4. You may have to try out different J-hook heights to determine which setting is best for you.
4. Place the bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks.
    1. Initially leave the bar unloaded to check that the bench and J-hooks are positioned correctly.
5. Sit down with your buttocks and back in contact with the bench. Firmly place your feet flat on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart with your knees bent.
    1. Your hips should be fully back on the seat.
    2. If your bench’s backrest reaches your head, rest your head against it as well.
6. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
7. Reach up overhead and firmly grasp the bar with your hands slightly outside shoulder width as your palms are facing forward.
    1. Situating your index fingers directly outside the outer aspects of your shoulders is generally an effective approach, but what is personally your ideal grip may be a bit wider or closer. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
8. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of overhead press reps with the form described under the exercise technique section prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
    1. If you cannot comfortably unrack the bar and avoid bumping the J-hooks during these reps, adjust your bench placement and/or J-hook height and repeat this step until you can do so.
9. If you have access to adjustable safety pins, position the pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase.
    1. This will entail placing the pins just below the height of your upper chest (when seated) if you can comfortably lower the bar to your upper chest.
10. Add plates of your desired load to the bar, and repeat steps 5-7 before commencing your working set.

### **Setting up an overhead press station**

1. Place the bar on top of the J-hooks behind the seat that will allow you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are seated on the bench.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks without having to shrug your shoulders up.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the top of the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. You may have to try out different J-hook heights to determine which setting is best for you, so you can initially leave the bar unloaded to check if you can comfortably unrack the bar.
2. Sit down with your buttocks and back in contact with the bench. Firmly place your feet flat on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart with your knees bent.
    1. Your hips should be fully back on the seat.
    2. If your bench’s backrest reaches your head, rest your head against it as well.
3. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
4. Reach up overhead and firmly grasp the bar with your hands slightly outside shoulder width as your palms are facing forward.
    1. Situating your index fingers directly outside the outer aspects of your shoulders is generally an effective approach, but what is personally your ideal grip may be a bit wider or closer. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of overhead press reps with the form described under the exercise technique section prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
    1. If you cannot comfortably unrack the bar, you can situate the bar on a different pair of J-hooks and try again.
    2. If you lack the shoulder mobility to unrack the bar from the J-hooks behind the bench, you can situate the bar on top of the J-hooks in front of you that are slightly above shoulder height (when seated). To unrack the bar from these J-hooks, you could initially scoot forward on the seat until your shoulders are close to being under the bar, lift the bar up off the J-hooks, and scoot back to the back rest. Note that this approach to unrack the bar from the front J-hooks differs from the standard unrack method described in the exercise technique section.
6. Add plates of your desired load to the bar, and repeat steps 2-4 before commencing your working set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position and throughout the exercise, your feet should be firmly planted on the ground, while your buttocks and upper back are snugly contacting the bench.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward until it is just in front of the front edge of the J-hooks. Hold the bar in this position for a moment.
    1. Maintain your “proud chest” posture to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar in a controlled manner until you are able to tap near your upper chest lightly with the bar, or until you have fully moved through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. If your bench permits you to do so, tuck your chin back to move your face away from the bar and allow you to lower the bar in a close to fully vertical path. If your bench restricts your head, you will have to move the bar slightly forward to avoid hitting your head. Try not to move the bar any further in front of you than is required to clear your head.
    2. Keep your elbows mostly stacked under the bar rather than meaningfully tracking in front of the bar or behind. However, you can allow your elbows to track slightly forward in front of the bar at the bottom of the rep if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    3. Your elbows should neither be fully flared, such that they are pointing completely out to your sides, nor should they be fully tucked, such that they are pointing directly forward. Aligning your elbows close to directly under the bar will naturally promote the appropriate balance between elbow flare and elbow tuck.
    4. Most lifters can comfortably lower the bar to their upper chest, but certain individuals with limited shoulder mobility may not be able to touch their chest with the bar without discomfort. If this applies to you, lower the bar as far as you can without discomfort.
    5. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up overhead until your elbows are fully straightened.
    1. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    2. Keep your hip bones snugly against the bench as you avoid scooting your hips forward or excessively arching your lower back.
    3. Continue keeping your elbows mostly stacked under the bar.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a high incline with an angle that is at least 60 degrees but less than 90 degrees.
    1. If your bench lacks a high incline setting, you can alternatively select the [45° incline barbell press](45%C2%B0%20incline%20barbell%20press%201a05c6f170d880198e1aceac084f30eb.md) or [seated barbell overhead press](Seated%20barbell%20overhead%20press%201a05c6f170d8803c86effb7acb6ade56.md) as a substitution that you can perform with your bench.
2. Place the bench centered within a power rack with the head of the bench in between the posts, where you will adjust the J-hooks.
    1. You should position the bench in a spot that allows your shoulders to be a little in front of the J-hooks after setting up the rack and lying down on the bench.
3. Position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the incline bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. Then place the bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the top of the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater than ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of incline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your incline press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins.
    2. Certain power rack models have fairly wide spaces between safety pinholes that may result in the highest setting not restricting your incline press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. It is not ideal if this applies to your rack, but the safety pins can still enhance safety if they are high enough to receive the bar if you dump it forward, in case you are completely pinned without anyone to assist you.
6. After loading the bar with your intended weight, lie down with your buttocks, back, and head on the incline bench. Firmly place your feet flat on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart with your knees bent.
    1. With the appropriate bench placement, your shoulders should be a little in front of the front edge of the J-hooks. If your shoulders are under the J-hooks from the bench being situated too far back, you may bump the J-hooks with the bar when pressing the bar up. If the J-hooks are excessively behind your shoulders from the bench being situated too far forward, it can be difficult to unrack the bar.
    2. Based on what feels most stable, you can position your heels directly under your knees with vertical shins, or you can bend your knees a bit beyond this point to position your heels slightly behind your knees with slightly angled shins.
    3. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
    4. If you are not training with safety pins that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
7. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for bench press variations is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
8. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your upper chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other. Descend until you are able to tap your upper chest or collarbone lightly with the bar or until you have fully moved through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom, but certain individuals with limited shoulder mobility may not be able to touch their upper chest or collarbone with the bar without discomfort. If this applies to you, lower the bar as far as you can without discomfort.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists (when viewed from the side). This will keep your forearms close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set and naturally promote the appropriate balance between elbow flare and elbow tuck.
    3. Avoid fully flaring your elbows out away from your sides or completely tucking them. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, set the arms so that their ends are about the length of your wingspan apart from each other.

    1. You want to be sufficiently positioned in front of the cables that the cables exert resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise. This will involve your hands being in front of the cable pulleys with tension still present from the cables when you are fully spread apart in the starting position of each rep.
4. While mildly bending your knees, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other.

    2. Keep your chest up throughout the set as you avoid hunching over with your shoulders slouched forward.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your hands to spread apart from each other in a controlled manner as they move diagonally backward and upward in line with the resistance from the cables until you have returned to the starting position with your arms fully spread apart.
    1. At the end of this movement, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulders, but the end range should not be painful.
    2. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to allow their arms to pull back until their elbows are slightly behind the torso, but your shoulder mobility will determine what your individual end range is.

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell, and sit down on a flat exercise bench while lifting the dumbbell onto your upper thigh near your abdomen with your palm facing inward.
    1. Position yourself so that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    2. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    3. To move the dumbbell into the proper position, you can situate the dumbbell on the front of your thigh while standing up against the end of the bench, and you can rest it on your thighs while sitting down.
2. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbell back toward your chest with your elbow bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. Even though only one thigh will be initially against the weight, marching both thighs up can help you rock your torso back.
    2. Throughout the exercise, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting on your thigh or chest.
    3. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training first.
    4. Once you are lying down, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    5. You should now be holding the dumbbell right by your chest with your forearm in a vertical position, and your wrist stacked over your elbow as the handle of the dumbbell is parallel to your upper arm.
    6. You should be holding the dumbbell on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a mostly straight wrist that allows for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
4. Flare your elbow moderately out to your side such that your upper arm forms an approximately 45-75-degree angle with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arm is tucked by your side, and 90 degrees means your upper arm forms half of a “T-shape” with your torso).
    1. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable for your shoulders, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbow out within this range.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Press the dumbbell up by driving your elbow upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten it until your arm is directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbow, keep your forearm in a vertical position throughout the press, as your wrist and dumbbell remain stacked over your elbow.
    2. Throughout your set, keep your feet flat on the floor and your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbell should be situated vertically over your shoulder.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner toward the side of your chest through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Let your elbow moderately flare out to your side as it descends and bends enough to keep your wrist stacked above it with a vertical forearm. Lifters often find that at least a mild degree of elbow tuck makes this exercise feel most comfortable for the shoulder compared to fully flaring the elbow straight out to the side.
    2. How far you can lower the dumbbell with a vertical forearm will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hand is at least level with their chest.
    3. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of the shoulder at the bottom.
    4. There is no need to lower the dumbbell extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. It can be awkward to transfer the weight to your other hand with proper positioning while lying down if you are using a weight that is at least fairly heavy to you, so you can initially return to an upright position to transfer the weight before resetting to train your other side.
5. After the dumbbell is by your chest following the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arm in line with your side to tuck your elbow and position the dumbbell closer to your thigh.
    1. Once you are in this position, you can optionally reach across your body with your free hand to place it around your hand holding the dumbbell for extra stability.
6. March your thighs up until they are close to being vertical, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbell on your upper thigh before standing up with the dumbbell.
7. Place the dumbbell onto the bench, and pick it up with your other side before repeating the exercise with that side.

2. Position your hands by the front of your outer thighs and direct your palms so that they are facing backward.

    1. Your mobility will affect how high you are comfortably able to lift the dumbbells, and there is no need to force your shoulders into a range that provokes any discomfort.
    2. While different individuals may be able to lift higher up and others not quite as high, people often can lift their upper arms until they are close to parallel to the ground for a comfortable and effective range of motion.
    3. The dumbbells should remain close to your torso throughout the exercise as they move vertically.

    1. At the end of the lowering phase, the dumbbells should be situated in front of your thighs.

## Setting up
1. Position the safety pins of a power rack slightly below the height of your shoulders when you are seated on the ground with an upright torso.
    1. Ideally, the pins should be set to a height that is high enough to pick up the bar (once it is on the pins) comfortably, but low enough so that the pins do not restrict your pressing range of motion.
    2. Certain power racks have fairly wide spaces between safety pinholes that can make it difficult to perform this exercise. For some racks, the lowest pin height that would not meaningfully restrict your pressing range of motion may be too low to pick up the bar comfortably. If this is the case for you, you can set the pins to the higher setting and perform this exercise through a somewhat reduced range of motion. Alternatively, you can position the pins to the lower setting and place J-hooks at the higher setting, where you would set the barbell and sit down just far enough away that the J-hooks will not interfere with your bar path during the press. With this approach, it could be challenging to unrack the bar independently since you will have to reach out in front of you. Consequently, you can have a partner assist you in lifting the bar off the J-hooks and positioning it over your upper chest if you are using a load that you cannot unrack by yourself.
2. Symmetrically place a barbell onto the middle of the safety pins and load it with your desired weight.
3. Sit down on the ground with an upright torso as the center of the barbell is directly in front of your chest. Your knees should be straight with the back of your heels on the ground.
    1. You can determine how wide apart you position your legs based on your preference. Spreading your legs fairly wide apart may assist with maintaining your balance, but you can alternatively position your legs closer together if you wish to do so.
    2. Rather than being slouched forward, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with your hands slightly outside shoulder width as your palms are facing away from you.
    1. Situating your index fingers directly outside the outer aspects of your shoulders is generally an effective approach, but what is personally your ideal grip may be a bit wider or closer. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Position your elbows under the bar and just slightly in front of it. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists stacked under the bar.
    1. This step can be performed simultaneously with step 4.
    2. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    3. Your forearms should now be close to a vertical position when viewed from the front.
    4. From this position, your elbows should be reasonably close to being flared 45 degrees out from your sides. 0 degrees of flare would mean your elbows are directly aligned with your shoulders when viewed from the front. 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows are directly aligned with your shoulders when viewed from the side.
6. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension that provides a stable platform from which to press.
2. Tuck or tilt your chin back to move your head behind the bar.
    1. The goal is to move your head out of the bar’s way so that you can press straight upward without hitting your face with the bar.
3. While keeping your torso upright, press the bar upward with as close to a straight bar path as you can perform.
    1. To the best of your ability, avoid pushing the bar forward out in front of your shoulders. This can be challenging if you are new to this exercise, since you want to avoid hitting your face with the bar. You can still meaningfully increase your strength and grow muscle if the bar drifts a bit forward, but strive to minimize any forward bar motion as well as you can for an efficient press.
    2. Keep the back of your heels firmly planted on the ground throughout your set.
    3. Avoid leaning back at any point during this exercise. If you start doing so, it can be difficult to stop your torso from tipping backward and falling to the ground.
4. Immediately after the bar clears the top of your head, mildly push your head forward until your ears are close to being under the bar.
    1. Rather than pushing your head excessively forward, you primarily should be reversing the backward chin tuck/tilt you previously performed.
5. Finish the press with your elbows straightened as the bar is overhead.
    1. You should be able to draw a straight line down from the bar that passes through your shoulders and hips.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath during your set, you can breathe after locking out the weight overhead. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to lowering the bar.
6. Reverse the movement by tucking your chin back and lowering the bar toward your collarbone in a controlled manner.
    1. Continue keeping your torso fully upright.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down.
    3. If the safety pins are at the height of your collarbone or slightly higher, lower the bar as close as you can to your collarbone without bumping the pins.
7. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down onto the safety pins.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. Lift the dumbbells up near the front of your shoulders with your elbows bent by curling the weights and using momentum from your lower body as needed.
    1. You can perform a cheat curl-like motion to move the dumbbells into position if they are too heavy to lift without momentum. To do so, first sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and simultaneously rocking the dumbbells mildly backward. Then drive your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body while bending your elbows to curl the weights upward while swinging your elbows forward. The hip drive motion, which is similar to the lockout of a deadlift, will bring your torso into a vertical position with your knees straightened.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your shoulders with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, pull your shoulder blades back together, and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    3. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back along with your neck, like when you are normally standing upright.
4. In the starting position, your palms should be facing in toward each other as your upper arms are close to being parallel to each other in front of your body (as opposed to being flared out away from your sides).
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes like you are trying to crush a walnut, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core and tightening your glutes throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. While keeping your palms facing in toward each other, press the dumbbells upward by driving your elbows upward as you progressively straighten them until your elbows are fully straightened with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your forearms should be in a vertical position throughout the press as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your knees and hips straightened as you avoid using your legs to help lift the weights or leaning your torso back via lower back arching.
    3. Since they will naturally arc back toward your shoulders as you press up, your elbows and dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders at the end of the lifting phase.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner as your elbows progressively bend while simultaneously moving downward until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbells in front of your shoulders.
    1. Lower the dumbbells as far as you can while keeping your wrists in a straight position stacked over your elbows as your forearms remain vertical, which should result in your elbows being lower than your shoulders.
    2. Avoid descending beyond the point at which you can keep your forearms vertical.
    3. If you are using heavy, bulky dumbbells, the dumbbells contacting your shoulders may also determine your end range of the lowering phase.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your dumbbells are by your shoulders following the lowering phase of the last rep, lower the dumbbells to your sides as you straighten your elbows and swing your elbows back by your sides.

Gripping the bar with your hands near these two points can be an appropriate starting grip width for many people. However, the specific grip width that is best to use for this exercise will vary among different individuals. To personally find your ideal placement, feel free to try out different hand widths over time while noting how your shoulders feel. The hand placement that is best for you should feel comfortable on your shoulders while enabling you to train through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility permits.
    3. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Slightly bend your knees, and step forward to situate your collarbone or upper chest directly under the bar. Simultaneously, position your elbows under the bar. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists stacked under the bar.
    1. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Relative to when you overhead press to the front with a closer grip, which normally involves a greater degree of elbow tuck (pointing forward), your elbows should naturally be flared out (pointing out to the side) to a greater extent during this variation.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
2. Fully stand upright while holding the bar.
    1. With your knees straightened, the bar should now be above the tops of the J-hooks.
3. Take a couple of steps backward and set your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable to you, you can point your toes straight ahead or rotate them slightly out to the side.
4. Squeeze your glutes and quads from now until you finish your last rep.
    1. This will create a stable platform from which to press.
5. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Avoid leaning back into an excessively arched position.
6. Press the bar upward just in front of your face without hitting your face with the bar.
    1. In contrast to a standard overhead press, you will not be meaningfully moving your head during the Bradford press. Since you are not tucking your chin back, you will have to arc the bar slightly forward to clear your face instead of pressing straight up. This is an inefficient bar path for pressing maximal weights, but pressing maximal weights is not the goal for this variation.
    2. Do not lean back any further or excessively arch your lower back. Your lower back should stay locked in the same position.
7. Once the bar clears the top of your head, drive your elbows back to move the bar back behind your head.
    1. Your elbows should remain stacked under the bar.

However, you can still be pressing the bar mildly upward as you move it back, resulting in a smooth arcing motion as opposed to the bar path forming a 90-degree angle from completely stopping any vertical motion during this step.
8. Lower the bar behind your head through the range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.

Training this exercise over time may progressively improve your shoulder mobility and gradually permit you to descend through a greater range, but there is no need to force yourself into a position that currently does not feel right for your shoulders.
    3. With sufficient shoulder mobility, you should not have to push your head meaningfully forward to avoid scraping your head or neck with the bar. However, you can slightly tuck your chin toward your chest if you wish to do so for additional clearance. ## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, you will find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench as your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor approximately shoulder width apart from each other.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. You can similarly decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) as your hands are well outside shoulder width, with the bar on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A wide grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be near twice your shoulder width, and this involves somewhat of a range of grip widths, so you can feel free to try out mildly different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. What is personally considered a wide grip to you can also be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard bench press, which you can somewhat widen to individualize your wide grip. For instance, for your wide grip, you can place your index finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your little finger when performing your standard bench press.
    3. For stability, your thumbs should be wrapped around the bar from the opposite side of your other fingers, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands in contrast to if you positioned your thumbs on the same side of your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip that is also called a “suicide grip”).

Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. ## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together as you avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them naturally to flare out away from each other while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists rather than letting your elbows track in front of your wrists (closer to your hips) or behind them. Maintaining this alignment as you touch the bar to your lower chest will promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare.
    2. Near the bottom of the rep, the appropriate amount of elbow flare should result in your upper arms forming reasonably close to 75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are touching your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    3. Compared to a closer grip bench press, your elbows should flare out further away from your sides during a wide grip bench press.
    4. When aiming to touch the bar to your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    5. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up as you progressively drive your elbows upward and inward while straightening them until you have returned to the starting position with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is situated above your shoulders.
    1. To finish with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest, the bar will now arc slightly backward as you lift it up.
    2. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows mildly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a low incline with an angle up to 30 degrees.
    1. If your bench can be adjusted to a moderate incline near 45 degrees but does not have a low incline setting, you can alternatively select the moderate incline barbell bench press from this database.
2. Place the bench centered within a power rack with the head of the bench in between the posts, where you will adjust the J-hooks.
    1. You should position the bench in a spot that allows your mouth to be directly under the barbell after setting up the rack and lying down on the bench.
3. Position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the incline bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. Then place the bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of incline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your incline press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins.
    2. Certain power rack models have fairly wide spaces between safety pinholes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your incline press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. It is not ideal if this applies to your rack, but the safety pins can still enhance safety if they are high enough to receive the bar if you dump it forward, in case you are completely pinned without anyone to assist you.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and lie down with your back and head on the incline bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Firmly situate the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    2. Based on what feels most stable, you can position your heels directly under your knees with vertical shins, or you can bend your knees a bit beyond this point to position your heels slightly behind your knees with slightly angled shins.
    3. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
    4. If you are not training with safety pins that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
7. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for bench press variations is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
8. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development.

## Setting up
1. At a cable station, adjust the cable to be near the height of your lower chest, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at the weight stack.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you will also position the arm furthest back such that it is directed out to the side of the machine.
    2. Dual cable stations that have their two weight stacks facing each other (often with a pull-up in between them) normally lack adjustable arms.
2. While standing with the side of one shoulder facing the cable station, reach to the side and grasp the handle firmly with the hand closer to the cable station as your palm is facing forward.
    1. Throughout the exercise, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side or on top of your hip bone.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the handle since that is the side you will be training first.
3. Step out to the side away from the cable station until you feel tension from the cable (as the weight stack separates) while keeping your arm aligned with the cable.
    1. In this position, your arm should be outstretched away from your side such that your arm and torso resemble half of a “T-shape.”
4. Pivot your feet about 45 degrees away from the cable station as you keep the center of your hips and chest facing the same direction, while allowing the cable’s tension to pull your arm back behind your torso through a range that your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. You will now be facing near a 135-degree angle away from the cable station, which will allow you to train through a full range of motion.
    2. How far you can position your arm behind your torso will be influenced by your individual shoulder mobility.
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulder in this position, but it should not be painful.
    4. Throughout the exercise, avoid letting the cable’s resistance twist your trunk toward the cable, which would result in your chest facing a different direction than the center of your hips.
5. While mildly bending your knees and your elbow, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other.
    1. In this position, you should feel stable and balanced.
6. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow mildly bent and your torso stationary, sweep your arm forward and inward in an arcing motion until your arm is outstretched in front of your chest.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, your hand should be close to chest height, and your arm should be close to facing the same direction as your chest.
    2. Keep your chest up throughout the set as you avoid hunching over with your shoulders slouched forward.
    3. As a cue to avoid letting the cable twist your torso, you can think about imaginary laser beams shooting out from your breastbone and where you would wear a belt buckle above your hips. Throughout the set, the lasers from your breastbone and belt buckle should be facing the same direction as they normally would when standing upright without being twisted toward either side.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your arm to sweep out to the side and back toward the cable station in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your elbow behind your torso through the range of motion your shoulder mobility allows.
    1. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to allow their arm to pull back until the elbow is at least slightly behind the torso, but your shoulder mobility will determine what your individual end range is.
    2. Continue keeping your torso stationary and your elbow mildly bent, as the movement comes from shoulder motion rather than elbow motion or trunk twisting motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

    2. How far you can lower the dumbbell with a vertical forearm will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hand is at least level with their chest.
    3. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of the shoulder at the bottom.
    4. There is no need to lower the dumbbell extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. It can be awkward to transfer the weight to your other hand with proper positioning while lying down if you are using a weight that is at least fairly heavy to you, so you can initially return to an upright position to transfer the weight before resetting to train your other side.
5. After the dumbbell is by your chest following the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arm in line with your side to tuck your elbow and position the dumbbell closer to your thigh.
    1. Once you are in this position, you can optionally reach across your body with your free hand to place it around your hand holding the dumbbell for extra stability.
6. March your thighs up, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbell on your upper thigh before standing up with the dumbbell.
7. Place the dumbbell onto the seat of the bench, and pick it up with your other side before repeating the exercise with that side.
