## Setting up
1. Follow the set-up instructions for the [single arm kettlebell clean](Single%20arm%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d880ba964ffcbd097f377d.md), and perform the lifting phase of the [single arm kettlebell clean](Single%20arm%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d880ba964ffcbd097f377d.md) described in steps 1-5 of its exercise technique instructions.
    1. After doing so, you should now be holding the kettlebell in the front rack position. This involves situating it in front of your shoulder with your elbow bent slightly in front of your ribcage, palm facing in toward your other side, and the weight resting on your forearm, which is mostly vertically with your wrist slightly closer to the midline of your body than your elbow. The handle should also be diagonally contacting your palm, such that the side of the handle by your thumb is angled mildly higher than the side of the handle by your little finger.
    2. As an alternative to cleaning the kettlebell, you can curl it up while using your free hand to help lift the weight up under its base and guide the kettlebell into the same front rack position described above. Initially grasp the handle with your little finger closer to one of the corner horns than your thumb to help the handle rest diagonally across your palm in the front rack position. Feel free to perform a cheat curl-like motion where you initially generate some momentum by swinging the weight mildly backward with a straight elbow before swinging your elbow forward while curling it and assisting with your free hand. This is a less technically complicated means of moving the kettlebell into the front rack, but it is not as efficient when using a heavy weight for lifters who are proficient with cleaning the kettlebell.
    3. Once the kettlebell is in the front rack position, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the kettlebell.
2. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, keep your chest up in a “proud chest” posture, rather than letting your shoulders and upper back round forward into a hunched position.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain its natural curvature like when you are normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes like you are trying to crush a walnut. Simultaneously, brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue keeping your glutes tightened and core braced throughout your set.
2. While simultaneously flaring your elbow out away from your side and directing your palm forward, press the kettlebell upward.
    1. Strive to finish with your arm directed straight up toward the ceiling with your elbow fully straightened, and your biceps by your ear.
    2. While your forearm starts slightly angled in the front rack position, it should otherwise remain essentially in a vertical position with your elbow stacked under your wrist throughout the press.
    3. Rather than turning the exercise into a segmented movement where you flare your elbow fully outward and then drive it upward, aim to have the outward elbow flare fluidly occur while pressing up. 
    4. Continue keeping your knees and wrist straight as the kettlebell contacts your forearm throughout the set.
    5. Avoid leaning your torso back via lower back arching, which may be more likely to occur if you relax your abs or glutes.
    6. Allow your shoulder blade to move naturally.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the kettlebell in a controlled manner as you let your elbow bend while descending and arcing forward toward the front rack position. 
    1. Finish with your wrist in front of your shoulder, palm facing in toward your side, and elbow bent slightly in front of your ribcage.
    2. While keeping it vertical throughout most of this step, allow your forearm to angle slightly inward at the end, resulting in your straight wrist being slightly closer to your midline than your elbow.
    3. There is no need to lower the kettlebell very slowly, but you should avoid letting it drop down abruptly in an uncontrolled fashion.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. After the kettlebell is in the front rack position after your final rep, set it down in the opposite manner to how you initially lifted it into position.
    2. If you initially cleaned the kettlebell, you can let the kettlebell fall forward as you swing your arm down while straightening your elbow and hinging at your hips to absorb the force of the lowering phase.
    3. If you initially curled the kettlebell up with assistance from your free hand, you can similarly use your free hand to help guide the kettlebell down while letting your working arm’s elbow straighten in a controlled manner.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. If you are using an adjustable incline bench, position it in the fully upright setting. Otherwise, proceed to the next step.
    1. You can interchangeably use an adjustable bench that is positioned fully upright or a seated bench that is permanently fixed in an upright position.
    2. Alternatively, you can use a bench that is permanently fixed in a flat position. This will preclude you from resting your back against the bench, but otherwise allow you to use the same technique that the exercise involves when using back support.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and hold them with your palms facing in toward your sides.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
3. Sit down on a seated bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your lower thighs without leaning back onto the back rest.
    1. To move the dumbbells into the proper position, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up against the end of the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
    2. When seated, your elbows should be tucked by your sides with your palms facing in toward each other.
4. March your thighs up one at a time as you lift the dumbbells up near your shoulders with your elbows bent. Simultaneously lean back to situate your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench.
    1. After doing so, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your shoulders with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
5. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling, and maintain this posture throughout your set.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
6. Flare your elbows at least moderately out to your sides to a degree that feels comfortable for your shoulders.
    1. When 0 degrees of elbow flare means that your wrists are directly in front of your shoulders with your palms facing each other, and 90 degrees of elbow flare means that your wrists are fully out to your sides with your palms facing straight forward, using about 60-75 degrees of elbow flare is commonly appropriate. In this position, your elbows will point more out to the side than forward, but they will not be fully flared out.
    2. If your shoulders feel comfortable when pressing with a greater degree of elbow flare, you can certainly flare your elbows beyond that point, but some people find that utilizing a closer to moderate degree of elbow flare feels most comfortable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbells upward by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten your elbows until they are fully straightened with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your forearms should be in a vertical position throughout the press as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your feet flat on the floor along with your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner as your elbows progressively bend while simultaneously moving outward and downward until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbells by the sides of your shoulders.
    1. Lower the dumbbells as far as you can while keeping your wrists in a straight position stacked over your elbows as your forearms remain vertical, which should result in your elbows being lower than your shoulders.
    2. Avoid descending beyond the point at which you can keep your forearms vertical.
    3. If you are using heavy, bulky dumbbells, the dumbbells contacting your shoulders may also determine your end range of the lowering phase.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your dumbbells are by your shoulders following the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arms in line with your sides to tuck your elbows and position the dumbbells closer to your thighs.
    2. Then march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to situate the dumbbells on your thighs before standing up with them.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable decline bench at a decline angle of 15-30 degrees.
    1. As the decline angle becomes more pronounced, transitioning into the starting position can become more awkward, so a relatively mild decline is typically appropriate.
    2. Utilizing an approximately 15-degree decline angle is recommended if you are new to this exercise.
    3. Some adjustable benches have a mild decline setting along with incline settings, but lack a pad to secure your feet. Using a decline bench with a foot/ankle pad is recommended for stability during this exercise.
2. Pick up one dumbbell on the side you will be training, and sit down on the higher end of the bench while lifting the dumbbell onto your upper thigh.
    1. The directions describe how to assume the starting position for this exercise independently, but you can alternatively have a spotter transfer the dumbbell to you after you lie down on the bench, which can be ideal if you are using a heavy dumbbell.
3. Snugly position the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
4. On the side firmly holding the dumbbell, tuck your elbow by your side. Tightly wrap your free hand around the hand holding the dumbbell.
5. Lean back in a controlled manner to lie down while keeping your elbow tucked by your side and the dumbbell close to your torso.
    1. While using both arms to help control weight, move your torso and arms together as one unit to minimize any shoulder stress when lying down.
    2. Your head and upper back should now be in contact with the bench, along with your buttocks and feet (which remain hooked under the pad). Maintain this body position until you have finished your set.
    3. Strive to have the dumbbell be vertically stacked over your elbow once you are lying down, resulting in your forearm being in a vertical position.
6. Unwrap your outer hand, not directly holding the dumbbell, and move it into a comfortable position away from the weight, such as resting on your torso.
    1. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training.
    2. You should be holding the dumbbell on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a mostly straight wrist that allows for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
7. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
8. Flare your elbow moderately out to your side such that your upper arm forms near a 45-75-degree angle with your torso.
    1. Keep your forearm vertical while doing so.
    2. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable for your shoulder, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbow out within this range.
    3. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbow is completely tucked by your side, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your upper arm would form half of a “T-shape” with your torso.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbell upward until your elbow is fully straightened with your arm directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. It may help to focus on driving your elbow upward and inward.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulder and elbow, your forearm should be in a vertical position throughout the press. This will result in your wrist and dumbbell remaining stacked over your elbow.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbell should be situated vertically over your shoulder.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner. Move through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits while keeping your wrist stacked over your elbow.
    1. Let your elbow flare out moderately away from your side so that your upper arm forms an approximately 45-75-degree angle with your torso at the bottom. Lifters often find that at least a mild degree of elbow tuck makes this exercise feel most comfortable for the shoulder compared to fully flaring the elbow straight out to the side.
    2. People commonly can lower the weight until their elbows are somewhat lower than their shoulders while keeping their forearms vertical, but your specific end range will be determined by your individual shoulder mobility. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulder at your end range.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the entire movement.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. It can be awkward to transfer the weight to your other hand with proper positioning while lying down if you are using a weight that is at least fairly heavy to you, so you can initially return to an upright position to transfer the weight before resetting to train your other side.
5. After finishing the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arm in line with your side to tuck your elbow and position the dumbbell closer to your torso.
6. Wrap your free hand around the hand holding the dumbbell for additional stability.
7. If you are able to do so, rock forward in a sit-up motion until you are sitting upright and can place the dumbbell on top of your thigh before grasping the dumbbell with your opposite side and repeating the exercise.
    1. This maneuver is only feasible if you have the core strength to perform a sit-up with the weight you selected. Compared to if you decline pressed two dumbbells simultaneously, repositioning yourself will be easier with this single arm variation due to the lighter total load.
    2. If you cannot sit up with the weight, you can have a spotter take the dumbbell from your hand while you are lying down on the bench. This option can be ideal if you are using a heavy weight, but it naturally requires another person. When using this approach, make sure to communicate what you want your spotter to do before starting the set.
    3. Alternatively, you can set the dumbbell directly onto the floor while still lying down before picking up the weight with your other side and resetting. Compared to the other options, this approach potentially may involve a higher risk of injury if you move your shoulder into a disadvantaged position with a heavy weight, but you can assist with your free hand. Relative to setting the weight down under control, dumping the weight forward may be less demanding on your shoulder, but it involves the risk of having a dumbbell ricochet and potentially injuring someone nearby or damaging equipment. For these reasons, it is recommended to use a spotter or to sit up with the dumbbell when possible.

## Setting up
1. With a cable station positioned to its lowest height, connect an attachment with a straight bar body, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down or hinge at your hips with extended elbows.
3. Grasp the bar with approximately a shoulder-width grip and an overhand grip (AKA reverse grip) such that your palms are directed back toward you.
4. While keeping your elbows straight, stand upright while gripping the bar.
5. Make sure tension is present from the cable station while your elbows are straight, rather than slack being present in the cable.
    1. Depending on your arm length relative to your height and which specific cable station you are using, you may have to take a small step backward to take out the slack of the cable.
    2. When taking a small step backwards, the cable will now have a mildly diagonal line of pull rather than being completely vertical.
    3. To maintain a straight elbow position with a diagonal line of pull, you will position your upper arms slightly in front of your body rather than keeping them directly at your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift the bar upward by driving your elbows upward and out to your sides through a range of motion that feels comfortable to your shoulders while bending your elbows.
    1. Your mobility will affect how high you are comfortably able to lift the bar, and there is no need to force your shoulders into a range that provokes any discomfort.
    2. While different individuals may be able to lift higher up and others not quite as high, people often can lift their upper arms until they are close to parallel to the ground for a comfortable and effective range of motion.
    3. The bar should move predominantly vertically, but it will also move slightly back toward you if you are positioned a step back from the cable station, resulting in a slight diagonal line of pull from the cable.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your elbows to descend in toward your sides as you lower the bar in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with straight elbows.
    1. At the end of the lowering phase, the bar should be situated in front of your thighs.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, you will find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your rep.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could relax your upper back and flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench as your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet flat on the floor, approximately shoulder width apart from each other.
    1. Starting with your feet on the floor, as you would with a standard bench press, can help you set up optimally and feel more stable when unracking the weight compared to if you lifted your feet off the ground before unracking the bar.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) as your hands are moderately outside shoulder width apart from each other, with the bar on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be near 1.5 times your shoulder width, and this involves somewhat of a range of grip widths, so you can feel free to try out mildly different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, your thumbs should be wrapped around the bar from the opposite side of your other fingers, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands in contrast to if you positioned your thumbs on the same side of your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip that is also called a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists meaningfully cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together, which is a position you will maintain throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades, which should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting, like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together as you avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. One at a time, lift your feet off the ground and straighten your knees with your legs close together while keeping the bar stationary above your shoulders.
    1. Keep your legs in this position until you finish your set.
    2. While your thighs are on the bench, your calves may or may not be resting on the bench as well, depending on your height and the length of your bench.
4. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. Except for keeping your knees straight with your feet off the ground, you will otherwise perform your set like you would with a standard bench press.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set.
    3. When aiming to touch the bar to your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    4. To touch your lower chest, you will have to keep your elbows tucked to a degree instead of being fully flared out, and the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar to your lower chest. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    5. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
5. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up as you progressively drive your elbows upward and inward while straightening them until you have returned to the starting position with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is situated above your shoulders.
    1. To finish with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest, the bar will now arc slightly backward as you lift it up.
    2. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together and your feet off the ground as your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench.
6. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
7. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
8. Bend your elbows mildly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on a flat exercise bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your upper thighs near your abdomen with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Position yourself so that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    2. If you can curl the weight of the dumbbells, you can sit down on the bench with the dumbbells by your sides before curling them up onto your lap
    3. With heavier dumbbells, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs with your palms facing each other while standing over the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
2. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent, and you will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest, as you would be in the starting position for a dumbbell bench press.
3. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
4. Press the dumbbells up until your elbows are straight, and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. In this starting position, your wrists should be straight, and you will keep them straight throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your elbows to bend mildly, spread your arms apart from each other as you lower the dumbbells out away from your sides in a slow and controlled arcing manner through the available range of motion of your shoulders.
    1. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to lower the dumbbells at least until their elbows are level with their shoulders and often a little beyond this point, but what is specifically your full range of motion will be dependent on your mobility.
    2. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulders at the bottom, but the end range should not be painful.
    3. After fully spreading your arms apart, your upper arms should form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    4. While your elbows should not be locked into a fully straightened position, they also should be notably less bent than when you are bench pressing, so the dumbbells should be clearly further out to the sides than your elbows (as opposed to being stacked over your elbows like at the bottom of a bench press).
2. Reverse the movement by pulling your arms in toward each other in a hug-like motion to lift the dumbbells upward until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbells being approximately over your shoulders.
    1. Near the end of the lifting phase, the resistance from the dumbbells is minimal, and there is no purpose of touching the dumbbells to each other.
    2. Toward the end of the lifting phase, you can straighten your elbows, or you can maintain the same degree of mild elbow bend throughout the set.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your last rep, lower the dumbbells toward the sides of your chest and abdomen as you allow your elbows to bend like you would during the lowering phase of a dumbbell bench press.
    2. Once the dumbbells are by your chest, you can rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs before placing them down onto the ground one at a time or standing up with them.

Flaring out such that your upper arms form approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso is appropriate for many lifters, but feel free to try out different angles to determine what feels best for you. In this context, 0 degrees of elbow flare means your upper arms are fully tucked by your sides, and 90 degrees means your upper arms would form a “T-shape” with your torso.

1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.

Then let the kettlebells fall forward as you swing your arms down while straightening your elbows and hinging at your hips to absorb the force of the lowering phase.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a moderate incline near 45 degrees.
    1. Alternatively, you can also use a fixed moderate incline bench for this exercise.
    2. Any bench angle that is greater than 30 degrees but less than 60 degrees can be considered a moderate incline. 
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on the incline bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your lower thighs near your abdomen with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    2. To move the dumbbells into the proper position, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up against the end of the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
3. While marching your thighs up one at a time in quick succession to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench.
    1. Once you are inclined, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
4. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    3. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
5. Flare your elbows moderately out to your sides such that your upper arms form approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    1. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable on your shoulders, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbows out within this range.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Press the dumbbells up by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten them until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press, as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, keep your feet flat on the floor and your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner toward the sides of your chest through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Let your elbows moderately flare out to your sides as they descend and bend enough to keep your wrists stacked above them with vertical forearms. Lifters often find that at least a mild degree of elbow tuck makes this exercise feel most comfortable for the shoulders compared to fully flaring the elbows straight out to the sides.
    2. How far you can lower the dumbbells with vertical forearms will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hands are at least level with their chest.
    3. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom.
    4. There is no need to lower the dumbbells extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your dumbbells are by your chest following the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arms in line with your sides to tuck your elbows and position the dumbbells closer to your thighs.
    2. Then march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs before standing up with them.

## Setting up
1. Position the J-hooks of a power rack (or squat stand) near the height of your upper chest.
    1. As an alternative to starting from a rack, you can begin with the barbell on the floor and power clean it into position. However, this page will describe how to set up from a rack.
2. Place a barbell onto the J-hooks and load it with your desired weight.
3. Stand in front of the middle of the bar with your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with your hands moderately outside shoulder width as your palms are facing away from you.
    1. What is personally considered a wide grip to you can be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard overhead press, which you can somewhat widen to individualize your wide grip. For instance, for your wide grip, you can place your index finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your little finger when performing your standard overhead press. This approach provides many lifters with an appropriately wide grip, but there is a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine specifically where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Slightly bend your knees, and step forward to situate your collarbone or upper chest directly under the bar. Simultaneously, position your elbows under the bar and just slightly in front of it. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists stacked under the bar.
    1. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Relative to when you overhead press with a closer grip, which normally involves a greater degree of elbow tuck (pointing forward), your elbows should naturally be flared out (pointing out to the side) to a greater extent during this wide grip variation.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
2. Fully stand upright while holding the bar.
    1. With your knees straightened, the bar should now be above the tops of the J-hooks.
3. Take a couple of steps backward and set your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable to you, you can point your toes straight ahead or rotate them slightly out to the side.
4. Squeeze your glutes and quads from now until you finish your last rep.
    1. This will create a stable platform from which to press.
5. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Avoid leaning back into an excessively arched position.
6. Tuck or tilt your chin back to move your head behind the bar.
    1. The goal is to move your head out of the bar’s way so that you can press straight upward without hitting your face with the bar.
7. While keeping your legs straight, press the bar upward with as close to a straight bar path as you can perform.
    1. To the best of your ability, avoid pushing the bar forward out in front of your shoulders. This can be challenging if you are new to this exercise, since you want to avoid hitting your face with the bar. You can still meaningfully increase your strength and grow muscle if the bar drifts a bit forward, but strive to minimize any forward bar motion as well as you can for an efficient overhead press.
    2. Do not lean back any further or excessively arch your lower back. Your lower back should stay locked in the same position throughout your rep.
    3. Avoid using your legs to help with driving the bar up. This is not a push press.
8. Immediately after the bar clears the top of your head, mildly push your head forward until your ears are close to being under the bar.
    1. Rather than pushing your head excessively forward, you primarily should be reversing the backward chin tuck/tilt you previously performed.
9. Finish the press with your elbows straightened as the bar is overhead.
    1. You should be able to draw a straight line down from the bar that passes through your shoulders, hips, knees, and the middle of your feet.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath during your set, you can breathe after locking out the weight overhead. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to lowering the bar.
10. Reverse the movement by tucking your chin back and lowering the bar toward your collarbone in a controlled manner.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down.
11. Alternate between steps 7-10 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
12. After completing the lowering phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second before walking forward.
13. After the bar contacts the back of both J-hooks, bend your knees slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks.

## Setting up
You have the option of performing this exercise within a specific incline press station (in which the bench is fused to the rack) or within an adjustable power rack using a mobile incline bench. Specifically how you will set up will differ depending on which equipment you use, so the setup for each approach is described separately. However, the exercise technique is the same for either option. A power rack normally takes longer to prepare than an incline press station, but power racks typically have safety pins in contrast to incline press stations. It is recommended to have a spotter behind you if you will incline press without safety pins.

### Setting up in a power rack

## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform for pressing.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your upper chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other. Descend until you are able to tap your upper chest lightly with the bar or until you have fully moved through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom, but certain individuals with limited shoulder mobility may not be able to touch their upper chest with the bar without discomfort. If this applies to you, lower the bar as far as you can without discomfort.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath (when viewed from the side) your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set.
    3. Avoid fully flaring your elbows out away from your sides or completely tucking them. The appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Once you have fully lowered the bar, pause in that bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., 1-2 seconds) while staying tight.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
6. Alternate between steps 3-5 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
7. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
8. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a pair of securely anchored gymnastic rings to be slightly outside shoulder width apart.
2. Set the rings to a height that allows your elbows to be aligned with the center of the rings or to whatever is your preferred starting height. Set up a step (like a plyometric box, aerobic step on risers, or a couple of bumper plates stacked on each other) slightly behind the rings so that you can grasp the rings with straight elbows once you are standing on it while mildly leaning your torso forward.
    1. The appropriate ring height should allow you to train dips through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits, while also allowing you to get into the proper starting position with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. The right ring height should also enable you to set your feet onto the ground or step while holding onto the rings if you fail a rep.
    3. While setting up the rings so that their centers are near elbow height is an appropriate starting point for many people, the ideal ring height can vary among different individuals. Someone’s shoulder mobility and preferred knee position during dips can affect where it is best to set the rings.
    4. While not required since you can jump up into the starting position, setting up a step is highly recommended if you are not already accustomed to performing ring dips, where you jump up from the ground. Correspondingly, the directions will describe the usage of the step.
3. Step up onto the step while facing the rings.
4. Firmly grasp the rings with your palms facing each other. Hold the rings directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the rings tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
5. Step forward off the step, and hold yourself up with straight elbows.
    1. Keep your knees as straight as you can without your feet restricting your range of motion from contacting the ground before you reach the bottom of your rep. Initially, you can maintain a slight knee bend and then adjust your knee position during your set if warranted.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back and down to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. You chiefly want to prevent your shoulders from rolling forward or shrugging up during this exercise.
    2. It is not required to keep your shoulder blades packed down further than they normally are at rest, but the intent to pack them down will prevent your torso from sagging down, which would place you into a shrugged shoulder position.
    3. Similarly, you do not necessarily need to have your shoulder blades fully back in the starting position, but pulling them back can make it easier to avoid tilting your shoulders forward, which is undesirable.
7. Rather than keeping your torso fully upright, mildly lean your torso forward and maintain this mild lean throughout your set.
    1. The appropriate degree of lean should result in your chest being slightly in front of your hips (when viewed from the side) while helping your shoulders feel comfortable throughout the set.
    2. Feel free to try out different degrees of torso lean over time to determine what personally feels best to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Throughout your set, avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up. If you notice that either motion starts occurring, strive to pull your shoulder blades further backward and/or downward.
    2. Your elbows should be predominantly pointing backward rather than out to your sides from excessive elbow flare. However, you do not have to keep your elbows completely tucked by your sides, and you can allow them to flare mildly outward if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    3. Rather than letting them swing, keep your legs stationary relative to your hips until you finish your set.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point in which their upper arms are at least parallel to the ground, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Reverse the movement by pushing through the rings to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your hands and elbows downward to lift your body upward.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step back onto the step before releasing the rings.

1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that places the handles near your lower chest or slightly lower once you are seated.
    1. This is an appropriate starting point for most people, but the ideal seat height specifically should allow you to train through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably allows.

3. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your feet flat on the ground.
    1. If your machine has a back pad, position your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against it.

    1. Either option will help you anchor your body.
    2. Certain machines lack a thigh pad or seat belt, which can contribute to the exercise being less stable.

    3. Even if your body does not restrict your range of motion with the closer handle setting, you can also select the wider setting if it just feels more comfortable to you.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back, and move your elbows fully back behind your torso while bending them by at least 90 degrees.
    1. Position your elbows close to being directly behind your wrists and the handles. Keeping your elbows tucked close to your sides rather than flaring them out away from your sides will limit the degree to which this exercise trains the pec major.
    2. If the handles are now just within your reach, the seat height you initially selected is appropriate.
    3. If you cannot reach the handles without shrugging your shoulders up or tipping them forward, raise the seat before resuming your setup.
    4. If the handles are lower than what you can comfortably reach from this position, you can lower the seat to facilitate a greater degree of elbow bend before resuming your setup.
7. Firmly grasp the handles with the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) against them.
    1. While almost all machines allow you to use a neutral grip with your palms facing in toward each other, some machines also have handles that allow you to use an overhand grip with your palms facing backward. If your machine enables you to use both grips, select whichever feels most comfortable to you.
    2. Hold the handles with mostly straight wrists. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Push the handles down by driving your elbows down until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. Throughout your set, continue keeping your torso fully upright and feet planted on the ground.
    2. You should finish with your elbows close to your sides and your arms directed down toward the ground.
    3. While driving downward and straightening, your elbows will simultaneously move forward.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing the handles to lift up to the starting position. Bend your elbows while arcing them upward and backward.
    1. Keep your elbows tucked so that they remain behind your wrists rather than flaring them out away from your sides.
    2. Avoid letting your shoulders shrug up or roll forward.
    3. With the appropriate seat height, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders at the end range, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain. If you feel joint discomfort at the end range, increase the seat height before resuming your set.
    4. At the end range, you can allow the weights you selected to tap the rest of the weight stack. A light tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [lateral](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Lateral%20Head%2018f5c6f170d880c0a504d0d644758f40.md) and [medial](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Medial%20Head%201905c6f170d880fbb6e9e7e7ca37f2d1.md) heads of your triceps while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, you will find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you, and the optimal J-hook height for a close grip bench press may be slightly higher compared to when you use a wider grip.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench as your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor approximately shoulder width apart from each other.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. You can similarly decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) as your hands are near shoulder width apart from each other, with the bar on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. Positioning your hands near shoulder-width apart results in somewhat of a range, but you can initially start with a shoulder-width grip and try out mildly different hand widths over time to determine where specifically you feel best.
    2. What is personally considered a close grip to you can also be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard bench press, which you can somewhat narrow to individualize your close grip. For instance, for your close grip, you can place your little finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your index finger when performing your standard bench press.  
    3. For stability, your thumbs should be wrapped around the bar from the opposite side of your other fingers, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands in contrast to if you positioned your thumbs on the same side of your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip that is also called a “suicide grip”).
    4. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists meaningfully cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort.
    5. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together, which is a position you will maintain throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades, which should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting, like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together as you avoid losing your upper back tightness.
    2. In this position, your wrist should be stacked above your elbows, which should be stacked above your shoulders as your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and keeping them reasonably tucked in toward your sides while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set, which will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow tuck as you touch the bar to your lower chest.
    2. Near the bottom of the rep, the appropriate amount of elbow tuck should result in your upper arms forming close to 30-45-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are touching your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    3. Compared to a wider grip bench press, your elbows should not flare out away from your sides as much during a close grip bench press.
    4. When aiming to touch the bar to your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    5. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up as you progressively drive your elbows upward and inward while straightening them until you have returned to the starting position with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is situated above your shoulders.
    1. To finish with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest, the bar will now arc slightly backward as you lift it up.
    2. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows mildly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
While still training the chest’s [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) and [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) effectively, this exercise can preferentially train the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) to a greater degree than wider grip bench press variations.
