## Setting up
Certain chest press machines have a foot pedal that you can press to move the machine’s arms while setting up. Other machines lack a foot pedal but commonly allow you to modify the starting position with adjustable arms or a back pad that can be moved forward and backward. Some of the specific setup details differ depending on which type of machine you are using, so the setup for each approach is described separately. However, the exercise technique can be very similar for either option, so one technique section is provided with a couple of details that depend on which type of machine you utilize.

### Setting up a machine without a foot pedal

1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that situates the handles level with the lower half of your chest once you are seated.
    1. This is an appropriate starting point for most people, and it can result in somewhat of a range of viable seat heights. Feel free to try out different settings to determine what personally feels best to your body.
    2. The seat height that is ideal for you as an individual should allow your shoulders to feel comfortable throughout the exercise while simultaneously allowing you to feel meaningful tension in your chest.
    3. If the seat is too low (placing the handles near shoulder level or above), some lifters may be more likely to feel shoulder discomfort from having to flare their elbows outward excessively.
    4. If the seat is excessively high (placing the handles below the lowest part of the chest), the exercise may be suboptimal for developing the chest.
2. If your machine allows you to adjust either aspect, position its arms or back pad to a setting that enables you to press through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. Some machines allow you to increase the range of motion by placing the arms further back toward the back pad, while others allow you to move the back pad forward, closer toward the arms. However, certain machine models may not permit you to adjust either part.
    2. If you have normal shoulder mobility, you can initially position the arms or the seat to a setting that results in the handles being near the front of your chest (when viewed from the side) once you are seated. This commonly involves setting the arms as far backward or the seat as far forward as the machine enables.
    3. If you cannot comfortably grasp the handles with proper positioning during step 5, you can adjust the machine to increase the distance between the back pad and the handles until you can do so.
    4. The ideal setting should allow your elbows to start as far behind your torso as is comfortable for your shoulders while keeping your elbows level with the handles.
3. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
4. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against the back pad.
    1. Your feet should be flat on the ground.
    2. You can optionally rest your head against the back pad if it is tall enough, or you can simply keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
5. With your palms facing down and elbows bent, firmly grasp the handles that are directed out to the sides. Position your elbows directly behind the handles, resulting in your elbows being level with the handles when viewed from the side.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. If you cannot comfortably grasp the handles and position your elbows level with them, you may have to position the machine’s arms further forward or the back pad further back before resuming your setup.
    3. Aligning your elbows directly behind (rather than being above or below) the handles will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare during this exercise, provided that you selected a proper seat height.
    4. If your machine has sufficiently long handles, you may be able to adjust your grip width with different hand placements. Placing your hands moderately outside shoulder width can work well for many people, but you can try out different grip widths to determine where you personally feel best.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.

### Setting up a machine with a foot pedal

1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that situates the handles level with the lower half of your chest once you are seated.
    1. This is an appropriate starting point for most people, and it can result in somewhat of a range of viable seat heights. Feel free to try out different settings to determine what personally feels best to your body.
    2. The seat height that is ideal for you as an individual should allow your shoulders to feel comfortable throughout the exercise while simultaneously allowing you to feel meaningful tension in your chest.
    3. If the seat is too low (placing the handles near shoulder level or above), some lifters may be more likely to feel shoulder discomfort from having to flare their elbows outward excessively.
    4. If the seat is excessively high (placing the handles below the lowest part of the chest), the exercise may be suboptimal for developing the chest.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against the back pad.
    1. You can optionally rest your head against the back pad if it is tall enough, or you can simply keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
4. Place one foot against the machine’s foot pedal, and push the pedal forward with your leg.
    1. This brings the handles forward to a position you can comfortably reach.
    2. Keep the pedal pushed away during the next two steps, while keeping your other foot on the ground.
5. With your palms facing down and elbows bent, firmly grasp the horizontally directed handles. Position your elbows directly behind the handles, resulting in your elbows being level with the handles when viewed from the side.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. Aligning your elbows directly behind (rather than being above or below) the handles will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare during this exercise, provided that you selected a proper seat height.
    3. If your machine has sufficiently long handles, you may be able to adjust your grip width with different hand placements. Placing your hands moderately outside shoulder width can work well for many people, but you can try out different grip widths to determine where you personally feel best.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
7. Bring the foot pedal back to its starting position by bending your knee, which will shift the machine’s resistance to your upper body. Simultaneously, allow your elbows to move backward through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Keep your elbows level with the handles, not lifting above them or dropping below them when viewed from the side.
    2. How far your elbows can comfortably move backward while keeping them aligned with the handles will be dependent on your mobility.
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and/or the front of your shoulders at the end range, but you should not allow the machine to pull you into a position that causes shoulder discomfort.
8. Lift your foot off the foot pedal and place it flat on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the handles forward until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows forward and inward in an arcing manner.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your elbows should remain level with your wrists and the handles when viewed from the side.
    3. Throughout your set, continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together, back snugly against the back pad, and feet planted on the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by allowing the handles to move backward in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows and wrists aligned as they remain level with the handles when viewed from the side.
    2. Move through the full range of motion that your mobility comfortably permits. Some machines will limit the range of motion before reaching this point, even when set up ideally.
    3. If your machine lacks a foot pedal, you can lightly tap the weights you selected against the rest of the weight stack at the end range to confirm that you have moved through the full range in a controlled manner. If your machine has a foot pedal, you can finish the lowering phase once you can no longer comfortably move your elbows backward while keeping your elbows at the height of the handles.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. If your machine has a foot pedal, push the pedal forward with your leg until you are no longer supporting any of the machine’s resistance with your upper body. Then let go of the handles and bend your knee to bring the foot pedal back to its initial position.
    2. If your machine lacks a foot pedal, simply rest the machine’s arms on the stoppers after the lowering phase of your last rep before letting go of the handles.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a pair of sturdy, flat, mildly elevated objects that you will use for your deficit onto the ground mildly outside shoulder width apart from each other.
    1. So long as they can support your bodyweight with your hands on top of them and will not slide, you have multiple options that you can use based on your equipment availability.
    2. The height of the objects should allow you to descend through your full available shoulder range of motion without the ground restricting your push-up range of motion. The minimum height required to achieve this full range will vary from person to person, depending on someone's shoulder mobility, but a height of about 4in (10cm) should permit a full range for most people.
    3. Yoga blocks, deadlift blocks, aerobic steps, and thick bumper plates can all be similarly used with your palms flat on top of them.
    4. Alternatively, you can stack standard metal weight plates on top of each other to provide a similar elevation. If you do so, it is recommended to use fairly heavy weights for stability.
2. Position yourself with your palms mildly outside shoulder width apart from each other on the elevated objects with straight elbows as your knees and toes are on the ground with bent knees.
    1. In this position, your elbows should be a little outside and underneath your shoulders rather than being in front of your shoulders (i.e., horizontally closer to your head) or behind your shoulders (i.e., horizontally closer to your hips).
3. Spread your fingers somewhat apart from each other, and shift your bodyweight into your hands.
    1. Your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
4. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you, and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. How far you can descend depends on your individual shoulder mobility, but you should be able to reach the point where your chest is at least slightly lower than your hands. Otherwise, the deficit serves no function compared to a standard push-up.
    2. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom.
    3. Let your elbows flare out moderately away from your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you. This commonly results in the upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with the torso (when viewed from above) at the bottom of the push-up. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbows are fully tucked to your sides, remaining shoulder-width the whole rep, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows point straight out to your sides, letting your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    4. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” at the bottom instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    5. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    6. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    7. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ground to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), which is assisted by your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), and [pec minor](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Minor%201905c6f170d88030b03dd3f99706ecb0.md).

## Setting up
1. In an approximately hip-width stance, face the stable object with a flat, elevated surface that you will use for this push-up variation.
    1. So long as the object can support your bodyweight and will not slide, you can use a variety of objects based on the degree of difficulty you wish to have and what is available to you.
    2. As the height of the surface decreases, the difficulty of the exercise will increase from being able to adopt a closer to horizontal torso position, where gravity can provide greater resistance during a push-up.
    3. A flat exercise bench (which typically has a surface near 18in (46cm) above the ground) can be appropriate to use in a gym as an initial starting point for many people who struggle to perform more than a couple of reps of standard push-ups through a full range of motion.
    4. In addition to a plyometric box, an aerobic step elevated on top of risers can also be a quality object to use, since you can adjust the height (typically in 2in (5cm) increments) to match the specific level of difficulty you wish to have.
    5. For a lower intensity variation at home, furniture like a bed can alternatively be used to elevate your hands.
2. After leaning forward at your hips, place your palms on top of the elevated object with the base of your palms on the corner as your elbows are straight, and your hands are mildly outside shoulder width apart from each other.
    1. In this position, your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
    2. Based on your preference, you can spread your fingers somewhat apart from each other or keep them close together.
3. While bearing weight through your hands and allowing your heels to lift off the ground, walk your feet back until your hips and knees are straightened as your arms form approximately 90-degree angles with your torso.
    1. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    2. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    3. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest in a controlled manner until it lightly touches the elevated surface.
    1. Let your elbows flare out moderately away from your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you. This commonly results in the upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with the torso (when viewed from above) at the bottom of the push-up. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbows are fully tucked to your sides, remaining shoulder-width the whole rep, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows point straight out to your sides, letting your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ground instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    5. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the surface to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise trains your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) like a standard [push-up](Push-up%201a05c6f170d880a5b43fe13bcb1b6f3a.md) but with a lower intensity.

    1. In this position, your knees should be approximately hip-width apart, with your elbows stacked under your shoulders and your arms pointing straight down toward the ground.

## Setting up
1. Place one dumbbell on the ground.
    1. Both of its weighted ends should be on the ground.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground, with the dumbbell by the side of your body you are about to train. When your upper arm (closer to the dumbbell) is by your side, the dumbbell’s handle should be parallel with your upper arm and out to the side of your elbow.
    1. Specifically, the dumbbell should be slightly greater than the length of your forearm away from your elbow to help you pick it up.
3. On the side closer to the dumbbell, bend your elbow by about 90 degrees with your upper arm right by your side.
4. Roll onto your side toward the dumbbell.
5. Firmly grasp the dumbbell with your palm on the side of your lower arm facing up toward the ceiling. Tightly wrap your other hand over your lower hand, so that your palms are facing each other.
6. While pulling the dumbbell up with your top arm, roll over onto your back. Move your torso and arms together as one unit, such that the dumbbell remains directly in front of your elbow (on the side holding the dumbbell directly) throughout the roll.
    1. When appropriately transitioning to lying on your back, you should not feel that you are stressing your shoulder on the side directly holding the dumbbell. You are primarily using the rest of your body to reposition yourself and lift the dumbbell rather than using your shoulder muscles (on the side directly holding the dumbbell) to rotate the forearm.
    2. Once you are on your back, you should be holding the dumbbell on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a mostly straight wrist that allows for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. On the side holding the dumbbell, your upper arm should be resting on the ground, and your forearm should be vertical.
7. Move your arm that is not directly holding the dumbbell into a comfortable position, such as resting by your side.
    1. Some lifters may prefer to use the free hand to hold onto a sturdy object (like the beam of a power rack) for additional stability, but you can position that hand wherever you like.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training first.
8. If you have not already, position your legs straight out in front of you with straight knees.
    1. The back of your heels should now be on the ground along with your buttocks, upper back, and head.
9. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
10. Flare your elbow moderately out to your side such that your upper arm forms an approximately 45-75-degree angle with your torso.
    1. Keep your forearm vertical while doing so.
    2. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable for your shoulder, you can decide how far you flare your elbow within this range.
    3. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbow is completely tucked by your side, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your upper arm would form half of a “T-shape” with your torso.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbell upward until your elbow is fully straightened with your arm directed straight up toward the ceiling. It may help to focus on driving your elbow upward and inward.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulder and elbow, your forearm should be in a vertical position throughout the press. This will result in your wrist and dumbbell remaining stacked over your elbow.
    2. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbell should be situated vertically over your shoulder.
    3. Throughout your set, continue keeping your heels, buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner. Move your elbow outward and downward while bending it.
    1. Continue keeping your wrist stacked over your elbow as your forearm remains vertical.
    2. Allow your elbow to flare out moderately away from your side so that your upper arm forms an approximately 45-75-degree angle with your torso at the bottom.
    3. You should finish with the back of your upper arm and elbow contacting the ground.
    4. While you do not have to finish the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you certainly should avoid slamming your arm onto the ground. You will not be bouncing your arm off the ground.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. It can be awkward to transfer the weight to your other hand with proper positioning while lying down if you are using a weight that is at least fairly heavy to you.
    2. Consequently, you can set the dumbbell down in an opposite manner to how you initially set up before switching to your other side.
5. After finishing the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arm in line with your side to tuck your elbow and position the dumbbell closer to your torso.
6. Wrap your free hand around your hand holding the dumbbell.
7. Roll onto your side (in which you are holding the dumbbell) while using your outer hand’s arm to help control the weight onto the ground. Move your torso and arms together as one unit, such that the dumbbell remains directly in front of your elbow (on the side holding the dumbbell directly) throughout the roll.
8. Let go of the dumbbell before setting up on the opposite side of the dumbbell to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

## Setting up
1. Position the safety pins of a power rack at the height of your collarbone or slightly above this point.
    1. For this variation, the goal is to position the pins in a manner that results in the bar (once it is on the pins) being as close to your starting position for the standard overhead press as possible. Ideally, the pins should allow the bar to start below your chin.
    2. While the pins can be slightly above your collarbone, it is not feasible to situate the pins slightly below your collarbone.
    3. Certain power racks have fairly wide spaces between safety pinholes. This may result in the lowest pin height that is at least at collarbone height, placing the bar closer toward the midpoint of the press rather than the start of the press. If this is the case for you, it is not feasible for you to train the overhead low pin press with your current rack. However, you may be able to perform the overhead midpoint pin press.
2. Symmetrically place a barbell in the middle of the safety pins and load it with your desired weight.
3. Stand in front of the middle of the bar.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with your hands slightly outside shoulder width as your palms are facing away from you.
    1. Situating your index fingers directly outside the outer aspects of your shoulders is generally an effective approach, but what is personally your ideal grip may be a bit wider or closer. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Step forward to situate your collarbone directly under the bar with your feet approximately shoulder-width apart. The middle of your feet should be under the bar, and your knees should be straight.
    1. Based on what feels most stable to you, you can point your toes straight ahead or rotate them slightly out to the side.
    2. You can perform this step simultaneously with step 6.
6. Position your elbows under the bar and just slightly in front of it. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists stacked under the bar.
    1. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    2. Your forearms should now be close to a vertical position when viewed from the front.
    3. From this position, your elbows should be reasonably close to being flared 45 degrees out from your sides. 0 degrees of flare would mean your elbows are directly aligned with your shoulders when viewed from the front. 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows are directly aligned with your shoulders when viewed from the side.
7. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Avoid leaning back into an excessively arched position.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
2. Squeeze your glutes and quads from now until you finish your last rep.
    1. This will create a stable platform from which to press.
3. Tuck or tilt your chin back to move your head behind the bar.
    1. The goal is to move your head out of the bar’s way so that you can press straight upward without hitting your face with the bar.
4. While keeping your legs straight, press the bar upward with as close to a straight bar path as you can perform.
    1. To the best of your ability, avoid pushing the bar forward out in front of your shoulders. This can be challenging if you are new to this exercise, since you want to avoid hitting your face with the bar. You can still meaningfully increase your strength and grow muscle if the bar drifts a bit forward, but strive to minimize any forward bar motion as well as you can for an efficient overhead press.
    2. Do not lean back any further or excessively arch your lower back. Your lower back should stay locked in the same position throughout your rep.
5. Immediately after the bar clears the top of your head, mildly push your head forward until your ears are close to being under the bar.
    1. Rather than pushing your head excessively forward, you primarily should be reversing the backward chin tuck/tilt you previously performed.
6. Finish the press with your elbows straightened as the bar is overhead.
    1. You should be able to draw a straight line down from the bar that passes through your shoulders, hips, knees, and the middle of your feet.
7. Reverse the movement by tucking your chin back and lowering the bar toward your collarbone in a controlled manner.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down. Do not let the bar crash into the pins.
8. Once the bar contacts the pins, allow the weight to transmit fully into the pins. Remain completely stationary with the bar resting on the pins for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds).
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath during your set, you can breathe when the bar is resting on the pins. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating your next.
9. Alternate between steps 4-8 until you have completed your set.
    1. In contrast to a standard overhead press, you will finish your set with the bar resting on the pins rather than racking it onto J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also meaningfully training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of standard bench press reps to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended plate weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Based on the type of equipment you have, securely attach a sufficiently anchored pair of long looped elastic bands or a single band to the bar through your preferred set-up method.
    1. Ultimately, you want to make sure that whatever you use as your anchor point will not move during your set. Your anchor point should have a smooth surface that will not tear the band.
    2. The appropriate set-up should result in the bands remaining taut at the bottom of each rep. If the bands become slack at any point during your reps, you did not stretch them sufficiently in the starting position.
    3. Once positioned, the bands should be flat rather than having any twists.
    4. If you have access to band pegs and a pair of bands with equal tensions, anchoring the bands to the pegs and looping them around each side of the bar will be the ideal method of setting up. The bands should be set up where they are pulling vertically downward rather than being angled to one side. Other methods are less stable and not recommended if you can use band pegs.
    5. Without band pegs, you can anchor the bands to heavy dumbbells on each end of the bar. To reduce the risk that they move, the dumbbells should ideally be as heavy as possible. It can help to place a pair of weight plates on the sides of each dumbbell to reduce the likelihood that they will roll. If you are using bands with a high enough tension that they move the heaviest dumbbells you have, this method is simply not practical to use.
    6. Without band pegs or a pair of equal bands, you can loop each end of one band through the bar and anchor it under the bench pad. With this approach, it is generally recommended to anchor the band at a point on the bench that will result in the band being slightly further away horizontally from the head of the bench compared to your shoulders. After anchoring the band, you should pull the bottom of the band down under the bench to check whether it is applying the same resistance on each side of the bar.
    7. Prior to using them, it is recommended that you inspect the bands to confirm they do not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
6. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
7. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning to bench press, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
8. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set.
    2. When aiming to touch the bar to your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    3. To touch your lower chest, you will have to keep your elbows tucked to a degree instead of being fully flared out, and the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar to your lower chest. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest.
    3. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
    4. As you lift the bar higher up, the band tension will progressively increase.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

## Setting up
1. Use the machine’s loading pin to select your desired level of assistance, and ensure that the machine’s knee pad or foot bar is positioned down.
    1. In contrast to most machines, the difficulty of this exercise decreases as you select heavier loads from the assisted dip machine, since the weight determines the extent to which the machine will support your bodyweight.
    2. Certain machine models have a knee pad, and others have a foot bar, but essentially the same exercise technique can be used with either type of machine.
2. Step up onto the machine’s elevated foot plates.
3. If your machine allows you to rotate its parallel handles inward or outward, position them inward unless your body’s width restricts the range of motion for the closer setting.
    1. The closer setting facilitates a greater degree of elbow tuck, which is typically desirable when striving to emphasize the triceps and/or the front delts to a greater degree than the chest during this exercise.
    2. However, the closer setting may position the handles excessively close for individuals with rather wide body types.

    4. Note that a variety of machines do not allow you to adjust the handle position.
4. Firmly grasp the parallel handles with your palms facing each other. Hold the handles directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
5. One leg at a time, kneel onto the machine’s knee pad (if your machine has a knee pad) or step onto the machine’s foot bar (if your machine has a foot bar) while continuing to grasp the handles firmly. Maintain straight elbows when doing so.
    1. If using a machine with a knee pad, you will keep your knees bent on the pad throughout your set, but if you are using a machine with a foot bar, you will keep your knees straight while standing on the bar throughout your set.
6. Assume a “proud chest” posture as you pull your shoulder blades back with an upright torso.
    1. Avoid letting your shoulders shrug up throughout the exercise.
    2. In contrast to a “chest dip,” you want to avoid leaning forward at your hips during this “triceps dip.”
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. While keeping them tucked close to your sides, bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Throughout your set, continue keeping your torso upright and avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up.
    2. Avoid flaring your elbows out away from your sides. When viewed from behind, your elbows should remain stacked over your wrists and the handles rather than having your elbows move outside your wrists.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.

4. Reverse the movement by pushing through the handles to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows straight down.
    2. You should finish with your elbows close to your sides and your arms directed down toward the ground.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.
    1. In this position, your elbows should be stacked underneath your shoulders with your arms pointing straight down toward the ground. 
2. Situate your hands clearly outside shoulder width apart from each other (i.e., about twice shoulder width distance apart), with your fingers spread somewhat apart from each other.
    1. So long as your hands are wider apart than during your standard push-up with a moderate grip width, you can use somewhat of a range of hand placements for your wide grip, but you should place your hands in a position that feels right to your shoulders.
    2. Your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
3. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you, and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest in a controlled manner until it lightly touches the ground.
    1. Rather than trying to keep your elbows tucked in by your sides, allow your elbows to flare out away from your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you.  This commonly results in the upper arms forming at least 60-degree angles with the torso (when viewed from above) at the bottom of a wide grip push-up. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbows are fully tucked to your sides, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows point straight out to your sides, letting your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ground instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    5. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ground to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

This will involve your hands being in front of the pulleys with tension still present from the cables when you are fully spread apart in the starting position of each rep.
    2. If your shoulder mobility comfortably allows your arms to move further behind your torso than they initially are, you can take another step forward to be able to train through a full range of motion.

5. While mildly bending your knees, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip-width apart from each other.
    1. In this position, you should feel stable and balanced.
6. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.

1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to use a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position an incline bench within the rack, or within a specific incline press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. For this variation, you will use a bench with a moderate incline near 45 degrees. Any bench angle (which includes most incline press stations) that is greater than 30 degrees but less than 60 degrees can be considered a moderate incline.
    2. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    3. Incline bench press stations typically lack spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to incline press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it more difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    4. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and an incline press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it normally takes longer to prepare compared to an incline press station. It is recommended to have a spotter behind you if you will incline press without safety pins.
2. If you are using a power rack, place the moderate incline bench centered within the power rack. The head of the bench should be between the posts, where you will adjust the J-hooks.
    1. You should position the bench in a spot that allows your nose to be directly under the barbell after setting up the rack and lying down on the bench.
3. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the incline bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With an incline press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will require a greater-than-needed pressing range of motion, which will increase effort and fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
4. Place the bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks. If you are training in a power rack with safety pins, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of incline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
    1. If you are training in an incline press station without spotter arms, proceed to step 6.
5. If you are training in a power rack, position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your incline press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins.
    2. Certain power rack models have fairly wide spaces between safety pinholes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your incline press range of motion, being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. It is not ideal if this applies to your rack, but the safety pins can still enhance safety if they are high enough to receive the bar if you dump it forward in the event that you become completely pinned without anyone to assist you.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and lie down with your back and head on the incline bench. Position yourself so that your nose is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Firmly situate the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    2. Based on what feels most stable, you can position your heels directly under your knees with vertical shins, or you can bend your knees a bit beyond this point to position your heels slightly behind your knees with slightly angled shins.
    3. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
    4. If you are not training with safety pins that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
7. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands near shoulder width apart. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. You can initially start with a shoulder-width grip, but positioning your hands near shoulder-width apart results in a bit of a range of possible hand placements. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. What is personally considered a close grip to you can also be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard incline press, which you can narrow somewhat to individualize your close grip. For instance, for your close grip, you can place your little finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your index finger when performing your standard incline press.
    3. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    4. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    5. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
8. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your upper chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and keeping them reasonably tucked in toward your sides. Descend until you are able to tap your upper chest lightly with the bar or until you have fully moved through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom, but certain individuals with limited shoulder mobility may not be able to touch their upper chest with the bar without discomfort. If this applies to you, lower the bar as far as you can without discomfort.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists (when viewed from the side). This will keep your forearms close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set and naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow tuck.
    3. You should not completely tuck your elbows, but your elbows should not flare out away from your sides as much during a close grip incline press compared to a wider grip incline press. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming close to 30-45-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on a flat exercise bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your upper thighs near your abdomen with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Position yourself so that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    2. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    3. To move the dumbbells into the proper position, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up against the end of the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
2. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    3. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
4. In the starting position, your palms should face each other, and your elbows should be tucked fairly close to your sides.
    1. Keeping your elbows tucked to the extent that your upper arms form near 30-degree angles with your torso (when viewed from above) is generally appropriate.
    2. If you completely tuck your elbows, you will likely reduce how effectively this exercise can train your chest compared to using a mild degree of elbow flare.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbells upward by driving your elbows upward as you progressively straighten them until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your palms facing each other as you avoid notably flaring your elbows out away from your sides, like you otherwise do with a standard dumbbell bench press.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press, as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    3. Keep your feet flat on the floor and your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench throughout the exercise. 
    4. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
3. While keeping your elbows tucked fairly close to your sides, reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. While they descend, let your elbows bend enough to keep your wrists stacked above them with vertical forearms.
    2. Strive to finish with your upper arms forming close to 30-degree angles with your torso.
    3. How far you can lower the dumbbells with vertical forearms will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hands are at least level with their chest.
    4. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders at the bottom.
    5. There is no need to lower the dumbbells extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After the lowering phase of the last rep, fully tuck your elbows by your sides to position the dumbbells closer to your thighs.
    2. Then march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs before standing up with them.
