## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, you will find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
    1. In addition to setting up safety pins/spotter arms, it is strongly recommended that you use a spotter, since the reverse grip bench press does not typically enable you to have as secure a grip on the bar compared to a standard overhand grip bench press.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench as your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor approximately shoulder width apart from each other.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. You can similarly decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing backward (resulting in an underhand grip) as your hands are mildly wider apart than your grip for a standard bench press. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands).
    1. As a general rule of thumb for your reverse grip, you can place your index finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your little finger when performing your standard bench press. Based on how that feels, you can try out mildly different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best. 
    2. Securely holding the bar with an underhand grip requires that you somewhat cock your wrists back rather than keeping them fully straight. However, you should avoid excessively cocking them back into a fully extended position, which may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort.
    3. For stability, your thumbs should be wrapped around the bar from the opposite side of your other fingers, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands in contrast to if you positioned your thumbs on the same side of your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip that is also called a “suicide grip”).
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together, which is a position you will maintain throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades, which should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting, like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together as you avoid losing your upper back tightness.
    2. In this position, your wrist should be stacked above your elbows, which should be stacked above your shoulders as your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest or upper abdomen in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and keeping them tucked in toward your sides. Descend until you are able to tap a little below your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. A reverse grip bench press will normally allow you to contact the bar lower on your body than a standard bench press. You could decide specifically where you touch the bar based on what feels more comfortable to you. 
    2. The bar should track mildly forward away from your shoulders, rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    3. Compared to a standard bench press, which involves a greater degree of elbow flare, your elbows should be tucked closer toward your sides during a reverse grip bench press.
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your body with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your body.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up as you progressively drive your elbows upward while straightening them until you have returned to the starting position with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is situated above your shoulders.
    1. To finish with the bar over your shoulders instead of your upper abdomen, the bar will now arc mildly backward as you lift it up.
    2. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows mildly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

    4. Compared to positioning your legs further backward or forward, keeping your thighs close to vertical can generally promote an upright torso.

    1.     2. Throughout your set, avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up.

4. Reverse the movement by pushing through the bars to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows straight down.
    2. You should finish with your elbows close to your sides and your arms directed down toward the ground.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step down from the bars.

4. While keeping your elbows straightened and torso upright, lift your feet off the ground, and position your legs against the weight (if you are using a dip belt).
    1. Depending on the equipment you use, you may have to bend your knees in order for your feet to clear the ground, or you may be able to keep your knees straight.
    2. Based on your preference, you can spread your legs just enough to position the weight between them, or you can position your legs together with the weight just in front of them. Which option is most comfortable will be influenced by how you set up your belt and the shape of your weight(s). Contacting the weight with your legs can help you prevent the weight from excessively swinging during your set.
    3. If you opt to bend your knees, you can cross your ankles for additional stability
    4. Compared to positioning your legs further backward or forward, keeping your thighs close to vertical can generally promote an upright torso.
5. Pull your shoulder blades back and down to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. You chiefly want to prevent your shoulders from rolling forward or shrugging up during this exercise.
    2. It is not required to keep your shoulder blades packed down further than they normally are at rest, but the intent to pack them down will prevent your torso from sagging down, which would place you into a shrugged shoulder position.
    3. Similarly, you do not necessarily need to have your shoulder blades fully back in the starting position, but pulling them back can make it easier to avoid tilting your shoulders forward, which is undesirable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. As you keep them tucked close to your sides, bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. While you do not have to maintain a completely upright torso, keep your torso mostly upright for this triceps dip rather than more prominently leaning your torso forward like you would during a chest dip. A mild degree of torso lean can naturally occur without striving to lean forward and often contributes to the exercise feeling more comfortable than if you focus on being fully upright.
    2. Throughout your set, avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up.
    3. Avoid flaring your elbows out away from your sides. When viewed from behind, your elbows should remain stacked over your wrists and the bars rather than having your elbows move noticeably outside your wrists.
    4. Rather than swinging them, continue keeping your legs stationary relative to your hips until you finish your set. If you are using a dip belt, keeping your legs in contact with the weight can help you stabilize it. If the weight is between your legs, squeezing your thighs together can stop the weight from swinging.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point at which their elbows are bent by at least 90 degrees, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Once you have finished lowering to your end range, pause in that bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds).
    1. Continue to stay braced with your shoulder blades pulled back and down.
    2. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Reverse the movement by pushing through the bars to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows straight down.
    2. You should finish with your elbows close to your sides and your arms directed down toward the ground.
6. Alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step down from the bars.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [lateral](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Lateral%20Head%2018f5c6f170d880c0a504d0d644758f40.md) and [medial](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Medial%20Head%201905c6f170d880fbb6e9e7e7ca37f2d1.md) heads of your triceps while also training its [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md) to a lesser degree, along with your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md).

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a multi-grip Swiss bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
    1. If your Swiss bar has angled handles instead of purely parallel handles, you can position the bar so that the end of the handles closer toward your feet are wider apart than the end of the handles closer toward your head. This will allow you to grasp the handles with your handles angled in toward each other and somewhat forward.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the center of the Swiss bar, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor approximately shoulder width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. With your palms facing each other, firmly grasp the handles that are near shoulder width apart or mildly wider. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. Depending on the specific Swiss bar you are using and your body proportions, sometimes you may feel that your ideal grip width is between two handle pairs that are available to you. Feel free to try out different grips over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the handles, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands.
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and keeping them reasonably tucked in toward your sides. Lower it until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set. This will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow tuck as you touch the bar to your lower chest.
    2. Near the bottom of the rep, the appropriate amount of elbow tuck should result in your upper arms forming close to 30-45-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are touching your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    3. When aiming to touch the bar to your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest.
    3. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have  already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
While still training the chest’s [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) and [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) effectively, this exercise likely can preferentially train the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) to a greater degree than a standard barbell bench press.

## Setting up
1. Position the J-hooks of a rack near the height of your upper chest.
    1. As an alternative to starting from a rack, you can begin with the barbell on the floor and power clean it into position. However, this page will describe how to set up from a rack.
2. Place a barbell onto the J-hooks and load it with your desired weight.
3. Stand in front of the middle of the bar with your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with your hands slightly outside shoulder width as your palms are facing away from you.
    1. Situating your index fingers directly outside the outer aspects of your shoulders is generally an effective approach, but what is personally your ideal grip may be a bit wider or closer. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Slightly bend your knees, and step forward to situate your collarbone or upper chest directly under the bar. Simultaneously, position your elbows under the bar and just slightly in front of it. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists stacked under the bar.
    1. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    2. Your forearms should now be close to a vertical position when viewed from the front.
    3. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    4. From this position, your elbows should be reasonably close to being flared 45 degrees out from your sides. 0 degrees of flare would mean your elbows are directly aligned with your shoulders when viewed from the front. 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows are directly aligned with your shoulders when viewed from the side.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
2. Fully stand upright while holding the bar.
    1. With your knees straightened, the bar should now be above the tops of the J-hooks.
3. Take a couple of steps backward and set your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable to you, you can point your toes straight ahead or rotate them slightly out to the side.
4. Squeeze your glutes and quads from now until you finish your last rep.
    1. This will create a stable platform from which to press.
5. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Avoid leaning back into an excessively arched position.
6. Tuck or tilt your chin back to move your head behind the bar.
    1. The goal is to move your head out of the bar’s way so that you can press straight upward without hitting your face with the bar.
7. While keeping your legs straight, press the bar upward with as close to a straight bar path as you can perform.
    1. To the best of your ability, avoid pushing the bar forward out in front of your shoulders. This can be challenging if you are new to this exercise, since you want to avoid hitting your face with the bar. You can still meaningfully increase your strength and grow muscle if the bar drifts a bit forward, but strive to minimize any forward bar motion as well as you can for an efficient overhead press.
    2. Do not lean back any further or excessively arch your lower back. Your lower back should stay locked in the same position throughout your rep.
    3. Avoid using your legs to help with driving the bar up. This is not a push press.
8. Immediately after the bar clears the top of your head, mildly push your head forward until your ears are close to being under the bar.
    1. Rather than pushing your head excessively forward, you primarily should be reversing the backward chin tuck/tilt you previously performed.
9. Finish the press with your elbows straightened as the bar is overhead.
    1. You should be able to draw a straight line down from the bar that passes through your shoulders, hips, knees, and the middle of your feet.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath during your set, you can breathe after locking out the weight overhead. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to lowering the bar.
10. Reverse the movement by tucking your chin back and lowering the bar toward your collarbone in a controlled manner.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down.
11. Alternate between steps 7-10 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
12. After completing the lowering phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second before walking forward.
13. After the bar contacts the back of both J-hooks, bend your knees slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [upper pec major,](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md) [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. At a cable station, adjust the cable to be near the height of your lower chest, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at the weight stack.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you will also position the arm furthest back, such that it is directed out to the side of the machine.
    2. Dual cable stations that have their two weight stacks facing each other (often with a pull-up in between them) normally lack adjustable arms.
2. Stand with the handle just in front of the arm you are going to train as you are facing away from the cable station.
3. With the hand closer to the cable station, firmly grasp the handle and direct your palm to face downward and inward at an angle.
    1. Your elbow should be bent with your forearm pointing straight ahead.
4. Walk forward a little beyond the point where the weight stack separates and starts providing you resistance from the cable.
    1. The goal is to be far enough from the cable station that you will experience resistance throughout the full range of motion of this exercise.
    2. Keep your chest and imaginary belt buckle pointing straight ahead rather than letting the cable twist your body when walking out.
    3. You can optionally use your free arm to help you stabilize the arm holding the cable when walking out. To do so, you could place your free hand firmly around your other hand until you finish setting your feet (which is when you will be more stable than walking out).
5. With the leg opposite to the side in which you are holding the cable, step forward to adopt a staggered stance while mildly bending your knees.
    1. In this position, you should feel stable and balanced.
    2. You can keep your free arm wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side or held out to the side for balance assistance.
    3. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the handle since that is the side you will be training first.
6. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
7. If you did not do so already, allow the cable’s tension to pull your elbow back behind your torso through a range that your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. This will be the starting position of your arm, and you can assume it at any point from step 4 onward.
    2. How far you can position your elbow behind your torso will be influenced by your individual shoulder mobility.
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulder in this position, but it should not be painful.
    4. Throughout the exercise, avoid letting the cable’s resistance twist your trunk toward the cable, which would result in your chest facing a different direction than the center of your hips.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the handle forward until your arm is outstretched in front of you with a straight elbow.
    1. Drive your elbow forward and inward in an arcing manner.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulder and elbow, strive to keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
    3. Continue keeping your chest and imaginary belt buckle pointing straight ahead in the same direction as you avoid twisting your body.
    4. Keep your mostly straight wrist stacked in front of your elbow throughout the rep.
    5. Keep your chest up as you avoid hunching over with your shoulders slouched forward.
3. Reverse the movement by bending your elbow and moving it outward and backward in a controlled arcing manner.
    1. Allow the cable to pull your elbow back through your shoulder’s full range of motion to return to the starting position.
    2. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to allow the arm to pull back until the elbow is at least slightly behind the torso, but your shoulder mobility will determine what your individual end range is.
    3. Do not let your chest twist toward the cable station.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
While statically training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md), this exercise will develop your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), which is assisted by your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a moderate incline near 45 degrees.
    1. Any bench angle that is greater than 30 degrees but less than 60 degrees can be considered a moderate incline.
2. Center the incline bench underneath a Smith machine’s bar in a spot that will allow you to touch your upper chest with the bar at the bottom of the press.
    1. After initially estimating which bench placement allows this to occur, you may have to move the bench a bit forward or backward during later steps if you notice the bar does not reach your upper chest.
    2. Specifically how you should set up can be influenced by whether your Smith machine has sliding rails that are purely vertical or angled.
    3. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, place the side of the bench where you will place your feet on the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends. This will result in the top of the rails being horizontally closer to your head than the bottom of the rails when lying down on the bench. An angled Smith machine will prompt the bar to track mildly back toward your head when pressing the bar up.
    4. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which side of the bar you place your feet.
3. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to grasp it with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently.
    1. The ideal height allows you to unrack the bar while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together without requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    2. If the bar is situated too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart to lift the bar off the safety bars (on which the safety hooks that are attached to the bar rest). This can place you in a less stable position to start your set since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    3. If the bar is situated excessively low, you will have to grasp the bar initially with a greater degree of elbow bend, and unracking it will involve a greater than ideal pressing range of motion. This will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    4. If neither of the two closest bar heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    5. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best starting bar height for you.
4. After positioning the bar to the appropriate height, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of incline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section. Use these reps to determine the appropriate height of the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails under the bar) prior to re-racking the bar.
5. Position the safety stops slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your incline press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could untuck your shoulder blades and flatten out your back to lose your arch. This will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety stops.
    2. Certain Smith machine models have fairly wide spaces between where you could position safety stops. This may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your Smith machine, it is not ideal, and you have the option of using a spotter.
    3. If you cannot press the bar fully up and lack a spotter or safety stops that are able to receive the bar when flattening your back, you may be able to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars above your chest if you are able to complete part of the press. If you happen to become pinned in this situation and are initially unable to reach the nearest safety bars above you, you can let the bar rest on your chest until you feel recovered enough to press the bar up high enough to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and lie down with your buttocks, back, and head on the incline bench. Firmly place your feet flat on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart with your knees bent.
    1. With the appropriate bench placement, your upper chest should be under the bar if your Smith machine has vertical slide rails. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, your upper chest should be mildly horizontally in front of the bar.
    2. Based on what feels most stable, you can position your heels directly under your knees with vertical shins, or you can bend your knees a bit beyond this point to position your heels slightly behind your knees with slightly angled shins.
7. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for bench press variations is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
8. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform for pressing.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the safety bars by straightening your elbows before rotating the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion. After unracking it, hold the bar stationary for a moment before starting to lower it.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your upper chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other. Descend until you are able to tap your upper chest lightly with the bar or until you have fully moved through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom, but certain individuals with limited shoulder mobility may not be able to touch their upper chest or collarbone with the bar without discomfort. If this applies to you, lower the bar as far as you can without discomfort.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists (when viewed from the side). This will keep your forearms close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set and naturally promote the appropriate balance between elbow flare and elbow tuck.
    3. Avoid fully flaring your elbows out away from your sides or completely tucking them. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up until you have fully straightened your elbows. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together as your feet and buttocks remain firmly planted respectively on the ground and bench.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
    1. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second.
6. Rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars by flicking your wrists before bending your elbows to lower the safety hooks securely onto the safety bars.

## Setting up
1. Stand with your back facing the stable object with a flat elevated surface that you will use for this push-up variation.
    1. So long as the object can support your bodyweight and will not slide, you can use a variety of objects based on the degree of decline you wish to use and what is available to you.
    2. As the height of the surface increases, the exercise will function closer to a vertical press (like a shoulder press) than a horizontal press (like a flat bench press), which will increase its difficulty.
    3. Initially selecting an object near mid-shin in height or lower is recommended if you are new to decline push-ups.
    4. For a steeper decline that will be more challenging, you can select an object near knee height.
    5. An aerobic step that can be elevated on top of risers can be a quality object to use, since you can adjust the height (typically in 2in (5cm) increments) to match the specific decline and level of difficulty you wish to have.
    6. Thick bumper plates, which can be stacked on top of each other, can be useful to provide a low to moderately low height that can be adjusted.
    7. A flat exercise bench (which typically has a surface near 18in (46cm) above the ground) or plyometric box can additionally be used.
    8. At home, you can also use sturdy furniture like a bed or couch.
2. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.
    1. In this “on all fours” position, your elbows should be stacked underneath your shoulders with your arms pointing straight down toward the ground.
    2. You should be situated close enough to the elevated surface that you will be able to place your feet on top of it after you straighten your knees.
3. Situate your hands mildly outside shoulder width apart from each other, with your fingers spread somewhat apart from each other.
    1. Your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
4. One at a time, lift your legs off the ground and place the balls of your feet and toes on top of the elevated surface.
    1. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the ground in a controlled manner until.
    1. A low to moderate decline can often allow you to touch your chest lightly to the ground, but your head may obstruct how far you can descend if you use a steeper decline. Consequently, you can aim to move through the full range of motion you can while keeping your neck in a neutral position.
    2. Let your elbows flare out moderately away from your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you. This commonly results in the upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with the torso (when viewed from above) at the bottom of the push-up. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbows are fully tucked to your sides, remaining shoulder-width the whole rep, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows point straight out to your sides, letting your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    3. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” at the bottom instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    4. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    5. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    6. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ground to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to return your feet to the ground.

## Setting up
In addition to situating a mobile bench within a power rack or squat stand, you have the option of setting up this exercise within a seated overhead press station in which a seated bench is fused to a rack. The exercise technique is the same for either option, but the set-up details differ depending on which equipment you use, so each set-up is described separately.

### **Setting up a power rack or squat stand**

1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a 90-degree angle, or approach a mobile exercise bench that is permanently fixed with an upright backrest.
    1. If you have access to one, a seated bench with a backrest that does not reach your head is ideal, because a taller backrest can interfere with your bar path.
2. Place the bench centered within a power rack or squat stand with the backrest in between the uprights, where you will adjust the J-hooks.
    1. The proper placement of the bench should allow you to unrack the bar comfortably without bumping the J-hooks with the bar during your set. This may require some trial and error.
    2. If the backrest is situated in front of where the bar will start, you will have to reach back behind your head to unrack the bar, which requires greater than typical shoulder mobility.
    3. If the backrest is situated too far behind where the bar will start, you may bump the J-hooks with the bar when pressing the bar up.
3. Position the J-hooks at a height that will allow you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are seated on the bench.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks without having to shrug your shoulders up.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the top of the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If neither of the two J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little lower than optimal, since it may not be feasible to unrack the bar with proper positioning if the J-hooks are excessively high.
    4. You may have to try out different J-hook heights to determine which setting is best for you.
4. Place the bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks.
    1. Initially leave the bar unloaded to check that the bench and J-hooks are positioned correctly.
5. Sit down with your buttocks and back in contact with the bench. Firmly place your feet flat on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart with your knees bent.
    1. Your hips should be fully back on the seat.
    2. If your bench’s backrest reaches your head, rest your head against it as well.
6. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
7. Reach up overhead and firmly grasp the bar with your hands at least moderately outside shoulder width as your palms are facing forward.
    1. Relative to a standard overhead press performed to the front of your body, a wider grip will normally be more comfortable when pressing behind your head.
    2. If you raise your arms straight out to your sides until they are parallel to the ground, note the midway points between your elbows and the outer aspect of your shoulders. Gripping the bar with your hands near these two points can be an appropriate starting grip width for many people. However, the specific grip width that is best to use for this exercise will vary among different individuals. To personally find your ideal placement, feel free to try out different hand widths over time while noting how your shoulders feel. The hand placement that is best for you should feel comfortable on your shoulders while enabling you to train through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility permits.
    3. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
8. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of reps with the form described under the exercise technique section prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
    1. If you cannot comfortably unrack the bar and avoid bumping the J-hooks during these reps, adjust your bench placement and/or J-hook height and repeat this step until you can do so.
    2. If you are using an adjustable bench with a tall backrest and notice that the top of the backrest restricts your range of motion, you can position the bench to its flat setting and simply perform the exercise without any back support. This is a modification to the standard technique, so you will ignore the directions to keep your back against the backrest if you use this approach and otherwise use the same pressing technique.
9. If you have access to adjustable safety pins, position the pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase.
    1. This will entail placing the pins slightly below shoulder height (when seated) if you can comfortably lower the bar to your upper back.
10. Add plates of your desired load to the bar, and repeat steps 5-7 before commencing your working set.

### **Setting up an overhead press station**

1. Place the bar on top of the J-hooks behind the seat that will allow you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are seated on the bench.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks without having to shrug your shoulders up.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the top of the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. You may have to try out different J-hook heights to determine which setting is best for you, so you can initially leave the bar unloaded to check if you can comfortably unrack the bar.
2. Sit down with your buttocks and back in contact with the bench. Firmly place your feet flat on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart with your knees bent.
    1. Your hips should be fully back against the seat.
3. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
4. Reach up overhead and firmly grasp the bar with your hands at least moderately outside shoulder width as your palms are facing forward.
    1. Relative to a standard overhead press performed to the front of your body, a wider grip will normally be more comfortable when pressing behind your head.
    2. If you raise your arms straight out to your sides until they are parallel to the ground, note the midway points between your elbows and the outer aspect of your shoulders. Gripping the bar with your hands near these two points can be an appropriate starting grip width for many people. However, the specific grip width that is best to use for this exercise will vary among different individuals. To personally find your ideal placement, feel free to try out different hand widths over time while noting how your shoulders feel. The hand placement that is best for you should feel comfortable on your shoulders while enabling you to train through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility permits.
    3. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of overhead press reps with the form described under the exercise technique section prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
    1. If you cannot comfortably unrack the bar, you can situate the bar on a different pair of J-hooks and try again.
    2. If you lack the shoulder mobility to unrack the bar from the J-hooks behind the bench, you can situate the bar on top of the J-hooks in front of you that are slightly above shoulder height (when seated). To unrack the bar from these J-hooks, you could initially scoot forward on the seat until your shoulders are close to being under the bar, lift the bar up off the J-hooks, and scoot back to the back rest. Then you would have to press the bar overhead before lowering it behind your head. Note that this approach to unrack the bar from the front J-hooks differs from the standard unrack method described in the exercise technique section.
6. Add plates of your desired load to the bar, and repeat steps 2-4 before commencing your working set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position and throughout the exercise, your feet should be firmly planted on the ground.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward until it is just in front of the front edge of the J-hooks. Hold the bar in this position for a moment.
    1. Maintain your “proud chest” posture to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. In a slow and controlled manner, lower the bar behind your head through the range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. If you have the mobility to do so comfortably, you can lower the bar until it lightly contacts your upper back muscles just under the base of your neck. However, what constitutes your end range will be determined by your individual shoulder mobility.
    2. If you start experiencing shoulder pain or joint discomfort at the bottom of the lowering phase, you likely are moving beyond the current limit of your shoulder mobility. Training this exercise over time may progressively improve your shoulder mobility and gradually permit you to descend through a greater range, but there is no need to force yourself into a position that currently does not feel right for your shoulders.
    3. With sufficient shoulder mobility, you should not have to push your head meaningfully forward to avoid scraping your head or neck with the bar. However, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest if you wish to do so for additional clearance.
    4. Strive to keep your elbows stacked under the bar when viewed from the side. To do so, your elbows should be pointing out away from your sides.
    5. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up overhead until your elbows are fully straightened.
    1. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows stacked under the bar.
    3. Maintain an upright torso as you avoid arching your lower back excessively.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the seat so that your upper arms can be parallel with the floor or a little lower while grasping the handles.
    1. After initially adjusting the seat height, spread your arms outward so that your hands are level with the handles.
    2. You may have to re-adjust the seat if your upper arms are not parallel with the floor or a little lower.
    3. Some people will find their shoulders feel more comfortable when the seat is set to a height that allows their hands to be a bit lower than their shoulders, compared to when their hands are completely level with their shoulders.
2. While sitting with your back against the backrest, spread your arms backward into a “T-position” through your available range of motion.
3. Adjust the pins above the handles to a position that allows you to grasp the horizontal handles with an overhand grip (i.e., palms facing down) when your arms are in this “T-position.”
    1. You may have to readjust the handles and recheck to see that the handles are not positioned too far behind, such that you cannot grab the handles, or positioned too far in front, such that your arms are not as far back into the “T-position” as your mobility allows.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Keep your shoulder blades in this tucked back position throughout the set.
2. Spread your arms apart into the “T-position” with a slight bend in your elbows before grasping the handles with an overhand grip (i.e., palms facing down).
3. Pull your arms together as the handles move toward each other until they are just about to contact each other or until they lightly contact each other.
4. Reverse the motion by spreading your arms in a controlled manner until you have returned to your starting position (i.e., the “T-position”).
5. Alternate between pulling your arms together and spreading them apart until you have completed the set.

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, adjust each cable to be near the height of your lower chest, connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you will also position the arms furthest back, such that they are directed out to the sides of the machine.
    2. Dual cable stations that have their two weight stacks facing each other (often with a pull-up in between them) normally lack adjustable arms.
2. While standing to the side of one cable, grasp its handle, and then walk over to grasp the handle of the other cable.
3. With your palms facing forward and your elbows slightly bent, center yourself between the cables, and step forward while allowing the cables to spread your arms apart and pull your arms back behind your torso through a range that your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. You want to be sufficiently positioned in front of the cables that the cables exert resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise. This will involve your hands being in front of the cable pulleys with tension still present from the cables when you are fully spread apart in the starting position of each rep.
    2. If your shoulder mobility comfortably allows your arms to move further behind your torso than they initially are, you can take another step forward to be able to train through a full range of motion.
    3. In line with the resistance from the cables, your upper arms should look like they form a “T-shape” with your torso as your elbows are close to shoulder height.
4. While mildly bending your knees, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other.
    1. In this position, you should feel stable and balanced.
5. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows mildly bent, sweep your arms forward and in toward each other in an arcing motion before mildly crossing your forearms over each other in front of your chest.
    1. To cross your forearms, you will naturally need to lift one arm slightly higher than the other arm, and you can decide which side you place in each position.
    2. At the end of the lifting phase, your forearms should form an “X-shape” with each other as your right hand is in front of your left shoulder, and your left hand is in front of your right shoulder.
    3. Keep your chest up throughout the set as you avoid hunching over with your shoulders slouched forward.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your hands to spread apart from each other in a controlled manner as they move backward and out away from your sides in line with the resistance from the cables until you have returned to the starting position with your arms fully spread apart.
    1. At the end of this movement, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulders, but the end range should not be painful.
    2. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to allow their arms to pull back until their elbows are slightly behind the torso, but your shoulder mobility will determine what your individual end range is.
    3. Continue keeping your elbows mildly bent as the movement comes from shoulder motion rather than elbow motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Based on your preference, you can alternate which arm crosses over the other during each rep, or you can use the same position throughout the set. If you prefer to use the same position throughout the set, you can alternate which arm crosses over the other from set to set, or you can use the same position during each set. Each side is being trained in an extremely similar manner, so there is little reason to be concerned about developing any meaningful side-to-side imbalance, regardless of whether you decide to alternate which arm crosses over the other.
