## Setting up
1. If your decline press station allows you to adjust them, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench. If your decline press station has fixed J-hook heights, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
2. After situating a bar on top of the J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of decline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to confirm they are the appropriate height prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
3. Load the bar with your intended weight.
    1. It is recommended to avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would permit you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
4. Sit down on the bench while snugly positioning the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
    2. Most decline press stations do not allow you to adjust this pad.
5. Lie down with your back and head on the bench.
    1. Ideally, the bar should now be reasonably close to being above your eyes. However, decline press stations do not allow you to adjust where you position your body on the bench as you could do on a flat bench or an incline press station (which typically has an adjustable seat).
    2. When locking your feet and ankles under the pad, you cannot meaningfully adjust where your body will be in relation to the bar. Consequently, a decline bench press station may not be well suited to accommodate every body type. Rather short people may find that the bar is positioned behind the back of their head, which can make it quite difficult to unrack the bar. In this instance, a spotter may be required to provide meaningful assistance when unracking and racking the bar. Alternatively, if you happen to be tall enough that the bar is positioned above your shoulders when lying down, it may simply not be practical to use a decline press station since the J-hooks will interfere with your bar path.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands near shoulder width apart. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. Positioning your hands near shoulder-width apart results in somewhat of a range, but you can initially start with a shoulder-width grip and try out mildly different hand widths over time to determine where specifically you feel best.
    2. What is personally considered a close grip to you can also be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard decline press, which you can mildly narrow to individualize your close grip. For instance, for your close grip, you can place your little finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your index finger when performing your standard decline press.
    3. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    4. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    5. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, but avoid exaggerating this arch any further.
## Exercise technique
1. While squeezing your glutes, brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, as if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be securely locked in place, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and keeping them reasonably tucked in toward your sides. Descend until you are able to tap your lower chest or lower breastbone lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists (when viewed from the side) rather than letting your elbows track in front of your wrists (closer to your hips) or behind them. This should result in your forearms remaining close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set.
    2. Keeping your wrists stacked over your elbows while touching near your lower chest will naturally promote the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare. At the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming reasonably close to 45-30-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso). This should involve a lesser degree of elbow flare compared to if you used a wider grip.
    3. When aiming to touch the bar near your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up until it is situated above your shoulders with your elbows fully straightened.
    1. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and in toward each other.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest.
    3. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

This exercise can effectively develop your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) with a focus on its [middle and lower regions](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md)  while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable decline bench at a decline angle near 15-30 degrees.
    1. As the decline angle becomes more pronounced, the range of motion for this exercise decreases, so a relatively mild decline is typically appropriate.
    2. Some adjustable benches have a mild decline setting along with incline settings, but lack a pad to secure your feet. Using a decline bench with a foot/ankle pad is recommended for stability during this exercise.
2. Center the decline bench underneath a Smith machine’s bar in a spot that will allow you to touch near your lower chest with the bar at the bottom of the press.
    1. After initially estimating which bench placement allows this to occur, you may have to move the bench a bit forward or backward during later steps if you notice the bar does not reach near your lower chest.
    2. Specifically how you should set up can be influenced by whether your Smith machine has sliding rails that are purely vertical or angled.
    3. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, place the side of the bench where you will place your feet on the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends. This will result in the top of the rails being horizontally closer to your head than the bottom of the rails when lying down on the bench. An angled Smith machine will prompt the bar to track mildly back toward your head when pressing the bar up.
    4. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which side of the bar you place your feet.
3. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to grasp it with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench.
    1. The ideal height allows you to unrack the bar while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together without requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    2. If the bar is situated too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart to lift the bar off the safety bars (on which the safety hooks that are attached to the bar rest). This can place you in a less stable position to start your set since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    3. If the bar is situated excessively low, you will have to grasp the bar initially with a greater degree of elbow bend, and unracking it will involve a greater than ideal pressing range of motion. This will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    4. If neither of the two closest bar heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    5. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best starting bar height for you.
4. After positioning the bar to the appropriate height, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of decline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section. Use these reps to determine the appropriate height of the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails under the bar) prior to re-racking the bar.
5. Position the safety stops slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your decline press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could untuck your shoulder blades. This will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety stops if the safety stops are just under your lower chest.
    2. Certain Smith machine models have fairly wide spaces between where you could position safety stops. This may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your decline press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you untuck your shoulder blades. If this applies to your Smith machine, you have the option of using a spotter.
    3. If you cannot press the bar fully up and lack a spotter or safety stops that are able to receive the bar, you may be able to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars above your chest if you are able to complete part of the press. If you happen to become pinned in this situation and are initially unable to reach the nearest safety bars above you, you can let the bar rest on your chest until you feel recovered enough to press the bar up high enough to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars.
6. After loading the bar with your intended weight, sit down on the bench while snugly positioning the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
7. Lie down with your back and head on the bench.
    1. With the appropriate bench placement, your lower chest should now be under the bar if your Smith machine has vertical slide rails. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, your lower chest should be mildly horizontally in front of the bar.
8. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for a bench press variation is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
9. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, but avoid exaggerating this arch any further.
## Exercise technique
1. While squeezing your glutes, brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, as if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be securely locked in place, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the safety bars by straightening your elbows before rotating the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion. After unracking it, hold the bar stationary for a moment before starting to lower it.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other. Descend until you are able to tap near your lower chest lightly with the bar
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set.
    2. Avoid fully flaring your elbows out away from your sides or completely tucking them. The appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar near your lower chest. At the bottom of the rep, your upper arms should be reasonably close to forming 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    3. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up until you have fully straightened your elbows. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
    1. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second.
6. Rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars by flicking your wrists before bending your elbows to lower the safety hooks securely onto the safety bars.

## Setting up
1. Follow the set-up instructions for the [dual kettlebell clean](Dual%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d88030b58fd481d9951983.md), and perform the lifting phase of the [dual kettlebell clean](Dual%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d88030b58fd481d9951983.md) described in steps 1-5 of its exercise technique instructions.
    1. After doing so, you should now be holding the kettlebell in the front rack position. This involves situating them in front of your shoulders with your elbows bent slightly in front of your ribcage, palms facing in toward each other, and the weights resting on your forearms, which are mostly vertically with your wrists slightly closer to the midline of your body than your elbows. The handle should also be diagonally contacting your palms, such that the sides of the handles by your thumbs are angled mildly higher than the sides of the handles by your little fingers.
    2. As an alternative to cleaning the kettlebells, you can curl them up into the same front rack position described above if you are using loads that are light enough to do so. With this technique, initially grasp the handles with your little fingers directly next to one of the horns (i.e., side handles) on each kettlebell to help the handles rest diagonally across your palms in the front rack position. Feel free to perform a cheat curl-like motion where you initially generate some momentum by swinging the weights mildly backward with straight elbows before swinging your elbows forward while curling them. This is a less technically complicated means of moving the kettlebells into the front rack, but it is not as efficient when using heavy weights for lifters who are proficient with cleaning kettlebells.
2. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, keep your chest up in a “proud chest” posture, rather than letting your shoulders and upper back round forward into a hunched position.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain its natural curvature like when you are normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes like you are trying to crush a walnut. Simultaneously, brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue keeping your glutes tightened and core braced throughout your set.
2. While simultaneously flaring your elbows out away from your sides and directing your palms forward, press the kettlebells upward.
    1. Strive to finish with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling with your elbows fully straightened, and your biceps by your ears.
    2. Rather than turning the exercise into a segmented movement where you flare your elbows fully outward and then drive them upward, aim to have the outward elbow flare fluidly occur while pressing up.
    3. While your forearms start slightly angled in the front rack position, they should otherwise remain essentially in a vertical position with your elbows stacked under your wrists throughout the press.
    4. Continue keeping your knees and wrists straight as the kettlebells contact your forearms throughout the set.
    5. Avoid leaning your torso back via lower back arching, which may be more likely to occur if you relax your abs or glutes.
    6. Allow your shoulder blades to move naturally.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the kettlebells in a controlled manner as you let your elbows bend while descending and arcing forward toward the front rack position.
    1. Finish with your wrists in front of your shoulders, palms facing in toward each other, and elbows bent slightly in front of your ribcage.
    2. While keeping them vertical throughout most of this step, allow your forearms to angle slightly inward at the end, resulting in your straight wrists being slightly closer to your midline than your elbows.
    3. There is no need to lower the kettlebells very slowly, but you should avoid letting them drop down abruptly in an uncontrolled fashion.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the kettlebells down in the opposite manner to how you initially lifted them into the front rack position.
    1. If you initially cleaned the kettlebells, you can let the kettlebells fall forward as you swing your arms down while straightening your elbows and hinging at your hips to absorb the force of the lowering phase.
    2. If you initially curled the kettlebells up, you can similarly guide them down by letting your elbows straighten and swinging your elbows mildly back to help control the weights.

## Setting up
1. Position the J-hooks of a power rack (or squat stand) near the height of your upper chest.
    1. As an alternative to starting from a rack, you can begin with the barbell on the floor and power clean it into position. However, this page will describe how to set up from a rack.
2. Place a barbell onto the J-hooks and load it with your desired weight.
3. Stand in front of the middle of the bar with your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with your hands near shoulder width apart, as your palms are facing away from you.
    1. What is personally considered a close grip to you can be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard overhead press, which you can narrow somewhat to individualize your close grip. For instance, for your close grip, you can place your little finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your index finger when performing your standard overhead press. However, if you already use a shoulder-width grip for your standard overhead press rather than a slightly outside shoulder-width grip, overhead pressing may feel awkward with your hands any closer than shoulder-width apart.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Slightly bend your knees, and step forward to situate your collarbone or upper chest directly under the bar. Simultaneously, position your elbows under the bar and just slightly in front of it. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists stacked under the bar.
    1. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    2. Your forearms should now be close to a vertical position when viewed from the front.
    3. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    4. Relative to when you overhead press with a wider grip, which normally involves a greater degree of elbow flare (pointing out to the side), your elbows should naturally be tucked in (pointing forward) to a greater extent during this close-grip variation.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
2. Fully stand upright while holding the bar.
    1. With your knees straightened, the bar should now be above the tops of the J-hooks.
3. Take a couple of steps backward and set your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable to you, you can point your toes straight ahead or rotate them slightly out to the side.
4. Squeeze your glutes and quads from now until you finish your last rep.
    1. This will create a stable platform from which to press.
5. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Avoid leaning back into an excessively arched position.
6. Tuck or tilt your chin back to move your head behind the bar.
    1. The goal is to move your head out of the bar’s way so that you can press straight upward without hitting your face with the bar.
7. While keeping your legs straight, press the bar upward with as close to a straight bar path as you can perform.
    1. To the best of your ability, avoid pushing the bar forward out in front of your shoulders. This can be challenging if you are new to this exercise, since you want to avoid hitting your face with the bar. You can still meaningfully increase your strength and grow muscle if the bar drifts a bit forward, but strive to minimize any forward bar motion as well as you can for an efficient overhead press.
    2. Do not lean back any further or excessively arch your lower back. Your lower back should stay locked in the same position throughout your rep.
    3. Avoid using your legs to help with driving the bar up. This is not a push press.
8. Immediately after the bar clears the top of your head, mildly push your head forward until your ears are close to being under the bar.
    1. Rather than pushing your head excessively forward, you primarily should be reversing the backward chin tuck/tilt you previously performed.
9. Finish the press with your elbows straightened as the bar is overhead.
    1. You should be able to draw a straight line down from the bar that passes through your shoulders, hips, knees, and the middle of your feet.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath during your set, you can breathe after locking out the weight overhead. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to lowering the bar.
10. Reverse the movement by tucking your chin back and lowering the bar toward your collarbone in a controlled manner.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down.
    2. Compared to if you used a moderate grip width, it may be more difficult to touch your collarbone with the bar when using a close grip. If it feels awkward to reach your collarbone with this variation, there is no need to force yourself into that position.
11. Alternate between steps 7-10 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
12. After completing the lowering phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second before walking forward.
13. After the bar contacts the back of both J-hooks, bend your knees slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [upper pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, adjust each cable to be near the height of your lower chest, connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, set the arms so that their ends are about the length of your wingspan apart from each other.
2. While standing to the side of one cable, grasp its handle, and then walk over to grasp the handle of the other cable.
3. With your palms facing forward and your elbows slightly bent, center yourself between the cables, and step forward while allowing the cables to spread your arms apart and pull your arms back behind your torso through a range that your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. You want to be sufficiently positioned in front of the cables that the cables exert resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise. This will involve your hands being in front of the cable pulleys with tension still present from the cables when you are fully spread apart in the starting position of each rep.
    2. If your shoulder mobility comfortably allows your arms to move further behind your torso than they initially are, you can take another step forward to be able to train through a full range of motion.
    3. In line with the resistance from the cables, your upper arms should look like they form a “T-shape” with your torso as your elbows are close to shoulder height.
4. While mildly bending your knees, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other.
    1. In this position, you should feel stable and balanced.
5. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows mildly bent, pull your hands in toward each and forward in an arcing motion until they are close to touching with your arms out in front of your torso.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, your hands should be close to shoulder height, and your arms should look like you are hugging a barrel.
    2. Keep your chest up throughout the set as you avoid hunching over with your shoulders slouched forward.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your hands to spread apart from each other in a controlled manner as they move backward and out away from your sides in line with the resistance from the cables until you have returned to the starting position with your arms fully spread apart.
    1. At the end of this movement, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulders, but the end range should not be painful.
    2. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to allow their arms to pull back until their elbows are slightly behind the torso, but your shoulder mobility will determine what your individual end range is.
    3. Continue keeping your elbows mildly bent as the movement comes from shoulder motion rather than elbow motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can set up on an exercise mat.
2. Spread your fingers somewhat apart from each other as your hands are situated directly underneath your shoulders (i.e., shoulder-width apart).
    1. Your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
3. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you, and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest in a controlled manner until it lightly touches the ground.
    1. Rather than excessively flaring your elbows out away from your sides, keep your elbows reasonably tucked by your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you as you descend.
    2. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ground instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    5. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ground to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), which is assisted by your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), and [pec minor](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Minor%201905c6f170d88030b03dd3f99706ecb0.md).

## Setting up
1. Approach the pair of bars/handles that you will use for your dip.
    1. While you do not have to maintain a completely upright torso, keep your torso mostly upright for this triceps dip rather than more prominently leaning your torso forward like you would during a chest dip. A mild degree of torso lean can naturally occur without striving to lean forward and often contributes to the exercise feeling more comfortable than if you focus on being fully upright.
2. Firmly grasp the bars with your palms facing each other and your elbows straight. Hold the handles directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
    2. If you are using angled bars, you can grasp the bars at the point where they are near shoulder width apart for you.
    3. Depending on the equipment you use, you initially may have to step up onto the equipment or a step you position nearby before you can grasp the bars with straight elbows.
3. While keeping your elbows straightened and torso upright, lift your feet off the ground.
    1. Depending on the equipment you use, you may have to bend your knees in order for your feet to clear the ground, or you may be able to keep your knees straight.
    2. With straight knees, you can keep the inner aspect of your feet against each other. If you bend your knees, you can cross your ankles.
    3. Compared to positioning your legs further backward or forward, keeping your thighs close to vertical can generally promote an upright torso.
4. Pull your shoulder blades back and down to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. You chiefly want to prevent your shoulders from rolling forward or shrugging up during this exercise.
    2. It is not required to keep your shoulder blades packed down further than they normally are at rest, but the intent to pack them down will prevent your torso from sagging down, which would place you into a shrugged shoulder position.
    3. Similarly, you do not necessarily need to have your shoulder blades fully back in the starting position, but pulling them back can make it easier to avoid tilting your shoulders forward, which is undesirable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. As you keep them tucked close to your sides, bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. While you do not have to maintain a completely upright torso, keep your torso mostly upright for this triceps dip rather than more prominently leaning your torso forward like you would during a chest dip. A mild degree of torso lean can naturally occur without striving to lean forward and often contribute to the exercise feeling more comfortable than if you focused on being fully upright.
    2. Throughout your set, keep your legs stationary relative to your hips (rather than swinging them) and avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up.
    3. Avoid flaring your elbows out away from your sides. When viewed from behind, your elbows should remain stacked over your wrists and the bars rather than having your elbows move noticeably outside your wrists.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point at which their elbows are bent by at least 90 degrees, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Reverse the movement by pushing through the bars to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows straight down.
    2. You should finish with your elbows close to your sides and your arms directed down toward the ground.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step down from the bars.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [lateral](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Lateral%20Head%2018f5c6f170d880c0a504d0d644758f40.md) and [medial](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Medial%20Head%201905c6f170d880fbb6e9e7e7ca37f2d1.md) heads of your triceps while also training its [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md) to a lesser degree, along with your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while holding the dumbbell at your side with a straight elbow as your palm faces in toward your thigh.
    1. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    2. Throughout the exercise, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side or held out to the side for balance assistance.
    3. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training first.
2. Lift the dumbbell up near the front of your shoulder with your elbow bent by curling the weight and using momentum from your lower body as needed.
    1. You can perform a cheat curl-like motion to move the dumbbell into position if it is too heavy to lift without momentum. To do so, first sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and simultaneously rocking the dumbbell mildly backward. Then drive your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body while bending your elbow to curl the weight upward while swinging your elbow forward. The hip drive motion, which is similar to the lockout of a deadlift, will bring your torso into a vertical position with your knees straightened.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbell right by your shoulder with your forearm in a vertical position, and your wrist stacked over your elbow as the handle of the dumbbell is parallel to your upper arm.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbell on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a mostly straight wrist that allows for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, pull your shoulder blades back together to adopt a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back along with your neck, like when you are normally standing upright.
4. In the starting position, your palm should be facing inward (with a neutral grip) as your upper arm is in front of your body with the back of your elbow pointing downward and forward (as opposed to being flared out away from your side).
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Without moving your arm, mildly bend your knees in a quarter squat-like manner to dip down while maintaining an upright torso position with your chest up.
    1. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground during this dip phase.
    2. Your knees should track straight forward toward your toes rather than caving inward.
3. Directly after reaching the bottom of your dip, forcibly push through your feet as you rapidly extend (straighten) your knees and hips to generate upward momentum.
    1. The intent of this leg drive phase should be akin to a jump without lifting your feet fully off the ground.
    2. At the end of this drive, you can either keep the soles of your feet fully on the ground, or you can allow your heels to lift up slightly off the ground while keeping the front of your feet firmly in contact with the ground if a slight heel lift feels natural to you.
4. Immediately after you have finished extending your legs, explosively push the dumbbell upward by forcibly driving your elbow upward as you swiftly straighten your elbow.
    1. At the end of the pressing phase, your knees, hips, and elbow should be fully straightened, and your arm should be directed straight up toward the ceiling with your elbow and dumbbell situated vertically over your shoulder.
    2. To transfer your leg drive into pushing the dumbbell upward in an explosive manner, you should perform steps 3 and 4 as a continuous movement.
    3. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulder and elbow, your forearm should be in a vertical position throughout the rep as your wrist and dumbbell remain stacked over your elbow.
    4. Throughout the exercise, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back.
    5. Regardless of whether you lifted your heels up off the ground after extending your legs during the leg drive phase, your heels should be flat on the ground with the rest of your feet at the end of the pressing phase.
5. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner as your elbow progressively bends while simultaneously moving downward.
6. As you approach the end of the lowering phase, shallowly bend your knees and hips as you did during step 2 (the dip phase) to help control the weight until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbell in front of your shoulder.
    1. Lower the dumbbell as far as you can while keeping your wrist in a straight position stacked over your elbow as your forearm remains vertical, which should result in your elbow being lower than your shoulder.
    2. Avoid descending beyond the point at which you can keep your forearm vertical.
    3. If you are using a heavy, bulky dumbbell, the dumbbell contacting your shoulder may also determine your end range of the lowering phase.
7. After you have fully lowered the weight, extend your knees and hips to stand upright before initiating your next rep.
8. Alternate between steps 2-7 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
9. After your dumbbell is by your shoulder following the lowering phase of the last rep, lower the dumbbell to your side as you straighten your elbow and swing your elbow back by your side.
10. Set the dumbbell down and pick it up with your other side before repeating the exercise with that side.

While developing explosive overhead pressing strength and engaging the [quads](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md) to generate leg drive, this exercise can train  your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md),  and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a pair of dumbbells on the ground next to each other with their handles vertical, if possible for the dumbbells you are using.
    1. Positioning them in this manner will result in one weighted end of each dumbbell being off the ground.
    2. However, you will have to situate both ends of each dumbbell on the ground (with their handles parallel to the ground) if you are using dumbbells that do not have flat ends (such as with a plate-loaded adjustable dumbbell). You can still floor press these dumbbells, but it can be more difficult to move them into the starting position, particularly if you are using heavy loads.
    3. You can optionally place an exercise mat on the ground behind the dumbbells for comfort.
2. Sit down on the ground with your thighs spread apart just outside the dumbbells.
    1. Your knees should be straight as you are sitting with an upright torso and the back of your heels on the ground.
3. One at a time, firmly grasp the dumbbells and position them on top of your upper thighs with their handles vertical and your elbows tucked close to your sides.
    1. When using dumbbells with flat ends, place them on the middle part of your thighs.
    2. If you are using plate-loaded adjustable dumbbells with protruding sleeves, you can rest the outer part of the dumbbells on the inner aspect of the front of your thighs. This will result in the lower sleeve contacting the inner aspect of your thighs
4. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back in a controlled manner to lie down.
    1. Move your torso and arms together as one unit. This will result in your upper arms remaining by your sides throughout the transition and contacting the ground at the same time as your back.
    2. When appropriately moving into position, you should not feel that you are meaningfully stressing your shoulders.
    3. When marching your thighs up, your thighs should be close to vertical with your knees bent once your back contacts the ground.
    4. Strive to have the dumbbells vertically stacked over your elbows when lying on the ground, resulting in your forearms being in a vertical position.
    5. Once you are on your back, you should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists. This should promote a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
5. Position your legs straight out in front of you with straight knees.
    1. The back of your heels should now be on the ground along with your buttocks, upper back, and head.
6. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
7. Flare your elbows moderately out to your sides such that your upper arms form approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso.
    1. Keep your forearms vertical while doing so.
    2. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable for your shoulders, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbows out within this range.
    3. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbows are completely tucked by your sides, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your upper arms would form a “T-shape” with your torso.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbells upward until your elbows are fully straightened with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your wrists mostly straight and stacked under your elbows throughout the press. This will result in your forearms remaining in a vertical position.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
    4. Throughout your set, continue keeping your heels, buttock, upper back, and head in contact with the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner until your elbows and upper arms softly contact the ground.
    1. Allow your elbows to flare out moderately away from your sides so that your upper arms form close to 45-75-degree angles with your torso at the bottom.
    2. Continue keeping your wrists stacked over your elbows as your forearms remain vertical.
    3. While you do not have to finish the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you certainly should avoid slamming your arms onto the ground. You will not be bouncing your arms off the ground.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the reverse manner to how you initially set up.
5. After finishing the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arms in line with your sides to tuck your elbows and position the dumbbells closer to your torso.
6. March your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs before setting them down.

## Setting up
1. Position the J-hooks of a power rack (or squat stand) near the height of your upper chest.
2. Place a barbell onto the J-hooks and load it with your desired weight.
    1. It is recommended to use an empty barbell if you are new to this exercise.
3. Stand in front of the middle of the bar with your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with your hands at least moderately outside shoulder width as your palms are facing away from you.
    1. Relative to a standard overhead press performed to the front of your body, a wider grip will normally be more comfortable when pressing behind your head.
    2. If you raise your arms straight out to your sides until they are parallel to the ground, note the midway points between your elbows and the outer aspect of your shoulders. Gripping the bar with your hands near these two points can be an appropriate starting grip width for many people. However, the specific grip width that is best to use for this exercise will vary among different individuals. To personally find your ideal placement, feel free to try out different hand widths over time while noting how your shoulders feel. The hand placement that is best for you should feel comfortable on your shoulders while enabling you to train through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility permits.
    3. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Slightly bend your knees, and step forward to situate your collarbone or upper chest directly under the bar. Simultaneously, position your elbows under the bar and just slightly in front of it. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists stacked under the bar.
    1. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Relative to when you overhead press to the front with a closer grip, which normally involves a greater degree of elbow tuck (pointing forward), your elbows should naturally be flared out (pointing out to the side) to a greater extent during this variation.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
2. Fully stand upright while holding the bar.
    1. With your knees straightened, the bar should now be above the tops of the J-hooks.
3. Take a couple of steps backward and set your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable to you, you can point your toes straight ahead or rotate them slightly out to the side.
4. Squeeze your glutes and quads from now until you finish your last rep.
    1. This will create a stable platform from which to press.
5. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Avoid leaning back into an excessively arched position.
6. Tuck your chin back to move your head behind the bar.
    1. The goal is to move your head out of the bar’s way so that you can press straight upward without hitting your face with the bar.
7. Press the bar upward with as close to a straight bar path as you can perform.
    1. Do not lean back any further or excessively arch your lower back. Your lower back should stay locked in the same position.
8. Immediately after the bar clears the top of your head, mildly push your head forward until your ears are close to being under the bar. Simultaneously, arc the bar slightly backward while pressing it up.
    1. Rather than pushing your head excessively forward, you primarily should be reversing the backward chin tuck/tilt you previously performed.
9. Finish the initial press with your elbows straightened as the bar is overhead.
    1. You should be able to draw a straight line down from the bar that passes through your shoulders, hips, knees, and the middle of your feet.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath during your set, you can breathe after locking out the weight overhead. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to lowering the bar.
    3. You are now in the starting position for your behind-the-neck press.
10. In a slow and controlled manner, lower the bar behind your head through the range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. If you have the mobility to do so comfortably, you can lower the bar until it lightly contacts your upper back muscles just under the base of your neck. However, what constitutes your end range will be determined by your individual shoulder mobility.
    2. If you start experiencing shoulder pain or joint discomfort at the bottom of the lowering phase, you likely are moving beyond the current limit of your shoulder mobility. Training this exercise over time may progressively improve your shoulder mobility and gradually permit you to descend through a greater range, but there is no need to force yourself into a position that currently does not feel right for your shoulders.
    3. With sufficient shoulder mobility, you should not have to push your head meaningfully forward to avoid scraping your head or neck with the bar. However, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest if you wish to do so for additional clearance.
    4. Strive to keep your elbows stacked under the bar when viewed from the side. To do so, your elbows should be pointing out away from your sides.
    5. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down.
11. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up until you have fully straightened your elbows with the bar overhead.
12. Alternate between steps 10 and 11 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
13. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, tuck your chin back and lower the bar to your collarbone.
14. With the bar now in front of your body, walk forward until the bar contacts the back of both J-hooks
15. Bend your knees slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks.

    1. The intent of this leg drive phase should be akin to a jump without lifting your feet fully off the ground.
    2. At the end of this drive, you can either keep the soles of your feet fully on the ground, or you can allow your heels to lift up slightly off the ground while keeping the front of your feet firmly in contact with the ground if a slight heel lift feels natural to you.
4. Immediately after you have finished extending your legs, explosively push the dumbbells upward by forcibly driving your elbows upward as you swiftly straighten your elbows.
    1. At the end of the pressing phase, your knees, hips, and elbows should be fully straightened, and your arms should be directed straight up toward the ceiling with your elbows and dumbbells situated vertically over your shoulders.
    2. To transfer your leg drive into pushing the dumbbells upward in an explosive manner, you should perform steps 3 and 4 as a continuous movement.
    3. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your forearms should be in a vertical position throughout the rep as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    4. Throughout the exercise, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back.
    5. Regardless of whether you lifted your heels up off the ground after extending your legs during the leg drive phase, your heels should be flat on the ground with the rest of your feet at the end of the pressing phase.
5. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner as your elbows progressively bend while simultaneously moving downward.
6. As you approach the end of the lowering phase, shallowly bend your knees and hips like you did during step 2 (the dip phase) to help control the weight until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbells in front of your shoulders.
    1. Lower the dumbbells as far as you can while keeping your wrists in a straight position stacked over your elbows as your forearms remain vertical, which should result in your elbows being lower than your shoulders.
    2. Avoid descending beyond the point at which you can keep your forearms vertical.
    3. If you are using heavy, bulky dumbbells, the dumbbells contacting your shoulders may also determine your end range of the lowering phase.
7. After you have fully lowered the weights, extend your knees and hips to stand upright before initiating your next rep.
8. Alternate between steps 2-7 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your dumbbells are by your shoulders following the lowering phase of the last rep, lower the dumbbells to your sides as you straighten your elbows and swing your elbows back by your sides.
## Description
While developing explosive overhead pressing strength and engaging the [quads](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md) to generate leg drive, this exercise can train  your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md),  and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. If your decline press station allows you to adjust them, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench. If your decline press station has fixed J-hook heights, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
2. After situating a bar on top of the J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of decline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to confirm they are the appropriate height prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
3. Load the bar with your intended weight.
    1. It is recommended to avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would permit you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
4. Sit down on the bench while snugly positioning the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
    2. Most decline press stations do not allow you to adjust this pad.
5. Lie down with your back and head on the bench.
    1. Ideally, the bar should now be reasonably close to being above your eyes. However, decline press stations do not allow you to adjust where you position your body on the bench as you could do on a flat bench or an incline press station (which typically has an adjustable seat).
    2. When locking your feet and ankles under the pad, you cannot meaningfully adjust where your body will be in relation to the bar. Consequently, a decline bench press station may not be well suited to accommodate every body type. Rather short people may find that the bar is positioned behind the back of their head, which can make it quite difficult to unrack the bar. In this instance, a spotter may be required to provide meaningful assistance when unracking and racking the bar. Alternatively, if you happen to be tall enough that the bar is positioned above your shoulders when lying down, it may simply not be practical to use a decline press station since the J-hooks will interfere with your bar path.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands well outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A wide grip width for a bench press variation is commonly considered to be near twice your shoulder width, and this involves somewhat of a range of grip widths, so you can feel free to try out mildly different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. What is personally considered a wide grip to you can also be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard decline press, which you can somewhat widen to individualize your wide grip. For instance, for your wide grip, you can place your index finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your little finger when performing your standard decline press.
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, but avoid exaggerating this arch any further.
## Exercise technique
1. While squeezing your glutes, brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, as if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be securely locked in place, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them naturally to flare out moderately away from each other. Descend until you are able to tap your lower chest or lower breastbone lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists (when viewed from the side) rather than letting your elbows track in front of your wrists (closer to your hips) or behind them. This should result in your forearms remaining close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set.
    2. When aiming to touch the bar near your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    3. To touch that point, you will not fully flare your elbows out away from your side to the extent that your upper arms form 90-degree angles with your torso. However, keeping your wrists stacked over your elbows will naturally promote a greater degree of elbow flare during this wide grip variation compared to when pressing with a closer grip. Near the bottom of the rep, the appropriate amount of elbow flare should result in your upper arms forming reasonably close to 75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are touching your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest.
    3. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) with a focus on its [middle and lower regions](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).
