## Setting up
1. Adjust a pair of securely anchored gymnastic rings to be near shoulder width apart with the bottom of the rings at hand height.
    1. For a more advanced fly variation, you can alternatively situate the rings closer to the ground, but this page will describe how to set up for an intermediate difficulty.
2. Grasp the rings with your palms facing in toward each other and your elbows straight. Hold the rings directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
3. How you subsequently position your body will be affected by the degree of difficulty you wish each to have. For a lower intensity fly, raise your arms so that they are directed diagonally forward and downward. For higher intensity fly, keep your arms directed down toward the ground.
    1. The difficulty of each rep will directly increase as your torso becomes closer to horizontal, which is facilitated by keeping your arms directed closer to straight down.
    2. As you angle your arms forward, you will be able to set up with a more vertical torso, which makes the exercise easier.
    3. The appropriate position should allow you to perform your fly through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits for your target number of reps.
    4. If you are new to this exercise, it is recommended to angle your arms diagonally forward to let you use a more vertical torso position during your set.
4. While bearing weight through the rings, step backward while allowing your torso to lean forward as one unit until your arms form approximately 90-degree angles with your torso when viewed from the side.
    1. Finish with your knee straight and your legs fully aligned with your torso, allowing you to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulder when viewed from the side.
    2. You should now look like you are in a tall plank position.
## Exercise technique
1. Tighten your abdominal muscles to brace your core and squeeze your glutes to maintain a flat back position while keeping your elbows and knees straight.
    1. Continue keeping your abs and glutes tensed throughout the set, like you would during a plank.
    2. Throughout the set, avoid letting your lower back arch excessively, which could occur if your hips start sagging.
2. Spread your arms apart from each other in a controlled manner while letting the rest of your body lean forward as one unit. Simultaneously, let your shoulder blades pull back together and your elbows mildly bend.
    1. Maintain the approximately 90-degree angles between your arms and torso as you avoid moving your arms closer toward your sides or further away from your sides.
    2. While motion chiefly occurs at your shoulders and mildly at your elbows, you should keep the rest of your body in a plank position as you avoid moving your legs or torso, besides allowing them to lean forward together.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point at which their elbows are at least level with their shoulders when viewed from the side, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders and chest, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility or have adopted an excessively horizontal torso relative to your current strength. Training this exercise over time may improve your mobility and strength, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Reverse the movement by driving your arms in toward each other to lift your body up toward a more vertical position.
    1. Allow your elbows to straighten naturally, and finish this lifting phase once the rings are shoulder width apart.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have finished your last rep, step forward to return to an upright torso position.

## Setting up
1. If you are using an adjustable incline bench, position it in the fully upright setting. Otherwise, proceed to the next step.
    1. You can interchangeably use an adjustable bench that is positioned fully upright or a seated bench that is permanently fixed in an upright position.
    2. Alternatively, you can use a bench that is permanently fixed in a flat position. This will preclude you from resting your back against the bench, but otherwise allow you to use the same technique that the exercise involves when using back support.
2. After picking up one dumbbell, sit down on a seated bench while lifting the dumbbell onto your lower thigh without leaning back onto the back rest.
    1. To move the dumbbell into the proper position, you can situate the dumbbell on the front of your thigh while standing up against the end of the bench, and you can rest it on your thigh while sitting down.
3. On the side firmly holding the dumbbell, tuck your elbow by your side. Tightly wrap your free hand around the hand holding the dumbbell.
4. March your thigh up as you lift the dumbbell up near your shoulder with your elbow bent. Simultaneously lean back to situate your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench.
    1. You can use both arms to help you lift the weight.
    2. After doing so, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    3. You should now be holding the dumbbell right by your shoulder with your forearm in a vertical position, and your wrist stacked over your elbow as the handle of the dumbbell is parallel to your upper arm.
5. Unwrap your outer hand, not directly holding the dumbbell, and move it into a comfortable position away from the weight, such as resting by your side.
    1. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training.
    2. You should be holding the dumbbell on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a mostly straight wrist that allows for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
6. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling, and maintain this posture throughout your set.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
7. Flare your elbow at least moderately out to your side to a degree that feels comfortable for your shoulder.
    1. When 0 degrees of elbow flare means your wrist is directly in front of your shoulder, and 90 degrees of elbow flare means your wrist is fully out to your side with your palm facing straight forward, about 60-75 degrees of elbow flare is commonly appropriate. In this position, your elbow will point more out to the side than forward, but it will not be fully flared out.
    2. If your shoulder feels comfortable when pressing with a greater degree of elbow flare, you can certainly flare your elbow beyond that point, but some people find that utilizing a closer to moderate degree of elbow flare feels most comfortable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbell upward by driving your elbow upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten your elbow until it is fully straightened with your arm directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulder and elbow, your forearm should be in a vertical position throughout the press as your wrist and dumbbell remain stacked over your elbow.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your feet flat on the floor along with your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbell should be situated vertically over your shoulder.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner as your elbow progressively bends while simultaneously moving outward and downward until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbell by the side of your shoulder.
    1. Lower the dumbbell as far as you can while keeping your wrist in a straight position stacked over your elbow as your forearm remains vertical, which should result in your elbow being lower than your shoulder.
    2. Avoid descending beyond the point at which you can keep your forearm vertical.
    3. If you are using a heavy, bulky dumbbell, the dumbbell contacting your shoulder may also determine your end range of the lowering phase.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
5. After the dumbbell is by your shoulder following the lowering phase of the last rep, bring your upper arm in line with your side to tuck your elbow and position the dumbbell closer to your thigh.
6. Wrap your free hand around the hand holding the dumbbell for additional stability.
7. March your thigh up, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbell on your upper thigh before standing up with the dumbbell.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a moderate incline near 45 degrees.
    1. Alternatively, you can also use a fixed moderate incline bench for this exercise.
    2. Any bench angle that is greater than 30 degrees but less than 60 degrees can be considered a moderate incline. 
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on the incline bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your lower thighs near your abdomen with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. If you can curl the weight of the dumbbells, you can sit down on the bench with the dumbbells by your sides before curling them up onto your lap
    2. With heavier dumbbells, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs with your palms facing each other while standing over the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
3. While marching your thighs up one at a time to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench.
    1. Once you are inclined, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent, and you will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest, as you would be in the starting position for a dumbbell incline press.
4. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
5. Press the dumbbells up until your elbows are straight, and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. In this starting position, your wrists should be straight, and you will keep them straight throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your elbows to bend mildly, spread your arms apart from each other as you lower the dumbbells out away from your sides in a slow and controlled arcing manner through the available range of motion of your shoulders.
    1. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to lower the dumbbells at least until their elbows are level with their shoulders and often a little beyond this point, but what is specifically your full range of motion will be dependent on your mobility.
    2. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulder at the bottom, but the end range should not be painful.
    3. After fully spreading your arms apart, your upper arms should form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    4. While your elbows should not be locked into a fully straightened position, they also should be notably less bent than when you are bench pressing, so the dumbbells should be clearly further out to the sides than your elbows (as opposed to being stacked over your elbows like at the bottom of a bench press).
2. Reverse the movement by pulling your arms in toward each other in a hug-like motion to lift the dumbbells upward until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbells being approximately over your shoulders.
    1. Near the end of the lifting phase, the resistance from the dumbbells is minimal, and there is no purpose of touching the dumbbells to each other.
    2. Toward the end of the lifting phase, you can straighten your elbows, or you can maintain the same degree of mild elbow bend throughout the set.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your last rep, lower the dumbbells toward the sides of your chest as you allow your elbows to bend like you would during the lowering phase of a dumbbell incline press.
    2. Once the dumbbells are by your chest, you can rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your thighs before placing them down onto the ground one at a time or standing up with them.

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to a barbell situated in a landmine attachment (or a viable substitute), stand in a shoulder width stance near the end of the barbell’s sleeve that is loaded with plates with one side facing the barbell.
    1. As an alternative to using a landmine attachment, landmine exercises can be performed with one end of the barbell situated in a wall corner.
    2. While the scraping can be lessened by placing a towel in between the wall corner and the barbell, be aware that performing landmine exercises in a wall corner can easily damage the wall corner, so this approach is not appropriate in every environment.
    3. The diameter of the plates you select can influence the range of motion of this exercise, so you can use smaller diameter plates if you wish to row through a longer range of motion.
    4. Plates weighing 45lb or 20kg (which differ slightly) along with bumper plates of various weights typically have a diameter near 45cm (slightly under 18 inches) that can physically constrain the range of motion for your row by contacting the ground at the end of the lowering phase.
2. Adopt a moderately staggered stance with your foot on the side closer to the bar positioned behind you and the inner aspect of your opposite foot in line with the barbell.
3. Simultaneously bend your hips and knees in a lunging motion to descend until you are low enough to grasp the end of the barbell’s sleeve with an extended elbow and an overhand grip resulting in your palm facing backward
    1. You will naturally grasp the bar with your hand on the side closer to the bar.
4. While firmly holding the bar, brace your core and stand upright with the bar by extending your hips and knees while keeping your elbow extended.
    1. Throughout this movement, keep your lower back reasonably close to a neutral position like you have when you are normally standing upright rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so.
    2. To brace effectively, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    3. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    4. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    5. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    6. While your lower back muscles will be working to maintain a rigid trunk position, lifting the bar upward should chiefly occur from your hip and thigh muscles extending your hips and knees.
5. Hinge at your hips through your available range of motion while you mildly bend your knees to position your torso at an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    1. Continue keeping your elbow extended, core braced, and lower back near a neutral position while doing so.
    2. Your buttock should move backward while you hinge at your hips as if you were closing a car door with your buttock while your hands are carrying something.
    3. How close to horizontal you are able to position your torso without meaningfully rounding your lower back will be dependent on your mobility.
    4. In the hinged position, it is natural to feel a stretching sensation in the hamstrings of your forward leg.
    5. Maintain this hinged position throughout your set.
    6. If using large diameter plates, the plates have the potential to contact the ground before you have finished hinging through your available range of motion, therefore requiring a relatively more upright trunk position.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar upward by driving your elbow upward and out to your side while progressively bending your elbow and pulling your shoulder blade backward .
    1. Allow your elbow naturally to flare out away from your side in a manner that feels comfortable to you.
    2. Keep your torso in a fixed hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set while keeping your core braced and your lower back near a neutral position.
    3. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your upper arm being close to parallel with the ground at the end of the lifting phase.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner by allowing your elbow to move downward and inward until your elbow has finished extending and the bar has returned to the starting position.
    1. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blade will naturally move forward.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up and firmly grasp it with your palms facing backward (i.e., an underhand grip) and your hands shoulder-width apart.
    1. Specifically, how closely you position your hands is up to your preference. Still, they should be clearly closer than for a standard chin-up with a moderate grip width (i.e., approximately shoulder width).
    2. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    3. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up onto a sturdy box, an aerobic step, or a bumper plate to place the bar within reach.
    4. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar than if you jumped up from the ground to reach it.
    5. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    6. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
2. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will place you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up by your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back puts you in a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending your elbows.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows naturally will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps; however, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

### **How Your Grip and Pull-Up Technique Influence Back Muscle Development**

Somewhat of a range of grip widths can fall within what is closer than shoulder width, but whether you opt to position your hands as close together as possible or only mildly within shoulder width is unlikely to alter to any meaningful degree which muscles are trained from this chin-up variation. Nonetheless, when repeatedly performing this exercise over time, you can feel free to try out different grip widths to determine if any particular position feels most comfortable to you and/or allows you to perceive your target muscles working particularly well. Pull-ups can be performed with a variety of hand grips including different grip widths and whether an overhand, underhand (resulting in the exercise being called a chin-up), neutral, or hybrid (i.e., a combination between neutral and underhand or overhand) grip is utilized. Additionally, the shoulder motion occurring during a pull-up can be performed predominantly in the sagittal (front to back) plane, frontal (side to side) plane, or in a combination between the sagittal and frontal planes. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the sagittal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out in front of you), the upper arms remain parallel to each other and do not deviate away from the mid-line of your body. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the frontal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out to your sides such as with a snow angle motion), the upper arms move away from the mid-line of your body until they are parallel to the ground, and then they move closer to the mid-line of your body with further elevation. During the lifting phase of a pull-up, the shoulders could extend when moving in the sagittal plane, adduct when moving in the frontal plane, or exhibit a combination of extension and adduction when moving at a hybrid between the sagittal and frontal planes. Rather than moving the shoulders exclusively through one plane, pull-up variations are commonly performed with a technique that allows for the shoulders to move in between these two planes, but one plane of shoulder motion often makes a greater contribution than the other.

Muscles acting on the shoulder joint have different leverage to generate extension torque in the sagittal plane versus adduction torque in the frontal plane, and the nervous system is most likely to recruit the particular muscles that are best leveraged to produce the intended joint action during any active movement. Correspondingly, the plane of motion in which the shoulders move during a pull-up can affect how well different muscles are likely to be trained. With any particular grip for a pull-up, you can intentionally rotate your shoulders in a manner that allows you to move your shoulder relatively more in the sagittal or frontal plane. However, most people will typically find that a particular path of shoulder motion feels most comfortable and stable to their shoulders, elbows, and wrists when using a specific grip. For instance, people will normally perform a wide overhand grip pull-up with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the frontal plane, while they will normally perform a close grip chin-up (using an underhand grip) with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the sagittal plane. To perform either variation in the alternative plane of motion would require greater than normal rotational range of motion in the shoulders and forearms, and attempting to do so could feel very awkward and uncomfortable. People will typically feel most comfortable when positioning themselves in a manner that, at the portion of the pull-up when their upper arms are situated parallel with the ground, results in their elbows and wrists being vertically aligned or their elbows lying somewhat lateral (outside) to their wrists.

In general, widening a grip facilitates relatively more frontal plane shoulder motion, while narrowing a grip facilitates relatively more sagittal plane shoulder motion. An overhand, underhand, or neutral grip may be used with any grip width, but the combination of these grip variables will influence comfort and which plane of shoulder motion feels most natural. When pulling predominantly in the sagittal plane with a rather close grip, an underhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable than an overhand grip. Similarly, when pulling predominantly in the frontal plane with a rather wide grip, an overhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable and enable more frontal plane motion than an underhand grip. With a moderate width grip, people may commonly find that pulling mostly in the sagittal plane feels natural with an underhand or neutral grip, but pulling relatively more in the frontal plane feels natural with an overhand grip. Fundamentally, the shoulder motion is what matters to the back muscles, and the grip is only relevant to the back muscles based on how it influences which shoulder motion is performed. When performing this chin-up with a close grip width, you most likely will pull in a way that predominantly trains shoulder extension in the sagittal plane as your elbows remain close to being aligned with your shoulders rather than flaring out to the sides.

The lat and teres major in the back function both as primary adductors and extensors and are consequently highly likely to be trained very effectively by pull-up variations regardless of the grip or plane of shoulder motion. However, the preponderance of available evidence indicates that the rear deltoid lacks meaningful leverage to contribute to shoulder adduction, but it clearly has favorable leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. The rear deltoid is correspondingly likely to be trained better with a closer grip emphasizing shoulder extension, which would be most comfortable when using an underhand or neutral grip. Alternatively the middle and lower regions of the pectoralis major (that constitute the sternoclavicular head) have large moment arms to function as shoulder adductors, but only the lower portion exhibits a shoulder extension moment arm, and this moment arm is quite small and only present in flexed shoulder positions. Consequently, wider grip pull-ups (that will be most comfortable with an overhand or neutral grip) involving greater frontal plane shoulder motion are likely to train the pectoralis major more effectively than closer grip pulldowns. Which regions of the lats are preferentially biased by a pull-up variation may also potentially be influenced by how much shoulder motion occurs in the frontal or sagittal planes. The middle and lower regions have relatively greater leverage to function as shoulder adductors, while the upper region of the lat has relatively greater leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. Plausibly, these biomechanical differences may facilitate the middle and lower regions of the lats being preferentially trained by wider grip pull-ups, while the upper region may be preferentially trained by closer grip pulling variations. With that said, the degree to which any preferential biasing may occur among different regions of the lats when comparing different pull-up grips is more speculative in nature and has not been tested by any longitudinal training interventions.

### **Why Overhand Grip Pull-Ups may be More Difficult than Chin-Ups or Neutral Grip Pull-Ups**

While exceptions exist, people often find overhand grip pull-ups to be more difficult on a per rep basis than chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. The discrepancy is most likely influenced by chin-ups and neutral grip pull-ups typically being performed with a technique that emphasizes shoulder extension in the sagittal plane, while overhand grip pull-ups are typically performed with relatively more shoulder adduction in the frontal plane. As demonstrated by studies such as those from Mayer et al. (1994) along with Shklar and Dvir (1995), on average, maximal torque for shoulder extension exceeds maximal torque for shoulder adduction. The sample of participants, velocity, and type of muscle action tested can all influence the degree to which torque differs between these two actions, but maximal shoulder adduction torque has been measured to be 63-90% of maximal shoulder extension depending on the specific test conditions. In addition to the effect from how the shoulder moves, the forearm position can also affect how much elbow flexion torque you can generate during your pull. Guenzkofer et al. (2012) found that up to 15% greater elbow flexion torque can be generated when the forearm is in supinated (used for an underhand grip) or neutral position compared to a pronated (used with an overhand grip) position. Together these relationships mean that most people should be able to generate greater torque at the shoulders and elbows while performing chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups in comparison to overhand grip pull-ups, which are likely to be more challenging when performing the same number of reps. Consequently, it is common not to be able to complete as many reps of overhand grip pull-ups in a set as you would be able to complete when performing chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. Nonetheless, individual differences among factors such as training history and the relative strength of different muscle groups can result in some people not noticing a difference in difficulty between these variations or even finding overhand grip pull-ups to be somewhat easier on a per rep basis.

### **Chin Over Bar?**

The technique instructions do not specify where any particular part of your body should be situated in relation to the bar at the end of the lifting phase because your full range of motion can differ from someone else’s full range of motion. Pulling until your chin is above the bar is a common standard that is utilized for pull-up testing by the United States Marines or competitions held by the World Pull-Up Organization (which permits use of an underhand or overhand grip), and you certainly can use this standard if you wish. However, when focusing on chin clearance, some people have a tendency to extend their necks in a manner that lifts their chins upward in order to clear the bar with lower range of motion through the pull itself compared to if they retained a neutral neck position. In this instance, focusing on the proxy for a full range of motion may lead to a different movement compared to focusing on what is the full range of motion for the individual. When competing or performing a standardized test that affects professional prospects, it is only sensible to perform the minimum amount of work required to complete each rep per the rules provided, but training to build muscle and strength is a different endeavor.

### **The Most Challenging Part of the Pull-Up**

The end range of the lifting phase will typically be the most challenging portion of chin-ups in large part due to how the torque our pulling muscles can generate meaningfully varies across different joint angles. When the elbow is flexed to 120 degrees, Bober et al. (2002) found maximal elbow flexion torque to be approximately 35% of the peak torque that can be generated in a moderately flexed elbow position (i.e., near 60-75 degrees of elbow flexion). With your elbows approaching full flexion toward the end range of a chin-up, your elbow flexor muscles are correspondingly operating from a rather disadvantaged position to help you complete the rep. On average, maximal shoulder extension torque is also lower when the shoulder is mildly elevated (like at the end of a chin-up’s lifting phase) compared to when it is moderately elevated (like during the middle range of a chin-up). The difference can be of a notable magnitude as indicated by Bober et al. (2002) finding maximal shoulder extension in a neutral shoulder position to be only 60% of its peak value that could be generated in 90 degrees of shoulder flexion. Together these strength curves of the muscle groups acting on the elbow and shoulder can contribute to your chin-ups consistently feeling the most difficult during the last quarter of the lifting phase.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your back muscle strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your back muscles. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

## Setting up
1. Stand under a very stable pull-up bar that is at least slightly above what you can reach with your feet on the ground.
    1. The bar should provide enough clearance so that your feet do not touch the ground when you hang from it with straight legs.
    2. In contrast to standard pull-ups, it is inherently unsafe to use a door frame pull-up bar for a kipping pull-up; these types of bars can be dislodged from the horizontal forces imparted by swinging. A pull-up bar from a power rack or rig will be much more secure.
2. Reach up overhead toward the bar with your hands slightly outside shoulder width and your palms facing forward.
    1. While a slightly outside shoulder-width grip is normally appropriate, you can try out somewhat different grip widths over time to determine where you personally feel best.
3. Jump up and firmly grasp the bar to hang on it with straight elbows and straight legs as your feet are together.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your shoulder blades down, which will lift your chest slightly up.
    1. This will prevent your torso from sagging, which would leave you in a shrugged-shoulder position.
2. While keeping your elbows and knees straightened, drive through your arms to push your chest back as you simultaneously sweep your legs moderately forward.
    1. You can think of this motion as starting with you lying on your back, with your arms fully back overhead, aligned with your legs. The movement on the bar should be akin to if you lifted your arms and legs up off the ground from that position. Since you are holding onto the bar, the arm motion (which is like the start of a straight arm lat pulldown) pushes your chest backward.
    2. From this position, which is known as a hollow body, your shoulders should be mildly behind the bar as your feet are in front of it.
    3. As soon as you have achieved this position, strive to fluidly transition into the next step, utilizing the momentum you just generated.
3. Actively reverse the movement into the opposite direction as you drive through your arms to push your chest forward while swinging your legs back.
    1. Now you are achieving the arched body position, where your shoulders are slightly ahead of the bar (if your mobility permits), while your feet are behind it.
4. Swing back into the hollow body position you adopted from step 2 as you push your chest back while sweeping your legs forward.
    1. Use the momentum you have already developed to allow a more vigorous swing back than you were able to achieve during step 1.
5. As you reach the apex of step 4’s swing, explosively pull your chest up toward the bar. While bending them progressively, drive your elbows down and toward your sides until your chin is above the bar.
    1. As you begin driving your elbows to pull yourself up, you can simultaneously march your knees mildly to generate even more momentum.
    2. Swinging into this step should allow your body to move in an arc rather than straight up, as you would during a standard pull-up.
    3. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows won't actually drive downward, but having that intention helps you use your back muscles to pull yourself up.
    4. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
6. Quickly reverse the arcing movement by lowering your body in preparation to swing fluidly into step 3’s arched body position with straight elbows.
    1. Strive to transfer momentum from the descent directly into the start of the next rep.
    2. To utilize momentum most effectively, you need to strike a proper balance between being sufficiently controlled and quick. If you lower yourself slowly, you will lose momentum, but if you drop into an uncontrolled free fall, you will be unable to transfer the momentum with appropriate technique.
7. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set and are ready to stop swinging before letting go of the bar.
    1. Fluidly moving from step 6’s descent into step 3’s arching requires fairly precise timing that can take some time to learn. If you have to learn that coordinated motor skill proficiently, you can allow yourself to settle into the dead hang position after the descent of each rep before completing each rep as a discrete cycle of steps 2-6. With repeated practice, smoothly stringing together consecutive reps can feel more natural.
## Description
This exercise can train your ability to pull your chin up above the bar efficiently using momentum generated from your [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md) and [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) to assist your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md).
1a15c6f170d88003b147f2f4c4910437:
## Setting up
1. Pick a pair of weight plates with your desired load.
    1. Weight plates (like cast iron plates or calibrated steel plates) that have a completely flat surface on one side are ideal.
2. Position the plates upright and together on a sturdy elevated object (e.g., plyometric box, flat bench, aerobic step on risers) or the ground.
    1. If you are using plates that have a flat surface on one side and a textured surface with a lip on the other side, have the flat surfaces of the plates facing outward.
    2. If you are using plates that have grip holes (cutouts that allow the rim of a plate to function as a handle), rotate the plates to have a portion of their solid bodies directed upward. For a pinch grip, you want to be able to grasp the solid body directly rather than having your fingers contact the grip holes.
    3. Placing them on an elevated surface can make it easier to pick the plates up with the pinch grip and set them down at the end of the set, but you can perform the same exercise from the ground.
3. While holding the plates together with one hand from the side, use your other hand to grasp the top of the plates with flat fingers.
    1. Position your thumb against one plate and your other four fingers against the other plate.
    2. Your palm should be directed down toward the ground while your elbow is straight.
4. Release your hand from the side while continuing to grip the plates with your top hand.
    1. You can now keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side.
## Exercise technique
1. Stand upright to lift the plates off the elevated object or ground, and hold the plates with your working arm by your side.
    1. You can think about trying to crush the weight plates as you squeeze your thumb and your other four fingers in toward each other.
2. Continue firmly holding the plates together while standing upright until you have completed your set’s target duration.
    1. This is a static exercise, so you will simply hold the plates together without moving.
    2. Keep your fingers fully straightened as you avoid letting them curl.
    3. Keep the plates completely pressed into each other rather than letting the bottom of the plates tilt away from each other.
    4. If you notice that the plates begin sliding slightly, end your set and use your free hand to help you guide the plates down to the ground or an elevated surface. Be careful not to lose your grip and drop the plates, which can rapidly occur if the plates start sliding.
3. Set the plates down and repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively strengthen your hand’s [intrinsic finger flexors](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md) while also training your forearm’s three [extrinsic finger flexors](../Muscles/Extrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d88050a550fbeff6041573.md).

## Setting up
1. Load an adjustable EZ bar with your desired weight, or approach a fixed-weight EZ bar.
    1. Either type of EZ bar can be used interchangeably for this exercise.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down and firmly grasp it with your palms angled backward and in toward each other (resulting in a semi-overhand grip). Your hands should be about shoulder-width apart or mildly closer.
    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it before a shoulder-width or mildly closer semi-overhand grip is accessible on the bar.
    2. The proper hand placement should result in your wrists and elbows feeling comfortable during this exercise.
3. Stand upright with the bar, walk over to a flat exercise bench, and stand over one end of the bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space behind you. With this equipment, you would straddle the bench and walk forward toward the J-hooks.
    2. With a portable exercise bench, your back should be facing the head of the bench, like when you would bench press.
4. Lift the bar up slightly above your waist, and sit down on the bench with the bar on your lap.
    1. Ensure that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie down with your head on the end of the bench.
5. While keeping your elbows bent and the bar close to your torso, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench. Your head should be right by the end of the bench.
    1. As you transition from sitting to lying down, you optionally can march your thighs up against the bar to help reposition yourself. This can be helpful when using heavier loads.
    2. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent. You will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
6. In a bench pressing motion, press the bar up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a bench press rep), the bar should be sitting on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists. You will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
    2. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar hard will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the bar in a controlled arcing manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Based on what feels most natural and comfortable to you, you can allow your elbows to flare out to your sides to a degree, or you can keep your elbows tucked in.
    2. Avoid letting your elbows drift back and down with the bar through shoulder motion. When viewed from the side, the proper elbow position should result in your upper arms remaining in a vertical position.
    3. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
2. Finish lowering the bar just before it reaches your forehead.
    1. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way, especially when the bar approaches your head.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the bar into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is vertically above your shoulders.
    2. Continue keeping your upper arms in a vertical position as you avoid pushing your elbows forward (toward your chest) through shoulder motion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
5. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the bar toward your lower chest or upper abdomen like you would during a bench press.
6. March your thighs up toward the weight, and then rock forward to sit up with the weight on your upper thighs.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to the machine’s weight sleeve, straddle the machine by standing on the foot plates as you are facing toward the weights.
    1. This variation specifically uses a T-bar row machine without any chest support, and other exercises using chest-supported T-bar row machines are included in this database.
    2. You will be most stable when the entirety of the soles of your feet are in contact with the foot plates.
    3. The foot plates of most machines will require you to adopt a close to hip-width stance.
    4. Position your feet in a manner that places the machine’s handles just in front of you so that you do not have to reach far forward in order to grasp the handles initially.
2. With your arms pointing down toward the handles, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the handles. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track far forward. However, you can let your knees shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
3. Firmly grasp the parallel handles with a neutral grip so your palms face each other.
    1. Different T-bar row machines have different handle designs, which can affect the specific grip you can use.
    2. If your machine lacks parallel handles but has handles that angle diagonally backward and outward, you can select a different over T-bar variation from this database, such as the [bent-over semi-neutral grip T-bar row](Bent-over%20semi-neutral%20grip%20T-bar%20row%201cf5c6f170d880b7a988c5c82888660c.md).
4. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from now on.
5. While keeping your lower back flat, chest up, and elbows straight, drive through your legs to lift the bar slightly up and assume a slightly more upright torso position.
    1. The objective is to use your hip and thigh muscles to lift the bar just high enough that you can experience resistance from the weight when your elbows are fully straight in the starting position of each rep.
    2. In this position, your torso should still be meaningfully inclined closer to horizontal than vertical, with your hips mostly bent.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar upward and back toward your torso by driving your elbows simultaneously upward and backward while progressively bending your elbows and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. Move your elbows through a path of motion that feels comfortable to you, which will typically involve keeping them tucked fairly close to your sides with this neutral grip rather than notably flaring your elbows away from your sides (which is typically more comfortable with a wider overhand grip).
    2. Keep your torso in a fixed hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set while keeping your core braced and your lower back near a neutral position.
    3. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner by allowing your elbows to move downward and forward until your elbows have finished extending and the bar has returned to the starting position.
    1. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to return the bar to its initial position by bending your knees and hips to lower the bar.
## Description
This row can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), which are assisted by your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
1a15c6f170d880098bcbe64c93b3cf31:
## Setting up
1. Prepare the barbell with your desired load by adding weight plates to it or leaving the barbell unloaded, which is recommended if performing this exercise for the first time.
    1. If you have access to one, you can also use a fixed-weight straight barbell, which may be lighter than a typical 20kg (44lb) barbell that has sleeves on which to add weight plates.
2. Pick up the barbell with an underhand grip where your palms are facing forward away from you.
3. While holding the barbell, sit down on a flat exercise bench or chair and position your forearms on top of your thighs with your palms facing up and your wrists situated slightly in front of your knees.
    1. To achieve this position, you will be leaning forward at your hips when seated with your elbows bent.
4. Allow the force from the bar to bend your wrists and bring your hands downward such that your palms are facing forward.
    1. In this position, the bar should not be contacting your legs, so scoot your forearms forward if it is initially contacting your legs.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift the bar upward by curling your wrists through their available range of motion while keeping your forearms resting on your thighs.
    1. All motion should come from your wrists.
    2. About halfway through the lifting phase, your palms should be facing straight up when your hands are aligned with your forearms.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, when the bar is fully raised, your palms should be angled back toward you.
    4. When performing this exercise appropriately, you should feel tension in the muscles on the palm side of your forearms.
2. Reverse the motion by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your palms directed forward away from you.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the six [wrist flexor muscles](../Muscles/Wrist%20flexor%20muscles%202c85c6f170d880a49749f7d7a9f307c8.md) on the palm side of your forearm.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, and sit down on the seat.
2. Adjust the height of the machine’s thigh pad to a level that allows you to fit the lowest portion of your thigh just underneath it, while the front half of your foot is situated on the foot plate.
    1. To help find this point, you can initially place the front half of your foot on the foot plate while your heel is lower than your toes.
    2. Avoid setting the pad to a height that requires you to lift your heel up higher than your toes in order for your thigh to press snugly into the pad. The weakest portion of a calf raise occurs when your heel is fully raised. Consequently, it can be difficult to re-rack the weight at the end of a set if your calf is fatigued, and you have to raise your heel meaningfully before adjusting the machine’s stopper to accept the weight.
3. With the front half of your foot on the foot plate, scoot your knee under and in front of the thigh pad until your lower thigh is securely under the pad.
    1. You can optionally use your hands to help pull the thigh pad up as you scoot forward.
    2. Because this is a single leg variation, you can leave your other foot resting on the ground. All the instructions will apply to the leg on the foot plate, since that is the side you are about to train.
4. Raise your heel up just enough to disengage the machine’s stopper by operating its lever with one of your hands.
    1. You should be primarily bearing weight through the ball of your foot as the back half of your foot is hanging off the foot plate.
    2. For tracking purposes, you can consider your first full rep to start after you have completely lowered your heel when performing step 1 of the exercise technique for the first time in a set. The initial short range of motion heel raise you perform to disengage the stopper does not constitute a full rep.
## Exercise technique
1. In a controlled manner, allow your heel to descend toward the ground through the available range of motion of your ankle while continuing to keep the front half of your foot on top of the foot plate.
    1. Strive to lower your heel as far as you can, and you will likely feel a stretching sensation in your calf and/or ankle at the bottom position.
    2. Specifically how far you are able to lower your heel will be dependent on your mobility, but individuals with normal ankle mobility can position their heels lower than the balls of their feet at the bottom.
2. Push through the ball of your foot to raise your heel into the air through the available range of motion of your ankle.
    1. At the top, your heel should be higher than the ball of your foot.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. At times during a set, you may feel that your foot slides back on the foot plate. If that occurs, you can use your hands to pull up the bottom of the thigh pad to make it easier for you to re-position your foot forward on the foot plate.
4. After finishing the lowering phase of your rep, raise your heel high enough to engage the machine’s stopper with your hand.
    1. If you performed as many reps as you possibly could during your set, you may have to rest in the bottom position for several seconds until your calf is ready to lift your heel high enough to engage the stopper.
5. With the stopper engaged, lower your heel to let the weight rest on the stopper before repeating the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md), but it will not train your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) nearly as well as calf raise variations performed with straight knees.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while holding the dumbbells by your thighs with straight elbows as your palms face your thighs.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hand while holding them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
    3. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    4. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    5. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back flat, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Shrug your shoulders upward through your available range of motion to lift the dumbbells upward while keeping your elbows straight.
    1. Throughout the exercise, look straight ahead to keep your neck near a neutral position.
    2. As a cue, you can think about driving your shoulders up toward your earlobes.
    3. While you shrug your shoulders upward, the rest of your body should remain stationary as you continue standing upright with straight legs.
3. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulders to descend fully in a controlled manner to lower the dumbbells.
    1. At the bottom, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the dumbbells can provide.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the dumbbells abruptly yank you downward.
4. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have finished your last rep, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back flat rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).
1a15c6f170d8800abe49f4321d63a1ef:
## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground.
    1. To set up for this row, you can use an underhand grip and perform the lifting phase of a [conventional deadlift](Conventional%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880f7a755cd3780a63371.md), followed by the lowering phase of a [Romanian deadlift](Barbell%20Romanian%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880bebc64f4dce0d5f5f1.md).
2. In a near hip-width stance, stand with the middle of your feet under the middle of the bar.
3. With your arms pointing down toward the bar, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can reach the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up throughout the exercise.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. Throughout the exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, as when you are looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with a near shoulder-width underhand grip such that your palms are facing forward.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue keeping your core braced from this point on.
6. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.
    1. While motion occurs at your hips and knees, your back should remain rigid.
7. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and incline your torso as close to horizontal as your hamstring flexibility permits with a flat back.
    1. To avoid rounding your lower back, you should think about sitting back rather than bending over.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something. 
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical (or close to vertical) throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively pushing your knees forward depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    5. If you have the mobility to hinge until the plates touch the ground, hinge at your hips until the plates are just above the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar up toward your upper abdomen by driving your elbows simultaneously backward and upward while progressively bending your elbows and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. As you do so, keep your torso in a fixed hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set while keeping your core braced and your lower back near a neutral position.
    2. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your lower body should remain nearly stationary.
    3. You can aim to row the bar until it touches near your upper abdomen or is close to doing so, which will result in your elbows being behind your torso (or at least aligned with your torso) at the end of the lifting phase.
    4. Rather than flaring your elbows out away from your sides, keep them tucked close to your sides as you lift the bar.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner by allowing your elbows to move downward and forward until your arms are directed down toward the ground with extended elbows.
    1. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another.
    2. The plates should not touch the ground when lowering the bar.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down onto the floor by bending your knees further.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).
1a15c6f170d8800ba699c5125f79af15:
## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat height to a comfortable position that will allow the lower aspect of your triceps to rest against the machine’s upper arm pads.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin, and sit down on its seat with an upright posture, your feet flat on the floor, and your back against the backrest.
3. After positioning your triceps against the machine’s upper arm pads, grasp the handles with an underhand grip that results in your palms facing forward.
## Exercise technique
1. Starting from a position where your elbows are straight, curl the handles upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms pinned against the machine’s arm pads (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully bent, reverse the motion by lowering the handles in a controlled manner until your elbows have straightened.
    1. Continue to keep your upper arms in contact with the arm pads.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
1a15c6f170d8800d8e3eee8e00854767:
## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable to approximately hip height, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. Based on your preference, either connect a rope attachment to the cable or leave the cable without any attachment.
    1. Either option allows you to perform this exercise with essentially the same technique.
3. Stand facing the cable station with the cable just in front of one of your arms.
4. With the hand in front of the cable, firmly grasp the rope or the ball-shaped stopper with a neutral grip such that your palm is facing in toward your other side.
    1. If you decide to use the rope attachment, pull the rope to one side of the attachment and grip its end with your little finger and the adjacent aspect of your hand contacting the flat surface of the attachment’s rubber stopper as your thumb wraps over the outside of your other fingers.
    2. If you decide not to use any cable attachment, grasp the ball-shaped stopper at the end of the cable in the palm of your hand by wrapping your four smaller fingers around it and positioning your thumb on top of these fingers.
5. Take a step backward so that you feel tension from the cable as the weight stack separates.
6. As you keep your upper arm aligned with your torso, hinge at your hips to sit your buttocks back, and incline your torso so that it is fairly close to being in a horizontal position.
    1. If you wish to do so, you can place your free hand up against the cable station’s beam for additional stability.
    2. Maintain this bent-over-torso position throughout your set.
7. Drive your elbow backward and upward until your upper arm is approximately parallel to the ground while you allow tension from the cable to keep your elbow bent.
    1. Your elbow should now be somewhat above the side of your torso (which would look like behind your torso if you were standing upright) rather than being aligned with your torso.
    2. In this starting position, your elbow should be bent by at least 90 degrees.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your upper arm parallel to the ground, progressively straighten your elbow to drive the cable backward and upward in an arcing motion until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. As you move your elbow, you should keep the rest of your body stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbow to bend in a controlled manner as you bring the cable downward and forward in an arcing fashion until you have returned to the starting position with your elbow bent by at least 90 degrees.
    1. Allow your elbow to continue bending as long as you feel tension from the cable pulling you toward a greater degree of bending.
    2. Continue keeping your upper arm parallel to the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise trains all three heads of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), which together constitute the majority of muscle mass in your upper arms.

## Setting up
1. Connect a lat pulldown bar to the cable, select your weight with the loading pin, and adjust the thigh pad to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. If you do not have a standard lat pulldown bar attachment, which has a straight body and mildly angled ends, you can use a different attachment that lets you grasp it with an overhand grip.
2. While facing the bar and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside shoulder-width overhand grip, such that your palms face forward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
3. While holding the bar, sit down on the machine’s seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to straighten and your arms to raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
4. In the seated position, slightly lean your torso backward at your hips.
    1. Maintain this slight backward lean throughout your set.
    2. From this position, your elbows should be straight, with your arms overhead and slightly forward (rather than completely vertical), and you should feel tension from the cable station holding your arms in this position.
    3. If you notice the cable remains slack in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), widening out your grip may be needed to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down toward your sides as you progressively bend them.
    1. Simultaneosuly pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears.
    2. Maintain the slight backward lean of your torso you adopted while setting up, rather than leaning further backward.
    3. When pulling through your full range of motion, you should finish with the bar touching your upper chest or very close to doing so.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the bar in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your arms overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
