## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and sit down on a bench with your feet flat on the floor while holding the dumbbells at your sides with slightly bent elbows as your palms are facing in toward your sides (i.e., in a neutral grip position).
    1. You can opt to sit down on a flat bench without any back support or sit down on a seated bench with back support.
2. Assume a bent-over torso position by flexing forward at your hips and back until your torso is close to parallel with the ground.
    1. How far you are able to bend over will be affected by your mobility.
    2. If your mobility permits, you can bend over until your torso is parallel with the ground, but you can still effectively perform this exercise if you are not able to descend as far.
    3. While bent over, your arms should be approximately perpendicular to the ground with the dumbbells situated in front of your knees.
    4. Maintain this bent-over position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Raise the dumbbells away from each other and straight out to your sides until your arms and torso form a “T-shape.”
2. Reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells toward each other in a controlled manner back until they have returned to their starting position in front of your knees.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which is assisted by your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), along with your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).
1a15c6f170d880129623ecf7b410009b:
## Setting up
1. After loading your desired amount of weight onto the machine, stand centered between its handles in a shoulder-width stance with your back facing the machine.
2. With extended elbows and your arms positioned by your sides, hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the handles.
    1. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so.
3. Firmly grasp each handle with a neutral grip such that your palms are facing in toward each other.
4. By extending your hips and knees, stand upright with the handles while continuing to keep your elbows extended and your lower back near a neutral position.
## Exercise technique
1. Shrug your shoulders upward through your available range of motion while keeping your elbows extended, which will lift the handles upward.
    1. While doing so, keep your neck in a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulders to descend in a controlled manner through your available range of motion, which will lower the handles.
    1. At the end of this motion, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the weight can provide.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).
1a15c6f170d8801383bce169e240d03c:
## Setting up
1. Stand upright with your back against a wall.
2. While keeping your buttocks and back against the wall, walk your feet forward before straightening your knees with your soles flat on the ground.
    1. As you walk your feet farther forward, the difficulty of the exercise can increase, so you can select your positioning based on the challenge you wish to have, which may take some trial and error.
    2. At any point during the exercise, you can walk your feet closer toward the wall or farther away from it if you wish to adjust the difficulty.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your heels on the ground, lift up the rest of your feet off the ground through your available ankle range of motion.
    1. As only your ankles move, continue keeping your knees straight while your buttocks and back remain in contact with the wall.
    2. You will likely feel the muscles on the front of your shins engage while doing so.
    3. With the balls of your feet lifting up rather than your heels, this is the opposite movement of a calf raise.
2. Reverse the motion by lowering your feet in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with the soles of your feet fully contacting the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can train the four muscle ankle dorsiflexor muscles on the front of your lower leg, the largest of which is the [tibialis anterior](../Muscles/Tibialis%20Anterior%201925c6f170d880f78c80c47a8fbb2627.md).
1a15c6f170d880148cade872878baf4c:
## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable bench at a low incline angle (e.g., near 30 degrees) and set a pair of dumbbells under the head of the bench.
    1. As a different variation, which you can use if your bench does not have a low incline setting, you can alternatively select a moderate incline angle (e.g., near 45 degrees) and otherwise use the same technique for this exercise.
2. Lie down with your chest contacting the head of the bench and your legs spread out as you position the balls of your feet on the ground.
3. Grasp the dumbbells and position your arms so that they are perpendicular to the ground with extended elbows.
    1. In this position, you can direct your palms to face whichever direction feels most comfortable to you.
    2. Most individuals will feel comfortable when positioning their palms such that they face in toward each other (i.e., a neutral grip), backward (i.e., an overhand grip), or at some angle in between these two positions.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your shoulder blades backward and toward each other as far as you can while you continue to keep your elbows extended and your chest in contact with the bench.
    1. This will lift the dumbbells upward.
    2. As a cue, you can imagine pinching a pencil between your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulder blades to move forward and spread apart from each other as far as they can while you continue to keep your elbows extended and your chest in contact with the bench.
    1. While doing so, the dumbbells will descend toward the ground.
    2. At the end of this motion, your shoulder girdles should resemble a slouched posture as they are pulled forward beyond their typical resting position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise effectively trains your [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md) and all three regions of your [trapezius](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) in a more isolated manner than row variations do.

## Setting up
1. After loading your desired weight onto the machine, adjust the seat or thigh pad height to a level that allows you to position your thighs snugly against the thigh pad while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. Certain machine models have an adjustable seat, while others have an adjustable thigh pad, and some have both an adjustable seat and an adjustable thigh pad.
    2. Depending on the specific model, plate-loaded lat pulldown machines may have the thigh pads positioned so you face toward or away from the weights, and these models often include a chest pad.
    3. While exceptions exist, the machines you sit facing away from the weights tend to have handles angled in a way that makes an overhand grip uncomfortable and awkward to use, whereas those facing the weights are typically preferable for this variation.
2. While facing the thigh pads and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the handles with an overhand grip, with your palms facing forward and away from you.
    1. The grip width you can use will depend on the specific machine model you use, and you can feel free to select whichever grip width you prefer within the range your machine supports.
    2. Situating your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, or even wider, will typically be most comfortable with this overhand grip variation.
3. While holding the handles, sit down on the machine’s seat, with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the thigh pad, then slightly lean your torso backward by moving your hips.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to extend in a controlled manner and your arms to raise up overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
    2. If you do not feel tension from the machine in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), lowering the seat height or widening out your grip may be needed to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows down toward the sides of your torso while progressively bending them to pull the handles downward.
    1. Simultaneosuly pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears.
    2. Maintain the same slight backward lean of your torso that you adopted while setting up, rather than progressively leaning further backward.
    3. Allow your elbows to naturally flare out from the midline of your body, in a manner that feels comfortable to you, during the initial portion of the pull.
    4. Pull through your available range of motion until you can no longer drive your elbows closer toward your torso, which often results in the handles finishing below the height of your ears and a little higher than the top of your shoulders.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the handles in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your arms overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to be near chest height, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Connect to the cable a rope attachment that is ideally a long rope attachment, or two standard rope attachments that are each fully pulled to one side of the attachment.
    1. Compared to using one standard length rope attachment, using a long rope attachment or two standard rope attachments (that together replicate the length of a long rope attachment) can help you emphasize shoulder external rotation at the end of this exercise’s lifting phase. However, this exercise can still be effectively performed with a single standard-length rope attachment, so you do not need to use a long rope or a combination of two standard ropes.
    2. In addition to the attachments that are just longer versions of the standard rope attachments, long rope attachments functionally include the long strap attachments (that can be used for cable crunches) that have a pair of looped ends into which you can place your hands.
3. While facing the cable station, grasp each end of the rope with your index fingers and adjacent aspects of your hands contacting the flat surfaces of the attachment’s rubber stoppers. Wrap your thumbs over the rounded outer aspects of the stoppers.
    1. If you are using a long strap attachment with looped ends rather than ropes, you naturally will situate your hands within the loops and grasp the inner part of each loop.
4. With your elbows straightened and arms raised to be parallel with the cable, step backward until the machine’s weight plates separate and you feel tension from the cable.
    1. In this position, your palms should be directed down as your arms are outstretched in front of your torso while you are standing upright with your hands close to each other.
5. With your feet near hip width apart, slightly bend your knees, and adopt a staggered stance with one foot mildly in front of the other, or keep your feet symmetrical with each other.
    1. Utilize whichever stance helps you feel the most stable and balanced.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows backward while flaring them out away from your sides. Simultaneously pull your hands upward and apart from each other as you pull the cable up toward your eyes.
    1. At the end of this motion, your elbows should be pointing straight out to your sides, and your upper arms should be approximately parallel with the ground as they form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. The end position should resemble a double biceps flexing pose with your hands pulled as far backward as your elbows, as opposed to your hands remaining in front of your elbows like they would during a row.
    3. Finish pulling with your shoulder blades fully pulled back together and your chest up in a “proud chest” posture.
    4. If you are using a long rope attachment or two ropes together, strive to finish with your hands vertically above your elbows with your elbows bent by about 90 degrees. With a single standard rope attachment, you will not be able to spread your hands as far apart and will finish the pull with a greater degree of elbow bend.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your hands to move diagonally forward, downward, and in toward each other. Simultaneously, allow your elbows to move forward toward each other as they straighten.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart naturally and move forward as your arms move in line with the cable’s resistance.
    2. You should finish in the starting position with your elbows straightened and arms outstretched in front of you.
    3. You do not have to perform this step with an extremely slow tempo, but you should actively control it the entire time rather than letting the cable abruptly pull your arms forward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While also meaningfully training your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), this exercise can effectively develop your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md) and [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), along with the [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. If using an adjustable bench, position it at a moderate incline angle, which is near 45 degrees.
    1. The available incline angles will vary among different benches, with some benches having several angle configurations, while others may only be set to flat, upright, or a 45-degree angle.
    2. You can also use a fixed moderate incline bench for this exercise.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and sit down on the incline bench with your feet flat on the floor while holding the dumbbells at your sides with extended elbows.
    1. Keep your upper back and the back of your head in contact with the bench throughout the set.
3. Direct your palms so that they are facing in toward your sides (i.e., in a neutral grip position).
    1. Maintain this neutral grip on the dumbbells throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl both dumbbells upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed at your sides (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms positioned by your sides.
3. Alternate between curling the dumbbells up and lowering them down until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Prepare the barbell with your desired load by adding weight plates to it or leaving the barbell unloaded, which is recommended if performing this exercise for the first time.
    1. You can initially set the bar up on the floor or from an elevated position, such as from a power rack.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down or hinge at your hips with extended elbows.
3. Grasp the bar with approximately a shoulder width grip and an underhand grip such that your palms are directed forward.
4. While keeping your elbows extended, stand upright while gripping the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl the bar upward by bending at your elbows while simultaneously driving your upper arms back behind your torso.
    1. The combined motion at your shoulders and elbows should result in the bar moving vertically upward in a straight line (as opposed to the arcing bar path that occurs with a typical barbell biceps curl).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed and your upper arms are positioned behind your torso, reverse the motion by lowering the bar in a controlled manner by simultaneously bringing your upper arms forward and extending your elbows.
    1. After finishing the lower phase of this exercise, your elbows should have returned to a fully extended position, and your upper arms should once again be positioned at your sides.
3. Alternate between curling the bar up and lowering it down until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and sit down on a flat exercise bench or chair.
2. While holding the dumbbells, lean forward at your hips and position your forearms on top of your thighs with your palms facing upward and your wrists situated slightly in front of your knees.
3. Allow the force from the dumbbells to bend your wrists and bring your hands downward such that your palms are facing forward.
    1. In this position, the dumbbells should not be contacting your legs, so scoot your forearms forward if they are initially contacting your legs.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift the dumbbells upward by curling your wrists through their available range of motion while keeping your forearms resting on your thighs.
    1. All motion should come from your wrists.
    2. About halfway through the lifting phase, your palms should be facing straight up when your hands are aligned with your forearms.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, when the dumbbells are fully raised, your palms should be angled back toward you.
    4. When performing this exercise appropriately, you should feel tension in the muscles on the palm side of your forearms.
2. Reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your palms directed forward away from you.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the six [wrist flexor muscles](../Muscles/Wrist%20flexor%20muscles%202c85c6f170d880a49749f7d7a9f307c8.md) on the palm side of your forearm.
1a15c6f170d8801ab4e9f6fd8b9576fb:
## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground.
    1. The initial steps of the setup are the same as a [conventional deadlift](Conventional%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880f7a755cd3780a63371.md).
2. Stand close to the middle of the bar with approximately a hip-width stance with straight elbows.
    1. You can set up with the bar approximately over the middle of your feet, which should situate the bar close to one inch or 2.5cm away from most individuals’ shins while initially standing upright.
3. Hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. Throughout this movement, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with a near shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
6. Stand upright with the bar by extending your hips and knees while continuing to keep your elbows straight and your lower back near a neutral position.
    1. While your lower back muscles will be working to maintain a rigid trunk position, lifting the bar upward should chiefly occur from your hip and thigh muscles extending your hips and knees.
    2. Keep the bar very close to your legs as you lift the bar rather than allowing the bar to drift forward.
7. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and incline your torso through the range of motion you can move without rounding your back.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight, back flat, and core braced.
    2. Allow your knees to bend naturally while sitting your hips back as if you were closing a car door with your buttocks, while your hands are carrying something.
    3. How close to horizontal you are able to position your torso without rounding your lower back will be dependent on your mobility.
    4. If you can hinge low enough that the plates touch the ground, adopt a slightly shallower hinged position to keep the plates off the ground.
    5. In the hinged position, it is natural to feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings.
## Exercise technique
1. Explosively pull the bar up toward your abdomen by driving your elbows backward and upward. Simultaneously generate momentum from your lower body by letting your hips snap forward.
    1. Rather than focusing on driving the hips forward, focusing on pulling the bar toward your abdomen while allowing your lower body to assist naturally is often a viable strategy. Using your lower body to build momentum is more mechanically efficient than keeping your lower body completely stationary with a strict row. Without consciously thinking about your lower body, you naturally may be able to “cheat” appropriately when emphasizing the outcome (moving the bar to your abdomen) while letting your hips move freely.
    2. Snapping your hips forward will lift your torso into a more upright position, but your torso should still be somewhat inclined at the top rather than completely upright like you would be when fully thrusting your hips forward to lock out a deadlift. An appropriate degree of torso lean at the top of the row should allow you to finish with your elbows at least slightly behind your torso while the bar touches your lower abdomen. This will not be feasible if you lift your torso excessively upright.
    3. Keep your back flat and core braced throughout your set. When your torso transitions to a moderately more upright position through hip motion, your spine should stay rigid.
    4. Your shoulder blades should naturally pull back to allow you to finish the row with your chest up.
    5. A sweet spot exists in terms of how much “cheating” is appropriate. If you do not feel meaningful tension in the back muscles you normally do during a strict row, you may be using excessive momentum from your lower body. When initially learning this exercise, it can be helpful to start with only mild assistance from your lower body to ensure that you are still training your back muscles primarily.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar as you sit your hips back. Allow your elbows to move downward and forward until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. At the end of the lowering phase, you should be in the hinged position with the bar just in front of your legs and the plates above the ground.
    2. Keep your lower back tight as you avoid rounding it.
    3. It is natural to lower the bar more quickly than you would during a strict row, but strive to control the bar to the best of your ability rather than letting gravity abruptly yank the bar down. A quick lowering phase does not necessitate an uncontrolled lowering phase.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
4. Set the bar down onto the ground by reversing the technique you used to pick it up (i.e., bending at your hips and knees as opposed to just rounding over at your lower back).
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your abdomen contacting the ground (i.e., in the prone position) and your head lifted slightly off the ground as you maintain a tucked chin position with your face directed toward the ground
2. With extended elbows, raise your arms straight out to your sides so that they form a “T-shape” with your torso while resting on the ground.
3. Rotate your arms so that your palms face forward.
    1. If you make a thumbs-up gesture in this position, your thumb should be pointing up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your arms up off the ground through your available shoulder range of motion while maintaining the “T-shape” and keeping your chest in contact with the ground.
    1. Your shoulder mobility will affect how high you can raise your arms.
    2. If you notice your chest lifting up off the ground during this movement, that indicates that you most likely are dynamically extending your lumbar spine, which can occur as a compensation pattern instead of lifting your arm only with your shoulder girdle muscles.
2. Reverse the motion by lowering your arms in a controlled manner until your hands lightly contact the ground while maintaining the “T-shape.”
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise trains your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), which are assisted by your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance. Hold the kettlebells at your sides with straight elbows and your palms facing in toward your thighs.
    1. If you are using kettlebells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both kettlebells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one kettlebell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other kettlebell onto the bench before picking up both kettlebells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the kettlebells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue keeping your core braced from this point on.
3. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and incline your torso as close to horizontal as your hamstring flexibility permits. Keep your back flat and chest up.
    1. To avoid rounding your lower back, you should think about sitting back rather than bending over.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something. 
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical (or close to vertical) throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively pushing your knees forward depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    5. If you have the mobility to hinge until the weights touch the ground, hinge at your hips until the weights are just above the ground.
4. With your arms hanging straight down toward the ground, direct your palms to angle inward and backward, resulting in a semi-overhand grip.
    1. The bony bump on the back of each elbow should point diagonally outward and backward, which is the direction in which you will row.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows in an arcing motion backward, upward, and moderately out away from your sides to row the kettlebells. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Aim to flare your elbows about 45 degrees away from your sides as you move them equally backward and out to the side. Zero degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows purely backward and keeping them completely tucked by your sides, while 90 degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows straight out to the sides, which would result in your upper arms and torso forming a “T-shape” at the top.
    2. Throughout the set, rigidly maintain a flat lower back with the same degree of bend in your hips and knees. All the motion should occur from your upper body.
    3. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being slightly above your sides at the top.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
    5. When allowing your elbows to bend naturally, your forearms should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    6. The kettlebells should move in an arcing motion rather than move straight up toward your shoulders.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the kettlebells in a controlled arcing motion until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. Allow the weights to pull your shoulder blades apart and forward to stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. Move your elbows diagonally inward and forward at a near 45-degree angle while they descend to reverse the moderate elbow flare you just utilized during the lifting phase.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weights pull your arms down rapidly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the weights down by bending your knees further.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to pick it up with straight elbows from a position where your knees are mildly bent, and your torso is mildly hinged forward at your hips.
    1. Your individual limb lengths and the specific type of machine you are using will influence how high the bar will be in this position, but the bar will be above the knees for many people.
    2. For some people, the lowest machine setting that places the bar above their knees may be too high for them to pick up the bar with extended elbows, so they may have to situate the bar closer to knee height.
    3. You will naturally have to position the machine’s safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) below the height of the bar.
2. After loading your desired amount of weight onto the machine, stand with your back facing the middle of the bar in a shoulder-width stance and hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so.
3. With extended elbows, firmly grasp the bar with a near shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
4. By extending your hips and knees, start standing up with the bar and rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion prior to standing fully upright with the bar.
    1. While doing, continue to keep your lower back near a neutral position.
## Exercise technique
1. Shrug your shoulders upward through your available range of motion while keeping your elbows extended, which will lift the bar upward.
    1. While doing so, keep your neck in a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. If your buttock obstructs the upward movement of the bar, you can re-rack the bar and position yourself slightly farther away from the bar before resuming your set.
    3. If your buttock still obstructs the upward movement of the bar after repositioning yourself, you can proceed to use a limited range of motion for this exercise or select another shrug variation. 
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulders to descend in a controlled manner through your available range of motion, which will lower the bar.
    1. At the end of this motion, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the machine’s weight can provide.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to re-rack the bar.

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, adjust each cable to its lowest height.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you can position the arms so that they form an approximately 90-degree angle with each other. This would result in the arms being midway between pointing straight forward and straight out to the side.
    2. Dual cable stations that have their two weight stacks facing each other (often with a pull-up in between them) normally lack adjustable arms.
2. Connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.
3. Squat down with one cable station by your side, and firmly grasp its handle with a straight elbow as your palm is directed in toward you.
4. While keeping your elbow straight, stand upright with the handle, and walk over to grasp the handle from the other cable in the same manner.
    1. You can allow the resistance from the first cable you grasped to lift your arm out to the side before doing the same with the other cable during the next step.
5. Step to the side to center yourself between the cables.
6. Step forward while allowing your arms and palms to rotate in line with the resistance from the cables. Stop moving once the cables are angled diagonally by about 30-45 degrees.
    1. When you are initially standing with your torso directly between the pulleys, the cables will exert resistance directly out to your sides. This is the 0-degree starting point from which you will move forward to angle the cables by about 30-4545 degrees.
    2. As you step forward, the cables will progressively apply more of a backward-directed force.
    3. If your pulleys are situated close together, you will not have to step as far forward to achieve the intended line of pull compared to if your cable stations are positioned farther apart.
    4. On each side, the back of your hand and the bony bump on the back of your elbow should be directed toward the cable station. This will allow the cables to resist your biceps most directly.
    5. Your wrists should be mostly straight throughout the exercise.
7. While mildly bending your knees, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other.
    1. In this position, you should feel stable and balanced.
8. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to curl the handles upward, forward, and in toward each other. Keep your upper arms stationary as you avoid swinging them forward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully bent as your forearms contact your biceps.
    2. While you move your forearms through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to straighten in a controlled manner.
    1. Finish the lowering phase with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. The handles should simultaneously spread apart from each other while arcing downward and back toward the pulleys.
    3. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cables abruptly yank the handles back in an uncontrolled manner.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its highest level, select your desired weight with the loading pin, and attach a bar with a straight (or mostly straight) body to the cable.
    1. Any bar that enables you to perform this exercise with an overhand grip can be similarly used, including a standard straight bar, a lat pulldown bar (with a long straight body and angled ends), and a multi-grip EZ bar.
2. While facing the cable station, reach up and grasp the bar with an overhand grip such that your palms are facing away from you.
3. Take a step backward and slightly lean forward by hinging at your hips.
    1. Maintain this slight torso lean throughout your set.
4. Pull your upper arms down and back until they are positioned at your sides with your elbows close to fully bent.
    1. Maintain this upper arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Push the bar downward by extending your elbows until they are straightened.
    1. At the end of this motion, the bar should be situated in front of your thighs.
2. Reverse the motion by bending your elbows through your available range of motion to raise the bar in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. Strive to have your elbows as close to fully bent as you can by the time you have finished this motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. Prepare the barbell with your desired load by adding weight plates to it or leaving the barbell unloaded, which is recommended if performing this exercise for the first time.
    1. As an alternative to a standard barbell, in which you can load plates onto its sleeves, you can similarly use a fixed-weight barbell for this exercise.
    2. If you do not have any experience training Jefferson curls, it is recommended that you initially try out the [bodyweight Jefferson curl](Bodyweight%20Jefferson%20curl%201ec5c6f170d880ba8e43cf305531982d.md) to determine how your body feels with this movement prior to performing a loaded variation.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down or hinge at your hips with straight elbows.
3. Firmly grasp the bar with approximately a shoulder-width overhand grip, such that your palms are directed toward you.
4. While keeping your elbows straight, stand upright with the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. Tuck your chin to your chest, and lower the bar in a slow and controlled manner by bending over and rounding your whole back through your comfortable range of motion while keeping your knees and elbows straight.
    1. As a cue, you can think about rounding forward each segment of your spine successively until your entire spine has achieved a rounded posture.
    2. As you progressively descend, it is natural to feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings and back muscles.
    3. How far you can descend will be influenced by your hamstring flexibility and the available bending range of motion in your spine.
    4. With a sufficient amount of mobility, you may be able to descend until the weight contacts the floor, but only move through a range that is painless and feels right to your body.
    5. Your arms should be directed down toward the ground throughout the exercise.
2. Reverse the movement by gradually transitioning from the bent over position to the upright position in which you started by uncoiling your back, which will lift the bar up.
    1. At the end of the ascent, untuck your chin and look straight ahead.
    2. Continue keeping your knees and elbows in a straightened position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) that run along your entire back, while also training your spinal mobility and hamstring flexibility.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that places the handles near shoulder level once you are seated.
    1. This seat height is an appropriate starting point for most people, but the ideal seat height specifically should allow you to press through your full range of motion while initially gripping the handles with your elbows stacked under the handles.
    2. If the seat is excessively high, you will not be able to position your elbows directly under the handles (when viewed from the side).
    3. If the seat is excessively low, your range of motion for this exercise will be limited.
    4. Some trial and error may be needed to find the best height for you as an individual.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against the backrest.
    1. Your feet should be flat on the ground.
    2. You can optionally rest your head against the backrest if it is tall enough, or you can simply keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
4. With your palms facing forward and elbows bent, firmly grasp the handles that are directed out to the sides. Position your elbows directly under the handles, resulting in your forearms being vertical when viewed from the side.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. If you cannot comfortably position your elbows under the handles, mildly lower the seat height before resuming your setup.
    3. Situating your elbows under the handles and maintaining this alignment will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare during this exercise.
5. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling, and maintain this posture throughout your set.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the handles up overhead until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your elbows should remain stacked under your wrists when viewed from the side.
    3. Throughout your set, continue keeping your back snuggly against the backrest and your feet planted on the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the handles in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. With the appropriate seat height, you should finish the lowering phase with the handles near shoulder level, as your elbows are lower than your shoulders.
    2. At the bottom, you can lightly tap the machine’s arms against the stoppers underneath them. A gentle tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
    3. Continue keeping your elbows stacked underneath the handles, resulting in your forearms remaining in a vertical position when viewed from the side.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a trap bar in a location where you have sufficient space to carry it, and position its high handles up if your bar has high handles.
    1. The setup for this exercise mirrors that of a [trap bar deadlift](High%20handle%20trap%20bar%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880e09409ca60499f2367.md), with the lifting phase of one trap bar deadlift rep.
    2. You can certainly use a trap bar without elevated handles, but it is easier to lift into the starting position when using high handles.
2. Add weight plates to the bar, and stand within the middle of the bar with a near hip-width stance and your arms at your sides.
3. Hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the handles when your elbows are straight, and your arms are lifted slightly out to your sides (to position your hands directly over the handles).
    1. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back flat and chest up, rather than meaningfully rounding your back.
4. Firmly grasp the center of the handles with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Keep your elbows straight throughout the exercise.
5. While keeping your elbows straight, press your legs into the ground with enough force to feel the trap bar’s sleeves push up into the weight plates, but not enough force to lift the bar off the ground.
    1. Applying this pre-tension to the bar will likely produce an audible “clinking” sound.
    2. The initial submaximal pull allows you to check if you have grasped the handles correctly, which will be indicated by the handles not rotating forward or backward when applying the pre-tension.
    3. If you pick up a trap bar with your hands positioned slightly away from the middle of the handles, the trap bar can start rotating in a manner that makes it very difficult to hold and lift appropriately.
    4. Even for experienced lifters, it can be easy to grasp a trap bar’s handles without having their hands truly centered initially, so applying the pre-tension can make sure you are in your ideal starting position.
    5. If the bar starts rotating when you apply the pre-tension, re-center your grip, and apply the pre-tension again until the bar no longer rotates.
6. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
7. Drive through the ground to lift the bar upward as you extend (straighten) your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright.
    1. Continue keeping your back flat as you lift the bar with your hip and thigh muscles.
## Exercise technique
1. Walk forward while holding the trap bar while maintaining an upright posture with your shoulders approximately level with each other.
    1. While you will not swing your arms like you would when walking normally, your torso and lower body should look similar to how they would when you walk normally.
    2. Walk at a pace where you feel stable and balanced throughout the carry.
    3. If you use a weight that is fairly heavy to you, it is natural to take shorter strides compared to how you typically walk.
    4. Keep the tops of your hip bones approximately level throughout your set rather than letting them drop down to one side when taking each step.
2. Continue walking with the trap bar until you have completed your set and are ready to set it down by reversing the movement you used to pick it up initially.
    1. Remember to lower the weight by hinging at your hips while bending your knees and keeping your lower back near a neutral position.
## Description
Rather than concentrating the workload on one body region, this exercise trains a variety of muscle groups throughout your body in an integrated manner, including the muscles in your forearms, upper back, core, and lower body.

### **Straps for Carries**

Even when using chalk, the weight you can use or distance you can complete with a particular weight will commonly be limited by grip strength while performing a farmer’s carry, so this carry can be a viable means of training static grip strength. However, if you wish to increase the stimulus provided to muscles besides the forearm and hand muscles, you have the option of performing this carry with lifting straps. With the heavier loads or longer distances that straps typically facilitate, the exercise can be more challenging to your upper back and core muscles as they support your trunk and shoulder girdle in addition to your lower body muscles that stabilize your pelvis and propel you forward.

### **Training Many Muscles Simultaneously**

McGill et al. (2009) measured EMG activity of several core and lower body muscles as competitive strongmen performed a variety of movements that appear in strongman competitions, including the farmer’s walk, which was performed for several steps with a 75kg (167.6lb) weight in each hand. During the farmer’s walk, peak EMG activity was high for the internal abdominal obliques, lats, thoracic erector spinae, lumbar erector spinae, gluteus medius, gluteus maximus, and rectus femoris. The external abdominal obliques and biceps femoris also exhibited moderate peak EMG activity, while the rectus abdominis exhibited low EMG activity. The abdominal muscles and rectus femoris demonstrated their peak activity during the walking portion of the carry, while the lats, erector spinae and biceps femoris demonstrated their peak activity during the initial lifting phase. The gluteal muscles exhibited peak activity during the initial lifting phase and during the first step of the carry. As indicated by these findings, the farmer’s carry can train a large amount of musculature simultaneously, which can result in this exercise being metabolically demanding when performed at a high relative intensity, especially for longer duration sets. Correspondingly, challenging sets of farmer’s carries may be able to train your cardiovascular system more robustly than most resistance training exercises that localize the workload to a smaller amount of total muscle mass.

## Setting up
1. Connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, select your weight with the loading pin, and sit down facing the cable station.
    1. You can readily perform this exercise with essentially the same technique whether you use a seated cable row machine or an adjustable cable station.
    2. If you use a seated cable row machine, you naturally will sit down on its seat, but if you are using an adjustable cable station, you will sit down on the ground after adjusting the cable to a height that is approximately level with your shoulders when seated on the floor with an upright torso.
2. Slightly scoot to one side to situate the shoulder on the side you are about to train in front of the cable.
    1. As opposed to keeping the center of your chest aligned with the cable (like you would when rowing with both sides simultaneously), this asymmetrical sitting position will allow you to row straight backward in line with the cable’s resistance.
    2. Cable row machines often have pulleys that do not pivot side to side, and pulling their cables at an angle out to the side could result in excess friction, deleterious to the cables, while increasing the risk that a cable slips out of its pulley’s groove.
3. On the side you are about to train, position your foot in contact with the machine’s foot plate or the base of the adjustable cable station. Position your other foot similarly, or flat on the ground with a bent knee, based on what feels comfortable and stable to you when using your specific cable machine.
    1. Allow your knees to bend to an angle that allows you to feel stable and comfortable.
4. Lean forward at your hips until you are able to use one hand to grasp the handle firmly with an extended elbow before leaning backward until you are sitting with an upright torso.
    1. With greater knee bend, you will be able to sit closer toward the cable, so you can bend your knees further if you initially cannot reach the handles when leaning forward.
    2. When seated upright, you should feel tension from the cable, so if the cable is still slack, you can extend your knees to scoot yourself backward until the machine’s weight stack separates and you feel the resistance.
5. Based on your preference and what feels most comfortable, you can rotate the handle in a manner that allows you to use an underhand grip with your palm facing up, an overhand grip with your palm facing down, or a neutral grip with your palm facing in toward the midline of your body.
    1. People often find that the neutral grip feels most natural.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handle back toward your torso by driving your elbow backward while simultaneously bending and pulling your shoulder blade backward.
    1. Move your elbow through a path of motion that feels comfortable to you, which will typically involve keeping it tucked close to your side with this variation rather than notably flaring your elbow up and away from your side.
    2. Movement should occur at your shoulder, shoulder blade, and elbow, but your knees, hips, and lower back should remain nearly stationary in a stable position throughout the set.
    3. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your elbow being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbow to move forward in a controlled manner as it progressively straightens to move the handle forward.
    1. Finish with your arm fully outstretched in front of you with a straight elbow.
    2. Your shoulder blade will naturally move forward, but you have the option of exaggerating this motion by intentionally allowing the weight to pull it further forward than your resting position at the bottom. This will stretch your upper back muscles and may help you to train them more effectively.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
While also training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md), this row can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that allows you to rest your elbows and most of the back of your upper arms (i.e., triceps) on the sloped arm pad when sitting on the seat.
    1. The proper setting will typically result in the top of the pad being close to your armpits.
    2. Some trial and error may be needed to find the ideal seat height.
2. After selecting your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin, sit down on the seat with your feet on the ground.
3. With one arm, position the back of your upper arm and elbow on top of the arm pad as your elbow is aligned with the machine’s pivot point, which is the center about which the machine’s lever arm rotates. That is denoted by a small dot or circle in some machines.
    1. For additional stability, you can use your other hand to hold onto the top of the arm pad, or you can place it wherever you prefer, so long as it does not touch the handle.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm on top of the arm pad since that is the arm you will be training first.
4. While your arm is aligned with the front of your shoulder, firmly grasp the handle with your palm angled upward.
    1. If the handle is a little out of your reach, you could slightly stand up and lean forward to reach the handle before sitting back down after you have grasped the handle.
    2. Your wrist should be mostly straight throughout your set after grasping the handles.
    3. Machines commonly have angled handles that allow you to grasp them with your palm angled inward and upward (resulting in a hybrid between an underhand and neutral grip), but certain models may have horizontal handles that will allow you to use a purely underhand grip.
5. In the starting position, your elbow should be fully straightened to allow you to train through a full range of motion.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow and the back of your upper arm in contact with the arm pad, curl the handle upward and back toward you in an arcing motion by bending at your elbow until it is fully bent.
    1. While your one forearm moves through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout your set.
2. After your elbow has fully bent, reverse the motion by lowering the handle in a slow and controlled manner until your elbow has returned to a fully straightened position.
    1. Continue keeping your elbow and the back of your upper arm in contact with the arm pad.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other arm.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance. Hold the dumbbells by your sides with your palms facing in toward your thighs.
2. Lift the dumbbells up near the front of your shoulders with your elbows bent by curling the weights and using momentum from your lower body as needed.
    1. You can perform a cheat curl-like motion to move the dumbbells into position if they are too heavy to lift without momentum. To do so, first sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and simultaneously rocking the dumbbells mildly backward. Then drive your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum while bending your elbows and mildly swinging them forward to lift the weight up.
    2. Your elbows should now be underneath and slightly in front of the dumbbells.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. Press the dumbbells up overhead in a shoulder press motion until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can point the back of your elbows forward with your palms facing in toward each other.
    2. The dumbbells should be vertically stacked over your shoulder.
    3. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the dumbbells behind your head in a controlled manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Predominantly keep your elbows tucked in as they are chiefly pointing forward rather than out to your side. However, you can allow your elbows to flare slightly out away from your sides if that feels natural and comfortable to you. If the dumbbells bump into each other, you are flaring your elbows excessively.
    2. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
    3. As you keep your elbows up, your upper arms should remain in a vertical position by the sides of your head.
2. Continue lowering the dumbbells until you have fully bent your elbows or can lightly tap the back of your shoulders with the dumbbells.
    1. It is normal to be able to bend the elbows beyond 90 degrees, but specifically how far you can bend your elbows may be limited by the flexibility of your long head of the triceps.
    2. While some lifters have the flexibility to reach their shoulders with the dumbbells, wherever you feel a notable stretching sensation in your triceps can be an appropriate end range.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weights the entire way.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the dumbbells into the starting position overhead.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the dumbbells are vertically stacked above your shoulders.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows up as all the motion occurs from your elbows without moving your shoulders.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
5. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the dumbbells toward the front of your shoulders like you would during a shoulder press.
6. Lower the dumbbells to your sides as you straighten your elbows and swing your elbows back by your sides.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. Securely attach your desired weight to your wrist roller.
    1. Depending on the model of your wrist roller, you may have to use weight plates (if your model uses a loading pin), or you may be able to use weight plates, kettlebells, or dumbbells (if your model uses a strap that you can loop around the weight).
    2. Leave enough of the rope initially uncoiled so that you can stand up with the roller without the weight lifting off the ground.
2. While the weight is on the ground, firmly grasp the roller’s handles with your palms facing toward you (i.e., an overhand grip) and the uncoiled part of the rope on the side of the roller that is farther away from you.
    1. If the uncoiled part of the rope is on the side of the roller closer toward you, you would be able to train wrist flexion when using an overhand grip, but this is the wrist extension variation.
3. Stand upright while grasping the roller and raise your arms out in front of you with straight elbows until your arms are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. You will maintain this arm position throughout your set.
4. Take up the slack from the roller’s rope with alternating twisting motions of your wrists until you feel that the rope is taught from the weight’s resistance.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your arms held out in front of you, extend one wrist by pointing that side’s palm down toward the ground as you curl your other wrist in the opposite direction by pointing that hand’s palm up and back toward you.
    1. You should grasp the handle loosely with the hand whose palm is curling toward you, as you grasp the handle firmly with the hand whose palm is pointing toward the ground.
    2. The hand whose palm is directed down is what rotates the roller to lift the weight up via wrist extension, while the other side’s wrist is repositioned into a flexed position in preparation to perform the lifting motion through wrist extension.
2. Alternate the motions in step 1 with the opposite hands as you lift the weight up by cyclically repeating these twisting movements with your wrists until you have fully coiled the rope around the roller.
3. Lower the weight in a controlled manner by reversing the same motions you just performed until the weight lightly taps the ground or is just about to do so.
4. Repeatedly perform steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the seven [wrist extensor muscles](../Muscles/Wrist%20extensors%202c35c6f170d8804ab377fe1e53371f25.md) on the side of your forearm opposite to your palm.

## Setting up
1. With a cable station’s pulley positioned near hip height, connect a d-handle attachment, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Position yourself to one side of the cable station while facing away from it.
3. Squat down or hinge at your hips with an extended elbow before using your closer hand to grasp the handle with an underhand grip such that your palm is directed forward.
4. While keeping your elbow extended, stand upright while gripping the handle.
5. Step forward while keeping your elbow fully extended and allowing the cable’s resistance to pull your upper arm backward at an angle behind your torso.
    1. In this position, your forearm and upper arm should form a straight line with the cable that is diagonally angled forward and upward, and you should also feel tension from the cable rather than slack being present in the cable.
    2. How far you step forward from the cable station will be based on your personal preference, since you can effectively perform this exercise with variable shoulder positions.
        1. If you step forward further, you will be able to have your upper arm pulled further behind your body, which will place your biceps into a more lengthened position.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl the handle upward by bending at your elbow while keeping your upper arm fixed in the same position that allowed your elbow to be fully extended at the start of the rep (rather than allowing your upper arm to swing forward).
2. After your elbow has fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the handle in a controlled manner until your elbow has returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arm in the same position used to start the rep.
3. Alternate between curling the handle upwards and lowering it down until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
While also meaningfully developing your [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md) and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md), this exercise can effectively train [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md) from a notably lengthened position.

## Setting up
1. Load a bar with your desired weight, and firmly grasp it with a near shoulder-width overhand grip that results in your palms facing back toward you
    1. In addition to a standard barbell to which you can add weight plates, you can also utilize a fixed-weight bar, which can be useful if you wish to use a load that is lighter than 45lb (20kg), which is the typical weight of an unloaded standard barbell.
2. Stand upright with the bar, walk over to a flat exercise bench, and stand over one end of the bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space behind you. With this equipment, you would straddle the bench and walk forward toward the J-hooks.
    2. With a portable exercise bench, your back should be facing the head of the bench, like when you would bench press.
3. Lift the bar up slightly above your waist, and sit down on the bench with the bar on your lap.
    1. Ensure that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie down with your head on the end of the bench.
4. While keeping your elbows bent and the bar close to your torso, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench. Your head should be right by the end of the bench.
    1. As you transition from sitting to lying down, you optionally can march your thighs up against the bar to help reposition yourself. This can be helpful when using heavier loads.
    2. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent. You will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
5. In a bench pressing motion, press the bar up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a bench press rep), the bar should be sitting on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists. You will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
    2. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar hard will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the bar in a controlled arcing manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Based on what feels most natural and comfortable to you, you can allow your elbows to flare out to your sides to a degree, or you can keep your elbows tucked in.
    2. Avoid letting your elbows drift back and down with the bar through shoulder motion. When viewed from the side, the proper elbow position should result in your upper arms remaining in a vertical position.
    3. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
2. Finish lowering the bar just before it reaches your forehead.
    1. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way, especially when the bar approaches your head.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the bar into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is vertically above your shoulders.
    2. Continue keeping your upper arms in a vertical position as you avoid pushing your elbows forward (toward your chest) through shoulder motion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
5. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the bar toward your lower chest or upper abdomen like you would during a bench press.
6. March your thighs up toward the weight, and then rock forward to sit up with the weight on your upper thighs.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.
