## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance. Hold the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows and your palms facing in toward your thighs.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue keeping your core braced from this point on.
3. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and incline your torso as close to horizontal as your hamstring flexibility permits. Keep your back flat and chest up.
    1. To avoid rounding your lower back, you should think about sitting back rather than bending over.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical (or close to vertical) throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively pushing your knees forward depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    5. If you have the mobility to hinge until the weights touch the ground, hinge at your hips until the weights are just above the ground.
4. With your arms hanging straight down toward the ground, direct your palms to angle inward and backward, resulting in a semi-overhand grip.
    1. The bony bump on the back of each elbow should point diagonally outward and backward, which is the direction in which you will row.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows in an arcing motion backward, upward, and moderately out away from your sides to row the dumbbells. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Aim to flare your elbows about 45 degrees away from your sides as you move them equally backward and out to the side. Zero degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows purely backward and keeping them completely tucked by your sides, while 90 degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows straight out to the sides, which would result in your upper arms and torso forming a “T-shape” at the top.
    2. Throughout the set, rigidly maintain a flat lower back with the same degree of bend in your hips and knees. All the motion should occur from your upper body.
    3. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being slightly above your sides at the top.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
    5. When allowing your elbows to bend naturally, your forearms should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    6. The dumbbells should move in an arcing motion rather than move straight up toward your shoulders.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled arcing motion until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. Allow the weights to pull your shoulder blades apart and forward to stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. Move your elbows diagonally inward and forward at a near 45-degree angle while they descend to reverse the moderate elbow flare you just utilized during the lifting phase.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weights pull your arms down rapidly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the weights down by bending your knees further.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).
1a15c6f170d8802c8fcac7ee0b4ff011:
## Setting up
1. Use the machine’s loading pin to select your desired level of assistance, and ensure that the machine’s knee pad or foot bar is positioned down.
    1. In contrast to most machines, the difficulty of this exercise decreases as you select heavier loads from the assisted pull-up machine since the weight determines the extent to which the machine will support your bodyweight.
    2. Certain machine models have a knee pad, and others have a foot bar, but essentially the same exercise technique can be used with either type of machine.
2. Step up onto the machine’s elevated foot plates and reach up overhead to grasp the machine’s handles firmly with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip) and your hands situated near shoulder-width apart or somewhat wider apart.
    1. If your machine has multiple handles, you can specifically select the handles that are most comfortable for you to grasp with your palms facing forward, which will typically be the outer handles on machines with multiple handles.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
3. One leg at a time, kneel onto the machine’s knee pad (if your machine has a knee pad) or step onto the machine’s foot bar (if your machine has a foot bar) while continuing to grasp the handles firmly.
    1. If using a machine with a knee pad, you will keep your knees bent on the pad throughout your set, but if you are using a machine with a foot bar, you will keep your knees straight while standing on the bar throughout your set.
    2. Certain machines with knee pads may not allow shorter individuals to pull through a full range of motion when kneeling on the pad, so you can switch to standing on the knee pad if the machine does not allow you to pull yourself fully up when kneeling on the pad.
4. Allow your body to descend in a controlled manner until your arms are fully overhead with straight elbows.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will place you in a more advantageous position to start your pull compared to if you kept your chest facing exclusively horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up from the force of your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back places you into a position akin to a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the handles by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending your elbows.
    1. Since the handles are fixed, your elbows naturally will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. If you are using a machine with a knee pad and you notice the machine restricts your range of motion when kneeling on the pad, switch to standing on the pad before resuming your set to pull through your full range of motion.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable bench at a low incline angle (e.g., near 30 degrees) and set a pair of dumbbells under the head of the bench.
    1. You can alternatively set your bench at a moderate incline (e.g., near 45 degrees) if your bench lacks a low incline setting, or if you personally prefer to use a mildly greater incline.
    2. The dumbbells may be easiest to grasp while lying on the bench if you initially place one end of each dumbbell on top of the bench’s horizontal base leg (which is where wheels may be located) and the other end of each dumbbell on the floor closer to where you will be on the bench.
2. Lie down with your chest contacting the head of the bench and your legs spread out as you position the balls of your feet on the ground.
3. Firmly grasp one dumbbell at a time, and angle your palms in toward each other while your arms hang down with straight elbows.
    1. The bony bump on the back of each elbow should be pointing backward, which is the direction in which you will row.
    2. Maintain this neutral grip throughout your set.
    3. To row through a full range of motion, the dumbbells should not contact the ground or the base of the bench, which may be more challenging to avoid for individuals with longer arms.
    4. To create greater clearance between the dumbbells and the ground, you can scoot further up toward the head of the bench.
    5. If it is difficult for you to grasp the dumbbells, which may be more likely if you have shorter arms, you can initially place the dumbbells closer to the bench’s seat before setting up with your torso scooted further down on the bench to situate your hands closer to the floor. After grasping the dumbbells, you can then press your feet into the ground to scoot further up on the bench so that your head can hang off the bench rather than having your face pressed into the head of the bench.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows backward and upward in an arcing motion to pull the dumbbells toward your hip. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Keep your elbows tucked by your sides, rather than flaring them outward.
    2. Progressively bend your elbows to the extent that keeps your forearms close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    3. Keep your torso in contact with the bench throughout the set rather than arching your lower back to lift your chest up off the bench.
    4. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    5. While performing this arcing motion, the dumbbells should not move straight upward in a vertical path.
    6. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled arcing forward motion until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. Allow the weights to pull your shoulder blades apart to stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weights rapidly pull your arms down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to place the dumbbells back onto the ground.
## Description
While also training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md), this row can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up one kettlebell, and hold it directly next to your chest with bent elbows as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. There are multiple ways in which you transfer the kettlebell to this position based on your preference.
    2. One such way is to tilt a kettlebell onto its side with the bottom of its base facing you, firmly grasp its horns (i.e., the corner handles) with the middle handle facing away from you, stand upright, and curl the kettlebell toward your chest.
    3. With a heavier weight, you can alternatively pick it up by its middle handle in a deadlift motion before setting it on top of a flat exercise bench with its handle facing up. Then you can squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it by the horns, and squat up with it close to your chest.
2. With your back facing the head of the position, sit down on a flat exercise bench while keeping the kettlebell close to your chest.
    1. Ensure that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie down with your head on the end of the bench.
3. Lean back to lie down on the bench while marching your thighs up to help when transitioning. Continue keeping the kettlebell close to your torso with your elbows by your sides.
    1. Let your elbows lower toward the ground when leaning back, which will allow the kettlebell to move slightly further away from your head compared to when you were sitting upright. When sitting upright, this would be the same motion as moving your elbows back slightly back toward your ribcage.
    2. Once you are lying down, return your feet to the ground in a stable position with your knees bent.
4. In a bench pressing motion, press the kettlebell up until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling with straight elbows.
    1. In this starting position, you should be holding the kettlebell's horns with mostly straight wrists as the bottom of the kettlebell’s base is directed forward (away from your head).
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the kettlebell’s handle toward your head in a controlled arcing manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Aim to keep your wrists straight throughout the set, which should result in the bottom of the kettlebell’s base angling upward and its handle angling downward while lowering the weight.
    2. Based on what feels most natural and comfortable, you can keep your elbows tucked in, or you can allow your elbows to flare out to your sides slightly.
    3. Movement should chiefly occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows as you strive to avoid letting your elbows drift back and down with the kettlebells through shoulder motion. When viewed from the side, your elbows should remain aligned over your shoulders rather than moving behind (closer to your head) them.
    4. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
2. Finish lowering the kettlebell once its handle is just above your forehead.
    1. Most lifters will be able to finish with their elbows bent by approximately 90 degrees.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way, particularly as it approaches your head.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the kettlebell into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. Continue keeping your upper arms in a vertical position as you avoid pushing your elbows forward (toward your chest) through shoulder motion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, lower your elbows toward your sides while bending them to bring the kettlebell toward your chest.
    2. March your thighs up before rocking forward to sit upright while keeping the kettlebell close to your chest.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the entirety of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. With its heavier side facing backward, firmly grasp an asymmetrical weighted implement (or a viable alternative) by its lighter end at a position that can provide your desired level of resistance.
    1. Asymmetrical weighted implements include adjustable dumbbells with plates loaded only on one side, hammers, and end-loaded baseball bats.
    2. As an alternative to an asymmetrical weighted implement, you can grasp certain symmetrically weighted cylindrical implements closer toward one end, which can provide the same training effect. Examples include a fixed-weight straight bar, a fixed-weight EZ bar, an adjustable EZ bar, and a cable straight bar attachment (like a lat pulldown bar).
    3. The resistance your forearm muscles experience during this exercise will be dictated by how closely to one end you grasp the implement.
    4. For greater resistance, you can grasp farther away from the weighted end with an asymmetrically loaded implement or closer to whichever end you are holding with a symmetrically loaded implement.
    5. When performing this exercise for the first time with a particular implement, you may have to try out different grip positions to determine specifically where you should grasp the implement to provide the magnitude of resistance you wish to have.
2. Hold the implement by your side with your palm facing in toward your side and your elbow straight. Based on your preference, you can stand or sit down with an upright torso.
    1. Hold the implement with your thumb bent and wrapped around your other fingers, like the standard grip for many exercises.
## Exercise technique
1. Allow the implement’s heavier end to tilt down through your wrist’s comfortable range of motion to assume the starting position of the exercise.
2. Tilt your hand back toward the little finger-side of your forearm (which is facing backward) through your wrist’s full range of motion.
    1. This will angle your knuckles at least mildly backward.
    2. The part of the lighter part of the implement in front of your thumb and index finger should now be angled diagonally downward and forward.
    3. Similarly, the heavier part of the implement behind your little finger should now be angled diagonally upward and backward.
    4. How far you can tilt your hand will be affected by your wrist mobility, and this exercise does not involve a particularly long range of motion.
    5. While you move your hand through wrist motion, keep the rest of your body stationary throughout the exercise.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your hand to tilt toward the thumb-side of your forearm through your wrist’s comfortable range of motion.
    1. This will angle your knuckles at least slightly forward.
    2. The lighter part of the implement in front of your thumb and index finger should now be angled at least slightly upward.
    3. On the other hand, the heavier part of the implement behind your little finger should now be angled at least slightly downward.
    4. There is no need to perform this extremely slowly, but you should actively control the movement rather than letting the weight swing your hand.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise will primarily train your forearm’s [flexor carpi ulnaris](../Muscles/Flexor%20Carpi%20Ulnaris%201905c6f170d880dba90bee3febf9486a.md) and [extensor carpi ulnaris](../Muscles/Extensor%20Carpi%20Ulnaris%2018f5c6f170d880349a23da380715c6e5.md).

## Setting up
1. Connect an attachment with a straight bar shaft to the cable, select your weight with the loading pin, and sit down facing the cable station.
    1. You can use any attachment that allows you to hold it comfortably with an overhand grip.
    2. The most commonly available attachment appropriate for this exercise is a standard lat pulldown bar attachment, which has a straight shaft with mildly angled ends and may be found attached to a cable lat pulldown machine.
    3. You can perform this exercise with essentially the same technique whether you use a seated cable row machine or an adjustable cable station, but a seated cable row machine is typically more stable and therefore the ideal option. 
    4. If you use a seated cable row machine, you naturally will sit down on its seat, but if you are using an adjustable cable station, you will sit down on the ground after adjusting the cable to a height that is approximately level with your shoulders when seated on the floor with an upright torso.
2. Position your feet in contact with the machine’s foot plates or the base of the adjustable cable station.
    1. Allow your knees to bend to an angle that allows you to feel stable and comfortable, which can be a mild to moderately mild knee bend for many people.
    2. With greater knee bend, you will be able to sit closer toward the cable, so you can bend your knees further if you initially cannot reach the bar when leaning forward by bending at your hip
3. Lean forward at your hips until you are able to grasp the bar firmly with straight elbows. Grasp it with a slightly outside shoulder-width overhand grip, as your palms face down.
4. While holding the bar with straight elbows, lean your torso backward at your hips until you are sitting with an upright torso.
    1. When seated upright, you should feel tension from the cable, so if the cable is still slack, you can extend your knees to scoot yourself backward until the machine’s weight stack separates and you feel the resistance.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar back toward your torso by driving your elbows backward while simultaneously bending them and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. Let your elbows naturally flare out away from your sides in a way that feels comfortable to you.
    2. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your knees, hips, and lower back should remain nearly stationary in a stable position throughout the set.
    3. Pull through your available range of motion or until the bar is directly in front of your torso, which will typically result in your elbows being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to move forward in a controlled manner as they progressively straighten to move the bar forward.
    1. Finish with your arms fully outstretched in front of you.
    2. Your shoulder blades will naturally move apart, but you can exaggerate this motion by intentionally allowing the weight to pull them further apart than your resting position at the end, without rounding your lower back. This will stretch your upper back muscles and may help you to train them more effectively.
    3. While you do not have to perform this step extremely slowly, you should avoid letting the weight abruptly yank your arms forward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable cable station’s pulley to its highest setting, or approach a cable lat pulldown machine.
    1. Either type of equipment can be used interchangeably for this exercise.
2. Select your desired weight with the loading pin, and connect a straight bar attachment to the cable.
    1. As an alternative to a standard straight bar or a lat pulldown bar (with a long straight body and angled ends), you can use a multi-grip EZ bar if you wish to do so.
3. While facing the cable station, reach up and firmly grasp the bar with an approximately shoulder-width overhand grip, such that your palms are angled forward and downward.
    1. Keep your elbows and wrists straight.
4. While keeping your arms outstretched with straight elbows in line with the cable, walk backward until you feel tension from the cable as the weight stack separates.
5. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and moderately incline your torso while keeping your arms in line with the cable and your back flat.
    1. The appropriate degree of torso incline should allow you to draw a mostly straight line from your arms through your shoulders to your hips when viewed from the side. From this position, the cable’s resistance should situate your arms fully overhead relative to what your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows straightened and your torso inclined, sweep your arms down and back toward your sides in an arcing motion until your hands are right by your thighs.
    1. During the initial half of this movement, you can focus on driving down, while you can focus on pulling back during the latter half of this movement.
    2. As your arms move through motion at your shoulders, the rest of your body should be stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your arms to sweep forward and upward in a controlled arcing manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms fully overhead in line with the cable.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straightened and your torso inclined.
    2. While you do not have to reverse the movement with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the cable abruptly swing your arms upward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, you can stand upright and walk forward to return the cable to its initial position.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which are assisted by the [lowest portion of your pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) and the [long head of your triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md) in the overhead position of each rep.

## Setting up
1. At a cable station, adjust the cable height to near the top of your head when standing, clip in a D-handle attachment, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. While facing away from the cable station and standing slightly to its side (such that the back of one shoulder is in line with the cable station), use your hand on the side closer to the cable to grasp the handle and take a step forward.
3. On the side holding the handle, raise your upper arm approximately 90 degrees out to your side (so that it is parallel to the ground) while bending your elbow to approximately 90 degrees and keeping your wrist in a fairly straight position.
    1. Maintain this position throughout your set.
4. Rotate your forearm through your available range of motion so that it is near a vertical position (or as close to that position as is comfortable for your shoulder), which will result in your palm facing forward.
    1. In this position, you should feel tension from the cable, so if that is not the case, take another step backward away from the cable station.
    2. Your shoulder mobility will affect how far you can rotate.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handle downward and forward by rotating your forearm away from the cable station until your forearm is situated parallel to the ground, as you continue to keep your upper arm held out to your side and parallel to the ground.
    1. All of this movement should occur from shoulder rotation as the bony prominence on the back of your elbow continues pointing straight out to the side throughout the rep.
    2. When thinking about this technique, it can be helpful to view your forearm as a clock’s hand, while your elbow is the center about which rotation occurs without any side-to-side motion.
2. Reverse the motion by rotating your forearm toward the cable station as you move the handle upward and backward in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set with one side and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your rotator cuff’s [subscapularis](../Muscles/Subscapularis%201905c6f170d88064bf36d328969a3679.md), while also training your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md).

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up overhead and firmly grasp it with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip) and your hands situated near shoulder-width apart or somewhat wider.
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the bar.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide upward during the dead hang, which pulls on your hand skin in a manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
    1. A dead hang is a static exercise, so you will simply hang on the bar while keeping your feet off the ground and not moving your body to perform it.
2. Continue hanging on the bar until you have completed your set’s target duration.
    1. Following the set, lower your feet onto the ground (or step) and let go of the bar.
## Description
While simultaneously improving overhead shoulder mobility, this exercise can increase your grip strength by training your [forearm](../Muscles/Extrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d88050a550fbeff6041573.md) and [hand](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md) muscles that function as finger flexors.

## Setting up
1. Approach a surface (e.g., hand rail, wall, power rack) where you can place one hand to assist with maintaining your balance while performing this exercise.
2. Place your hand onto the nearby surface for balance assistance.
    1. Maintain this hand contact throughout the set.
3. On the side you are not about to train, lift the foot up off the ground by bending that knee.
    1. Keep this foot in this position off the ground throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. With the leg that is standing on the ground, raise your heel into the air through your ankle’s available range of motion while keeping that side’s knee straight and your trunk upright.
2. In a controlled manner, allow your heel to descend toward the ground while continuing to keep the knee straight on your working side.
    1. Gently tap the ground with your heel at the bottom.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat this exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise offers you a convenient way to train your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md)  in nearly any environment.

## Setting up
1. After adding your desired load (in the form of weight plates or kettlebells) to a pull-up/dip belt you have around your waist, stand upright under a pull-up bar.

The back of your belt should be securely resting on top of your buttocks, and the belt’s chain or strap (depending on the belt model) should be looped through the center hole of a weight plate or under the handle of a kettlebell. If you have a loading pin for your belt, you can alternatively loop the chain or strap through it after adding weight plates.
    2. It will be easiest if you carry the weight over to the pull-up bar and add it to your belt while you are under the bar, rather than adding it farther away from the bar before walking over.
    3. As an alternative to using a pull-up/dip belt, you can wear a weighted vest.
    4. While less stable and more awkward than using a belt or weighted vest, you also have the option of holding a dumbbell between your thighs or feet, but you will be limited in how much weight you can add when using a dumbbell.
2. Reach overhead and firmly grasp the pull-up bar with your palms facing backward (i.e., an underhand grip) and your hands shoulder-width apart.
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. Particularly with this weighted variation, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar than if you jumped up from the ground.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
3. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will place you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up by your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back places you into a position akin to a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending your elbows.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows naturally will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps; however, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

### **How Your Grip and Pull-Up Technique Influence Back Muscle Development**

When repeatedly performing this exercise over time, you can feel free to try out mildly different grip widths to determine if any particular position feels most comfortable to you and/or allows you to perceive your target back muscles working particularly well. Pull-ups can be performed with a variety of hand grips, including different grip widths and overhand, underhand (resulting in the exercise being called a chin-up), neutral, or hybrid (i.e., a combination of neutral and underhand or overhand) grips. Additionally, shoulder motion during a pull-up can occur predominantly in the sagittal (front-to-back) plane, the frontal (side-to-side) plane, or a combination of the two. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the sagittal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out in front of you), the upper arms remain parallel to each other and do not deviate away from the mid-line of your body. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the frontal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out to your sides, such as with a snow angle motion), the upper arms move away from the mid-line of your body until they are parallel to the ground. Then they move closer to the mid-line of your body with further elevation. During the lifting phase of a pull-up, the shoulders could extend in the sagittal plane, adduct in the frontal plane, or exhibit a combination of extension and adduction at a hybrid angle between the sagittal and frontal planes. Rather than moving the shoulders exclusively through one plane, pull-up variations are commonly performed with a technique that allows for the shoulders to move in between these two planes, but one plane of shoulder motion often makes a greater contribution than the other.

Muscles acting on the shoulder joint have different leverage to generate extension torque in the sagittal plane versus adduction torque in the frontal plane, and the nervous system is most likely to recruit the particular muscles that are best leveraged to produce the intended joint action during any active movement. Correspondingly, the plane of motion in which the shoulders move during a pull-up can affect how well different muscles are likely to be trained. With any particular grip for a pull-up, you can intentionally rotate your shoulders in a manner that allows you to move your shoulder relatively more in the sagittal or frontal plane. However, most people will typically find that a particular path of shoulder motion feels most comfortable and stable to their shoulders, elbows, and wrists when using a specific grip. For instance, people will normally perform a wide overhand grip pull-up with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the frontal plane. In contrast, they will normally perform a close-grip chin-up (using an underhand grip) with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the sagittal plane. Performing either variation in the alternative plane of motion would require greater-than-normal rotational range of motion in the shoulders and forearms, and attempting to do so could feel very awkward and uncomfortable. People will typically feel most comfortable when positioning themselves so that, at the point in the pull-up when their upper arms are parallel to the ground, their elbows and wrists are vertically aligned or their elbows are slightly lateral (outside) to their wrists.

In general, widening a grip facilitates relatively more frontal plane shoulder motion, while narrowing a grip facilitates relatively more sagittal plane shoulder motion. An overhand, underhand, or neutral grip may be used with any grip width. Still, the combination of these grip variables will influence comfort and which plane of shoulder motion feels most natural. When pulling predominantly in the sagittal plane with a rather close grip, an underhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable than an overhand grip. Similarly, when pulling predominantly in the frontal plane with a rather wide grip, an overhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable and allow more frontal-plane motion than an underhand grip. With a moderate-width grip, people may commonly find that pulling mostly in the sagittal plane feels natural with an underhand or neutral grip, but pulling relatively more in the frontal plane feels natural with an overhand grip. Fundamentally, the shoulder motion is what matters to the back muscles, and the grip is only relevant to the back muscles based on how it influences which shoulder motion is performed. When performing this overhand grip pull-up with a moderate grip width, you most likely will pull in a way that biases shoulder adduction somewhat more than shoulder extension. Still, you can also perform the exercise in a way that results in a fairly even balance between these two motions.

The lat and teres major in the back function both as primary adductors and extensors and are therefore highly likely to be trained effectively with pull-up variations regardless of the grip or plane of shoulder motion. However, the preponderance of available evidence indicates that the rear deltoid lacks meaningful leverage to contribute to shoulder adduction, but it clearly has favorable leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. The rear deltoid is correspondingly likely to be trained better with a closer grip emphasizing shoulder extension, which would be most comfortable when using an underhand or neutral grip. Alternatively, the middle and lower regions of the pectoralis major (that constitute the sternoclavicular head) have large moment arms to function as shoulder adductors, but only the lower portion exhibits a shoulder extension moment arm, and this moment arm is quite small and only present in flexed shoulder positions. Consequently, wider grip pull-ups (which are most comfortable with an overhand or neutral grip) that involve greater frontal-plane shoulder motion are likely to train the pectoralis major more effectively than closer grip pulldowns. Which regions of the lats are preferentially biased by a pull-up variation may also potentially be influenced by how much shoulder motion occurs in the frontal or sagittal planes. The middle and lower regions have relatively greater leverage to function as shoulder adductors, while the upper region of the lat has relatively greater leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. Plausibly, these biomechanical differences may facilitate the middle and lower regions of the lats being preferentially trained by wider grip pull-ups, while the upper region may be preferentially trained by closer grip pulling variations. With that said, the degree to which any preferential biasing may occur across different regions of the lats when comparing pull-up grips is more speculative and has not been tested in any longitudinal training interventions.

### Why Overhand Grip Pull-Ups may be More Difficult than Chin-Ups or Neutral Grip Pull-Ups

While exceptions exist, people often find overhand grip pull-ups to be more difficult per rep than chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. The discrepancy is most likely influenced by chin-ups and neutral grip pull-ups typically being performed with a technique that emphasizes shoulder extension in the sagittal plane, while overhand grip pull-ups are typically performed with relatively more shoulder adduction in the frontal plane. As demonstrated by studies such as those by Mayer et al. (1994) and Shklar and Dvir (1995), on average, maximal torque for shoulder extension exceeds that for shoulder adduction. The sample of participants, velocity, and type of muscle action tested can all influence the degree to which torque differs between these two actions, but maximal shoulder adduction torque has been measured at 63-90% of maximal shoulder extension, depending on the specific test conditions. In addition to the effect of how the shoulder moves, the forearm position can also affect how much elbow flexion torque you can generate during your pull. Guenzkofer et al. (2012) found that up to 15% greater elbow flexion torque can be generated when the forearm is in a supinated (used for an underhand grip) or neutral position compared to a pronated (used with an overhand grip) position. Together, these relationships suggest that most people can generate greater torque at the shoulders and elbows during chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups than during overhand grip pull-ups, which are likely to be more challenging when performing the same number of reps. Consequently, it is common not to be able to complete as many reps of overhand grip pull-ups in a set as you would be able to complete when performing chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. Nonetheless, individual differences in factors such as training history and the relative strength of different muscle groups can result in some people not noticing a difference in difficulty between these variations, or even finding overhand grip pull-ups to be somewhat easier per rep.

### Chin Over Bar?

The technique instructions do not specify where any particular part of your body should be situated in relation to the bar at the end of the lifting phase because your full range of motion can differ from someone else’s full range of motion. Pulling until your chin is above the bar is a common standard used for testing by the United States Marines and for competitions held by the World Pull-Up Organization, and you can certainly use it if you wish. However, when focusing on chin clearance, some people tend to extend their necks, lifting their chins, to clear the bar with less range of motion through the pull, compared to when they retain a neutral neck position. In this instance, focusing on the proxy for a full range of motion may result in a different movement than focusing on the individual's full range of motion. When competing or taking a standardized test that affects professional prospects, it is only sensible to do the minimum required to complete each rep per the rules, but training to build muscle and strength is a different endeavor.

### **The Most Challenging Part of the Chin-Up**

The end range of the lifting phase is typically the most challenging portion of chin-ups, in large part because the torque our pulling muscles can generate meaningfully varies across different joint angles. When the elbow is flexed to 120 degrees, Bober et al. (2002) found maximal elbow flexion torque to be approximately 35% of the peak torque that can be generated in a moderately flexed elbow position (i.e., near 60-75 degrees of elbow flexion). With your elbows approaching full flexion toward the end range of a chin-up, your elbow flexor muscles are correspondingly operating from a rather disadvantaged position to help you complete the rep. On average, maximal shoulder extension torque is also lower when the shoulder is mildly elevated (like at the end of a chin-up’s lifting phase) compared to when it is moderately elevated (like during the middle range of a chin-up). The difference can be of notable magnitude, as indicated by Bober et al. (2002), who found that maximal shoulder extension in a neutral shoulder position was only 60% of the peak value achievable at 90 degrees of shoulder flexion. Together these strength curves of the muscle groups acting on the elbow and shoulder can contribute to your chin-ups consistently feeling the most difficult during the last quarter of the lifting phase.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your back muscle strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your back muscles. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

## Setting up
1. With its heavier side facing forward, firmly grasp an asymmetrical weighted implement (or a viable alternative) by its lighter end at a position that can provide your desired level of resistance.
    1. Asymmetrical weighted implements include adjustable dumbbells with plates loaded only on one side, hammers, and end-loaded baseball bats.
    2. As an alternative to an asymmetrical weighted implement, you can grasp certain symmetrically weighted cylindrical implements closer toward one end, which can provide the same training effect. Examples include a fixed-weight straight bar, a fixed-weight EZ bar, an adjustable EZ bar, and a cable straight bar attachment (like a lat pulldown bar).
    3. The resistance your forearm muscles experience during this exercise will be dictated by how closely to one end you grasp the implement.
    4. For greater resistance, you can grasp farther away from the weighted end with an asymmetrically loaded implement or closer to whichever end you are holding with a symmetrically loaded implement.
    5. When performing this exercise for the first time with a particular implement, you may have to try out different grip positions to determine specifically where you should grasp the implement to provide the magnitude of resistance you wish to have.
2. Hold the implement by your side with your palm facing in toward your side and your elbow straight. Based on your preference, you can stand or sit down with an upright torso.
    1. You have the option of holding the implement with your thumb bent and wrapped around your other fingers, like the standard grip for many exercises. Alternatively, you can situate your thumb flat against the implement as it is pointing forward. While not inherently injurious, certain individuals may experience thumb discomfort in the bottom position of this exercise when using a bent thumb position due to the loaded stretch it provides to a thumb muscle.
## Exercise technique
1. Allow the weight to tilt your hand down through your wrist’s comfortable range of motion to assume the starting position of the exercise.
2. Tilt your hand up toward the thumb-side of your forearm (which is facing forward) through your wrist’s full range of motion.
    1. This will angle your knuckles at least slightly forward.
    2. The heavier part of the implement in front of your thumb and index finger should now be angled at least slightly upward while mostly pointing forward.
    3. Similarly, the lighter part of the implement behind your little finger should now be angled at least slightly downward while mostly pointing backward.
    4. Individuals with normal wrist mobility can typically only tilt their hands mildly beyond a neutral wrist position (like it normally is when standing at rest with your knuckles pointing straight down) during this exercise. Consequently, this exercise does not involve a particularly long range of motion.
    5. While you move your hand through wrist motion, keep the rest of your body stationary throughout the exercise.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your hand to tilt away from the thumb-side of your forearm through your wrist’s comfortable range of motion.
    1. This will angle your knuckles at least mildly backward.
    2. The heavier part of the implement in front of your thumb and index finger should now be angled diagonally downward and forward.
    3. On the other hand, the lighter part of the implement behind your little finger should now be angled diagonally upward and backward.
    4. Only move through the range of motion that is comfortable to your wrist and thumb.
    5. There is no need to perform this extremely slowly, but you should actively control the movement rather than letting the weight swing your hand down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train five forearm muscles, namely the two [extensor carpi radialis muscles](../Muscles/Extensor%20Carpi%20Radialis%20Muscles%201b95c6f170d880b49202f1bf7521fa58.md), [flexor carpi radialis](../Muscles/Flexor%20Carpi%20Radialis%201905c6f170d880bea472f97a5bce0b64.md), [extensor pollicis brevis](../Muscles/Extensor%20Pollicis%20Brevis%201905c6f170d880079d14c018a5133bbd.md), and [abductor pollicis longus](../Muscles/Abductor%20Pollicis%20Longus%201905c6f170d8807b89e7c7ca3c8c19d3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to position the bar on your upper back and un-rack it in a stable position.
    1. As an initial approximation, you can position the bar such that it is a few finger widths below the height of your collarbone.
2. Add your desired weight to the bar and position the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) so that they are just below the height of the bar.
3. After adjusting the bar height, face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder width stance, and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
    3. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to then walk under the bar and situate the bar on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    4. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    5. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar up excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    6. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    7. If you are not accustomed to having a bar on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
    8. If you need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground in order to position the bar on your upper back, you can lower the height of the bar and the stop pads before repositioning the bar on your back.
## Exercise technique
1. With the hand placement and bar positioning determined while setting up, un-rack the bar by standing up in a squat-like manner by extending your knees and hips while pulling down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back.
2. After the bar is resting on your upper back rather than the safety bars, rotate the safety hooks backward by extending your wrists backward.
3. Raise your heels into the air through the available range of motion of your ankles while keeping your knees straight and your trunk upright.
4. In a controlled manner, allow your heels to descend toward the ground while continuing to keep your knees straight.
5. After your heels touch the ground, alternate between raising and lowering your heels until you have completed your set.
6. To rerack the bar, rotate the safety hooks forward by flexing your wrists forward before once again bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to return the bar to resting on the safety bars.
## Description
This exercise can develop your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md).

## Setting up
In contrast to pin-loaded pullover machines, it is not unusual for plate-loaded pullover machines to lack a foot pedal that you can press to move the machine’s arms while setting up. Some of the specific setup details differ depending on whether your machine has a foot pedal, so the setup for each type of machine is described separately. However, the exercise technique can be very similar for either option, so one technique section is provided with a couple of details that depend on which type of machine you utilize.

### **Setting up a machine with a foot pedal**

1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that aligns your shoulders with the machine’s pivot points and allows you to rest your triceps (the back of your upper arms) and elbows comfortably on the arm pads once you are seated.
    1. On each side of the machine, the pivot point (which is also known as the axis of rotation) is the center about which the machine’s lever arm will rotate during the exercise. Aligning your shoulders with these pivot points can help the exercise feel smooth and natural.
    2. The same seat height that aligns your shoulders with the pivot points is what should allow you to rest your triceps and elbows on the arm pads throughout the exercise.
    3. Finding the ideal seat height for you may initially require some trial and error, since you can only determine if the height is appropriate by sitting on the seat and checking to see if the center of your shoulders is level with the pivot points.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit on the seat with an upright torso and a “proud chest” posture, as your back and the back of your hip bones are resting against the backrest.
    1. Situate your feet on the stationary foot bar if your machine has one. Otherwise, situate your feet flat on the ground if you can do so. If your feet cannot reach a foot bar or the ground, you can simply let your feet hang down or place a step or bumper plate under your feet if you prefer them not to dangle.
4. If your machine has one, fasten the seat belt securely around your waist for additional stability.
5. Place one foot against the machine’s foot pedal, and push the pedal forward with your leg.
    1. This lowers the arm pads and moves the handle forward to a position you can comfortably reach.
    2. Keep the pedal pushed away during the next two steps.
6. With bent elbows, raise your arms to situate your elbows and triceps snugly against the arm pads while grasping the handles.
    1. Different machines have different handle types that will influence specifically how you should grasp the handle (such as with an overhand or semi-neutral grip), but what chiefly matters is that your grip feels comfortable and stable.
    2. While uncommon, certain machines may have handles without any arm pads. If you are using one of these atypical machines, you will simply grasp the handles and ignore the details about arm pad usage while otherwise performing the exercise as instructed.
7. Slowly bring the foot pedal back to its starting position by bending your knee, which will shift the machine’s resistance to your arms. Simultaneously, allow the machine’s resistance to lift your elbows upward and backward through the full range of motion that is comfortable to your shoulders.
    1. Maintain the natural curvature of your lower back rather than excessively arching your lower back and flaring your ribs upward and away from your hip bones as you raise your elbows.
    2. The degree to which you can comfortably allow your elbows to lift upward will be influenced by your individual shoulder mobility, but it is common to be able to reach near the point at which the upper arms are fully vertical.
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your shoulders and/or back muscles in the starting position, but you should move through the range in which you do not feel any shoulder joint pain or discomfort.
8. Once your arms are fully lifted up, lift your foot off the foot pedal and place it symmetrically with your other foot, whether that be on the stationary foot bar, on the ground, or hanging under the seat.

### **Setting up a machine without a foot pedal**

1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that aligns your shoulders with the machine’s pivot points and allows you to rest your triceps (the back of your upper arms) and elbows comfortably on the arm pads once you are seated.
    1. On each side of the machine, the pivot point (which is also known as the axis of rotation) is the center about which the machine’s lever arm will rotate during the exercise. Aligning your shoulders with these pivot points can help the exercise feel smooth and natural.
    2. The same seat height that aligns your shoulders with the pivot points is what should allow you to rest your triceps and elbows on the arm pads throughout the exercise.
    3. Finding the ideal seat height for you may initially require some trial and error, since you can only determine if the height is appropriate by sitting on the seat and checking to see if the centers of your shoulders are level with the pivot points.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit on the seat with an upright torso and a “proud chest” posture, as your back and the back of your hip bones are resting against the backrest.
    1. Situate your feet on the stationary foot bar if your machine has one. Otherwise, situate your feet flat on the ground if you can do so. If your feet cannot reach a foot bar or the ground, you can simply let your feet hang down or place a step or bumper plate under your feet if you prefer them not to dangle.
4. If your machine has one, fasten the seat belt securely around your waist for additional stability.
5. With bent elbows, raise your arms up overhead until your triceps are behind the arm pads.
    1. Maintain the natural curvature of your lower back rather than excessively arching your lower back and flaring your ribs upward and away from your hip bones as you raise your elbows.
    2. You cannot modify the starting position of the arm pads when using a machine without a foot pedal, which is not particularly problematic for the majority of lifters, since these machines are designed to have a starting position that is accessible for people with normal shoulder mobility. However, certain individuals with meaningful shoulder mobility limitations may not be able to raise their arms high enough to reach the pads without pushing into a position that causes shoulder joint discomfort or pain. If this applies to you, you can select an alternative variation (such as the [straight arm cable lat pulldown](Cable%20bar%20straight%20arm%20lat%20pulldown%201a15c6f170d880308073fc37f580cda4.md)) that allows you to individualize the starting position and train the same movement pattern through a comfortable range of motion.
6. Situate your elbows and triceps snugly against the arm pads while grasping the handles.
    1. Different machines have different handle types that will influence specifically how you should grasp the handle (such as with an overhand or semi-neutral grip), but what chiefly matters is that your grip feels comfortable and stable.
    2. While uncommon, certain machines may have handles without any arm pads. If you are using one of these atypical machines, you will simply grasp the handles and ignore the details about arm pad usage while otherwise performing the exercise as instructed.
    3. Certain unconventional machines may also have a foot brake that you need to press with your foot to disengage before starting your set to enable you to train through a full range of motion.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows down toward your sides in an arcing motion until your elbows are by your sides.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up and back in contact with the backrest rather than slumping forward into a slouched posture.
    2. During the initial half of this movement, you can focus on pulling down, while you can focus on pulling back during the latter half of this movement.
    3. Emphasize driving your elbows down into the arm pads rather than pulling the handle with your hands.
    4. As your arms move through motion at your shoulders, the rest of your body should be stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to sweep upward in a controlled arcing manner through the full range of motion that is comfortable to your shoulders.
    1. You should return to the starting position with your elbows lifted as high up as your shoulder mobility comfortably permits. If you are using a machine without a foot pedal, the machine’s lever arms contacting the stoppers underneath them may restrict your end range before your shoulder mobility does, so you can lightly tap the lever arms against the stoppers to confirm that you have moved through your full range of motion.
    2. Like when setting up, avoid letting your lower back excessively arch from flaring your ribs upward and away from your hip bones.
    3. While you do not need to perform this phase with an extremely slow tempo, avoid letting the machine’s resistance abruptly swing your arms upward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. If your machine has a foot pedal, push it forward with your leg (once your arms are fully overhead following your last rep) until you are no longer supporting any of the machine’s resistance with your upper body. Then let go of the handles while lifting your arms off the arm pads before bending your knee to bring the foot pedal back to its initial position.
    2. If your machine lacks a foot pedal or foot brake, simply rest the machine’s lever arms on the stoppers underneath them (after your arms are fully overhead following your last rep) before letting go of the handles while lifting arms off the arm pads.
    3. If your machine has a foot brake rather than a foot pedal, engage it with your foot before letting go of the handles.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which are assisted by the [lowest portion of your pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) in the overhead position of each rep.

## Setting up
1. You can select either a fixed-weight EZ bar or an adjustable plate-loaded EZ bar, which are functionally interchangeable for this exercise.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down or hinge at your hips with extended elbows.
    1. If the EZ bar is already positioned in an elevated rack at mid-thigh level or above, you naturally would not have to squat down or hinge at your hips before picking it up.
3. Grasp the bar with approximately a shoulder width grip and a semi-underhand grip (AKA semi-neutral grip) such that your palms are directed at an angle that is facing forward and inward.
    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it before a shoulder width semi-underhand grip is accessible on the bar.
4. While keeping your elbows extended, stand fully upright while gripping the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl the bar upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed at your sides (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms positioned by your sides.
3. Alternate between curling the bar upwards and lowering it down until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. After selecting your desired weight with the loading pin, adjust the height of the machine’s shoulder pad to a level that allows you to perform full range of motion calf raises.
    1. If the pad is too high, the machine may not be able to provide tension when your heels are fully lowered.
    2. If the pad is too low, the machine may restrict you from fully raising your heels.
2. With your knees slightly bent, position the front halves of your feet onto the step with your heels hanging off the edge while your shoulders are snugly resting under the shoulder pads.
3. Stand upright with your knees extended to receive the weight from the machine.
    1. Maintain this upright position throughout the set.
    2. Depending on their mobility, some people may be able to adopt a position of knee hyperextension, which is when the knees bend backward beyond a straight position. Being able to reach a mildly hyperextended knee position is normal for many individuals and is not inherently problematic. However, certain individuals may experience knee discomfort if they utilize a hyperextended knee position during this exercise, so keeping a straight knee position instead of a hyperextended knee position may be preferable.
4. While keeping one foot on the step, lift your other foot off the step by bending that knee.
    1. Keep this foot in this position off the step throughout the set while you keep the front half of your working leg’s foot on the step.
## Exercise technique
1. Raise your heel into the air through your ankle’s available range of motion.
2. In a controlled manner, allow your heel to descend toward the ground through your ankle’s available range of motion while continuing to keep the front half of your foot on top of the step.
    1. How far you are able to lower your heel will be dependent on your mobility.
    2. Strive to lower your heel as far as you can, and you will likely feel a stretching sensation in your calf at the bottom position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md) while simultaneously improving calf flexibility through loaded stretching.
