## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable bench at a moderate incline angle, which is near 45 degrees.
    1. Whether the bench is set to a 45-degree angle or a somewhat steeper angle will not meaningfully affect the stimulus this exercise provides to your biceps and other arm muscles.  However, using an angle closer to 60 degrees may result in setting up being easier if you are using heavy weights.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and straddle the bench as you face toward the elevated head of the bench.
3. While keeping your toes on the ground, position the front of your torso on top of the bench with your chest at the head of the bench, so that your head is above the end of the bench.
    1. Transitioning to lying on top of the bench may be easier if you initially position the dumbbells against the head of the bench, lower your torso to the bench in a push-up-like motion, and then lift the dumbbells out to the sides off the bench to hang down.
    2. Once on the bench, your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are looking straight ahead when normally standing upright.
4. With your arms hanging straight down toward the ground with straight elbows, direct your palms to face forward as you hold the dumbbells with an underhand grip.
    1. You will maintain this underhand grip throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your upper arms directed straight down toward the ground, curl the dumbbells upward in an arcing motion by bending your elbows until they are fully bent.
    1. While your forearms move through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout your set.
    2. Avoid swinging your elbows forward.
2. After your elbows have fully bent, reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled arcing manner until your elbows have returned to a fully straightened position with your forearms directed straight down toward the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your upper arms directed straight down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hand while holding them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
    2. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    3. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    4. With the aforementioned strategy, make sure to set the dumbbells down onto the bench in a manner where they do not risk rolling off the bench.
    5. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
## Exercise technique
1. Walk forward while holding the dumbbells at your sides, maintaining an upright posture with your shoulders approximately level.
    1. While you will not swing your arms like you would when walking normally, your torso and lower body should look similar to how they would when you walk normally.
    2. Walk at a pace where you feel stable and balanced throughout the carry.
    3. If you use a weight that is fairly heavy to you, it is natural to take shorter strides compared to how you typically walk.
    4. Keep the tops of your hip bones approximately level throughout your set rather than letting them drop down to one side when taking each step.
2. Continue walking with the dumbbells until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down.
    1. Similar to the setup, it may be easiest to set the dumbbells down one at a time onto a flat exercise (or sturdy box) prior to picking up one dumbbell and reracking it, and then doing the same with the other dumbbell.
    2. The above approach can be particularly useful if you are rather fatigued after completing your set and could use a rest break prior to reracking the dumbbells.
## Description
Rather than concentrating the workload on one body region, this exercise trains a variety of muscle groups throughout your body in an integrated manner, including the muscles in your forearms, upper back, core, and lower body.

### **Straps for Carries**

Even when using chalk, the weight you can use or distance you can complete with a particular weight will commonly be limited by grip strength while performing a farmer’s carry, so this carry can be a viable means of training static grip strength. However, if you wish to increase the stimulus provided to muscles besides the forearm and hand muscles, you have the option of performing this carry with lifting straps. With the heavier loads or longer distances that straps typically facilitate, the exercise can be more challenging to your upper back and core muscles as they support your trunk and shoulder girdle in addition to your lower body muscles that stabilize your pelvis and propel you forward.

### Training Many Muscles Simultaneously

McGill et al. (2009) measured EMG activity of several core and lower body muscles as competitive strongmen performed a variety of movements that appear in strongman competitions, including the farmer’s walk, which was performed for several steps with a 75kg (167.6lb) weight in each hand. During the farmer’s walk, peak EMG activity was high for the internal abdominal obliques, lats, thoracic erector spinae, lumbar erector spinae, gluteus medius, gluteus maximus, and rectus femoris. The external abdominal obliques and biceps femoris also exhibited moderate peak EMG activity, while the rectus abdominis exhibited low EMG activity. The abdominal muscles and rectus femoris demonstrated their peak activity during the walking portion of the carry, while the lats, erector spinae and biceps femoris demonstrated their peak activity during the initial lifting phase. The gluteal muscles exhibited peak activity during the initial lifting phase and during the first step of the carry. As indicated by these findings, the farmer’s carry can train a large amount of musculature simultaneously, which can result in this exercise being metabolically demanding when performed at a high relative intensity, especially for longer duration sets. Correspondingly, challenging sets of farmer’s carries may be able to train your cardiovascular system more robustly than most resistance training exercises that localize the workload to a smaller amount of total muscle mass.

1. After ensuring that your suspension trainer is appropriately anchored to a sufficiently sturdy elevated structure (such as the top of a power rack or a pull-up bar), adjust its straps to a length that situates the handles approximately at the level of your waist.
    1. If you are familiar with TRX straps but unfamiliar with the term “suspension trainer,” TRX is a specific brand name that popularized suspension trainers (the general type of equipment) to enough of a degree that people may colloquially refer to suspension trainers in general as TRX straps.
    2. To check that your suspension trainer is anchored firmly, you can tug down on the straps and make sure they are stable before continuing to set up for this exercise.

    2. Pull through your full range of motion while aiming for the front of your chest to reach near the level of the handles, which will typically result in your elbows being aligned with your torso or a little behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    3. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your torso and lower body should remain nearly stationary in the bridged position that is akin to holding a [reverse plank](Reverse%20plank%201a45c6f170d880faa555d3e604efa65f.md).
2. Reverse the movement by letting your chest move down away from the handles in a controlled manner as your elbows progressively straighten.
    1. Fully return to the starting position with your arms outstretched up in front of you.
    2. Continue keeping your knees, hips, and shoulders aligned.
    3. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart naturally.
    4. While you do not have to lower yourself extremely slowly, you should actively resist the descent rather than abruptly dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a dumbbell with one hand, carry it over to a flat bench, and position yourself near the base of the bench and directly to its side with your side that is holding the dumbbell farther away from the bench.
    1. If you have to carry the dumbbell a meaningful distance before reaching your bench and your grip is somewhat fatigued, you can place the dumbbell on the bench before picking it up with your opposite hand to start your set with the side that does not have a fatigued grip.
2. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips, reach out with your free arm to place its hand on the bench with a straight elbow, and place your knee (on the side not holding the dumbbell) onto the bench.
    1. In this position, your torso should now be reasonably close to being parallel to the ground, and your lower back should be flat rather than being meaningfully rounded.
    2. While setting up, keep your elbow straight on the side holding the dumbbell and allow that arm to hang down toward the ground with your shoulder blade naturally pulled forward toward the ground from the weight.
    3. Based on your comfort and preference, you can place the open palm of your free hand onto the bench, or you can make a fist and place your knuckles onto the bench.
    4. Your foot on the side of the dumbbell should remain firmly in contact with the floor and be sufficiently far behind the dumbbell that your leg does not restrict your row. If you initially do not feel well-balanced, you can try positioning this foot somewhat further out to the side to widen your base of support.
3. Direct your palm so that it is facing forward, and keep it facing forward to use an underhand grip throughout the row.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Drive your elbow backward and upward in an arcing motion to pull the dumbbell toward your hip. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blade backward, and keep your elbow tucked by your side rather than flaring it outward.
    1. When allowing your elbow to bend naturally, your forearm should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    2. At the top of the row, your elbow should be aligned with your torso or slightly behind your torso.
    3. Keep your torso in a mostly fixed position with your chest facing a similar direction throughout this movement. A mild degree of torso rotation is not problematic, but avoid letting it become excessive and turning the exercise into a cheat row.
    4. While performing this arcing motion, the dumbbell should not move straight upward in a vertical path.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled arcing motion until your arm is directed down toward the ground with your elbow straightened.
    1. Allow the weight to pull your shoulder blade forward, which will stretch your upper back muscles and result in your working side’s shoulder being mildly closer to the ground than your other side’s shoulder at the bottom of the row.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weight rapidly pull your arm down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up overhead and firmly grasp it with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip) and your hands situated near shoulder-width apart or somewhat wider.
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the bar.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
2. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, raise your legs up and out in front of you with straight knees until your legs are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. In this position, your torso and legs should resemble an “L-shape” when viewed from the side, which results from your legs forming a right angle with your torso.
    2. If you do not have the hamstring flexibility to utilize what is considered the standard “textbook form” with your knees fully straight as your legs are parallel to the ground, you can situate your legs as closely as you can to this position.
    3. Individuals with limited hamstring flexibility can either keep their thighs parallel to the ground with their knees mildly bent, or they can lift their legs up as close to parallel to the ground as they can reach with straight knees.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending your elbows and continuing to keep your legs lifted parallel to the ground.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows naturally will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows being bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps, but different individuals may have different ranges of motion that their bodies enable.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md), and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a pair of securely anchored gymnastic rings to be fairly close to shoulder width apart and elevated above your head.
    1. Ideally, the rings should be reasonably close to the height of your palms when standing upright with your arms raised straight up overhead. However, a lower height can be appropriate as long as you can hang on the rings without your legs touching the ground when your knees are bent.
    2. You may also use rings beyond your reach if you initially place a sturdy box, an aerobic step, or a bumper plate on the ground as a step to reach the rings. While not required, elevating yourself to reach high rings may help you set up with a more stable hand position compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the rings.
    3. If the rings have not been previously anchored, you will naturally have to anchor them to a sturdy structure that is able to support your bodyweight. Potential anchor points include the top of a power rack, a pull-up bar, a monkey rig, and a ceiling-mounted anchor that is designed for rings or suspension trainers.
    4. While positioning the rings at shoulder width is appropriate, you can adjust the exact distance between them to your preference.
2. Stand under the rings, reach up overhead, and firmly grasp them with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip)
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the rings with the rings pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the rings closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the rings can slide up your hands while hanging on them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
3. Lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the rings with straight elbows.
    1. You only need to bend your knees as much as is required to keep your feet above the ground.
    2. If you initially used a step to reach the rings and the step is positioned somewhat behind the rings, you may be able to keep your knees straight and still keep your feet off the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the rings with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will place you in a more advantageous position to start your pull compared to if you kept your chest facing exclusively horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to shrug up from the force of your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back places you into a position akin to a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the rings by driving your elbows down and toward your sides as you progressively bend them. Allow your palms to rotate naturally in a manner that feels comfortable to you.
    1. People commonly perform this exercise by progressively turning their palms toward each other, so that they face each other at the top of the pull-up, after facing forward at the bottom. That can certainly be an effective technique, but it is not the only viable technique, since rotating your palms in a way that feels right to you as an individual is most important.
    2. Since the rings are anchored, your elbows will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    3. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms near the sides of the torso and elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, individuals may have different ranges of motion that their bodies allow.
    4. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. If you rotate your palms to face each other while pulling yourself up, you can let them rotate forward as you descend.
    2. You do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than just letting gravity pull you down abruptly.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to return your feet to the ground.

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell on the side you are about to train, and stand over one end of a flat exercise bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space behind you. With this equipment, you would straddle the bench and walk forward toward the J-hooks.
    2. With a portable exercise bench, your back should face the head of the bench, as you would with a dumbbell bench press.
    3. All the directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training first.
    4. Throughout the exercise, you can situate your free arm wherever is comfortable to you.
2. Sit down on the bench while lifting the dumbbell onto your upper thigh near your abdomen.
    1. Ensure that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie down with your head on the end of the bench.
    2. Your palm should be facing inward with your upper arm by your side.
    3. To move a heavy dumbbell efficiently into the proper position, you can initially situate the dumbbell on the front of your thigh while standing up. Then you can rest it on your thigh while sitting down.
3. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbell back toward your chest with your elbow bent, lean back to lie down on the bench. Your head should be right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent. You will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
4. In a bench pressing motion, press the dumbbell up until your elbow is straight and your arm is directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a single arm dumbbell bench press rep), the dumbbell should be sitting on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a reasonably straight wrist. You will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
    2. While your wrist does not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the dumbbell with your wrist cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the dumbbell hard will usually keep your wrist from cocking back excessively.
    3. Based on what feels most comfortable, you can have your palm facing in toward your other side (with a neutral grip), forward (with an overhand grip), or angled inward and forward. During your set, you can similarly allow your palm to rotate within this range if that feels comfortable to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbow to lower the dumbbell in a controlled arcing manner while keeping your elbow up.
    1. Predominantly keep your elbow tucked in, but you can allow it to flare slightly out away from your side if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    2. Avoid letting your elbow drift back and down with the dumbbells through shoulder motion. When viewed from the side, the proper elbow position should result in your upper arm remaining in a vertical position.
    3. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearm hinging at your elbow without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbow as the center of an analog clock, while your forearm is the hand that rotates about the center elbow during this exercise.
2. Finish lowering the dumbbell just before it reaches your forehead or the bench.
    1. If you are using an overhand grip (with your palm facing forward to start), you will finish with the dumbbell just above your forehead.
    2. If you are using a neutral grip (with your palms facing inward), your head may not be in the way of the dumbbell, so you can finish with the dumbbell just above the end of the bench.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way, especially when the weight approaches your head.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbow to lift the dumbbell into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbow fully straightened as the dumbbell is vertically above your shoulder.
    2. Continue keeping your upper arm in a vertical position as you avoid pushing your elbow forward (toward your chest) through shoulder motion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
5. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the dumbbell toward your side like you would during a neutral grip dumbbell bench press.
    1. Regardless of the palm position you used for your set, it is easier to reposition yourself when your palm is facing in toward your other side.
6. Transfer the dumbbell to your other side and repeat the exercise.
    1. Once you have finished training your other side and have performed step 5, march your thighs up until they are close to being vertical before rocking forward to sit up with the dumbbell on your upper thigh.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar with parallel handles that are near shoulder-width apart, reach up and firmly grasp the handles with your palms facing in toward each other (i.e., a neutral grip).
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar than if you jumped up from the ground to reach it.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
2. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will put you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up by your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back puts you in a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending them.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows will not actually drive downward, but having this intent helps pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates to the machine and adjust the seat to a height that allows your chest to rest comfortably against the chest pad.
    1. While you can initially adjust the seat to a height that situates your shoulders approximately level with the horizontal handles, the seat height that is best for you depends on the specific machine you use, and trying out different positions may be helpful.
2. If your machine has an adjustable chest pad, adjust it to a position that allows you to grasp the horizontal handles when your arms are fully outstretched forward in front of you with extended elbows.
    1. To row through your full range of motion, ideally place the chest pad far enough back that you have to push your shoulder blades forward and apart to grasp the handles with your elbows fully straight.
3. Sit down with your chest resting snugly against the chest pad and your feet flat on the floor.
4. Reach fully forward with straight elbows to grasp the horizontally directed handles firmly with your palms facing down (i.e., an overhand grip).
    1. If your machine does not have an adjustable chest pad and the handles are far enough from you to make it difficult to grasp both of them simultaneously, it may be easier for you to grasp one handle at a time.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handles back toward you by driving your elbows backward while simultaneously bending them and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. Allow your elbows naturally to flare out away from your sides in a manner that feels comfortable to you, rather than trying to keep them tucked close to your sides (which is typically more comfortable with a closer underhand or neutral grip).
    2. Keep your chest in contact with the chest pad throughout the set.
    3. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.

2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to move forward in a controlled manner, progressively straightening until they are outstretched in front of you.
    1. Your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another, but you can exaggerate this motion by intentionally allowing the weight to pull them further apart than your resting position at the bottom. This will stretch your upper back muscles and may help you train them more effectively.
    2. While you do not have to perform this step extremely slowly, you should avoid letting the weight abruptly yank your arms forward in an uncontrolled fashion.

### **Notes**

### **How Your Grip and Pull-Up Technique Influence Back Muscle Development**

When repeatedly performing this exercise over time, you can feel free to try out mildly different grip widths to determine if any particular position feels most comfortable to you and/or allows you to perceive your target back muscles working particularly well. Pull-ups can be performed with a variety of hand grips, including different grip widths and overhand, underhand (resulting in the exercise being called a chin-up), neutral, or hybrid (i.e., a combination of neutral and underhand or overhand) grips. Additionally, shoulder motion during a pull-up can occur predominantly in the sagittal (front-to-back) plane, the frontal (side-to-side) plane, or a combination of the two. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the sagittal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out in front of you), the upper arms remain parallel to each other and do not deviate away from the mid-line of your body. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the frontal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out to your sides, such as with a snow angle motion), the upper arms move away from the mid-line of your body until they are parallel to the ground. Then they move closer to the mid-line of your body with further elevation. During the lifting phase of a pull-up, the shoulders could extend in the sagittal plane, adduct in the frontal plane, or exhibit a combination of extension and adduction at a hybrid angle between the sagittal and frontal planes. Rather than moving the shoulders exclusively through one plane, pull-up variations are commonly performed with a technique that allows for the shoulders to move in between these two planes, but one plane of shoulder motion often makes a greater contribution than the other.

Muscles acting on the shoulder joint have different leverage to generate extension torque in the sagittal plane versus adduction torque in the frontal plane, and the nervous system is most likely to recruit the particular muscles that are best leveraged to produce the intended joint action during any active movement. Correspondingly, the plane of motion in which the shoulders move during a pull-up can affect how well different muscles are likely to be trained. With any particular grip for a pull-up, you can intentionally rotate your shoulders in a manner that allows you to move your shoulder relatively more in the sagittal or frontal plane. However, most people will typically find that a particular path of shoulder motion feels most comfortable and stable to their shoulders, elbows, and wrists when using a specific grip. For instance, people will normally perform a wide overhand grip pull-up with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the frontal plane. In contrast, they will normally perform a close-grip chin-up (using an underhand grip) with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the sagittal plane. Performing either variation in the alternative plane of motion would require greater-than-normal rotational range of motion in the shoulders and forearms, and attempting to do so could feel very awkward and uncomfortable. People will typically feel most comfortable when positioning themselves so that, at the point in the pull-up when their upper arms are parallel to the ground, their elbows and wrists are vertically aligned or their elbows are slightly lateral (outside) to their wrists.

In general, widening a grip facilitates relatively more frontal plane shoulder motion, while narrowing a grip facilitates relatively more sagittal plane shoulder motion. An overhand, underhand, or neutral grip may be used with any grip width. Still, the combination of these grip variables will influence comfort and which plane of shoulder motion feels most natural. When pulling predominantly in the sagittal plane with a rather close grip, an underhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable than an overhand grip. Similarly, when pulling predominantly in the frontal plane with a rather wide grip, an overhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable and allow more frontal-plane motion than an underhand grip. With a moderate-width grip, people may commonly find that pulling mostly in the sagittal plane feels natural with an underhand or neutral grip, but pulling relatively more in the frontal plane feels natural with an overhand grip. Fundamentally, the shoulder motion is what matters to the back muscles, and the grip is only relevant to the back muscles based on how it influences which shoulder motion is performed. When performing this overhand grip pull-up with a moderate grip width, you most likely will pull in a way that biases shoulder adduction somewhat more than shoulder extension. Still, you can also perform the exercise in a way that results in a fairly even balance between these two motions.

The lat and teres major in the back function both as primary adductors and extensors and are therefore highly likely to be trained effectively with pull-up variations regardless of the grip or plane of shoulder motion. However, the preponderance of available evidence indicates that the rear deltoid lacks meaningful leverage to contribute to shoulder adduction, but it clearly has favorable leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. The rear deltoid is correspondingly likely to be trained better with a closer grip emphasizing shoulder extension, which would be most comfortable when using an underhand or neutral grip. Alternatively, the middle and lower regions of the pectoralis major (that constitute the sternoclavicular head) have large moment arms to function as shoulder adductors, but only the lower portion exhibits a shoulder extension moment arm, and this moment arm is quite small and only present in flexed shoulder positions. Consequently, wider grip pull-ups (which are most comfortable with an overhand or neutral grip) that involve greater frontal-plane shoulder motion are likely to train the pectoralis major more effectively than closer grip pulldowns. Which regions of the lats are preferentially biased by a pull-up variation may also potentially be influenced by how much shoulder motion occurs in the frontal or sagittal planes. The middle and lower regions have relatively greater leverage to function as shoulder adductors, while the upper region of the lat has relatively greater leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. Plausibly, these biomechanical differences may facilitate the middle and lower regions of the lats being preferentially trained by wider grip pull-ups, while the upper region may be preferentially trained by closer grip pulling variations. With that said, the degree to which any preferential biasing may occur across different regions of the lats when comparing pull-up grips is more speculative and has not been tested in any longitudinal training interventions.

### Why Overhand Grip Pull-Ups may be More Difficult than Chin-Ups or Neutral Grip Pull-Ups

While exceptions exist, people often find overhand grip pull-ups to be more difficult per rep than chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. The discrepancy is most likely influenced by chin-ups and neutral grip pull-ups typically being performed with a technique that emphasizes shoulder extension in the sagittal plane, while overhand grip pull-ups are typically performed with relatively more shoulder adduction in the frontal plane. As demonstrated by studies such as those by Mayer et al. (1994) and Shklar and Dvir (1995), on average, maximal torque for shoulder extension exceeds that for shoulder adduction. The sample of participants, velocity, and type of muscle action tested can all influence the degree to which torque differs between these two actions, but maximal shoulder adduction torque has been measured at 63-90% of maximal shoulder extension, depending on the specific test conditions. In addition to the effect of how the shoulder moves, the forearm position can also affect how much elbow flexion torque you can generate during your pull. Guenzkofer et al. (2012) found that up to 15% greater elbow flexion torque can be generated when the forearm is in a supinated (used for an underhand grip) or neutral position compared to a pronated (used with an overhand grip) position. Together, these relationships suggest that most people can generate greater torque at the shoulders and elbows during chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups than during overhand grip pull-ups, which are likely to be more challenging when performing the same number of reps. Consequently, it is common not to be able to complete as many reps of overhand grip pull-ups in a set as you would be able to complete when performing chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. Nonetheless, individual differences in factors such as training history and the relative strength of different muscle groups can result in some people not noticing a difference in difficulty between these variations, or even finding overhand grip pull-ups to be somewhat easier per rep.

### Chin Over Bar?

The technique instructions do not specify where any particular part of your body should be situated in relation to the bar at the end of the lifting phase because your full range of motion can differ from someone else’s full range of motion. Pulling until your chin is above the bar is a common standard used for testing by the United States Marines and for competitions held by the World Pull-Up Organization, and you can certainly use it if you wish. However, when focusing on chin clearance, some people tend to extend their necks, lifting their chins, to clear the bar with less range of motion through the pull, compared to when they retain a neutral neck position. In this instance, focusing on the proxy for a full range of motion may result in a different movement than focusing on the individual's full range of motion. When competing or taking a standardized test that affects professional prospects, it is only sensible to do the minimum required to complete each rep per the rules, but training to build muscle and strength is a different endeavor.

### The Most Challenging Part of the Pull-Up

The end range of the lifting phase is typically the most challenging portion of pull-ups, in large part because the torque our pulling muscles can generate meaningfully varies across different joint angles. When the elbow is flexed to 120 degrees, Bober et al. (2002) found maximal elbow flexion torque to be approximately 35% of the peak torque that can be generated in a moderately flexed elbow position (i.e., near 60-75 degrees of elbow flexion). With your elbows approaching full flexion toward the end range of a pull-up, your elbow flexor muscles are correspondingly operating from a rather disadvantaged position to help you complete the rep. On average, maximal shoulder extension and adduction (a combination of which occurs during a pull-up) torques are also lower when the shoulder is mildly elevated (like at the end of a pull-up’s lifting phase) compared to when it is moderately elevated (like during the middle range of a pull-up). Together, these strength curves of the muscle groups acting on the elbow and shoulder can contribute to your pull-ups consistently feeling the most difficult during the last quarter of the lifting phase.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your back muscle strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your back muscles. As a simple approach, if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure you use the same technique for each condition, which means the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how the performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep's performance across these conditions on a second day, in which you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps on the first day, perform the set with straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue from the first set may influence the second. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting the performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, select your weight with the loading pin, and connect a D-handle attachment to the cable.
2. Stand with the side of one shoulder (on the same side of your body you intend to train) facing the cable station.
3. Squat down and grasp the handle firmly with the hand closer to the cable station.
    1. Keep your elbow straight and your palm facing in toward your side.
    2. When squatting down (and up during the next step), keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back.
4. By extending (straightening) your hips and knees, stand upright with the handle while continuing to keep your elbow straight.
    1. You can situate your resting hand wherever you feel helps maintain your balance, such as raised out to the side or resting on your hip.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the side in which you are holding the cable.
5. Take a step out to the side against the cable’s resistance while keeping your straight arm aligned with the cable. Simultaneously allow the cable’s resistance to pull your shoulder blade downward and out toward the pulley.
    1. Your arm should naturally be directed diagonally out to the side and downward in line with the cable.
    2. Due to the cable’s resistance, your working side’s shoulder blade should be a bit lower and further away from the midline of your back compared to your resting side’s shoulder blade.
    3. You should currently feel resistance from the cable, so take another step away from the cable station if you do not feel resistance.
6. Position your feet about shoulder width apart with your knees slightly bent in an athletic stance and your chest up.
    1. Ultimately, you want to adopt a stance that helps you feel stable and balanced, so you can modify your stance based on what helps accomplish that for you personally.
## Exercise technique
1. As you keep your elbow straight, shrug your shoulder and shoulder blade upward while simultaneously pulling them in toward your body’s midline.
    1. The objective is to move your shoulder and shoulder blade diagonally in the opposite direction to which the cable is pulling them.
    2. Once you can no longer shrug upward and inward, you have reached the end range. In this position, your working side’s shoulder should be higher than your resting side’s shoulder.
    3. Throughout the set, keep your neck in a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    4. Keep your torso upright as you avoid letting the cable’s resistance bend your torso toward the pulley, as would otherwise occur during a side-bend exercise.
2. Reverse the motion in a controlled manner by allowing your shoulder and shoulder blade to move diagonally downward and to the side toward the pulley.
    1. Move through your full range of motion, which may prompt you to feel a stretching sensation in the region of your upper trap (on the back of your neck and uppermost upper back) at the bottom.
    2. At the end of this motion, your working side’s shoulder should be positioned a little lower than your resting side’s shoulder due to the downward stretch that the cable can provide.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm toward the pulley.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md) while also training your [middle trap](../Muscles/Middle%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880ae812dc1cacf02f16f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md) to a greater degree than purely vertical shrugs.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up overhead with one arm to firmly grasp the bar with your palm facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip).
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the bar.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palm (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide upward during the dead hang, which pulls on your hand skin in a manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. With your elbow straight and your hand firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
    1. A dead hang is a static exercise, so you will simply hang on the bar while keeping your feet off the ground to perform it.
2. Continue hanging on the bar until you have completed your set’s target duration and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. Following the set, lower your feet onto the ground (or step) and let go of the bar.
## Description
While simultaneously improving overhead shoulder mobility, this exercise can increase your grip strength by training your [forearm](../Muscles/Extrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d88050a550fbeff6041573.md) and [hand](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md) muscles that function as finger flexors.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with extended elbows.
2. Direct your palms so that they are facing in toward your sides (i.e., in a neutral grip position).
    1. Maintain this neutral grip on the dumbbells throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl both dumbbells upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed at your sides (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms positioned by your sides.
3. Alternate between curling the dumbbells up and lowering them down until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a barbell in the J-cups of a power rack set approximately to the height of your hips while standing or alternatively position a Smith machine’s bar to the same height.
    1. This exercise can be performed with the same technique whether you use a barbell and power rack or a Smith machine.
    2. If you use a power rack, situate the barbell snugly in contact with the back corner of the J-cups since the middle portion of certain J-cups can be wide enough to allow the barbell to roll forward or backward, which is undesirable for this exercise.
2. Stand in front of the middle of the bar with your back facing the back of the power rack/Smith machine and firmly grasp the bar with an approximately shoulder-width underhand grip that results in your palms facing up.
3. While holding the bar, walk your feet forward to recline your torso into a more horizontal position until your chest is underneath the bar. Simultanesouly allow your elbows to straighten, and bridge your hips up by squeezing your glutes.
    1. In the bridged position, which you will maintain throughout your set, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    2. For the standard technique, you will walk your feet forward until you can fully extend your knees with the back of your heels on the ground, while the soles of your feet are off the ground and facing forward.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your chest toward the bar by driving your elbows simultaneously downward and backward while progressively bending them and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. Move your elbows through a path of motion that feels comfortable to you, which will typically involve keeping them tucked close to your sides with this underhand grip rather than notably flaring your elbows away from your sides (which is typically more comfortable with a wider overhand grip).
    2. Pull through your full range of motion while aiming for your chest to reach the bar.
    3. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your torso and lower body should remain nearly stationary in the bridged position that is akin to holding a [reverse plank](Reverse%20plank%201a45c6f170d880faa555d3e604efa65f.md).
2. Reverse the movement by letting your chest move down away from the bar in a controlled manner as your elbows progressively straighten.
    1. Fully return to the starting position with your arms outstretched up in front of you.
    2. Continue keeping your knees, hips, and shoulders aligned.
    3. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart naturally.
    4. While you do not have to lower yourself extremely slowly, you should actively resist the descent rather than abruptly dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This row can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), which are assisted by your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates to a barbell situated in a landmine attachment (or a viable substitute).
    1. As an alternative to using a landmine attachment, landmine exercises can be performed with one end of the barbell situated in a wall corner.
    2. While the scraping can be lessened by placing a towel between the wall corner and the barbell, be aware that performing landmine exercises in a wall corner can easily damage the wall corner, so this approach is not appropriate in every environment.
2. Stand upright in a near hip-width stance with the free end of the bar between the middle of your feet.
3. Simultaneously bend your hips and knees to squat down until you are low enough to grasp the bar.
    1. Keep your back flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your back.
4. Firmly grasp the end of the bar with your fingers cupped around it, as one hand is directly in front of the other.
    1. The little finger of one hand should be touching the index finger of your other hand.
    2. Your palms should be facing in toward the bar.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
6. Explosively lift the bar up to chest height while rapidly repositioning your hands under the bar with your elbows bent. Allow the end of the bar to rest on the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with your fingers cupped around the bar as one hand is directly in front of the other.
    1. Your knees and hips should now be straight, like when you are normally standing upright, but allow your body to lean mildly forward at your ankles.
    2. Avoid leaning back with an excessively arched lower back position throughout the rest of the setup and during your set.
7. Move the bar to the side you are about to train so that its end is slightly in front of that side’s shoulder.
8. Maintain a firm grip on the end of the bar with the hand on the side you are about to train while releasing your other hand.
    1. You can now keep your free arm in whichever position you prefer, such as resting by your side.
    2. The subsequent directions will apply to the side on which you continue holding the bar, since that is the side you will be training.
9. Pivot your feet and your whole body so that the front of your shoulder is directly facing the base of the landmine.
    1. Your elbow should be positioned by your side or slightly in front of it, rather than being behind your side.
    2. Your wrist should be mostly straight rather than cocked back. Squeezing the bar hard can help you maintain the appropriate wrist position.
10. Take a small step forward on the side you are not training to adopt a staggered stance for greater stability.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes like you are trying to crush a walnut. Simultaneously, brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core and tightening your glutes throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the bar upward and mildly forward until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. As a cue, you think about punching upward and outward while driving your elbow in this direction.
    2. Your hand will move diagonally since the bar will naturally move in an arcing manner rather than in a purely vertical path. At the top, your arm should be angled upward and forward.
    3. Rather than intentionally trying to keep it pulled back and packed down, allow your shoulder blade to move freely. It is natural for the shoulder blade on your working side to move forward as you press.
    4. Keep your shoulder, elbow, and wrist stacked in alignment with the bar from your perspective of looking forward.
    5. Continue keeping your knees and hips stationary rather than using them to help you lift the weight.
    6. Throughout your set, avoid leaning your torso back via excessive lower back arching.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until its end is slightly in front of your shoulder.
    1. Move your elbow downward and back toward your side while progressively bending it.
    2. At the bottom, your elbow should be tucked near your side or slightly in front of it. Avoid bringing it back to the extent that it is behind your back, which would require lowering the bar excessively.
    3. Allow your shoulder blade to move naturally backward with your elbow.
    4. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
5. Once you have completed the lowering phase of your last rep, transfer the bar to your other side and repeat the exercise.
6. After finishing the set with your other side, firmly grasp the bar with your free hand as you pivot toward the side in which you just finished the set.
7. Guide the bar toward the ground as if you were performing the lowering phase of a row while sitting your hips back like during a deadlift.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [upper pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a dumbbell in one hand and sit down on a flat exercise bench with enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space.
2. Lift the dumbbell up onto your thigh and grasp its handle with both hands as your palms face inward.
3. While simultaneously marching your thigh up to help lift the dumbbell back toward your upper abdomen, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench, as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent, and you will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbell with both hands right above your upper abdomen.
4. Press the weight up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
5. Reposition your hands so that both of your palms are firmly contacting one end of the dumbbell with your thumbs crossed over each other and your index fingers crossed over each other, which can result in your thumbs and index fingers resembling close to a diamond shape.
    1. In this position, the dumbbell’s handle should be vertical as one end of the weight is below your hands, while the other end is above your hands.
    2. You will continue securely gripping the dumbbell in this manner throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows fairly straight, lower the weight behind your head in a controlled arcing manner through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. You should avoid meaningfully bending your elbows, but you can allow them to bend mildly as your arms move through motion at your shoulders while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
    2. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back during the descent.
    3. People can often lower the weight until their upper arms are close to parallel with the ground, but how far you can descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    4. Once you feel that you have reached the end range to which your shoulders can safely stretch, you have reached the end range for you as an individual.
2. Reverse the movement by pulling your arms upward and forward in an arcing motion to lift the weight up until you have returned to the starting position with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows fairly straight as you move your arms through shoulder motion while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
3. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can train your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which are assisted by the [lowest portion of your pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) in the overhead position of each rep.

## Setting up
1. Connect a V-bar lat pulldown/row attachment (or a similar neutral grip attachment) to the cable and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. You can use any attachment that lets you grasp it with a closer-than-shoulder-width neutral grip.
    2. Note that a V-bar for pulldowns or rows, which is also known as a double-D handle attachment, differs from the V-bar attachment that can be used for triceps pushdowns.
2. Adjust the thigh pad to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
3. While facing the bar and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the bar with a neutral grip, such that your palms face each other.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
4. While holding the bar, sit down on the machine’s seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to straighten and your arms to raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
5. In the seated position, slightly lean your torso backward at your hips.
    1. Maintain this slight backward lean throughout your set.
    2. From this position, your elbows should be straight, with your arms overhead and slightly forward (rather than completely vertical), and you should feel tension from the cable station holding your arms in this position.
    3. If you notice the cable remains slack in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), you may need to use a different attachment and a wider grip to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for your lat pulldown.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down toward your sides as you progressively bend them.
    1. Simultaneosuly pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears.
    2. After the initial half of the pull, when your upper arms are approximately parallel with the ground, the bony prominence on the back of each elbow should be pointing predominantly forward as your upper arms are situated in front of your body, rather than having your elbows and upper arms predominantly flared out to your sides.
    3. During the second half of this pull, drive your elbows simultaneously backward and downward until they are in line with your torso or slightly behind it.
    4. Maintain the slight backward lean of your torso you adopted while setting up, rather than leaning further backward.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the bar in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your arms overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground.
    1. The initial steps of the setup are the same as a [conventional deadlift](Conventional%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880f7a755cd3780a63371.md) with an underhand grip.
2. In a near hip-width stance, stand with the middle of your feet under the middle of the bar.
3. Hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. Throughout this movement, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with a near shoulder-width underhand grip such that your palms are facing forward.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
6. Stand upright with the bar by extending your hips and knees while continuing to keep your elbows straight and your lower back near a neutral position.
    1. While your lower back muscles will be working to maintain a rigid trunk position, lifting the bar upward should chiefly occur from your hip and thigh muscles extending your hips and knees.
    2. Keep the bar very close to your legs as you lift the bar rather than allowing the bar to drift forward.
7. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and moderately incline your torso until you have lowered the bar near your knees.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight, back flat, and core braced.
    2. Allow your knees to bend naturally while sitting your hips back as if you were closing a car door with your buttocks, while your hands are carrying something.
    3. Maintain this hinged position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar up toward your lower abdomen by driving your elbows simultaneously backward and upward as you pull your shoulder blades back.
    1. Throughout your set, maintain the same degree of torso inclination while keeping your back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    2. As movement occurs at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, your lower body should remain essentially stationary. Resist the urge to use your legs to lift your torso into a more upright position at the end of the lifting phase, which is the most difficult part of the exercise.
    3. Keep your elbows tucked close to your sides as they bend rather than meaningfully flaring your elbows out away from your sides.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner. Allow your elbows to move downward and forward until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. At the end of the lowering phase, you should be in the starting position with the bar just in front of your knees.
    2. Let your shoulder blades naturally spread apart.
    3. There is no need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but make sure that you actively control the weight rather than simply letting gravity abruptly yank the bar down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
4. Set the bar down onto the ground by reversing the technique you used to pick it up (i.e., bending at your hips and knees as opposed to just rounding over at your lower back).
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).
