## Setting up
1. Prepare the barbell with your desired load by adding weight plates while the barbell is on the ground or in an elevated position, such as a power rack.
    1. Setting up will be easier when using an elevated position, especially if you are using relatively heavy loads for this exercise.
    2. The bar will be easiest to pick up if positioned at a height slightly lower than the level of your hands when standing upright with your arms relaxed at your sides.
2. Stand close in front of the middle of the bar with a hip-width stance and extended elbows before hinging at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so.
3. Firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
4. By extending your hips and knees, stand upright with the bar while continuing to keep your elbows extended and your lower back near a neutral position.
## Exercise technique
1. Mildly hinge at your hips while slightly bending your knees to lower the bar until it is positioned slightly above your knees.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows extended and your lower back near a neutral position.
2. Vigorously extend your hips and knees while simultaneously shrugging your shoulders upward in an explosive manner through your available range of motion to lift the bar upward.
    1. While doing so, keep your elbows extended, your lower back near a neutral position, and your neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
3. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulders to descend through your available range of motion while hinging at your hips and bending your knees until the bar has returned to slightly above your knees.
    1. At the end of this motion, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the weight can provide.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).
1a15c6f170d8808fbb71ec4a23bd16a8:
## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance. Hold the dumbbell at your side with a straight elbow as your palm faces in toward your thigh.
    1. Throughout the exercise, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side. You can optionally  set up near a sturdy surface (like a power rack) where you can place your free hand for additional stability if you wish to do so.
    2. All the directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training first.
2. Lift the dumbbell up near the front of your shoulder with your elbow bent by curling the weight and using momentum from your lower body as needed.
    1. You can perform a cheat curl-like motion to move the dumbbell into position if it is too heavy to lift without momentum. To do so, first sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and simultaneously rocking the dumbbell mildly backward. Then drive your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body while bending your elbow and mildly swinging it forward to lift the weight up.
    2. Your elbow should now be underneath and slightly in front of the dumbbell.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbell on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a mostly straight wrist that allows for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. Press the dumbbell up overhead in a shoulder press motion until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. You can point the back of your elbow forward and out to the side at an angle.
    2. The dumbbell should be vertically stacked over your shoulder.
    3. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbow to lower the dumbbell behind your head in a controlled manner while keeping your elbow up.
    1. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearm hinging at your elbow without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbow as the center of an analog clock, while your forearm is the hand that rotates about this center elbow during the exercise.
    2. As you keep your elbow up, your upper arm should remain in a vertical position by the side of your head.
2. Continue lowering the dumbbell until you have fully bent your elbow or can lightly tap your upper back with the dumbbell.
    1. It is normal to be able to bend the elbow beyond 90 degrees, but specifically how far you can bend your elbow may be limited by the flexibility of your long head of the triceps.
    2. While some lifters have the flexibility to reach their upper back with the dumbbell, wherever you feel a notable stretching sensation in your triceps can be an appropriate end range.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbow to lift the dumbbell into the starting position overhead.
    1. You should finish with your elbow fully straightened as the dumbbell is vertically above your shoulder.
    2. Continue keeping your elbow up as all the motion occurs from your elbow without moving your shoulder.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
5. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the dumbbell toward your shoulder like you would during a shoulder press.
6. Lower the dumbbell to your side as you straighten your elbow and swing your elbow back by your side.
7. Transfer the dumbbell to your other hand and repeat the exercise with that side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells, and stand over one end of a flat exercise bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space behind you. With this equipment, you would straddle the bench and walk forward toward the J-hooks.
    2. With a portable exercise bench, your back should be facing the head of the bench like when you would during a kettlebell bench press.
2. Sit down on the bench while holding the kettlebells by your sides with your palms facing forward.
    1. Ensure that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie down with your head on the end of the bench.
3. Curl the kettlebells up toward the front of your shoulders by bending your elbows, turning your palms to face in toward each other at the top. Move your elbows slightly in front of your ribcage, and allow the bodies of the kettlebells to rest against your forearms while keeping your wrists straight.
    1. You will be able to rest the bodies of the kettlebells against your forearms by angling them slightly inward as your wrists are slightly closer to the midline of your body than your elbows.
    2. To help get the weights into position, feel free to perform a cheat curl-like motion where you initially generate some momentum by swinging the weights mildly backward with straight elbows before swinging your elbows forward while curling them.
4. Lean back to lie down on the bench while marching your thighs up to help when transitioning. Keep your forearms in a mostly vertical position with the kettlebells contacting them as your elbows remain bent and close to your torso.
    1. To maintain a mostly vertical forearm position, you should let your elbows lower toward the ground when leaning back. When sitting upright, this would be the same motion as moving your elbows back slightly behind your ribcage.
    2. Once you are lying down, return your feet to the ground in a stable position with your knees bent.
    3. After completing this step, you should now be in essentially the same position as the bottom of a kettlebell bench press.
5. In a bench pressing motion, press the kettlebells up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling. Direct your palms forward at the top.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the top of a bench press rep), your wrists should be mostly straight while you are holding the kettlebells’ handles across your palms.
    2. Based on what feels most comfortable, you can have your palms facing in toward each other (with a neutral grip), forward (with an overhand grip), or angled inward and forward. During your set, you can similarly allow your palms to rotate within this range if that feels comfortable to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the kettlebells in a controlled arcing manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Based on what feels most natural and comfortable, you can keep your elbows tucked in, or you can allow your elbows to flare out to your sides slightly.
    2. Movement should chiefly occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows as you strive to avoid letting your elbows drift back and down with the kettlebells through shoulder motion. When viewed from the side, your elbows should remain aligned over your shoulders rather than moving behind (closer to your head) them.
    3. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
2. Finish lowering the kettlebells just before they reach the bench or until you have fully bent your elbows.
    1. When not letting the elbows drift back, the bench will determine how far the kettlebells can be lowered for most lifters.
    2. Normally, you should be able to finish with your elbows bent by greater than 90 degrees, but the size of your kettlebells may influence specifically how much you can bend your elbows.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weights the entire way.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the kettlebells into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as your wrists are vertically stacked above your shoulders.
    2. Continue keeping your upper arms in a vertical position as you avoid pushing your elbows forward (toward your chest) through shoulder motion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, lower your elbows and the kettlebells toward your sides like you would during a kettlebell bench press.
    2. March your thighs up before rocking forward while keeping your forearms mostly vertical to sit up with the kettlebells close to your shoulders.
    3. Turn your palms back toward your shoulders, and guide them down by letting your elbows straighten and swinging your elbows mildly back to help control the weights.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the entirety of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up and firmly grasp it with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip), with your hands shoulder-width apart or slightly wider.
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position than if you jumped up from the ground to reach it.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
2. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will put you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up by your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back puts you in a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. After hanging from the bar with your body stationary for a brief period of time (i.e., about two seconds), pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending your elbows.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows will not actually drive downward, but having this intent helps pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
    4. Keep your neck in a neutral position (like when you are standing upright and looking straight ahead) rather than arching it backward.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. To perform the dead hang pull-up specifically, make sure that you briefly pause at the bottom with your elbows fully straightened after the lowering phase of each rep before commencing your next rep.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
You can set up for this exercise in essentially the same way you would for a close grip bench that situates your hands shoulder-width apart without arching your back.

1. Determine whether you will set up within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench. With a bench press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. Some trial and error may be needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of JM press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descended by the end of the lowering phase of your JM press.
    1. The safety pins/spotter arms should be high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    2. While the safety pins/spotter arms can provide additional safety, you should be able to close grip bench press the bar up if you happen to fail a JM press rep.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned above your neck, you can also avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your eyes are close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands near shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A shoulder-width grip is an appropriate starting point, but you can try mildly different grip widths over time to determine where you personally feel best. The proper grip width should allow your elbows, wrists, and shoulders to feel comfortable while emphasizing the triceps to a greater degree than your close grip bench press.
    2. The traditional technique for this exercise involves a thumbless grip with the thumbs placed on the same side of the bar as the other fingers. However, if you are new to this exercise, you have the option of wrapping your thumbs around the bar to fully enclose the bar with your hands, which can make it easier to hold the bar securely.
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
7. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Maintain the natural curvature of your lower back, like when you are normally standing upright. Regardless of whether you meaningfully arch your lower back when bench pressing, the JM press involves a mostly flat back position.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
3. Lower the bar toward your throat or chin in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows. Keep your elbows higher than your chest (when viewed from the side) while flaring your elbows out about 45 degrees from your sides.
    1. Avoid letting your wrist cock back, which would point your palms away from your forearms. Rather, curl your wrists mildly to angle your palms closer toward your forearms while securely holding the bar.
    2. In contrast to a strict lying triceps extension, you will somewhat lower your elbows, but to a meaningfully lesser degree than with a close grip bench press.
    3. The degree to which your forearms are angled relative to the ground can indicate whether you are moving your elbows (through shoulder motion) appropriately. By the end of the lowering phase, your forearms should be closer to horizontal than vertical. If your forearms remain closer to vertical at the bottom, you are excessively lowering your elbows and performing too much of a pressing movement. If your forearms angle beyond horizontal (with your wrists lower than your elbows), you are keeping your elbows excessively high and performing an exercise closer to a strict triceps extension than is intended.
    4. The amount of elbow flare is similar to what you can use for a close grip bench press. Strive to reach the middle ground between 90 degrees of elbow flare (which would cause your upper arms to form a “T-shape” with your torso) and 0 degrees of elbow flare (which would result in your upper arms being completely parallel to your torso).
    5. When lowering the bar toward your throat or chin, the bar will track slightly backward (toward your face) but to a notably lesser degree than with a strict triceps extension.
4. Continue lowering the bar until you have fully bent your elbows or until the bar is just about to contact your chin or throat.
    1. The end range can be determined by when your biceps contact your forearms, so what constitutes your personal end range can be influenced by the circumference of your arms.
    2. If the bar is about to touch your chin or throat before you have fully bent your elbows, you naturally can finish lowering the bar before achieving a full elbow bend.
5. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the bar up into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. Your elbows will move upward and inward during the lifting phase, but you can predominantly focus on extending your elbows to lift the weight.
    3. Uncurl your wrists while lifting the bar to maintain a secure grip.
6. Alternate between steps 3-5 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
7. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
8. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
While training the [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) and [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) to a lesser degree than a [close grip bench press](Close%20grip%20bench%20press%201a05c6f170d8807c9f16f226db24074d.md), this exercise can develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) particularly well.

## Setting up
1. Firmly grasp an asymmetrical weighted implement (or a viable alternative) by its lighter end at a position that can provide your desired level of resistance.
    1. Asymmetrical weighted implements include adjustable dumbbells with plates loaded only on one side, hammers, and end-loaded baseball bats.
    2. As an alternative to an asymmetrical weighted implement, you can grasp certain symmetrically weighted cylindrical implements closer toward one end, which can provide the same training effect. Examples include a fixed-weight straight bar, a fixed-weight EZ bar, an adjustable EZ bar, and a cable straight bar attachment (like a lat pulldown bar).
    3. The resistance your forearm pronator muscles experience during this exercise will be dictated by how closely to one end you grasp the implement.
    4. For greater resistance, you can grasp farther away from the weighted end with an asymmetrically loaded implement or closer to whichever end you are holding with a symmetrically loaded implement.
    5. When performing this exercise for the first time with a particular implement, you may have to try out different grip positions to determine specifically where you should grasp the implement to provide the magnitude of resistance you wish to have.
2. Sit down on a seat (e.g., chair, flat exercise bench, plyometric box), and position your forearm (on the side holding the weight) on top of your thigh with a bent elbow and your hand slightly in front of your knee.
    1. You can situate your wrist just above your kneecap, which should allow the weighted implement to rotate freely without contacting any part of your leg.
3. If not already in this position, direct your palm to face in toward your opposite side with a straight wrist position and the heavier end of your weighted implement directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. From here, your wrist and forearms are in a neutral position as they would normally be when standing upright with your palms facing in toward your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your forearm resting on your thigh, progressively rotate your palm up toward the ceiling in a controlled manner through your available range of motion.
    1. Doing so will rotate the weighted end (if using an asymmetrically loaded object) or longer end (if using a symmetrically loaded object) out to your side, such that this end moves away from the midline of your body.
    2. How far you are able to rotate will be influenced by your individual forearm mobility, and you should aim to move through what is your comfortable full range of motion.
    3. Most people will have the forearm mobility to rotate until their palm is close to facing straight up, which will result in the weight’s handle being close to parallel to the floor, but some people may not be able to rotate quite as far, while others can rotate beyond that point.
    4. As you rotate your forearm, keep your wrist in a straight (neutral) position rather than letting the weight bend your wrist and pull your hand downward (which would bring the back of your hand closer toward your knee if the wrist extends).
2. After reaching your end range, reverse the movement until you have returned to the starting position by turning your palm to face in toward your opposite side.
    1. Doing so will lift the weighted end or longer end of the implement upward and inward in an arcing manner until the handle is vertically oriented.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the [pronator teres](../Muscles/Pronator%20Teres%201905c6f170d880469c68dcf80a241445.md) and [pronator quadratus](../Muscles/Pronator%20Quadratus%201905c6f170d8805d864ff866cf803c77.md) on the palm side of your forearm.

## Setting up
1. Securely attach your desired weight to your wrist roller.
    1. Depending on the model of your wrist roller, you may have to use weight plates (if your model uses a loading pin), or you may be able to use weight plates, kettlebells, or dumbbells (if your model uses a strap that you can loop around the weight).
    2. Leave enough of the rope initially uncoiled so that you can stand up with the roller without the weight lifting off the ground.
2. While the weight is on the ground, firmly grasp the roller’s handles with your palms facing toward you (i.e., an overhand grip) and the uncoiled part of the rope on the side of the roller that is closer toward you.
    1. If the uncoiled part of the rope is on the side of the roller farther away from you, you would be able to train wrist extension when using an overhand grip, but this is the wrist flexion variation.
3. Stand upright while grasping the roller and bend your elbows by approximately 90 degrees while keeping your upper arms tucked by your sides.
    1. You will maintain this bent elbow position throughout your set.
4. Take up the slack from the roller’s rope with alternating twisting motions of your wrists until you feel that the rope is taught from the weight’s resistance.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows bent, bend one wrist to curl that side’s hand toward you as you extend your other wrist in the opposite direction by pointing that hand’s palm down toward the ground.
    1. You should grasp the handle firmly with the hand whose palm is curling toward you, as you grasp the handle loosely with the hand whose palm is pointing toward the ground.
    2. The hand whose palm is curling toward you is what rotates the roller to lift the weight up, while the other side’s wrist is repositioning in preparation to perform the curling motion.
2. Alternate the motions in step 1 with the opposite hands as you lift the weight up by cyclically repeating these twisting movements with your wrists until you have fully coiled the rope around the roller.
3. Lower the weight in a controlled manner by reversing the same motions you just performed until the weight lightly taps the ground or is just about to do so.
4. Repeatedly perform steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the six [wrist flexor muscles](../Muscles/Wrist%20flexor%20muscles%202c85c6f170d880a49749f7d7a9f307c8.md) on the palm side of your forearm.
1a15c6f170d8809a878dd1577bac5536:
## Setting up
1. Pick up a hand gripper with your desired resistance level. Initially hold it with what will be your non-working hand to help you set the gripper firmly within the hand you will be training.
    1. Based on your preference, you can be standing or seated for this exercise.
    2. For direction clarity, the set-up will be described with your working side’s elbow bent by 90 degrees as your upper arm is by your side, palm is facing in toward your other side, and forearm pointing forward. This can help communicate directionality (such as what “forward” involves), but you can optionally set up with your arm in a different position.
2. With the middle coil (where the handles meet) facing up, position one handle in your working hand’s palm as your thumb is directed forward
    1. The bottom end of the handle should be near the base of your palm on the side of your little finger.
    2. The handle should be deep enough in the middle of your palm that it is not resting on the wad of muscle at the base of your thumb.
3. Tightly wrap your index, middle, ring, and little fingers around the other handle with these four fingers close together. Position your little finger at the lowest point of the handle.
    1. To help you wrap your little finger firmly around the end of the handle, you can optionally use your non-working hand to squeeze the gripper until the front handle is close enough for your working hand’s little finger. This involves using your non-working hand’s thumb to press the back handle into your palm to stabilize it. Then use your non-working hand’s index finger to squeeze the front handle in toward your palm, so that you can tightly wrap your little finger around the front handle.
4. With the gripper now fully set, situate your arm in your preferred position.
    1. You can have your elbow straightened or bent, and you can keep your upper arm by your side or raised out in front of you. Over time, you can try out different arm positions to determine where the exercise feels best to you.
    2. So long as it does not touch the gripper or your working hand, you can place your non-working hand wherever you wish.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze the handles together until they touch.
    1. Hearing the clinking sound of the ends of the handles contacting each other confirms you have moved through the full range of motion.
    2. Strive to crush the gripper with all five fingers simultaneously. While your four long fingers pull the front handle toward the back handle, having the intent to crush with your thumb will keep the back handle stabilized.
    3. The back handle should remain firmly dug into your palm throughout the set.
    4. Allow your wrist to move naturally. Grip strength is normally greatest when the wrist is mildly cocked back, so your wrist may naturally cock back when squeezing the gripper without thinking about moving your wrist.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner as you allow the handles to separate into the starting position.
    1. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow opening phase, do not let the gripper abruptly yank your hand open.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively strengthen your forearm’s [flexor digitorum superficialis](../Muscles/Flexor%20Digitorum%20Superficialis%201905c6f170d880f7b5c4d319b5fbe7e9.md) and [flexor digitorum profundus](../Muscles/Flexor%20Digitorum%20Profundus%201905c6f170d880f7bfa5f786584c4f71.md), along with your hand’s [intrinsic finger flexors](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md).
1a15c6f170d8809a927ed538bf683443:
## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder width stance while holding the kettlebells at your sides with extended elbows.
2. Direct your palms so that they are facing forward.
    1. Maintain this underhand grip on the kettlebells throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl both kettlebells upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed at your sides (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the kettlebells in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms positioned by your sides.
3. Alternate between curling the kettlebells up and lowering them down until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to a barbell situated in a landmine attachment (or a viable substitute), grab a V-bar row grip attachment (or attach a specific neutral grip landmine attachment to the bar before adding plates).
    1. Note that a V-bar for rows or pulldowns, which is also known as a double D-handle attachment, differs from the V-bar attachment that can be used for triceps pushdowns.
    2. As an alternative to using a landmine attachment, landmine exercises can be performed with one end of the barbell situated in a wall corner.
    3. While the scraping can be lessened by placing a towel between the wall corner and the barbell, be aware that performing landmine exercises in a wall corner can easily damage the wall corner, so this approach is not appropriate in every environment.
    4. The diameter of the plates you select can influence the range of motion of this exercise, so you can use smaller diameter plates if you wish to row through a longer range of motion.
    5. Plates weighing 45lb or 20kg (which differ slightly), along with bumper plates of various weights, have a diameter near 18in (45cm) that can physically constrain the range of motion for your row by contacting your torso at the end of the lifting phase or by contacting the ground at the end of the lowering phase.
2. While holding the V-bar, straddle the barbell by standing a little behind the weight plates as your chest is directed toward the weight and your back is facing the landmine’s pivot point.
3. Sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can position the V-bar to the end of the barbell’s shaft, such that the V-bar contacts the bearing (the cylinder separating the shaft from the sleeve where you add plates) with its handles directed upward.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track far forward. However, you can let your knees shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. In this position, the V-bar should be situated under and just in front of you such that you can grasp it without having to reach meaningfully forward.
4. Firmly grasp the V-bar’s handles with your palms facing each other, elbows straight, lower back flat, and chest up.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from now on.
6. While keeping your lower back flat, chest up, and elbows straight, drive through your legs to lift the bar slightly up and assume a slightly more upright torso position.
    1. The objective is to use your hip and thigh muscles to lift the bar just high enough that you can experience resistance from the weight when your elbows are fully straight in the bottom position of each rep, rather than having the plates touch the ground.
    2. In this position, your torso should ideally remain inclined closer to horizontal than to vertical, with your hips mostly bent. However, large-diameter plates may require a more upright torso to keep them off the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar upward and back toward your torso by driving your elbows simultaneously upward and backward while progressively bending your elbows and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. Move your elbows through a path of motion that feels comfortable to you, which will typically involve keeping them tucked fairly close to your sides with this neutral grip rather than notably flaring your elbows away from your sides (which is typically more comfortable with a wider overhand grip).
    2. Keep your torso in a fixed hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set while keeping your core braced and your lower back near a neutral position.
    3. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    4. If using large diameter plates, you may not be able to row as far backward compared to if you use smaller diameter plates.
    5. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner by allowing your elbows to move downward and forward until your elbows have finished extending and the bar has returned to the starting position.
    1. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to return the bar to its initial position by bending your knees and hips to lower the bar.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. With a cable station positioned to its lowest height, clip in a straight bar attachment and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down or hinge at your hips with extended elbows.
3. Grasp the bar with approximately a shoulder width grip and an underhand grip such that your palms are directed forward.
4. While keeping your elbows extended, stand upright while gripping the bar.
5. Make sure tension is present from the cable station while your elbows are fully extended, rather than slack being present in the cable.
    1. Depending on your arm length relative to your height and which specific cable station you are using, you likely will have to take a small step backward to take out the slack of the cable.
    2. When taking a small step backward, the cable will now have a mildly diagonal line of pull rather than being vertical.
    3. To maintain a fully extended elbow position with a diagonal line of pull, you will position your upper arms slightly in front of your body by flexing at your shoulders instead of keeping your upper arms pinned to your sides (like you would with a curl that has a vertically directed resistance, such as free weights).
## Exercise technique
1. Curl the bar upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed in the same position that allowed your elbows to be fully extended at the start of the rep (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing further forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms in the same position used to start the rep.
3. Alternate between curling the bar upwards and lowering it down until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Connect a lat pulldown bar to the cable, select your weight with the loading pin, and adjust the thigh pad to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. If you do not have a standard lat pulldown bar attachment, which has a straight body and mildly angled ends, you can use a different attachment that lets you grasp it with an overhand grip.
2. While facing the bar and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the bar with a well outside shoulder width overhand grip, such that your palms are directed forward, and your arms form a “Y-shape” with your torso.
    1. Positioning your hands about 50% further apart than your shoulder width is appropriate, but a wide grip can encompass a range of grip widths, and specifically how wide you grasp the bar is up to your preference.
    2. What is personally considered a wide grip to you can also be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard pulldown, which you can somewhat widen to individualize your wide grip. For instance, for your wide grip, you can place your index finger on the bar just outside where you would otherwise place your little finger when performing your standard pulldown.
    3. Feel free to try out mildly different grip widths to determine if any particular position feels best to you.
3. While holding the bar, sit down on the machine’s seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to extend and your arms to raise overhead in line with the cable's resistance.
4. In the seated position, slightly lean your torso backward at your hips.
    1. Maintain this slight backward lean throughout your set.
    2. From this position, your elbows should be straight, with your arms overhead and slightly forward (rather than completely vertical), and you should feel tension from the cable station holding your arms in this position.
    3. If you notice the cable remains slack in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), widening out your grip even further may be needed to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down toward your sides as you progressively bend them.
    1. Simultaneosuly pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears.
    2. Maintain the slight backward lean of your torso you adopted while setting up, rather than leaning further backward.
    3. When pulling through your full range of motion, you should finish with the bar touching your upper chest or very close to doing so.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the bar in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your arms overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates to the machine and adjust the seat to a height that allows your chest to rest comfortably against the chest pad.
    1. While you can initially adjust the seat to a height that situates your shoulders approximately level with the parallel handles, the seat height that is best for you depends on the specific machine you use, and trying out different positions may be helpful.
2. If your machine has an adjustable chest pad, adjust it to a position that allows you to grasp the parallel handles when your arms are fully outstretched forward in front of you with extended elbows.
    1. To row through your full range of motion, ideally place the chest pad far enough back that you have to push your shoulder blades forward and apart to grasp the handles with your elbows fully straight.
3. Sit down with your chest resting snugly against the chest pad and your feet flat on the floor.
4. Reach fully forward with straight elbows to grasp the parallel handles firmly with your palms facing each other (i.e., a neutral grip).
    1. If your machine does not have an adjustable chest pad and the handles are far enough from you to make it difficult to grasp both of them simultaneously, it may be easier for you to grasp one handle at a time.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handles back toward the sides of your torso by driving your elbows backward while simultaneously bending them and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. Move your elbows through a path of motion that feels comfortable to you, which will typically involve keeping them tucked close to your sides with this grip rather than notably flaring your elbows away from your sides (which is typically more comfortable with a wider overhand grip).
    2. Keep your chest in contact with the chest pad throughout the set.
    3. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to move forward in a controlled manner, progressively straightening until they are outstretched in front of you.
    1. Your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another, but you can exaggerate this motion by intentionally allowing the weight to pull them further apart than your resting position at the bottom. This will stretch your upper back muscles and may help you train them more effectively.
    2. While you do not have to perform this step extremely slowly, you should avoid letting the weight abruptly yank your arms forward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

This row primarily trains your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), which are assisted by your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that places the handles slightly above shoulder level once you are seated.
    1. This seat height is an appropriate starting point for most people, but the ideal seat height specifically should allow you to press through your full range of motion while initially gripping the handles with your elbows stacked under the handles.
    2. If the seat is excessively high, you will not be able to position your elbows directly under the handles (when viewed from the side).
    3. If the seat is excessively low, your range of motion for this exercise will be limited.
    4. Some trial and error may be needed to find the best height for you as an individual.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against the backrest.
    1. Your feet should be flat on the ground.
    2. You can optionally rest your head against the backrest if it is tall enough, or you can simply keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
4. With your palms facing in toward each other and elbows bent, firmly grasp the handles that are directed forward. Position your elbows directly under the handles, resulting in your forearms being vertical when viewed from the side.
    1. If your machine only has handles directed out to the sides that can allow an overhand grip but not a neutral grip, you cannot perform this specific variation. However, you can select the “[overhand grip pin-loaded machine shoulder press](Pin-loaded%20machine%20shoulder%20press%201a15c6f170d880fc9e97e840aa8098c7.md)” from this database as an alternative.
    2. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    3. If you cannot comfortably position your elbows under the handles, mildly lower the seat height before resuming your setup.
    4. Situating your elbows under the handles and maintaining this alignment will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow tuck during this exercise.
5. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling, and maintain this posture throughout your set.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the handles up overhead until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your elbows should remain stacked under your wrists when viewed from the side. This will result in your elbows driving up in front of your body rather than being excessively flared out away from your sides.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your back snuggly against the backrest and your feet planted on the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the handles in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. With the appropriate seat height, you should finish the lowering phase with the handles slightly above shoulder level, as your elbows are lower than your shoulders.
    2. At the bottom, you can allow the weights you selected to tap the rest of the weight stack. A light tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
    3. Continue keeping your elbows stacked underneath the handles, resulting in your forearms remaining in a vertical position when viewed from the side.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [upper pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates to the machine’s weight sleeve, and straddle the machine as you are facing toward the weights.
2. Place your feet onto the foot plates and your chest onto the chest pad such that your whole body is inclined forward.
    1. You will be most stable when the entirety of the soles of your feet are in contact with the foot plates.
3. Depending upon your height and leg lengths, you may want to bend your knees somewhat or keep them straight to determine where your torso is situated on the chest pad.
    1. How you position your knees will be based on what feels most comfortable and stable to you, but you can initially see how you feel when positioning your knees to allow the uppermost aspect of the chest pad to be approximately level with your collarbone.
    2. Individuals who have longer legs will typically feel more comfortable when using a somewhat more bent knee position, while those with shorter legs will typically feel more comfortable with straighter knees.
4. Firmly grasp the outer horizontally directed handles with a mildly outside shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are directed behind you.
    1. During the row, the appropriate grip width should allow your elbows to flare naturally out away from your sides. This should result in a fairly even balance between having them fully tucked by your sides (which can naturally occur with a close grip) and having them fully flared out away from your sides (which can naturally occur with a wide grip).
5. Lift the bar up off the machine’s stopper, center the bar so that it no longer lies above the stopper, and lower it until your elbows are extended.
    1. In this bottom position, allow the weight to pull your shoulder blades apart from one another, which will likely prompt you to feel a stretching sensation in your upper back.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar upward and back toward your torso by driving your elbows simultaneously upward and backward. Simultaneously bend your elbows and pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Allow your elbows to flare out moderately away from your sides to a degree that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    2. Keep your torso in contact with the chest pad throughout the set rather than arching your lower back to lift your chest up off the pad.
    3. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner by allowing your elbows to move downward and forward until your elbows have finished straightening and the bar has returned to the starting position.
    1. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another, but you can exaggerate this motion by intentionally allowing the weight to pull them further apart than your resting position at the bottom, which will stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. While you do not have to lower the bar extremely slowly, you should avoid letting the bar drop abruptly in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to return the bar back onto the machine’s stopper.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance. Firmly hold the handle with both hands in front of your body as your hands are wrapped around each other.
2. Lift the dumbbell up to shoulder level with your elbows bent by curling the weight and using momentum from your lower body as needed.
    1. You can perform a cheat curl-like motion to move the dumbbell into position if it is too heavy to lift without momentum. To do so, first sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly. Then drive your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body while bending your elbows and mildly swinging them forward to lift the weight.
3. Press the dumbbell up overhead with both arms in a shoulder press motion until your arms are vertical.
    1. The back of your elbows should be pointing forward.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
4. While keeping your elbows up, slightly bend your elbows to tilt one end of the dumbbell down.
5. Reposition your hands so that both palms are firmly contacting the higher end of the dumbbell. Cross your thumbs over each other firmly around the handle. Simultaneously cross your index fingers over each other, resulting in your thumbs and index fingers resembling close to a diamond shape.
    1. In this position, one end of the dumbbell should be above your hands, while the other end is below your hands.
    2. You will continue securely gripping the dumbbell in this manner throughout your set. Make sure that your thumbs stay wrapped around the handle for stability.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the dumbbell behind your head in a controlled manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
    2. Predominantly keep your elbows tucked in as they are chiefly pointing forward rather than out to your side. However, you can allow your elbows to flare slightly out away from your sides if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    3. As you keep your elbows up, your upper arms should remain in a vertical position by the sides of your head.
2. Continue lowering the dumbbell until you have fully bent your elbows or can lightly tap your upper back with the dumbbell.
    1. It is normal to be able to bend the elbows beyond 90 degrees during this exercise, but specifically how far you can bend your elbows may be limited by the flexibility of your long head of the triceps.
    2. While some lifters have the flexibility to reach their upper back with the dumbbell, wherever you feel a notable stretching sensation in your triceps can be an appropriate end range.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the dumbbell overhead.
    1. You can finish the lifting phase with a slight bend in your elbows rather than fully straightening them. A slight bend will keep one end of the dumbbell tilted down and make it easier to maintain a secure grip with the higher end of the dumbbell resting on your palms.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows up as all the motion occurs from your elbows without moving your shoulders.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
5. After you have completed the lifting phase of your last rep, firmly grasp the handle with your lower hand while keeping the palm of your upper hand against the side of the dumbbell.
    1. Grasping the handle with one hand will make it easier for you to lower the weight compared to if you kept both palms against one end of the dumbbell.
6. Use both hands to lower the dumbbell toward your chest before setting it down.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. With a cable station positioned to its lowest height, select your weight with the loading pin, and connect a straight bar attachment.
2. Situate a flat exercise bench or chair a little in front of the cable station.
3. Squat down to pick up the bar attachment with an overhand grip where your palms are facing back toward you.
4. While holding the bar, sit down on a flat exercise bench or chair and position your forearms on top of your thighs with your palms facing down and your wrists situated slightly in front of your knees.
    1. To achieve this position, you will lean forward at your hips when seated, with your elbows bent.
5. Allow the force from the cable to bend your wrists and bring your hands downward such that your palms are directed at an angle down and back toward you.
    1. In this position, the bar should not be contacting your legs, so scoot your forearms forward if it is initially contacting your legs.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift the bar upward by extending your wrists through their available range of motion while keeping your forearms resting on your thighs.
    1. All motion should come from your wrists as your hands move upward.
    2. About halfway through the lifting phase, your palms should be facing straight down toward the floor when your hands are aligned with your forearms.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, when the bar is fully raised, your palms should be angled forward.
    4. When performing this exercise appropriately, you should feel tension in the muscles on the top side of your forearms.
2. Reverse the motion by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your palms directed at an angle down and back toward you.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up overhead and firmly grasp it with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip), with your hands shoulder-width apart or slightly wider apart.
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up onto a sturdy box, an aerobic step, or a bumper plate to place the bar within reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar than if you jumped up from the ground to reach it.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
2. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will put you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up by your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back puts you in a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending your elbows.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows will not actually drive downward, but having this intent helps pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
Certain machines have a foot pedal that you can press to move the machine’s handle while setting up, but other machine models lack a foot pedal. Some of the specific setup details differ depending on which type of machine you are using, so the setup for each approach is described separately. However, the exercise technique can be essentially the same for either option, so one technique section is provided with a couple of details that depend on which type of machine you utilize.

### Setting up a machine without a foot pedal

1. Adjust the seat to a height that comfortably allows you to grasp the handle behind your head with your elbows fully bent once you are seated.
    1. This seat height commonly allows the base of someone’s neck to be reasonably close to being level with the handle once seated. However, your flexibility can influence where your ideal position lies, so trying out different seat heights may initially be required.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on its seat with an upright torso as your back is resting against the backrest.
    1. If your machine has a foot plate, position your soles against it. Otherwise, place your feet flat on the floor.
4. Raise your arms up with your elbows fully bent to grasp the handle firmly with fairly straight wrists.
    1. Different machines have different handle types that will influence specifically how you should grasp the handle, but handles that allow you to grasp them with your palms angled in toward each other are common. Some machines also allow you to connect various cable attachments, such as a multi-grip angled bar or a rope attachment, depending on what you prefer.
    2. What chiefly matters is that your grip feels stable and comfortable.
    3. From this position, your upper arms should be near the sides of your head with your elbows held high and tucked in (rather than being meaningfully flared out away from your sides).
    4. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your triceps.

### Setting up a machine with a foot pedal

1. Adjust the seat to a height that positions the handle at least a little lower than what you can reach behind your head with your elbows lifted up and fully bent once you are seated.
    1. This seat height commonly allows the base of someone’s neck to be at least mildly higher than the handle once seated. However, the foot pedal allows a range of seat heights to be viable for this exercise.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on its seat with an upright torso as your back is resting against the backrest.
4. Place one foot against the machine’s foot pedal, and push the pedal forward with your leg.
    1. This brings the handles up to a position you can comfortably reach.
    2. Keep the pedal pushed away during the next step, while keeping your other foot on the ground.
5. Raise your upper arms up near the sides of your head with your elbows bent enough to grasp the handle firmly with fairly straight wrists.
    1. Different machines have different handle types that will influence specifically how you should grasp the handle, but handles that allow you to grasp them with your palms angled in toward each other are common.
    2. What chiefly matters is that your grip feels stable and comfortable.
    3. From this position, hold your elbows high while keeping tucked in rather than being meaningfully flared out away from your sides.
6. Bring the foot pedal back to its starting position by bending your knee, which will shift the machine’s resistance to your arms. Simultaneously, lower the handle behind your head by fully bending your elbows while keeping your upper arms stationary.
    1. The degree to which you can bend your elbows while keeping your upper arms raised up will be dependent on your triceps flexibility.
    2. Allow your elbows to bend through the full range that feels comfortable, and you will normally feel a stretching sensation in your triceps.
7. Lift your foot off the foot pedal and place it flat on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Press the handle up overhead by straightening your elbows while keeping your upper arms stationary.
    1. At the top of the movement, your elbows should be fully straightened with your upper arms in the same position in which they started.
    2. While you move your forearms through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by bending your elbows to lower the handle behind your head in a controlled manner.
    1. Lower the bar to the starting position with your elbows fully bent through your full range of motion.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows tucked in rather than meaningfully flaring them out to your sides.
    3. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the machine’s resistance rapidly pull the handle back down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you are using a machine with a foot pedal, push the pedal forward with your leg until you are no longer supporting any of the machine’s resistance with your arms. Then let go of the handle and bend your knee to return the foot pedal to its initial position.

## Setting up
1. You can select either a fixed weight EZ bar or an adjustable plate-loaded EZ bar, which are functionally interchangeable for this exercise.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down or hinge at your hips with extended elbows.
    1. If the EZ bar, if already positioned in an elevated rack at mid-thigh level or above, you naturally would not have to squat down or hinge at your hips before picking it up.

    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it before a closer than shoulder width semi-underhand grip is accessible on the bar.
4. While keeping your elbows extended, stand fully upright while gripping the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl the bar upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed at your sides (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms positioned by your sides.
3. Alternate between curling the bar upwards and lowering it down until you have completed your set.

Like other curls, this exercise can effectively train the biceps and brachialis in your upper arm along with the brachioradialis in your forearm.
