## Setting up
1. Load a barbell with your desired weight, or approach a fixed weight straight bar.
2. While facing the middle of the bar in a near shoulder-width stance, squat down and firmly grasp it with an overhand grip (as your palms face backward). Your hands should be about shoulder-width apart or mildly closer.
3. Stand upright with the bar just in front of your thighs.
4. Move the bar up to your shoulders with your elbows fully bent underneath and slightly in front of the bar.
    1. If the load is light enough to do so, you can just curl the bar up.
    2. With a heavier load, you can perform a cheat curl, where you generate momentum with your hips to help you curl the bar up. Initially sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and your torso to incline slightly forward. Then drive your hips forcefully forward while bending your elbows and mildly swinging them forward.
    3. The bar should now be in essentially the same position it would be for an overhead press.
    4. The bar should be sitting on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists. You will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
    5. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar hard will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
5. Press the bar up overhead in a shoulder press motion until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. The bar should be vertically stacked above your shoulders, hips, and knees.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the bar behind your head in a controlled manner. Based on your preference and what feels most comfortable to your elbows, you can select one of two approaches with respect to your elbow position.
    1. Option 1: Keep your elbows completely up with your upper arms in a vertical position throughout the rep. This will result in the bar moving in an arcing manner exclusively from your forearms hinging at your elbows.
    2. Option 2: Mildly arc your elbows forward and down while bending your elbows to lower the bar. You can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest to create additional space for the bar. This option will result in the bar moving in a closer to vertical path from a combination of shoulder and elbow motion.
    3. Neither of the approaches is inherently superior to the other, so you can feel free to try out both ways and continue using the technique you prefer.
    4. With either option, predominantly keep your elbows tucked in. However, you can allow them to flare slightly out away from your sides if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
2. Continue lowering the bar until you have fully bent your elbows or can lightly tap the base of your neck or your upper back muscles with the bar.
    1. How far you can lower the bar may be limited by the flexibility of your long head of the triceps, particularly if you keep your elbows completely up. While some lifters have the flexibility to reach near their upper back with the bar, others will reach the limit to which they can comfortably bend their elbows before that point. Do not lower the bar beyond the range that your flexibility permits without discomfort.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the bar into the starting position overhead.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is vertically above your shoulders.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
5. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the bar in front of your head toward your shoulders like you would during an overhead press.

This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that allows you to rest your elbows and most of the back of your upper arms (i.e., triceps) on the sloped arm pad when sitting on the seat.
    1. The proper setting will typically result in the top of the pad being close to your armpits.
    2. Some trial and error may be needed to find the ideal seat height.
2. After selecting your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin, sit down on the seat with your feet on the ground.
3. Position the back of your upper arms and elbows on top of the arm pad as your elbows are aligned with the machine’s pivot point, which is the center about which the machine’s lever arm rotates that is denoted by a small dot or circle in some machines.
4. Firmly grasp the handles with your hands approximately shoulder width apart from each other as your palms are angled upward.
    1. If the handles are a little out of your reach, you could slightly stand up and lean forward to reach the handles before sitting back down after you have grasped the handles.
    2. Your wrists should be mostly straight throughout your set after grasping the handles.
    3. Machines commonly have angled handles that allow you to grasp them with your palms angled inward and upward (resulting in a hybrid between an underhand and neutral grip), but certain models may have horizontal handles that will allow you to use a purely underhand grip.
5. In the starting position, your elbows should be fully straightened to allow you to train through a full range of motion.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows and the back of your upper arms in contact with the arm pad, curl the handles upward and back toward you in an arcing motion by bending at your elbows until they are fully bent.
    1. While your forearms move through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout your set.
2. After your elbows have fully bent, reverse the motion by lowering the handles in a slow and controlled manner until your elbows have returned to a fully straightened position.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows and the back of your upper arms in contact with the arm pad.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable bench at a low incline angle (e.g., near 30 degrees) and set a pair of dumbbells under the head of the bench.
    1. As a different variation, which you can use if your bench does not have a low incline setting, you can alternatively select a moderate incline angle (e.g., near 45 degrees) and otherwise use the same technique for this exercise.
2. Lie down with your chest contacting the head of the bench and your legs spread out as you position the balls of your feet on the ground.
3. Grasp the dumbbells, position your arms so that they are perpendicular to the ground with extended elbows, and rotate your arms so that your palms are facing at an angle in toward each other and somewhat forward.
    1. Keep your elbows extended and your palms facing this direction throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Raise your arms upward and outward through your available shoulder range of motion so that they form a “Y-shape” with your torso as you continue to keep your chest in contact with the bench.
    1. You can strive to raise your arms until they are close to parallel with the incline bench, but your shoulder mobility will affect how high you can raise your arms.
    2. If you notice your chest lifting up off the bench during this movement, that indicates that you most likely are dynamically extending your lumbar spine, which can occur as a compensation pattern instead of lifting your arm only with your shoulder girdle muscles.
2. Reverse the motion by lowering your arms in a controlled manner until your arms have returned to being perpendicular to the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise trains your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) along with your [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [side delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell and sit down on a seated bench or a flat exercise bench with your feet flat on the ground.
    1. If you use a seated bench, the back rest should be low enough that it will not be within the path of the dumbbell and restrict your range of motion for this exercise.
    2. The tall back rest of an adjustable bench positioned fully upright may be more likely to limit your range than a fixed seated bench with a back rest that does not reach your head.
    3. Throughout the exercise, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side.
    4. All the directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training first.
2. Lift the dumbbell up near the front of your shoulder with your elbow bent by curling the weight and swinging your elbow mildly forward.
    1. If the weight is too heavy for you to lift with a typical curling motion, you can initially situate the dumbbell on your lower thigh and march it up into position with assistance from your free hand.
    2. You should be holding the dumbbell on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a mostly straight wrist that allows for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
    3. Your forearm should now be in a close to vertical position.
3. While sitting fully upright, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
4. Press the dumbbell up overhead in a shoulder press motion until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. You can point the back of your elbow forward and out to the side at an angle.
    2. The dumbbell should be vertically stacked over your shoulder.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbow to lower the dumbbell behind your head in a controlled manner while keeping your elbow up.
    1. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearm hinging at your elbow without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbow as the center of an analog clock, while your forearm is the hand that rotates about this center elbow during the exercise.
    2. As you keep your elbow up, your upper arm should remain in a vertical position by the side of your head.
2. Continue lowering the dumbbell until you have fully bent your elbow or can lightly tap your upper back with the dumbbell.
    1. It is normal to be able to bend the elbow beyond 90 degrees, but specifically how far you can bend your elbow may be limited by the flexibility of your long head of the triceps.
    2. While some lifters have the flexibility to reach their upper back with the dumbbell, wherever you feel a notable stretching sensation in your triceps can be an appropriate end range.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbow to lift the dumbbell into the starting position overhead.
    1. You should finish with your elbow fully straightened as the dumbbell is vertically above your shoulder.
    2. Continue keeping your elbow up as all the motion occurs from your elbow without moving your shoulder.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
5. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the dumbbell toward your shoulder like you would during a shoulder press.
6. Lower the dumbbell to your side as you straighten your elbow and swing your elbow back by your side.
7. Transfer the dumbbell to your other hand and repeat the exercise with that side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. At a cable station, adjust the cable to near the height of your elbows when standing with your arms at your sides, clip in a D-handle attachment, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. While standing with your chest facing near a 135-degree angle away from the cable station, grasp the handle with your hand on the side farther away from the cable.
3. On the side holding the handle, position your upper arm by your side and slightly forward while bending your elbow to approximately 90 degrees and keeping your wrist in a fairly straight position.
    1. Maintain this position throughout your set.
    2. Situating your upper arm slightly forward rather than having it be completely vertical at your side can limit your torso from restricting your range of motion during this exercise.
4. Have your forearm rotated inward across the front of your torso such that your forearm is contacting or close to contacting your abdomen while your palm is facing backward.
    1. Your shoulder mobility will affect how far you can rotate, and you should use as much range as feels comfortable for your shoulder.
    2. In this position, you should feel tension from the cable, so if that is not the case, take a step to the side away from the cable stack.
## Exercise technique
1. Rotate your forearm outward by pulling the handle away from the cable station while moving through your shoulder’s available range of motion as you continue to keep your upper arm positioned slightly in front of your side.
    1. If the cable contacts your arm that is closer to the cable stack during this motion, you can position this arm away from the cable behind you with its elbow bent to near 90 degrees as its forearm rests on your lower back.
    2. All of this movement should occur from shoulder rotation, and your upper arm should not raise away from your torso.
    3. When thinking about this technique, it can be helpful to view your forearm as a clock’s hand, while your elbow is the center about which rotation occurs without any side-to-side motion.
2. Reverse the motion by rotating your forearm inward across your body as you bring the handle closer toward the cable station in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set with one side and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md) and [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), along with a portion of the [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Connect a lat pulldown bar to the cable, select your weight with the loading pin, and adjust the thigh pad to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. If you do not have a standard lat pulldown bar attachment, which has a straight body and mildly angled ends, you can use a different attachment that lets you comfortably grasp it with an underhand grip.
2. While facing the bar and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the bar with a near shoulder-width underhand grip, such that your palms face backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
3. While holding the bar, sit down on the machine’s seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to straighten and your arms to raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
4. In the seated position, slightly lean your torso backward at your hips.
    1. Maintain this slight backward lean throughout your set.
    2. From this position, your elbows should be straight, with your arms overhead and slightly forward (rather than completely vertical), and you should feel tension from the cable station holding your arms in this position.
    3. If you notice the cable remains slack in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), widening out your grip may be needed to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down toward your sides as you progressively bend them.
    1. Simultaneosuly pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears.
    2. Predominantly keep your elbows aligned with your wrists, rather than meaningfully flaring them out away from your sides.
    3. Maintain the slight backward lean of your torso you adopted while setting up, rather than leaning further backward.
    4. When pulling through your full range of motion, you should finish with the bar touching your upper chest or very close to doing so.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the bar in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your arms overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while holding the kettlebells at your sides with extended elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs.
    1. If you are using kettlebells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both kettlebells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one kettlebell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other kettlebell onto the bench before picking up both kettlebells from a mechanically advantaged position.

1. Shrug your shoulders upward through your available range of motion while keeping your elbows extended, which will lift the kettlebells upward.
    1. While doing so, keep your neck in a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulders to descend in a controlled manner through your available range of motion, which will lower the kettlebells.
    1. At the end of this motion, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the weight can provide.

This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your abdomen contacting the ground (i.e., in the prone position) and your head lifted slightly off the ground as you maintain a tucked chin position with your face directed toward the ground.
2. Position your arms straight out in front of you with straight elbows such that your hands are approximately shoulder-width apart while resting on the ground.
    1. Your body position should resemble how you would look if you were reaching up with your arms fully overhead while standing.
3. Rotate your arms so that your palms face down toward the ground if they are not already doing so.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your arms straight up off the ground through your full available shoulder range of motion while keeping your chest in contact with the ground.
    1. You will keep your arms lifted off the ground throughout your set.
    2. Your shoulder mobility will affect how high you can raise your arms.
    3. Most people will not be able to lift their arms particularly high before reaching the end of their available range of motion.
    4. If you notice your chest lifting up off the ground during this movement, that indicates that you most likely are dynamically extending your lumbar spine, which can occur as a compensation pattern instead of lifting your arms only with your shoulder girdle muscles.
2. Bring your arms toward your sides in an arcing motion akin to the lowering phase of a jumping jack as you continue keeping your arms as high off the ground as your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. Partway through this motion, your arms will point straight away from your sides as they form a “T-shape” with your torso.
3. After you have moved beyond the “T-shape” position, rotate your arms to point your palms up as you simultaneously continue moving your arms toward your sides.
4. Once your arms are near your sides, bend your elbows and continue to bring your hands together behind your back until one hand is on top of the other or as close to this position as your shoulder range of motion permits.
    1. The end range of this exercise places you into a position that resembles the position in which someone may be handcuffed while lying on the ground, which is why this exercise is sometimes called a prone handcuff.
5. Reverse the motions you just performed by bringing your arms out away from your sides, straightening your elbows, and rotating your arms to point your palms down before bringing your arms into the overhead starting position.
    1. You should move your arms in an arcing fashion akin to the upward phase of a jumping jack.
6. Alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. After learning the technique, you should be able to perform the different components of this exercise in a fluid motion.
## Description
This exercise can train your ability to move your shoulders actively through multiple motions while engaging various muscles throughout your shoulder girdle that allow you to do so.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up overhead and firmly grasp it with your palms facing backward (underhand grip) and your hands spaced about shoulder-width apart.
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the bar.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
2. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will place you in a more advantageous position to start your pull compared to if you kept your chest facing exclusively horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up from the force of your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back places you into a position akin to a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending them.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows naturally will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

### **How Your Grip and Pull-Up Technique Influence Back Muscle Development**

When repeatedly performing this exercise over time, you can feel free to try out mildly different grip widths to determine if any particular position feels most comfortable to you and/or allows you to perceive your target back muscles working particularly well. Pull-ups can be performed with a variety of hand grips, including different grip widths and overhand, underhand (resulting in the exercise being called a chin-up), neutral, or hybrid (i.e., a combination of neutral and underhand or overhand) grips. Additionally, shoulder motion during a pull-up can occur predominantly in the sagittal (front-to-back) plane, the frontal (side-to-side) plane, or a combination of the two. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the sagittal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out in front of you), the upper arms remain parallel to each other and do not deviate away from the mid-line of your body. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the frontal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out to your sides, such as with a snow angle motion), the upper arms move away from the mid-line of your body until they are parallel to the ground. Then they move closer to the mid-line of your body with further elevation. During the lifting phase of a pull-up, the shoulders could extend in the sagittal plane, adduct in the frontal plane, or exhibit a combination of extension and adduction at a hybrid angle between the sagittal and frontal planes. Rather than moving the shoulders exclusively through one plane, pull-up variations are commonly performed with a technique that allows for the shoulders to move in between these two planes, but one plane of shoulder motion often makes a greater contribution than the other.

Muscles acting on the shoulder joint have different leverage to generate extension torque in the sagittal plane versus adduction torque in the frontal plane, and the nervous system is most likely to recruit the particular muscles that are best leveraged to produce the intended joint action during any active movement. Correspondingly, the plane of motion in which the shoulders move during a pull-up can affect how well different muscles are likely to be trained. With any particular grip for a pull-up, you can intentionally rotate your shoulders in a manner that allows you to move your shoulder relatively more in the sagittal or frontal plane. However, most people will typically find that a particular path of shoulder motion feels most comfortable and stable to their shoulders, elbows, and wrists when using a specific grip. For instance, people will normally perform a wide overhand grip pull-up with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the frontal plane. In contrast, they will normally perform a close-grip chin-up (using an underhand grip) with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the sagittal plane. Performing either variation in the alternative plane of motion would require greater-than-normal rotational range of motion in the shoulders and forearms, and attempting to do so could feel very awkward and uncomfortable. People will typically feel most comfortable when positioning themselves so that, at the point in the pull-up when their upper arms are parallel to the ground, their elbows and wrists are vertically aligned or their elbows are slightly lateral (outside) to their wrists.

In general, widening a grip facilitates relatively more frontal plane shoulder motion, while narrowing a grip facilitates relatively more sagittal plane shoulder motion. An overhand, underhand, or neutral grip may be used with any grip width. Still, the combination of these grip variables will influence comfort and which plane of shoulder motion feels most natural. When pulling predominantly in the sagittal plane with a rather close grip, an underhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable than an overhand grip. Similarly, when pulling predominantly in the frontal plane with a rather wide grip, an overhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable and allow more frontal-plane motion than an underhand grip. With a moderate-width grip, people may commonly find that pulling mostly in the sagittal plane feels natural with an underhand or neutral grip, but pulling relatively more in the frontal plane feels natural with an overhand grip. Fundamentally, the shoulder motion is what matters to the back muscles, and the grip is only relevant to the back muscles based on how it influences which shoulder motion is performed. When performing this overhand grip pull-up with a moderate grip width, you most likely will pull in a way that biases shoulder adduction somewhat more than shoulder extension. Still, you can also perform the exercise in a way that results in a fairly even balance between these two motions.

The lat and teres major in the back function both as primary adductors and extensors and are therefore highly likely to be trained effectively with pull-up variations regardless of the grip or plane of shoulder motion. However, the preponderance of available evidence indicates that the rear deltoid lacks meaningful leverage to contribute to shoulder adduction, but it clearly has favorable leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. The rear deltoid is correspondingly likely to be trained better with a closer grip emphasizing shoulder extension, which would be most comfortable when using an underhand or neutral grip. Alternatively, the middle and lower regions of the pectoralis major (that constitute the sternoclavicular head) have large moment arms to function as shoulder adductors, but only the lower portion exhibits a shoulder extension moment arm, and this moment arm is quite small and only present in flexed shoulder positions. Consequently, wider grip pull-ups (which are most comfortable with an overhand or neutral grip) that involve greater frontal-plane shoulder motion are likely to train the pectoralis major more effectively than closer grip pulldowns. Which regions of the lats are preferentially biased by a pull-up variation may also potentially be influenced by how much shoulder motion occurs in the frontal or sagittal planes. The middle and lower regions have relatively greater leverage to function as shoulder adductors, while the upper region of the lat has relatively greater leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. Plausibly, these biomechanical differences may facilitate the middle and lower regions of the lats being preferentially trained by wider grip pull-ups, while the upper region may be preferentially trained by closer grip pulling variations. With that said, the degree to which any preferential biasing may occur across different regions of the lats when comparing pull-up grips is more speculative and has not been tested in any longitudinal training interventions.

### Why Overhand Grip Pull-Ups may be More Difficult than Chin-Ups or Neutral Grip Pull-Ups

While exceptions exist, people often find overhand grip pull-ups to be more difficult per rep than chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. The discrepancy is most likely influenced by chin-ups and neutral grip pull-ups typically being performed with a technique that emphasizes shoulder extension in the sagittal plane, while overhand grip pull-ups are typically performed with relatively more shoulder adduction in the frontal plane. As demonstrated by studies such as those by Mayer et al. (1994) and Shklar and Dvir (1995), on average, maximal torque for shoulder extension exceeds that for shoulder adduction. The sample of participants, velocity, and type of muscle action tested can all influence the degree to which torque differs between these two actions, but maximal shoulder adduction torque has been measured at 63-90% of maximal shoulder extension, depending on the specific test conditions. In addition to the effect of how the shoulder moves, the forearm position can also affect how much elbow flexion torque you can generate during your pull. Guenzkofer et al. (2012) found that up to 15% greater elbow flexion torque can be generated when the forearm is in a supinated (used for an underhand grip) or neutral position compared to a pronated (used with an overhand grip) position. Together, these relationships suggest that most people can generate greater torque at the shoulders and elbows during chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups than during overhand grip pull-ups, which are likely to be more challenging when performing the same number of reps. Consequently, it is common not to be able to complete as many reps of overhand grip pull-ups in a set as you would be able to complete when performing chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. Nonetheless, individual differences in factors such as training history and the relative strength of different muscle groups can result in some people not noticing a difference in difficulty between these variations, or even finding overhand grip pull-ups to be somewhat easier per rep.

### Chin Over Bar?

The technique instructions do not specify where any particular part of your body should be situated in relation to the bar at the end of the lifting phase because your full range of motion can differ from someone else’s full range of motion. Pulling until your chin is above the bar is a common standard used for testing by the United States Marines and for competitions held by the World Pull-Up Organization, and you can certainly use it if you wish. However, when focusing on chin clearance, some people tend to extend their necks, lifting their chins, to clear the bar with less range of motion through the pull, compared to when they retain a neutral neck position. In this instance, focusing on the proxy for a full range of motion may result in a different movement than focusing on the individual's full range of motion. When competing or taking a standardized test that affects professional prospects, it is only sensible to do the minimum required to complete each rep per the rules, but training to build muscle and strength is a different endeavor.

### **The Most Challenging Part of the Chin-Up**

The end range of the lifting phase is typically the most challenging portion of chin-ups, in large part because the torque our pulling muscles can generate meaningfully varies across different joint angles. When the elbow is flexed to 120 degrees, Bober et al. (2002) found maximal elbow flexion torque to be approximately 35% of the peak torque that can be generated in a moderately flexed elbow position (i.e., near 60-75 degrees of elbow flexion). With your elbows approaching full flexion toward the end range of a chin-up, your elbow flexor muscles are correspondingly operating from a rather disadvantaged position to help you complete the rep. On average, maximal shoulder extension torque is also lower when the shoulder is mildly elevated (like at the end of a chin-up’s lifting phase) compared to when it is moderately elevated (like during the middle range of a chin-up). The difference can be of notable magnitude, as indicated by Bober et al. (2002), who found that maximal shoulder extension in a neutral shoulder position was only 60% of the peak value achievable at 90 degrees of shoulder flexion. Together these strength curves of the muscle groups acting on the elbow and shoulder can contribute to your chin-ups consistently feeling the most difficult during the last quarter of the lifting phase.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your back muscle strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your back muscles. As a simple approach, if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure you use the same technique for each condition, which means the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how the performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep's performance across these conditions on a second day, in which you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps on the first day, perform the set with straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue from the first set may influence the second. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting the performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with extended elbows as your palms are facing in toward your sides (i.e., in a neutral grip position).
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout the set.
2. Raise the dumbbells out in front of you until your upper arms are approximately parallel with the ground.
    1. If you wish to do so, elevating the dumbbells higher up, beyond when your upper arms are parallel to the floor, is a completely viable modification to this exercise’s technique.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner back to your sides.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [upper pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and sit down on a bench with an upright posture and your feet flat on the floor while holding the dumbbells at your sides with extended elbows.
    1. You can opt to sit down on a flat bench without any back support or sit down on a seated bench with back support.
2. Direct your palms so that they are facing in toward your sides (i.e., in a neutral grip position)
    1. Maintain this neutral grip on the dumbbells throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl both dumbbells upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed at your sides (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms positioned by your sides.
3. Alternate between curling the dumbbells up and lowering them down until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with extended elbows.
2. Direct your palms so that they are facing in toward your sides (i.e., using a neutral grip position).
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one dumbbell resting at your side with an extended elbow, curl the other dumbbell upward by bending at your elbow while keeping your upper arm fixed at your side (rather than allowing your upper arm to swing forward).
    1. While curling the dumbbell upward, simultaneously rotate your forearm into an underhand grip position that results in your palm facing back toward you when your elbow is fully flexed.
2. After your elbow has fully flexed and your forearm has rotated from a neutral grip to an underhand grip, reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner until your elbow has returned to an extended position.
    1. While lowering the dumbbell, simultaneously rotate your forearm back into a neutral grip position that results in your palm facing in toward your side when your elbow is fully extended.
    2. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arm positioned by your side.
3. With your other arm, repeat steps 3 and 4.
4. Alternate between curling with each side until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to the machine, sit down with your back in full contact with the backrest.
    1. The machine’s safety stoppers (which can be moved with one or two safety handles, depending upon the specific machine) should already be locked, and you will keep them locked throughout your set.
    2. If your machine has an adjustable seat, you can also initially adjust the seat to whichever position feels most comfortable to you, but the seat position is unlikely to affect this exercise meaningfully.
    3. Your low back should be in a fairly flat position rather than being meaningfully rounded, like in a slouched position, which could occur if you sit your hips excessively forward.
2. Place the front half of one foot onto the bottom of the foot plate with your heel hanging off the edge.
    1. Keep your other foot in a comfortable position, such as resting on the ground.
3. While grasping the hand grips, press the platform away from you by extending your knee until it is straight or only slightly bent.
    1. You should maintain this knee position (rather than bending and extending your knee) while performing this exercise until you are ready to finish your set.
    2. Depending on their mobility, some people may be able to adopt a position of knee hyperextension, which is when the knees bend backward beyond a straight position. Being able to reach a mildly hyperextended knee position is normal for many individuals and is not inherently problematic. However, certain individuals may experience knee discomfort if they utilize a hyperextended knee position during this exercise, so keeping a straight or slightly bent knee position instead of a hyperextended knee position may be preferable.
## Exercise technique
1. Press the platform away from you by pointing the ball of your foot away from you (in a manner similar to stepping on a car’s gas pedal) through your ankle’s available range of motion.
    1. Motion should occur exclusively at your ankle, while your knee and hip do not move.
2. In a controlled manner, reverse the motion by allowing the front half of your foot to move back toward you through your ankle’s available range of motion.
    1. How far you are able to move will be dependent on your mobility.
    2. Strive to lower your heels as far as you can, and you will likely feel a stretching sensation in your calf at the bottom position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. After completing your last rep with your other side, lower the platform back into its starting position by bending your knee.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop both your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md) while simultaneously improving calf flexibility through loaded stretching.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to near waist height, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. Based on your preference, connect a rope attachment to the cable with the rope pulled fully to one side of the attachment, connect a D-handle to the cable, or leave the cable without any attachment.
    1. Essentially the same exercise can be performed with any of those options, so you can select whichever feels most comfortable for you to hold.
    2. Except for the next step, which includes details about how to grasp the cable without an attachment as an alternative option, the subsequent instructions refer to the usage of the rope as one example.
3. While facing the cable station, firmly grasp the end of the rope with the side you wish to train during this set.
    1. Your little finger and the adjacent aspect of your hand should be in contact with the flat surface of the rope attachment’s rubber stopper as your thumb wraps over the outside of your other fingers.
    2. If you opt to use the cable without any attachment, you can grasp the ball at the end of the cable, or you can grasp the end of the cable directly with your little finger, and the adjacent side of your hand in contact with the ball. If you decide to grasp the cable directly, be aware to avoid pinching any fingers when returning the cable to its initial position after finishing your set.
4. Directly above your hand already holding the rope, grasp the rope with the hand on the side you will not be training.
5. Pivot your body 180 degrees while simultaneously lifting your upper arms fully up with your elbows fully bent to reposition the rope behind your head.
    1. The arm movement performed during this step is akin to a controlled swinging-like motion.
    2. How high you are able to raise your upper arms and bend your elbows will be influenced by your mobility.
    3. In this position, you should feel tension from the cable pulling downward, so if that is not the case, you should walk forward until you feel tension from the cable.
6. On the side you will not be training, let go of the rope while continuing to hold the rope firmly with your other side.
    1. The purpose of initially holding the rope with both hands was to help reposition it behind your head.
    2. From this point onward, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side or on the cable station’s beam for balance assistance.
    3. All the subsequent directions will refer to the arm that is holding the rope.
7. While slightly bending your knees, take a step forward with your foot on the side opposite the one holding the cable.
    1. In this staggard stance, you should feel stable and balanced with an upright torso.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched from leaning back toward the cable station, your lower back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow up, press the rope upward by extending your elbow until it is fully straightened.
    1. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearm hinging at your elbow without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbow as the center of an analog clock, while your forearm is the hand that rotates about this stationary center elbow.
    2. As you keep your elbow up, your upper arm should remain in a vertical position by the side of your head.
2. Reverse the motion in a controlled manner by bending your elbow and lowering the rope until you have returned to the starting position with your elbow fully bent.
    1. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your triceps at the end range.
    2. It is typical to be able to bend your elbow beyond 90 degrees during this exercise, but specifically how far you can bend it can be affected by the flexibility of the long head of your triceps.
    3. Continue keeping your elbow raised up with your biceps by the side of your head.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all three heads of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including its large [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which may not be trained as well by compound pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. After adding your desired load (in the form of weight plates or a kettlebell) to a pull-up/dip belt you have around your waist, stand upright under a pull-up bar.
    1. The back of your belt should be securely resting on top of your buttocks, and the belt’s chain or strap (depending on the belt model) should be looped through the center hole of a weight plate or under the handle of a kettlebell. If you have a loading pin for your belt, you can alternatively loop the chain or strap through it after adding weight plates.
    2. It will be easiest if you carry the weight over to the pull-up bar and add the weight to your belt while you are under the bar, rather than adding the weight to your belt farther away from the bar before walking over to the bar.
    3. As an alternative to using a pull-up/dip belt, you can wear a weighted vest.
    4. While less stable and more awkward than using a belt or weighted vest, you also have the option of holding a dumbbell between your thighs or feet, but you will be limited in how much weight you can add when using a dumbbell.
2. Reach up overhead and firmly grasp the pull-up bar with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip), with your hands shoulder-width apart, slightly wider.
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the bar.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
3. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will put you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and let your bodyweight pull your shoulder blades up.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back places you into a position akin to a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending your elbows.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows will not actually drive downward, but having this intent helps pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps; however, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can train your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) especially well while also effectively training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up one kettlebell and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while holding the kettlebell just in front of your thighs. Direct your palms back toward you with your elbows straight.
    1. If you do not have any experience training Jefferson curls, it is recommended that you initially try out the [bodyweight Jefferson curl](Bodyweight%20Jefferson%20curl%201ec5c6f170d880ba8e43cf305531982d.md) to determine how your body feels with this movement prior to performing a loaded variation.
## Exercise technique
1. Tuck your chin to your chest and lower the kettlebell in a slow and controlled manner by bending over and rounding your whole back through what is your comfortable range of motion while keeping your knees and elbows straight.
    1. As a cue, you can think about rounding forward each segment of your spine successively until your entire spine has achieved a rounded posture.
    2. As you progressively descend, it is natural to feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings and back muscles.
    3. How far you can descend will be influenced by your hamstring flexibility and the available bending range of motion in your spine.
    4. If you have a high degree of mobility, you may be able to descend until the kettlebell contacts the floor, but only move through a range that is painless and feels right to your body.
    5. Your arms should be directed down toward the ground throughout the exercise.
2. Reverse the movement by gradually transitioning from the bent over position to the upright position in which you started by uncoiling your back, which will lift the kettlebell up.
    1. At the end of the ascent, untuck your chin and look straight ahead.
    2. Continue keeping your knees and elbows in a straightened position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) that run along your entire back, while also training your spinal mobility and hamstring flexibility.
1a15c6f170d880c2bf39d2f4b0fd7b97:
## Setting up
1. Securely attach your desired weight to your wrist roller.
    1. Depending on the model of your wrist roller, you may have to use weight plates (if your model uses a loading pin), or you may be able to use weight plates, kettlebells, or dumbbells (if your model uses a strap that you can loop around the weight).
    2. Leave enough of the rope initially uncoiled so that you can stand up with the roller without the weight lifting off the ground.
2. While the weight is on the ground, firmly grasp the roller’s handles with your palms facing toward you (i.e., an overhand grip) and the uncoiled part of the rope on the side of the roller that is closer toward you.
    1. If the uncoiled part of the rope is on the side of the roller farther away from you, you would be able to train wrist extension when using an overhand grip, but this is the wrist flexion variation.
3. Stand upright while grasping the roller as your elbows are straight, and your hands are slightly in front of your thighs with your arms directed down toward the ground.
4. Take up the slack from the roller’s rope with alternating twisting motions of your wrists until you feel that the rope is taught from the weight’s resistance.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows straightened, bend one wrist to curl that side’s hand toward you as you extend your other wrist in the opposite direction by pointing that hand’s palm down toward the ground.
    1. You should grasp the handle firmly with the hand whose palm is curling toward you as you grasp the handle loosely with the hand whose palm is pointing toward the ground.
    2. The hand whose palm is curling toward you is what rotates the roller to lift the weight up, while the other side’s wrist is repositioning in preparation to perform the curling motion.
2. Alternate the motions in step 1 with the opposite hands as you lift the weight up by cyclically repeating these twisting movements with your wrists until you have fully coiled the rope around the roller.
3. Lower the weight in a controlled manner by reversing the same motions you just performed until the weight lightly taps the ground or is just about to do so.
4. Repeatedly perform steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the six [wrist flexor muscles](../Muscles/Wrist%20flexor%20muscles%202c85c6f170d880a49749f7d7a9f307c8.md) on the palm side of your forearm.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its highest setting, connect a rope attachment to the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. While standing directly in front of the cable station and facing away from it, reach up overhead with bent elbows to grasp the ends of the rope with a neutral grip such that your palms are facing in toward each other.
    1. Your little fingers and the adjacent aspects of your hands should be in contact with the flat surfaces of the attachment’s rubber stoppers as your thumbs wrap over the outside of your other fingers.
3. While keeping your hands overhead and elbows bent, step forward and adopt a staggered stance with one foot forward in front of the other before moderately leaning forward by hinging at your hips.
    1. Maintain this forward torso lean throughout your set.
    2. In this position, your hands should be behind your head, and you should feel tension from the cable. If that is not the case, walk forward until you feel tension from the cable.
4. Tuck your chin toward your chest and make sure your upper arms are situated parallel to the ground or raised up a little higher.
    1. Doing so will reduce the likelihood that the back of your head obstructs the path of the cable during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Press the rope forward and somewhat downward by extending your elbows until they are straightened, while not moving your upper arms.
    1. At the end of this motion, the rope should be situated in front of you.
    2. If the cable contacts the back of your head during this motion, you can lean forward a little more for additional clearance.
2. Reverse the motion by bending your elbows through your available range of motion to move the rope backward and somewhat upward in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. Strive to continue keeping your upper arms stationary while all of the movement occurs from elbow motion rather than also involving shoulder motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all three heads of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including its large [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which may not be trained as well by compound pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. If you wish to use a precise snatch grip rather than a general approximation, you can start by determining your individual hand placement with an empty barbell or dowel rod.
    1. A true snatch grip results in the bar being level with the crease of your hip when holding the bar in a fully upright position.
    2. You can find which hand placement specifically places the bar in the aforementioned position by trying out different grip widths with an empty barbell or dowel rod until determining what precisely is your individual snatch grip width.
    3. As a general starting point, you can see where a bar is situated relative to your hip crease when grasping it with your arms spread out away from your sides with extended elbows so that each arm forms close to a 45-degree angle with your torso.
    4. Rather than trying out different grip widths, you can alternatively use that arm position as a general approximation to train this exercise effectively.
2. Prepare the barbell with your desired load by adding weight plates while the barbell is on the ground or in an elevated position, such as a power rack.
    1. Setting up will be easier when using an elevated position, especially if you are using relatively heavy loads for this exercise.
    2. The bar will be easiest to pick up if positioned near mid-thigh height.
3. Stand close in front of the middle of the bar with a hip-width stance and spread your arms out away from your sides with straight elbows until reaching what you determined to be your snatch grip width (or until each arm forms close to a 45-degree angle with your torso if you opt to use a general approximation).
4. Hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar prior to firmly grasping the bar with an overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so.
5. By extending your hips and knees, stand upright with the bar while continuing to keep your elbows extended and your lower back near a neutral position.
## Exercise technique
1. Shrug your shoulders upward through your available range of motion while keeping your elbows extended, which will lift the bar upward.
    1. While doing so, keep your neck in a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulders to descend in a controlled manner through your available range of motion, which will lower the bar.
    1. At the end of this motion, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the weight can provide.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a dumbbell with one hand, carry it to a flat bench, and position yourself near the base of the bench, directly to its side, with the side holding the dumbbell farther from the bench.
2. Hinge at your hips to lean your torso forward. Simultaneously reach out with your free arm to place your hand on the bench with a straight elbow, and place your knee on the side not holding the dumbbell onto the bench.
    1. Based on your comfort and preference, you can place the open palm of your free hand onto the bench, or you can make a fist and place your knuckles onto the bench.
    2. In this position, your torso should be fairly close to being parallel to the ground.
    3. Your foot on the side of the dumbbell should remain in contact with the floor, which, with your free hand and knee on the bench, results in three points of contact to stabilize yourself during the exercise.
3. On the side holding the dumbbell, direct your palm so that it is facing in toward the opposite side of your body, and maintain this neutral grip position throughout your set.
    1. From this position, your arm on the side of the dumbbell should be directed down toward the ground.
4. Drive your elbow backward and upward in an arcing motion until your upper arm is parallel to the ground while allowing your elbow to bend and keeping your forearm directed down toward the ground.
    1. After performing this rowing motion, your elbow should be bent by approximately 90 degrees, placing you into the starting position for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your upper arm parallel to the ground, progressively straighten your elbow to drive the dumbbell backward and upward in an arcing motion until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. As you move your elbow, you should keep the rest of your body stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbow to bend in a controlled manner as you bring the dumbbell downward and forward in an arcing fashion until you have returned to the starting position with your forearm directed straight down toward the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your upper arm stationary as it remains parallel to the ground.
    2. At the end of the lowering phase, your elbow should be bent by approximately 90 degrees.
    3. There is no need to bend your elbow beyond 90 degrees (when your forearm is perpendicular to the ground) since that additional bending motion would be training your biceps rather than your triceps.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise trains all three heads of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), but other exercises can likely train the triceps more effectively.

## Setting up
1. After selecting your desired weight with the loading pin, adjust the height of the machine’s back pad to a level that allows you to perform full range of motion calf raises.
    1. If the pad is too high, the machine may not be able to provide tension when your heels are fully lowered.
    2. If the pad is too low, it may be difficult for you to assume your starting position.
2. With your knees mildly bent and your torso flexed forward at your hips while facing toward the handles, position the front halves of your feet onto the foot plate. While grasping the handles and resting forearms on the nearby pad, let your heels hang off the edge of the foot plate.
    1. In this position, your lower back should be snugly resting under the back pad.
3. If your lower back is not snugly resting under the back pad or you find it challenging to situate your body into the starting position, you can re-adjust the height of the back pad.
4. Lift your hips up by extending your knees to receive the weight from the machine.
    1. Maintain your knees in a position of extension or a slight bend with the front halves of your feet on the foot plate throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Raise your heels into the air through the available range of motion of your ankles.
2. In a controlled manner, allow your heels to descend toward the ground through the available range of motion of your ankles while continuing to keep the front halves of your feet on top of the foot plate.
    1. How far you are able to lower your heels will be dependent on your mobility.
    2. Strive to lower your heels as far as you can, and you will likely feel a stretching sensation in your calf at the bottom position.
3. After your heels have fully descended, alternate between raising and lowering your heels until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md) while simultaneously improving calf flexibility through loaded stretching.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its highest level, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. While standing with the cable station positioned in front of one of your shoulders, reach up with your closer hand to grasp the handle with an overhand grip such that your palm is facing forward and away from you while keeping your wrist fairly straight.
    1. Keep your wrist in a fairly straight position throughout your set.
3. Take a step backward and slightly lean forward by hinging at your hips.
    1. Maintain this slight torso lean throughout your set.
4. Pull your upper arm down and back until it is positioned at your sides with your elbow being close to fully bent.
    1. Maintain this upper arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Push the handle downward by extending your elbow until it is straightened.
    1. At the end of this motion, the handle should be situated by your side.
2. Reverse the motion by bending your elbow through your available range of motion to raise the handle in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. Strive to have your elbow as close to fully bent as you can by the time you have finished this motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.
