## Setting up
You have the option of setting up this exercise with the plates resting on the ground or an elevated surface like the top of an exercise bench or plyometric box. Using the elevated set-up will make it easier to get into the starting position and set the weight down at the end of the set. While useful for heavy loads, the elevated setup requires more equipment, takes more time, and is not needed for lighter loads. The setup for each approach is described separately, but the exercise technique is the same for both options.

### Setting up from the ground

1. Add weight plates to a barbell situated in a landmine attachment (or a viable substitute).
    1. As an alternative to using a landmine attachment, landmine exercises can be performed with one end of the barbell situated in a wall corner.
    2. While the scraping can be lessened by placing a towel between the wall corner and the barbell, be aware that performing landmine exercises in a wall corner can easily damage the wall corner, so this approach is not appropriate in every environment.
2. Stand upright in a near shoulder-width stance with the free end of the bar between the middle of your feet.
3. Simultaneously bend your hips and knees to squat down until you are low enough to grasp the bar.
    1. Keep your back flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your back.
4. Firmly grasp the end of the bar with your fingers cupped around it, as one hand is directly in front of the other.
    1. The little finger of one hand should be touching the index finger of your other hand.
    2. Your palms should be facing in toward the bar.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
6. Quickly lift the bar up to chest height while rapidly repositioning your hands under the bar with your elbows bent. Allow the end of the bar to rest on the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with your fingers interlocked and your thumbs against the tip of the bar.
    1. The tip of the bar should now be directly in front of your upper chest.
    2. Rather than being flared out or completely by your sides, your elbows should be mildly in front of your sides.
    3. Your knees and hips should now be straight, like when you are normally standing upright, but allow your body to lean mildly forward at your ankles.
    4. With the appropriate positioning, you should feel stable holding the bar.
7. While tucking your chin slightly back, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this position throughout your set.
    2. Avoid leaning back with an excessively arched lower back position.

### Setting up from an elevated position

1. Place a barbell in a landmine attachment or a viable substitute.
    1. As an alternative to using a landmine attachment, landmine exercises can be performed with one end of the barbell situated in a wall corner.
    2. While the scraping can be lessened by placing a towel between the wall corner and the barbell, be aware that performing landmine exercises in a wall corner can easily damage the wall corner, so this approach is not appropriate in every environment.
2. Load the bar with one full diameter plate (such as a 45lb (20kg) plate or any bumper plate) or whichever plate will have the largest diameter of the plates you will use for your working weight.
3. Position a sturdy object with an elevated surface directly next to the plate you loaded onto the bar. Select an object that is tall enough to allow you to squat the weight up while holding it in front of your chest once the bar’s plate is resting on the object.
    1. Viable objects include a plyometric box at least 18in (46cm) in height, a flat exercise bench, or an aerobic step elevated on risers.
    2. How high the object needs to be for you to be able to squat the bar up will be influenced by your height and mobility.
    3. If the object you selected is too low for you, you can increase its height by stacking bumper plates on top of it. With an aerobic step, you can naturally increase its height by adding risers.
4. Lift the bar up by the free end and rest the weight plate on top of the elevated object.
5. Finish adding weight plates to the bar with your desired load.
6. Stand upright with the free end of the bar above the center point between the middle of your feet. Position your feet near shoulder width apart with your toes pointing mildly out to the sides or in whatever is your preferred squat stance.
7. Simultaneously bend your hips and knees to squat down until the tip of the bar is just in front of your upper chest.
    1. Keep your back flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your back.
8. With your elbows bent, position the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) firmly against the bottom of the end of the bar. Interlock your fingers, and place your thumbs against the tip of the bar.
    1. Rather than being flared out or completely by your sides, your elbows should be mildly in front of your sides.
9. Drive through the ground to stand upright while keeping the bar end of the bar directly in front of your chest.
    1. Your knees and hips should now be straight, like when you are normally standing upright, but allow your body to lean mildly forward at your ankles. A mild forward lean should feel natural due to the angle of the landmine.
10. While tucking your chin slightly back, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this position throughout your set.
    2. Avoid leaning back with an excessively arched lower back position.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes like you are trying to crush a walnut. Simultaneously, brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core and tightening your glutes throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the bar upward and outward by driving your elbows upward as you progressively straighten them.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as your arms are angled upward and forward.
    2. Your hands will move diagonally since the bar will naturally move in an arcing manner rather than in a purely vertical path.
    3. Continue keeping your knees and hips straightened rather than using them to help you lift the weight.
    4. Throughout your set, avoid leaning your torso back via excessive lower back arching.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until its end is directly in front of your upper chest.
    1. Move your elbows downward and backward toward your sides while progressively bending them.
    2. At the bottom, your elbows should be tucked slightly in front of where they would be when standing with your arms by your sides.
    3. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
5. Once you have completed the lowering phase of your last rep, set the weight down in the opposite manner to how you initially picked it up.
    1. If you set up from the floor, quickly and sequentially reposition your hands under the bar while guiding the bar down until you are holding it in front of you with straight elbows. After returning your hands to the cupping grip you used when initially setting up, squat down to set the weight onto the ground.
    2. If you set up with the plates on top of an elevated object, squat down until you can return the plates to fully resting on the object before letting go of the bar.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [upper pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and stand over one end of a flat exercise bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space behind you. With this equipment, you would straddle the bench and walk forward toward the J-hooks.
    2. With a portable exercise bench, your back should be facing the head of the bench, as you would when dumbbell bench pressing.
2. Sit down on the bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your upper thighs near your abdomen.
    1. Ensure that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie down with your head on the end of the bench.
    2. Your palms should be facing in toward each other with your upper arms by your sides.
    3. To move heavy dumbbells efficiently into the proper position, you can initially situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up. Then you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
3. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down on the bench. Your head should be right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent. You will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
4. In a bench pressing motion, press the dumbbells up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a bench press rep), the dumbbells should be sitting on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists. You will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
    2. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the dumbbells with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the dumbbells hard will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    3. Based on what feels most comfortable, you can have your palms facing in toward each other (with a neutral grip), forward (with an overhand grip), or angled inward and forward. During your set, you can similarly allow your palms to rotate within this range if that feels comfortable to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the dumbbells in a controlled arcing manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Based on what feels most natural and comfortable, you can keep your elbows tucked in, or you can allow your elbows to flare out to your sides slightly.
    2. Avoid letting your elbows drift back and down with the dumbbells through shoulder motion. When viewed from the side, the proper elbow position should result in your upper arms remaining in a vertical position.
    3. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
2. Finish lowering the dumbbells just before they reach your forehead or the bench.
    1. If you are using an overhand grip (with your palms facing forward to start), you will finish with the dumbbells just above your forehead.
    2. If you are using a neutral grip (with your palms facing inward), your head may not be in the way of the dumbbells, so you can finish with the dumbbells just above the end of the bench.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way, especially when the weights approach your head.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the dumbbells into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the dumbbells are vertically above your shoulders.
    2. Continue keeping your upper arms in a vertical position as you avoid pushing your elbows forward (toward your chest) through shoulder motion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
5. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the dumbbells toward your sides like you would during a neutral grip dumbbell bench press.
    1. Regardless of the palm position you used for your set, it is easier to sit up with the dumbbells when your palms are facing in toward each other.
6. March your thighs up toward the weights, and then rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with slightly bent elbows as your palms are facing in toward your sides (i.e., in a neutral grip position).
2. Assume a bent-over torso position by hinging at your hips and mildly bending your knees until your torso is close to parallel with the ground.
    1. How far you are able to bend over will be affected by your mobility.
    2. If your mobility permits, you can bend over until your torso is parallel with the ground, but you can still effectively perform this exercise if you are not able to descend as far.
    3. While bent over, your arms should be approximately perpendicular to the ground with the dumbbells situated in front of your knees.
    4. Maintain this bent-over position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Raise the dumbbells away from each other and straight out to your sides until your arms and torso form a “T-shape” without moving your hips or knees.
2. Reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells toward each other in a controlled manner back until they have returned to their starting position in front of your knees.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which is assisted by your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), along with your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with extended elbows.
2. Direct your palms so that they are facing in toward your sides (i.e., using a neutral grip position).
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one dumbbell resting at your side with an extended elbow, curl the other dumbbell upward and across the front of your torso toward your opposite shoulder by bending at your elbow.
    1. As you start curling across your body, you will naturally rotate your shoulder inward such that your palm is directed toward the front of your torso.
    2. To allow the dumbbell to clear your torso, you will have to position your upper arm slightly in front of your body while curling (rather than keeping your upper arm right next to your side like you could with a standard hammer curl).
2. After your elbow has fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner until your elbow has returned to an extended position with the dumbbell and your upper back at your side.
3. With your other arm, repeat steps 3 and 4.
4. Alternate between curling with each side until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

1. If you have experience performing the [dual kettlebell clean](Dual%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d88030b58fd481d9951983.md) and [kettlebell overhead press](Standing%20kettlebell%20overhead%20press%201a05c6f170d880d983adf3f27171db52.md), you can set up by cleaning a pair of kettlebells and pressing them overhead. Otherwise, pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright in a near hip-width stance while holding the kettlebells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms are facing forward.
    1. The set-up described here will be less complicated than the technique for a [dual kettlebell clean](Dual%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d88030b58fd481d9951983.md), but can be less efficient if you are using rather heavy weights that are difficult to curl for even one rep.
2. Curl the kettlebells up toward the front of your shoulders by bending your elbows and turning your palms to face in toward each other at the top. Allow the bodies of the kettlebells to rest against your forearms while keeping wrists straight.
    1. To help get the weights into position, feel free to perform a cheat curl-like motion where you initially generate some momentum by swinging the weights mildly backward with straight elbows before swinging your elbows forward while curling them.
3. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, keep your chest up in a “proud chest” posture, rather than letting your shoulders and upper back round forward into a hunched position.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain its natural curvature (like when you are normally standing upright) throughout the exercise.
4. Press the kettlebells up overhead by driving your elbows upward while straightening them. Direct your palms to face forward at the top.
    1. Strive to finish with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling with your elbows fully straightened, and your biceps by your ears.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the kettlebells behind your head in a controlled arcing manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Predominantly keep your elbows tucked in as they are chiefly pointing forward rather than out to your side. However, you can allow your elbows to flare slightly out away from your sides if that feels natural and comfortable to you. If the kettlebells bump into each other, you are flaring your elbows excessively.
    2. Movement should chiefly occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows as you strive to avoid lowering your elbows through shoulder motion.
    3. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
2. Continue lowering the kettlebells until you have fully bent your elbows or can lightly tap the back of your shoulders with the kettlebells.
    1. It is normal to be able to bend the elbows beyond 90 degrees, but specifically how far you can bend your elbows may be limited by the flexibility of the long head of your triceps.
    2. While some lifters have the flexibility to reach their shoulders with the kettlebells, wherever you feel a notable stretching sensation in your triceps can be an appropriate end range.
    3. You do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, but you should be actively controlling the weights the entire way.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the kettlebells up into the starting position overhead.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as your wrists are vertically stacked above your shoulders.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows up as you aim to avoid moving your shoulders.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the kettlebells down in the opposite manner to how you initially lifted them into the starting position.
    1. After your last rep, lower the kettlebells toward the front of your shoulders while bending your elbows like you would during an overhead press. Then lower the kettlebells to your sides as you straighten your elbows in a controlled manner and swing your elbows mildly back to help control the weights.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground.
    1. To set up for this row, you can perform the lifting phase of a [conventional deadlift](Conventional%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880f7a755cd3780a63371.md), followed by the lowering phase of a [Romanian deadlift](Barbell%20Romanian%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880bebc64f4dce0d5f5f1.md).
2. In a near hip-width stance, stand with the middle of your feet under the middle of the bar.
3. With your arms pointing down toward the bar, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can reach the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up throughout the exercise.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. Throughout the exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, as when you are looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue keeping your core braced from this point on.
6. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.
    1. While motion occurs at your hips and knees, your back should remain rigid.
7. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and incline your torso as close to horizontal as your hamstring flexibility permits with a flat back.
    1. To avoid rounding your lower back, you should think about sitting back rather than bending over.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something. 
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical (or close to vertical) throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively pushing your knees forward depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    5. If you have the mobility to hinge until the plates touch the ground, hinge at your hips until the plates are just above the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar up toward your upper abdomen by driving your elbows simultaneously backward and upward while progressively bending your elbows and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. As you do so, keep your torso in a fixed hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set while keeping your core braced and your lower back near a neutral position.
    2. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your lower body should remain nearly stationary.
    3. You can aim to row the bar until it touches near your upper abdomen or is close to doing so, which will result in your elbows being behind your torso (or at least aligned with your torso) at the end of the lifting phase.
    4. While lifting the bar, allow your elbows naturally to flare out away from your sides in a manner that feels comfortable to you, which may result in your upper arms forming near a 45-degree angle with your torso toward the end of the lifting phase.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner by allowing your elbows to move downward and forward until your arms are directed down toward the ground with extended elbows.
    1. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another.
    2. The plates should not touch the ground when lowering the bar.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down onto the floor by bending your knees further.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to near shoulder height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Stand facing the cable, slightly to the side, with one of your shoulders in line with it
    1. Stand with the side of your body you wish to train in line with the cable. The subsequent directions will refer to that side’s arm, while you can position your opposite arm wherever you prefer throughout the exercise.
3. Grasp the handle firmly with a straight elbow and your arm elevated to the height of the pulley. 
4. Step backward until the machine’s weight stack separates and you feel the resistance.
5. Mildly bend your hips and knees by sitting your buttocks somewhat backward with your feet approximately shoulder-width apart to assume a stable stance.
    1. In this position, the center of your breastbone should be facing the same way as the center of your hips, rather than having your trunk rotated toward one side.
6. Unless you prefer a different grip, direct your palm inward to hold the handle with a neutral grip.
    1. If you wish, you can alternatively rotate the handle to use an underhand grip with your palm facing up or an overhand grip with your palm facing down.
    2.  However, many people find the neutral grip feels most natural, so it is an appropriate starting point.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbow back toward your side while simultaneously bending it and pulling your shoulder blade backward to pull the handle back toward you.
    1. Rather than notably flaring your elbow up and away from your side, keep your elbow tucked near your side, which should naturally feel comfortable.
    2. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbow being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    3. Keep your forearm mostly aligned with the cable, which naturally promotes the appropriate degree of elbow bend.
    4. Movement should occur at your shoulder, shoulder blade, and elbow, but your knees, hips, and lower back should remain nearly stationary in a stable position as the center of your breastbone faces the same direction throughout the set.
    5. The cable will impart a rotational force to your trunk that your core muscles will resist to prevent your trunk from twisting during the row.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbow to move forward in a controlled manner as it progressively straightens to move the handle forward.
    1. Without rotating your torso, simultaneously let the cable’s resistance pull your shoulder blade beyond its resting position to stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. Finish this step with your elbow fully straightened and your whole arm aligned with the cable
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arm up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This row primarily trains your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), which are assisted by your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that aligns your shoulders with the machine’s pivot points and allows you to rest your triceps (the back of your upper arms) and elbows comfortably on the arm pads once you are seated.
    1. On each side of the machine, the pivot point (which is also known as the axis of rotation) is the center about which the machine’s lever arm will rotate during the exercise. Aligning your shoulders with these pivot points can help the exercise feel smooth and natural.
    2. The same seat height that aligns your shoulders with the pivot points is what should allow you to rest your triceps and elbows on the arm pads throughout the exercise.
    3. Finding the ideal seat height for you may initially require some trial and error, since you can only determine if the height is appropriate by sitting on the seat and checking to see if the centers of your shoulders are level with the pivot points.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit on the seat with an upright torso and a “proud chest” posture, as your back and the back of your hip bones are resting against the backrest.
    1. Situate your feet flat on the ground if you can do so, but some lifters may not be able to reach the ground with their feet when using certain machines. If that applies to you, you can simply let your feet hang down or place a step or bumper plate under your feet if you prefer them not to dangle.
4. If your machine has one, fasten the seat belt securely around your waist for additional stability.
5. Place one foot against the machine’s foot pedal, and push the pedal forward with your leg.
    1. This lowers the arm pads and moves the handle forward to a position you can comfortably reach.
    2. Keep the pedal pushed away during the next two steps.
6. With bent elbows, raise your arms to situate your elbows and triceps snugly against the arm pads while grasping the handles.
    1. Different machines have different handle types that will influence specifically how you should grasp the handle (such as with an overhand or semi-neutral grip), but what chiefly matters is that your grip feels comfortable and stable.
    2. While uncommon, certain machines may have handles without any arm pads. If you are using one of these atypical machines, you will simply grasp the handles and ignore the details about arm pad usage while otherwise performing the exercise as instructed.
7. Slowly bring the foot pedal back to its starting position by bending your knee, which will shift the machine’s resistance to your arms. Simultaneously, allow the machine’s resistance to lift your elbows upward and backward through the full range of motion that is comfortable to your shoulders.
    1. Maintain the natural curvature of your lower back rather than excessively arching your lower back and flaring your ribs upward and away from your hip bones as you raise your elbows.
    2. The degree to which you can comfortably allow your elbows to lift upward will be influenced by your individual shoulder mobility, but it is common to be able to reach near the point at which the upper arms are fully vertical.
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your shoulders and/or back muscles in the starting position, but you should move through the range in which you do not feel any shoulder joint pain or discomfort.
8. Once your arms are fully lifted up, lift your foot off the foot pedal and place it flat on the ground with your other foot.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows down toward your sides in an arcing motion until your elbows are by your sides.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up and back in contact with the backrest rather than slumping forward into a slouched posture.
    2. During the initial half of this movement, you can focus on pulling down, while you can focus on pulling back during the latter half of this movement.
    3. Emphasize driving your elbows down into the arm pads rather than pulling the handle with your hands.
    4. As your arms move through motion at your shoulders, the rest of your body should be stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to sweep upward in a controlled arcing manner through the full range of motion that is comfortable to your shoulders.
    1. You should return to the starting position with your elbows lifted as high up as your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    2. Like when setting up, avoid letting your lower back excessively arch from flaring your ribs upward and away from your hip bones.
    3. While you do not need to perform this phase with an extremely slow tempo, avoid letting the machine’s resistance abruptly swing your arms upward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once your arms are fully overhead following your last rep, push the pedal forward with your leg until you are no longer supporting any of the machine’s resistance with your upper body.
    2. Then let go of the handles while lifting your arms off the arm pads before bending your knee to bring the foot pedal back to its initial position.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which are assisted by the [lowest portion of your pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) in the overhead position of each rep.

## Setting up
1. With a cable station positioned to its lowest height, select your weight with the loading pin, and connect a straight bar attachment.
2. Situate a flat exercise bench or chair a little in front of the cable station.
3. Squat down to pick up the bar attachment with an underhand grip where your palms are facing forward away from you.
4. While holding the bar, sit down on a flat exercise bench or chair and position your forearms on top of your thighs with your palms facing up and your wrists situated slightly in front of your knees.
    1. To achieve this position, you will lean forward at your hips when seated, with your elbows bent.
5. Allow the force from the cable to bend your wrists and bring your hands downward such that your palms are facing forward.
    1. In this position, the bar should not be contacting your legs, so scoot your forearms forward if it is initially contacting your legs.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift the bar upward by curling your wrists through their available range of motion while keeping your forearms resting on your thighs.
    1. All motion should come from your wrists.
    2. About halfway through the lifting phase, your palms should be facing straight up when your hands are aligned with your forearms.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, when the bar is fully raised, your palms should be angled back toward you.
    4. When performing this exercise appropriately, you should feel tension in the muscles on the palm side of your forearms.
2. Reverse the motion by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your palms directed forward away from you.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the six [wrist flexor muscles](../Muscles/Wrist%20flexor%20muscles%202c85c6f170d880a49749f7d7a9f307c8.md) on the palm side of your forearm.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that places the handles near shoulder level once you are seated.
    1. This seat height is an appropriate starting point for most people, but the ideal seat height specifically should allow you to press through your full range of motion while initially gripping the handles with your elbows stacked under the handles.
    2. If the seat is excessively high, you will not be able to position your elbows directly under the handles (when viewed from the side).
    3. If the seat is excessively low, your range of motion for this exercise will be limited.
    4. Some trial and error may be needed to find the best height for you as an individual.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against the backrest.
    1. Your feet should be flat on the ground.
    2. You can optionally rest your head against the backrest if it is tall enough, or you can simply keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
4. With your palms facing forward and elbows bent, firmly grasp the handles that are directed out to the sides. Position your elbows directly under the handles, resulting in your forearms being vertical when viewed from the side.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. If you cannot comfortably position your elbows under the handles, mildly lower the seat height before resuming your setup.
    3. Situating your elbows under the handles and maintaining this alignment will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare during this exercise.
5. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling, and maintain this posture throughout your set.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the handles up overhead until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your elbows should remain stacked under your wrists when viewed from the side.
    3. Throughout your set, continue keeping your back snuggly against the backrest and your feet planted on the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the handles in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. With the appropriate seat height, you should finish the lowering phase with the handles near shoulder level, as your elbows are lower than your shoulders.
    2. At the bottom, you can allow the weights you selected to tap the rest of the weight stack. A light tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
    3. Continue keeping your elbows stacked underneath the handles, resulting in your forearms remaining in a vertical position when viewed from the side.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with extended elbows.
2. Direct your palms so that they are facing behind you, which positions you with a reverse (AKA overhand) grip.
    1. Maintain this reverse grip on the dumbbells throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl both dumbbells upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed at your sides (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms positioned by your sides.
3. Alternate between curling the dumbbells up and lowering them down until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can develop your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md), but it may train your biceps somewhat less effectively than a curl with an underhand or neutral grip.
1a25c6f170d88002af2fe9c5835b7524:
## Setting up
1. With the empty bar, perform a couple of reps of the [standard back squat](Barbell%20back%20squat%201a25c6f170d8803d8231d083fdd65458.md) or [pause back squat](Pause%20back%20squat%201a25c6f170d880db8636d9788926a62d.md) through the full range of motion that your mobility permits with high-quality technique. Relative to the pinholes available in your rack, note the lowest point at which the bar descends during these reps.
2. Adjust the power rack’s safety pins to be mildly above the lowest point at which the bar descended during those reps.
    1. This height is generally an appropriate starting point, but you specifically want to set the pins near the lowest height that allows you to set up under the bar (once the bar is on pins) with high-quality positioning, which typically requires some trial and error to find.
    2. Setting up with high-quality positioning means that you can start under the bar with your back flat, heels fully on the ground, and each knee aligned with your second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or third toe of that side’s foot. If you round your back, lift your heels off the ground, or cave your knees inward once you are fully set up under the bar, you most likely set the pins lower than what is currently ideal for your mobility and body control.
    3. Particularly if you are not accustomed to this variation, it can be more difficult to set up with optimal positioning from the bottom of the squat compared to a standard back squat. Consequently, beginning with the bar set to the lowest point at which lifters normally can squat through a full range of motion may preclude them from setting up with optimal technique.
    4. For instance, people who have the mobility to squat no deeper than when their thighs are parallel to the ground often are not able to set up with the same quality of body positioning when setting the pins to a level that results in them starting with their thighs parallel to the ground. Setting the pins mildly above that position commonly allows them to set up with better technique.
3. Place the bar centered on the pins, and perform a couple of warm-up reps with the empty bar to confirm whether you selected the appropriate pin height.
    1. If you were unable to keep your back flat, heels down, and knees aligned with your toes, elevate the pins before repeating this step until you find the right pin height for you.
    2. If you think that you can begin from a lower pin height with quality technique, lower the pins before repeating this step.
4. Load the bar with your desired weight, and face the middle of the bar.
5. Grasp the bar with your standard back squat grip width, which commonly is a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
6. Squat down and move under the bar until the middle of your feet and upper back are directly under the bar. Simultaneously, bend your elbows and pull them down by your sides.
    1. Aim to contact the bar specifically with the part of your upper back on which you normally rest the bar during your standard back squat, which varies from person to person.
    2. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck or contacting any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    3. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after starting to squat up with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
7. With the soles of your feet fully on the ground, position your feet in your standard back squat stance, which commonly is reasonably near shoulder width apart with the toes angled mildly outward.
    1. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when squatting, which could involve a different stance width and a different degree of outward toe flare for you than other lifters prefer.
    2. Whatever stance feels best for your typical back squat is appropriate to use for this variation.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar as you tighten your back muscles with your chest up in a “proud chest” posture and your back flat.
    1. While they are presented distinctly for clarity, you can perform steps 1, 2, and 3 simultaneously with each other as they collectively serve to generate full-body tension before starting to squat up.
2. With your weight evenly distributed throughout your feet, “screw your feet into the ground” with the intent to push your knees out while developing tension through your hip muscles.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core throughout your rep.
4. Drive through the ground to stand upright with the bar by extending (straightening) your knees and hips while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. Since you have no momentum to help you, the bar may remain motionless for a moment as you begin driving through the ground before it starts moving.
    2. Maintain the full body tightness you develop throughout the set.
    3. Continue keeping the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground throughout the set.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
5. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back, and progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your 2nd-3rd toes.
6. After you have squatted deep enough for the bar to contact the pins in a controlled manner, allow the weight from the bar to transmit into the pins fully as you completely come to a dead stop with the bar resting on the pins.
    1. While you do not have to finish the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you certainly should avoid crashing the bar into the pins in a jarring manner.
7. With the bar no longer transmitting any load into your back, relax in the bottom position for at least a couple of seconds to ensure you are able to train the subsequent rep in the same manner as the first.
    1. This is distinct from the standard pin squat, where you pause with the bar on the pins for a brief period while staying tight in between reps.
    2. Part of the objective of this variation is to train your ability to develop full-body tightness in a challenging position and lift each rep from a total dead stop.
    3. This is the ideal time to breathe fully during each rep, and the end of step 3 is also an appropriate time to breathe without losing your brace.
8. Alternate between steps 1-7 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while firmly holding the kettlebells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using kettlebells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both kettlebells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one kettlebell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other kettlebell onto the bench before picking up both kettlebells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the kettlebells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    4. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one foot on the ground, take a fairly long step straight forward with your other foot far enough ahead that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee when lunging down.
    1. Like when you step forward while walking, you can initially contact the ground with your front foot’s heel prior to lowering the entirety of your sole onto the ground in a fluid motion, which will likely occur naturally without having to think about it.
    2. When your front foot contacts the ground, you can allow your rear leg’s heel to start lifting up off the ground, which is also likely to occur naturally.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Strive to step forward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    6. Continue keeping your elbows straight and arms directed straight down, which you will do throughout the entire duration of your set.
    7. If you are new to forward lunges, you may have to try out different step lengths to determine which step length places you in the appropriate position.
2. After contacting the ground with your front foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep your rear leg’s forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes) and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot’s sole in contact with the ground.
    2. Continue keeping your torso upright and your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step forward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step forward during your next rep.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step backward with your front leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging forward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the kettlebells down.
    1. After finishing the last rep, set the kettlebells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad muscles](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a sturdy object (such as a thick bumper plate, aerobic step, or plyometric box) that you will use as a step onto the floor or approach the bottom step of a staircase.
    1. You can use a range of different heights for your step, and the difficulty of the exercise will increase as the height increases.
    2. If you are new to forward step-downs, selecting an object that is near four inches (10cm) high (which is a typical height of many aerobic steps without additional risers) can be an appropriate starting point, and you can subsequently adjust the height based on how challenging this height is for you.
    3. For reference, a step of a typical staircase is normally near seven inches (18cm) in height.
    4. If you have balance limitations, you can situate your step near a surface (e.g., handrail, wall, power rack) where you can place one hand to assist with maintaining your balance while performing this exercise.
    5. When feasible, setting up where you can face a mirror is recommended to be able to receive visual feedback about your technique.
2. Step up onto the step with your feet hip-width apart, toes pointing straight ahead, and heels right by the edge.
    1. Your soles should be fully on the step.
    2. Throughout the exercise, keep your hands in your preferred position, such as resting by your sides, on top of your hips, crossed in front of your chest, or outstretched in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot, then lift your other foot up and back so it hangs over the edge of the step.
    1. Naturally, the side of your body to which you shift your weight will be the working side during this set.
2. On the side hovering off the step, pull your toes and the ball of your foot up toward your shin through an ankle motion that brings your heel closer to the ground than the ball of your foot.
    1. This is the opposite of the ankle motion that occurs when lifting your heels up during a calf raise, and you should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract.
    2. Throughout your set, maintain this foot position and the knee of your non-working side straight.
    3. You are now in the starting position for your first rep.
3. Sit your buttocks back to initiate the descent. Then progressively bend your working leg’s knee and hip in a controlled manner until you can gently tap the ground with the heel of your other foot.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hip to maintain your balance, but keep your back flat and chest up. When starting to descend, you can think about beginning to sit on a chair, which cues the intended hip motion that loads your glute.
    2. Keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down. Imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    3. While letting your working leg’s knee naturally track forward, strive to keep it aligned with your middle toes, rather than letting it inward relative to your foot (which you can check in a mirror, along with how level your hip bones are). Think about driving your knees out to the side if it starts drifting inward.
    4. Keep your elevated heel firmly planted on the step, along with the rest of your sole.
    5. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your free leg’s heel, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram). Lowering yourself slowly can help achieve this very light tap at the bottom.
4. Reverse the movement by driving through your elevated foot to step up into an upright position.
    1. By extending (straightening) your knee and hip, lift your body up completely through your working leg, as you avoid pushing off the ground with your other side’s foot.
    2. Continue keeping your hip bones level and your working leg’s knee aligned with your middle toes.
5. Alternate steps 3 and 4 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side on the step.
    1. Based on your preference, you can keep your non-working side’s foot hovering in the air between reps, or briefly place it on the step before lifting it off for the next rep. The latter approach can be useful if you feel that you need to reset your balance between reps, but either option is valid.
## Description
While training your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [glutes](../Muscles/Glutes%201b95c6f170d88002885bca53f30406d5.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), this exercise can improve your single leg stability.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the rack’s J-hooks to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on top of them.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
    3. If you need to bend your knees and hips beyond a mild degree (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) initially to place the bar on your back, you positioned the J-hooks excessively low. This can make it more challenging to rerack the bar at the end of your set.
2. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance, and grasp the bar with your palms facing down as your hands are slightly outside shoulder width.
    1. For the full clean grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your 2nd-5th fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
3. While simultaneously bending your elbows, shallowly bend at your knees and hips with an upright torso to walk under the bar and situate it on the front of your shoulders just in front of the base of your neck.
    1. The bar should be resting on your front delts (which are the muscles on the front of your shoulders that attach to the outer aspects of your collarbones) and the outer portions of your collarbones, which together form a shelf with the base of your neck to cradle the bar.
    2. While the bar should be directly in front of your neck, it should not be pressing into your neck to the extent that it feels like it is choking you.
    3. If you are not accustomed to front squats, it is normal to experience discomfort from the pressure the bar places on the front of your shoulders (which may cause some skin bruising), but it should not be painful with proper bar placement.
4. With the bar now on the front of your shoulders, lift your elbows up until your upper arms are parallel to the ground while keeping your fingers wrapped around the bar.
    1. You can perform steps 3 and 4 simultaneously with each other.
    2. The bony prominence on the back of each elbow should now be pointing straight forward.
    3. Your hands can assist in keeping the bar balanced, but the bar should first and foremost be resting on the front of your shoulders without necessarily needing your hands to hold it there.
    4. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your wrists and/or forearm muscles in this position. However, if you find this position to be painful or lack the mobility to use a full clean grip, you can select a different front squat variation from this database that requires less mobility (such as the [cross-arm grip front squat](Cross-arm%20grip%20front%20squat%201a25c6f170d88038b559cf1d5dbd8366.md) or [fingertip clean grip front squat](Fingertip%20clean%20grip%20front%20squat%202165c6f170d880048694f9a5579ba6ab.md)).
5. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of front squat reps with the form described in the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins before reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends when front squatting.
7. Repeat steps 2-4 of the setup before proceeding to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your upper arms parallel to the ground, stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the bar resting on your shoulders throughout the set.
2. Take a couple of steps back, and position your feet near shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing slightly out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip-width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside shoulder width and their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. Throughout your set, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest and elbows up.
    1. Throughout the set, avoid dropping your elbows or letting your chest cave down.
    2. As you descend, it is natural for your torso to lean forward mildly at your hips to maintain your balance, but maintain a mostly upright torso position with your back flat.
    3. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    5. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
6. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
7. Alternate between steps 4-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
8. Walk forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.

## Setting up
1. Position your shoulders snugly underneath the shoulder pads as your back is fully in contact with the back pad.
    1. The back of your hip bones should also be contacting the back pad.
    2. Rather than being rounded in a slouched posture, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
2. Place your feet fully on the middle of the foot plate, near shoulder width apart, with your toes pointing slightly outward.
    1. Many people find that setting up with a stance reasonably close to this allows them to hack press effectively. However, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Some people will feel that they can move their hips more freely with a wider stance, while others may prefer a closer stance. Similarly, certain lifters may feel better with their toes pointing straight up, while others may feel more comfortable with their toes pointing moderately further outward.
    3. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when hack squatting through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different stances over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    4. While recognizing that near the middle of the foot plate works well for many people, you can also adjust how high up on the platform you position your feet based on your preference. Wherever you select should allow your heels (along with the rest of your feet) to be firmly on the foot plate throughout the whole set. Your foot placement should also allow you to keep the back of your hips snugly against the back pad at the bottom of each rep. The proper position should additionally feel comfortable for your knees.
    5. Placing your feet higher up may make it easier to keep your heels in contact with the foot plate, more difficult to keep your back flat against the back pad, and potentially bias the gluteus maximus to a greater degree. Placing your feet lower down may make it more difficult to keep your heels in contact with the foot plate, easier to keep your back flat against the back pad, and potentially bias the quads to a degree. Avoid positioning your feet toward either end of the platform if doing so feels awkward and/or limits your range of motion.
    6. In the starting position, your knees should be at least slightly bent to allow you to unlock the sled and begin your set. If you have very short legs, you potentially may have to situate your feet lower on the foot plate to start with slightly bent knees.
3. Without having any weight plates added to the machine, perform a few reps with the technique described in the “exercise technique” section before finishing your setup.
    1. These initial reps will help you determine what your full range of motion entails and inform you if any adjustments (such as to your foot placement or machine settings) are warranted.
    2. If you make any adjustments to your foot placement or the machine, it is recommended to try out a couple of reps without additional weights to make sure the adjustments were appropriate before adding weights.
4. If your machine allows you to adjust it, angle the foot plate to a setting that comfortably allows you to train through a full range of motion with your feet fully on the foot plate.
    1. Angling the foot plate closer toward a horizontal position can reduce the amount of ankle mobility required to keep your heels in contact with the foot plate at the bottom of the rep. If you noticed that your ability to keep your heels fully on the foot plate limited how deeply you were able to hack squat, it may be appropriate to try angling the foot plate closer toward a horizontal position. This may allow you to hack squat with a deeper knee bend compared to if the foot plate were angled more vertically.
    2. However, your feet may feel unstable and risk sliding if the foot plate is angled excessively close to being horizontal, so you want to find an appropriate balance.
5. If your machine has them, position the safety stoppers slightly under the lowest point at which the sled reaches at the bottom of your hack squat rep.
    1. Depending on how deeply you hack squat and the machine you use, the lowest safety stoppers available potentially may not be sufficiently low to allow you to descend through your full range of motion.
6. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, and repeat steps 1 and 2 to assume the starting position with the foot placement you determined is appropriate for you.
    1. Note that the machine will provide resistance even without any additional weight plates. The weight of the sled will vary depending on the specific model, but it commonly weighs reasonably close to 100lb (45kg).
    2. Avoid adding so much weight that you no longer are able to train through your full range of motion.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your feet into the platform to push it away from you by straightening your knees.
    1. After doing so, the sled should no longer be resting on the machine’s safety stoppers.
    2. Your knees should now be straight or just slightly bent.
3. Unlock the safety handles with your hands to move the safety stoppers out of the sled’s way.
    1. The specific location of the safety handles and how to unlock them can vary among different machine models. However, the safety handles are often near where your hands will be when resting by your sides, and rotating the handles outward will commonly disengage the safety stoppers.
4. For additional stability, firmly grasp the fixed handles (not the movable safety handles) and continue holding them throughout your set.
    1. The fixed handles are commonly located near the shoulder pads.
5. Squat down in a controlled manner by simultaneously bending at your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the foot plate.
    2. Continue keeping your back and the back of your hip bones snugly in contact with the back pad.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet. It can help to think about pushing your knees out if you notice them starting to drift inward.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively in control the entire time.
6. Continue squatting down through the full pain-free range of motion you can while keeping your heels fully on the foot plate, along with the back of your hips and back flat against the back pad.
    1. People can commonly descend until their knees are bent by at least 90 degrees, and some lifters can reach the point at which their thighs touch their calves with their knees fully bent. However, what constitutes a full range of motion will vary from person to person and be influenced by your individual hip and ankle mobility, along with your foot placement.
    2. With certain machine models, you alternatively may reach the end range to which the machine permits before reaching the deepest position that your mobility enables.
    3. If you reached the end range to which your ankle mobility allows your knees to track over your toes, hack squatting any deeper would cause your heels to start lifting off the foot plate.
    4. If you reached the end range to which your hips can bend, lowering the sled any further would cause your lower back to start rounding. This would be demonstrated by your hip bones starting to curl forward off the back pad.
    5. Hack squatting into a deep position is not inherently problematic to the knees, but there is no need to force yourself into the lowest position possible if you experience knee discomfort at your end range.
7. Reverse the movement by driving your feet into the foot plate to squat up as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees when hack squatting, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. Rather than pushing all through your heels or all through your toes, you should be pushing evenly throughout your feet.
    3. Continue keeping your feet fully on the platform, knees aligned over your feet, and your back and the back of your hip bones fully against the back pad.
8. Alternate between steps 5-7 until you have completed your set.
9. After your knees are straightened following the lifting phase of your last rep, lock the safety handles with your hands to return the safety stoppers to being fully under the sled.
10. Lower the sled onto the safety stoppers by bending your knees.
