## Setting up
1. Stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance in a location that has sufficient space in front of you for lunging forward repeatedly.
    1. You can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides, on top of your hips, in front of your chest, etc.
    2. Keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
    3. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one foot on the ground, take a fairly long step straight forward with your other foot far enough ahead that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee when lunging down.
    1. Like when you step forward while walking, you can initially contact the ground with your front foot’s heel prior to lowering the entirety of your sole onto the ground in a fluid motion, which will likely occur naturally without having to think about it.
    2. When your front foot contacts the ground, you can allow your rear leg’s heel to start lifting up off the ground, which is also likely to occur naturally.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Strive to step forward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    6. If you are new to walking lunges, you may have to try out different step lengths to determine which step length places you in the appropriate position.
2. After contacting the ground with your front foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep your rear leg’s forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes) and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot’s sole in contact with the ground.
    2. Continue keeping your torso upright and your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step forward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step forward during your next rep.
3. Progressively extend (straighten) your knees to lift your body up until you can repeat step 1 to step forward with your rear leg past your stationary leg in the same manner that you initially performed with your other side.
    1. Strive to begin stepping forward as you are lunging up in a fluid manner, which will advance your body forward.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat step 2 with your other side now in the forward position, as you lunge down just like you previously did.
5. Continue repeating steps 1-4 as you progressively lunge forward with alternating legs until you have completed your set or have to turn around and continue lunging in the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Determine what you hold with your hands for balance assistance.
    1. So long as what you use for assistance is sturdy and will be within your reach to hold throughout the exercise, you have multiple options for what you can select.
    2. With two hands, you can hold objects like the vertical posts of a rack, a door frame, anchored suspension trainer straps, or gymnastic rings.
    3. If you feel that you only require one hand for assistance, you can also use those objects in addition to a variety of others, such as a bedpost, couch, dumbbell rack, incline exercise bench, part of an exercise machine, etc.
2. Stand upright in a hip-width stance with your toes pointing straight ahead as you are close to what you hold onto to provide assistance with your arms. Grasp that object with one or two hands.
    1. Ensure that there is sufficient room for you to lift one of your legs forward and that you will be able to continue holding the object at the bottom of your rep, along with the top of it.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight into the foot on the side of your body you will train. Simultaneously pick your other foot up off the ground by lifting that thigh up until it is parallel to the ground with your knee as straight as your hamstring flexibility permits.
    1. Throughout the set, keep this leg close to parallel to the ground without letting its foot touch the ground.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the leg whose foot is on the ground.
2. Bend at your hip and knee to squat down in a controlled manner while assisting with your arms as needed.
    1. Throughout the rep, you can adjust how much assistance you use from your upper body, which will likely need to be greater near the bottom of the rep (where the exercise is more challenging) compared to near the top of the rep. Some people will simply use their hands to assist with balance, while others may need to utilize greater upper body involvement to reduce the demands on their lower body muscles.
    2. Keep the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your foot firmly in contact with the ground throughout your set.
    3. Strive to have your knee track straight forward in line with your second and third toes (when counting your big toe as your first toe) as you descend, while not letting your knee cave inward.
    4. To the best of your ability, keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Aim to keep your torso mostly upright within the constraints of your mobility and balance. The vast majority of people can only move through a full range of motion during this exercise if they let their backs round during the descent.
    6. Through motion at your working leg’s hip, your torso should naturally transition to an inclined position rather than remaining completely upright, but strive to keep your back near a neutral position (where it retains its natural curvature or looks flat) as you avoid excessively rounding your lower back.
3. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion that your mobility comfortably enables without letting your heel lift up off the ground or your knee cave inward.
    1. The greatest possible depth involves descending until your knee is fully bent with your hamstrings contacting your calves. If you have ankle mobility limitations, you will not be able to reach this point, but training this exercise over time can help improve your depth.
    2. If you start experiencing knee discomfort in the deepest position, you can abbreviate the range of motion to what feels right to your knee. This exercise is not inherently dangerous to the knees, but it can take some time to adapt to very deep pistol squats if you are unaccustomed to exercises that concentrate a high degree of loading into a fully bent knee position.
    3. While an extremely slow descent is unnecessary, controlling the entirety of the lowering phase is recommended rather than dropping down rapidly in an effort to bounce out of the bottom position.
4. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knee and hip to squat up until you have returned to standing upright.
    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your foot fully in contact with the ground and your hip bones level as you avoid letting your knee cave inward.
    2. Greater assistance from your hands is commonly needed when squatting up compared to squatting down.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. You can optionally place a soft object (like a cushioned balance pad, yoga block, folded thick towel, folded yoga mat, or a pillow) on the ground directly behind where you will stand if you are not confident in your ability to control the descent and tap your knee to the ground in a gentle manner.
    2. If you opt to place a soft object on the ground, you will use your knee to tap that object instead of the ground, and doing so will mildly reduce the range of motion and difficulty of this exercise compared to if you would lightly contact the ground with your knee.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot and pick the other foot up off the ground by bending that side’s knee by greater than 90 degrees while keeping its thigh directed down toward the ground.
    1. The goal is to bend your knee enough that your foot will not contact the ground before your knee reaches the ground during the descent.
    2. Keep your free leg in this position throughout your set.
2. While simultaneously reaching the dumbbells mildly forward, progressively bend at your knee and hip with the leg in contact with the ground to squat down in a controlled manner until you can gently tap the ground with your free leg’s knee.
    1. It can be helpful to initiate the descent by mildly sitting your buttocks back through a hip hinge motion that mildly inclines your torso, as if you are closing a car door with your buttocks as your hands are carrying something.
    2. The forward movement of the dumbbells should come from your shoulders (as if you started to perform a front raise) as you keep your elbows fairly straight, and it should be a relatively small movement primarily to help you maintain your balance.
    3. Keep the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your working leg’s foot firmly in contact with the ground throughout your set.
    4. Strive to have your knee track straight forward in line with your second and third toes (when counting your big toe as your first toe) as you descend, while not letting your knee cave inward.
    5. To the best of your ability, keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down.
    6. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    7. Through motion at your working leg’s hip, your torso should naturally transition to a somewhat inclined position rather than remaining completely upright, but strive to keep your back near a neutral position (where it retains its natural curvature or looks flat) as you avoid excessively rounding your lower back.
    8. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your free leg’s knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
3. Reverse the motion you just performed by progressively extending (straightening) your working leg's knee and hip to squat yourself up as you simultaneously pull your arms back until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your working leg’s foot fully in contact with the ground as you keep your hip bones level and avoid letting your knee cave inward.
    2. At the end of the ascent, your arms should once again be by your sides as they are directed down toward the ground.
4. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise after switching which foot is in contact with the ground.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the dumbbells with a deadlift or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    4. Positioning yourself in a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, take a fairly long step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Slightly bend the knee on the side of your stationary foot while doing so.
    2. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to split squats.
    3. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. Keep your arms by your sides, directed down toward the ground throughout the duration of your set.
2. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. While the forefoot of your rear leg will stay in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground with your knee, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and step somewhat farther backward after you ascend before performing your next rep.
3. While keeping both of your feet planted on the ground, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which leg is in the forward position.
    1. After finishing the set with your other leg forward, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad muscles](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the lower leg pad to be level with your upper calf, just below the back of your knees, when standing on the foot plate.
    1. The ideal pad height will allow your knees to move freely (which may not be the case if the pad is too high) during the exercise while appropriately supporting your lower legs (which may not be the case if the pad is too low).
2. Step onto the foot plate in an approximately hip-width stance with the tops of your feet under the machine’s foot roller and your upper calves snugly against the pad.
    1. The soles of your feet should be fully in contact with the foot plate as your toes are pointing straight ahead.
3. If your machine permits you to do so, adjust the foot roller so that it is snugly on top of your feet just in front of your ankles.
    1. Your feet and lower legs should now be securely locked into the machine in a position where they will not move during the exercise.
    2. While many do, certain machine models lack an adjustable foot roller.
4. Stand fully upright and place your arms in your preferred position, which may be crossed in front of your chest or held outstretched in front of you parallel to the ground.
    1. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your torso in a vertical position and your calves in contact with the leg pad, bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner until your thighs are approximately parallel to the ground or somewhat below this point.
    1. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the foot plate.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot.
    3. Strive to keep your shoulders vertically stacked over your hips, as you resist any forward torso lean. 
    4. When your thighs are parallel to the ground, your knees and hips should be bent by approximately 90 degrees (as demonstrated by the angle between your thighs and trunk for your hips and the angle between your shins and thighs for your knees).
    5. The intensity of this exercise will increase as your squat depth increases, so you can adjust your depth based on your ability if you currently cannot descend until your thigh is parallel to the ground for the number of reps you intend to perform during this set.
2. Reverse the movement by pressing through the foot plate to squat up as you extend (straighten) your knees and hips until you have returned to the starting position with your torso fully lifted up and your knees straightened.
    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your torso in a vertical position, calves in contact with the leg pad, feet fully in contact with the ground, and knees in line with your feet.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md) with relatively low loading of your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and [hip adductors](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md), in contrast to most squat variations.

## Setting up
1. Position a sturdy object (such as a thick bumper plate, aerobic step, or plyometric box) that you will use as a step onto the floor.
    1. You can use a range of different heights for your step, and the difficulty of the exercise will increase as the height increases.
    2. If you are new to weighted lateral step-downs, selecting an object that is near four inches (10cm) high (which is a typical height of many aerobic steps without additional risers) can be an appropriate starting point, and you can subsequently adjust the height based on how challenging this height is for you.
    3. Alternatively, you can perform this exercise on the lowest step of a staircase, which is normally near seven inches (18cm) in height.
    4. When feasible, setting up where you can face a mirror is recommended to be able to receive visual feedback about your technique.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
3. Stand directly to the side of the step, and place one foot fully onto the step while leaving your other foot on the ground. Situate your feet about hip-width apart, and point your toes straight ahead.
    1. The entire sole (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) of your elevated foot should be firmly planted on the step throughout your set.
    2. Continue holding the dumbbells by your sides throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive through your elevated leg and straighten your knee to step up until your feet are level, keeping your non-working leg’s foot hanging off the step.
    1. Finish fully upright with the tops of your hip bones and shoulders level, while you bear all your bodyweight through the foot on the step.
2. On the side hovering off the step, pull your toes and the ball of your foot up toward your shin through an ankle motion that brings your heel closer to the ground than the ball of your foot.
    1. This is the opposite of the ankle motion that occurs when lifting your heels up during a calf raise, and you should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract.
    2. Throughout your set, maintain this foot position and the knee of your non-working side straight.
    3. You are now in the starting position for your first rep.
3. Sit your buttocks back to initiate the descent. Then progressively bend your working leg’s knee and hip in a controlled manner until you can gently tap the ground with the heel of your other foot.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hip to maintain your balance, but keep your back flat and chest up. When starting to descend, you can think about beginning to sit on a chair, which cues the intended hip motion that loads your glute.
    2. Keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down. Imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    3. While letting your working leg’s knee naturally track forward, strive to keep it aligned with your middle toes, rather than letting it inward relative to your foot (which you can check in a mirror, along with how level your hip bones are). Think about driving your knees out to the side if it starts drifting inward.
    4. Keep your elevated heel firmly planted on the step, along with the rest of your sole.
    5. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your free leg’s heel, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram). Lowering yourself slowly can help achieve this very light tap at the bottom.
4. Reverse the movement by driving through your elevated foot to step up into a fully upright position.
    1. By extending (straightening) your knee and hip, lift your body up completely through your working leg, as you avoid pushing off the ground with your other side’s foot.
    2. Continue keeping your hip bones level and your working leg’s knee aligned with your middle toes.
    3. Finish your free foot hovering in the air, not in contact with the step.
5. Alternate steps 3 and 4 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side on the step.
    1. Since each rep starts with the lowering phase, completion of step 2 does not constitute a full rep.
## Description
While training your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [glutes](../Muscles/Glutes%201b95c6f170d88002885bca53f30406d5.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), this exercise can improve your single leg stability.

## Setting up
1. Position a sturdy object (such as a thick bumper plate or an aerobic step) that you will use as a step onto the floor in a location that has sufficient space behind it for your split squat.
    1. You can use a range of different heights for your stepping surface, but selecting an object that is near four inches (10cm) high (which is a typical height of many aerobic steps without additional risers) can be an appropriate starting point.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the dumbbells with a deadlift or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
3. In approximately a hip-width stance, stand with the foot that you will first step up onto the step aligned with the middle of your step (which is primarily relevant if you are using a bumper plate to provide the greatest surface area for your foot).
## Exercise technique
1. With the foot aligned with the middle of your step, step up onto the step with the entirety of its sole in contact with the step while leaving your other foot on the ground.
    1. The knee on the side of your elevated foot should be mildly bent once on the step.
    2. Keep your arms by your sides, directed down toward the ground throughout the duration of your set.
2. Shift your bodyweight into your elevated foot before taking a fairly long step backward with your other foot and contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. To shift your bodyweight into your elevated foot, you can lean your torso mildly forward by hinging at your hip as you bend that side’s knee slightly more.
    2. Once you step back and resume transferring some of your weight into your rear leg, you can return to keeping your torso in an upright position.
    3. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to split squats.
    4. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    5. Keep the entire sole of your elevated foot firmly planted on the step and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    6. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
3. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the step.
    2. While the forefoot of your rear leg will stay in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground with your knee, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and step somewhat farther backward after you ascend before performing your next rep.
4. While keeping both of your feet planted, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which leg is in the forward position on top of the step.
    1. After finishing the set with your other leg forward, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

While statically training your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md) and [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), this exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance in a location that has sufficient space in front of you for lunging forward.
    1. You can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides, on top of your hips, in front of your chest, etc.
    2. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
    3. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one foot on the ground, take a fairly long step straight forward with your other foot far enough ahead that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee when lunging down.
    1. Like when you step forward while walking, you can initially contact the ground with your front foot’s heel prior to lowering the entirety of your sole onto the ground in a fluid motion, which will likely occur naturally without having to think about it.
    2. When your front foot contacts the ground, you can allow your rear leg’s heel to start lifting up off the ground, which is also likely to occur naturally.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Strive to step forward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    6. If you are new to forward lunges, you may have to try out different step lengths to determine which step length places you in the appropriate position.
2. After contacting the ground with your front foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep your rear leg’s forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes) and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot’s sole in contact with the ground.
    2. Continue keeping your torso upright and your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step forward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step forward during your next rep.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step backward with your front leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging forward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates to a barbell situated in a landmine attachment (or a viable substitute).
    1. As an alternative to using a landmine attachment, landmine exercises can be performed with one end of the barbell situated in a wall corner.
    2. While the scraping can be lessened by placing a towel between the wall corner and the barbell, be aware that performing landmine exercises in a wall corner can easily damage the wall corner, so this approach is not appropriate in every environment.
2. Stand upright with the free end of the bar between the middle of your feet. Position your feet near shoulder width apart with your toes pointing mildly out to the sides.
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside of shoulder width with their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. In the starting position, your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, and you will keep your neck in this position throughout your set.
3. Simultaneously bend your hips and knees to squat down until you are low enough to grasp the bar.
    1. Keep your back flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your back.
4. Firmly grasp the end of the bar with your fingers cupped around it, as one hand is directly in front of the other.
    1. The little finger of one hand should be touching the index finger of your other hand.
    2. Your palms should be facing in toward the bar.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
6. Explosively lift the bar up to chest height while rapidly repositioning your hands under the bar with your elbows bent. Allow the end of the bar to rest on the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with your fingers interlocked and your thumbs against the tip of the bar.
    1. The tip of the bar should now be directly in front of your chest.
    2. Your elbows should be tucked slightly in front of your sides.
    3. Your knees and hips should now be straight, like when you are normally standing upright, but allow your body to lean mildly forward at your ankles.
    4. With the appropriate positioning, you should feel stable holding the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner.
    1. Avoid rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    5. Keep the tip of the bar directly in front of your chest throughout your set.
2. Continue to squat down through the available range of motion that your mobility enables without rounding your back, lifting your heels up off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, heels lift off the ground, or knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting excessively deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively standing up as you drive through the ground. Extend (straighten) your knees and hips until you have returned to the upright starting position.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, knees stacked over your feet, and the weight held close to your chest as you squat up.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
5. Once you have completed the lifting phase of your last rep, quickly reposition your hands under the bar sequentially while guiding the bar down until you are holding it in front of you with straight elbows.
    1. You are returning your hands to the cupping grip you used when initially setting up.
6. Squat down to set the weight onto the ground.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a kettlebell or dumbbell and hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows, as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. You can use either a kettlebell or a dumbbell, but some people find holding a kettlebell in the goblet position to feel more stable and comfortable, especially with a fairly heavy weight.
    2. Based on your preference and the load you use, you can transfer your kettlebell or dumbbell into the goblet position through a couple of different approaches.
    3. An effective approach is initially to pick up the weight by the handle through a deadlift motion and set it on an elevated surface (like a bench or plyometric box) with the handle facing up if you use a kettlebell or the handle directed vertically if using a dumbbell (as only one end of the dumbbell is on the surface). Then squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it in the goblet position, and squat up with the weight. If you use a kettlebell, grasp it by its horns (i.e., side handles). If you use a dumbbell, cup your hands around the top end of the weight with the base of your palms by the handle, and your fingers wrapped around the rest of that end of the weight.
    4. With a lighter kettlebell, you can tilt it onto its side with the weight base directed toward you, squat down to grasp its horns, stand upright with it, and curl it into the goblet position.
    5. With a lighter dumbbell, you can also pick it up with one hand and curl it up across your body to be in front of your chest. Then cup your free hand around the top end of the dumbbell with the base of its palm by the handle and fingers wrapped around the top end of the weight before repositioning your other hand to cup the other side of the weight in the same manner.
2. While holding the weight to your chest and looking straight ahead, stand upright with your feet near shoulder-width apart from each other as your toes are pointing somewhat out to the sides (rather than pointing straight ahead).
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside of shoulder width with their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. In the starting position, your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, and you will keep your neck in this position throughout your set.
    5. Continue holding the weight close to your chest in the goblet position throughout your set.

1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward, leaving your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Strive to create tension throughout the entirety of your core to form a “360-degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. Continue bracing your core throughout your set to help you maintain a rigid trunk position.
2. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your knees aligned with your feet.

3. Continue to squat down through the available range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.

    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, knees stacked over your feet, and the weight held close to your chest as you squat up.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat to a distance away from the foot platform that allows you to leg press through a full range of motion without rounding your lower back.
    1. Finding the ideal setting for you as an individual typically takes some trial and error. The only way to know if the seat setting is appropriate is to sit down on the seat and situate your feet on the platform in the same position you will use for your set.
    2. The appropriate setting will allow you to assume the starting position as your lower back maintains close to its natural curvature (like when you are normally standing upright). It should also allow you to keep your feet fully on the platform.
    3. If the seat is excessively close to the foot platform relative to your hip mobility, your lower back may have to round to place your feet on the platform while seated. Alternatively, you may not be able to place your heels firmly in contact with the platform if it is too close.
    4. You should ideally place the seat as close to the foot platform as you can without having to round your lower back or lift your heels off the platform. Placing the seat meaningfully farther back beyond this point may decrease how much muscle growth the exercise is likely to stimulate.
    5. As a general starting point, you can find the seat setting that allows your knees to be bent by about 90 degrees when your feet are on the platform. If you are able to avoid rounding your lower back when set up with this setting, you can incrementally bring the seat closer until you find your optimal starting position. Alternatively, if you have to round your lower back to set up with your knees bent by about 90 degrees, you can incrementally bring the seat back until you can assume the starting position without rounding your lower back.
2. Select your weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on the seat with your back firmly supported by the backrest.
    1. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Place your feet fully on the middle of the foot platform, near shoulder width apart, with your toes pointing slightly outward.
    1. Many people find that setting up with a stance reasonably close to this allows them to leg press effectively. However, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Some people will feel that they can move their hips more freely with a wider stance, while others may prefer a closer stance. Similarly, certain lifters may feel better with their toes pointing straight up, while others may feel more comfortable with their toes pointing moderately further outward.
    3. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when leg pressing through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different stances over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    4. While recognizing that near the middle of the platform works well for many people, you can also adjust how high up on the platform you position your feet based on your preference. Wherever you select, your heels should be firmly on the platform along with the rest of your feet. Placing your feet higher up potentially may bias the gluteus maximus to a degree, while placing your feet lower down potentially may train the quads preferentially. Avoid positioning your feet toward either end of the platform if doing so feels awkward or limits your range of motion.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
3. Drive your feet into the platform to push it away from you as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees when leg pressing, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.

A sign of an appropriately controlled movement is having the weights you selected lightly contact the rest of the weight stack at the end range. Having the weights lightly touch down will also confirm that you have moved through your full range of motion.
    3. With the appropriate seat position, you should be able to avoid rounding your lower back at the end range of this motion. If you notice your lower back starts rounding at the end, you could finish your rep and mildly move the seat backward before resuming your set.

This exercise can effectively train your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and multiple [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the rack’s J-hooks to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on top of them.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
    3. If you need to bend your knees and hips beyond a mild degree (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) initially to place the bar on your back, you positioned the J-hooks excessively low. This can make it more challenging to rerack the bar at the end of your set.
2. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of squat reps through the full range of motion your mobility allows, without rounding your back or lifting your heels off the ground
    1. Use the technique for a standard [barbell back squat](Barbell%20back%20squat%201a25c6f170d8803d8231d083fdd65458.md) to help you determine the appropriate height of the safety pins for your pin squats.
3. Rerack the bar onto the J-hooks before loading the bar with your intended weight.
4. Position the safety pins slightly above the lowest point at which the bar descends during your typical back squat.
    1. If you wish to train through a shorter range of motion to address a specific weak point, you can alternatively set the pins a little higher.
    2. Your safety pins should be positioned to a height that allows you to set the bar on them at the end of each rep’s descent without having to descend beyond the range of motion in which you can squat with quality technique (e.g., keeping your back flat and feet fully on the ground).
5. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
6. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on your upper back in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should be securely resting on the muscles of your upper back when squeezing your shoulder blades together.
    2. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    5. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. Take a couple of steps back, and position your feet near shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing slightly out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip-width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside shoulder width and their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. Throughout your set, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    4. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. After you have squatted deep enough for the bar to contact the pins in a controlled manner, allow the weight from the bar to transmit into the pins as you come to a dead stop with the bar resting on the pins for a brief period of time (e.g., about two seconds).
    1. While you do not have to finish the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you certainly should avoid crashing the bar into the pins in a jarring manner.
    2. Continue keeping your core braced and your back flat while you remain stationary.
6. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
7. Alternate between steps 4-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
8. Walk forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    4. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to backward lunges.
    2. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position with your arms directed down toward the ground as you do so.
    4. Strive to keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
2. After contacting the ground with your rear foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    7. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step backward during your next rep.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step forward with your rear leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright, arms directed down toward the ground, and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging backward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down.
    1. After finishing the last rep, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a kettlebell or dumbbell and hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows, as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. You can use either a kettlebell or a dumbbell, but some people find holding a kettlebell in the goblet position to feel more stable and comfortable, especially with a fairly heavy weight.
    2. Based on your preference and the load you use, you can transfer your kettlebell or dumbbell into the goblet position through a couple of different approaches.
    3. An effective approach is initially to pick up the weight by the handle through a deadlift motion and set it on an elevated surface (like a bench or plyometric box) with the handle facing up if you use a kettlebell or the handle directed vertically if using a dumbbell (as only one end of the dumbbell is on the surface). Then squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it in the goblet position, and squat up with the weight. If you use a kettlebell, grasp it by its horns (i.e., side handles). If you use a dumbbell, cup your hands around the top end of the weight with the base of your palms by the handle, and your fingers wrapped around the rest of that end of the weight.
    4. With a lighter kettlebell, you can tilt it onto its side with the weight base directed toward you, squat down to grasp its horns, stand upright with it, and curl it into the goblet position.
    5. With a lighter dumbbell, you can also pick it up with one hand and curl it up across your body to be in front of your chest. Then cup your free hand around the top end of the dumbbell with the base of its palm by the handle and fingers wrapped around the top end of the weight before repositioning your other hand to cup the other side of the weight in the same manner.
2. While keeping your chest up, position your feet approximately hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight ahead.
    1. In this starting position, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you are keeping your chest up and looking straight ahead.
    2. You will continue holding the weight close to your chest in the goblet position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Take a long step out to the side as you keep the toes of your stepping foot pointing forward.
    1. How wide a stance may be ideal for you will be influenced by your hip mobility, and some trial and error may be needed to find which stance feels best to you.
    2. As a general guideline, your feet should be further apart than one and a half times your shoulder width, but not so wide that you feel unstable.
    3. While you step to the side, your torso will shift over to that side.
2. As your stepping foot contacts the ground, bend at that side’s knee and hip while sitting your buttock somewhat backward to squat down with your stepping leg in a controlled manner through your available range of motion while keeping your other knee straight.
    1. While doing so, drive your stepping side’s knee out to the side to keep it aligned over your foot as opposed to letting your knee cave inward relative to your foot.
    2. Keep the entirety of the soles of both feet in contact with the ground as you descend.
    3. As you sit your buttocks back (like if you started to sit on a chair), allow your torso naturally to lean somewhat forward at your hips to maintain your balance. Simultaneously keep your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    4. People can commonly descend until the stepping leg’s thigh is close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes your full range of motion will be affected by your mobility.
    5. Descend as far as you can while keeping your stepping leg’s knee aligned with your foot, soles fully on the ground, and back near a neutral position.
    6. Strive to perform steps 1 and 2 fluidly as a continuous movement.
3. Reverse the movement by squatting up with your stepping leg as you drive through the ground by progressively extending (straightening) your knee and hip until you can push through the ground to step back with your feet together and your torso upright.
    1. Continue keeping your stepping leg’s knee aligned with your foot and your back near a neutral position as you squat up.
    2. At the end of this movement, you should have returned to the starting position as you are standing upright with your feet approximately hip-width apart from each other.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 as you use your other leg to step out to the side while performing your lateral lunge.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the weight down.

    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    4. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
6. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
7. Alternate between steps 4-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
8. Walk forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Stand upright with your feet approximately width apart from each other as your toes are pointing straight forward, and lift your arms up so that they are parallel to the ground.
    1. In this starting position, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you are keeping your chest up and looking straight ahead.
    2. Keep your arms outstretched parallel to the ground throughout your set to provide a counterbalance that helps keep your torso upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Take a long step out to the side as you keep the toes of your stepping foot pointing forward.
    1. The ideal stance width will be influenced by hip mobility, and some trial and error may be needed to determine which stance feels best to you.
    2. As a general guideline, your feet should be further apart than one and a half times your shoulder width, but not so wide that you feel unstable.
    3. While you step to the side, your torso will shift over to that side.
2. As your stepping foot contacts the ground, bend at that side’s knee and hip while sitting your buttock somewhat backward to squat down with your stepping leg in a controlled manner through your available range of motion while keeping your other knee straight.
    1. While doing so, drive your stepping side’s knee out to the side to keep it aligned over your foot as opposed to letting your knee cave inward relative to your foot.
    2. Keep the entirety of the soles of both feet in contact with the ground as you descend.
    3. As you sit your buttocks back (like if you started to sit on a chair), allow your torso naturally to lean somewhat forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but keep your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    4. People can commonly descend until the stepping leg’s thigh is close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes your full range of motion will be affected by your mobility.
    5. Descend as far as you can while keeping your stepping leg’s knee aligned with your foot, soles fully on the ground, and back near a neutral position.
    6. Strive to perform steps 1 and 2 fluidly as a continuous movement.
3. Reverse the movement by squatting up with your stepping leg as you drive through the ground by progressively extending (straightening) your knee and hip until you can push through the ground to step back with your feet together and your torso upright.
    1. Continue keeping your stepping leg’s knee aligned with your foot and your back near a neutral position as you squat up.
    2. At the end of this movement, you should have returned to the starting position as you are standing upright with your feet approximately hip-width apart from each other.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 as you use your other leg to step out to the side while performing your lateral lunge.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a kettlebell or dumbbell and hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows, as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. You can use either a kettlebell or a dumbbell, but some people find holding a kettlebell in the goblet position to feel more stable and comfortable, especially with a fairly heavy weight.
    2. Based on your preference and the load you use, you can transfer your kettlebell or dumbbell into the goblet position through a couple of different approaches.
    3. An effective approach is initially to pick up the weight by the handle through a deadlift motion and set it on an elevated surface (like a bench or plyometric box) with the handle facing up if you use a kettlebell or the handle directed vertically if using a dumbbell (as only one end of the dumbbell is on the surface). Then squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it in the goblet position, and squat up with the weight. If you use a kettlebell, grasp it by its horns (i.e., side handles). If you use a dumbbell, cup your hands around the top end of the weight with the base of your palms by the handle, and your fingers wrapped around the rest of that end of the weight.
    4. With a lighter kettlebell, you can tilt it onto its side with the weight base directed toward you, squat down to grasp its horns, stand upright with it, and curl it into the goblet position.
    5. With a lighter dumbbell, you can also pick it up with one hand and curl it up across your body to be in front of your chest. Then cup your free hand around the top end of the dumbbell with the base of its palm by the handle and fingers wrapped around the top end of the weight before repositioning your other hand to cup the other side of the weight in the same manner.
2. Once you are standing upright while holding the weight to your chest, position your feet into a rather wide stance by taking a large step out to the side with one foot while keeping your other foot on the ground.
    1. How wide a stance may be ideal for you will be influenced by your hip mobility, and some trial and error may be needed to find which stance feels best to you.
    2. As a general guideline, your feet should be further apart than one and a half times your shoulder width, but not so wide that you feel unstable.
3. Point your toes somewhat outward in a position that feels comfortable to you.
    1. In this starting position, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you are keeping your chest up and looking straight ahead.
    2. You will continue holding the weight close to your chest in the goblet position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot. On the side to which you shift your weight, start bending at your knee and hip to squat down toward that side as you push your knee out to that side while keeping your other knee straight.
    1. While doing so, your torso will move closer to the foot on which you shifted your weight as it simultaneously descends.
    2. In the starting position, your knees are inside your feet, and one of the objectives of the descent is to drive your bending knee out toward that side’s foot until your knee is stacked over the middle of your foot.
2. Continue to squat down in a controlled manner to that side through the full range of motion comfortably permitted by your hip mobility and muscle flexibility.
    1. Throughout your rep, keep the sole of the foot to which you shifted your weight fully in contact with the ground as you keep that side’s knee aligned with your foot (as opposed to letting your knee cave inward relative to your foot).
    2. Based on your preference and what feels most comfortable, you can keep the sole of your other foot fully on the ground, or you can keep its heel on the ground while allowing the rest of the foot to lift up off the ground.
    3. As you descend, allow your torso naturally to lean somewhat forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but strive to keep your lower back flat and chest up
    4. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your thigh muscles the deeper you squat.
    5. If you wish, you can pause at the bottom to extend the time you spend stretching your muscles.
3. Reverse the movement by squatting up as you progressively extend (straighten) your knee and hip to drive your torso upward and back toward the center of your stance.
    1. Finish in the same position in which you started, where both knees are straight, and your torso is upright, symmetrically situated between your feet.
    2. If you opted to lift part of your foot (on the side with the straight knee) off the ground during the descent, you will return the entirety of its sole onto the ground during the ascent.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 as you perform your Cossack squat toward your opposite foot.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to bring your feet back together to a near hip-width stance.
