This exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md) while also being able to improve your hip mobility due to the loaded stretch it provides.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the J-hooks of a rack to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on the J-hooks.
    1. The setup for this exercise is essentially the same as for a [back squat](Barbell%20back%20squat%201a25c6f170d8803d8231d083fdd65458.md).
    2. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    3. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
2. Face the center of the bar with approximately hip-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
3. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on your upper back muscles, slightly below the base of your neck, in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Aim for the bar to rest on the muscular shelf formed by your traps above your rear delts on the back of your shoulders and above the bony ridge running across your shoulder blades (known as the scapular spine). This is the high bar position, which is generally recommended over the low bar position for split squats and lunges.
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable on your traps will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back as you squeeze your shoulder blades back together.
    3. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    4. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    5. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    6. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase.
    1. While not required, setting up safety pins is recommended in case you lose your balance or fail a rep during your work sets.
6. Repeat steps 2 and 3 of the setup and proceed to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. While keeping your chest up, take a couple of steps backward and position your feet approximately hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight ahead.
    1. Make sure that you walk far enough backward that the barbell will not contact the rack when lunging forward.
3. While keeping one foot on the ground, take a fairly long step straight forward with your other foot far enough ahead that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee when lunging down.
    1. Like when you step forward while walking, you can initially contact the ground with your front foot’s heel prior to lowering the entirety of your sole onto the ground in a fluid motion, which will likely occur naturally without having to think about it.
    2. When your front foot contacts the ground, you can allow your rear leg’s heel to start lifting up off the ground, which is also likely to occur naturally.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Strive to step forward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    6. If you are new to forward lunges, you may have to try out different step lengths to determine which step length places you in the appropriate position.
4. After contacting the ground with your front foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep your rear leg’s forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes) and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot’s sole in contact with the ground.
    2. Continue keeping your torso upright and your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step forward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step forward during your next rep.
5. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step backward with your front leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
6. Repeat steps 3-5 while lunging forward with your opposite side.
7. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set.
8. Walk forward until the bar contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. Adopt an approximately hip-width stance in a location that has sufficient space in front of you for lunging forward repeatedly.
    1. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one foot on the ground, take a fairly long step straight forward with your other foot far enough ahead that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee when lunging down.
    1. Like when you step forward while walking, you can initially contact the ground with your front foot’s heel prior to lowering the entirety of your sole onto the ground in a fluid motion, which will likely occur naturally without having to think about it.

    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Strive to step forward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    6. Continue keeping your elbows straight and arms directed straight down by your sides, which you will do throughout the entire duration of your set.
    7. If you are new to walking lunges, you may have to try out different step lengths to determine which step length places you in the appropriate position.
2. After contacting the ground with your front foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep your rear leg’s forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes) and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot’s sole in contact with the ground.
    2. Continue keeping your torso upright and your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step forward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step forward during your next rep.
3. Progressively extend (straighten) your knees to lift your body up until you can repeat step 1 to step forward with your rear leg past your stationary leg in the same manner that you initially performed with your other side.
    1. Strive to begin stepping forward as you are lunging up in a fluid manner, which will advance your body forward.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat step 2 with your other side now in the forward position, as you lunge down just like you previously did.
5. Continue repeating steps 1-4 as you progressively lunge forward with alternating legs until you have completed your set or have to turn around and continue lunging in the opposite direction.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to position the bar on your upper back and un-rack it in a stable position.
    1. As an initial approximation, you can position the bar such that it is a few finger widths below the height of your collarbone.
2. Position the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) so that they are slightly below the height of the bar when your rear knee taps the ground at the end of the lowering phase of your split squat.
    1. To find this point for your body, you can perform a rep or two of the split squat with the unloaded bar as described in the “exercise technique” section, but you initially can put the safety stops a little below the top of your hip bones when standing upright as an approximation.
3. Add your desired weight to the bar and face the center of the bar with approximately a hip width stance.
    1. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, position yourself to face the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends (which results in the bottom of the rails being farther in front of you than the top of the rails).
    2. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face.
4. Grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
5. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees to then walk under the bar and situate it on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    2. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar up excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
    5. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a bar on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
    7. If you need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground in order to position the bar on your upper back, you can remove the weights from the bar, lower the height of the bar, and add the weight plates back before repositioning the bar on your upper back.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to tighten your upper back muscles, and unrack it by starting to stand up as you straighten your knees.
2. After the bar rests fully on your upper back rather than the safety bars, rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars with a slight wrist flick before standing fully upright with the bar.
3. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to backward lunges.
    2. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
4. After contacting the ground with your rear foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    7. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step backward during your next rep.
5. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step forward with your rear leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
6. Repeat steps 3-5 while lunging forward with your opposite side.
7. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set and are ready to re-rack the bar.
    1. Re-rack the bar by bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner as you rotate the safety hooks onto the safety bars and return the bar to resting on the safety bars.

## Setting up
1. Stand upright with your back, pelvis (hip bone), and heels against a wall.
    1. Continue keeping your back and pelvis against the wall throughout the rest of your setup and while you perform your wall squat.
2. Step forward with one foot until its heel is just in front of your other foot’s big toe before doing the same with your opposite foot.
3. Step forward with your rear foot to position it symmetrically with your front foot, resulting in your feet now being about two “foot lengths” in front of the wall.
    1. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, somewhat of a range of foot placements can be effectively used for this exercise.
4. Situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other and position your toes so that they are either facing straight ahead or rotated somewhat out based on what feels comfortable to you.
    1. So long as you do not place them on your legs, you can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides or crossed on your shoulders.
    2. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
    3. After finishing adjusting your foot position, your knees should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend at your knees and hips to squat down as you slide your back down the wall in a controlled manner until your thighs are approximately parallel to the ground or somewhat below that point.
    1. Avoid descending beyond the point where you can still keep your pelvis in contact with the wall.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot.
    3. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground as you continue keeping your upper back and pelvis in contact with the wall.
    4. If you wish to prioritize training your quads, focus on transmitting pressure to the wall through your pelvis while minimizing how much pressure you transmit into the wall through your upper back.

    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your pelvis and upper back in contact with the wall, feet fully in contact with the ground, and your knees in line with your feet.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the rack’s J-hooks to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on top of them.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
    3. If you need to bend your knees and hips beyond a mild degree (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) initially to place the bar on your back, you positioned the J-hooks excessively low. This can make it more challenging to rerack the bar at the end of your set.
2. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
3. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on the back of your shoulder muscles and shoulder blades in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. For the low bar squat, you are aiming for the bar to rest on your rear delts on the back of your shoulders, just below the bony ridge running across your shoulder blades (known as the scapular spine).
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable on your rear delts will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back as you squeeze your shoulder blades back together.
    3. If you feel the bar may slide down your back after standing upright, you most likely have it placed too low.
    4. If you notice discomfort from the bar pressing on a bony ridge on your shoulder blades, shifting the bar slightly lower may be more comfortable.
    5. The bar should be clearly lower than the base of your neck, so you should not feel pressure on your neck from the weight pressing on any bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    6. When positioning the bar, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    7. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends when squatting.
6. Repeat steps 2 and 3 of the setup before proceeding to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. Take a couple of steps back, and position your feet near shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing slightly out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip-width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside shoulder width and their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. Throughout your set, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    4. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
6. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
7. Alternate between steps 4-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
8. Walk forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to position the bar on your upper back and un-rack it in a stable position.
    1. As an initial approximation, you can position the bar such that it is a few finger widths below the height of your collarbone.
2. Position a sturdy object near knee height (like a flat exercise bench, split squat roller stand, aerobic step with risers, or plyometric box) behind the Smith machine’s bar at a distance that is about twice the length of your feet.
    1. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you will face the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends (which results in the bottom of the rails being farther in front of you than the top of the rails) during this exercise, so you will place the object behind where you will face.
    2. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face, so it does not matter which side you place the elevated object.
    3. To determine an appropriate distance, you can stand with the middle of your feet directly under the bar, step backward with one foot until its big toe is just behind the heel of your other foot, and do the same with your other foot.
    4. Where the heel of your rear foot reaches after taking these two steps backward is where you can place your elevated object just behind.
    5. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, a range of foot placements can be effectively used, including having the object foot two and a half “foot lengths” behind the bar (which may be even more comfortable for some people).
    6. If it is available, a split squat roller stand will normally be the most comfortable object you can use to elevate your foot during this exercise.
    7. If you are using an angled Smith machine, a bench may potentially be too wide to fit behind you within the machine.
3. Position the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) so that they are slightly below the height of the bar when your rear knee taps the ground at the end of the lowering phase of your split squat.
    1. To find this point for your body, you can perform a rep or two of the split squat with the unloaded bar as described in the “exercise technique” section, but you can initially put the safety stops a little below the top of your hip bones when standing upright as an approximation.
4. Add your desired weight to the bar and face the center of the bar with approximately a hip-width stance.
5. Grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
6. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees to then walk under the bar and situate the bar on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    2. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
    5. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a bar on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
    7. If you need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground in order to position the bar on your upper back, you can remove the weights from the bar, lower the height of the bar, and add the weight plates back before repositioning the bar on your upper back.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to tighten your upper back muscles, and unrack it by starting to stand up as you straighten your knees.
2. After the bar rests fully on your upper back rather than the safety bars, rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars with a slight wrist flick before standing fully upright with the bar.
3. Shift your bodyweight into your front foot before placing the top surface (on the side of your shoe laces) of your rear foot on top of the elevated surface with that side’s knee bent.
    1. To help shift your bodyweight into your front foot, you can lean your torso mildly forward by hinging at your hip as you slightly bend that side’s knee.
    2. Once you have situated your rear foot into the elevated position, you can return to keeping your torso in a fairly upright position, which should involve you maintaining the natural curvature of your lower back, like when you are normally standing upright (rather than excessively arching beyond that position).
    3. Strive to move your rear foot backward in a straight line to keep your feet approximately hip width apart rather than bringing your rear foot closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep the entire sole of your front foot firmly planted on the ground and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. If you are using a split squat roller to elevate your foot, you can contact the surface with the front of your ankle along with your foot, but only your foot will contact the elevated surface if it is flat, like a bench.
4. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep most of your weight shifted onto your front foot while you are primarily using your rear foot to assist with balance.
    2. Continue keeping your torso fairly upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. If you initially situated your elevated object excessively far behind you, you may reach the end of your available hip range of motion before your rear knee reaches the ground.
    7. If you initially situated your elevated object excessively close to you, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. In either case of suboptimal foot placement, you do not need to force your rear knee to tap the ground, and you can adjust how far in front your front foot is situated after finishing your rep.
5. While keeping your front foot firmly planted on the ground and your rear foot in its elevated position, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso fairly upright and knees aligned with your feet while having most of your weight shifted onto the front foot.
6. Repeat steps 4 and 5 until you have finished your set and are ready to step forward with your rear leg prior to repeating the exercise by switching which leg is in the forward position and which leg is in the elevated position.
7. After finishing the set with your other leg forward, step forward with your rear leg before you rerack the bar by bending at your hips and knees as you rotate the safety hooks onto the safety bars and return the bar to resting on the safety bars.

While statically training your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md) and [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), this exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a sturdy object (such as a thick bumper plate, aerobic step, or plyometric box) that you will use as a step onto the floor or approach the bottom step of a staircase.
    1. You can use a range of different heights for your step, and the difficulty of the exercise will increase as the height increases.
    2. If you are new to forward step-ups, selecting an object that is near four inches (10cm) high (which is a typical height of many aerobic steps without additional risers) can be an appropriate starting point, and you can subsequently adjust the height based on how challenging this height is for you.
    3. For reference, a step of a typical staircase is normally near seven inches (18cm) in height.
    4. If you have balance limitations, you can situate your step near a surface (e.g., handrail, wall, power rack) where you can place one hand to assist with maintaining your balance while performing this exercise.
    5. When feasible, setting up where you can face a mirror is recommended to be able to receive visual feedback about your technique.
2. Face the step with your feet approximately hip width apart from each other, as your toes are pointing straight ahead.
    1. You can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides, on top of your hips, crossed in front of your chest, or outstretched in front of you.
    2. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While leaving one foot on the ground, lift your other foot up to place its sole fully in contact with the step.
    1. Make sure that your lead leg’s heel is not hanging off the step.
2. Shift your weight into your lead foot as you mildly lean your torso forward from hinging at your hip.
    1. The forward torso should occur from you moving about your hip while you keep your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    2. In this starting position for the exercise, your rear leg’s knee should be straight.
3. Without pushing off the ground through your rear foot, drive through your lead leg as you push down into the step by extending (straightening) your knee and hip to lift yourself upward until you can place your rear foot onto the step.
    1. Your lead leg’s knee should be straight, and your torso should be upright by the time you place your other foot onto the step.
    2. Aim to lift yourself exclusively through your lead leg as you refrain from performing a calf raise-like motion to push off with your rear leg.
    3. Keep the entire sole (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) of your elevated foot firmly planted on the step and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your rear leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
4. While you are bearing your weight into the foot that started on the step, lift your other foot up and back off the step as you pull that foot’s toes upward through an ankle motion that results in your heel being closer to the ground than the ball of your foot.
    1. This is the opposite of the ankle motion that occurs when lifting your heels up during a calf raise.
5. With your leg that is on the step, sit your buttocks backward to initiate the descent, and bend your knee to lower yourself in a controlled manner until you can contact the ground with the heel of your other foot.
    1. As you sit your buttocks back (like if you started to sit on a chair), allow your torso naturally to lean mildly forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid rounding your back excessively.
    2. Continue keeping your working leg’s knee stacked over your foot, the sole of your foot fully on the step, and your hip bones level.
    3. While the descent does not have to be extremely slow, your lower body muscles should be actively lowering your body rather than gravity simply plopping you down onto the ground.
6. Repeat steps 3-5 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which foot starts elevated on top of the step.

4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of split squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase.
    1. While not required, setting up safety pins is recommended in case you lose your balance or fail a rep during your work sets.
6. Repeat steps 2 and 3 of the setup and proceed to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. While keeping your chest up, take a couple of steps backward and position your feet approximately hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight ahead.
3. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, take a fairly long step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Slightly bend the knee on the side of your stationary foot while doing so.
    2. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to split squats.
    3. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
4. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. While the forefoot of your rear leg will stay in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground with your knee, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and step somewhat farther backward after you ascend before performing your next rep.
5. While keeping both of your feet planted on the ground, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
6. Repeat steps 4 and 5 until you have finished your set. Then step forward with your rear leg to position your feet symmetrically.
    1. Now you have the option of proceeding directly into your next set with your other leg in the forward position, or you can rerack the bar and rest before doing so.
    2. When you are ready to rerack the bar, walk forward until it contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.

This exercise can effectively develop your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat to the most reclined position that allows your back to be well-supported by the backrest when seated with your feet on the foot platform.
    1. Starting with the most reclined position (which tilts the seat down in a closer to horizontal position) generally works well for most people.
    2. Compared to using a closer to upright seat angle, using an appropriately reclined position will allow you to leg press through a longer range of motion without rounding your lower back.
    3. The most reclined setting on certain machine models may be excessively reclined to the extent that the backrest may no longer be able to stabilize your body when leg pressing. If this occurs, your buttocks may lift off the seat, and your torso may slide back along the backrest due to the backrest being angled too close to a horizontal position. However, most leg press machines will not have an excessively reclined seat setting available.
    4. To determine if the seat angle you initially selected is appropriate for you, you can perform a couple of reps with the technique described in the “exercise technique” section without adding any weight plates to the leg press. If you feel stable and well-supported by the backrest, the seat is not excessively reclined, and you have selected a viable seat angle.
    5. Most machines allow you to adjust the seat angle, but some models may not permit you to adjust it.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
    1. Note that the sled will provide resistance even without any additional weight plates. The weight of the sled will vary depending on the specific model, but it commonly weighs near 120lb (54kg).
3. Sit down with your buttocks fully on the seat and your whole back firmly supported by the backrest.
    1. Rather than being rounded in a slouched posture, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Place your feet fully on the middle of the foot platform, hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight up.
    1. While not required, initially placing both feet on the platform before lifting one foot off the platform during the next step can help with positioning your working leg’s foot appropriately.
    2. Many people find that positioning their feet in this manner allows them to leg press effectively. However, specifically what is ideal foot placement may vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility. Some people will feel that they can move their hips more freely with a shoulder-width stance compared to a hip-width stance. Similarly, certain lifters may feel better with pointing their toes slightly out to the side instead of straight up.
    3. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when leg pressing through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different foot placements over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    4. While recognizing that near the middle of the platform works well for many people, you can also adjust how high up on the platform you position your feet based on your preference. Wherever you select should let your heels remain firmly planted on the platform along with the rest of your feet. Placing your feet higher up potentially may bias the gluteus maximus to a degree, while placing your feet lower down potentially may train the quads preferentially. Avoid positioning your feet toward either end of the platform if doing so feels awkward or limits your range of motion.
    5. In the starting position, your knees should be at least slightly bent to allow you to unlock the sled and begin your set. If you have short legs, you potentially may have to situate your feet lower on the platform to reach the platform with slightly bent knees. If your legs are too short to achieve this position with a leg press that has multiple safety stopper heights, you can ask a taller lifter to reposition the platform to a lower starting height that you can reach. If you are using a machine that does not permit a lower starting height of the sled, that particular machine may not be feasible for your body type.
5. Lift one foot off the platform and place it in a comfortable position that will keep that leg from contacting the platform throughout your set.
    1. Situating the resting leg’s foot under the platform with a bent knee is commonly a comfortable position for a variety of machines.
    2. However, where it is best to position your resting leg can vary depending on the specific machine model you are using.
    3. The subsequent directions will apply to the leg whose foot is on the platform, since you will just keep your other leg out of the way during your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your foot into the platform to push it away from you by straightening your knee.
    1. After doing so, the sled should no longer be resting on the machine’s safety stoppers.
    2. Your knee should now be straight or just slightly bent.
3. Unlock the safety handles with your hands to move the safety stoppers out of the sled’s way.
    1. The specific location of the safety handles and how to unlock them can vary among different machine models. However, the safety handles are often near where your hands will be when resting by your sides, and rotating the handles outward will commonly disengage the safety stoppers.
4. For additional stability, firmly grasp the fixed handles (not the movable safety handles) and continue holding them throughout your set.
5. Lower the sled toward you in a controlled manner by simultaneously bending at your knee and hip.
    1. Keep the entire sole of your foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the platform.
    2. Continue keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the seat and your back snugly up against the backrest.
    3. Strive to keep your knee aligned with your second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or third toe as you avoid letting your knee cave inward relative to your foot. It can help to think about pushing your knee out if you notice it starting to drift inward.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively in control the entire time.
6. Continue lowering the sled through the full range of motion you can while keeping your buttocks firmly on the seat, lower back flat against the back rest, and heel fully on the platform.
    1. People can commonly lower the sled until reaching at least 90 degrees of knee bend. However, what constitutes a full range of motion will vary from person to person and be influenced by your individual hip and ankle mobility, along with your foot placement.
    2. If you reached the end range to which your hip can bend, lowering the sled any further would cause your lower back to start rounding. This would be demonstrated by your buttocks starting to curl up off the seat.
    3. If you reached the end range to which your ankle mobility allows your knee to track over your toes, lowering the sled any further would cause your heel to start lifting off the platform.
7. Drive your foot into the platform to push the sled away from you as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knee and hip.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knee fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knee when leg pressing, but avoid forcibly snapping your knee into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. Rather than pushing all through your heel or all through your toes, you should be pushing evenly throughout your foot.
    3. Continue keeping your foot fully on the platform, buttocks on the seat, back against the back rest, and knee aligned over your foot.
8. Alternate between steps 5-7 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
9. After your knee is straightened following the lifting phase of your last rep, lock the safety handles with your hands to return the safety stoppers to being fully under the sled.
10. Lower the sled onto the safety stoppers by bending your knee.
11. Switch which leg is on the platform and perform a set with that side.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. While holding the dumbbells, stand upright with your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, with your toes pointing somewhat out to the sides rather than pointing straight ahead.
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside of shoulder width with their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. Continue holding the dumbbells by your sides throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your knees aligned with your feet.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but keep your back flat and chest up, as you avoid rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
3. Continue to squat down through the available range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
4. Reverse the movement by progressively standing up as you drive through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips until you have returned to a fully upright position.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees stacked over your feet as you squat up.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.

    1. People can commonly lower the sled until their knees are bent by at least 90 degrees. However, what constitutes a full range of motion will vary from person to person and be influenced by your individual hip and ankle mobility, along with your foot placement.
    2. If you reached the end range to which your hips can bend, lowering the sled any further would cause your lower back to start rounding. This would be demonstrated by your buttocks starting to curl up off the seat.
    3. If you reached the end range to which your ankle mobility allows your knees to track over your toes, lowering the sled any further would cause your heels to start lifting off the platform.
7. Drive your feet into the platform to push the sled away from you as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees when leg pressing, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. Rather than pushing all through your heels or all through your toes, you should be pushing evenly throughout your feet.
    3. Continue keeping your feet fully on the platform, buttocks on the seat, back against the back rest, and knees aligned over your feet.
8. Alternate between steps 5-7 until you have completed your set.
9. After your knees are straightened following the lifting phase of your last rep, lock the safety handles with your hands to return the safety stoppers to being fully under the sled.
10. Lower the sled onto the safety stoppers by bending your knees.

## Setting up
1. Place a cushioned object like a Pilates mat or foam pillow onto the ground.
    1. You can use any object that is comfortable for kneeling.
2. Kneel on the cushioned object with your knees approximately hip width apart from each other and your shoelaces (or the top surface of your feet) in contact with the ground as your heels are facing backward.
    1. Your ankles will be in the same position that they would be at the top of a calf raise.
    2. If you have limited ankle mobility and/or find this ankle position uncomfortable, you can place a half foam roller underneath the front of your ankles, which will allow you to adopt a closer to neutral ankle position.
3. Assume an upright torso position while kneeling and position your arms by your sides with straight elbows or in your preferred position.
    1. Where you position your arms can influence the difficulty of the exercise.
    2. If you wish to increase the intensity of the exercise beyond what is present when your arms are by your sides, you can cross your arms across your chest with bent elbows or hold them overhead with straight elbows for an even greater challenge.
    3. Keep your arms in your preferred position throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Keep your glutes squeezed and your core braced throughout the set to help you maintain a rigid trunk position.
2. Lean your torso backward in a controlled manner by bending at your knees through the range of motion that your strength and mobility permit.
    1. The motion should exclusively come from your knees, while your hips and lower back remain near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, which is facilitated by step 1.
    2. Throughout the exercise, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your torso, indicating that you are maintaining an appropriately rigid trunk position without moving your hips.
    3. In particular, avoid letting your lower back excessively arch, which can occur if you do not keep your glutes squeezed and core braced.
    4. The intensity of this exercise will increase as you lean back further, so you can adjust how far you descend based on your ability.
    5. The greatest possible range of motion involves leaning back until your upper back lightly contacts the ground with your knees fully bent, but most people cannot reach this depth without consistently training this exercise over time.
    6. As you progressively lean back, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in one of the quad muscles on the front of your upper thigh, and the flexibility of this muscle can limit how far backward certain individuals can move.
3. Reverse the movement by lifting your torso up through motion at your knees until you have returned to the starting position, where your torso is fully upright.
    1. Continue keeping your thighs and torso aligned with each other as you resist any back or hip motion, as you did not during the descent.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. While standing upright, position your feet into a rather wide stance by taking a large step out to the side with one foot while keeping your other foot on the ground.
    1. How wide a stance may be ideal for you will be influenced by your hip mobility, and some trial and error may be needed to find which stance feels best to you.
    2. As a general guideline, your feet should be further apart than one and a half times your shoulder width, but not so wide that you feel unstable.
    3. If you have balance limitations, you can situate yourself with a surface (e.g., power rack beam) in front of you where you can place one hand to assist with maintaining your balance while performing this exercise.
2. Point your toes somewhat outward in a position that feels comfortable to you and lift your arms up so that they are parallel to the ground.
    1. In this starting position, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you are keeping your chest up and looking straight ahead.
    2. You will keep your arms outstretched parallel to the ground throughout your set to provide you with a counterbalance that can assist with keeping your torso upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot. On the side to which you shift your weight, start bending at your knee and hip to squat down toward that side as you push your knee out to that side while keeping your other knee straight.
    1. While doing so, your torso will move closer to the foot on which you shifted your weight as it simultaneously descends.
    2. In the starting position, your knees are inside your feet, and one of the objectives of the descent is to drive your bending knee out toward that side’s foot until your knee is stacked over the middle of your foot.
2. Continue to squat down in a controlled manner to that side through the full range of motion comfortably permitted by your hip mobility and muscle flexibility.
    1. Throughout your rep, keep the sole of the foot to which you shifted your weight fully in contact with the ground as you keep that side’s knee aligned with your foot (as opposed to letting your knee cave inward relative to your foot).
    2. Based on your preference and what feels most comfortable, you can keep the sole of your other foot fully on the ground, or you can keep its heel on the ground while allowing the rest of the foot to lift up off the ground.
    3. As you descend, allow your torso naturally to lean somewhat forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but strive to keep your lower back flat and chest up
    4. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your thigh muscles the deeper you squat.
    5. If you wish, you can pause at the bottom to extend the time you spend stretching your muscles.
3. Reverse the movement by squatting up as you progressively extend (straighten) your knee and hip to drive your torso upward and back toward the center of your stance.
    1. Finish in the same position in which you started, where both knees are straight, and your torso is upright, symmetrically situated between your feet.
    2. If you opted to lift part of your foot (on the side with the straight knee) off the ground during the descent, you will return the entirety of its sole onto the ground during the ascent.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 as you perform your Cossack squat toward your opposite foot.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to bring your feet back together to a near hip-width stance.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while firmly holding the kettlebells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using kettlebells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both kettlebells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one kettlebell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other kettlebell onto the bench before picking up both kettlebells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the kettlebells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    4. Positioning yourself in a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to backward lunges.
    2. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position with your arms directed down toward the ground as you do so.
    4. Strive to keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
2. After contacting the ground with your rear foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    7. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step backward during your next rep.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step forward with your rear leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright, arms directed down toward the ground, and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging backward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the kettlebells down.
    1. After finishing the last rep, set the kettlebells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).
