## Setting up
1. Adjust the J-hooks of a rack to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on the J-hooks.
    1. The setup for this exercise is essentially the same as for a [back squat](Barbell%20back%20squat%201a25c6f170d8803d8231d083fdd65458.md).
    2. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    3. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
2. Face the center of the bar with approximately hip-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
3. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on your upper back muscles, slightly below the base of your neck, in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Aim for the bar to rest on the muscular shelf formed by your traps above your rear delts on the back of your shoulders and above the bony ridge running across your shoulder blades (known as the scapular spine). This is the high bar position, which is generally recommended over the low bar position for split squats and lunges.
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable on your traps will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back as you squeeze your shoulder blades back together.
    3. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    4. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    5. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    6. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase.
    1. While not required, setting up safety pins is recommended in case you lose your balance or fail a rep during your work sets.
6. Repeat steps 2 and 3 of the setup and proceed to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. While keeping your chest up, take a couple of steps backward and position your feet approximately hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight ahead.
3. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to backward lunges.
    2. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
4. After contacting the ground with your rear foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    7. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step backward during your next rep.
5. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step forward with your rear leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
6. Repeat steps 3-5 while lunging backward with your opposite side.
7. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set.
8. Walk forward until the bar contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance with the back of your legs against the edge of the sturdy elevated object you will use to elevate your foot.
    1. If available, a padded cylindrical object positioned near knee height will normally be most comfortable and is recommended.
    2. A Smith machine bar with a squat/hip thrust pad on it, a barbell on top of the J-cups of a power rack, the leg pad of a lying hamstring curl machine, and a split squat roller stand are all high-quality cylindrical options that you can position to knee height.
    3. Alternatively, you can use an object like a flat exercise bench, couch, or plyometric box with a somewhat compliant surface, but objects with a flat surface tend not to be as comfortable for this exercise.
2. While keeping your feet approximately hip-width apart, step forward with one foot until its heel is just in front of your other foot’s big toe before doing the same with your opposite foot.
    1. This results in your front foot now being about two “foot lengths” in front of where you started when your calves were touching the object you will use to elevate your rear foot.
    2. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, a range of foot placements can be effectively used, including having your front foot two and a half “foot lengths” in front of where you started (which may be even more comfortable for some people).
    3. You can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides, on top of your hips, in front of your chest, etc.
    4. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your bodyweight into your front foot before placing the top surface (on the side of your shoe laces) of your rear foot on top of the elevated surface with that side’s knee bent.
    1. To help shift your bodyweight into your front foot, you can lean your torso mildly forward by hinging at your hip as you slightly bend that side’s knee.
    2. Once you have situated your rear foot into the elevated position, you can return to keeping your torso in a fairly upright position, which should involve you maintaining the natural curvature of your lower back, like when you are normally standing upright (rather than excessively arching beyond that position).
    3. Strive to move your rear foot backward in a straight line to keep your feet approximately hip-width apart, rather than bringing your rear foot closer toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep the entire sole of your front foot firmly planted on the ground and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. If you are using a cylindrical object to elevate your foot, you can contact the surface with the front of your ankle along with your foot, but only your foot will contact the elevated surface if it is flat, like a bench.
2. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep most of your weight shifted onto your front foot while you are primarily using your rear foot to assist with balance.
    2. Continue keeping your torso fairly upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. If you initially positioned your front foot excessively far in front of your elevated object, you may reach the end of your available hip range of motion before your rear knee reaches the ground.
    7. If you initially positioned your front foot too close to the elevated object, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. In either case of suboptimal foot placement, you do not need to force your rear knee to tap the ground, and you can adjust how far in front your front foot is situated after finishing your rep.
3. While keeping your front foot firmly planted on the ground and your rear foot in its elevated position, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso fairly upright and knees aligned with your feet while having most of your weight shifted onto the front foot.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which leg is in the forward position and which leg is in the elevated position.
## Description
While statically training your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md) and [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), this exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Anchor a long looped band at knee height around a power rack’s beam or similarly sturdy object with a smooth surface to which you can anchor your band.
    1. To anchor the band, you can initially fold the band around the beam while holding each end, loop one end of the band into the middle of the other end, and pull that end until it is taught.
    2. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
    3. You can optionally select an anchor point that, after you walk backward, places you near an elevated surface where you can place a hand to provide balance assistance during the exercise.
2. Step into the band with one foot and situate the band on the back of your knee.
    1. If you are wearing shorts, you can situate a hand towel between the back of your knee and the band for comfort since the band pulling on the skin can be uncomfortable (especially for individuals with notable leg hair).
3. Walk backward until the band provides the level of tension you wish to experience.
    1. Up to a certain point, you can progressively increase the band’s resistance by walking back farther. However, be careful not to walk back so far that you overstretch the band, which can be indicated by an abrupt increase in resistance from the band.
    2. The capacity to which a band can safely stretch can vary depending on the company that made it, but avoid stretching the band three times its resting length or greater as a general rule of thumb to minimize the risk of tearing the band.
    3. Naturally, you will not be measuring the length to which you elongate the band. Nonetheless, if the band does not provide sufficient resistance after taking a few steps back from the point at which you started feeling resistance, it may be appropriate to switch to a higher tension band instead of walking any farther back.
4. Position your feet about hip width apart as you are facing the band’s anchor point while standing fully upright.
    1. If you are near a surface that you can reach, you can place one hand on that surface to assist with maintaining your balance throughout the exercise, which can be helpful if you are using a high-tension band.
## Exercise technique
1. Through the leg that is banded, allow the band to pull your knee forward in a controlled manner as your heel lifts up off the ground while you keep the ball of your foot on the ground and maintain an upright torso position.
    1. As you bend your working leg’s knee, keep your other leg’s knee straight with its foot fully in contact with the ground.
    2. Once you feel that your working leg’s knee can no longer track forward with the previously described technique, you have reached the end range of this exercise.
2. Reverse the movement by pulling your knee backward until you have fully straightened your knee with your working leg’s foot flat on the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright as your resting leg’s knee straight.
3. Fully squeeze your quad muscles on the front of your working leg’s thigh for approximately 1-2 seconds in the fully straightened knee position.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the J-hooks of a rack to be slightly below the height of your elbows when standing with your arms at your sides.
2. Place a barbell on the J-hooks, and add weight plates of your desired load.
3. Optionally place a squat pad or hip thrust pad around the center of the bar to provide cushioning for your elbows.
    1. Wearing a fairly thick long-sleeved shirt (like a hoodie) or elbow sleeves can be another means of cushioning your elbows.
4. Face the center of the bar in a near shoulder-width stance.
5. Mildly bend your knees, and hook your elbows under the bar as your elbows are bent and pointing down toward the ground.
    1. Based on your preference, you can clasp your hands together or leave them unclasped.
6. Stand upright with the bar by straightening your knees and hips.
7. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of Zercher squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
8. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of the Zercher squat.
    1. If you train without safety pins and fail a rep, you can dump the weight forward, which may require shooting your hips up and pushing your knees into a more hinged position so that you can dump the bar without hitting your legs. This maneuver increases loading on your lower back (which is not inherently problematic but may be uncomfortable for some people), and it has the potential to damage certain types of flooring, so using the safety pins is recommended.
9. Repeat steps 4-6 of the setup and proceed to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Take a couple of steps backward, and position your feet shoulder-width apart or wider with your toes pointing somewhat out to the sides.
    1. The specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. In the starting position, your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright. Keep your neck in this position throughout your set.
2. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to create tension throughout the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
3. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your knees aligned with your feet.
    1. As you descend, it is natural for your torso to lean forward mildly at your hips to maintain balance, but aim to keep your torso mostly upright, with your back flat and chest up.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot, as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    5. Keep the bar close to your torso with your bent elbows hooked under it throughout your set.
4. Continue to squat down through the available range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
5. Reverse the movement by progressively standing up as you drive through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips until you have returned to a fully upright position.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees stacked over your feet as you squat up.
6. Alternate between steps 3-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
7. Rerack the bar by walking forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup, and you are ready to rest the bar on the J-hooks by once again bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner.

## Setting up
1. If your machine allows you to adjust it, angle the foot plate to a setting that comfortably allows you to train through a full range of motion with your feet fully on the foot plate.
    1. Angling the foot plate closer toward a horizontal position can reduce the amount of ankle mobility required to keep your heels in contact with the foot plate at the bottom of the rep. However, your feet may feel unstable and risk sliding if the foot plate is angled excessively close to being horizontal, so you want to find an appropriate balance.
    2. Some trial and error may be needed to find the ideal foot plate angle for you, but you can initially select an angle that is about halfway in between the two extremes before trying out different settings over time to determine which one you prefer.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
    1. When learning the exercise, you can alternatively leave the machine unloaded, since it will still provide resistance without additional weight plates.
3. Stand on the foot plate, and position your shoulders snugly underneath the shoulder pads as your back is fully in contact with the back pad.
    1. Rather than being rounded in a slouched posture, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. Based on your preference, you can rest your head against the pad or keep it slightly in front of the pad. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    3. If your machine’s back pad extends low enough, you should also be resting the back of your hip bones against the back pad.
4. Place your feet fully on the middle of the foot plate, near shoulder width apart, with your toes pointing mildly outward and the soles of your feet fully on the foot plate.
    1. People commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, but the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Some people will feel that they can move their hips more freely with a wider stance, while others may prefer a closer stance. Similarly, certain lifters may feel better with their toes pointing straight up, while others may feel more comfortable with their toes pointing moderately further outward.
    3. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable while being able to train through a long range of motion, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    4. While recognizing that near the middle of the foot plate works well for many people, you can also adjust how high up on the platform you position your feet based on your preference. Wherever you select should allow your heels (along with the rest of your feet) to be firmly on the foot plate throughout the whole set. Your foot placement should also feel comfortable on your knees and allow you to keep your whole back snugly against the back pad at the bottom of each rep.
    5. Placing your feet higher up may make it easier to keep your heels in contact with the foot plate, more difficult to keep your back flat against the back pad, and potentially bias the gluteus maximus to a greater degree. Placing your feet lower down may make it more difficult to keep your heels in contact with the foot plate, easier to keep your back flat against the back pad, and potentially bias the quads to a degree. Avoid positioning your feet toward either end of the plate if doing so feels awkward and/or limits your range of motion.
    6. In the starting position, your knees should be at least slightly bent to allow you to unlock the machine and begin your set. While exceptions may exist, V-squat machines often do not allow you to adjust the starting height of the pads, so certain machines may not be suitable for rather short lifters.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your feet into the foot plate to push yourself away from it by straightening your knees.
    1. Your knees should now be straight or just slightly bent.
3. Unlock the safety handle with your hand before firmly grasping the hand grips for additional stability.
4. Squat down in a controlled manner by simultaneously bending at your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the foot plate.
    2. Continue keeping your back snugly in contact with the back pad.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet. It can help to think about pushing your knees out if you notice them starting to drift inward.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should avoid dropping down in an uncontrolled fashion.
5. Continue squatting down through the full range of motion you can comfortably perform while keeping your heels fully on the foot plate, along with your back flat against the back pad.
    1. People can commonly descend until their knees are bent by at least 90 degrees, and some lifters can reach the point at which their thighs touch their calves with their knees fully bent. However, what constitutes a full range of motion will vary from person to person and be influenced by your individual hip and ankle mobility, along with your foot placement.
    2. If you reach the end range to which your ankle mobility allows your knees to track forward over your toes, squatting any deeper can cause your heels to start lifting off the foot plate.
    3. If you reach the end range to which your hips can bend, descending any further can cause your lower back to start rounding. This would be demonstrated by your hip bones starting to curl forward off the back pad.
    4. Squatting into a deep position is not inherently problematic to the knees, but there is no need to force yourself into the lowest position possible if you experience knee discomfort at your end range.
6. Reverse the movement by driving your feet into the foot plate to squat up as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees during this exercise, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. Rather than pushing all through your heels or all through your toes, you should be pushing evenly throughout your feet.
    3. Continue keeping your feet fully on the platform, knees aligned over your feet, and your back fully against the back pad.
7. Alternate between steps 4-6 until you have completed your set.
8. After your knees are straightened following the lifting phase of your last rep, engage the safety handle with one of your hands.
9. Bend your knees to lower the weight fully onto the safety arm before stepping off the foot plate.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the dumbbells with a deadlift or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. Stand in approximately a hip-width stance with the back of your legs against the edge of the sturdy elevated object you will use to elevate your foot.
    1. If available, a padded cylindrical object positioned near knee height will normally be most comfortable and is recommended.
    2. A Smith machine bar with a squat/hip thrust pad on it, a barbell on top of the J-cups of a power rack, the leg pad of a lying hamstring curl machine, and a split squat roller stand are all high-quality cylindrical options that you can position to knee height.
    3. Alternatively, you can use an object like a flat exercise bench, couch, or plyometric box with a somewhat compliant surface, but objects with a flat surface tend not to be as comfortable for this exercise.
3. While keeping your feet approximately hip width apart, step forward with one foot until its heel is just in front of your other foot’s big toe before doing the same with your opposite foot.
    1. This results in your front foot now being about two “foot lengths” in front of where you started when your calves were touching the object you will use to elevate your rear foot.
    2. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, somewhat of a range of foot placements can be effectively used including having your front foot two and a half “foot lengths” in front of where you started (which may be even more comfortable for some people).
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your bodyweight into your front foot before placing the top surface (on the side of your shoelaces) of your rear foot on top of the elevated surface with that side’s knee bent.
    1. To help shift your bodyweight into your front foot, you can lean your torso mildly forward by hinging at your hip as you slightly bend that side’s knee.
    2. Once you have situated your rear foot into the elevated position, you can return to keeping your torso in a fairly upright position, which should involve you maintaining the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright (rather than excessively arching beyond that position).
    3. Strive to move your rear foot backward in a straight line to keep your feet approximately hip-width apart, rather than bringing your rear foot closer toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep the entire sole of your front foot firmly planted on the ground and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. If you are using a cylindrical object to elevate your foot, you can contact the surface with the front of your ankle along with your foot, but only your foot will contact the elevated surface if it is flat, like a bench.
    7. Keep your arms by your sides, directed down toward the ground, as you continue holding the dumbbells throughout the duration of your set.
2. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep most of your weight shifted onto your front foot while you are primarily using your rear foot to assist with balance.
    2. Continue keeping your torso fairly upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. If you initially positioned your front foot excessively far in front of your elevated object, you may reach the end of your available hip range of motion before your rear knee reaches the ground.
    7. If you initially positioned your front foot too close to the elevated object, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. In either case of suboptimal foot placement, you do not need to force your rear knee to tap the ground, and you can adjust how far in front your front foot is situated after finishing your rep.
    9. If you initially positioned your front foot excessively far in front of your elevated object, you may reach the end of your available hip range of motion before your rear knee can tap the ground. If you initially positioned your front foot too close to the elevated object, your depth may be limited by your ability to keep your front foot’s heel on the ground. In either case of suboptimal foot placement, you can simply descend through the range of motion in which you can move with proper technique before adjusting how far in front your front foot is situated after finishing your rep.
3. While keeping your front foot firmly planted on the ground and your rear foot in its elevated position, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso fairly upright and knees aligned with your feet while having most of your weight shifted onto the front foot.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which leg is in the forward position and which leg is in the elevated position.
    1. After finishing the set with your other leg forward, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

## Setting up
1. Wrap a thick, long, looped band around a power rack’s beam (or similarly sturdy object with a smooth surface) just below knee height.
    1. Because the purpose of the band is to keep your lower legs upright in a stationary position, a high-tension band will be required (unless you have a viable inelastic substitute like a Spanish squat strap made of polyester).
    2. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
    3. The floor on which you perform this exercise should have sufficient traction so that your feet do not slide forward during your Spanish squat.
2. Step inside each end of the band’s loop with your feet, and situate the band on the top of your calves just below your knees.
    1. If you are wearing shorts, you can situate a hand towel between the back of your knees and the band for comfort since the band pulling on the skin can be uncomfortable (especially for individuals with notable leg hair).
3. Walk backward until the band is fully tensed, which should not require many steps when using an appropriately thick band.
    1. Up to a certain point, you can progressively increase the band’s resistance by walking back farther, but be careful not to walk back so far that you overstretch the band, which can be indicated by an abrupt increase in resistance from the band.
    2. The capacity to which a band can safely stretch can vary depending on the company that made it, but avoid stretching the band three times its resting length or greater as a general rule of thumb to minimize the risk of tearing the band.
    3. Naturally, you will not be measuring the length to which you elongate the band, but if the band does not provide sufficient resistance after taking a few steps back from the point at which you started feeling resistance, it may be appropriate to switch to a higher tension band instead of walking any farther back.
4. Position your feet about shoulder width apart as you are facing the band’s anchor point while standing fully upright with your toes either facing straight ahead or rotated slightly outward based on your preference.
    1. So long as you do not place them on your legs, you can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides or crossed on your shoulders.
    2. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your torso and lower legs in a vertical position, bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner until your thighs are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot.
    3. Strive to keep your shoulders vertically stacked over your hips, as you resist any forward torso lean. 
2. Reverse the movement by pressing through the ground to squat up as you extend (straighten) your knees and hips until you have returned to the starting position with your torso fully lifted up and your knees straightened.
    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your torso and lower legs in a vertical position, feet fully in contact with the ground, and knees in line with your feet.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md) with relatively low loading of your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and [hip adductors](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md), in contrast to most squat variations.

## Setting up
1. Firmly grasp one dumbbell with both hands interlocked around the handle before standing upright with it.
    1. Keep your elbows straight with your arms just in front of your torso. This will position the dumbbell between the inner aspect of your upper thighs. You will continue holding the dumbbell in this position throughout your set.
    2. The two weighted ends of the dumbbells should be horizontally level with each other.
    3. Some people may perform this exercise while holding one weighted end of the dumbbell with its handle in a vertical position. Holding it this way will limit your range of motion, since the lower end of the dumbbell will contact the floor and prevent you from squatting any deeper unless you are standing on a pair of aerobic steps.
2. Position your feet moderately outside shoulder width apart with your toes angled forward and moderately out to your sides.
    1. Initially situating your feet near 1.5 times your shoulder width apart can be an appropriate stance width for many lifters.
    2. Pointing your toes about 30-45 degrees out to the side is an appropriate amount of toe flare for most people. Zero degrees of toe flare would mean your toes are pointing straight forward, while 90 degrees would mean your toes are pointing directly out to your side.
    3. Ultimately, your feet should be situated in a manner that allows you to feel stable and comfortable (particularly in your hips) during this exercise.
    4. Specifically where it is optimal to position your feet can be influenced by your individual body structure and hip mobility. Consequently, you can try out different stance widths and degrees of toe flare over time to determine where you personally feel best.
3. In the starting position, your back and neck should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Start squatting down by sitting your buttocks back while bending at your hips and knees in a controlled manner. Drive your knees outward as you keep your back flat and chest up.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground.
    3. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance. However, you should focus on sitting your hips back rather than pushing your knees forward.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
3. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion that your mobility enables without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a sumo squat will vary among different individuals. Your hip mobility will often determine how deeply you can sumo squat.
    2. If your back starts rounding, heels lift off the ground, or knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting excessively deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
4. Reverse the movement by progressively standing up. Drive your feet through the ground and thrust your hips forward until you are fully upright.
    1. Continue keeping your knees pushed out over your feet, chest up, back flat, and feet fully on the ground.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat’s back pad to a position that aligns your knees with the machine’s pivot point while sitting up against the back pad with your thighs resting on the seat.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to its furthest back position that allows you to begin each rep with the greatest knee bend you can achieve.
    1. Certain machines can be used for leg extensions or hamstring curls based on how the lever arm is positioned.
3. Adjust the shin pad to a position that places it slightly above the front of your ankles on the lowest aspect of your shins when seated with your legs behind the shin pad with your knees bent.
    1. Adjusting this setting exclusively moves the shin pad without moving the lever arm in contrast to step 2, where the machine lever arm and shin pad move together.
4. Add weight plates to the machine, and sit down on its seat with your lower shins behind the shin pad, knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point, and back resting against the back pad.
    1. With the appropriate positioning, it should be comfortable for you to have your knees bent.
    2. Your knees are aligned with the machine’s pivot point if you can draw a straight line through the center of both knees to the pivot point.
5. Adjust the thigh pad to press down snugly against your lower thighs.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Through a controlled kicking motion, progressively extend (straighten) one knee to lift up the shin pad until you have fully straightened your knee while you keep your other knee bent.
    1. While you should not lift the weight in an intentionally slow manner, avoid kicking up in an uncontrolled, jerky motion.
    2. As your lower leg moves through motion at your knee, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set as your thighs remain in contact with the seat.
3. Reverse the movement as you allow your working leg’s knee to bend progressively in a controlled manner to lower the leg pad until you have returned to the starting position with your knee bent as much as the machine permits.
    1. Keep your resting leg’s knee bent as you lower the weight with your other leg.
    2. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower leg down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all four of your [quad muscles](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md), including your [rectus femoris](../Muscles/Rectus%20Femoris%201925c6f170d880f080b7cda6f5f3f0ee.md), which may not be trained as effectively by most squat, leg press, and lunge variations.

### **Training the entirety of your quad**

Exercises that exclusively resist knee extension like machine leg extensions or exercises that chiefly load knee extension while imparting minimal hip extensor loading (like reverse Nordic curls and sissy squats) can serve a distinct role in a training program. A wide array of exercises will train knee extension and hip extension simultaneously such as squats, lunges, step ups, and leg presses. These multi-joint exercises can certainly stimulate meaningful increases in the size and strength of the quads, but they are not ideal for training the rectus femoris, which is the one quad muscle that crosses the hip and functions as a hip flexor along with functioning as a knee extensor. Notably, the rectus femoris does not just weakly assist in flexing the hip, but rather functions as a primary hip flexor that has greater leverage for producing hip flexion torque than any other muscle in the human body at certain joint angles. Because contraction of the rectus femoris can produce a substantial amount of hip flexion torque, its recruitment during a movement that requires both hip and knee extension is less biomechanically efficient than recruitment of the other muscle bellies of the quadriceps. As the rectus femoris contracts more forcefully during a movement like the squat, the hip extensors must work harder to resist the hip flexion torque it produces. Striving to maximize efficiency, the nervous system preferentially recruits the three monoarticular (crossing only the knee joint) muscles of the quad to a greater degree than the rectus femoris during compound exercises where extension simultaneously occurs at the hip and knee joints.

Although some research indicates the rectus femoris does not grow significantly from multi-joint exercises like squats, other studies have reported statistically significant growth in this muscle following such training. When a fairly small magnitude of growth occurs (which is the case even in studies reaching the level of statistical significance), it is unsurprising that the change reaches statistical significance in certain studies but not in others. While the rectus femoris will be trained to a degree during these types of multi-joint exercises, the available body of evidence indicates that the monoarticular quad muscles are much more likely to experience a robust hypertrophy response. Correspondingly, your rectus femoris will almost certainly lag behind your other quad muscles if all of your quad training is performed through multi-joint exercises like squats.

However, during a single joint knee extension exercise where no movement occurs at the hip joint, the rectus femoris is just as active as the monoarticular muscles of the quad, if not more so. This is logical since the hip flexion torque that rectus femoris contraction generates is essentially inconsequential during an exercise that does not simultaneously resist the hip extensor muscles. Congruent with what would be expected, machine seated leg extensions have been demonstrated to produce a considerable degree of hypertrophy of the rectus femoris that is similar to or even more pronounced than that of the three monoarticular quad muscles. While much less studied than machine leg extensions, reverse Nordic curls have been found to yield significant increases in rectus femoris size and the biomechanically similar sissy squat would likely yield a similar result, although it has not been directly studied.

### **Modifying the leg extension for greater muscle growth**

When performed with a sufficiently high relative intensity and appropriate load, machine leg extensions can grow the rectus femoris regardless of how you position the seat, but the seat position can influence the magnitude to which the muscle may grow. Larsen et al. (2025) assessed changes in the thickness of the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis after untrained participants trained single leg machine leg extensions for 10 weeks. For each participant, one leg was trained with an upright torso positioning the hip into 90 degrees of flexion, while the other leg trained with a recline torso positioning the hip into only 40 degrees of flexion. The two interventions resulted in similar vastus lateralis growth, which is unsurprising since that muscle does not cross the hip joint. However, the rectus femoris experienced significantly greater growth from the leg extensions using a reclined torso position compared to the upright torso position. Because the rectus femoris functions as a hip flexor, it shortens in progressively greater angles of hip flexion, while it lengthens as the hip extends. When you are able to lean your torso back when seated, your hip is in a lower angle of flexion compared to when you are seated upright or leaned forward, so your rectus femoris can operate at a longer muscle length when you lean back. The available body of evidence indicates that biarticular muscles (which cross two joints) are likely to experience greater hypertrophy when trained at long lengths compared to shorter lengths, and the rectus femoris fits this trend along with the hamstrings, calves, and triceps.

If you wish to train your rectus femoris at longer lengths during machine leg extensions, you can intentionally position the back pad as far back as you can to allow you to lean further back at your hips when performing the exercise. With this approach, you would still want to align your knee joint with the machine’s pivot point, so you would position your thighs at the same part of the seat as you would if you had the back pad further forward to maintain an upright torso. When using the reclined technique, your upper back would still rest against the back pad, but your lower back would no longer contact the back pad in contrast to if you positioned the seat further forward. While Larsen et al. (2025) specifically utilized a machine that allowed participants to be meaningfully reclined, many leg extensions are not constructed in a manner that would allow users to set up appropriately with only 40 degrees of hip flexion. Consequently, the degree to which you practically can modify your hip position during a machine leg extension will likely be smaller than what was studied by Larsen et al. (2025). This may potentially result in using a reclined torso position on your leg extension machine having a smaller effect on rectus femoris hypertrophy compared to what was reported by Larsen et al. (2025).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the J-hooks of a power rack or squat stand to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on the J-hooks.
    1. Other than setting up an object you use as a step during the next step, the setup for this exercise is the same as for a [back squat](Barbell%20back%20squat%201a25c6f170d8803d8231d083fdd65458.md).
2. Centered under the bar, position what you will use as your sturdy step that will not slide.
    1. As an alternative to a thick bumper plate (which can be the ideal option), you may be able to use an aerobic step that is situated in a manner ensuring that part of the step does not get in your way when setting up.
    2. When using a long aerobic step, it is typically most practical to position the step so that the back end is directly under the bar, while the front end is further in front of the bar outside the rack. Strive to avoid positioning the step where it can interfere with walking out the weight.
    3. You can use a range of different heights for your stepping surface, but selecting an object that is near 3-4 inches (7-10cm) high can be an appropriate starting point, which typically includes 45lb (20kg) bumper plates and aerobic steps without risers.
3. Face the center of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
4. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to then walk under the bar with your feet on each side of the step.
5. Situate the bar on your upper back muscles slightly below the base of your neck in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Aim for the bar to rest on the muscular shelf formed by your traps above your rear delts on the back of your shoulders and above the bony ridge running across your shoulder blades (known as the scapular spine). This is the high bar position, which is generally recommended over the low bar position for split squats and lunges.
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable on your traps will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back as you squeeze your shoulder blades back together.
    3. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back and should situate the bar lower on your traps.
    4. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    5. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
6. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
7. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of split squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
8. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase.
    1. While not required, setting up safety pins is recommended in case you lose your balance or fail a rep during your work sets.
9. Repeat steps 3-6 of the setup and proceed to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your chest up, take a couple of steps backward and position your feet approximately hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight ahead.
    1. Strive to step back far enough that you will be able to lower your rear knee below the height of your front foot during your set.
2. Step up onto the step with the entirety of your sole in contact with the step while leaving your other foot on the ground.
    1. To keep the feet hip-width apart with the front foot’s sole fully on the step (rather than part of the sole hanging off the step), some lifters may initially have to take a very small step to the side, so that one foot is fully aligned with the step.
3. From your split stance position, bend your knees to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the step.
    2. While the balls of your rear foot will stay in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    3. Keep your knees tracking forward in line with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
4. Continue descending through the full range of motion you can while keeping your front foot’s sole fully in contact with the step.
    1. For some lifters, this may involve lightly tapping the ground with the rear knee in the bottom position.
    2. Other lifters may find that they reach the end of their hip’s available range of motion before the rear knee reaches the ground, which will produce a notable stretching sensation in the front leg’s glute as the hip is fully bent.
    3. If you feel a blocked sensation in your front ankle at the bottom before your rear knee descends below the level of your front foot, your rear foot is likely excessively close to your front foot, resulting in your ankle mobility restricting your range of motion. To descend any further would require lifting up your front foot’s heel off the step in this situation. To correct this, you should move your rear foot a bit further back once you are upright between reps.
5. While keeping both of your feet planted, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees and hips to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
6. Repeat steps 3-5 until you have finished your set. Then step down from the step to position your feet symmetrically.
    1. Now you have the option of proceeding directly into your next set with your other leg in the forward position, or you can rerack the bar and rest before doing so.
    2. When you are ready to rerack the bar, walk forward until it contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.

## Setting up
To perform this exercise, you naturally have to position a bar on your back and have sufficient space available for you without any objects or people getting in your way. With a heavy load, it will be easiest to initially set up an Olympic barbell at mid-chest height in a squat stand or the outside of a power rack. However, many gyms will not have the necessary space to perform walking lunges starting from a squat stand/power rack. Alternatively, you can reverse curl or power clean a bar (whether that be an Olympic bar with weight plates or a fixed weight straight bar) to your shoulders, press it up overhead, and lower it onto your upper back. With a fixed-weight straight bar, you will not require as much space width to perform this exercise, but you will be limited in terms of your load potential. Regardless of how you set up, the exercise technique will be the same, but the different set-up methods are described in separate sections based on which one you wish to select.

### **Setting up with a fixed-weight straight bar**

1. Stand upright with a fixed weight straight bar while holding with straight elbows and a mildly outside shoulder width overhand grip, such that your palms are directed toward you.
2. Walk over with the bar to the spot where you could begin your walking lunges.
3. While keeping your elbows straight, sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and your torso to incline slightly forward.
4. As you simultaneously drive your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body, curl the bar upward in an arcing manner by bending at your elbows while allowing your elbows to swing a bit forward.
    1. The hip drive motion, which is similar to the lockout of a deadlift, will bring your torso into a vertical position with your knees straightened.
5. Tuck your chin back to move your head behind the bar.
6. Press the bar upward with as close to a straight bar path as you can perform.
    1. If you wish to do so, you can press the bar overhead with a [push press](Barbell%20push%20press%201a05c6f170d8802d9233da6c4897b8e7.md) technique, where you use leg drive.
7. Immediately after the bar clears the top of your head, mildly push your head forward until your ears are close to being under the bar.
8. Finish the press with your elbows straightened as the bar is overhead.
9. Lower the bar behind your head onto your upper back muscles slightly below the base of your neck in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Aim for the bar to rest on the muscular shelf formed by your traps above your rear delts on the back of your shoulders and above the bony ridge running across your shoulder blades (known as the scapular spine). This is the high bar position, which is generally recommended over the low bar position for walking lunges.
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable on your traps will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back as you squeeze your shoulder blades back together.
    3. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back and should situate the bar lower on your traps.
    4. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.

## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one foot on the ground, take a fairly long step straight forward with your other foot far enough ahead that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee when lunging down.
    1. Like when you step forward while walking, you can initially contact the ground with your front foot’s heel prior to lowering the entirety of your sole onto the ground in a fluid motion, which will likely occur naturally without having to think about it.
    2. When your front foot contacts the ground, you can allow your rear leg’s heel to start lifting up off the ground, which is also likely to occur naturally.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Strive to step forward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    6. If you are new to walking lunges, you may have to try out different step lengths to determine which step length places you in the appropriate position.
2. After contacting the ground with your front foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep your rear leg’s forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes) and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot’s sole in contact with the ground.
    2. Continue keeping your torso upright and your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step forward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step forward during your next rep.
3. Progressively extend (straighten) your knees to lift your body up until you can repeat step 1 to step forward with your rear leg past your stationary leg in the same manner that you initially performed with your other side.
    1. Strive to begin stepping forward as you are lunging up in a fluid manner, which will advance your body forward.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat step 2 with your other side now in the forward position, as you lunge down just like you previously did.
5. Continue repeating steps 1-4 as you progressively lunge forward with alternating legs until you have completed your set or have to turn around and continue lunging in the opposite direction.
    1. After finishing the last rep, set the weight down in the opposite manner to how you initially set up.
    2. You can press the weight up overhead, lower it to the front of your shoulders, and then lower it to the front of your thighs, or you can rerack the bar in a rack (if you initially set up in a rack).

2. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright while firmly holding the kettlebells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using kettlebells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both kettlebells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one kettlebell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other kettlebell onto the bench before picking up both kettlebells from a mechanically advantaged position.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat’s back pad to a position that aligns your knees with the machine’s pivot point while sitting up against the back pad with your thighs resting on the seat.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to its furthest back position that allows you to begin each rep with the greatest knee bend you can achieve.
    1. Certain machines can be used for leg extensions or hamstring curls based on how the lever arm is positioned.
3. Adjust the shin pad to a position that places it slightly above the front of your ankles on the lowest aspect of your shins when seated with your legs behind the shin pad with your knees bent.
    1. Adjusting this setting exclusively moves the shin pad without moving the lever arm in contrast to step 2, where the machine lever arm and shin pad move together.
4. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin and sit down on its seat with your lower shins behind the shin pad, knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point, and back resting against the back pad.
    1. With the appropriate positioning, it should be comfortable for you to have your knees bent.
    2. Your knees are aligned with the machine’s pivot point if you can draw a straight line through the center of both knees to the pivot point.
5. Adjust the thigh pad to press down snugly against your lower thighs.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Through a controlled kicking motion, progressively extend (straighten) your knees to lift up the shin pad until you have fully straightened your knees.
    1. While you do not lift the weight in an intentionally slow manner, avoid kicking up in an uncontrolled, jerky motion.
    2. As your lower legs move through motion at your knees, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set as your thighs remain in contact with the seat.
3. Reverse the movement as you allow your knees to bend progressively in a controlled manner to lower the shin pad until you have returned to the starting position with your knees bent as much as the machine permits.
    1. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower legs down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all four of your [quad muscles](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md), including your [rectus femoris](../Muscles/Rectus%20Femoris%201925c6f170d880f080b7cda6f5f3f0ee.md), which may not be trained as effectively by most squat, leg press, and lunge variations.

### **Training the entirety of your quad**

Exercises that exclusively resist knee extension like machine leg extensions or exercises that chiefly load knee extension while imparting minimal hip extensor loading (like reverse Nordic curls and sissy squats) can serve a distinct role in a training program. A wide array of exercises will train knee extension and hip extension simultaneously such as squats, lunges, step ups, and leg presses. These multi-joint exercises can certainly stimulate meaningful increases in the size and strength of the quads, but they are not ideal for training the rectus femoris, which is the one quad muscle that crosses the hip and functions as a hip flexor along with functioning as a knee extensor. Notably, the rectus femoris does not just weakly assist in flexing the hip, but rather functions as a primary hip flexor that has greater leverage for producing hip flexion torque than any other muscle in the human body at certain joint angles. Because contraction of the rectus femoris can produce a substantial amount of hip flexion torque, its recruitment during a movement that requires both hip and knee extension is less biomechanically efficient than recruitment of the other muscle bellies of the quadriceps. As the rectus femoris contracts more forcefully during a movement like the squat, the hip extensors must work harder to resist the hip flexion torque it produces. Striving to maximize efficiency, the nervous system preferentially recruits the three monoarticular (crossing only the knee joint) muscles of the quad to a greater degree than the rectus femoris during compound exercises where extension simultaneously occurs at the hip and knee joints.

Although some research indicates the rectus femoris does not grow significantly from multi-joint exercises like squats, other studies have reported statistically significant growth in this muscle following such training. When a fairly small magnitude of growth occurs (which is the case even in studies reaching the level of statistical significance), it is unsurprising that the change reaches statistical significance in certain studies but not in others. While the rectus femoris will be trained to a degree during these types of multi-joint exercises, the available body of evidence indicates that the monoarticular quad muscles are much more likely to experience a robust hypertrophy response. Correspondingly, your rectus femoris will almost certainly lag behind your other quad muscles if all of your quad training is performed through multi-joint exercises like squats.

However, during a single joint knee extension exercise where no movement occurs at the hip joint, the rectus femoris is just as active as the monoarticular muscles of the quad, if not more so. This is logical since the hip flexion torque that rectus femoris contraction generates is essentially inconsequential during an exercise that does not simultaneously resist the hip extensor muscles. Congruent with what would be expected, machine seated leg extensions have been demonstrated to produce a considerable degree of hypertrophy of the rectus femoris that is similar to or even more pronounced than that of the three monoarticular quad muscles. While much less studied than machine leg extensions, reverse Nordic curls have been found to yield significant increases in rectus femoris size and the biomechanically similar sissy squat would likely yield a similar result, although it has not been directly studied.

### Modifying the leg extension for greater muscle growth

When performed with a sufficiently high relative intensity and appropriate load, machine leg extensions can grow the rectus femoris regardless of how you position the seat, but the seat position can influence the magnitude to which the muscle may grow. Larsen et al. (2025) assessed changes in the thickness of the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis after untrained participants trained single leg machine leg extensions for 10 weeks. For each participant, one leg was trained with an upright torso positioning the hip into 90 degrees of flexion, while the other leg trained with a recline torso positioning the hip into only 40 degrees of flexion. The two interventions resulted in similar vastus lateralis growth, which is unsurprising since that muscle does not cross the hip joint. However, the rectus femoris experienced significantly greater growth from the leg extensions using a reclined torso position compared to the upright torso position. Because the rectus femoris functions as a hip flexor, it shortens in progressively greater angles of hip flexion, while it lengthens as the hip extends. When you are able to lean your torso back when seated, your hip is in a lower angle of flexion compared to when you are seated upright or leaned forward, so your rectus femoris can operate at a longer muscle length when you lean back. The available body of evidence indicates that biarticular muscles (which cross two joints) are likely to experience greater hypertrophy when trained at long lengths compared to shorter lengths, and the rectus femoris fits this trend along with the hamstrings, calves, and triceps.

If you wish to train your rectus femoris at longer lengths during machine leg extensions, you can intentionally position the back pad as far back as you can to allow you to lean further back at your hips when performing the exercise. With this approach, you would still want to align your knee joint with the machine’s pivot point, so you would position your thighs at the same part of the seat as you would if you had the back pad further forward to maintain an upright torso. When using the reclined technique, your upper back would still rest against the back pad, but your lower back would no longer contact the back pad in contrast to if you positioned the seat further forward. While Larsen et al. (2025) specifically utilized a machine that allowed participants to be meaningfully reclined, many leg extensions are not constructed in a manner that would allow users to set up appropriately with only 40 degrees of hip flexion. Consequently, the degree to which you practically can modify your hip position during a machine leg extension will likely be smaller than what was studied by Larsen et al. (2025). This may potentially result in using a reclined torso position on your leg extension machine having a smaller effect on rectus femoris hypertrophy compared to what was reported by Larsen et al. (2025).
