## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
    1. You can alternatively leave the machine initially unloaded if you are new to this exercise and have yet to determine which belt attachment points are best for you.
2. Connect the belt to the machine’s carabiner at the belt’s attachment points that will allow you to squat through your full range of motion.
    1. This exercise’s potential range of motion and ease of setting up can be determined by the specific attachment point you select.
    2. While you may have to switch to different ones later on, you can initially try the attachment points closest to the middle of the belt, since using them will allow you to squat through the longest range of motion.
    3. Trying out different attachment points may be required because you have to continue setting up to determine if the pair you selected is ideal for you as an individual.
    4. If you select attachment points too close to the ends of the belt, the end of the cable that is linked to the belt will bottom out prematurely when squatting down, which will restrict you to performing partial range of motion squats.
    5. The con of using attachment points close to the middle of the belt is that they can make it more difficult to get into the starting position. Consequently, you ideally do not want to select attachments that are any closer toward the middle of the belt than what is needed for you to squat through a full range of motion.
3. Move the belt toward the front of the machine (away from the weights) on the ground.
4. Step both feet into the belt, and situate it around your hips while squatting down as needed to move the belt into position.
    1. The back of the belt should be securely resting on top of your buttocks in a comfortable position.
    2. Avoid pulling the cable to the extent that you have to work against the machine’s resistance when moving the belt.
    3. Rather than standing on the platform, it can often be easier to get the belt into position while standing on the ground, particularly with machines that have a platform that is noticeably elevated above the ground. However, it may be easier to get the belt around your hips while standing on the platform with certain machines, so you can try that approach if you initially have a difficult time setting the belt around your hips while standing on the ground.
    4. If you are unable to get the belt around your hips regardless of whether you are standing on the ground or platform, you may have to switch to belt attachment points closer toward the ends of the belt.
5. Step up onto the center of the platform with the cable pulling directly downward (rather than being angled forward or backward) between the middle of your feet.
    1. When stepping up, you can hold the machine's uprights for balance assistance if they are within your reach.
6. Position your feet reasonably near shoulder width apart with your toes pointing somewhat out to the sides and the soles of your feet fully on the platform.
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up close to this stance allows them to belt squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when belt squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. Using a stance that is mildly wider than your typical squat stance may sometimes reduce discomfort from the pressure the belt can exert on the groin.
7. Raise your arms and grasp the handle with your hands near shoulder width apart.
8. While standing upright, pull the handle back toward you to disengage the safety arm.
    1. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. Your neck should similarly be near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner.
    1. Lightly use the handles to help you feel stable with a mostly upright torso while allowing your torso naturally to lean mildly forward at your hips to maintain your balance.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the platform as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your entire set.
    3. Allow your knees to track forward to load your quads and help you maintain your balance.
    4. Aim to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    5. As you would during other squats, strive to keep your chest up and lower back flat rather than meaningfully rounding your back.
3. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion that is comfortably enabled by your mobility and your machine.
    1. When setting up appropriately and following the technique points listed under step 2, people can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground. However, what constitutes a full range of motion for a belt squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your heels lift off the platform or knees cave inward at the bottom, you may be squatting excessively deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
4. Reverse the movement by progressively standing up as you drive through the platform to extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Avoid pulling down on the handle with your arms, as you simply hold the handle for stability rather than using your upper body to help your legs.
    2. Continue keeping your feet fully on the platform, knees stacked over your feet, chest up, and lower back mostly flat.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
6. Once you are upright after your last rep, push the handle forward to engage the safety arm before squatting down to return the weight onto the safety arm.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the rack’s J-hooks to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on top of them.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back.

If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. 2. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
3. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on your upper back in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should be securely resting on the muscles of your upper back when squeezing your shoulder blades together.
    2. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    5. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends when squatting.
6. Repeat steps 2 and 3 of the setup before proceeding to the “exercise technique” section.

1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. Take a couple of steps back, and position your feet near shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing slightly out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip-width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside shoulder width and their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.

3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in an intentionally slow and controlled manner while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. Aim for your descent to take a few seconds as you actively control every moment of the lowering phase with a tempo that is clearly slower than your standard squat.
    2. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down.

    1. Strive to perform the lifting phase explosively with quality technique.

## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all four of your [quad muscles](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md), including your [rectus femoris](../Muscles/Rectus%20Femoris%201925c6f170d880f080b7cda6f5f3f0ee.md), which may not be trained as effectively by most squat, leg press, and lunge variations.

### **Training the entirety of your quad**

Exercises that exclusively resist knee extension like machine leg extensions or exercises that chiefly load knee extension while imparting minimal hip extensor loading (like reverse Nordic curls and sissy squats) can serve a distinct role in a training program. A wide array of exercises will train knee extension and hip extension simultaneously such as squats, lunges, step ups, and leg presses. These multi-joint exercises can certainly stimulate meaningful increases in the size and strength of the quads, but they are not ideal for training the rectus femoris, which is the one quad muscle that crosses the hip and functions as a hip flexor along with functioning as a knee extensor. Notably, the rectus femoris does not just weakly assist in flexing the hip, but rather functions as a primary hip flexor that has greater leverage for producing hip flexion torque than any other muscle in the human body at certain joint angles. Because contraction of the rectus femoris can produce a substantial amount of hip flexion torque, its recruitment during a movement that requires both hip and knee extension is less biomechanically efficient than recruitment of the other muscle bellies of the quadriceps. As the rectus femoris contracts more forcefully during a movement like the squat, the hip extensors must work harder to resist the hip flexion torque it produces. Striving to maximize efficiency, the nervous system preferentially recruits the three monoarticular (crossing only the knee joint) muscles of the quad to a greater degree than the rectus femoris during compound exercises where extension simultaneously occurs at the hip and knee joints.

Although some research indicates the rectus femoris does not grow significantly from multi-joint exercises like squats, other studies have reported statistically significant growth in this muscle following such training. When a fairly small magnitude of growth occurs (which is the case even in studies reaching the level of statistical significance), it is unsurprising that the change reaches statistical significance in certain studies but not in others. While the rectus femoris will be trained to a degree during these types of multi-joint exercises, the available body of evidence indicates that the monoarticular quad muscles are much more likely to experience a robust hypertrophy response. Correspondingly, your rectus femoris will almost certainly lag behind your other quad muscles if all of your quad training is performed through multi-joint exercises like squats.

However, during a single joint knee extension exercise where no movement occurs at the hip joint, the rectus femoris is just as active as the monoarticular muscles of the quad, if not more so. This is logical since the hip flexion torque that rectus femoris contraction generates is essentially inconsequential during an exercise that does not simultaneously resist the hip extensor muscles. Congruent with what would be expected, machine seated leg extensions have been demonstrated to produce a considerable degree of hypertrophy of the rectus femoris that is similar to or even more pronounced than that of the three monoarticular quad muscles. While much less studied than machine leg extensions, reverse Nordic curls have been found to yield significant increases in rectus femoris size and the biomechanically similar sissy squat would likely yield a similar result, although it has not been directly studied.

### **Modifying the leg extension for greater muscle growth**

When performed with a sufficiently high relative intensity and appropriate load, machine leg extensions can grow the rectus femoris regardless of how you position the seat, but the seat position can influence the magnitude to which the muscle may grow. Larsen et al. (2025) assessed changes in the thickness of the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis after untrained participants trained single leg machine leg extensions for 10 weeks. For each participant, one leg was trained with an upright torso positioning the hip into 90 degrees of flexion, while the other leg trained with a recline torso positioning the hip into only 40 degrees of flexion. The two interventions resulted in similar vastus lateralis growth, which is unsurprising since that muscle does not cross the hip joint. ## Setting up
1. Adjust the J-hooks of a power rack or squat stand to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on the J-hooks.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
2. Set up the sturdy object near knee height that you will use to elevate your rear foot sufficiently behind the bar.
    1. A cylindrical split squat roller pad is ideal to use if you have one, but flat exercise benches are most commonly used due to their availability, and a plyometric box with a somewhat compliant surface can also be viable. Objects with a flat hard surface (like a metal plyometric box or aerobic step elevated on risers) can be used to elevate the foot, but they can feel uncomfortable, so they are not the best options.
    2. With respect to placement, you could place the object about two “foot lengths” behind where your heels will be after you unrack the bar and take a couple of steps back away from the J-cups. When initially walking back with the bar, the goal is to move far enough away that the bar will not risk bumping the J-cups when your torso leans mildly forward during the exercise. From this position, step backward with one foot until its big toe is just behind your other foot’s heel before doing the same with your opposite foot. You can situate the front of the elevated object where the back of your rear foot’s heel is situated after those steps. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, a range of foot placements can be effectively used, including having your front foot two and a half “foot lengths” in front of where you started (which may be even more comfortable for some people).
3. Face the center of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
4. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on your upper back muscles, slightly below the base of your neck, in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Aim for the bar to rest on the muscular shelf formed by your traps above your rear delts on the back of your shoulders and above the bony ridge running across your shoulder blades (known as the scapular spine). This is the high bar position, which is generally recommended over the low bar position for split squats and lunges.
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable on your traps will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back as you squeeze your shoulder blades back together.
    3. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    4. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    5. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    6. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
5. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
    1. Additionally, use these initial reps to check if you have situated your elevated object an appropriate distance behind the bar. The right distance will typically allow your rear knee to tap the ground lightly at the bottom of the rep while keeping your front foot’s heel fully on the ground.

    3. If the object is not far enough behind you, you may feel a blocked sensation in your front ankle at the bottom before your rear knee reaches the ground, indicating that you have reached the limit of your front ankle’s mobility from your knee having to track far forward. To descend any further would require lifting up your front foot’s heel off the ground in this situation.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase.
    1. While not required, setting up safety pins is recommended in case you lose your balance or fail a rep during your work sets.
7. Repeat steps 3 and 4 of the setup and proceed to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. While keeping your chest up, take a couple of steps backward and position your feet approximately hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight ahead.
    1. Strive to step back far enough that your heels are now about “two foot lengths” in front of the object behind you.
3. Shift your bodyweight into one foot (that will be your front foot) before placing the top surface (on the side of your shoelaces) of your other foot on top of the elevated surface with that side’s knee bent.
    1. Strive to move your rear foot backward in a straight line to keep your feet approximately hip-width apart, rather than bringing your rear foot closer toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    2. Throughout the set, keep the entire sole of your front foot firmly planted on the ground and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    3. If you are using a cylindrical object to elevate your foot, you can contact the surface with the front of your ankle along with your foot, but only your foot will contact the elevated surface if it is flat, like a bench.
4. From your split stance position, bend your knees and hips to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Rather than letting your back round, keep your back flat and chest up throughout the exercise.
    2. You should keep your torso mostly upright, but you can allow your torso to lean forward mildly if that feels natural to you.
    3. Continue keeping the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground throughout the rep.
    4. Keep your knees tracking forward in line with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
5. Continue descending through the full range of motion you can while keeping your front foot’s sole fully in contact with the ground and your back flat.
    1. With the right set-up, this commonly involves lightly tapping the ground with the rear knee in the bottom position. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    2. Alternatively, some people may notice that their front leg’s hip reaches the end of its mobility before the rear knee can tap the ground, which will produce a notable stretching sensation in the front leg’s glute.
    3. What chiefly matters is moving through your individual full range of motion with high-quality technique.
    4. More important than whether you tap the ground with your rear knee
    5. Regardless of where you end the descent, you should strive to move through the full range of motion you can with high-quality technique.
6. While keeping both of your feet planted, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees and hips to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso mostly upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
7. Repeat steps 4-6 until you have finished your set. Then lift your rear foot off the object and step forward to position your feet symmetrically.
    1. Now you have the option of proceeding directly into your next set with your other leg in the forward position, or you can rerack the bar and rest before doing so.
    2. When you are ready to rerack the bar, walk forward until it contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.

    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.

Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.

    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.

    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.

    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat’s back pad to a position that aligns your knees with the machine’s pivot point while sitting up against the back pad with your thighs resting on the seat.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to its furthest back position that allows you to begin each rep with the greatest knee bend you can achieve.
    1. Certain machines can be used for leg extensions or hamstring curls based on how the lever arm is positioned.
3. Adjust the shin pad to a position that places it slightly above the front of your ankles on the lowest aspect of your shins when seated with your legs behind the shin pad with your knees bent.
    1. Adjusting this setting exclusively moves the shin pad without moving the lever arm in contrast to step 2, where the machine lever arm and shin pad move together.
4. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin and sit down on its seat with your lower shins behind the shin pad, knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point, and back resting against the back pad.
    1. With the appropriate positioning, it should be comfortable for you to have your knees bent.
    2. Your knees are aligned with the machine’s pivot point if you can draw a straight line through the center of both knees to the pivot point.
5. Adjust the thigh pad to press down snugly against your lower thighs.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Through a controlled kicking motion, progressively extend (straighten) one knee to lift up the shin pad until you have fully straightened your knee while you keep your other knee bent.
    1. While you should not lift the weight in an intentionally slow manner, avoid kicking up in an uncontrolled, jerky motion.
    2. As your lower leg moves through motion at your knee, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set as your thighs remain in contact with the seat.
3. Reverse the movement as you allow your working leg’s knee to bend progressively in a controlled manner to lower the leg pad until you have returned to the starting position with your knee bent as much as the machine permits.
    1. Keep your resting leg’s knee bent such that this leg does not touch the lower leg pad until you have finished lowering it with your other leg.
    2. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower leg down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

### **Training the entirety of your quad**

Exercises that exclusively resist knee extension like machine leg extensions or exercises that chiefly load knee extension while imparting minimal hip extensor loading (like reverse Nordic curls and sissy squats) can serve a distinct role in a training program. A wide array of exercises will train knee extension and hip extension simultaneously such as squats, lunges, step ups, and leg presses. These multi-joint exercises can certainly stimulate meaningful increases in the size and strength of the quads, but they are not ideal for training the rectus femoris, which is the one quad muscle that crosses the hip and functions as a hip flexor along with functioning as a knee extensor. Notably, the rectus femoris does not just weakly assist in flexing the hip, but rather functions as a primary hip flexor that has greater leverage for producing hip flexion torque than any other muscle in the human body at certain joint angles. Because contraction of the rectus femoris can produce a substantial amount of hip flexion torque, its recruitment during a movement that requires both hip and knee extension is less biomechanically efficient than recruitment of the other muscle bellies of the quadriceps. As the rectus femoris contracts more forcefully during a movement like the squat, the hip extensors must work harder to resist the hip flexion torque it produces. Striving to maximize efficiency, the nervous system preferentially recruits the three monoarticular (crossing only the knee joint) muscles of the quad to a greater degree than the rectus femoris during compound exercises where extension simultaneously occurs at the hip and knee joints.

Although some research indicates the rectus femoris does not grow significantly from multi-joint exercises like squats, other studies have reported statistically significant growth in this muscle following such training. When a fairly small magnitude of growth occurs (which is the case even in studies reaching the level of statistical significance), it is unsurprising that the change reaches statistical significance in certain studies but not in others. While the rectus femoris will be trained to a degree during these types of multi-joint exercises, the available body of evidence indicates that the monoarticular quad muscles are much more likely to experience a robust hypertrophy response. Correspondingly, your rectus femoris will almost certainly lag behind your other quad muscles if all of your quad training is performed through multi-joint exercises like squats.

However, during a single joint knee extension exercise where no movement occurs at the hip joint, the rectus femoris is just as active as the monoarticular muscles of the quad, if not more so. This is logical since the hip flexion torque that rectus femoris contraction generates is essentially inconsequential during an exercise that does not simultaneously resist the hip extensor muscles. Congruent with what would be expected, machine seated leg extensions have been demonstrated to produce a considerable degree of hypertrophy of the rectus femoris that is similar to or even more pronounced than that of the three monoarticular quad muscles. While much less studied than machine leg extensions, reverse Nordic curls have been found to yield significant increases in rectus femoris size and the biomechanically similar sissy squat would likely yield a similar result, although it has not been directly studied.

### **Modifying the leg extension for greater muscle growth**

When performed with a sufficiently high relative intensity and appropriate load, machine leg extensions can grow the rectus femoris regardless of how you position the seat, but the seat position can influence the magnitude to which the muscle may grow. Larsen et al. (2025) assessed changes in the thickness of the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis after untrained participants trained single leg machine leg extensions for 10 weeks. For each participant, one leg was trained with an upright torso positioning the hip into 90 degrees of flexion, while the other leg trained with a recline torso positioning the hip into only 40 degrees of flexion. The two interventions resulted in similar vastus lateralis growth, which is unsurprising since that muscle does not cross the hip joint. However, the rectus femoris experienced significantly greater growth from the leg extensions using a reclined torso position compared to the upright torso position. Because the rectus femoris functions as a hip flexor, it shortens in progressively greater angles of hip flexion, while it lengthens as the hip extends. When you are able to lean your torso back when seated, your hip is in a lower angle of flexion compared to when you are seated upright or leaned forward, so your rectus femoris can operate at a longer muscle length when you lean back. The available body of evidence indicates that biarticular muscles (which cross two joints) are likely to experience greater hypertrophy when trained at long lengths compared to shorter lengths, and the rectus femoris fits this trend along with the hamstrings, calves, and triceps.

If you wish to train your rectus femoris at longer lengths during machine leg extensions, you can intentionally position the back pad as far back as you can to allow you to lean further back at your hips when performing the exercise. With this approach, you would still want to align your knee joint with the machine’s pivot point, so you would position your thighs at the same part of the seat as you would if you had the back pad further forward to maintain an upright torso. When using the reclined technique, your upper back would still rest against the back pad, but your lower back would no longer contact the back pad in contrast to if you positioned the seat further forward. While Larsen et al. (2025) specifically utilized a machine that allowed participants to be meaningfully reclined, many leg extensions are not constructed in a manner that would allow users to set up appropriately with only 40 degrees of hip flexion. Consequently, the degree to which you practically can modify your hip position during a machine leg extension will likely be smaller than what was studied by Larsen et al. (2025). This may potentially result in using a reclined torso position on your leg extension machine having a smaller effect on rectus femoris hypertrophy compared to what was reported by Larsen et al. (2025).

## Setting up
1. Position a sturdy object (such as a thick bumper plate, aerobic step, or plyometric box) that you will use as a step onto the floor.
    1. You can use a range of different heights for your step, and the difficulty of the exercise will increase as the height increases.
    2. If you are new to weighted forward step-ups, selecting an object that is near four inches (10cm) high (which is a typical height of many aerobic steps without additional risers) can be an appropriate starting point, and you can subsequently adjust the height based on how challenging this height is for you.
    3. Alternatively, you can perform this exercise on the lowest step of a staircase, which is normally near seven inches (18cm) in height.
    4. When feasible, setting up where you can face a mirror is recommended to be able to receive visual feedback about your technique.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
3. Face the step with your feet approximately hip width apart from each other, as your toes are pointing straight ahead.
    1. You will continue holding the dumbbells by your sides throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While leaving one foot on the ground, lift your other foot up to place its sole fully in contact with the step.
    1. Make sure that your lead leg’s heel is not hanging off the step.
2. Shift your weight into your lead foot as you mildly lean your torso forward from hinging at your hip.
    1. The forward torso should occur from you moving about your hip while you keep your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    2. In this starting position for the exercise, your rear leg’s knee should be straight.
3. Without pushing off the ground through your rear foot, drive through your lead leg as you push down into the step by extending (straightening) your knee and hip to lift yourself upward until you can place your rear foot onto the step.
    1. Your lead leg’s knee should be straight, and your torso should be upright by the time you place your other foot onto the step.
    2. Aim to lift yourself exclusively through your lead leg as you refrain from performing a calf raise-like motion to push off with your rear leg.
    3. Keep the entire sole (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) of your elevated foot firmly planted on the step and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your rear leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
4. While you are bearing your weight into the foot that started on the step, lift your other foot up and back off the step as you pull that foot’s toes upward through an ankle motion that results in your heel being closer to the ground than the ball of your foot.
    1. This is the opposite of the ankle motion that occurs when lifting your heels up during a calf raise.
5. With your leg that is on the step, sit your buttocks backward to initiate the descent, and bend your knee to lower yourself in a controlled manner until you can contact the ground with the heel of your other foot.
    1. As you sit your buttocks back (like if you started to sit on a chair), allow your torso naturally to lean mildly forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid rounding your back excessively.
    2. Continue keeping your working leg’s knee stacked over your foot, the sole of your foot fully on the step, and your hip bones level.
    3. While the descent does not have to be extremely slow, your lower body muscles should be actively lowering your body rather than gravity simply plopping you down onto the ground.
6. Repeat steps 3-5 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which foot starts elevated on top of the step.
## Description

## Setting up
1. Position a sturdy object (such as a thick bumper plate, aerobic step, or plyometric box) that you will use as a step onto the floor or approach the bottom step of a staircase.
    1. You can use a range of different heights for your step, and the difficulty of the exercise will increase as the height increases.
    2. If you are new to forward step-downs, selecting an object that is near four inches (10cm) high (which is a typical height of many aerobic steps without additional risers) can be an appropriate starting point, and you can subsequently adjust the height based on how challenging this height is for you.
    3. For reference, a step of a typical staircase is normally near seven inches (18cm) in height.
    4. If you have balance limitations, you can situate your step near a surface (e.g., handrail, wall, power rack) where you can place one hand to assist with maintaining your balance while performing this exercise.
    5. When feasible, setting up where you can face a mirror is recommended to be able to receive visual feedback about your technique.
2. Step up onto the step with both feet and position them approximately hip-width apart from each other, with your toes pointing straight ahead, as the soles of your feet are fully on the step, with your toes right by the edge of the step.
3. Raise your arms out in front of you until they are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. You will keep your arms outstretched in this position throughout your set to provide a counterbalance that can assist in keeping your torso upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight into one foot and lift your other foot up and forward so that it is hanging over the edge of the step.
2. On the side hovering off the step, pull your toes and the ball of your foot upward through an ankle motion that results in your heel being closer to the ground than the ball of your foot.
    1. This is the opposite of the ankle motion that occurs when lifting your heels up during a calf raise.
    2. You will keep your foot in this position and that side’s knee straight throughout your set.
    3. Now you are in the starting position for your first rep.
3. With your leg that is on the step, bend your knee as you drive your knee forward over your foot while keeping your torso upright to lower yourself in a controlled manner until you can gently tap the ground with the heel of your other foot.
    1. Keep the entire sole (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) of your elevated foot firmly planted on the step and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down.
    2. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    3. Keep your working leg’s knee aligned with your foot rather than letting your knee cave inward relative to your foot (which you can check in a mirror, along with how level your hip bones are).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your free leg’s heel, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
4. Reverse the movement by driving through your elevated foot as you straighten your knee to lift yourself up until you have returned to the starting position with your knee fully straightened.
    1. During the ascent, continue keeping your working leg’s knee stacked over your foot, the sole of your foot fully on the step, hip bones level, and torso upright.
    2. While you lift yourself up through your elevated leg, avoid pushing off the ground with your foot.
5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which foot is elevated on top of the step.

While biasing your [quads](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md) to a greater degree than your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), this exercise can help train your dynamic single leg stability.

## Setting up
1. Stand upright with your back, pelvis (hip bone), and heels against a wall.
    1. Continue keeping your back and pelvis against the wall throughout the rest of your setup and while you perform your wall squat.
2. Step forward with one foot until its heel is just in front of your other foot’s big toe before doing the same with your opposite foot.
3. Step forward with your rear foot to position it symmetrically with your front foot, resulting in your feet now being about two “foot lengths” in front of the wall.
    1. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, somewhat of a range of foot placements can be effectively used for this exercise.
4. Situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other and position your toes so that they are either facing straight ahead or rotated somewhat out based on what feels comfortable to you.
    1. So long as you do not place them on your legs, you can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides or crossed on your shoulders.
    2. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
    3. After finishing adjusting your foot position, your knees should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend at your knees and hips to squat down as you slide your back down the wall in a controlled manner until your thighs are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. If you wish to prioritize training your quads, focus on transmitting pressure to the wall through your pelvis while minimizing how much pressure you transmit into the wall through your upper back.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot.
    3. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground as you continue keeping your back and pelvis in contact with the wall.
2. Statically maintain this wall squat position until you have finished your set and are ready to squat up by extending (straightening) your knees and hips until you have returned to the starting position.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md) with relatively low loading of your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and [hip adductors](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md), in contrast to most squat variations.

## Setting up
1. Determine what you hold with your hands for balance assistance during your sissy squat.
    1. So long as what you use for assistance is sturdy and will be within your reach to hold throughout the exercise, you have multiple options for what you can select.
    2. With two hands, you can hold objects such as a Smith machine bar locked in place near chest height, an elastic band anchored near a similar level, a door frame, or the posts of a power rack.
    3. If you feel that you only require one hand for assistance, you can also use a variety of objects such as a bedpost, couch, dumbbell rack, incline exercise bench, part of an exercise machine, etc.
2. Stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance with your toes pointing straight ahead, as you are close to what you hold onto to provide assistance with your arms. Simultaneously grasp that object with one or two hands.
    1. Ensure that there is sufficient room for your knee to track forward during the exercise and that you will be able to continue holding the object at the bottom of your rep, along with the top of it.
    2. If you use an object that you will hold with both hands, position yourself a little behind the object.
    3. If you use an object that you will hold with only one hand, you can position yourself to the side of the object.
    4. Specifically how you should hold the object will be dependent on what you selected
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Keep your glutes squeezed and your core braced throughout the set to help you maintain a rigid trunk position.
2. In a controlled manner, push your knees forward while leaning your torso backward. While bending your knees and keeping your thighs aligned with your torso, bear your weight through the balls of your feet while allowing your heels to lift off the ground.
    1. Throughout the exercise, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side, indicating that you are maintaining an appropriately rigid trunk position without moving your hips.
    2. Rather than letting your lower back excessively arch, strive to keep your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright. If you notice your lower back starting to arch beyond this point, it can help to emphasize further bracing your core and squeezing your glutes.
    3. While an extremely slow descent is unnecessary, using a fairly slow tempo is generally recommended to help you focus on achieving high-quality technique through the range of motion that feels right to your knees.
3. Continue slowly descending with step 2’s technique through the full range of motion that is both comfortable to your knees and permitted by your current level of strength and mobility.
    1. The greatest possible range of motion for this exercise involves fully bending the knee to the point where the hamstrings contact the calves, and the knees are able to tap the ground gently. Most individuals are not able to achieve this maximal depth if they are new to this exercise and can consequently move through an abbreviated range of motion.
    2. Prioritize moving through a range that does not produce knee discomfort. This exercise is not inherently dangerous to the knees, but it can meaningfully load the knees, especially in deeper degrees of knee bend. This can increase the risk of experiencing knee discomfort if you immediately move through a long range of motion without progressively building up to that point by training incrementally greater ranges of motion within your comfort zone.
    3. Only descend through the range in which you can avoid bending your hips. For some individuals, the range of motion will be limited by the flexibility of one of the quad muscles, which will be demonstrated by feeling a deep stretching sensation on the front of your hip and thigh.
4. Reverse the movement by straightening your knees to lift your thighs and torso as one unit into an upright position.
    1. Continue keeping your hips straightened so that you can still draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    2. Your knees should track backward until they finish vertically stacked under your hips, like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. Allow your heels to return to the ground naturally.
    4. Aim to use your hands merely for balance assistance rather than pulling yourself up through your arms.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all four of your [quad muscles](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md), including the [rectus femoris](../Muscles/Rectus%20Femoris%201925c6f170d880f080b7cda6f5f3f0ee.md), which may not be trained as effectively by most squat, leg press, and lunge variations.

If you are new to weighted lateral step-downs, selecting an object that is near four inches (10cm) high (which is a typical height of many aerobic steps without additional risers) can be an appropriate starting point, and you can subsequently adjust the height based on how challenging this height is for you.
    3. Alternatively, you can perform this exercise on the lowest step of a staircase, which is normally near seven inches (18cm) in height.
    4. When feasible, setting up where you can face a mirror is recommended to be able to receive visual feedback about your technique.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
3. Step up onto the step with your feet hip-width apart, toes pointing straight ahead, and heels right by the edge.
    1. Your soles should be fully on the step.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot, then lift your other foot up and back so it hangs over the edge of the step.
    1. Continue holding the dumbbells by your sides throughout your set.
    2. Naturally, the side of your body to which you shift your weight will be the working side during this set.
2. On the side hovering off the step, pull your toes and the ball of your foot up toward your shin through an ankle motion that brings your heel closer to the ground than the ball of your foot.
    1. This is the opposite of the ankle motion that occurs when lifting your heels up during a calf raise, and you should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract.
    2. Throughout your set, maintain this foot position and the knee of your non-working side straight.
    3. You are now in the starting position for your first rep.
3. Sit your buttocks back to initiate the descent. Then progressively bend your working leg’s knee and hip in a controlled manner until you can gently tap the ground with the heel of your other foot.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hip to maintain your balance, but keep your back flat and chest up. When starting to descend, you can think about beginning to sit on a chair, which cues the intended hip motion that loads your glute.
    2. Keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down. Imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    3. While letting your working leg’s knee naturally track forward, strive to keep it aligned with your middle toes, rather than letting it inward relative to your foot (which you can check in a mirror, along with how level your hip bones are). Think about driving your knees out to the side if it starts drifting inward.
    4. Keep your elevated heel firmly planted on the step, along with the rest of your sole.
    5. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your free leg’s heel, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram). Lowering yourself slowly can help achieve this very light tap at the bottom.
4. Reverse the movement by driving through your elevated foot to step up into an upright position.
    1. By extending (straightening) your knee and hip, lift your body up completely through your working leg, as you avoid pushing off the ground with your other side’s foot.
    2. Continue keeping your hip bones level and your working leg’s knee aligned with your middle toes.
5. Alternate steps 3 and 4 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side on the step.
    1. Based on your preference, you can keep your non-working side’s foot hovering in the air between reps, or briefly place it on the step before lifting it off for the next rep. The latter approach can be useful if you feel that you need to reset your balance between reps, but either option is valid.

## Setting up
1. Stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance in a location that has sufficient space behind you for lunging backward.
    1. You can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides, on top of your hips, in front of your chest, etc.
    2. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
    3. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to backward lunges.
    2. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
2. After contacting the ground with your rear foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    7. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step backward during your next rep.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step forward with your rear leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging backward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).
1a25c6f170d880f6a715f65d5e8b425b:
## Setting up
1. Adjust the rack’s J-hooks to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on top of them.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
    3. If you need to bend your knees and hips beyond a mild degree (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) initially to place the bar on your back, you positioned the J-hooks excessively low. This can make it more challenging to rerack the bar at the end of your set.
2. Position a sturdy box of your desired height centered within the rack, a couple of step lengths behind the J-hooks.
    1. To train your lower body muscles most effectively, you want to pick a box height that enables you to squat near the depth of what is your full range of motion back squat (i.e., the lowest point at which you can squat with quality technique while keeping your back flat and feet fully on the floor). This depth will vary from person to person, but people can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground.
    2. A squat box or plyometric box is an ideal choice for your box. You can position either type of box with one of its corners directed to the middle point between the J-hooks to give you the greatest freedom in how you situate your feet when box squatting.
    3. Plyometric boxes are often available in gyms at heights of 12in (31cm), 18in (46cm), and 24in (61cm). Box squatting with an 18in (46cm) box, which is near the typical height of a flat exercise bench, restricts the range of motion for most people who are not clearly taller than six feet (183cm). If you currently do not have the mobility to squat down to a 12in (31cm) box with proper form, you can increase the height of the box by placing a thick bumper plate on top of the box to elevate it.
    4. While others have fixed heights like plyometric boxes, the height of certain squat box models can be adjusted to accommodate how deeply you wish to box squat.
    5. If you do not have access to a squat box or plyometric box, you can use an aerobic step provided that the step is rated to withstand at least half the combined load of your bodyweight and the bar weight. You can adjust its height based on how many pairs of risers you stack underneath it.
    6. Alternatively, you may be able to use a flat exercise bench as your box. A bench is excessively tall for many lifters to squat through a full range of motion, but it can be suitable for rather tall individuals, people with limited mobility, and anyone who intentionally wishes to train through a partial range of motion. To fit either a bench or an aerobic step within a rack, you may have to position it with the shorter side facing the side of the rack where you will place the barbell.
    7. While not ideal due to its lower stability, you can also stack bumper plates on top of each other to form a “box” of your desired height. If you opt to do so, make sure that the plates are completely centered on top of each other.
3. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
4. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on your upper back in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should be securely resting on the muscles of your upper back when squeezing your shoulder blades together.
    2. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    5. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
5. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of box squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends when squatting.
7. Repeat steps 3 and 4 of the setup before proceeding to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. Take a couple of steps backward until the box is just behind you. Position your feet near shoulder width apart from each other or mildly wider as your toes are pointing somewhat out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to box squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when box squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Based on your preference, you can use the same stance that you would when back squatting without a box, or you can use a somewhat wider stance, which can facilitate sitting back a bit more.
    4. Throughout your set, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    4. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down until you can sit onto the box in a controlled manner, as you avoid plopping onto the box or rocking back onto the box.
    1. As you sit on the box, your torso should maintain the same degree of forward lean that you had right before reaching the box.
    2. If your torso transitions to a more upright position after sitting on the box compared to at the end of your descent, you have rocked back onto the box.
6. While keeping your core braced and back flat, and feet fully on the ground, allow about half of your weight to deload into the box as you pause on the box for approximately one second.
    1. As a cue, you can think about a scale being on top of the box. If you weigh 200lb (91kg) and have 100lb (45kg) on the bar, the scale should read within the vicinity of 150lb (136kg).
7. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Avoid rocking your torso forward to generate momentum before you start squatting upward.
    2. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
8. Alternate between steps 4-7 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
9. Walk forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise primarily trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat to a distance away from the foot platform that allows you to leg press through a full range of motion without rounding your lower back.
    1. Finding the ideal setting for you as an individual typically takes some trial and error. The only way to know if the seat setting is appropriate is to sit down on the seat and situate your foot on the platform in the same position you will use for your set.
    2. The appropriate setting will allow you to assume the starting position as your lower back maintains close to its natural curvature (like when you are normally standing upright). It should also allow you to keep your foot fully on the platform.
    3. If the seat is excessively close to the foot platform relative to your hip mobility, your lower back may have to round to place your feet on the platform while seated. Alternatively, you may not be able to place your heel firmly in contact with the platform if it is too close.
    4. You should ideally place the seat as close to the foot platform as you can without having to round your lower back or lifting your heel off the platform. Placing the seat meaningfully farther back beyond this point may decrease how much muscle growth the exercise is likely to stimulate.
    5. As a general starting point, you can find the seat setting that allows your knee to be bent by about 90 degrees when your foot is on the platform. If you are able to avoid rounding your lower back when set up with this setting, you can incrementally bring the seat closer until you find your optimal starting position. Alternatively, if you have to round your lower back to set up with your knee bent by about 90 degrees, you can incrementally bring the seat back until you can assume the starting position without rounding your lower back.
2. Select your weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on the seat with your back firmly supported by the backrest.
    1. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Place your feet fully on the middle of the foot platform, hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight up.
    1. While not required, initially placing both feet on the platform before lifting one foot off the platform during the next step can help with positioning your working leg’s foot appropriately.
    2. Many people find that positioning their feet in this manner allows them to leg press effectively. However, specifically what is ideal foot placement may vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility. Some people will feel that they can move their hips more freely with a shoulder-width stance compared to a hip-width stance. Similarly, certain lifters may feel better with pointing their toes slightly out to the side instead of straight up.
    3. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when leg pressing through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different foot placements over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    4. While recognizing that near the middle of the platform works well for many people, you can also adjust how high up on the platform you position your feet based on your preference. Wherever you select should let your heels remain firmly planted on the platform along with the rest of your feet. Placing your feet higher up potentially may bias the gluteus maximus to a degree, while placing your feet lower down potentially may train the quads preferentially. Avoid positioning your feet toward either end of the platform if doing so feels awkward or limits your range of motion.
5. Lift one foot off the platform and place it in a comfortable position that will keep that leg from contacting the platform throughout your set.
    1. Situating the resting leg’s foot under the platform with a bent knee is commonly a comfortable position for a variety of machines.
    2. However, where it is best to position your resting leg can vary depending on the specific machine model you are using.
    3. The subsequent directions will apply to the leg whose foot is on the platform, since you will just keep your other leg out of the way during your set.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
3. Drive your foot into the platform to push it away from you as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knee and hip.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knee fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knee when leg pressing, but avoid forcibly snapping your knee into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner. 
    2. Keep the entire sole of your foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the platform. Rather than pushing all through your heel or all through your toes, you should be pushing evenly throughout your foot.
    3. Continue keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the seat and your back snugly up against the backrest.
    4. Strive to keep your knee aligned with your second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or third toe as you avoid letting your knee cave inward relative to your foot.
    5. Certain machine models will involve you pressing yourself away from a stationary foot platform rather than pressing the platform away from you. The technique remains the same regardless.
4. Reverse the movement by bending at your knee and hip in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. Continue keeping your foot fully on the platform, buttocks on the seat, back against the back rest, and knee aligned over your foot.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively in control the entire time. A sign of an appropriately controlled movement is having the weights you selected lightly contact the rest of the weight stack at the end range. Having the weights lightly touch down will also confirm that you have moved through your full range of motion.
    3. With the appropriate seat position, you should be able to avoid rounding your lower back at the end range of this motion. If you notice your lower back starts rounding at the end, you could finish your rep and mildly move the seat backward before resuming your set.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

This exercise can effectively train your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and multiple [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md).
