## Setting up
1. Stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance with your toes pointing straight ahead.
    1. You can optionally place a soft object (like a cushioned balance pad, yoga block, folded thick towel, folded yoga mat, or a pillow) on the ground directly behind where you will stand if you are not confident in your ability to control the descent and tap your knee to the ground in a gentle manner.
    2. If you opt to place a soft object on the ground, you will use your knee to tap that object instead of the ground, and doing so will mildly reduce the range of motion and difficulty of this exercise compared to if you would lightly contact the ground with your knee.
    3. If you lack the strength or mobility to perform a full range of motion skater squat, you can select the “partial range of motion bodyweight skater squat” from this database.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot and pick the other foot up off the ground by bending that side’s knee by greater than 90 degrees while keeping its thigh directed down toward the ground.
    1. The goal is to bend your knee enough that your foot will not contact the ground before your knee reaches the ground during the descent.
    2. Keep your free leg in this position throughout your set.
2. Raise your arms up with straight elbows until they are approximately parallel with the ground.
    1. Keep your arms parallel to the ground throughout your set.
3. With the leg in contact with the ground, progressively bend at your hip and knee to squat down in a controlled manner until you can gently tap the ground with your free leg’s knee.
    1. It can be helpful to initiate the descent by mildly sitting your buttocks back through a hip hinge motion that somewhat inclines your torso, as if you are closing a car door with your buttocks as your hands are carrying something. 
    2. Keep the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your working leg’s foot firmly in contact with the ground throughout your set.
    3. Strive to have your knee track straight forward in line with your second and third toes (when counting your big toe as your first toe) as you descend, while not letting your knee cave inward.
    4. To the best of your ability, keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. Through motion at your working leg’s hip, your torso should naturally transition to an inclined position rather than remaining completely upright, but strive to keep your back near a neutral position (where it retains its natural curvature or looks flat) as you avoid excessively rounding your lower back.
    7. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your free leg’s knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
4. Reverse the motion you just performed by progressively extending (straightening) your working leg's knee and hip to squat yourself up until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your working leg’s foot fully in contact with the ground as you keep your hip bones level and avoid letting your knee cave inward.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise after switching which foot is in contact with the ground.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable decline bench to your desired decline angle.
    1. An angle near 30 degrees is an appropriate starting point, but you can effectively perform this exercise with a range of decline angles.
    2. The difficulty of this exercise will increase as the decline becomes steeper, so you can adjust the angle to modify the intensity.
    3. Some adjustable benches have a mild decline setting along with incline settings but lack a pad to secure your feet. This exercise specifically uses a decline with a foot/ankle pad.
2. Pick up your desired weight and hold it on one side.
    1. A weight plate, dumbbell, or kettlebell is a viable option that you can use. Select whichever option you find most comfortable to hold to your chest.
3. Sit down on the bench while snugly positioning the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
    2. You can use your free hand to help you get into position.
4. Hold the weight just above your chest with bent elbows as you firmly grasp each side of the weight.
5. Lie down in a controlled manner to position your back and head on the bench.
## Exercise technique
1. As you tighten your abdominal muscles, lift your back and head up off the bench by curling your back. Bring your chest toward your thighs.
    1. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that you have fully rounded your back and cannot bring your chest closer toward your thighs.
    2. Continue holding the weight close to your chest throughout your set.
    3. Given that this is a sit-up rather than a crunch, you will lift the entirety of your back up off the bench.
    4. To train your abdominal muscles dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain in a flat position (which could occur if you predominantly lift your torso up through your hip flexor muscles).
    5. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    6. As a cue for your engaging abdominal muscles, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs toward your hip bones.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your back to the starting position.
    1. Rather than fully relaxing at the bottom, strive to tap the bench lightly with your upper back while keeping your abdominals tensed.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the entire movement.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, or leave the machine unloaded.
2. Confirm that the center of the knee pad is pointing straight forward toward the handles rather than pointing out to either side of the machine.
    1. The knee pad may be swiveled to either side to perform an asymmetrical exercise that emphasizes your obliques, but the pad should be centered for this symmetrical variation.
    2. Machine models commonly permit you to adjust only the load and the knee pad orientation. If your machine has any additional modifiable features (such as handle height), you can adjust them to your preferred settings at this time.
3. Stand directly to the side of the knee pad while facing the handles.
4. Grasp the handles for balance assistance, and kneel on the knee pad, one leg at a time, while resting your forearms and elbows on the arm pads.
    1. Situate your knees near the front of the pad to allow your shins to rest on the pad for stability.
    2. You should be in a tall kneeling position with your chest up and your hips reasonably slightly behind your knees, as opposed to sitting your buttocks onto your heels with your knees fully bent.
    3. Your neck and back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. This should result in your lower back having its natural curvature rather than being excessively arched or rounded.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your knees upward while curling your hip bones up toward your ribs through the range of motion permitted by your mobility and the machine.
    1. To train your abs dynamically, you should be intentionally rounding your lower back by curling your hip bones closer toward your ribs, since this motion is performed by contraction of your abs. As you drive your knees higher up, you will be able to curl your hip bones to a greater degree.
    2. If you lift your knees up while keeping your lower back flat or mildly arched, you may be emphasizing your hip flexors to a greater degree than your abs.
    3. When curling your hip bones appropriately, you should feel meaningful tension in your abs.
    4. You can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the midpoint between your hips, a little below where you would wear a belt buckle. Strive to angle this laser beam upward by curling your hip bones
    5. Keep your chest and arms stationary throughout the exercise as you avoid pulling through your arms or moving your upper body.
    6. Where you precisely end the lifting phase can be influenced by the specific machine you are using, along with your mobility, but finishing with your knees being close to level with your hips is often an appropriate end range.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering your knees and uncurling your lower back until your knees have returned to being slightly in front of your hips.
    1. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should avoid letting gravity rapidly swing you down.
    2. With an appropriately controlled descent, your knees should not rock back behind your hips.
    3. Your lower back should initially uncurl from a rounded position into a flat position before finishing with the mild arch it naturally has. At the end of the lowering phase, your lower back should not be arched beyond what it normally is when standing upright. If your lower back is arching excessively, you most likely are letting your knees rock too far backward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to dismount the machine.
    1. When transitioning from rep to rep, minimize any momentum to the best of your ability as you prioritize controlled movement and avoid swinging.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your back on the ground near an exercise bench or similar sturdy elevated surface, such as a plyometric box or bed.
2. Lift up your legs to position the back of your heels on top of the bench with straight knees.
    1. If you are too close to keep your knees straight on top of the bench, you can scoot backward until you can do so.
    2. You can situate your feet near shoulder-width apart from each other, but it is up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    3. In this position, you can rest the back of your head on the ground and leave your arms on the ground by your sides.
    4. As a modification, you can alternatively perform this exercise with your knees slightly bent if you wish to do so.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels into the ground until your hips are fully extended.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your torso.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

This exercise will primarily train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and three of your four [hamstring muscles](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the lower leg pad to a position that places it slightly above the back of your heels (i.e., on your Achilles tendons) when lying down on the machine with your knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to a position that allows you to begin each rep with your knees straightened.
    1. If the lever arm is too high, you will start each rep with your knees somewhat bent rather than fully straightened. This would prevent you from training through a full range of motion.
    2. Certain machines may allow you to position the lever arm low enough that it could situate your knees beyond fully straightened into a hyperextended position (where your knees are bent in the opposite direction in which they normally bend). This may increase the likelihood of experiencing knee discomfort during this exercise.
    3. The optimal position will allow you to draw a straight line through your knees from your lower legs to your thighs once you are in the starting position.
3. If your machine allows you to do so, adjust the forearm pad to a height that allows you to rest your forearms on it comfortably without excessively arcing your lower back.
4. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
5. Lie down on the body pad with your lower legs under the lower leg pad and your knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point (which will typically result in your knees hanging just off the edge of the body pad).
    1. The front of your thighs, hips, and torso should be in contact with the body pad.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. Your neck should similarly be near a neutral position with its natural curvature like when you are normally standing upright.
    4. In this starting position, your knees should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
    1. If your machine has forearm pads, you should also rest your forearms on them.
2. Pull your toes and feet back toward your shins by moving at your ankles, and maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shins contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankles in the same position in which they would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heels up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankles in this position can increase your hamstring curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
3. Drive your heels toward your buttocks by bending your knees through the full range of motion you can perform. You should typically be able to contact your buttocks or upper thighs with the lower leg pad at the end range.
    1. While your lower legs move through motion at your knees, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
    2. Avoid lifting your hips up off the pad or excessively arching your lower back.
4. Reverse the movement as you allow your knees to straighten progressively in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your knees fully straightened.
    2. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower legs down.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your back on the ground, and your knees bent at least 90 degrees.
    1. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
2. Position the soles of your feet flat against each other while allowing your knees to spread out to your sides and descend closer toward the ground.
    1. When you press your soles together, your knees will naturally spread out, and you do not have to try to push them further apart than this point.
    2. Your knees should be in a comfortable position, and the degree to which your knees will spread out will be influenced by your hip mobility.
    3. The outer aspect of your feet (on the side of your little toes) should be firmly in contact with the ground.
3. Tuck your chin toward your chest and lift your head slightly off the ground.
    1. This can help you keep your lower back flat rather than excessively arched during the exercise, but you have the option of resting your head on the ground if you wish to do so.
    2. You can position your arms in whichever comfortable position you prefer, such as resting by your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving the outer aspects of your feet into the ground and squeezing your glutes. Keep the soles of your feet pressed together and your knees spread apart.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you ideally should be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side if you have the mobility to perform the full range of motion. If your hips feel “stuck” or quite uncomfortable before reaching this point, you may not have the hip mobility to move through the full range with your current knee position. Bringing your knees somewhat higher up and closer together may allow you to lift your hips up higher in a more comfortable manner.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively. Tensing your abdominal muscles may help limit your lower back from arching.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glutes engage during this exercise.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
    1. Continue keeping your soles in contact with each other.
    2. After determining which knee position allows you to comfortably move through your full range of motion, strive to keep your knees in the same position throughout your set.
3. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise will predominantly train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) in a rather shortened position.

## Setting up
1. Place a dumbbell on the ground next to the side of an exercise bench via a squatting motion and sit down on the ground with the side of one of your hips directly next to the dumbbell and your upper back in contact with the bench.
    1. For an easier setup with a heavier dumbbell that has flat sides, you can position the dumbbell with one end on the ground and its handle directed vertically, resulting in one end remaining off the ground.
2. Position your feet out in front of you with your soles flat on the floor and your knees bent to at least 90 degrees.
    1. You can situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, but it is up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can opt to point your toes forward or somewhat out to the sides.
    3. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is also up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
3. Tip the dumbbell onto the crease of your hips in a controlled manner using both hands to have the ends of the dumbbell symmetrically in contact with your upper thighs and the front of your hip bones.
    1. Use your hands to keep the dumbbell in the crease of your hips throughout your set.
4. Tuck your chin mildly toward your chest, and maintain this neck position throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels into the ground and squeezing your buttock muscles.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your torso.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glutes engage during this exercise.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your hip mobility comfortably permits without rounding or excessively arching your lower back.
    1. Some people can descend all the way down until they lightly contact the ground with their glutes, but you can prioritize lowering through the range in which you can achieve through hip motion rather than lower back motion.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Select your weight with the loading pin and position the footplates as closely together as the machine permits.
2. If your machine’s knee pads rotate (which is the case for combo machines that can be adjusted to train hip adduction or abduction), position the pads so that they are facing in toward each other.
    1. The knee pads may permanently face in toward each other in machines that exclusively permit you to train hip abduction.
3. If your machine allows you to adjust the backrest angle, position it fully upright.
    1. Most machines have backrests fixed in an upright position.
4. Sit down on the machine's seat with your torso upright against the backrest. Place your feet on the footplates with the outer aspect of your knees and/or lower thighs contacting the knee pads.
    1. If you have rather short legs, you may have to scoot slightly forward for your knees to reach the pads, which will require you to lean your torso somewhat backward to keep your back against the backrest.
## Exercise technique
1. Spread your legs apart from each other through your hips’ available range of motion.
    1. How far apart you can spread your legs will be affected by your hip mobility.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your legs to move in toward each other in a controlled manner.
    1. At the end range, you can allow the weights you selected to tap the rest of the weight stack. A light tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
    2. After doing so, you should now be in the starting position with your legs as close together as the machine permits.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

While also training several other smaller muscles on the side of your hip, this exercise can dynamically train your [glutes](../Muscles/Glutes%201b95c6f170d88002885bca53f30406d5.md), likely with an emphasis on the [upper region](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%20Upper%20Region%201925c6f170d88070b08aeccda6e5ac88.md) of your gluteus maximus.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the lower leg pad to a position that places it slightly above the back of your heels (i.e., on your Achilles tendons) when lying down on the machine with your knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
2. If your machine allows you to do so, adjust its lever arm (that will align with your shins) to a position that lets you begin each rep with your knees straightened.
    1. If the lever arm is too high, you will start each rep with your knees somewhat bent rather than fully straightened. This would prevent you from training through a full range of motion.
    2. Certain machines may allow you to position the lever arm low enough that it could situate your knees beyond fully straightened into a hyperextended position (where your knees are bent in the opposite direction in which they normally bend). This may increase the likelihood of experiencing knee discomfort during this exercise.
    3. The optimal position will allow you to draw a straight line through your knees from your lower legs to your thighs once you are in the starting position.
3. Add weight plates to the machine.
4. Lie down on the body pad with your lower legs under the lower leg pad and your knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point (which will typically result in your knees hanging just off the edge of the body pad).
    1. The front of your thighs, hips, and torso should be in contact with the body pad.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. Your neck should similarly be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
    4. In this starting position, your knees should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. On the side you are about to train, pull your toes and foot back toward your shin by moving at your ankle. Maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankle in the same position in which it would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heel up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankle in this position can increase your hamstring curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
3. While keeping one knee straightened, use your other leg to drive your heel toward your buttock by bending your knee through the full range of motion you can perform. You should typically be able to contact your buttocks or upper thighs with the lower leg pad at the end range.
    1. While your lower leg moves through motion at your one knee, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
    2. Avoid lifting your hips up off the pad or excessively arching your lower back.
4. Reverse the movement as you allow your knee to straighten progressively in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your knee fully straightened.
    2. Continue keeping your other knee straightened.
    3. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower leg down.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the Roman chair’s pad to a level that positions the top of your hip bones somewhat above the top of the pads when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. This position will allow you to move freely about your hips in contrast to if the pad is contacting the top of your hip bones, which would restrict hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    2. If the top of the pad is positioned much lower than the top of the hip bones (rather than only somewhat lower), some individuals may feel knee discomfort, so a sweet spot can exist for pad placement.
    3. Some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position after initially completing step 2.
2. While placing your hands onto the handles for balance support, step onto the foot plate one leg at a time with the back of your heels in contact with the back of the foot plate, so that the entirety of your soles are in contact with the foot plate.
    1. Position your feet symmetrically in a stance that feels comfortable to you, which can involve pointing your toes somewhat outward or pointing them fairly straight forward.
    2. Situating your feet approximately hip width to shoulder apart from each other will result in a viable stance width, but how wide of a stance you can use will be influenced by the width of your Roman chair’s foot plate.
    3. Your knees should be straight after you have finished setting your feet on the foot plate.
3. Check to make sure that the pad is positioned as described by step 1, and readjust the pad height if it is not prior to resuming your setup. 
4. Cross your arms across your chest with bent elbows to position each hand on the front of the opposite shoulder.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes to keep your torso up such that you can draw approximately a straight line from your legs through your hip and to your torso as opposed to having your torso bent over.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. This is the starting position of the exercise, where your body should look like it does when normally standing upright except at an incline.
2. Begin bracing your core by taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
3. While keeping your core braced, hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner.
    1. Nearly all of the motion should occur from you moving at your hips as you keep your trunk in a static position that maintains the natural curvature of your lower back (as opposed to bending over by rounding your lower back).
    2. Maintain a straight knee position, but you should avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads. 
    3. While hinging at your hips and keeping your hands on your shoulders, you should feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings that progressively intensifies.
    4. Most people will be able to descend until their shoulders are lower than their hips, but how deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    5. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch, you have finished descending through your available hip range of motion.
4. Reverse the movement by lifting your torso up through your hips until you have returned to the starting positio,n where your torso is aligned with your legs.
    1. You can finish the lifting phase by fully squeezing your glutes, which helps cue hip movement at the top as opposed to spinal movement.
    2. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the hip motion you just performed during the lowering phase. 
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.

    1. In this starting position, your knees should be straight and aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Pull your toes and feet back toward your shins by moving at your ankles, and maintain this ankle position throughout your set.

    1. At some point, the machine will stop you from bending your knees any further, but most machines will allow you to bend your knees by at least 90 degrees.
    2. While your lower legs move through motion at your knees, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.

## Setting up
1. Set the foot plate to a height that aligns the machine’s pivot point with your hips while standing on the center of the foot plate with your knees slightly bent.
    1. The pivot point will be the center of the machine’s wheel, about which the lever arm rotates.
    2. Strive to align the pivot point specifically with the bony bump (greater trochanter) that you could feel on the side of your hip.
    3. Some machines do not allow you to adjust the foot plate.
2. Position the machine’s lever arm to point straight down.
    1. This will help you adjust the machine to your body proportions before moving the lever arm into the exercise’s starting position.
3. Adjust the machine’s roller pad to be slightly above knee height when standing on the foot plate.
4. Kick one leg up as high as you can with a straight knee and note the height of your knee before lowering your leg.
5. Rotate the lever arm to arc the roller pad to the height at which you were able to lift your knee.
    1. This will commonly involve rotating the lever arm until it is close to parallel to the ground.
    2. The appropriate setting will enable the machine to provide resistance throughout the full range of motion your hamstring flexibility allows.
6. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
7. Stand in the center of the foot plate while facing the roller pad to align your hips with the machine’s pivot point.
    1. The roller should be in front of your leg that is closer to the weight stack.
    2. The leg further away from the weight stack should not be in the way of the roller pad when it arcs back toward the center of the machine during the exercise.
8. On the side closer to the weight stack, position the back of your knee on top of the roller pad with your knee fairly straight. Firmly grasp the handlebar in front of you with both hands.
    1. To move it into position, you can use your hands to pull down on the roller pad as you swing this leg in toward your other side while marching up before swinging it out onto the roller pad. It can be easier to march your leg with your knee bent before straightening it once it is on top of the roller pad.
    2. Your knee does not have to be completely straight, but it should be sufficiently close to fully straight that you feel a meaningful stretching sensation in your hamstrings. This can be achieved with a mild knee band.
    3. The leg further away from the weight stack should be standing with a slightly bent knee as its foot is flat on the foot plate.
    4. Based on what feels most stable to you, your torso should be upright or mildly leaned forward at your hips.
    5. In this starting position, your hips and shoulders should be level.
    6. The subsequent technique directions will apply to the leg on top of the roller pad, since that is the side you will train with this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your leg down and back in an arcing manner through your hip’s full range of motion. Keep your knee fairly straight throughout your set.
    1. Most people should be able to finish a little beyond the point at which the thigh is in a vertical position. However, how far you personally can drive your leg back will be influenced by your hip mobility.
    2. Strive to have all the motion come from your hip while keeping the rest of your body stationary. The foot of your other leg should remain firmly planted on the foot plate throughout your set.
    3. In particular, avoid excessively arching your lower back, which is a common technique error that can occur when trying to move the roller pad further back than what your hip mobility permits. Appropriately bracing your core can help limit unintended arching.
    4. At the end range, you should feel your glute contract. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glute engage during this exercise.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by bringing your leg forward and upward in an arcing motion.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your knee fairly straight and fully lifted up in front of you. In this position, you should feel a notable stretching sensation in your hamstrings.
    2. Avoid letting the weight rapidly swing your leg forward in an uncontrolled manner.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. To train your other side, you will face the opposite direction.
## Description
While training other lower body muscles to a lesser degree, this exercise will predominantly develop your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).
1a35c6f170d88025a7a1f34e94c394c5:
## Setting up
1. In a location where you have sufficient room to side-step, position a short looped elastic band around both of your lower shins just above your ankles.
    1. Initially inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
2. Stand upright with your feet near shoulder-width apart from each other and your toes pointing straight forward.
    1. Position your arms where you prefer. People often clasp their hands in front of their chest or rest them on their hips, but there is no single correct arm position.
    2. In the starting position, you ideally should feel tension from the band. The band may be slack for some people if they place it around their middle thighs instead of just above their knees.
## Exercise technique
1. Assume an athletic stance by mildly sitting your buttocks back while bending your hips and knees.
    1. Rather than being fully upright, your torso should now be mildly inclined.
    2. Keep your chest up and your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as opposed to being rounded or excessively arched.
    3. Maintain this mild bend in your hips and knees throughout your set.
2. Drive your knees out against the band’s resistance with the intent to align your knees with the middle of your feet.
    1. If you do not resist the band, it can pull your shins and knees inward to the extent that your knees are no longer stacked over the middle of your feet.
    2. Resist letting the band pull your shins or knees inward throughout the set.
3. Take a small step to the side while keeping both knees aligned with the middle of your feet.
    1. This requires continuing to drive both knees out to your sides, which should prompt you to feel meaningful tension in the muscles on the sides of your hips.
    2. Rather than leading with your foot, emphasize pushing out to the side with your lead leg’s knee as your foot remains vertically stacked under your knee.
    3. Your foot should not travel further out to the side than your knee. If it does (which can occur when leading with your foot instead of your knee and/or taking a long step), you will notice that your knee no longer remains aligned with the middle of your foot.
    4. At any moment during your set, including the moment in which your lead foot contacts the ground, you should be able to draw a straight line down from your knee through the middle of your foot. Achieving this alignment is typically only feasible with rather short steps.
    5. Keep your hips and shoulders level throughout the exercise as you avoid letting your trunk tilt to one side.
    6. Maintain the same degree of mild torso inclination rather than bobbing up and down.
4. Once your initial lead leg’s foot contacts the ground, step inward with your trail leg to return to an approximately shoulder-width stance.
    1. The appropriate step length should result in the band remaining tensed the entire set.
    2. If you notice the band becomes slack, you have taken an excessively long inward step with the trailing leg, resulting in your feet being too close together.
    3. As you step inward with your trailing leg, you need to continue driving your other knee outward to prevent the band from pulling it inward.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 to side-step until you are ready to switch which side is your lead leg, and repeat the exercise.
    1. If you reach the end of the space through which you can side-step and do not yet wish to switch your lead leg, you can simply pivot 180 degrees and walk back to the starting position to continue using the same lead leg.
    2. Based on your preference, you could complete all the distance you intend to complete in a set with one lead leg before switching to the other side, or you can switch lead legs multiple times in a set. For instance, you have the option of walking 20yd (18.3m) with your right leg leading before walking 20yd (18.3m) with your left leg leading. Alternatively, you can walk 10yd (9.1m) with your right leg leading before walking 10yd (9.1m) with your left leg leading, and then repeating this for another cycle.

This exercise can train your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), and the [upper region of your gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%20Upper%20Region%201925c6f170d88070b08aeccda6e5ac88.md), along with several smaller muscles on the side of your hip.

    2. While your lower legs move through motion at your knees, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
4. Reverse the movement as you allow your knees to straighten progressively in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your knees fully straightened.
    2. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower legs up.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.

This exercise can effectively train all your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Hamstrings%201b95c6f170d88055a462c40b686f381a.md), which are assisted by your [gracilis](../Muscles/Gracilis%201925c6f170d880938681fbbe8f075831.md), [sartorius](../Muscles/Sartorius%201925c6f170d8801c8493cac115de0546.md), and [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while holding the dumbbells by your thighs with straight elbows as your palms face your thighs.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hand while holding them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
    3. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    4. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    5. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. Once upright, you can situate your palms right next to the outer aspect of the front of your thighs so that your palms face at an angle between backward and in toward each other.
    1. This results in a semi-overhand grip, which is a hybrid between an overhand grip that would direct your palms straight backward (with the dumbbells directly in front of your body) and a neutral grip that would direct your palms straight in toward your sides (with the dumbbells directly to the sides of your body).
    2. You will keep your palms facing this way throughout your set.
    3. Your neck should be near a neutral position when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead, and you will keep your neck in this position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, as if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Bracing will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hip throughout your set.
2. While allowing the other side’s foot to lift up off the floor, begin hinging at the hip on the side to which you shifted your weight by sitting your buttocks back as you let your knee mildly bend.
    1. As you do so, the dumbbells will naturally descend, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    2. Allow your free leg to swing backward as it moves with your torso in a see-saw-like manner, but focus on hinging at the hip of your working leg instead of kicking your other leg back.
    3. Continue keeping your elbows straightened, core braced, lower back near a neutral position, and working leg’s sole fully in contact with the ground while doing so.
    4. To the best of your ability, keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down.
    5. Most of the motion should come from your hip, and your shin should remain in a fairly vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knee fully straightened.
    6. You do not need to focus on bending your knee, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks back while not intentionally keeping your knee locked.
3. Continuing hinging at your hip in a controlled manner until you have reached the end of your available range of motion.
    1. While some people can descend until their torsos are close to parallel to the ground, how deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knee will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer descend without rounding your lower back, you have finished descending through your available range of motion.
4. Reverse the hinge movement by driving through your working leg’s hip to lift yourself up until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straightened, core braced, lower back near a neutral position, hip bones level, and working leg’s sole fully in contact with the ground.
    2. After you are fully upright, you could place your free leg’s foot back onto the ground if you could use some additional balance assistance.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which foot remains in contact with the ground.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
    3. After finishing the last rep with your other side, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

## Setting up
1. Position a pair of deadlift blocks (or a similarly sturdy substitute capable of safely withstanding the load you will use) on the ground far enough apart from each other that the weight plates on a bar will be able to rest fully on the blocks in a stable position.
    1. For this block pull variation, your blocks should be of a low height that situates the bar near the middle of your shins when the loaded bar is resting on the blocks, which often involves no greater than a few inches of elevation  for most people.
    2. To appropriately position the blocks, it can be helpful to have a barbell on the ground and align the blocks about the same distance apart from each other as is the length of the barbell’s shaft (which is the middle part of the bar in between the two thick circular collars).
    3. Aerobic steps can often be used for block pulls while having the option to adjust the height by changing the number of risers you use, but you should be aware of the recommended weight limit if you opt to use heavy loads. The weight limit for aerobic steps will vary by brand, but some of the common brands recommend not exceeding 300lb (136kg) per step, which would result in a 600lb (272kg) limit when using a pair of steps for a block pull. The height of the aerobic step will also vary by brand, but the step itself is commonly near 4in (10cm) in height, with the risers being near 2in (5cm) in height.
    4. With thickness typically ranging from about 1-3.5in (2.5-8.9cm), depending on the weight and brand, bumper plates can also function as blocks that can be stacked on top of each other to provide a range of different heights.
2. After placing a barbell onto the blocks and loading weight plates to the bar, stand upright in approximately a hip width stance close in front of the middle of the bar as the bar is over the middle of your feet with your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly turned out to the sides.
    1. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    2. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
3. With your arms directed down toward the ground, straight elbows, and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward to bring your shins right next to the bar.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    5. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat with the bar close to your shins, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. Immediately after the bar lifts off the blocks, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. The “push the floor away” cue only applies to the very start of the rep since thrusting your hips forward is chiefly what will allow you to lift the weight during this variation.
    2. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    3. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
5. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the blocks.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track slightly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the blocks for a moment (rather than simply tapping the blocks and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the blocks for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferring between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the blocks.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. Connect a straight bar attachment or whichever attachment you prefer to the cable.
    1. As an alternative to a straight bar, you can use a multi-grip curl bar, two D-handles, or a V-bar row grip attachment.
    2. This page will describe the usage of the straight bar attachment, but the exercise can be performed in the same manner with the other attachments, except for how you hold them.
3. While standing directly in front of the middle of the bar, squat down with straight elbows to grasp it firmly with approximately a shoulder-width grip as your palms are directed back toward you (i.e., an overhand grip).
    1. When squatting down, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back.
4. Extend (straighten) your hips and knees to squat upright with the bar while keeping your elbows straight and your lower back near a neutral position.
5. Take a couple of steps backward while allowing your straight arms to lift up in line with the cable’s resistance.
    1. The purpose of stepping backward is to ensure that the cable can provide resistance throughout the full range of motion of your Romanian deadlift.
    2. If you lose resistance from the weights you selected contacting the rest of the weight stack during the exercise, you should take another step backward.
6. Position your feet approximately hip width apart with your soles fully on the ground and toes pointing toward the pulley.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to stabilize your back and maximize performance.
2. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner while keeping your straight arms aligned with the cable.
    1. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal, and your arms will naturally move away from you and toward the pulley.
    2. Avoid trying to push or pull the cable with your arms. Your arms should function merely to transmit force from the cable to your torso, which transmits force to your hips.
    3. Avoid rounding your lower back as you keep your lower back mildly arched or flat throughout the exercise.
    4. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    5. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something, as you keep your chest up (rather than letting your chest collapse through back rounding).
    6. Keep the soles of your feet fully planted on the ground the entire time.
3. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move.
    1. How deeply you are able to hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
4. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so you should continue keeping your arms aligned with the cable, feet fully on the ground, and lower back flat or mildly arched.
    2. Once you have returned to the starting position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid driving your hips in front of your shoulders at the top, which would prompt your lower back to arch excessively. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips appropriately stacked under your shoulders to prevent excessive arching.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
6. Once you are fully upright following your last rep, walk forward until you are directly in front of the pulley before squatting down to return the bar to the ground.

## Setting up
1. Position a short, looped elastic band around both thighs.
    1. The band will provide the greatest resistance to your hip muscles if you place it just above your knees, while it will provide less resistance if you place it higher up your thighs.
    2. You can choose where you situate the band on your thighs based on the level of resistance you wish to experience, and if you are using a particular band for this exercise for the first time, you can adjust its placement during the set if you wish to change the difficulty after starting the set.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground or an exercise mat. Bend your knees to at least 90 degrees to position the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can position your feet shoulder-width apart, but it is up to you whether you would like them closer together or farther apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can point your toes forward or slightly out to the sides.
    3. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is also up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
    4. You can rest the back of your head on the ground and leave your arms on the ground by your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. Push your knees outward against the band’s resistance to have them in line with your feet (as opposed to letting the band pull your knees closer together), and maintain this knee position throughout your set.
    1. You will most likely feel tension in the muscles on the sides of your hips while doing so.
2. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels into the ground and squeezing your glutes.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thighs and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glutes.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glutes engage.
    4. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them at the top.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you can lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 while continuing to keep your knees aligned with your feet until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. In a [deadlift](Kettlebell%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880828c2be446fb07ecff.md) motion, pick up a kettlebell and set it onto the ground with its handle facing up.
    1. Particularly when using what you consider to be a heavy weight, initially lift it up using your hips and knees with your lower back near a flat position rather than being excessively rounded over at your lower back.
2. Stand upright with the kettlebell centered just in front of your toes.
3. Take a step back with one foot until its big toe is just behind the heel of your front foot, before stepping back the same distance with your front foot.
    1. This results in the kettlebell now being about one “foot length” in front of your toes.
4. Position your feet near shoulder width apart, with your toes slightly turned out to the sides or pointing straight ahead. Direct your arms toward the handle with straight elbows.
    1. While using a near shoulder-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility. Feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    2. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
5. Hinge at your hips while allowing your knees to bend until your hands are level with the handle. This will incline your torso forward with a flat back.
    1. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something. After you have hinged through your available hip range of motion (which should prompt you to feel a hamstring stretch), you can bend your knees further to reach the handle.
    2. More motion should come from your hips than your knees, and you should minimize forward knee tracking, since you are not squatting. Try to keep your shins as close to vertical as you can without rounding your back.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
6. With your hands close together and your elbows still straight, firmly grasp the handle with an overhand grip, resulting in your facing backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the handle with the handle pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handle closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handle can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Pack your shoulder blades down to tilt the kettlebell slightly toward you on the closer edge of its base.
    1. In this starting position, you should have your back locked into a stable position with the muscles running up the length of your back fully tensed.
    2. The edge of the kettlebell’s base further in front of you should now be just off the ground
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you lift the weight with your hips.
3. Sweep the kettlebell back between your legs while keeping your torso inclined, lower back flat, and chest up.
    1. You should look like you are hiking a football (referring to American football).
    2. This is the only part of the exercise where you are intentionally using your upper body to move the weight. You should be moving your shoulders as you would during a straight arm lat pulldown.
    3. The objective is to generate some momentum and shift the weight into a position that loads your hips.
4. Once your forearms contact your inner thighs, explosively thrust your hips forward to drive your body into an upright position and swing the kettlebell out in front of you.
    1. Your arms and hands should respectively function as ropes and hooks that are attached to the kettlebell. While they maintain a tight grip and transmit force from your hips to the kettlebell, do not intentionally try to lift the weight with your arms.
    2. With an appropriate load, the power from your hips should be able to drive the kettlebell up until your arms are reasonably close to being parallel to the ground. It is common for the swing height from the first rep or two to be somewhat lower than during later reps since the initial reps help build momentum.
    3. Finish thrusting forward by momentarily squeezing your glutes as you avoid arching your lower back excessively. Stay tall while looking straight ahead rather than leaning back or tilting your head up at the top.
    4. While you focus on driving your hips, your knees will naturally straighten as well. At the top of your swing, you should essentially be able to draw a straight line (when viewed from the side) from your shoulders to your feet that moves through your hips and knees.
    5. Throughout your set, keep your neck and back locked in the same position in which you started while keeping the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground.
5. Allow the kettlebell to swing down and back between your legs while simultaneously hinging your hips with the intent of “catching” the weight.
    1. Rather than waiting for the weight to snap you down, start sitting your buttocks back to hinge as soon as the kettlebell begins arcing downward.
    2. Allow your knees naturally to bend from sitting your hips back while keeping your knees unlocked, but keep your shins close to vertical. You should be sitting back rather than squatting down. The appropriate amount of knee bend should allow you to feel a hamstring stretch at the bottom of the swing.
    3. Continue keeping your core braced, back flat, and chest up while your torso inclines forward from hinging your hips. Particularly avoid letting your lower back round, which may easily occur if you lose core tightness.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 in a rhythmic pendulum-like manner until you have completed your set.
    1. After completing the lowering phase of your last rep, stay tight while allowing the kettlebell to slow to a stop before setting it down.
## Description
This exercise can develop explosive hip extension strength while dynamically training your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the lower leg pad to a position that places it slightly above the back of your heels (i.e., on your Achilles tendons) when lying down on the machine with your knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to a position that allows you to begin each rep with your knees straightened.
    1. If the lever arm is too high, you will start each rep with your knees somewhat bent rather than fully straightened. This would prevent you from training through a full range of motion.
    2. Certain machines may allow you to position the lever arm low enough that it could situate your knees beyond fully straightened into a hyperextended position (where your knees are bent in the opposite direction in which they normally bend). This may increase the likelihood of experiencing knee discomfort during this exercise.
    3. The optimal position will allow you to draw a straight line through your knees from your lower legs to your thighs once you are in the starting position.
3. If your machine allows you to do so, adjust the forearm pad to a height that allows you to rest your forearms on it comfortably without excessively arcing your lower back.
4. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
5. Lie down on the body pad with your lower legs under the lower leg pad and your knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point (which will typically result in your knees hanging just off the edge of the body pad).
    1. The front of your thighs, hips, and torso should be in contact with the body pad.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. Your neck should similarly be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
    4. In this starting position, your knees should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
    1. If your machine has forearm pads, you should also rest your forearms on them.
2. On the side you are about to train, pull your toes and foot back toward your shin by moving at your ankle. Maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankle in the same position in which it would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heel up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankle in this position can increase your hamstring curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
3. While keeping one knee straightened, use your other leg to drive your heel toward your buttock by bending your knee through the full range of motion you can perform. You should typically be able to contact your buttocks or upper thighs with the lower leg pad at the end range.
    1. While your lower leg moves through motion at your one knee, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
    2. Avoid lifting your hips up off the pad or excessively arching your lower back.
4. Reverse the movement as you allow your knee to straighten progressively in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your knee fully straightened.
    2. Continue keeping your other knee straightened.
    3. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower leg down.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your back on the ground or an exercise mat. Bend your knees to at least 90 degrees to position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your feet near hip-width apart.
    1. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is also up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
    2. In this position, you can have your toes pointing forward, rest the back of your head on the ground, and leave your arms on the ground by your sides.
2. While leaving one foot on the ground, lift the other foot off the ground by marching that side’s thigh up while keeping your knee bent, or by straightening your knee while leaving that side’s thigh aligned with the thigh of your other leg.
    1. Either position for the free leg is viable, so you can go with whichever you prefer, but keeping the knee straight may make the exercise mildly more challenging than keeping it bent.
    2. Keep one foot off the ground in the static position of your choice throughout the set you perform with your other side.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heel into the ground and squeezing your glute.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side (on the side of your body with the foot contacting the ground). Your thigh and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glute.
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glute engage.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to contact the ground with your buttocks lightly.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
