## Setting up
1. Position a short looped elastic band around both of your lower thighs in a location where you have sufficient room to side-step.
    1. The band will provide the greatest resistance to your hip muscles if you place it just above your knees, while it will provide less resistance if you place it higher up your thighs.
    2. You can choose specifically where you situate the band on your thighs based on the level of resistance you wish to experience. If you are using a particular band for this exercise for the first time, you can adjust its placement during the set if you wish to change the difficulty after starting the set.
    3. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
2. Stand upright with your feet near shoulder-width apart from each other and your toes pointing straight forward.
    1. Position your arms where you prefer. People often clasp their hands in front of their chest or rest them on their hips, but there is no single correct arm position.
    2. In the starting position, you ideally should feel tension from the band. The band may be slack for some people if they place it around their middle thighs instead of just above their knees.
## Exercise technique
1. Assume an athletic stance by mildly sitting your buttocks back while bending your hips and knees.
    1. Rather than being fully upright, your torso should now be mildly inclined.
    2. Keep your chest up and your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as opposed to being rounded or excessively arched.
    3. Maintain this mild bend in your hips and knees throughout your set.
2. Drive your knees out against the band with the intent to align your knees with the middle of your feet.
    1. If you do not resist the band, it can pull your knees inward to the extent that they are no longer stacked over the middle of your feet.
    2. Resist letting the band pull your knees inward throughout the set.
3. Take a small step to the side while keeping both knees aligned with the middle of your feet.
    1. This requires continuing to drive both knees out to your sides against the band, which should prompt you to feel meaningful tension in the muscles on the sides of your hips.
    2. Rather than leading with your foot, emphasize pushing out to the side with your lead leg’s knee as your foot remains vertically stacked under your knee.
    3. Your foot should not travel further out to the side than your knee. If it does (which can occur when leading with your foot instead of your knee and/or taking a long step), you will notice that your knee no longer remains aligned with the middle of your foot.
    4. At any moment during your set, including the moment in which your lead foot contacts the ground, you should be able to draw a straight line down from your knee through the middle of your foot. Achieving this alignment is typically only feasible with rather short steps.
    5. Keep your hips and shoulders level throughout the exercise as you avoid letting your trunk tilt to one side.
    6. Maintain the same degree of mild torso inclination rather than bobbing up and down.
4. Once your initial lead leg’s foot contacts the ground, step inward with your trail leg to return to an approximately shoulder width stance.
    1. The appropriate step length should result in the band remaining tensed the entire set.
    2. If you notice the band becomes slack, you have taken an excessively long inward step with the trail leg, resulting in your feet being too close together.
    3. As you step inward with your trail leg, you need to continue driving your other knee outward to prevent the band from pulling it inward.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 to side-step until you are ready to switch which side is your lead leg and repeat the exercise.
    1. If you reach the end of the space through which you can side-step and do not yet wish to switch your lead leg, you can simply pivot 180 degrees and walk back to the starting position to continue using the same lead leg.
    2. Based on your preference, you could complete all the distance you intend to complete in a set with one lead leg before switching to the other side, or you can switch lead legs multiple times in a set. For instance, you have the option of walking 20yd (18.3m) with your right leg leading before walking 20yd (18.3m) with your left leg leading. Alternatively, you can walk 10yd (9.1m) with your right leg leading before walking 10yd (9.1m) with your left leg leading, and then repeating this for another cycle.

## Setting up
1. Determine what you will use to anchor your feet securely during the exercise.
    1. You want to have something very stable positioned slightly above the back of your heels (i.e., on your Achilles tendons) while you are able to kneel comfortably on a relatively soft surface such as a foam pad, pillow, or rolled-up exercise mat.
    2. A person who is sufficiently strong and heavy can anchor your feet if you have access to an appropriate partner.
    3. Without specialized equipment, you can alternatively anchor your feet under a barbell with a squat pad that is sufficiently loaded with at least bodyweight. The barbell should be loaded with large-diameter plates to provide room for you to fit your lower legs under it with your toes on the ground. The bar should also be anchored so that it does not roll forward. Placing the barbell inside a power rack against the posts or placing heavy bumper plates in front of the barbell weight plates can stop it from rolling.
    4. If you have access to specialized Nordic hamstring curl equipment (e.g., a Nordic hamstring curl bench or strap), you can set that up. A strap will also require using an anchor point, like a flat exercise bench, power rack, or door, depending on which type of strap you are using. Specifically how you would set up different types of specialized equipment will vary based on what you are using.
2. Securely anchor your lower legs while kneeling on a comfortable surface with an upright torso. The anchor point should snugly contact the back of your lower leg, slightly above the back of your heels.
    1. The soles of your feet should be facing backward while not contacting the ground.
    2. Your knees should be approximately hip width apart as your thighs are completely vertical.
    3. You should be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your torso.
    4. Your back and neck should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    5. You can position your feet in the way that feels most comfortable with your setup. One option involves pointing your feet like when hitting the gas pedal, which will result in your toes being behind your heels. Alternatively, you can situate your feet in a closer to vertical position with your toes under your heels.
    6. You can situate your arms by your side or have your palms facing forward a little in front of your chest with your elbows bent. Wherever you position your arms should allow you to be ready to use them for a push-up motion to control the end of this exercise’s lowering phase.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes and tighten your abdominal muscles to brace your core.
    1. Continue doing so throughout the lowering phase to prevent your hips from bending or your lower back from excessively arching.
2. While your lower legs remain stationary, slowly lean the rest of your body forward as one unit through motion at your knees. Lean forward as far as you can in a controlled manner,
    1. Keep your torso and hips in a rigid position, while all the movement occurs from your knees gradually transitioning to a less bent position. You can think of your knees as the center of an analog clock, while the rest of your body above your knees forms one of its hands that arcs forward beyond twelve o’clock.
    2. Throughout your descent, you should be able to continue drawing a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders. To do so, you will have to avoid bending forward at your hips or dynamically arching your lower back.
    3. The degree of difficulty required to control the descent will markedly increase as your body progressively becomes closer to horizontal.
3. Once you can no longer control the descent, extend your hands out in front of you to catch yourself through the same upper body movement you perform during the lowering phase of a push-up.
    1. You can initially contact the ground with slightly bent elbows as your arms are raised to form about 90-degree angles with your torso.
    2. How much of the descent you can control before your body starts to fall rapidly (which is known as the break point) will naturally be dependent on your hamstring strength and experience with Nordic hamstring curls. Certain individuals who are remarkably proficient at this exercise may be able to control the descent all the way to the ground without having to catch themselves with their hands, but the ability to do so is extremely rare.
4. After catching yourself and reaching the bottom of your push-up position, rock your buttocks back toward your heels while bending your hips and knees, and walking yourself back with your hands.
    1. The purpose of this step is to reposition yourself and allow you to return to the starting position rather than training your hamstrings on the way up.
    2. This standard version of the Nordic hamstring curl exclusively trains the hamstrings during the lowering phase.
5. Return to the starting position with your torso fully upright above your knees.
6. Alternate between steps 1-5 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while holding the dumbbells by your thighs with straight elbows as your palms face your thighs.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hand while holding them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
    3. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    4. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    5. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back flat, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back.
2. Situate your palms right next to the outer aspect of the front of your thighs so that your palms face at an angle between backward and in toward each other.
    1. This results in a semi-overhand grip, which is a hybrid between an overhand grip that would direct your palms straight backward (with the dumbbells directly in front of your body) and a neutral grip that would direct your palms straight in toward your sides (with the dumbbells directly to the sides of your body).
    2. Keep your palms facing this way throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Bracing your core will help you maintain a rigid torso position as you subsequently move about your hips rather than your back.
2. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight with the dumbbells just in front of your legs. Avoid letting the dumbbells drift forward away from you, which may be more likely to occur if you think about “bending over” rather than “sitting back.”
    2. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the dumbbells.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    5. Throughout the set, keep the soles of your feet fully planted on the ground and your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
3. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move.
    1. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the dumbbells at least below their knees, but how deeply you are able to hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    3. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be in clear control of the entire descent.
4. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so you should continue keeping your lower back flat, chest up, core braced, feet fully on the ground, and the dumbbells close to your legs.
    2. When you have finished lifting the dumbbells, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back at the top through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips appropriately stacked under your shoulders to prevent excessive arching.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
    2. Once you have finished your last rep, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back flat rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

### Learning how to hip hinge

If you have minimal experience training hip hinge exercises such as Romanian deadlift and good morning variations, it is normal to have difficulty performing this movement pattern. Like riding a bicycle or shooting a basketball, hip hinging is a motor skill that may require repeated practice before you feel comfortable consistently using it. Broadly speaking, there are two types of movement substitution patterns that individuals who are in the process of learning how to hip hinge commonly perform when attempting to execute a hip hinge exercise.

One of these is using a stoop lift, which involves dynamically rounding the back (through flexion of the lumbar and thoracic spine) to bend over prior to uncoiling the spine into an upright position during the ascent. This often is accompanied by the buttock not moving particularly far backward and the arms drifting out in front of the legs in contrast to a strict hip hinge, which utilizes a visibly flat back position (with close to a neutral lumbar spine) and has the buttock noticeably moving backward during the descent. In terms of similarity, a stoop lift and a hip hinge both involve only a mild magnitude of knee bend during the descent while keeping the hips high. A clue that you may be performing more of a stoop lift than a hip hinge is feeling a stretching sensation in your back rather than feeling your back muscles remain statically tight throughout your set as these muscles function to maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips. With a properly performed hip hinge, you should certainly feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the bottom of the lift, but you may also feel this stretching sensation during a stoop lift. Nonetheless, a hip hinge can allow you to feel the hamstring stretch earlier during the descent compared to a stoop lift since the hamstrings are shortened by the posterior pelvic tilt (tucking the tailbone under) that is coupled with lumbar spine flexion.

In addition to performing a stoop lift unintentionally when attempting to hip hinge, people can commonly utilize more of a squatting motion that is characterized by greater knee bend and forward tracking of the knees during the descent. Compared to a hip hinge, using more of a squatting movement can result in the buttock moving downward during the descent as opposed to backward, and the shins can also incline forward as opposed to remaining vertical. Because the hamstrings shorten as the knees bend, someone moving in a squat pattern when attempting to perform a hip hinge exercise is unlikely to feel much of a stretching sensation in the hamstrings at the bottom of the lift. Not feeling a hamstring stretch is the most straightforward indicator that you may be squatting your hip hinge exercise, but an additional clue would be if you perceive your quads to be working (e.g., feeling a “burning” sensation or lots of tension) more intensely than your hamstrings during the exercise.

When thinking about moving through hip hinge, stoop lift, and squat patterns, it is important to recognize that these movements can occur along a spectrum. You can perform a hip hinge exercise with a technique that is mostly a hip hinge while still utilizing elements of a stoop lift or a squat that may not be ideal for what you wish to accomplish from the exercise. Similarly, your technique can incrementally progress from being stoop lift-dominant or squat-dominant to becoming progressively more of a hip hinge as your body learns how to move in a different way through repeated practice. If your hip hinge technique currently has much room for improvement, it can be beneficial to start with lighter loads that may not be especially challenging to your muscles until you developed a reasonable level of competency with the movement itself. There is no need to let perfect be the enemy of good, so you do not need to wait to load a movement meaningfully until you have immaculate technique, but it would also be inadvisable to push your body to the limit without initially learning the basic fundamentals of the movement.

Depending on which element of hip hinging in which you currently are challenged, certain external cues can expedite how quickly you can learn how to hinge. When unintentionally moving in a manner that involves a greater degree of squatting or stoop lifting than is intended, a wall may help provide tactile feedback to cue sitting your buttock backward. To do so, you can perform your hip hinge with your back facing a nearby wall, and you will be able to receive confirmation as to whether you are actually sitting your hips backward by feeling the wall contact your buttock at the end of the descent. As an initial starting point, you can set up with a heel-to-toe tandem stance as the back of one heel contacts the wall. Then you can bring your rear foot forward to be aligned with your front foot in the symmetrical stance you will utilize for your hip hinge. This can provide a reasonable approximation as to how far people may commonly be able to sit their hips back when hinging, but you can adjust from there how far away you position yourself from the wall to individualize it to you.

Specifically if you have a tendency to perform a “squatty” hip hinge, practicing your hip hinge with your calves up against something like a flat exercise bench (or even a couch or chair at home) can be a rather productive means of honing your hinge. As you descend, you will receive immediate tactile feedback if your knees track forward from no longer feeling the contact with your calves, so it can be a great way to reinforce keeping your shins vertical throughout the movement. When using this method, make sure that you maintain full contact between the soles of your feet and the ground while you avoid leaning your bodyweight into the bench to the extent that you would fall backward if the bench was removed. If you successfully keep your calves in contact with the bench throughout the movement and feel a pronounced stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the end of the descent, you are right on track to achieving a high quality hip hinge.

As an additional learning tool, you can situate a long object like a dowel rod, PVC pipe, or yardstick on your back while hip hinging if you have a tendency to utilize more of a stoop lift technique with excessive back rounding. Either the calf-to-bench technique or the buttock-to-wall technique can be incorporated into an actual Romanian deadlift where you use weights, but using a rod as a cue without a partner will require you to hold the rod in place, so you would not be able to load this drill independently. To perform this movement, you would hold the rod behind against your back with one hand higher up near your head and your other hand lower down near your buttock. While standing fully upright and looking straight ahead, you should feel the rod contacting your sacrum (the bone that lies between your upper buttock cheeks and right above your tailbone), upper back between your shoulder blades, and the back of your head. You will then hip hinge while maintaining these three points of contact throughout the entirety of the movement. If you start rounding your back or moving your neck beyond the neutral position you adopt when standing fully upright, you will feel the rod lose contact with one of those three spots. This can be a rather effective form of instant feedback to help develop your ability to move predominantly through your lower body while keeping your trunk in a rigid position throughout the movement, which can transfer to improved technique for an array of different exercises. When maintaining those three contact points, you potentially can still perform a squatting motion rather than a hip hinge since moving through your lower body while minimizing back motion is also a component of squatting technique. However, if you maintain those three contact points and additionally feel your hamstrings notably stretched at the bottom of the descent, those two factors indicate that you have successfully hip hinged in all likelihood. If you find that the rod cuing shifts your movement from a stoop lift to more of a squat, you can use the rod cuing simultaneously with the calf-to-bench cuing, which can address multiple aspects of the hip hinge concurrently.

In the context of performing a hip hinge exercise, using a form that resembles more of a squat or stoop lift rather than a hip hinge can be considered technique errors, but squatting and stoop lifting are by no means faulty movement patterns inherently. They simply differ from a hip hinge, so they can be suboptimal means of performing an exercise that you intend to train specifically for the benefits that hip hinging can provide as opposed to other movements. The hip hinge can take some practice to learn, but investing the time and effort into doing so can be a prudent investment given that having the motor skill of hip hinging can meaningfully expand your freedom in how you can move both inside and outside of the gym.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your lower body or lower back strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your lower body and back muscles. Among trained lifters, grip strength can very commonly limit performance of Romanian deadlifts if they do not utilize straps since the posterior chain has the potential to move rather heavy loads for this exercise. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least a few minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

### Romanian deadlift vs stiff-leg deadlift

The terms “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” are often used interchangeably to describe the same exercise by scholarly articles and lifters in general. The nomenclature of the Romanian deadlift has been attributed to this exercise being performed by Nicu Vlad, a Romanian weightlifter who won gold, silver, and bronze medals respectively in the 1984, 1988, and 1996 Olympic games in addition to medaling in seven World Weightlifting Championships (with three of them being gold). American weightlifting coach Jim Schmitz reportedly saw Vlad performing the barbell hip hinge exercise and subsequently called it the Romanian deadlift since Vlad did not have a particular name for the variation he was performing.

While they may be commonly used to refer to the same exercise, some people will use the names “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” to refer to different variations. They consider the stiff-leg deadlift to be what is described in this database as the “barbell stiff-leg deadlift from floor,” which involves each rep starting with the plates fully on the floor like a conventional deadlift. This variation differs from the Romanian deadlift, which starts from the upright position and uses a range of motion individualized to someone’s flexibility as the plates often do not contact the floor. If someone has the hamstring flexibility for the plates to contact the floor during a Romanian deadlift, a light tap to the ground is utilized, but the full weight of the bar is not transferred into the ground like how the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor is performed. In contrast to the Romanian deadlift, which is typically performed with a controlled lowering phase, this conception of the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor often involves a quicker lower phase with a tempo akin to how conventional deadlifts are commonly performed, which is to say a controlled drop. Both variations can involve a mild amount of knee flexion at the bottom of the hinge, but the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor can require that someone adopts a more flexed lumbar position in order to pull from the floor with the knee position while maintaining high hips. This differs from the Romanian deadlift being performed only through the range of motion where someone can maintain close to a neutral lumbar spine or a flat back position. 

As demonstrated by sources such as Hegyi et al. (2018) along with Piper and Waller (2001), another interpretation of the stiff-leg deadlift also exists as a truly straight leg deadlift. Under this conception of the exercise, the knees are kept extended to the extent that they are completely straight but not fully locked (which could otherwise allow for knee hyperextension in individuals with the mobility to do so). Such a technique would result in a movement that is more akin to “bending over” rather than “sitting back,” and the bar would correspondingly be likely to drift further in front of the legs compared to a Romanian deadlift, which utilizes a mild knee bend that allows you to “sit back.” In light of the different ways in which these names may be interpreted, hopefully this note provides some clarification if you have ever been confused by how different individuals may view Romanian deadlifts and stiff-leg deadlifts exercises as the same exercise or distinct variations.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your side with the side of your body that you are about to train facing up.
    1. In this side-lying position, you can rest the bottom side of your head on the hand of your bottom arm for comfort by situating your upper arm out to the side with your elbow bent.
    2. For extra stability, you can bend the elbow of your top arm and place that side’s hand on the ground in front of your torso.
2. Bend your knees by approximately 90 degrees and bring your thighs forward so they form near a 45-60-degree angle with your torso.
    1. Based on preference and what feels comfortable to you, you can position your thighs further forward so that they are closer to forming a right angle with your torso, or you can position them further backward so that they are closer to being aligned with your torso.
    2. In this position, the inner aspects of your knees and feet should be in contact with each other.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your top leg’s knee upward away from your bottom knee while keeping the inner aspect of your feet in contact with each other and the rest of your body stationary.
    1. Move through your hip’s available range of motion, and avoid rolling your hips backward during this exercise, which is a common technical error.
    2. To help prevent your hips from rolling, you can imagine that you are wearing a belt with a buckle that has a laser beam shooting out of it. Strive to keep the laser beam pointing straight forward, parallel to the ground, throughout the movement.
    3. If you start to roll your hips backward, your belt buckle’s laser beam will start to angle upward, the exercise will feel easier, and you will be able to lift your knee higher up than if you had avoided rolling backward.
    4. While performing this movement with the appropriate technique, you will likely feel the muscles on the side of your top hip contracting.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your top knee to descend in a controlled manner until it is low enough to contact the inner aspect of your lower knee.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side by lying on your opposite side.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains the [upper region of your gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%20Upper%20Region%201925c6f170d88070b08aeccda6e5ac88.md) and the [short hip external rotator muscles](../Muscles/Short%20Hip%20External%20Rotators%201b95c6f170d880c79035ce63a7c5f540.md) situated underneath your glutes.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your knees bent, as the soles of your feet are flat on the ground, approximately hip width apart.
    1. You can rest your head on the ground.
    2. You can optionally hook the tops of your feet under a sturdy object, such as a couch (while your soles remain flat on the ground), to help stabilize your body during this exercise.
2. Cross your arms across your chest with bent elbows to position each hand on the front of the opposite shoulder.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground while you lift your head and shoulder blades up off the ground by curling your middle back.
    1. Given that this is a crunch rather than a sit-up, the lower half of your back should remain in contact with the ground while you only lift up the upper half of your back mildly off the floor.
    2. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    3. As a cue, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the top of your hip bones, which is the action that contraction of your abdominal muscles can produce.
    4. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that crunching up any further would require the lower half of your back to lift off the floor.
    5. At the end of the lifting phase, your chest should be facing at an angle between forward and upward, rather than only facing upward as it did in the starting position.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your middle back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your head and shoulder blades back to the starting position on the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and especially your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md), which is the “six-pack muscle.”

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that allows you to hold the handles comfortably with bent elbows once you are seated.
    1. If your machine has elbow pads, the proper seat height should also permit you to rest your elbows on them comfortably while grasping the handles.
    2. The appropriate setting should allow you to keep your arms mostly relaxed when grasping the handles.
    3. You should not have to shrug your shoulders up to reach the handles.
    4. Some trial and error may be required to find a seat height that feels appropriate for you.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit on the seat with your back snugly against the back pad as your lower back is comfortably arched.
    1. The degree to which you can comfortably arch your lower back can be affected by your mobility.
    2. Starting with an appropriate degree of lower back arching will situate your abs in a lengthened position that can facilitate training them through an extended range of motion during this exercise.
4. Position your feet in the stable position permitted by your machine, which will vary based on the specific model you are using.
    1. This may involve hooking your feet snugly under the foot roller pads, situating your feet on foot pegs, resting your feet on a foot plate, or placing your feet directly on the ground.
    2. Machines that allow your legs to move during the exercise will normally have foot roller pads, and certain machines allow you to adjust them. When using one of these models, you can situate the front of your ankles against the back of the pads and the top of your feet against the bottom of the pads
    3. Ultimately, you want to set up in a manner that allows your feet to feel stable throughout the exercise.
5. Reach up and grasp the handles with your palms facing in toward each other. If your machine has elbow pads, rest your elbows against them as well.
    1. In the starting position, your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Maintain this neck position during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl your spine as you pull the bottom of your ribs toward the tops of your hip bones in a controlled manner.
    1. Once you feel that you can no longer curl your spine through a range permitted by the machine that feels comfortable to your back, you have reached your end range. The machine may physically restrict your range of motion at a certain point, even if you have the mobility to crunch further.
    2. Depending on the specific model you are using, the bottom of the machine may lift up with your legs as you crunch, or it may remain stationary with your legs not moving. When using the former category of machines, moving the top of the machine through the crunching action will naturally prompt your knees and feet to lift upward, even if you do not consciously try to march your knees up. If you wish to train your hip flexors simultaneously with your abs, you can also intentionally think about driving your knees up, but make sure that you do so in addition to curling your spine rather than as an alternative to curling your spine.
    3. Avoid pulling down with your arms. Your arms should only move because they are attached to your torso, which is what you are directly moving. The function of your arms is merely to transmit force from your abs into the machine. You should not feel your back muscles contract like they would during a pulling exercise (such as a straight arm lat pulldown). If you feel like your back muscles are driving the movement, you can try loosening your grip to the minimum required to hold the handles in a stable fashion.
    4. To train your abs dynamically, you should be intentionally rounding your entire back, since this motion is performed by contraction of your abs. When rounding your back appropriately, you should feel meaningful tension in your abs. If you do not feel your abs engaging, you may be substituting hip or shoulder motion for the intended spinal motion.
    5. If you finish the movement with your back fairly flat as opposed to rounded, you most likely are primarily bending at your hips rather than curling your spine.
    6. It can help to think about crunching your elbows toward your knees.
    7. You can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the middle of your chest, and you are trying to point that closer toward the middle point between your knees.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner as you uncurl your back by flaring your ribs up and away from your hip bones.
    1. Move through the full range of motion permitted by the machine that feels comfortable to your lower back. This may involve allowing the weights you selected to tap the rest of the stack lightly at the end of this movement if the full range that the machine allows feels comfortable to you.
    2. When uncurling your spine, your lower back will initially move into a flat position before moving into an arched position.
    3. Depending on your mobility and the range of motion your machine permits, you may feel a stretching sensation in your abs as you allow your lower back to arch.
    4. The imaginary laser beam shooting out from your chest should angle progressively higher up as you uncurl your back and flare your ribs away from your hip bones.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you feel lower back discomfort at the end of either step, you can abbreviate the range of motion to what feels best to you. Performing this exercise through a full range of motion is by no means inherently injurious to the lower back, but certain individuals with pre-existing conditions may experience discomfort in rather rounded or rather arched positions.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md), which is assisted by your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md).

## Setting up
1. If your machine allows you to adjust the height of the footplate, select a height that will allow your legs to be in an approximately horizontal position once you are in the starting position.
    1. After estimating where this setting may be, you can adjust it during later steps if warranted.
    2. Not all machines permit you to adjust the footplate height.
2. Horizontally adjust the machine’s footplate to a setting that will allow the pad to support your thighs without contacting your hip bones when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. The appropriate position should allow your hips to move freely while sufficiently stabilizing your legs.
    2. If the footplate is positioned excessively far back (resulting in your hips resting on the pad), the pad can restrict your hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    3. If the footplate is positioned excessively far forward to the extent that your knees are near the middle of the pad rather than your thighs, the exercise may provoke knee discomfort in some people.
    4. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position.
3. Climb up onto the machine, and position your feet against the footplate with your lower legs between the leg rollers while the front of your hips are resting on the pad.
    1. The back of your lower legs should be snugly pressed into the top pair of leg rollers slightly above your heels.
    2. Your knees should be straight, and your soles should be firmly contacting the footplate.
    3. While you are setting your feet, you can use the handles for assistance.
    4. Some machines have a step that you can use to help you get into position.
    5. With the appropriate footplate setting, the front of your hip bones should not be resting on the pad.
4. Cross your arms across your chest with bent elbows to position each hand on the front of the opposite shoulder.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes to keep your torso up such that you can draw approximately a straight line from your legs through your hips and to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. This is the starting position of the exercise, where your body should look like it does when normally standing upright, except rotated to be horizontal.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips.
3. Without rounding your back, hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner to angle your torso downward.
    1. As opposed to bending over at your back, nearly all the motion should occur from you moving at your hips as you statically keep your trunk near a neutral position with your lower back mildly arched or flat.
    2. Maintain a straight knee position, but avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads.
    3. While hinging at your hips and keeping your hands on your shoulders, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings that progressively intensifies.
    4. How deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility. If you have the flexibility to hinge until your torso is completely vertical, stop once you reach this point. Otherwise, stop descending once you feel like you have reached the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch.
    5. If you initially did not position the footplate sufficiently forward, the pad may alternatively limit how deeply you can hinge.
4. Reverse the movement by lifting your torso up through your hips and squeezing your glutes.
    1. When moving through your hips, your entire torso should move together as one unit. You can think of your hips as the center of an analog clock, while your rigid torso is a hand that rotates about the center.
    2. At the end of the lifting phase, your torso should be close to a horizontal position aligned with your legs.
    3. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the hip motion you just performed during the lowering phase. Focusing on finishing the movement by squeezing your glutes can help prevent excessive back arching.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
6. After your last rep, you can grasp the handles to help you dismount the machine.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
Standing pin-loaded glute kickback machines usually have an adjustable chest pad that permits a fairly upright torso position. A minority of machines lack a chest and have a fixed forearm pad as an alternative, which involves a more leaned-forward torso position to use. The exercise technique with either machine can be essentially the same, but certain setup details differ, which is why two different setup sections are provided for you to select based on the specific type of machine you have.

### Setting up a machine with an adjustable chest pad

1. Adjust the chest pad to a position that allows you to rest your chest comfortably on it while holding the handles after leaning forward onto the pad.
    1. The appropriate setting should allow you to feel stable and well-supported during the exercise.
    2. Some trial and error may be required to find a position that feels best to your body.
2. If your machine has a narrow adjustable foot bar (that can be moved to the right or left side), set it to the side you intend to train during this set.
    1. Other machine models have a wide foot bar that does not need to be adjusted to train your right or left sides.
3. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin, and stand directly next to the chest pad facing the handles.
    1. Depending on the machine you have, you may be able to stand with your feet hip-width apart, or you may have to angle your working leg wider out to the side if the foot bar is underneath where you would otherwise place that leg.
4. Lean forward at your hips to rest your chest on the chest pad, and firmly grasp the handles. Rest your forearms on the forearm pads if your machine has these pads.
    1. When you lean forward, keep your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright. You should lean forward at your hips rather than simply rounding over at your back.
    2. How far you have to lean forward will be influenced by your machine model and body type. With certain machines, only a rather slight forward lean may be needed to contact the chest pad, while others may involve a greater degree of forward lean.
5. On the side you intend to train, bend your knee to lift your foot off the ground, and position the back half of its sole in contact with the foot bar.
    1. Based on your preference and what feels stable to you, you can contact the foot bar with your heel or a little closer to your midfoot. The appropriate foot position should ensure that your foot does not slide during the exercise while also helping you to feel meaningful tension in your glute.
    2. When viewed from the front, your foot should be aligned with your knee rather than being positioned to either the right or left side of your knee.
    3. With a machine that has the foot bar starting under you, you will have to march your working side’s knee upward and forward to reach the foot bar. With a machine that has the foot bar starting behind you, you may be able to reach the foot bar by simply bending your knee without marching your thigh up.
    4. Keep the foot of your non-working leg firmly planted on the ground from this point onward.
    5. All the subsequent directions will apply to your working leg.

### Setting up a machine with a fixed forearm pad

1. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
2. Stand directly in front of the foot bar, facing the handles, with your feet hip-width apart.
    1. The machine may have a pair of footprint outlines indicating where it is appropriate to stand initially.
3. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, lean forward at your hips to rest your forearms on the forearm pad and grasp the handles.
    1. If you feel that you have to reach forward excessively to hold the handles (which may be more likely for short individuals), move your feet forward until you find that you can comfortably hold the handles and rest on the forearm pad. Because the pad is not adjustable, you have to modify the stance if the initial position does not suit your body.
    2. The appropriate position should allow you to feel stable throughout the exercise. Avoid walking any further forward than is needed to feel stable, since the exercise’s range of motion shortens when moving further away from the foot bar.
    3. When you lean forward, keep your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright. You should lean forward at your hips rather than simply rounding over at your back.
4. On the side you intend to train, bend your knee to lift your foot off the ground, and position the back half of its sole in contact with the foot bar.
    1. Based on your preference and what feels stable to you, you can contact the foot bar with your heel or a little closer to your midfoot. The appropriate foot position should ensure that your foot does not slide during the exercise while also helping you to feel meaningful tension in your glute.
    2. When viewed from the front, your foot should be aligned with your knee rather than being positioned to either the right or left side of your knee.
    3. Keep the foot of your non-working leg firmly planted on the ground from this point onward.
    4. All the subsequent directions will apply to your working leg.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your knee backward in an arcing manner to push your heel and the foot bar backward through the full range of motion that your hip mobility permits.
    1. Allow your knee to straighten naturally while focusing on moving your knee backward through hip motion.
    2. How far you personally can drive your knee backward will be influenced by your hip mobility.
    3. Strive to have all the movement come from your working leg while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
    4. During the entire set, keep your chest snugly against the chest pad and your imaginary belt buckle pointing straight ahead.
    5. Particularly avoid excessively arching your lower back or turning your imaginary belt buckle to the side, both of which are common technique errors that can occur when striving to push the foot bar further backward than what your hip mobility permits.
    6. At the end range, you should feel your glute contract. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glute engage during this exercise and help cue the intended hip motion.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your knee to arc forward while naturally bending.
    1. Avoid letting the weight rapidly swing your knee forward in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. You should finish in the starting position with your knee positioned as far forward as the machine permits while keeping your foot on the foot bar.
    3. To confirm you have moved through your full range of motion, you can lightly tap the weights you selected against the rest of the weight stack without allowing the weights to rest on the stack.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise will chiefly train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), which may be assisted by your [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md) and [piriformis](../Muscles/Piriformis%201925c6f170d88068a670ce338a8215cf.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to the barbell situated on the ground, stand upright close in front of the middle of the bar as the bar is approximately over the middle of your feet.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
    2. The size of the weight plates you add to the bar will determine how high the bar lies above the ground, which consequently affects your range of motion. Adding a pair of 45lb (20kg) plates (or 25kg plates common in gyms outside the USA) or bumper plates will elevate the bar to the standard height (about 9in (23cm)) when deadlifting from the floor. When only using smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a deficit sumo deadlift with a greater range of motion that may exceed the range of motion in which some people wish to train if they lack the mobility to perform a deficit deadlift with appropriate technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize the largest diameter plates, you can perform a sumo block pull or rack pull with the bar elevated to where it would be when deadlifting from the floor with large diameter plates.
2. Spread your legs apart into a wide stance that is clearly outside shoulder width, with your feet moderately rotated out away from your sides.
    1. Provided that your feet are wider apart than your shoulders but closer together than the plates, you can use a range of stance widths for your sumo deadlift.
    2. The ideal stance width can meaningfully vary among different individuals based on someone’s body structure and hip mobility.
    3. Trying out different foot positions will normally be required to determine which stance specifically feels best to you.
    4. As a starting point, you can widen your feet as far apart as you feel comfortable and stable while being able to push your knees out approximately over your heels, resulting in close to vertical shins. You will push your knees out when descending to reach the bar, so subsequent aspects of the setup can help you gauge if you should adjust your stance.
    5. The ideal amount of toe flare also varies among different lifters, but you can start with your toes pointing about 30-45 degrees out to the side before adjusting from there based on what feels best to you. Zero degrees of toe flare would mean your toes are pointing straight forward, while 90 degrees would mean your toes are pointing directly out to your side.
3. Direct your arms straight down toward the ground with straight elbows as your shoulders are packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up).
    1. Maintain this position from here onward.
4. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips while bending your knees and pushing your knees out until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees, and your knees should essentially not track forward (although a slight degree of forward knee tracking can be used if that feels best to you).
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something. After you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Try to push your knees far enough out to the sides that they are vertically stacked over your heels.
    4. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    5. Similarly, keep your chest up in a “proud chest” posture and your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    6. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
    7. The bar should be directly in front of your shins.
5. With your shoulders stacked vertically above the bar, firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath). This should expand the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles, like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360-degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. Continue bracing your core throughout your set. This will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. This can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” by extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. Keep your chest up, back flat, and knees pushed out.
    2. As your hips and chest rise at the same rate, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull. Avoid letting your torso incline further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
    3. Keep the bar very close to your legs throughout the rep.
    4. Try to avoid slowing down the start of your sumo deadlift just because you know you will be pausing very soon. You ideally should start your rep just like you would when performing a standard sumo deadlift.
4. Just after the plates lift off the floor, pause in that position for a brief period of time (e.g., 1-2 seconds) while staying tight with your chest up and back flat.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability as you visibly remain stationary.
5. Resume “pushing the floor away” until the bar reaches near your knees. Then focus on thrusting your hips forward until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back when viewed from the side.
6. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips and bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your hips back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally. After the bar has cleared your knees, you can further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
    2. Continue keeping your back flat and chest up.
7. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again. Then continue to alternate between steps 2-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the ground.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.
## Description
While also training your [spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can train much of your lower body musculature, including your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), and [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md).

## Setting up
1. Situate a barbell in front of a sufficiently anchored flat exercise bench (or viable alternative). The length of the bar should be parallel to the length of the bench.
    1. A specific hip thrust bench is ideal to use, but it is not commonly available.
    2. If you use a mobile exercise bench, make sure that it will not slide back during the exercise. To do so, you can position it against a power rack. Alternatively, you can position the bench against a plyometric box or bumper plates that are contacting a wall. When using a wall to anchor the bench, the intermediate objects are required to provide clearance for your head.
    3. You may also be able to use a soft plyometric box near knee height that is anchored in the same manner as a flat bench.
    4. What ultimately matters is selecting an object that is sturdy, stable, and reasonably close to being knee height while being comfortable enough to support your upper back.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the barbell.
    1. The diameter of the weight plates you select can influence how easily you can set up.
    2. It will be easiest to assume the starting position with at least one pair of full diameter plates, such as typical 45lb (20kg) Olympic plates or bumper plates. With full diameter plates, certain individuals who are very thick may need to utilize one of the strategies discussed below to set up under the bar.
    3. If you exclusively load the bar with smaller diameter plates, you may have to modify the standard setup in order to position your hips under the bar. When only using smaller diameter plates, you can elevate the bar just enough to fit your hips under it by situating the plates on top of deadlift blocks, aerobic steps, or stacks of full diameter weight plates. Alternatively, you may have a partner place the bar on top of your hip bones and load it with weight plates after you have assumed the starting position. If neither of these approaches is practical to you, you lack bumper plates that allow you to elevate the bar fully with light loads, and you do not currently have the strength to use 135lb (or 60kg) for this exercise, you have the option of performing other hip thrust variations. For instance, you can select a [single leg bodyweight hip thrust](Single%20leg%20bodyweight%20hip%20thrust%201a35c6f170d880e5a5e5fc58d493ca07.md) or a [dumbbell hip thrust](Dumbbell%20hip%20thrust%201a35c6f170d8801d8819ce2fc219c047.md) to train the glutes in essentially the same manner as the barbell variation, but with an easier setup.
3. Optionally, obtain a pad (or an object that can function as a pad) that you will place between the bar and your hips.
    1. Using a pad is not required but strongly recommended because it can be very uncomfortable to have a barbell directly resting on your hip bones with a meaningful load.
    2. You can wrap a hip thrust pad or a squat pad around the middle of the bar.
    3. Alternatively, you can place a thick foam or folded exercise mat on the crease of your hip during the next step and subsequently keep it there to cushion your hip bones. Be aware that foam pads not specifically designed for hip thrusts may be somewhat damaged from this exercise.
4. Sit down on the ground with your upper back against the edge of the bench and your legs straight out in front of you under the bar.
    1. Specifically place the lower part of your shoulder blades against the edge of the bench. Feel free to adjust your upper back positioning mildly from this point based on what feels most stable to you.
    2. The middle of the bar should be aligned with the midline of your body.
5. Grasp the bar with your palms facing down and roll it toward the crease of your hips.
    1. So long as your hands are wider apart than your hips, you can adjust your grip width based on what feels stable and comfortable to you during this exercise.
    2. Continue holding the bar from this point onward.
6. Tuck your chin mildly toward your chest, and maintain this neck position throughout the exercise.
7. Bring your heels toward your buttocks by bending your knees greater than 90 degrees with the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, but it is up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can opt to point your toes forward or somewhat out to the sides.
    3. The optimal degree of knee bend should allow your feet to feel stable while being firmly planted on the ground throughout the set. It is normally appropriate to position your feet far enough back that your knees will be bent by approximately 90 degrees at the top of your hip thrust. From this placement, you can adjust specifically where you situate your feet based on your preference.
8. Confirm that the bar is directly above the crease of your hips and completely centered before initiating the set.
    1. Positioning the bar appropriately will help you avoid the excessive discomfort that may arise from positioning the bar too high (i.e., directly on your lower abdomen) or too low (i.e., directly on your groin).
    2. Some people may experience discomfort when the bar looks aligned with the crease of their hips if the bar is directly resting on the bony bumps on the front of their hip bones. If you notice that this occurs for you during your set, you can roll the bar slightly further down away from your abdomen to shift the pressure away from these bony bumps. When making any adjustments during a set, only do so in between reps when the weights are resting on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
    2. From this starting position, your back should either be flat or exhibit its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
2. Lift your hips up by driving your heels into the ground and squeezing your glutes. Keep the bar balanced on the crease of your hips the entire set.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thighs and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glutes.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glutes engage during this exercise.
    4. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them at the top.
    5. Throughout the exercise, the soles of your feet should remain fully planted on the ground, and your upper back should remain firmly in contact with the bench.
    6. The purpose of holding the bar with your hands is to keep it stabilized on the crease of your hips. Avoid trying to lift the bar up or push it down with your hands.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your hip mobility comfortably permits without rounding or excessively arching your lower back.
    1. Some people can descend all the way down until they lightly contact the ground with the plates or their glutes, but you can prioritize lowering through the range in which you can achieve through hip motion rather than lower back motion.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly. If you hear the plates crashing into the ground, you are not lowering the bar with sufficient control.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps. The bar should come to a dead stop on the ground after each rep.
    2. After completing the lowering phase of your last rep, roll the bar forward before getting up in the reversed manner to how you set up initially.

This exercise will predominantly develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) while also training your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the lower leg pad to a position that places it slightly above the back of your heels (i.e., on your Achilles tendons) when lying down on the machine with your knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
2. If your machine allows you to do so, adjust its lever arm (that will align with your shins) to a position that lets you begin each rep with your knees straightened.
    1. If the lever arm is too high, you will start each rep with your knees somewhat bent rather than fully straightened. This would prevent you from training through a full range of motion.
    2. Certain machines may allow you to position the lever arm low enough that it could situate your knees beyond fully straightened into a hyperextended position (where your knees are bent in the opposite direction in which they normally bend). This may increase the likelihood of experiencing knee discomfort during this exercise.
    3. The optimal position will allow you to draw a straight line through your knees from your lower legs to your thighs once you are in the starting position.
3. Add weight plates to the machine.
4. Lie down on the body pad with your lower legs under the lower leg pad and your knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point (which will typically result in your knees hanging just off the edge of the body pad).
    1. The front of your thighs, hips, and torso should be in contact with the body pad.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. Your neck should similarly be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
    4. In this starting position, your knees should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Pull your toes and feet back toward your shins by moving at your ankles, and maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shins contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankles in the same position in which they would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heels up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankles in this position can increase your hamstring curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
3. Drive your heels toward your buttocks by bending your knees through the full range of motion you can perform. You should typically be able to contact your buttocks or upper thighs with the lower leg pad at the end range.
    1. While your lower legs move through motion at your knees, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
    2. Avoid lifting your hips up off the pad or excessively arching your lower back.
4. Reverse the movement as you allow your knees to straighten progressively in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your knees fully straightened.
    2. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower legs down.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your back on the ground behind a sturdy object with an elevated surface, such as a flat exercise bench, stackable aerobic steps, plyometric box, stairs, or bed.
2. Lift up your legs to position your feet on top of the elevated surface with your knees bent by at least 90 degrees.
    1. If you are too far away from the elevated surface to achieve this bent knee position, you can scoot forward until you can do so.
    2. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (by scooting toward the elevated surface) is up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
    3. Based on what feels stable to you, you can either position the back of your heels on top of the elevated surface or position the middle of your soles on the corner of the elevated surface.
    4. You can situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, but it is also up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    5. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can opt to point your toes forward or somewhat out to the sides.
    6. In this position, you can rest the back of your head on the ground and leave your arms on the ground by your sides.
3. While leaving one foot on the elevated surface, lift the other foot off the elevated surface by marching that side’s thigh up while bending your knee, or by lifting that leg a little above the elevated surface while keeping your knee straight.
    1. Either position for the free leg is similarly viable, so you can go with whichever you prefer, but keeping the knee straight may make the exercise mildly more challenging compared to keeping it bent.
    2. Keep one foot off the elevated surface or ground in the static position of your choice throughout the set you perform with your other side.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your foot into the elevated surface and squeezing your glute.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side (on the side of your body with the foot contacting the surface). Your thigh and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glute.
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glute engage.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to contact the ground with your buttocks lightly.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
