## Setting up
1. With a cable station positioned to its lowest height, connect a rope attachment and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. In approximately a shoulder-width stance, stand above the rope with your back toward the cable station.
3. Squat down or hinge at your hips to grasp the ends of the rope firmly with your palms facing in toward each other and your elbows straightened.
    1. For a particularly stable grip, you can place the outside of your index fingers in contact with the flat surface of the hard plastic end caps of the rope attachment.
    2. Whether you wrap your thumbs around your other fingers or place your thumbs on top of the rope’s end caps will be based on your personal preference.
4. With your arms directed down toward the floor, take a few steps forward so that you can feel resistance from the cable station during the pull-through you are about to perform.
    1. After walking forward, you can adopt a near shoulder-width stance or a wider stance based on what feels comfortable and stable to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    4. Bracing will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips throughout your set.
2. Hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner to move your buttocks backward while you allow your knees to bend mildly.
    1. Continue keeping your soles flat on the floor, elbows straightened, core braced, and lower back near a neutral position while doing so.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a close to vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened.
    4. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    5. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    6. While you hinge at your hips, the rope will naturally move backward, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    7. How deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    8. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit your buttocks any farther back, you have finished hinging through your available range of motion.
    9. Tension from the cable should be present throughout the entire movement, so if you lose resistance from the cable while sitting back, you should take another step forward after completing the rep and returning to an upright position.
3. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. Continue keeping your lower back and neck near a neutral position while you move through your hips.
    2. If you wish to do so, you can squeeze your glutes for a moment at the end of this motion.
    3. When completing your rep, avoid excessively arching your back into a position that is hyperextended beyond the natural curvature of your spine (like you have when normally standing upright).
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to walk backward with the rope before setting it down.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise dynamically trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

### **Learning how to hip hinge**

If you have minimal experience training hip hinge exercises such as Romanian deadlift and good morning variations, it is normal to have difficulty performing this movement pattern. Like riding a bicycle or shooting a basketball, hip hinging is a motor skill that may require repeated practice before you feel comfortable consistently using it. Broadly speaking, there are two types of movement substitution patterns that individuals who are in the process of learning how to hip hinge commonly perform when attempting to execute a hip hinge exercise.

One of these is using a stoop lift, which involves dynamically rounding the back (through flexion of the lumbar and thoracic spine) to bend over prior to uncoiling the spine into an upright position during the ascent. This often is accompanied by the buttock not moving particularly far backward and the arms drifting out in front of the legs in contrast to a strict hip hinge, which utilizes a visibly flat back position (with close to a neutral lumbar spine) and has the buttock noticeably moving backward during the descent. In terms of similarity, a stoop lift and a hip hinge both involve only a mild magnitude of knee bend during the descent while keeping the hips high. A clue that you may be performing more of a stoop lift than a hip hinge is feeling a stretching sensation in your back rather than feeling your back muscles remain statically tight throughout your set as these muscles function to maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips. With a properly performed hip hinge, you should certainly feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the bottom of the lift, but you may also feel this stretching sensation during a stoop lift. Nonetheless, a hip hinge can allow you to feel the hamstring stretch earlier during the descent compared to a stoop lift since the hamstrings are shortened by the posterior pelvic tilt (tucking the tailbone under) that is coupled with lumbar spine flexion.

In addition to performing a stoop lift unintentionally when attempting to hip hinge, people can commonly utilize more of a squatting motion that is characterized by greater knee bend and forward tracking of the knees during the descent. Compared to a hip hinge, using more of a squatting movement can result in the buttock moving downward during the descent as opposed to backward, and the shins can also incline forward as opposed to remaining vertical. Because the hamstrings shorten as the knees bend, someone moving in a squat pattern when attempting to perform a hip hinge exercise is unlikely to feel much of a stretching sensation in the hamstrings at the bottom of the lift. Not feeling a hamstring stretch is the most straightforward indicator that you may be squatting your hip hinge exercise, but an additional clue would be if you perceive your quads to be working (e.g., feeling a “burning” sensation or lots of tension) more intensely than your hamstrings during the exercise.

When thinking about moving through hip hinge, stoop lift, and squat patterns, it is important to recognize that these movements can occur along a spectrum. You can perform a hip hinge exercise with a technique that is mostly a hip hinge while still utilizing elements of a stoop lift or a squat that may not be ideal for what you wish to accomplish from the exercise. Similarly, your technique can incrementally progress from being stoop lift-dominant or squat-dominant to becoming progressively more of a hip hinge as your body learns how to move in a different way through repeated practice. If your hip hinge technique currently has much room for improvement, it can be beneficial to start with lighter loads that may not be especially challenging to your muscles until you developed a reasonable level of competency with the movement itself. There is no need to let perfect be the enemy of good, so you do not need to wait to load a movement meaningfully until you have immaculate technique, but it would also be inadvisable to push your body to the limit without initially learning the basic fundamentals of the movement.

Depending on which element of hip hinging in which you currently are challenged, certain external cues can expedite how quickly you can learn how to hinge. When unintentionally moving in a manner that involves a greater degree of squatting or stoop lifting than is intended, a wall may help provide tactile feedback to cue sitting your buttock backward. To do so, you can perform your hip hinge with your back facing a nearby wall, and you will be able to receive confirmation as to whether you are actually sitting your hips backward by feeling the wall contact your buttock at the end of the descent. As an initial starting point, you can set up with a heel-to-toe tandem stance as the back of one heel contacts the wall. Then you can bring your rear foot forward to be aligned with your front foot in the symmetrical stance you will utilize for your hip hinge. This can provide a reasonable approximation as to how far people may commonly be able to sit their hips back when hinging, but you can adjust from there how far away you position yourself from the wall to individualize it to you.

Specifically if you have a tendency to perform a “squatty” hip hinge, practicing your hip hinge with your calves up against something like a flat exercise bench (or even a couch or chair at home) can be a rather productive means of honing your hinge. As you descend, you will receive immediate tactile feedback if your knees track forward from no longer feeling the contact with your calves, so it can be a great way to reinforce keeping your shins vertical throughout the movement. When using this method, make sure that you maintain full contact between the soles of your feet and the ground while you avoid leaning your bodyweight into the bench to the extent that you would fall backward if the bench was removed. If you successfully keep your calves in contact with the bench throughout the movement and feel a pronounced stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the end of the descent, you are right on track to achieving a high quality hip hinge.

As an additional learning tool, you can situate a long object like a dowel rod, PVC pipe, or yardstick on your back while hip hinging if you have a tendency to utilize more of a stoop lift technique with excessive back rounding. Either the calf-to-bench technique or the buttock-to-wall technique can be incorporated into an actual Romanian deadlift where you use weights, but using a rod as a cue without a partner will require you to hold the rod in place, so you would not be able to load this drill independently. To perform this movement, you would hold the rod behind against your back with one hand higher up near your head and your other hand lower down near your buttock. While standing fully upright and looking straight ahead, you should feel the rod contacting your sacrum (the bone that lies between your upper buttock cheeks and right above your tailbone), upper back between your shoulder blades, and the back of your head. You will then hip hinge while maintaining these three points of contact throughout the entirety of the movement. If you start rounding your back or moving your neck beyond the neutral position you adopt when standing fully upright, you will feel the rod lose contact with one of those three spots. This can be a rather effective form of instant feedback to help develop your ability to move predominantly through your lower body while keeping your trunk in a rigid position throughout the movement, which can transfer to improved technique for an array of different exercises. When maintaining those three contact points, you potentially can still perform a squatting motion rather than a hip hinge since moving through your lower body while minimizing back motion is also a component of squatting technique. However, if you maintain those three contact points and additionally feel your hamstrings notably stretched at the bottom of the descent, those two factors indicate that you have successfully hip hinged in all likelihood. If you find that the rod cuing shifts your movement from a stoop lift to more of a squat, you can use the rod cuing simultaneously with the calf-to-bench cuing, which can address multiple aspects of the hip hinge concurrently.

In the context of performing a hip hinge exercise, using a form that resembles more of a squat or stoop lift rather than a hip hinge can be considered technique errors, but squatting and stoop lifting are by no means faulty movement patterns inherently. They simply differ from a hip hinge, so they can be suboptimal means of performing an exercise that you intend to train specifically for the benefits that hip hinging can provide as opposed to other movements. The hip hinge can take some practice to learn, but investing the time and effort into doing so can be a prudent investment given that having the motor skill of hip hinging can meaningfully expand your freedom in how you can move both inside and outside of the gym.

## Setting up
1. Set the foot plate to a height that aligns the machine’s pivot point with your hips while standing on the center of the foot plate with your knees slightly bent.
    1. The pivot point will be the center of the machine’s wheel, about which the lever arm rotates.
    2. Strive to align the pivot point specifically with the bony bump (greater trochanter) that you could feel on the side of your hip.
    3. Some machines do not allow you to adjust the foot plate.
2. Position the machine’s lever arm to point straight down.
    1. This will help you adjust the machine to your body proportions before moving the lever arm into the exercise’s starting position.
3. Adjust the machine’s roller pad to be slightly above knee height when standing on the foot plate.
4. March one knee up as high as you can and note the height of your knee before lowering your leg.
5. Rotate the lever arm to arc the roller pad to the height at which you were able to march your knee. When facing the middle of the machine, you will rotate the lever away from the side you are about to train
    1. This will commonly involve rotating the lever arm up a little beyond the point at which it is parallel to the ground.
    2. The appropriate setting will enable the machine to provide resistance throughout the full range of motion your hip mobility allows.
6. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
7. Stand in the center of the foot plate while facing the roller pad to align your hips with the machine’s pivot point.
    1. The roller should be in front of your leg that is closer to the weight stack.
    2. The leg further away from the weight stack should not be in the way of the roller pad when it arcs back toward the center of the machine during the exercise.
8. On the side closer to the weight stack, position the back of your knee on top of the roller pad with your knee bent by about 90 degrees. Firmly grasp the handlebar in front of you with both hands.
    1. To move it into position, you can use your hands to pull down on the roller pad as you swing this leg in toward your other side while marching up before swinging it out onto the roller pad.
    2. The leg further away from the weight stack should be standing with a slightly bent knee as its foot is flat on the foot plate.
    3. Based on what feels most stable to you, your torso should be upright or mildly leaned forward at your hips.
    4. In this starting position, your hips and shoulders should be level.

## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your knee down and back in an arcing manner through your hip’s full range of motion. Keep your knee bent throughout your set.
    1. Most people should be able to finish a little beyond the point at which the thigh is in a vertical position. However, how far you personally can drive your knee back will be influenced by your hip mobility.
    2. Strive to have all the motion come from your hip while keeping the rest of your body stationary. The foot of your other leg should remain firmly planted on the foot plate throughout your set.
    3. In particular, avoid excessively arching your lower back, which is a common technique error that can occur when trying to move the roller pad further back than what your hip mobility permits. Appropriately bracing your core can help limit unintended arching.
    4. At the end range, you should feel your glute contract. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glute engage during this exercise.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by bringing your knee forward and upward in an arcing motion.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your knee bent and fully lifted up in front of you.
    2. Avoid letting the weight rapidly swing your knee forward in an uncontrolled manner.

## Setting up
1. If you wish to use a precise snatch grip rather than a general approximation, you can start by determining your individual hand placement with an empty barbell or dowel rod.
    1. A true snatch grip results in the bar being level with the crease of your hip when holding the bar in a fully upright position.
    2. You can find which hand placement specifically places the bar in the aforementioned position by trying out different grip widths with an empty barbell or dowel rod until determining what precisely is your individual snatch grip width.
    3. As a general starting point, you can see where a bar is situated relative to your hip crease when grasping it with your arms spread out away from your sides with straight elbows so that each arm forms close to a 45-degree angle with your torso.
    4. Rather than trying out different grip widths, you can alternatively use that arm position as a general approximation to train this exercise effectively.
2. After adding weight plates to the barbell situated on the ground, stand upright close in front of the middle of the bar as the bar is over the middle of your feet.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
    2. The size of the weight plates you add to the bar will determine how high the bar lies above the ground, which consequently affects your range of motion. Adding a pair of 45lb (20kg) plates (or 25kg plates common in gyms outside the USA) or bumper plates will elevate the bar to the standard height (about 9in (23cm)) when deadlifting from the floor. When only using smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a snatch grip deficit deadlift with a greater range of motion that may exceed the range of motion in which some people wish to train if they lack the mobility to perform a deficit deadlift with appropriate technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize the largest diameter plates, you can perform a snatch grip block pull or rack pull with the bar elevated to where it would be when deadlifting from the floor with large diameter plates.
3. Situate your feet near hip width apart from each other or slightly wider, and position your toes slightly turned out to the sides or pointing straight ahead based on what feels best to you
    1. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
4. Spread your arms apart with straight elbows until your arms form close to 45-degree angles with your torso (if you opt to approximate your snatch grip width) or however far apart you determined from step 1 results in your specific snatch grip width.
5. With your arms held in that position and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track very far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift mildly forward to help you reach the bar rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    5. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
6. With your hands wide apart in the aforementioned snatch grip width, firmly grasp the bar with an overhand grip, resulting in your palms facing backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat with the bar close to your shins, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the bar reaches near the middle of your shins, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
5. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the ground.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.

## Setting up
1. Horizontally adjust the machine’s footplate to a setting that will allow you to position part of your buttocks just off the front edge of the pad when you set up with your feet on the footplate.
    1. The appropriate position should allow your thighs to rest comfortably on the pad.
    2. If the footplate is positioned excessively far from the pad, you will have to sit closer toward the middle of the pad rather than just off the front edge.
    3. If the footplate is positioned excessively close to the pad, the back of your upper thighs will not be in contact with the pad.
    4. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position.
2. If your machine allows you to adjust the footplate height, select a height that lets you feel comfortable and secure with slightly bent knees once you are in the starting position.
    1. As a starting point, you can select a height that positions the lower pair of leg rollers level with the pad and the upper pair of leg rollers higher than the pad.
    2. Not all machines permit you to adjust the footplate height.
3. Climb up onto the machine, and hook your lower legs between the leg rollers with the top of your feet snugly pressed into the top roller as your soles are facing the footplate. Sit upright with your buttocks just hanging off the front edge of the pad.
    1. Your feet should be securely anchored so that they will not slide during the exercise. The top rollers should be just above the lowest part of your shins by your ankles, while the bottom rollers should be just under your Achilles tendons (which attach to the top of your heels).
    2. Depending on the machine you are using, you can step up onto a middle beam or a step to help you get into position.
    3. While you are setting your feet, you can reach back with your hands to hold the handles for stability.
4. Place the fingertips of each hand lightly in contact with the sides of the back of your head as your upper arms and elbows are directed out away from your sides.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
    2. Your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, looking straight ahead. Keep your neck in this position during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Lean your torso back in a controlled manner until your torso is approximately parallel to the ground or slightly beyond this point.
    1. Allow your lower back to arch to a degree that feels comfortable to you.
    2. Specifically how much of an arch is comfortable will vary from person to person, but it is often appropriate to finish the lowering phase with your lower back arched to a similar degree as when you are normally standing upright. It is not inherently injurious to arch beyond this point, but meaningfully arching the lower back beyond this point can provoke lower back discomfort in some people.
    3. If you feel lower back discomfort at the bottom, you can strive to keep your lower back closer to a flat position with less of an arch, or you can reduce the range in which you lean back. Thinking about keeping your ribs tucked down to a greater degree as you avoid flaring them can help limit excessive arching.
2. Reverse the movement by curling your back to lift your torso up until your shoulders are vertically above your hips.
    1. To train your abs dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain in a flat position (which could occur if you predominantly lift your torso up through your hip flexor muscles).
    2. As a cue to emphasize your abs, think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the tops of your hip bones while tightening your abs.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
4. After your last rep, you can grasp the handles to help you dismount the machine.

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Securely attach an ankle cuff just above the ankle of the leg you will train. Position the cuff so that one of its attachment rings is directed toward the inside of your leg.
3. Stand sideways directly next to the pulley with your working leg further away from the pulley and your feet together.
    1. For instance, if you are going to train your left side, the side of your right shoulder should be facing the cable station.
4. Take a step forward with the leg closer to the pulley.
    1. The goal is to have your non-working leg’s heel slightly in front of your working leg’s toes to provide sufficient clearance for your working leg to sweep inward across toward the pulley.
5. Bend over and connect the cable to your cuff’s attachment ring before standing upright.
    1. It will be easiest to connect the cable when your working leg is close enough to the pulley that the cable does not provide resistance when connecting it.
6. Grasp the cable station’s beam with your closer hand and continue holding it from now onward for balance assistance.
7. Take a step out to the side with your working leg against the cable’s resistance before taking a step with your other leg.
    1. Your feet should now be hip-width apart, with your non-working leg’s foot still in front of your working leg’s foot.
    2. The goal of this step is to step out just far enough so that the cable can provide resistance throughout the exercise’s full range of motion. If you notice that you lose resistance from the cable when your working leg is in the starting position of a rep, you should step a bit further out away from the pulley.
    3. Your chest and imaginary belt buckle should be pointing straight ahead.
    4. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Keep your back near this neutral position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Mildly lean your torso forward by hinging at your front leg’s hip until your working leg’s foot can lift off the ground with a straight knee.
    1. Keep your working leg’s thigh aligned with your torso when viewed from the side.
    2. To help your foot clear the ground, you can pull the top of your foot upward through ankle motion. This is the opposite motion that occurs during the lifting phase of a calf raise, and you should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract when performing it.
    3. Only lean as far forward as is required for you to be able to lift your foot off the ground.
    4. All the subsequent directions will apply to your working leg.
3. Allow your leg to sweep inward in line with the cable’s resistance while keeping your hip bones and shoulder level with each other.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your knee cap pointing straight ahead rather than rotating it inward or outward.
    2. Allow your leg to sweep inward through the full range that your hip mobility permits, which commonly prompts a stretching sensation on the side of your hip.
    3. People commonly have the mobility to let their working leg’s foot be pulled slightly horizontally closer to the pulley than the non-working leg’s foot.
4. Drive your leg straight out to the side and upward in an arcing manner through your hip’s available range of motion.
    1. During the entirety of the exercise, continue keeping the tops of your hip bones and shoulders level with each other as your chest and imaginary belt buckle are pointing straight ahead. Avoid twisting your torso, bending your torso to the side, or hiking up either hip bone.
    2. While the rest of your body remains stationary, the only motion that should occur is your leg arcing out to the side, like the hand of an analog clock moving about the center point that is your hip.
    3. Most people should be able to finish with the thigh angled at least 30 degrees from a vertical position. However, how far you personally can lift your leg out to the side will be influenced by your hip mobility, and you should only move as far as you can without using the rest of your body to compensate for hip motion.
    4. You should feel the muscles on the side of your hip contract.
5. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your leg to sweep downward and inward in an arcing motion.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your leg crossed across the midline of your body.
    2. Allow your leg to sweep back in through the full range that your hip mobility permits while keeping your knee cap, chest, and imaginary belt buckle pointing straight forward with your hip bones and shoulders level.
    3. Avoid letting the weight rapidly swing your leg inward in an uncontrolled manner.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. To train your other side, you will switch the cuff to your other leg and face the opposite direction.

## Setting up
1. Position a short looped elastic band around both of your lower thighs.
    1. The band will provide the greatest resistance to your hip muscles if you place it just above your knees, while it will provide less resistance if you place it higher up your thighs.
    2. You can choose specifically where you situate the band on your thighs based on the level of resistance you wish to experience. If you are using a particular band for this exercise for the first time, you can adjust its placement during the set if you wish to change the difficulty after starting the set.
    3. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
2. Stand upright with your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, as your toes are pointing somewhat out to the sides rather than pointing straight ahead.
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside of shoulder width with their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
3. Raise your arms out in front of you until they are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. You can alternatively keep your arms in a different position if you wish to do so, but keeping your arms outstretched throughout the set provides a counterbalance that often allows people to reach a greater squat depth.
## Exercise technique
1. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down, while driving your knees out against the band to keep your knees stacked over your feet.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but keep your back flat and chest up, as you avoid rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting the band pull your knees inward past this point.
2. Continue to squat down through the available range of motion that your mobility enables without rounding your back, lifting your heels up off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, heels lift off the ground, or knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting excessively deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively standing up as you drive through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips until you have returned to a fully upright position.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees stacked over your feet as you squat up.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable to its highest level, connect a rope attachment to it, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
    1. You optionally can place a foam pad (or similarly soft object) that is comfortable for kneeling a little in front of the cable station.
2. Stand under the rope with your back facing the cable station.
3. Reach up and grasp each end of the rope with your little fingers and adjacent aspects of your hands contacting the flat surfaces of the attachment’s rubber stoppers. Wrap your thumbs over the outside of your other fingers.
4. Pull your hands down until they are approximately in front of your shoulders with your elbows bent.
    1. You will keep your hands in this position throughout your set.
5. Kneel down with both knees on the ground (or the soft object you placed on the ground) about hip width apart from each other.
6. While keeping your back flat, moderately bend at your hips to position your torso closer to horizontal to the ground.
    1. The appropriate degree of hip bend should allow you to feel stable and balanced throughout your set. You can initially try bending your hips until your torso is approximately 45 degrees inclined and adjust from there based on what feels best to you.
    2. In this position, you should feel tension from the cable. If you do not, you should set up a little further away from the cable to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion of each rep.
## Exercise technique
1. Without moving your hips or arms, arch your back in a controlled manner through the range of motion that feels comfortable to your lower back.
    1. How far you can comfortably arch your back will be influenced by your mobility.
    2. Some people may experience lower back discomfort in a fully arched position, and there is no need to arch beyond the point that feels right to you.
    3. When thinking about an imaginary laser beam shooting out from the middle of your chest, the beam should angle progressively higher up as you arch your back.
    4. The bottom of your ribs should lift up and away from the top of your hip bones.
2. Curl your spine as you pull the bottom of your ribs toward the tops of your hip bones in a controlled manner. Avoid moving your hips or arms as you round your entire back.
    1. Once you feel that you can no longer curl your spine through a range that feels comfortable to your back, you have reached your end range.
    2. Try to point the imaginary laser beam shooting out from the middle of your chest closer toward the middle point between your knees.
    3. It can help to think about crunching your elbows toward your knees.
    4. If you finish the movement with your back fairly flat as opposed to rounded, you most likely are bending at your hips rather than curling your spine.
    5. Making sure to avoid sitting your buttocks back can help limit unintended hip motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md), which is assisted by your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md).

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your knees bent, as the soles of your feet are flat on the ground, approximately hip width apart. Place your arms by your sides and your palms on the ground.
    1. You can rest your head on the ground.
    2. You can optionally hook the tops of your feet under a sturdy object, such as a couch (while your soles remain flat on the ground), to help stabilize your body during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground while you lift your head and shoulder blades up off the ground by curling your middle back.
    1. Given that this is a crunch rather than a sit-up, the lower half of your back should remain in contact with the ground while you only lift up the upper half of your back mildly off the floor.
    2. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    3. As you progressively crunch up, allow your hands to slide forward slightly while remaining on the ground.
    4. As a cue, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the top of your hip bones, which is the action that contraction of your abdominal muscles can produce.
    5. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that crunching up any further would require the lower half of your back to lift off the floor.
    6. At the end of the lifting phase, your chest should be facing at an angle between forward and upward, rather than only facing upward as it did in the starting position.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your middle back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your head and shoulder blades back to the starting position on the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and especially your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md), which is the “six-pack muscle.”

## Setting up
1. In a deadlift motion (like what is subsequently described in the technique section), pick up a kettlebell and set it onto the ground with its handle facing up.
    1. Particularly when using what you consider to be a heavy weight, initially lift it up using your hips and knees with your lower back near a flat position rather than being excessively rounded over at your lower back.
2. Stand upright in a near shoulder-width stance with the handle of the kettlebell between the middle of your feet, as your toes are slightly turned out to the sides or pointing straight ahead.
    1. While using a near shoulder-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    2. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
3. With your arms directed down toward the ground, straight elbows, and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the handle.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the handle.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    5. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
4. With your hands close together and your elbows still straight, firmly grasp the handle with an overhand grip, resulting in your facing palms backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the handle with the handle pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handle closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handle can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the kettlebell, apply “pre-tension” into the handle as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force that would lift the weight if it were only half as heavy
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position and pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat, drive through your legs to begin lifting the kettlebell as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the handle reaches near the middle of your shins, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
5. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the kettlebell until it has returned to resting on the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the handle has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the kettlebell.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the kettlebell up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the kettlebell on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the kettlebell on the ground.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to position the bar on your upper back and unrack it in a stable position.
    1. As an initial approximation, you can position the bar such that it is a few finger widths below the height of your collarbone.
2. Stand upright, facing the center of the unloaded bar.
    1. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you can position yourself to face the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends (which results in the bottom of the rails being farther in front of you than the top of the rails). Facing this way can often feel more natural for good mornings, but you can alternatively face the other direction if you personally prefer to do so.
    2. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face.
3. Grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
4. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to then walk under the bar and situate the bar on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    2. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
    5. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a bar on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
5. Position the middle of your feet under the bar in an approximately shoulder-width to hip-width stance with your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly out to the sides.
    1. You can determine specifically how wide a stance and where you point your toes based on what personally feels most comfortable and stable to you, since the ideal stance can vary among different individuals.
6. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of good morning reps with the form described under the exercise technique section before reracking the bar to determine the appropriate height of the safety stops.
7. Position the safety stops slightly under the lowest point or directly at the lowest point at which the bar descended during your good morning.
    1. The appropriate safety stop position should allow you to hinge through your full range of motion while being high enough to receive the bar if you fail a rep and bend your knees a bit more to set the bar on the safety stops.
8. Load the bar with your desired weight, and repeat steps 2-5.
## Exercise technique
1. While pulling down on the bar to keep it stable on your upper back, un-rack the bar by starting to stand up as you extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the bar on your upper back throughout your set.
2. After the bar is fully resting on your upper back rather than the safety bars, rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion prior to standing fully upright with the bar.
    1. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. Your neck should similarly be near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
    3. Keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position throughout your set.
3. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
4. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner.
    1. Avoid rounding your lower back as you keep your lower back mildly arched or flat throughout the exercise.
    2. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    3. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something, as you keep your chest up (rather than letting your chest collapse through back rounding).
    4. Keep the soles of your feet fully planted on the ground the entire time.
    5. While you hinge at your hips, the bar will naturally descend, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    6. How deeply you are able to hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    7. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range.
    8. If your end range corresponds to where you positioned the safety stops, you can gently tap the bar against the safety stops without resting the bar on the safety stops at the bottom.
5. Reverse the movement by driving your hips forward until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so you should continue keeping your chest up without any back rounding.
    2. Once you have returned to the starting position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid driving your hips in front of your shoulders at the top, which would prompt your lower back to arch excessively. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips appropriately stacked under your shoulders to prevent excessive arching.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
7. After finishing the set, rerack the bar by bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner as you rotate the safety hooks onto the safety bars and return the bar to resting on the safety bars.

1a35c6f170d880918125e6387c3849d5:
## Setting up
1. Lie down on your side with the side of your body that you are about to train facing up.
    1. In this side-lying position, you can rest the bottom side of your head on the hand of your bottom arm for comfort by situating your upper arm out to the side with your elbow bent.
    2. For extra stability, you can bend the elbow of your top arm and place that side’s hand on the ground in front of your torso.
2. While keeping the knee of your top leg straight and that side’s thigh aligned with your torso (like it would be when you are standing upright), march the thigh of your bottom leg toward your chest while moderately bending that side’s knee.
    1. After doing so, your bottom leg and foot should no longer be situated underneath your top leg, allowing your top leg’s foot to rest on the ground as that side’s thigh crosses in toward the midline of your body.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your top leg straight upward through your hip’s available range of motion while keeping that side’s knee straight and the rest of your body stationary.
    1. Avoid rolling your hips backward or bringing your top leg forward toward your chest during this exercise, which are common technical errors.
    2. To help prevent your hips from rolling, you can imagine that you are wearing a belt with a buckle that has a laser beam shooting out of it. Strive to keep the laser beam pointing straight forward, parallel to the ground, throughout the movement.
    3. If you start to roll your hips backward, your belt buckle’s laser beam will start to angle upward.
    4. When you lift your top leg straight upward rather than also bringing that leg forward in front of you, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your torso when your top thigh is parallel with the ground.
    5. While performing this movement with the appropriate technique, you will likely feel the muscles on the side of your top hip contracting.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your top leg to descend in a controlled manner until the inner aspect of its foot lightly contacts the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side by lying on your opposite side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the musculature on the side of your hip, including your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), and [tensor fascia latae](../Muscles/Tensor%20Fascia%20Latae%201925c6f170d8806fb83bf08142d940fc.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Securely attach an ankle cuff just above the ankle of the leg you will train. Position the cuff so that one of its attachment rings is directed toward the inside of your leg.
3. Stand sideways directly next to the pulley with your working leg further away from the pulley and your feet together.
    1. For instance, if you are going to train your left side, the side of your right shoulder should be facing the cable station.
4. Take a step backward with the leg closer to the pulley.
    1. The goal is to have your non-working leg’s toes slightly behind your working leg’s heel to provide sufficient clearance for your working leg to sweep inward across your body toward the pulley.
5. Bend over and connect the cable to your cuff’s attachment ring before standing upright.
    1. It will be easiest to connect the cable when your working leg is close enough to the pulley that the cable does not provide resistance when connecting it.
6. Grasp the cable station beam with your closer hand and continue holding it from now onward for balance assistance.
7. Take a step out to the side with your working leg against the cable’s resistance before taking a step with your other leg.
    1. Your feet should now be hip-width apart, with your non-working leg’s foot still in front of your working leg’s foot.
    2. The goal of this step is to step out just far enough so that the cable can provide resistance throughout the exercise’s full range of motion. If you notice that you lose resistance from the cable when your working leg is in the starting position of a rep, you should step a bit further out away from the pulley.
    3. Your chest and imaginary belt buckle should be pointing straight ahead.
    4. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Keep your back near this neutral position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Shift your bodyweight into your non-working leg, and lift your working leg’s foot off the ground with a straight knee.
    1. All the subsequent directions will apply to your working leg.
3. Allow your leg to sweep inward in line with the cable’s resistance while keeping your hip bones and shoulder level with each other.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your knee cap pointing straight ahead rather than rotating it inward or outward.
    2. Allow your leg to sweep inward through the full range that your hip mobility permits, which commonly prompts a stretching sensation on the side of your hip.
    3. People commonly have the mobility to let their working leg’s foot be pulled slightly horizontally closer to the pulley than the non-working leg’s foot.
4. Drive your leg straight out to the side and upward in an arcing manner through your hip’s available range of motion.
    1. During the entirety of the exercise, continue keeping the tops of your hip bones and shoulders level with each other as your chest and imaginary belt buckle are pointing straight ahead. Avoid twisting your torso, bending your torso to the side, or hiking up either hip bone.
    2. While the rest of your body remains stationary, the only motion that should occur is your leg arcing out to the side, like the hand of an analog clock moving about the center point that is your hip.
    3. Most people should be able to finish with the thigh angled at least 30 degrees from a vertical position. However, how far you personally can lift your leg out to the side will be influenced by your hip mobility, and you should only move as far as you can without using the rest of your body to compensate for hip motion.
    4. You should feel the muscles on the side of your hip contract.
5. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your leg to sweep downward and inward in an arcing motion.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your leg crossed across the midline of your body.
    2. Allow your leg to sweep back in through the full range that your hip mobility permits while keeping your knee cap, chest, and imaginary belt buckle pointing straight forward with your hip bones and shoulders level.
    3. Avoid letting the weight rapidly swing your leg inward in an uncontrolled manner.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. To train your other side, you will switch the cuff to your other leg and face the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the musculature on the side of your hip, including your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), and [tensor fascia latae](../Muscles/Tensor%20Fascia%20Latae%201925c6f170d8806fb83bf08142d940fc.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell in a spot where you have sufficient space to lie down on the ground.
    1. The diameter of the weight plates you select can influence how easily you can set up while also affecting the range of motion for this exercise.
    2. It will be easiest to assume the starting position with at least one pair of full diameter plates, such as typical 45lb (20kg) Olympic plates or bumper plates. With full diameter plates, certain individuals who are very thick may need to utilize one of the strategies discussed below to set up under the bar.
    3. If you exclusively load the bar with smaller diameter plates, you may have to modify the standard setup in order to position your hips under the bar. When only using smaller diameter plates, you can elevate the bar just enough to fit your hips under it by situating the plates on top of deadlift blocks, aerobic steps, or stacks of full diameter weight plates. Alternatively, you may have a partner place the bar on top of your hip bones and load it with weight plates after you have assumed the starting position. If neither of these approaches is practical to you, you lack bumper plates that allow you to elevate the bar fully with light loads, and you do not currently have the strength to use 135lb (or 60kg) for this exercise, you have the option of performing other glute bridge variations. For instance, you can select a [single leg bodyweight glute bridge](Single%20leg%20bodyweight%20glute%20bridge%201a35c6f170d88042b608da098f0a9af6.md) or a [dumbbell glute bridge](Dumbbell%20glute%20bridge%201a35c6f170d880c5867ce22eefbc7cb7.md) from this database to train the glutes in essentially the same manner as the barbell variation, but with an easier setup.
2. Optionally, obtain a pad (or an object that can function as a pad) that you will place between the bar and your hips.
    1. Using a pad is not required but strongly recommended because it can be very uncomfortable to have a barbell directly resting on your hip bones with a meaningful load.
    2. You can wrap a hip thrust pad or a squat pad around the middle of the bar.
    3. Alternatively, you can place a thick foam or folded exercise mat on the crease of your hip during the next step and subsequently keep it there to cushion your hip bones. Be aware that foam pads not specifically designed for glute bridges or hip thrusts may be somewhat damaged from this exercise.
3. Sit down on the ground with an upright torso and your legs straight out in front of you under the bar.
    1. The middle of the bar should be aligned with the midline of your body.
4. Grasp the bar with your palms facing down and roll it toward the crease of your hips.
    1. So long as your hands are wider apart than your hips, you can adjust your grip width based on what feels stable and comfortable to you during this exercise.
    2. Continue holding the bar from this point onward.
5. Lie down with your back and head resting on the ground.
    1. Tuck your chin slightly toward your chest while resting the back of your head on the ground throughout the exercise.
6. Bend your knees until your shins are in an approximately vertical position with the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can position your feet shoulder-width apart, but it is up to you whether you would like them closer together or farther apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can point your toes forward or slightly out to the sides.
    3. The optimal degree of knee bend should allow your feet to feel stable while being firmly planted on the ground throughout the set. Bringing your heels toward your buttocks until they are vertically stacked under your knees is normally appropriate, but you can adjust how much you bend your knees if a different position feels more stable to you.
7. Confirm that the bar is directly above the crease of your hips and completely centered before initiating the set.
    1. Positioning the bar appropriately will help you avoid the excessive discomfort that may arise from positioning the bar too high (i.e., directly on your lower abdomen) or too low (i.e., directly on your groin).
    2. Some people may experience discomfort when the bar looks aligned with the crease of their hips if the bar is directly resting on the bony bumps on the front of their hip bones. If you notice that this occurs for you during your set, you can roll the bar slightly further down away from your abdomen to shift the pressure away from these bony bumps. When making any adjustments during a set, only do so in between reps when the weights are resting on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
2. Lift your hips up by driving your heels into the ground and squeezing your glutes. Keep the bar balanced on the crease of your hips the entire set.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thighs and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glutes.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glutes engage during this exercise.
    4. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them at the top.
    5. The soles of your feet and your upper back should remain firmly in contact with the ground throughout the exercise.
    6. The purpose of holding the bar with your hands is to keep it stabilized on the crease of your hips. Avoid trying to lift the bar up or push it down with your hands.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid simply letting gravity pull the bar down abruptly, as opposed to you using your glutes to control the descent actively.
    2. If you hear the plates crashing into the ground, you are not lowering the bar with sufficient control.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps. The bar should come to a dead stop on the ground after each rep.
    2. After completing the lowering phase of your last rep, roll the bar forward before sitting up in the reversed manner to how you set up initially.
## Description
While your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md) and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md) can assist to a degree, this exercise primarily targets your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md).
