## Setting up
1. If your machine allows you to adjust the height of the footplate, select a height that will allow your legs to be in an approximately horizontal position once you are in the starting position.
    1. After estimating where this setting may be, you can adjust it during later steps if warranted.
    2. Not all machines permit you to adjust the footplate height.
2. Horizontally adjust the machine’s footplate to a setting that will allow the pad to support your thighs without contacting your hip bones when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. The appropriate position should allow your hips to move freely while sufficiently stabilizing your legs.
    2. If the footplate is positioned excessively far back (resulting in your hips resting on the pad), the pad can restrict your hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    3. If the footplate is positioned excessively far forward to the extent that your knees are near the middle of the pad rather than your thighs, the exercise may provoke knee discomfort in some people.
    4. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position.
3. Position the weight you intend to use in a spot that you can comfortably reach after you set your feet on the footplate.
    1. For this variation, you can hold a weight close to your chest or hold it with straight arms that are directed down toward the ground. The position in which you hold it is up to preference, along with whether you use a weight plate, dumbbell, kettlebell, or medicine ball.
    2. Based on the weight you use, the machine model you have, your body proportions, and your mobility, you have multiple options for where you can place the weight.
    3. You may be able to place certain weights on top of the pad before picking up the weight after you mount the machine. However, not all weights can remain balanced on top of the pad, and this approach is not practical for some pad designs.
    4. With a sufficiently light weight plate or kettlebell, you may be able to hang the weight on one of the handles.
    5. Alternatively, you can place the weight on the ground just in front of the pad and pick it up at the bottom of your hip hinge after you finish setting up on the machine. This option naturally requires that you are able to reach the weight on the ground, which is not feasible for everyone.
    6. As an additional approach, you can have a partner hand you the weight after you are set up, which can be useful if you are using a heavy weight.
4. Climb up onto the machine, and position your feet against the footplate with your lower legs between the leg rollers while the front of your hips are resting on the pad.
    1. The back of your lower legs should be snugly pressed into the top pair of leg rollers slightly above your heels.
    2. Your knees should be straight, and your soles should be firmly contacting the footplate.
    3. While you are setting your feet, you can use the handles for assistance.
    4. Some machines have a step that you can use to help you get into position.
    5. With the appropriate footplate setting, the front of your hip bones should not be resting on the pad.
5. Pick up the weight, and hold it with both hands either close to your chest or with straight arms directed down toward the ground.
    1. The precise way in which you will pick up and hold it may vary based on the specific implement you selected and where you placed it initially. What matters is that you have a firm grip on the weight and are able to keep it in a stable position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes to keep your torso up such that you can draw approximately a straight line from your legs through your hips and to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. This is the starting position of the exercise, where your body should look like it does when normally standing upright, except rotated to be horizontal.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips.
3. Without rounding your back, hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner to angle your torso downward.
    1. As opposed to bending over at your back, nearly all the motion should occur from you moving at your hips as you statically keep your trunk near a neutral position with your lower back mildly arched or flat.
    2. Maintain a straight knee position, but avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads.
    3. While hinging at your hips and keeping your hands on your shoulders, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings that progressively intensifies.
    4. How deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility. If you have the flexibility to hinge until your torso is completely vertical, stop once you reach this point. Otherwise, stop descending once you feel like you have reached the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch.
    5. If you initially did not position the footplate sufficiently forward, the pad may alternatively limit how deeply you can hinge.
4. Reverse the movement by lifting your torso up through your hips and squeezing your glutes.
    1. When moving through your hips, your entire torso should move together as one unit. You can think of your hips as the center of an analog clock, while your rigid torso is a hand that rotates about the center.
    2. At the end of the lifting phase, your torso should be close to a horizontal position aligned with your legs.
    3. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the hip motion you just performed during the lowering phase. Focusing on finishing the movement by squeezing your glutes can help prevent excessive back arching.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
6. After your last rep, return the weight to the position in which you initially placed it before dismounting the machine.
    1. You can grasp the handles to help you dismount the machine.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, and secure the weights with collars.
    1. In contrast to most machines, the weight plates may slide if you do not connect collars on a reverse hyper with a center pendulum and two sleeves.
2. If your machine has adjustable handles, position them at a setting that allows you to hold with mostly straight elbows during step 4.
    1. This can require some trial and error to find the ideal handle setting.
    2. A variety of machine models lack adjustable handles, but some have multiple pairs of handles that allow you to select the ones that you can grasp with mostly straight elbows.
3. Stand directly in front of the pad and the weights. If you are using leg straps rather than rollers, step into the straps.
4. After climbing on the pad, lie down with your abdomen on the pad, and firmly grasp the handles. Position the top of your hip bones just on the edge of the pad.
    1. The appropriate positioning should allow your legs to move freely throughout the exercise.
    2. If you position yourself excessively far forward, the pad will restrict your hip motion.
    3. If you position yourself excessively far backward, you will be less stable and may round your lower back more than intended.
    4. Some machine models will have a pair of steps to help you climb onto the pad.
5. If you are using leg straps, move your legs backward until your lower legs are snugly contacting the straps slightly above your ankles. If you are using leg rollers, position your lower legs snugly between the rollers slightly above your ankles.
    1. In the starting position, the straps should be taught rather than slacked (if you are using straps).
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Drive your legs backward and upward in an arcing motion as you squeeze your glutes.
    1. Rather than aiming to lift your legs to a particular height, you can focus on forcefully squeezing your glutes, which can naturally promote the appropriate range.
    2. It is normal for the range of motion of the initial rep or two to be lower than subsequent reps, since the initial reps help build momentum.
    3. Throughout your set, keep your torso fully in contact with the pad and your neck near a normal position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    4. As a cue, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between your glutes.
3. Reverse the movement by allowing your legs to arc downward and forward in a controlled manner.
    1. Keep the strap snugly against your lower legs the entirety of each rep if you are using a strap.
    2. The standard technique for this exercise involves a controlled swinging motion that the machine’s pendulum facilitates, but you optionally can use a very strict technique where you emphasize slowing the descent as much as you can. 
    3. While you can work with the pendulum’s momentum, avoid letting the momentum take over the movement in an uncontrolled manner. If you feel that the momentum is excessive despite your effort to control it, it may be appropriate to try a lighter load.
4. After your legs are close to pointing straight down, drive your legs backward and upward while squeezing your glutes.
    1. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable to you, you can begin driving your legs back once they are vertical or once they move mildly forward beyond this point. Do not let the pendulum yank your legs any further forward.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
    1. It is normal for some lower back motion to occur simultaneously with hip motion during this exercise. However, your lower back should not fully arch at the top or excessively round at the bottom when appropriately using your glutes through the proper range of motion.
6. While keeping your legs snugly against the strap or roller, allow the pendulum’s momentum to subside until it stops swinging before dismounting the machine.
    1. Guiding the pendulum through a few cycles of progressively shorter swings may be required for it to come to a dead stop.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) while also training your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and [spinal erectors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md).

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to the barbell situated on the ground, position a large diameter weight plate (or a viable alternative) under the center of the bar that you will use to create a deficit.
    1. While you can use a variety of deficit heights, selecting a low deficit height (under 4in (10cm)) is initially recommended to facilitate the appropriate technique.
    2. You want to pick a height that allows you to keep your lower back flat at the bottom of the rep, and the height should still allow you to use a deadlift technique rather than squatting the weight up (which can occur with an excessively large deficit).
    3. A large diameter (e.g., 45lb (20kg)) cast iron weight plate with the flat surface facing up can be a suitable option to select since these plates are normally near 1.5in (3.8cm) thick.
    4. A bumper plate or stackable deadlift block can also be used for your deficit.
    5. Depending on your preferred stance width, you can also position two plates directly next to each other if the soles of your feet do not fit fully onto one plate.
    6. As an alternative to standing on a plate or step, you can also pull through an extended range of motion by exclusively loading smaller diameter plates onto the bar and standing on the ground.
2. Stand upright on the plate in approximately a hip-width stance, close in front of the middle of the bar, as the bar is over the middle of your feet, with your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly turned out to the sides.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
    2. The soles of your feet should be fully in contact with the plate for maximal stability.
    3. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    4. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
3. With your arms directed down toward the ground, straight elbows, and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    5. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat with the bar close to your shins, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the bar reaches near the middle of your shins, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
5. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the ground.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.

## Setting up
This exercise can be performed with an ankle weight strapped to your ankle or a weight plate, dumbbell, or kettlebell held on top of your lower thigh. The technique is essentially the same regardless of which equipment you use, but certain setup details differ, which is why two different setup sections are presented.

### Setting up with ankle weights

1. Strap an ankle weight to each of your ankles and lie down on your side with the side of your body that you are about to train facing up.
    1. In this side-lying position, you can rest the bottom side of your head on the hand of your bottom arm for comfort by situating your upper arm out to the side with your elbow bent.
    2. For extra stability, you can bend the elbow of your top arm and place that side’s hand on the ground in front of your torso.
2. While keeping the knee of your top leg straight and that side’s thigh aligned with your torso (like it would be when you are standing upright), march the thigh of your bottom leg toward your chest while moderately bending that side’s knee.
    1. After doing so, your bottom leg and foot should no longer be situated underneath your top leg, allowing your top leg’s foot to rest on the ground as that side’s thigh crosses in toward the midline of your body.

### Setting up without ankle weights

1. Place the weight you will use for resistance on the ground next to where you will lie.
2. Lie down on your side with the side of your body that you are about to train facing up.
    1. In this side-lying position, you can rest the bottom side of your head on the hand of your bottom arm for comfort by situating your upper arm out to the side with your elbow bent.
    2. For extra stability, you can bend the elbow of your top arm and place that side’s hand on the ground in front of your torso.
3. While keeping the knee of your top leg straight and that side’s thigh aligned with your torso (like it would be when you are standing upright), march the thigh of your bottom leg toward your chest while moderately bending that side’s knee.

4. Place the weight on top of your thigh (that is facing up). Throughout the exercise, continue holding the weight in place with your hand as your top arm is by your side and your elbow is straight.

1. Lift your top leg straight upward through your hip’s available range of motion while keeping that side’s knee straight and the rest of your body stationary.

    2. To help prevent your hips from rolling, you can imagine that you are wearing a belt with a buckle that has a laser beam shooting out of it. Strive to keep the laser beam pointing straight forward, parallel to the ground, throughout the movement.
    3. If you start to roll your hips backward, your belt buckle’s laser beam will start to angle upward.
    4. When you lift your top leg straight upward rather than also bringing that leg forward in front of you, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your torso when your top thigh is parallel with the ground.
    5. While performing this movement with the appropriate technique, you should feel the muscles on the side of your top hip contracting.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your top leg to descend in a controlled manner until the inner aspect of its foot lightly contacts the ground.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground.
    1. The setup for this exercise is simply performing the lifting phase of a [conventional deadlift](Conventional%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880f7a755cd3780a63371.md).
2. In a near hip-width stance, stand with the middle of your feet under the middle of the bar.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the ground, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track far forward. However, you can let your knees shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
4. With straight elbows, firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip, such that your palms face backward.
    1. As an alternative to the double overhand grip, you can use a mixed grip (with one palm facing forward and the other facing backward) or lifting straps with the double overhand grip if you wish.
    2. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    3. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    4. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than at the base of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hands while you hold it, which pulls on your hand skin uncomfortably and increases the risk of tearing a callus.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
6. While keeping your lower back flat and chest up, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.
    1. Keep your elbows straight and the bar very close to your legs as you lift the bar, rather than letting the bar drift forward.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight with the bar just in front of your legs. Avoid letting the bar drift forward away from you, which may be more likely to occur if you think about “bending over” rather than “sitting back.”
    2. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the bar.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    5. Throughout the set, keep your feet fully planted on the ground and your neck near a neutral position, as when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move.
    1. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    3. If you have high hamstring flexibility and can hinge until the plates contact the ground, descend until you can tap the plates very lightly on the ground, but do not let the weight rest on the ground.
    4. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should clearly be in control of the entire descent.
3. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward to lift your torso upright into the starting position.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so keep your lower back flat, chest up, core braced, feet fully on the ground, and the bar close to your legs.
    2. When you have finished lifting the bar, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back at the top through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips properly stacked under your shoulders, preventing excessive arching.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down onto the floor.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe between reps in the fully upright position, rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
    2. After finishing the last rep, set the bar down in the same manner in which you initially picked it up (e.g., keeping your lower back flat rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

### Learning how to hip hinge

If you have minimal experience training hip hinge exercises such as Romanian deadlift and good morning variations, it is normal to have difficulty performing this movement pattern. Like riding a bicycle or shooting a basketball, hip hinging is a motor skill that may require repeated practice before you feel comfortable consistently using it. Broadly speaking, there are two types of movement substitution patterns that individuals who are in the process of learning how to hip hinge commonly perform when attempting to execute a hip hinge exercise.

One of these is using a stoop lift, which involves dynamically rounding the back (through flexion of the lumbar and thoracic spine) to bend over prior to uncoiling the spine into an upright position during the ascent. This often is accompanied by the buttock not moving particularly far backward and the arms drifting out in front of the legs in contrast to a strict hip hinge, which utilizes a visibly flat back position (with close to a neutral lumbar spine) and has the buttock noticeably moving backward during the descent. In terms of similarity, a stoop lift and a hip hinge both involve only a mild magnitude of knee bend during the descent while keeping the hips high. A clue that you may be performing more of a stoop lift than a hip hinge is feeling a stretching sensation in your back rather than feeling your back muscles remain statically tight throughout your set as these muscles function to maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips. With a properly performed hip hinge, you should certainly feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the bottom of the lift, but you may also feel this stretching sensation during a stoop lift. Nonetheless, a hip hinge can allow you to feel the hamstring stretch earlier during the descent compared to a stoop lift since the hamstrings are shortened by the posterior pelvic tilt (tucking the tailbone under) that is coupled with lumbar spine flexion.

In addition to performing a stoop lift unintentionally when attempting to hip hinge, people can commonly utilize more of a squatting motion that is characterized by greater knee bend and forward tracking of the knees during the descent. Compared to a hip hinge, using more of a squatting movement can result in the buttock moving downward during the descent as opposed to backward, and the shins can also incline forward as opposed to remaining vertical. Because the hamstrings shorten as the knees bend, someone moving in a squat pattern when attempting to perform a hip hinge exercise is unlikely to feel much of a stretching sensation in the hamstrings at the bottom of the lift. Not feeling a hamstring stretch is the most straightforward indicator that you may be squatting your hip hinge exercise, but an additional clue would be if you perceive your quads to be working (e.g., feeling a “burning” sensation or lots of tension) more intensely than your hamstrings during the exercise.

When thinking about moving through hip hinge, stoop lift, and squat patterns, it is important to recognize that these movements can occur along a spectrum. You can perform a hip hinge exercise with a technique that is mostly a hip hinge while still utilizing elements of a stoop lift or a squat that may not be ideal for what you wish to accomplish from the exercise. Similarly, your technique can incrementally progress from being stoop lift-dominant or squat-dominant to becoming progressively more of a hip hinge as your body learns how to move in a different way through repeated practice. If your hip hinge technique currently has much room for improvement, it can be beneficial to start with lighter loads that may not be especially challenging to your muscles until you developed a reasonable level of competency with the movement itself. There is no need to let perfect be the enemy of good, so you do not need to wait to load a movement meaningfully until you have immaculate technique, but it would also be inadvisable to push your body to the limit without initially learning the basic fundamentals of the movement.

Depending on which element of hip hinging in which you currently are challenged, certain external cues can expedite how quickly you can learn how to hinge. When unintentionally moving in a manner that involves a greater degree of squatting or stoop lifting than is intended, a wall may help provide tactile feedback to cue sitting your buttock backward. To do so, you can perform your hip hinge with your back facing a nearby wall, and you will be able to receive confirmation as to whether you are actually sitting your hips backward by feeling the wall contact your buttock at the end of the descent. As an initial starting point, you can set up with a heel-to-toe tandem stance as the back of one heel contacts the wall. Then you can bring your rear foot forward to be aligned with your front foot in the symmetrical stance you will utilize for your hip hinge. This can provide a reasonable approximation as to how far people may commonly be able to sit their hips back when hinging, but you can adjust from there how far away you position yourself from the wall to individualize it to you.

Specifically if you have a tendency to perform a “squatty” hip hinge, practicing your hip hinge with your calves up against something like a flat exercise bench (or even a couch or chair at home) can be a rather productive means of honing your hinge. As you descend, you will receive immediate tactile feedback if your knees track forward from no longer feeling the contact with your calves, so it can be a great way to reinforce keeping your shins vertical throughout the movement. When using this method, make sure that you maintain full contact between the soles of your feet and the ground while you avoid leaning your bodyweight into the bench to the extent that you would fall backward if the bench was removed. If you successfully keep your calves in contact with the bench throughout the movement and feel a pronounced stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the end of the descent, you are right on track to achieving a high quality hip hinge.

As an additional learning tool, you can situate a long object like a dowel rod, PVC pipe, or yardstick on your back while hip hinging if you have a tendency to utilize more of a stoop lift technique with excessive back rounding. Either the calf-to-bench technique or the buttock-to-wall technique can be incorporated into an actual Romanian deadlift where you use weights, but using a rod as a cue without a partner will require you to hold the rod in place, so you would not be able to load this drill independently. To perform this movement, you would hold the rod behind against your back with one hand higher up near your head and your other hand lower down near your buttock. While standing fully upright and looking straight ahead, you should feel the rod contacting your sacrum (the bone that lies between your upper buttock cheeks and right above your tailbone), upper back between your shoulder blades, and the back of your head. You will then hip hinge while maintaining these three points of contact throughout the entirety of the movement. If you start rounding your back or moving your neck beyond the neutral position you adopt when standing fully upright, you will feel the rod lose contact with one of those three spots. This can be a rather effective form of instant feedback to help develop your ability to move predominantly through your lower body while keeping your trunk in a rigid position throughout the movement, which can transfer to improved technique for an array of different exercises. When maintaining those three contact points, you potentially can still perform a squatting motion rather than a hip hinge since moving through your lower body while minimizing back motion is also a component of squatting technique. However, if you maintain those three contact points and additionally feel your hamstrings notably stretched at the bottom of the descent, those two factors indicate that you have successfully hip hinged in all likelihood. If you find that the rod cuing shifts your movement from a stoop lift to more of a squat, you can use the rod cuing simultaneously with the calf-to-bench cuing, which can address multiple aspects of the hip hinge concurrently.

In the context of performing a hip hinge exercise, using a form that resembles more of a squat or stoop lift rather than a hip hinge can be considered technique errors, but squatting and stoop lifting are by no means faulty movement patterns inherently. They simply differ from a hip hinge, so they can be suboptimal means of performing an exercise that you intend to train specifically for the benefits that hip hinging can provide as opposed to other movements. The hip hinge can take some practice to learn, but investing the time and effort into doing so can be a prudent investment given that having the motor skill of hip hinging can meaningfully expand your freedom in how you can move both inside and outside of the gym.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your lower body or lower back strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your lower body and back muscles. Among trained lifters, grip strength can very commonly limit performance of Romanian deadlifts if they do not utilize straps since the posterior chain has the potential to move rather heavy loads for this exercise. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least a few minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

### Romanian deadlift vs stiff-leg deadlift

The terms “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” are often used interchangeably to describe the same exercise by scholarly articles and lifters in general. The nomenclature of the Romanian deadlift has been attributed to this exercise being performed by Nicu Vlad, a Romanian weightlifter who won gold, silver, and bronze medals respectively in the 1984, 1988, and 1996 Olympic games in addition to medaling in seven World Weightlifting Championships (with three of them being gold). American weightlifting coach Jim Schmitz reportedly saw Vlad performing the barbell hip hinge exercise and subsequently called it the Romanian deadlift since Vlad did not have a particular name for the variation he was performing.

While they may be commonly used to refer to the same exercise, some people will use the names “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” to refer to different variations. They consider the stiff-leg deadlift to be what is described in this database as the “barbell stiff-leg deadlift from floor,” which involves each rep starting with the plates fully on the floor like a conventional deadlift. This variation differs from the Romanian deadlift, which starts from the upright position and uses a range of motion individualized to someone’s flexibility as the plates often do not contact the floor. If someone has the hamstring flexibility for the plates to contact the floor during a Romanian deadlift, a light tap to the ground is utilized, but the full weight of the bar is not transferred into the ground like how the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor is performed. In contrast to the Romanian deadlift, which is typically performed with a controlled lowering phase, this conception of the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor often involves a quicker lower phase with a tempo akin to how conventional deadlifts are commonly performed, which is to say a controlled drop. Both variations can involve a mild amount of knee flexion at the bottom of the hinge, but the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor can require that someone adopts a more flexed lumbar position in order to pull from the floor with the knee position while maintaining high hips. This differs from the Romanian deadlift being performed only through the range of motion where someone can maintain close to a neutral lumbar spine or a flat back position. 

As demonstrated by sources such as Hegyi et al. (2018) along with Piper and Waller (2001), another interpretation of the stiff-leg deadlift also exists as a truly straight leg deadlift. Under this conception of the exercise, the knees are kept extended to the extent that they are completely straight but not fully locked (which could otherwise allow for knee hyperextension in individuals with the mobility to do so). Such a technique would result in a movement that is more akin to “bending over” rather than “sitting back,” and the bar would correspondingly be likely to drift further in front of the legs compared to a Romanian deadlift, which utilizes a mild knee bend that allows you to “sit back.” In light of the different ways in which these names may be interpreted, hopefully this note provides some clarification if you have ever been confused by how different individuals may view Romanian deadlifts and stiff-leg deadlifts exercises as the same exercise or distinct variations.

## Setting up
1. Fully lower the Smith machine’s safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails), and position the bar somewhat below knee height with the safety hooks resting on the safety bars.
    1. The proper starting height of the bar should comfortably allow you to get into the starting position. If the bar is too low, it can be difficult initially to move your hips under the bar with a bench behind you. If the bar is too high, you will be unable to lift your hips high enough to receive the bar initially without arching your back excessively.
2. Determine whether your Smith machine has angled or purely vertical sliding rails.
    1. If your machine has angled sliding rails, it will be ideal for you to position your bench (or other object during the next step) on the side that allows the bar to track slightly forward when lifting the bar up and slightly backward when lowering it. This means that the bottom of the rails should be horizontally closer to the bench than the top of the rails. However, the direction in which the rails angle can vary among different machines, and you may be restricted from setting up on a bench on the side of the machine’s frame. You can still hip thrust with the bar tracking backward during the lifting phase, but it may not feel as natural compared to if the bar tracks forward while lifting up.
    2. If your machine has angled sliding rails, it does not matter which side you face during this exercise.
3. Situate a flat exercise (or viable alternative) in front of the bar with the length of the bench parallel to the length of the bar.
    1. Position the bench at a distance from the bar that specifically enables you to rest your upper back comfortably on the edge of the bench while the bar is on the crease of your hips. Finding this position may require some trial and error, which is why it is recommended to perform a couple of hip thrust reps with the empty bar before you add weight plates.
    2. A specific hip thrust bench is ideal to use if you can move it, but it is not commonly available.
    3. If you use a mobile exercise bench, make sure that it will not slide back during the exercise. In contrast to a barbell hip thrust, it is not normally feasible to anchor a bench against a rack or wall when using an immobile Smith machine. However, you can place some heavy weight plates against the back of your bench if you are concerned it may slide back during your set. Note that certain benches may be more likely to slide than others.
    4. You may also be able to use a soft plyometric box near knee height that is anchored in the same manner as a flat bench.
    5. What ultimately matters is selecting an object that is sturdy, stable, and reasonably close to being knee height while being comfortable enough to support your upper back.
4. Optionally, obtain a pad (or an object that can function as a pad) that you will place between the bar and your hips.
    1. Using a pad is not required but strongly recommended because it can be very uncomfortable to have a barbell directly resting on your hip bones with a meaningful load.
    2. You can wrap a hip thrust pad or a squat pad around the middle of the bar.
    3. Alternatively, you can place a thick foam or folded exercise mat on the crease of your hip during the next step and subsequently keep it there to cushion your hip bones. Be aware that foam pads not specifically designed for hip thrusts may be somewhat damaged from this exercise.
5. Sit down on the ground with your upper back against the edge of the bench and your legs straight out in front of you under the bar.
    1. Specifically place the lower part of your shoulder blades against the edge of the bench. Feel free to adjust your upper back positioning mildly from this point based on what feels most stable to you.
    2. The middle of the bar should be aligned with the midline of your body.
6. Bring your heels toward your buttocks by bending your knees mildly greater than 90 degrees, with the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, but it is up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can opt to point your toes forward or somewhat out to the sides.
    3. The optimal degree of knee bend should allow your feet to feel stable while being firmly planted on the ground throughout the set. It is normally appropriate to position your feet far enough back that your knees will be bent by approximately 90 degrees at the top of your hip thrust. From this placement, you can adjust specifically where you situate your feet based on your preference.
7. Grasp the bar with your palms facing down, and tuck your chin mildly toward your chest.
    1. So long as your hands are wider apart than your hips, you can adjust your grip width based on what feels stable and comfortable to you during this exercise.
    2. Continue holding the bar and keeping your chin mildly tucked throughout the exercise.
8. Using the form described in the exercise technique section, perform a couple of hip thrust reps with the empty bar to confirm that your bench placement lets the bar comfortably rest on the crease of your hips.
    1. If the bar is not positioned appropriately relative to your hips, adjust your bench placement prior to checking again until you have determined that you are set up correctly.
    2. Positioning the bar appropriately will help you avoid the excessive discomfort that may arise from positioning the bar too high (i.e., directly on your lower abdomen) or too low (i.e., directly on your groin).
    3. Some people may experience discomfort when the bar looks aligned with the crease of their hips if the bar is directly resting on the bony bumps on the front of their hip bones. If you notice that this occurs for you, you can move the bench slightly further back away from the bar to shift the pressure away from these bony bumps.
9. Load the bar with your intended weight, and assume the starting position by repeating steps 5-7.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
    2. From this starting position, your back should either be flat or exhibit its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
2. Lift your hips up until the bar is fully resting on the crease of your hips and the safety hooks are no longer resting on the safety bars.
3. Rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion.
4. Squeeze your glutes to continue lifting up until you can draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side.
    1. Since the bar begins from an elevated position, you may not have to lift your hips up much further from when you initially received the bar to reach this position.
5. Lower your hips in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your machine permits.
    1. With most Smith machines, the depth to which you can lower your hips will be determined by when the bar reaches the bottom of the slide rails. These Smith machines reach their lowest position before the weight plates or your buttocks can contact the ground, resulting in a shorter range of motion than a barbell hip thrust. If you are using one of these machines, you can aim to lightly tap the bar to the bottom of the machine.
    2. Certain Smith machines permit you to lower the bar through the same range as if you used a barbell. With one of these less common machines, you can finish the lowering phase when either the weight plates lightly contact the ground, or you have reached the end point permitted by your hip mobility.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid simply letting gravity pull the bar down abruptly, as opposed to you using your glutes to control the descent actively. Do not bounce the bar out of the bottom position.
6. Lift your hips up by driving your heels into the ground and squeezing your glutes.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thighs and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glutes.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glutes engage during this exercise.
    4. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them at the top.
    5. Throughout the exercise, the soles of your feet should remain fully planted on the ground, and your upper back should remain firmly in contact with the bench.
    6. Continue holding the bar for stability, but avoid trying to lift the bar up or push it down with your hands.
7. Alternate between steps 5 and 6 until you have completed your set.
    1. For tracking purposes, each rep finishes after you have fully lifted your hips from the bottom position. The initial movement you performed during step 4 does not constitute a full rep.
8. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars and lower your hips until the safety hooks are fully resting on the safety bars.

## Setting up
The key goal of your setup is to adjust the machine and position yourself in a manner that results in your knee joint being aligned with the machine’s pivot point, which is the center about which the machine’s lever arm rotates, that is denoted by a small dot or circle in some machines. After setting up appropriately, you should be in a position that results in you feeling comfortable and stable during the exercise. The features you can adjust will vary based on the specific machine model you use, so certain setup steps described in the instructions may not be applicable to a particular machine model. As you set up, some trial and error may be needed while you adjust the machine and position yourself to find what works best for your individual body proportions.

1. Adjust the lower leg pad to a position that places it slightly above the back of your heel (i.e., on your Achilles tendons) when leaning on the machine with your knee aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
    1. Certain machine models have an adjustable foot plate rather than an adjustable lower leg pad. If your machine has the adjustable foot plate, you should adjust its height until the lower leg pad is situated slightly above the back of your heel when standing on the foot plate.
2. Adjust the thigh pad to a position that allows you to place your lower thigh snugly against it when your knee is aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
    1. This pad may be adjusted vertically or horizontally (or not at all) depending on which machine you are using.
3. Add weight plates to the machine.
4. Stand in front of the lower leg pad with the back of your lower legs contacting this pad and your thighs contacting the thigh pad.
5. Lean forward at your hips until you can firmly grasp the handles in a comfortable position. Continue holding them throughout your set.
    1. If your machine has forearm pads, you should also rest your forearms on them.
    2. If your machine has a torso pad (for your lower abdomen or chest) in addition to a thigh pad, you should also rest your torso on it while leaning forward.
    3. In this starting position, your knees should be straight and aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
    4. Rather than being excessively arched or rounded, your lower back should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
    5. Your neck should similarly be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. On the side you are about to train, pull your toes and foot up toward your shin by moving at your ankle. Maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankle in the same position in which it would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heel up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankle in this position can increase your hamstring curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
2. Drive your heel toward your buttock by bending your knee through the full range of motion you can perform without moving your other leg.
    1. Some machines may allow you to contact your buttock or upper thigh with the lower leg pad at the end range, but other models may limit you from bending your knee to this extent.
    2. If you experience a notable cramping sensation in your hamstrings at the end range, you can stop curling the weight up just before the point where your hamstrings may cramp.
    3. While your lower leg moves through motion at your one knee, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
    4. Avoid lifting your thigh off the pad or excessively arching your lower back.
3. Reverse the movement as you allow your knee to straighten progressively in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your knee straightened.
    2. Continue keeping the foot of your resting leg planted on the ground/foot plate.
    3. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower leg down.
4. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your back on the ground near a sturdy object with an elevated surface that is no higher than the height of your upper thighs while standing.
    1. Objects like exercise flat benches, stackable aerobic steps, plyometric boxes, stairs, and beds may be used.
    2. The height of the object will affect the range of motion you can use for this exercise, and selecting an object that is near mid-thigh height for you may be preferable over shorter objects to train through a longer range of motion.
2. Lift up your legs to position the back of your heels on top of the elevated surface with your knees straight or slightly bent.
    1. If you are too close to keep your knees straight or slightly bent on top of the elevated surface, you can scoot backward until you can do so.
    2. In this position, you can rest the back of your head on the ground and leave your arms on the ground by your sides.
3. While leaving one foot on the elevated surface, lift the other foot off the elevated surface by marching that side’s thigh up while bending your knee, or by lifting that leg a little above the elevated surface while keeping your knee straight.
    1. Either position for the free leg is viable, so you can go with whichever you prefer, but keeping the knee straight may make the exercise mildly more challenging than keeping it bent.
    2. Keep one foot off the elevated surface in the static position of your choice throughout the set you perform with your other side.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heel into the elevated surface until your hip is fully extended.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your torso.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Place one weighted end of a dumbbell on the ground with its handle directed vertically, resulting in one end remaining off the ground.
    1. Placing a dumbbell on the ground in this manner will make it easier to position onto your lap compared to if you placed both ends of the dumbbell on the ground. However, if the ends of your dumbbell are not flat (such as with a plate-loaded adjustable dumbbell), you will alternatively have to place both ends of the dumbbell on the ground with a horizontal handle.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground (or an exercise mat) and the side of one of your hips directly next to the dumbbell.
3. Roll onto your side toward the dumbbell, hold the dumbbell in contact with the front of your waist with both hands, and roll onto your back with the dumbbell situated in the crease of your hips.
4. While using both hands to keep the dumbbell in the crease of your hips, bend your knees to at least 90 degrees to position the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can position your feet shoulder-width apart, but it is up to you whether you would like them closer together or farther apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can point your toes forward or slightly out to the sides.
    3. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is also up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
    4. In this position, you can rest the back of your head on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels into the ground and squeezing your glutes while continuing to hold the dumbbell in the crease of your hips.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thighs and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glutes.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glutes engage.
    4. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them at the top.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you can lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. To remove the dumbbell from your lap, roll over to your side as you did when setting it up, and then place it on the ground.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your knees bent and the soles of your feet flat on the ground, approximately hip width apart. 
    1. You can rest your head on the ground.
    2. You optionally can hook the tops of your feet under a sturdy object like a couch (while your soles are still flat on the ground), which is recommended to help stabilize your body during this exercise.
2. Cross your arms across your chest with bent elbows to position each hand on the front of the opposite shoulder.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. As you tighten your abdominal muscles, lift your back and head up off the ground by curling your back to bring your chest toward your thighs.
    1. Given that this is a sit-up rather than a crunch, you will lift the entirety of your back off the ground.
    2. To train your abdominal muscles dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain in a flat position (which could occur if you predominantly lift your torso up through your hip flexor muscles).
    3. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    4. As a cue, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the top of your hip bones, which is the action that contraction of your abdominal muscles can produce.
    5. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that you have fully rounded your back and cannot bring your chest closer toward your thighs.
    6. At the end of the lifting phase, your chest should be facing forward.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your head and back to the starting position on the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md), which is assisted by your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

1. Position an adjustable decline bench to your desired decline angle.
    1. An angle near 30 degrees is an appropriate starting point, but you can effectively perform this exercise with a range of decline angles.
    2. The difficulty of this exercise will increase as the decline becomes steeper, so you can adjust the angle to modify the intensity.
    3. Some adjustable benches have a mild decline setting along with incline settings but lack a pad to secure your feet. This exercise specifically uses a decline with a foot/ankle pad.
2. Sit down on the bench while snugly positioning the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
3. Lie down in a controlled manner to position your back and head on the bench.
4. Place the fingertips of each hand lightly in contact with the sides of the back of your head as your upper arms and elbows are directed out away from your sides.
    1. Keeping your hands and arms in this position can help you avoid inadvertently pulling down on your head during the exercise, which would otherwise be easier to do if you interlocked your fingers and directed your upper arms up toward the ceiling.
    2. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. As you tighten your abdominal muscles, lift your back and head up off the bench by curling your back. Bring your chest toward your thighs.
    1. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that you have fully rounded your back and cannot bring your chest closer toward your thighs.
    2. Given that this is a sit-up rather than a crunch, you will lift the entirety of your back up off the bench.
    3. To train your abdominal muscles dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain in a flat position (which could occur if you predominantly lift your torso up through your hip flexor muscles).
    4. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    5. If a scale were fixed to your head, it should not detect any force from your fingertips as you keep your hands relaxed throughout the exercise, rather than pulling your head.
    6. As a cue for your engaging abdominal muscles, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs toward your hip bones.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your back to the starting position.
    1. Rather than fully relaxing at the bottom, strive to tap the bench lightly with your upper back while keeping your abdominals tensed.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the entire movement.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable to its highest level, connect a rope attachment to it, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. In a near shoulder width stance, stand under the rope with your back facing the cable station.
3. Reach up and grasp each end of the rope with your little fingers and adjacent aspects of your hands contacting the flat surfaces of the attachment’s rubber stoppers. Wrap your thumbs over the outside of your other fingers.
4. Pull your hands down until they are approximately in front of your shoulders with your elbows bent.
    1. You will keep your hands in this position throughout your set.
5. While allowing your knees to bend slightly, mildly lean forward at your hips. Simultaneously sit your buttocks back to contact the cable station’s beam.
    1. In this position, you should feel tension from the cable. If you do not, you should lean forward further by bending your hips until you feel tension to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion of each rep.
    2. You will continue keeping your backside against the cable station for additional stability throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Without moving your hips or arms, arch your back in a controlled manner through the range of motion that feels comfortable to your lower back.
    1. How far you can comfortably arch your back will be influenced by your mobility.
    2. Some people may experience lower back discomfort in a fully arched position, and there is no need to arch beyond the point that feels right to you.
    3. When thinking about an imaginary laser beam shooting out from the middle of your chest, the beam should angle progressively higher up as you arch your back.
    4. The bottom of your ribs should lift up and away from the top of your hip bones.
2. Curl your spine as you pull the bottom of your ribs toward the tops of your hip bones in a controlled manner. Avoid moving your hips or arms as you round your entire back.
    1. Once you feel that you can no longer curl your spine through a range that feels comfortable to your back, you have reached your end range.
    2. Try to point the imaginary laser beam shooting out from the middle of your chest closer toward the middle point between your feet.
    3. It can help to think about crunching your elbows toward your thighs.
    4. If you finish the movement with your back fairly flat as opposed to rounded, you most likely are bending at your hips rather than curling your spine.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Determine what you will use to anchor your looped elastic bands securely. You can use a variety of approaches based on your equipment availability, and the specific details for the setup can differ depending on which option you select.
    1. Ultimately you want to make sure that whatever you use as your anchor point will not move during your set. Your anchor point should have a smooth surface that will not tear the band.
    2. A deadlift platform with band pegs can provide ideal anchor points for long bands, but it is not available at most gyms.
    3. A power rack with band pegs at the bottom is also a very stable choice that allows you to use short or long bands within the rack. A power rack with base beams elevated above the ground can additionally be used to loop the bands around the base beams as anchor points.
    4. Without any of the aforementioned equipment, you can anchor a single long band by draping it around the center of the bar and standing with the middle of your feet on top of it. This method is convenient because it only requires a band, a barbell, and weight plates. However, it may be less stable compared to if you are able to anchor the bands to band pegs.
    5. Bands can alternatively be anchored to a pair of heavy dumbbells on each end of the bar, but this approach also requires that you use other weights to anchor the four dumbbells. This can be a more time-intensive set-up, and it may be difficult to keep the dumbbells stationary with a certain level of band tension. If you use dumbbells, you can place a pair of weight plates on the sides of each dumbbell to reduce the likelihood that they will roll.
2. After adding weight plates to the barbell situated on the ground, anchor your bands to the barbell with your chosen method.
    1. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
    2. Once positioned, the bands should be flat rather than twisted.
    3. Ideally the bands should be mildly tensed while the weight is on the ground. If the bands are slack, they will not be as stable and may move during your set.
    4. The bands should provide the same amount of tension on each side of the bar.
3. Stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance close in front of the middle of the bar, as the bar is over the middle of your feet, with your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly turned out to the sides.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
    2. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    3. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
    4. The size of the weight plates you add to the bar will determine how high the bar lies above the ground, which consequently affects your range of motion. Adding a pair of 45lb (20kg) plates (or 25kg plates common in gyms outside the USA) or bumper plates will elevate the bar to the standard height (about 9in (23cm)) when deadlifting from the floor. When only using smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a deficit deadlift with a greater range of motion that may exceed the range of motion in which some people wish to train if they lack the mobility to perform a deficit deadlift with appropriate technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize the largest diameter plates, you can perform a block pull or rack pull with the bar elevated to where it would be when deadlifting from the floor with large diameter plates.
4. With your arms directed down toward the ground, straight elbows, and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    5. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
5. Firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat with the bar close to your shins, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the bar reaches near the middle of your shins, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
    3. As you lift the bar higher up, the band tension will progressively increase.
5. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the ground.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.

## Setting up
1. Place a stability ball (which is also known as a Swiss ball or physio ball) on the ground.
2. After lying down with your back on the ground, place your heels and calves close together on top of the ball with straight knees.
    1. Make sure that your heels are on the half of the ball, further away from you, to provide sufficient room for you to drive your heels back without sliding off the ball.
    2. While the back of your heels are in contact with the ball, the soles of your feet should be facing forward and not contacting the ball.

1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels into the ball as you keep your knees straight. Squeeze your glutes and tighten your abdominal muscles while doing so.
