3. Reverse the movement by progressively straightening your knees in a controlled manner to roll the ball away from you.
    1. You should finish with your knees fully straightened, allowing you to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso.
    2. Continue keeping your hips bridged up.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. The initial submaximal pull allows you to check if you have grasped the handles correctly, which will be indicated by the handles not rotating forward or backward when applying the pre-tension.
    2. If you pick up a trap bar with your hands positioned slightly away from the middle of the handles, the trap bar can start rotating in a manner that makes it very difficult to hold and lift appropriately.
    3. Even for experienced lifters, it can be easy to grasp a trap bar’s handles without having their hands truly centered initially, so applying the pre-tension can make sure you are in your ideal starting position.
    4. If the bar starts rotating when you apply the pre-tension, re-center your grip, and apply the pre-tension again until the bar no longer rotates.
3. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees. Prioritize keeping your chest up, lower back flat, and your core braced throughout the entire exercise.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. Once the bar is moving, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
5. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. Just like when lifting the bar, keep your lower back flat and chest up as you descend while actively avoiding letting your lower back round or chest collapse.
    2. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees. Then you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is on the ground rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before the next rep.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), along with your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) to a lesser degree.

### **Hip Hinging versus Squatting Your Trap Bar Deadlift**

Relative to conventional deadlifts or block pulls with a straight barbell, trap bar deadlifts can allow you greater liberty in how you perform them with respect to biasing more of a hip hinge or squat movement pattern. A conventional deadlift keeps the load in front of you and constrains forward knee travel, while a trap bar deadlift positions the load closer to your center of mass and permits pushing your knees farther forward than you would do during a conventional deadlift. Trap bar deadlifting with greater forward knee travel makes the movement more squat-like in nature compared to maintaining a closer to vertical shin position, which results in a comparatively more hip-hinge dominant movement. As discussed by Greg Nuckols in his Stronger By Science article “Trap Bar Deadlifts are Underrated”, squat and deadlift variations can be analyzed as existing along a “squat-hinge continuum” based on the demands they impart to the hip extensor muscles (e.g., gluteus maximus, hamstrings, adductor magnus) relative to the quads, which extend the knees. Compared to trap bar deadlifting with a vertical shin, the lever arm of the resistance acting on the knees is greater when deadlifting with your knees situated farther forward, resulting in a greater ratio of loading imparted to the quads relative to the hip extensor muscles. In contrast, the lever arm of the resistance acting on the hips is greater when deadlifting with vertical shins, which prompts you to sit your hips farther back and experience a lower ratio of loading imparted to the quads relative to the hip extensor muscles. While people tend to perform trap bar deadlifts with their knees situated farther forward than when they conventional deadlift, you certainly have the ability to trap bar deadlift with the same knee position you would use for conventional deadlifts. Correspondingly, you can trap bar deadlift with whichever technique you prefer in congruence with your training goals.

Based on research assessing participants using their self-selected technique (which likely is the technique in which they were most efficient for pulling), it is worth noting that low handle trap bar deadlifts have been found to be more hip-dominant than knee-dominant. Swinton et al. (2011) specifically assessed male powerlifters performing low handle trap bar deadlifts and conventional dreadlifts. Both exercises imparted meaningfully greater loading to the hip extensors and lumbar spinal extensors than the quads, but conventional deadlifts were relatively more hip dominant. When lifting 80% of the participants’ conventional deadlift one-rep maxes, the ratio of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee was 3.7 for conventional deadlifts and 1.8 for low handle trap bar deadlifts. This difference was mainly attributed to the low handle trap bar deadlift having greater peak resistive torque acting on the knee, which was 190% of the conventional deadlift. A smaller gap was present for hip extensor loading as the peak resistive torque acting on the hip for the low handle trap bar deadlift was 92% that of conventional deadlift. These findings indicate that the degree to which low handle trap bar deadlifts train the quads more than conventional deadlifts most likely exceeds the degree to which conventional deadlifts train the hip extensor muscles more than low handle trap bar deadlifts. In terms of which hip extensor muscles may be less involved during trap bar deadlifts, the biarticular hamstrings in particular will likely receive a lesser stimulus. Camara et al. (2016) and Andersen et al. (2018) both found the hamstring’s biceps femoris to exhibit lower EMG activity during the low handle trap bar deadlift compared to the conventional deadlift, which is congruent with what be anticipated in light of the mechanical differences between these two exercises. Since the trap bar deadlift imparts greater loading to the knee, the knee flexion torque that results from hamstring contraction will have more of a deleterious effect on performance than during the conventional deadlift. While the hip extension torque that the hamstrings produce is beneficial, their knee flexion torque will oppose the quads as they extend the knee, so the hamstrings are not the most efficient hip extensor muscles for the nervous system to recruit during an exercise that imparts meaningful resistance to the quads. To a lesser extent, this is the same principle that results in the hamstrings experiencing minimal hypertrophy after interventions of squatting, which imparts even greater loading of the quads relative to the hip extensor muscles. Accompanying the lower hamstring EMG activity,  Camara et al. (2016) found the quad’s vastus lateralis (which was not assessed by Andersen et al.) to exhibit greater activity with the trap bar deadlift compared to the conventional deadlift. In contrast to the difference in hamstring EMG activity, Andersen et al. (2018) also found the gluteus maximus (which was not assessed by Camara et al.) to exhibit similar EMG activity during the two deadlift variations, which makes sense given that the gluteus maximus is able to generate hip extension without simultaneously generating knee flexion torque.

While the previously discussed data indicates that low handle trap bar deadlifts are typically performed with a more squat-like technique than conventional deadlifts, it is natural to wonder how they may compare to back squats. Choe et al. (2021) did not assess trap bar deadlifts, but they studied conventional deadlifts and back back squats performed with 70-85% of the mixed sex participants’ one-rep maxes. The researchers found the ratio of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee to be 3.0 for conventional deadlifts and 1.4 for squats. The participants of this study had some squat and deadlift training experience as the males had average deadlift and squat maxes that were respectively 143.3kg and 122.7kg, while the females had average deadlift and squat maxes that were respectively 95.0kg and 88.0kg. However, they were not nearly as strong as the powerlifter participants partaking in the study from Swinton et al. (2011) who had average conventional deadlift and low handle trap bar deadlift maxes that were respectively 244.5kg and 265.0kg. The participants from Swinton et al. (2011) correspondingly most likely used more efficient techniques, which may explain why they exhibited a higher ratio (3.8 versus 3.0) of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee when conventional deadlifting relative to the participants from Choe et al. (2021). When comparing the low handle trap bar deadlift findings from Swinton et al. (2011) to the back squat findings from Choe et al. (2021), the back squat was more knee dominant than the low handle trap bar deadlift, but the previously mentioned hip to knee torque ratio difference (1.7 versus 1.4) was not particularly pronounced.

This data suggests that the ratio of hip to knee loading of the low handle trap bar may be more similar to back squats than conventional deadlifts, but the strengths of our conclusions are limited when comparing findings from different studies assessing meaningfully different participants. For the most valid comparison of trap bar deadlifts to back squats, we ideally would want to analyze the findings from a study that assessed the same participants performing both exercises, which is what Stahl et al. (2024) precisely investigated. The researchers specifically compared the high handle trap bar deadlift (permitting chalk use but not straps) to the back squat (performed until thighs were parallel with the floor) as moderately trained mixed-sex participants lifted loads up to 100% of their maxes. They found the ratio of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee to be 0.9 for high trap bar deadlifts and 1.4 for squats (which was the same value determined by Choe et al.), indicating that high handle trap bar deadlifts can be even more knee-dominant than back squats. This difference was influenced by the resistive lever arm acting on the hip during back squats exceeding that during high trap bar deadlifts, while the resistive lever arm acting on the knee was similar between the two exercises. Comparing the data from Stahl et al. (2024) to the data from Swinton et al. (2011), high handle trap bar deadlifts appear to be more knee-dominant than low handle trap bar deadlifts with self-selected techniques, while back squats fall in between these two variations along the spectrum of hip to knee loading.

With that said, it is important to reiterate that you have the ability to perform trap bar deadlifts with either handle height in a more hip-dominant fashion if you wish to do so. Furthermore, it is also worth emphasizing that the aforementioned findings do not mean that high handle trap bar deadlifts are superior to back squats for training the quads. While the knee to hip loading ratios are relevant when appraising the ability of a deadlift or squat variation to train particular muscle groups, the capacity of an exercise to induce muscle hypertrophy is multi-factorial in nature. Multiple studies involving back squat training interventions have found back squats to induce significant quad growth, but the effect that high handle or low handle trap bar deadlifts may have on quad development has yet to be studied.

### **Trap Bar Deadlift versus Conventional Deadlift Strength**

Two different studies from Lockie et al. (2018) have compared one rep maxes without straps between conventional deadlifts and trap bar deadlifts with 4-inch (10.2cm) higher handles. Together they assessed a total of 54 mixed sex participants with at least two years of lifting experience that included conventional and trap bar deadlifts in addition to hitting maxes. Pooling the data from the two studies together, the average high handle trap bar max was 12% greater than the conventional deadlift max, resulting in a 39lb (17.7kg) mean difference. When comparing 1-rep maxes of the conventional deadlift to the low handle trap bar deadlift, Camara et al. (2016) found the maxes to be nearly identical to each other for the two lifts, but Swinton et al. (2011) and Lake et al. (2017) found their participants to lift an average of 6-8% greater loads during the low handle trap bar deadlift.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your lower body and spinal extensor muscles. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

## Setting up
1. Position a short looped elastic band around both of your thighs.
    1. The band will provide the greatest resistance to your hip muscles if you place it just above your knees, while it will provide less resistance if you place it higher up your thighs.
    2. You can choose where you situate the band on your thighs based on the level of resistance you wish to experience, and if you are using a particular band for this exercise for the first time, you can adjust its placement during the set if you wish to change the difficulty after starting the set.
2. Lie down with your upper back on a flat exercise bench (or a sturdy object of similar height), your buttocks on the floor, and your feet out in front of you with your soles flat on the floor and your knees bent to at least 90 degrees.
    1. You can situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, but it is up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can opt to point your toes forward or somewhat out to the sides.
    3. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is also up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
    4. In this position, you can cross your arms across your chest or hold your upper arms somewhat out to your sides.
    5. You can keep your neck near a neutral position, like you normally would when standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Push your knees outward against the band’s resistance to have them in line with your feet (as opposed to letting the band pull your knees closer together), and maintain this knee position throughout your set.
    1. You will most likely feel tension in the muscles on the sides of your hips while doing so.
2. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels into the ground and squeezing your buttock muscles.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your torso.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glutes engage during this exercise.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your hip mobility comfortably permits without rounding or excessively arching your lower back.
    1. Some people can descend all the way down until they lightly contact the ground with their glutes, but you can prioritize lowering through the range in which you can achieve through hip motion rather than lower back motion.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 while continuing to keep your knees aligned with your feet until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise dynamically trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) while statically training your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), and [short hip external rotator muscles](../Muscles/Short%20Hip%20External%20Rotators%201b95c6f170d880c79035ce63a7c5f540.md).

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to the barbell situated on the ground, stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance close in front of the middle of the bar, as the bar is over the middle of your feet, with your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly turned out to the sides.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
    2. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    3. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
    4. The size of the weight plates you add to the bar will determine how high the bar lies above the ground, which consequently affects your range of motion. Adding a pair of 45lb (20kg) plates (or 25kg plates common in gyms outside the USA) or bumper plates will elevate the bar to the standard height (about 9in (23cm)) when deadlifting from the floor. When only using smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a deficit deadlift with a greater range of motion that may exceed the range of motion in which some people wish to train if they lack the mobility to perform a deficit deadlift with appropriate technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize the largest diameter plates, you can perform a block pull or rack pull with the bar elevated to where it would be when deadlifting from the floor with large diameter plates.
2. With your arms directed down toward the ground, straight elbows, and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    5. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
3. Firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat with the bar close to your shins, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the bar reaches near the middle of your shins, pause in that position for a brief period of time (e.g., 1-2 seconds) while staying tight with your chest up and back flat.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability as you visibly remain stationary.
5. Following the pause, thrust your hips forward as you resume extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
6. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
7. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the ground.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.

    1. The band will provide the greatest resistance to your hip muscles if you place it just above your knees, while it will provide less resistance if you place it higher up your thighs.
    2. You can choose where you situate the band on your thighs based on the level of resistance you wish to experience. If you are using a particular band for this exercise for the first time, you can adjust its placement during the set if you wish to change the difficulty after starting the set.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground, and your knees bent at least 90 degrees.
    1. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
3. Position the soles of your feet flat against each other while spreading your knees apart to bring them closer to the ground.
    1. Spread your knees as far apart as is comfortable to your hips, but there is no need to push them further apart than they would naturally fall during a frog pump without a band. The degree to which your knees will spread out comfortably will be influenced by your hip mobility.
    2. The band exerts a force that will pull your knees together unless you actively push your knees out against the band to assume the appropriate position.
    3. The outer aspect of your feet (on the side of your little toes) should be firmly in contact with the ground.
4. Tuck your chin toward your chest and lift your head slightly off the ground.
    1. This can help you keep your lower back flat rather than excessively arched during the exercise, but you have the option of resting your head on the ground if you wish to do so.
    2. You can position your arms in whichever comfortable position you prefer, such as resting by your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving the outer aspects of your feet into the ground and squeezing your glutes. Keep the soles of your feet pressed together and your knees spread apart.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you ideally should be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side if you have the mobility to perform the full range of motion. If your hips feel “stuck” or quite uncomfortable before reaching this point, you may not have the hip mobility to move through the full range with your current knee position. Bringing your knees somewhat higher up and closer together may allow you to lift your hips up higher in a more comfortable manner.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively. Tensing your abdominal muscles may help limit your lower back from arching.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glutes engage during this exercise.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
    1. Continue keeping your soles in contact with each other.
    2. After determining which knee position allows you to comfortably move through your full range of motion, strive to keep your knees in the same position throughout your set.
3. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright with approximately a hip width stance while holding the kettlebells by your thighs with straight elbows as your palms face your thighs.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hand while holding them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
    3. If you are using kettlebells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent over position to pick up both kettlebells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    4. For an easier setup, you can pick up one kettlebell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other kettlebell onto the bench before picking up both kettlebells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    5. Pick up the kettlebells with a hip hinge or squat motion where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. Once upright, you can situate your palms right next to the outer aspect of the front of your thighs so that your palms face at an angle between backward and in toward each other.
    1. This results in a semi-overhand grip, which is a hybrid between an overhand grip that would direct your palms straight backward (with the kettlebells directly in front of your body) and a neutral grip that would direct your palms straight in toward your sides (with the kettlebells directly to the sides of your body).
    2. You will keep your palms facing this way throughout your set.
    3. Your neck should be near a neutral position when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead, and you will keep your neck in this position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, as if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Bracing will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hip throughout your set.
2. While allowing the other side’s foot to lift up off the floor, begin hinging at the hip on the side to which you shifted your weight by sitting your buttocks back as you let your knee mildly bend.
    1. As you do so, the kettlebells will naturally descend, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    2. Allow your free leg to swing backward as it moves with your torso in a see-saw-like manner, but focus on hinging at the hip of your working leg instead of kicking your other leg back.
    3. Continue keeping your elbows straightened, core braced, lower back near a neutral position, and working leg’s sole fully in contact with the ground while doing so.
    4. To the best of your ability, keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down.
    5. Most of the motion should come from your hip, and your shin should remain in a fairly vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knee fully straightened.
    6. You do not need to focus on bending your knee, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks back while not intentionally keeping your knee locked.
3. Continuing hinging at your hip in a controlled manner until you have reached the end of your available range of motion.
    1. While some people can descend until their torsos are close to parallel to the ground, how deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knee will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer descend without rounding your lower back, you have finished descending through your available range of motion.
4. Reverse the hinge movement by driving through your working leg’s hip to lift yourself up until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straightened, core braced, lower back near a neutral position, hip bones level, and working leg’s sole fully in contact with the ground.
    2. After you are fully upright, you could place your free leg’s foot back onto the ground if you could use some additional balance assistance.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which foot remains in contact with the ground.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
    3. After finishing the last rep with your other side, set the kettlebells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to a trap bar situated on the ground and positioning the high handles up, stand within the middle of the trap bar with approximately a hip-width to shoulder-width stance and your arms at your sides.
    1. Specifically how wide you situate your feet apart can be based on what feels most comfortable to you when picking up a weight off the floor with a deadlifting motion.
    2. Many trap bar models have a pair of high handles that allow you to grasp the bar with your hands elevated more than when grasping a barbell on the ground, but certain trap bars lack a pair of high handles.
    3. If your trap bar does not have high handles, you can select the [trap bar block pull](Trap%20bar%20block%20pull%201e25c6f170d8809193e0e6ead5da5816.md) from this database to be able to train essentially the same movement.
2. With your arms pointing straight down toward the bar and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from hinging at your hips than bending your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift moderately forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something. After you have fully sat back and feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    4. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and help engage your back muscles.
3. With your elbows fully straightened, firmly grasp the center of the handles with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hands while holding the bar, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. The initial submaximal pull allows you to check if you have grasped the handles correctly, which will be indicated by the handles not rotating forward or backward when applying the pre-tension.
    2. If you pick up a trap bar with your hands positioned slightly away from the middle of the handles, the trap bar can start rotating in a manner that makes it very difficult to hold and lift appropriately.
    3. Even for experienced lifters, it can be easy to grasp a trap bar’s handles without having their hands truly centered initially, so applying the pre-tension can make sure you are in your ideal starting position.
    4. If the bar starts rotating when you apply the pre-tension, re-center your grip, and apply the pre-tension again until the bar no longer rotates.
3. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees. Prioritize keeping your chest up, lower back flat, and your core braced throughout the entire exercise.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. Once the bar is moving, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
5. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. Just like when lifting the bar, keep your lower back flat and chest up as you descend while actively avoiding letting your lower back round or chest collapse.
    2. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees. Then you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is on the ground rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before the next rep.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this can meaningfully train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), along with your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) to a lesser degree.

### **Hip Hinging versus Squatting Your Trap Bar Deadlift**

Relative to conventional deadlifts or block pulls with a straight barbell, trap bar deadlifts can allow you greater liberty in how you perform them with respect to biasing more of a hip hinge or squat movement pattern. A conventional deadlift keeps the load in front of you and constrains forward knee travel, while a trap bar deadlift positions the load closer to your center of mass and permits pushing your knees farther forward than you would do during a conventional deadlift. Trap bar deadlifting with greater forward knee travel makes the movement more squat-like in nature compared to maintaining a closer to vertical shin position, which results in a comparatively more hip-hinge dominant movement. As discussed by Greg Nuckols in his Stronger By Science article “Trap Bar Deadlifts are Underrated”, squat and deadlift variations can be analyzed as existing along a “squat-hinge continuum” based on the demands they impart to the hip extensor muscles (e.g., gluteus maximus, hamstrings, adductor magnus) relative to the quads, which extend the knees. Compared to trap bar deadlifting with a vertical shin, the lever arm of the resistance acting on the knees is greater when deadlifting with your knees situated farther forward, resulting in a greater ratio of loading imparted to the quads relative to the hip extensor muscles. In contrast, the lever arm of the resistance acting on the hips is greater when deadlifting with vertical shins, which prompts you to sit your hips farther back and experience a lower ratio of loading imparted to the quads relative to the hip extensor muscles. While people tend to perform trap bar deadlifts with their knees situated farther forward than when they conventional deadlift, you certainly have the ability to trap bar deadlift with the same knee position you would use for conventional deadlifts. Correspondingly, you can trap bar deadlift with whichever technique you prefer in congruence with your training goals.

Based on research assessing participants using their self-selected technique (which likely is the technique in which they were most efficient for pulling), it is worth noting that low handle trap bar deadlifts have been found to be more hip-dominant than knee-dominant. Swinton et al. (2011) specifically assessed male powerlifters performing low handle trap bar deadlifts and conventional dreadlifts. Both exercises imparted meaningfully greater loading to the hip extensors and lumbar spinal extensors than the quads, but conventional deadlifts were relatively more hip dominant. When lifting 80% of the participants’ conventional deadlift one-rep maxes, the ratio of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee was 3.7 for conventional deadlifts and 1.8 for low handle trap bar deadlifts. This difference was mainly attributed to the low handle trap bar deadlift having greater peak resistive torque acting on the knee, which was 190% of the conventional deadlift. A smaller gap was present for hip extensor loading as the peak resistive torque acting on the hip for the low handle trap bar deadlift was 92% that of conventional deadlift. These findings indicate that the degree to which low handle trap bar deadlifts train the quads more than conventional deadlifts most likely exceeds the degree to which conventional deadlifts train the hip extensor muscles more than low handle trap bar deadlifts. In terms of which hip extensor muscles may be less involved during trap bar deadlifts, the biarticular hamstrings in particular will likely receive a lesser stimulus. Camara et al. (2016) and Andersen et al. (2018) both found the hamstring’s biceps femoris to exhibit lower EMG activity during the low handle trap bar deadlift compared to the conventional deadlift, which is congruent with what be anticipated in light of the mechanical differences between these two exercises. Since the trap bar deadlift imparts greater loading to the knee, the knee flexion torque that results from hamstring contraction will have more of a deleterious effect on performance than during the conventional deadlift. While the hip extension torque that the hamstrings produce is beneficial, their knee flexion torque will oppose the quads as they extend the knee, so the hamstrings are not the most efficient hip extensor muscles for the nervous system to recruit during an exercise that imparts meaningful resistance to the quads. To a lesser extent, this is the same principle that results in the hamstrings experiencing minimal hypertrophy after interventions of squatting, which imparts even greater loading of the quads relative to the hip extensor muscles. Accompanying the lower hamstring EMG activity,  Camara et al. (2016) found the quad’s vastus lateralis (which was not assessed by Andersen et al.) to exhibit greater activity with the trap bar deadlift compared to the conventional deadlift. In contrast to the difference in hamstring EMG activity, Andersen et al. (2018) also found the gluteus maximus (which was not assessed by Camara et al.) to exhibit similar EMG activity during the two deadlift variations, which makes sense given that the gluteus maximus is able to generate hip extension without simultaneously generating knee flexion torque.

While the previously discussed data indicates that low handle trap bar deadlifts are typically performed with a more squat-like technique than conventional deadlifts, it is natural to wonder how they may compare to back squats. Choe et al. (2021) did not assess trap bar deadlifts, but they studied conventional deadlifts and back back squats performed with 70-85% of the mixed sex participants’ one-rep maxes. The researchers found the ratio of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee to be 3.0 for conventional deadlifts and 1.4 for squats. The participants of this study had some squat and deadlift training experience as the males had average deadlift and squat maxes that were respectively 143.3kg and 122.7kg, while the females had average deadlift and squat maxes that were respectively 95.0kg and 88.0kg. However, they were not nearly as strong as the powerlifter participants partaking in the study from Swinton et al. (2011) who had average conventional deadlift and low handle trap bar deadlift maxes that were respectively 244.5kg and 265.0kg. The participants from Swinton et al. (2011) correspondingly most likely used more efficient techniques, which may explain why they exhibited a higher ratio (3.8 versus 3.0) of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee when conventional deadlifting relative to the participants from Choe et al. (2021). When comparing the low handle trap bar deadlift findings from Swinton et al. (2011) to the back squat findings from Choe et al. (2021), the back squat was more knee dominant than the low handle trap bar deadlift, but the previously mentioned hip to knee torque ratio difference (1.7 versus 1.4) was not particularly pronounced.

This data suggests that the ratio of hip to knee loading of the low handle trap bar may be more similar to back squats than conventional deadlifts, but the strengths of our conclusions are limited when comparing findings from different studies assessing meaningfully different participants. For the most valid comparison of trap bar deadlifts to back squats, we ideally would want to analyze the findings from a study that assessed the same participants performing both exercises, which is what Stahl et al. (2024) precisely investigated. The researchers specifically compared the high handle trap bar deadlift (permitting chalk use but not straps) to the back squat (performed until thighs were parallel with the floor) as moderately trained mixed-sex participants lifted loads up to 100% of their maxes. They found the ratio of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee to be 0.9 for high trap bar deadlifts and 1.4 for squats (which was the same value determined by Choe et al.), indicating that high handle trap bar deadlifts can be even more knee-dominant than back squats. This difference was influenced by the resistive lever arm acting on the hip during back squats exceeding that during high trap bar deadlifts, while the resistive lever arm acting on the knee was similar between the two exercises. Comparing the data from Stahl et al. (2024) to the data from Swinton et al. (2011), high handle trap bar deadlifts appear to be more knee-dominant than low handle trap bar deadlifts with self-selected techniques, while back squats fall in between these two variations along the spectrum of hip to knee loading.

With that said, it is important to reiterate that you have the ability to perform trap bar deadlifts with either handle height in a more hip-dominant fashion if you wish to do so. Furthermore, it is also worth emphasizing that the aforementioned findings do not mean that high handle trap bar deadlifts are superior to back squats for training the quads. While the knee to hip loading ratios are relevant when appraising the ability of a deadlift or squat variation to train particular muscle groups, the capacity of an exercise to induce muscle hypertrophy is multi-factorial in nature. Multiple studies involving back squat training interventions have found back squats to induce significant quad growth, but the effect that high handle or low handle trap bar deadlifts may have on quad development has yet to be studied.

### **Trap Bar Deadlift versus Conventional Deadlift Strength**

Two different studies from Lockie et al. (2018) have compared one rep maxes without straps between conventional deadlifts and trap bar deadlifts with 4-inch (10.2cm) higher handles. Together they assessed a total of 54 mixed sex participants with at least two years of lifting experience that included conventional and trap bar deadlifts in addition to hitting maxes. Pooling the data from the two studies together, the average high handle trap bar max was 12% greater than the conventional deadlift max, resulting in a 39lb (17.7kg) mean difference. When comparing 1-rep maxes of the conventional deadlift to the low handle trap bar deadlift, Camara et al. (2016) found the maxes to be nearly identical to each other for the two lifts, but Swinton et al. (2011) and Lake et al. (2017) found their participants to lift an average of 6-8% greater loads during the low handle trap bar deadlift.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your lower body and spinal extensor muscles. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

## Setting up
1. Set a weight on the ground and lie down on your back next to it.
    1. A weight plate, medicine ball, dumbbell, or kettlebell is a viable option. Select whichever option you find most comfortable to hold to your chest.
2. Pick up the weight and hold it just above your chest with bent elbows as you are firmly grasping each side of the weight.
3. Bend your knees to position the soles of your feet flat on the ground approximately hip width apart, and rest your head on the ground.
    1. You optionally can hook the tops of your feet under a sturdy object like a couch (while your soles are still flat on the ground), which is recommended to help stabilize your body during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. As you tighten your abdominal muscles, lift your back and head up off the ground by curling your back. Bring your chest toward your thighs.
    1. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that you have fully rounded your back and cannot bring your chest closer toward your thighs. At the top, your chest should be facing forward.
    2. Continue holding the weight close to your chest throughout your set.
    3. Given that this is a sit-up rather than a crunch, you will lift the entirety of your back up off the ground.
    4. To train your abdominal muscles dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain in a flat position (which could occur if you predominantly lift your torso up through your hip flexor muscles).
    5. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    6. As a cue for your engaging abdominal muscles, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs toward your hip bones.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your back to the starting position.
    1. Rather than fully relaxing at the bottom, strive to tap the bench lightly with your upper back while keeping your abdominals tensed.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the entire movement.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Position the weight you intend to use at the base of the Roman chair in between its handles such that you can reach the weight when your feet are on its foot plate.
    1. Based on your equipment availability and preference, you can select essentially any type of weight that you can hold with straight elbows. Dumbbells and kettlebells (which can be held as a pair or as one weight in both hands) can be used in addition to a weight plate, barbell, EZ curl bar, and medicine ball.
    2. Ideally select a weight that does not physically restrict you from hinging through your full range of motion when holding it.
    3. If you use a barbell to which you add plates, small diameter plates may be preferable over larger diameter plates to prevent the plates from limiting your motion.
    4. A fixed weight bar can be a quality choice since its weights are of a small diameter, and holding it with a wide grip can reduce the likelihood that it contacts the ground prematurely while you hinge.
2. Adjust the height of the Roman chair’s pad to a level that positions the top of your hip bones somewhat above the top of the pads when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. This position will allow you to move freely about your hips in contrast to if the pad is contacting the top of your hip bones, which would restrict hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    2. If the top of the pad is positioned much lower than the top of the hip bones (rather than only somewhat lower), some individuals may feel knee discomfort, so a sweet spot can exist for pad placement.
    3. Some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position after initially completing step 2.
3. While placing your hands onto the handles for balance support, step onto the foot plate one leg at a time with the back of your heels in contact with the back of the foot plate, so that the entirety of your soles are in contact with the foot plate.
    1. Position your feet symmetrically in a stance that feels comfortable to you, which can involve pointing your toes somewhat outward or pointing them fairly straight forward.
    2. Situating your feet approximately hip width to shoulder apart from each other will result in a viable stance width, but how wide of a stance you can use will be influenced by the width of your Roman chair’s foot plate.
    3. Your knees should be straight after you have finished setting your feet on the foot plate.
4. Check to make sure that the pad is positioned as described by step 1, and readjust the pad height if it is not prior to resuming your setup.
## Exercise technique
1. Begin bracing your core by taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
2. Hinge at your hips until you are low enough to firmly grasp the weight you selected with straight elbows as your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. Nearly all of the motion should occur from you moving at your hips as you keep your trunk in a static position that maintains the natural curvature of your lower back (as opposed to bending over by rounding your lower back).
    3. Maintain a straight knee position throughout your set, but you should avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads.
    4. Depending on your limb lengths and the height of your Roman chair, you may have to round your upper back somewhat to grasp the weight initially.
    5. The precise way in which you will hold the weight to your chest may vary based on the specific implement you selected, but what matters is that you have a firm grip on the weight and are able to keep it in a stable position.
3. While holding the weight with your arms hanging down, lift your torso up through your hips until you can draw approximately a straight line from your legs through your hips and to your torso.
    1. You can finish the lifting phase by fully squeezing your glutes, which helps cue hip movement at the top as opposed to spinal movement.
    2. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the hip motion you just performed during the lowering phase.
4. Lower your torso by hinging at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner as you continue keeping your trunk in a statically braced position.
    1. While hinging at your hips, you should feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings that progressively intensifies.
    2. Most people will be able to descend until their shoulders are lower than their hips, but how deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    3. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch, you have finished descending through your available hip range of motion.
    4. If you notice that the weight contacts the ground before you have reached the end of your hip hinge range of motion, bend your elbows just enough to permit your full range of motion without the weight contacting the ground.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the weight back down on the ground.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.

    3. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    4. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    5. While your lower back muscles will be working to maintain a rigid trunk position, lifting the bar upward should chiefly occur from your hip and thigh muscles extending your hips and knees.
    6. Keep the bar very close to your legs as you lift the bar rather than allowing the bar to drift forward.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight with the bar just in front of your legs. Avoid letting the bar drift forward away from you, which may be more likely to occur if you think about “bending over” rather than “sitting back.”
    2. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the bar.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    5. Throughout the set, keep your feet fully planted on the ground and your neck near a neutral position, as when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move.
    1. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    3. If you have sufficient hamstring flexibility and can hinge until the bar reaches the bottom of the machine, tap the bottom lightly with the bar, but do not let the weight rest on the bottom.
    4. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should clearly be in control of the entire descent.
3. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward to lift your torso upright into the starting position.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so keep your lower back flat, chest up, core braced, feet fully on the ground, and the bar close to your legs.
    2. When you have finished lifting the bar, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back at the top through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips properly stacked under your shoulders, preventing excessive arching.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
    3. After finishing the last rep, set the bar down in the same manner in which you initially picked it up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).
