### **Learning how to hip hinge**

If you have minimal experience training hip hinge exercises such as Romanian deadlift and good morning variations, it is normal to have difficulty performing this movement pattern. Like riding a bicycle or shooting a basketball, hip hinging is a motor skill that may require repeated practice before you feel comfortable consistently using it. Broadly speaking, there are two types of movement substitution patterns that individuals who are in the process of learning how to hip hinge commonly perform when attempting to execute a hip hinge exercise.

One of these is using a stoop lift, which involves dynamically rounding the back (through flexion of the lumbar and thoracic spine) to bend over prior to uncoiling the spine into an upright position during the ascent. This often is accompanied by the buttock not moving particularly far backward and the arms drifting out in front of the legs in contrast to a strict hip hinge, which utilizes a visibly flat back position (with close to a neutral lumbar spine) and has the buttock noticeably moving backward during the descent. In terms of similarity, a stoop lift and a hip hinge both involve only a mild magnitude of knee bend during the descent while keeping the hips high. A clue that you may be performing more of a stoop lift than a hip hinge is feeling a stretching sensation in your back rather than feeling your back muscles remain statically tight throughout your set as these muscles function to maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips. With a properly performed hip hinge, you should certainly feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the bottom of the lift, but you may also feel this stretching sensation during a stoop lift. Nonetheless, a hip hinge can allow you to feel the hamstring stretch earlier during the descent compared to a stoop lift since the hamstrings are shortened by the posterior pelvic tilt (tucking the tailbone under) that is coupled with lumbar spine flexion.

In addition to performing a stoop lift unintentionally when attempting to hip hinge, people can commonly utilize more of a squatting motion that is characterized by greater knee bend and forward tracking of the knees during the descent. Compared to a hip hinge, using more of a squatting movement can result in the buttock moving downward during the descent as opposed to backward, and the shins can also incline forward as opposed to remaining vertical. Because the hamstrings shorten as the knees bend, someone moving in a squat pattern when attempting to perform a hip hinge exercise is unlikely to feel much of a stretching sensation in the hamstrings at the bottom of the lift. Not feeling a hamstring stretch is the most straightforward indicator that you may be squatting your hip hinge exercise, but an additional clue would be if you perceive your quads to be working (e.g., feeling a “burning” sensation or lots of tension) more intensely than your hamstrings during the exercise.

When thinking about moving through hip hinge, stoop lift, and squat patterns, it is important to recognize that these movements can occur along a spectrum. You can perform a hip hinge exercise with a technique that is mostly a hip hinge while still utilizing elements of a stoop lift or a squat that may not be ideal for what you wish to accomplish from the exercise. Similarly, your technique can incrementally progress from being stoop lift-dominant or squat-dominant to becoming progressively more of a hip hinge as your body learns how to move in a different way through repeated practice. If your hip hinge technique currently has much room for improvement, it can be beneficial to start with lighter loads that may not be especially challenging to your muscles until you developed a reasonable level of competency with the movement itself. There is no need to let perfect be the enemy of good, so you do not need to wait to load a movement meaningfully until you have immaculate technique, but it would also be inadvisable to push your body to the limit without initially learning the basic fundamentals of the movement.

Depending on which element of hip hinging in which you currently are challenged, certain external cues can expedite how quickly you can learn how to hinge. When unintentionally moving in a manner that involves a greater degree of squatting or stoop lifting than is intended, a wall may help provide tactile feedback to cue sitting your buttock backward. To do so, you can perform your hip hinge with your back facing a nearby wall, and you will be able to receive confirmation as to whether you are actually sitting your hips backward by feeling the wall contact your buttock at the end of the descent. As an initial starting point, you can set up with a heel-to-toe tandem stance as the back of one heel contacts the wall. Then you can bring your rear foot forward to be aligned with your front foot in the symmetrical stance you will utilize for your hip hinge. This can provide a reasonable approximation as to how far people may commonly be able to sit their hips back when hinging, but you can adjust from there how far away you position yourself from the wall to individualize it to you.

Specifically if you have a tendency to perform a “squatty” hip hinge, practicing your hip hinge with your calves up against something like a flat exercise bench (or even a couch or chair at home) can be a rather productive means of honing your hinge. As you descend, you will receive immediate tactile feedback if your knees track forward from no longer feeling the contact with your calves, so it can be a great way to reinforce keeping your shins vertical throughout the movement. When using this method, make sure that you maintain full contact between the soles of your feet and the ground while you avoid leaning your bodyweight into the bench to the extent that you would fall backward if the bench was removed. If you successfully keep your calves in contact with the bench throughout the movement and feel a pronounced stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the end of the descent, you are right on track to achieving a high quality hip hinge.

As an additional learning tool, you can situate a long object like a dowel rod, PVC pipe, or yardstick on your back while hip hinging if you have a tendency to utilize more of a stoop lift technique with excessive back rounding. Either the calf-to-bench technique or the buttock-to-wall technique can be incorporated into an actual Romanian deadlift where you use weights, but using a rod as a cue without a partner will require you to hold the rod in place, so you would not be able to load this drill independently. To perform this movement, you would hold the rod behind against your back with one hand higher up near your head and your other hand lower down near your buttock. While standing fully upright and looking straight ahead, you should feel the rod contacting your sacrum (the bone that lies between your upper buttock cheeks and right above your tailbone), upper back between your shoulder blades, and the back of your head. You will then hip hinge while maintaining these three points of contact throughout the entirety of the movement. If you start rounding your back or moving your neck beyond the neutral position you adopt when standing fully upright, you will feel the rod lose contact with one of those three spots. This can be a rather effective form of instant feedback to help develop your ability to move predominantly through your lower body while keeping your trunk in a rigid position throughout the movement, which can transfer to improved technique for an array of different exercises. When maintaining those three contact points, you potentially can still perform a squatting motion rather than a hip hinge since moving through your lower body while minimizing back motion is also a component of squatting technique. However, if you maintain those three contact points and additionally feel your hamstrings notably stretched at the bottom of the descent, those two factors indicate that you have successfully hip hinged in all likelihood. If you find that the rod cuing shifts your movement from a stoop lift to more of a squat, you can use the rod cuing simultaneously with the calf-to-bench cuing, which can address multiple aspects of the hip hinge concurrently.

In the context of performing a hip hinge exercise, using a form that resembles more of a squat or stoop lift rather than a hip hinge can be considered technique errors, but squatting and stoop lifting are by no means faulty movement patterns inherently. They simply differ from a hip hinge, so they can be suboptimal means of performing an exercise that you intend to train specifically for the benefits that hip hinging can provide as opposed to other movements. The hip hinge can take some practice to learn, but investing the time and effort into doing so can be a prudent investment given that having the motor skill of hip hinging can meaningfully expand your freedom in how you can move both inside and outside of the gym.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your lower body or lower back strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your lower body and back muscles. Among trained lifters, grip strength can very commonly limit performance of Romanian deadlifts if they do not utilize straps since the posterior chain has the potential to move rather heavy loads for this exercise. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least a few minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

### **Romanian deadlift vs stiff-leg deadlift**

The terms “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” are often used interchangeably to describe the same exercise by scholarly articles and lifters in general. The nomenclature of the Romanian deadlift has been attributed to this exercise being performed by Nicu Vlad, a Romanian weightlifter who won gold, silver, and bronze medals respectively in the 1984, 1988, and 1996 Olympic games in addition to medaling in seven World Weightlifting Championships (with three of them being gold). American weightlifting coach Jim Schmitz reportedly saw Vlad performing the barbell hip hinge exercise and subsequently called it the Romanian deadlift since Vlad did not have a particular name for the variation he was performing.

While they may be commonly used to refer to the same exercise, some people will use the names “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” to refer to different variations. They consider the stiff-leg deadlift to be what is described in this database as the “barbell stiff-leg deadlift from floor,” which involves each rep starting with the plates fully on the floor like a conventional deadlift. This variation differs from the Romanian deadlift, which starts from the upright position and uses a range of motion individualized to someone’s flexibility as the plates often do not contact the floor. If someone has the hamstring flexibility for the plates to contact the floor during a Romanian deadlift, a light tap to the ground is utilized, but the full weight of the bar is not transferred into the ground like how the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor is performed. In contrast to the Romanian deadlift, which is typically performed with a controlled lowering phase, this conception of the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor often involves a quicker lower phase with a tempo akin to how conventional deadlifts are commonly performed, which is to say a controlled drop. Both variations can involve a mild amount of knee flexion at the bottom of the hinge, but the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor can require that someone adopts a more flexed lumbar position in order to pull from the floor with the knee position while maintaining high hips. This differs from the Romanian deadlift being performed only through the range of motion where someone can maintain close to a neutral lumbar spine or a flat back position.

As demonstrated by sources such as Hegyi et al. (2018) along with Piper and Waller (2001), another interpretation of the stiff-leg deadlift also exists as a truly straight leg deadlift. Under this conception of the exercise, the knees are kept extended to the extent that they are completely straight but not fully locked (which could otherwise allow for knee hyperextension in individuals with the mobility to do so). Such a technique would result in a movement that is more akin to “bending over” rather than “sitting back,” and the bar would correspondingly be likely to drift further in front of the legs compared to a Romanian deadlift, which utilizes a mild knee bend that allows you to “sit back.” In light of the different ways in which these names may be interpreted, hopefully this note provides some clarification if you have ever been confused by how different individuals may view Romanian deadlifts and stiff-leg deadlifts exercises as the same exercise or distinct variations.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your upper back on a flat exercise bench (or a sturdy object of similar height), your buttocks on the floor, and your feet out in front of you with your soles flat on the floor and your knees bent to at least 90 degrees.
    1. You can situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, but it is up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can opt to point your toes forward or somewhat out to the sides.
    3. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is also up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
    4. In this position, you can cross your arms across your chest or hold your upper arms somewhat out to your sides.
    5. You can keep your neck near a neutral position, like you normally would when standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. While leaving one foot on the ground, lift the other foot off the ground by marching that side’s thigh up while keeping your knee bent, or by straightening your knee while leaving that side’s thigh aligned with the thigh of your other leg.
    1. Either position for the free leg is similarly viable, so you can go with whichever you prefer, but keeping the knee straight may make the exercise mildly more challenging compared to keeping it bent.
    2. Keep your one foot off the ground in the static position of your choice throughout the set you perform with your other side.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heel into the ground and squeezing your glute.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your torso (on the side of your body with the foot contacting the ground)
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid arching your lower back excessively.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glutes engage during this exercise.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your hip mobility comfortably permits without rounding or excessively arching your lower back.
    1. Some people can descend all the way down until they lightly contact the ground with their glutes, but you can prioritize lowering through the range in which you can achieve through hip motion rather than lower back motion.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your knees bent, as the soles of your feet are flat on the ground, approximately hip width apart.
    1. You can rest your head on the ground.
    2. You can optionally hook the tops of your feet under a sturdy object, such as a couch (while your soles remain flat on the ground), to help stabilize your body during this exercise.
2. Place the fingertips of each hand lightly in contact with the sides of the back of your head as your upper arms and elbows are directed out away from your sides.
    1. Since you are not interlocking your fingers along the middle of the back of your head, you should not have to lift your head up off the ground to situate your hands in the appropriate position.
    2. Keeping your hands and arms in this position can help you avoid inadvertently pulling your head down during the exercise, which would be easier to do if you interlocked your fingers and raised your upper arms toward the ceiling.
    3. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Without applying pressure to your head with your hands, tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back into the ground while you lift your head and shoulder blades off the ground by curling your middle back.
    1. Given that this is a crunch rather than a sit-up, the lower half of your back should remain in contact with the ground while you only lift up the upper half of your back mildly off the floor.
    2. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    3. If a scale were fixed to the back of your head, it should not detect any force from your fingertips as you keep your hands relaxed throughout the exercise, rather than pulling your head.
    4. As a cue, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the top of your hip bones, which is the action that contraction of your abdominal muscles can produce.
    5. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that crunching up any further would require the lower half of your back to lift off the floor.
    6. At the end of the lifting phase, your chest should be facing at an angle between forward and upward, rather than only facing upward as it did in the starting position.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your middle back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your head and shoulder blades back to the starting position on the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the power rack’s J-hooks to a height that allows you to position the bar on your upper back and walk out the weight comfortably.
    1. As an initial approximation, you can position the J-hooks such that they are a few finger widths below the height of your collarbone.
    2. You may have to re-adjust the height of the J-hooks later.
2. After placing the barbell on top of the J-hooks, face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
3. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to then walk under the bar and situate the bar on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    2. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
    5. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
    7. If you find that deeper than a mild bend at your hips and knees is (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) is required to position the bar on your back, you can lift the bar out of the J-hooks, set it down, raise the height of the J-hooks, and place the bar back onto the J-hooks.
4. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back and stand up in a quarter squat-like manner by extending your knees and hips.
5. After standing upright with the bar, check if you selected an appropriate height for the J-hooks.
    1. The bar should be above the tops of the J-hooks such that they would not contact the bar when walking out backward.
    2. If you need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too low.
    3. If this is the case, lift the bar out of the J-hooks, set it down, lower the height of the J-hooks, place the bar back onto the J-hooks, and recheck to ensure you can walk out the weight without rising onto the balls of your feet.
    4. Walking out with your heels raised up will increase the risk of you losing your balance and should consequently be avoided whenever you have a barbell on your back.
6. After confirming the J-hooks are positioned appropriately, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of good morning reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
7. Load the bar with your intended weight and position the safety pins to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of the good morning.
## Exercise technique
1. With the hand placement and bar positioning determined while setting up, un-rack the bar standing up in a quarter squat-like manner by extending your knees and hips while pulling down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back.
2. Take a couple of steps backward and position your feet into approximately a shoulder-width stance with the soles of your feet fully contacting the floor.
3. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    4. Bracing will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips throughout your set.
4. Hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner to move your buttocks backward while you allow your knees to bend mildly.
    1. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than rounding your lower back while doing so.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened.
    4. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    5. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something, as you keep your chest up (rather than letting your chest collapse through back rounding).
    6. While you hinge at your hips, the bar will naturally descend, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    7. How deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    8. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit your buttocks any farther back, you have finished descending through your available range of motion.
    9. If you positioned them appropriately, the safety pins should not restrict how far you can hip hinge, but if you are able to hinge until the bar contacts the safety pins, you can lightly tap the safety pins with the bar without resting the bar on the pins.
5. Reverse the movement by pulling your hips forward until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. Since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, all of the technique points from the lowering phase apply to how to perform the lifting phase, except for the details on how deeply to hip hinge.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
7. Re-rack the bar by walking forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup, and you are ready to rest the bar on the J-hooks by once again bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner.

### Reducing set up time

Relative to a variety of other exercises, exercises performed with a barbell on your back can require more time initially to set them up appropriately as is demonstrated by the fairly lengthy “setting up” section. However, subsequent sessions in which you perform the same exercise can involve a quicker set up relative to the first time in which you use this exercise. To save time during future sessions, you can record the height that you determined was appropriate to position the J-cups and safety pins. If your power rack has numbered pin holes, you can simply note the positions you used. Without numbered holes, you can note how many holes were above your J-cup position and how many holes were between your safety pin position and your J-cup position. Consequently, you will not need to take a trial and error approach when setting up your power rack each session.

### Use the safety pins

It is by no means rare for people to perform exercises with a bar on their back without setting up safety pins, but using safety pins when appropriate is strongly recommended. Positioning safety pins for an exercise such as the barbell good morning is the equivalent of wearing a seat belt when driving. In either situation, you may not actually intend to have to use them, but both safety mechanisms can reduce the risk of injury if an accident occurs. While you can try to refrain from performing a set of barbell good mornings with a load or number of reps that is beyond your capacity, sometimes lifters can overestimate what is left in the tank and unintentionally fail a rep. Furthermore a non-zero risk of injury exists during any reasonably challenging physical activity even when using high quality technique and an intelligently designed program that utilizes appropriate volumes, intensities, and rates of progression. For instance, the likelihood may be very low on a per rep basis, but it is certainly possible to sustain a sudden strain injury to a hamstring or a spinal extensor muscle during the descent of a good morning. If such an acute injury occurs, you can simply set the bar down onto the safety pins when the safety pins are positioned appropriately. However, if you did not previously set up the safety pins, you face a risk of sustaining further injury if an unforeseen injury acutely occurs while your torso is in an inclined position with a bar on your back. That unfortunate predicament can easily be avoided when investing a moment of time into just positioning the safety pins beforehand. As demonstrated by competitive powerlifters, weightlifters, and bodybuilding having lower rates of reported injuries than athletes in many other sports, strenuous resistance training is not uniquely dangerous and there is no need to be fearful about lifting weights. Nonetheless, the potential for an injury to occur acutely while training can never be eliminated, and it is prudent to take the simple precautionary actions that promote your safety in the weight room.

### Standardizing range of motion

As an alternative to positioning the safety pins just under the lowest point in which the bar would descend during your good morning, you can intentionally position them directly at the lowest point in which the bar reaches when you have finished fully sitting your buttock back and reaching your full hamstring stretch. With this approach, you can lightly tap the safety pins with the bar during each rep, which will provide confirmation that you reached the same depth every rep. Doing so can help you standardize your technique and know that any progressions in your reps per set or load do not come at the expense of reducing your range of motion, which can help with tracking your improvement over time. During exercises that lack an external stopping point such as barbell good mornings, people may have a tendency to reduce depth unintentionally during challenging reps, so you can know that will not be occurring if you lightly tap the pins at the bottom of each rep. It is worth noting using pins in this manner is distinct from the barbell pin good morning, which involves letting the bar come to a dead stop and fully resting on the pins at the bottom of each rep.

### **Learning how to hip hinge**

If you have minimal experience training hip hinge exercises such as Romanian deadlift and good morning variations, it is normal to have difficulty performing this movement pattern. Like riding a bicycle or shooting a basketball, hip hinging is a motor skill that may require repeated practice before you feel comfortable consistently using it. Broadly speaking, there are two types of movement substitution patterns that individuals who are in the process of learning how to hip hinge commonly perform when attempting to execute a hip hinge exercise.

One of these is using a stoop lift, which involves dynamically rounding the back (through flexion of the lumbar and thoracic spine) to bend over prior to uncoiling the spine into an upright position during the ascent. This often is accompanied by the buttock not moving particularly far backward and the arms drifting out in front of the legs in contrast to a strict hip hinge, which utilizes a visibly flat back position (with close to a neutral lumbar spine) and has the buttock noticeably moving backward during the descent. In terms of similarity, a stoop lift and a hip hinge both involve only a mild magnitude of knee bend during the descent while keeping the hips high. A clue that you may be performing more of a stoop lift than a hip hinge is feeling a stretching sensation in your back rather than feeling your back muscles remain statically tight throughout your set as these muscles function to maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips. With a properly performed hip hinge, you should certainly feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the bottom of the lift, but you may also feel this stretching sensation during a stoop lift. Nonetheless, a hip hinge can allow you to feel the hamstring stretch earlier during the descent compared to a stoop lift since the hamstrings are shortened by the posterior pelvic tilt (tucking the tailbone under) that is coupled with lumbar spine flexion.

In addition to performing a stoop lift unintentionally when attempting to hip hinge, people can commonly utilize more of a squatting motion that is characterized by greater knee bend and forward tracking of the knees during the descent. Compared to a hip hinge, using more of a squatting movement can result in the buttock moving downward during the descent as opposed to backward, and the shins can also incline forward as opposed to remaining vertical. Because the hamstrings shorten as the knees bend, someone moving in a squat pattern when attempting to perform a hip hinge exercise is unlikely to feel much of a stretching sensation in the hamstrings at the bottom of the lift. Not feeling a hamstring stretch is the most straightforward indicator that you may be squatting your hip hinge exercise, but an additional clue would be if you perceive your quads to be working (e.g., feeling a “burning” sensation or lots of tension) more intensely than your hamstrings during the exercise.

When thinking about moving through hip hinge, stoop lift, and squat patterns, it is important to recognize that these movements can occur along a spectrum. You can perform a hip hinge exercise with a technique that is mostly a hip hinge while still utilizing elements of a stoop lift or a squat that may not be ideal for what you wish to accomplish from the exercise. Similarly, your technique can incrementally progress from being stoop lift-dominant or squat-dominant to becoming progressively more of a hip hinge as your body learns how to move in a different way through repeated practice. If your hip hinge technique currently has much room for improvement, it can be beneficial to start with lighter loads that may not be especially challenging to your muscles until you developed a reasonable level of competency with the movement itself. There is no need to let perfect be the enemy of good, so you do not need to wait to load a movement meaningfully until you have immaculate technique, but it would also be inadvisable to push your body to the limit without initially learning the basic fundamentals of the movement.

Depending on which element of hip hinging in which you currently are challenged, certain external cues can expedite how quickly you can learn how to hinge. When unintentionally moving in a manner that involves a greater degree of squatting or stoop lifting than is intended, a wall may help provide tactile feedback to cue sitting your buttock backward. To do so, you can perform your hip hinge with your back facing a nearby wall, and you will be able to receive confirmation as to whether you are actually sitting your hips backward by feeling the wall contact your buttock at the end of the descent. As an initial starting point, you can set up with a heel-to-toe tandem stance as the back of one heel contacts the wall. Then you can bring your rear foot forward to be aligned with your front foot in the symmetrical stance you will utilize for your hip hinge. This can provide a reasonable approximation as to how far people may commonly be able to sit their hips back when hinging, but you can adjust from there how far away you position yourself from the wall to individualize it to you.

Specifically if you have a tendency to perform a “squatty” hip hinge, practicing your hip hinge with your calves up against something like a flat exercise bench (or even a couch or chair at home) can be a rather productive means of honing your hinge. As you descend, you will receive immediate tactile feedback if your knees track forward from no longer feeling the contact with your calves, so it can be a great way to reinforce keeping your shins vertical throughout the movement. When using this method, make sure that you maintain full contact between the soles of your feet and the ground while you avoid leaning your bodyweight into the bench to the extent that you would fall backward if the bench was removed. If you successfully keep your calves in contact with the bench throughout the movement and feel a pronounced stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the end of the descent, you are right on track to achieving a high quality hip hinge.

As an additional learning tool, you can situate a long object like a dowel rod, PVC pipe, or yardstick on your back while hip hinging if you have a tendency to utilize more of a stoop lift technique with excessive back rounding. Either the calf-to-bench technique or the buttock-to-wall technique can be incorporated into an actual Romanian deadlift where you use weights, but using a rod as a cue without a partner will require you to hold the rod in place, so you would not be able to load this drill independently. To perform this movement, you would hold the rod behind against your back with one hand higher up near your head and your other hand lower down near your buttock. While standing fully upright and looking straight ahead, you should feel the rod contacting your sacrum (the bone that lies between your upper buttock cheeks and right above your tailbone), upper back between your shoulder blades, and the back of your head. You will then hip hinge while maintaining these three points of contact throughout the entirety of the movement. If you start rounding your back or moving your neck beyond the neutral position you adopt when standing fully upright, you will feel the rod lose contact with one of those three spots. This can be a rather effective form of instant feedback to help develop your ability to move predominantly through your lower body while keeping your trunk in a rigid position throughout the movement, which can transfer to improved technique for an array of different exercises. When maintaining those three contact points, you potentially can still perform a squatting motion rather than a hip hinge since moving through your lower body while minimizing back motion is also a component of squatting technique. However, if you maintain those three contact points and additionally feel your hamstrings notably stretched at the bottom of the descent, those two factors indicate that you have successfully hip hinged in all likelihood. If you find that the rod cuing shifts your movement from a stoop lift to more of a squat, you can use the rod cuing simultaneously with the calf-to-bench cuing, which can address multiple aspects of the hip hinge concurrently.

In the context of performing a hip hinge exercise, using a form that resembles more of a squat or stoop lift rather than a hip hinge can be considered technique errors, but squatting and stoop lifting are by no means faulty movement patterns inherently. They simply differ from a hip hinge, so they can be suboptimal means of performing an exercise that you intend to train specifically for the benefits that hip hinging can provide as opposed to other movements. The hip hinge can take some practice to learn, but investing the time and effort into doing so can be a prudent investment given that having the motor skill of hip hinging can meaningfully expand your freedom in how you can move both inside and outside of the gym.

## Setting up
1. If your machine allows you to adjust the height of the footplate, select a height that will allow your legs to be in an approximately horizontal position once you are at the bottom of a rep.
    1. After estimating where this setting may be, you can adjust it during later steps if warranted.
    2. If you wish to increase the intensity of the exercise beyond the typical version, you can elevate the footplate beyond this standard setting.
2. Horizontally adjust the machine’s footplate to a setting that will allow the lowest point of your thighs to contact the back (i.e., the end closer to the foot plate) of the pad once you are in the starting position.
    1. This is the standard set-up for a glute ham raise, as demonstrated by certain machines having a knee pad (in addition to the thigh pad) onto which you can kneel in the starting position when setting the foot plate in this manner.
    2. The proper footplate position should permit your knees to move freely throughout the exercise while feeling stable and comfortable.
    3. If your knees are resting on top of the thigh pad in the starting position, the footplate is excessively far forward for a standard glute ham raise, and the exercise can function more like a higher-intensity Nordic hamstring curl.
    4. If your middle or upper thighs are resting on the thigh pad in the starting position, the footplate is excessively far backward for a standard glute ham raise.
    5. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal footplate position.
3. Climb up onto the machine, and position the soles of your feet fully against the footplate with your lower legs between the leg rollers and your lower thigh resting against the thigh pad.
    1. The back of your lower legs should be snugly pressed into the top pair of leg rollers slightly above your heels.
    2. While you are setting your feet, you can use the handles for assistance.
    3. Some machines have a step that you can use to help you get into position.
4. Assume an upright torso position, where your shoulders and hips are vertically stacked above your knees when viewed from the side.
    1. Your back and neck should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
5. Situate your arms by your sides with straight elbows, so that they are aligned with your torso and thighs.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set to minimize the difficulty of each rep compared to other arm positions.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Keep your glutes squeezed and your core braced throughout the set to help you maintain a rigid trunk position.
2. In a controlled manner, lean your thighs and torso forward as one unit exclusively through knee motion.
    1. As all the movement occurs from your knees transitioning to a less bent position, keep your torso and hips in a rigid position while keeping your feet firmly against the footplate.
    2. Throughout your set, you should be able to continue drawing a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders. To do so, you will have to avoid bending forward at your hips or dynamically arching your lower back, either of which may occur if you do not appropriately continue squeezing your glutes and bracing your core.
    3. While you do not need to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should actively be in control the entire time rather than letting gravity rapidly pull you downward.
    4. As you lean forward, your knees will gradually slide upward and become closer to being vertically level with your feet.
3. Continue leaning forward until you have straightened your knees with your whole body in a horizontal position or until you have reached the end range that you can control.
    1. The exercise will become progressively more difficult as you descend, so not every lifter has the strength to lower through the full range of motion with quality technique, which includes keeping the thighs and torso aligned.
    2. If you are currently unable to control the descent until your knees have straightened, you can gradually increase the range of motion across multiple sessions to progress over time, or you can train through a full range of motion with the lower intensity [band-assisted glute ham raise](Band-assisted%20glute%20ham%20raise%202995c6f170d8803d8ec1c1d7f755a8d9.md).
4. Reverse the movement by bending your knees to lift your torso and thighs as one unit until you have returned to having your hips and shoulders vertically stacked above your knees.
    1. It can help to think about driving the balls of your feet into the footplate.
    2. Since you are continuing to keep your thighs and torso aligned, your hips and shoulders should lift upward and backward in an arcing motion at the same rate. Avoid bending over at your torso while shooting your hips backward, which is a common error people make.
    3. Strive to have your torso and thighs form the hand of an analog clock that is arcing from 9 o’clock to 12 o’clock about the center point formed by your knees.
    4. During the lifting phase, your knees will naturally descend mildly toward the bottom of the thigh pad.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, you can bend at your hips and grasp the handles to help you dismount the machine.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Hamstrings%201b95c6f170d88055a462c40b686f381a.md), [gracilis](../Muscles/Gracilis%201925c6f170d880938681fbbe8f075831.md), and [sartorius](../Muscles/Sartorius%201925c6f170d8801c8493cac115de0546.md), which are assisted by your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a short looped elastic band around both of your thighs.
    1. The band will provide the greatest resistance to your hip muscles if you place it just above your knees, while it will provide less resistance if you place it higher up on your thighs.
    2. You can choose where you situate the band on your thighs based on the level of resistance you wish to experience, and if you are using a particular band for this exercise for the first time, you can adjust its placement during the set if you wish to change the difficulty after starting the set.
2. Lie down on your side with the side of your body that you are about to train facing up.
    1. In this side-lying position, you can rest the bottom side of your head on the hand of your bottom arm for comfort by situating your upper arm out to the side with your elbow bent.
    2. For extra stability, you can bend the elbow of your top arm and place that side’s hand on the ground in front of your torso.
3. Bend your knees by approximately 90 degrees and bring your thighs forward so they form near a 45-60-degree angle with your torso.
    1. Based on preference and what feels comfortable to you, you can position your thighs further forward so that they are closer to forming a right angle with your torso, or you can position them further backward so that they are closer to being aligned with your torso.
    2. In this position, the inner aspects of your knees and feet should be in contact with each other.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your top leg’s knee upward away from your bottom knee while keeping the inner aspect of your feet in contact with each other and the rest of your body stationary.
    1. Move through your hip’s available range of motion, and avoid rolling your hips backward during this exercise, which is a common technical error.
    2. To help prevent your hips from rolling, you can imagine that you are wearing a belt with a buckle that has a laser beam shooting out of it. Strive to keep the laser beam pointing straight forward, parallel to the ground, throughout the movement.
    3. If you start to roll your hips backward, your belt buckle’s laser beam will start to angle upward, the exercise will feel easier, and you will be able to lift your knee higher up than if you had avoided rolling backward.
    4. While performing this movement with the appropriate technique, you will likely feel the muscles on the side of your top hip contracting.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your top knee to descend in a controlled manner until it is low enough to contact the inner aspect of your lower knee.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side by lying on your opposite side.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains the [upper region of your gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%20Upper%20Region%201925c6f170d88070b08aeccda6e5ac88.md) and the [short hip external rotator muscles](../Muscles/Short%20Hip%20External%20Rotators%201b95c6f170d880c79035ce63a7c5f540.md) situated underneath your glutes.

## Setting up
1. Position the weight you intend to use at the base of the Roman chair in between its handles such that you can reach the weight when your feet are on its foot plate.
    1. For this variation, you will be holding the weight to your chest, so a weight plate, dumbbell, kettlebell, or medicine ball is a viable option that you can select based on equipment availability and preference.
2. Adjust the height of the Roman chair’s pad to a level that positions the top of your hip bones somewhat above the top of the pads when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. This position will allow you to move freely about your hips in contrast to if the pad is contacting the top of your hip bones, which would restrict hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    2. If the top of the pad is positioned much lower than the top of the hip bones (rather than only somewhat lower), some individuals may feel knee discomfort, so a sweet spot can exist for pad placement.
    3. Some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position after initially completing step 2.
3. While placing your hands onto the handles for balance support, step onto the foot plate one leg at a time with the back of your heels in contact with the back of the foot plate, so that the entirety of your soles are in contact with the foot plate.
    1. Position your feet symmetrically in a stance that feels comfortable to you, which can involve pointing your toes somewhat outward or pointing them fairly straight forward.
    2. Situating your feet approximately hip width to shoulder apart from each other will result in a viable stance width, but how wide of a stance you can use will be influenced by the width of your Roman chair’s foot plate.
    3. Your knees should be straight after you have finished setting your feet on the foot plate.
4. Check to make sure that the pad is positioned as described by step 1, and readjust the pad height if it is not prior to resuming your setup.
## Exercise technique
1. Begin bracing your core by taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    4. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the upright position.
    5. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
2. Hinge at your hips until you are low enough to pick up your weight and hold it to your chest.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. Nearly all of the motion should occur from you moving at your hips as you keep your trunk in a static position that maintains the natural curvature of your lower back (as opposed to bending over by rounding your lower back).
    3. Maintain a straight knee position throughout your set, but you should avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads.
    4. Depending on your limb lengths and the height of your Roman chair, you may have to round your upper back somewhat to grasp the weight initially.
    5. The precise way in which you will hold the weight to your chest may vary based on the specific implement you selected, but what matters is that you have a firm grip on the weight and are able to keep it in a stable position.
3. While keeping the weight held to your chest, lift your torso up through your hips until you can draw approximately a straight line from your legs through your hips and to your torso.
    1. You can finish the lifting phase by fully squeezing your glutes, which helps cue hip movement at the top as opposed to spinal movement.
    2. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the hip motion you just performed during the lowering phase.
4. Lower your torso by hinging at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner as you continue keeping your trunk in a statically braced position.
    1. While hinging at your hips and keeping the weight by your chest, you should feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings that progressively intensifies.
    2. Most people will be able to descend until their shoulders are lower than their hips, but how deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    3. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch, you have finished descending through your available hip range of motion.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the weight back down on the ground.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise dynamically trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a pair of deadlift blocks (or a similarly sturdy substitute capable of safely withstanding the load you will use) on the ground far enough apart from each other that the weight plates on a bar will be able to rest fully on the blocks in a stable position.
    1. For this block pull variation, your blocks should be of a height that situates the bar near the middle of your shins when the loaded bar is resting on the blocks. This can be considered a moderate height sumo block pull that elevates the bar to a greater degree than the sumo low block pull.
    2. To appropriately position the blocks, it can be helpful to have a barbell on the ground and align the blocks about the same distance apart from each other as is the length of the barbell’s shaft (which is the middle part of the bar in between the two thick circular collars).
    3. Aerobic steps can often be used for block pulls while having the option to adjust the height by changing the number of risers you use, but you should be aware of the recommended weight limit if you opt to use heavy loads. The weight limit for aerobic steps will vary by brand, but some of the common brands recommend not exceeding 300lb (136kg) per step, which would result in a 600lb (272kg) limit when using a pair of steps for a block pull. The height of the aerobic step will also vary by brand, but the step itself is commonly near 4in (10cm) in height, and risers are often near 2in (5cm) in height.
    4. With thickness typically ranging from about 1-3.5in (2.5-8.9cm), depending on the weight and brand, bumper plates can also function as blocks that can be stacked on top of each other to provide a range of different heights.
    5. It may be worthwhile to try out different block heights to determine which height places you in your intended starting position. However, you can initially try out a pair of approximately 4in (10cm) deadlift blocks, aerobic steps without risers, or thick 45lb (20kg) bumper plates, which should situate a bar loaded with large diameter plates (e.g., 45lb (20kg) plates or any jumper plates) reasonably close to mid-shin for many people. If one set-up places you mildly above mid-shin, while another set-up places you mildly below this point, utilizing the lower height set-up is generally recommended when training for muscle growth or to strengthen your sumo deadlift from the floor. If you are going to add only smaller diameter plates onto the bar, higher blocks will naturally be needed to position the bar near the middle of your shins.
2. After placing a barbell onto the blocks and loading weight plates to the bar, stand upright close in front of the middle of the bar as the bar is approximately over the middle of your feet.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
3. Spread your legs apart into a wide stance that is clearly outside shoulder width, with your feet moderately rotated out away from your sides.
    1. Provided that your feet are wider apart than your shoulders but closer together than the plates, you can use a range of stance widths for your sumo deadlift.
    2. The ideal stance width can meaningfully vary among different individuals based on someone’s body structure and hip mobility.
    3. Trying out different foot positions will normally be required to determine which stance specifically feels best to you.
    4. As a starting point, you can widen your feet as far apart as you feel comfortable and stable while being able to push your knees out approximately over your heels, resulting in close to vertical shins. You will push your knees out when descending to reach the bar, so subsequent aspects of the setup can help you gauge if you should adjust your stance.
    5. The ideal amount of toe flare also varies among different lifters, but you can start with your toes pointing about 30-45 degrees out to the side before adjusting from there based on what feels best to you. Zero degrees of toe flare would mean your toes are pointing straight forward, while 90 degrees would mean your toes are pointing directly out to your side.
4. Direct your arms straight down toward the ground with straight elbows as your shoulders are packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up).
    1. Maintain this position from here onward.
5. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips while bending your knees and pushing your knees out until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees, and your knees should essentially not track forward (although a slight degree of forward knee tracking can be used if that feels best to you).
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something. After you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Try to push your knees far enough out to the sides that they are vertically stacked over your heels.
    4. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    5. Similarly, keep your chest up in a “proud chest” posture and your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    6. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
    7. The bar should be directly in front of your shins.
6. With your shoulders stacked vertically above the bar, firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down, such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath). This should expand the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles, like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360-degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. Continue bracing your core throughout your set. This will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. This can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” by extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. Keep your chest up, back flat, and knees pushed out.
    2. As your hips and chest rise at the same rate, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull. Avoid letting your torso incline further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
    3. Keep the bar very close to your legs throughout the rep.
4. After the bar reaches near your knees, focus on thrusting your hips forward until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back when viewed from the side.
5. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips and bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the blocks.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your hips back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally. After the bar has cleared your knees, you can further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
    2. Continue keeping your back flat and chest up.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the blocks for a moment rather than simply tapping the blocks and immediately deadlifting the bar up again. Then continue to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the blocks for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferring between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the blocks.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.

## Setting up
1. Horizontally adjust the machine’s footplate to a setting that will allow you to position part of your buttocks just off the front edge of the pad when you set up with your feet on the footplate.
    1. The appropriate position should allow your thighs to rest comfortably on the pad.
    2. If the footplate is positioned excessively far from the pad, you will have to sit closer toward the middle of the pad rather than just off the front edge.
    3. If the footplate is positioned excessively close to the pad, the back of your upper thighs will not be in contact with the pad.
    4. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position.
2. If your machine allows you to adjust the height of the footplate, select a height that allows you to feel comfortable and secure with slightly bent knees once you are in the starting position.
    1. As a starting point, you can select a height that positions the lower pair of leg rollers level with the pad and the upper pair of leg rollers higher than the pad.
    2. Not all machines permit you to adjust the footplate height.
3. Climb up onto the machine, and hook your lower legs between the leg rollers with the top of your feet snugly pressed into the top roller as your soles are facing the footplate. Sit upright with your buttocks just hanging off the front edge of the pad.
    1. Your feet should be securely anchored so that they will not slide during the exercise. The top rollers should be just above the lowest part of your shins by your ankles, while the bottom rollers should be just under your Achilles tendons (which attach to the top of your heels).
    2. Depending on the machine you are using, you can step up onto a middle beam or a step to help you get into position.
    3. While you are setting your feet, you can reach back with your hands to hold the handles for stability.
4. Cross your arms across your chest with bent elbows to position each hand on the front of the opposite shoulder.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
    2. Your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, looking straight ahead. Keep your neck in this position during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Lean your torso back in a controlled manner until your torso is approximately parallel to the ground or slightly beyond this point.
    1. Allow your lower back to arch to a degree that feels comfortable to you.
    2. Specifically how much of an arch is comfortable will vary from person to person, but it is often appropriate to finish the lowering phase with your lower back arched to a similar degree as when you are normally standing upright. It is not inherently injurious to arch beyond this point, but meaningfully arching the lower back beyond this point can provoke lower back discomfort in some people.
    3. If you feel lower back discomfort at the bottom, you can strive to keep your lower back closer to a flat position with less of an arch, or you can reduce the range in which you lean back. Thinking about keeping your ribs tucked down to a greater degree as you avoid flaring them can help limit excessive arching.
2. Reverse the movement by curling your back to lift your torso up until your shoulders are vertically above your hips.
    1. To train your abs dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain in a flat position (which could occur if you predominantly lift your torso up through your hip flexor muscles).
    2. As a cue to emphasize your abs, think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the tops of your hip bones while tightening your abs.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
4. After your last rep, you can grasp the handles to help you dismount the machine.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance while holding the kettlebells with straight elbows.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you are using kettlebells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both kettlebells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    3. For an easier setup, you can pick up one kettlebell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other kettlebell onto the bench before picking up both kettlebells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    4. Pick up the kettlebells with a deadlift or squat motion, where you lift them by extending (straightening) your hips and knees while keeping your back flat.
2. Position your palms right next to the outer aspect of the front of your thighs so that your palms angle diagonally backward and in toward each other.
    1. Keep your palms facing this way throughout the exercise.
    2. This results in a semi-overhand grip, which is a hybrid between an overhand grip that would direct your palms straight backward (with the kettlebells directly in front of your body) and a neutral grip that would direct your palms straight in toward your sides (with the kettlebells directly to the sides of your body).
    3. Your neck should be near a neutral position, as when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Maintain this neck position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Bracing your core will help you maintain a rigid torso position as you subsequently move about your hips rather than your back.
2. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    2. Without thinking about “bending over,” your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the kettlebells when focusing on “sitting back.”
    3. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    4. Keep the kettlebells just in front of your legs and your feet fully planted on the ground throughout the set.
3. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move without rounding your back or excessively bending your knees.
    1. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    2. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically hinge until their hands are at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your back or excessively bending your knees depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    3. If you have the flexibility to hinge until the kettlebells contact the ground, descend until you can tap the weights very lightly on the ground, but do not let the weights rest on the ground.
    4. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should clearly be in control of the entire descent.
4. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward to lift your torso upright into the starting position.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    2. When you have finished lifting the kettlebells, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back at the top through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips properly stacked under your shoulders, preventing excessive arching.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the kettlebells down.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
    2. After finishing the last rep, set the kettlebells down in a deadlift motion by bending your hips and knees while keeping your back flat.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your knees bent and the soles of your feet flat on the ground, approximately hip width apart. Place your arms by your sides with your palms on the ground.
    1. You can rest your head on the ground.
    2. You optionally can hook the tops of your feet under a sturdy object like a couch (while your soles are still flat on the ground), which is recommended to help stabilize your body during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. As you tighten your abdominal muscles, lift your back and head up off the ground by curling your back to bring your chest toward your thighs.
    1. Given that this is a sit-up rather than a crunch, you will lift the entirety of your back off the ground.
    2. To train your abdominal muscles dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain in a flat position (which could occur if you predominantly lift your torso up through your hip flexor muscles).
    3. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    4. Allow your hands to slide forward on the ground progressively as your torso lifts up.
    5. As a cue, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the top of your hip bones, which is the action that contraction of your abdominal muscles can produce.
    6. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that you have fully rounded your back and cannot bring your chest closer toward your thighs.
    7. At the end of the lifting phase, your chest should be facing forward.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your head and back to the starting position on the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
