## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat’s back pad to a position that aligns your knees with the machine’s pivot point while sitting up against the back pad with your thighs resting on the seat.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to its highest position that allows you to begin each rep with your knees fully straightened.
    1. Certain machines can be used for leg extensions or hamstring curls based on how the lever arm is positioned.
3. Adjust the lower leg pad to a position that places it slightly above the back of your heels (i.e., on your Achilles tendons) when seated against the backrest, with your legs on top of the lower leg pad and your knees straightened.
    1. Adjusting this setting exclusively moves the lower leg pad without moving the lever arm, in contrast to step 2, where the machine lever arm and shin pad move together.
4. After selecting your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin, sit down on its seat with your back against the back pad and your lower legs on top of the lower leg pad.
5. Adjust the thigh pad to press down snugly against your lower thighs.
    1. In this starting position, your knees should be straight and aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. On the side you are about to train, pull your toes and foot back toward your shin by moving at your ankle. Maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankle in the same position in which it would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heel up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankle in this position can increase your hamstring curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
3. While keeping one knee fully straightened, use your other leg to drive your heel down and back toward you as you bend your knee to pull the lower leg pad under your thighs. Drive back through the available range of motion that the machine allows.
    1. At some point, the machine will stop you from bending your knee any further, but most machines will allow you to bend your knee by at least 90 degrees.
    2. While your lower leg moves through motion at your one knee, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
4. Reverse the movement as you allow your knee to straighten progressively in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your knee fully straightened.
    2. Continue keeping your other knee straightened.
    3. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower legs up.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that allows you to hold the handles comfortably with bent elbows once you are seated.
    1. If your machine has elbow pads, the proper seat height should also permit you to rest your elbows on them comfortably while grasping the handles.
    2. The appropriate setting should allow you to keep your arms mostly relaxed when grasping the handles.
    3. You should not have to shrug your shoulders up to reach the handles.
    4. Some trial and error may be required to find a seat height that feels appropriate for you.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit on the seat with your back snugly against the back pad as your lower back is comfortably arched.
    1. The degree to which you can comfortably arch your lower back can be affected by your mobility.
    2. Starting with an appropriate degree of lower back arching will situate your abs in a lengthened position that can facilitate training them a long range of motion during this exercise.
4. Hook your feet snugly under the foot roller pads in a secure position.
    1. Specifically how you should set your feet may vary from machine to machine, but situating the front of your ankles against the back of the pads and the top of your feet against the bottom of the pads can commonly promote a stable position. If your machine allows you to adjust these pads, you can set them to where you achieve this position.
    2. Certain machine models may have foot pegs onto which you simply rest your feet, rather than roller pads that can lock your feet into position.
    3. Ultimately, you want to set up in a manner that allows your feet to feel stable throughout the exercise.
5. Reach up and grasp the handles with your palms facing in toward each other. If your machine has elbow pads, rest your elbows against them as well.
    1. In the starting position, your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Maintain this neck position during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl your spine as you pull the bottom of your ribs toward the tops of your hip bones in a controlled manner.
    1. This action will naturally prompt your knees and feet to lift upward, even if you do not consciously try to march your knees up. If you wish to train your hip flexors simultaneously with your abs, you can also intentionally think about driving your knees up, but make sure that you do so in addition to curling your spine rather than as an alternative to curling your spine.
    2. Once you feel that you can no longer curl your spine through a range permitted by the machine that feels comfortable to your back, you have reached your end range. The machine may physically restrict your range of motion at a certain point, even if you have the mobility to crunch further.
    3. Avoid pulling down with your arms. Your arms should only move because they are attached to your torso, which is what you are directly moving. The function of your arms is merely to transmit force from your abs into the machine. You should not feel your back muscles contract like they would during a pulling exercise (such as a straight arm lat pulldown). If you feel like your back muscles are driving the movement, you can try loosening your grip to the minimum required to hold the handles in a stable fashion.
    4. To train your abs dynamically, you should be intentionally rounding your entire back, since this motion is performed by contraction of your abs. When rounding your back appropriately, you should feel meaningful tension in your abs. If you do not feel your abs engaging, you may be substituting hip or shoulder motion for the intended spinal motion.
    5. If you finish the movement with your back fairly flat as opposed to rounded, you most likely are primarily bending at your hips rather than curling your spine.
    6. It can help to think about crunching your elbows toward your knees.
    7. You can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the middle of your chest, and you are trying to point that closer toward the middle point between your knees.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner as you uncurl your back by flaring your ribs up and away from your hip bones.
    1. Allow your knees to descend away from your elbows.
    2. Move through the full range of motion permitted by the machine that feels comfortable to your lower back. This may involve letting the machine’s lever arms (onto which you loaded weight plates) lightly tap the stoppers underneath them if the full range enabled by the machine feels comfortable to you.
    3. When uncurling your spine, your lower back will initially move into a flat position before moving into an arched position.
    4. Depending on your mobility and the range of motion your machine permits, you may feel a stretching sensation in your abs as you allow your lower back to arch.
    5. The imaginary laser beam shooting out from your chest should angle progressively higher up as you uncurl your back and flare your ribs away from your hip bones.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you feel lower back discomfort at the end of either step, you can abbreviate the range of motion to what feels best to you. Performing this exercise through a full range of motion is by no means inherently injurious to the lower back, but certain individuals with pre-existing conditions may experience discomfort in rather rounded or rather arched positions.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground.
    1. The size of the weight plates you add to the bar will determine how high the bar lies above the ground, which consequently affects your range of motion. Adding a pair of full-diameter plates (like 45lb (20kg) plates or any bumper plates) will elevate the bar to the standard height (about 9in (23cm)) when deadlifting from the floor. If you only use smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a deficit deadlift with a greater range of motion that may exceed the range of motion in which some people wish to train if they lack the mobility to perform a [deficit deadlift](Deficit%20conventional%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d8809f90f5d4f2e2273493.md) with appropriate technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize 45lb (20kg) plates, you can perform a [block pull](Conventional%20mid-shin%20block%20pull%201a35c6f170d880349a3beab3040acdc9.md) or [rack pull](Mid-shin%20rack%20pull%201a35c6f170d880fd8a71e340d039d10a.md) with the bar elevated to where it would be when deadlifting from the floor with full diameter plates.
2. While facing the center of the bar, stand in an approximately hip-width stance with the middle of your feet under the bar and your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly out to the sides.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
    2. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    3. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the bar and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from hinging at your hips than bending your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something. After you have fully sat back and feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    4. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and help engage your back muscles.
4. With your elbows fully straightened, firmly grasp the bar with an approximately shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. As an alternative to the double overhand grip, you can naturally use a mixed grip (with one palm facing forward and the other facing backward) or lifting straps with the double overhand grip if you wish to do so.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees. Prioritize keeping your chest up, lower back flat, the bar close to your legs, and your core braced throughout the entire exercise.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the bar reaches near the middle of your shins, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
5. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. Just like when lifting the bar, keep your lower back flat and chest up as you descend while actively avoiding letting your lower back round or chest collapse.
    2. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees. Then you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is on the ground rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before the next rep.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable decline bench to your desired decline angle.
    1. An angle near 30 degrees is an appropriate starting point, but you can effectively perform this exercise with a range of decline angles.
    2. The difficulty of this exercise will increase as the decline becomes steeper, so you can adjust the angle to modify the intensity.
    3. Some adjustable benches have a mild decline setting along with incline settings, but they lack a pad to secure your feet. This exercise specifically uses a decline with a foot/ankle pad.
2. Sit down on the bench while snugly positioning the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
3. Lie down in a controlled manner to position your back and head on the bench.
4. Cross your arms across your chest with bent elbows to position each hand on the front of the opposite shoulder.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. As you tighten your abdominal muscles, lift your back and head up off the bench by curling your back. Bring your chest toward your thighs.
    1. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that you have fully rounded your back and cannot bring your chest closer toward your thighs.
    2. Given that this is a sit-up rather than a crunch, you will lift the entirety of your back off the bench.
    3. To train your abdominal muscles dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain in a flat position (which could occur if you predominantly lift your torso up through your hip flexor muscles).
    4. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    5. As a cue for your engaging abdominal muscles, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs toward your hip bones.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your back to the starting position.
    1. Rather than fully relaxing at the bottom, strive to tap the bench lightly with your upper back while keeping your abdominals tensed.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the entire movement.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat’s back pad to a position that aligns your knees with the machine’s pivot point while sitting up against the back pad with your thighs resting on the seat.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to its highest position that allows you to begin each rep with your knees fully straightened.
    1. Certain machines can be used for leg extensions or hamstring curls based on how the lever arm is positioned.
3. Adjust the lower leg pad to a position that places it slightly above the back of your heels (i.e., on your Achilles tendons) when seated against the backrest, with your legs on top of the lower leg pad and your knees straightened.
    1. Adjusting this setting exclusively moves the lower leg pad without moving the lever arm, in contrast to step 2, where the machine lever arm and shin pad move together.
4. After adding weight plates to the machine, sit down on its seat with your back against the back pad and your lower legs on top of the lower leg pad.
5. Adjust the thigh pad to press down snugly against your lower thighs.
    1. In this starting position, your knees should be straight and aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. On the side you are about to train, pull your toes and foot back toward your shin by moving at your ankle. Maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankle in the same position in which it would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heel up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankle in this position can increase your hamstring curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
3. While keeping one knee fully straightened, use your other leg to drive your heel down and back toward you as you bend your knee to pull the lower leg pad under your thighs. Drive back through the available range of motion that the machine allows.
    1. At some point, the machine will stop you from bending your knee any further, but most machines will allow you to bend your knee by at least 90 degrees.
    2. While your lower leg moves through motion at your one knee, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
4. Reverse the movement as you allow your knee to straighten progressively in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your knee fully straightened.
    2. Continue keeping your other knee straightened.
    3. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower legs up.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train all your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Hamstrings%201b95c6f170d88055a462c40b686f381a.md), which are assisted by your [gracilis](../Muscles/Gracilis%201925c6f170d880938681fbbe8f075831.md), [sartorius](../Muscles/Sartorius%201925c6f170d8801c8493cac115de0546.md), and [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a power rack’s safety pins near the height of the middle of your shins when standing upright.
    1. Certain power racks will not allow you to position safety pins near this level, so this variation will not be feasible in every power rack. If your rack is not suitable for this variation, you can select the “conventional mid-shin block pull” from this database to provide a similar training effect.
    2. If the closest safety pin setting of your rack situates the bar somewhat higher than mid-shin, you may be able to perform a mid-shin block pull by elevating your feet like you would for a deficit deadlift. To do so, you can place a large diameter weight plate or deadlift block in the center of your rack, and you will stand on top of it to perform your rack pull from a closer to mid-shin starting position. Depending on your preferred stance width, you can also position two plates or deadlift blocks directly next to each other if the soles of your feet do not fit fully onto one plate or deadlift block.
2. Place a barbell centered on top of the safety pins, and add your desired weight plates to it.
    1. Particularly as the load on the bar increases, rack pulls risk damaging a bar if you do not utilize a well-controlled lowering phase, which people often do not.
    2. Certain gyms have bars that were previously bent from rack pulls and are now specifically designated to be used for rack pulls to avoid damaging other bars.
    3. When using a well-controlled lowering phase during every rep, you most likely can avoid damaging the bar when performing a rack pull.
    4. If you do not feel confident in your ability to avoid damaging a bar when performing a rack pull, it is not recommended to perform rack pulls with a bar you do not own unless you receive approval from the gym owner or are using a bar designated for rack pulls.
3. Stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance close in front of the middle of the bar, as the bar is over the middle of your feet, with your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly turned out to the sides.
    1. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    2. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
4. With your arms directed down toward the ground, straight elbows, and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward to bring your shins right next to the bar.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    5. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
5. Firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down, such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force that would lift the bar if it were only half as heavy.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat with the bar close to your shins, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. Immediately after the bar lifts off the pins, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. The “push the floor away” cue only applies to the very start of the rep, since thrusting your hips forward is chiefly what will allow you to lift the weight during this variation.
    2. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    3. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
5. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar in a controlled manner until the bar has returned to resting on the pins.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track slightly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you absolutely should not slam the bar onto the pins in a jarring manner.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the pins for a moment (rather than simply tapping the pins and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the pins for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferring between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the pins.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise dynamically trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Sit on the ground with your knees bent by approximately 90 degrees and feet together.
2. Moderately lean your torso back at your hips, and lift your feet slightly off the ground.
    1. Keep your feet off the ground, and your torso reclined throughout this exercise.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
3. Place your hands together in front of your chest with your elbows bent and your upper arms by your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. Rotate your torso to one side through your trunk’s available range of motion as you direct your chest toward that side.
    1. You can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the center of your chest as you rotate that laser beam out to the side. This should result in your elbow (on the side to which you are twisting) moving behind your torso.
    2. People often emphasize tapping the ground with their hands rather than actually rotating their torsos during this exercise. It is not inherently problematic to tap the ground with your hands, but focusing on your hands can prompt you to move your arms through shoulder motion rather than actually twisting your trunk (which is the function of your obliques).
    3. How far you can rotate will be influenced by your spinal mobility.
    4. Continue keeping your legs stationary throughout your set as you avoid letting your legs swing to the side.
2. Reverse the movement by rotating your torso back to the starting position.
3. Cyclically perform steps 1 and 2 as you alternate to which side you are rotating until you have completed your set.
    1. Strive to rotate fluidly from one side to the other rather than pausing once you have returned to the center position.
    2. Move in a controlled manner the entire time.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) while statically training your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s chest pad to a setting that will situate it at chest height once you are kneeling on the knee pad.
    1. To confirm if the chest pad is positioned appropriately, you will have to be kneeling on the knee pad.
    2. A minority of machine models may lack a chest pad and simply have fixed handles for you to hold. If you are using one of those machines, disregard the instructions about the chest pad and just aim to keep your chest pointing straight forward throughout the exercise while holding the handles.
2. Rotate the kneeling pad toward one direction. Select a setting that allows you to perform this exercise through the full range of motion that is comfortable to you.
    1. If you have normal back mobility and a healthy back, you can initially rotate it fully to one side. If you cannot comfortably assume the starting position from this setting, you can rotate the pad closer toward the center (where your imaginary belt buckle and chest are both facing forward) until you can set up comfortably.
    2. As you rotate the pad further away from the centered position, you will be able to train your core muscles in more lengthened positions that may be conducive to developing them effectively.
    3. It is up to you whether you begin with the pad rotated to your right or left, since you will adjust it to the opposite side after your first set to train both sides equally.
    4. Your optimal setting will be affected by your back mobility, and finding this ideal setting may require some trial and error.
3. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
4. Kneel on the knee pad with an upright torso as your thighs are vertical. Squeeze your glutes to promote the proper posture.
    1. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Keeping your glutes squeezed from this point onward can help you maintain the appropriate lower back position throughout the exercise.
    2. Your knees should be vertically stacked underneath your hips.
5. Rotate your chest toward the chest pad and snugly contact the pad with your chest while firmly gripping the handles.
    1. In the starting position, it is common to feel a stretching sensation in your back when the machine is adjusted to train through your full range of motion. However, you should not feel lower back discomfort in this position, so you should adjust the degree to which the knee pad is rotated if you experience discomfort when moving into the starting position. If you cannot rotate your chest enough to reach the chest pad, you naturally should adjust the knee  pad as well until you can reach it.
## Exercise technique
1. Rotate your imaginary belt buckle in a controlled manner away from the side it initially faces. Move through the full range of motion your mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your chest snug against the chest pad and your glutes squeezed while you maintain the tall kneeling position with your knees firmly on the knee pad.
    2. Your legs should only turn because you are rotating your torso, and your legs are connected to your torso.
    3. Focusing on turning your imaginary belt buckle can help cue the rotational trunk motion that your core muscles perform. 
    4. During the first half of the movement, you will rotate your imaginary belt buckle so that it faces straight forward with your chest. Then you will continue rotating to have your imaginary belt buckle face the opposite direction from which it started.
2. Reverse the movement as you rotate your imaginary belt buckle in the opposite direction to return to the starting position.
    1. While you do not need to utilize an extremely slow tempo, you should actively control the entire movement rather than letting the machine’s resistance abruptly twist you back into the starting position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with the knee pad rotated toward the opposite side from which you started.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and your small [rotatores muscles](../Muscles/Rotatores%20Muscles%201b95c6f170d8800188c7db2ca87b8b54.md) through a long range of motion.

## Setting up
1. Approach a flat exercise bench or a similarly sturdy object with an elevated surface that can support your foot.
    1. As an alternative to a bench, you can use a plyometric box or an aerobic step stacked on risers. At home, you can use pieces of furniture such as a bed, couch, or chair that will not slide. If the object you use has a hard surface, placing a cushioned object (such as a foam pad) on top of it may make this exercise more comfortable.
    2. The difficulty of this exercise will increase as the object’s height increases, so you can utilize a taller object for a greater intensity. However, a height near 18in (46cm), which applies to a typical flat exercise bench, is recommended to use as a minimum for most people.
2. Lie down on your side with the inner aspect of your top foot and ankle on top of the elevated surface, as that leg’s knee is straight. Align your leg with your torso so that you can draw a straight line from your leg through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from above.
    1. The outer aspect of your lower hip should be resting on the ground.
    2. If you are on a hard surface, you can set up on an exercise mat for comfort. You chiefly want a comfortable surface to be under the forearm that you will be placing on the ground.
3. Align your lower thigh directly under your top thigh.
    1. If the object you are using has open space underneath its top surface (like with a bench), keep your knee straight on your lower leg.
    2. If your object lacks space for your lower foot under its top surface (like with a soft plyometric box), keep your bottom knee bent.
4. Position your bottom forearm on the ground with your elbow bent by about 90 degrees. Your elbow should be close to being stacked directly underneath your shoulder.
    1. With your bottom hand, you can make a fist and keep the little finger-side of your hand in contact with the ground. Alternatively, you can keep your palm flat on the ground if you find that to feel more comfortable and stable.
    2. You can keep your top arm in a comfortable position, such as resting on top of your side with a straight elbow. Alternatively, you can reach that arm toward the ceiling with a straight elbow or place that side’s hand on your top hip with a bent elbow.
    3. Your bottom upper arm should be in a vertical position.
    4. You can perform steps 2-4 simultaneously.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your bottom hip and leg fully off the ground by driving your top leg down into the bench while pushing your bottom forearm into the ground.
    1. At the top, you should now be able to draw a straight line from your head through your belly button to the center point between your knees when viewed from the front.
    2. You should also be able to draw a straight line from your heel through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the top.
    3. Your thighs (which should be close together), torso, and head should be in essentially the same alignment as they would be when standing upright.
    4. The intent to pull your top leg down is what should lift your bottom leg, rather than simply lifting your bottom leg up by itself. Since the bench stops your top leg from moving down, this intent lifts you up.
    5. An indicator that you are appropriately driving through your top leg is when your top hip becomes approximately level with your top foot. If you lift your bottom leg by itself, your top hip will remain lower than your top foot, which you do not want.
2. Slowly reverse the movement by lowering your hips until your bottom leg lightly taps the ground. Keep your bottom thigh close to parallel to the ground throughout the exercise.
    1. At the bottom, your top hip should now be lower than your top foot, since you should be moving through your top hip.
    2. Avoid lowering your bottom leg by itself, which would result in your bottom knee being lower than your bottom hip. Your bottom knee should remain essentially level with your bottom hip throughout the set.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your opposite side elevated.
    1. When learning this exercise, it can be useful to face a mirror to receive visual feedback about your positioning.
    2. Avoid letting your buttocks drift backward during the set by bending your hips. This would prevent you from being able to draw a straight line through your whole body when viewed from the top. Squeezing your glutes can help prevent you from unintentionally bending your hips.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train all your [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md) and a variety of core muscles, including your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [quadratus lumborum](../Muscles/Quadratus%20Lumborum%201965c6f170d880b89d4fc43238472b46.md).

## Setting up
1. If your machine has an adjustable seat, position it to a height that allows you to contact the lower back pad with the back of your hip bones and your lower back.
    1. Most machines lack an adjustable seat.
2. Initially position the roller pad far enough back that you can comfortably sit on the seat.
3. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
4. Sit down on the seat with the back of your hip bones snugly against the lower back pad. 
5. Place your feet on the foot bar, and adjust the foot bar to a comfortable setting if it is adjustable on your machine.
    1. If your machine permits you to adjust the foot bar or presents multiple foot bars that cannot be adjusted, the ideal foot bar position should allow your feet to feel stable while your hip bones are well-supported by the lower back pad. The optimal foot bar position should also readily enable you to perform this exercise through spinal motion while limiting hip motion.
    2. Some people may find it easier to emphasize training the back muscles through spinal motion when setting the foot bar far enough back to allow their knees to be bent by about 90 degrees or somewhat greater. However, you may still be able to perform this exercise when setting the foot bar further in front to a position that allows your knees to be mildly bent. A range of foot bar positions can be viable, so you can feel free to try out different positions over time to determine where you personally feel best if you can utilize different settings with your machine.
6. Securely fasten the seat belt around your waist if your machine has a belt.
7. Round your lower and middle back through the full range of motion that is comfortable for you. Set the roller pad so that it contacts your upper back in this rounded position or is as close to doing so as your machine permits.
    1. You may notice that setting the roller pad as far forward as you can results in the pad not contacting your back when you have rounded your back through your full comfortable range. If this occurs with your machine, you will have to start each rep from a less rounded back position in order to reach the pad.
    2. As you move the roller pad further forward, you will be able to achieve a greater degree of back rounding in the starting position, which allows you to train your back muscles in a more lengthened position that may be conducive to developing them effectively.
    3. Your mobility can affect the degree to which you can comfortably round your back and, consequently, which roller pad starting position is ideal for you.
    4. Throughout this exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Uncurl your back by flaring your ribs up and away from your hip bones through a comfortable range of motion. Avoid leaning your torso backward primarily through hip motion as you emphasize moving the roller pad backward through spinal motion.
    1. If you just focus on driving the roller pad backward rather than on how you move it, you most likely will be meaningfully using your hip muscles to lift the weight rather than using your back muscles in a more targeted manner. Regardless of your intent, the hip muscles (like your glutes) will inevitably be engaged to at least some degree, since a normal rhythm exists between hip and spinal motions, and the machine does not fully stabilize the hips. However, you should strive to move predominantly at your spine while minimizing hip motion to the best of your ability when you are striving to target your back muscles.
    2. When uncurling your spine, your lower back will initially move into a flat position before moving into an arched position.
    3. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable to you as an individual, you can finish the lifting phase once your lower back is close to having the mild curvature it naturally has when sitting upright, or you can finish with a greater degree of lower back arching. What chiefly matters is moving through a range that does not prompt you to feel lower back discomfort.
    4. When you are appropriately moving your spine, you should feel tension in the lower back muscles running along each side of your spine. Thinking about flaring your ribs up and away from your hip bones can help cue you to move at your spine rather than your hips.
    5. Both during this lifting phase and the subsequent lowering phase, it is recommended to move in a slow and controlled manner while prioritizing technique quality.
    6. Throughout your set, keep your buttocks on the seat, hip bones snugly against the lower back pad, and feet on the foot bar.
2. Reverse the movement by rounding your back through the full range of motion that is comfortable to you to bring the roller pad forward.
    1. Continue emphasizing spinal motion while minimizing hip motion. If you finish the movement with your lower back flat or arched as opposed to rounded, you most likely are primarily bending at your hips rather than rounding your spine.
    2. It can help to think about crunching your ribs down toward your hip bones as you move into a slouched position with your chest angled closer toward your knees.
    3. If you initially positioned the roller pad to the appropriate setting, you should return to the starting position, where you can gently tap the weights you selected against the rest of the weight stack to confirm you have moved through your full range of motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you feel lower back discomfort at the end of either step, you can abbreviate the range of motion to what feels best to you. Performing this exercise through a full range of motion is by no means inherently injurious to the lower back, but certain individuals with pre-existing conditions may experience discomfort in rather rounded or rather arched positions.
    2. If you experience lower back discomfort specifically at the end of step 2, you can pause your set and adjust the starting position of the roller pad to be further back to limit you from training beyond your comfortable range of motion.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) in your lower and middle back.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with straight legs, as your feet are approximately hip width apart.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can lie down on an exercise mat.
2. Place the fingertips of each hand lightly in contact with the sides of the back of your head as your upper arms and elbows are directed out away from your sides.
    1. Since you are not interlocking your fingers along the middle of the back of your head, you should not have to lift your head up off the ground to situate your hands in the appropriate position.
    2. Keeping your hands and arms in this position can help you avoid inadvertently pulling down on your head during the exercise, which would otherwise be easier to do if you interlocked your fingers and directed your upper arms up toward the ceiling.
    3. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Tighten your abs to flatten your lower back and press it lightly into the ground. Keep your lower back flattened against the ground throughout all subsequent steps.
    1. In contrast to if your abs were relaxed and your lower back exhibited its natural arch, you should not be able to slide a hand under your lower back.
2. March your left leg up and back toward your chest while bending its knee.
    1. How far you can march this leg back will be affected by your hip mobility.
    2. So long as you follow the same movement pattern described here, you can choose whether you begin with your left or right leg marched, but mentioning the sides as an example can help with technique clarity.
3. With a straight knee, lift your right leg slightly off the ground or higher up for a lower intensity.
    1. As you lift this leg higher up, the difficulty of the exercise will decrease, so you can determine specifically how high you lift it based on your current ability.
    2. If you notice that you cannot keep your lower back flat with your leg slightly off the ground, you can try lifting it up to a height that allows you to avoid aching your lower back.
4. Tuck your chin slightly toward your chest to lift your head just above the ground.
5. In a crunch-like motion, mildly curl your upper back to lift your shoulder blades slightly up off the ground.
    1. While they are presented as distinct steps for instructional clarity, you can perform the actions from steps 1-5 simultaneously with each other once you understand the proper positioning that each step achieves.
6. March your right leg up and back toward your chest while bending its knee as you lower your left leg while straightening its knee. Simultaneously rotate your chest to the right to bring your left elbow toward your right knee.
    1. Strive to move your legs reciprocally at the same speed in sync with your torso rotation. This should result in you finishing lowering your left leg at the same time you have finished marching your right leg and turning your chest to the right.
    2. Move through the range of motion permitted by your spine and hip mobility. You have reached your end range once you feel that you can no longer rotate your chest to the right while marching your right leg back. ## Setting up
1. After initially standing in the center of the captain’s chair with your back facing its back pad, step up onto its foot plates while placing your hands against the arm pads for any balance assistance as needed.
2. Bend your elbows and place the bottom of your forearms onto the arm pads while firmly grasping the handles with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Your back should be contacting the backrest while your torso is in an upright position.
3. While bearing the force from your bodyweight through your elbows into the arm pads, pick your feet up off the foot plates and allow them to hang straight down toward the ground.
    1. Keep your shoulder blades and shoulders near the natural position in which they are when normally standing upright, rather than letting your shoulder blades and shoulders shrug up from gravity pulling your torso down.
    2. You should be able to draw a straight line vertically down from your torso through your legs.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your legs up and toward your torso through your available range of motion while curling your hips forward and only allowing your knees to bend mildly.
    1. If you keep your knees locked in a fully straightened position throughout the movement, your hamstring flexibility can limit how high you can lift your legs.
    2. Ideally keep your knees as close to straight as you can without your hamstring flexibility restricting your range of motion, which should result in your feet clearly being in front of your knees.
    3. You can keep your knees completely straight during the initial portion of the movement and allow them to bend as needed while progressively lifting your legs, since the hamstrings progressively lengthen as the thighs lift higher up (through hip flexion).
    4. Curling your hips forward will round your lower back and result in your buttocks facing forward at the end of the lifting phase.
    5. Keep your upper body stationary.
    6. Your legs should move in an arcing manner as they initially move upward and forward before moving upward and backward after they lift beyond being parallel to the ground.
    7. How high you are able to raise your legs up will be influenced by the mobility in your hips and lower back, along with your strength.
    8. Whenever you feel like you cannot bring your legs any higher up without excessively bending your knees, you have reached the end of the lifting phase.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your legs to descend while uncurling your lower back until you have returned to the starting position with your thighs directed straight down toward the ground.
    1. Actively lower your legs throughout the descent rather than letting gravity rapidly pull you back down, which could result in your legs swinging back behind the starting position as momentum takes over.
    2. Your knees can progressively straighten as you descend.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to return your feet onto the foot plates and step down from the captain’s chair.

### Straight knee leg raise versus bent knee leg raise

With the exception of utilizing a straighter knee position, the technique for the straight knee leg raise is otherwise essentially the same as the bent knee leg raise, so both variations primarily train the same muscle groups. In terms of the training effect these exercises provide, the main difference is that the straight knee leg raise is a higher intensity variation due to how it shifts the center of mass of your legs farther forward relative to your trunk and hip. This results in a longer lever arm of resistance acting on your trunk and hip, which requires your abdominal muscles and hip flexor muscles respectively generating greater trunk flexion and hip flexion torque to overcome. Resistive torque can be increased by increasing the weight you move or by increasing the lever arm in which the weight acts on a particular joint, so the straight knee leg raise can function similar to a weighted knee raise without requiring additional weights. The greater magnitude of resistance from the straight knee leg raise almost certainly explains why McGill et al. (2014) found this variation to yield noticeably greater EMG activity of the abdominal muscles than the bent knee leg raise when participants performed three reps of each exercise.

Nonetheless, this does not mean that the straight knee leg raise is inherently superior to the bent knee leg raise for developing the abdominal muscles in the same way that squatting 200lb (91kg) is not necessarily better than squatting 150lb (68kg) for inducing quad hypertrophy. If you have the strength to perform both leg raise variations with sound technique, you simply will have to perform greater reps per set with the bent knee position compared to the straight knee position to achieve the same hypertrophic stimulus. If an equal number of sets are performed until the same proximity failure (e.g., performing as many reps as you can with each condition), a very similar degree of muscle growth may be produced by 6-rep sets, 30-rep sets, or anywhere in between. Correspondingly, the bent knee variation that provides less resistance can still be just as productive for developing the abdominals as the straight knee variation for most people when leaving the same number of reps in reserve for sets of either exercise. The one exception may be for individuals with especially strong abdominals who are able to perform a very high number of bent knee leg raise reps per set before reaching a pronounced degree of muscle fatigue, indicating that the resistance from these reps are very low relative to their strength. At some point an exercise may just be providing too low of a resistance to optimize how much muscle growth that a set can stimulate even if the set is performed until failure. Specifically where that threshold lies is currently unclear, but that should not be any concern for you unless you are able to perform over 30 reps per set, which will not be an issue for the vast majority of people performing bent knee leg raises with a controlled technique through a full range of motion.

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.

1. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.

## Setting up
1. Anchor a long looped band at chest height around a power rack’s beam or similarly sturdy object with a smooth surface to which you can anchor your band.
    1. To anchor the band, you can initially fold it around the beam while holding each end, then loop one end into the middle of the other, and pull that end until it is taut.
    2. Inspect the band to confirm it has no small tears, as a small tear can quickly become a full tear when stretching a band.
    3. If you have a D-handle attachment that you can connect to the band, you can optionally use it and grasp it during step 3 instead of grasping the band directly.
2. Stand with the side of one shoulder facing the band’s anchor point, and take a small step backward so that the band is directly in front of you.
3. Firmly grasp the free end of the band with your hands interlocked and palms facing each other. Your elbows should be bent with your upper arms by your sides, and your hands should be just in front of your chest.
    1. One palm should face toward the anchor point, while the other faces straight out to the side, away from the anchor point.
4. While keeping your hands close to your chest, side-step away from the anchor point until you feel the degree of tension you wish to experience from the band.
    1. Prevent your torso from rotating when side-stepping.
    2. The two halves of the band should be flat rather than twisted.
    3. Up to a certain point, you can progressively increase the band’s resistance by stepping out farther. However, be careful not to step out so far that you overstretch the band, which an abrupt increase in band resistance can indicate.
    4. The capacity to which a band can safely stretch varies depending on the manufacturer, but, as a general rule of thumb, avoid stretching the band three times its resting length or more to minimize the risk of tearing.
    5. Naturally, you will not be measuring the length to which you elongate the band. Nonetheless, if the band does not provide sufficient resistance after taking a few steps out from the point at which you started feeling resistance, it may be appropriate to switch to a higher tension band instead of stepping out any farther.
5. Position your feet near shoulder-width apart, and slightly sit your buttocks backward to bend your hips and knees slightly.
    1. Rather than being excessively arched or rounded, your back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. In this starting position, you should be able to form a 90-degree angle between the band and an imaginary laser beam shooting straight forward from the center of your chest. You should also be able to draw a straight line between your shoulders that is parallel to the band.
    3. The purpose of the slight hip and knee bend is to help you feel stable and balanced during your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forceful slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. While keeping your chest facing straight ahead, press your hands forward, away from your chest.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as your arms are outstretched in front of you close to parallel to the ground.
    2. All the motion should occur from your arms moving at your shoulders and elbows, while the rest of your body remains completely stationary.
    3. Particularly avoid letting the band's resistance rotate your torso. If your core muscles do not stabilize your trunk sufficiently, the imaginary laser beam shooting out from the center of your chest will start angling closer toward the band’s anchor point. The center of your chest should be facing the same direction throughout your entire set.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by bringing your hands straight back toward your chest as you bend your elbows.
    1. You should now be back to the starting position, with your hands directly in front of your chest and your upper arms by your sides.
    2. Continue keeping the center of your chest facing straight forward, with your shoulders aligned when viewed from the side.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise, this time facing the opposite direction.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your side with straight legs as one leg is resting on top of the other. Align your legs with your torso so that you can draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso when viewed from above.
    1. The outer aspect of your lower foot and lower hip should be resting on the ground.
    2. If you are on a hard surface, you can set up on an exercise mat for comfort. You chiefly want a comfortable surface to be under the forearm that you will be placing on the ground.
    3. This side plank will simultaneously train the hip muscles on both sides of your body along with the core and shoulder muscles on the side closer to the ground.
2. Position your bottom forearm on the ground with your elbow bent to about 90 degrees. Your elbow should be close to being stacked directly underneath your shoulder.
    1. With your bottom hand, you can make a fist and keep the little finger-side of your hand in contact with the ground. Alternatively, you can keep your palm flat on the ground if you find that to feel more comfortable and stable.
    2. You can keep your top arm in a comfortable position, such as resting on top of your side with a straight elbow. Alternatively, you can reach that arm toward the ceiling with a straight elbow or place that side’s hand on your top hip with a bent elbow.
    3. Your bottom upper arm should be in a vertical position.
    4. You can perform this step simultaneously with step 1.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your bottom hip off the ground by pushing through your bottom foot and forearm. You should now be able to draw a straight line from your head through your belly button to the center point between your feet when viewed from the front.
    1. You should also be able to draw a straight line from your heel through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the top.
    2. Your legs, torso, and head should be in the same alignment in which they would be when standing upright with your feet together.
2. Lift your top leg straight up through your hip’s available range of motion. Keep the rest of your body completely stationary in the same position you assumed from step 1.
    1. Specifically how high you are able to lift your top leg will be influenced by your hip mobility and strength.
    2. Avoid rotating your top leg when lifting it up. Your kneecap and toes should be pointing straight forward the whole time. If your kneecap and toes are pointing diagonally up and forward instead of straight forward, you have rotated your leg while lifting it up.
3. Statically hold this position in proper alignment until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your opposite side contacting the ground.
    1. Avoid letting your lower hip sag down, which would prevent you from being able to draw the line through the midline of your body when viewed from the front. If you notice your hip starting to drop down, it can help to think about pushing more forcefully through your bottom foot. When learning this exercise, it can be useful to face a mirror to receive visual feedback if your lower hip begins sagging down.
    2. Avoid letting your buttocks drift backward or letting your top leg drift forward by bending your hips. This would prevent you from being able to draw the straight line through your whole body when viewed from the top. Squeezing your glutes can help prevent you from unintentionally bending your hips.
    3. To the best of your ability, strive to limit your top leg from drifting down. However, it is natural for this leg to descend gradually as your hip muscles become fatigued, and you do not necessarily need to end your set if this starts occurring. The key is that you are able to keep your top leg high enough that it does not touch your bottom leg.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), [lateral deltoid](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), and a variety of core muscles, including your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [quadratus lumborum](../Muscles/Quadratus%20Lumborum%201965c6f170d880b89d4fc43238472b46.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to approximately chest height, connect a D-handle attachment to it, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. As an alternative to the D-handle attachment, you can also use a rope attachment, but this page will describe the usage of the D-handle.
2. Stand with the side of one shoulder facing the cable station, as the handle is just in front of your chest.
3. Firmly grasp the handle with your hands interlocked and palms facing each other. Your elbows should be bent with your upper arms by your sides, and the handle in front of your chest.
    1. One palm should be facing in toward the cable, as the other palm faces straight out to the side, away from the cable.
4. While keeping your chest pointing straight ahead and the handle close to it, take a few steps to the side away from the cable station against its resistance.
    1. Walk far enough outward that the cable can still provide resistance at the point during the exercise when your torso is twisted toward the cable station. If you lose resistance at any point during this exercise, you can take another step away.
    2. Do not let the cable’s resistance twist your chest when stepping outward.
5. Position your feet near shoulder width apart, and slightly sit your buttocks backward to bend your hips and knees slightly.
    1. Rather than being excessively arched or rounded, your back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. In this starting position, two imaginary laser beams shooting out from the center of your chest and where you would wear a belt buckle should be pointing straight forward, parallel to each other. These two laser beams should form approximately 90-degree angles with the cable.
## Exercise technique
1. Press the handle straight forward away from your chest. Keep your elbows straight throughout the later steps.
    1. Your arms should now be outstretched in front of you and close to parallel to the ground.
2. Rotate your chest toward the cable station to move the handle toward the station in a controlled manner. Keep your imaginary belt buckle pointing straight ahead and the handle directly in front of your chest throughout the set.
    1. Rotate your chest in a controlled manner through the full range of motion that your spinal mobility comfortably permits. Because spinal mobility varies among people, the end range will vary among different individuals.
    2. When appropriately rotating your trunk, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your back at your end range.
    3. As you move, a progressively greater angle should form between the mobile imaginary laser beam exiting your chest and the stationary imaginary laser beam shooting out from your belt buckle.
    4. If your imaginary belt buckle turns with your chest, you are rotating at your hips rather than rotating your trunk in an isolated manner.
    5. If your hands no longer remain directly in front of your chest’s imaginary laser beam, you are moving your arms through shoulder motion.
3. Rotate your chest fully away from the cable station to move the handle away from the station in an arcing manner.
    1. Continue keeping your imaginary belt buckle facing straight ahead and the handle directly aligned with the center of your chest.
    2. When rotating your trunk (rather than just your hips), you should feel the muscles on the sides of your torso contract.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise while facing the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and your small [rotatores muscles](../Muscles/Rotatores%20Muscles%201b95c6f170d8800188c7db2ca87b8b54.md) through a long range of motion.

1. Pick up one kettlebell and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while firmly holding the kettlebell at your side with your elbow straight, as your palm faces in toward your thigh.
    1. Initially pick up the kettlebell with a hip hinge or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).

3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forceful slap.
    1. In this starting position, your lower back should be near a neutral position with the natural mild curvature you have when normally standing upright rather than being excessively arched or flattened.
2. Sweep your right arm backward and downward while simultaneously straightening your left leg and lowering it toward the ground. Rigidly maintain the natural curvature of your lower back throughout the entire exercise.
    1. As you lower your arm and leg, you will have to continue bracing your core to prevent your lower back from arching to a greater degree. Unintended arching would be demonstrated by an increase in the space between the ground and your lower back, so you can focus on maintaining this space each rep.
    2. Strive to move your arm and leg at the same rate through the full range of motion that you can without letting your lower back dynamically arch.
    3. With sufficient core control, you can finish with your arm and leg parallel to the ground as they are fully straightened. From this position, you can gently tap the ground with your hand and heel simultaneously. If your lower back starts arching to a greater degree before this point, shorten the range of motion to what you can perform without letting your lower back arch further.
    4. All the movement should occur from your right shoulder, left hip, and left knee as your spine remains motionless.
    5. Move in a slow and controlled manner throughout your set as you focus on high quality technique through every degree of motion.
    6. Keep your left arm and right leg completely stationary.
    7. So as long as you move an arm and leg on opposite sides of your body, you can choose which sides in which you will move to begin your set, but mentioning the sides as an example can help with technique clarity.
3. Reverse the movement by lifting your right arm and left leg up to return to the starting position.
    1. Since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the lowering phase, no motion should occur at your lower back as you continue bracing your core.
    2. While keeping your elbow straight, bend your left knee as you lift that thigh up to finish with your knee bent by approximately 90 degrees.
    3. At the top, both of your knees should be stacked vertically above your hips, and your arms should be vertically stacked above your shoulders.
4. Proceed to perform steps 2 and 3 with your left arm and right leg with the same technique you just utilized for your right arm and left leg.
5. Alternate between steps 2 through 4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) to maintain a rigid back position as you refine your ability to move through your hips and shoulders with a stable trunk.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to near the height of your head, connect a rope attachment to it, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. As an alternative to the rope attachment, you can also use a D-handle attachment, but this page will describe the usage of the rope attachment.
2. Pull the rope fully to one side of the attachment.
3. Stand with the cable station at your side, and firmly grasp the rope with your palms about shoulder-width apart while facing down.
4. While keeping your chest pointing straight ahead and the rope close to it, take a couple of steps to the side away from the cable station against its resistance.
    1. Allow the rope to align diagonally with the cable, which will result in your hand that is closer to the cable being higher than your hand on the other side.
    2. Step far enough outward that the cable can still provide resistance at the point during the exercise when your torso is twisted toward the cable station. If you lose resistance at any point during this exercise, you can set up farther away.
5. Lunge backward with your foot closer to the station to assume a half-kneeling position with your knee on the side closer to the station on the ground. Simultaneously straighten your elbows so that the rope stays in close to the same position while you lunge your torso back away from it.
    1. You can optionally rest your lower knee on a comfortable surface (e.g., exercise mat, foam cushion, folded towel) in this position.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched or rounded, your back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Rotate your chest diagonally up and toward the cable station to move the rope diagonally up toward the station in a controlled manner. Keep your chest facing the rope and your elbows straightened throughout the set.
    1. Rotate your chest in a controlled manner through the full range of motion that your spinal mobility comfortably permits. Because spinal mobility varies among people, the end range will vary among different individuals.
    2. During this exercise, you can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the middle of your chest, and you want to keep that laser beam pointing toward the middle of the rope. Turn that laser beam diagonally up toward the cable station during this step.
    3. If the middle of the rope no longer remains directly in front of your chest’s imaginary laser beam, you are moving your arms through shoulder motion rather than exclusively moving your trunk.
    4. Keep your imaginary belt buckle pointing straight ahead with your legs planted on the ground throughout this exercise.
2. Rotate your chest diagonally down and away from the cable station to move the rope diagonally down and away from the station.
    1. Continue keeping your imaginary belt buckle facing straight ahead and the rope directly aligned with the center of your chest.
    2. Avoid focusing on pulling with your arms to emphasize training your core. Your arms function to link the cable to your torso, and you are chiefly turning your chest to move the cable.
    3. When rotating your trunk appropriately (rather than only moving through your shoulders and/or hips), you should feel the muscles on the sides of your torso contract, particularly on the side further away from the cable station.
3. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise while facing the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) while also training your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) to a lesser degree.
