## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground, as your elbows are straight and your knees are bent.
    1. Your upper arms should be directed straight down under your shoulders such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    2. You can spread your fingers apart for stability. Depending upon which hand position feels most comfortable, you can point your middle fingers straight ahead or mildly out to the sides.
## Exercise technique
1. While bearing weight through your arms, straighten one knee to move your foot behind you and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. You should now look like you are at the top of a push-up.
2. Tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes to flatten your lower back.
    1. From this tall plank position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    2. Contracting your abs and glutes appropriately will prevent your hips from sagging down, which would prompt your lower back to arch rather than remain flat.
    3. During the entire set, do not allow your chest to sag down, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together. If you notice your chest starting to sag, push down into the ground more forcefully through your straight arms to spread your shoulder blades apart.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position as you would normally do when standing upright.
3. March one knee forward and up toward your chest while keeping the opposite leg on the ground and maintaining the same stable trunk position you assumed during step 2.
    1. Continue keeping your lower back flat while the only movement occurs from your marching leg as the rest of your body remains stationary.
    2. Particularly avoid letting your hip bones sag down, hike up, or tilt to either side.
    3. How far you can march your knee forward will be influenced by your hip mobility.
4. Reverse the movement by driving your knee (that you just marched) backward and straightening it until you are once again in a tall plank position with both feet on the ground.
    1. Move your leg in a controlled manner as you emphasize keeping your torso and hip bones stable.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 while switching which leg you march up each time until you have completed your set.
    1. During this variation, you are moving only one leg at a time while focusing on maintaining a strict plank position with your trunk.
    2. Wait to begin marching forward your opposite side’s knee until your other side’s foot has returned to the ground.
## Description
While also dynamically training your [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md), this exercise can statically train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. Pick up an ab wheel and kneel on a comfortable surface (e.g., exercise mat, foam cushion, pillow, folded towel) with your knees approximately hip-width apart.
    1. A comfortable surface is optional but definitely preferred by most people.
2. Place the ab wheel on the ground directly in front of you, then firmly grip the handles with your palms facing back toward you (i.e., an overhand grip).
    1. Keep your wrists straight throughout this exercise.
3. With your hips stacked vertically above your knees, position the ab wheel directly under your shoulders as your elbows are straight.
    1. Your thighs and arms should now be directed straight down, such that they are perpendicular to the ground, which places your torso closer to a horizontal position than a vertical position.
    2. Your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Maintain this neck position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Scoop your hip bones toward your ribs, while keeping your ribs pulled down toward your hip bones and tightening your abs. Maintain this position throughout your set.
    1. When starting with your lower back in its natural mild arch, this motion (known as posterior pelvic tilting) will flatten your lower back, since it is the opposite of arching it.
    2. Your abs attach to your pubic bone (which you can feel as a bony ridge in the middle of your pubic region) and your ribs, and this scooping motion should tilt your pubic bone up toward your ribs as you contract your abs.
    3. It can help to imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the midpoint between your hip bones, slightly below where you would wear a belt buckle. Before you scoop your hips, this laser beam will point down toward your abdomen. Scooping your hips appropriately should angle this laser beam forward toward the ab wheel.
2. Slowly push the ab wheel forward by simultaneously moving your hips and arms forward in unison. Keep your torso rigidly braced as you avoid letting your lower back arch throughout the movement.
    1. Only move the ab wheel as far forward as you can while maintaining a flat lower back position.
    2. Keeping your lower back flat will become progressively more difficult as you roll out further, so you can determine your range of motion based on your current ability.
    3. If you are new to this exercise, a rather short range may be appropriate. If you have the strength to do so with proper form, you can finish rolling out when your chest is almost touching the ground.
    4. Keep your elbows fully straightened as you move your hips and shoulders together.
    5. Avoid letting your hips sag down or your ribs flare up, as this can arch your lower back. If you can roll out until you are reasonably close to being able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your lower back, squeezing your glutes at this point can help you prevent your hips from sagging.
3. Reverse the movement by pulling the ab wheel back toward the starting position. Drive your arms down and back while allowing your hips to rock back in a controlled manner.
    1. Continue keeping your lower back in the same flat position you maintained while rolling out.
    2. In contrast to the exaggerated hip motion people often perform by rocking their back behind their knees, your hips should finish vertically above your knees with your thighs perpendicular to the ground.
    3. To avoid rocking your hips back excessively, focus on sweeping your arms back while letting your hips rock back naturally, rather than pulling through your hips.
    4. Your arms should finish directly under your shoulders, pointing straight down toward the ground.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while statically training your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. Hold a weight plate to your chest with both hands, and carry it toward a flat exercise bench.
    1. For comfort, you can optionally wear a beanie on your head or hold a small towel against the inner aspect of the plate. Resting the plate directly on your head without a soft fabric over your head can be uncomfortable, so using a beanie or towel is recommended.
    2. If you are new to this exercise, it is recommended to use a light plate, such as a 2.5-5lb (or 1.25-2.5kg).
2. Lie down with your back and buttocks on the bench. Rest your shoulder blades on the head of the bench with your head and neck fully off the bench.
    1. Place your legs and feet in a position that feels comfortable and stable to you. This may involve positioning your feet flat on the ground or the bench with your knees bent. flat on the bench with your knees bent. 
3. While securely holding the plate with both hands, position the center of the weight plate against the middle of your forehead.
    1. Throughout the set, you will use your hands to help keep the plate in contact with your forehead.
## Exercise technique
1. Slowly tilt your head down and back to bring your chin away from your chest. Move through your neck’s comfortable range of motion.
    1. How far you can comfortably tilt your head back will be affected by your neck mobility, so the end position will vary from person to person.
    2. At the bottom position, your face should be directed primarily backward rather than upward, like in the starting position.
    3. Do not exceed the range of motion that is comfortable for your neck.
    4. This is the same neck motion that you would perform when standing up and looking up toward the ceiling.
    5. Continue holding the plate against your forehead.
2. Reverse the movement by slowly nodding your head up. Bring your chin toward your collarbone without using your arms to lift the weight.
    1. Aim to lift the weight exclusively with your neck muscles as your arms simply hold the plate against your head.
    2. People can commonly perform this movement until the chin is very close to touching the collarbone, but your neck mobility will also influence the degree to which you can nod.
    3. When performing this movement correctly, you should feel the muscles on the front of your neck contract.
    4. Prioritize actively controlling the weight throughout the entirety of your set. This is an intentionally slow exercise.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After completing your last rep, use your arms to lift the plate off your forehead and bring it to your chest before sitting up.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train several muscles on the front of your neck, the largest and strongest of which is your [sternocleidomastoid](../Muscles/Sternocleidomastoid%2019a5c6f170d8806e81bdd0b1d1242785.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while firmly holding the dumbbell at your side with your elbow straight, as your palm faces in toward your thigh.
    1. Initially pick up the dumbbell with a hip hinge or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow, hips, and knees extended, slowly lower the dumbbell toward the side of your knee in a controlled manner as you bend your torso toward the side of the dumbbell.
    1. Move through your comfortable full range of motion, which will normally result in you experiencing a stretching sensation in the muscles on the opposite side of your torso (including your lower back).
    2. Your mobility will affect how far you can side bend, as some people will reach their end range when the dumbbell is at the level of the lower thigh, while others may be able to reach knee level or even a little lower.
    3. The motion should exclusively involve your trunk bending to the side, so you should not be bending your lower back forward or arching it backward during this exercise.
    4. The tops of your hip bones should remain level throughout this movement, like they do when you are normally standing upright.
2. Reverse the motion by bringing the dumbbell back up your side as you bend your torso toward the opposite side in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your torso upright and your shoulders approximately level with each other.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [quadratus lumborum](../Muscles/Quadratus%20Lumborum%201965c6f170d880b89d4fc43238472b46.md), while also training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [intertransversarii lumborum](../Muscles/Intertransversarii%20Lumborum%201b95c6f170d880f6902cf3d4a6d61511.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while holding the dumbbell at your side with a straight elbow as your palm faces in toward your thigh.
    1. Initially pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    2. Throughout the exercise, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side or held out to the side for balance assistance.
    3. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training first.
2. Lift the dumbbell up near the front of your shoulder with your elbow bent by curling the weight and using momentum from your lower body as needed.
    1. You can perform a cheat curl-like motion to move the dumbbell into position if it is too heavy to lift without momentum. To do so, first sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and simultaneously rocking the dumbbell mildly backward. Then drive your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body while bending your elbow to curl the weight upward while swinging your elbow forward. The hip drive motion, which is similar to the lockout of a deadlift, will bring your torso into a vertical position with your knees straightened.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbell right by your shoulder with your forearm in a vertical position, and your wrist stacked over your elbow as the handle of the dumbbell is parallel to your upper arm.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbell on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a mostly straight wrist that allows for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, pull your shoulder blades back together to adopt a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back along with your neck, like when you are normally standing upright.
4. Now your palm should be facing inward (with a neutral grip) as your upper arm is in front of your body with the back of your elbow pointing downward and forward (as opposed to being flared out away from your side).
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. Prior to walking with the weight, you will press it up through a push press or strict overhead press without leg drive. The directions describe how to perform a push press, since it will efficiently allow you to assume the overhead position with a heavy weight, but you can alternatively press the weight up without leg drive if you have the strength to do so.
2. Without moving your arm, mildly bend your knees in a quarter squat-like manner to dip down while maintaining an upright torso position with your chest up.
    1. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground during this dip phase.
    2. Your knees should track straight forward toward your toes rather than caving inward.
3. Directly after reaching the bottom of your dip, forcibly push through your feet as you rapidly extend (straighten) your knees and hips to generate upward momentum.
    1. The intent of this leg drive phase should be akin to a jump without lifting your feet fully off the ground.
    2. At the end of this drive, you can either keep the soles of your feet fully on the ground, or you can allow your heels to lift up slightly off the ground while keeping the front of your feet firmly in contact with the ground if a slight heel lift feels natural to you.
4. Immediately after you have finished extending your legs, explosively push the dumbbell upward by forcibly driving your elbow upward as you swiftly straighten your elbow.
    1. At the end of the pressing phase, your knees, hips, and elbow should be fully straightened, and your arm should be directed straight up toward the ceiling with your elbow and dumbbell situated vertically over your shoulder.
    2. To transfer your leg drive into pushing the dumbbell upward in an explosive manner, you should perform steps 3 and 4 as a continuous movement.
    3. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulder and elbow, your forearm should be in a vertical position throughout the rep as your wrist and dumbbell remain stacked over your elbow.
    4. Throughout the exercise, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back.
    5. Regardless of whether you lifted your heels up off the ground after extending your legs during the leg drive phase, your heels should be flat on the ground with the rest of your feet at the end of the pressing phase.
5. While keeping the dumbbell overhead with your elbow straightened and your chest up, walk forward in a controlled manner while maintaining an upright posture with your shoulders approximately level with each other.
    1. You will not swing your arm like you would when normally walking, and you will keep your trunk in a rigidly braced position, but your lower body should look similar to how it would when you walk normally.
    2. Based on your preference and what feels natural to you, you can either swing your free arm back and forth as you walk or keep it by your side.
    3. Walk at a pace where you feel stable and balanced throughout the carry.
    4. If you use a weight that is fairly heavy to you, it is natural to take shorter strides compared to how you typically walk.
    5. You should feel your core muscles on the side opposite to the dumbbell working to maintain an upright torso, as these muscles prevent the weight from bending your torso to the side of the dumbbell.
    6. Avoid leaning your torso away from the dumbbell, and keep the tops of your hip bones approximately level throughout your set rather than letting them drop down to one side when taking each step.
6. Continue walking with the dumbbell overhead until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the carry while holding the dumbbell with your other side.
7. Lower the dumbbell in a controlled manner as your elbow progressively bends while simultaneously moving downward.
8. As you approach the end of the lowering phase, shallowly bend your knees and hips as you did during step 2 (the dip phase) to help control the weight until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbell in front of your shoulders.
    1. Lower the dumbbell as far as you can while keeping your wrist in a straight position stacked over your elbow as your forearm remains vertical, which should result in your elbow being lower than your shoulder.
    2. Avoid descending beyond the point at which you can keep your forearm vertical.
    3. If you are using a heavy, bulky dumbbell, the dumbbell contacting your shoulder may also determine your end range of the lowering phase.
9. After you have fully lowered the weight, extend your knees and hips to stand upright before initiating your next rep.
10. After your dumbbell is by your shoulder, lower the dumbbell to your side as you straighten your elbow and swing your elbow back by your side.
11. Set the dumbbell down and pick it up with your other side before repeating the exercise with that side.
## Description
While also engaging your [thoracic erectors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can statically train much of your shoulder girdle musculature, including your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rotator cuff muscles](../Muscles/Rotator%20Cuff%201b95c6f170d880b3b0d8eab69c3a7683.md).

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up overhead and firmly grasp it with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip) and your hands situated near shoulder-width apart or somewhat wider.
    1. Ideally use a bar that is high enough to allow you to hang from it with straight legs without your feet touching the ground.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground and lifting your heels up, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the bar.
    4. If you use an object as a step to reach the bar, position that object a little behind the bar so that your feet do not touch that object when you are hanging from the bar with straight legs.
    5. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    6. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide upward during the dead hang, which pulls on your hand skin in a manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
2. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet off the ground to begin hanging on the bar. Allow your legs to hang down toward the ground with straight knees.
    1. While hanging, you should be able to draw a straight line vertically down from your torso through your legs.
    2. You will maintain a firm grip on the bar with straightened elbows throughout your set.
    3. If your bar is not high enough to keep your feet off the ground when your legs are directed straight down toward the ground (which may often be the case with doorway pull-up bars), bend your knees by the minimum needed to lift your feet just off the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your legs up and toward your torso through your available range of motion while curling your hips forward and only allowing your knees to bend mildly.
    1. If you keep your knees locked in a fully straightened position throughout the movement, your hamstring flexibility can limit how high you can lift your legs.
    2. Ideally keep your knees as close to straight as you can without your hamstring flexibility restricting your range of motion, which should result in your feet clearly being in front of your knees.
    3. You can keep your knees completely straight during the initial portion of the movement and allow them to bend as needed while progressively lifting your legs, since the hamstrings progressively lengthen as the thighs lift higher up (through hip flexion).
    4. Curling your hips forward will round your lower back and result in your buttocks facing forward at the end of the lifting phase.
    5. Keep your chest facing straight ahead rather than leaning your torso backward.
    6. Your legs should move in an arcing manner as they initially move upward and forward before moving upward and backward after they lift beyond being parallel to the ground.
    7. How high you are able to raise your legs up will be influenced by the mobility in your hips and lower back, along with your strength.
    8. Whenever you feel like you cannot bring your legs any higher up without excessively bending your knees, you have reached the end of the lifting phase.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your legs to descend while uncurling your lower back until you have returned to the starting position with your thighs directed straight down toward the ground.
    1. Actively lower your legs throughout the descent rather than letting gravity rapidly pull you back down, which could result in your legs swinging back behind the starting position as momentum takes over.
    2. Your knees can progressively straighten as you descend.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to return your feet to the ground.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

### **Straight knee leg raise versus bent knee leg raise**

With the exception of utilizing a straighter knee position, the technique for the straight knee leg raise is otherwise essentially the same as the bent knee leg raise, so both variations primarily train the same muscle groups. In terms of the training effect these exercises provide, the main difference is that the straight knee leg raise is a higher intensity variation due to how it shifts the center of mass of your legs farther forward relative to your trunk and hip. This results in a longer lever arm of resistance acting on your trunk and hip, which requires your abdominal muscles and hip flexor muscles respectively generating greater trunk flexion and hip flexion torque to overcome. Resistive torque can be increased by increasing the weight you move or by increasing the lever arm in which the weight acts on a particular joint, so the straight knee leg raise can function similar to a weighted knee raise without requiring additional weights. The greater magnitude of resistance from the straight knee leg raise almost certainly explains why McGill et al. (2014) found this variation to yield noticeably greater EMG activity of the abdominal muscles than the bent knee leg raise when participants performed three reps of each exercise.

Nonetheless, this does not mean that the straight knee leg raise is inherently superior to the bent knee leg raise for developing the abdominal muscles in the same way that squatting 200lb (91kg) is not necessarily better than squatting 150lb (68kg) for inducing quad hypertrophy. If you have the strength to perform both leg raise variations with sound technique, you simply will have to perform greater reps per set with the bent knee position compared to the straight knee position to achieve the same hypertrophic stimulus. If an equal number of sets are performed until the same proximity failure (e.g., performing as many reps as you can with each condition), a very similar degree of muscle growth may be produced by 6-rep sets, 30-rep sets, or anywhere in between. Correspondingly, the bent knee variation that provides less resistance can still be just as productive for developing the abdominals as the straight knee variation for most people when leaving the same number of reps in reserve for sets of either exercise. The one exception may be for individuals with especially strong abdominals who are able to perform a very high number of bent knee leg raise reps per set before reaching a pronounced degree of muscle fatigue, indicating that the resistance from these reps are very low relative to their strength. At some point an exercise may just be providing too low of a resistance to optimize how much muscle growth that a set can stimulate even if the set is performed until failure. Specifically where that threshold lies is currently unclear, but that should not be any concern for you unless you are able to perform over 30 reps per set, which will not be an issue for the vast majority of people performing bent knee leg raises with a controlled technique through a full range of motion.

### Hanging ab straps

If you have access to hanging ab straps, you have the option of using them for this exercise by hanging them from your pull-up bar about shoulder width apart from each other and resting your upper arms on top of the straps as you otherwise use the same form described under the exercise technique section. Using straps would ensure that your grip strength would not be able to function as the limiting factor during your set without otherwise affecting how your abdominal and hip flexor muscles are trained. Correspondingly, utilizing straps would remove the stimulus this exercise can provide to your forearm and hand muscles involved with gripping. Performing the exercise with straps would also result in the shoulders maintaining a moderately flexed position (as the upper arms remain parallel to the ground) in contrast to the fully flexed shoulder position that is adopted when hanging on the bar. This can result in strap usage removing the stimulus to improve or maintain shoulder mobility in an overhead position that can be experienced when hanging on the bar. On the other hand, the shoulder extensor muscles (e.g., lats, teres major, rear delt) will have to act isometrically (statically) to maintain the moderately flexed shoulder position when using straps. While these muscles are likely more engaged when performing the exercise with straps compared to without straps, they are still unlikely to be loaded enough to provide any meaningful training effect for most lifters.

### Is your grip strength limiting you?

As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance rather than abdominal muscle strength, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual. If you find that you can complete meaningfully more reps when using straps, your grip strength is likely limiting you during this exercise, which can consequently limit the stimulus it provides to your abdominal muscles.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a kettlebell or dumbbell and hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows, as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. You can use either a kettlebell or a dumbbell, but some people find holding a kettlebell in the goblet position to feel more stable and comfortable, especially with a fairly heavy weight.
    2. Based on your preference and the load you use, you can transfer your kettlebell or dumbbell into the goblet position through a couple of different approaches.
    3. An effective approach is initially to pick up the weight by the handle through a deadlift motion and set it on an elevated surface (like a bench or plyometric box) with the handle facing up if you use a kettlebell or the handle directed vertically if using a dumbbell (as only one end of the dumbbell is on the surface). Then squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it in the goblet position, and squat up with the weight. If you use a kettlebell, grasp it by its horns (i.e., side handles). If you use a dumbbell, cup your hands around the top end of the weight with the base of your palms by the handle, and your fingers wrapped around the rest of that end of the weight.
    4. With a lighter kettlebell, you can tilt it onto its side with the weight base directed toward you, squat down to grasp its horns, stand upright with it, and curl it into the goblet position.
    5. With a lighter dumbbell, you can also pick it up with one hand and curl it up across your body to be in front of your chest. Then cup your free hand around the top end of the dumbbell with the base of its palm by the handle and fingers wrapped around the top end of the weight before repositioning your other hand to cup the other side of the weight in the same manner.
## Exercise technique
1. Walk forward, holding the weight close to your chest in the goblet position, maintaining an upright posture with your shoulders approximately level.
    1. Walk at a pace where you feel stable and balanced throughout the carry.
    2. If you use a weight that is fairly heavy to you, it is natural to take shorter strides compared to how you typically walk.
    3. While you will not swing your arms like you would when walking normally, your torso and lower body should look similar to how they would when you walk normally.
    4. Focus on keeping your chest up, which will help engage your upper back muscles to prevent the weight from excessively rounding your upper back into a slouched posture.
    5. Maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like you have when normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back, which would lean your torso backward. 
    6. Keep the tops of your hip bones approximately level throughout your set rather than letting them drop down to one side when taking each step.
2. Continue walking with the weight in the goblet position using the technique described in step 1 until you have completed your set or have to turn around and walk in the opposite direction.
    1. After finishing the set, set the weight down in the same manner in which you initially picked it up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).
## Description
This exercise primarily trains the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) in your upper and middle back, which help keep your chest up.

## Setting up
1. Position the footplates far enough apart that you can fully spread your legs apart when you are seated with your feet on the footplates.
    1. If your machine’s knee pads rotate (which is the case for combo machines that can be adjusted to train hip adduction or abduction), position the pads so that they are facing away from each other.
    2. Determining specifically where you should position the footplates can take some trial and error if you are not accustomed to this exercise. The ideal position will allow you to feel resistance from the machine when your legs are spread as far apart as your flexibility comfortably permits. Avoid placing the footplates any further apart than that point to help you more easily transition into and out of the starting position.
2. If your machine allows you to adjust the backrest angle, position it fully upright.
    1. Most machines have backrests fixed in an upright position.
3. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
4. Sit down on the machine's seat with your torso upright against the backrest.
5. Spread your legs apart to place your feet on the footplates with the inner aspect of your knees and/or lower thighs contacting the knee pads.
    1. It may be easiest initially to position one leg and then use your arms to help pull the knee pads inward before positioning your other leg. The stretching force from the machine typically allows you to spread your legs further apart than you actively could by yourself, so it can be difficult to achieve the fully spread position for this exercise without using your arms to assist in setting up.
    2. If you have rather short legs, you may have to scoot slightly forward on the seat for your knees to reach the pads, which will require you to lean your torso somewhat backward to keep your upper back against the backrest.
6. If you feel that you can spread your legs further apart than is permitted by the initial machine setting you selected, you can adjust the pads to be further away from each other until you feel that your inner thigh muscles are sufficiently stretched.
    1. It is recommended to remove at least one leg from the footplate when adjusting the machine.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your knees in toward each other until your legs are situated directly in front of you.
    1. You can tap the inner aspect of the knee pads against each other at the end of this motion.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your knees to move out and away from each other in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your flexibility comfortably permits.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your legs spread fully apart.
    2. With the appropriate machine setting, you should feel a stretching sensation in your inner thighs.
    3. While you do not have to perform this phase of the movement with an extremely slow tempo, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach your end range is recommended.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Like when setting up, you can use your hands to apply an inward pressure to the knee pads to assist with lifting your legs up one at a time.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train all your [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md) in an isolated manner.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your abdomen contacting the ground (i.e., in the prone position) and your head lifted slightly off the ground as you maintain a mildly tucked chin position with your face directed toward the ground.
2. Position your arms straight out in front of you with straight elbows such that your hands are approximately shoulder-width apart while resting on the ground.
    1. Your body position should resemble how you would look if you were reaching up with your arms fully overhead while standing.
3. Rotate your arms so that your palms face in toward each other.
    1. If you make a thumbs-up gesture in this position, your thumb should be pointing up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your chest, arms, and feet as high off the ground as you comfortably can by arching your lower back in a controlled manner and squeezing your glutes while keeping your knees and elbows straight.
    1. How far you are able to lift up will be influenced by your back mobility, and you can aim to lift up through the full range of motion that your mobility comfortably permits, but it is normal for the range of motion to be fairly small overall.
    2. You should feel the muscles running up and down your back on each side of the spine contract, especially in your lower back.
    3. Throughout the set, continue keeping your chin mildly tucked without moving your neck as your abdomen and the front of your hips remain in contact with the ground.
2. After you have fully lifted up, statically hold this position for a brief period of time, such as about two seconds.
3. Reverse the movement by gradually lowering your chest, arms, and feet back onto the ground.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically and statically train the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep intrinsic spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) that run along the length of your entire back.

## Setting up
1. Pick up one kettlebell and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while firmly holding the kettlebell at your side with your elbow straight as your palm faces in toward your thigh.
    1. Initially pick up the kettlebell with a hip hinge or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back flat, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back.
    2. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handle with the handle pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the handle closer toward the middle of your palm (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handle can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.

1. Walk forward while holding the kettlebell at your side while maintaining an upright posture with your shoulders approximately level with each other.
    1. While you will not swing your arm like you would when walking normally, your torso and lower body should look similar to how they would when you walk normally.
    2. Based on your preference and what feels natural to you, you can either swing your free arm back and forth as you walk or keep it by your side.
    3. Walk at a pace where you feel stable and balanced throughout the carry.
    4. If you use a weight that is fairly heavy to you, it is natural to take shorter strides compared to how you typically walk.

    6. Avoid leaning your torso away from the kettlebell, which can be a common compensation to rest the kettlebell partially on the outside of your thigh.
    7. Keep the tops of your hip bones approximately level throughout your set rather than letting them drop down to one side when taking each step.
2. Continue walking with the kettlebell until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the suitcase carry while holding the kettlebell with your other side.
## Description

## Setting up
1. With a cable station positioned to its lowest height, select your weight with the loading pin, and connect a D-handle attachment to the cable.
2. While standing with the side of one shoulder facing the cable station, squat down to grasp the handle firmly with the hand closer to the cable station as you keep your elbow straight and your palm facing in toward your side (i.e., a neutral grip).
    1. When squatting down, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back.
3. By extending your hips and knees, stand upright with the handle while continuing to keep your elbow straight and your lower back near a neutral position.
    1. When upright, you should feel resistance from the cable.
4. Take a step to the side away from the cable station and allow the cable’s tension to raise your arm somewhat out away from your side, such that your arm is directed in a straight line with the cable.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow, hips, and knees extended, slowly lower the handle toward the base of the cable station in a controlled manner as you bend your torso toward the side of the cable station.
    1. Move through your comfortable full range of motion, which will normally result in you experiencing a stretching sensation in the muscles on the opposite side of your torso (including your lower back).
    2. Continue to keep your arm directed in a straight line with the cable, which should naturally occur and result in the handle moving in a diagonal path involving motion directed both downward and out away from your side.
    3. Your mobility will affect how far you can side bend.
    4. Avoid bending your lower back forward or arching it backward during this exercise.
    5. The tops of your hip bones should remain level throughout this movement, like they do when you are normally standing upright.
2. Reverse the motion by bending your torso away from the cable station in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your torso upright and your shoulders approximately level with each other.
    1. Doing so will pull the handle diagonally out and away from the cable station.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [quadratus lumborum](../Muscles/Quadratus%20Lumborum%201965c6f170d880b89d4fc43238472b46.md), while also training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [intertransversarii lumborum](../Muscles/Intertransversarii%20Lumborum%201b95c6f170d880f6902cf3d4a6d61511.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a weight plate on the ground directly in front of the head of a flat exercise bench.
    1. For comfort, you can optionally wear a beanie on your head or place a small towel on top of the plate. Resting the plate directly on your head without a soft fabric over your head can be uncomfortable, so using a beanie or towel is recommended.
    2. If you are new to this exercise, it is recommended to learn the proper technique while using a light weight, such as a 2.5-5lb (or 1.25-2.5kg) plate. For lifters opting to use heavier weights, it is worth noting that a large diameter plate (e.g., a bumper plate or a 45lb (20kg) plate) may limit the range of motion for this exercise’s lifting phase by contacting the back of your neck.
2. Lie down with your abdomen on the bench. Rest your chest on the head of the bench with your head and neck fully off the bench.
    1. Place your legs and feet in a position that feels comfortable and stable to you. This may involve placing your legs close together on the bench with your feet hanging off the bench, which may be practical for people with relatively narrow statures. Alternatively, you can spread your legs mildly apart to straddle the bench with your toes on the ground, which may be more suitable for individuals with wider frames.
3. Firmly grasp the weight plate (with the towel on top of it if you are using a towel) with both hands.
4. Nod your head by bringing your chin toward your collarbone.
    1. This will be the starting position for your head during each rep.
5. Position the center of the weight plate against the back of your head while securely holding the plate with both hands.
    1. The plate should not be touching your upper neck, since it should be directly on the back of your skull.
    2. During the exercise, you will use your hands to help keep the plate in contact with your head.
## Exercise technique
1. Slowly tilt your head up to bring your chin away from your chest without using your arms to lift the weight. Move through your neck’s comfortable range of motion.
    1. How far you can comfortably lift your head will be affected by your neck mobility, so the end position will vary from person to person.
    2. At the top position, your face should be angled forward.
    3. Do not exceed the range of motion that is comfortable to your neck.
    4. This is the same neck motion that you would perform when standing up and looking up toward the ceiling.
    5. Aim to lift the weight exclusively with your neck muscles as you use your arms simply to hold the plate against your head throughout your set.
    6. When performing this movement correctly, you should feel the muscles on the back of your neck contract.
    7. Continue keeping your chest on the bench.
2. Reverse the movement by slowly nodding your head down. Bring your chin toward your collarbone to return to the starting position.
    1. People can commonly perform this movement until the chin is very close to touching the collarbone, but your neck mobility will also influence the degree to which you can nod down.
    2. Prioritize actively controlling the weight throughout the entirety of your set. This is an intentionally slow exercise.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After completing your last rep, use your arms to lift the plate off your head and set it on the ground before sitting up.

### **Description**

This exercise can effectively develop the musculature on the back of your neck, including the [splenius muscles](../Muscles/Splenius%20Muscles%201b95c6f170d8804eaebad2422eead478.md), [semispinalis muscles](../Muscles/Semispinalis%20Muscles%201b95c6f170d88068a729f9e025be3c3b.md), and cervical portions of the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Erector%20Spinae%201b95c6f170d880f38250f60ce2c8b4ba.md) and [multifidus](../Muscles/Multifidus%201995c6f170d8805ca532c98856405055.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up an ab wheel and kneel on a comfortable surface (e.g., exercise mat, foam cushion, pillow, folded towel) with your knees approximately hip-width apart.
    1. A comfortable surface is optional but definitely preferred by most people.
2. Place the ab wheel on the ground directly in front of you, then firmly grip the handles with your palms facing back toward you (i.e., an overhand grip).
    1. Keep your wrists straight throughout this exercise.
3. With your hips stacked vertically above your knees, position the roller directly under your shoulders, keeping your elbows straight.
    1. Your thighs and arms should now be directed straight down, such that they are perpendicular to the ground, which places your torso closer to a horizontal position than a vertical position.
    2. Your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Maintain this neck position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Scoop your hip bones forward toward your ribs, while keeping your ribs pulled down toward your hip bones and tightening your abs. Maintain this position throughout your set.
    1. When starting with your lower back exhibiting its natural mild arch, this motion (known as posterior pelvic tilting) will flatten your lower back, since it is the opposite of arching your lower back.
    2. Your abs attach to your pubic bone (which you can feel as a bony ridge in the middle of your pubic region) and your ribs, and this scooping motion should tilt your pubic bone up toward your ribs as you contract your abs.
    3. It can help to imagine a laser beam shooting out to the midpoint between your hip bones, slightly below where you would wear a belt buckle. Before you scoop your hips, this laser beam will point down toward your abdomen. Scooping your hips appropriately should angle this laser beam forward toward the ab wheel.
2. Lower your hips forward until you can draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your lower back when viewed from the side. Keep the ab wheel under your shoulders and your lower back flat.
    1. This lower-body motion will push the ab wheel moderately forward, but you are not moving your shoulders during this step. Your arms move forward simply because they are connected to the rest of your body.
    2. Your thighs, torso, and arms should now resemble a tall plank position.
    3. Avoid lowering your hips so far forward that your lower back begins arching. Your lower back position should not change from the last step.
3. Squeeze your glutes, and keep them squeezed for the rest of your set.
    1. Actively squeezing your glutes can help you avoid arching your lower back.
    2. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them.
4. Slowly push the ab wheel forward by sweeping your arms forward. Keep your torso rigidly braced as you avoid letting your lower back arch throughout the set.
    1. Only move the ab wheel as far forward as you can while maintaining a flat lower back position.
    2. Keeping your lower back flat will become progressively more difficult as you roll out further, so you can determine your range of motion based on your current ability.
    3. If you are new to this exercise, a rather short range may be appropriate. If you have the strength to do so with proper form, you can finish rolling out when your chest is almost touching the ground.
    4. Keep your elbows fully straightened.
    5. While you push the ab wheel forward through shoulder motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    6. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag or your ribs flare, as this can arch your lower back. Continuing to squeeze your glutes and tighten your abs will help you keep your lower back flat.
5. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by pulling the ab wheel back toward the starting position. Drive your arms back until they are once again under your shoulders without moving your hips.
    1. In contrast to the traditional rollout technique, you will not bend your hips or move them back during each rep with this variation.
    2. Your arms should now be pointing straight down toward the ground.
    3. Continue keeping your lower back in the same flat position you maintained while rolling out.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set and are ready to move your hips back before standing up.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while statically training your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your legs straight and your feet approximately hip-width apart.
    1. On the ground, your legs and torso should be in the same position you exhibit when normally standing upright.
    2. While you can leave your arms resting on the ground by your sides, you can feel free to situate your hands wherever you prefer.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your knees straight, lift both feet slightly (about 6 inches (or 15 centimeters)) off the ground, tightening your abdominal muscles to press your lower back into the ground.
    1. Pressing your lower back into the ground will flatten it out from abdominal muscle contraction and prevent you from sliding a hand under it.
    2. If you do not contract your abdominals, lifting both legs up would prompt your lower back to develop an exaggerated arch that would allow you to slide a hand under your lower back.
2. As you hold the position described in step 1, tuck your chin toward your chest to lift your head off the ground and mildly curl your upper back (in a crunch-like motion) to lift your shoulder blades slightly up off the ground.
    1. Doing so should prompt you to feel your upper abdominal muscles further tightening up.
3. Statically hold the position you reached after performing steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Along with training your hip flexor muscles on the front of your thigh, this exercise can statically train your abdominal muscles, including your obliques and rectus abdominis, which is the “si-pack muscle.”

### How the abdominal and hip flexor muscles work together

As with many other abdominal exercises, the six-inch leg raise trains the abdominal muscles concurrently with the hip flexor muscles due to the opposing forces these muscles can generate at the lumbopelvic region (i.e., the pelvis and lower back). For the sake of having clearer directions when referring to “up” or “down” during this explanation, we can imagine that you are standing upright rather than lying down, as you would when performing this exercise. To lift the thigh via hip flexion, the hip flexor muscles contract, creating a pulling force from the front of the pelvis toward the thigh. Muscle contraction generates a force at both ends to which a muscle attaches, and the hip flexor muscles either originate on the front of the pelvis or cross the front of the pelvis as they course toward their insertion on the femur (thigh bone) or tibia (shin bone). If left unopposed, the force from the hip flexor muscles will rotate the front of the pelvis down toward the thigh as the back of the pelvis rotates up toward the lower back via a motion known as anterior (forward) pelvic tilting. When the pelvis tilts in this manner, the lumbar spine extends correspondingly as the natural arch of the lower back becomes exaggerated into a sway-back posture.

Contraction of the abdominal muscles is able to produce the opposite motions, given that they arise from the ribs and attach to the top surface of the front aspect of the pelvis. To pull the ribs closer to the top of the pelvis, the lumbar spine flexes, initially flattening the natural curvature of the lower back and then rounding it with further flexion. Contraction of the abdominal muscles can also pull the top surface of the front aspect of the pelvis up toward the ribs as the back of the pelvis rotates down toward the thigh via a motion known as posterior (backward) pelvic tilting. Due to the posterior pelvic tilt function of the abdominals and the anterior pelvic tilt function of the hip flexors, these two muscle groups can operate in tandem. Whenever the legs lift off the ground via hip flexion, the abdominal muscles stabilize the lumbopelvic region by preventing the lower back from arching beyond its natural curvature, through a combination of anterior pelvic tilt and lumbar spine extension that would otherwise occur with abdominal muscle contraction.

### Six-inch leg raise progression

Performing the six-inch leg raise with the head and upper back lifted up off the ground serves as a more advanced variation of the six-inch leg raise with the head on the ground. When the upper back is off the ground, the abdominals have to work to prevent the thoracic spine from extending, while also functioning to prevent the lumbar spine from extending, which increases the intensity of the exercise.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, connect a rope attachment to it, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. As an alternative to the rope attachment, you can also use a D-handle attachment, but this page will describe the usage of the rope attachment.
2. Pull the rope fully to one side of the attachment.
3. Squat down with the cable station at your side and firmly grasp the rope with an overhand grip as your palms are about shoulder-width apart.
4. Stand upright while allowing the rope to align diagonally with the cable, which will result in your hand that is closer to the cable being lower than your hand on the other side.
5. While keeping your chest pointing straight ahead and the rope close to your body, take a couple of steps to the side away from the cable station against its resistance.
    1. Step far enough outward that the cable can still provide resistance at the point during the exercise when your torso is twisted toward the cable station. If you lose resistance at any point during this exercise, you can set up farther away.
6. Lunge backward with your foot closer to the station to assume a half-kneeling position with your knee on the side closer to the station on the ground. Simultaneously straighten your elbows so that the rope stays in close to the same position while you lunge your torso back away from it.
    1. You can optionally rest your lower knee on a comfortable surface (e.g., exercise mat, foam cushion, folded towel) in this position.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched or rounded, your back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Rotate your chest diagonally down and toward the cable station to move the rope diagonally down toward the station in a controlled manner. Keep your chest facing the rope and your elbows straightened throughout the set.
    1. Rotate your chest in a controlled manner through the full range of motion that your spinal mobility comfortably permits. Because spinal mobility varies among people, the end range will vary among different individuals.
    2. During this exercise, you can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the middle of your chest, and you want to keep that laser beam pointing toward the middle of the rope. Turn that laser beam diagonally down toward the cable station during this step.
    3. If the middle of the rope no longer remains directly in front of your chest’s imaginary laser beam, you are moving your arms through shoulder motion rather than exclusively moving your trunk.
    4. Keep your imaginary belt buckle pointing straight ahead with your legs planted on the ground throughout this exercise.
2. Rotate your chest diagonally up and away from the cable station to move the rope diagonally up and away from the station.
    1. Continue keeping your imaginary belt buckle facing straight ahead and the rope directly aligned with the center of your chest.
    2. Avoid focusing on pulling with your arms to emphasize training your core. Your arms function to link the cable to your torso, and you are chiefly turning your chest to move the cable.
    3. When rotating your trunk appropriately (rather than only moving through your shoulders and/or hips), you should feel the muscles on the sides of your torso contract.
3. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise while facing the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise will primarily train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [rotatores muscles](../Muscles/Rotatores%20Muscles%201b95c6f170d8800188c7db2ca87b8b54.md), which are assisted by your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and other [deep spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md).

## Setting up
1. Position yourself on your hands, knees, and toes, with your elbows straight and your knees bent.
2. Prop your forearms onto the ground with your upper arms directed straight down such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    1. Based on your preference, you can either make a fist with each hand and direct your palms in toward each other or place your palms flat on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. You should be bearing your bodyweight into the ground through your elbows and feet.
2. Tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes to maintain a flat back position while keeping your knees straight and elbows bent.
    1. Doing so keeps your hips up (but not excessively hiked) rather than letting them sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch in your lower back.
    2. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, as this can cause your shoulder blades to pinch together.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
3. Press through your feet to rock your body back forward as you move at your ankles like you would during the lifting phase of a calf raise (also known as a heel raise).
    1. Doing so will prompt your elbows to bend further.
    2. Continue keeping your abdominal muscles and glutes tightened to maintain the same rigid trunk position you adopted in step 2.
4. Reverse the motion you just performed by rocking your body backward at your ankles as you continue keeping your abdominal muscles and glutes tightened.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your core muscles, including your rectus abdominis (AKA  the “six-pack muscle”) and your abdominal obliques as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. After initially standing in the center of the captain’s chair with your back facing its back pad, step up onto its foot plates while placing your hands against the arm pads for any balance assistance as needed.
2. Bend your elbows and place the bottom of your forearms onto the arm pads while firmly grasping the handles with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Your back should be contacting the backrest while your torso is in an upright position.
3. While bearing the force from your bodyweight through your elbows into the arm pads, pick your feet up off the foot plates and allow them to hang straight down toward the ground.
    1. Keep your shoulder blades and shoulders near the natural position in which they are when normally standing upright, rather than letting your shoulder blades and shoulders shrug up from gravity pulling your torso down.
    2. You should be able to draw a straight line vertically down from your torso through your legs.
## Exercise technique
1. March up both knees toward your chest through your available range of motion while curling your hips forward and allowing your knees to progressively bend as they lift higher up.
    1. Curling your hips forward will round your lower back and result in your buttocks facing forward at the end of the lifting phase.
    2. You do not consciously need to think about progressively bending your knees since they will naturally bend when marching your knees up unless you intentionally try to straighten them.
    3. How closely you are able to raise your knees up toward your chest will be influenced by the mobility in your hips and lower back, along with your strength.
    4. Whenever you feel like you cannot bring your knees any closer toward your chest, you have reached the end of the lifting phase.
    5. Keep your upper body stationary.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your knees to descend while uncurling your lower back until you have returned to the starting position with your thighs directed straight down toward the ground.
    1. Actively lower your legs throughout the descent rather than letting gravity rapidly pull you back down, which could result in your legs swinging back behind the starting position as momentum takes over.
    2. Your knees can naturally transition to a less bent position as you lower your legs.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to return your feet onto the foot plates and step down from the captain’s chair.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

### Straight knee leg raise versus bent knee leg raise

With the exception of utilizing a straighter knee position, the technique for the straight knee leg raise is otherwise essentially the same as the bent knee leg raise, so both variations primarily train the same muscle groups. In terms of the training effect these exercises provide, the main difference is that the straight knee leg raise is a higher intensity variation due to how it shifts the center of mass of your legs farther forward relative to your trunk and hip. This results in a longer lever arm of resistance acting on your trunk and hip, which requires your abdominal muscles and hip flexor muscles respectively generating greater trunk flexion and hip flexion torque to overcome. Resistive torque can be increased by increasing the weight you move or by increasing the lever arm in which the weight acts on a particular joint, so the straight knee leg raise can function similar to a weighted knee raise without requiring additional weights. The greater magnitude of resistance from the straight knee leg raise almost certainly explains why McGill et al. (2014) found this variation to yield noticeably greater EMG activity of the abdominal muscles than the bent knee leg raise when participants performed three reps of each exercise.

Nonetheless, this does not mean that the straight knee leg raise is inherently superior to the bent knee leg raise for developing the abdominal muscles in the same way that squatting 200lb (91kg) is not necessarily better than squatting 150lb (68kg) for inducing quad hypertrophy. If you have the strength to perform both leg raise variations with sound technique, you simply will have to perform greater reps per set with the bent knee position compared to the straight knee position to achieve the same hypertrophic stimulus. If an equal number of sets are performed until the same proximity failure (e.g., performing as many reps as you can with each condition), a very similar degree of muscle growth may be produced by 6-rep sets, 30-rep sets, or anywhere in between. Correspondingly, the bent knee variation that provides less resistance can still be just as productive for developing the abdominals as the straight knee variation for most people when leaving the same number of reps in reserve for sets of either exercise. The one exception may be for individuals with especially strong abdominals who are able to perform a very high number of bent knee leg raise reps per set before reaching a pronounced degree of muscle fatigue, indicating that the resistance from these reps are very low relative to their strength. At some point an exercise may just be providing too low of a resistance to optimize how much muscle growth that a set can stimulate even if the set is performed until failure. Specifically where that threshold lies is currently unclear, but that should not be any concern for you unless you are able to perform over 30 reps per set, which will not be an issue for the vast majority of people performing bent knee leg raises with a controlled technique through a full range of motion.

## Setting up
1. Add a pair of round weight plates to a barbell situated on the ground with sufficient room in front of the bar for you to roll out.
    1. If you roll out through the full range of motion, using small-diameter weight plates can make this exercise slightly more difficult than using large-diameter plates.
    2. If you stop rolling out before your arms are fully outstretched, the plate diameter is inconsequential.
    3. Your bodyweight will primarily provide the resistance for this exercise, so the weight of the plates you select is not particularly impactful.
    4. Hexagonal weight plates cannot be used for this exercise.
2. Optionally place a comfortable surface (e.g., an exercise mat, foam cushion, pillow, or folded towel) slightly behind the middle of the bar.
3. Kneel behind the bar as your body is completely centered with the bar and your knees are approximately hip-width apart.
4. With your elbows and wrists straightened, firmly grasp the bar with your hands at least slightly outside shoulder width.
    1. Use an overhand grip with your palms facing back toward you.
    2. So long as it is at least slightly outside shoulder width, you decide specifically how wide a grip you will use.
    3. Keep your wrists and elbows straight throughout this exercise.
5. With your hips stacked vertically above your knees, position the bar directly under your shoulders.
    1. Your thighs and arms should now be directed straight down, such that they are perpendicular to the ground, which places your torso closer to a horizontal position than a vertical position.
    2. Your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Maintain this neck position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Scoop your hip bones forward toward your ribs, while keeping your ribs pulled down toward your hip bones and tightening your abs. Maintain this position throughout your set.
    1. When starting with your lower back its natural mild arch, this motion (known as posterior pelvic tilting) will flatten your lower back, since it is the opposite of arching your lower back.
    2. Your abs attach to your pubic bone (which you can feel as a bony ridge in the middle of your pubic region) and your ribs, and this scooping motion should tilt your pubic bone up toward your ribs as you contract your abs.
    3. It can help to imagine a laser beam is shooting out for the midpoint between your hip bones, slightly below where you would wear a belt buckle. Before you scoop your hips, this laser beam will point down toward your abdomen. Scooping your hips appropriately should angle this laser beam forward toward the bar.
2. Slowly push the bar forward by simultaneously moving your hips and arms forward in unison. Keep your torso rigidly braced as you avoid letting your lower back arch throughout the set.
    1. Only move the bar as far forward as you can while maintaining a flat lower back position.
    2. Keeping your lower back flat will become progressively more difficult as you roll out further, so you can determine your range of motion based on your current ability.
    3. If you are new to this exercise, a rather short range may be appropriate. If you have the strength to do so with proper form, you can finish rolling out when your arms are fully outstretched in line with your torso, and your chest is close to the ground.
    4. Keep your elbows fully straightened as you move your hips and shoulders together.
    5. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag down or your ribs flare up, which will arch your lower back. If you can roll out until you are reasonably close to drawing a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your lower back, squeezing your glutes at this point can help prevent your hips from sagging.
3. Reverse the movement by pulling the bar back toward the starting position. Drive your arms down and back while allowing your hips to rock back in a controlled manner.
    1. Continue keeping your lower back in the same flat position you maintained while rolling out.
    2. In contrast to the exaggerated hip motion people often perform by rocking their back behind their knees, your hips should finish vertically above your knees with your thighs perpendicular to the ground.
    3. To avoid rocking your hips back excessively, focus on sweeping your arms back while letting your hips rock back naturally, rather than pulling through your hips.
    4. Your arms should finish directly under your shoulders as they are pointing straight down toward the ground.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while statically training your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.
