## Setting up
If your sled has vertical posts, you have the option of grasping the posts directly as handles, or you can connect a pair of straps with handles to the sled. Without vertical posts, you will naturally have to connect straps to the sled to drag it. For clarity, the setup for each method is described separately, but the exercise technique is the same. If you have the ability to utilize either setup, using the straps is recommended.

### **Setting up with straps**

1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a sled situated in an area where you have sufficient space for pulling it backward.
    1. With certain wheeled sleds, you may also be able to adjust your resistance level with a lever that changes its friction. For these sleds, increasing the friction will increase the intensity of the exercise, similar to adding weight plates.
    2. Note that the type of surface on which you will move the sled will affect how much resistance you experience during this exercise. When tracking progress, it is consequently best to compare sets performed on the same surface.
2. Attach to the base of the sled a pair of straps with handles like TRX suspension trainer straps.
    1. Since a range of strap lengths can be used for this exercise, you can adjust the straps to a length that feels comfortable to use and is practical with the space that is available to you.
3. While standing centered behind the sled, firmly grasp the handles.
4. Walk backward until the straps have become taut with your arms aligned with the straps, elbows straight, and palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Your arms should now be angled diagonally toward the base of the sled.
5. Position your feet approximately hip-width apart with your toes pointing straight ahead.
6. Adopt a “proud chest” posture with your shoulder blades pulled mildly backward.
7. While keeping your torso upright, bend your knees into a near half squat position or your preferred degree of knee bend.
    1. For stimulating increases in quad muscle size and developing strength through a longer range of motion, it is appropriate to reach at least a moderate degree (i.e., about 60 degrees) of knee bend during this exercise. However, you have the option of utilizing a milder degree of knee bend if you wish to do so.

### **Setting up without straps**

1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a sled situated in an area where you have sufficient space for pulling it backward.
    1. With certain wheeled sleds, you may also be able to adjust your resistance level with a lever that changes its friction. For these sleds, increasing the friction will increase the intensity of the exercise, similar to adding weight plates.
    2. Note that the type of surface on which you will move the sled will affect how much resistance you experience during this exercise. When tracking progress, it is consequently best to compare sets performed on the same surface.
2. Stand centered behind the sled with your feet approximately hip width apart and your toes pointing straight ahead.
3. With your palms facing in toward each other and elbows mildly bent, firmly grasp the posts near waist height.
4. While keeping your torso mostly upright, bend your knees until your arms are approximately parallel to the ground. Simultaneously allow your elbows to straighten and take a step backward if needed to have room to straighten them.
    1. This places most people reasonably near a half squat position. If you wish to perform your sled drag with a deeper or shallower angle of peak knee bend, you have the option of gripping the posts lower or higher, respectively, while bending your knees to the point that places your arms in a horizontal position.
5. Adopt a “proud chest” posture with your shoulder blades pulled mildly backward.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Begin dragging the sled backward by straightening one leg’s knee while simultaneously bending your other leg’s knee to step backward with its foot.
    1. While using your legs to move the sled, the rest of your body should remain in essentially a static position during your set.
    2. Keep your back flat and chest up to maintain an upright torso position throughout the drag.
    3. Rather than using your upper body muscles to pull the sled, your arms should simply function to transmit force from your legs to the sled, so you should keep your elbows straight during this exercise.
3. At the moment you finish fully straightening your one knee, plant your other foot onto the ground.
    1. While straightening your knee, you should feel tension in that side’s quad.
    2. With the proper technique, you should first and foremost be using your quads to drag the sled.
4. Continue fluidly dragging the sled backward as you reciprocally straighten one leg’s knee while stepping backward with your other leg’s foot until you have reached your target distance or the end of your available space and have to switch to dragging it the opposite direction.
    1. Throughout the set, be aware of any individuals who may potentially enter the path in which you are pulling to avoid an unintended collision.
    2. If your sled has an attachment point or a pair of vertical posts on each side of the sled, you can connect the straps to the other side or grasp the posts on the other side before dragging the sled in the opposite direction. Otherwise, you naturally will have to rotate your sled 180 degrees before dragging it back in the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise will chiefly train your [quads](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md) while being easier from which to recover compared to most quad exercises.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a sled situated in an area where you have sufficient space for pushing it.
    1. With certain wheeled sleds, you may also be able to adjust your resistance level with a lever that changes its friction. For these sleds, increasing the friction will increase the intensity of the exercise, similar to adding weight plates.
    2. Note that the type of surface on which you will move the sled will affect how much resistance you experience during this exercise. When tracking progress, it is consequently best to compare sets performed on the same surface.
2. Stand centered directly behind the sled in a hip-width stance with your toes pointing straight ahead.
3. With mostly straight wrists, firmly grasp the handles in a position that is comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Position the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) directly behind the handles so that you can push primarily through the bases of your palms.
    2. Sleds commonly have vertical posts that function as handles, but some models have horizontal handles.
    3. With vertical handles, you can direct your palms in toward each other and adjust how high up you grasp them. Initially gripping the handles a little below hip height is an appropriate starting point. However, a range of grip heights can be viable, so feel free to try out different hand positions over time to determine what feels best to you.
    4. With horizontal handles, you can situate your hands about shoulder width apart with your palms facing down.
4. Take a step backward with one foot and lean your torso forward while moderately bending your front leg’s knee and keeping your rear leg’s knee mildly bent. Keep your elbows straight, chest up, and back flat.
    1. Rather than simply rounding your back, the forward torso lean should arise from you hinging at your front leg’s hip.
    2. The degree to which you should lean your torso will be affected by the height of your hands when holding the handles. As a general rule of thumb, it is often appropriate to lean your torso forward by about 45 degrees when grasping handles a little below hip height, but you should feel free to try out different degrees of forward lean to determine what personally feels best to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position as you push through your legs.
2. Begin pushing the sled forward by pushing through your rear leg. Drive your rear knee backward while straightening it and pushing off through your foot in a calf raise-like ankle motion.
    1. It can help to think about pushing the ground away from you.
    2. Strive to push through your rear leg until you can draw a straight line from that leg through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side.
    3. While the toes and the ball of your foot remain on the ground, the rest of your rear foot’s sole should be off the ground and facing backward.
    4. Since you are starting with your rear knee only mildly bent, this initial step involves a short range of motion to start moving the sled
3. As you finish driving through your rear leg, push through your front leg to continue pushing the sled forward. Simultaneously, march what initially was your rear leg forward as you drive that knee forward while bending it.
    1. Keep your back flat and chest up the whole time while you maintain the same degree of forward torso lean.
    2. All the motion should come from your hips, knees, and ankles while the rest of your body remains in essentially a static position throughout your set.
    3. Rather than using your upper body to push the sled, your arms should simply function to transmit force from your legs to the sled.
4. Continue pushing the sled forward as you reciprocally move your legs until you have reached your target distance or the end of your available space, and have to switch to pushing it in the opposite direction.
    1. With some sled models, you may have to rotate your sled 180 degrees to be able to access the same type of handles before pushing the sled in the opposite direction. With other models, you may be able to walk to the other side of the sled and access another pair of handles.
## Description
This exercise will train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md), and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md) as they function to extend your hips, knees, and ankles simultaneously.

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while firmly holding the dumbbell at your side with your elbow straight as your palm faces in toward your thigh.
    1. Initially pick up the dumbbell with a hip hinge or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back flat, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back.
    2. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handle with the handle pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the handle closer toward the middle of your palm (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handle can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Walk forward while holding the dumbbell at your side while maintaining an upright posture with your shoulders approximately level with each other.
    1. While you will not swing your arm like you would when walking normally, your torso and lower body should look similar to how they would when you walk normally.
    2. Based on your preference and what feels natural to you, you can either swing your free arm back and forth as you walk or keep it by your side.
    3. Walk at a pace where you feel stable and balanced throughout the carry.
    4. If you use a weight that is fairly heavy to you, it is natural to take shorter strides compared to how you typically walk.
    5. You should feel your core muscles on the side opposite to the dumbbell working to maintain an upright torso, as these muscles prevent the weight from bending your torso to the side of the dumbbell.
    6. Avoid leaning your torso away from the dumbbell, which can be a common compensation to rest the dumbbell partially on the outside of your thigh.
    7. Keep the tops of your hip bones approximately level throughout your set rather than letting them drop down to one side when taking each step.
2. Continue walking with the dumbbell until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the suitcase carry while holding the dumbbell with your other side.
## Description
This exercise statically trains your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md), [quadratus lumborum](../Muscles/Quadratus%20Lumborum%201965c6f170d880b89d4fc43238472b46.md), and [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) as they work to keep your trunk upright. 

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your core muscle strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your core muscles. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

## Setting up
1. Place a stability ball (also known as a Swiss ball or physio ball) on the ground.
    1. Ideally, select a ball with a diameter exceeding your shoulder width.
2. Kneel with the ball in front of you as your elbows are bent to approximately 90 degrees.
3. Hinge at your hips to lean your torso forward, and position your bent elbows on top of the ball about shoulder width apart.
    1. Lean forward enough that you can stack your shoulders directly above your elbows.
    2. With a sufficiently large ball, your forearms can rest on the ball with your elbows, but you will chiefly be bearing weight through your elbows.
    3. The appropriate elbow placement should ensure that the ball does not roll when you press down through your elbows.
    4. Once on the ball, you can optionally clench each hand into a fist to promote full-body tension.
## Exercise technique
1. Walk your legs back until your knees are fully straightened with the bottom of your toes dug into the ground.
    1. Position your feet approximately hip-width apart with your soles facing backward.
    2. You should be bearing your bodyweight into the ground through your feet and into the ball through your elbows.
2. Tighten your abs and squeeze your glutes to maintain a rigid back position while pushing your elbows into the ball and keeping your knees straight.
    1. Doing so keeps your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting them sag downward, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, as this can cause your shoulder blades to pinch together. Thinking about pushing your elbows down into the ball can help keep your shoulder blades apart.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like you would normally do when standing upright.
3. Smoothly move both elbows in a small circular motion on the ball in a controlled manner. Otherwise, maintain the same plank position you adopted from step 2.
    1. Only your arms should be moving through shoulder motion while you keep the rest of your body rigidly stationary.
    2. If someone were to watch your body from your middle back through your feet, you should ideally look like you are performing a static stability ball plank.
    3. The difficulty of this exercise will increase as the circumference of the circular motion increases, so you can determine the range of this movement based on your current ability. Only move through a range that allows you to execute all the technical aspects from step 2. If your hips or chest start sagging down, you may be moving through a range that presently exceeds what you can currently stabilize effectively. Moving in a very small circle is recommended if you are new to this exercise.
    4. You decide whether you start with a clockwise or counterclockwise motion, since you will be training both directions.
4. Cyclically repeat step 3 for your desired number of reps, then start stirring your elbows in the opposite direction.
    1. Specifically, how many revolutions you complete in a particular direction before switching is up to your preference. For instance, if you are striving to perform 20 total reps, you may perform five clockwise reps before performing five counterclockwise reps and then repeat this for another round. Alternatively, you may perform 10 clockwise reps followed by 10 counterclockwise reps. If you wish to do so, you can even switch directions every rep.
5. Alternate between bouts of stirring clockwise and counterclockwise until you have completed your set and are ready to bend your knees to return to kneeling on the ground.

    2. Strive to have your torso and lower body look the same during the last second of your set as they did during the first second after getting into position

## Setting up
1. Using an underhand grip, grasp an elastic band with both hands in front of your torso while standing upright with your feet in approximately a shoulder-width stance.
    1. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
2. Position your hands so that they are somewhat greater than shoulder width apart from each other, with slack taken out of the band.
3. With straight elbows, elevate your arms in front of your torso until they are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. In this position, your palms should be directed down toward the ground.
    2. Maintain this position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your hands apart and backward until your arms and torso form a “T-shape.”
    1. If you set up by grasping the band with your hands too close together, you may reach the limit of the band’s extensibility (as indicated by an abrupt increase in resistance from the band) prior to your hands being pulled entirely apart from each other. If you notice this, bring your hands back together and adjust your setup by gripping the band with your hands farther apart. Continuing to pull the band apart once a portion has fully stretched may cause the band to tear.
2. Reverse the motion by bringing your hands forward and toward each other until they have returned to their starting position.
    1. You should feel tension from the band throughout the entire range of motion.
    2. Do not bring your hands so close together that the band becomes slack.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise trains your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which is assisted by your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), along with your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that will situate the chest pad to chest height once you are seated.
    1. You will have to sit down to check if you selected the appropriate seat height, so you may have to adjust the seat height multiple times before finding the right setting for you.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit on the seat with an upright torso as your knees are snugly contacting the knee pads.
    1. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. If your machine has foot plates, situate your feet on top of them, but if your machine lacks foot plates, place your feet on the ground.
4. Rotate the chest pad toward one direction. Select a setting that allows you to perform this exercise through the full range of motion that is comfortable to you.
    1. If you have normal back mobility and a healthy back, you can initially rotate it fully to one side. If you cannot comfortably assume the starting position from this setting, you can rotate the pad closer toward the center (where your imaginary belt buckle and chest are both facing forward) until you can set up comfortably.
    2. As you rotate the pad further away from the centered position, you will be able to train your core muscles in more lengthened positions that may be conducive to developing them effectively.
    3. It is up to you whether you begin with the pad rotated to your right or left, since you will adjust it to the opposite side after your first set to train both sides equally.
    4. Your optimal setting will be affected by your back mobility, and finding this ideal setting may require trying out different settings.
5. Rotate your chest toward the chest pad and snugly contact the pad with your chest while firmly gripping the handles.
    1. In the starting position, it is common to feel a stretching sensation in your back when the machine is adjusted to train through your full range of motion. However, you should not feel lower back discomfort in this position, so you should adjust the degree to which the seat is rotated if you experience discomfort when moving into the starting position. If you cannot rotate your chest enough to reach the chest pad, you naturally should adjust the seat as well until you can reach it.
## Exercise technique
1. In a controlled manner, rotate your chest away from the side that it is initially facing. Move through the full range of motion your mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your chest snugly against the chest pad, buttocks on the seat, knees against the knee pads, and feet stationary.
    2. Continue holding the handles for stability, but do not actively try to push or pull the machine with your arms. The function of your arms is merely to help transmit force from your core muscles into the machine.
    3. As a cue, you can think about turning an imaginary laser beam that is shooting out from the middle of your chest without moving your imaginary belt buckle.
    4. During the first half of the movement, you will rotate your chest so that it faces straight forward with your imaginary belt buckle. Then you will continue rotating to have your chest face the opposite direction from which it started.
2. Reverse the movement as you rotate your chest in the opposite direction to return to the starting position.
    1. While you do not need to utilize an extremely slow tempo, you should actively control the entire movement rather than letting the machine’s resistance abruptly twist you back into the starting position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with the chest pad rotated toward the opposite side from which you started.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and your small [rotatores muscles](../Muscles/Rotatores%20Muscles%201b95c6f170d8800188c7db2ca87b8b54.md) through a long range of motion.

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your hands, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight and your knees are bent.
2. Prop your forearms onto the ground with your upper arms directed straight down such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    1. Based on your preference, you can either make a fist with each hand and direct your palms in toward each other or place your palms flat on the ground.
3. One at a time, move your arms forward so that your upper arms are now directed forward and downward at an angle while your forearms are in contact with the ground.
    1. Positioning your elbows so that they are under your eyes (while still being shoulder width apart) is an appropriate starting point.
    2. However, it is up to you specifically how far forward you wish to position your arms so long as you are still able to keep your forearms and elbows on the ground.
    3. The difficulty of this exercise will progressively increase as you shift your arms farther forward, so you could determine your specific arm position based on the intensity you intend this exercise to have.
## Exercise technique
1. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. You should be bearing your bodyweight into the ground through your elbows and feet.
2. Tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes to maintain a flat back position while keeping your knees straight and elbows bent.
    1. Doing so keeps your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting them sag downward, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag down, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
3. Statically hold the position you adopted after performing steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your core muscles, including your rectus abdominis (AKA  the “six-pack muscle”) and your abdominal obliques as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with straight legs as your feet are together.
2. Raise your arms straight back behind your head with straight elbows so that your arms are aligned with your legs and torso.
    1. Except for being rotated by 90 degrees, your body should be in the same position when you are standing upright and reaching your arms straight up overhead.
    2. Your palms should be facing up away from the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. While only allowing your knees to bend mildly, lift both legs up simultaneously with your torso as you crunch up to touch your feet with your hands.
    1. Sweep your arms toward your feet in an arcing manner until you can touch them with your arms reaching forward and upward. Avoid rapidly swinging your arms in an effort to build momentum.
    2. To touch your feet, sweep your arms forward until they are angled upward and forward.
    3. Keep your elbows straight and your knees as close to straight as your hamstring flexibility permits.
    4. Lift the entirety of your back off the ground, resulting in only your buttocks contacting the ground at the top of the movement.
    5. Rather than trying to keep your back flat, you should intentionally curl your spine to train your abs dynamically.
    6. Keep your neck near a neutral position throughout the exercise, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering your legs and torso at the same time.
    1. At the bottom, lightly tap your heels to the ground, and keep your abs tensed to avoid excessively arching your lower back.
    2. Fluidly lower your legs and torso at the same rate, resulting in your upper back contacting the ground at the same time as your heels.
    3. Finish with your whole body forming a straight line like the starting position.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, make sure that you actively control the entire movement rather than letting gravity rapidly pull you down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) (the “six-pack muscle”) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and hip flexors.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your back and head on the ground as your legs are straight and your feet are together.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can lie down on an exercise mat.
2. Place your arms straight out to your sides with your palms on the ground and elbows straight.
    1. When viewed from above, your arms should now form a “T-shape” with your torso.
## Exercise technique
1. Press your hands into the ground, and tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground. Continue keeping your hands pressed into the ground and your abs tensed throughout the set.
    1. Pressing your hands into the ground will enhance your stability during the exercise.
    2. Pressing your lower back into the ground will flatten it out from abdominal muscle contraction and prevent you from being able to slide a hand under your lower back.
2. While keeping your knees mostly straight, lift your legs up off the ground until your thighs are approximately vertical.
    1. Strive to keep your knees as close to straight as your hamstring flexibility comfortably permits.
    2. If you do not keep your abdominals contracted, lifting both legs up would prompt your lower back to develop an exaggerated arch that would allow you to slide a hand under your lower back.
3. While keeping your hips bent and knees as straight as your hamstring flexibility enables, rotate your legs toward one side.
    1. Rotate through the full range of motion your mobility comfortably permits while keeping your upper back on the ground. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your back.
    2. While some lifters will naturally be able to rotate their legs closer to the ground than others, you should be able to rotate your legs at least 45 degrees beyond vertical if you have normal mobility.
    3. There is no need to rotate your legs extremely slowly, but you should lower them in a controlled manner rather than letting them drop down abruptly.
4. Reverse the movement as you sweep your legs up toward your midline and then fully to the other side in the same manner you just performed during step 3.
5. Cyclically rotate your legs from side to side in a windshield wiper-like fashion until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise chiefly trains your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) while your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md) serve a stabilizing role.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up overhead and firmly grasp it with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip) and your hands situated near shoulder-width apart or somewhat wider.
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the bar.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide upward during the dead hang, which pulls on your hand skin in a manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
2. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
    1. So long as your feet are above the ground, it is up to you how bent your knees initially are when hanging on the bar.
    2. While hanging, your thighs should be directed straight down toward the ground, and your torso should be in a vertical position.
    3. You will maintain a firm grip on the bar with straightened elbows throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. March up both knees toward your chest through your available range of motion while curling your hips forward and allowing your knees to progressively bend as they lift higher up.
    1. Curling your hips forward will round your lower back and result in your buttocks facing forward at the end of the lifting phase.
    2. Keep your chest facing straight ahead rather than leaning your torso backward.
    3. You do not consciously need to think about progressively bending your knees since they will naturally bend when marching your knees up unless you intentionally try to straighten them.
    4. How closely you are able to raise your knees up toward your chest will be influenced by the mobility in your hips and lower back, along with your strength.
    5. Whenever you feel like you cannot bring your knees any closer toward your chest, you have reached the end of the lifting phase.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your knees to descend while uncurling your lower back until you have returned to the starting position with your thighs directed straight down toward the ground.
    1. Actively lower your legs throughout the descent rather than letting gravity rapidly pull you back down, which could result in your legs swinging back behind the starting position as momentum takes over.
    2. Your knees can naturally transition to a less bent position as you lower your legs.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to return your feet to the ground.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

### **Straight knee leg raise versus bent knee leg raise**

With the exception of utilizing a straighter knee position, the technique for the straight knee leg raise is otherwise essentially the same as the bent knee leg raise, so both variations primarily train the same muscle groups. In terms of the training effect these exercises provide, the main difference is that the straight knee leg raise is a higher intensity variation due to how it shifts the center of mass of your legs farther forward relative to your trunk and hip. This results in a longer lever arm of resistance acting on your trunk and hip, which requires your abdominal muscles and hip flexor muscles respectively generating greater trunk flexion and hip flexion torque to overcome. Resistive torque can be increased by increasing the weight you move or by increasing the lever arm in which the weight acts on a particular joint, so the straight knee leg raise can function similar to a weighted knee raise without requiring additional weights. The greater magnitude of resistance from the straight knee leg raise almost certainly explains why McGill et al. (2014) found this variation to yield noticeably greater EMG activity of the abdominal muscles than the bent knee leg raise when participants performed three reps of each exercise.

Nonetheless, this does not mean that the straight knee leg raise is inherently superior to the bent knee leg raise for developing the abdominal muscles in the same way that squatting 200lb (91kg) is not necessarily better than squatting 150lb (68kg) for inducing quad hypertrophy. If you have the strength to perform both leg raise variations with sound technique, you simply will have to perform greater reps per set with the bent knee position compared to the straight knee position to achieve the same hypertrophic stimulus. If an equal number of sets are performed until the same proximity failure (e.g., performing as many reps as you can with each condition), a very similar degree of muscle growth may be produced by 6-rep sets, 30-rep sets, or anywhere in between. Correspondingly, the bent knee variation that provides less resistance can still be just as productive for developing the abdominals as the straight knee variation for most people when leaving the same number of reps in reserve for sets of either exercise. The one exception may be for individuals with especially strong abdominals who are able to perform a very high number of bent knee leg raise reps per set before reaching a pronounced degree of muscle fatigue, indicating that the resistance from these reps are very low relative to their strength. At some point an exercise may just be providing too low of a resistance to optimize how much muscle growth that a set can stimulate even if the set is performed until failure. Specifically where that threshold lies is currently unclear, but that should not be any concern for you unless you are able to perform over 30 reps per set, which will not be an issue for the vast majority of people performing bent knee leg raises with a controlled technique through a full range of motion.

### Hanging ab straps

If you have access to hanging ab straps, you have the option of using them for this exercise by hanging them from your pull-up bar about shoulder width apart from each other and resting your upper arms on top of the straps as you otherwise use the same form described under the exercise technique section. Using straps would ensure that your grip strength would not be able to function as the limiting factor during your set without otherwise affecting how your abdominal and hip flexor muscles are trained. Correspondingly, utilizing straps would remove the stimulus this exercise can provide to your forearm and hand muscles involved with gripping. Performing the exercise with straps would also result in the shoulders maintaining a moderately flexed position (as the upper arms remain parallel to the ground) in contrast to the fully flexed shoulder position that is adopted when hanging on the bar. This can result in strap usage removing the stimulus to improve or maintain shoulder mobility in an overhead position that can be experienced when hanging on the bar. On the other hand, the shoulder extensor muscles (e.g., lats, teres major, rear delt) will have to act isometrically (statically) to maintain the moderately flexed shoulder position when using straps. While these muscles are likely more engaged when performing the exercise with straps compared to without straps, they are still unlikely to be loaded enough to provide any meaningful training effect for most lifters.

### Is your grip strength limiting you?

As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance rather than abdominal muscle strength, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual. If you find that you can complete meaningfully more reps when using straps, your grip strength is likely limiting you during this exercise, which can consequently limit the stimulus it provides to your abdominal muscles.

## Setting up
1. Approach a flat exercise bench or a similarly sturdy object with an elevated surface that can support your foot.
    1. As an alternative to a bench, you can use a plyometric box or an aerobic step stacked on risers. At home, you can use pieces of furniture such as a bed, couch, or chair that will not slide. If the object you use has a hard surface, placing a cushioned object (such as a foam pad) on top of it may make this exercise more comfortable.
    2. The difficulty of this exercise will increase as the object’s height increases, so you can utilize a taller object for a greater intensity. However, a height of around 18in (46cm), which applies to a typical flat exercise bench, is recommended to use as a minimum for most people.
2. Lie down on your side with the inner aspect of your top knee (which is bent by about 90 degrees) and lower leg on top of the elevated surface. Align this thigh with your torso so that you can draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from above.
    1. The outer aspect of your lower hip should be resting on the ground.
    2. If you are on a hard surface, you can set up on an exercise mat for comfort. You chiefly want a comfortable surface to be under the forearm that you will be placing on the ground.
3. Align your lower thigh directly under your top thigh.
    1. If the object you are using has open space underneath its top surface (like with a bench), keep your knee straight on your lower leg.
    2. If your object lacks space for your lower foot under its top surface (like with a soft plyometric box), keep your bottom knee bent.
4. Position your bottom forearm on the ground with your elbow bent by about 90 degrees. Your elbow should be close to being stacked directly underneath your shoulder.
    1. With your bottom hand, you can make a fist and keep the little finger-side of your hand in contact with the ground. Alternatively, you can keep your palm flat on the ground if you find that to feel more comfortable and stable.
    2. You can keep your top arm in a comfortable position, such as resting on top of your side with a straight elbow. Alternatively, you can reach that arm toward the ceiling with a straight elbow or place that side’s hand on your top hip with a bent elbow.
    3. Your bottom upper arm should be in a vertical position.
    4. You can perform steps 2-4 simultaneously.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your bottom hip and leg fully off the ground by driving your top knee down into the bench while pushing your bottom forearm into the ground.
    1. At the top, you should now be able to draw a straight line from your head through your belly button to the center point between your knees when viewed from the front.
    2. You should also be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the top.
    3. Your thighs (which should be close together), torso, and head should be in essentially the same alignment as they would be when standing upright.
    4. The intent to pull your top knee down toward your bottom knee is what should lift your bottom leg, rather than simply lifting your bottom leg up by itself. Since the bench stops your knee from moving down, this intent lifts you up.
    5. An indicator that you are appropriately driving through your top leg is when your top hip becomes approximately level with your top knee. If you lift your bottom leg by itself, your top hip will remain lower than your top foot, which you do not want.
2. Slowly reverse the movement by lowering your hips until your bottom leg lightly taps the ground. Keep your bottom thigh close to parallel to the ground throughout the exercise.
    1. At the bottom, your top hip should now be lower than your top knee, since you should be moving through your top hip.
    2. Avoid lowering your bottom leg by itself, which would result in your bottom knee being lower than your bottom hip. Your bottom knee should remain essentially level with your bottom hip throughout the set.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your opposite side elevated.
    1. When learning this exercise, it can be useful to face a mirror to receive visual feedback about your positioning.
    2. Avoid letting your buttocks drift backward during the set by bending your hips. This would prevent you from being able to draw a straight line through your whole body when viewed from the top. Squeezing your glutes can help prevent you from unintentionally bending your hips.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train all your [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md) and a variety of core muscles, including your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [quadratus lumborum](../Muscles/Quadratus%20Lumborum%201965c6f170d880b89d4fc43238472b46.md).

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with straight legs and your feet approximately hip-width apart. The back of your head should either rest on the ground or on your hands, which you can clasp behind your head.
    1. If you do not want to position your hands behind your head, feel free to place your arms wherever you prefer (e.g., resting on the ground by your sides).
    2. On the ground, your legs and torso should be in the same position in which you exhibit when normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your knees straightened, lift both of your feet mildly (i.e., approximately 6 inches (15 centimeters)) up off the ground while you tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground.
    1. Pressing your lower back into the ground will flatten it out from abdominal muscle contraction and prevent you from being able to slide a hand under your lower back.
    2. If you do not contract your abdominals, lifting both legs would prompt your lower back to develop an exaggerated arch, allowing you to slide a hand under it.
    3. For this variation, you will either rest your head on the ground or on your hands (as you prefer).
2. As you keep one leg stationary, lift your other leg somewhat (e.g., about 6 to 10 inches (15 to 25 centimeters)) higher up while keeping both knees straight.
    1. Specifically how high you lift this leg is up to your preference since a range of heights can effectively be used for this exercise.
3. In a scissor-like manner, lower your top leg toward the starting position (about 6 inches (15 centimeters)) off the ground while simultaneously lifting up your lower leg to the same height you just did with your other leg in step 2.
    1. How quickly you move is up to you, but strive to move each leg at the same speed such that they finish switching positions at the same time.
    2. Continue keeping your lower back pressed into the ground with your abdominal muscles tensed throughout your set as you avoid arching your lower back.
4. Cyclically repeat step 3 while switching which leg moves up and down each time until you have completed your set.
## Description
Along with training your hip flexor muscles on the front of your thigh, this exercise can statically train your abdominal muscles including your obliques and particularly your rectus abdominis, which is the “six-pack muscle.”

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station to approximately chest height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. As an alternative to the D-handle attachment, you also can perform a Pallof press with a rope attachment, but this page will describe use of the D-handle.
2. Stand with the side of one shoulder facing the cable station as the handle is just in front of your chest.
3. Firmly grasp the handle with your hands interlocked and palms facing each other. Your elbows should be bent with your upper arms by your sides and the handle in front of your chest.
    1. One palm should be facing in toward the cable as the other palm faces straight out to the side away from the cable.
4. While keeping the handle close to your chest, side-step away from the cable station until you feel tension from the cable.
    1. Prevent your torso from rotating when side-stepping.
5. Position your feet near shoulder-width apart, and slightly sit your buttocks backward to bend your hips and knees slightly.
    1. Rather than being excessively arched or rounded, your back and neck should be near a neutral position like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. In this starting position, you should be able to form a 90-degree angle between the cable and an imaginary laser beam shooting straight forward from the center of your chest. You should also be able to draw a straight line between your shoulders that is parallel to the cable.
    3. The purpose of the slight hip and knee bend is to help you feel stable and balanced during your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forceful slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full body tension, and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. While keeping the center of your chest facing straight ahead, press the handle straight forward away from your chest.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as your arms are outstretched in front of you close to parallel to the ground.
    2. All the motion should occur from your arms moving at your shoulders and elbows while the rest of your body remains completely stationary.
    3. Particularly avoid letting the resistance from the cable rotate your torso. If your core muscles do not stabilize your trunk sufficiently, the imaginary laser beam shooting out from the center of your chest will start angling closer toward the cable station. The center of your chest should be facing the same direction throughout your entire set.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by bringing the handle straight back toward your chest as you bend your elbows.
    1. You should now be back to the starting position with the handle directly in front of your chest as your upper arms are right by your sides.
    2. Continue keeping the center of your chest facing straight forward as your shoulders remain aligned when viewed from the side.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise while facing the opposite direction.
## Description
While also engaging your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), this exercise will statically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they function to resist trunk rotation.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a weighted exercise ball of your desired weight that is appropriate to slam onto the ground.
    1. Not every medicine ball is designed to withstand the impact of slamming. Balls with a soft shell (which includes balls specifically known as slam balls) are typically suitable to slam, but balls with a rigid coat are often inappropriate for a high-impact exercise.
    2. If you are unsure whether the ball you have is appropriate to slam, you can look up the details of the model you have or ask the gym staff.
    3. It is recommended to use a ball that does not bounce if you have access to one.
2. Carry the ball to an area with sufficient space around you and a surface appropriate for slamming.
3. While standing upright with your feet near shoulder width apart, firmly hold the ball in front of your thighs with both hands and your fingers spread apart.
    1. Your palms should be facing in toward each other on each side of the ball.
    2. Your back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Quickly lift the ball up until it is directly overhead with mildly bent elbows.
    1. Rather than overhead pressing the ball up, you can sweep it up out in front of you with mildly bent elbows as you could do during a front raise that ends overhead.
    2. You can optionally lift your heels up as you lift the ball up.
    3. While you should have a “proud chest” posture with your chest up, avoid arching your lower back excessively.
    4. If you do not have the shoulder mobility to lift the ball directly overhead without leaning back, simply raise your arms up as high as you can without letting your ribs flare up (which occurs from lower back arching). Strive to position your biceps close to your ears.
2. Explosively slam the ball down with the intent to break the ground. Simultaneously sweep your arms down while sitting your buttocks back as you hinge at your hips and bend your knees.
    1. To fully benefit from this exercise, it is paramount that you slam the ball as forcefully as you physically can.
    2. The arm motion you perform is akin to a straight arm lat pulldown performed as explosively as possible.
    3. Make sure to fully follow through with your arms rather than halting the slam after releasing the ball. If you can stop moving directly after the ball leaves your hands, you are not slamming the ball as violently as you can. You should drive your arms down so forcefully that they inevitably fly fully back behind your torso after letting go of the ball.
    4. Finish the slam with your elbows fully straightened.
    5. The slamming motion should look similar to when someone dips down in preparation to perform a vertical jump. At the end of the slamming phase, your body should look like you are ready to jump up.
    6. As your torso transitions closer to a horizontal angle from sitting your buttocks back, avoid collapsing your chest or rounding your shoulders forward into a slumped posture.
    7. If you opted to lift your heels up during the lifting phase, you naturally will bring your heels to the ground during the slamming phase.
3. Allow the ball to come to a dead stop on the ground before picking it up and assuming the same position you did while setting up.
    1. Certain balls will stop immediately as they hit the ground, while other balls will bounce up.
    2. When using a ball that bounces up, people often catch the ball right after it bounces following the impact, but this can be suboptimal. Aiming to catch the ball very soon after releasing it can interfere with the maximally explosive intent when initially slamming the ball. It can be difficult to catch the ball in front of you after fully following through with the slam, so striving to catch the ball can prompt people to stop the slamming motion prematurely, which contributes to reduced explosiveness.
    3. Use your lower body to pick up the ball in a squat or hip hinge movement rather than excessively rounding and straightening your lower back to do so.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While engaging a variety of muscles throughout the body, this exercise can particularly improve explosive strength of your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) as they function to extend the shoulders.
1a45c6f170d880f7a1bdff9807752d71:
## Setting up
1. Follow the setup instructions for the [single arm kettlebell clean](Single%20arm%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d880ba964ffcbd097f377d.md), and perform the lifting phase of the [single arm kettlebell clean](Single%20arm%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d880ba964ffcbd097f377d.md) described in steps 1-5 of its exercise technique instructions.
    1. After doing so, you should now be holding the kettlebell in the front rack position. This involves situating it in front of your shoulder with your elbow bent slightly in front of your ribcage, palm facing in toward your other side, and the weight resting on your forearm, which is mostly vertically with your wrist slightly closer to the midline of your body than your elbow. The handle should also be diagonally contacting your palm, such that the side of the handle by your thumb is angled mildly higher than the side of the handle by your little finger.
    2. As an alternative to cleaning the kettlebell, you can curl it up while using your free hand to help lift the weight up under its base and guide the kettlebell into the same front rack position described above. Initially grasp the handle with your little finger closer to one of the corner horns than your thumb to help the handle rest diagonally across your palm in the front rack position. Feel free to perform a cheat curl-like motion where you initially generate some momentum by swinging the weight mildly backward with a straight elbow before swinging your elbow forward while curling it and assisting with your free hand. This is a less technically complicated means of moving the kettlebell into the front rack, but it is not as efficient when using a heavy weight for lifters who are proficient with cleaning the kettlebell.
    3. Once the kettlebell is in the front rack position, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the kettlebell.
2. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, keep your chest up in a “proud chest” posture, rather than letting your shoulders and upper back round forward into a hunched position.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain its natural curvature like when you are normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue keeping your core braced throughout your set.
2. Based on your preference and familiarity with each technique, you can press the kettlebell fully up overhead through a [push press](Single%20arm%20kettlebell%20push%20press%202cf5c6f170d8805498c1ec358b498bbc.md) using leg drive or a [strict overhead press](Standing%20single%20arm%20kettlebell%20overhead%20press%201a05c6f170d88060b7f3f259ca3140b0.md) without leg drive.
    1. The following directions describe how to perform a push press, since it will efficiently allow you to assume the overhead position with a heavy weight, but you can alternatively press the weight up without leg drive if you have the strength to do so.
3. Without moving your arm, mildly bend your knees in a quarter squat-like manner to dip down while maintaining an upright torso position with your chest up.
    1. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground during this dip phase.
    2. Your knees should track straight forward toward your toes rather than caving inward.
4. Directly after reaching the bottom of your dip, forcibly push through your feet as you rapidly extend (straighten) your knees and hips to generate upward momentum.
    1. The intent of this leg drive phase should be akin to a jump without lifting your feet fully off the ground.
    2. At the end of this drive, you can either keep the soles of your feet fully on the ground, or you can allow your heels to lift up slightly off the ground while keeping the front of your feet firmly in contact with the ground if a slight heel lift feels natural to you.
5. Immediately after you have finished extending your legs, explosively push the kettlebell upward by forcibly driving your elbow upward as you swiftly straighten your elbow. Allow your elbow to flare out away from your side when driving up, so that your palm faces forward at the top.
    1. At the end of the pressing phase, your knees, hips, and elbow should be fully straightened, and your arm should be directed straight up toward the ceiling with your elbow and wrist situated vertically over your shoulder.
    2. To transfer your leg drive into pushing the kettlebell upward in an explosive manner, you should perform steps 4 and 5 as a continuous movement.
    3. While your forearm starts slightly angled in the front rack position, it should otherwise remain essentially in a vertical position with your elbow stacked under your wrist throughout the press.
    4. Throughout the exercise, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back.
    5. Regardless of whether you lifted your heels up off the ground after extending your legs during the leg drive phase, your heels should be flat on the ground with the rest of your feet at the end of the pressing phase.
6. While keeping the kettlebell overhead with your elbow straightened and your chest up, walk forward in a controlled manner while maintaining an upright posture with your shoulders approximately level with each other.
    1. You will not swing your working arm like you would when normally walking, and you will keep your trunk in a rigidly braced position, but your lower body should look similar to how it would when you walk normally.
    2. Based on your preference and what feels natural to you, you can either swing your free arm back and forth as you walk or keep it by your side.
    3. Walk at a pace where you feel stable and balanced throughout the carry.
    4. If you use a weight that is fairly heavy to you, it is natural to take shorter strides compared to how you typically walk.
    5. You should feel your core muscles on the side opposite to the kettlebell working to maintain an upright torso, as these muscles prevent the weight from bending your torso to the side of the kettlebell.
    6. Avoid leaning your torso away from the kettlebell, and keep the tops of your hip bones approximately level throughout your set rather than letting them drop down to one side when taking each step.
7. Continue walking with the kettlebell overhead until you have completed your target distance and are ready to repeat the carry while holding the kettlebell with your other side.
    1. Based on the space available to you, you naturally may have to pivot around and walk the opposite direction after covering a particular distance, depending on the distance you are striving to reach during this set.
8. Lower the kettlebell in a controlled manner as you let your elbow bend while descending and arcing forward toward the front rack position.
9. As you approach the end of the lowering phase, shallowly bend your knees and hips as you did during step 3 (the dip phase) to help control the weight until you have returned to the starting position with the kettlebell in front of your shoulder.
10. Set the kettlebell down in the opposite manner to how you lifted it into the front rack position when setting up.
    1. If you initially cleaned the kettlebell up, you can let the kettlebell fall forward as you swing your arm down while straightening your elbow and hinging at your hips to absorb the force of the lowering phase.
    2. If you initially curled the kettlebell up with assistance from your free hand, you can similarly use your free hand to help guide the kettlebell down while letting your working arm’s elbow straighten in a controlled manner.
11. Transfer the kettlebell to your other side before repeating the exercise with that side.
## Description
While also engaging your [thoracic erectors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can statically train much of your shoulder girdle musculature, including your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rotator cuff muscles](../Muscles/Rotator%20Cuff%201b95c6f170d880b3b0d8eab69c3a7683.md).
1a45c6f170d880faa555d3e604efa65f:
## Setting up
1. Sit on the ground with an upright torso and your legs straight out in front of you.
    1. The back of your heels should be on the ground as your feet are close together.
2. Place your hands on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart, slightly behind your hips, with your fingers spread apart and elbows straight.
    1. Rotating your hands such that your middle fingers point straight out to your sides is appropriate. However, you can feel free to rotate your hands to point in whichever direction you find most comfortable.
    2. The proper hand placement should allow your arms to point straight down toward the ground during the exercise.
3. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. Rather than being slumped forward, your chest should be directed slightly upward.
    2. As a cue, you can think about pinching a pencil with your shoulder blades.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels into the ground and squeezing your glutes.
    1. At the top, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    2. Keep your elbows straight as the weight you bear through your arms predominantly goes through the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) rather than closer to your knuckles.
    3. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back with a “proud chest” as you avoid letting your shoulders round forward.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    5. Squeezing your glutes can help you avoid excessively arching your lower back, which should exhibit its natural mild curvature. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them.
2. Statically hold the rigid position you adopted from step 1 until you have completed your set’s target duration.
    1. Strive to have your body look the same during the last second of your set as it did during the first second after getting into position.
    2. Resist letting your hips gradually lower toward the ground as time elapses.
3. After completing your set, bend your hips to return to sitting on the ground.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) that run along your entire back.
1a45c6f170d880fabcebd578763b9c46:
## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your hands, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight and your knees are bent.
2. Prop your forearms onto the ground with your upper arms directed straight down such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    1. Based on your preference, you can make a fist with each hand and direct your palms in toward each other, or you can place your palms flat on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. You should be bearing your bodyweight into the ground through your elbows and feet.
2. Tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes to maintain a flat back position while keeping your knees straight and elbows bent.
    1. Doing so keeps your hips up (but not excessively hiked) rather than letting them sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch in your lower back.
    2. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag down, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
3. Statically hold the position you adopted after performing steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your core muscles, including your rectus abdominis (AKA the “six-pack muscle”) and your abdominal obliques, which help maintain a rigid trunk position.
1a45c6f170d880ff8f44dfd8ac3f86a2:
## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your knees bent and the soles of your feet  flat on the ground, approximately hip width apart.
    1. You can rest your head on the ground while your arms are by your sides with your palms in contact with the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift both legs off the ground and back toward you until your thighs are approximately vertical. Keep your knees bent, and tighten your abs to press your lower back down into the ground.
    1. Pressing your lower back into the ground will flatten it out from abdominal muscle contraction and prevent you from being able to slide a hand under your lower back.
    2. If you do not contract your abdominals, lifting both legs up would prompt your lower back to develop an exaggerated arch that would allow you to slide a hand under your lower back.
2. Continue driving your bent knees toward your face while lifting your buttocks and hip bones up off the floor as you curl up your lower back.
    1. Doing so will prompt your buttocks to face forward rather than face straight down toward the ground.
    2. Move through what feels like your full range of motion that is comfortable to you, which will be influenced by the mobility in your hips and lower back.
    3. Aim to transition fluidly from step 1 to step 2 in a continuous motion rather than pausing after completing step 1.
    4. You should naturally feel your abdominal muscles further tighten while doing so.
3. Reverse the movement from step 2 by allowing your buttocks and hip bones to lower down to the floor in a controlled manner as you uncurl your lower back.
4. Reverse the movement from step 1 by allowing your legs to descend in a controlled manner until the soles of your feet lightly contact the ground.
    1. Continue tightening your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground as you lower your legs.
5. Alternate between performing steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a dumbbell with one hand, carry it over to a flat bench, and position yourself near the base of the bench and directly to its side with your side that is holding the dumbbell farther away from the bench.
    1. If you have to carry the dumbbell a meaningful distance before reaching your bench and your grip is somewhat fatigued, you can place the dumbbell on the bench before picking it up with your opposite hand to start your set with the side that does not have a fatigued grip.
2. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips, reach out with your free arm to place its hand on the bench with a straight elbow, and place your knee (on the side not holding the dumbbell) onto the bench.
    1. In this position, your torso should now be reasonably close to being parallel to the ground, and your lower back should be flat rather than being meaningfully rounded.
    2. While setting up, keep your elbow straight on the side holding the dumbbell and allow that arm to hang down toward the ground with your shoulder blade naturally pulled forward toward the ground from the weight.
    3. Based on your comfort and preference, you can place the open palm of your free hand onto the bench, or you can make a fist and place your knuckles onto the bench.
    4. Your foot on the side of the dumbbell should remain firmly in contact with the floor and be sufficiently far behind the dumbbell that your leg does not restrict your row. If you initially do not feel well-balanced, you can try positioning this foot somewhat further out to the side to widen your base of support.
3. Direct your palm so that it is facing in toward the opposite side of your body, and maintain this neutral grip position throughout your set.
    1. The bony bump on the back of your elbow should be directed backward, which is the direction you will row.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Drive your elbow backward and upward in an arcing motion to pull the dumbbell toward your hip. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blade backward, and keep your elbow tucked by your side rather than flaring it outward.
    1. When allowing your elbow to bend naturally, your forearm should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    2. At the top of the row, your elbow should be aligned with your torso or slightly behind your torso.
    3. Keep your torso in a mostly fixed position with your chest facing a similar direction throughout this movement. A mild degree of torso rotation is not problematic, but avoid letting it become excessive and turning the exercise into a cheat row.
    4. While performing this arcing motion, the dumbbell should not move straight upward in a vertical path.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled arcing motion until your arm is directed down toward the ground with your elbow straightened.
    1. Allow the weight to pull your shoulder blade forward, which will stretch your upper back muscles and result in your working side’s shoulder being mildly closer to the ground than your other side’s shoulder at the bottom of the row.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weight rapidly pull your arm down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).
