## Setting up
1. While placing one hand on each of a kettlebell’s horns (i.e, the side handles) with your palms facing in toward each other, pick up the kettlebell and stand upright in a near hip-width stance. Hold the kettlebell in front of your thighs with straight elbows.
    1. It may be awkward to use this grip to pick up a kettlebell directly from the floor (especially if you are using a heavier weight), so you have the option of initially deadlifting the kettlebell with a double overhand grip from the top handle and setting it on an elevated surface like a bench before grasping its horns with your palms facing in.
    2. Due to the shape of the kettlebell, it is not feasible to have the top handle pointing straight upward (like it would when the bottom base of the kettlebell is resting on the ground) while your elbows are fully extended, so you will have to angle the kettlebell’s base toward you.
    3. To hold the kettlebell in front of your upper thighs with extended elbows, you will need to move your upper arms slightly in front of your torso (rather than keeping your upper arm positioned directly by your sides like you could when curling two kettlebells or dumbbells).
## Exercise technique
1. Curl the kettlebell upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms fixed just in front of your torso (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the kettlebell in a controlled manner until your elbows have returned to an extended position.
    1. During the lowering phase, continue to keep your upper arms in the same position with which you started.
3. Alternate between curling the kettlebell up and lowering it down until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise will effectively train the biceps and brachialis in your upper arm along with the brachioradialis in your forearm with the practical benefit of only requiring one kettlebell.
1aa5c6f170d880b9ab00ea8320731145:
## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with extended elbows.
2. Direct your palms so that they are facing in toward your sides (i.e., using a neutral grip position).
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one dumbbell resting at your side with an extended elbow, curl the other dumbbell upward and across the front of your torso toward your opposite shoulder by bending at your elbow.
    1. As you start curling across your body, you will naturally rotate your shoulder inward such that your palm is directed toward the front of your torso.
    2. To allow the dumbbell to clear your torso, you will have to position your upper arm slightly in front of your body while curling (rather than keeping your upper arm right next to your side like you could with a standard hammer curl).
2. After your elbow has fully flexed, reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner until your elbow has returned to an extended position with the dumbbell and your upper back at your side.
3. Alternate between curling the dumbbell upwards and lowering it down until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
1ac5c6f170d8803f915fec32a9820548:
## Setting up
1. Select your desired weight with the loading pin and adjust the machine’s seat to a position that allows your knees to be mildly bent when your feet are on the foot plate.
    1. If the seat is positioned too far back, the machine may not be able to provide tension throughout your full ankle range of motion.
2. Sit down with your back in full contact with the backrest.
    1. Your low back should be in a fairly flat position rather than being meaningfully rounded, like in a slouched position, which could occur if you sit your hips excessively forward.
3. With approximately a shoulder width stance, place the front halves of your feet onto the bottom of the foot plate with your heels hanging off the edge.
    1. Maintain this foot position throughout your set.
4. While grasping the hand grips, press the platform away from you by extending your knees until they are straight or only slightly bent.
    1. Maintain this knee position (rather than bending and extending your knees) while performing this exercise until you are ready to finish your set.
    2. Depending on their mobility, some people may be able to adopt a position of knee hyperextension, which is when the knees bend backward beyond a straight position. Being able to reach a mildly hyperextended knee position is normal for many individuals and is not inherently problematic. However, certain individuals may experience knee discomfort if they utilize a hyperextended knee position during this exercise, so keeping a straight or slightly bent knee position instead of a hyperextended knee position may be preferable.
## Exercise technique

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that aligns the machine’s pivot points with the height of your shoulders once you are seated.
    1. On each side of the machine, the pivot point is the center about which the lever arm rotates, and it is denoted by a small dot or circle in some machines.
    2. Aligning the center of your shoulders with the pivot points can help this exercise feel more comfortable and natural compared to if the seat height resulted in your shoulders being above or below the pivot points.
    3. To confirm whether you selected an appropriate seat height, you will have to sit down and visually check where your shoulders are positioned relative to the pivot points, so you may have to try out different settings before finding one that best suits your body.
    4. A seat height that aligns your shoulders with the pivot points will commonly allow you to contact the arm pads with the outer aspects of your arms just above your elbows when keeping your upper arms near your sides.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit on the seat with your upper arms by your sides and your elbows bent to near 90 degrees. Place the outer aspects of your arms against the arm pads, and grasp the handles with your palms facing in toward each other if your machine has handles.
    1. Seated lateral raise machines may be constructed with handles situated closer toward the machine's weight stack or further away in front of the machine’s weight stack.
    2. With a machine that has handles closer toward its weight stack, you should sit down with your chest facing the stack. These machines often have a chest pad onto which you can rest your chest.
    3. With a machine that has handles further away in front of its weight stack, you should sit down with your back directed toward the stack. These machines often have a back pad onto which you can rest your back.
    4. Some machine models lack handles for you to hold, but have a chest pad or a larger back pad that could inform you which is the standard direction for you to face while using them.
    5. A minority of machines may lack a chest pad, back pad, or handles, and correspondingly not have a clear way for you to face besides what may be presented on an instructional image on the side of the machine.
4. Based on your preference, you can sit with a fully upright torso, or you can lean slightly forward at your hips.
    1. Either torso position can allow you to perform this exercise effectively, so you can utilize whichever one feels most comfortable for your shoulders.
    2. You can try out each posture during a different set to determine your personal preference.
    3. If you opt to lean slightly forward and are using a machine with a chest pad, you may have to scoot slightly backward on the seat.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows out and away from your sides until your upper arms are close to parallel with the ground.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to move naturally rather than trying to keep them in any particular position.
    2. Focusing on moving your elbows in an arcing manner throughout this exercise can help you target the appropriate shoulder muscles.
2. Reverse the motion in a controlled manner by lowering your elbows in toward your sides until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. To confirm you have moved through your full range of motion, you can lightly tap the machine lever arms (onto which you loaded the plates) to the stoppers underneath them.
    2. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time. Do not let the weight abruptly swing your arms downward.
    3. Keep your arms snugly in contact with the arm pads throughout your set.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. As the side of your shoulder (that you will not train during this set) is facing the cable station, stand in a staggered stance with one foot a little in front of the pulley and your other foot a little behind the pulley.
    1. If you step forward with your foot on the side that is closer to the pulley, the cable may be less likely to brush up against your leg during the exercise.
3. Lunge down and grasp the handle between your legs with your hand on the side opposite the cable.
    1. Your palm should be facing in toward the pulley.
4. Grasp the cable station’s vertical beam for stability with your closer free hand, and stand up while maintaining a slight bend in your knees.
    1. Your working side’s arm should now be in a vertical position close to your body with a straight or slightly bent elbow (depending on what feels most comfortable to you).
    2. In this position, you should feel tension from the cable, so if that is not the case, take a step away from the cable stack.
    3. Continue using your free hand to assist with stabilizing yourself throughout the exercise.

1. Sweep the handle out and away from your side until your upper arm is close to parallel with the ground.
    1. At the top of the raise, your working arm should form half of a “T-shape” with your torso when viewed from the front or back.
    2. While you raise your arm through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blade to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your arm in toward your side in a controlled arcing manner until your arm lightly contacts your torso.
    1. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm downward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

    2. If your mobility permits, you can bend over until your torso is parallel with the ground, but you can still effectively perform this exercise if you are not able to descend as far.

    4. Maintain this bent-over position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Raise the dumbbells away from each other and straight out to your sides until your arms and torso form a “T-shape.”
2. Reverse the motion by lowering the dumbbells toward each other in a controlled manner back until they have returned to their starting position in front of your knees.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which is assisted by your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), along with your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, adjust each cable to a height approximately level with your shoulders or slightly above them, remove any handle attachment if it is clipped onto the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pins.
2. After standing centered between the cables with your sides facing the cable stacks, take a step backward, raise your arms in front of you until they are approximately parallel with the ground, and side step toward one cable.
3. Reach across your body with your arm that is opposite to the cable to grasp the ball at the end of the cable with an overhand grip as your palm is facing down, before side-stepping toward the other cable and grasping its ball with your free hand.
    1. Alternatively, you have the option to grasp the end of the cable directly with your little finger and the adjacent side of your hand contacting the ball.
    2. Use whichever hand placement feels most comfortable and stable to you, but if you decide to grasp the cable directly, be aware to avoid pinching any fingers when returning the cable to its initial position after finishing your set.
4. Return to being centered between the cables with your arms crossed in front of your torso, with slightly bent elbows, as the cable stacks are situated a little in front of you.
    1. In this position, your arms should resemble an “X-shape” with each other.
    2. Maintain slightly bent elbows throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your arms out and away from each other as you move your arms backward until they form a “T-shape” with your torso.
2. Reverse the motion by bringing your arms inward and toward each other in a controlled manner until your arms have crossed and returned to their starting position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable to a height that is approximately level with your elbows when your arms are resting at your sides while standing.
2. Connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
3. While facing the cable station, grasp the handle with one hand and direct your palm downward as you raise your arm to be parallel with the cable.
4. With your elbow in an extended position, step backward until the machine’s weight plates separate and you feel tension from the cable
    1. In this position, your arm should be outstretched in front of your torso.
## Exercise technique
1. While bending your elbow, pull the handle backward and upward simultaneously until your upper arm is in line with your torso and approximately parallel with the ground while your palm is facing forward.
    1. While doing so, the cable should move in a diagonal motion that involves more horizontal motion than vertical motion.
    2. At the end of this motion, your elbow should be bent to near a 90-degree angle.
2. Reverse the motion by moving the handle forward and downward simultaneously as your elbow extends until you have returned to the starting position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
While also meaningfully training your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), this exercise can effectively develop your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md) and [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), along with the [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its highest level, connect a straight bar attachment to the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable to approximately hip height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. Stand facing the cable station with the cable just in front of one of your arms.
3. With the hand in front of the cable, firmly grasp the handle with an underhand grip that directs your palm up with a bent elbow.
4. Take a step backward so that you feel tension from the cable as the weight stack separates.
5. As you keep your upper arm aligned with your torso, hinge at your hips to sit your buttocks back, and incline your torso so that it is fairly close to being in a horizontal position.
    1. If you wish to do so, you can place your free hand up against the cable station’s beam for additional stability.
    2. Maintain this bent-over-torso position throughout your set.
6. Drive your elbow backward and upward until your upper arm is approximately parallel to the ground while you allow tension from the cable to keep your elbow bent.
    1. Your elbow should now be somewhat above the side of your torso (which would look like behind your torso if you were standing upright) rather than being aligned with your torso.
    2. In this starting position, your elbow should be bent by at least 90 degrees.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your upper arm parallel to the ground, progressively straighten your elbow to drive the handle backward and upward in an arcing motion until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. As you move your elbow, you should keep the rest of your body stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbow to bend in a controlled manner as you bring the handle downward and forward in an arcing fashion until you have returned to the starting position with your elbow bent by at least 90 degrees.
    1. Allow your elbow to continue bending as long as you feel tension from the cable pulling you toward a greater degree of bending.
    2. Continue keeping your upper arm parallel to the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise trains all three heads of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), which together constitute the majority of muscle mass in your upper arms.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable to its highest setting, clip in a V-bar attachment, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. While standing directly in front of the cable station and facing away from it, reach up overhead with bent elbows and fairly straight wrists to grasp the V-bar with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Maintain fairly straight wrists throughout your set.
3. While keeping your hands overhead and elbows bent, step forward and adopt a staggered stance with one foot forward in front of the other before moderately leaning forward by hinging at your hips.
    1. Maintain this forward torso lean throughout your set.
    2. In this position, your hands should be behind your head, and you should feel tension from the cable. If that is not the case, walk forward until you feel tension from the cable.
4. Tuck your chin toward your chest and make sure your upper arms are situated parallel to the ground or raised up a little higher.
    1. Doing so will reduce the likelihood that the back of your head obstructs the path of the cable during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Press the V-bar forward and somewhat downward by extending your elbows until they are straightened, while not moving your upper arms.
    1. At the end of this motion, the V-bar should be situated in front of you.
    2. If the cable contacts the back of your head during this motion, you can lean forward a little more for additional clearance.
2. Reverse the motion by bending your elbows through your available range of motion to move the V-bar backward and somewhat upward in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. Strive to continue keeping your upper arms stationary while all of the movement occurs from elbow motion rather than also involving shoulder motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up and grasp it with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip) and your hands situated near shoulder-width apart or somewhat wider.
    1. If you wish to do so, you can use a different grip, such as an underhand or a neutral (i.e., palms facing toward each other) grip, while otherwise using the same technique for this exercise.
2. Hang on the bar with straight elbows by bending your knees and lifting your heels off the ground while keeping the balls of your feet and your toes in contact with the ground.
    1. In this position, you can adjust how much of your bodyweight you are supporting through your legs and how much you are supporting through hanging on the bar.
    2. At any time during your set, you can shift how much of the force from your bodyweight is transmitted through the ground as opposed to the bar to alter the difficulty of this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows straight and part of your feet on the ground, pull your shoulder blades downward through your available range of motion.
    1. This will move your shoulders away from your ears, while the rest of your body, except for your arms, lifts upward to a small extent.
    2. While the range of motion for this exercise may vary among different individuals, this exercise involves a low amplitude of total movement.
    3. You can think about packing your armpits down into your pockets as a technique cue.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulder blades to move upward in a controlled manner until you have reached a position that is akin to when you shrug your shoulders upward.
    1. This will move your shoulders closer toward your ears, while the rest of your body, except for your arms, moves downward to a small extent.
    2. Continue to keep your elbows straight.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise will train your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [lower traps](../Muscles/Lower%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d88092b0bfc88e7ed9e50a.md), and [pec minor](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Minor%201905c6f170d88030b03dd3f99706ecb0.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that situates its handles slightly below the level of your hands when seated with your arms resting at your sides.
2. After loading your desired amount of weight onto the machine, sit down facing away from the machine with your feet flat on the floor.
3. With extended elbows, lean forward by hinging at your hips until your hands are low enough to grasp the handles firmly with a neutral grip such that your palms are facing in toward each other.
    1. While leaning forward, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back into a slouched posture.
4. Sit upright by moving about your hips while continuing to keep your elbows extended and your lower back near a neutral position.
## Exercise technique
1. Shrug your shoulders upward through your available range of motion while keeping your elbows extended, which will lift the handles upward.
    1. While doing so, keep your neck in a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulders to descend in a controlled manner through your available range of motion, which will lower the handles.
    1. At the end of this motion, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the weight can provide.
    2. If you lose resistance from the machine (from its mobile arms contacting its base beams) when your shoulders are fully depressed, you can set the handles down, elevate the seat height, and resume your set with resistance throughout the full range of motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).

## Setting up
1. Connect to the lat pulldown cable an attachment with a pair of parallel handles that are approximately shoulder-width apart
    1. For this variation, you can use any neutral grip attachment that allows you to grip it with your hands about shoulder-width apart.
    2. If you do not have access to this type of attachment, you can select a similar lat pulldown variation (such as the [neutral close grip cable lat pulldown](Neutral%20close%20grip%20cable%20lat%20pulldown%201a15c6f170d8808bbb8ecd9aae199152.md) or [underhand grip cable lat pulldown](Underhand%20grip%20cable%20lat%20pulldown%201a15c6f170d880b2a97ec3d948120f99.md)) from this database to train the same muscles.
2. Select your weight with the loading pin, and adjust the thigh pad to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
3. While facing the bar and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the bar with a neutral grip, such that your palms face each other.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
4. While holding the bar, sit down on the machine’s seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to straighten and your arms to raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
5. In the seated position, slightly lean your torso backward at your hips.
    1. Maintain this slight backward lean throughout your set.
    2. From this position, your elbows should be straight, with your arms overhead and slightly forward (rather than completely vertical), and you should feel tension from the cable station holding your arms in this position.
    3. If you notice the cable remains slack in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), you may need to use a different attachment and a wider grip to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for your lat pulldown.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down toward your sides as you progressively bend them.
    1. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears.
    2. Predominantly keep your elbows aligned with your wrists, rather than meaningfully flaring them out away from your sides.
    3. Pull through your full range of motion, which should result in your elbows finishing in line with your torso or slightly behind it at the bottom.
    4. Maintain the slight backward lean of your torso you adopted while setting up, rather than leaning further backward.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the bar in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your arms overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable above the height of your shoulders when standing, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. Whether you position the cable to its highest setting or only moderately above your shoulder height is up to your preference.
    2. As an alternative to using an adjustable cable station, you can also perform this exercise with the same technique on a cable lat pulldown machine.
2. Stand facing in front of the cable and slightly to the side such that one of your shoulders is in line with the cable.
3. With your arm that is in front of the cable, grasp the handle firmly with an extended elbow and your arm elevated to be aligned with the cable before stepping backward until the machine’s weight stack separates and you feel the resistance.
4. Mildly bend your hips and knees by sitting your buttocks somewhat backward with your feet approximately shoulder-width apart to assume a stable stance.
    1. In this position, the center of your breastbone should be facing the same way as the center of your hips, rather than having your trunk rotated toward one side.
5. Based on your preference and what feels most comfortable, you can rotate the handle to use an underhand grip with your palm facing up, an overhand grip with your palm facing down, or a neutral grip with your palm facing in toward the midline of your body.
    1. People often find that the neutral grip feels most natural.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handle back toward your torso by driving your elbow simultaneously downward and backward while progressively bending your elbow.
    1. Move your elbow through a path of motion that feels comfortable to you, which will typically involve keeping it tucked close to your side with this variation rather than notably flaring your elbow up and away from your side.
    2. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your elbow being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    3. Keep your forearm aligned in the same direction as the cable, which will naturally occur with the appropriate degree of elbow bend.
    4. Your shoulder blade will naturally move backward with your elbow.
    5. Movement should occur at your shoulder, shoulder blade, and elbow, but your knees, hips, and lower back should remain nearly stationary in a stable position as the center of your breastbone faces the same direction throughout the set.
    6. The cable will impart a rotational force to your trunk that your core muscles will resist to prevent your trunk from twisting during the row.
2. Reverse the movement by bringing the handle toward the cable station in a controlled manner by allowing your elbow to move forward and upward while it progressively extends until the handle has returned to the starting position.
    1. Your shoulder blade will naturally move forward with your elbow.
    2. At the end of this motion, your elbow should be in an extended position, and your arm should be aligned in the same direction as the cable.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable bench at a low incline angle (e.g., near 30 degrees) and set a pair of dumbbells under the head of the bench.
    1. You can alternatively set your bench at a moderate incline (e.g., near 45 degrees) if your bench lacks a low incline setting, or if you personally prefer to use a mildly greater incline.
    2. The dumbbells may be easiest to grasp while lying on the bench if you initially place one end of each dumbbell on top of the bench’s horizontal base leg (which is where wheels may be located) and the other end of each dumbbell on the floor closer to where you will be on the bench.
2. Lie down with your chest contacting the head of the bench and your legs spread out as you position the balls of your feet on the ground.
3. Grasp one dumbbell at a time, position your arms so that they are perpendicular to the ground with extended elbows, and direct your palms backward to utilize an overhand grip.
    1. The bony bump on the back of each elbow should point directly out to the side (which is the direction you will row), rather than pointing backward.
    2. To be able to row through a full range of motion, the dumbbells should not be in contact with the ground or the base of the bench, which may be more challenging to avoid for individuals with longer arms.
    3. To create greater clearance between the dumbbells and the ground, you can scoot further up toward the head of the bench.
    4. If it is difficult for you to grasp the dumbbells, which may be more likely if you have shorter arms, you can initially place the dumbbells closer to the bench’s seat before setting up with your torso scooted further down on the bench to situate your hands closer to the floor. After grasping the dumbbells, you can then press your feet into the ground to scoot further up on the bench so that your head can hang off the bench rather than having your face pressed into the head of the bench.

1. Drive your elbows straight out to your sides and upward in an arcing motion to row the dumbbells up. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. To focus on your upper back, emphasize flaring your elbows straight out from your sides so your upper arms and torso form a “T-shape” at the top of the row. 
    2. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being approximately level with your shoulders at the end of the lifting phase.
    3. Keep your palms facing backward and torso in contact with the chest pad throughout the set.
    4. When allowing your elbows to bend naturally, your forearms should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    5. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells inward in a controlled arcing motion until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. Allow the weights to pull your shoulder blades apart and forward to stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. Avoid tucking your elbows back toward your sides to keep the emphasis on your upper back.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weights pull your arms down rapidly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to place the dumbbells back onto the ground.

## Setting up
1. After loading your desired weight onto the machine, adjust the seat or thigh pad height to a level that allows you to position your thighs snugly against the thigh pad while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. Some machine models have an adjustable seat, others have an adjustable thigh pad, and some have both.
    2. Depending on the specific model, plate-loaded lat pulldown machines may have the thigh pads positioned so you face toward or away from the weights, and these models often include a chest pad.
    3. The machines in which you sit facing toward the weights may be more likely to have handles angled in a manner that results in an underhand grip being uncomfortable and awkward to use, in contrast to machines where you face away from weights, which often have handles well-suited for an underhand grip.
2. While facing the thigh pads and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the handles with an underhand grip, with your palms facing backward.
    1. The grip width you can use will depend on the specific machine model you use, and you can feel free to select whichever grip width you prefer within the range your machine allows. An approximately shoulder-width grip will often be quite comfortable.
3. While holding the handles, sit down on the machine’s seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to extend in a controlled manner and your arms to raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
    2. If you do not feel tension from the machine in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), you may need to lower the seat height to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows down toward your sides while progressively bending them to pull the handles downward.
    1. Simultaneosuly pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears.
    2. Keep your torso in the same position throughout your set rather than progressively leaning backward during the pull.
    3. During the initial portion of the pull, you will drive your elbows downward, but you will drive your elbows simultaneously backward and downward during the second half of the pull.
    4. Pull through your available range of motion, which will typically leave your elbows level with or slightly behind your torso at the end of the pull.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the handles in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your arms overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your back on the ground and moderately bend your knees to a degree that lifts up the back of your legs off the ground but does not allow you to contact the ground with the soles of your feet.
    1. Compared to a standard glute bridge (where the soles of your feet would contact the ground), your knees will not be as bent with this hamstring bridge, so only the back of your heels will be in contact with the ground.
    2. You can situate your feet near shoulder-width apart from each other, but it is up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    3. In this position, you can rest the back of your head on the ground and leave your arms on the ground by your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels into the ground until your hips are fully extended.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your torso.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. With an approximately shoulder-width overhand grip that results in your palms facing back toward you, firmly grasp a bar loaded with your desired weight and stand upright.
    1. In addition to a standard barbell to which you can add weight plates, you can also utilize a fixed-weight bar, which can be useful if you wish to use a load that is lighter than 45lb (20kg), which is the typical weight of an unloaded standard barbell.
2. After walking over to a flat exercise bench with the bar, lift the bar up slightly above your waist and sit down on the bench with the bar on your lap and enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space.
3. While keeping your elbows bent and the bar close to your torso, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. As you transition from sitting to lying down, you optionally can march your thighs up against the bar to help reposition yourself.
    2. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent, and you will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Press the bar up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a bench press rep), your wrist should be fairly straight rather than bent backward, and you should keep your wrist fairly straight throughout the exercise.
2. While keeping your elbows fairly straight, lower the bar back behind your head in a controlled arcing manner through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. You should avoid meaningfully bending your elbows, but you can allow them to bend mildly as your arms move through motion at your shoulders while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
    2. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back during the descent.
    3. People can often lower the bar until their upper arms are close to parallel with the ground, but how far you can descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    4. Once you feel that you have reached the end range to which your shoulders can safely stretch, you have reached the end range for you as an individual.
3. Reverse the movement by pulling your arms upward and forward in an arcing motion to lift the bar until you have returned to the starting position with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows fairly straight as you move your arms through shoulder motion while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can train your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which are assisted by the [lowest portion of your pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) in the overhead position of each rep.

## Setting up
1. Position a short, looped elastic band around both thighs.
    1. The band will provide the greatest resistance to your hip muscles if you place it just above your knees, while it will provide less resistance if you place it higher up your thighs.
    2. You can choose where you situate the band on your thighs based on the level of resistance you wish to experience, and if you are using a particular band for this exercise for the first time, you can adjust its placement during the set if you wish to change the difficulty after starting the set.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground or an exercise mat behind a sturdy object with an elevated surface, such as a flat exercise bench, aerobic step with risers, plyometric box, stairs, or bed.
    1. So long as you can position your feet on the object while still lying on the ground, a range of heights can be used for your object, but selecting something near knee height is typically appropriate.
3. Lift up your legs to position your feet on top of the elevated surface with your knees bent by at least 90 degrees.
    1. If you are too far away from the elevated surface to achieve this bent knee position, you can scoot forward until you can do so.
    2. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (by scooting toward the elevated surface) is up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
    3. Based on what feels stable to you, you can either position the back of your heels on top of the elevated surface or position the middle of your soles on the corner of the elevated surface.
    4. You can situate your feet near shoulder-width apart from each other, but it is also up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    5. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can opt to point your toes forward or somewhat out to the sides.
    6. In this position, you can rest the back of your head on the ground and leave your arms on the ground by your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. Push your knees outward against the band’s resistance to have them in line with your feet (as opposed to letting the band pull your knees closer together), and maintain this knee position throughout your set.
    1. You will most likely feel tension in the muscles on the sides of your hips while doing so.
2. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your feet into the elevated surface and squeezing your buttock muscles.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thighs and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glutes.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glutes engage.
    4. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them at the top.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you can lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 while continuing to keep your knees aligned with your feet until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise dynamically trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) while statically training your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), and [short hip external rotator muscles](../Muscles/Short%20Hip%20External%20Rotators%201b95c6f170d880c79035ce63a7c5f540.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a short looped elastic band around both of your legs.
    1. The band will provide the greatest resistance to your hip muscles if you place it at ankle level, while it will provide less resistance if you place it higher up on your legs.
    2. You can choose where you situate the band on your thighs based on the level of resistance you wish to experience, and if you are using a particular band for this exercise for the first time, you can adjust its placement during the set if you wish to change the difficulty after starting the set.
2. Lie down on your side with the side of your body that you are about to train facing up and your legs aligned with your torso with straight knees (like they would be when you are standing upright).
    1. In this side-lying position, you can rest the bottom side of your head on the hand of your bottom arm for comfort by situating your upper arm out to the side with your elbow bent.
    2. For extra stability, you can bend the elbow of your top arm and place that side’s hand on the ground in front of your torso.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your top leg straight upward through your hip’s available range of motion while keeping that side’s knee straight and the rest of your body stationary.
    1. Avoid rolling your hips backward or bringing your top leg forward toward your chest during this exercise, which are common technical errors.
    2. To help prevent your hips from rolling, you can imagine that you are wearing a belt with a buckle that has a laser beam shooting out of it. Strive to keep the laser beam pointing straight forward, parallel to the ground, throughout the movement.
    3. If you start to roll your hips backward, your belt buckle’s laser beam will start to angle upward.
    4. When you lift your top leg straight upward rather than also bringing that leg forward in front of you, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your torso when your top thigh is parallel with the ground.
    5. While performing this movement with the appropriate technique, you will likely feel the muscles on the side of your top hip contracting.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your top leg to descend in a controlled manner until your leg is low enough that the band becomes slack or until the inner aspect of your top foot contacts your bottom foot.
    1. If you lower your leg until beyond the point when the band becomes slack, you naturally will no longer be experiencing resistance from the band, but the weight of your top leg will still be resisting your hip muscles, so you have the option of deciding when you finish the rep.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side by lying on your opposite side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the musculature on the side of your hip, including your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), and [tensor fascia latae](../Muscles/Tensor%20Fascia%20Latae%201925c6f170d8806fb83bf08142d940fc.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while holding the kettlebells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hand while holding them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
    2. If you are using kettlebells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both kettlebells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    3. For an easier setup, you can pick up one kettlebell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other kettlebell onto the bench before picking up both kettlebells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    4. Pick up the kettlebells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
## Exercise technique
1. Walk forward while holding the kettlebells at your sides, maintaining an upright posture with your shoulders approximately level.
    1. While you will not swing your arms like you would when walking normally, your torso and lower body should look similar to how they would when you walk normally.
    2. Walk at a pace where you feel stable and balanced throughout the carry.
    3. If you use a weight that is fairly heavy to you, it is natural to take shorter strides compared to how you typically walk.
    4. Keep the tops of your hip bones approximately level throughout your set rather than letting them drop down to one side when taking each step.
2. Continue walking with the kettlebells until you have completed your set and are ready to set the kettlebells down.
    1. Similar to the setup, it may be easiest to set the kettlebells down one at a time onto a flat exercise (or sturdy box) prior to picking up one kettlebell and reracking it, and then doing the same with the other kettlebell.
    2. The above approach can be particularly useful if you are rather fatigued after completing your set and could use a rest break prior to reracking the kettlebells.
## Description
Rather than concentrating the workload on one body region, this exercise trains a variety of muscle groups throughout your body in an integrated manner, including the muscles in your forearms, upper back, core, and lower body.

### **Straps for Carries**

Even when using chalk, the weight you can use or distance you can complete with a particular weight will commonly be limited by grip strength while performing a farmer’s carry, so this carry can be a viable means of training static grip strength. Relative to performing a farmer’s walk with dumbbells or a trap bar, your grip may be especially challenged when carrying kettlebells since their handles typically lack knurling, and heavy kettlebells can also have handle diameters that are larger than dumbbells or trap bars. However, if you wish to increase the stimulus provided to muscles besides the forearm and hand muscles, you have the option of performing this carry with lifting straps. With the heavier loads or longer distances that straps typically facilitate, the exercise can be more challenging to your upper back and core muscles as they support your trunk and shoulder girdle in addition to your lower body muscles that stabilize your pelvis and propel you forward.

### **Training Many Muscles Simultaneously**

McGill et al. (2009) measured EMG activity of several core and lower body muscles as competitive strongmen performed a variety of movements that appear in strongman competitions, including the farmer’s walk, which was performed for several steps with a 75kg (167.6lb) weight in each hand. During the farmer’s walk, peak EMG activity was high for the internal abdominal obliques, lats, thoracic erector spinae, lumbar erector spinae, gluteus medius, gluteus maximus, and rectus femoris. The external abdominal obliques and biceps femoris also exhibited moderate peak EMG activity, while the rectus abdominis exhibited low EMG activity. The abdominal muscles and rectus femoris demonstrated their peak activity during the walking portion of the carry, while the lats, erector spinae and biceps femoris demonstrated their peak activity during the initial lifting phase. The gluteal muscles exhibited peak activity during the initial lifting phase and during the first step of the carry. As indicated by these findings, the farmer’s carry can train a large amount of musculature simultaneously, which can result in this exercise being metabolically demanding when performed at a high relative intensity, especially for longer duration sets. Correspondingly, challenging sets of farmer’s carries may be able to train your cardiovascular system more robustly than most resistance training exercises that localize the workload to a smaller amount of total muscle mass.

## Setting up
1. To elevate the bar to your desired height, position a trap bar on top of a pair of deadlift blocks or a similarly sturdy substitute capable of safely withstanding the load you will use.
    1. If your trap bar has a pair of high handles and low handles, you can decide which handles to situate facing up based on the position in which you wish to start your trap bar block pull, which will also be influenced by the height of the blocks you select. It is generally recommended to use a block height that will position the handles you will use at least below your knees once you have placed the trap bar on top of the blocks.   
    2. Aerobic steps can often be used for block pulls while having the option to adjust the height by changing the number of risers you use, but you should be aware of the recommended weight limit if you opt to use heavy loads.
    3. The weight limit for aerobic steps will vary by brand, but some of the common brands recommend not exceeding 300lb (136kg) per step, which would result in a 600lb (272kg) limit when using a pair of steps for a block pull.
    4. The height of the aerobic step will also vary by brand, but the step itself is commonly near 4in (10cm) in height, with the risers being near 2in (5cm) in height.
    5. With thickness typically ranging from about 1-3.5in (2.5-8.9cm), depending on the weight and brand, bumper plates can also function as blocks that can be stacked on top of each other to provide a range of different heights.
2. Add weight plates to the trap bar, and stand within the middle of it with approximately a hip-width to shoulder-width stance and your arms at your sides.
    1. Specifically how wide you situate your feet apart can be based on what feels most comfortable to you when picking up a weight off the floor with a deadlifting motion.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the bar and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from hinging at your hips than bending your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift moderately forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something. After you have fully sat back and feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    4. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and help engage your back muscles.
4. With your elbows fully straightened, firmly grasp the center of the handles with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hands while holding the bar, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. The initial submaximal pull allows you to check if you have grasped the handles correctly, which will be indicated by the handles not rotating forward or backward when applying the pre-tension.
    2. If you pick up a trap bar with your hands positioned slightly away from the middle of the handles, the trap bar can start rotating in a manner that makes it very difficult to hold and lift appropriately.
    3. Even for experienced lifters, it can be easy to grasp a trap bar’s handles without having their hands truly centered initially, so applying the pre-tension can make sure you are in your ideal starting position.
    4. If the bar starts rotating when you apply the pre-tension, re-center your grip, and apply the pre-tension again until the bar no longer rotates.
3. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees. Prioritize keeping your chest up, lower back flat, and your core braced throughout the entire exercise.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. Once the bar is moving, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
5. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the blocks.
    1. Just like when lifting the bar, keep your lower back flat and chest up as you descend while actively avoiding letting your lower back round or chest collapse.
    2. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees. Then you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the blocks for a moment (rather than simply tapping the blocks and immediately lifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the blocks for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is on the blocks rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before the next rep.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this can meaningfully train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), along with your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) to a lesser degree.

### Why Pull from Blocks Instead of the Floor?

When performing a low handle trap bar deadlift from the floor, your body proportions will determine the magnitude of hip flexion and knee flexion that is required in order to grasp the handles. Along with bumper plates, plates weighing 45lb or 20kg (which differ slightly) typically have a diameter near 45cm (17.7in) that result in the center of a bar (and a trap bar’s low handles) to which they are loaded being about 22.5cm (8.9in) above the ground. Based on differences in body proportions such as arm length relative to height, certain individuals may find that the handles at this level of elevation require deeper joint angles than they wish to train. In light of a particular person’s mobility, training goals, and injury history, the ideal starting height of any deadlift variation will vary among different individuals. For instance someone with short arms relative to his/her height and limited hip mobility may find pulling from the floor to be quite awkward, but elevating the handles mildly allows for a more comfortable starting position that feels better to that individual. Many trap models have a pair of high handles that allow for a lifter to pull from a height akin to a block pull, but some models lack such handles, so you can perform a trap bar block pull to replicate the high handle trap bar deadlift if you do not have access to a trap bar with high handles. Even when using a trap bar with high handles, a trap bar block pull can still serve a purpose because the height of the handles is fixed. The high handles of trap bars are commonly elevated 4in (10.2cm) above the low handles, but some models have slightly lower high handles, while others have high handles that are up to about 8in (20.3cm) above the low handles. Based on your specific trap bar, body dimensions, and training goals, high handle trap deadlifting from the floor may not provide quite enough handle elevation or it may provide excessive elevation. Correspondingly, you can adjust the starting position to your preference by determining the height of the blocks and which handles you use. 

### **Hip Hinging versus Squatting Your Trap Bar Deadlift**

Relative to conventional deadlifts or block pulls with a straight barbell, trap bar deadlifts can allow you greater liberty in how you perform them with respect to biasing more of a hip hinge or squat movement pattern. A conventional deadlift keeps the load in front of you and constrains forward knee travel, while a trap bar deadlift positions the load closer to your center of mass and permits pushing your knees farther forward than you would do during a conventional deadlift. Trap bar deadlifting with greater forward knee travel makes the movement more squat-like in nature compared to maintaining a closer to vertical shin position, which results in a comparatively more hip-hinge dominant movement. As discussed by Greg Nuckols in his Stronger By Science article “Trap Bar Deadlifts are Underrated”, squat and deadlift variations can be analyzed as existing along a “squat-hinge continuum” based on the demands they impart to the hip extensor muscles (e.g., gluteus maximus, hamstrings, adductor magnus) relative to the quads, which extend the knees. Compared to trap bar deadlifting with a vertical shin, the lever arm of the resistance acting on the knees is greater when deadlifting with your knees situated farther forward, resulting in a greater ratio of loading imparted to the quads relative to the hip extensor muscles. In contrast, the lever arm of the resistance acting on the hips is greater when deadlifting with vertical shins, which prompts you to sit your hips farther back and experience a lower ratio of loading imparted to the quads relative to the hip extensor muscles. While people tend to perform trap bar deadlifts with their knees situated farther forward than when they conventional deadlift, you certainly have the ability to trap bar deadlift with the same knee position you would use for conventional deadlifts. Correspondingly, you can trap bar deadlift with whichever technique you prefer in congruence with your training goals.

Based on research assessing participants using their self-selected technique (which likely is the technique in which they were most efficient for pulling), it is worth noting that low handle trap bar deadlifts have been found to be more hip-dominant than knee-dominant. Swinton et al. (2011) specifically assessed male powerlifters performing low handle trap bar deadlifts and conventional dreadlifts. Both exercises imparted meaningfully greater loading to the hip extensors and lumbar spinal extensors than the quads, but conventional deadlifts were relatively more hip dominant. When lifting 80% of the participants’ conventional deadlift one-rep maxes, the ratio of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee was 3.7 for conventional deadlifts and 1.8 for low handle trap bar deadlifts. This difference was mainly attributed to the low handle trap bar deadlift having greater peak resistive torque acting on the knee, which was 190% of the conventional deadlift. A smaller gap was present for hip extensor loading as the peak resistive torque acting on the hip for the low handle trap bar deadlift was 92% that of conventional deadlift. These findings indicate that the degree to which low handle trap bar deadlifts train the quads more than conventional deadlifts most likely exceeds the degree to which conventional deadlifts train the hip extensor muscles more than low handle trap bar deadlifts. In terms of which hip extensor muscles may be less involved during trap bar deadlifts, the biarticular hamstrings in particular will likely receive a lesser stimulus. Camara et al. (2016) and Andersen et al. (2018) both found the hamstring’s biceps femoris to exhibit lower EMG activity during the low handle trap bar deadlift compared to the conventional deadlift, which is congruent with what be anticipated in light of the mechanical differences between these two exercises. Since the trap bar deadlift imparts greater loading to the knee, the knee flexion torque that results from hamstring contraction will have more of a deleterious effect on performance than during the conventional deadlift. While the hip extension torque that the hamstrings produce is beneficial, their knee flexion torque will oppose the quads as they extend the knee, so the hamstrings are not the most efficient hip extensor muscles for the nervous system to recruit during an exercise that imparts meaningful resistance to the quads. To a lesser extent, this is the same principle that results in the hamstrings experiencing minimal hypertrophy after interventions of squatting, which imparts even greater loading of the quads relative to the hip extensor muscles. Accompanying the lower hamstring EMG activity,  Camara et al. (2016) found the quad’s vastus lateralis (which was not assessed by Andersen et al.) to exhibit greater activity with the trap bar deadlift compared to the conventional deadlift. In contrast to the difference in hamstring EMG activity, Andersen et al. (2018) also found the gluteus maximus (which was not assessed by Camara et al.) to exhibit similar EMG activity during the two deadlift variations, which makes sense given that the gluteus maximus is able to generate hip extension without simultaneously generating knee flexion torque.

While the previously discussed data indicates that low handle trap bar deadlifts are typically performed with a more squat-like technique than conventional deadlifts, it is natural to wonder how they may compare to back squats. Choe et al. (2021) did not assess trap bar deadlifts, but they studied conventional deadlifts and back back squats performed with 70-85% of the mixed sex participants’ one-rep maxes. The researchers found the ratio of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee to be 3.0 for conventional deadlifts and 1.4 for squats. The participants of this study had some squat and deadlift training experience as the males had average deadlift and squat maxes that were respectively 143.3kg and 122.7kg, while the females had average deadlift and squat maxes that were respectively 95.0kg and 88.0kg. However, they were not nearly as strong as the powerlifter participants partaking in the study from Swinton et al. (2011) who had average conventional deadlift and low handle trap bar deadlift maxes that were respectively 244.5kg and 265.0kg. The participants from Swinton et al. (2011) correspondingly most likely used more efficient techniques, which may explain why they exhibited a higher ratio (3.8 versus 3.0) of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee when conventional deadlifting relative to the participants from Choe et al. (2021). When comparing the low handle trap bar deadlift findings from Swinton et al. (2011) to the back squat findings from Choe et al. (2021), the back squat was more knee dominant than the low handle trap bar deadlift, but the previously mentioned hip to knee torque ratio difference (1.7 versus 1.4) was not particularly pronounced.

This data suggests that the ratio of hip to knee loading of the low handle trap bar may be more similar to back squats than conventional deadlifts, but the strengths of our conclusions are limited when comparing findings from different studies assessing meaningfully different participants. For the most valid comparison of trap bar deadlifts to back squats, we ideally would want to analyze the findings from a study that assessed the same participants performing both exercises, which is what Stahl et al. (2024) precisely investigated. The researchers specifically compared the high handle trap bar deadlift (permitting chalk use but not straps) to the back squat (performed until thighs were parallel with the floor) as moderately trained mixed-sex participants lifted loads up to 100% of their maxes. They found the ratio of peak resistive torque acting on the hip to the peak resistive torque acting on the knee to be 0.9 for high trap bar deadlifts and 1.4 for squats (which was the same value determined by Choe et al.), indicating that high handle trap bar deadlifts can be even more knee-dominant than back squats. This difference was influenced by the resistive lever arm acting on the hip during back squats exceeding that during high trap bar deadlifts, while the resistive lever arm acting on the knee was similar between the two exercises. Comparing the data from Stahl et al. (2024) to the data from Swinton et al. (2011), high handle trap bar deadlifts appear to be more knee-dominant than low handle trap bar deadlifts with self-selected techniques, while back squats fall in between these two variations along the spectrum of hip to knee loading.

With that said, it is important to reiterate that you have the ability to perform trap bar deadlifts with either handle height in a more hip-dominant fashion if you wish to do so. Furthermore, it is also worth emphasizing that the aforementioned findings do not mean that high handle trap bar deadlifts are superior to back squats for training the quads. While the knee to hip loading ratios are relevant when appraising the ability of a deadlift or squat variation to train particular muscle groups, the capacity of an exercise to induce muscle hypertrophy is multi-factorial in nature. Multiple studies involving back squat training interventions have found back squats to induce significant quad growth, but the effect that high handle or low handle trap bar deadlifts may have on quad development has yet to be studied.

### **Trap Bar Deadlift versus Conventional Deadlift Strength**

Two different studies from Lockie et al. (2018) have compared one rep maxes without straps between conventional deadlifts and trap bar deadlifts with 4-inch (10.2cm) higher handles. Together they assessed a total of 54 mixed sex participants with at least two years of lifting experience that included conventional and trap bar deadlifts in addition to hitting maxes. Pooling the data from the two studies together, the average high handle trap bar max was 12% greater than the conventional deadlift max, resulting in a 39lb (17.7kg) mean difference. When comparing 1-rep maxes of the conventional deadlift to the low handle trap bar deadlift, Camara et al. (2016) found the maxes to be nearly identical to each other for the two lifts, but Swinton et al. (2011) and Lake et al. (2017) found their participants to lift an average of 6-8% greater loads during the low handle trap bar deadlift.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your lower body and spinal extensor muscles. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up overhead and firmly grasp it with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip) and your hands situated near shoulder-width apart or somewhat wider.
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    4. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide upward during the dead hang, which pulls on your hand skin in a manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, bend your knees to lift your heels up off the ground while keeping the balls of your feet and your toes in contact with the ground.
2. While supporting some of your bodyweight through your feet on the ground, hang on the bar to support the rest of your bodyweight.
    1. Based on the proportion of your bodyweight you wish to use for your dead hang, you can adjust how much of your bodyweight you are supporting through your legs as opposed to your hands.
    2. A dead hang is a static exercise, so you will simply hang on the bar while not moving your body to perform it.
3. Continue hanging on the bar until you have completed your set’s target duration.
## Description
While simultaneously improving overhead shoulder mobility, this exercise can increase your grip strength by training your [forearm](../Muscles/Extrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d88050a550fbeff6041573.md) and [hand](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md) muscles that function as finger flexors.
