## Setting up
1. Stand under a pull-up bar with parallel handles that are closer than shoulder-width apart.
    1. While not necessarily rare for multi-grip pull-up bars to have, these parallel handles that allow you to use a neutral close grip are not as commonly available as parallel handles that enable you to use a moderate-width neutral grip (i.e., approximately shoulder width).
    2. If you lack a pull-up bar with close parallel handles, you can select from this database the [neutral grip pull-up](Neutral%20grip%20pull-up%201a15c6f170d8808281eec44bc9b7fd67.md) that uses a moderate grip width to train the same muscle groups as would be trained by this close grip variation.
2. Reach up overhead and firmly grasp the close parallel handles with your palms facing in toward each other (i.e., a neutral grip).
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up on a sturdy box, aerobic step, or bumper plate to place the bar within your reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the bar.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
3. With your elbows straight and your hands firmly grasping the bar, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will place you in a more advantageous position to start your pull compared to if you kept your chest facing exclusively horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up from the force of your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back places you into a position akin to a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending them.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows naturally will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

### **How Your Grip and Pull-Up Technique Influence Back Muscle Development**

When repeatedly performing this exercise over time, you can feel free to try out mildly different grip widths to determine if any particular position feels most comfortable to you and/or allows you to perceive your target back muscles working particularly well. Pull-ups can be performed with a variety of hand grips, including different grip widths and overhand, underhand (resulting in the exercise being called a chin-up), neutral, or hybrid (i.e., a combination of neutral and underhand or overhand) grips. Additionally, shoulder motion during a pull-up can occur predominantly in the sagittal (front-to-back) plane, the frontal (side-to-side) plane, or a combination of the two. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the sagittal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out in front of you), the upper arms remain parallel to each other and do not deviate away from the mid-line of your body. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the frontal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out to your sides, such as with a snow angle motion), the upper arms move away from the mid-line of your body until they are parallel to the ground. Then they move closer to the mid-line of your body with further elevation. During the lifting phase of a pull-up, the shoulders could extend in the sagittal plane, adduct in the frontal plane, or exhibit a combination of extension and adduction at a hybrid angle between the sagittal and frontal planes. Rather than moving the shoulders exclusively through one plane, pull-up variations are commonly performed with a technique that allows for the shoulders to move in between these two planes, but one plane of shoulder motion often makes a greater contribution than the other.

Muscles acting on the shoulder joint have different leverage to generate extension torque in the sagittal plane versus adduction torque in the frontal plane, and the nervous system is most likely to recruit the particular muscles that are best leveraged to produce the intended joint action during any active movement. Correspondingly, the plane of motion in which the shoulders move during a pull-up can affect how well different muscles are likely to be trained. With any particular grip for a pull-up, you can intentionally rotate your shoulders in a manner that allows you to move your shoulder relatively more in the sagittal or frontal plane. However, most people will typically find that a particular path of shoulder motion feels most comfortable and stable to their shoulders, elbows, and wrists when using a specific grip. For instance, people will normally perform a wide overhand grip pull-up with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the frontal plane. In contrast, they will normally perform a close-grip chin-up (using an underhand grip) with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the sagittal plane. Performing either variation in the alternative plane of motion would require greater-than-normal rotational range of motion in the shoulders and forearms, and attempting to do so could feel very awkward and uncomfortable. People will typically feel most comfortable when positioning themselves so that, at the point in the pull-up when their upper arms are parallel to the ground, their elbows and wrists are vertically aligned or their elbows are slightly lateral (outside) to their wrists.

In general, widening a grip facilitates relatively more frontal plane shoulder motion, while narrowing a grip facilitates relatively more sagittal plane shoulder motion. An overhand, underhand, or neutral grip may be used with any grip width. Still, the combination of these grip variables will influence comfort and which plane of shoulder motion feels most natural. When pulling predominantly in the sagittal plane with a rather close grip, an underhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable than an overhand grip. Similarly, when pulling predominantly in the frontal plane with a rather wide grip, an overhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable and allow more frontal-plane motion than an underhand grip. With a moderate-width grip, people may commonly find that pulling mostly in the sagittal plane feels natural with an underhand or neutral grip, but pulling relatively more in the frontal plane feels natural with an overhand grip. Fundamentally, the shoulder motion is what matters to the back muscles, and the grip is only relevant to the back muscles based on how it influences which shoulder motion is performed. When performing this overhand grip pull-up with a moderate grip width, you most likely will pull in a way that biases shoulder adduction somewhat more than shoulder extension. Still, you can also perform the exercise in a way that results in a fairly even balance between these two motions.

The lat and teres major in the back function both as primary adductors and extensors and are therefore highly likely to be trained effectively with pull-up variations regardless of the grip or plane of shoulder motion. However, the preponderance of available evidence indicates that the rear deltoid lacks meaningful leverage to contribute to shoulder adduction, but it clearly has favorable leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. The rear deltoid is correspondingly likely to be trained better with a closer grip emphasizing shoulder extension, which would be most comfortable when using an underhand or neutral grip. Alternatively, the middle and lower regions of the pectoralis major (that constitute the sternoclavicular head) have large moment arms to function as shoulder adductors, but only the lower portion exhibits a shoulder extension moment arm, and this moment arm is quite small and only present in flexed shoulder positions. Consequently, wider grip pull-ups (which are most comfortable with an overhand or neutral grip) that involve greater frontal-plane shoulder motion are likely to train the pectoralis major more effectively than closer grip pulldowns. Which regions of the lats are preferentially biased by a pull-up variation may also potentially be influenced by how much shoulder motion occurs in the frontal or sagittal planes. The middle and lower regions have relatively greater leverage to function as shoulder adductors, while the upper region of the lat has relatively greater leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. Plausibly, these biomechanical differences may facilitate the middle and lower regions of the lats being preferentially trained by wider grip pull-ups, while the upper region may be preferentially trained by closer grip pulling variations. With that said, the degree to which any preferential biasing may occur across different regions of the lats when comparing pull-up grips is more speculative and has not been tested in any longitudinal training interventions.

### Why Overhand Grip Pull-Ups may be More Difficult than Chin-Ups or Neutral Grip Pull-Ups

While exceptions exist, people often find overhand grip pull-ups to be more difficult per rep than chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. The discrepancy is most likely influenced by chin-ups and neutral grip pull-ups typically being performed with a technique that emphasizes shoulder extension in the sagittal plane, while overhand grip pull-ups are typically performed with relatively more shoulder adduction in the frontal plane. As demonstrated by studies such as those by Mayer et al. (1994) and Shklar and Dvir (1995), on average, maximal torque for shoulder extension exceeds that for shoulder adduction. The sample of participants, velocity, and type of muscle action tested can all influence the degree to which torque differs between these two actions, but maximal shoulder adduction torque has been measured at 63-90% of maximal shoulder extension, depending on the specific test conditions. In addition to the effect of how the shoulder moves, the forearm position can also affect how much elbow flexion torque you can generate during your pull. Guenzkofer et al. (2012) found that up to 15% greater elbow flexion torque can be generated when the forearm is in a supinated (used for an underhand grip) or neutral position compared to a pronated (used with an overhand grip) position. Together, these relationships suggest that most people can generate greater torque at the shoulders and elbows during chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups than during overhand grip pull-ups, which are likely to be more challenging when performing the same number of reps. Consequently, it is common not to be able to complete as many reps of overhand grip pull-ups in a set as you would be able to complete when performing chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. Nonetheless, individual differences in factors such as training history and the relative strength of different muscle groups can result in some people not noticing a difference in difficulty between these variations, or even finding overhand grip pull-ups to be somewhat easier per rep.

### Chin Over Bar?

The technique instructions do not specify where any particular part of your body should be situated in relation to the bar at the end of the lifting phase because your full range of motion can differ from someone else’s full range of motion. Pulling until your chin is above the bar is a common standard used for testing by the United States Marines and for competitions held by the World Pull-Up Organization, and you can certainly use it if you wish. However, when focusing on chin clearance, some people tend to extend their necks, lifting their chins, to clear the bar with less range of motion through the pull, compared to when they retain a neutral neck position. In this instance, focusing on the proxy for a full range of motion may result in a different movement than focusing on the individual's full range of motion. When competing or taking a standardized test that affects professional prospects, it is only sensible to do the minimum required to complete each rep per the rules, but training to build muscle and strength is a different endeavor.

### The Most Challenging Part of the Pull-Up

The end range of the lifting phase is typically the most challenging portion of pull-ups, in large part because the torque our pulling muscles can generate meaningfully varies across different joint angles. When the elbow is flexed to 120 degrees, Bober et al. (2002) found maximal elbow flexion torque to be approximately 35% of the peak torque that can be generated in a moderately flexed elbow position (i.e., near 60-75 degrees of elbow flexion). With your elbows approaching full flexion toward the end range of a pull-up, your elbow flexor muscles are correspondingly operating from a rather disadvantaged position to help you complete the rep. On average, maximal shoulder extension and adduction (a combination of which occurs during a pull-up) torques are also lower when the shoulder is mildly elevated (like at the end of a pull-up’s lifting phase) compared to when it is moderately elevated (like during the middle range of a pull-up). Together, these strength curves of the muscle groups acting on the elbow and shoulder can contribute to your pull-ups consistently feeling the most difficult during the last quarter of the lifting phase.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your back muscle strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your back muscles. As a simple approach, if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure you use the same technique for each condition, which means the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how the performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep's performance across these conditions on a second day, in which you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps on the first day, perform the set with straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue from the first set may influence the second. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting the performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

### **How Your Grip and Pull-Up Technique Influence Back Muscle Development**

When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the sagittal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out in front of you), the upper arms remain parallel to each other and do not deviate away from the mid-line of your body. When symmetrically moving the shoulders strictly in the frontal plane (like would occur when lifting your arms straight out to your sides, such as with a snow angle motion), the upper arms move away from the mid-line of your body until they are parallel to the ground. Then they move closer to the mid-line of your body with further elevation. During the lifting phase of a pull-up, the shoulders could extend in the sagittal plane, adduct in the frontal plane, or exhibit a combination of extension and adduction at a hybrid angle between the sagittal and frontal planes. Rather than moving the shoulders exclusively through one plane, pull-up variations are commonly performed with a technique that allows for the shoulders to move in between these two planes, but one plane of shoulder motion often makes a greater contribution than the other.

Muscles acting on the shoulder joint have different leverage to generate extension torque in the sagittal plane versus adduction torque in the frontal plane, and the nervous system is most likely to recruit the particular muscles that are best leveraged to produce the intended joint action during any active movement. Correspondingly, the plane of motion in which the shoulders move during a pull-up can affect how well different muscles are likely to be trained. With any particular grip for a pull-up, you can intentionally rotate your shoulders in a manner that allows you to move your shoulder relatively more in the sagittal or frontal plane. However, most people will typically find that a particular path of shoulder motion feels most comfortable and stable to their shoulders, elbows, and wrists when using a specific grip. For instance, people will normally perform a wide overhand grip pull-up with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the frontal plane. In contrast, they will normally perform a close-grip chin-up (using an underhand grip) with shoulder motion predominantly occurring in the sagittal plane. Performing either variation in the alternative plane of motion would require greater-than-normal rotational range of motion in the shoulders and forearms, and attempting to do so could feel very awkward and uncomfortable. People will typically feel most comfortable when positioning themselves so that, at the point in the pull-up when their upper arms are parallel to the ground, their elbows and wrists are vertically aligned or their elbows are slightly lateral (outside) to their wrists.

In general, widening a grip facilitates relatively more frontal plane shoulder motion, while narrowing a grip facilitates relatively more sagittal plane shoulder motion. An overhand, underhand, or neutral grip may be used with any grip width. Still, the combination of these grip variables will influence comfort and which plane of shoulder motion feels most natural. When pulling predominantly in the sagittal plane with a rather close grip, an underhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable than an overhand grip. Similarly, when pulling predominantly in the frontal plane with a rather wide grip, an overhand or neutral grip will typically be more comfortable and allow more frontal-plane motion than an underhand grip. With a moderate-width grip, people may commonly find that pulling mostly in the sagittal plane feels natural with an underhand or neutral grip, but pulling relatively more in the frontal plane feels natural with an overhand grip. Fundamentally, the shoulder motion is what matters to the back muscles, and the grip is only relevant to the back muscles based on how it influences which shoulder motion is performed. When performing this overhand grip pull-up with a moderate grip width, you most likely will pull in a way that biases shoulder adduction somewhat more than shoulder extension. Still, you can also perform the exercise in a way that results in a fairly even balance between these two motions.

The lat and teres major in the back function both as primary adductors and extensors and are therefore highly likely to be trained effectively with pull-up variations regardless of the grip or plane of shoulder motion. However, the preponderance of available evidence indicates that the rear deltoid lacks meaningful leverage to contribute to shoulder adduction, but it clearly has favorable leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. The rear deltoid is correspondingly likely to be trained better with a closer grip emphasizing shoulder extension, which would be most comfortable when using an underhand or neutral grip. Alternatively, the middle and lower regions of the pectoralis major (that constitute the sternoclavicular head) have large moment arms to function as shoulder adductors, but only the lower portion exhibits a shoulder extension moment arm, and this moment arm is quite small and only present in flexed shoulder positions. Consequently, wider grip pull-ups (which are most comfortable with an overhand or neutral grip) that involve greater frontal-plane shoulder motion are likely to train the pectoralis major more effectively than closer grip pulldowns. Which regions of the lats are preferentially biased by a pull-up variation may also potentially be influenced by how much shoulder motion occurs in the frontal or sagittal planes. The middle and lower regions have relatively greater leverage to function as shoulder adductors, while the upper region of the lat has relatively greater leverage to function as a shoulder extensor. Plausibly, these biomechanical differences may facilitate the middle and lower regions of the lats being preferentially trained by wider grip pull-ups, while the upper region may be preferentially trained by closer grip pulling variations. With that said, the degree to which any preferential biasing may occur across different regions of the lats when comparing pull-up grips is more speculative and has not been tested in any longitudinal training interventions.

### Why Overhand Grip Pull-Ups may be More Difficult than Chin-Ups or Neutral Grip Pull-Ups

While exceptions exist, people often find overhand grip pull-ups to be more difficult per rep than chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. The discrepancy is most likely influenced by chin-ups and neutral grip pull-ups typically being performed with a technique that emphasizes shoulder extension in the sagittal plane, while overhand grip pull-ups are typically performed with relatively more shoulder adduction in the frontal plane. As demonstrated by studies such as those by Mayer et al. (1994) and Shklar and Dvir (1995), on average, maximal torque for shoulder extension exceeds that for shoulder adduction. The sample of participants, velocity, and type of muscle action tested can all influence the degree to which torque differs between these two actions, but maximal shoulder adduction torque has been measured at 63-90% of maximal shoulder extension, depending on the specific test conditions. In addition to the effect of how the shoulder moves, the forearm position can also affect how much elbow flexion torque you can generate during your pull. Guenzkofer et al. (2012) found that up to 15% greater elbow flexion torque can be generated when the forearm is in a supinated (used for an underhand grip) or neutral position compared to a pronated (used with an overhand grip) position. Together, these relationships suggest that most people can generate greater torque at the shoulders and elbows during chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups than during overhand grip pull-ups, which are likely to be more challenging when performing the same number of reps. Consequently, it is common not to be able to complete as many reps of overhand grip pull-ups in a set as you would be able to complete when performing chin-ups or neutral grip pull-ups. Nonetheless, individual differences in factors such as training history and the relative strength of different muscle groups can result in some people not noticing a difference in difficulty between these variations, or even finding overhand grip pull-ups to be somewhat easier per rep.

### Chin Over Bar?

The technique instructions do not specify where any particular part of your body should be situated in relation to the bar at the end of the lifting phase because your full range of motion can differ from someone else’s full range of motion. Pulling until your chin is above the bar is a common standard used for testing by the United States Marines and for competitions held by the World Pull-Up Organization, and you can certainly use it if you wish. However, when focusing on chin clearance, some people tend to extend their necks, lifting their chins, to clear the bar with less range of motion through the pull, compared to when they retain a neutral neck position. In this instance, focusing on the proxy for a full range of motion may result in a different movement than focusing on the individual's full range of motion. When competing or taking a standardized test that affects professional prospects, it is only sensible to do the minimum required to complete each rep per the rules, but training to build muscle and strength is a different endeavor.

### The Most Challenging Part of the Pull-Up

The end range of the lifting phase is typically the most challenging portion of pull-ups, in large part because the torque our pulling muscles can generate meaningfully varies across different joint angles. When the elbow is flexed to 120 degrees, Bober et al. (2002) found maximal elbow flexion torque to be approximately 35% of the peak torque that can be generated in a moderately flexed elbow position (i.e., near 60-75 degrees of elbow flexion). With your elbows approaching full flexion toward the end range of a pull-up, your elbow flexor muscles are correspondingly operating from a rather disadvantaged position to help you complete the rep. On average, maximal shoulder extension and adduction (a combination of which occurs during a pull-up) torques are also lower when the shoulder is mildly elevated (like at the end of a pull-up’s lifting phase) compared to when it is moderately elevated (like during the middle range of a pull-up). ### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your back muscle strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your back muscles. As a simple approach, if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least three minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how the performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep's performance across these conditions on a second day, in which you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps on the first day, perform the set with straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue from the first set may influence the second. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting the performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

2. Step up onto the machine’s elevated foot plates and reach up overhead to grasp the machine’s parallel handles firmly with your palms facing in toward each other (i.e., a neutral grip).
    1. While fairly common, not all assisted pull-up machines have a pair of parallel handles.

1. While hanging with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.

    1. Since the handles are fixed, your elbows naturally will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. If you are using a machine with a knee pad and you notice the machine restricts your range of motion when kneeling on the pad, switch to standing on the pad before resuming your set to pull through your full range of motion.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.

## Setting up
1. Stand upright with a shoulder-width stance, straight elbows, and your palms resting on the front of your thighs.
    1. This variation will not utilize any weights, as it can serve as a primer to loaded Jefferson curls by allowing you to determine how your body feels during the movement itself.
## Exercise technique
1. Tuck your chin to your chest and lower your hands toward the floor in a slow and controlled manner by bending over and rounding your whole back through what is your comfortable range of motion while keeping your knees and elbows straight.
    1. As a cue, you can think about rounding forward each segment of your spine successively until your entire spine has achieved a rounded posture.
    2. As you progressively descend, it is natural to feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings and back muscles.
    3. How far you can descend will be influenced by your hamstring flexibility and the available bending range of motion in your spine.
    4. If you have a high degree of mobility, you may be able to descend until your hands contact the floor, but only move through a range that is painless and feels right to your body.
    5. If you can touch the floor with your fingertips and feel that you have greater available range of motion, you can bend your wrists to point your palms toward the floor, which will allow you to descend past when your fingertips would contact the ground with straight wrists.
    6. Your arms should be directed down toward the ground throughout the exercise.
2. Reverse the movement by gradually transitioning from the bent-over position to the upright position in which you started by progressively uncoiling your back.
    1. At the end of the ascent, untuck your chin and look straight ahead.
    2. Continue keeping your knees and elbows in a straightened position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

This exercise can dynamically train the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) that run along your entire back, while also training your spinal mobility and hamstring flexibility.

## Setting up
1. Securely attach your desired weight to your wrist roller.
    1. Depending on the model of your wrist roller, you may have to use weight plates (if your model uses a loading pin), or you may be able to use weight plates, kettlebells, or dumbbells (if your model uses a strap that you can loop around the weight).
    2. Leave enough of the rope initially uncoiled so that you can stand up with the roller without the weight lifting off the ground.
2. While the weight is on the ground, firmly grasp the roller’s handles with your palms facing toward you (i.e., an overhand grip) and the uncoiled part of the rope on the side of the roller that is closer toward you.
    1. If the uncoiled part of the rope is on the side of the roller farther away from you, you would be able to train wrist extension when using an overhand grip, but this is the wrist flexion variation.
3. Stand upright while grasping the roller and raise your arms out in front of you with straight elbows until your arms are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. You will maintain this arm position throughout your set.
4. Take up the slack from the roller’s rope with alternating twisting motions of your wrists until you feel that the rope is taught from the weight’s resistance.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your arms held out in front of you, bend one wrist to curl that side’s hand toward you as you extend your other wrist in the opposite direction by pointing that hand’s palm down toward the ground.
    1. You should grasp the handle firmly with the hand whose palm is curling toward you, as you grasp the handle loosely with the hand whose palm is pointing toward the ground.
    2. The hand whose palm is curling toward you is what rotates the roller to lift the weight up, while the other side’s wrist is repositioning in preparation to perform the curling motion.
2. Alternate the motions in step 1 with the opposite hands as you lift the weight up by cyclically repeating these twisting movements with your wrists until you have fully coiled the rope around the roller.
3. Lower the weight in a controlled manner by reversing the same motions you just performed until the weight lightly taps the ground or is just about to do so.
4. Repeatedly perform steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the six [wrist flexor muscles](../Muscles/Wrist%20flexor%20muscles%202c85c6f170d880a49749f7d7a9f307c8.md) on the palm side of your forearm.

## Setting up
1. Firmly grasp an asymmetrical weighted implement (or a viable alternative) by its lighter end at a position that can provide your desired level of resistance.
    1. Asymmetrical weighted implements include adjustable dumbbells with plates loaded only on one side, hammers, and end-loaded baseball bats.
    2. As an alternative to an asymmetrical weighted implement, you can grasp certain symmetrically weighted cylindrical implements closer toward one end, which can provide the same training effect. Examples include a fixed-weight straight bar, a fixed-weight EZ bar, an adjustable EZ bar, and a cable straight bar attachment (like a lat pulldown bar).
    3. The resistance your forearm pronator muscles experience during this exercise will be dictated by how closely to one end you grasp the implement.
    4. For greater resistance, you can grasp farther away from the weighted end with an asymmetrically loaded implement or closer to whichever end you are holding with a symmetrically loaded implement.
    5. When performing this exercise for the first time with a particular implement, you may have to try out different grip positions to determine specifically where you should grasp the implement to provide the magnitude of resistance you wish to have.
2. Sit down on a seat (e.g., chair, flat exercise bench, plyometric box), and position your forearm (on the side holding the weight) on top of your thigh with a bent elbow and your hand slightly in front of your knee.
    1. You can situate your wrist just above your kneecap, which should allow the weighted implement to rotate freely without contacting any part of your leg.
3. If not already in this position, direct your palm to face in toward your opposite side with a straight wrist position and the heavier end of your weighted implement directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. From here, your wrist and forearms are in a neutral position as they would normally be when standing upright with your palms facing in toward your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your forearm resting on your thigh, progressively rotate your palm down toward the floor in a controlled manner through your available range of motion.
    1. Doing so will rotate the weighted end (if using an asymmetrically loaded object) or longer end (if using a symmetrically loaded object) in toward the midline of your body, such that this end moves in front of your torso rather than out to the side.
    2. Most people will have the forearm mobility to rotate until their palm is close to facing straight up, which will result in the weight’s handle being close to parallel to the floor, but some people may not be able to rotate quite as far, while others can rotate beyond that point.
    3. As you rotate your forearm, keep your wrist in a straight (neutral) position rather than letting the weight bend your wrist and pull your hand downward (which would bring the palm of your hand closer toward your knee if the wrist flexes).
2. After reaching your end range, reverse the movement until you have returned to the starting position by turning your palm to face in toward your opposite side.
    1. Doing so will lift the weighted end or longer end of the implement upward and outward in an arcing manner until the handle is vertically oriented.
3. Continue rotating your palm up toward the ceiling in a controlled manner through your available range of motion.
    1. Doing so will rotate the weighted end (if using an asymmetrically loaded object) or longer end (if using a symmetrically loaded object) out to your side, such that this end moves away from the midline of your body.
    2. Most people will have the forearm mobility to rotate until their palm is close to facing straight up, which will result in the weight’s handle being close to parallel to the floor, but how far you can move will be influenced by your individual forearm mobility.
    3. Continue keeping your wrist in a straight (neutral) position rather than letting the weight bend your wrist and pull your hand downward (which would bring the back of your hand closer toward your knee if the wrist extends).
4. After reaching your end range, reverse the movement until you have returned to the starting position by turning your palm to face in toward your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
While also training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), this exercise can effectively develop your forearm’s [pronator teres](../Muscles/Pronator%20Teres%201905c6f170d880469c68dcf80a241445.md), [pronator quadratus](../Muscles/Pronator%20Quadratus%201905c6f170d8805d864ff866cf803c77.md), and [supinator](../Muscles/Supinator%201905c6f170d88034845dfa135173a9ef.md). 

### **How to progressively overload**

Resistive torque is what fundamentally determines the challenge any particular muscle group experiences during an exercise. To increase resistive torque, you can increase the weight of the resistance you use, or you can increase the lever arm in which the resistance acts on the joints (and the muscles acting on those joints) you are training. Either variable can be adjusted as a form of progressive overload to increase the torque that your muscles must overcome as they become stronger (i.e., are able to generate greater torque) over time. Whether you modify the load or the lever arm of the resistance is inconsequential to your muscles since the product of those two variables (torque) is what directly matters to the muscles you train. With a forearm pronation and supination exercise such as this, you correspondingly can progress by using a heavier load or by incrementally grasping the implement closer toward one end as you increase your pronation and supination strength. If you have reached the end of your implement and wish to continue increasing the resistance you provide your pronator and supinator muscles, you naturally will have to add load to your implement (which is easiest to do so when using an adjustable dumbbell) or switch to an implement that has a longer handle or a greater weight.

### Training forearm pronation and supination with one exercise

This variation combines the asymmetrical weight forearm pronation and asymmetrical weight forearm supination exercises into one, which can readily be done in part because those two exercises utilize the same starting position. As you transition from the neutral forearm position (with your palm facing in toward your opposite side) to your palm facing down, you are eccentrically training your supinators as your forearm pronates. When moving from the fully pronated position (with your palm down) to the neutral position, you subsequently are concentrically training supination. As you transition from the neutral forearm position to your palm facing up, you are eccentrically training your pronators as your forearm supinates. When moving from the fully supinated position (with your palm up) to the neutral position, you are then concentrically training pronation.

When combining two movements that train different different muscle groups together into one exercise, it is worth noting that whichever muscle group is most fatigued by the time you finish the set will likely be the muscle group that receives the greatest stimulus. Depending on which movements are paired together, you can risk one of the movements being considerably underloaded to the extent that it provides a magnitude of stimulus that is simply insufficient to promote increases in strength or muscle size. For instance, if you combine a dumbbell squat and dumbbell biceps curl into one exercise where you perform a squatting movement followed by a curling movement, you would be noticeably limited by your curling strength in all likelihood. People can normally squat markedly more weight than they curl, and the lower body muscles would not experience remotely close to the same stimulus that they could receive from a squat using loads that are not constrained by curling strength.

However, average forearm pronation and supination strength have been found to be fairly similar in the general population. When pooling the results together from nine studies that measured both pronation and supination strength, Kotte et al. (2018) found average pronation strength to be 93% of supination strength for the dominant arm and 98% of supination strength for the non-dominant arm among males. Females exhibited a mildly greater discrepancy as their average pronation strength was 90% of their supination strength for the dominant arm and 89% of supination strength for the non-dominant arm. Correspondingly, forearm pronation strength will more likely serve as the limiting factor than supination strength during an exercise training both functions, but the difference may be fairly small. Relative to the general population, the discrepancy between supination strength and pronation strength will likely be greater among lifters who commonly perform any curling, vertical pulling (e.g., lat pulldown, pull-up), or rowing variations since these exercises can strengthen the biceps. With the exception of the brachioradialis, which can contribute to both pronation and supination while being effectively trained along with the biceps by exercises resisting elbow flexion, the other muscles that function as forearm pronators or supinators are unlikely to be meaningfully trained by exercises that people most commonly perform. Compared to the general population, lifters consequently will likely have proportionally greater forearm supination strength relative to pronation strength. If your pronation strength limits performance of this combined exercise before you feel your supinators are meaningfully fatigued, you simply can finish the set by performing reps through the half of the movement that resists supination (i.e., alternating between the neutral start position and the palm down position). With that approach, you can ensure that both your supinators and your pronators are effectively trained by the time you finish the exercise.

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to the barbell situated on the ground, position a large diameter weight plate (or a viable alternative) under the center of the bar that you will use to create a deficit.
    1. While you can use a variety of deficit heights based on your hamstring flexibility, selecting a low deficit height (under 4in (10cm)) is initially recommended to facilitate the appropriate technique.
    2. Pick a height that keeps your lower back flat and shins vertical at the bottom of the rep.
    3. A large diameter (e.g., 45lb (20kg)) cast iron weight plate with the flat surface facing up can be a suitable option to select since these plates are normally near 1.5in (3.8cm) thick.
    4. A bumper plate or stackable deadlift block can also be used for your deficit.
    5. Depending on your hip width, you can also position two plates directly next to each other if the soles of your feet do not fit fully onto one plate in a hip-width stance.
    6. As an alternative to standing on a plate or step, you can also train through an extended range of motion by exclusively loading smaller diameter plates onto the bar and standing on the ground.
2. With your feet fully planted on the sturdy elevated surface, stand close to the middle of the bar in approximately a hip-width stance.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the ground, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track far forward. However, you can let your knees shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
4. With straight elbows, firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip, such that your palms face backward.
    1. As an alternative to the double overhand grip, you can use a mixed grip (with one palm facing forward and the other facing backward) or lifting straps with the double overhand grip if you wish.
    2. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    3. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    4. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than at the base of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hands while you hold it, which pulls on your hand skin uncomfortably and increases the risk of tearing a callus.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
6. While keeping your lower back flat and chest up, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.
    1. Keep your elbows straight and the bar very close to your legs as you lift the bar, rather than letting the bar drift forward.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight with the bar just in front of your legs. Avoid letting the bar drift forward away from you, which may be more likely to occur if you think about “bending over” rather than “sitting back.”
    2. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the bar.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    5. Throughout the set, keep your feet fully planted on the ground and your neck near a neutral position, as when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.

### Learning how to hip hinge

If you have minimal experience training hip hinge exercises such as Romanian deadlift and good morning variations, it is normal to have difficulty performing this movement pattern. Like riding a bicycle or shooting a basketball, hip hinging is a motor skill that may require repeated practice before you feel comfortable consistently using it. Broadly speaking, there are two types of movement substitution patterns that individuals who are in the process of learning how to hip hinge commonly perform when attempting to execute a hip hinge exercise.

One of these is using a stoop lift, which involves dynamically rounding the back (through flexion of the lumbar and thoracic spine) to bend over prior to uncoiling the spine into an upright position during the ascent. This often is accompanied by the buttock not moving particularly far backward and the arms drifting out in front of the legs in contrast to a strict hip hinge, which utilizes a visibly flat back position (with close to a neutral lumbar spine) and has the buttock noticeably moving backward during the descent. In terms of similarity, a stoop lift and a hip hinge both involve only a mild magnitude of knee bend during the descent while keeping the hips high. A clue that you may be performing more of a stoop lift than a hip hinge is feeling a stretching sensation in your back rather than feeling your back muscles remain statically tight throughout your set as these muscles function to maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips. With a properly performed hip hinge, you should certainly feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the bottom of the lift, but you may also feel this stretching sensation during a stoop lift. Nonetheless, a hip hinge can allow you to feel the hamstring stretch earlier during the descent compared to a stoop lift since the hamstrings are shortened by the posterior pelvic tilt (tucking the tailbone under) that is coupled with lumbar spine flexion.

In addition to performing a stoop lift unintentionally when attempting to hip hinge, people can commonly utilize more of a squatting motion that is characterized by greater knee bend and forward tracking of the knees during the descent. Compared to a hip hinge, using more of a squatting movement can result in the buttock moving downward during the descent as opposed to backward, and the shins can also incline forward as opposed to remaining vertical. Because the hamstrings shorten as the knees bend, someone moving in a squat pattern when attempting to perform a hip hinge exercise is unlikely to feel much of a stretching sensation in the hamstrings at the bottom of the lift. Not feeling a hamstring stretch is the most straightforward indicator that you may be squatting your hip hinge exercise, but an additional clue would be if you perceive your quads to be working (e.g., feeling a “burning” sensation or lots of tension) more intensely than your hamstrings during the exercise.

When thinking about moving through hip hinge, stoop lift, and squat patterns, it is important to recognize that these movements can occur along a spectrum. You can perform a hip hinge exercise with a technique that is mostly a hip hinge while still utilizing elements of a stoop lift or a squat that may not be ideal for what you wish to accomplish from the exercise. Similarly, your technique can incrementally progress from being stoop lift-dominant or squat-dominant to becoming progressively more of a hip hinge as your body learns how to move in a different way through repeated practice. If your hip hinge technique currently has much room for improvement, it can be beneficial to start with lighter loads that may not be especially challenging to your muscles until you developed a reasonable level of competency with the movement itself. There is no need to let perfect be the enemy of good, so you do not need to wait to load a movement meaningfully until you have immaculate technique, but it would also be inadvisable to push your body to the limit without initially learning the basic fundamentals of the movement.

Depending on which element of hip hinging in which you currently are challenged, certain external cues can expedite how quickly you can learn how to hinge. When unintentionally moving in a manner that involves a greater degree of squatting or stoop lifting than is intended, a wall may help provide tactile feedback to cue sitting your buttock backward. To do so, you can perform your hip hinge with your back facing a nearby wall, and you will be able to receive confirmation as to whether you are actually sitting your hips backward by feeling the wall contact your buttock at the end of the descent. As an initial starting point, you can set up with a heel-to-toe tandem stance as the back of one heel contacts the wall. Then you can bring your rear foot forward to be aligned with your front foot in the symmetrical stance you will utilize for your hip hinge. This can provide a reasonable approximation as to how far people may commonly be able to sit their hips back when hinging, but you can adjust from there how far away you position yourself from the wall to individualize it to you.

Specifically if you have a tendency to perform a “squatty” hip hinge, practicing your hip hinge with your calves up against something like a flat exercise bench (or even a couch or chair at home) can be a rather productive means of honing your hinge. As you descend, you will receive immediate tactile feedback if your knees track forward from no longer feeling the contact with your calves, so it can be a great way to reinforce keeping your shins vertical throughout the movement. When using this method, make sure that you maintain full contact between the soles of your feet and the ground while you avoid leaning your bodyweight into the bench to the extent that you would fall backward if the bench was removed. If you successfully keep your calves in contact with the bench throughout the movement and feel a pronounced stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the end of the descent, you are right on track to achieving a high quality hip hinge.

As an additional learning tool, you can situate a long object like a dowel rod, PVC pipe, or yardstick on your back while hip hinging if you have a tendency to utilize more of a stoop lift technique with excessive back rounding. Either the calf-to-bench technique or the buttock-to-wall technique can be incorporated into an actual Romanian deadlift where you use weights, but using a rod as a cue without a partner will require you to hold the rod in place, so you would not be able to load this drill independently. To perform this movement, you would hold the rod behind against your back with one hand higher up near your head and your other hand lower down near your buttock. While standing fully upright and looking straight ahead, you should feel the rod contacting your sacrum (the bone that lies between your upper buttock cheeks and right above your tailbone), upper back between your shoulder blades, and the back of your head. You will then hip hinge while maintaining these three points of contact throughout the entirety of the movement. If you start rounding your back or moving your neck beyond the neutral position you adopt when standing fully upright, you will feel the rod lose contact with one of those three spots. This can be a rather effective form of instant feedback to help develop your ability to move predominantly through your lower body while keeping your trunk in a rigid position throughout the movement, which can transfer to improved technique for an array of different exercises. When maintaining those three contact points, you potentially can still perform a squatting motion rather than a hip hinge since moving through your lower body while minimizing back motion is also a component of squatting technique. However, if you maintain those three contact points and additionally feel your hamstrings notably stretched at the bottom of the descent, those two factors indicate that you have successfully hip hinged in all likelihood. If you find that the rod cuing shifts your movement from a stoop lift to more of a squat, you can use the rod cuing simultaneously with the calf-to-bench cuing, which can address multiple aspects of the hip hinge concurrently.

In the context of performing a hip hinge exercise, using a form that resembles more of a squat or stoop lift rather than a hip hinge can be considered technique errors, but squatting and stoop lifting are by no means faulty movement patterns inherently. They simply differ from a hip hinge, so they can be suboptimal means of performing an exercise that you intend to train specifically for the benefits that hip hinging can provide as opposed to other movements. The hip hinge can take some practice to learn, but investing the time and effort into doing so can be a prudent investment given that having the motor skill of hip hinging can meaningfully expand your freedom in how you can move both inside and outside of the gym.

### **Straps**

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your lower body or lower back strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your lower body and back muscles. Among trained lifters, grip strength can very commonly limit performance of Romanian deadlifts if they do not utilize straps since the posterior chain has the potential to move rather heavy loads for this exercise. As a simple approach you can use if you are unsure whether grip strength is limiting your performance, you can perform a set of as many quality reps as you can with a particular weight without using straps and compare your rep total to a set using straps. To perform an appropriate comparison, you would want to ensure that you are using the same technique for each condition, which will mean using the same range of motion and tempo. Additionally, you would want to perform each condition when you are similarly recovered. Practically, resting at least a few minutes between the two sets should allow most fatigue to dissipate by the time you perform the second set, therefore enabling a useful comparison in terms of how performance of this exercise may be affected by your grip strength. However, if you really wish to optimize the validity of your self-assessment, you can compare your rep performance between these conditions on a second day where you reverse the order of the conditions. If you performed the set without straps prior to the set using straps on the first day, you perform the set using straps before the set without straps on a different day to control for how any fatigue resulting from the first set may influence the second set. When comparing how many reps you complete during each condition, you will be well informed as to how grip strength may be affecting performance of this exercise for you as an individual.

### **Romanian deadlift vs stiff-leg deadlift**

The terms “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” are often used interchangeably to describe the same exercise by scholarly articles and lifters in general. The nomenclature of the Romanian deadlift has been attributed to this exercise being performed by Nicu Vlad, a Romanian weightlifter who won gold, silver, and bronze medals respectively in the 1984, 1988, and 1996 Olympic games in addition to medaling in seven World Weightlifting Championships (with three of them being gold). American weightlifting coach Jim Schmitz reportedly saw Vlad performing the barbell hip hinge exercise and subsequently called it the Romanian deadlift since Vlad did not have a particular name for the variation he was performing.

While they may be commonly used to refer to the same exercise, some people will use the names “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” to refer to different variations. They consider the stiff-leg deadlift to be what is described in this database as the “barbell stiff-leg deadlift from floor,” which involves each rep starting with the plates fully on the floor like a conventional deadlift. This variation differs from the Romanian deadlift, which starts from the upright position and uses a range of motion individualized to someone’s flexibility as the plates often do not contact the floor. If someone has the hamstring flexibility for the plates to contact the floor during a Romanian deadlift, a light tap to the ground is utilized, but the full weight of the bar is not transferred into the ground like how the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor is performed. In contrast to the Romanian deadlift, which is typically performed with a controlled lowering phase, this conception of the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor often involves a quicker lower phase with a tempo akin to how conventional deadlifts are commonly performed, which is to say a controlled drop. Both variations can involve a mild amount of knee flexion at the bottom of the hinge, but the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor can require that someone adopts a more flexed lumbar position in order to pull from the floor with the knee position while maintaining high hips. This differs from the Romanian deadlift being performed only through the range of motion where someone can maintain close to a neutral lumbar spine or a flat back position.

As demonstrated by sources such as Hegyi et al. (2018) along with Piper and Waller (2001), another interpretation of the stiff-leg deadlift also exists as a truly straight leg deadlift. Under this conception of the exercise, the knees are kept extended to the extent that they are completely straight but not fully locked (which could otherwise allow for knee hyperextension in individuals with the mobility to do so). Such a technique would result in a movement that is more akin to “bending over” rather than “sitting back,” and the bar would correspondingly be likely to drift further in front of the legs compared to a Romanian deadlift, which utilizes a mild knee bend that allows you to “sit back.” In light of the different ways in which these names may be interpreted, hopefully this note provides some clarification if you have ever been confused by how different individuals may view Romanian deadlifts and stiff-leg deadlifts exercises as the same exercise or distinct variations.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground.
    1. The size of the weight plates you add to the bar will determine how high the bar lies above the ground, which consequently affects your range of motion. Adding a pair of full diameter plates (like 45lb (20kg) plates or any bumper plates) will elevate the bar to the standard height (about 9in (23cm)) when deadlifting from the floor. If you only use smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a deficit stiff-leg deadlift with an extended range of motion that requires greater than average mobility to perform with quality technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize 45lb (20kg) plates, you can elevate the bar like you would for a [block pull](Conventional%20mid-shin%20block%20pull%201a35c6f170d880349a3beab3040acdc9.md) or [rack pull](Mid-shin%20rack%20pull%201a35c6f170d880fd8a71e340d039d10a.md) and otherwise use the same stiff-leg deadlift technique described by this page.
2. While facing the center of the bar, stand in an approximately hip-width stance with the middle of your feet under the bar and your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly out to the sides.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
    2. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    3. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
3. While only allowing your knees to bend minimally and keeping your hips up, sit your hips backward to incline your torso until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. As you keep your shins vertical, the vast majority of motion should occur from you hinging at your hips, which should result in you feeling a notable stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the bottom. However, you should not keep your knees locked in a completely straight position. A mild degree of knee bend will naturally occur as you focus on sitting your hips backward without intentionally locking your knees.
    2. As a cue for hip hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    3. Without lowering their hips and bending their knees further to turn this exercise into a conventional deadlift, most individuals will have to experience a mild degree of back rounding to reach the bar. Strive to have this modest rounding distributed throughout the entirety of your lower, middle, and upper back rather than only rounding your lower back.
    4. Throughout this exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. With your elbows fully straightened, firmly grasp the bar with an approximately shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. As an alternative to the double overhand grip, you can naturally use a mixed grip (with one palm facing forward and the other facing backward) or lifting straps with the double overhand grip if you wish to do so.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a stable back position.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” into the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your back tight, drive your hips forward to lift your torso up until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Avoid letting your back dynamically round when starting to lift the bar. Rather than amplifying the mildly rounded back position you adopted when setting up, your back should straighten toward a neutral position (like when you are normally upright) during this step. Recognizing that your lower back may not be fully flat in the bottom position, it can help to think about keeping your lower back flat and chest up to resist rounding your lower back or collapsing your chest when lifting the bar through your hips.
    2. Rather than letting the bar drift forward, keep it over the middle of your feet throughout the set to move the bar in a straight line.
    3. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    4. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
4. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips via sitting your buttocks backward to lower the bar in a controlled manner. Keep your hips up and your shins vertical as you use essentially the same technique during step 3 of the setup.
    1. While you can let your back mildly round while staying tight and chiefly bending your hips, avoid letting your back excessively round in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. There is no need to lower the bar extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the bar drop into a free fall.
    3. Your knees should only bend by a mild degree, resulting in you feeling a hamstring stretch.
5. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is on the ground rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.

However, some people consider these names to refer to different hip variations, and this database includes three different exercises to allow you to select whichever specific variation you wish to utilize. Under this usage of the terms, the straight-leg deadlift utilizes a literally straight knee position in contrast to the mild knee bend that is involved with the Romanian or still-leg deadlift from the floor. This conception of the straight-leg deadlift, which has been demonstrated by sources such as Hegyi et al. (2018) along with Piper and Waller (2001), may be utilized less commonly than the other two variations. 

Both the straight-leg deadlift and the Romanian deadlift start from the upright position and use a range of motion individualized to someone’s flexibility as the plates often do not contact the floor. If someone has the hamstring flexibility for the plates to contact the floor during either of these variations (which is much rarer with the straight-leg deadlift), a light tap to the ground is utilized. In contrast, the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor involves each rep starting with the plates fully on the floor like a conventional deadlift and results in the full weight of the bar being transferred into the ground at the end of each rep. All three of these variations are hip hinge exercises that train the same muscle groups, but how different muscles are emphasized may mildly differ depending on the variation. Relative to the other two variations, the straight-leg deadlift will result in a lower range of motion for most people since the hamstrings are lengthened to a greater with completely straight knees compared to mildly bent knees. Correspondingly, someone can reach maximal hamstring elongation sooner during the descent of a straight-leg deadlift, which limits the degree to which the hips can flex before someone starts the lifting phase of the exercise. Compared to using a mild knee bend, a straight-leg deadlift also constrains how far you can sit your buttock backward and results in the bar drifting farther out in front of your legs during the descent.

Compared to a hip hinge, using more of a squatting movement can result in the buttock moving downward during the descent as opposed to backward, and the shins can also incline forward as opposed to remaining vertical. Because the hamstrings shorten as the knees bend, someone moving in a squat pattern when attempting to perform a hip hinge exercise is unlikely to feel much of a stretching sensation in the hamstrings at the bottom of the lift. 4. Hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar, while your elbows are straight.
    1. You can set up with the bar approximately over the middle of your feet, which should situate the bar close to one inch (2.5cm) away from most individuals’ shins while initially standing upright.
    2. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    3. Throughout this movement, keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so.
5. Firmly grasp the bar with an approximately shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.

    1. To brace effectively, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.

    3. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    4. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    5. While your lower back muscles will be working to maintain a rigid trunk position, lifting the bar upward should chiefly occur from your hip and thigh muscles extending your hips and knees.

1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight with the bar just in front of your legs. Avoid letting the bar drift forward away from you, which may be more likely to occur if you think about “bending over” rather than “sitting back.”
    2. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the bar.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.

2. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move.

    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.

If you find that your grip strength functions as the limiting factor as opposed to your lower body or lower back strength when performing this exercise, you can utilize chalk or straps in an effort to amplify the stimulus each set provides your lower body and back muscles. The terms “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” are often used interchangeably to describe the same exercise by scholarly articles and lifters in general.
