American weightlifting coach Jim Schmitz reportedly saw Vlad performing the barbell hip hinge exercise and subsequently called it the Romanian deadlift since Vlad did not have a particular name for the variation he was performing.

While they may be commonly used to refer to the same exercise, some people will use the names “Romanian deadlift” and “stiff-leg deadlift” to refer to different variations. They consider the stiff-leg deadlift to be what is described in this database as the “barbell stiff-leg deadlift from floor,” which involves each rep starting with the plates fully on the floor like a conventional deadlift. This variation differs from the Romanian deadlift, which starts from the upright position and uses a range of motion individualized to someone’s flexibility as the plates often do not contact the floor. If someone has the hamstring flexibility for the plates to contact the floor during a Romanian deadlift, a light tap to the ground is utilized, but the full weight of the bar is not transferred into the ground like how the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor is performed. In contrast to the Romanian deadlift, which is typically performed with a controlled lowering phase, this conception of the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor often involves a quicker lower phase with a tempo akin to how conventional deadlifts are commonly performed, which is to say a controlled drop. Both variations can involve a mild amount of knee flexion at the bottom of the hinge, but the stiff-leg deadlift from the floor can require that someone adopts a more flexed lumbar position in order to pull from the floor with the knee position while maintaining high hips. This differs from the Romanian deadlift being performed only through the range of motion where someone can maintain close to a neutral lumbar spine or a flat back position.

As demonstrated by sources such as Hegyi et al. (2018) along with Piper and Waller (2001), another interpretation of the stiff-leg deadlift also exists as a truly straight leg deadlift. Under this conception of the exercise, the knees are kept extended to the extent that they are completely straight but not fully locked (which could otherwise allow for knee hyperextension in individuals with the mobility to do so). Such a technique would result in a movement that is more akin to “bending over” rather than “sitting back,” and the bar would correspondingly be likely to drift further in front of the legs compared to a Romanian deadlift, which utilizes a mild knee bend that allows you to “sit back.” In light of the different ways in which these names may be interpreted, hopefully this note provides some clarification if you have ever been confused by how different individuals may view Romanian deadlifts and stiff-leg deadlifts exercises as the same exercise or distinct variations.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the power rack’s J-hooks to a height that allows you to position the bar on your upper back and walk out the weight comfortably.
    1. As an initial approximation, you can position the J-hooks such that they are a few finger widths below the height of your collarbone. 
    2. You may have to re-adjust the height of the J-hooks later.
2. After placing the barbell on top of the J-hooks, face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
3. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to then walk under the bar and situate the bar on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    2. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
    5. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
    7. If you find that deeper than a mild bend at your hips and knees is (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) is required to position the bar on your back, you can lift the bar out of the J-hooks, set it down, raise the height of the J-hooks, and place the bar back onto the J-hooks.
4. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back and stand up in a quarter squat-like manner by extending your knees and hips.
5. After standing upright with the bar, check if you selected an appropriate height for the J-hooks.
    1. The bar should be above the tops of the J-hooks such that they would not contact the bar when walking out backward.
    2. If you need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too low.
    3. If this is the case, lift the bar out of the J-hooks, set it down, lower the height of the J-hooks, place the bar back onto the J-hooks, and recheck to ensure you can walk out the weight without rising onto the balls of your feet.
    4. Walking out with your heels raised up will increase the risk of you losing your balance and should consequently be avoided whenever you have a barbell on your back.
6. After confirming the J-hooks are positioned appropriately, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of good morning reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
7. Load the bar with your intended weight and position the safety pins to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of the good morning.
## Exercise technique
1. With the hand placement and bar positioning determined while setting up, un-rack the bar standing up in a quarter squat-like manner by extending your knees and hips while pulling down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back.
2. Take a couple of steps backward, and position your feet into a clearly outside shoulder-width stance with your feet rotated mildly to moderately to point your toes outward and the soles of your feet fully contacting the floor.
    1. Specifically how wide a stance and how much you point your toes outward can be based on what feels comfortable and stable to you as an individual.
3. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    4. Bracing will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips throughout your set.
4. Hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner to move your buttocks backward while you allow your knees to bend mildly.
    1. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than rounding your lower back while doing so.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened.
    4. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    5. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something, as you keep your chest up (rather than letting your chest collapse through back rounding).
    6. While you hinge at your hips, the bar will naturally descend, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    7. How deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    8. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit your buttocks any farther back, you have finished descending through your available range of motion.
    9. If you positioned them appropriately, the safety pins should not restrict how far you can hip hinge, but if you are able to hinge until the bar contacts the safety pins, you can lightly tap the safety pins with the bar without resting the bar on the pins.
5. Reverse the movement by pulling your hips forward until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. Since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, all of the technique points from the lowering phase apply to how to perform the lifting phase, except for the details on how deeply to hip hinge.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
7. Re-rack the bar by walking forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup, and you are ready to rest the bar on the J-hooks by once again bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner.
    1. Depending on how wide a stance you adopted, you may feel more balanced if you initially bring your feet closer together before walking forward to re-rack the weight.

It is by no means rare for people to perform exercises with a bar on their back without setting up safety pins, but using safety pins when appropriate is strongly recommended. It is worth noting using pins in this manner is distinct from the barbell pin good morning, which involves letting the bar come to a dead stop and fully resting on the pins at the bottom of each rep.

3. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.

While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise dynamically trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

### **Reducing set up time**

Relative to a variety of other exercises, exercises performed with a barbell on your back can require more time initially to set them up appropriately as is demonstrated by the fairly lengthy “setting up” section. However, subsequent sessions in which you perform the same exercise can involve a quicker set up relative to the first time in which you use this exercise. To save time during future sessions, you can record the height that you determined was appropriate to position the J-cups and safety pins. If your power rack has numbered pin holes, you can simply note the positions you used. Without numbered holes, you can note how many holes were above your J-cup position and how many holes were between your safety pin position and your J-cup position. Consequently, you will not need to take a trial and error approach when setting up your power rack each session.

### **Learning how to hip hinge**

If you have minimal experience training hip hinge exercises such as Romanian deadlift and good morning variations, it is normal to have difficulty performing this movement pattern. Like riding a bicycle or shooting a basketball, hip hinging is a motor skill that may require repeated practice before you feel comfortable consistently using it. Broadly speaking, there are two types of movement substitution patterns that individuals who are in the process of learning how to hip hinge commonly perform when attempting to execute a hip hinge exercise.

One of these is using a stoop lift, which involves dynamically rounding the back (through flexion of the lumbar and thoracic spine) to bend over prior to uncoiling the spine into an upright position during the ascent. This often is accompanied by the buttock not moving particularly far backward and the arms drifting out in front of the legs in contrast to a strict hip hinge, which utilizes a visibly flat back position (with close to a neutral lumbar spine) and has the buttock noticeably moving backward during the descent. In terms of similarity, a stoop lift and a hip hinge both involve only a mild magnitude of knee bend during the descent while keeping the hips high. A clue that you may be performing more of a stoop lift than a hip hinge is feeling a stretching sensation in your back rather than feeling your back muscles remain statically tight throughout your set as these muscles function to maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips. With a properly performed hip hinge, you should certainly feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the bottom of the lift, but you may also feel this stretching sensation during a stoop lift. Nonetheless, a hip hinge can allow you to feel the hamstring stretch earlier during the descent compared to a stoop lift since the hamstrings are shortened by the posterior pelvic tilt (tucking the tailbone under) that is coupled with lumbar spine flexion.

In addition to performing a stoop lift unintentionally when attempting to hip hinge, people can commonly utilize more of a squatting motion that is characterized by greater knee bend and forward tracking of the knees during the descent. Compared to a hip hinge, using more of a squatting movement can result in the buttock moving downward during the descent as opposed to backward, and the shins can also incline forward as opposed to remaining vertical. Because the hamstrings shorten as the knees bend, someone moving in a squat pattern when attempting to perform a hip hinge exercise is unlikely to feel much of a stretching sensation in the hamstrings at the bottom of the lift. Not feeling a hamstring stretch is the most straightforward indicator that you may be squatting your hip hinge exercise, but an additional clue would be if you perceive your quads to be working (e.g., feeling a “burning” sensation or lots of tension) more intensely than your hamstrings during the exercise.

You can perform a hip hinge exercise with a technique that is mostly a hip hinge while still utilizing elements of a stoop lift or a squat that may not be ideal for what you wish to accomplish from the exercise. Similarly, your technique can incrementally progress from being stoop lift-dominant or squat-dominant to becoming progressively more of a hip hinge as your body learns how to move in a different way through repeated practice. If your hip hinge technique currently has much room for improvement, it can be beneficial to start with lighter loads that may not be especially challenging to your muscles until you developed a reasonable level of competency with the movement itself. Specifically if you have a tendency to perform a “squatty” hip hinge, practicing your hip hinge with your calves up against something like a flat exercise bench (or even a couch or chair at home) can be a rather productive means of honing your hinge. As you descend, you will receive immediate tactile feedback if your knees track forward from no longer feeling the contact with your calves, so it can be a great way to reinforce keeping your shins vertical throughout the movement. When using this method, make sure that you maintain full contact between the soles of your feet and the ground while you avoid leaning your bodyweight into the bench to the extent that you would fall backward if the bench was removed. If you successfully keep your calves in contact with the bench throughout the movement and feel a pronounced stretching sensation in your hamstrings at the end of the descent, you are right on track to achieving a high quality hip hinge.

As an additional learning tool, you can situate a long object like a dowel rod, PVC pipe, or yardstick on your back while hip hinging if you have a tendency to utilize more of a stoop lift technique with excessive back rounding. Either the calf-to-bench technique or the buttock-to-wall technique can be incorporated into an actual Romanian deadlift where you use weights, but using a rod as a cue without a partner will require you to hold the rod in place, so you would not be able to load this drill independently. To perform this movement, you would hold the rod behind against your back with one hand higher up near your head and your other hand lower down near your buttock. While standing fully upright and looking straight ahead, you should feel the rod contacting your sacrum (the bone that lies between your upper buttock cheeks and right above your tailbone), upper back between your shoulder blades, and the back of your head. You will then hip hinge while maintaining these three points of contact throughout the entirety of the movement. If you start rounding your back or moving your neck beyond the neutral position you adopt when standing fully upright, you will feel the rod lose contact with one of those three spots. This can be a rather effective form of instant feedback to help develop your ability to move predominantly through your lower body while keeping your trunk in a rigid position throughout the movement, which can transfer to improved technique for an array of different exercises. When maintaining those three contact points, you potentially can still perform a squatting motion rather than a hip hinge since moving through your lower body while minimizing back motion is also a component of squatting technique. However, if you maintain those three contact points and additionally feel your hamstrings notably stretched at the bottom of the descent, those two factors indicate that you have successfully hip hinged in all likelihood. ## Setting up
1. Strap an ankle weight to each of your ankles, and lie down on your back with straight legs as your feet are hip-width apart.
    1. On the ground, your legs and torso should be in the same position in which you exhibit when normally standing upright.
    2. As an alternative to keeping both knees straight, you have the option of keeping one knee (on the side that you are not about to train) bent with that side’s foot flat on the floor if you are more comfortable in that position.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one foot on the ground, lift the other leg up off the ground through your hip’s available range of motion. Keep your knee straight and the rest of your body stationary.
    1. How high you are able to lift the leg will be influenced by your hamstring flexibility, since flexing your hip with a straight knee position stretches your hamstrings.
    2. While performing this movement with the appropriate technique, you will likely feel the muscles on the front of your upper thigh contracting.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your working leg to descend in a controlled manner until the back of its heel lightly contacts the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [hip flexor muscles](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md), including your [psoas major](../Muscles/Psoas%20Major%201925c6f170d880d9bd8ff7b80b3b3368.md), [iliacus](../Muscles/Iliacus%201925c6f170d880dbbf66e6d67529db1e.md), [rectus femoris](../Muscles/Rectus%20Femoris%201925c6f170d880f080b7cda6f5f3f0ee.md), and [tensor fascia latae](../Muscles/Tensor%20Fascia%20Latae%201925c6f170d8806fb83bf08142d940fc.md).

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your legs straight, feet approximately hip-width apart, and the back of your head either resting on the ground or on top of your hands, which you can clasp behind your head.
    1. If you do not want to position your hands behind your head, feel free to place your arms wherever you prefer (e.g., resting on the ground by your sides).
    2. On the ground, your legs and torso should be in the same position you exhibit when normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your knees straight, lift both feet slightly (about 6 inches (or 15 centimeters)) off the ground, tightening your abdominal muscles to press your lower back into the ground.
    1. Pressing your lower back into the ground will flatten it out from abdominal muscle contraction and prevent you from sliding a hand under it.
    2. If you do not contract your abdominals, lifting both legs would prompt your lower back to develop an exaggerated arch, allowing you to slide a hand under it.
    3. For this variation, you will either rest your head on the ground or on your hands (as you prefer).
2. Statically hold the position you reached from step 1 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Along with training your hip flexor muscles on the front of your thigh, this exercise can statically train your abdominal muscles, including your obliques and rectus abdominis, which is the “six-pack muscle.”

### How the abdominal and hip flexor muscles work together

As with many other abdominal exercises, the six-inch leg raise trains the abdominal muscles concurrently with the hip flexor muscles due to the opposing forces these muscles can generate at the lumbopelvic region (i.e., the pelvis and lower back). For the sake of having clearer directions when referring to “up” or “down” during this explanation, we can imagine that you are standing upright rather than lying down, like you would when performing this exercise. To lift the thigh via hip flexion, the hip flexor muscles contract, creating a pulling force from the front of the pelvis toward the thigh. Muscle contraction generates a force at both ends to which a muscle attaches, and the hip flexor muscles either originate on the front of the pelvis or cross the front of the pelvis as they course toward their insertion on the femur (thigh bone) or tibia (shin bone). If left unopposed, the force from the hip flexor muscles will rotate the front of the pelvis down toward the thigh as the back of the pelvis rotates up toward the lower back via a motion known as anterior (forward) pelvic tilting. When the pelvis tilts in this manner, the lumbar spine extends correspondingly as the natural arch of the lower back becomes exaggerated into a sway-back posture.

Contraction of the abdominal muscles is able to produce the opposite motions, given that they arise from the ribs and attach to the top surface of the front aspect of the pelvis. To pull the ribs closer to the top of the pelvis, the lumbar spine flexes, initially flattening the natural curvature of the lower back and then rounding it with further flexion. Contraction of the abdominal muscles can also pull the upper surface of the front of the pelvis up toward the ribs as the back of the pelvis rotates down toward the thigh, a motion known as posterior (backward) pelvic tilting. Due to the posterior pelvic tilt function of the abdominals and the anterior pelvic tilt function of the hip flexors, these two muscle groups can operate in tandem. Whenever the legs lift off the ground via hip flexion, the abdominal muscles stabilize the lumbopelvic region by preventing the lower back from arching beyond its natural curvature, through a combination of anterior pelvic tilt and lumbar spine extension that would otherwise occur with abdominal muscle contraction.

### Six-inch leg raise progression

As you progressively increase your abdominal strength, you can progress from the six-inch leg raise with the head on the ground to the six-inch leg raise with the head and upper back lifted up off the ground. When the upper back is off the ground, the abdominals have to work to prevent the thoracic spine from extending, while they are already working to prevent the lumbar spine from extending, which increases the intensity of the exercise.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with straight legs and your feet hip width apart. Rest your head on the ground with your arms by your sides in contact with the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift both legs off the ground until your thighs are approximately vertical. Only allow your knees to bend mildly, and tighten your abs  to press your lower back down into the ground.
    1. Ideally keep your knees as close to straight as you can without your hamstring flexibility restricting your range of motion.
    2. Pressing your lower back into the ground will flatten it out from abdominal muscle contraction and prevent you from being able to slide a hand under your lower back.
    3. If you do not contract your abdominals, lifting both legs up would prompt your lower back to develop an exaggerated arch that would allow you to slide a hand under your lower back.
2. Drive your buttocks and hip bones up off the floor while curling up your lower back, which will lift your legs higher up.
    1. Without locking them, continue keeping your knees as straightened as your hamstring flexibility permits.
    2. You should naturally feel your abdominal muscles further tighten while doing so.
3. Reverse the movement from step 2 by allowing your buttocks and hip bones to lower down to the floor in a controlled manner as you uncurl your lower back.
4. Reverse the movement from step 1 by allowing your legs to descend in a controlled manner until the backs of your heels lightly contact the ground.
    1. Continue tightening your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground as you lower your legs.
5. Alternate between performing steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Position yourself on your palms, knees, and toes, with your elbows straight and your knees bent.
    1. In this “on all fours” position, your upper arms and thighs should be directed straight down such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    2. Your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position with the natural curvature you have when normally standing upright rather than being rounded or excessively arched.
## Exercise technique
1. Begin bracing your core by taking a deep “belly breath” (also known as a diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
2. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    1. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forceful slap.
3. While keeping your core braced, simultaneously sweep your right leg backward and your left arm forward in a slow, controlled manner, lifting these two limbs slightly off the ground as you straighten your right knee and left elbow.
    1. As you do so, you can squeeze your right glute while squeezing your left hand into a fist to create whole body tension that promotes a rigid trunk position.
    2. While you move your right leg at your hip and left arm at your shoulder, the rest of your body should be as close to stationary as is physically possible for you.
    3. When maintaining the appropriately rigid trunk position, someone should be able to place an object such as a mug of water on top of your back without the object falling off your back as you lift your leg and arm.
    4. Particularly avoid dynamically arching your lower back or tilting your right hip bone up.
    5. Do not lift your leg and arm any higher beyond a range that allows you to keep your trunk in a rigidly static position.
    6. As long as you move an arm and a leg on opposite sides of your body, you can choose which sides you move first in your set, but mentioning the sides as an example can help clarify technique.
4. Statically hold your right leg and left arm in the position you just adopted, then slowly return them to their initial position, with your right knee and left hand on the floor as your upper arms and thighs are directed straight down toward the ground.
    1. You can aim to hold your leg and arm off the ground for at least a couple of seconds, but it is up to you specifically how long you wish to maintain that position before returning them to the ground.
    2. After returning to having both your legs and arms on the ground, take a breath before resuming to brace your core.
5. Proceed to perform steps 3 and 4 with your left leg and right arm in the same manner you just utilized with your other sides.
6. Alternate between steps 3 and 5 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your core muscles to maintain a rigid trunk position as you refine your ability to move through your hips and shoulders with a stable trunk.

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.
    1. Your upper arms should be directed straight down such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. You should now be in the same position as the top of a push-up.
2. Tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes to maintain a flat back position while keeping your elbows and knees straight.
    1. Doing so keeps your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting them sag downward, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
    4. Keep your neck in a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright.
3. While keeping your knees straightened, lift one foot slightly up off the ground and hold it in that position briefly as you keep your abdominal muscles and glutes tightened to maintain the same rigid trunk position you adopted in step 2.
    1. While you move your leg at your hip, the rest of your body should be as close to stationary as is physically possible for you.
    2. When maintaining the appropriately rigid trunk position, someone should be able to place an object, such as a mug of water, on top of your back without the object falling off your back as you lift your leg.
    3. Do not lift your leg any higher than the range that allows you to keep your trunk in a rigid, static position.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your lower back dynamically arch or letting your hip bone (on the side of the leg you are lifting) tilt up, which can easily occur if you lift your leg up too far.
4. Lower your foot back onto the ground in a controlled manner before repeating step 3 with your other leg.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise statically trains your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they work to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your hands, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight and your knees are bent.
2. Prop your forearms onto the ground with your upper arms directed straight down such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    1. Based on your preference, you can either make a fist with each hand and direct your palms in toward each other or place your palms flat on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. You should be bearing your bodyweight into the ground through your elbows and feet.
2. Tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes to maintain a flat back position while keeping your knees straight and elbows bent.
    1. Doing so keeps your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting them sag downward, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag down, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
3. While keeping your knees straightened, lift one foot slightly up off the ground and hold it in that position briefly (such as for approximately two seconds).
    1. Continue keeping your abdominal muscles and glutes tightened to maintain the same rigid trunk position you adopted in step 2.
    2. Except for the one leg you are moving, the rest of your body should be as close to stationary as is physically possible for you.
    3. When maintaining the appropriately rigid trunk position, someone should be able to place an object such as a mug of water on top of your back without the object falling off your back as you lift your leg.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your lower back dynamically arch or letting your hip bone (on the side of the leg you are lifting) tilt up.
    5. Lifting your leg until it is approximately parallel to the ground is an appropriate range of motion, but you can lift it up slightly higher if you are able to do so without arching your lower back, which can otherwise easily occur if you lift it up too far.
4. Lower your foot back onto the ground before repeating step 3 with your other leg.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your core muscles, including your rectus abdominis (AKA  the “six pack muscle”) and your abdominal obliques as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back next to your weight with your knees bent as the soles of your feet are flat on the ground and approximately hip width apart.
    1. In addition to using a weight plate, a medicine ball, a dumbbell, or a kettlebell is a viable option that you can use.
    2. You optionally can hook the tops of your feet under a sturdy object like a couch (while your soles are still flat on the ground) to help stabilize your body during this exercise.
2. Pick up the weight, firmly grasp each side of it, and press it up until your arms are directed up toward the ceiling with straight elbows.
    1. After doing so, you can rest your head on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your arms directed straight up, tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground while you lift your head and shoulder blades up off the ground by curling your middle back.
    1. Given that this is a crunch rather than a sit-up, the lower half of your back should remain in contact with the ground while you only lift up the upper half of your back mildly off the floor.
    2. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    3. As a cue, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the top of your hip bones, which is the action that contraction of your abdominal muscles can produce.
    4. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that crunching up any further would require the lower half of your back to start lifting up off the floor.
    5. At the end of the lifting phase, your chest should be facing at an angle between forward and upward as opposed to only facing upward as it did in the starting position.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your middle back to uncurl in a controlled manner as you lower your head and shoulder blades back to the starting position on the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the Roman chair’s pad to a level that positions the top of your hip bones somewhat above the top of the pads when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. This position will allow you to move freely about your hips in contrast to if the pad is contacting the top of your hip bones, which would restrict hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    2. If the top of the pad is positioned much lower than the top of the hip bones (rather than only somewhat lower), some individuals may feel knee discomfort, so a sweet spot can exist for pad placement.
    3. Some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position after initially completing step 2.
2. While placing your hands onto the handles for balance support, step onto the foot plate one leg at a time with the back of your heels in contact with the back of the foot plate, so that the entirety of your soles are in contact with the foot plate.
    1. Position your feet symmetrically in a stance that feels comfortable to you, which can involve pointing your toes somewhat outward or pointing them fairly straight forward.
    2. Situating your feet approximately hip width to shoulder apart from each other will result in a viable stance width, but how wide of a stance you can use will be influenced by the width of your Roman chair’s foot plate.
    3. Your knees should be straight after you have finished setting your feet on the foot plate.
3. Check to make sure that the pad is positioned as described by step 1, and readjust the pad height if it is not prior to resuming your setup.
4. Place the fingertips of each hand lightly in contact with the sides of the back of your head as your upper arms and elbows are directed out away from your sides.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes to keep your torso up such that you can draw approximately a straight line from your legs through your hip and to your torso as opposed to having your torso bent over.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. This is the starting position of the exercise, where your body should look like it does when normally standing upright except at an incline.
2. Begin bracing your core by taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
3. While keeping your core braced, hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner.
    1. Nearly all of the motion should occur from you moving at your hips as you keep your trunk in a static position that maintains the natural curvature of your lower back (as opposed to bending over by rounding your lower back).
    2. Maintain a straight knee position, but you should avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads.
    3. While hinging at your hips and keeping your hands behind your head, you should feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings that progressively intensifies.
    4. Most people will be able to descend until their shoulders are lower than their hips, but how deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    5. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch, you have finished descending through your available hip range of motion.
4. Reverse the movement by lifting your torso up through your hips until you have returned to the starting position, where your torso is aligned with your legs.
    1. You can finish the lifting phase by fully squeezing your glutes, which helps cue hip movement at the top as opposed to spinal movement.
    2. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the hip motion you just performed during the lowering phase.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    4. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, take a fairly long step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. As you do so, start hinging at your front leg’s hip to incline your torso forward while keeping your lower back near a neutral position as opposed to rounding it.
    2. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to backward lunges.
    3. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep your arms directed down toward the ground.
    5. Strive to keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    6. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
2. After contacting the ground with your rear foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue hinging at your front leg’s hip through your available hip range of motion, which will incline your torso further forward while keeping your lower back near a neutral position.
    2. Continue keeping the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    6. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground, and you will likely feel a stretching sensation in your front leg’s buttock.
    7. You should aim to perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    8. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    9. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step backward during your next rep.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step forward with your rear leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. As you extend your knees, reverse the hip hinge motion you just performed to lift your torso up from the inclined angle so that your torso is facing straight ahead.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your arms directed down toward the ground, knees aligned with your feet, and lower back near a neutral position.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging backward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down.
    1. After finishing the last rep, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a kettlebell or dumbbell and hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows, as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. You can use either a kettlebell or a dumbbell, but some people find holding a kettlebell in the goblet position to feel more stable and comfortable, especially with a fairly heavy weight.
    2. Based on your preference and the load you use, you can transfer your kettlebell or dumbbell into the goblet position through a couple of different approaches.
    3. An effective approach is initially to pick up the weight by the handle through a deadlift motion and set it on an elevated surface (like a bench or plyometric box) with the handle facing up if you use a kettlebell or the handle directed vertically if using a dumbbell (as only one end of the dumbbell is on the surface). Then squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it in the goblet position, and squat up with the weight. If you use a kettlebell, grasp it by its horns (i.e., side handles). If you use a dumbbell, cup your hands around the top end of the weight with the base of your palms by the handle, and your fingers wrapped around the rest of that end of the weight.
    4. With a lighter kettlebell, you can tilt it onto its side with the weight base directed toward you, squat down to grasp its horns, stand upright with it, and curl it into the goblet position.
    5. With a lighter dumbbell, you can also pick it up with one hand and curl it up across your body to be in front of your chest. Then cup your free hand around the top end of the dumbbell with the base of its palm by the handle and fingers wrapped around the top end of the weight before repositioning your other hand to cup the other side of the weight in the same manner.
2. While keeping your chest up, position your feet approximately hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight ahead.
    1. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise.
    2. While holding the weight in the goblet position throughout your set, your upper back muscles will have to work to prevent the weight from rounding your upper back, which would prompt your chest to cave.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one foot on the ground, take a fairly long step straight forward with your other foot far enough ahead that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee when lunging down.
    1. Like when you step forward while walking, you can initially contact the ground with your front foot’s heel prior to lowering the entirety of your sole onto the ground in a fluid motion, which will likely occur naturally without having to think about it.
    2. When your front foot contacts the ground, you can allow your rear leg’s heel to start lifting up off the ground, which is also likely to occur naturally.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Strive to step forward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    6. If you are new to forward lunges, you may have to try out different step lengths to determine which step length places you in the appropriate position.
2. After contacting the ground with your front foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep your rear leg’s forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes) and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot’s sole in contact with the ground.
    2. Continue keeping your torso upright and your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step forward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step forward during your next rep.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step backward with your front leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging forward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the weight down.
    1. When setting the weight down, you can just perform the reverse of whichever technique you initially used to place it into the goblet position.

## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad muscles](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md).

### **Can you make your lunge more glute-dominant or quad-dominant?**

When lunging, you can utilize somewhat of a range of varying step lengths while being able to contact the ground with your rear knee as you keep the entirety of your front foot’s sole on the ground. At the short end of this step range, you will be able to drive your front knee farther forward relative to your foot, which will result in your shin being inclined forward. With a long step, you can keep your front shin in a vertical position as the knee stays stacked above the ankle, which requires less knee flexion (bending) range of motion. A longer step may also allow the thigh of the rear leg to be angled further backward (via greater hip extension) compared to the more vertical position of the rear thigh with a shorter step. Since the rear knee can initially be positioned higher up off the floor when the thigh is angled backward, a long step can permit someone to move through a mildly greater hip flexion range of motion during the descent until the rear knee contacts the floor.

These differences can enable a lifter to train the quads in a somewhat more lengthened position when lunging with a short step since the quads are lengthened in increasing angles of knee flexion. On the other hand, a long step may allow someone to train the gluteus maximus and adductor magnus at somewhat longer muscle lengths since these primary hip extensor muscles are lengthened in increasing angles of hip flexion. This has the potential to be relevant because the available body of evidence indicates that the peak length in which a muscle is trained during a particular exercise can most likely influence how much growth the exercise may stimulate. Plenty of muscles have yet to be studied in terms of how their growth may be affected by the lengths in which they are loaded during exercise, but several studies have investigated this topic for the quads. The findings of five of these studies align with each other in the sense that training the quads at moderately long peak lengths (involving up to 90-120 degrees of knee flexion) stimulates greater quad growth than training the quads at moderately short peak lengths (involving up to 50-65 degrees of knee flexion). With at least four separate studies (involving squat interventions, machine leg extension interventions, and a multi-exercise intervention that included lunges) reporting the same outcome, there is fairly strong justification to perform lunges until the rear knee gently taps the ground rather than training through a meaningfully more shallow range of motion. However, the quads can already be trained at moderately long lengths when lunging with a long step, and using a short step changes that by only a fairly small magnitude. This was demonstrated by Escamalla et al. (2025), who reported peak knee flexion angles to be approximately 90-100 degrees when participants lunged with a long step until their rear knee contacted the ground, while they reached about 100-110 degrees of knee flexion with a short step.

Up to a certain point training the quads at longer peak lengths than shorter peak lengths is likely to promote greater hypertrophy, but this effect may have a ceiling. Kubo et al. (2019) found similar quad growth to occur after participants performed a half squat intervention involving 90 degrees of peak knee flexion or a full squat intervention involving 140 degrees of knee flexion. Larsen et al. (2025) also found similar quad growth to occur whether leg pressing until 100 degrees of knee flexion or until the end range of knee flexion for each participant (which was 154 degrees of knee flexion on average). While new evidence may emerge in the future indicating otherwise, these findings suggest that training into very high angles of knee flexion to highly lengthen the quads is not necessarily a superior means of developing the quads than training to approximately 90-100 degrees of knee flexion. Furthermore, the previously mentioned study from Escamalla et al. (2025) found EMG activity of the quads generally to be greater when using a long step compared to a short step. This does not mean that lunging with a long step is necessarily more effective for training the quads than lunging with a short step, but the preponderance of evidence suggests that using a short step is unlikely to train the quads better than lunging with a long step.

On the other hand, it is worth noting that Kubo et al. (2019) found the aforementioned full squat group to experience about three times as much gluteus maximus growth and a little over twice the hip adductor muscle (involving the primary hip extensor adductor magnus) growth relative to the half squat group. With a compound exercise that meaningfully trains knee extension and hip extension simultaneously (like lunge and squat variations), training into high angles of hip flexion may consequently may be beneficial to amplify the hypertrophy stimulus to the hip extensor muscles compared to reaching only a moderately high degree of hip flexion. The findings from one squat study do not guarantee that the same relationship will exist when lunging, but it is certainly plausible that lunges can be similar in this respect. While there is no legitimate reason to think that lunging with a long step would train the hip extensor muscles less effectively than lunging with a short step, the difference in hip range of motion between step lengths potentially may be of a low enough magnitude to be inconsequential for many people. The directionality may be similar, but lunging with a long step as opposed to a short step increases the hip range of motion to a smaller degree than full squatting instead of half squatting. In isolation, the small effect that lunge step length has on the length of hip extensor muscles may limit the degree to which step length influences hip extensor muscle growth, but step length is not the only variable you can modify in an effort to amplify the stimulus you provide to these muscles.

Just as moderately different step lengths can be used when lunging, so too can somewhat different trunk positions be utilized when performing lunge variations. On one end of the spectrum, you can maintain a fully upright trunk as your torso faces straight ahead throughout your lunge like it would face when normally standing upright. Alternatively you can incline your trunk forward by hinging at the hip of your front leg, which results in your torso facing at an angle between forward and downward. It should be noted that this forward trunk lean occurs from hip motion as you maintain the natural curvature of your lower back rather than spinal motion that can occur from simply rounding your lower back. Relative to if you held weights in your hands, lunging with a forward trunk lean can be quite difficult when holding a weight in the goblet position, so other variations may be preferable if you opt to use a forward trunk lean. Compared to lunging with an upright trunk position, lunging with an inclined trunk can allow you to reach a greater angle hip flexion for the front leg, which will allow you to train your hip extensor muscles (e.g., gluteus maximus and adductor magnus) at longer muscle lengths. When you use this forward trunk lean simultaneously with a long step, you may be able to reach a meaningfully greater angle (such as near 40 degrees more) of hip flexion than could otherwise be achieved with a short step and an upright trunk position. The discrepancy between these two lunge approaches could correspondingly be fairly close to the difference between half squats and full squats in terms of the peak lengths in which the gluteus maximus and adductor magnus are trained. Besides affecting the length in which these muscles are trained, the trunk position used while lunging can affect the resistance imparted to the hip extensor muscles. Relative to an upright trunk, an inclined trunk shifts your upper body’s center of mass forward along with any weights you may be using. Doing so increases the lever arm through which resistance acts on your front leg’s hip joint while simultaneously decreasing the lever arm through which resistance acts on your front leg’s knee joint. Consequently, your front leg’s hip extensor muscles will be loaded to a relatively greater degree when lunging with an inclined trunk, while your front leg’s quads will receive comparatively greater loading when lunging with an upright trunk. While not directly proven, the combination of subjecting your hip extensor muscles to relatively greater resistance while they are trained at longer muscle lengths can likely contribute to lunges with a long step and forward trunk lean being more effective for developing your gluteus maximus and adductor magnus than lunging with a short step and upright trunk. On the other hand, keeping your trunk upright while using whichever step length that feels most comfortable to you potentially may be somewhat more effective if you prioritize quad development.

### **Forward versus backward lunges**

Forward and backward lunges are much more similar than different as they both involve similar movement patterns that resist knee extension to train the quads while resisting hip extension to train gluteus maximus and adductor magnus. While you can consciously strive to reach the same knee and hip positions during each variation, people may naturally tend to perform these two exercises with somewhat different knee and hip motions. Comfort et al. (2015) and Goulette et al. (2021) both compared bodyweight forward lunges to backward lunges and found participants to reach a slightly greater angle of peak knee flexion and peak ankle dorsiflexion (which results in a greater forward lean of the shin) during the forward lunge. The differences were significantly different for Goulette et al. (2021) but not significantly different for Comfort et al. (2015). While not significantly different, Comfort et al. (2015) also found reverse lunges to involve slightly greater peak hip flexion, and Goulette et al. (2021) found reverse lunges to involve significantly greater forward trunk lean despite participants being instructed to maintain an upright trunk position. When taking a step backward, people may naturally be more likely to adopt somewhat of a forward trunk lean to maintain balance during a reverse lunge, which may contribute to a slightly greater hip flexion angle during the descent even without consciously striving to do so. This difference in average trunk position may contribute to why Song and Woo (2021) found the lumbar erector spinae to exhibit significantly higher EMG activity during bodyweight backward lunges compared to bodyweight forward lunges.

The available evidence also demonstrates that loading parameters may differ between the forward and backward lunge. Comfort et al. (2015) calculated resistive torque acting on the knee and hip to be greater during forward lunges. Because resistive torque acting on the knee and hip is what your lower body muscles must oppose while lunging, this suggests that forward lunges may tend to be more challenging than backward lunges when performed for the same number of reps with the same resistance. If a similar relationship applies to weighted lunges, heavier loads may be required when reverse lunging to achieve the same level of resistive torque when forward lunging. Goulette et al. (2021) additionally reported the patellofemoral joint (of the knee) to experience significantly greater forces, stress, and loading rates during forward lunges, which also resulted in higher quad force. Along with the difference in resistive torque that Comfort et al. (2015) identified, these differences in knee loading may arise in part from greater momentum being present when the lead leg begins being loaded during the forward lunge compared to the backward lunge. With a backward lunge, you can start loading your lead leg with your entire sole flat on the ground the moment you lift your other foot up off the ground. In contrast, your center of mass has forward momentum by the time the heel of your lead leg contacts the ground during a forward lunge, which may increase the demands imposed onto your lead leg. Of any of the differences identified, the discrepancy in patellofemoral joint loading rate was the greatest given that the loading rate of the forward lunge was 2.2 times that of the backward lunge. Having a higher loading rate and magnitude of forces imparted into the knee does not necessarily mean that forward lunges are problematic to the knee, but these factors may be relevant to lifters who have pre-existing knee issues. While there is no reason to fear forward lunges, certain individuals may find forward lunges to provoke knee discomfort but backward lunges may feel better especially if utilizing a slower descent that can be more readily performed with backward lunges than forward lunges. Because they are quite similar to one another, if one lunge variation simply feels better to your body than the other, that can be a completely legitimate justification to train that variation.

### **Are lunges unilateral, bilateral, or something in between?**

Lunge variations are commonly considered to be unilateral exercises which have been defined by Fountaine (2018) to be exercises where “each limb works independently of the other to create the desired movement.” Unilateral exercises differ from bilateral exercises where “both limbs are used in unison to contract the muscles, which create forces, and subsequently move a given load.” Exercises can clearly be bilateral when both limbs are symmetrically loaded as they simultaneously move in the same manner (such as during a barbell back squat) or unilateral when one limb limb is loaded as the other limb remains suspended in space (such as during a pistol squat). However, both legs function simultaneously against resistance in an asymmetrical manner to move your body (and any weights you may add) during lunge variations.

The front leg may be loaded to a greater extent than the rear leg, but the rear leg can still be meaningfully loaded when lunging as demonstrated by Hefzy et al. (1997) finding the rear leg to receive about one quarter of the total load during a forward lunge. Hofmann et al. (2017) provided further evidence supporting the notable involvement of the rear leg when assessing forward lunges performed with a vertical trunk and vertical shin, a vertical trunk and inclined shin, or an inclined trunk and inclined shin. The researchers found that knee loading (measured as knee extensor impulse) was similar between the front and rear legs when lunging with the trunk and front shin both inclined forward, but the rear knee experienced meaningfully greater loading when using either technique with a vertical trunk position. In light of this data, Hofmann et al. (2017) considered lunges to be bilateral exercises along with split squats, which Schultz et al. (2014) also reported to impart greater loading to the rear knee than the front knee while simultaneously transferring more weight into the front leg. The specific technique in which someone performs a lunge can certainly affect how load is distributed between the two sides. Besides modifying the trunk angle, people may intentionally be able to shift almost all of their weight into the lead leg while using the rear leg lightly for balance assistance or they may be able to focus on pushing off forcibly through the rear leg to perform much of the ascent through work from the rear leg. The ability to lunge with variable techniques can further amplify the ambiguity with respect to whether lunges should be classified as unilateral or bilateral. What someone considers to be a unilateral or bilateral exercise can also be notably influenced by specifically how the terms are operationally defined, and there can be legitimate reasons to classify lunges either way. Given this lack of clarity, this database seeks a middle road by classifying lunge variations simply as asymmetrical exercises since both legs are simultaneously loaded in an asymmetrical fashion.

### **Lunges versus split squats**

Forward and backward lunges are quite similar to split squats given that they train the same muscle groups and can look identical to each other at the bottom of the lowering phase. The distinction between them is that your feet remain stationary throughout a split squat set except for the initial step you take into the split stance position and the step you take to reposition your feet near each other to conclude the set. With lunges, you start each rep with your feet in a symmetrical stance, step backward or forward (depending on the variation) with one foot during a rep, and then reverse the step to bring your feet back together at the end of each rep. This difference contributes to a lunge set involving a greater proportion of time in which your balance can be most challenged since the least stable portion of either exercise is when one foot is briefly off the ground when taking a step, which occurs much less frequently during split squats. However, a lunge set also involves a greater proportion of time in which your balance can be least challenged since you are in a highly stable position whenever you are standing in a symmetrical hip width stance, which you adopt between each lunge rep but not in between each split squat rep. Correspondingly, lunges can have a greater fluctuation in the balance demands throughout a set with both more frequent moments of maximal balance difficulty and more frequent moments of minimal balance difficulty. In comparison, split squats can involve a fairly constant level of moderate instability throughout most of the set, which contributes to split squats having a reputation of being relatively less challenging from a balance perspective than lunges. Nonetheless, certain individuals may actually find that it is more difficult to sustain balance throughout a split squat set since they do not receive the brief “balance break” after each rep that lunges allow when the feet are returned to the highly stable symmetrical stance.

    1. Avoid rocking your torso forward to generate momentum before you start squatting upward.
    2. Like during the descent, continue keeping your working leg’s foot fully in contact with the ground as you keep your hip bones level and avoid letting your knee cave inward.
