## Setting up
1. Pick up a kettlebell or dumbbell and hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows, as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. You can use either a kettlebell or a dumbbell, but some people find holding a kettlebell in the goblet position to feel more stable and comfortable, especially with a fairly heavy weight.
    2. Based on your preference and the load you use, you can transfer your kettlebell or dumbbell into the goblet position through a couple of different approaches.
    3. An effective approach is initially to pick up the weight by the handle through a deadlift motion and set it on an elevated surface (like a bench or plyometric box) with the handle facing up if you use a kettlebell or the handle directed vertically if using a dumbbell (as only one end of the dumbbell is on the surface). Then squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it in the goblet position, and squat up with the weight. If you use a kettlebell, grasp it by its horns (i.e., side handles). If you use a dumbbell, cup your hands around the top end of the weight with the base of your palms by the handle, and your fingers wrapped around the rest of that end of the weight.
    4. With a lighter kettlebell, you can tilt it onto its side with the weight base directed toward you, squat down to grasp its horns, stand upright with it, and curl it into the goblet position.
    5. With a lighter dumbbell, you can also pick it up with one hand and curl it up across your body to be in front of your chest. Then cup your free hand around the top end of the dumbbell with the base of its palm by the handle and fingers wrapped around the top end of the weight before repositioning your other hand to cup the other side of the weight in the same manner.
2. Stand in approximately a hip-width stance with the back of your legs against the edge of the sturdy elevated object you will use to elevate your foot.
    1. If available, a padded cylindrical object positioned near knee height will normally be most comfortable and is recommended.
    2. A Smith machine bar with a squat/hip thrust pad on it, a barbell on top of the J-cups of a power rack, the leg pad of a lying hamstring curl machine, and a split squat roller stand are all high-quality cylindrical options that you can position to knee height.
    3. Alternatively, you can use an object like a flat exercise bench, couch, or plyometric box with a somewhat compliant surface, but objects with a flat surface tend not to be as comfortable for this exercise.
3. While keeping your feet approximately hip-width apart, step forward with one foot until its heel is just in front of your other foot’s big toe before doing the same with your opposite foot.
    1. This results in your front foot now being about two “foot lengths” in front of where you started when your calves were touching the object you will use to elevate your rear foot.
    2. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, somewhat of a range of foot placements can be effectively used including having your front foot two and a half “foot lengths” in front of where you started (which may be even more comfortable for some people).
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your bodyweight into your front foot before placing the top surface (on the side of your shoe laces) of your rear foot on top of the elevated surface with that side’s knee bent.
    1. To help shift your bodyweight into your front foot, you can lean your torso mildly forward by hinging at your hip as you slightly bend that side’s knee.
    2. Once you have situated your rear foot into the elevated position, you can return to keeping your torso in a fairly upright position, which should involve you maintaining the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright (rather than excessively arching beyond that position).
    3. Strive to move your rear foot backward in a straight line to keep your feet approximately hip-width apart, rather than bringing your rear foot closer toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep the entire sole of your front foot firmly planted on the ground and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. If you are using a cylindrical object to elevate your foot, you can contact the surface with the front of your ankle along with your foot, but only your foot will contact the elevated surface if it is flat, like a bench.
    7. Keep the weight close to your chest in the goblet position throughout the duration of your set.
2. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep most of your weight shifted onto your front foot while you are primarily using your rear foot to assist with balance.
    2. Continue keeping your torso fairly upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. If you initially positioned your front foot excessively far in front of your elevated object, you may reach the end of your available hip range of motion before your rear knee reaches the ground.
    7. If you initially positioned your front foot too close to the elevated object, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. In either case of suboptimal foot placement, you do not need to force your rear knee to tap the ground, and you can adjust how far in front your front foot is situated after finishing your rep.
3. While keeping your front foot firmly planted on the ground and your rear foot in its elevated position, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso fairly upright and knees aligned with your feet while having most of your weight shifted onto the front foot.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which leg is in the forward position and which leg is in the elevated position.
    1. After finishing the set with your other leg forward, set the weight down in the same manner in which you initially picked it up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat’s back pad to a position that aligns your knees with the machine’s pivot point while sitting up against the back pad with your thighs resting on the seat.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to its highest position that allows you to begin each rep with your knees fully straightened.
    1. Certain machines can be used for leg extensions or hamstring curls based on how the lever arm is positioned.
3. Adjust the lower leg pad to a position that places it slightly above the back of your heels (i.e., on your Achilles tendons) when seated against the backrest, with your legs on top of the lower leg pad and your knees straightened.
    1. Adjusting this setting exclusively moves the lower leg pad without moving the lever arm, in contrast to step 2, where the machine lever arm and shin pad move together.
4. After selecting your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin, sit down on its seat with your back against the back pad and your lower legs on top of the lower leg pad.
5. Adjust the thigh pad to press down snugly against your lower thighs.
    1. In this starting position, your knees should be straight and aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Pull your toes and feet back toward your shins by moving at your ankles, and maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shins contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankles in the same position in which they would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heels up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankles in this position can increase your hamstring curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
3. Drive both heels down and back toward you as you bend your knees to pull the lower leg pad under your thighs through the available range of motion that the machine allows.
    1. At some point, the machine will stop you from bending your knees any further, but most machines will allow you to bend your knees by at least 90 degrees.
    2. While your lower legs move through motion at your knees, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
4. After you have fully bent your knees, fully straighten one knee to lift that side’s leg off the lower leg pad, leaving only one leg in contact with the pad.
5. With the leg still in contact with the lower leg pad, allow that side’s knee to straighten progressively in a controlled manner while resisting the weight on the way up. Continue doing so until you have returned to the starting position with both knees fully straightened.
    1. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower leg up.
6. Repeatedly perform steps 3-5 as you alternate each rep which leg you keep in contact with the lower leg pad during steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you wish to do so, you can alternatively complete one set where you perform step 5 of each rep exclusively with one side, rest, and then complete another set where you perform step 5 of every rep with your opposite side. 
    2. During each rep, continue to move the leg pad down with both legs as you control it on the way up with only one leg.

While emphasizing eccentric strength training, this exercise can effectively train all your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Hamstrings%201b95c6f170d88055a462c40b686f381a.md), which are assisted by your [gracilis](../Muscles/Gracilis%201925c6f170d880938681fbbe8f075831.md), [sartorius](../Muscles/Sartorius%201925c6f170d8801c8493cac115de0546.md), and [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md).

    3. If you feel that you only require one hand for assistance, you can also use a variety of objects, such as a power rack post, bed post, couch, dumbbell rack, etc.
    4. If you use an object that you will hold with both hands, position yourself a little behind the object.
    5. If you use an object that you will hold with only one hand, you can position yourself to the side of the object.
    6. You can optionally place a soft object (like a cushioned balance pad, yoga block, folded thick towel, folded yoga mat, or a pillow) on the ground directly behind where you will stand if you are not confident in your ability to control the descent and tap your knee to the ground in a gentle manner.
    7. If you opt to place a soft object on the ground, you will use your knee to tap that object instead of the ground, and doing so will mildly reduce the range of motion and difficulty of this exercise compared to if you would lightly contact the ground with your knee.

1. Grasp the object you selected to use for assistance with either one or two hands based on your preference.
    1. If you are only holding onto the object with one hand, raise your other arm up with a straight elbow until it is approximately parallel with the ground, and maintain this arm position throughout your set.
    2. Continue holding that object throughout your set while using as much assistance as you need from your upper body.
    3. Throughout a rep, you can adjust how much assistance you use from your upper body, which will likely need to be greater near the bottom of the rep (where the exercise is more challenging) compared to near the top of the rep.
2. Shift your weight onto one foot and pick the other foot up off the ground by bending that side’s knee by greater than 90 degrees while keeping its thigh directed down toward the ground.
    1. The goal is to bend your knee enough that your foot will not contact the ground before your knee reaches the ground during the descent.
    2. Keep your free leg in this position throughout your set.

    1. It can be helpful to initiate the descent by mildly sitting your buttocks back through a hip hinge motion that somewhat inclines your torso, as if you are closing a car door with your buttocks as your hands are carrying something.

## Setting up
1. Position a sturdy object (such as a thick bumper plate or an aerobic step) that you will use as a step onto the floor in a location that has sufficient space behind it for your split squat.

2. Pick up one kettlebell and stand upright while firmly holding the kettlebell at your side with a straight elbow, as your palm faces in toward your thighs and your arm is directed down toward the ground.
    1. You can pick up the kettlebell with a deadlift or squat motion, where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
3. In approximately a hip-width stance, stand with the foot opposite to the side in which you are holding the kettlebell aligned with the middle of your step (which is primarily relevant if you are using a bumper plate to provide the greatest surface area for your foot).
## Exercise technique
1. With the foot opposite to the side in which you are holding the kettlebell, step up onto the step with the entirety of its sole in contact with the step while leaving your other foot on the ground.
    1. The knee on the side of your elevated foot should be mildly bent once on the step.
    2. Continue holding the kettlebell by your side as your arm is directed down toward the ground throughout the duration of your set.
2. Shift your bodyweight into your elevated foot before taking a fairly long step backward with your other foot and contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. To shift your bodyweight into your elevated foot, you can lean your torso mildly forward by hinging at your hip as you bend that side’s knee slightly more.
    2. Once you step back and resume transferring some of your weight into your rear leg, you can return to keeping your torso in an upright position.

    4. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    5. Keep the entire sole of your elevated foot firmly planted on the step and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    6. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
3. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.

## Setting up
1. Position an object on the floor to which you will tap your free leg’s knee at the end of the skater squat’s lowering phase.
    1. While the object must be lower than knee height, you can determine specifically how tall an object you wish to use based on your current ability.
    2. The difficulty of the exercise will directly increase as you decrease the height of your object.
    3. If you are new to skater squats and are unsure what height to use, you can start with an object with a height near mid-shin or a little lower and simply progress to a lower object if that feels easy.
    4. Commonly available objects you can use include aerobic steps that can be adjusted in height through risers and thick bumper plates that can be stacked on top of each other if you wish to use a greater height.
    5. You can optionally place a soft object like a cushioned balance pad, yoga block, folded thick towel, or a pillow on top of your elevated object if you are not confident in your ability to tap your knee to the object in a gentle manner.
2. Stand directly in front of your elevated object with an upright torso in approximately a hip-width stance with your toes pointing straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot and pick the other foot up off the ground by bending that side’s knee greater than 90 degrees while keeping its thigh directed down toward the ground.
    1. The goal is to bend your knee enough that your foot will not contact the elevated object before your knee reaches the ground during the descent.
    2. Keep your free leg in this position throughout your set.
2. Raise your arms up with straight elbows until they are approximately parallel with the ground.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
3. With the leg in contact with the ground, progressively bend at your knee and hip to squat down in a controlled manner until you can gently tap the elevated object with your free leg’s knee.
    1. It can be helpful to initiate the descent by mildly sitting your buttocks back through a hip hinge motion that somewhat inclines your torso, as if you are closing a car door with your buttocks as your hands are carrying something.
    2. Keep the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your working leg’s foot firmly in contact with the ground throughout your set.
    3. Strive to have your knee track straight forward in line with your second and third toes (when counting your big toe as your first toe) as you descend, while not letting your knee cave inward.
    4. To the best of your ability, keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. Through motion at your working leg’s hip, your torso should naturally transition to an inclined position rather than remaining completely upright, but strive to keep your back near a neutral position (where it retains its natural curvature or looks flat) as you avoid excessively rounding your lower back.

    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your working leg’s foot fully in contact with the ground as you keep your hip bones level and avoid letting your knee cave inward.

    1. This results in your front foot (which will be on the side not holding the weight) now being about two “foot lengths” in front of where you started when your calves were touching the object you will use to elevate your rear foot.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a kettlebell or dumbbell and hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows, as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. You can use either a kettlebell or a dumbbell, but some people find holding a kettlebell in the goblet position to feel more stable and comfortable, especially with a fairly heavy weight.
    2. Based on your preference and the load you use, you can transfer your kettlebell or dumbbell into the goblet position through a couple of different approaches.
    3. An effective approach is initially to pick up the weight by the handle through a deadlift motion and set it on an elevated surface (like a bench or plyometric box) with the handle facing up if you use a kettlebell or the handle directed vertically if using a dumbbell (as only one end of the dumbbell is on the surface). Then squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it in the goblet position, and squat up with the weight. If you use a kettlebell, grasp it by its horns (i.e., side handles). If you use a dumbbell, cup your hands around the top end of the weight with the base of your palms by the handle, and your fingers wrapped around the rest of that end of the weight.
    4. With a lighter kettlebell, you can tilt it onto its side with the weight base directed toward you, squat down to grasp its horns, stand upright with it, and curl it into the goblet position.
    5. With a lighter dumbbell, you can also pick it up with one hand and curl it up across your body to be in front of your chest. Then cup your free hand around the top end of the dumbbell with the base of its palm by the handle and fingers wrapped around the top end of the weight before repositioning your other hand to cup the other side of the weight in the same manner.
2. While keeping your chest up, position your feet approximately hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight ahead.
    1. You can optionally place a soft object (like a cushioned balance pad, yoga block, folded thick towel, folded yoga mat, or a pillow) on the ground directly behind where you will stand if you are not confident in your ability to control the descent and tap your knee to the ground in a gentle manner.
    2. If you opt to place a soft object on the ground, you will use your knee to tap that object instead of the ground, and doing so will mildly reduce the range of motion and difficulty of this exercise compared to if you would lightly contact the ground with your knee.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot and pick the other foot up off the ground by bending that side’s knee by greater than 90 degrees while keeping its thigh directed down toward the ground.
    1. The goal is to bend your knee enough that your foot will not contact the ground before your knee reaches the ground during the descent.
    2. Keep your free leg in this position as you continue holding your weight in the goblet position throughout your set.
2. With the leg in contact with the ground, progressively bend at your knee and hip to squat down in a controlled manner until you can gently tap the ground with your free leg’s knee.
    1. It can be helpful to initiate the descent by mildly sitting your buttocks back through a hip hinge motion that mildly inclines your torso, as if you are closing a car door with your buttocks as your hands are carrying something.
    2. Keep the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your working leg’s foot firmly in contact with the ground throughout your set.

    4. To the best of your ability, keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. Through motion at your working leg’s hip, your torso should naturally transition to a somewhat inclined position rather than remaining completely upright, but strive to keep your back near a neutral position (where it retains its natural curvature or looks flat) as you avoid excessively rounding your lower back or letting your upper back cave.
    7. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your free leg’s knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
3. Reverse the motion you just performed by progressively extending (straightening) your working leg's knee and hip to squat yourself up until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your working leg’s foot fully in contact with the ground as you keep your hip bones level and avoid letting your knee cave inward.

## Setting up
1. Pick up your weight of choice, which may be a pair of dumbbells or kettlebells that you hold in each hand, or it can be a single dumbbell, kettlebell, or weight plate that you simultaneously hold with both hands.
    1. When using a pair of dumbbells or kettlebells, hold them at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    2. When using a single weight, you can hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
2. Stand upright with your back, pelvis (hip bone), and heels against a wall.
    1. Continue keeping your back and pelvis against the wall throughout the rest of your setup and while you perform your wall squat.
3. Step forward with one foot until its heel is just in front of your other foot’s big toe before doing the same with your opposite foot.
4. Step forward with your rear foot to position it symmetrically with your front foot, resulting in your feet now being about two “foot lengths” in front of the wall.
    1. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, somewhat of a range of foot placements can be effectively used for this exercise.
5. Situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other and position your toes so that they are either facing straight ahead or rotated somewhat out based on what feels comfortable to you.
    1. After finishing adjusting your foot position, your knees should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend at your knees and hips to squat down as you slide your back down the wall in a controlled manner until your thighs are approximately parallel to the ground or somewhat below that point.
    1. Avoid descending beyond the point where you can still keep your pelvis in contact with the wall.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot.
    3. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground as you continue keeping your upper back and pelvis in contact with the wall.
    4. If you wish to prioritize training your quads, focus on transmitting pressure to the wall through your pelvis while minimizing how much pressure you transmit into the wall through your upper back.
2. Reverse the movement by pressing through the ground to squat up as you extend (straighten) your knees and hips until you have returned to the starting position with your torso fully lifted up and your knees straightened.
    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your pelvis and upper back in contact with the wall, feet fully in contact with the ground, and your knees in line with your feet.

## Setting up
1. Wrap a thick, long, looped band around a power rack’s beam (or similarly sturdy object with a smooth surface) just below knee height.
    1. Because the purpose of the band is to keep your lower legs upright in a stationary position, a high-tension band will be required (unless you have a viable inelastic substitute like a Spanish squat strap made of polyester).
    2. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
    3. The floor on which you perform this exercise should have sufficient traction so that your feet do not slide forward during your Spanish squat.
2. Position a weight (such as a kettlebell, dumbbell, weight plate, or medicine ball) by the band so that it will be within your reach after stepping into the band.
    1. If you are using a light weight (which will be sufficiently challenging for most people), you can similarly use any weighted implement that you can hold to your chest.
    2. If you have very strong quads and are using at least a moderately heavy weight, a kettlebell or dumbbell can be most practical for you to select.
3. Step inside each end of the band’s loop with your feet, and situate the band on the top of your calves just below your knees.
    1. If you are wearing shorts, you can situate a hand towel between the back of your knees and the band for comfort since the band pulling on the skin can be uncomfortable (especially for individuals with notable leg hair).
4. Pick up the weight and hold it with both hands right next to your chest with bent elbows as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
5. Walk backward until the band is fully tensed, which should not require many steps when using an appropriately thick band.
    1. Up to a certain point, you can progressively increase the band’s resistance by walking back farther, but be careful not to walk back so far that you overstretch the band, which can be indicated by an abrupt increase in resistance from the band.
    2. The capacity to which a band can safely stretch can vary depending on the company that made it, but avoid stretching the band three times its resting length or greater as a general rule of thumb to minimize the risk of tearing the band.
    3. Naturally, you will not be measuring the length to which you elongate the band, but if the band does not provide sufficient resistance after taking a few steps back from the point at which you started feeling resistance, it may be appropriate to switch to a higher tension band instead of walking any farther back.
6. Position your feet about shoulder width apart as you are facing the band’s anchor point while standing fully upright with your toes either facing straight ahead or rotated slightly outward based on your preference.

1. While keeping your torso and lower legs in a vertical position, bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner until your thighs are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground.

## Setting up
1. Wrap a thick, long, looped band around a power rack’s beam (or similarly sturdy object with a smooth surface) just below knee height.
    1. Because the purpose of the band is to keep your lower legs upright in a stationary position, a high-tension band will be required (unless you have a viable inelastic substitute like a Spanish squat strap made of polyester).
    2. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
    3. The floor on which you perform this exercise should have sufficient traction so that your feet do not slide forward during your Spanish squat.
2. Step inside each end of the band’s loop with your feet, and situate the band on the top of your calves just below your knees.
    1. If you are wearing shorts, you can situate a hand towel between the back of your knees and the band for comfort since the band pulling on the skin can be uncomfortable (especially for individuals with notable leg hair).
3. Walk backward until the band is fully tensed, which should not require many steps when using an appropriately thick band.
    1. Up to a certain point, you can progressively increase the band’s resistance by walking back farther, but be careful not to walk back so far that you overstretch the band, which can be indicated by an abrupt increase in resistance from the band.
    2. The capacity to which a band can safely stretch can vary depending on the company that made it, but avoid stretching the band three times its resting length or greater as a general rule of thumb to minimize the risk of tearing the band.
    3. Naturally, you will not be measuring the length to which you elongate the band, but if the band does not provide sufficient resistance after taking a few steps back from the point at which you started feeling resistance, it may be appropriate to switch to a higher tension band instead of walking any farther back.
4. Position your feet about shoulder width apart as you are facing the band’s anchor point while standing fully upright with your toes either facing straight ahead or rotated slightly outward based on your preference.
    1. So long as you do not place them on your legs, you can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides or crossed on your shoulders.
    2. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your torso and lower legs in a vertical position, bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner until your thighs are approximately parallel to the ground or as close to this position as your strength permits.
    1. The difficulty of the exercise will meaningfully increase as your squat depth increases, so you can adjust your depth based on your ability and the duration in which you intend to hold the position.
    2. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the ground.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot.
    4. Strive to keep your shoulders vertically stacked over your hips, as you resist any forward torso lean. 
2. Statically maintain this squat position with a fully vertical torso position until you have finished your set and are ready to squat up by extending (straightening) your knees and hips until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. As you hold this position for your target duration, continue keeping your shins vertical, feet fully in contact with the ground, and knees in line with your feet.
    2. If you notice that the position in which you are initially holding is too difficult to maintain for the minimum set duration you are seeking (e.g., you can only hold for several seconds but intend to hold for at least 30 seconds), you can reduce the depth of your Spanish squat to reduce the intensity.

## Setting up
1. Anchor a long looped elastic band around a pull-up bar (or a similar elevated object with a smooth surface, such as the beam of a power rack).
    1. To anchor the band, you can initially drape the band over the bar, loop one end of the band into the middle of the other end, and pull that end until it is taught.
    2. Inspect the band to confirm it does not have any small tears, since a small tear can swiftly become a full tear when stretching a band.
2. Grasp the band with both hands and walk backward until you begin feeling tension from the band with your elbows straightened and arms aligned with the band.
3. Let go of the band, and place a cushioned object that is comfortable for kneeling, like a Pilates mat or foam pillow, onto the ground at the location where you started feeling tension from the band.
4. Grasp the band with both hands, and kneel on the cushioned object with your knees approximately hip width apart from each other and your shoelaces (or the top surface of your feet) in contact with the ground as your heels are facing backward.
    1. Your ankles will be in the same position that they would be at the top of a calf raise.
    2. If you have limited ankle mobility and/or find this ankle position uncomfortable, you can place a half foam roller underneath the front of your ankles, which will allow you to adopt a closer to neutral ankle position.
5. Assume an upright torso position while kneeling and align your arms with the band so that you can draw a straight line from your arms to the band with straight elbows.
    1. You will keep your arms aligned with the band throughout the exercise.
    2. If there is any slack in the band in this position, you need to situate yourself further away from the band’s anchor point until you feel tension in the starting position.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Keep your glutes squeezed and your core braced throughout the set to help you maintain a rigid trunk position.
2. While holding the band with outstretched arms, lean your torso backward in a controlled manner by bending at your knees through the range of motion that your strength and mobility permit.
    1. The motion should exclusively come from your knees, while your hips and lower back remain near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, which is facilitated by step 1.
    2. Throughout the exercise, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your torso, indicating that you are maintaining an appropriately rigid trunk position without moving your hips.
    3. In particular, avoid letting your lower back excessively arch, which can occur if you do not keep your glutes squeezed and core braced.
    4. Depending on how much assistance you receive from the band, the intensity of this exercise may increase as you lean back further, so you can adjust how far you descend based on your ability.
    5. The greatest possible range of motion involves leaning back until your upper back lightly contacts the ground with your knees fully bent.
    6. As you progressively lean back, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in one of the quad muscles on the front of your upper thigh, and the flexibility of this muscle can limit how far backward certain individuals can move.
3. Reverse the movement by lifting your torso up through motion at your knees until you have returned to the starting position, where your torso is fully upright.
    1. Continue holding the band and keeping your thighs and torso aligned with each other as you resist any back or hip motion, as you did not during the descent.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Position a weight (such as a kettlebell, dumbbell, weight plate, or medicine ball) by the sissy squat machine so that it will be within your reach when standing on the foot plate.
    1. If you are using a light weight (which will be sufficiently challenging for most people), you can similarly use any weighted implement that you can hold to your chest.
    2. If you have very strong quads and are using at least a moderately heavy weight, a kettlebell or dumbbell can be most practical for you to select.
2. Adjust the height of the lower leg pad to be level with your upper calf, just below the back of your knees, when standing on the foot plate.
    1. The ideal pad height will allow your knees to move freely (which may not be the case if the pad is too high) during the exercise while appropriately supporting your lower legs (which may not be the case if the pad is too low).
3. Step onto the foot plate in an approximately hip-width stance with the tops of your feet under the machine’s foot roller and your upper calves snugly against the pad.
    1. The soles of your feet should be fully in contact with the foot plate as your toes are pointing straight ahead.
4. If your machine permits you to do so, adjust the foot roller so that it is snugly on top of your feet just in front of your ankles.
    1. Your feet and lower legs should now be securely locked into the machine in a position where they will not move during the exercise.
    2. While many do, certain machine models lack an adjustable foot roller.
5. Squat or hinge down to pick up the weight and hold it with both hands right next to your chest with bent elbows as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. If the weight you selected is heavy enough to make it difficult for you to pick it up when you are locked into the machine, you can walk out of the machine, pick it up, and then reposition yourself in the machine.
6. Stand fully upright while holding the weight close to your chest.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your torso in a vertical position and your calves in contact with the leg pad, bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner until your thighs are approximately parallel to the ground or somewhat below this point.
    1. Keep the soles of your feet fully in contact with the foot plate.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot.
    3. As you keep your chest up and hold the weight close to your chest, strive to keep your shoulders vertically stacked over your hips while resisting any forward torso lean. 
    4. When your thighs are parallel to the ground, your knees and hips should be bent by approximately 90 degrees (as demonstrated by the angle between your thighs and trunk for your hips and the angle between your shins and thighs for your knees).
    5. The intensity of this exercise will increase as your squat depth increases, so you can adjust your depth based on your ability if you currently cannot descend until your thigh is parallel to the ground for the number of reps you intend to perform during this set.
2. Reverse the movement by pressing through the foot plate to squat up as you extend (straighten) your knees and hips until you have returned to the starting position with your torso fully lifted up and your knees straightened.
    1. Like during the descent, continue keeping your torso in a vertical position, calves in contact with the leg pad, feet fully in contact with the ground, and knees in line with your feet while holding the weight close to your chest.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a weight plate and firmly hold it close to your chest with both hands as your palms are facing in toward each other.
2. While holding the weight to your chest, lie down with your back on a flat exercise bench, with the back of your head on the bench right by the end of the bench.
    1. Your feet should be on the ground with your knees bent, and you will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
    2. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should position your head on the side further away from the base of the rack, since you will be moving your arms backward.
## Exercise technique
1. Press the weight up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
2. While keeping your elbows fairly straight, lower the plate back behind your head in a controlled arcing manner through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. You should avoid meaningfully bending your elbows, but you can allow them to bend mildly as your arms move through motion at your shoulders while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
    2. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back during the descent.
    3. People can often lower the weight until their upper arms are close to parallel with the ground, but how far you can descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    4. Once you feel that you have reached the end range to which your shoulders can safely stretch, you have reached the end range for you as an individual.
3. Reverse the movement by pulling your arms upward and forward in an arcing motion until you have returned to the starting position with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows fairly straight as you move your arms through shoulder motion while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can train your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which are assisted by the [lowest portion of your pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) in the overhead position of each rep.

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while firmly holding the dumbbell at your side with a straight elbow.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handle with the handle pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. You can pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion, where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back flat.
2. Once upright, you can situate your palm right next to the outer aspect of the front of your thigh so that your palm faces at an angle between backward and inward.
    1. Your neck should be near a neutral position when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Keep your neck in this position throughout the exercise.
3. If you wish to use your free hand to assist your balance, stand with your side opposite the dumbbell near a surface where you can place your hand during this exercise.
    1. Using your free hand for balance assistance is optional.
    2. A variety of objects can be used as a support point, provided they let you maintain hand contact throughout your set, which typically involves the surface being between hip-height and shoulder-height. Examples include a post from a squat rack or Smith machine, the head of an inclined bench, a doorframe, and a bedpost.
4. If you want to receive balance assistance, lightly grasp the support surface with your free hand and maintain this hand contact until you finish the set. Otherwise, keep your free hand in a comfortable position throughout the exercise.
    1. If you use your free hand for balance assistance, use the least amount of assistance that is needed for you to feel sufficiently stable during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto the foot opposite to the side in which you are holding the dumbbell and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, as if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Bracing will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hip throughout your set.
2. While allowing the foot on the side of the dumbbell to lift up off the floor, begin hinging at the hip on the side to which you shifted your weight by sitting your buttocks back as you let your knee mildly bend.
    1. As you do so, the dumbbell will naturally descend, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    2. Allow your free leg to swing backward as it moves with your torso in a see-saw-like manner, but focus on hinging at the hip of your working leg instead of kicking your other leg back.
    3. Continue keeping your elbow straightened, core braced, lower back flat, and working leg’s sole fully in contact with the ground.
    4. To the best of your ability, keep the top of your hip bones and your shoulders level with each other rather than letting the hip bone or shoulder on either side drop down.
    5. Most of the motion should come from your hip, and your shin should remain in a fairly vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knee fully straightened.
    6. You do not need to focus on bending your knee, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks back while not intentionally keeping your knee locked.
3. Continuing hinging at your hip in a controlled manner until you have reached the end of your available range of motion.
    1. While some people can descend until their torsos are close to parallel to the ground, how deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knee will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer descend without rounding your lower back, you have finished descending through your available range of motion.
4. Reverse the hinge movement by driving through your working leg’s hip to lift yourself up until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. Continue keeping your elbow straightened, core braced, lower back flat, hip bones level, and working leg’s sole fully in contact with the ground.
    2. After you are fully upright, you could place your free leg’s foot back onto the ground if you could use some additional balance assistance.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which hand you use to hold the weight and which foot remains in contact with the ground.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
    3. After finishing the last rep with your other side, set the dumbbell down in the same manner in which you initially picked it up (e.g., keeping your lower back flat rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), and [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), this exercise dynamically trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs.
2. While holding the dumbbells by your legs, hinge at your hips by sitting your buttocks back, and mildly bend your knees to position your torso at an angle fairly close to horizontal.
    1. Keep your lower back flat as you hinge at your hips, rather than just rounding your back.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    3. Maintain this bent-over position throughout your set.
3. Drive your elbows backward and upward in an arcing motion until your upper arms are close to parallel to the ground while allowing your elbows to bend and keeping your forearms directed down toward the ground.
    1. After performing this rowing motion, your elbows should be bent by approximately 90 degrees, placing you into the starting position for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your upper arms parallel to the ground, progressively straighten your elbows to drive the dumbbells backward and upward in an arcing motion until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. As you move your elbows, you should keep the rest of your body stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to bend in a controlled manner as you bring the dumbbells downward and forward in an arcing fashion until you have returned to the starting position with your forearms directed straight down toward the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your upper arms stationary as they remain parallel to the ground.
    2. At the end of the lowering phase, your elbows should be bent by approximately 90 degrees.
    3. There is no need to bend your elbows beyond 90 degrees (when your forearms are perpendicular to the ground) since that additional bending motion would be training your biceps rather than your triceps.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down.
## Description
This exercise trains all three heads of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), but other exercises can likely train the triceps more effectively.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a short looped elastic band and sit down on the ground.
    1. You will remain seated throughout this exercise.
2. Position the band around both of your feet with the band under and on top of the balls of your feet.
    1. The appropriate positioning will keep the band in place during the exercise.
3. Straighten your knees to move your feet out in front of you with only your heels remaining on the ground, while the rest of your soles are off the ground.
    1. While sitting with your knees straight (which is known as long sitting), you can place your hands on the ground for additional stability and either keep your torso upright or somewhat reclined based on your preference.
4. If the band is slack, spread your thighs apart from each other until you feel meaningful tension from the band while allowing the band to rotate your feet inward (through ankle inversion).
    1. In this starting position for the exercise, the soles of your feet should be angled in toward the midline of your body, which is an imaginary line that extends forward from your navel and divides your body into right and left halves.
    2. When imagining a laser pointer shooting out from the middle of your soles, the lasers should intersect in an “X-shape” in front of you from your feet being inwardly rotated.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your legs stationary, rotate your feet outward (via ankle eversion) against the band’s resistance through your available ankle motion.
    1. When imagining a laser pointer shooting out from the middle of your soles, the outward rotation of your feet should prompt the laser pointer to point out away from the midline of your body.
    2. When performing this exercise correctly, you should feel tension in the muscles on the outer aspects of your lower legs near the outer aspect of your calf muscles.
    3. Particularly avoid letting your thighs rotate via hip motion, which would result in your knee caps moving.
    4. If you have difficulty keeping your legs stationary, you can hold onto your thighs to stabilize them while the motion exclusively comes from your ankles.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing the band to rotate your feet inward (via ankle inversion) in a controlled manner through your available ankle range of motion as you continue keeping your thighs stationary.
    1. When imagining a laser pointer shooting out from the middle of your soles, the inward rotation of your feet should prompt the laser pointer to point in toward the midline of your body as the lasers intersect in front of you.
    2. If the band becomes slack toward the end of this movement, you can spread your thighs somewhat further apart in order to experience resistance from the band throughout your full range of motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the [fibularis muscles](../Muscles/Fibularis%20muscles%201b95c6f170d8801da142f6e7458238a0.md) on the outer aspect of your lower leg that assist in actively stabilizing the ankle.

## Setting up
1. Position a sturdy object (such as a thick bumper plate, aerobic step, or plyometric box) that you will use as a step onto the floor.
    1. You can use a range of different heights for your step, and the difficulty of the exercise will increase as the height increases.
    2. If you are new to weighted lateral step-downs, selecting an object that is near four inches (10cm) high (which is a typical height of many aerobic steps without additional risers) can be an appropriate starting point, and you can subsequently adjust the height based on how challenging this height is for you.
    3. Alternatively, you can perform this exercise on the lowest step of a staircase, which is normally near seven inches (18cm) in height.
    4. When feasible, setting up where you can face a mirror is recommended to be able to receive visual feedback about your technique.
2. Pick up a kettlebell or dumbbell and hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows, as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. You can use either a kettlebell or a dumbbell, but some people find holding a kettlebell in the goblet position to feel more stable and comfortable, especially with a fairly heavy weight.
    2. Based on your preference and the load you use, you can transfer your kettlebell or dumbbell into the goblet position through a couple of different approaches.
    3. An effective approach is initially to pick up the weight by the handle through a deadlift motion and set it on an elevated surface (like a bench or plyometric box) with the handle facing up if you use a kettlebell or the handle directed vertically if using a dumbbell (as only one end of the dumbbell is on the surface). Then squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it in the goblet position, and squat up with the weight. If you use a kettlebell, grasp it by its horns (i.e., side handles). If you use a dumbbell, cup your hands around the top end of the weight with the base of your palms by the handle, and your fingers wrapped around the rest of that end of the weight.
    4. With a lighter kettlebell, you can tilt it onto its side with the weight base directed toward you, squat down to grasp its horns, stand upright with it, and curl it into the goblet position.
    5. With a lighter dumbbell, you can also pick it up with one hand and curl it up across your body to be in front of your chest. Then cup your free hand around the top end of the dumbbell with the base of its palm by the handle and fingers wrapped around the top end of the weight before repositioning your other hand to cup the other side of the weight in the same manner.
3. While holding the weight to your chest, stand directly to the side of the step, and place one foot fully onto the step while leaving your other foot on the ground as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other, and toes are pointing straight ahead.
    1. The entire sole (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) of your elevated foot should be firmly planted on the step throughout your set.
    2. You will continue holding the weight close to your chest in the goblet position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Step up as you straighten your knee on the side of your elevated foot until your feet are level with each other and both of your knees are straight while standing upright with one foot hanging off the step.
    1. After stepping up, the tops of your hip bones and shoulders should be level with each other as you are bearing all of your bodyweight through the foot on the step.
2. On the side hovering off the step, pull your toes and the ball of your foot upward through an ankle motion that results in your heel being closer to the ground than the ball of your foot.
    1. This is the opposite of the ankle motion that occurs when lifting your heels up during a calf raise.
    2. You will keep your foot in this position and that side’s knee straight throughout your set.
    3. Now you are in the starting position for your first rep.
3. With your leg that is on the step, sit your buttocks slightly backward to initiate the descent, and bend your knee to lower yourself in a controlled manner until you can gently tap the ground with the heel of your other foot.
    1. As you sit your buttocks back (like if you started to sit on a chair), allow your torso naturally to lean mildly forward at your hips to maintain your balance. Simultaneosuly keep your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    2. Keep the entire sole of your elevated foot firmly planted on the step and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down.
    3. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    4. Keep your working leg’s knee aligned with your foot rather than letting your knee cave inward relative to your foot (which you can check in a mirror, along with how level your hip bones are).
    5. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your free leg’s heel, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
4. Reverse the movement by driving through your elevated foot as you straighten your knee and pull your hips forward to lift yourself up until you have returned to an upright torso position with your knee fully straightened.
    1. During the ascent, continue keeping your working leg’s knee stacked over your foot, the sole of your foot fully on the step, and hip bones level.
    2. While you lift yourself up through your elevated leg, avoid pushing off the ground with your foot.
5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which foot is elevated on top of the step.
## Description
While training your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [glutes](../Muscles/Glutes%201b95c6f170d88002885bca53f30406d5.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), this exercise can improve your single leg stability.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the rack’s J-hooks to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on top of them.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
    3. If you need to bend your knees and hips beyond a mild degree (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) initially to place the bar on your back, you positioned the J-hooks excessively low. This can make it more challenging to rerack the bar at the end of your set.
2. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
3. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on your upper back muscles, slightly below the base of your neck, in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. For the high bar squat, you are aiming for the bar to rest on the muscular shelf formed by your traps above your rear delts (on the back of your shoulders) and above the bony ridge running across your shoulder blades (known as the scapular spine).
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable on your traps will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back as you squeeze your shoulder blades back together.
    3. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    4. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    5. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    6. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    7. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends when squatting.
6. Repeat steps 2 and 3 of the setup before proceeding to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. Take a couple of steps back, and position your feet near shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing slightly out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip-width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside shoulder width and their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. Throughout your set, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back slightly. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    4. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
6. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
7. Alternate between steps 4-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
8. Walk forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.

## Exercise technique
1. Stand upright with the bar snugly on your upper back by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Continue holding the handles while keeping the bar on your upper back throughout your set.
2. While keeping your chest up, take a couple of steps backward and position your feet approximately hip-width apart, with your toes pointing straight ahead.
3. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, take a fairly long step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Slightly bend the knee on the side of your stationary foot while doing so.
    2. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to split squats.
    3. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
4. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. While the forefoot of your rear leg will stay in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground with your knee, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and step somewhat farther backward after you ascend before performing your next rep.
5. While keeping both of your feet planted on the ground, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
6. Repeat steps 4 and 5 until you have finished your set. Then step forward with your rear leg to position your feet symmetrically.
    1. Now you have the option of proceeding directly into your next set with your other leg in the forward position, or you can rerack the bar and rest before doing so.
    2. When you are ready to rerack the bar, walk forward until it contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.

## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your upper arms parallel to the ground, stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the bar resting on your shoulders throughout the set.
2. Take a couple of steps back, and position your feet near shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing slightly out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip-width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside shoulder width and their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. Throughout your set, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest and elbows up.
    1. Throughout the set, avoid dropping your elbows or letting your chest cave down.
    2. As you descend, it is natural for your torso to lean forward mildly at your hips to maintain your balance, but maintain a mostly upright torso position with your back flat.
    3. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    5. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
6. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
7. Alternate between steps 4-6 until you have completed your set.

    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
