If you currently do not have the mobility to squat to a 12in (31cm) box with proper form, you can increase the height of the box by placing a thick bumper plate on top of the box to elevate it.
    4. While others have fixed heights like plyometric boxes, the height of certain squat box models can be adjusted to accommodate how deeply you wish to squat.
    5. If you do not have access to a squat box or plyometric box, you can use an aerobic step and adjust its height based on how many risers you stack underneath it.
    6. Alternatively, you may be able to use a flat exercise bench as your box. A bench is excessively tall for many lifters to squat through a full range of motion, but it can be suitable for rather tall individuals, people with limited mobility, and anyone who intentionally wishes to train through a partial range of motion. To fit either a bench or an aerobic step within a rack, you may have to position it with the shorter side facing the side of the rack where you will place the barbell.
    7. As another option, you can also stack bumper plates on top of each other to form a “box” of your desired height. If you opt to do so, make sure that the plates are completely centered on top of each other.
3. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
4. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on your upper back in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should be securely resting on the muscles of your upper back when squeezing your shoulder blades together.
    2. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    5. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
5. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends when squatting.
7. Repeat steps 3 and 4 of the setup before proceeding to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. Take a couple of steps back, and position your feet near shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing slightly out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip-width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside shoulder width and their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. Throughout your set, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    4. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down until you can lightly contact the box with your buttocks.
    1. You are gently tapping the box to provide tactile feedback as to when you reach your desired squat depth with the same squat technique you would use without the box, but you are not actually sitting on the box.
6. Immediately after touching the box, reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
7. Alternate between steps 4-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
8. Walk forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.

## Setting up
1. Add your desired weight to an adjustable plate-loaded EZ bar on top of the preacher curl bench, or place a fixed weight EZ bar on top of the preacher curl bench.
2. Adjust the seat to a height that allows you to rest your elbows and most of the back of your upper arms (i.e., triceps) on the sloped arm pad when sitting on the seat.
    1. The proper setting will typically result in the top of the pad being close to your armpits.
    2. Some trial and error may be needed to find the ideal seat height.
3. Sit down on the seat, and position the back of your upper arms and elbows on top of the arm pad with your feet on the ground.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with a wider than shoulder width grip as your palms are directed at an angle that is facing forward and inward, resulting in a semi-underhand grip (AKA semi-neutral grip).
    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it initially before a wider than shoulder width semi-underhand grip is accessible on the bar.
    2. If the bar is a little out of your reach, you could slightly stand up and lean forward to reach the bar before sitting back down after you have grasped the bar.
    3. Your wrists should be mostly straight throughout your set after grasping the bar.
5. In the starting position, your elbows should be fully straightened with the bar no longer in contact with the bench so that you can train through a full range of motion.
    1. If this is not the case, you can mildly scoot back with an upright torso until you have reached this starting position.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows and the back of your upper arms in contact with the bench, curl the bar upward and back toward you in an arcing motion by bending at your elbows until they are fully bent.
    1. While your forearms move through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout your set.
    2. If your preacher bench allows you to curl the bar past the point when your forearms are completely vertical and perpendicular to the ground, you can finish the lifting phase after your forearms are vertical since the biceps would no longer be working beyond this point.
2. After your elbows have fully bent, reverse the motion by lowering the bar in a slow and controlled manner until your elbows have returned to a fully straightened position.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows and the back of your upper arms in contact with the bench.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar back down onto the preacher bench.
## Description
Like other curls, this exercise can effectively train the biceps and brachialis in your upper arm along with the brachioradialis in your forearm.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a low incline with an angle up to 30 degrees.
    1. If your bench can be adjusted to a moderate incline near 45 degrees but does not have a low incline setting, you can alternatively select the moderate incline dumbbell fly from this database.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on the incline bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your lower thighs near your abdomen with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. If you can curl the weight of the dumbbells, you can sit down on the bench with the dumbbells by your sides before curling them up onto your lap
    2. With heavier dumbbells, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs with your palms facing each other while standing over the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
3. While marching your thighs up one at a time to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench.
    1. Once you are inclined, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent, and you will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest, as you would be in the starting position for a dumbbell incline press.
4. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
5. Press the dumbbells up until your elbows are straight, and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. In this starting position, your wrists should be straight, and you will keep them straight throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your elbows to bend mildly, spread your arms apart from each other as you lower the dumbbells out away from your sides in a slow and controlled arcing manner through the available range of motion of your shoulders.
    1. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to lower the dumbbells at least until their elbows are level with their shoulders and often a little beyond this point, but what is specifically your full range of motion will be dependent on your mobility.
    2. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulder at the bottom, but the end range should not be painful.
    3. After fully spreading your arms apart, your upper arms should form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    4. While your elbows should not be locked into a fully straightened position, they also should be notably less bent than when you are bench pressing, so the dumbbells should be clearly further out to the sides than your elbows (as opposed to being stacked over your elbows like at the bottom of a bench press).
2. Reverse the movement by pulling your arms in toward each other in a hug-like motion to lift the dumbbells upward until you have returned to the starting position with the dumbbells being approximately over your shoulders.
    1. Near the end of the lifting phase, the resistance from the dumbbells is minimal, and there is no purpose of touching the dumbbells to each other.
    2. Toward the end of the lifting phase, you can straighten your elbows, or you can maintain the same degree of mild elbow bend throughout the set.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After your last rep, lower the dumbbells toward the sides of your chest as you allow your elbows to bend like you would during the lowering phase of a dumbbell incline press.
    2. Once the dumbbells are by your chest, you can rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your thighs before placing them down onto the ground one at a time or standing up with them.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also training your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).

## Setting up
1. At a cable station, adjust the cable to be between knee and hip height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at the weight stack.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you will also position the arm furthest back such that it is directed out to the side of the machine.
    2. Dual cable stations that have their two weight stacks facing each other (often with a pull-up in between them) normally lack adjustable arms.
2. While standing with the side of one shoulder facing the cable station, reach to the side and grasp the handle firmly with the hand closer to the cable station, as your palm is facing forward.
    1. Throughout the exercise, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side or on top of your hip bone.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the handle, since that is the side you will be training first.
3. Step out to the side away from the cable station until you feel tension from the cable (as the weight stack separates) while keeping your arm aligned with the cable.
    1. In this position, your arm should form an approximately 45-60-degree angle with your torso (when 0 degrees means your arms are straight by your sides, and 90 degrees means your arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
4. Pivot your feet about 45 degrees away from the cable station as you keep the center of your hips and chest facing the same direction, while allowing the cable’s tension to pull your arm back behind your torso through a range that your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. You will now be facing near a 135-degree angle away from the cable station, which will allow you to train through a full range of motion.
    2. How far you can position your arm behind your torso will be influenced by your individual shoulder mobility.
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of your shoulder in this position, but it should not be painful.
    4. Throughout the exercise, avoid letting the cable’s resistance twist your trunk toward the cable, which would result in your chest facing a different direction than the center of your hips.
5. While mildly bending your knees and your elbow, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other.
    1. In this position, you should feel stable and balanced.
6. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow mildly bent and your torso stationary, sweep your arm inward in an arcing motion as it moves diagonally forward and upward until your arm is outstretched in front of you.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, your hand should be close to shoulder height, and your arm should be close to facing the same direction as your chest.
    2. Keep your chest up throughout the set as you avoid hunching over with your shoulders slouched forward.
    3. As a cue to avoid letting the cable twist your torso, you can think about imaginary laser beams shooting out from your breastbone and where you would wear a belt buckle above your hips. Throughout the set, the lasers from your breastbone and belt buckle should be facing the same direction as they normally would when standing upright without being twisted toward either side.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your arm to sweep out to the side toward the cable station as it moves diagonally backward and downward in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your elbow behind your torso through the range of motion your shoulder mobility allows.
    1. People commonly have the shoulder mobility to allow their arm to pull back until the elbow is at least slightly behind the torso, but your shoulder mobility will determine what your individual end range is.
    2. Continue keeping your torso stationary and your elbow mildly bent, as the movement comes from shoulder motion rather than elbow motion or trunk twisting motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) with an emphasis on the [upper pec](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md) while still training the [middle and lower pec](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md).

### **Notes**

The shoulder motion that is trained by the low-to-high cable fly is very similar to what occurs during an incline dumbbell fly or an incline press variation. Lowering the height of the cables is also akin to increasing the angle for an incline fly or press. When positioned near hip level, the low-to-high cable fly likely results in a training effect that is similar to a low incline (e.g., near 30 degrees) fly, while situating the cables near knee height likely results in a training effect that is similar to a moderate incline (e.g., near 45 degrees) fly.

## Setting up
1. With a cable station’s pulley positioned near hip height, connect a d-handle attachment and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Position yourself to one side of the cable station while facing away from it, resulting in the cable’s handle being underneath one of your arms when your arms are by your sides.
3. After squatting down, use your hand closer to the cable to grasp the handle with your palm facing back toward the cable (i.e., an overhand grip) while your elbow is straight.
    1. Throughout the exercise, you can keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side or on top of your hip bone.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the handle, since that is the side you will be training first.
4. While keeping your elbow straight, stand upright with the handle.
5. Walk forward while keeping your elbow straight and allowing the cable’s resistance to pull your arm backward at an angle behind your torso through a range that your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. You can continue walking forward until you feel that you have reached the end range to which your arm can comfortably be pulled behind your torso, which will be influenced by your individual shoulder mobility.
    2. With your arm positioned behind your torso, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulder, but it should not be painful.
    3. In this position, you should feel tension from the cable, and your forearm and upper arm should form a straight line with the cable that is diagonally angled forward and upward from the pulley.
6. While mildly bending your knees, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other, and your chest is up in an upright position.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow straight, sweep your arm forward and upward in an arcing manner until your arm is approximately parallel to the ground, outstretched in front of you, which will result in your palm facing down toward the ground.
    1. While your arm moves from motion at your shoulder, the rest of your body should remain stationary, and your wrist should be straight throughout your set.
    2. As a cue, you can think about the side of your shoulder being the center of a clock, and your arm is the hand of a clock that rotates about this point.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your arm to sweep downward and backward in a controlled arcing manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arm positioned behind your body through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility allows.
    1. Continue keeping your elbow straightened.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [upper pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

    1. You will now be facing near a 135-degree angle away from the cable station, which will allow you to train through a full range of motion.

    3. Throughout the exercise, avoid letting the cable’s resistance twist your trunk toward the cable, which would result in your chest facing a different direction than the center of your hips.

## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow mildly bent and your torso stationary, sweep your arm inward in an arcing motion as it moves diagonally forward and downward until your arm is outstretched in front of you.

Throughout the set, the lasers from your breastbone and belt buckle should be facing the same direction as they normally would when standing upright without being twisted toward either side.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your arm to sweep out to the side toward the cable station as it moves diagonally backward and upward in a controlled manner until you have moved through your shoulder’s full range of motion and have returned to the starting position.
    1. Continue keeping your torso stationary and your elbow mildly bent, as the movement comes from shoulder motion rather than elbow motion or trunk twisting motion.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on a flat exercise bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your upper thighs near your abdomen, with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Position yourself so that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    2. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    3. To move heavy dumbbells efficiently into the proper position, you can initially situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up. Then you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
2. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
4. Flare your elbows moderately out to your sides such that your upper arms form approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    1. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable for your shoulders, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbows out within this range.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Press both dumbbells up by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten them until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press, as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, keep your feet flat on the floor and your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
3. While keeping one arm stationary with a straight elbow, lower the other side’s dumbbell in a controlled manner toward the side of your chest through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Let your elbow moderately flare out to your side as it descends and bends enough to keep your wrist stacked above it with a vertical forearm. Lifters often find that at least a mild degree of elbow tuck makes this exercise feel most comfortable for the shoulder compared to fully flaring the elbow straight out to the side.
    2. How far you can lower the dumbbell with a vertical forearm will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hand is at least level with their chest.
    3. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of the shoulder at the bottom.
    4. There is no need to lower the dumbbell extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.
4. As you continue keeping your higher arm motionless and directed straight up toward the ceiling, use the same technique from step 2 to press the other dumbbell upward until that arm is symmetrical with your stationary arm.
    1. Except for the start and end of the set, you will only be moving one arm at a time.
5. Repeat steps 3 and 4 while switching which arm remains stationary and which arm moves the dumbbell.
6. Alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After lowering both dumbbells near your chest following the last rep, bring your upper arms in line with your sides to tuck your elbows and position the dumbbells closer to your thighs.
    2. Then march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs before standing up with them.
## Description
While not loading your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) as effectively as a barbell bench press, this exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also meaningfully training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md).

When only using smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a deficit deadlift with a greater range of motion that may exceed the range of motion in which some people wish to train if they lack the mobility to perform a deficit deadlift with appropriate technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize the largest diameter plates, you can perform a block pull with the bar elevated to where it would be when deadlifting from the floor with large diameter plates.
2. With your arms directed down toward the ground, straight elbows, and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    5. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
3. Firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat with the bar close to your shins, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the bar reaches near the middle of your shins, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
5. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement in a controlled manner by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates contact the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Immediately after the plates touch the ground in a controlled fashion, fluidly initiate your next rep by repeating step 3 while staying braced with full body tension before continuing onto steps 4 and 5 again.
    1. Using this touch-and-go deadlift technique should provide a mild rebound from the plates tapping the ground that helps make the start of the next rep a bit easier compared to if you let the plates come to a dead stop on the ground between reps.
    2. Do not bounce the plates off the ground in an uncontrolled manner that contributes to technique degradation.
    3. Throughout the entirety of the set, you should be in complete control over the bar as you prioritize using essentially the same form for your touch-and-go reps as you did with the first rep.
7. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in the fully upright position after locking out a rep before you resume fully bracing your core.

While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), along with your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.
    1. In this position, your knees should be approximately hip-width apart, with your elbows stacked under your shoulders and your arms pointing straight down toward the ground. 
    2. For comfort, you can optionally place a fitness mat, cushion, or pillow under your knees.
2. Situate your hands clearly outside shoulder width apart from each other (i.e., about twice shoulder width distance apart), with your fingers spread somewhat apart from each other.
    1. So long as your hands are wider apart than during your standard push-up with a moderate grip width, you can use somewhat of a range of hand placements for your wide grip, but you should place your hands in a position that feels right to your shoulders.
    2. Your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
3. Walk your hands forward while allowing your hips to straighten until you can draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your torso, like when you are normally standing upright.
    1. After doing so, your hands should still be outside and underneath your shoulders rather than being in front of your shoulders (i.e., horizontally closer to your head) or behind your shoulders (i.e., horizontally closer to your hips).
    2. Rather than being directly above your knees like they were in step 1, your hips should now be horizontally in front of your knees.
    3. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
4. Lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees further, and keep them off the ground throughout your set.
    1. How much you bend your knees is up to preference, and whether you cross your ankles or leave them uncrossed is also up to your preference.
## Exercise technique
1. Tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes, which you will continue doing throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag downward, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag toward the ground, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso in a rigid position, lower your chest toward the ground in a controlled manner as you bend your elbows until you are able to contact the ground with your chest.
    1. Rather than trying to keep your elbows tucked in by your sides, allow your elbows to flare out away from your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you as you descend. For many people, this can result in the upper arms forming at least 60-degree angles with the torso at the bottom of a wide grip push-up (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    2. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ground instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ground to lift your body as you progressively straighten your elbows until you have returned to the starting position with fully straightened elbows.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your thighs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still allow you to draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your torso.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), which is assisted by your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), and [pec minor](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Minor%201905c6f170d88030b03dd3f99706ecb0.md).

## Setting up
1. Determine what you will use as your weight that can securely rest on your middle and upper back while performing your push-up.
    1. Wearing a weighted vest is an excellent option if you have one due to its stability and ease of setting up, but most people lack a weighted vest.
    2. If someone can assist you, a partner can also place a weight plate or stack of weight plates on your back once you have completed step 4 and assumed the tall plank position. With this approach, a rubber-coated plate is best since it is less likely to slide than a purely iron plate. If you are in a gym without a designated training partner, many lifters would be open to lending a hand if you just politely ask them to do so. Communicate to the other person that you would like him/her to lift the plate off your back after finishing your last rep, in addition to placing it on your middle back to begin the set.
    3. As a substitute for a weighted vest, you can add weighted objects to a sufficiently sturdy backpack. If you do so, you would want to try to have the weight as evenly distributed as possible to reduce the likelihood of it sliding around or shifting to rest on your lower back, which may be difficult to avoid with weight plates in many backpacks. Chains may be more likely to fill up a backpack evenly, and textbooks can also be viable when using lighter loads. When present, securely fastening chest straps and hip straps on a backpack can increase its stability.
    4. If you decide to use a vest or a loaded backpack to carry your weight, put it on yourself now. If you decide to use a weight plate, make sure your partner is standing nearby with your desired weight and understands what to do before proceeding to step 2.
2. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.
    1. Your elbows should be stacked under your shoulders with your arms pointing straight down toward the ground.
3. Situate your hands mildly outside shoulder width apart from each other, with your fingers spread somewhat apart from each other.
    1. Your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
4. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you, and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. If you are using a weight plate for your resistance, have your partner now position it symmetrically on your middle and upper back, but you will naturally ignore this step if you are using a vest or backpack.
3. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest in a controlled manner until it lightly touches the ground.
    1. Let your elbows flare out moderately away from your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you. This commonly results in the upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with the torso (when viewed from above) at the bottom of the push-up. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your elbows are fully tucked to your sides, remaining shoulder-width the whole rep, while 90 degrees of flare would mean your elbows point straight out to your sides, letting your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ground instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    5. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
    6. If you are wearing a weighted vest, its thickness may slightly limit your range of motion and preclude you from touching the ground with your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ground to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you are using a weight plate, direct your partner to remove the weight after finishing your last rep.
## Description
This  exercise primarily trains your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), which is assisted by your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), and [pec minor](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Minor%201905c6f170d88030b03dd3f99706ecb0.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a flat exercise bench centered underneath a Smith machine’s bar in a spot that will situate the bar over your chest when lying down on the bench.
    1. Specifically how you should set up can be influenced by whether your Smith machine has sliding rails that are purely vertical or angled. With either type, you want to set up in a manner that results in the bar being able to touch your lower chest at the bottom of the press.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, place the side of the bench where you will place your feet on the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends. This will result in the top of the rails being horizontally closer to your head than the bottom of the rails when lying down on the bench. An angled Smith machine will allow you to use a bar path that most closely resembles that of a standard barbell bench press.
    3. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which side of the bar you place your feet.
2. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to grasp it with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently.
    1. The ideal height allows you to unrack the bar while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together without requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    2. If the bar is situated too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart to lift the bar off the safety bars (on which the safety hooks that are attached to the bar rest). This can place you in a less stable position to start your set since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    3. If the bar is situated excessively low, you will have to grasp the bar initially with a greater degree of elbow bend, and unracking it will involve a greater than ideal pressing range of motion. This will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    4. If neither of the two closest bar heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    5. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best starting bar height for you.
3. After positioning the bar to the appropriate height, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section. Use these reps to determine the appropriate height of the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails under the bar) prior to re-racking the bar.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety stops to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could untuck your shoulder blades and flatten out your back to lose your arch. This will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety stops.
    2. Certain Smith machine models have fairly wide spaces between where you could position safety stops. This may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your Smith machine, it is not ideal, and you have the option of using a spotter. However, the safety stops can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck if you are pinned under a bar and try to scoot out.
    3. If you cannot press the bar fully up and lack a spotter or safety stops that are able to receive the bar when flattening your back, you may be able to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars above your chest if you are able to complete part of the press. If you happen to become pinned in this situation and are initially unable to reach the nearest safety bars above you, you can let the bar rest on your chest until you feel recovered enough to press the bar up high enough to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your chest is underneath the bar, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor approximately shoulder width apart.
    1. If your Smith machine has vertical slide rails, situate your lower chest under the bar.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, situate your upper chest under the bar to allow the bar to reach your lower chest at the bottom of the rep.
    3. With the fixed bar path from the Smith machine, it may be worthwhile to try scooting slightly forward or backward on the bench if the exercise feels a bit awkward with your initial positioning.
    4. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    5. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands well outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A wide grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around two times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. What is personally considered a wide grip to you can also be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard bench press, which you can somewhat widen to individualize your wide grip. For instance, for your wide grip, you can place your index finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your little finger when performing your standard bench press.
    3. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning to bench press, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    4. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    5. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the safety bars by straightening your elbows before rotating the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion. After unracking it, hold the bar stationary for a moment before starting to lower it.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them naturally to flare out  away from each other while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists rather than letting your elbows track meaningfully in front of your wrists (closer to your hips) or behind them.
    2. Near the bottom of the rep, the appropriate amount of elbow flare should result in your upper arms forming reasonably close to 75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are touching your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    3. Compared to a closer grip bench press, your elbows should flare out further away from your sides during a wide grip bench press.
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up until you have fully straightened your elbows. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
    1. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second.
6. Rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars by flicking your wrists before bending your elbows to lower the safety hooks securely onto the safety bars.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.

## Setting up
1. Load an adjustable EZ bar with your desired weight or approach a fixed-weight EZ bar.
    1. Either type of EZ bar can be used interchangeably for this exercise.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down and firmly grasp it with your palms angled backward and in toward each other (resulting in a semi-overhand grip) as your hands are about shoulder width apart or somewhat closer.
    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it before a shoulder-width or closer semi-overhand grip is accessible on the bar.
    2. Since a range of grip widths can be effectively used for this exercise, you can determine your specific grip width based on what feels most comfortable to you.
3. Stand upright with the bar, and walk over to a flat exercise bench before turning your back to the bench.
4. Lift the bar up slightly above your waist and sit down on the bench with the bar on your lap and enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space.
5. While keeping your elbows bent and the bar close to your torso, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. As you transition from sitting to lying down, you optionally can march your thighs up against the bar to help reposition yourself.
    2. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent, and you will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Press the bar up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a bench press rep), your wrist should be reasonably straight rather than bent backward, and you should keep your wrist reasonably straight throughout the exercise.
2. While keeping your elbows fairly straight, lower the bar back behind your head in a controlled arcing manner through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. You should avoid meaningfully bending your elbows, but you can allow them to bend mildly as your arms move through motion at your shoulders while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
    2. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, as you avoid excessively arching your lower back during the descent.
    3. People can often lower the bar until their upper arms are close to parallel with the ground, but how far you can descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    4. Once you feel that you have reached the end range to which your shoulders can safely stretch, you have reached the end range for you as an individual.
3. Reverse the movement by pulling your arms upward and forward in an arcing motion to lift the bar until you have returned to the starting position with your arms directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows fairly straight as you move your arms through shoulder motion while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can train your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which are assisted by the [lowest portion of your pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) in the overhead position of each rep.

## Setting up
1. Position a pair of deadlift blocks (or a similarly sturdy substitute capable of safely withstanding the load you will use) on the ground far enough apart from each other that the weight plates on a bar will be able to rest fully on the blocks in a stable position.
    1. For this block pull variation, your blocks should be of a height that situates the bar close to slightly below your knees when the loaded bar is resting on the blocks. This results in a moderate height block pull with a somewhat greater elevation than the mid-shin block pull also present in this database.
    2. To appropriately position the blocks, it can be helpful to have a barbell on the ground and align the blocks about the same distance apart from each other as is the length of the barbell’s shaft (which is the middle part of the bar in between the two thick circular collars).
    3. Aerobic steps can often be used for block pulls while having the option to adjust the height by changing the number of risers you use, but you should be aware of the recommended weight limit if you opt to use heavy loads. The weight limit for aerobic steps will vary by brand, but some of the common brands recommend not exceeding 300lb (136kg) per step, which would result in a 600lb (272kg) limit when using a pair of steps for a block pull. The height of the aerobic step will also vary by brand, but the step itself is commonly near 4in (10cm) in height, with the risers being near 2in (5cm) in height.
    4. With thickness typically ranging from about 1-3.5in (2.5-8.9cm), depending on the weight and brand, bumper plates can also function as blocks that can be stacked on top of each other to provide a range of different heights.
    5. It may be worthwhile to try out different block heights to determine which height places you in your intended starting position. However, you can initially try out a pair of approximately 6-8in (15-20cm) deadlift blocks, aerobic steps with 1-2 pairs of risers, or a pair of two thick 45lb (20kg) bumper plates stacked on top of each other. Your individual body proportions will dictate where the bar is specifically positioned relative to your knees, but the aforementioned set-up options should situate a bar loaded with large diameter plates (e.g., 45lb (20kg) plates or any jumper plates) reasonably close to slightly below the knees for many people and allow you to adjust the height as needed. If you are going to add only smaller diameter plates onto the bar, higher blocks will naturally be needed to position the bar at the appropriate height.
2. After placing a barbell onto the blocks and loading weight plates to the bar, stand upright in approximately a hip width stance close in front of the middle of the bar as the bar is over the middle of your feet with your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly turned out to the sides.
    1. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    2. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
3. With your arms directed down toward the ground, straight elbows, and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while allowing your knees to bend until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your shins should remain close to being vertical, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward to bring your shins right next to the bar.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees a bit further to reach the bar.
    3. When hinging your hips properly, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings on the back of your thighs at the bottom of your hip hinge.
    4. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    5. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    6. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent (i.e., the quadruped position, which is also known as being “on all fours”).
    1. In this position, your elbows should be stacked underneath your shoulders with your arms pointing straight down toward the ground.
2. Situate your hands mildly outside shoulder width apart from each other, with your fingers spread somewhat apart from each other.
    1. Your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
3. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you, and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart from each other as your heels are facing backward.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes, which you will continue doing throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag downward, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should allow you to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag down, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso in a rigid position and your legs straight, lower your chest toward the ground in a controlled manner as you bend your elbows until you are able to contact the ground with your chest.
    1. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ground instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    2. As you descend, allow your elbows to flare out moderately away from your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you. This can result in the upper arms forming approximately 30-60-degree angles with the torso for many people at the bottom of the push-up (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag down below your chest or hike up excessively above your chest.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ground to lift your whole body as you progressively straighten your elbows until you have returned to the starting position with fully straightened elbows.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart naturally from each other as you push up.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will allow you to still draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso.
4. Immediately after you finish straightening your elbows, continue pushing the ground away from you as you further spread your shoulder blades apart as far as you can while keeping your elbows straight.
    1. While prompting your upper back to round mildly, this will cause your chest to lift up a little higher above the ground, but it is a fairly small amplitude of motion.
    2. If you performed this shoulder blade motion when standing with your arms outstretched parallel to the ground, your shoulder blades would move forward.
    3. As a cue, you can imagine what it would feel like if you were leaning forward with your arms outstretched in front of you, and you are trying to touch something just beyond your reach with your elbows fully straightened. Pushing your shoulder blades forward as they spread apart would push your hands slightly forward to touch that object, and you should be performing the same shoulder blade motion during this step.
    4. Steps 3 and 4 should occur as a fluid movement.
5. Allow your shoulder blades to move back and toward each other until they have returned to being near their typical neutral position, like at the top of a standard push-up.
    1. Doing so will lower your chest slightly closer to the ground.
6. Alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. You should fluidly transition from step 5 back to the lowering phase of step 2.
    2. Steps 2 and 3 are the same as during a standard push-up, so the “plus” of a push-up plus simply refers to the additional shoulder blade motion performed at the top of each rep.

## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the kettlebell, apply “pre-tension” into the handle as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force that would lift the weight if it was only half as heavy
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position and pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat, drive through your legs to begin lifting the kettlebell as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the handle reaches near the middle of your shins, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
5. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the kettlebell until it has returned to resting on the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttock back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the handle has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the kettlebell.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the kettlebell up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the kettlebell on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferring between reps.

## Description
While also training your back’s spinal extensor muscles, this exercise can train much of lower body musculature including your buttock’s gluteus maximus along with the hamstrings, quads, and hip adductor muscles in your thighs.
