## Setting up
1. Position a pair of deadlift blocks (or a similarly sturdy substitute capable of safely withstanding the load you will use) on the ground far enough apart from each other that the weight plates on a bar will be able to rest fully on the blocks in a stable position.
    1. For this block pull variation, your blocks should be of a height that situates the bar slightly above your knees when the loaded bar is resting on the blocks. This results in a high block pull with a greater elevation than the other block pulls included in this database.
    2. To appropriately position the blocks, it can be helpful to have a barbell on the ground and align the blocks about the same distance apart from each other as is the length of the barbell’s shaft (which is the middle part of the bar in between the two thick circular collars).
    3. Aerobic steps can often be used for block pulls while having the option to adjust the height by changing the number of risers you use, but you should be aware of the recommended weight limit if you opt to use heavy loads. The weight limit for aerobic steps will vary by brand, but some of the common brands recommend not exceeding 300lb (136kg) per step, which would result in a 600lb (272kg) limit when using a pair of steps for a block pull. The height of the aerobic step will also vary by brand, but the step itself is commonly near 4in (10cm) in height, with the risers being near 2in (5cm) in height.
    4. With thickness typically ranging from about 1-3.5in (2.5-8.9cm), depending on the weight and brand, bumper plates can also function as blocks that can be stacked on top of each other to provide a range of different heights.
    5. It may be worthwhile to try out different block heights to determine which height places you in your intended starting position. However, you can initially try out a pair of approximately 10in (15-20cm) deadlift blocks, aerobic steps with three pairs of risers, or a pair of three thick 45lb (20kg) bumper plates stacked on top of each other. Your individual body proportions will dictate where the bar is specifically positioned relative to your knees, but the aforementioned set-up options should situate a bar loaded with large diameter plates (e.g., 45lb (20kg) plates or any jumper plates) reasonably close to slightly above the knees for many people and allow you to adjust the height as needed. If you are going to add only smaller diameter plates onto the bar, higher blocks will naturally be needed to position the bar at the appropriate height.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with straight legs and your feet approximately hip-width apart. The back of your head should either rest on the ground or on your hands, which you can clasp behind your head.
    1. If you do not opt to position your hands behind your head, you can feel free to situate your arms wherever you prefer (e.g., resting on the ground by your sides).
    2. On the ground, your legs and torso should be in the same position you exhibit when normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your knees straightened, lift both of your feet mildly (i.e., approximately 6 inches (15 centimeters)) up off the ground while you tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground.
    1. Pressing your lower back into the ground will flatten it out from abdominal muscle contraction and prevent you from being able to slide a hand under your lower back.
    2. If you do not contract your abdominals, lifting both legs up would prompt your lower back to develop an exaggerated arch that would allow you to slide a hand under your lower back.
2. As you hold the position described in step 1, tuck your chin toward your chest to lift your head off the ground and mildly curl your upper back (in a crunch-like motion) to lift your shoulder blades slightly up off the ground.
    1. Doing so should prompt you to feel your upper abdominal muscles further tightening up.
    2. Maintain this head position throughout your set.
3. As you keep one leg stationary, lift your other leg somewhat (e.g., about 6 to 10 inches (15 to 25 centimeters)) higher up while keeping both knees straight.
    1. Specifically how high you lift this leg is up to your preference since a range of heights can effectively be used for this exercise.
4. In a scissor-like manner, lower your top leg toward the starting position (about 6 inches (15 centimeters)) off the ground) while simultaneously lifting up your lower leg to the same height you just did with your other leg in step 3.
    1. How quickly you move is up to you, but strive to move each leg at the same speed such that they finish switching positions at the same time.
    2. Continue keeping your head up and lower back pressed into the ground with your abdominal muscles tensed throughout your set as you avoid arching your lower back.
5. Cyclically repeat step 3 while switching which leg moves up and down each time until you have completed your set.
## Description
Along with training your hip flexor muscles on the front of your thigh, this exercise can statically train your abdominal muscles including your obliques and particularly your rectus abdominis, which is the “six-pack muscle.”

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, you will find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you, and the optimal J-hook height for a close grip bench press may be slightly higher compared to when you use a wider grip.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench as your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor approximately shoulder width apart from each other.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. You can similarly decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) as your hands are near shoulder width apart from each other, with the bar on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. Positioning your hands near shoulder-width apart results in somewhat of a range, but you can initially start with a shoulder-width grip and try out mildly different hand widths over time to determine where specifically you feel best.
    2. What is personally considered a close grip to you can also be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard bench press, which you can somewhat narrow to individualize your close grip. For instance, for your close grip, you can place your little finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your index finger when performing your standard bench press.  
    3. For stability, your thumbs should be wrapped around the bar from the opposite side of your other fingers, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands in contrast to if you positioned your thumbs on the same side of your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip that is also called a “suicide grip”).
    4. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists meaningfully cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort.
    5. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together, which is a position you will maintain throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades, which should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting, like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together as you avoid losing your upper back tightness.
    2. In this position, your wrist should be stacked above your elbows, which should be stacked above your shoulders as your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and keeping them reasonably tucked in toward your sides while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set, which will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow tuck as you touch the bar to your lower chest.
    2. Near the bottom of the rep, the appropriate amount of elbow tuck should result in your upper arms forming close to 30-45-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are touching your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    3. Compared to a wider grip bench press, your elbows should not flare out away from your sides as much during a close grip bench press.
    4. When aiming to touch the bar to your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    5. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Once the bar contacts your chest, pause in that bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., 1-2 seconds) while staying tight.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up as you progressively drive your elbows upward and inward while straightening them until you have returned to the starting position with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is situated above your shoulders.
    1. To finish with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest, the bar will now arc slightly backward as you lift it up.
    2. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
6. Alternate between steps 3-5 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
7. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
8. Bend your elbows mildly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
While still training the chest’s [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) and [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) effectively, this exercise can preferentially train the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) to a greater degree than wider grip bench press variations.

1. Drive your feet into the ground, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins/spotter arms.
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your rack, it is not ideal, but the safety pins/spotter arms can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck.
    3. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning to bench press, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.

Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. ## Setting up
1. Position a pair of low deadlift blocks (or a similarly sturdy substitute capable of safely withstanding the load you will use) on the ground far enough apart from each other that the weight plates on a bar will be able to rest fully on the blocks in a stable position.
    1. For this low block pull, your blocks should be of a height that elevates the bar mildly (about 1-2in (2.5-5cm)) above the ground when the bar is resting on the blocks after being loaded with full diameter plates (like 45lb (20kg) plates or bumper plates). If you are going to add only smaller diameter plates onto the bar, higher blocks will naturally be needed to position the bar to the equivalent height.
    2. To appropriately position the blocks, it can be helpful to have a barbell on the ground and align the blocks about the same distance apart from each other as is the length of the barbell’s shaft (which is the middle part of the bar in between the two thick circular collars).
    3. With thickness typically ranging from about 1-3.5in (2.5-8.9cm), depending on the weight and brand, bumper plates can also function as a substitute for deadlift blocks.
    4. You can alternatively stack EVA foam mats on top of each other to serve as your blocks.
    5. While they often can be used for higher block pulls, aerobic steps are typically too tall to use for a sumo low block pull.
2. After placing a barbell onto the blocks and loading weight plates onto the bar, stand upright close in front of the middle of the bar as the bar is approximately over the middle of your feet.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
3. Spread your legs apart into a wide stance that is clearly outside shoulder width, with your feet moderately rotated out away from your sides.
    1. Provided that your feet are wider apart than your shoulders but closer together than the plates, you can use a range of stance widths for your sumo deadlift.
    2. The ideal stance width can meaningfully vary among different individuals based on someone’s body structure and hip mobility.
    3. Trying out different foot positions will normally be required to determine which stance specifically feels best to you.
    4. As a starting point, you can widen your feet as far apart as you feel comfortable and stable while being able to push your knees out approximately over your heels, resulting in close to vertical shins. You will push your knees out when descending to reach the bar, so subsequent aspects of the setup can help you gauge if you should adjust your stance.
    5. The ideal amount of toe flare also varies among different lifters, but you can start with your toes pointing about 30-45 degrees out to the side before adjusting from there based on what feels best to you. Zero degrees of toe flare would mean your toes are pointing straight forward, while 90 degrees would mean your toes are pointing directly out to your side.
4. Direct your arms straight down toward the ground with straight elbows as your shoulders are packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up).
    1. Maintain this position from here onward.
5. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips while bending your knees and pushing your knees out until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees, and your knees should essentially not track forward (although a slight degree of forward knee tracking can be used if that feels best to you).
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something. After you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Try to push your knees far enough out to the sides that they are vertically stacked over your heels.
    4. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    5. Similarly, keep your chest up in a “proud chest” posture and your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    6. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
    7. The bar should be directly in front of your shins.
6. With your shoulders stacked vertically above the bar, firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down, such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath). This should expand the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles, like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360-degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. Continue bracing your core throughout your set. This will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. This can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” by extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. Keep your chest up, back flat, and knees pushed out.
    2. As your hips and chest rise at the same rate, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull. Avoid letting your torso incline further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
    3. Keep the bar very close to your legs throughout the rep.
4. After the bar reaches near your knees, focus on thrusting your hips forward until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back when viewed from the side.
5. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips and bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the blocks.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your hips back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally. After the bar has cleared your knees, you can further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
    2. Continue keeping your back flat and chest up.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the blocks for a moment rather than simply tapping the blocks and immediately deadlifting the bar up again. Then continue to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the blocks for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferring between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the blocks.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.

2. Then perform the lifting phase of a [sumo deadlift](Sumo%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d8807aae84e2c6eb136395.md) to assume an upright position.
    1. With your knees and hips fully straightened, you are now ready to start your set of sumo Romanian deadlifts.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath). This should expand the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles, like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360-degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. Continue bracing your core throughout your set. This will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips.
2. Sit your buttocks backward while allowing your knees to bend mildly to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straightened, core braced, and lower back near a neutral position throughout your set.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Avoid letting the bar drift forward away from being just in front of your legs, which may be more likely to occur if you think about “bending over” rather than “sitting back.”
    4. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened.
    5. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit back without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    6. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    7. While you hinge at your hips, the bar will naturally descend, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
3. Continue to sit your buttocks back through your full range of motion while keeping your back flat with mildly bent knees.
    1. How deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit your buttocks any farther back, you have finished descending through your available range of motion.
    3. If you have sufficiently high hamstring flexibility and are able to hinge until the plates contact the ground, hinge until you are able to tap the plates lightly on the ground. Do not bounce the plates off the ground or let the weight rest on the ground.
4. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed.
    2. Continue keeping your lower back and neck near neutral position while staying braced with the bar close to your legs.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down onto the floor.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
    3. After finishing the last rep, set the bar down in the same manner in which you initially picked it up (e.g., keeping your back flat rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath). This should expand the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles, like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360-degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. Continue bracing your core throughout your set. This will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. This can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” by extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. Keep your chest up, back flat, and knees pushed out.
    2. As your hips and chest rise at the same rate, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull. Avoid letting your torso incline further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
    3. Keep the bar very close to your legs throughout the rep.
4. After the bar reaches near your knees, focus on thrusting your hips forward until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back when viewed from the side.
5. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by hinging at your hips and bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates lightly contact the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your hips back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally. After the bar has cleared your knees, you can further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
    2. Continue keeping your back flat and chest up.
6. Immediately after the plates touch the ground, fluidly initiate your next rep by repeating step 3 before continuing onto steps 4 and 5 again.
    1. Stay braced with full body tension when transitioning to your next rep.
    2. Using this touch-and-go deadlift technique should provide a mild rebound from the plates tapping the ground. This can make the start of the next rep a bit easier compared to if you let the plates come to a dead stop on the ground between reps.
    3. Do not bounce the plates off the ground in an uncontrolled manner that contributes to technique degradation.
    4. Throughout the entirety of the set, you should be in complete control over the weight as you prioritize using essentially the same form for your touch-and-go reps as you did with the first rep.
7. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in the fully upright position after locking out a rep before you resume fully bracing your core.

## Setting up
1. Position a flat exercise bench centered underneath a Smith machine’s bar in a spot that will situate the bar over your chest when lying down on the bench.
    1. Specifically how you should set up can be influenced by whether your Smith machine has sliding rails that are purely vertical or angled. With either type, you want to set up in a manner that results in the bar being able to touch your lower chest at the bottom of the press.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, place the side of the bench where you will place your feet on the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends. This will result in the top of the rails being horizontally closer to your head than the bottom of the rails when lying down on the bench. An angled Smith machine will allow you to use a bar path that most closely resembles that of a standard barbell bench press.
    3. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which side of the bar you place your feet.
2. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to grasp it with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently.
    1. The ideal height allows you to unrack the bar while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together without requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    2. If the bar is situated too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart to lift the bar off the safety bars (on which the safety hooks that are attached to the bar rest). This can place you in a less stable position to start your set since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    3. If the bar is situated excessively low, you will have to grasp the bar initially with a greater degree of elbow bend, and unracking it will involve a greater than ideal pressing range of motion. This will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    4. If neither of the two closest bar heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    5. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best starting bar height for you.
3. After positioning the bar to the appropriate height, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section. Use these reps to determine the appropriate height of the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails under the bar) prior to re-racking the bar.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety stops to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could untuck your shoulder blades and flatten out your back to lose your arch. This will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety stops.
    2. Certain Smith machine models have fairly wide spaces between where you could position safety stops. This may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your Smith machine, it is not ideal, and you have the option of using a spotter. However, the safety stops can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck if you are pinned under a bar and try to scoot out.
    3. If you cannot press the bar fully up and lack a spotter or safety stops that are able to receive the bar when flattening your back, you may be able to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars above your chest if you are able to complete part of the press. If you happen to become pinned in this situation and are initially unable to reach the nearest safety bars above you, you can let the bar rest on your chest until you feel recovered enough to press the bar up high enough to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your chest is underneath the bar, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor approximately shoulder width apart.
    1. If your Smith machine has vertical slide rails, situate your lower chest under the bar.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, situate your upper chest under the bar to allow the bar to reach your lower chest at the bottom of the rep.
    3. With the fixed bar path from the Smith machine, it may be worthwhile to try scooting slightly forward or backward on the bench if the exercise feels a bit awkward with your initial positioning.
    4. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    5. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands near shoulder width apart. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. You can initially start with a shoulder-width grip, but positioning your hands near shoulder-width apart results in a bit of a range of possible hand placements. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning to bench press, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the safety bars by straightening your elbows before rotating the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion. After unracking it, hold the bar stationary for a moment before starting to lower it.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and keeping them reasonably tucked in toward your sides while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set. This will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow tuck when touching the bar to your lower chest.
    2. Near the bottom of the rep, the appropriate amount of elbow tuck should result in your upper arms forming close to 30-45-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are touching your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    3. Compared to a wider grip bench press, your elbows should not flare out away from your sides as much during a close grip bench press.
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up until you have fully straightened your elbows. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward.
    1. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
    1. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second.
6. Rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars by flicking your wrists before bending your elbows to lower the safety hooks securely onto the safety bars.
## Description
While still training the chest’s [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) and [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) effectively, this exercise can preferentially train the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) to a greater degree than wider grip bench press variations.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a high incline with an angle that is at least 60 degrees but less than 90 degrees.
    1. If your bench lacks a high incline setting, you can alternatively select the [45° incline Smith machine press](45%C2%B0%20incline%20Smith%20machine%20press%201a05c6f170d880ccbf5aeb7f1b3fcee5.md) or [seated Smith machine overhead press](Smith%20machine%20overhead%20press%2024f5c6f170d88077beffc838033a5eea.md) as a substitution that you can perform with your bench.
2. Center the incline bench underneath a Smith machine’s bar in a spot that will allow you to touch near your upper chest with the bar at the bottom of the press.
    1. After initially estimating which bench placement allows this to occur, you may have to move the bench a bit forward or backward during later steps if you notice the bar does not reach near your upper chest.
    2. Specifically how you should set up can be influenced by whether your Smith machine has sliding rails that are purely vertical or angled.
    3. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, place the side of the bench where you will place your feet on the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends. This will result in the top of the rails being horizontally closer to your head than the bottom of the rails when lying down on the bench. An angled Smith machine will prompt the bar to track mildly back toward your head when pressing the bar up.
    4. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which side of the bar you place your feet.
3. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to grasp it with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently.
    1. The ideal height allows you to unrack the bar while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together without requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    2. If the bar is situated too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart to lift the bar off the safety bars (on which the safety hooks that are attached to the bar rest). This can place you in a less stable position to start your set since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    3. If the bar is situated excessively low, you will have to grasp the bar initially with a greater degree of elbow bend, and unracking it will involve a greater than ideal pressing range of motion. This will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    4. If neither of the two closest bar heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    5. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best starting bar height for you.
4. After positioning the bar to the appropriate height, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of incline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section. Use these reps to determine the appropriate height of the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails under the bar) prior to re-racking the bar.
5. Position the safety stops slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your incline press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could untuck your shoulder blades and flatten out your back to lose your arch. This will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety stops.
    2. Certain Smith machine models have fairly wide spaces between where you could position safety stops. This may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion, being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your Smith machine, it is not ideal, and you have the option of using a spotter.
    3. If you cannot press the bar fully up and lack a spotter or safety stops that are able to receive the bar when flattening your back, you may be able to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars above your chest if you are able to complete part of the press. If you happen to become pinned in this situation and are initially unable to reach the nearest safety bars above you, you can let the bar rest on your chest until you feel recovered enough to press the bar up high enough to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars.
6. After loading the bar with your intended weight, lie down with your back and head on the incline bench. Firmly place your feet flat on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart with your knees bent and buttocks resting on the seat of the bench.
    1. With the appropriate bench placement, your upper chest should be under the bar if your Smith machine has vertical slide rails. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, your upper chest should be mildly horizontally in front of the bar.
    2. Based on what feels most stable, you can position your heels directly under your knees with vertical shins, or you can bend your knees a bit beyond this point to position your heels slightly behind your knees with slightly angled shins.
7. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for bench press variations is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
8. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the safety bars by straightening your elbows before rotating the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion. After unracking it, hold the bar stationary for a moment before starting to lower it.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other. Descend until you are able to tap your upper chest or collarbone lightly with the bar or until you have fully moved through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom, but certain individuals with limited shoulder mobility may not be able to touch their chest with the bar without discomfort. If this applies to you, lower the bar as far as you can without discomfort.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists (when viewed from the side). This will keep your forearms close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set and naturally promote the appropriate balance between elbow flare and elbow tuck.
    3. Avoid fully flaring your elbows out away from your sides or completely tucking them. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up until you have fully straightened your elbows. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together as your feet and buttocks remain firmly planted respectively on the ground and bench.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
    1. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second.
6. Rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars by flicking your wrists before bending your elbows to lower the safety hooks securely onto the safety bars.

    2. When lowering the bar toward your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    3. To touch your lower chest, you will have to keep your elbows tucked to a degree instead of being fully flared out, and the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar to your lower chest. ## Setting up
1. Place a stability ball (also known as a Swiss ball or physio ball) on the ground.
2. After lying down with your back on the ground, place the heel and calf of one leg on top of the ball with a straight knee.
    1. Make sure that your heel is centered on the half of the ball, further away from you, to provide sufficient room for you to drive your heel back without sliding off the ball.
    2. While the back of your heel is in contact with the ball, the sole of your foot should be facing forward and not contacting the ball.
    3. In this position, you can rest the back of your head on the ground and leave your arms on the ground by your sides.
3. With your leg not on the ball, march your thigh up off the ground. Keep it lifted throughout your set.
    1. Your leg should be marched up high enough that it will not contact the ball throughout your set.
    2. Based on your preference, you can keep your knee bent or straight, which may be mildly more difficult.
    3. The subsequent directions will apply to the leg in contact with the ball, since that is the side you will train with this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heel into the ball as you keep your knee straight. Squeeze your glute and tighten your abdominal muscles while doing so.
    1. You should now be able to draw a straight line from your leg through your hip to your torso.
    2. Avoid arching your lower back excessively as you move about your hip.
2. While keeping your hips lifted up, drive your heel toward your buttock to bend your knee and roll the ball back toward you.
    1. Once the sole of your foot is flat on the ball and you feel that you can no longer bend your knee, you have reached your end range. People can typically drive their heel back until their knee is bent by at least 90 degrees, but what constitutes a full range of motion may vary somewhat among different individuals.
    2. At the end range, you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your torso.
    3. If you experience a notably uncomfortable cramping sensation in your hamstring when your knee is fully bent, you can stop bending your knee just before reaching that point.
    4. Continue keeping your glute and abdominal muscles tightened throughout your set. This will help prevent you from excessively arching your lower back or letting your hips sag down.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively straightening your knee in a controlled manner to roll the ball away from you.
    1. You should finish with your knee fully straightened, allowing you to draw a straight line from your leg through your hip to your torso.
    2. Continue keeping your hips bridged up.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other leg on the ball.

4. Continue lowering the bar until it contacts the pins above your middle-to-upper chest in a controlled manner and comes to a dead stop.
    1. While you do not have to finish the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you certainly should avoid crashing the bar into the pins in a jarring manner.
5. Allow the weight from the bar to transmit fully into the pins, and remain completely stationary with the bar resting on the pins for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds).
    1. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back, glutes squeezed, and core braced rather than losing tightness in this position.
6. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up with explosive intent. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your chest.
    3. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
7. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
8. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
9. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after youhave  already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to pin press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Whatever you select must have safety pins or spotter arms to perform this variation.
    2. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    3. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a viable J-hook height, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of reps of a standard bench press to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Position the safety pins/spotter arms to be near the end (i.e., within the final third) of the lifting phase of your standard bench press.
    1. This is intentionally a very short range of motion variation. However, for it to transfer effectively to improved lockout strength of your standard bench press, the pins should generally allow you to press the bar greater than one inch (2.5cm).
    2. Certain power rack and bench press station models have fairly wide spaces between safety pin/spotter arm holes that may result in the highest setting that is low enough to receive the bar being near the midpoint of your press. If this applies to you, and you cannot set them reasonably close to your lockout (i.e., within the final third of the press), it may not be feasible to perform a lockout pin press. However, you can select the midpoint pin press as an alternative variation you can perform with your equipment.
5. After loading the bar with your intended weight, lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning to bench press, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you prefer to perform your standard bench press with a greater arch, you can also use the same degree of arching for this variation.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar straight down by bending your elbows in a controlled manner until it contacts the pins and comes to a dead stop.
    1. Strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists (when viewed from the side). This will keep your forearms close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set.
    2. The bony bump on the back of each elbow should be pointing straight out to the side as the bar moves vertically toward your shoulders.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you certainly should avoid crashing the bar into the pins in a jarring manner.
4. Allow the weight from the bar to transmit fully into the pins, and remain completely stationary with the bar resting on the pins for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds).
    1. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back, glutes squeezed, and core braced rather than losing tightness in this position.
5. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar straight up with explosive intent.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
6. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
7. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
8. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have  already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
