## Setting up
1. Lie down on your side with straight legs as one leg is resting on top of the other. Align your legs with your torso so that you can draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso when viewed from above.
    1. The outer aspect of your lower foot and lower hip should be resting on the ground.
    2. If you are on a hard surface, you can set up on an exercise mat for comfort. You chiefly want a comfortable surface to be under the forearm that you will be placing on the ground.
    3. This side plank will simultaneously train the hip muscles on both sides of your body along with the core and shoulder muscles on the side closer to the ground.
2. Position your bottom forearm on the ground with your elbow bent to about 90 degrees. Your elbow should be close to being stacked directly underneath your shoulder.
    1. With your bottom hand, you can make a fist and keep the little finger-side of your hand in contact with the ground. Alternatively, you can keep your palm flat on the ground if you find that to feel more comfortable and stable.
    2. You can keep your top arm in a comfortable position, such as resting on top of your side with a straight elbow. Alternatively, you can reach that arm toward the ceiling with a straight elbow or place that side’s hand on your top hip with a bent elbow.
    3. Your bottom upper arm should be in a vertical position.
    4. You can perform this step simultaneously with step 1.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your bottom hip off the ground by pushing through your bottom foot and forearm. You should now be able to draw a straight line from your head through your belly button to the center point between your feet when viewed from the front.
    1. You should also be able to draw a straight line from your heel through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the top.
    2. Your legs, torso, and head should be in the same alignment in which they would be when standing upright with your feet together.
2. Lift your top leg straight up through your hip’s available range of motion. Keep the rest of your body completely stationary in the same position you assumed from step 1.
    1. Specifically how high you are able to lift your top leg will be influenced by your hip mobility and strength.
    2. Avoid rotating your top leg when lifting it up. Your kneecap and toes should be pointing straight forward the whole time. If your kneecap and toes are pointing diagonally up and forward instead of straight forward, you have rotated your leg while lifting it up.
3. In a controlled manner, lower your top leg straight down until the inner aspect of its foot lightly contacts the inner aspect of your bottom foot.
    1. At the end of the lowering phase, you should be in the position of a standard side plank, like you assumed during step 1.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 while statically maintaining the side plank position until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your opposite side contacting the ground.
    1. Avoid letting your lower hip sag down, which would prevent you from being able to draw the line through the midline of your body when viewed from the front. If you notice your hip starting to drop down, it can help to think about pushing more forcefully through your bottom foot. When learning this exercise, it can be useful to face a mirror to receive visual feedback if your lower hip begins sagging down.
    2. Avoid letting your buttocks drift backward or letting your top leg drift forward by bending your hips. This would prevent you from being able to draw the straight line through your whole body when viewed from the top. Squeezing your glutes can help prevent you from unintentionally bending your hips.
    3. To the best of your ability, strive to maintain the same height of your leg lift each rep. However, it is natural for the height of your leg lift to decrease gradually as your hip muscles become fatigued, and you do not necessarily need to end your set if this starts occurring.

## Setting up
1. Place one weighted end of a dumbbell on the ground with its handle directed vertically, resulting in one end remaining off the ground.
    1. Placing a dumbbell on the ground in this manner will make it easier to position onto your lap compared to if you placed both ends of the dumbbell on the ground. However, if the ends of your dumbbell are not flat (such as with a plate-loaded adjustable dumbbell), you will alternatively have to place both ends of the dumbbell on the ground with a horizontal handle.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground and the side of one of your hips directly next to the dumbbell. Your knees should be bent at least 90 degrees.
    1. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
3. Roll onto your side toward the dumbbell, hold the dumbbell in contact with the front of your waist with both hands, and roll onto your back with the dumbbell situated in the crease of your hips.
    1. From this point onward, you will continue holding the dumbbell in front of your hips with both hands.
4. Position the soles of your feet flat against each other while allowing your knees to spread out to your sides and descend closer toward the ground.
    1. When you press your soles together, your knees will naturally spread out, and you do not have to try to push them further apart than this point.
    2. Your knees should be in a comfortable position, and the degree to which your knees will spread out will be influenced by your hip mobility.
    3. The outer aspect of your feet (on the side of your little toes) should be firmly in contact with the ground.
5. Tuck your chin toward your chest and lift your head slightly off the ground.
    1. This can help you keep your lower back flat rather than excessively arched during the exercise, but you have the option of resting your head on the ground if you wish to do so.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving the outer aspects of your feet into the ground and squeezing your glutes. Keep the soles of your feet pressed together and your knees spread apart.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you ideally should be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side if you have the mobility to perform the full range of motion. If your hips feel “stuck” or quite uncomfortable before reaching this point, you may not have the hip mobility to move through the full range with your current knee position. Bringing your knees somewhat higher up and closer together may allow you to lift your hips up higher in a more comfortable manner.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively. Tensing your abdominal muscles may help limit your lower back from arching.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glutes engage during this exercise.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
    1. Continue keeping your soles in contact with each other.
    2. After determining which knee position allows you to comfortably move through your full range of motion, strive to keep your knees in the same position throughout your set.
3. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. To remove the dumbbell from your lap, you can roll over to your side like you did when initially setting up before placing it on the ground.

## Setting up
1. Set the foot plate to a height that aligns the machine’s pivot point with your hips while standing on the center of the foot plate with your knees slightly bent.
    1. The pivot point will be the center of the machine’s wheel, about which the lever arm rotates.
    2. Strive to align the pivot point specifically with the bony bump (greater trochanter) that you could feel on the side of your hip.
    3. Some machines do not allow you to adjust the foot plate.
2. Position the machine’s lever arm to point straight down.
    1. This will help you adjust the machine to your body proportions before moving the lever arm into the exercise’s starting position.
3. Adjust the machine’s roller pad to be slightly above knee height when standing on the foot plate.
4. Rotate the lever arm about 35-45 degrees out to the side. When facing the middle of the machine, you will rotate the lever toward the side you are about to train.
    1. The appropriate setting will enable the machine to provide resistance throughout the full range of motion your hip mobility allows.
    2. Rotating the lever arm 35-45 degrees should allow most people to train through a full range of motion, but you can adjust specifically how far you rotate the lever arm based on your individual hip mobility.
5. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
6. Stand to the side of the machine, closer to the roller pad, with the roller pad just in front of your lower thigh on the leg closer to the weight stack.
    1. The leg further away from the weight stack should be just outside of the roller pad’s way.
7. While using your hands to help you push the roller pad forward, walk forward to the center of the foot plate.
    1. Your hips should now be aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
8. Firmly grasp the handlebar in front of you with both hands.
9. On the side closer to the weight stack, bend your knee by about 90 degrees to lift your foot off the foot plate while allowing the machine’s resistance to sweep your knee back.
    1. Allow your knee to move back until you have reached the end range that your hip mobility allows. This should provide a stretching sensation to the muscles in the front of your hip.
    2. The leg further away from the weight stack should be standing with a slightly bent knee as its foot is flat on the foot plate.
    3. Based on what feels most stable to you, your torso should be upright or mildly leaned forward at your hips. Rather than being excessively arched, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    4. In this starting position, your hips and shoulders should be level.
    5. The subsequent technique directions will apply to the leg contacting the roller pad, since that is the side you will train with this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your knee forward and upward in an arcing manner through your hip’s full range of motion. Keep your knee bent throughout your set.
    1. Most people should be able to finish with the thigh close to being parallel to the ground. However, how far you personally can march your knee up will be influenced by your hip mobility.
    2. Strive to have all the motion come from your hip while keeping the rest of your body stationary. The foot of your other leg should remain firmly planted on the foot plate throughout your set.
    3. You should feel the muscles on the front of your upper thigh contract.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by bringing your knee downward and backward in an arcing motion.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your working leg’s bent knee behind your stance leg’s knee.
    2. Allow your knee to sweep back through the full range that your hip mobility permits without excessively arching your lower back. When trying to move the roller pad further back than what your hip mobility permits, excessive lower back arching is a common error that is easier to avoid when you appropriately brace your core.
    3. Avoid letting the weight rapidly swing your knee backward in an uncontrolled manner.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. To train your other side, you will face the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [hip flexor muscles](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md), including your [psoas major](../Muscles/Psoas%20Major%201925c6f170d880d9bd8ff7b80b3b3368.md), [iliacus](../Muscles/Iliacus%201925c6f170d880dbbf66e6d67529db1e.md), [rectus femoris](../Muscles/Rectus%20Femoris%201925c6f170d880f080b7cda6f5f3f0ee.md), and [tensor fascia latae](../Muscles/Tensor%20Fascia%20Latae%201925c6f170d8806fb83bf08142d940fc.md).

## Setting up
1. Place one dumbbell on the ground.
    1. Both of its weighted ends should be on the ground.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground, with the dumbbell by the side of your body you are about to train. When your upper arm (closer to the dumbbell) is by your side, the dumbbell’s handle should be parallel with your upper arm and out to the side of your elbow.
    1. Specifically, the dumbbell should be slightly greater than the length of your forearm away from your elbow to help you pick it up.
3. On the side closer to the dumbbell, bend your elbow by about 90 degrees with your upper arm right by your side.
4. Roll onto your side toward the dumbbell.
5. Firmly grasp the dumbbell with your palm on the side of your lower arm facing up toward the ceiling. Tightly wrap your other hand over your lower hand, so that your palms are facing each other.
6. While pulling the dumbbell up with your top arm, roll over onto your back. Move your torso and arms together as one unit, such that the dumbbell remains directly in front of your elbow (on the side holding the dumbbell directly) throughout the roll.
    1. When appropriately transitioning to lying on your back, you should not feel that you are stressing your shoulder on the side directly holding the dumbbell. You are primarily using the rest of your body to reposition yourself and lift the dumbbell rather than using your shoulder muscles (on the side directly holding the dumbbell) to rotate the forearm.
    2. Once you are on your back, you should be holding the dumbbell on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a mostly straight wrist that allows for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. On the side holding the dumbbell, your upper arm should be resting on the ground with your palm facing in toward your opposite side, your elbow tucked close to your side, and your forearm vertical.
7. Move your arm that is not directly holding the dumbbell into a comfortable position, such as resting by your side.
    1. Some lifters may prefer to use the free hand to hold onto a sturdy object (like the beam of a power rack) for additional stability, but you can position that hand wherever you like.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training first.
8. If you have not already, position your legs straight out in front of you with straight knees.
    1. The back of your heels should now be on the ground along with your buttocks, upper back, and head.
9. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the dumbbell upward until your elbow is fully straightened with your arm directed straight up toward the ceiling. It may help to focus on driving your elbow upward.
    1. Your palm should continue facing in toward your opposite side as you avoid flaring your elbow out away from your side.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulder and elbow, your forearm should be in a vertical position throughout the press. This will result in your wrist and dumbbell remaining stacked over your elbow.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbell should be situated vertically over your shoulder.
    4. Throughout your set, continue keeping your heels, buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner. Move your elbow downward while bending it and keeping it tucked fairly close to your side.
    1. Continue keeping your wrist stacked over your elbow as your forearm remains vertical.
    2. You should finish with the back of your upper arm and elbow contacting the ground.
    3. While you do not have to finish the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you certainly should avoid slamming your arm onto the ground. You will not be bouncing your arm off the ground.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. It can be awkward to transfer the weight to your other hand with proper positioning while lying down if you are using a weight that is at least fairly heavy to you.
    2. Consequently, you can set the dumbbell down in an opposite manner to how you initially set up before switching to your other side.
5. After finishing the lowering phase of the last rep, wrap your free hand around your hand holding the dumbbell.
6. Roll onto your side (in which you are holding the dumbbell) while using your outer hand’s arm to help control the weight onto the ground. Move your torso and arms together as one unit, such that the dumbbell remains directly in front of your elbow (on the side holding the dumbbell directly) throughout the roll.

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to board press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, board pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, determine what you will use as your two-board.
    1. If you are using a standard wooden two-board, a partner will hold the board on your chest after you unrack the weight. The partner should stand next to you out of the bar’s way.
    2. Alternatively, you may use a specialized board press attachment that you would connect to the middle of the bar to board press without a partner. This type of equipment commonly allows you to perform variable height board presses based on which side you connect to the bar. For this variation, the thickness of the attachment under the bar should be approximately 3in (7.6cm), which is the standard thickness of a two-board.
4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of board press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your board press.
6. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
7. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
8. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you prefer to perform your standard bench press with a greater arch, you can also use the same degree of arching for this variation.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your middle chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other while descending.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists (when viewed from the side). This will keep your forearms close to vertical (when viewed from the side) throughout the set and promote the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare.
    2. When lowering the bar toward your middle chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line. Relative to when you perform a standard bench press, you can aim to lower the bar slightly higher up on your chest with this board press.
    3. To reach that point with the bar, you will have to keep your elbows tucked to a degree instead of being fully flared out (which would result in your upper arms forming a “T-shape” with your torso).
4. Continue lowering the bar until you are able to tap the board with the bar (if you are using a wooden board) or able to tap the board attachment to your chest.
    1. You should be in full control of your light tap, since you will not be bouncing out of the bottom position.
5. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your chest.
    3. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
6. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
7. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
8. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.

While primarily training your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), this exercise can improve bench press strength throughout the range of motion it trains.

## Setting up
1. Load an adjustable EZ bar with your desired weight, or approach a fixed-weight EZ bar.
    1. Either type of EZ bar can be used interchangeably for this exercise.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down and firmly grasp it with your palms angled backward and in toward each other (resulting in a semi-overhand grip). Your hands should be about shoulder-width apart or mildly closer.
    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it before a shoulder-width or mildly closer semi-overhand grip is accessible on the bar.
    2. The proper hand placement should result in your wrists and elbows feeling comfortable during this exercise.
3. Stand upright with the bar, walk over to a flat exercise bench, and stand over one end of the bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space behind you. With this equipment, you would straddle the bench and walk forward toward the J-hooks.
    2. With a portable exercise bench, your back should be facing the head of the bench, like when you would bench press.
4. Lift the bar up slightly above your waist, and sit down on the bench with the bar on your lap.
    1. Ensure that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie down with your head on the end of the bench.
5. While keeping your elbows bent and the bar close to your torso, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench. Your head should be right by the end of the bench.
    1. As you transition from sitting to lying down, you optionally can march your thighs up against the bar to help reposition yourself. This can be helpful when using heavier loads.
    2. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent. You will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
6. In a bench pressing motion, press the bar up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a bench press rep), the bar should be sitting on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists. You will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
    2. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar hard will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
## Exercise technique
1. Lower the bar behind your head in a controlled manner by bending your elbows while simultaneously moving your elbows backward. Based on your preference, you can select one of two approaches with respect to specifically where you lower the bar.
    1. Option 1: Lower the bar until it lightly taps the bench just behind your head. While the back muscles will still be engaged, this technique will predominantly train the triceps.
    2. Option 2: Set up with your head near the edge of the bench, lower the bar just behind your head while flexing your elbows, and then continue lowering the bar through the full range that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits. This option involves more of a pullover movement (arising from shoulder motion) than the former and will more heavily engage the back muscles along with the triceps.
    3. Neither of the approaches is inherently superior to the other, so you can feel free to try out both ways and continue using the technique you prefer.
    4. With either option, predominantly keep your elbows tucked in. However, you can allow them to flare slightly out away from your sides if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    5. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way.
2. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows while arcing them forward to lift the bar into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is vertically above your shoulders.
    2. For targeting the triceps, it can be helpful to focus on straightening your elbows to a greater degree than arcing your elbows forward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
4. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the bar toward your lower chest or upper abdomen like you would during a bench press.
5. March your thighs up toward the weight, and then rock forward to sit up with the weight on your upper thighs.

## Setting up
1. Position the safety pins of a power rack within the final third of the range of motion for your standard overhead press.
    1. For this variation, the pins should be higher than the top of your head, but somewhat of a range of pin heights can fall within the final third of your standard press. Within this range, you can decide specifically where you set the pins based on your preferences and the pin heights your rack permits.
    2. This is intentionally a short range of motion variation. However, for it to transfer effectively to improved lockout strength of your standard overhead press, the pins should generally allow you to press the bar at least 2in (5cm) up.
    3. Certain power racks have fairly wide spaces between safety pinholes that may not allow you to set the pins at an appropriate height for a lockout pin press. If this applies to you, it may not be feasible to perform a lockout pin press with your rack. However, you may be able to select the overhead midpoint pin press as an alternative that you can perform with your equipment.
2. Symmetrically place a barbell in the middle of the safety pins and load it with your desired weight.
3. Stand in front of the middle of the bar.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with your hands slightly outside shoulder width as your palms are facing away from you.
    1. Situating your index fingers directly outside the outer aspects of your shoulders is generally an effective approach, but what is personally your ideal grip may be a bit wider or closer. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Step forward until the bar is directly over your head and the middle of your feet. Situate your feet near shoulder width apart with your knees straight.
    1. Based on what feels most stable to you, you can point your toes straight ahead or rotate them slightly out to the side.
    2. You can perform this step simultaneously with step 6.
6. Position your elbows under the bar. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists stacked under the bar.
    1. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    2. Your forearms should now be in close to a vertical position.
7. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Avoid leaning back into an excessively arched position.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Since the bar is already starting overhead, you will not have to tuck your chin back during this variation, in contrast to a standard overhead press.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
2. Squeeze your glutes and quads from now until you finish your last rep.
    1. This will create a stable platform from which to press.
3. While keeping your legs straight, press the straight bar up until your elbows are fully straightened.
    1. Do not lean back any further or excessively arch your lower back. Your lower back should stay locked in the same position throughout your rep.
    2. At the top of the press, you should be able to draw a straight line down from the bar that passes through your shoulders, hips, knees, and the middle of your feet.
4. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar straight down in a controlled manner.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down. Do not let the bar crash into the pins.
5. Once the bar contacts the pins, allow the weight to transmit fully into the pins. Remain completely stationary with the bar resting on the pins for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds).
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath during your set, you can breathe when the bar is resting on the pins. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating your next.
6. Alternate between steps 3-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. In contrast to a standard overhead press, you will finish your set with the bar resting on the pins rather than racking it onto J-hooks.

While training the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and other shoulder girdle muscles, this exercise can improve lockout strength for your overhead press.

11. Once the bar is on your collarbone, pause in that position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds) while staying tight.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
12. Alternate between steps 7-11 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
13. After completing the lowering phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second before walking forward.
14. After the bar contacts the back of both J-hooks, bend your knees slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and stand over one end of a flat exercise bench.
    1. If you are using a bench that is built into a rack, you should set up facing toward the base of the rack for sufficient space behind you. With this equipment, you would straddle the bench and walk forward toward the J-hooks.
    2. With a portable exercise bench, your back should be facing the head of the bench, like when you would dumbbell bench press.
2. Sit down on the bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your upper thighs near your abdomen.
    1. Ensure that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie down with your head on the end of the bench.
    2. Your palms should be facing in toward each other with your upper arms by your sides.
    3. To move heavy dumbbells efficiently into the proper position, you can initially situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up. Then you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
3. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down on the bench. Your head should be right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent. You will keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
4. In a bench pressing motion, press the dumbbells up until your elbows are straight and your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a bench press rep), the dumbbells should be sitting on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists. You will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
    2. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the dumbbells with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the dumbbells hard will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    3. Based on what feels most comfortable, you can have your palms facing in toward each other (with a neutral grip), forward (with an overhand grip), or angled inward and forward. During your set, you can similarly allow your palms to rotate within this range if that feels comfortable to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Lower the dumbbells behind your head in a controlled manner by bending your elbows while simultaneously moving your elbows backward. Based on your preference, you can select one of two approaches with respect to specifically where you lower the dumbbells.
    1. Option 1: Lower the dumbbells until they lightly tap the bench just behind your head. While the back muscles will still be engaged, this technique will predominantly train the triceps.
    2. Option 2: Set up with your head near the edge of the bench, lower the dumbbells just behind your head while flexing your elbows, and then continue lowering the dumbbells through the full range that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits. This option involves more of a pullover movement (arising from shoulder motion) than the former and will more heavily engage the back muscles along with the triceps.
    3. Neither of the approaches is inherently superior to the other, so you can feel free to try out both ways and continue using the technique you prefer.
    4. With either option, predominantly keep your elbows tucked in. However, you can allow them to flare slightly out away from your sides if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    5. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way.
2. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows while arcing them forward to lift the dumbbells into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the dumbbells are vertically above your shoulders.
    2. For targeting the triceps, it can be helpful to focus on straightening your elbows to a greater degree than arcing your elbows forward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
4. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the dumbbells toward your sides like you would during a neutral grip dumbbell bench press.
    1. Regardless of the palm position you used for your set, it is easier to sit up with the dumbbells when your palms are facing in toward each other.
5. March your thighs up toward the weights, and then rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a 90-degree angle, or approach a mobile exercise bench with a permanently fixed upright backrest.
    1. If you have access to one, a seated bench with a backrest that does not reach your head is ideal because it can allow you to move your head back away from the bar during the exercise.
2. Center the bench underneath a Smith machine’s bar in a spot that will allow you to touch near your upper chest with the bar at the bottom of the press.
    1. After initially estimating which bench placement allows this to occur, you may have to move the bench a bit forward or backward during later steps if you notice the bar does not reach near your upper chest.
    2. Specifically how you should set up can be influenced by whether your Smith machine has sliding rails that are purely vertical or angled.
    3. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, place the side of the bench where you will place your feet on the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends. This will result in the top of the rails being horizontally closer to your head than the bottom of the rails when seated on the bench. An angled Smith machine will prompt the bar to track mildly back toward your head when pressing the bar up.
    4. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which side of the bar you place your feet.
3. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to grasp it with slightly bent elbows once you are sitting on the bench.
    1. The ideal height will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently.
    2. If the bar is situated too high, you may have to shrug your shoulders excessively to lift the bar off the safety bars (on which the safety hooks that are attached to the bar rest). This can place you in a less stable position to start your set.
    3. If the bar is situated excessively low, you will have to grasp the bar initially with a greater degree of elbow bend, and unracking it will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    4. If neither of the two closest bar heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    5. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best starting bar height for you.
4. After positioning the bar to the appropriate height, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of overhead press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section. Use these reps to confirm that you positioned the bench the ideal distance away from the bar prior to reracking the bar and adjusting the bench as needed.
    1. The bench should not be any further away from the bar than what is required for the bar to clear your head when pressing up.
    2. Even a small magnitude of additional distance between the bar and your face can contribute to the exercise feeling awkward.
    3. At this time, you can optionally place the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails under the bar) slightly under the height of your upper chest when seated.
5. After loading the bar with your intended weight, sit down with your buttocks, back, and head in contact with the bench. Firmly place your feet flat on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart with your knees bent.
    1. Your hips should be fully back on the seat.
6. Tuck your chin back to move your head slightly further back away from the bar.
7. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
8. Reach up and firmly grasp the bar with your hands slightly outside shoulder width as your palms are facing forward.
    1. Situating your index fingers directly outside the outer aspects of your shoulders is generally an effective approach, but what is personally your ideal grip may be a bit wider or closer. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
2. Press the bar up off the safety bars by straightening your elbows before rotating the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion. After unracking it, hold the bar stationary for a moment before starting to lower it.
3. Lower the bar in a controlled manner until you are able to tap near your upper chest lightly with the bar, or until you have fully moved through your available shoulder range of motion.
    1. Keep your elbows mostly stacked under the bar rather than meaningfully tracking in front of the bar or behind. However, you can allow your elbows to track slightly forward in front of the bar at the bottom of the rep if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    2. Your elbows should neither be fully flared, such that they are pointing completely out to your sides, nor should they be fully tucked, such that they are pointing directly forward. Aligning your elbows close to directly under the bar will naturally promote the appropriate balance between elbow flare and elbow tuck.
    3. Most lifters can comfortably lower the bar to their upper chest, but certain individuals with limited shoulder mobility may not be able to touch their chest with the bar without discomfort. If this applies to you, lower the bar as far as you can without discomfort.
    4. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up overhead until your elbows are fully straightened.
    1. Keep your buttocks pressed up against the bench as you avoid scooting your hips forward or excessively arching your lower back.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows stacked under the bar.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
    1. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second.
6. Rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars by flicking your wrists before bending your elbows to lower the safety hooks securely onto the safety bars.

## Setting up
1. Position the J-hooks of a power rack (or squat stand) near the height of your upper chest.
2. Place a barbell onto the J-hooks and load it with your desired weight.
    1. It is recommended to use an empty barbell if you are new to this exercise.
3. Stand in front of the middle of the bar with your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
4. Firmly grasp the bar with your hands clearly outside shoulder width as your palms are facing away from you (i.e., with an overhand grip).
    1. What is personally considered a wide grip to you can be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard behind-the-neck press, which you can somewhat widen to individualize your wide grip. For instance, for your wide grip, you can place your index finger on the bar where you would otherwise place your little finger when performing your standard behind-the-neck press. This approach provides many lifters with an appropriately wide grip, but there is a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine specifically where you feel best.
    2. The standard behind-the-neck press normally uses a wider grip than when overhead pressing to the front. Consequently, the wide grip behind the neck press can have a meaningfully wider grip than where you feel strongest when overhead pressing to the front.
    3. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re new to this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip).
5. Slightly bend your knees, and step forward to situate your collarbone or upper chest directly under the bar. Simultaneously, position your elbows under the bar and just slightly in front of it. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists stacked under the bar.
    1. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Your elbows should naturally be flared out (pointing out to the side) to a greater extent during this variation compared to your standard behind-the-neck press.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to help create full-body tension.
2. Fully stand upright while holding the bar.
    1. With your knees straightened, the bar should now be above the tops of the J-hooks.
3. Take a couple of steps backward and set your feet approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable to you, you can point your toes straight ahead or rotate them slightly out to the side.
4. Squeeze your glutes and quads from now until you finish your last rep.
    1. This will create a stable platform from which to press.
5. While naturally allowing your lower back to arch mildly, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Avoid leaning back into an excessively arched position.
6. Tuck your chin back to move your head behind the bar.
    1. The goal is to move your head out of the bar’s way so that you can press straight upward without hitting your face with the bar.
7. Press the bar upward with as close to a straight bar path as you can perform.
    1. Do not lean back any further or excessively arch your lower back. Your lower back should stay locked in the same position.
8. Immediately after the bar clears the top of your head, mildly push your head forward until your ears are close to being under the bar. Simultaneously arc the bar slightly backward while pressing it up.
    1. Rather than pushing your head excessively forward, you primarily should be reversing the backward chin tuck/tilt you previously performed.
9. Finish the initial press with your elbows straightened as the bar is overhead.
    1. You should be able to draw a straight line down from the bar that passes through your shoulders, hips, knees, and the middle of your feet.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath during your set, you can breathe after locking out the weight overhead. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to lowering the bar.
    3. You are now in the starting position for your behind-the-neck press.
10. In a slow and controlled manner, lower the bar behind your head through the range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. If you have the mobility to do so comfortably, you can lower the bar until it lightly contacts your upper back muscles just under the base of your neck. However, what constitutes your end range will be determined by your individual shoulder mobility.
    2. If you start experiencing shoulder pain or joint discomfort at the bottom of the lowering phase, you likely are moving beyond the current limit of your shoulder mobility. Training this exercise over time may progressively improve your shoulder mobility and gradually permit you to descend through a greater range, but there is no need to force yourself into a position that currently does not feel right for your shoulders.
    3. With sufficient shoulder mobility, you should not have to push your head meaningfully forward to avoid scraping your head or neck with the bar. However, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest if you wish to do so for additional clearance.
    4. Strive to keep your elbows stacked under the bar when viewed from the side. To do so, your elbows should be pointing out away from your sides.
    5. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the bar the entire way down.
11. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up until you have fully straightened your elbows with the bar overhead.
12. Alternate between steps 10 and 11 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
13. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, tuck your chin back and lower the bar to your collarbone.
14. With the bar now in front of your body, walk forward until the bar contacts the back of both J-hooks
15. Bend your knees slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md) while also training your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), and [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a weight plate under the base of a flat exercise bench (on the end where you place your feet) to position the head of the bench at a slight decline.

    2. If your plate has different surfaces, place the flat part of the weight plate facing up against the bench.
    3. The bench should be very stable once it is on the plate.
    4. This variation intentionally uses a degree of decline that should allow you to feel stable once you are lying down with your feet flat on the ground. If you feel like you may slide back on the bench once you are lying down, the decline is excessively high to use without a bench that has a foot/ankle pad to secure your feet.

    1. Position yourself so that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    2. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    3. To move heavy dumbbells efficiently into the proper position, you can initially situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up. Then you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
3. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
4. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
5. Flare your elbows moderately out to your sides such that your upper arms form approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    1. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable for your shoulders, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbows out within this range.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Press the dumbbells up by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten them until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press, as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, keep your feet flat on the floor and your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner toward the sides of your chest through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.

Let your elbows moderately flare out to your sides as they descend and bend enough to keep your wrists stacked above them with vertical forearms. Lifters often find that at least a mild degree of elbow tuck makes this exercise feel most comfortable for the shoulders compared to fully flaring the elbows straight out to the sides.
    2. How far you can lower the dumbbells with vertical forearms will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hands are at least level with their chest.
    3. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom.
    4. There is no need to lower the dumbbells extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable decline bench to your desired decline angle.
    1. An angle near 30 degrees is an appropriate starting point, but you can effectively perform this exercise with a range of decline angles.
    2. The difficulty of this exercise will increase as the decline becomes steeper, so you can adjust the angle to modify the intensity.
    3. Some adjustable benches have a mild decline setting along with incline settings, but they lack a pad to secure your feet. This exercise specifically uses a decline with a foot/ankle pad.
2. Sit down on the bench while snugly positioning the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
3. Lie down in a controlled manner to position your back and head on the bench.
4. Cross your arms across your chest with bent elbows to position each hand on the front of the opposite shoulder.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the bench. Simultaneously lift your head and shoulder blades up off the bench by curling your middle back.
    1. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that crunching up any further would require the lower half of your back to start lifting up off the bench.
    2. Given that this is a crunch rather than a sit-up, the lower half of your back should remain in contact with the bench while you only lift up the upper half of your back mildly up.
    3. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
    4. As a cue for your engaging abdominal muscles, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs toward your hip bones.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your back to uncurl in a controlled manner until you can lightly tap the bench with your shoulder blades.
    1. Rather than fully relaxing at the bottom, keep your abdominals tensed at the bottom.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the entire movement.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Avoid using momentum to rock your body from rep to rep.

## Setting up
1. Approach a flat exercise bench or a similarly sturdy object with an elevated surface that can support your foot.
    1. As an alternative to a bench, you can use a plyometric box or an aerobic step stacked on risers. At home, you can use pieces of furniture such as a bed, couch, or chair that will not slide. If the object you use has a hard surface, placing a cushioned object (such as a foam pad) on top of it may make this exercise more comfortable.
    2. The difficulty of this exercise will increase as the object’s height increases, so you can utilize a taller object for a greater intensity. However, a height near 18in (46cm), which applies to a typical flat exercise bench, is recommended to use as a minimum for most people.
2. Lie down on your side with the inner aspect of your top knee (which is bent by about 90 degrees) and lower leg on top of the elevated surface. Align this thigh with your torso so that you can draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from above.
    1. The outer aspect of your lower hip should be resting on the ground.
    2. If you are on a hard surface, you can set up on an exercise mat for comfort. You chiefly want a comfortable surface to be under the forearm that you will be placing on the ground.
3. Align your lower thigh directly under your top thigh.
    1. If the object you are using has open space underneath its top surface (like with a bench), keep your knee straight on your lower leg.
    2. If your object lacks space for your lower foot under its top surface (like with a soft plyometric box), keep your bottom knee bent.
4. Position your bottom forearm on the ground with your elbow bent by about 90 degrees. Your elbow should be close to being stacked directly underneath your shoulder.
    1. With your bottom hand, you can make a fist and keep the little finger-side of your hand in contact with the ground. Alternatively, you can keep your palm flat on the ground if you find that to feel more comfortable and stable.
    2. You can keep your top arm in a comfortable position, such as resting on top of your side with a straight elbow. Alternatively, you can reach that arm toward the ceiling with a straight elbow or place that side’s hand on your top hip with a bent elbow.
    3. Your bottom upper arm should be in a vertical position.
    4. You can perform steps 2-4 simultaneously.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your bottom hip and leg fully off the ground by driving your top knee down into the bench while pushing your bottom forearm into the ground.
    1. At the top, you should now be able to draw a straight line from your head through your belly button to the center point between your knees when viewed from the front.
    2. You should also be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the top.
    3. Your thighs (which should be close together), torso, and head should be in essentially the same alignment as they would be when standing upright.
    4. The intent to pull your top knee down toward your bottom knee is what should lift your bottom leg, rather than simply lifting your bottom leg up by itself. Since the bench stops your knee from moving down, this intent lifts you up.
    5. An indicator that you are appropriately driving through your top leg is when your top hip becomes approximately level with your top knee. If you lift your bottom leg by itself, your top hip will remain lower than your top knee, which you do not want.
2. Statically hold this position in proper alignment until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your opposite side elevated.
    1. Avoid letting your hips sag down, which would prevent you from being able to draw the line through the midline of your body when viewed from the front. If you notice your hips starting to drop down, it can help to think about driving more forcefully through your top knee. When driving through your top leg, you should feel its inner thigh muscles contract.
    2. When learning this exercise, it can be useful to face a mirror to receive visual feedback if your hips begin sagging.
    3. Avoid letting your buttocks drift backward by bending your hips. This would prevent you from being able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the top. Squeezing your glutes can help prevent you from unintentionally bending your hips.
## Description
This exercise can statically train all your [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md) and a variety of core muscles, including your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [quadratus lumborum](../Muscles/Quadratus%20Lumborum%201965c6f170d880b89d4fc43238472b46.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a barbell in a landmine attachment or a viable substitute.
    1. As an alternative to using a landmine attachment, landmine exercises can be performed with one end of the barbell situated in a wall corner.
    2. While the scraping can be lessened by placing a towel between the wall corner and the barbell, be aware that performing landmine exercises in a wall corner can easily damage the wall corner, so this approach is not appropriate in every environment.
2. Load the bar with one full diameter plate (such as a 45lb (20kg) plate or any bumper plate) or whichever plate will have the largest diameter of the plates you will use for your working weight.
3. Position a sturdy object with an elevated surface directly next to the plate you loaded onto the bar. Select an object with a height that will allow the bar to start at the bottom of your squat once the bar’s plate is resting on the object.
    1. The optimal object height will allow you to squat through your full range of motion. If it is excessively high, the plate will touch the object before you reach the end range of your squat, therefore restricting your squat depth.
    2. If the object’s height is excessively low relative to how deeply you can squat, you will not be able to pick it up initially in the goblet position, and it will be more difficult to set the weight down after your set.
    3. While not ideal, it is preferable to select an object that slightly limits your squat depth rather than an object that is too low for you to assume the appropriate starting positioning without meaningfully rounding your back.
    4. Trying out different object heights may be needed to determine which height is ideal for you as an individual. After you find what places you in your optimal position, you can make a note of what you used to expedite your set-up for subsequent sessions.
    5. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    6. As a general starting point, you can try out a flat exercise bench, a plyometric box with a height of 18in (46cm), or an aerobic step with seven risers on each side. With an aerobic step, you can naturally adjust the height via the addition or subtraction of risers. To increase the height with a bench or plyometric box, you can stack bumper plates on top of it. While more time-consuming, you can alternatively use a stack of only bumper plates to form your elevated object.
4. Lift the bar up by the free end and rest the weight plate on top of the elevated object.
5. Perform a couple of reps of this exercise with only one plate on the bar to confirm you selected the appropriate object height. If you initially selected an object that is too tall or too short, adjust the height of the object before proceeding to add more weight to the bar.
    1. Skip the next setup step and follow the subsequent setup steps before following the “exercise technique” section’s instructions to perform these couple of reps before adding plates to the bar.
    2. The proper starting height should allow you to keep your back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees in line with your feet at the bottom of your squat. If you cannot satisfy these criteria, a taller object is likely warranted. Alternatively, a lower object may be warranted if you feel that you can squat deeper with quality technique than what the object permits.
    3. If you only have access to objects near the height of a flat bench and find that you can squat deeper than they allow, you can exclusively load the bar with smaller diameter weight plates to extend your squat’s range of motion.
6. Finish adding weight plates to the bar with your desired load.
7. Stand upright with the free end of the bar above the center point between the middle of your feet. Position your feet shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing mildly out to the sides.
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside of shoulder width with their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. In the starting position, your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, and you will keep your neck in this position throughout your set.
8. Simultaneously bend your hips and knees to squat down until the tip of the bar is just in front of your upper chest.
    1. Keep your back flat, rather than meaningfully rounding it.
9. With your elbows bent, position the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) firmly against the bottom of the end of the bar. Interlock your fingers, and place your thumbs against the tip of the bar.
    1. Your elbows should be tucked slightly in front of your sides. They should be pointing slightly forward rather than pointing straight down, like they would if your upper arms were completely by your sides.
    2. You are now in the goblet position that you will maintain throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Drive through the ground to stand up while keeping the bar end of the bar directly in front of your chest. Push through your legs until you have straightened your knees and hips.
    1. Avoid rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    4. Allow your body to lean mildly forward at your ankles to keep the bar close to your chest at the end of the lifting phase.
3. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner until you can lightly tap the elevated object with the weight plates.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, knees aligned over your feet, and the weight held close to your chest as you squat up.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time.
    3. Avoid bouncing the plates off the elevated object instead of gently contacting it with the weight.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
5. Once you have completed the lowering phase of your last rep, allow the weight to fully rest on the elevated object before letting go of the bar.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).
