## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that places the handles near your lower chest or slightly lower once you are seated.
    1. This is an appropriate starting point for most people, but the ideal seat height specifically should allow you to train through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably allows.
    2. Individuals with limited mobility may have to position the seat higher to reach the handles, while those with greater mobility may benefit from positioning the seat lower to train through a full range of motion.
    3. If the seat is excessively high, your range of motion for this exercise will be limited.
    4. If the seat is excessively low, you may not be able to reach the handles with proper positioning. Forcing your elbows back beyond what your mobility permits in an effort to reach the handles may increase the risk of experiencing shoulder discomfort.
    5. Some trial and error may be needed to find the best height for you as an individual. When continuing to set up, you can always adjust the seat height if you determine the initial height is suboptimal for you.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your feet flat on the ground.
    1. If your machine has a back pad, position your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against it.
    2. If your machine lacks a back pad, sit with a fully upright torso.
4. If your machine has a thigh pad, snugly position it on top of your thighs. If your machine has a seat belt, securely fasten it around your waist.
    1. Either option will help you anchor your body.
    2. Certain machines lack a thigh pad or seat belt, which can contribute to the exercise being less stable.
5. If your machine allows you to rotate its handles inward or outward, position them inward unless your thighs restrict the range of motion for the closer setting or if you simply find the wider setting to feel more comfortable.
    1. The closer setting facilitates a greater degree of elbow tuck, which is typically desirable when striving to emphasize the triceps and/or the front delts to a greater degree than the pec major during this exercise.
    2. However, the closer setting may position the handles excessively close for individuals with rather wide body types.
    3. Even if your body does not restrict your range of motion with the closer handle setting, you can also select the wider setting if it just feels more comfortable to you.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back, and move your elbows fully back behind your torso while bending them by at least 90 degrees.
    1. Position your elbows close to being directly behind your wrists and the handles. Keeping your elbows tucked close to your sides rather than flaring them out away from your sides will limit the degree to which this exercise trains the pec major.
    2. If the handles are now just within your reach, the seat height you initially selected is appropriate.
    3. If you cannot reach the handles without shrugging your shoulders up or tipping them forward, raise the seat before resuming your setup.
    4. If the handles are lower than what you can comfortably reach from this position, you can lower the seat to facilitate a greater degree of elbow bend before resuming your setup.
7. Firmly grasp the handles with the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) against them.
    1. While almost all machines allow you to use a neutral grip with your palms facing in toward each other, some machines also have handles that allow you to use an overhand grip with your palms facing backward. If your machine enables you to use both grips, select whichever feels most comfortable to you.
    2. Hold the handles with mostly straight wrists. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Push the handles down by driving your elbows down until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. Throughout your set, continue keeping your torso fully upright and feet planted on the ground.
    2. You should finish with your elbows close to your sides and your arms directed down toward the ground.
    3. While driving downward and straightening, your elbows will simultaneously move forward.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing the handles to lift up to the starting position. Bend your elbows while arcing them upward and backward.
    1. Keep your elbows tucked so that they remain behind your wrists rather than flaring them out away from your sides.
    2. Avoid letting your shoulders shrug up or roll forward.
    3. With the appropriate seat height, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders at the end range, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain. If you feel joint discomfort at the end range, increase the seat height before resuming your set.
    4. At the end range, you can lightly tap the machine’s arms to the stoppers under them to confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [lateral](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Lateral%20Head%2018f5c6f170d880c0a504d0d644758f40.md) and [medial](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Medial%20Head%201905c6f170d880fbb6e9e7e7ca37f2d1.md) heads of your triceps while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
Certain machines have a foot pedal that you can press to move the machine’s handle while setting up, but other machine models lack a foot pedal. Some of the specific setup details differ depending on which type of machine you are using, so the setup for each approach is described separately. However, the exercise technique can be essentially the same for either option, so one technique section is provided with a couple of details that depend on which type of machine you utilize.

### **Setting up a machine without a foot pedal**

1. Adjust the seat to a height that comfortably allows you to grasp the handle behind your head with your elbows fully bent once you are seated.
    1. This seat height commonly allows the base of someone’s neck to be reasonably close to being level with the handle once seated. However, your flexibility can influence where your ideal position lies, so trying out different seat heights may initially be required.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit down on its seat with an upright torso as your back is resting against the backrest.
    1. If your machine has a foot plate, position your soles against it. Otherwise, place your feet flat on the floor.
4. Raise your arms up with your elbows fully bent to grasp the handle firmly with fairly straight wrists.
    1. Different machines have different handle types that will influence specifically how you should grasp the handle, but what chiefly matters is that your grip feels stable and comfortable.
    2. From this position, your upper arms should be near the sides of your head with your elbows held high and tucked in (rather than being meaningfully flared out away from your sides).
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your triceps.

### **Setting up a machine with a foot pedal**

1. Adjust the seat to a height that positions the handle at least a little lower than what you can reach behind your head with your elbows lifted up and fully bent once you are seated.
    1. This seat height commonly allows the base of someone’s neck to be at least mildly higher than the handle once seated. However, the foot pedal allows a range of seat heights to be viable for this exercise.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit down on its seat with an upright torso as your back is resting against the backrest.
4. Place one foot against the machine’s foot pedal, and push the pedal forward with your leg.
    1. This brings the handles up to a position you can comfortably reach.
    2. Keep the pedal pushed away during the next step, while keeping your other foot on the ground.
5. Raise your upper arms up near the sides of your head with your elbows bent enough to grasp the handle firmly with fairly straight wrists.
    1. Different machines have different handle types that will influence specifically how you should grasp the handle, but what chiefly matters is that your grip feels stable and comfortable.
    2. From this position, hold your elbows high while keeping tucked in rather than being meaningfully flared out away from your sides.
6. Bring the foot pedal back to its starting position by bending your knee, which will shift the machine’s resistance to your arms. Simultaneously, lower the handle behind your head by fully bending your elbows while keeping your upper arms stationary.
    1. The degree to which you can bend your elbows while keeping your upper arms raised up will be dependent on your triceps flexibility.
    2. Allow your elbows to bend through the full range that feels comfortable, and you will normally feel a stretching sensation in your triceps.
7. Lift your foot off the foot pedal and place it flat on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Press the handle up overhead by straightening your elbows while keeping your upper arms stationary.
    1. At the top of the movement, your elbows should be fully straightened with your upper arms in the same position in which they started.
    2. While you move your forearms through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by bending your elbows to lower the handle behind your head in a controlled manner.
    1. Lower the bar to the starting position with your elbows fully bent through your full range of motion.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows tucked in rather than meaningfully flaring them out to your sides.
    3. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the machine’s resistance rapidly pull the handle back down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you are using a machine with a foot pedal, push the pedal forward with your leg until you are no longer supporting any of the machine’s resistance with your arms. Then let go of the handle and bend your knee to return the foot pedal to its initial position.
    2. If your machine lacks a foot pedal, allow the machine’s arms to rest fully on the stoppers underneath them before releasing the handle.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train all three heads of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), which constitute the majority of muscle mass in your upper arms.

## Setting up
1. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin, and sit down on the seat.
2. Adjust the height of the machine’s thigh pad to a level that allows you to fit the lowest portion of your thigh just underneath it, while the front half of your foot is situated on the foot plate.
    1. To help find this point, you can initially place the front half of your foot on the foot plate while your heel is lower than your toes.
    2. Avoid setting the pad to a height that requires you to lift your heel up higher than your toes in order for your thigh to press snugly into the pad. The weakest portion of a calf raise occurs when your heel is fully raised. Consequently, it can be difficult to re-rack the weight at the end of a set if your calf is fatigued, and you have to raise your heel meaningfully before adjusting the machine’s stopper to accept the weight.
3. With the front half of your foot on the foot plate, scoot your knee under and in front of the thigh pad until your lower thigh is securely under the pad.
    1. You can optionally use your hands to help pull the thigh pad up as you scoot forward.
    2. Because this is a single leg variation, you can leave your other foot resting on the ground. All the instructions will apply to the leg on the foot plate, since that is the side you are about to train.
4. Raise your heel up just enough to disengage the machine’s stopper by operating its lever with one of your hands.
    1. You should be primarily bearing weight through the ball of your foot as the back half of your foot is hanging off the foot plate.
    2. For tracking purposes, you can consider your first full rep to start after you have completely lowered your heel when performing step 1 of the exercise technique for the first time in a set. The initial short range of motion heel raise you perform to disengage the stopper does not constitute a full rep.
## Exercise technique
1. In a controlled manner, allow your heel to descend toward the ground through the available range of motion of your ankle while continuing to keep the front half of your foot on top of the foot plate.
    1. Strive to lower your heel as far as you can, and you will likely feel a stretching sensation in your calf and/or ankle at the bottom position.
    2. Specifically how far you are able to lower your heel will be dependent on your mobility, but individuals with normal ankle mobility can position their heels lower than the balls of their feet at the bottom.
2. Push through the ball of your foot to raise your heel into the air through the available range of motion of your ankle.
    1. At the top, your heel should be higher than the ball of your foot.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. At times during a set, you may feel that your foot slides back on the foot plate. If that occurs, you can use your hands to pull up the bottom of the thigh pad to make it easier for you to re-position your foot forward on the foot plate.
4. After finishing the lowering phase of your rep, raise your heel high enough to engage the machine’s stopper with your hand.
    1. If you performed as many reps as you possibly could during your set, you may have to rest in the bottom position for several seconds until your calf is ready to lift your heel high enough to engage the stopper.
5. With the stopper engaged, lower your heel to let the weight rest on the stopper before repeating the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md), but it will not train your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) nearly as well as calf raise variations performed with straight knees.

## Setting up
1. With your hands close together and palms facing back toward you, firmly grasp the handle of one kettlebell.
2. In an approximately shoulder width stance, stand upright while holding the kettlebell in front of your legs with straight elbows.
3. Slightly (such as by about 10 degrees) lean forward at your hips by sitting your buttocks backward slightly.
    1. While performing a very small hip hinge motion that results in your knees barely bending, keep your chest up and lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. As an alternative to this slight forward lean, you can keep your torso completely upright if you prefer to do so, but some people find that slightly hinging their hips can help the exercise feel more comfortable for their shoulders.
    3. Regardless of whether you lean forward slightly or stay fully upright, you should maintain the same torso position throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the kettlebell upward by driving your elbows upward and out to your sides through a range of motion that feels comfortable to your shoulders.
    1. Your mobility will affect how high you are comfortably able to lift the kettlebell, and there is no need to force your shoulders into a range that causes any discomfort.
    2. While different individuals may be able to lift higher up and others not quite as high, people often can lift their upper arms until they are close to parallel to the ground for a comfortable and effective range of motion.
    3. For cuing your side delts, it can help to focus on leading with your elbows and allowing your hands to follow them naturally as your elbows naturally bend.
    4. Allow your shoulder blades to move naturally rather than trying to keep them in any particular position.
    5. Throughout the exercise, keep the kettlebell close to your body, and avoid moving your legs or lower back.
2. Reverse the motion by lowering your elbows in toward your sides in a controlled manner to lower the kettlebell.
    1. You finish in the starting position as your elbows are straight, and the kettlebell is directly in front of your legs.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the weight abruptly pull you down in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), which are assisted by your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md).

## Setting up
A chest press machine with vertical handles is required to perform this neutral grip variation. If your machine only has horizontal handles, you can select the “[seated overhand grip pin-loaded machine chest press](Pin-loaded%20machine%20chest%20press%201a05c6f170d8807cbae8c6f25fc1a3be.md)” from this database as an alternative.

Certain chest press machines have a foot pedal that you can press to move the machine’s arms while setting up. Other machines lack a foot pedal but commonly allow you to modify the starting position with adjustable arms or a back pad that can be moved forward and backward. Some of the specific setup details differ depending on which type of machine you are using, so the setup for each approach is described separately. However, the exercise technique can be very similar for either option, so one technique section is provided with a couple of details that depend on which type of machine you utilize.

### **Setting up a machine without a foot pedal**

1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that situates the handles level with the lower half of your chest once you are seated.
    1. This is an appropriate starting point for most people, and it can result in somewhat of a range of viable seat heights. Feel free to try out different settings to determine what personally feels best to your body.
    2. The seat height that is ideal for you as an individual should allow your shoulders to feel comfortable and the pressing motion to feel natural during the exercise.
2. If your machine allows you to adjust either aspect, position its arms or back pad to a setting that enables you to press through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. Some machines allow you to increase the range of motion by placing the arms further back toward the back pad, while others allow you to move the back pad forward, closer toward the arms. However, certain machine models may not permit you to adjust either part.
    2. If you have normal shoulder mobility, you can initially position the arms or the seat to a setting that results in the handles being near the front of your chest (when viewed from the side) once you are seated. This commonly involves setting the arms as far backward or the seat as far forward as the machine enables.
    3. If you cannot comfortably grasp the handles with proper positioning during step 5, you can adjust the machine to increase the distance between the back pad and the handles until you can do so.
    4. The ideal setting should allow your elbows to start as far behind your torso as is comfortable for your shoulders while keeping your elbows level with the handles.
3. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
4. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against the back pad.
    1. Your feet should be flat on the ground.
    2. You can optionally rest your head against the back pad if it is tall enough, or you can simply keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
5. With your palms facing in toward each other and elbows bent, firmly grasp the vertical handles. Position your elbows directly behind the handles, resulting in your elbows being level with the handles.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. If you cannot comfortably grasp the handles and position your elbows directly behind them, you may have to position the machine’s arms further forward or the back pad further back before resuming your setup.
    3. Aligning your elbows directly behind the handles will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow tuck during this exercise.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.

### **Setting up a machine with a foot pedal**

1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that situates the handles level with the lower half of your chest once you are seated.
    1. This is an appropriate starting point for most people, and it can result in somewhat of a range of viable seat heights. Feel free to try out different settings to determine what personally feels best to your body.
    2. The seat height that is ideal for you as an individual should allow your shoulders to feel comfortable and the pressing motion to feel natural during the exercise.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against the back pad.
    1. You can optionally rest your head against the back pad if it is tall enough, or you can simply keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
4. Place one foot against the machine’s foot pedal, and push the pedal forward with your leg.
    1. This brings the handles forward to a position you can comfortably reach.
    2. Keep the pedal pushed away during the next two steps, while keeping your other foot on the ground.
5. With your palms facing in toward each other and elbows bent, firmly grasp the vertical handles. Position your elbows directly behind the handles, resulting in your elbows being level with the handles.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. Aligning your elbows directly behind the handles will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow tuck during this exercise.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
7. Bring the foot pedal back to its starting position by bending your knee, which will shift the machine’s resistance to your upper body. Simultaneously, allow your elbows to move backward through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Keep your elbows level with your wrists and the handles.
    2. How far your elbows can comfortably move backward while keeping them aligned with the handles will be dependent on your mobility.
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and/or the front of your shoulders at the end range, but you should not allow the machine to pull you into a position that causes shoulder discomfort.
8. Lift your foot off the foot pedal and place it flat on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the handles forward until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. Keep your elbows stacked behind your wrists and the handles while driving your elbows forward.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together, back snugly against the back pad, and feet planted on the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by allowing the handles to move backward in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows and wrists aligned behind the handles as your elbows progressively move backward while bending.
    2. Move through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits. Some machines will limit the range of motion before reaching this point, even when set up ideally.
    3. If your machine lacks a foot pedal, you can lightly tap the weights you selected against the rest of the weight stack at the end range to confirm that you have moved through the full range in a controlled manner. If your machine has a foot pedal, you can finish the lowering phase once you can no longer comfortably move your elbows backward while keeping your elbows directly behind the handles.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. If your machine has a foot pedal, push the pedal forward with your leg until you are no longer supporting any of the machine’s resistance with your upper body. Then let go of the handles and bend your knee to bring the foot pedal back to its initial position.
    2. If your machine lacks a foot pedal, simply rest the machine’s arms on the stoppers after the lowering phase of your last rep before letting go of the handles.
## Description
This exercise predominantly trains your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) with a technique that some people find feels more comfortable for their shoulders compared to other presses.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
    1. You can alternatively leave the machine initially unloaded if you are new to this exercise and have yet to determine which lever arm and/or belt attachment points are best for you.
2. Grab the belt, and step up onto the center of the platform with the machine’s lever arm between your feet.
3. Situate the belt around your hips so that the back of the belt is securely resting on top of your buttocks in a comfortable position.
4. Squat down, and connect the belt to the lever arm’s attachment point in a way that will comfortably allow you to squat through your full range of motion.
    1. Different machine models vary in their design, since some machines have a lever arm with a single attachment point, while others have a lever arm with multiple attachment points. Similarly, some belts have a single attachment point that can be connected to the lever arm, while others have multiple attachment points.
    2. When using a lever arm with multiple attachment points, the machine will provide less resistance when using a point near the base of the lever arm compared to the free end of the lever arm. Consequently, the specific lever attachment point can affect the difficulty of each rep, in addition to how much weight you add to the machine via plates.
    3. Which lever arm attachment point you use may also affect how comfortable the exercise feels to you, and there is no way to know which one feels best to you without personally using them. If you are new to this exercise, you can initially pick one attachment point and then try out different points over time to find which one you most prefer.
    4. If your belt has multiple attachment points (including a chain that can be varied in length to form different attachment points), which one you select can affect the exercise’s range of motion. While you may have to switch to different ones later on, you can initially try the attachment points closest to the middle of the belt, since using them will allow you to squat through the longest range of motion. Trying out different belt attachment points may be required because you have to continue setting up to determine if the pair you selected is ideal for you as an individual.
    5. If you select attachment points too close to the ends of the belt, the end of the cable that is linked to the belt will bottom out prematurely when squatting down, which will restrict you to performing partial range of motion squats. The con of using attachment points close to the middle of the belt is that they can make it more difficult to get into the starting position. Consequently, you ideally do not want to select attachments that are any closer toward the middle of the belt than what is needed for you to squat through a full range of motion.
5. Stand upright, and align your feet so that the lever arm’s attachment point is between the middle of your feet (rather than being in front of your feet or behind them).
6. Position your feet reasonably near shoulder width apart with your toes pointing somewhat out to the sides and the soles of your feet fully on the platform.
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up close to this stance allows them to belt squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when belt squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. Using a stance that is mildly wider than your typical squat stance may sometimes reduce discomfort from the pressure the belt can exert on the groin.
7. Raise your arms and grasp the handle with your hands near shoulder width apart.
    1. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. Your neck should similarly be near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
8. Pull the handle back toward you to disengage the safety arm if you are using a machine that allows you to do so.
    1. Some machine models have the safety arm automatically disengage once you stand upright, but others require you to disengage it manually.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner.

## Setting up
While exceptions may exist, lying pin-loaded chest press machines normally have their handles in a fixed starting position. The starting height can be appropriate for many lifters, but may not be ideal for some people with pre-existing shoulder limitations who may benefit from being able to adjust the starting position.

1. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
2. Lie down with your back, buttocks, and head on the pad. Position yourself so that your lower-to-middle chest is aligned with the handles.
    1. Your elbows will naturally tuck closer to your sides as you position yourself further back on the pad (situating your shoulders horizontally further behind the handles).
    2. You can decide specifically where you lie down on the pad based on what feels comfortable to your shoulders throughout the exercise, while simultaneously allowing you to feel meaningful tension in your chest.
    3. If you experience shoulder discomfort when pressing with the handles near mid-chest, you can try positioning yourself with the handles by the lowest part of your chest to be able to press with a lower degree of elbow flare.
    4. Your feet should be flat on the ground in a stable position, stacked under your bent knees.
3. With your palms facing forward and elbows bent, firmly grasp the horizontally directed handles. Position your elbows directly under the handles, resulting in your forearms being in a vertical position.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. Aligning your elbows directly under (rather than being in front or behind when viewed from the side) the handles will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare during this exercise, provided that you positioned your body appropriately on the pad.
    3. If your machine has sufficiently long handles, you may be able to adjust your grip width with different hand placements. Placing your hands moderately outside shoulder width can work well for many people, but you can try out different grip widths to determine where you personally feel best while stacking your elbows under the handles.
4. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the handles upward until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your elbows should remain stacked under your wrists and the handles when viewed from the side.
    3. Throughout your set, continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together, back and buttocks snugly against the pad, and feet planted on the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the handles in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. Keep your elbows stacked under your wrists and the handles as you allow your elbows to move outward and downward while bending.
    2. Descend through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    3. If you can comfortably lower the handles fully to the starting position, you can lightly tap the weights you selected to the rest of the weight stack. A gentle tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that places the handles near your lower chest or slightly lower once you are seated.
    1. This is an appropriate starting point for most people, but the ideal seat height specifically should allow you to train through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably allows.
    2. Individuals with limited mobility may have to position the seat higher to reach the handles, while those with greater mobility may benefit from positioning the seat lower to train through a full range of motion.
    3. If the seat is excessively high, your range of motion for this exercise will be limited.
    4. If the seat is excessively low, you may not be able to reach the handles with proper positioning. Forcing your elbows back beyond what your mobility permits in an effort to reach the handles may increase the risk of experiencing shoulder discomfort.
    5. Some trial and error may be needed to find the best height for you as an individual. When continuing to set up, you can always adjust the seat height if you determine the initial height is suboptimal for you.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your feet flat on the ground.
    1. If your machine has a back pad, position the back of your hip bones against it.
    2. If your machine has a chest pad, sit down toward the back of the seat to provide some space for you to lean forward mildly during a subsequent step.
4. If your machine has a thigh pad, snugly position it on top of your thighs. If your machine has a seat belt, securely fasten it around your waist.
    1. Either option will help you anchor your body.
    2. Certain machines lack a thigh pad or seat belt, which can contribute to the exercise being less stable.
5. If your machine allows you to rotate its handles inward or outward, position them outward.
    1. Relative to the closer handle setting, the wider setting facilitates a greater degree of elbow flare that can help you train your chest more effectively during your dip.
6. Mildly lean forward at your hips while keeping your back flat and pulling your shoulder blades back.
    1. A mild forward lean can help you emphasize your chest to a greater degree compared to if you sat fully upright.
    2. Specifically how far you lean forward is up to your preference and what feels comfortable to you during the exercise.
    3. Pulling your shoulder blades back will place you into a “proud chest” posture and prevent your shoulders from rounding forward into a slouched position. Keep your shoulder blades pulled back while continuing to set up.
7. Move your elbows back behind your torso while flaring them somewhat out away from your sides and bending them reasonably close to 90 degrees.
    1. In contrast to a triceps-focused dip, you are intentionally flaring your elbows out to a degree for this variation rather than keeping them tucked very close to your sides. However, make sure to avoid excessively flaring them.
    2. The appropriate degree of elbow flare should feel comfortable to your shoulders while also permitting you to feel meaningful tension in your chest during the exercise. Specifically how much elbow flare someone should utilize will vary among different individuals and be influenced by shoulder mobility.
    3. Aiming to flare your elbows less than 45 degrees is generally appropriate for most people. Zero degrees of flare would mean your elbows are pointing straight back, parallel to each other, while 90 degrees of flare would mean they are pointing straight out to the sides.
8. After moving your arms to the end range that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits, confirm whether the handles are at an appropriate height for you.
    1. If the handles are now just within your reach, the seat height you initially selected is appropriate.
    2. If you cannot reach the handles without shrugging your shoulders up or tipping them forward, raise the seat before resuming your setup.
    3. If the handles are lower than what you can comfortably reach from this position, you can lower the seat to facilitate a greater degree of elbow bend before resuming your setup.
9. Firmly grasp the handles with the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) against them.
    1. While almost all machines allow you to use a neutral grip with your palms facing in toward each other, some machines also have handles that allow you to use an overhand grip with your palms facing backward. If your machine enables you to use both grips, select whichever feels most comfortable to you.
    2. Hold the handles with mostly straight wrists. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Push the handles down until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. While driving your elbows downward, they will simultaneously move forward and inward.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your torso mildly leaned forward and feet planted on the ground. Due to your torso lean, you should finish with your elbows in front of your sides rather than being directly by your sides.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing the handles to lift up to the starting position.
    1. Bend your elbows while allowing them to move upward, backward, and mildly to moderately out away from your sides.
    2. Avoid letting your shoulders shrug up or roll forward.
    3. With the appropriate seat height, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders and/or chest at the end range, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain. If you feel joint discomfort at the end range, increase the seat height before resuming your set.
    4. At the end range, you can lightly tap the machine’s arms against the stoppers under them to confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Use the machine’s loading pin to select your desired level of assistance, and ensure that the machine’s knee pad or foot bar is positioned down.
    1. In contrast to most machines, the difficulty of this exercise decreases as you select heavier loads from the assisted dip machine, since the weight determines the extent to which the machine will support your bodyweight.
    2. Certain machine models have a knee pad, and others have a foot bar, but essentially the same exercise technique can be used with either type of machine.
2. Step up onto the machine’s elevated foot plates.
3. If your machine allows you to rotate its parallel handles inward or outward, position them outward.
    1. Relative to the closer handle setting, the wider setting facilitates a greater degree of elbow flare that can help you train your chest more effectively during your dip.
    2. While using wider handles is standard when seeking to emphasize chest training during a dip, you have the option of selecting the closer setting if using the wide handles feels uncomfortable for your shoulders. The wide handle setting on certain machines may be wider than ideal for some lifters, particularly for people who have rather narrow frames and/or those with pre-existing shoulder issues.
    3. Note that a variety of machines do not allow you to adjust the handle position.
4. Firmly grasp the parallel handles with your palms facing each other. Hold the handles directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
5. One leg at a time, kneel onto the machine’s knee pad (if your machine has a knee pad) or step onto the machine’s foot bar (if your machine has a foot bar) while continuing to grasp the handles firmly. Maintain straight elbows when doing so.
    1. If using a machine with a knee pad, you will keep your knees bent on the pad throughout your set, but if you are using a machine with a foot bar, you will keep your knees straight while standing on the bar throughout your set.
6. Mildly lean forward at your hips while keeping your back flat and pulling your shoulder blades back. Avoid letting your shoulders shrug up.
    1. A mild forward lean can help you emphasize your chest more than if your torso were fully upright.
    2. Specifically how far you lean forward is up to your preference and what feels comfortable to you during the exercise.
    3. Pulling your shoulder blades back will place you into a “proud chest” posture and prevent your shoulders from rounding forward into a slouched position.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. While allowing them to flare out somewhat away from your sides, bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Throughout your set, continue keeping your torso mildly leaned forward and avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up.
    2. In contrast to a triceps-focused dip, you are intentionally flaring your elbows out to a degree for this variation rather than keeping them tucked very close to your sides. However, make sure to avoid excessively flaring them.
    3. The appropriate degree of elbow flare should feel comfortable for your shoulders while also permitting you to feel meaningful tension in your chest during the exercise. Specifically how much elbow flare someone should utilize will vary among different individuals and be influenced by shoulder mobility.
    4. Aiming to flare your elbows less than 45 degrees is generally appropriate for most people. Zero degrees of flare would mean your elbows are pointing straight back, parallel to each other, while 90 degrees of flare would mean they are pointing straight out to the sides.
    5. If your machine allows you to use moderately wide handles, the appropriate degree of elbow flare can often naturally occur without having to think about flaring your elbows out, provided that you do not intentionally try to tuck your elbows inward.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point at which their upper arms are at least parallel to the ground, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Reverse the movement by pushing through the handles to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows simultaneously in toward your sides and downward.
5. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step down onto the foot plate.

While also training the [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [upper pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), this exercise will particularly develop the [middle and lower regions of the pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md), along with the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

    1. Throughout your set, continue keeping your torso moderately leaned forward, and avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up.
    2. Rather than swinging them, continue keeping your legs stationary relative to your hips until you finish your set. If you are using a dip belt, keeping your legs in contact with the weight can help you stabilize it. If the weight is between your legs, squeezing your thighs together can stop the weight from swinging.
    3. In contrast to a triceps-focused dip, you are intentionally flaring your elbows out to a degree for this variation rather than keeping them tucked very close to your sides. However, make sure to avoid excessively flaring them.
    4. The appropriate degree of elbow flare should feel comfortable for your shoulders while also permitting you to feel meaningful tension in your chest during the exercise. Specifically how much elbow flare someone should utilize will vary among different individuals and be influenced by shoulder mobility.
    5. Aiming to flare your elbows less than 45 degrees is generally appropriate for most people. Zero degrees of flare would mean your elbows are pointing straight back, parallel to each other, while 90 degrees of flare would mean they are pointing straight out to the sides.
    6. Provided that you do not intentionally try to tuck your elbows inward, the appropriate degree of elbow flare can often naturally occur without having to think about flaring your elbows out if your bars are mildly outside shoulder width.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point at which their upper arms are at least parallel to the ground, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Reverse the movement by pushing through the bars to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows simultaneously in toward your sides and downward.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step down from the bars.

## Setting up
1. Set an adjustable exercise bench to a low incline, or determine a different object near hip height against which you can brace with your free hand.
    1. Viable alternatives to a low incline bench can include a plyometric box, dumbbell rack, racked Smith machine bar, or barbell on a rack’s J-cups, provided that any of those options are reasonably near hip height.
2. Place a dumbbell on the ground near the head of the incline bench.
    1. You should place the dumbbell where it will be under your working side’s shoulder after setting up, which may require adjusting the dumbbell while setting up.
3. Stand facing the head of the bench, and situate your feet mildly outside shoulder width.
4. With the foot on the same side of your body that you will train, step backward to adopt a staggered stance.
5. Place the hand on the side you will not train against the head of the bench.
    1. Throughout the exercise, use this hand to brace against the bench for stability.
6. Lean your torso forward by sitting your hips back while allowing your knees to bend mildly until you can reach the dumbbell with your other hand.
    1. While you rotate your torso to reach the dumbbell, avoid rounding your lower back when setting up or performing the exercise.
7. Firmly grasp the dumbbell, and angle your palm inward.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Explosively drive your elbow backward and upward in an arcing motion to pull the dumbbell toward your hip. Simultaneously rotate your chest moderately toward the dumbbell to help generate momentum.
    1. Pull your shoulder blade back at the same time to finish with a “proud chest.”
    2. When bending your elbow appropriately, your forearm should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    3. At the top of the row, your elbow should be aligned with your torso or slightly behind your torso.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell while letting your chest rotate moderately away from the dumbbell.
    1. While this variation purposely uses a “cheating” style, that does not mean you should just let the weight drop down abruptly. There is no need to lower the weight in a particularly slow manner, but you should strive to control the descent to a reasonable degree.
    2. Allow the weight to pull your shoulder blade forward, which will stretch your upper back muscles and result in your working side’s shoulder being mildly closer to the ground than your other side’s shoulder at the bottom of the row.
    3. Finish with your elbow straightened, hanging down toward the ground.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a weighted exercise ball of your desired weight that is appropriate to slam onto the ground.
    1. Not every medicine ball is designed to withstand the impact of slamming. Balls with a soft shell (which includes balls specifically known as slam balls) are typically suitable to slam, but balls with a rigid coat are often inappropriate for a high-impact exercise.
    2. If you are unsure whether the ball you have is appropriate to slam, you can look up the details of the model you have or ask the gym staff.
    3. It is recommended to use a ball that does not bounce if you have access to one.
2. Carry the ball to an area with sufficient space around you and a surface appropriate for slamming.
3. While standing upright with your feet near shoulder width apart, firmly hold the ball in front of your thighs with both hands and your fingers spread apart.
    1. Your palms should be facing in toward each other on each side of the ball.
    2. Your back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Quickly lift the ball up until it is directly overhead with mildly bent elbows. Simultaneously march one knee up.
    1. Aim to finish lifting the ball overhead and marching your knee at the same time. Immediately after you finish doing so, fluidly transition directly into the next step.
    2. Rather than overhead pressing the ball up, you can sweep it up out in front of you with mildly bent elbows as you could do during a front raise that ends overhead.
    3. While you should have a “proud chest” posture with your chest up, avoid arching your lower back excessively.
    4. If you do not have the shoulder mobility to lift the ball directly overhead without leaning back, simply raise your arms up as high as you can without letting your ribs flare up (which occurs from lower back arching). Strive to position your biceps close to your ears.
2. Explosively slam the ball down with the intent to break the ground as you drive your raised foot down to step into the slam. Simultaneously sweep your arms down while sitting your buttocks back as you hinge at your hips and bend your knees.
    1. To fully benefit from this exercise, it is paramount that you slam the ball as forcefully as you physically can.
    2. Finish the slam with your elbows fully straightened and your feet in a staggered stance.
    3. The arm motion you perform is akin to a straight arm lat pulldown performed as explosively as possible.
    4. Make sure to fully follow through with your arms rather than halting the slam after releasing the ball. If you can stop moving directly after the ball leaves your hands, you are not slamming the ball as violently as you can. You should drive your arms down so forcefully that they inevitably fly fully back behind your torso after letting go of the ball.
    5. Except for stepping into the slam with one leg, the slamming motion should look similar to when someone dips down in preparation to perform a vertical jump.
    6. As your torso transitions closer to a horizontal angle from hinging at your hips, avoid collapsing your chest or rounding your shoulders forward into a slumped posture.
3. Allow the ball to come to a dead stop on the ground before picking it up and assuming the same position you did while setting up.
    1. Certain balls will stop immediately as they hit the ground, while other balls will bounce up.
    2. When using a ball that bounces up, people often catch the ball right after it bounces following the impact, but this can be suboptimal. Aiming to catch the ball very soon after releasing it can interfere with the maximally explosive intent when initially slamming the ball. It can be difficult to catch the ball in front of you after fully following through with the slam, so striving to catch the ball can prompt people to stop the slamming motion prematurely, which contributes to reduced explosiveness.
    3. Use your lower body to pick up the ball in a squat or hip hinge movement rather than excessively rounding and straightening your lower back to do so.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 while switching which leg you march up during each rep until you have completed your set.
## Description
While engaging a variety of muscles throughout the body, this exercise can particularly improve explosive strength of the [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) as they function to extend the shoulders.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, and position the footplates as closely together as the machine permits.
2. If your machine’s knee pads rotate (which is the case for combo machines that can be adjusted to train hip adduction or abduction), position the pads so that they are facing in toward each other.
    1. The knee pads may permanently face in toward each other in machines that exclusively permit you to train hip abduction.
3. If your machine allows you to adjust the backrest angle, position it fully upright.
    1. Most machines have backrests fixed in an upright position.
4. Sit down on the machine's seat with the back of your hip bones against the back rest. Place your feet on the footplates with the outer aspect of your knees and/or lower thighs contacting the knee pads.
    1. If you have rather short legs, you may have to scoot slightly forward from the back rest for your knees to reach the pads.
    2. Keep your arms in whichever comfortable position you prefer.
5. Lean your torso forward by hinging at your hips through your available range of motion while keeping your back mostly flat.
    1. People can commonly lean forward at least by 30 degrees from a fully upright torso position, but the magnitude of lean will vary among different individuals.
    2. Specifically, how far you can lean forward will be influenced by your hip mobility, along with the size of your abdomen and thighs.
    3. To train your glutes and other hip muscles in a way that differs from when you maintain a fully upright torso, the forward lean should occur from hip motion rather than simply rounding your back.
## Exercise technique
1. Spread your legs apart from each other through your hips’ available range of motion.
    1. Maintain your leaned forward torso position throughout your set.
    2. How far apart you can spread your legs will be affected by your hip mobility.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your legs to move in toward each other in a controlled manner.
    1. After doing so, you should now be in the starting position with your legs as close together as the machine permits.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While also training several other smaller muscles on the side of your hip, this exercise can dynamically train your [glutes](../Muscles/Glutes%201b95c6f170d88002885bca53f30406d5.md), likely with an emphasis on the [upper region](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%20Upper%20Region%201925c6f170d88070b08aeccda6e5ac88.md) of your gluteus maximus.

## Setting up
1. Position the footplates far enough apart that you can fully spread your legs apart when you are seated with your feet on the footplates.
    1. If your machine’s knee pads rotate (which is the case for combo machines that can be adjusted to train hip adduction or abduction), position the pads so that they are facing away from each other.
    2. Determining specifically where you should position the footplates can take some trial and error if you are not accustomed to this exercise. The ideal position will allow you to feel resistance from the machine when your legs are spread as far apart as your flexibility comfortably permits. Avoid placing the footplates any further apart than that point to help you more easily transition into and out of the starting position.
2. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Adjust the backrest to its fully reclined position or move the backrest fully back.
4. Sit down on the machine's seat with an upright torso.
5. Spread your legs apart to place your feet on the footplates with the inner aspect of your knees and/or lower thighs contacting the knee pads.
    1. It may be easiest initially to position one leg and then use your arms to help pull the knee pads inward before positioning your other leg. The stretching force from the machine typically allows you to spread your legs further apart than you actively could by yourself, so it can be difficult to achieve the fully spread position for this exercise without using your arms to assist in setting up.
    2. If you have rather short legs, you may have to scoot slightly forward on the seat for your knees to reach the pads, which will require you to lean your torso somewhat backward to keep your upper back against the backrest.
6. If you feel that you can spread your legs further apart than is permitted by the initial machine setting you selected, you can adjust the pads to be further away from each other until you feel that your inner thigh muscles are sufficiently stretched.
    1. It is recommended to remove at least one leg from the footplate when adjusting the machine.
7. Lean back to position your back against the backrest, and firmly grasp the handles if they are within your reach.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your knees in toward each other until your legs are situated directly in front of you.
    1. You can tap the inner aspect of the knee pads against each other at the end of this motion.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your knees to move out and away from each other in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your flexibility comfortably permits.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your legs spread fully apart.
    2. With the appropriate machine setting, you should feel a stretching sensation in your inner thighs.
    3. While you do not have to perform this phase of the movement with an extremely slow tempo, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach your end range is recommended.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Like when setting up, you can use your hands to apply an inward pressure to the knee pads while sitting upright to assist with lifting your legs up one at a time.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train all your [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md) in an isolated manner.

## Setting up
A machine that allows you to adjust its backrest angle to a reclined position or move the backrest back (letting you lean back) is ideal for this variation, but many machine models lack this adjustable feature. If your machine does not permit you to adjust the backrest, you may alternatively bridge your hips up to place your hips in a similar position. Specifically how you will set up will differ depending on which equipment you use, so the set-up for each approach is described separately, but a single exercise technique section is provided. If you find this variation to feel awkward when using a machine without an adjustable backrest, you can select “[seated pin-loaded machine hip abduction](Seated%20machine%20hip%20abduction%201a35c6f170d8801e907be574e89e5c65.md)” as an alternative exercise from this database.

### Setting up with an adjustable backrest

1. Select your weight with the loading pin and position the footplates as closely together as the machine permits.
2. If your machine’s knee pads rotate (which is the case for combo machines that can be adjusted to train hip adduction or abduction), position the pads so that they are facing in toward each other.
    1. The knee pads may permanently face in toward each other in machines that exclusively permit you to train hip abduction.
3. Adjust the backrest to its fully reclined position, or position the backrest as far back as you can.
4. After sitting down on the machine's seat, place your feet on the footplates. The outer aspect of your knees and/or lower thighs should be contacting the knee pads.
    1. If you have rather short legs, you may have to scoot slightly forward from the back rest for your knees to reach the pads.
5. Lean back to position your back against the backrest, and firmly grasp the handles if they are within your reach.

### Setting up with an upright backrest

1. Select your weight with the loading pin and position the footplates as closely together as the machine permits.
2. If your machine’s knee pads rotate (which is the case for combo machines that can be adjusted to train hip adduction or abduction), position the pads so that they are facing in toward each other.
    1. The knee pads may permanently face in toward each other in machines that exclusively permit you to train hip abduction.
3. If your machine allows you to do so, move its back rest horizontally into the furthest back position.
    1. A variety of machines do not permit you to adjust the seat.
4. After sitting down on the machine's seat, place your feet on the footplates. The outer aspect of your knees and/or lower thighs should be contacting the knee pads.
    1. If you have rather short legs, you may have to scoot slightly forward from the back rest for your knees to reach the pads.
5. Position your shoulder blades against the backrest, and bridge your hips up above the seat while keeping your back flat. Simultaneously grasp the handles firmly for stability if they are within your reach.
    1. Avoid arching your lower back excessively when lifting your hips. Tightening your abdominal muscles to brace your core can help you keep your back flat.
    2. How far you can lift your hips up while maintaining a stable position can be influenced by your body proportions and the specific machine you are using. The appropriate degree of bridging should allow you to feel stable.
    3. You do not need to lift your hips fully up until your thighs are aligned with your torso (like you would do during a glute bridge) if you feel unstable doing so. Feel free to try out different bridge heights over time to determine what feels best to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Spread your legs apart from each other through your hips’ available range of motion.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your back snugly in contact with the back rest if you are using a reclined back rest, or keep your hips bridged up if you are not.
    2. If they are within your reach, continue holding the handles firmly until you finish the set.
    3. How far apart you can spread your legs will be affected by your hip mobility.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your legs to move in toward each other in a controlled manner.
    1. At the end range, you can allow the weights you selected to tap the rest of the weight stack. A light tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
    2. After doing so, you should now be in the starting position with your legs as close together as the machine permits.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the musculature on the side of your hip, including your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), and [tensor fascia latae](../Muscles/Tensor%20Fascia%20Latae%201925c6f170d8806fb83bf08142d940fc.md).

## Setting up
1. Position the footplates far enough apart that you can fully spread your legs apart when you are seated with your feet on the footplates.
    1. If your machine’s knee pads rotate (which is the case for combo machines that can be adjusted to train hip adduction or abduction), position the pads so that they are facing away from each other.
    2. Determining specifically where you should position the footplates can take some trial and error if you are not accustomed to this exercise. The ideal position will allow you to feel resistance from the machine when your legs are spread as far apart as your flexibility comfortably permits. Avoid placing the footplates any further apart than that point to help you more easily transition into and out of the starting position.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Adjust the backrest to its fully reclined position or move the backrest fully back.
4. Sit down on the machine's seat with an upright torso.
5. Spread your legs apart to place your feet on the footplates with the inner aspect of your knees and/or lower thighs contacting the knee pads.
    1. It may be easiest initially to position one leg and then use your arms to help pull the knee pads inward before positioning your other leg. The stretching force from the machine typically allows you to spread your legs further apart than you actively could by yourself, so it can be difficult to achieve the fully spread position for this exercise without using your arms to assist in setting up.
    2. If you have rather short legs, you may have to scoot slightly forward on the seat for your knees to reach the pads, which will require you to lean your torso somewhat backward to keep your upper back against the backrest.
6. If you feel that you can spread your legs further apart than is permitted by the initial machine setting you selected, you can adjust the pads to be further away from each other until you feel that your inner thigh muscles are sufficiently stretched.
    1. It is recommended to remove at least one leg from the footplate when adjusting the machine.
7. Lean back to position your back against the backrest, and firmly grasp the handles if they are within your reach.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your knees in toward each other until your legs are situated directly in front of you.
    1. You can tap the inner aspect of the knee pads against each other at the end of this motion.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your knees to move out and away from each other in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your flexibility comfortably permits.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your legs spread fully apart.
    2. With the appropriate machine setting, you should feel a stretching sensation in your inner thighs.
    3. While you do not have to perform this phase of the movement with an extremely slow tempo, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach your end range is recommended.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Like when setting up, you can use your hands to apply an inward pressure to the knee pads while sitting upright to assist with lifting your legs up one at a time.

## Setting up
1. If your machine allows you to adjust the height of the footplate, select a height that will allow your legs to be in an approximately horizontal position once you are in the starting position.
    1. After estimating where this setting may be, you can adjust it during later steps if warranted.
    2. Not all machines permit you to adjust the footplate height.
2. Horizontally adjust the machine’s footplate to a setting that will allow the pad to support your thighs without contacting your hip bones when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. The appropriate position should allow your hips to move freely while sufficiently stabilizing your legs.
    2. If the footplate is positioned excessively far back (resulting in your hips resting on the pad), the pad can restrict your hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    3. If the footplate is positioned excessively far forward to the extent that your knees are near the middle of the pad rather than your thighs, the exercise may provoke knee discomfort in some people.
    4. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position.
3. Climb up onto the machine, and position your feet against the footplate with your lower legs between the leg rollers while the front of your hips are resting on the pad.
    1. The back of your lower legs should be snugly pressed into the top pair of leg rollers slightly above your heels.
    2. Your knees should be straight, and your soles should be firmly contacting the footplate.
    3. While you are setting your feet, you can use the handles for assistance.
    4. Some machines have a step that you can use to help you get into position.
    5. With the appropriate footplate setting, the front of your hip bones should not be resting on the pad.
4. Place the fingertips of each hand lightly in contact with the sides of the back of your head as your upper arms and elbows are directed out away from your sides.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes to keep your torso up such that you can draw approximately a straight line from your legs through your hips and to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. This is the starting position of the exercise, where your body should look like it does when normally standing upright, except rotated to be horizontal.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips.
3. Without rounding your back, hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner to angle your torso downward.
    1. As opposed to bending over at your back, nearly all the motion should occur from you moving at your hips as you statically keep your trunk near a neutral position with your lower back mildly arched or flat.
    2. Maintain a straight knee position, but avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads.
    3. While hinging at your hips and keeping your hands behind your head, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings that progressively intensifies.
    4. How deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility. If you have the flexibility to hinge until your torso is completely vertical, stop once you reach this point. Otherwise, stop descending once you feel like you have reached the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch.
    5. If you initially did not position the footplate sufficiently forward, the pad may alternatively limit how deeply you can hinge.
4. Reverse the movement by lifting your torso up through your hips and squeezing your glutes.
    1. When moving through your hips, your entire torso should move together as one unit. You can think of your hips as the center of an analog clock, while your rigid torso is a hand that rotates about the center.
    2. At the end of the lifting phase, your torso should be close to a horizontal position aligned with your legs.
    3. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the hip motion you just performed during the lowering phase. Focusing on finishing the movement by squeezing your glutes can help prevent excessive back arching.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
6. After your last rep, you can grasp the handles to help you dismount the machine.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).
