## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the Roman chair’s pad to a level that positions its top slightly below the top of your hip bones when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. The appropriate position should allow you to move your lower back freely while supporting your hips.
    2. While it can effectively stabilize your hips, positioning the top of the pad higher than the top of your hip bones can restrict your lower back’s motion, which is suboptimal for training lower back muscles.
    3. If the top of the pad is positioned much lower than the top of the hip bones (rather than only slightly lower), the hips will not be stabilized as well, which can make it more challenging to emphasize training your back muscles.
    4. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position.
2. While placing your hands onto the handles for balance support, step onto the foot plate one leg at a time. Place the back of your heels against the back of the foot plate, as your soles fully contact the foot plate.
    1. Based on your preference, you can point your toes straight forward, or you can rotate them to point inward. Pointing the toes inward may help some people limit the hip muscle engagement while focusing on the back muscles.
    2. Situating your feet approximately hip width to shoulder apart from each other will result in a viable stance width, but how wide of a stance you can use will be influenced by the width of your Roman chair’s foot plate.
    3. Your knees should be straight after you have finished setting your feet on the foot plate.
3. Check to make sure that the pad is positioned as described by step 1, and readjust the pad height if warranted before resuming your setup.
4. Place the fingertips of each hand lightly in contact with the sides of the back of your head as your upper arms and elbows are directed out away from your sides.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
    2. Your back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your back mostly flat, hinge at your hips through the range of motion that is permitted by the pad and your flexibility.
    1. Only during this step are you intentionally moving about your hips to assume the starting position.
    2. Once you have reached the end range of your hip motion, it will be easier to emphasize back motion.
    3. Depending on specifically where you have the pad positioned, the pad may limit how far you can hinge, or your hamstring flexibility may limit it.
2. Round your entire back in a slow and controlled curling manner through the full range of motion that is comfortable for you.
    1. The degree to which you can round your back will be affected by your spinal mobility.
    2. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your back muscles in the bottom position, but you should not feel any discomfort at the end range. Only round your back as far as is comfortable.
    3. Rather than moving only one part of your back, strive to round your lower, middle, and upper back simultaneously.
    4. As a cue, you can think about bringing the bottom of your ribs toward the top of your hip bones.
3. Reverse the movement by extending (straightening) your back in a controlled manner without hinging at your hips.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, your back should be near a neutral position, which involves your lower back being mildly arched.
    2. For increasing the size and strength of your back muscles, there is no need to arch your back maximally like you would during a cobra yoga pose.
    3. Keep your glutes relaxed to the best of your ability as you focus on moving your spine rather than your hips.
    4. You should feel your spinal extensor muscles, which run along each side of the spine, contract to extend your back.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep intrinsic spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) that run along the length of your entire back.

    1. Continue keeping your core braced from this point on.
6. Stand upright with the bar by extending your hips and knees while continuing to keep your elbows straight and your lower back near a neutral position.
    1. While your lower back muscles will be working to maintain a rigid trunk position, lifting the bar upward should chiefly occur from your hip and thigh muscles, extending your hips and knees.
    2. Keep the bar very close to your legs as you lift the bar rather than allowing the bar to drift forward.
7. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and moderately incline your torso until you have lowered the bar near your knees.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight, back flat, and core braced.
    2. Allow your knees to bend naturally while sitting your hips back as if you were closing a car door with your buttocks, while your hands are carrying something.
    3. Maintain this hinged position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar up toward your lower abdomen by driving your elbows simultaneously backward and upward as you pull your shoulder blades back.
    1. Throughout your set, maintain the same degree of torso inclination while keeping your back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    2. As movement occurs at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, your lower body should remain essentially stationary. Resist the urge to use your legs to lift your torso into a more upright position at the end of the lifting phase, which is the most difficult part of the exercise.
    3. Keep your elbows tucked reasonably close to your sides as they bend, rather than meaningfully flaring your elbows out away from your sides.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner. Allow your elbows to move downward and forward until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. At the end of the lowering phase, you should be in the starting position with the bar just in front of your knees.
    2. Let your shoulder blades naturally spread apart.
    3. There is no need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but make sure that you actively control the weight rather than simply letting gravity abruptly yank the bar down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
4. Set the bar down onto the ground by reversing the technique you used to pick it up (i.e., bending at your hips and knees as opposed to just rounding over at your lower back).
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Horizontally adjust the machine’s footplate to a setting that will allow you to position part of your buttocks just off the front edge of the pad when you set up with your feet on the footplate.
    1. The appropriate position should allow your thighs to rest comfortably on the pad.
    2. If the footplate is positioned excessively far from the pad, you will have to sit closer toward the middle of the pad rather than just off the front edge.
    3. If the footplate is positioned excessively close to the pad, the back of your upper thighs will not be in contact with the pad.
    4. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position.
2. If your machine allows you to adjust  the footplate height, select a height that allows you to feel comfortable and secure with slightly bent knees once you are in the starting position.
    1. As a starting point, you can select a height that positions the lower pair of leg rollers level with the pad and the upper pair of leg rollers higher than the pad.
    2. Not all machines permit you to adjust the footplate height.
3. Climb up onto the machine, and hook your lower legs between the leg rollers with the top of your feet snugly pressed into the top roller as your soles are facing the footplate. Sit upright with your buttocks just hanging off the front edge of the pad.
    1. Your feet should be securely anchored so that they will not slide during the exercise. The top rollers should be just above the lowest part of your shins by your ankles, while the bottom rollers should be just under your Achilles tendons (which attach to the top of your heels).
    2. Depending on the machine you are using, you can step up onto a middle beam or a step to help you get into position.
    3. While you are setting your feet, you can reach back with your hands to hold the handles for stability.
4. Outstretch your arms and lean forward just enough to touch the top roller with your fingertips.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your knees slightly bent, lean your torso back until you can touch the ground with your fingertips. Mildly tuck your chin toward your chest as you do so.
    1. Most of the motion should come from you leaning back at your hips, but your back will naturally arch as well.
    2. Rather than reaching your arms straight back over your head to touch the ground, you can reach your arms out away from your sides through a motion resembling a jumping jack. This will be more mechanically efficient.
    3. Aim to be quick but simultaneously controlled.
2. Straighten your knees and rapidly reverse the movement by lifting your torso up through your hips until you can touch the top roller with both hands.
    1. As you predominantly pull yourself up through your hip flexors, you can simultaneously tighten your abs and drive the bottom of your ribs toward the top of your hip bones. This will shift you from an arched back position into a flat back position and then a mildly rounded back position at the top while you reach forward.
3. Quickly alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you tap the leg roller at the end of each rep, allow your knees to bend slightly as you transition to the lowering phase of your next rep.
4. After your last rep, you can grasp the handles to help you dismount the machine.
## Description
While also developing your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md), this exercise can meaningfully train your [iliopsoas](../Muscles/Iliopsoas%201b95c6f170d880e99c61fe85969fc3c9.md), [rectus femoris](../Muscles/Rectus%20Femoris%201925c6f170d880f080b7cda6f5f3f0ee.md), and other [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Sit on the ground with an upright torso and your legs straight out in front of you.
    1. The back of your heels should be on the ground as your feet are close together.
2. Place your hands on the ground approximately shoulder-width apart, slightly behind your hips, with your fingers spread apart and elbows straight.
    1. Rotating your hands such that your middle fingers point straight out to your sides is appropriate. However, you can feel free to rotate your hands to point in whichever direction you find most comfortable.
    2. The proper hand placement should allow your arms to point straight down toward the ground during the exercise.
3. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. Rather than being slumped forward, your chest should be directed slightly upward.
    2. As a cue, you can think about pinching a pencil with your shoulder blades.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels into the ground and squeezing your glutes.
    1. At the top, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    2. Keep your elbows straight as the weight you bear through your arms predominantly goes through the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) rather than closer to your knuckles.
    3. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back with a “proud chest” as you avoid letting your shoulders round forward.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    5. Squeezing your glutes can help you avoid excessively arching your lower back, which should exhibit its natural mild curvature. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them.
2. Shift your weight into one foot on the ground, and lift the other foot off the ground. Except for the leg you lift, keep the rest of your body in the same position you adopted from step 1.
    1. Based on your preference, you can lift your one leg up with a straight knee or a bent knee. Either position for the free leg is viable, but keeping the knee straight may make the exercise mildly more challenging compared to keeping it bent.
    2. So long as you lift the free leg high enough to keep its foot off the ground throughout the set, you can decide how high you lift it up.
    3. Focus on keeping your right and left hip bones level with each other as you avoid letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg tilt down. You can imagine balancing a mug of water on the middle of your waist. If laser beams were shooting out from the center of your chest and your imaginary belt buckle, the two lasers should be parallel to each other throughout your set.
3. Rigidly hold the position you adopted from completing steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set’s target duration.
    1. Strive to have your body look the same during the last second of your set as it did during the first second after finishing step 2.
    2. Prioritize keeping your grounded leg completely in line with your torso while you resist letting your hips gradually lower toward the ground as time elapses.
4. Bend your hips to return to sitting on the ground before repeating the exercise as you switch which foot remains on the ground.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) that run along your entire back.

## Setting up
1. Position the weight you intend to use on the ground.
    1. For this variation, you will be holding the weight to your chest, so a weight plate, dumbbell, kettlebell, or medicine ball is a viable option that you can select based on your equipment availability and preference.
2. Sit on the ground next to the weight before picking up the weight with both hands and holding it close to your chest.
    1. It will be easiest to pick up the weight if you sit with it to the side of one of your hips.
    2. The precise way in which you will hold the weight to your chest may vary based on the specific implement you selected, but what matters is that you have a firm grip on the weight and are able to keep it in a stable position.
3. Bend your knees by approximately 90 degrees with your feet together.
4. Moderately lean your torso back at your hips, and lift your feet slightly off the ground.
    1. Keep your feet off the ground, and your torso reclined throughout this exercise.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Rotate your torso to one side through your trunk’s available range of motion as you direct your chest toward that side.
    1. You can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the center of your chest as you rotate that laser beam out to the side. This should result in your elbow (on the side to which you are twisting) moving behind your torso.
    2. Continue holding the weight to your chest throughout the set.
    3. During this exercise, people often tap the weight to the ground and focus on moving the weight rather than actually rotating their torsos. It is not inherently problematic to tap the ground with the weight, but this can prompt you to move your arms through shoulder motion rather than actually twisting your trunk (which is the function of your obliques). Keeping the weight close to your chest and emphasizing turning your chest can help reinforce the intended torso rotation.
    4. How far you can rotate will be influenced by your spinal mobility.
    5. Continue keeping your legs stationary throughout your set as you avoid letting your legs swing to the side.
2. Reverse the movement by rotating your torso back to the starting position.
3. Cyclically perform steps 1 and 2 as you alternate to which side you are rotating until you have completed your set.
    1. Strive to rotate fluidly from one side to the other rather than pausing once you have returned to the center position.
    2. Move in a controlled manner the entire time.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) while statically training your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your knees bent to about 90 degrees.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can lie down on an exercise mat.
2. With straight elbows, raise both arms straight up toward the ceiling as your elbows and wrists are vertically stacked above your shoulders.
    1. You can point your palms in toward each other.
3. While keeping your knees bent to about 90 degrees, march both legs up until your knees are vertically stacked above your hips.
    1. In this position, your thighs should be perpendicular to the ground, and your shins should be parallel to the ground.
4. Based on your preference, you can keep your head resting on the ground, or you can slightly tuck your chin toward your chest to lift your head just barely off the ground.
    1. Lifting your head slightly off the ground can mildly increase the difficulty and allow you to train your neck muscles statically, but doing so is optional. If you opt to lift your head just off the ground, keep in that position throughout your set. Otherwise, continue resting your head on the ground during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forceful slap.
2. Press your lower back lightly into the floor to flatten it, and continue doing so throughout your set.
    1. This can prompt you to feel your abs contract further as they keep the bottom of your ribs pulled down toward your hip bones.
    2. It is the opposite of if you were to arch your lower back, which would flare the bottom of your ribs away from your hip bones.
    3. If you are relaxed while lying down, your lower back naturally has a mild arch, allowing you to slide a hand between the ground and your lower back. When you use your abs to flatten your lower back, there should be no space between your lower back and the ground, preventing you from sliding a hand between them.
    4. Before performing the next step, you optionally can attempt to slide one hand between your lower back and the ground. Being unable to slide your hand under your lower back confirms that you have effectively flattened your lower back. If you choose to do so, lift your arm to the starting position before beginning the next step.
3. Sweep your right arm backward and downward while simultaneously straightening your left leg and lowering it toward the ground.
    1. As you lower your arm and leg, you will have to continue bracing your core to prevent your lower back from arching up off the ground.
    2. Strive to move your arm and leg at the same rate through the full range of motion that you can while keeping your lower back flat against the ground.
    3. With sufficient core control, you can finish with your arm and leg parallel to the ground as they are fully straightened. From this position, you can gently tap the ground with your hand and heel simultaneously. If your lower backs start arching before this point, shorten the range of motion to what you can perform while maintaining a flat lower back.
    4. All the movement should occur from your right shoulder, left hip, and left knee as your spine remains motionless.
    5. Move slowly and deliberately throughout your set, focusing on high-quality technique at every degree of motion.
    6. Keep your left arm and right leg completely stationary.
    7. So as long as you move an arm and leg on opposite sides of your body, you can choose which sides in which you will move to begin your set, but mentioning the sides as an example can help with technique clarity.
4. Reverse the movement by lifting your right arm and left leg up to return to the starting position.
    1. Since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the lowering phase, no motion should occur at your lower back as you continue bracing your core.
    2. While keeping your elbow straight, bend your left knee as you lift that thigh up to finish with your knee bent to approximately 90 degrees.
    3. At the top, both of your knees should be stacked vertically above your hips, and your arms should be vertically stacked above your shoulders.
5. Proceed to perform steps 2 and 3 with your left arm and right leg with the same technique you just utilized for your right arm and left leg.
6. Alternate between steps 3 and 5 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) to maintain a rigid back position as you refine your ability to move through your hips and shoulders with a stable trunk.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your knees bent to about 90 degrees and your head resting on the ground.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can lie down on an exercise mat.
2. While keeping your knees bent to about 90 degrees, march both legs up until your knees are vertically stacked above your hips.
    1. In this position, your thighs should be perpendicular to the ground, and your shins should be parallel to the ground.
3. Slide one hand under your lower back with your palm facing down. Place your other hand on your abdomen.
    1. Throughout this exercise, you can use your hands as cues to know if you are effectively bracing your core and stabilizing your trunk.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forceful slap.
    1. In this starting position, your lower back should be near a neutral position with the natural mild curvature you have when normally standing upright rather than being excessively arched or flattened.
    2. The degree to which the lower back is naturally arched will vary among different individuals. However, a normal arch should allow you to feel your lower back with your hand while your hand remains on the ground.
    3. You should feel your core muscles tense outward into the hand you are resting on your abdomen.
2. While keeping one leg stationary, slowly lower your other leg toward the ground while straightening its knee. Rigidly maintain the natural curvature of your lower back throughout the entire exercise.
    1. As you lower your leg, you will have to continue bracing your core to prevent your lower back from arching to a greater degree. Unintended arching would be demonstrated by your lower back lifting up off your hand, so you can focus on maintaining contact between your lower back and hand each rep.
    2. Lower your leg as far as you can without letting your lower back dynamically arch, and gently tap the ground with your heel at the bottom.
    3. The difficulty of the exercise will progressively increase as your knee becomes closer to the ground.
    4. With sufficient core control, you can finish with your leg parallel to the ground as your knee is fully straightened. If your lower back starts arching before this point, you can maintain a degree of knee bend that shortens the range of motion to what you can perform without letting your lower back arch further. The movement will be easier with a moderate knee bend than a mild knee bend, so you can determine how much you will straighten your knee based on your current ability.
    5. All the movement should occur from your hip and knee as your spine remains motionless.
    6. Move in a slow and controlled manner throughout your set as you focus on high-quality technique through every degree of motion.
3. Reverse the movement by marching up your leg to return to the starting position.
    1. Bend your knee as you lift that thigh up to finish with your knee bent to approximately 90 degrees.
    2. Since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the lowering phase, no motion should occur at your lower back as you continue bracing your core.
    3. At the top, both of your knees should be stacked vertically above your hips.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 as you switch which leg you move each rep.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) to maintain a rigid back position as you refine your ability to move through your hips and shoulders with a stable trunk.

## Setting up
1. Pick a weight plate of your desired load.
    1. A thick bumper plate or a weight plate with a minimally raised lip can be quality options for this exercise.
    2. A cast iron plate with a notable lip on one side is better suited to use for a dual plate pinch, since a notable lip can interfere with your ability to grasp the body with flat fingers.
2. Position the plate upright and together on the ground or a sturdy elevated object (e.g., plyometric box, flat bench, aerobic step on risers).
    1. If you are using a plate that has grip holes (cutouts that allow the rim of a plate to function as a handle), rotate the plate to have a portion of its solid body directed upward. For a pinch grip, you want to be able to grasp the solid body directly rather than having your fingers contact the grip holes.
    2. Placing it on an elevated surface can make it easier to pick the plate up with the pinch grip and set it down at the end of the set, but you can perform the same exercise from the ground.
3. While keeping the plate upright with one hand from the side, use your other hand to grasp the top body of the plate with flat fingers.
    1. Position your thumb against one side of the plate and your other four fingers against the other side.
    2. Your palm should be directed down toward the ground while your elbow is straight.
    3. Avoid grasping the plate with your fingertips bent around its outer lip, as you emphasize placing your fingers flat against the body of the plate.
4. Release your hand from the side while continuing to grip the plate with your top hand.
    1. You can now keep your free hand wherever you prefer, such as resting by your side.
## Exercise technique
1. Stand upright to lift the plate off the ground or an elevated object, and hold the plate with your working arm by your side.
    1. You can think about trying to crush the weight plate as you squeeze your thumb and your other four fingers in toward each other.
2. Continue firmly holding the plate while standing upright until you have completed your set’s target duration.
    1. This is a static exercise, so you will simply hold the plate without moving.
    2. Keep your fingers fully straightened against the body plate as you avoid letting them curl.
    3. If you notice that the plate begins sliding slightly, end your set and use your free hand to help you guide the plate down to the ground or an elevated surface. Be careful not to lose your grip and drop the plate, which can rapidly occur if the plate starts sliding.
3. Set the plate down and repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively strengthen your hand’s [intrinsic finger flexors](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md) while also training your forearm’s three [extrinsic finger flexors](../Muscles/Extrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d88050a550fbeff6041573.md).

3. Try to slide your hand (that is not on your abdomen) under your lower back to confirm that you have appropriately flattened your lower back.
    1. If you are relaxed while lying down, your lower back naturally has a mild arch that can allow you to slide a hand between the ground and your lower back. When you use your abs to flatten your lower back, there should no longer should be any space between your lower back and the ground, preventing you from being able to slide a hand between them.
    2. Throughout your set, you can keep your hand resting on the ground touching the side of your lower back. If your lower back starts arching, you will feel it lifting up with your hand.
4. While keeping one leg stationary, slowly lower your other leg toward the ground while straightening its knee. Rigidly maintain this flattened lower back position throughout the entire exercise.
    1. Continue bracing your core to prevent your lower back from arching up off the ground.
    2. Lower your leg as far as you can without letting your lower back dynamically arch, and gently tap the ground with your heel at the bottom.
    3. The difficulty of the exercise will progressively increase as your knee becomes closer to the ground.
    4. With sufficient core control, you can finish with your leg parallel to the ground as your knee is fully straightened. If your lower back starts arching before this point, you can maintain a degree of knee bend that shortens the range of motion to what you can perform while keeping your lower back flat. The movement will be easier with a moderate knee bend than a mild knee bend, so you can determine how much you will straighten your knee based on your current ability.
    5. All the movement should occur from your hip and knee as your spine remains motionless.
    6. Move in a slow and controlled manner throughout your set as you focus on high-quality technique through every degree of motion.
5. Reverse the movement by marching up your leg to return to the starting position.
    1. Bend your knee as you lift that thigh up to finish with your knee bent to approximately 90 degrees.
    2. Since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the lowering phase, no motion should occur at your lower back as you continue bracing your core.
    3. At the top, both of your knees should be stacked vertically above your hips.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 as you switch which leg you move each rep.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) to maintain a rigid back position as you refine your ability to move through your hips and shoulders with a stable trunk.
2785c6f170d880e2a185cdf3fda20df9:
## Setting up
1. Place a stability ball (which is also known as a Swiss ball or physio ball) on the ground.
    1. Ideally, select a ball with a diameter exceeding your shoulder width.
2. Kneel with the ball in front of you as your elbows are bent by approximately 90 degrees.
3. Hinge at your hips to lean your torso forward, and position your bent elbows on top of the ball about shoulder width apart.
    1. Lean forward enough so that your shoulders are directly above your elbows.
    2. With a sufficiently large ball, your forearms can rest on the ball with your elbows, but you will chiefly be bearing weight through your elbows.
    3. The appropriate elbow placement should ensure that the ball does not roll when you press down through your elbows.
    4. Once on the ball, you optionally can clench each hand into a fist to promote full-body tension.
## Exercise technique
1. Walk your legs back until your knees are fully straightened with the bottom of your toes dug into the ground.
    1. Position your feet approximately hip-width apart with your soles facing backward.
    2. You should be bearing your bodyweight into the ground through your feet and into the ball through your elbows.
2. Tighten your abs and squeeze your glutes to maintain a rigid back position while pushing your elbows into the ball and keeping your knees straight.
    1. Doing so keeps your hips up (but not excessively hiked) rather than letting them sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch in your lower back.
    2. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, as this can cause your shoulder blades to pinch together. Thinking about pushing your elbows down into the ball can help keep your shoulder blades apart.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
3. Statically hold the position you adopted after performing two until you have completed your set, then bend your knees to return to the ground.
    1. Strive to have your body look the same during the last second of your set as it did during the first second after getting into position.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your core muscles, including your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) (AKA the “six-pack muscle”) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.
2795c6f170d88003959bf668d235bb04:
## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, adjust each cable to be slightly above shoulder height.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, position the ends of its arms further apart than your wingspan. The proper setting should allow you to feel tension from the cables when your arms are fully outstretched to your sides.
    2. Dual cable stations that have their two weight stacks facing each other (often with a pull-up in between them) normally lack adjustable arms. If the two pulleys are not situated further apart than your wingspan, this specific exercise may not be feasible for you to perform with that equipment. If that applies to your dual cable station, you can select an alternative cable curl variation from this database, such as the [low pulley dual cable biceps curl](../Alternative%20Name(s)/High%20pulley%20dual%20cable%20biceps%20curl%202795c6f170d880c994f8ca0b62506f0b.md).
2. Connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.
3. While standing with the sides of your shoulders facing the two pulleys, reach out to your side and firmly grasp one of the handles with a straight elbow.
4. While keeping your elbow straight, walk over to grasp the handle from the other cable in the same manner.
    1. Allow the resistance from the first cable you grasped to keep your arm raised out to the side before doing the same with the other cable during the next step.
5. Step to the side to center yourself between the cables while standing upright in a near shoulder width stance.
    1. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from one pulley through your head to the other pulley.
    2. Your arms should be fully aligned with the cables, such that you can draw a straight line from each shoulder through your arm to the cable and then the pulley.
    3. You should currently feel tension from both cables with your elbows straightened. If you are fairly tall, you may have to transition to a half-kneeling position (like at the bottom of a lunge) as a modification to experience resistance through the full range of motion for this exercise.
6. Rotate your palms to point up toward the ceiling if they are not already facing this way.
    1. Your wrists should be mostly straight and remain mostly straight throughout the exercise.
7. Pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to curl the handles in toward your ears. Keep your upper arms stationary as they remain directed toward the pulleys.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully bent as your forearms are contacting your biceps or are close to doing so. Depending on the length of your forearms, you may not be able to fully bend your elbows if your hands are about to contact your head.
    2. At the end of this movement, you should look like you are flexing for a double biceps pose.
    3. While you move your forearms through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to straighten to move the handles outward in a controlled manner.
    1. Finish with your elbows fully straightened, like they were in the starting position.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cables abruptly yank the handles outward in an uncontrolled manner.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
27f5c6f170d880a59b85fcf9ca2a0a2d:
## Setting up
1. Fully lower the Smith machine’s safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails), and position the bar somewhat below knee height with the safety hooks resting on the safety bars.
    1. The proper starting height of the bar should comfortably allow you to get into the starting position. If the bar is too low, it can be difficult initially to move your hips under the bar with a bench behind you. If the bar is too high, you will be unable to lift your hips high enough to receive the bar initially without arching your back excessively.
2. Determine whether your Smith machine has angled or purely vertical sliding rails.
    1. If your machine has angled sliding rails, it will be ideal for you to position your bench (or other object during the next step) on the side that allows the bar to track slightly forward when lifting the bar up and slightly backward when lowering it. This means that the bottom of the rails should be horizontally closer to the bench than the top of the rails. However, the direction in which the rails angle can vary among different machines, and you may be restricted from setting up on a bench on the side of the machine’s frame. You can still hip thrust with the bar tracking backward during the lifting phase, but it may not feel as natural compared to if the bar tracks forward while lifting up.
    2. If your machine has angled sliding rails, it does not matter which side you face during this exercise.
3. Situate a flat exercise (or viable alternative) in front of the bar with the length of the bench parallel to the length of the bar.
    1. Position the bench at a distance from the bar that specifically enables you to rest your upper back comfortably on the edge of the bench while the bar is on the crease of your hips. Finding this position may require some trial and error, which is why it is recommended to perform a couple of hip thrust reps with the empty bar before you add weight plates.
    2. A specific hip thrust bench is ideal to use if you can move it, but it is not commonly available.
    3. If you use a mobile exercise bench, make sure that it will not slide back during the exercise. In contrast to a barbell hip thrust, it is not normally feasible to anchor a bench against a rack or wall when using an immobile Smith machine. However, you can place some heavy weight plates against the back of your bench if you are concerned it may slide back during your set. Note that certain benches may be more likely to slide than others.
    4. You may also be able to use a soft plyometric box near knee height that is anchored in the same manner as a flat bench.
    5. What ultimately matters is selecting an object that is sturdy, stable, and reasonably close to being knee height while being comfortable enough to support your upper back.
4. Optionally, obtain a pad (or an object that can function as a pad) that you will place between the bar and your hips.
    1. Using a pad is not required but strongly recommended because it can be very uncomfortable to have a barbell directly resting on your hip bones with a meaningful load.
    2. You can wrap a hip thrust pad or a squat pad around the middle of the bar.
    3. Alternatively, you can place a thick foam or folded exercise mat on the crease of your hip during the next step and subsequently keep it there to cushion your hip bones. Be aware that foam pads not specifically designed for hip thrusts may be somewhat damaged from this exercise.
5. Sit down on the ground with your upper back against the edge of the bench and your legs straight out in front of you under the bar.
    1. Specifically place the lower part of your shoulder blades against the edge of the bench. Feel free to adjust your upper back positioning mildly from this point based on what feels most stable to you.
    2. The middle of the bar should be aligned with the midline of your body.
6. Bring your heels toward your buttocks by bending your knees mildly greater than 90 degrees, with the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can situate your feet near shoulder width apart from each other, but it is up to your preference if you would like to position them somewhat closer together or wider apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can opt to point your toes forward or somewhat out to the sides.
    3. The optimal degree of knee bend should allow your feet to feel stable while being firmly planted on the ground throughout the set. It is normally appropriate to position your feet far enough back that your knees will be bent by approximately 90 degrees at the top of your hip thrust. From this placement, you can adjust specifically where you situate your feet based on your preference.
7. Grasp the bar with your palms facing down, and tuck your chin mildly toward your chest.
    1. So long as your hands are wider apart than your hips, you can adjust your grip width based on what feels stable and comfortable to you during this exercise.
    2. Continue holding the bar and keeping your chin mildly tucked throughout the exercise.
8. Using the form described in the exercise technique section, perform a couple of hip thrust reps with the empty bar to confirm that your bench placement lets the bar comfortably rest on the crease of your hips.
    1. If the bar is not positioned appropriately relative to your hips, adjust your bench placement prior to checking again until you have determined that you are set up correctly.
    2. Positioning the bar appropriately will help you avoid the excessive discomfort that may arise from positioning the bar too high (i.e., directly on your lower abdomen) or too low (i.e., directly on your groin).
    3. Some people may experience discomfort when the bar looks aligned with the crease of their hips if the bar is directly resting on the bony bumps on the front of their hip bones. If you notice that this occurs for you, you can move the bench slightly further back away from the bar to shift the pressure away from these bony bumps.
9. Load the bar with your intended weight, and assume the starting position by repeating steps 5-7.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
    2. From this starting position, your back should either be flat or exhibit its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
2. Lift your hips up until the bar is fully resting on the crease of your hips and the safety hooks are no longer resting on the safety bars.
    1. By keeping both feet on the ground, you can initially use your right and left glutes to unrack the weight.
3. Rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion.
4. Squeeze your glutes to continue lifting up until you can draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side.
    1. Since the bar begins from an elevated position, you may not have to lift your hips up much further from when you initially received the bar to reach this position.
5. Shift your weight into one foot on the ground, and lift the other foot off the ground. Keep one foot off the ground while hip thrusting with your other side.
    1. Based on your preference, you can lift your one leg up with a straight knee or a bent knee. Either position for the free leg is viable, but keeping the knee straight may make the exercise mildly more challenging compared to keeping it bent.
    2. So long as you lift the free leg high enough to keep its foot off the ground throughout the set, you can decide how high you lift it up.
    3. During the set, keep your right and left hip bones level with each other as you avoid letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg tilt down. You can imagine balancing a mug of water on the middle of your waist. If laser beams were shooting out from the center of your chest and your imaginary belt buckle, the two lasers should be parallel to each other throughout your set.
6. Lower your hips in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your machine permits.
    1. With most Smith machines, the depth to which you can lower your hips will be determined by when the bar reaches the bottom of the slide rails. These Smith machines reach their lowest position before the weight plates or your buttocks can contact the ground, resulting in a shorter range of motion than a barbell hip thrust. If you are using one of these machines, you can tap the bar lightly against the bottom of the machine.
    2. Certain Smith machines permit you to lower the bar through the same range as if you used a barbell. With one of these less common machines, you can finish the lowering phase when either the weight plates lightly contact the ground, or you have reached the end range your hip mobility comfortably permits.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid simply letting gravity pull the bar down abruptly, as opposed to you using your glutes to control the descent actively. Do not bounce the bar out of the bottom position.
7. Lift your hips up by driving your heel into the ground and squeezing your glute.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your working leg’s knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thigh and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glute.
    2. Focus on moving at your hip and avoid arching your lower back excessively. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glute engage during this exercise.
    4. Throughout the exercise, the sole of your working side’s foot should remain fully planted on the ground, and your upper back should remain firmly in contact with the bench.
    5. Continue holding the bar for stability, but avoid trying to lift the bar up or push it down with your hands.
8. Alternate between steps 6 and 7 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. For tracking purposes, each rep finishes after you have fully lifted your hips from the bottom position. The initial movement you performed during step 4 does not constitute a full rep.
9. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, return your previously elevated foot to the ground before shifting your weight into that side, lifting your opposite foot off the ground, and performing a set with your other side.
10. Once you have finished the lifting phase of your last rep, rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars, and lower your hips until the safety hooks are fully resting on the safety bars.
## Description
This exercise will predominantly develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) while also training your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) to a lesser degree.
2815c6f170d8802483f6dec09280d25f:
## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with straight legs and your feet are together.
2. Raise your arms straight back behind your head with straight elbows so that your arms are aligned with your legs and torso.
    1. Except for being rotated by 90 degrees, your body should be in the same position when you are standing upright and reaching your arms straight up overhead.
    2. Based on your preference, you can point your palms in toward each other or up away from the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground.
    1. Continue doing so throughout the entire set, which will become progressively more difficult with the completion of each step.
    2. Pressing your lower back into the ground will flatten it out from abdominal muscle contraction and prevent you from being able to slide a hand under your lower back.
2. Tuck your chin slightly in toward your collarbone to lift your head just off the ground.
    1. This tucking motion should look like you are giving yourself a “double chin.”
3. Lift your shoulder blades just off the ground through a slight crunching motion that also lifts your arm slightly off the ground.
    1. Lifting the shoulder blades off the ground should naturally lift the arms off the ground for most people. If you have particularly high shoulder flexibility and notice that your arms do not naturally lift off the ground, you can intentionally lift them up just off the ground during this step.
    2. This step should pull your ribs slightly down toward your hip bones and prompt you to feel additional tension in your abs.
4. While keeping your knees straight and feet together, lift your heels up off the ground.
    1. The difficulty of this exercise will be greatest when keeping your heels just off the ground, while lifting them up higher will make it easier. Consequently, you can scale the challenge of this exercise to your current ability based on how high you lift your legs up.
5. Statically hold the position you reached after performing steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Prioritize keeping your lower back pressed into the ground as you avoid letting your lower back arch.
    2. Continue maintaining your slight chin tuck as you keep your shoulder blades, arms, and heels off the ground.
    3. If you can no longer maintain any of the positions you assumed from each step, you have finished your set.
    4. Once you understand the proper positioning that each step achieves, you can perform steps 1-4 simultaneously rather than as discrete steps, but it can be easier to learn this exercise when thinking about one step at a time.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) (the “six pack muscle”) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and hip flexors.
2815c6f170d88084baa6d985c5689827:
## Setting up
1. Adjust a pair of securely anchored gymnastic rings to be fairly close to shoulder-width apart and elevated above your head.
    1. Ideally, the rings should be reasonably close to the height of your palms when standing upright with your arms raised straight up overhead. However, a lower height can be appropriate as long as you can hang on the rings without your legs touching the ground when your knees are bent.
    2. You may also use rings beyond your reach if you initially place a sturdy box, an aerobic step, or a bumper plate on the ground as a step to reach the rings. While not required, elevating yourself to reach high rings may help you set up with a more stable hand position compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the rings.
    3. If the rings have not been previously anchored, you will naturally have to anchor them to a sturdy structure that is able to support your bodyweight. Potential anchor points include the top of a power rack, a pull-up bar, a monkey rig, and a ceiling-mounted anchor that is designed for rings or suspension trainers.
    4. While positioning the rings at shoulder width is appropriate, you can adjust the distance between them to your preference.
2. Stand under the rings, reach up overhead, and firmly grasp them with your palms facing in toward each other (i.e., a neutral grip)
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the rings with the rings pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the rings closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the rings can slide up your hands while hanging on them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
3. Lift your feet off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the rings with straight elbows.
    1. You only need to bend your knees as much as is required to keep your feet above the ground.
    2. If you initially used a step to reach the rings and the step is positioned somewhat behind the rings, you may be able to keep your knees straight while keeping your feet off the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the rings with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will put you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to shrug up from the force of your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back puts you in a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the rings by driving your elbows down and toward your sides as you progressively bend them. Allow your palms to rotate naturally backward in a manner that feels comfortable to you.
    1. People commonly perform this exercise by progressively turning their palms backward until they are facing fully backward at the top, but you can decide specifically how much you rotate your palms based on what feels best to you.
    2. Since the rings are anchored, your elbows will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    3. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms close to the sides of the torso and elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, individuals may have different ranges of motion that their bodies allow.
    4. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree).
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. Allow your palms to rotate in toward each other as you descend.
    2. You do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than just letting gravity pull you down abruptly.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to return your feet to the ground.
## Description
This exercise can train your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) especially well while also effectively training [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
2835c6f170d88068b256c47ea3cc7c8e:
## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s mobile chest pad to a setting that will situate it directly in front of your torso once you are seated with your lower back comfortably arched.
    1. The chest pad can commonly be moved forward or backward along an arc that affects the degree to which your lower back can be arched at the start of each rep.
    2. As the pad is set further back, a greater degree of lower back arching will be required to assume the starting position, which allows you to train your abs in a more lengthened position that may be conducive to training them effectively.
    3. The degree to which you can comfortably arch your lower back can be affected by your mobility, and you should not position the pad further back than you can reach during the exercise without lower back discomfort.
    4. Some trial and error may be required to find the chest pad setting that is best suited for you.
2. Adjust the seat to a height that will situate the chest pad at chest height once you are seated.
    1. The seat should neither be too high that the chest pad contacts your abdomen nor too low that the chest pad contacts your throat.
3. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
4. Sit on the seat with the back of your hip bones snugly against the hip pad as your lower back is comfortably arched.
    1. If you feel that you can comfortably lean back further by arching your lower back, you can set the chest pad further back.
5. If your machine has foot pegs that can help anchor your feet, hook your feet securely under them. If your machine lacks foot pegs, place your feet on the ground or on the foot plate (if your machine has a foot plate).
    1. Some machines allow you to adjust the foot pegs or foot plates to what feels most stable and comfortable to you.
    2. Keep your feet planted in a stationary position throughout your set.
6. Securely fasten the seat belt around your waist if your machine has a belt.
7. Position your arms in a manner that will allow you to keep the chest pad securely against your chest during the exercise.
    1. Precisely how you should position your arms will be dependent on the specific machine model you are using.
    2. Some machines have handles to hold with your hands.
    3. Certain machines have a cylindrical chest pad underneath which you can hook your arms, while others have a rectangular pad on top of which you can rest your upper arms with your hands crossed and resting on your shoulders.
    4. In the starting position, your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Maintain this neck position during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl your spine as you pull the bottom of your ribs toward the tops of your hip bones in a controlled manner.
    1. Once you feel that you can no longer curl your spine through a range permitted by the machine that feels comfortable to your back, you have reached your end range. The machine may physically restrict your range of motion at a certain point, even if you have the mobility to crunch further.
    2. Avoid pulling down with your arms. Your arms should only move indirectly because they are attached to your torso, which is what you are directly moving. The function of your arms is merely to help keep the chest pad stabilized against your chest. You should not feel your back muscles contract like they would during a pulling exercise (such as a lat pulldown). If you feel like your back muscles are driving the movement, you can try relaxing your arms to the minimum required to keep the chest pad against your chest.
    3. To train your abs dynamically, you should be intentionally rounding your entire back, since this motion is performed by contraction of your abs. When rounding your back appropriately, you should feel meaningful tension in your abs. If you do not feel your abs engaging, you may be substituting hip or shoulder motion for the intended spinal motion.
    4. If you finish the movement with your back fairly flat as opposed to rounded, you most likely are primarily bending at your hips rather than curling your spine.
    5. It can help to think about crunching your elbows toward your knees.
    6. You can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the middle of your chest, and you are trying to point that closer toward the middle point between your knees.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner as you uncurl your back by flaring your ribs up and away from your hip bones.
    1. Move through the full range of motion permitted by the machine that feels comfortable to your lower back. This may involve allowing the weights you selected to tap the rest of the stack lightly at the end of this movement if the full range that the machine allows feels comfortable to you.
    2. When uncurling your spine, your lower back will initially move into a flat position before moving into an arched position.
    3. Depending on your mobility and the range of motion your machine permits, you may feel a stretching sensation in your abs as you allow your lower back to arch.
    4. The imaginary laser beam shooting out from your chest should angle progressively higher up as you uncurl your back and flare your ribs away from your hip bones.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you feel lower back discomfort at the end of either step, you can abbreviate the range of motion to what feels best to you. Performing this exercise through a full range of motion is by no means inherently injurious to the lower back, but certain individuals with pre-existing conditions may experience discomfort in rather rounded or rather arched positions.
## Description

## Setting up

    1. Situate your knees near the front of the pad to allow your shins to rest on the pad for stability.
    2. You should be in a tall kneeling position with your chest up and your hips fairly close to being vertically above your knees, as opposed to sitting your buttocks onto your heels with your knees fully bent.
    3. Your neck and back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. This should result in your lower back having its natural curvature rather than being excessively arched or rounded.
4. While keeping your chest pointing straight forward, twist your torso to swivel the pad toward one side.
    1. Swivel the pad away from the side that you wish to predominantly train first. For instance, if you swivel the pad to the right by twisting your lower torso to the right, you will be in a position to train your left obliques predominantly.
    2. If laser beams were shooting out from your chest and the middle of your waist, where you would wear a belt buckle, those laser beams should now be angled in different directions.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping the pad swiveled to the side, drive your knees up across your body through the range of motion your mobility allows.
    1. On the side that you are primarily training, you can think about crunching your hip bone diagonally up toward your ribs, which is a primary function of your obliques. For instance, if you swiveled the pad to the right, you can strive to pull your left hip bone up toward your left ribs. Once you can no longer bring this hip bone closer toward these ribs, you have reached the end of the lifting phase.
    2. When keeping the pad rotated and your knees snugly on top of it, driving your knees up toward your elbows should naturally prompt you to feel meaningful tension in your working obliques (situated on the side of your abdomen).
    3. This exercise essentially trains a hybrid of a crunching motion with a side bending motion.
    4. Keep your chest and arms stationary throughout the exercise as you avoid pulling through your arms or moving your upper body.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering your knees until they are close to being under your hips.
    1. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should avoid letting gravity rapidly swing you down.
    2. With an appropriately controlled descent, your knees should not rock back behind the point at which they are directly under your hips.
    3. As you lower your knees, your working side’s hip bone will naturally move away from your ribs.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to swivel the pad to the opposite side and repeat the exercise.

## Setting up
1. Position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground, as your elbows are straight and your knees are bent.
    1. Your upper arms should be directed straight down under your shoulders such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    2. You can spread your fingers apart for stability. Depending upon which hand position feels most comfortable, you can point your middle fingers straight ahead or mildly out to the sides.
## Exercise technique
1. While bearing weight through your arms, straighten one knee to move your foot behind you and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. You should now look like you are at the top of a push-up.
2. Tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes to flatten your lower back.
    1. From this tall plank position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    2. Contracting your abs and glutes appropriately will prevent your hips from sagging down, which would prompt your lower back to arch rather than remain flat.
    3. During the entire set, do not allow your chest to sag down, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together. If you notice your chest starting to sag, push down into the ground more forcefully through your straight arms to spread your shoulder blades apart.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position as you would normally do when standing upright.
3. Explosively march one knee forward and up toward your chest while maintaining the same stable trunk position you assumed during step 2.
    1. How far you can march your knee forward will be influenced by your hip mobility.
4. Reverse the movement by quickly driving your knee (that you just marched) backward and straightening it. Simultaneously march your other knee explosively forward.
    1. Start marching one leg forward at the same time as you begin driving the other leg backward, which will result in both feet being off the ground for a brief moment until your foot moving backward reaches the ground.
    2. Move each leg reciprocally at the same speed as if you were running. This should result in one leg reaching its fully marched position at the same moment that the other leg’s foot contacts the ground.
    3. While you are moving your legs explosively through motion at your hip and knee joints, strive to keep the rest of your body stationary. Your trunk and hip bones should remain stable in a rigid position with your shoulders stacked over your wrists throughout the set. Moving your legs quickly is not an excuse to let your form become sloppy.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hip bones hike up, sag down, or tilt to either side.
    5. Also avoid letting your arms rock back and forth.
5. Cyclically repeat step 4 while switching which leg you march up and which leg you drive back each time until you have completed your set.
    1. Minimize how long either foot remains on the ground by rapidly marching your leg up immediately after its foot reaches the ground.
    2. Due to the speed of each rep, people commonly track set duration for this variation rather than the total number of reps.
    3. After finishing your last rep, return both feet to the ground before bending your knees and standing up.

## Setting up
1. Add a pair of round weight plates to a barbell situated on the ground with sufficient room in front of the bar for you to roll out.
    1. If you roll out through the full range of motion, using small-diameter weight plates can make this exercise slightly more difficult than using large-diameter plates.
    2. If you stop rolling out before your arms are fully outstretched, the plate diameter is inconsequential.
    3. Your bodyweight will primarily provide the resistance for this exercise, so the weight of the plates you select is not particularly impactful.
    4. Hexagonal weight plates cannot be used for this exercise.
2. Optionally place a comfortable surface (e.g., an exercise mat, foam cushion, pillow, or folded towel) slightly behind the middle of the bar.
3. Kneel behind the bar as your body is completely centered with the bar and your knees are approximately hip-width apart.
4. With your elbows and wrists straightened, firmly grasp the bar with your hands at least slightly outside shoulder width.
    1. Use an overhand grip with your palms facing back toward you.
    2. So long as it is at least slightly outside shoulder width, you decide specifically how wide a grip you will use.
    3. Keep your wrists and elbows straight throughout this exercise.
5. With your hips stacked vertically above your knees, position the bar directly under your shoulders.
    1. Your thighs and arms should now be directed straight down, such that they are perpendicular to the ground, which places your torso closer to a horizontal position than a vertical position.
    2. Your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Maintain this neck position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Scoop your hip bones forward toward your ribs, while keeping your ribs pulled down toward your hip bones and tightening your abs. Maintain this position throughout your set.
    1. When starting with your lower back in its natural mild arch, this motion (known as posterior pelvic tilting) will flatten your lower back, since it is the opposite of arching it.
    2. Your abs attach to your pubic bone (which you can feel as a bony ridge in the middle of your pubic region) and your ribs, and this scooping motion should tilt your pubic bone up toward your ribs as you contract your abs.
    3. It can help to imagine that a laser beam is shooting out for the midpoint between your hip bones, slightly below where you would wear a belt buckle. Before you scoop your hips, this laser beam will point down toward your abdomen. Scooping your hips appropriately should angle this laser beam forward toward the bar.
2. Lower your hips forward until you can draw a straight line from your thighs through your hips to your lower back when viewed from the side. Keep the bar under your shoulders and your lower back flat.
    1. This lower-body motion will push the bar moderately forward, but you are not moving your shoulders during this step. Your arms move forward simply because they are connected to the rest of your body.
    2. Your thighs, torso, and arms should now resemble a tall plank position.
    3. Avoid lowering your hips so far forward that your lower back begins arching. Your lower back position should not change from the last step.
3. Squeeze your glutes, and keep them squeezed for the rest of your set.
    1. Actively squeezing your glutes can help you avoid arching your lower back.
    2. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them.
4. Slowly push the bar forward by sweeping your arms forward. Keep your torso rigidly braced as you avoid letting your lower back arch throughout the set.
    1. Only move the bar as far forward as you can while maintaining a flat lower back position.
    2. Keeping your lower back flat will become progressively more difficult as you roll out further, so you can determine your range of motion based on your current ability.
    3. If you are new to this exercise, a rather short range may be appropriate. If you have the strength to do so with proper form, you can finish rolling out when your chest is almost touching the ground.
    4. Keep your elbows fully straightened.
    5. While you push the bar forward through shoulder motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    6. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag or your ribs flare, as this can arch your lower back. Continuing to squeeze your glutes and tighten your abs will help you keep your lower back flat.
5. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by pulling the bar back toward the starting position. Drive your arms back until they are once again under your shoulders without moving your hips.
    1. In contrast to the traditional rollout technique, you will not bend your hips or move them back during each rep with this variation.
    2. Your arms should now be pointing straight down toward the ground.
    3. Continue keeping your lower back in the same flat position you maintained while rolling out.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set and are ready to move your hips back before standing up.
