## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat to a height that allows your lower back to be aligned with the machine’s pivot point once you are seated.
    1. The proper alignment should place the top of your hip bones slightly above the pivot point when you are seated.
2. Initially position the roller pad far enough back that you can comfortably sit on the seat.
3. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
4. Sit down on the seat with your lower back aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
    1. If your machine has a lower back pad, position the back of your hip bones snugly against it, which should result in you being appropriately aligned.
5. Place your feet on the foot bar under the foot rollers (if present), and adjust the foot bar to a comfortable setting if it is adjustable on your machine.
    1. The ideal foot bar position should allow your feet to feel stable while your hip bones are well-supported by the lower back pad. The optimal foot bar position should also readily enable you to perform this exercise through spinal motion while limiting hip motion.
    2. Some people may find it easier to emphasize training the back muscles through spinal motion when setting the foot bar far enough back to allow their knees to be bent by about 90 degrees or somewhat greater. However, you may still be able to perform this exercise when setting the foot bar further in front to a position that allows your knees to be mildly bent. A range of foot bar positions can be viable, so you can feel free to try out different positions over time to determine where you personally feel best if you can utilize different settings with your machine.
6. Round your lower and middle back through the full range of motion that is comfortable for you. Set the roller pad so that it contacts your upper back in this rounded position, or is as close to doing so as your machine permits.
    1. You may notice that setting the roller pad as far forward as you can results in the pad not contacting your back when you have rounded your back through your full comfortable range. If this occurs with your machine, you will have to start each rep from a less rounded back position in order to reach the pad.
    2. As you move the roller pad further forward, you will be able to achieve a greater degree of back rounding in the starting position, which allows you to train your back muscles in a more lengthened position that may be conducive to developing them effectively.
    3. Your mobility can affect the degree to which you can comfortably round your back and, consequently, which roller pad starting position is ideal for you.
    4. Throughout this exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Uncurl your back by flaring your ribs up and away from your hip bones through a comfortable range of motion. Avoid leaning your torso backward primarily through hip motion as you emphasize moving the roller pad backward through spinal motion.
    1. If you just focus on driving the roller pad backward rather than on how you move it, you most likely will be meaningfully using your hip muscles to lift the weight rather than using your back muscles in a more targeted manner. Regardless of your intent, the hip muscles (like your glutes) will inevitably be engaged to at least some degree, since a normal rhythm exists between hip and spinal motions, and the machine does not fully stabilize the hips. However, you should strive to move predominantly at your spine while minimizing hip motion to the best of your ability when you are striving to target your back muscles.
    2. When uncurling your spine, your lower back will initially move into a flat position before moving into an arched position.
    3. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable to you as an individual, you can finish the lifting phase once your lower back is close to having the mild curvature it naturally has when sitting upright, or you can finish with a greater degree of lower back arching. What chiefly matters is moving through a range that does not prompt you to feel lower back discomfort.
    4. When you are appropriately moving your spine, you should feel tension in the lower back muscles running along each side of your spine. Thinking about flaring your ribs up and away from your hip bones can help cue you to move at your spine rather than your hips.
    5. Both during this lifting phase and the subsequent lowering phase, it is recommended to move in a slow and controlled manner while prioritizing technique quality.
    6. Avoid sliding your buttocks as you keep them planted on the seat, in addition to keeping your feet on the foot bar throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by rounding your back through the full range of motion that is comfortable to you to bring the roller pad forward.
    1. Continue emphasizing spinal motion while minimizing hip motion. If you finish the movement with your lower back flat or arched as opposed to rounded, you most likely are primarily bending at your hips rather than rounding your spine.
    2. It can help to think about crunching your ribs down toward your hip bones as you move into a slouched position with your chest angled closer toward your knees.
    3. If you initially positioned the roller pad to the appropriate setting, you should return to the starting position, where you can gently tap the machine’s lever arm (onto which you loaded weight plates) against the stopper underneath it to confirm you have moved through your full range of motion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you feel lower back discomfort at the end of either step, you can abbreviate the range of motion to what feels best to you. Performing this exercise through a full range of motion is by no means inherently injurious to the lower back, but certain individuals with pre-existing conditions may experience discomfort in rather rounded or rather arched positions.
    2. If you experience lower back discomfort specifically at the end of step 2, you can pause your set and adjust the starting position of the roller pad to be further back to limit you from training beyond your comfortable range of motion.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) in your lower and middle back.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that will situate the chest pad to chest height once you are seated.
    1. You will have to sit down to check if you selected the appropriate seat height, so you may have to adjust the seat height multiple times before finding the right setting for you.
2. Rotate the seat toward one direction. Select a setting that allows you to perform this exercise through the full range of motion that is comfortable to you.
    1. If you have normal back mobility and a healthy back, you can initially rotate it fully to one side. If you cannot comfortably assume the starting position from this setting, you can rotate the pad closer toward the center (where your imaginary belt buckle and chest are both facing forward) until you can set up comfortably.
    2. As you rotate the pad further away from the centered position, you will be able to train your core muscles in more lengthened positions that may be conducive to developing them effectively.
    3. It is up to you whether you begin with the pad rotated to your right or left, since you will adjust it to the opposite side after your first set to train both sides equally.
    4. Your optimal setting will be affected by your back mobility, and finding this ideal setting may require some trial and error.
3. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
4. Sit on the seat with an upright torso as your knees contact the knee pads and your feet rest on the foot plates.
    1. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
5. Rotate your chest toward the chest pad and snugly contact the pad with your chest while firmly gripping the handles.
    1. In the starting position, it is common to feel a stretching sensation in your back when the machine is adjusted to train through your full range of motion. However, you should not feel lower back discomfort in this position, so you should adjust the degree to which the seat is rotated if you experience discomfort when moving into the starting position. If you cannot rotate your chest enough to reach the chest pad, you naturally should adjust the seat as well until you can reach it.
## Exercise technique
1. Rotate your imaginary belt buckle in a controlled manner away from the side it initially faces. Move through the full range of motion your mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Throughout the set, continue keeping your chest snugly against the chest pad, buttocks on the seat, knees against the knee pads, and feet on the foot plates.
    2. Your legs should only turn because you are rotating your torso, and your legs are connected to your torso.
    3. Focusing on turning your imaginary belt buckle can help cue the rotational trunk motion that your core muscles perform.
    4. During the first half of the movement, you will rotate your imaginary belt buckle so that it faces straight forward with your chest. Then you will continue rotating to have your imaginary belt buckle face the opposite direction from which it started.
2. Reverse the movement as you rotate your imaginary belt buckle in the opposite direction to return to the starting position.
    1. While you do not need to utilize an extremely slow tempo, you should actively control the entire movement rather than letting the machine’s resistance abruptly twist you back into the starting position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with the seat rotated toward the opposite side from which you started.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and your small [rotatores muscles](../Muscles/Rotatores%20Muscles%201b95c6f170d8800188c7db2ca87b8b54.md) through a long range of motion.

    2. Continue holding the handles for stability, but do not actively try to push or pull the machine with your arms. The function of your arms is merely to help transmit force from your core muscles into the machine.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the rack’s J-hooks to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on top of them.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
    3. If you need to bend your knees and hips beyond a mild degree (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) initially to place the bar on your back, you positioned the J-hooks excessively low. This can make it more challenging to rerack the bar at the end of your set.
2. Face the center of the bar in approximately a shoulder-width stance.
3. Based on your preference, set up with a [full hand clean grip](Full%20hand%20clean%20grip%20front%20squat%201a25c6f170d880068daae293704193e0.md), [fingertip clean grip](Fingertip%20clean%20grip%20front%20squat%202165c6f170d880048694f9a5579ba6ab.md), [cross arm grip](Cross-arm%20grip%20front%20squat%201a25c6f170d88038b559cf1d5dbd8366.md), or [straps](Strap%20front%20squat%202165c6f170d88086b1b2c72025f4a497.md).
4. While simultaneously bending your elbows, shallowly bend at your knees and hips with an upright torso to walk under the bar and situate it on the front of your shoulders just in front of the base of your neck.
    1. The bar should be resting on your front delts (which are the muscles on the front of your shoulders that attach to the outer aspects of your collarbones) and the outer portions of your collarbones, which together form a shelf with the base of your neck to cradle the bar.
    2. While the bar should be directly in front of your neck, it should not be pressing into your neck to the extent that it feels like it is choking you.
    3. If you are not accustomed to front squats, it is normal to experience discomfort from the pressure the bar places on the front of your shoulders (which may cause some skin bruising), but it should not be painful with proper bar placement.
5. With the bar now on the front of your shoulders, lift your elbows up until your upper arms are parallel to the ground.
    1. You can perform steps 4 and 5 simultaneously with each other.
    2. The bony prominence on the back of each elbow should now be pointing straight forward.
    3. Your hands can assist in keeping the bar balanced, but the bar should first and foremost be resting on the front of your shoulders without necessarily needing your hands to hold it there.
6. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of front squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
7. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends when front squatting.
8. Repeat steps 2-5 of the setup before proceeding to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your upper arms parallel to the ground, stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the bar resting on your shoulders throughout the set.
2. Take a couple of steps back, and position your feet near shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing slightly out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip-width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside shoulder width and their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
    4. Throughout your set, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest and elbows up.
    1. Throughout the set, avoid dropping your elbows or letting your chest cave down.
    2. As you descend, it is natural for your torso to lean forward mildly at your hips to maintain your balance, but maintain a mostly upright torso position with your lower back flat.
    3. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    5. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your lower back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your lower back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
6. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
7. Alternate between steps 4-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
8. Walk forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the torso pad to a height that allows you to rest your torso comfortably on it while resting your forearms on the forearm pads and holding the handles.
    1. The appropriate setting should allow you to feel stable and well-supported during the exercise while distributing the pressure from your bodyweight comfortably throughout the forearms pads, torso pad, and knee pad.
    2. If the torso pad is too high, you may be unable to rest your forearms fully on the forearm pads without rounding your shoulders or back excessively forward. Without the ability to support a meaningful portion of your bodyweight through your forearms, you may feel that the torso pad applies excessive pressure through your abdomen or chest (depending on whether your machine has an abdomen or chest pad).
    3. If the torso pad is too low, it may not be able to support your torso unless you excessively arch your lower back, which could prompt you to feel less stable during the exercise.
    4. Some trial and error may be required to find the pad height that feels best to your body.
2. Set the knee pad to the side you intend to train during this set if it is adjustable.
3. Initially position the lever arm (to which the foot bar is attached) to the furthest forward setting if it is adjustable.
    1. If you cannot comfortably reach the foot bar when continuing to set up or notice that you have to round your back in order to reach the foot bar, you can move the lever arm further backward until you can comfortably reach the foot bar without rounding your back.
    2. Compared to setting it further backward, setting the lever arm further forward permits you to train through a longer range of motion that may amplify the muscle growth stimulus and increase your strength through a greater range of motion. Consequently, it is sensible to start with the furthest forward setting and adjust from there if warranted.
4. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
5. Kneel on the knee pad with the side you will not train during this set, and lean forward to rest your torso on the torso pad, rest your forearms on the forearm pads, and grasp the handles.
    1. With the proper set-up, your lower back should be near a neutral position (like when you are normally standing upright) rather than being excessively arched or rounded.
6. On the side you intend to train, bend your knee to lift your foot off the ground, and position its sole firmly against the foot bar or foot plate (depending on what your machine has).
    1. If your machine has a short foot bar (that is not tall enough for your entire sole to contact), position the back half of your sole against the foot bar. Based on your preference and what feels stable to you, you can contact the foot bar with your heel or a little closer to your midfoot. The appropriate foot position should ensure that your foot does not slide during the exercise while also helping you to feel meaningful tension in your glute.
    2. If your machine has a tall foot plate, place the entirety of your sole against it. Certain machines may also have a foot roller that can help secure the top part of your foot (where your shoelaces are) while the bottom of your foot contacts the foot plate.
    3. When viewed from the front, your foot should be aligned with your knee rather than being positioned to either the right or left side of your knee.
    4. Keep the knee of your non-working leg firmly planted on the knee pad from this point onward.
    5. All the subsequent directions will apply to your working leg.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your knee backward in an arcing manner to push your heel and the foot bar/plate backward through the full range of motion that your hip mobility permits.
    1. While focusing on moving your knee backward through hip motion, allow your knee to move naturally with respect to straightening or remaining bent. Depending on the specific machine you are using, your knee may naturally straighten, or it may continue to be fairly bent throughout the exercise.
    2. Strive to have all the movement come from your working leg while keeping the rest of your body stationary.
    3. During the entire set, keep your torso snugly against the torso pad and your imaginary belt buckle pointing in the same direction as it was in the starting position.
    4. Particularly avoid excessively arching your lower back or turning your imaginary belt buckle to the side, both of which are common technique errors that can occur when striving to push the foot bar/plate further backward than what your hip mobility permits.
    5. At the end range, you should feel your glute contract. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glute engage during this exercise and help cue the intended hip motion.
    6. If you are using a machine with a foot plate (rather than a foot bar), think about pushing through your heel instead of your toes to help cue the intended glute engagement.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your knee to arc forward while naturally bending.
    1. Avoid letting the weight rapidly swing your knee forward in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. You should finish in the starting position with your knee positioned as far forward as the machine permits while keeping your foot on the foot bar/plate.
    3. To confirm you have moved through your full range of motion, you can lightly tap the lever arm (onto which you loaded weight plates) to the stopper underneath it without allowing the lever arm to rest on the stopper.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise will chiefly train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), which may be assisted by your [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md) and [piriformis](../Muscles/Piriformis%201925c6f170d88068a670ce338a8215cf.md) to a lesser degree.

    1. If you cannot comfortably reach the foot bar when continuing to set up or notice that you have to round your back in order to reach the foot bar, you can move the lever arm further backward until you can comfortably reach the foot bar without rounding your back.

Compared to setting it further backward, setting the lever arm further forward permits you to train through a longer range of motion that may amplify the muscle growth stimulus and increase your strength through a greater range of motion. The appropriate foot position should ensure that your foot does not slide during the exercise while also helping you to feel meaningful tension in your glute.

    2. The proper position should feel comfortable and stable to you throughout the exercise.

    1. For this variation, you can effectively use an overhand grip (with handles directed out to the sides), a neutral grip (with the parallel handles), or a semi-neutral grip (with handles angled diagonally outward and backward).

## Exercise technique
1. Lift the bar up off the machine’s stopper in a short rowing motion by driving your elbows mildly backward while bending them.
2. Center the bar so that it no longer lies above the stopper, and lower it until your elbows are straight.
    1. In this bottom position, allow the weight to pull your shoulder blades fully apart from one another.
3. Pull your shoulder blades backward and in toward each other to lift the bar upward while keeping your elbows straight and your chest in contact with the pad.
    1. Pull your shoulder blades as far back as you can, which should result in you feeling your upper back muscles contracting.
    2. As a cue, you can imagine pinching a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    3. Like when performing a standard shrugging exercise, the bar will only move a short distance during this variation, since you are isolating motion of your shoulder blades without moving your arms directly.

    1. Continue keeping your elbows straightened and chest snugly in contact with the pad.
    2. At the end of this motion, your shoulder girdles should resemble a slouched posture as they are pulled forward beyond their normal resting position, which often produces a stretching sensation in your upper back muscles.

## Setting up
1. Add your desired load (in the form of weight plates or a kettlebell) to a pull-up/dip belt you have around your waist, and stand upright under a pull-up bar with parallel handles.
    1. The back of your belt should be securely resting on top of your buttocks, and the belt’s chain or strap (depending on the belt model) should be looped through the center hole of a weight plate or under the handle of a kettlebell. If you have a loading pin for your belt, you can alternatively loop the chain or strap through it after adding weight plates.
    2. It will be easiest if you carry the weight over to the pull-up bar and add the weight to your belt while you are under the bar, rather than adding the weight to your belt farther away from the bar before walking over to the bar.
    3. As an alternative to using a pull-up/dip belt, you can wear a weighted vest.
    4. While less stable and more awkward than using a belt or weighted vest, you also have the option of holding a dumbbell between your thighs or feet, but you will be limited in how much weight you can add when using a dumbbell.
2. Reach up overhead and firmly grasp the bar’s parallel handles with your palms facing in toward each other (i.e., a neutral grip).
    1. If your bar has greater than two parallel handles, grasp the two that situate your hands near your shoulders apart.
    2. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    3. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up onto a sturdy box, an aerobic step, or a bumper plate to place the bar within reach.
    4. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar compared to if you jumped up from the ground to reach the bar.
    5. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    6. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
3. Lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar with straight elbows.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will put you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up by your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back puts you in a “proud chest” posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending them.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows will not actually drive downward, but having this intent helps pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. It is up to your preference whether you would like to keep your thighs directed vertically downward (resulting in a similar hip position as when you stand) or whether you like to lift your knees moderately up (resulting in a more flexed hip position, like when you are seated, but to a lesser degree). Regardless, avoid swinging your legs during the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Move the back pad forward or backward to a setting that allows you to rest your upper back comfortably on it while your hips are aligned with the hip belt/pad and your feet are on the foot plate with your knees bent by at least 90 degrees.
    1. Depending on your machine model, you may be able to move the entire carriage, the upper back pad itself, or neither of them.
2. Adjust the seat to a height that can result in your thighs and torso forming reasonably close to a 90-degree angle (when viewed from the side) when you are in the starting position.
    1. Aiming to achieve near this 90-degree angle is an appropriate starting point for most people, but the ideal seat height specifically should allow you to set up with your lower back in a flat position while training through a meaningful range of motion.
    2. An excessively low seat can require you to round your lower back to move into the starting position.
    3. An excessively high seat can limit the degree to which your hips are initially bent and restrict the range of motion for this exercise.
    4. The seat height that is personally best for you can be affected by your stature and your hip mobility.
3. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
4. Lie down with your upper back on the back pad, hips aligned with the hip belt/pad, and the soles of your feet fully on the foot plate, with your knees bent at greater than 90-degree angles.
    1. If your machine has a fairly short upper back pad, you can place the lower part of your shoulder blades against the front of the pad. If your machine has a long back pad, you may be able to rest your middle and upper back against it.
    2. In addition to moving the back pad forward or backward, you can move your feet further forward or backward on the foot plate to modify the degree to which your knees are bent.
    3. The degree to which your knees are bent will decrease as you thrust your hips up during a rep, so initially setting up with a little over 90 degrees of knee bend can help you achieve about 90 degrees of knee bend at the top of the rep.
5. Situate your feet near shoulder width apart with your toes pointing straight ahead or mildly out to the sides, depending on what is most comfortable.
    1. A near shoulder-width stance is appropriate for most people, but feel free to adjust your stance based on what feels best to you, since what specifically is the most comfortable stance width can vary among different individuals, just like the most comfortable degree of toe flare.
6. Depending on what your machine has, snugly fasten the hip belt around the crease of your hips, or set the hip pad snugly on top of the crease of your hips.
    1. If you feel notable discomfort from the pressure of the belt/pad during your set, you can try shifting your hips slightly further forward or backward to adjust where the pressure is concentrated. When making any adjustments during a set, only do so in between reps when the machine’s lever arms (onto which you loaded plates) are resting on the stoppers underneath them.
    2. If you continue to feel discomfort from the pressure of the belt/pad, you can try cushioning your hip bones by placing a folded exercise mat or thick foam between your hips and the belt/pad.
7. Tuck your chin mildly toward your chest, and maintain this neck position throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
    2. From this starting position, your back should be flat.
2. Lift your hips up by driving your heels into the foot plate and squeezing your glutes.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thighs and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glutes.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glutes engage during this exercise.
    4. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to crush a walnut between them or tightly holding onto a million-dollar check with your glutes.
    5. Throughout the exercise, keep your upper back snugly in contact with the back pad and the soles of your feet fully planted on the foot plate while concentrating pressure through your heels.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering your hips through the full range of motion in which you can keep your lower back flat.
    1. If you were able to position the seat to a height that allowed you to assume the starting position with a flat lower back, you can lower your hips until you are able to tap the seat gently with your buttocks.
    2. If you do not have a seat under you that you can reach while maintaining a flat lower back position, simply lower your hips as much as you can without rounding your lower back. Most lifters will be able to reach the point at which their thighs and torso form at least a 90-degree angle, but your individual end range can be affected by your hip mobility.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid simply letting gravity pull you down abruptly, as opposed to using your glutes to control the descent actively.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After completing the lowering phase of your last rep, allow the machine’s lever arms to rest fully on the stoppers underneath them before unfastening the hip belt or lifting up the hip pad.

    1. If your machine has a fairly short upper back pad, you can place the lower part of your shoulder blades against the front of the pad. If your machine has a long back pad, you may be able to rest your middle and upper back against it.

    2. If you continue to feel discomfort from the pressure of the belt/pad, you can try cushioning your hip bones by placing a folded exercise mat or thick foam between your hips and the belt/pad.

1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
    2. From this starting position, your back should be flat.
2. Lift your hips up by driving your heel into the foot plate and squeezing your glute.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thigh and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glute.
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid arching your lower back excessively. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glute engage during this exercise.
    4. Throughout the exercise, keep your upper back snugly in contact with the back pad and your foot fully planted on the foot plate while concentrating pressure through your heel.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering your hips through the full range of motion in which you can keep your lower back flat.
    1. If you were able to position the seat to a height that allowed you to assume the starting position with a flat lower back, you can lower your hips until you are able to tap the seat gently with your buttocks.
    2. If you do not have a seat under you that you can reach while maintaining a flat lower back position, simply lower your hips as much as you can without rounding your lower back. Most lifters will be able to reach the point at which the thigh and torso form at least a 90-degree angle, but your individual end range can be affected by your hip mobility.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid simply letting gravity pull you down abruptly, as opposed to using your glute to control the descent actively.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Use the machine’s loading pin to select your desired level of assistance, and ensure that the machine’s knee pad or foot bar is positioned down.
    1. In contrast to most machines, the difficulty of this exercise decreases as you select heavier loads from the assisted dip machine, since the weight determines the extent to which the machine will support your bodyweight.
    2. Certain machine models have a knee pad, and others have a foot bar, but essentially the same exercise technique can be used with either type of machine.
2. Step up onto the machine’s elevated foot plates.
3. If your machine allows you to rotate its parallel handles inward or outward, position them to whichever setting is closest to being slightly outside shoulder width for you.
    1. A slightly outside shoulder-width grip is appropriate for many lifters, but a mildly wider grip or a shoulder-width grip may also be used. If they are adjustable on your machine, feel free to try out both handle positions to determine which one personally feels best to you.
4. Firmly grasp the parallel handles with your palms facing each other. Hold the handles directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
5. One leg at a time, kneel onto the machine’s knee pad (if your machine has a knee pad) or step onto the machine’s foot bar (if your machine has a foot bar) while continuing to grasp the handles firmly. Maintain straight elbows when doing so.
    1. If using a machine with a knee pad, you will keep your knees bent on the pad throughout your set, but if you are using a machine with a foot bar, you will keep your knees straight while standing on the bar throughout your set.
6. Rather than keeping your torso fully upright, mildly lean your torso forward and maintain this mild lean throughout your set.
    1. The appropriate degree of lean should result in your chest being slightly in front of your hips (when viewed from the side) while helping your shoulders feel comfortable throughout the set.
    2. Feel free to try out different degrees of torso lean over time to determine what personally feels best to you.
7. Pull your shoulder blades back and down to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. You chiefly want to prevent your shoulders from rolling forward or shrugging up during this exercise.
    2. It is not required to keep your shoulder blades packed down further than they normally are at rest, but the intent to pack them down will prevent your torso from sagging down, which would place you into a shrugged shoulder position.
    3. Similarly, you do not necessarily need to have your shoulder blades fully back in the starting position, but pulling them back can make it easier to avoid tilting your shoulders forward, which is undesirable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Throughout your set, avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up. If you notice that either motion starts occurring, strive to pull your shoulder blades further backward and/or downward.
    2. Your elbows should be predominantly pointing backward rather than out to your sides from excessive elbow flare. However, you do not have to keep your elbows completely tucked by your sides, and you can allow them to flare mildly outward if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point at which their upper arms are at least parallel to the ground, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Reverse the movement by pushing through the bars to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your hands and elbows downward to lift your body upward.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step down onto the foot plate.

## Setting up
1. Approach the pair of bars/handles that you will use for your dip.
    1. A pair of bars that enables you to use a slightly outside shoulder-width grip is an appropriate starting point, but a mildly wider grip or a shoulder-width grip may also be used. If you have access to equipment that permits you to use a range of grip widths, feel free to try out different grip widths over time to determine what feels most comfortable to your shoulders.
    2. A variety of pieces of equipment can be used to perform this exercise.
    3. You can use bars that are completely parallel to each other or angled “V-grip” bars that converge to be closer together near the base and wider apart at the free ends. In contrast to stationary parallel bars, angled bars allow you to adjust your grip width based on specifically where you grasp them. Gymnastics rings can also be used to train [weighted dips](Weighted%20ring%20dip%202ef5c6f170d880a59e8bd745a4365b27.md), but this specific variation uses straight bars.
    4. Gyms commonly have a power tower (which has dip bars protruding from its vertical frame and often has a pull-up bar and/or forearm pads to use for leg raises) or a dip stand/station (which is specifically designed for dips).
    5. You can alternatively use a dip attachment that is connected to a power rack.
    6. Some assisted dip/pull-up machines also permit you to flip the knee pad or foot bar up, therefore enabling you to train dips without machine assistance. Certain machine models allow you to adjust the distance between the bars and position them closer together or wider apart.
    7. Other options include portable parallettes (which can be positioned closer or wider apart to adjust your grip width) or parallel bars located at a playground.
2. While standing in front of the bars, add your desired load (in the form of weight plates or a kettlebell) to a dip/pull-up belt you have around your waist.
    1. The back of your belt should be securely resting on top of your buttocks. You can loop the belt’s chain or strap (depending on the belt model) through the center hole of a weight plate or under the handle of a kettlebell. If you have a loading pin for your belt, you would alternatively loop the chain or strap through the loading pin after adding weight plates to it.
    2. It will be easiest if you carry the weight over to the dip bars and add the weight to your belt while you are by them. Adding the weight to your belt farther away from the bar before walking over to the bar can be awkward.
    3. As an alternative to using a pull-up/dip belt, you can wear a weighted vest.
    4. While less stable and more awkward than using a belt or weighted vest, you also have the option of holding a dumbbell between your thighs or feet. This approach is suboptimal and will limit how much weight you can use.
3. Firmly grasp the bars with your palms facing each other and your elbows straight. Hold the handles directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
    2. If you are using angled bars, you can grasp the bars at the point where they are slightly outside shoulder width apart for you. Facing the ends of the bars that angle outward may also help the shoulders of some lifters feel more comfortable during dips compared to facing the base of the bars that angle inward.
    3. When using dip bars attached to a power rack, some people may have to face away from the rack to train through the full range of motion, since the base of the attachment has the potential to restrict dip depth.

2. Connect a rope attachment or a straight bar attachment to the cable.
    1. Except for specifically how you grasp the attachment, you can perform this exercise with the same technique with either implement, so you can select whichever one you prefer and feel free to try each one out to determine if one feels more comfortable than the other for you.

5. Stand upright while holding the attachment close to your body with straight elbows and your arms pointing down toward the ground.
6. For additional stability, sit your buttocks slightly backward to adopt a very mild forward torso lean.
    1. While performing a very small hip hinge motion that results in your knees barely bending, keep your chest up and lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. In the starting position, you should feel tension from the cable to provide resistance through this exercise’s full range of motion. If you do not currently feel tension from the cable, take a step forward to prompt the weight stack to separate.

## Setting up
1. If you wish to use a precise snatch grip rather than a general approximation, you can start by determining your individual hand placement with an empty barbell or dowel rod.
    1. A true snatch grip results in the bar being level with the crease of your hip when holding the bar in a fully upright position.
    2. You can find which hand placement specifically places the bar in the aforementioned position by trying out different grip widths with an empty barbell or dowel rod until determining what precisely is your individual snatch grip width.
    3. As a general starting point, you can see where a bar is situated relative to your hip crease when grasping it with your arms spread out away from your sides with straight elbows so that each arm forms close to a 45-degree angle with your torso.
    4. Rather than trying out different grip widths, you can alternatively use that arm position as a general approximation to train this exercise effectively.
2. After adding weight plates to the barbell situated on the ground, stand upright close in front of the middle of the bar as the bar is over the middle of your feet.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
    2. The size of the weight plates you add to the bar will determine how high the bar lies above the ground, which consequently affects your range of motion. Adding a pair of 45lb (20kg) plates (or 25kg plates common in gyms outside the USA) or bumper plates will elevate the bar to the standard height (about 9in (23cm)) when deadlifting from the floor. When only using smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a snatch grip deficit deadlift with a greater range of motion that may exceed the range of motion in which some people wish to train if they lack the mobility to perform a deficit deadlift with appropriate technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize the largest diameter plates, you can perform a snatch grip block pull or rack pull with the bar elevated to where it would be when deadlifting from the floor with large diameter plates.
3. Situate your feet near hip width apart from each other or slightly wider, and position your toes slightly turned out to the sides or pointing straight ahead based on what feels best to you
    1. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
4. Spread your arms apart with straight elbows until your arms form close to 45-degree angles with your torso (if you opt to approximate your snatch grip width) or however far apart you determined from step 1 results in your specific snatch grip width.
5. With your arms held in that position and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track very far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift mildly forward to help you reach the bar rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, and after you have hinged through your available hip range motion, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back looking flat near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, rather than excessively rounding your lower back while doing so.
    4. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    5. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and engage your back muscles.
6. With your hands wide apart in the aforementioned snatch grip width, firmly grasp the bar with an overhand grip, resulting in your palms facing backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward as you tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Strive to tighten the entirety of your core to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move through your hips and knees.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. While keeping your chest up and back flat with the bar close to your shins, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the bar reaches near the middle of your shins, pause in that position for a brief period of time (e.g., 1-2 seconds) while staying tight with your chest up and back flat.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability as you visibly remain stationary.
5. Following the pause, thrust your hips forward as you resume extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. You should lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your back.
6. While keeping your back flat, reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees, after which you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
7. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-6 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps with the bar on the ground.
    3. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can meaningfully train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), along with your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that allows you to rest your triceps (on the backs of your upper arms) comfortably on the angled arm pad when sitting on the seat with your elbows aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
    1. The pivot point (which is also known as the axis of rotation) is the center about which the machine’s lever arm will rotate during the exercise, and it may be denoted by a small dot or circle in a variety of machines. This exercise will feel the most comfortable when you align your elbows with the pivot point, such that you can draw a straight line between your elbows and the pivot point.
    2. The proper seat setting will typically result in the top of the pad being close to your armpits.
    3. If you have to shrug your shoulders up while getting into the starting position, the seat is too low.
    4. If you have to slump forward and round your back while getting into the starting position, the seat is too high.
    5. Some trial and error may be needed to find the ideal seat height for your body.
2. If your machine permits you to adjust the starting position of the handles, set them as far back as you can comfortably grip to start each rep with your elbows close to fully bent.
    1. They are always adjustable in combo machines that enable you to perform a preacher curl (when the handles are positioned forward) or a triceps extension (when the handles are positioned backward), but the handles often cannot be adjusted in dedicated triceps extension machines.
    2. The proper handle position should ensure that you can still align your elbows with the pivot point and rest your triceps comfortably on the arm pad.
3. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin.
4. Sit down on the seat with your feet resting on the foot bar (if your machine has one) or the ground.
    1. If your machine has a lower back pad, situate the back of your hip bones snugly against it.
    2. Remain seated with your feet planted on the foot bar or ground throughout your set.
5. Position the back of your upper arms and elbows on top of the arm pad as your elbows are aligned with the machine’s pivot point.
    1. You potentially may have to lean slightly forward at your hips to achieve this alignment.
    2. Maintain this position throughout your set.
6. Firmly grasp the handles with your elbows bent and palms facing in toward each other.
    1. With the appropriate set-up, you should now feel stable in the starting position
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your triceps in contact with the arm pad, press the handles away from you by straightening your elbows.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and your upper arms in the same position in which they started.
    2. As the rest of your body remains stationary, all the movement should occur from your forearms arcing forward through elbow motion, like the hands of an analog clock rotating about the center points formed by your elbows.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to bend in a controlled manner to bring the handles backward.
    1. Move through the full range of motion permitted by the machine to return to the starting position with your elbows as close to fully bent as you can achieve.
    2. To confirm you have moved through the full range in a controlled manner, you can let the weights you selected lightly tap the remainder of the weight stack without allowing the weights to rest at the bottom.
    3. While you do not need to perform this phase with an extremely slow tempo, avoid letting the weight abruptly swing your forearms backward in an unresisted fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to position the bar on your upper back and unrack it in a stable position.
    1. As an initial approximation, you can position the bar such that it is a few finger widths below the height of your collarbone when you are standing in a wide stance.
2. Face the center of the unloaded bar with your feet clearly outside shoulder width stance and your toes moderately to mildly pointing outward.
    1. You can determine specifically how wide apart you position your feet and the degree to which you rotate your toes outward based on what feels comfortable and stable to you, since what is ideal for a wide stance varies among different individuals. Avoid taking so wide a stance that you feel unbalanced.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you can position yourself to face the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends (which results in the bottom of the rails being farther in front of you than the top of the rails). Facing this way can often feel more natural for good mornings, but you can alternatively face the other direction if you personally prefer to do so.
    3. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face.
3. Grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
4. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to then walk under the bar and situate the bar on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. The soles of your feet should be fully planted on the ground.
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    3. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    4. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    5. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
    6. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    7. If you are not accustomed to having a bar on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
5. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of good morning reps with the form described under the exercise technique section before reracking the bar to determine the appropriate height of the safety stops.
6. Position the safety stops slightly under the lowest point or directly at the lowest point at which the bar descended during your good morning.
    1. The appropriate safety stop position should allow you to hinge through your full range of motion while being high enough to receive the bar if you fail a rep and bend your knees a bit more to set the bar on the safety stops.
7. Load the bar with your desired weight, and repeat steps 2-4.
## Exercise technique
1. While pulling down on the bar to keep it stable on your upper back, un-rack the bar by starting to stand up as you extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the bar on your upper back throughout your set.
2. After the bar is fully resting on your upper back rather than the safety bars, rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion prior to standing fully upright with the bar.
    1. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, your lower back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. Your neck should similarly be near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
    3. Keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position throughout your set.
3. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Tense these muscles like you would do if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or a forcible slap.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
4. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner.
    1. Avoid rounding your lower back as you keep your lower back mildly arched or flat throughout the exercise.
    2. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    3. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something, as you keep your chest up (rather than letting your chest collapse through back rounding).
    4. Keep the soles of your feet fully planted on the ground the entire time.
    5. While you hinge at your hips, the bar will naturally descend, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    6. How deeply you are able to hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    7. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range.
    8. If your end range corresponds to where you positioned the safety stops, you can gently tap the bar against the safety stops without resting the bar on the safety stops at the bottom.
5. Reverse the movement by driving your hips forward until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so you should continue keeping your chest up without any back rounding.
    2. Once you have returned to the starting position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid driving your hips in front of your shoulders at the top, which would prompt your lower back to arch excessively. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips appropriately stacked under your shoulders to prevent excessive arching.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
7. After finishing the set, rerack the bar by bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner as you rotate the safety hooks onto the safety bars and return the bar to resting on the safety bars.

## Setting up
1. If your machine allows you to adjust the height of the footplate, select a height that will allow your legs to be in an approximately horizontal position once you are at the bottom of a rep.
    1. After estimating where this setting may be, you can adjust it during later steps if warranted.
    2. If you wish to increase the intensity of the exercise beyond the typical version, you can elevate the footplate beyond this standard setting.
2. Horizontally adjust the machine’s footplate to a setting that will allow the lowest point of your thighs to contact the back (i.e., the end closer to the foot plate) of the pad once you are in the starting position.
    1. This is the standard set-up for a glute ham raise, as demonstrated by certain machines having a knee pad (in addition to the thigh pad) onto which you can kneel in the starting position when setting the foot plate in this manner.
    2. The proper footplate position should permit your knees to move freely throughout the exercise while feeling stable and comfortable.
    3. If your knees are resting on top of the thigh pad in the starting position, the footplate is excessively far forward for a standard glute ham raise, and the exercise can function more like a higher-intensity Nordic hamstring curl.
    4. If your middle or upper thighs are resting on the thigh pad in the starting position, the footplate is excessively far backward for a standard glute ham raise.
    5. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal footplate position.
3. Position the weight you intend to use in a spot that you can comfortably reach after you set your feet on the footplate.
    1. While a weight plate is most commonly used, you can select any type of weight that you can hold to your chest, including a medicine ball, kettlebell, or dumbbell.
    2. Based on the weight you use, the machine model you have, your body proportions, and your mobility, you have multiple options for where you can place the weight.
    3. You may be able to place certain weights on top of the pad before picking up the weight after you mount the machine. However, not all weights can remain balanced on top of the pad, and this approach is not practical for some pad designs.
    4. With a sufficiently light weight plate or kettlebell, you may be able to hang the weight on one of the handles.
    5. As an additional approach, you can have a partner hand you the weight after you are set up, which can be useful if you are using a heavy weight.
4. Climb up onto the machine, and position the soles of your feet fully against the footplate with your lower legs between the leg rollers and your lower thigh resting against the thigh pad.
    1. The back of your lower legs should be snugly pressed into the top pair of leg rollers slightly above your heels.
    2. While you are setting your feet, you can use the handles for assistance.
    3. Some machines have a step that you can use to help you get into position.
5. Pick up the weight, hold it with both hands close to your chest, and continue doing so throughout your set.
    1. The precise way in which you will pick up and hold it may vary based on the specific implement you selected and where you placed it initially. What matters is that you have a firm grip on the weight and are able to keep it in a stable position throughout your set.
6. Assume an upright torso position, where your shoulders and hips are vertically stacked above your knees when viewed from the side.
    1. Your back and neck should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Keep your glutes squeezed and your core braced throughout the set to help you maintain a rigid trunk position.
2. In a controlled manner, lean your thighs and torso forward as one unit exclusively through knee motion.
    1. As all the movement occurs from your knees transitioning to a less bent position, keep your torso and hips in a rigid position while keeping your feet firmly against the footplate.
    2. Throughout your set, you should be able to continue drawing a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders. To do so, you will have to avoid bending forward at your hips or dynamically arching your lower back, either of which may occur if you do not appropriately continue squeezing your glutes and bracing your core.
    3. While you do not need to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should actively be in control the entire time rather than letting gravity rapidly pull you downward.
    4. As you lean forward, your knees will gradually slide upward and become closer to being vertically level with your feet.
3. Continue leaning forward until you have straightened your knees with your whole body in a horizontal position.
4. Reverse the movement by bending your knees to lift your torso and thighs as one unit until you have returned to having your hips and shoulders vertically stacked above your knees.
    1. It can help to think about driving the balls of your feet into the footplate.
    2. Since you are continuing to keep your thighs and torso aligned, your hips and shoulders should lift upward and backward in an arcing motion at the same rate. Avoid bending over at your torso while shooting your hips backward, which is a common error people make.
    3. Strive to have your torso and thighs form the hand of an analog clock that is arcing from 9 o’clock to 12 o’clock about the center point formed by your knees.
    4. During the lifting phase, your knees will naturally descend mildly toward the bottom of the thigh pad.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, return the weight to the position in which you initially placed it, bend at your hips, and dismount the machine while using your hands for assistance.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Hamstrings%201b95c6f170d88055a462c40b686f381a.md), [gracilis](../Muscles/Gracilis%201925c6f170d880938681fbbe8f075831.md), and [sartorius](../Muscles/Sartorius%201925c6f170d8801c8493cac115de0546.md), which are assisted by your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md).
