## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Keep your glutes squeezed and your core braced throughout the set to help you maintain a rigid trunk position.
2. In a controlled manner, lean your thighs and torso forward as one unit exclusively through knee motion.
    1. As all the movement occurs from your knees transitioning to a less bent position, keep your torso and hips in a rigid position while keeping your feet firmly against the footplate.
    2. Throughout your set, you should be able to continue drawing a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders. To do so, you will have to avoid bending forward at your hips or dynamically arching your lower back, either of which may occur if you do not appropriately continue squeezing your glutes and bracing your core.
    3. While you do not need to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should actively be in control the entire time rather than letting gravity rapidly pull you downward.
    4. As you lean forward, your knees will gradually slide upward and become closer to being vertically level with your feet.
3. Continue leaning forward until you have straightened your knees with your whole body in a horizontal position.
    1. The exercise will become progressively more difficult as you descend, so not every lifter has the strength to lower through the full range of motion with quality technique, which includes keeping the thighs and torso aligned.
    2. If you are currently unable to control the descent until your knees have straightened with this variation, you can select the mildly lower intensity [glute ham raise, where you keep your arms by your sides](Glute%20ham%20raise%20with%20arms%20by%20sides%201a35c6f170d880edaf07d28f69c9da2e.md), or the [band-assisted glute ham raise](Band-assisted%20glute%20ham%20raise%202995c6f170d8803d8ec1c1d7f755a8d9.md) as an alternative.
4. Reverse the movement by bending your knees to lift your torso and thighs as one unit until you have returned to having your hips and shoulders vertically stacked above your knees.
    1. It can help to think about driving the balls of your feet into the footplate.
    2. Since you are continuing to keep your thighs and torso aligned, your hips and shoulders should lift upward and backward in an arcing motion at the same rate. Avoid bending over at your torso while shooting your hips backward, which is a common error people make.
    3. Strive to have your torso and thighs form the hand of an analog clock that is arcing from 9 o’clock to 12 o’clock about the center point formed by your knees.
    4. During the lifting phase, your knees will naturally descend mildly toward the bottom of the thigh pad.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, you can bend at your hips and grasp the handles to help you dismount the machine.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Hamstrings%201b95c6f170d88055a462c40b686f381a.md), [gracilis](../Muscles/Gracilis%201925c6f170d880938681fbbe8f075831.md), and [sartorius](../Muscles/Sartorius%201925c6f170d8801c8493cac115de0546.md), which are assisted by your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the power rack’s J-hooks to a height that allows you to position the safety squat bar on your upper back and walk out the weight comfortably.
    1. As an initial approximation, you can position the J-hooks just below the height of your collarbone.
    2. You may have to re-adjust the height of the J-hooks later.
2. Place the safety squat bar on top of the J-hooks with the handles angled down and toward the direction in which you will face during the good morning.
    1. When resting on J-hooks, most safety squat bar models are designed in a way that results in the handles being mildly angled forward or backward rather than being directed straight down.
    2. The direction in which the handles from those bars are directed will influence how far forward the weight is situated relative to the upper back pad, which influences the lever arm of the weight.
    3. If you set up with the handles angled back toward you, the weight will be pitched relatively farther forward and increase the difficulty of the exercise compared to positioning the bar in the standard way.
    4. If you wish to do so, you can intentionally position the bar in the opposite manner as its own variation, but be aware that lighter loads will be required with that approach.
    5. Certain safety squat bar models are designed with the front and back sides being identical, so their handles can be directed straight down, and how you place the bar on the J-hooks is irrelevant.
3. While facing the center of the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to then walk under the bar and grasp its handles while situating the bar on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Your palms should be facing in toward each other while grasping the handles with bent elbows.
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    3. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    4. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    5. If you are not accustomed to having a bar on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
    6. If you find that deeper than a mild bend at your hips and knees is (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) is required to position the bar on your back, you can lift the bar out of the J-hooks, set it down, raise the height of the J-hooks, and place the bar back onto the J-hooks.
4. With the bar resting on your upper back muscles, stand up in a quarter squat-like manner by extending your knees and hips before checking to see if you selected an appropriate height for the J-hooks.
    1. The bar should be above the tops of the J-hooks such that they would not contact the bar when walking out backward.
    2. If you need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too low.
    3. If this is the case, lift the bar out of the J-hooks, set it down, lower the height of the J-hooks, place the bar back onto the J-hooks, and recheck to ensure you can walk out the weight without rising onto the balls of your feet.
    4. Walking out with your heels raised up will increase the risk of you losing your balance and should consequently be avoided whenever you have a barbell on your back.
5. After confirming the J-hooks are positioned appropriately, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of good morning reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight and position the safety pins to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of the good morning.
## Exercise technique
1. With the hand placement and bar positioning determined while setting up, un-rack the bar standing up in a quarter squat-like manner by extending your knees and hips while keeping the bar positioned on your upper back.
2. Take a couple of steps backward, and position your feet clearly outside shoulder-width stance with your toes moderately to mildly pointing outward.
    1. You can determine specifically how wide apart you position your feet and the degree to which you rotate your toes outward based on what feels comfortable and stable to you, since what is ideal for a wide stance varies among different individuals. Avoid taking so wide a stance that you feel unbalanced.
    2. The soles of your feet should be fully planted on the ground.
3. Brace your core by initially taking a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward.
    1. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. After the deep “belly breath,” you can continue thinking about tensing the front of your abdominals, sides of your abdominals, and lower back muscles simultaneously in a manner that allows you to form a “360 degree brace” instead of only tensing the front of your core.
    3. As a helpful cue for your “360 degree brace,” you can tense the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you are bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    4. Bracing will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you move about your hips throughout your set.
4. Hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner to move your buttocks backward while you allow your knees to bend mildly.
    1. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than rounding your lower back while doing so.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened.
    4. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    5. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something, as you keep your chest up (rather than letting your chest collapse through back rounding).
    6. While you hinge at your hips, the bar will naturally descend, and your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    7. How deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    8. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit your buttocks any farther back, you have finished descending through your available range of motion.
    9. If you positioned them appropriately, the safety pins should not restrict how far you can hip hinge, but if you are able to hinge until the bar contacts the safety pins, you can lightly tap the safety pins with the bar without resting the bar on the pins.
5. Reverse the movement by driving your hips forward until you have returned to the starting position with an upright torso.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so you should continue keeping your chest up without any back rounding.
    2. Once you have returned to the starting position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid driving your hips in front of your shoulders at the top, which would prompt your lower back to arch excessively. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips appropriately stacked under your shoulders to prevent excessive arching.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
7. Re-rack the bar by walking forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup, and you are ready to rest the bar on the J-hooks by once again bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner.
    1. Depending on how wide a stance you adopted, you may feel more balanced if you initially bring your feet closer together before walking forward to re-rack the weight.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. If your machine has one, set the range limiter (situated in one of the machine’s back corners) just under the lowest point at which the lever arm will reach during your rep.
    1. If you are new to this exercise, you will have to perform a rep to determine which setting corresponds to this position. Consequently, you can initially set the range limiter toward the bottom, continue setting up, and then adjust from there if warranted.
    2. The range limiter should be low enough that you are able to train through the full range of motion (or very close to it) comfortably permitted by your shoulder mobility.
    3. The range limiter should be high enough that it will be able to receive the weight if you fail a rep and relax your upper back in the bottom position.
    4. After finding the appropriate setting, you can make a note of it and quickly know which one to use in the future, but initially finding it can take some trial and error.
    5. Prior to performing a challenging set, it is recommended to perform a warm-up set to confirm that you set the range limiter correctly if you are new to this machine.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Step on the footplate and stand upright in a hip-width to shoulder-width stance with your back fully against the back pad.
    1. If the pad is long enough for you to do so, rest your head and/or the back of your hip bones against the pad as well.
    2. Rather than being rounded or excessively arched, you should be standing with your lower back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. Note where the foot pedal is located, since you will have to press it at the end of your set.
4. Firmly grasp a pair of handles at chest height with your palms facing down. Position your elbows directly behind the handles, resulting in your elbows being level with the handles when viewed from the side.
    1. Machines typically have multiple pairs of handles at different heights from which you can select, but certain models may have a single pair of handles that you manually have to adjust to your desired height.
    2. It is recommended to pick a pair of handles that let your hands be close to level with your lower chest at the bottom of each rep. Finding this point may require trying out a couple of different handle heights, since the machine’s lever arms arc mildly downward during the rep’s lowering phase.
    3. The appropriate handles should allow your shoulders to feel comfortable throughout the set while also feeling meaningful tension in your chest.
    4. If the handles are excessively high, resulting in the hands being near shoulder height at the bottom of a rep, some people may be more likely to feel shoulder discomfort.
    5. If the handles are excessively low, resulting in the hands being fully below the chest at the bottom of a rep, the chest may not be trained as effectively.
    6. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    7. Aligning your elbows directly behind the handles will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare during this exercise.
5. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform for pressing.
2. Press the handles forward until you have straightened your elbows, which will disengage the safety arm (i.e., what the machine lever arms initially rest upon).
    1. Throughout your set, continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together, back snugly against the back pad, and feet planted on the footplate.
3. Let the handles move backward in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Keep your elbows and wrists aligned behind the handles as your elbows progressively move backward while bending.
    2. People commonly have the mobility to reach at least the point at which the handles are horizontally near chest level, but the end range will vary among different individuals.
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom, but you should not force yourself into an end range that causes any shoulder joint discomfort.
    4. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should actively control the weight the entire time, rather than letting it quickly swing your arms  back.
4. Reverse the movement as you press the handles forward by driving your elbows forward while straightening them.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows stacked behind your wrists and the handles.
    2. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
5. Alternate between steps 3-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Note that the initial press from step 2 does not constitute a full rep. Its function is to assume the starting position.
6. Once you have locked out your final rep, press the foot pedal with one foot to engage the safety arm.
7. Move the handles back until you can rest the weight on the safety arm before letting go of the handles.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your entire [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), which is assisted by your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
    1. Plates weighing 45lb (or 20kg) may be awkward to remove from this machine, especially if you are adding at least two of them, so using no greater than 35lb (or 15kg) plates is generally recommended.
2. In a hip-width to shoulder-width stance, stand centered directly in front of the handles.
3. Lift your arm slightly forward, so that your palms are just in front of the handles with your palms facing backward and elbows straight.
4. Mildly lean forward at your hips until you can hook the tips of your four long fingers around the bottom handle and firmly grasp it with straight wrists.
    1. Point your thumbs mildly forward so that they will be out of the way of the top handle.
    2. The handle should be resting on the joints of your fingers formed by your fingertip bones and the bones directly next to them that are closer toward your palms. These joints are most apparent when you make a fist.
## Exercise technique
1. Stand upright, using your hips to lift the bottom handle toward the top handle while keeping your elbows straight.
    1. Depending on your height, you may have to maintain a slight forward lean throughout your set, or you may be able to stand fully upright.
2. Move your thumbs over the top handle on its side closer to you, and snugly contact the top handle with the base of each palm.
    1. The appropriate grip should result in the webspaces between your thumbs and index fingers touching the bar.
3. Curl your four long fingers to lift the bottom handle upward until it taps the top handle.
    1. Throughout this exercise, you will predominantly be moving your fingers through motion at your knuckle joints.
    2. This motion is similar to the “come here” hand gesture performed with your four long fingers.
    3. Continue keeping your elbows and wrists straight while your thumb remains stationary around the top handles throughout your set.
4. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by uncurling your fingers to lower the bottom handle.
    1. You should finish with the finger bones attached to your knuckles pointing straight down while continuing to keep your fingertips hooked around the bottom handle.
    2. If you feel as if the bottom handle is sliding out of your finger, you should wrap your fingertips further around it to secure your grip.
    3. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the weight rapidly uncurl your fingers in an uncontrolled fashion.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
6. Lift the bases of your palms off the top handle and point your thumbs mildly forward before leaning forward at your hips to set the plates down.
    1. Release your four long fingers from the bottom handle after the plates are fully resting on the bottom of the machine.
## Description
While also effectively training the majority of your [intrinsic hand muscles](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md), this exercise can develop your forearms’s [flexor digitorum superficialis](../Muscles/Flexor%20Digitorum%20Superficialis%201905c6f170d880f7b5c4d319b5fbe7e9.md) and [flexor digitorum profundas](../Muscles/Flexor%20Digitorum%20Profundus%201905c6f170d880f7bfa5f786584c4f71.md).
29c5c6f170d880278b3ec11248f37c9f:
## Setting up
1. Position your shoulders snugly underneath the shoulder pads as your back is fully in contact with the back pad.
    1. The back of your hip bones should also be contacting the back pad.
    2. Rather than being rounded in a slouched posture, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
2. Place your feet fully on the middle of the foot plate, near shoulder width apart, with your toes pointing slightly outward.
    1. Many people find that setting up with a stance reasonably close to this allows them to hack press effectively. However, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Some people will feel that they can move their hips more freely with a wider stance, while others may prefer a closer stance. Similarly, certain lifters may feel better with their toes pointing straight up, while others may feel more comfortable with their toes pointing moderately further outward.
    3. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when hack squatting through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different stances over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    4. While recognizing that near the middle of the foot plate works well for many people, you can also adjust how high up on the platform you position your feet based on your preference. Wherever you select should allow your heels (along with the rest of your feet) to be firmly on the foot plate throughout the whole set. Your foot placement should also allow you to keep the back of your hips snugly against the back pad at the bottom of each rep. The proper position should additionally feel comfortable for your knees.
    5. Placing your feet higher up may make it easier to keep your heels in contact with the foot plate, more difficult to keep your back flat against the back pad, and potentially bias the gluteus maximus to a greater degree. Placing your feet lower down may make it more difficult to keep your heels in contact with the foot plate, easier to keep your back flat against the back pad, and potentially bias the quads to a degree. Avoid positioning your feet toward either end of the platform if doing so feels awkward and/or limits your range of motion.
    6. In the starting position, your knees should be at least slightly bent to allow you to unlock the sled and begin your set. If you have very short legs, you potentially may have to situate your feet lower on the foot plate to start with slightly bent knees.
3. Without having any weight plates added to the machine, perform a few reps with the technique described in the “exercise technique” section before finishing your setup.
    1. These initial reps will help you determine what your full range of motion entails and inform you if any adjustments (such as to your foot placement or machine settings) are warranted.
    2. If you make any adjustments to your foot placement or the machine, it is recommended to try out a couple of reps without additional weights to make sure the adjustments were appropriate before adding weights.
4. If your machine allows you to adjust it, angle the foot plate to a setting that comfortably allows you to train through a full range of motion with your feet fully on the foot plate.
    1. Angling the foot plate closer toward a horizontal position can reduce the amount of ankle mobility required to keep your heels in contact with the foot plate at the bottom of the rep. If you noticed that your ability to keep your heels fully on the foot plate limited how deeply you were able to hack squat, it may be appropriate to try angling the foot plate closer toward a horizontal position. This may allow you to hack squat with a deeper knee bend compared to if the foot plate were angled more vertically.
    2. However, your feet may feel unstable and risk sliding if the foot plate is angled excessively close to being horizontal, so you want to find an appropriate balance.
5. If your machine has them, position the safety stoppers slightly under the lowest point at which the sled reaches at the bottom of your hack squat rep.
    1. Depending on how deeply you hack squat and the machine you use, the lowest safety stoppers available potentially may not be sufficiently low to allow you to descend through your full range of motion.
6. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, and repeat steps 1 and 2 to assume the starting position with the foot placement you determined is appropriate for you.
    1. Note that the machine will provide resistance even without any additional weight plates. The weight of the sled will vary depending on the specific model, but it commonly weighs reasonably close to 100lb (45kg).
    2. Avoid adding so much weight that you no longer are able to train through your full range of motion.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your feet into the platform to push it away from you by straightening your knees.
    1. After doing so, the sled should no longer be resting on the machine’s safety stoppers.
    2. Your knees should now be straight or just slightly bent.
3. Unlock the safety handles with your hands to move the safety stoppers out of the sled’s way.
    1. The specific location of the safety handles and how to unlock them can vary among different machine models. However, the safety handles are often near where your hands will be when resting by your sides, and rotating the handles outward will commonly disengage the safety stoppers.
4. For additional stability, firmly grasp the fixed handles (not the movable safety handles) and continue holding them throughout your set.
    1. The fixed handles are commonly located near the shoulder pads.
5. Squat down in a controlled manner by simultaneously bending at your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the foot plate.
    2. Continue keeping your back and the back of your hip bones snugly in contact with the back pad.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet. It can help to think about pushing your knees out if you notice them starting to drift inward.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively in control the entire time.
6. Continue squatting down through the full range of motion you comfortably can while keeping your heels fully on the foot plate, along with the back of your hips and back flat against the back pad.
    1. People can commonly descend until their knees are bent by at least 90 degrees, and some lifters can reach the point at which their thighs touch their calves with their knees fully bent. However, what constitutes a full range of motion will vary from person to person and be influenced by your individual hip and ankle mobility, along with your foot placement.
    2. With certain machine models, you alternatively may reach the end range to which the machine permits before reaching the deepest position that your mobility enables.
    3. If you reached the end range to which your ankle mobility allows your knees to track over your toes, hack squatting any deeper would cause your heels to start lifting off the foot plate.
    4. If you reached the end range to which your hips can bend, lowering the sled any further would cause your lower back to start rounding. This would be demonstrated by your hip bones starting to curl forward off the back pad.
    5. Hack squatting into a deep position is not inherently problematic to the knees, but there is no need to force yourself into the lowest position possible if you experience knee discomfort at your end range.
7. Once you have reached the bottom of your hack squat, pause in that position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., 1-2 seconds) while staying tight.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
8. Reverse the movement by driving your feet into the foot plate to squat up as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees when hack squatting, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. Rather than pushing all through your heels or all through your toes, you should be pushing evenly throughout your feet.
    3. Continue keeping your feet fully on the platform, knees aligned over your feet, and your back and the back of your hip bones fully against the back pad.
9. Alternate between steps 5-8 until you have completed your set.
10. After your knees are straightened following the lifting phase of your last rep, lock the safety handles with your hands to return the safety stoppers to being fully under the sled.
11. Lower the sled onto the safety stoppers by bending your knees.
## Description
While also training your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and multiple [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md), this exercise primarily targets your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while holding the dumbbells by your thighs with straight elbows as your palms face your thighs.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hand while holding them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
    3. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    4. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.

## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Bracing your core will help you maintain a rigid torso position as you subsequently move about your hips rather than your back.
2. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight with the dumbbells just in front of your legs. Avoid letting the dumbbells drift forward away from you, which may be more likely to occur if you think about “bending over” rather than “sitting back.”
    2. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the dumbbells.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    5. Throughout the set, keep the soles of your feet fully planted on the ground and your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
3. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move.
    1. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the dumbbells at least below their knees, but how deeply you are able to hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    3. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be in clear control of the entire descent.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright while firmly holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows as your palms face in toward your thighs and your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    3. Pick up the dumbbells with a deadlift or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
2. Stand in approximately a hip-width stance with the back of your legs against the edge of the sturdy elevated object you will use to elevate your foot.
    1. If available, a padded cylindrical object positioned near knee height will normally be most comfortable and is recommended.
    2. A Smith machine bar with a squat/hip thrust pad on it, a barbell on top of the J-cups of a power rack, the leg pad of a lying hamstring curl machine, and a split squat roller stand are all high-quality cylindrical options that you can position to knee height.
    3. Alternatively, you can use an object like a flat exercise bench, couch, or plyometric box with a somewhat compliant surface, but objects with a flat surface tend not to be as comfortable for this exercise.
3. While keeping your feet approximately hip-width apart, step forward with one foot until its heel is just in front of your other foot’s big toe before doing the same with your opposite foot.
    1. This results in your front foot now being about two “foot lengths” in front of where you started when your calves were touching the object you will use to elevate your rear foot.
    2. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, somewhat of a range of foot placements can be effectively used including having your front foot two and a half “foot lengths” in front of where you started (which may be even more comfortable for some people).
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your bodyweight into your front foot before placing the top surface (on the side of your shoelaces) of your rear foot on top of the elevated surface with that side’s knee bent.
    1. To help shift your bodyweight into your front foot, you can lean your torso mildly forward by hinging at your hip as you slightly bend that side’s knee.
    2. Once you have situated your rear foot into the elevated position, you can return to keeping your torso in a fairly upright position, which should involve you maintaining the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright (rather than excessively arching beyond that position).
    3. Strive to move your rear foot backward in a straight line to keep your feet approximately hip-width apart, rather than bringing your rear foot closer toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep the entire sole of your front foot firmly planted on the ground and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. If you are using a cylindrical object to elevate your foot, you can contact the surface with the front of your ankle along with your foot, but only your foot will contact the elevated surface if it is flat, like a bench.
    7. Keep your arms by your sides, directed down toward the ground, as you continue holding the dumbbells throughout the duration of your set.
2. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until your rear leg’s kneecap is just barely above the ground.
    1. Keep most of your weight shifted onto your front foot while you are primarily using your rear foot to assist with balance.
    2. Continue keeping your torso fairly upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. If you initially positioned your front foot excessively far in front of your elevated object, you may reach the end of your available hip range of motion before your rear knee descends to just above the ground. If you initially positioned your front foot too close to the elevated object, your depth may be limited by your ability to keep your front foot’s heel on the ground. In either case of suboptimal foot placement, you can simply descend through the range of motion in which you can move with proper technique before adjusting how far in front your front foot is situated after finishing your rep.
3. Once your rear knee is just barely above the ground, pause in that position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., about two seconds).
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
4. While keeping your front foot firmly planted on the ground and your rear foot in its elevated position, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso fairly upright and knees aligned with your feet while having most of your weight shifted onto the front foot.
5. Repeat steps 2-4 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which leg is in the forward position and which leg is in the elevated position.
    1. After finishing the set with your other leg forward, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back near a neutral position rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, select your weight with the loading pin, and connect a D-handle attachment to the cable.
2. Stand with the side of one shoulder (on the same side of your body you intend to train) facing the cable station.
3. Squat down and grasp the handle firmly with the hand closer to the cable station.
    1. Keep your elbow straight and your palm facing in toward your side.
    2. When squatting down (and up during the next step), keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back.
4. By extending (straightening) your hips and knees, stand upright with the handle while continuing to keep your elbow straight.
    1. You can situate your resting hand wherever you feel helps maintain your balance, such as raised out to the side or resting on your hip.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the side in which you are holding the cable.
5. Take a step out to the side against the cable’s resistance while keeping your straight arm aligned with the cable. Simultaneously allow the cable’s resistance to pull your shoulder blade downward and out toward the pulley.
    1. Your arm should naturally be directed diagonally out to the side and downward in line with the cable.
    2. Due to the cable’s resistance, your working side’s shoulder blade should be a bit lower and further away from the midline of your back compared to your resting side’s shoulder blade.
    3. You should currently feel resistance from the cable, so take another step away from the cable station if you do not feel resistance.
6. Position your feet about shoulder-width apart with your knees slightly bent in an athletic stance and your chest up.
    1. Ultimately, you want to adopt a stance that helps you feel stable and balanced, so you can modify your stance based on what helps accomplish that for you personally.
## Exercise technique
1. As you keep your elbow straight, shrug your shoulder and shoulder blade upward while simultaneously pulling them in toward your body’s midline.
    1. The objective is to move your shoulder and shoulder blade diagonally in the opposite direction to which the cable is pulling them.
    2. Once you can no longer shrug upward and inward, you have reached the end range. In this position, your working side’s shoulder should be higher than your resting side’s shoulder.
    3. Throughout the set, keep your neck in a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    4. Keep your torso upright while avoiding letting the cable’s resistance bend your torso toward the pulley, as would occur during a side-bend exercise.
2. Continue squeezing your shoulder blade and shoulder upward and inward as you pause in the fully shrugged-in position for a brief period of time (e.g., about two seconds).
    1. You should feel meaningful tension in the region of your upper trap (at the base of your neck and uppermost upper back).
3. Reverse the motion in a controlled manner by allowing your shoulder and shoulder blade to move diagonally downward and to the side toward the pulley.
    1. Move through your full range of motion, which may prompt you to feel a stretching sensation in your upper trap at the bottom.
    2. At the end of this motion, your working side’s shoulder should be positioned a little lower than your resting side’s shoulder due to the downward stretch that the cable can provide.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm toward the pulley.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md) while also training your [middle trap](../Muscles/Middle%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880ae812dc1cacf02f16f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md) to a greater degree than purely vertical shrugs.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the preacher bench’s seat to a height that allows you to rest your elbow and most of your triceps (on the back of your upper arm) on the sloped arm pad when sitting on the seat.
    1. The appropriate seat height should allow the exercise to feel stable and comfortable, and it will also typically result in the top of the pad being close to your armpits once you are seated.
    2. Some trial and error may be needed to find the ideal seat height.
2. On the side you wish to train, pick up a dumbbell and straddle the seat. Hold the dumbbell firmly with your palm facing forward (resulting in an underhand grip).
    1. Initially stand with enough space between you and the pad that you will be able to curl the dumbbell upward.
    2. Maintain this underhand grip and avoid rotating your palm as you finish setting up and perform the exercise.
    3. Unless stated otherwise, the directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell.
3. Curl the dumbbell upward by fully bending your elbow while lifting it upward to point straight ahead.
    1. Your arm and dumbbell should now be fully above the arm pad, which will make it easier to get into the starting position.
4. Step forward until your torso is very close to the pad before sitting down on the seat and resting your triceps and elbow on the pad. Continue keeping your elbow bent.
    1. You can use your free hand to help guide your other arm into the starting position if you wish to do so.
    2. Once you are in position, you can hold the arm pad with your free hand for additional stability throughout the set.
    3. In the starting position and throughout the exercise, your wrist should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow and triceps in contact with the arm pad, lower the dumbbell in a slow and controlled manner until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. While your forearm arcs forward and downward through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the dumbbell down.
    3. After initially pointing back toward you in the starting position, your palm should be angled forward and upward at the bottom of the rep. 
2. Reverse the movement by bending your elbow to curl the dumbbell upward and back toward you in an arcing motion until your elbow is fully bent.
    1. Continue keeping your elbow and triceps snugly against the arm pad.
    2. If your preacher bench allows you to curl the dumbbell past the point when your forearm is completely vertical, you can finish curling once your forearm is fully vertical (rather than once your elbow is fully bent), since your biceps will not be loaded beyond this point.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other arm.
    1. Once you have finished your last rep with your elbow fully bent, stand upright to lift your arm off the pad, and step backward before lowering the dumbbell.
    2. If you become too fatigued to finish a rep during your set, you can use your free hand to assist with lifting it up and dismounting the preacher bench.

## Setting up
This page describes setting up a barbell hold the same way as an [above-the-knee rack pull](bove-the-knee%20rack%20pull%202335c6f170d880b2a5ecfddaa83b937c.md), since that is a common and efficient setup. However, you have the option of starting with the bar from a lower pin height, blocks, or the floor if you wish to do so, since all you need to do is wind up in the lockout position of a deadlift while holding the bar in front of you.

1. Position a power rack’s safety pins slightly above the height of your knees when standing upright.
    1. Specifically, you want to select the highest pin settings that allow you to hold the bar with straight elbows without the bar contacting the pins during this exercise.
    2. For some racks with large spaces between available pinholes, that point may result in the bar starting at or mildly below knee level. If these lower pinholes are the highest ones that you can use with your rack, you have the option of elevating your feet like you would for a deficit deadlift. To do so, you can place a large diameter weight plate or deadlift block in the center of your rack, and you will stand on top of it to perform your rack pull from a closer to above-the-knee starting position. Depending on your preferred stance width, you can also position two plates or deadlift blocks directly next to each other if the soles of your feet do not fit fully onto one plate or deadlift block.
2. Place a barbell centered on top of the safety pins, and add your desired weight plates to it.
3. Stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance, close in front of the middle of the bar with your toes pointing straight ahead.
    1. The bar should be touching your lower thighs.
4. With your arms directed down toward the ground, straight elbows, and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), hinge at your hips while allowing your knees to bend a bit until your hands are level with the bar.
    1. As a cue for hinging, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something, which will naturally facilitate a mild degree of knee bend.
    2. Throughout this exercise, keep your lower back flat rather than rounding over.
    3. Similarly, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
5. Firmly grasp the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. Your arms should be directed straight down, such that they form approximately 90-degree angles with the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position.
2. While keeping your lower back flat and chest up, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.
    1. Keep your elbows straight and the bar very close to your legs as you lift the bar rather than allowing the bar to drift forward.
    2. When you have finished lifting the bar, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the top can help you finish with your hips appropriately stacked under your shoulders to prevent excessive arching.
3. Statically grip the bar while staying upright and keeping your core braced until you have reached your target hold duration.
    1. Continue keeping your shoulders stacked above your hips as you avoid leaning back to rest the bar on your thighs.
    2. Whenever you take a breath, strive to take a belly breath rather than a chest breath to facilitate your core bracing.
4. Lower the bar onto the safety pins in a slow and controlled manner by sitting your hips backward and allowing your knees to bend mildly while keeping your lower back flat and chest up.
    1. A controlled descent is important to avoid permanently damaging the bar on the pins, so you should start lowering the bar if you feel it slipping from your hands to prevent you from dropping it.
## Description
This exercise can improve your grip strength by statically training your [forearm](../Muscles/Extrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d88050a550fbeff6041573.md) and [hand](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md) muscles that function as finger flexors.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the power rack’s J-hooks to a few finger widths below the height of your collarbone.
    1. Except for positioning the safety pins higher, the setup for this exercise should be the same as for your [back squat](Barbell%20back%20squat%201a25c6f170d8803d8231d083fdd65458.md).
2. Place a barbell on top of the J-hooks and load it with your desired weight.
    1. If you are not confident that you selected the ideal J-hook height for you, you should walk out with just the bar before adding weight plates, since it can be time-consuming to adjust the J-hooks after you load the bar with plates.
    2. The proper J-hook height should allow you to unrack the bar in no deeper than a quarter squat-like manner while ensuring that the bar will not bump the J-hooks when walking out without rising onto the balls of your feet.
3. Set the safety pins directly under the J-hooks.
4. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. Use whichever hand placement you prefer when back squatting.
    2. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility, so feel free to try out different hand placements.
5. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to then walk under the bar and situate it on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    2. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar up excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
    5. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position.
2. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand up in a quarter squat-like manner by extending (straightening) your knees and hips.
    1. The bar should now be above the tops of the J-hooks such that they would not contact the bar when walking out backward. If you need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too low. If this is the case, you need to lower the safety pins and J-hooks after reracking the bar, removing the plates, and lifting the bar off the J-hooks
3. Take a couple of steps backward, and position your feet near shoulder width apart from each other as your toes are pointing somewhat out to the sides (rather than pointing straight ahead).
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. For this variation to transfer most effectively to your standard squat, you should ultimately set up in your preferred squat stance.
    3. Keep the tops of your hip bones approximately level with each other when walking out, rather than letting either one drop down the side.
4. Continue standing upright with the bar on your back for your target duration while staying tight with your core braced, chest up, and lower back flat.
    1. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes).
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position as you are looking straight ahead.
    3. Whenever you take a breath, strive to take a belly breath rather than a chest breath to facilitate your core bracing.
5. Once you have reached your intended static hold time, walk forward until the bar firmly contacts the back of each J-cup.
6. Rerack the bar by bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner to rest the bar fully on the J-hooks.
## Description
While this exercise does not effectively increase the size of any particular muscle, it can train your ability to walk out and support heavy loads on your back.

## Setting up
1. Load an adjustable EZ bar with your desired weight, or approach a fixed-weight EZ bar.
    1. Either type of EZ bar can be used interchangeably for this exercise.

    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it before a shoulder width grip is accessible on the bar.

    1. Nothing else should move except for your forearms lowering in an arcing manner through elbow motion.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the rack’s J-hooks to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on top of them.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
    3. If you need to bend your knees and hips beyond a mild degree (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) initially to place the bar on your back, you positioned the J-hooks excessively low. This can make it more challenging to rerack the bar at the end of your set.
2. Position a sturdy box of your desired height centered within the rack, a couple of step lengths behind the J-hooks.
    1. To train your lower body muscles most effectively, you want to pick a box height that enables you to squat near the depth of what is your full range of motion back squat (i.e., the lowest point at which you can squat with quality technique while keeping your back flat and feet fully on the floor). This depth will vary from person to person, but people can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground.
    2. A squat box or plyometric box is an ideal choice for your box. You can position either type of box with one of its corners directed to the middle point between the J-hooks to give you the greatest freedom in how you situate your feet when box squatting.
    3. Plyometric boxes are often available in gyms at heights of 12in (31cm), 18in (46cm), and 24in (61cm). Box squatting with an 18in (46cm) box, which is near the typical height of a flat exercise bench, restricts the range of motion for most people who are not clearly taller than six feet (183cm). If you currently do not have the mobility to squat down to a 12in (31cm) box with proper form, you can increase the height of the box by placing a thick bumper plate on top of the box to elevate it.
    4. While others have fixed heights like plyometric boxes, the height of certain squat box models can be adjusted to accommodate how deeply you wish to box squat.
    5. If you do not have access to a squat box or plyometric box, you can use an aerobic step provided that the step is rated to withstand at least half the combined load of your bodyweight and the bar weight. You can adjust its height based on how many pairs of risers you stack underneath it.
    6. Alternatively, you may be able to use a flat exercise bench as your box. A bench is excessively tall for many lifters to squat through a full range of motion, but it can be suitable for rather tall individuals, people with limited mobility, and anyone who intentionally wishes to train through a partial range of motion. To fit either a bench or an aerobic step within a rack, you may have to position it with the shorter side facing the side of the rack where you will place the barbell.
    7. While not ideal due to its lower stability, you can also stack bumper plates on top of each other to form a “box” of your desired height. If you opt to do so, make sure that the plates are completely centered on top of each other.
3. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
4. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees walk under the bar. Situate the bar on your upper back muscles slightly below the base of your neck in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. For this high bar variation, you are aiming for the bar to rest on the muscular shelf formed by your traps above your rear delts (on the back of your shoulders) and above the bony ridge running across your shoulder blades (known as the scapular spine).
    2. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable on your traps will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back as you squeeze your shoulder blades back together.
    3. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    4. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    5. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    6. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    7. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
5. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of box squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends when squatting.
7. Repeat steps 3 and 4 of the setup before proceeding to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. Take a couple of steps backward until the box is just behind you. Position your feet near shoulder width apart from each other or mildly wider as your toes are pointing somewhat out to the sides.
    1. While people often find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to box squat effectively, the ideal stance width and degree of toe flare will vary among individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet where you feel comfortable and stable when box squatting, which typically requires trying different stances over time and assessing how you feel in them.
    3. Based on your preference, you can use the same stance that you would when back squatting without a box, or you can use a somewhat wider stance, which can facilitate sitting back a bit more.
    4. Throughout your set, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    4. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down until you can sit onto the box in a controlled manner, as you avoid plopping onto the box or rocking back onto the box.
    1. As you sit on the box, your torso should maintain the same degree of forward lean that you had right before reaching the box.

    1. Avoid rocking your torso forward to generate momentum before you start squatting upward.

    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the preacher bench’s seat to a height that allows you to rest your elbow and most of your triceps (on the back of your upper arm) on the sloped arm pad when sitting on the seat.
    1. The appropriate seat height should allow the exercise to feel stable and comfortable, and it will also typically result in the top of the pad being close to your armpits once you are seated.
    2. Some trial and error may be needed to find the ideal seat height.
2. On the side you wish to train, pick up a dumbbell and straddle the seat. Hold the dumbbell firmly with your palm facing backward (resulting in an overhand grip that is also called a reverse grip).
    1. Initially stand with enough space between you and the pad that you will be able to curl the dumbbell upward.
    2. Maintain this reverse grip and avoid rotating your palm as you finish setting up and perform the exercise.
    3. Unless stated otherwise, the directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell.
3. Curl the dumbbell upward by fully bending your elbow while lifting it upward to point straight ahead.
    1. Your arm and dumbbell should now be fully above the arm pad, which will make it easier to get into the starting position.
4. Step forward until your torso is very close to the pad before sitting down on the seat and resting your triceps and elbow on the pad. Continue keeping your elbow bent, which should result in your palm now facing forward.
    1. You can use your free hand to help guide your other arm into the starting position if you wish to do so.
    2. Once you are in position, you can hold the arm pad with your free hand for additional stability throughout the set.
    3. In the starting position and throughout the exercise, your wrist should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow and triceps in contact with the arm pad, lower the dumbbell in a slow and controlled manner until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. While your forearm arcs forward and downward through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the dumbbell down.
    3. After initially pointing forward away from you in the starting position, your palm should be angled backward and downward at the bottom of the rep. 
2. Reverse the movement by bending your elbow to curl the dumbbell upward and back toward you in an arcing motion until your elbow is fully bent.
    1. Continue keeping your elbow and triceps snugly against the arm pad.
    2. If your preacher bench allows you to curl the dumbbell past the point when your forearm is completely vertical, you can finish curling once your forearm is fully vertical (rather than once your elbow is fully bent), since the target muscles will not be resisted beyond this point.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other arm.
    1. Once you have finished your last rep with your elbow fully bent, stand upright to lift your arm off the pad, and step backward before lowering the dumbbell.
    2. If you become too fatigued to finish a rep during your set, you can turn your palm to switch to a stronger underhand grip in addition to using your free hand to assist with lifting the weight and dismounting the preacher bench.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows.
2. Direct your palms so that they are facing in toward your sides (i.e., in a neutral grip position).
    1. Maintain this neutral grip on the dumbbells throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout the exercise, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you use hip motion instead of lower back motion to help lift the dumbbells.
2. While keeping your elbows straight, sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and your torso to incline slightly forward.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your lower back flat or mildly arched rather than rounding it or excessively arching it.
3. As you simultaneously thrust your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body, curl the dumbbells upward by bending your elbows while allowing them to swing forward mildly.
    1. The hip drive motion, which is similar to the lockout of a deadlift, will bring your torso into a vertical position with your knees straightened.
    2. Refrain from leaning back through excessive lower back arching, which can be easier to avoid if you think about squeezing your glutes.
    3. While you are intentionally using momentum to help your arm muscles lift the weight, you should not be “cheating” to the extent that you feel out of control.
    4. You should finish the lifting phase with your elbows fully bent as your forearms contact your biceps and your palms are facing in toward each other.
4. Lower the dumbbells in a controlled manner as you progressively allow your elbows to straighten and return near your sides.
    1. You should finish with your elbows straight and the dumbbells by your sides.
    2. Keep your torso upright and hips stationary as only your arms move during the descent.
    3. Your muscles are noticeably stronger during the lowering phase of an exercise compared to the lifting phase, so “cheating” during the lifting phase allows your arm muscles to experience greater loading during the more controlled lowering phase.
    4. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should not let gravity just swing the dumbbells back down. If you are unable to control the lowering phase to any reasonable degree, you are likely using a weight that is excessively heavy relative to your current ability.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
