## Setting up
1. Stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance with your toes pointing straight ahead.
    1. Throughout this exercise, you can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides or in front of your chest.
    2. You can optionally set up near an elevated object where you can place your phone with a timer or stopwatch that you can start once you begin your lunge hold. Alternatively, you can use a wristwatch or position yourself in front of a clock with a second hand to track your set duration.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Step far enough backward that you will be able to descend until your rear knee is just above the ground with your front thigh close to parallel to the ground. This may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to backward lunges.
    2. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
2. After contacting the ground with your rear foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until your rear leg’s kneecap is just barely above the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet, rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    4. Perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
3. Hold the lunge position for your target duration as you remain completely stationary with your rear knee hovering above the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your knees aligned with your feet, the sole of your front foot fully on the ground, and your torso upright.
    2. Since this is a static exercise, you will track how many seconds you hold the lunge rather than reps.
4. Step forward with your rear leg while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to lift your body up into a standing position.
    1. If you are particularly fatigued following the completion of your lunge hold, you can alternatively just lower your rear knee to rest on the ground.
5. Repeat steps 1-4 while switching which leg you place in the lead position.
    1. Before proceeding to your next set, it is recommended to rest, since your rear leg can be meaningfully engaged during a lunge hold, which can result in fatigue interfering with the performance of your next set if you do not rest at all between them.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the rack’s J-hooks to near mid-chest height, and place a barbell on top of them.
    1. The optimal starting height should place the bar slightly above the tops of the J-hooks, with your feet flat on the floor, after you stand upright with the bar on your back. 
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground while walking out in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks, you initially positioned the J-hooks too high. Walking with your heels raised increases the risk of losing your balance and should be avoided when you have a barbell on your back.
    3. If you need to bend your knees and hips beyond a mild degree (e.g., more like a half squat than a quarter squat) initially to place the bar on your back, you positioned the J-hooks excessively low. This can make it more challenging to rerack the bar at the end of your set.
2. Position a sturdy box of your desired height centered within the rack, a couple of step lengths behind the J-hooks.
    1. To train your lower body muscles most effectively, you want to pick a box height that enables you to squat near the depth of what is your full range of motion back squat (i.e., the lowest point at which you can squat with quality technique while keeping your back flat and feet fully on the floor). This depth will vary from person to person, but people can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground.
    2. A squat box or plyometric box is an ideal choice for your box. You can position either type of box with one of its corners directed to the middle point between the J-hooks to give you the greatest freedom in how you situate your feet when box squatting.
    3. Plyometric boxes are often available in gyms at heights of 12in (31cm), 18in (46cm), and 24in (61cm). Box squatting with an 18in (46cm) box, which is near the typical height of a flat exercise bench, restricts the range of motion for most people who are not clearly taller than six feet (183cm). If you currently do not have the mobility to squat down to a 12in (31cm) box with proper form, you can increase the height of the box by placing a thick bumper plate on top of the box to elevate it.
    4. While others have fixed heights like plyometric boxes, the height of certain squat box models can be adjusted to accommodate how deeply you wish to box squat.
    5. If you do not have access to a squat box or plyometric box, you can use an aerobic step provided that the step is rated to withstand at least half the combined load of your bodyweight and the bar weight. You can adjust its height based on how many pairs of risers you stack underneath it.
    6. Alternatively, you may be able to use a flat exercise bench as your box. A bench is excessively tall for many lifters to squat through a full range of motion, but it can be suitable for rather tall individuals, people with limited mobility, and anyone who intentionally wishes to train through a partial range of motion. To fit either a bench or an aerobic step within a rack, you may have to position it with the shorter side facing the side of the rack where you will place the barbell.
    7. While not ideal due to its lower stability, you can also stack bumper plates on top of each other to form a “box” of your desired height. If you opt to do so, make sure that the plates are completely centered on top of each other.
3. Face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance and grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat outside shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width varies by person, and what feels best to you can depend on your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
4. Shallowly bend your hips and knees before walking under the bar and positioning it on your upper back in a spot that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should be securely resting on the muscles of your upper back when squeezing your shoulder blades together.
    2. If you feel the bar is putting pressure on your neck, it is most likely placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have it placed too low on your back.
    5. When positioning the bar on your upper back, you may need to adjust your grip if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a barbell on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
5. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of box squat reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to reracking the bar onto the J-hooks.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends when squatting.
7. Repeat steps 3 and 4 of the setup before proceeding to the “exercise technique” section.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to keep it positioned on your upper back, and stand upright by straightening your knees and hips.
    1. Maintain this bar position throughout your set.
2. Take a couple of steps backward until the box is just behind you. Position your feet clearly outside shoulder width apart as your toes are pointing moderately out to the sides.
    1. Ultimately, you want to use a wide stance for this variation, but what is ideal for a wide stance varies among different individuals, so trying out different stances over time can be helpful.
    2. You can determine specifically how wide apart you position your feet and the degree to which you rotate your toes outward based on what feels comfortable and stable to you.
    3. Unless you typically squat with a rather wide stance, you can also use your standard stance as a reference point and moderately widen your stance from there.
    4. As a general rule of thumb, a stance width that is at least 150% of your shoulder width with your toes pointing about 30-45 degrees out to the side is an appropriate starting point.
    5. The soles of your feet should be fully planted on the ground, while your lower back is flat and your head is looking straight ahead.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
4. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    4. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
5. Continue to squat down until you can sit onto the box in a controlled manner, as you avoid plopping onto the box or rocking back onto the box.
    1. As you sit on the box, your torso should maintain the same degree of forward lean that you had right before reaching the box.
    2. If your torso transitions to a more upright position after sitting on the box compared to at the end of your descent, you have rocked back onto the box.
6. While keeping your core braced and back flat, and feet fully on the ground, allow about half of your weight to deload into the box as you pause on the box for approximately one second.
    1. As a cue, you can think about a scale being on top of the box. If you weigh 200lb (91kg) and have 100lb (45kg) on the bar, the scale should read within the vicinity of 150lb (136kg).
7. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Avoid rocking your torso forward to generate momentum before you start squatting upward.
    2. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
8. Alternate between steps 4-7 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
9. Walk forward until the barbell contacts the back of each J-cup before mildly bending your knees and hips to rerack the bar onto the J-hooks.
    1. Depending on how wide a stance you adopted, you may feel more balanced if you initially bring your feet closer together before walking forward to re-rack the weight.

    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet, rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    4. Perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
3. Hold the lunge position for your target duration as you remain completely stationary with your rear knee hovering above the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your knees aligned with your feet, the sole of your front foot fully on the ground, and your torso upright.
    2. Since this is a static exercise, you will track how many seconds you hold the lunge rather than reps.
4. Step forward with your rear leg while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to lift your body up into a standing position.
    1. If you are particularly fatigued following the completion of your lunge hold, you can alternatively just lower your rear knee to rest on the ground and set the dumbbells down.
5. Repeat steps 1-4 while switching which leg you place in the lead position.
    1. Before proceeding to your next set, it is recommended to set the dumbbells down and rest, since your rear leg can be meaningfully engaged during a lunge hold, which can result in fatigue interfering with the performance of your next set if you do not rest at all between them.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad muscles](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to a little higher than your head, and select your desired load with the loading pin
2. Based on your preference, leave the cable without any handle attachment or connect a D-handle attachment to the cable.
    1. Either option allows you to train your rear delts with essentially the same technique except for the specific grip you will use, so feel free to try out both and use whichever feels most comfortable to you.
3. Stand with the side of your shoulder (on the side you will not train during this set) facing the cable station, and take a step backward.
4. With your arm that is opposite to the cable, reach across your body with a slightly bent elbow and firmly grasp the ball at the end of the cable (if you are not using any handle attachment) or the D-handle (if you are using a handle attachment). Simultaneously grasp the cable station’s beam with your free hand for additional stability.
    1. Continue using your free hand to help stabilize your body throughout the exercise.
    2. Keep your working side’s elbow slightly bent from this point onward.
5. If you do not currently feel resistance from the cable, take a small step backward out to the side away from the pulley until you do.
    1. You ideally want to experience resistance from the cable in the starting position of each rep.
    2. Rather than having your torso twisted with your chest facing the pulley, your chest and imaginary belt buckle should be facing the same direction. Having your chest rotated toward the pulley may prompt you not to feel tension from the cable in the starting position.
## Exercise technique
1. Sweep your arm out away from the pulley while driving it diagonally downward and backward
    1. Move through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility permits, which should result in your elbow being slightly behind your shoulder or at least horizontally level with your shoulder at the end range.
    2. Strive to achieve a roughly even balance between sweeping horizontally outward and vertically downward.
    3. Keep your torso upright with your chest up throughout the set, while all the motion occurs from your arm moving at your shoulder.
    4. Continue keeping your chest and imaginary belt buckle facing straight ahead in the same direction as you avoid twisting your torso.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your arm to move diagonally forward, upward, and in toward the pulley across your body until you have returned to the starting position.
    1. When you set up appropriately, the angle of resistance from the cable will naturally guide your arm through this intended diagonal path.
    2. You do not have to perform this movement with an extremely slow tempo, but you should avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm toward the pulley.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also training your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and two [rotator cuff](../Muscles/Rotator%20Cuff%201b95c6f170d880b3b0d8eab69c3a7683.md) muscles to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Use the machine’s loading pin to select your desired level of assistance, and ensure that the machine’s knee pad or foot bar is positioned down.
    1. In contrast to most machines, the difficulty of this exercise decreases as you select heavier loads from the assisted dip machine, since the weight determines the extent to which the machine will support your bodyweight.
    2. Certain machine models have a knee pad, and others have a foot bar, but essentially the same exercise technique can be used with either type of machine.
2. Step up onto the machine’s elevated foot plates.
3. If your machine allows you to rotate its parallel handles inward or outward, position them to whichever setting is closest to being slightly outside shoulder width for you.
    1. A slightly outside shoulder-width grip is appropriate for many lifters, but a mildly wider grip or a shoulder-width grip may also be used. If they are adjustable on your machine, feel free to try out both handle positions to determine which one personally feels best to you.
4. Firmly grasp the parallel handles with your palms facing each other. Hold the handles directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
5. One leg at a time, kneel onto the machine’s knee pad (if your machine has a knee pad) or step onto the machine’s foot bar (if your machine has a foot bar) while continuing to grasp the handles firmly. Maintain straight elbows when doing so.
    1. If using a machine with a knee pad, you will keep your knees bent on the pad throughout your set, but if you are using a machine with a foot bar, you will keep your knees straight while standing on the bar throughout your set.
6. Rather than keeping your torso fully upright, mildly lean your torso forward and maintain this mild lean throughout your set.
    1. The appropriate degree of lean should result in your chest being slightly in front of your hips (when viewed from the side) while helping your shoulders feel comfortable throughout the set.
    2. Feel free to try out different degrees of torso lean over time to determine what personally feels best to you.
7. Pull your shoulder blades back and down to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. You chiefly want to prevent your shoulders from rolling forward or shrugging up during this exercise.
    2. It is not required to keep your shoulder blades packed down further than they normally are at rest, but the intent to pack them down will prevent your torso from sagging down, which would place you into a shrugged shoulder position.
    3. Similarly, you do not necessarily need to have your shoulder blades fully back in the starting position, but pulling them back can make it easier to avoid tilting your shoulders forward, which is undesirable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Throughout your set, avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up. If you notice that either motion starts occurring, strive to pull your shoulder blades further backward and/or downward.
    2. Your elbows should be predominantly pointing backward rather than out to your sides from excessive elbow flare. However, you do not have to keep your elbows completely tucked by your sides, and you can allow them to flare mildly outward if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point at which their upper arms are at least parallel to the ground, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Once you have finished lowering to your end range, pause in that bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds).
    1. Continue to stay braced with your shoulder blades pulled back and down.
    2. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Reverse the movement by pushing through the bars to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your hands and elbows downward to lift your body upward.
6. Alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step down onto the foot plate.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) while being able to improve both your horizontal and vertical pressing strength.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to the height of your chest when you are in a half-kneeling position, which should correspond to being reasonably near hip height when standing.
2. Connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. As an alternative to the D-handle attachment, you also can perform a Pallof press with a rope attachment, but this page will describe the use of the D-handle.
3. Stand with the side of one shoulder facing the cable station, and grasp the handle with your closer hand.
4. Take a step to the side while keeping your arm (holding the handle) aligned with the cable.
5. Perform a controlled lunging motion into a half-kneeling position by stepping back with your leg closer to the cable and resting that side’s knee on the ground.
    1. In this position, your imaginary belt buckle should be facing about 90 degrees away from the cable station.
6. Turn your chest toward the cable station, and reach across your body with your free hand to firmly grasp the handle, interlocking your hands and facing your palms toward each other.
7. Pull the handle close to your chest with elbows bent and by your sides before turning your chest to face the same direction as your imaginary belt buckle.
    1. Rather than being bent to one side, twisted, rounded, or excessively arched, your torso should be in a symmetrical upright position aligned with your hips, like it would normally be when you are standing upright.
    2. In this starting position, you should be able to form close to a 90-degree angle between the cable and an imaginary laser beam shooting straight forward from the center of your chest. You should also be able to draw a straight line between your shoulders that is parallel to the cable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forceful slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension, and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. While keeping the center of your chest facing straight ahead, press the handle straight forward away from your chest.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as your arms are outstretched in front of you, close to parallel to the ground.
    2. All the motion should occur from your arms moving at your shoulders and elbows, while the rest of your body remains completely stationary.
    3. Particularly avoid letting the cable's resistance rotate your torso. If your core muscles do not stabilize your trunk sufficiently, the imaginary laser beam shooting out from the center of your chest will start angling closer toward the cable station. The center of your chest should be facing the same direction in line with your imaginary belt buckle throughout your entire set.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by bringing the handle straight back toward your chest as you bend your elbows.
    1. You should now be back to the starting position with the handle directly in front of your chest as your upper arms are right by your sides.
    2. Continue keeping the center of your chest facing straight forward as your shoulders remain aligned when viewed from the side.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise, this time facing the opposite direction.
## Description
While also engaging your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), this exercise will statically train your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they function to resist trunk rotation.

## Setting up
1. Bring a head harness and an elastic band to a flat exercise bench or any object on which you can comfortably sit.
    1. Either a tube elastic band or a long looped elastic band can be used for this exercise.
    2. You can alternatively perform this exercise standing, but this page will describe the seated position.
2. After optionally donning a beanie for comfort, place a head harness on top of your head, and adjust its straps as needed until it feels snug and secure.
    1. The appropriate fit should ensure that the harness does not slide when nodding your head up and down.
3. While sitting down, connect one end of the band to one of the harness's side attachment points before connecting the other end of the band to the other side attachment point.
4. Drape the band behind your body, and grasp the bottom of the band with your hands to tension the band with straight arms.
## Exercise technique
1. Slowly nod your head down as you tilt your chin toward your chest through your neck’s comfortable range of motion.
    1. People can commonly perform this movement until the chin is very close to touching the collarbone, but your neck mobility will also influence the degree to which you can nod down.
    2. It is natural to feel a stretching sensation in some of the muscles on the back of your neck in the bottom position, but you should not experience any neck discomfort.
    3. Prioritize actively controlling the weight throughout the entirety of your set. This is an intentionally slow exercise.
    4. While you move your head through neck motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary as you continue holding the band throughout the set.
2. Reverse the movement by nodding your head up in a controlled manner as you tilt your chin away from your chest through your neck’s comfortable range of motion.
    1. Finishing with the face angled diagonally forward and upward is generally an appropriate end position for many people, but the specific end point will vary among different individuals.
    2. What chiefly matters is finishing in a position that feels comfortable to your neck.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After completing your last rep, lift the band up with your hands by bending your elbows until the band becomes slack and you can remove the harness.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train several muscles on the front of your neck, the largest and strongest of which is your [sternocleidomastoid](../Muscles/Sternocleidomastoid%2019a5c6f170d8806e81bdd0b1d1242785.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an exercise bench at a low to moderate incline that will allow you to rest your chest against the head of the bench when you are bent over with your torso close to horizontal.
    1. The ideal bench angle should allow you to position your torso as close to horizontal as your mobility permits without your lower back.
    2. A lower incline may be appropriate for shorter lifters and/or those with good mobility, while a moderate incline may be better for taller lifters and/or those who have mobility limitations.
    3. You can optionally place a soft object (e.g., a squat pad, a rolled-up towel, or a rolled-up exercise mat) onto the head of the bench for cushioning.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and hold them by your sides with straight elbows.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    2. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
3. In a near hip-width stance, face the back of the bench while standing close enough to it that you will be able to rest your chest on it during the next step.
4. Sit your hips back while allowing your knees to bend mildly to hinge at your hips and incline your torso until you can rest your chest on the head of the bench.
    1. Keep your lower back flat throughout the exercise.
    2. The proper position should allow your head to be above the bench with your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
5. As your arms hang down toward the ground with straight elbows, angle your palms diagonally backward and in toward each other.
    1. Throughout your set, maintain this grip, which is a hybrid between an overhand grip and a neutral grip.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from now on.
2. Drive your elbows in an arcing motion backward, upward, and moderately out away from your sides to row the dumbbells. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Aim to flare your elbows about 45 degrees out away from your side as you move your elbows equal parts backward and out to the side. Zero degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows purely backward and keeping them completely tucked by your sides, while 90 degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows straight out to the sides, which would result in your upper arms and torso forming a “T-shape” at the top.
    2. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the top.
    3. Keep your chest in contact with the bench throughout the set, as all the motion occurs from your shoulder girdle and arms.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
    5. When allowing your elbows to bend naturally, your forearms should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    6. The dumbbells should move in an arcing motion rather than moving straight upward in a vertical path.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled arcing motion until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. Allow the weights to pull your shoulder blades apart and forward, which will stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. Move your elbows diagonally inward and forward at a near 45-degree angle while they descend to reverse the moderate elbow flare you just utilized during the lifting phase.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weights rapidly pull your arms down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, thrust your hips forward to stand upright with your chest off the bench before setting the dumbbells down.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Fully lower the Smith machine’s safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) and the machine’s bar.
    1. The safety hooks attached to the bar should be rotated out away from the safety bars (which are the bars onto which the safety hooks can latch).
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the bar, and stand close in front of the middle of the bar with approximately a hip width to shoulder width stance.
    1. Stand with the bar over the middle of your feet, which should situate the bar close to one inch (2.5cm) away from most individuals’ shins while initially standing upright.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you can position yourself to face the side in which the bar will track slightly backward when lifting it up (which results in the bottom of the rails being farther in front of you than the top of the rails). Facing this way will help the row feel most natural.
    3. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the ground, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
4. With straight elbows, firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside shoulder width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position.
2. Explosively pull the bar up toward your upper abdomen by driving your elbows simultaneously backward and upward as you pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Keep your torso in a hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set. All the movement should occur from motion at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows while your lower body remains stationary.
    2. Continue keeping your core braced, lower back flat, and chest up.
    3. Allow your elbows naturally to flare out away from your sides in a manner that feels comfortable to you, which may result in your upper arms forming near a 45-degree angle with your torso toward the end of the lifting phase.
    4. You can aim to row the bar until it touches near your upper abdomen or is close to doing so, which will result in your elbows being behind your torso (or at least aligned with your torso) at the end of the lifting phase.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar until it is fully resting on the bottom of the machine.
    1. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another, and your elbows will move downward and forward until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    2. Continue maintaining the same degree of forward torso lean with your chest up and lower back flat.
    3. The lowering phase of the Pendlay row is typically performed with a very quick tempo, but you can alternatively lower the bar in a more controlled manner if you wish to do so.
4. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop at the bottom for a moment (rather than using momentum) before continuing to alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is resting on the bottom of the machine. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, select your weight with the loading pin, and connect an EZ bar (also known as a multi-grip curl bar) attachment to the cable.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down or hinge at your hips to grasp the bar firmly with approximately a shoulder width semi-underhand grip such that your palms are directed at an angle that is facing forward and inward.
    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar attachment, you may have to rotate it initially before a near shoulder width semi-underhand grip is accessible on the bar.
3. While keeping your elbows straight, stand upright with the bar just in front of your legs.
4. If you do not currently feel resistance from the cable or are standing too close to the pulley to curl the bar without bumping the station, take a step backward while keeping your elbows straight.
    1. The appropriate positioning should allow you to feel resistance from the cable throughout the curl’s full range of motion.
    2. When stepping backward, the cable will now have a mildly diagonal line of the pull rather than being vertical. To maintain a straight elbow position with a mildly diagonal line of pull, you will have to raise your arms slightly in front of your body instead of keeping them pinned to your sides.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl the bar upward and back toward you in an arcing motion by bending your elbows until they are fully bent with your forearms contacting your biceps.
    1. Rather than swinging them further forward, keep your upper arms fixed in the same position in which they started (i.e., a little in front of you).
    2. While your forearms move through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. Nothing else should move except for your forearms lowering in an arcing manner through elbow motion.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should avoid letting the cable’s resistance abruptly swing the bar down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, step forward and squat down or hinge at your hips to set the bar down.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
2a05c6f170d88069a986ea15fb228983:
## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip width stance while holding the dumbbells at your sides with straight elbows.
2. Direct your palms so that they are facing in toward your sides (i.e., in a neutral grip position).
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout the exercise, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you use hip motion instead of lower back motion to help lift the dumbbells.
2. While keeping your elbows straight, sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and your torso to incline slightly forward.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your lower back flat or mildly arched rather than rounding it or excessively arching it.
3. Thrust your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body. Simultaneously curl the dumbbells upward by bending your elbows while turning your palms to face back toward you at the top.
    1. Allow your elbows to swing forward mildly rather than keeping them pinned to your sides, like during a strict curl.
    2. The hip drive motion, which is similar to the lockout of a deadlift, will bring your torso into a vertical position with your knees straightened.
    3. Refrain from leaning back through excessive lower back arching, which can be easier to avoid if you think about squeezing your glutes.
    4. While you are intentionally using momentum to help your arm muscles lift the weight, you should not be “cheating” to the extent that you feel out of control.
    5. You should finish the lifting phase with your elbows fully bent as your forearms are contacting your biceps and you are holding the dumbbells with an underhand grip (rather than the neutral grip with which you started).
4. Lower the dumbbells in a controlled manner as you progressively allow your elbows to straighten and return near your sides. Simultaneously turn your palms in toward each other.
    1. You should finish with your elbows straight while you are holding the dumbbells in a neutral grip by your sides.
    2. Keep your torso upright and hips stationary as only your arms move during the descent.
    3. Your muscles are noticeably stronger during the lowering phase of an exercise compared to the lifting phase, so “cheating” during the lifting phase allows your biceps to experience greater loading during the more controlled lowering phase.
    4. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should not let gravity just swing the dumbbells back down. If you are unable to control the lowering phase to any reasonable degree, you are likely using a weight that is excessively heavy relative to your current ability.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while holding the dumbbells by your thighs with straight elbows as your palms face your thighs.
    1. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hand while holding them, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
    3. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging.
    4. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position.
    5. Pick up the dumbbells with a hip hinge or squat motion, where you lift them by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back flat, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Dip down slightly by bending your knees while keeping your chest up.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your lower back flat or mildly arched rather than rounding it or excessively arching it.
    2. Quickly proceed to the next step as soon as you finish dipping down.
3. Forcefully drive your feet into the ground as you rapidly straighten your knees to generate momentum from your lower body. Simultaneously shrug your shoulders upward through your available range of motion to lift the dumbbells upward while keeping your elbows straight.
    1. While you are intentionally using momentum to help your upper traps lift the weight, you should not be “cheating” to the extent that you feel out of control.
    2. Throughout the exercise, look straight ahead to keep your neck near a neutral position.
    3. As a cue, you can think about driving your shoulders up toward your earlobes.
4. Allow your shoulders to descend fully in a controlled manner to lower the dumbbells while keeping your torso upright and legs stationary.
    1. Your muscles are noticeably stronger during the lowering phase of an exercise compared to the lifting phase, so “cheating” during the lifting phase allows your upper traps to experience greater loading during the more controlled lowering phase.
    2. At the bottom, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the dumbbells can provide.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the dumbbells abruptly yank you downward. If you are unable to control the lowering phase to any reasonable degree, you are likely using weights that are excessively heavy relative to your current ability.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have finished your last rep, set the dumbbells down in the same manner in which you initially picked them up (e.g., keeping your lower back flat rather than simply rounding over at your lower back).
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable cable station’s pulley to its highest setting, or approach a cable lat pulldown machine.
    1. Either type of equipment can be used interchangeably for this exercise.
2. Select your desired weight with the loading pin or add weight plates if you are using a plate-loaded cable machine.
3. Based on your preference, connect a rope attachment, straight bar attachment, or multi-grip EZ bar attachment to the cable.
    1. You can optionally place an exercise mat on the ground for comfort.
4. While facing the cable station, reach up and firmly grasp the cable attachment with straight elbows while keeping your wrists fairly straight.
    1. With a rope attachment, you can point your palms in toward each other and grasp each end of the rope with your little fingers and the adjacent aspects of your hands contacting the flat surfaces of the attachment’s rubber stoppers. Wrap your thumbs over the outside of your other fingers.
    2. With a straight bar or multi-grip EZ bar, you can grasp it with an approximately shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing away from you.
5. While keeping your arms outstretched with straight elbows in line with the cable, kneel down onto the ground.
    1. In this position, you should feel tension from the cable. If you do not, you should situate yourself further back away from the cable until the weight stack separates.
6. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and moderately incline your torso while keeping your arms in line with the cable and your back flat.
    1. The appropriate degree of torso incline should allow you to draw a mostly straight line from your arms through your shoulders to your hips when viewed from the side. From this position, the cable’s resistance should situate your arms fully overhead relative to what your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows straightened and your torso inclined, sweep your arms down and back toward your sides in an arcing motion until your hands are right by your thighs.
    1. During the initial half of this movement, you can focus on driving down, while you can focus on pulling back during the latter half of this movement.
    2. As your arms move through motion at your shoulders, the rest of your body should be stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your arms to sweep forward and upward in a controlled arcing manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms fully overhead in line with the cable.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straightened and your torso inclined.
    2. While you do not have to reverse the movement with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the cable abruptly swing your arms upward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, you can return to an upright torso position, step one leg forward to assume a lunge position, stand upright in a lunging motion, and return the cable to its initial position.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which are assisted by the [lowest portion of your pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) and the [long head of your triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md) in the overhead position of each rep.

## Setting up
1. In an approximately hip-width stance, face the stable object with a flat, elevated surface that you will use for this push-up variation.
    1. So long as the object can support your bodyweight and will not slide, you can use a variety of objects based on the degree of difficulty you wish to have and what is available to you.
    2. As the height of the surface decreases, the difficulty of the exercise will increase from being able to adopt a closer to horizontal torso position, where gravity can provide greater resistance during a push-up.
    3. A flat exercise bench (which typically has a surface near 18in (46cm) above the ground) can be appropriate to use in a gym as an initial starting point for many people who struggle to perform more than a couple of reps of standard push-ups through a full range of motion.
    4. In addition to a plyometric box, an aerobic step elevated on top of risers can also be a quality object to use, since you can adjust the height (typically in 2in (5cm) increments) to match the specific level of difficulty you wish to have.
    5. For a lower intensity variation at home, furniture like a bed can alternatively be used to elevate your hands.
2. After leaning forward at your hips, place your palms on top of the elevated object with the base of your palms on the corner as your elbows are straight, and your hands are about shoulder width apart.
    1. In this position, your middle fingers should be pointing slightly out to the sides or straight ahead, depending upon what hand position feels most comfortable and stable to you.
    2. Based on your preference, you can spread your fingers somewhat apart from each other or keep them close together.
3. While bearing weight through your hands and allowing your heels to lift off the ground, walk your feet back until your hips and knees are straightened as your arms form approximately 90-degree angles with your torso.
    1. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    2. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    3. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest in a controlled manner until it lightly touches the elevated surface.
    1. Rather than excessively flaring your elbows out away from your sides, keep your elbows reasonably tucked by your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you as you descend.
    2. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ground instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    5. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the surface to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    2. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise trains your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) like a standard [close grip push-up](Close%20grip%20push-up%201a05c6f170d880dfb02cf76f7519927d.md) but with a lower intensity.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground, and position a large diameter weight plate (or a viable alternative) under the center of the bar that you will use to create a deficit.
    1. While you can use a variety of deficit heights, selecting a low deficit height (under 4in (10cm)) is initially recommended to facilitate the appropriate technique.
    2. Ideally pick a height that allows you to keep your lower back flat at the bottom of the rep while fully hinging at your hips to incline your torso as close to horizontal as your flexibility permits.
    3. A large diameter (e.g., 45lb (20kg)) cast iron weight plate with the flat surface facing up can be a suitable option to select initially. For a greater deficit, you can alternatively select a thicker bumper plate, deadlift block, stack of two cast iron plates, or aerobic step rated to withstand the combined loads of your bodyweight and the bar’s weight.
    4. Whichever object you select should be stable when you are standing with the soles of your feet fully on it in a near hip-width stance. Some people may not be able to situate both feet fully on one plate and can alternatively situate two plates next to each other to enable full foot contact.
    5. As an alternative to standing on an elevated object, you can also achieve the same extended range of motion for your row by only adding smaller diameter weight plates to the bar instead of loading at least one pair of full diameter plates (like 45lb (20kg) plates or any bumper plates).
2. In a near hip-width stance, stand upright on the plate (or other object) with the middle of your feet directly under the middle of the bar as your toes are pointing straight ahead or slightly out to the sides (depending on what feels most comfortable).
    1. Throughout the exercise, the soles of your feet should be fully in contact with the plate (or other object) for maximal stability.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the ground, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something. Once you fully sit back and feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout the exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. With straight elbows, firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside shoulder-width overhand grip, such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position.
2. Explosively pull the bar up toward your upper abdomen by driving your elbows simultaneously backward and upward as you pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Keep your torso in a hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set. All the movement should occur from motion at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows while your lower body remains stationary.
    2. Continue keeping your core braced, lower back flat, and chest up.
    3. Allow your elbows naturally to flare out away from your sides in a manner that feels comfortable to you, which may result in your upper arms forming near 45-degree angles with your torso toward the end of the lifting phase.
    4. You can aim to row the bar until it touches near your upper abdomen or is close to doing so, which will result in your elbows being behind your torso (or at least aligned with your torso) at the end of the lifting phase.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar until it is fully resting on the ground.
    1. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another, and your elbows will move downward and forward until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    2. Continue maintaining the same degree of forward torso lean with your chest up and lower back flat.
    3. The lowering phase of the Pendlay row is typically performed with a very quick tempo, but you can alternatively lower the bar in a more controlled manner if you wish to do so.
4. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than using momentum) before continuing to alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is resting on the ground. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the next rep.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley near mid-shin height, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Securely attach an ankle cuff just above the ankle of the leg you will train. Position the cuff so that one of its attachment rings is directed out to the side (away from your other leg).
3. Stand sideways with your working leg directly next to the pulley, and connect the cable to your cuff’s outer attachment ring.
    1. It will be easiest to connect the cable when your cuffed ankle is close enough to the pulley that the cable does not provide resistance when connecting it. This may involve marching your cuffed side’s foot mildly above the ground when attaching the cable
4. Grasp the cable station’s beam near shoulder height with your closer hand, and continue holding it from now onward for additional stability.
5. Step out to the side away from the pulley until your elbow (of the arm holding the cable station) has fully straightened.
    1. Keeping your toes pointing straight forward, such that lines drawn from your toes to your heels can form approximately 90-degree angles with the cables.
    2. The objective is to situate yourself as far out to the side, away from the pulley, as you can while still being able to help stabilize your body with your arm.
6. Take a step backward with the leg that is not cuffed.
    1. The goal is to have your non-working leg’s toes slightly behind your cuffed leg’s heel to provide sufficient clearance for your cuffed leg to sweep across your body away from the pulley.
    2. In the starting position, your chest and imaginary belt buckle should be pointing straight ahead in the same direction, and your shoulders should be level.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Shift your bodyweight into your non-working side’s foot, and allow the cable’s resistance to sweep your cuffed leg out to the side toward the pulley. Keep your hip bones and shoulders level with each other throughout the exercise.
    1. Let your leg angle as far out to the side as the cable’s resistance enables.
    2. The subsequent directions will apply to your cuffed side’s leg as you keep your other leg still.
3. Sweep your leg inward away from the pulley and across your body while keeping your knee pointing straight forward.
    1. Individuals with normal hip mobility can typically finish with their legs slightly crossed over each other.
    2. As you move your leg via hip motion, strive to keep the rest of your body stationary throughout the set.
    3. With the appropriate technique, you should feel tension in your adductors within the inner aspect of your thigh.
4. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by letting your leg sweep out to the side toward the pulley, like during step 2.
    1. You can aim to let your leg move outward until the weights you selected are just about to tap the rest of the weight stack.
    2. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the cable abruptly swing your leg outward in an uncontrolled fashion.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train all your [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md) in an isolated manner.

## Setting up
1. While standing under a pull-up bar, reach up and firmly grasp it with a slightly outside shoulder-width grip, palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip).
    1. Depending on the specific pull-up bar you are using, your height, and your wingspan, the bar may be beyond your reach.
    2. If you cannot reach the bar while standing on the ground, you can initially step up onto a sturdy box, an aerobic step, or a bumper plate to place the bar within reach.
    3. While not required, elevating yourself to reach the bar may help you set up with a more stable hand position around the bar than if you jumped up from the ground to reach it.
    4. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    5. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
2. With your elbows straight, begin hanging on the bar by lifting your feet just off the ground (or the elevated object if you initially stood on something as a step to reach the bar).
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar, pull your shoulder blades down, which will pull your shoulders away from your ears.
    1. Maintain this shoulder position throughout the exercise as you avoid letting your shoulders shrug up toward your ears from the force of your bodyweight.
2. Sweep your legs up and out in front of you, keeping your knees straight, until your legs are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. Keep your torso vertical and your elbows straight as you avoid swinging your body to build momentum.
    2. In this position, your torso and legs should resemble an “L shape” when viewed from the side, which results from your legs forming a right angle with your torso.
    3. If you do not have the hamstring flexibility to utilize what is considered the standard textbook form with your knees fully straight as your legs are parallel to the ground, you can situate your legs as close as you can to this position.
    4. Individuals with limited hamstring flexibility can either keep their thighs parallel to the ground with their knees mildly bent, or lift their legs as close to parallel to the ground as they can reach with straight knees.
    5. Rather than remaining mildly arched like when you are normally standing upright, your lower back should naturally flatten from the contraction of your abs.
3. Hold the L-sit position for your target duration as you strive to remain completely stationary.
    1. Since this is a static exercise, you will track how many seconds you hold the position rather than reps.
4. After reaching your target hold duration, lower your legs in a controlled manner until you can return your feet to the ground (or the elevated object you used as a step to reach the bar).
## Description
This exercise will primarily train your [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md) and [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) (the “six pack muscle”) while also engaging your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) secondarily.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. In a mildly outside shoulder width stance, stand with the handle between your feet as your back is facing the cable station.
3. Hinge at your hips or squat down to firmly grasp the handle with the side of your body you will train during this set.
    1. Hold the handle with your palm facing forward and your elbow straight.
4. Take a step or two forward until the weight stack separates and you feel tension from the cable.
    1. You can keep your torso somewhat inclined forward while stepping forward.
5. On the same side of the body in which you are holding the cable, angle your knee and foot out to the side while situating your feet fairly wide apart.
6. Sit your hips back while allowing your knees to bend and torso to incline further forward until you can rest your working side’s elbow against the inside of your thigh. Simultaneously, brace your free arm’s forearm against your other side’s thigh for additional stability.
    1. Your working side’s arm should be directed down toward the ground with a straight elbow as the cable is exerting a pulling force backward.
    2. With the appropriate set-up, you should feel balanced in the starting position.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow pinned against your inner thigh, bend your elbow to curl the handle forward and upward in an arcing manner.
    1. You can finish curling once your forearm is approximately parallel to the ground. Resistance from the cable will be minimal when bending your elbow beyond that point.
    2. While you move your forearm through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbow to straighten in a controlled manner as you let your forearm arc downward and back toward the pulley.
    1. Finish this step with your elbow fully straightened.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank the handle back in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
