## Setting up
1. Add weight plates to the machine to utilize your desired level of assistance and ensure that the machine’s knee pad or foot bar is positioned down.
    1. In contrast to most machines, the difficulty of this exercise decreases as you add heavier loads to the assisted pull-up machine since the weight determines the extent to which the machine will support your bodyweight.
    2. Certain machine models have a knee pad, and others have a foot bar, but essentially the same exercise technique can be used with either type of machine.
2. Step up onto the machine’s elevated foot plates.
3. If your machine allows you to rotate its parallel handles inward or outward, position them to whichever setting is closest to being slightly outside shoulder width for you.
    1. A slightly outside shoulder-width grip is appropriate for many lifters, but a mildly wider grip or a shoulder-width grip may also be used. If they are adjustable on your machine, feel free to try out both handle positions to determine which one personally feels best to you.
4. Firmly grasp the parallel handles with your palms facing each other. Hold the handles directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the handles tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
5. One leg at a time, kneel onto the machine’s knee pad (if your machine has a knee pad) or step onto the machine’s foot bar (if your machine has a foot bar) while continuing to grasp the handles firmly. Maintain straight elbows when doing so.
    1. If using a machine with a knee pad, you will keep your knees bent on the pad throughout your set, but if you are using a machine with a foot bar, you will keep your knees straight while standing on the bar throughout your set.
6. Rather than keeping your torso fully upright, mildly lean your torso forward and maintain this mild lean throughout your set.
    1. The appropriate degree of lean should result in your chest being slightly in front of your hips (when viewed from the side) while helping your shoulders feel comfortable throughout the set.
    2. Feel free to try out different degrees of torso lean over time to determine what personally feels best to you.
7. Pull your shoulder blades back and down to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. You chiefly want to prevent your shoulders from rolling forward or shrugging up during this exercise.
    2. It is not required to keep your shoulder blades packed down further than they normally are at rest, but the intent to pack them down will prevent your torso from sagging down, which would place you into a shrugged shoulder position.
    3. Similarly, you do not necessarily need to have your shoulder blades fully back in the starting position, but pulling them back can make it easier to avoid tilting your shoulders forward, which is undesirable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Throughout your set, avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up. If you notice that either motion starts occurring, strive to pull your shoulder blades further backward and/or downward.
    2. Your elbows should be predominantly pointing backward rather than out to your sides from excessive elbow flare. However, you do not have to keep your elbows completely tucked by your sides, and you can allow them to flare mildly outward if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point where their upper arms are at least parallel to the ground, but how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Once you have finished lowering to your end range, pause in that bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds).
    1. Continue to stay braced with your shoulder blades pulled back and down.
    2. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Reverse the movement by pushing through the bars to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your hands and elbows downward to lift your body upward.
6. Alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step down onto the foot plate.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) while being able to improve both your horizontal and vertical pressing strength.

## Setting up
1. Situate a weight plate or kettlebell of your desired load next to a flat exercise bench or any object on which you can comfortably sit.
    1. You can alternatively perform this exercise standing with your torso hinged forward, but this page will describe the seated position.
2. After optionally donning a beanie for comfort, place a head harness on top of your head, and adjust its straps as needed until it feels snug and secure.
    1. The appropriate fit should ensure that the harness does not slide when nodding your head up and down.
3. Connect one end of a chain to one of the harness's side attachment points while sitting down with your legs moderately spread apart.
4. After picking up your weight, slide the free end of the chain through the center hole of a weight plate or under the handle of a kettlebell before connecting that end of the chain to the other side attachment point of the harness.
5. Moderately to mildly lean forward at your hips, and lower the weight until the chain is tensed.
    1. The weight should now be hanging between your legs.
## Exercise technique
1. Slowly nod your head down as you tilt your chin toward your chest through your neck’s comfortable range of motion.
    1. People can commonly perform this movement until the chin is very close to touching the collarbone, but your neck mobility will also influence the degree to which you can nod down.
    2. It is natural to feel a stretching sensation in some of the muscles on the back of your neck in the bottom position, but you should not experience any neck discomfort.
    3. Prioritize actively controlling the weight throughout the entirety of your set. This is an intentionally slow exercise.
    4. While you move your head through neck motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by nodding your head up in a controlled manner as you tilt your chin away from your chest through your neck’s comfortable range of motion.
    1. Based on your preference and what feels best to you, you can finish nodding up once you have returned to a neutral position (like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright), or you can extend a bit beyond that point.
    2. Regardless of which end range you opt to use, your face should be angled forward in the top position. There is no need to nod your head all the way up until you are looking up at the ceiling.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After completing your last rep, lift the weight up with your hand to unload the harness before unfastening the chain from one side of the harness and removing the chain from the weight.
## Description

## Setting up
1. Fully lower the Smith machine’s safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) and position the bar slightly below the height of your hands when standing with your arms at your sides.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the bar, and stand upright in a near hip-width stance with the middle of the bar just in front of your legs.
    1. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you can position yourself to face the side in which the bar will track slightly backward when lifting it up (which results in the bottom of the rails being farther in front of you than the top of the rails). Facing this way will help the row feel most natural.
    2. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the bar, sit your hips mildly backward while slightly bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
4. With straight elbows, firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside shoulder width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position.
2. By extending (straightening) your hips and knees, stand upright with the bar, and rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion.
3. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips as far as your flexibility comfortably permits without letting the bar contact the bottom of the machine.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight, lower back flat, chest up, core braced, and the soles of your feet fully on the ground.
    2. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    3. The degree to which you can hinge at your hips and consequently angle your torso closer to horizontal will be affected by your hamstring flexibility. If you have the flexibility to hinge until the bar reaches the bottom of the machine, you can stop just before you reach that point. Otherwise, you can sit your hips back as far as you comfortably can while keeping your back flat and shins vertical.
4. Pull the bar up toward your upper abdomen by driving your elbows simultaneously backward and upward as you pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Keep your torso in a hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set. All the movement should occur from motion at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows while your lower body remains stationary.
    2. Continue keeping your core braced, lower back flat, and chest up.
    3. Allow your elbows naturally to flare out away from your sides in a manner that feels comfortable to you, which may result in your upper arms forming near a 45-degree angle with your torso toward the end of the lifting phase.
    4. You can aim to row the bar until it touches near your upper abdomen or is close to doing so, which will result in your elbows being behind your torso (or at least aligned with your torso) at the end of the lifting phase.
5. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. Continue maintaining the same degree of forward torso lean with your chest up and lower back flat, which should result in the bar not reaching the bottom of the machine.
    2. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another as your elbows move downward and forward while straightening.
    3. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be in clear control of the entire descent.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set.
7. Following your last rep, thrust your hips forward to stand upright with the bar before rotating the safety hooks toward the safety bars, and mildly bending your hips and knees to rerack the bar onto the safety bars.

While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a firm medicine ball on the ground.
    1. The ball should have a diameter that is large enough for you to situate both hands on top of it.
2. With the ball under your shoulders, position yourself with your palms, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight, and your knees are bent.
3. Place your hands on top of the ball with the heels of your hands (i.e., bases of your palms) firmly pressed into the ball and your fingers spread somewhat apart.
    1. The proper hand placement should allow you to feel stable on top of the ball without wrist discomfort during this exercise. Determining the precise hand placement that personally feels best to you with the specific ball you are using may require some trial and error.
4. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you, and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. Rather than rolling, the ball should remain stationary under your shoulders throughout the exercise.
    2. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    3. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
## Exercise technique
1. From this tall plank position, tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes throughout your set.
    1. Contracting your abs and glutes will help you keep your back in a mostly flat position with your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting your hips sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. This should let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
2. While keeping your torso rigid and your legs straight, bend your elbows to lower your chest in a controlled manner until it lightly touches the ball.
    1. Rather than excessively flaring your elbows out away from your sides, keep your elbows reasonably tucked by your sides to a degree that feels comfortable and natural to you as you descend.
    2. Without shrugging your shoulders up toward your ears, allow your shoulder blades to pull back together as you lower yourself, which will result in you having a “proud chest posture” by the time you contact the ball instead of having your shoulders rounded forward.
    3. While motion occurs at your elbows and shoulder girdles, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the set, so you should still be able to draw a straight line from your thighs through your torso at the bottom of the rep.
    4. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag from lower back arching or hike up from bending your hips.
    5. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent, rather than dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by pressing into the ball to lift your whole body, progressively straightening your elbows until you return to the tall plank position.
    1. You can emphasize driving the heels of your hands into the ball with the intent to push the ball down through the ground, which will correspondingly push you up.
    2. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart from each other naturally as you push up, such that they are near their neutral position (like when you are normally relaxed) by the time you have finished the lifting phase.
    3. Continue keeping your legs aligned with your torso as your hips and chest lift up in unison, which will still let you draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    4. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, you can bend your knees to kneel on the ground before rocking your hips back and releasing the ball.
## Description
This exercise can train your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) to a preferentially greater degree than a standard push-up while also training your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md), and [pec minor](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Minor%201905c6f170d88030b03dd3f99706ecb0.md).

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, adjust each pulley to a little higher than your head, and select your desired load at the two with stacks.
2. Based on your preference, leave the cables without any handle attachments or connect a D-handle attachment to each cable.
    1. Either option allows you to train your rear delts with essentially the same technique except for the specific grip you will use, so feel free to try out both and use whichever feels most comfortable to you.
3. After standing centered between the cables with your sides facing the weight stacks, take a step backward before side-stepping toward one cable.
4. With your arm that is opposite to the cable, reach across your body and firmly grasp the ball at the end of the cable (if you are not using any handle attachment) or the D-handle (if you are using a handle attachment).
5. Side step toward the other cable, and reach across your body to grasp it with your free hand.
6. Return to being centered between the cables with your arms crossed in front of your torso, with slightly bent elbows, as the pulleys are situated a little in front of you.
    1. In this position, your arms should resemble an “X-shape” with each other as your hands are above shoulder height in line with the resistance from the cables.
    2. Maintain slightly bent elbows throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Sweep your arms out and away from each other while driving them diagonally downward and backward.
    1. Move through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility permits, which should result in your elbows being slightly behind your shoulders or at least horizontally level with your shoulders at the end range.
    2. Strive to achieve a roughly even balance between sweeping horizontally outward and vertically downward.
    3. Keep your torso upright with your chest up throughout the set, while all the motion occurs from your arms moving at your shoulder joints.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your arms to move diagonally forward, upward, and in toward each other until they have crossed each other and returned to the starting position.
    1. When you set up appropriately, the angle of resistance from the cables will naturally guide your arms through the intended diagonal crossing path.
    2. You do not have to perform this movement with an extremely slow tempo, but you should avoid letting the cables abruptly yank your arms in toward each other.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After completing your last rep, set the cables back in the opposite way in which you set up initially. Side-step toward one pulley until the cable loses tension, then release it and walk over to the other pulley to do the same.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also training your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and two [rotator cuff](../Muscles/Rotator%20Cuff%201b95c6f170d880b3b0d8eab69c3a7683.md) muscles to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, connect a rope attachment to a cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
    1. As an alternative to using an adjustable cable station, you can perform this exercise on a seated cable row machine that allows you to connect a rope attachment.
2. Sit down on the ground with your feet positioned against the base of the cable station.
3. Lean forward at your hips and reach forward to grasp each end of the rope with your index fingers and the adjacent aspects of your hands contacting the flat surfaces of the attachment’s rubber stoppers.
    1. Wrap your thumbs over the rounded outer aspects of the stoppers.
4. While holding the rope with straight elbows, lean your torso back until you are sitting with an upright torso. If you do not feel tension from the cable, straighten your knees to scoot back away from the pulley until the weight stack separates and you feel resistance.
    1. The appropriate position should prompt you to feel tension from the cable in the starting position of every rep.
## Exercise technique
1. While bending your elbows and progressively spreading your hands apart, pull the rope backward and upward simultaneously until the middle of the rope is situated close to your face at approximately eye level.
    1. At the end of this motion, each elbow should be bent by a mildly greater than 90-degree angle with your arms resembling a double biceps flexing pose. Your upper arms and torso should also form a “T-shape” while your upper arms are approximately parallel with the ground and your palms are facing your shoulders.
    2. The cable should move in a diagonal motion that involves more horizontal motion than vertical motion.
    3. Your shoulder blades should naturally pull back together when you drive your elbows backward.
2. Reverse the motion by moving the cable forward and downward simultaneously as your hands come closer together, and your elbows straighten.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart naturally and move forward.
    2. You should finish in the starting position with your elbows straightened and arms stretched out in front of you.
    3. You do not have to perform this reversal phase with an extremely slow tempo, but you should actively control it the entire time rather than letting the cable abruptly pull your arms forward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While also meaningfully training your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), this exercise can effectively develop your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md) and [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), along with the [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Position a flat exercise bench centered underneath a Smith machine’s bar in a spot that will allow the bar to descend toward your throat or chin when lying down on the bench.
    1. Specifically how you should set up can be influenced by whether your Smith machine has sliding rails that are purely vertical or angled.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, place the side of the bench where you will place your feet on the side in which the bar will track slightly backward as it descends. This will result in the bottom of the rails being horizontally closer to your head than the top of the rails when lying down on the bench. An angled Smith machine will allow you to use a bar path that most closely resembles that of a barbell JM press.
    3. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which side of the bar you place your feet.
2. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to grasp it with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently.
    1. The ideal height allows you to unrack the bar while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together without requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    2. If the bar is situated too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart to lift the bar off the safety bars (on which the safety hooks that are attached to the bar rest). This can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    3. Some trial and error may be needed to find the best starting bar height for you.
3. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of JM press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section. Use these reps to determine the appropriate height of the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails under the bar) prior to re-racking the bar.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety stops to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descended by the end of the lowering phase of your JM press.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench, knees bent, and feet on the floor approximately shoulder-width apart. Position yourself so that the bar can finish above your throat or chin (based on your preference) at the bottom of the JM press.
    1. If your Smith machine has vertical slide rails, situate your chin or throat directly under the bar.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you can alternatively set up with your upper chest under the bar.
    3. With the fixed bar path from the Smith machine, it may be worthwhile to try scooting slightly forward or backward on the bench in between sets if the exercise feels a bit awkward with your initial positioning.
    4. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    5. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with a near shoulder-width overhand grip, resulting in your palms facing forward. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A shoulder-width grip is an appropriate starting point, but you can try mildly different grip widths over time to determine where you personally feel best. The proper grip width should allow your elbows, wrists, and shoulders to feel comfortable while emphasizing the triceps to a greater degree than your close grip bench press.
    2. The traditional technique for this exercise involves a thumbless grip with the thumbs placed on the same side of the bar as the other fingers. However, if you are new to this exercise, you have the option of wrapping your thumbs around the bar to fully enclose the bar with your hands, which can make it easier to hold the bar securely.
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
7. Assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting, like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Maintain the natural curvature of your lower back, like when you are normally standing upright. Regardless of whether you meaningfully arch your lower back when bench pressing, the JM press involves a mostly flat back position.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the safety bars by straightening your elbows before rotating the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion. After unracking it, hold the bar stationary for a moment before starting to lower it.
    1. Keep your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your throat or chin in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows. Keep your elbows higher than your chest (when viewed from the side) while flaring your elbows out about 45 degrees from your sides.
    1. Avoid letting your wrist cock back, which would point your palms away from your forearms. Rather, curl your wrists mildly to angle your palms closer toward your forearms while securely holding the bar.
    2. In contrast to a strict lying triceps extension, you will somewhat lower your elbows, but to a meaningfully lesser degree than with a close grip bench press.
    3. The degree to which your forearms are angled relative to the ground can indicate whether you are moving your elbows (through shoulder motion) appropriately. By the end of the lowering phase, your forearms should be closer to horizontal than vertical. If your forearms remain closer to vertical at the bottom, you are excessively lowering your elbows and performing too much of a pressing movement. If your forearms angle beyond horizontal (with your wrists lower than your elbows), you are keeping your elbows excessively high and performing an exercise closer to a strict triceps extension than is intended.
    4. The amount of elbow flare is similar to what you can use for a close grip bench press. Strive to reach the middle ground between 90 degrees of elbow flare (which would cause your upper arms to form a “T-shape” with your torso) and 0 degrees of elbow flare (which would result in your upper arms being completely parallel to your torso).
4. Continue lowering the bar until you have fully bent your elbows or until the bar is just about to contact your chin or throat.
    1. The end range can be determined by when your biceps contact your forearms, so what constitutes your personal end range can be influenced by the circumference of your arms.
    2. If the bar is about to touch your chin or throat before you have fully bent your elbows, you naturally can finish lowering the bar before achieving a full elbow bend.
5. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the bar up into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. Your elbows will move upward and inward during the lifting phase, but you can predominantly focus on straightening your elbows to lift the weight with your triceps.
    3. Uncurl your wrists while lifting the bar to maintain a secure grip.
6. Alternate between steps 3-5 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
    1. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second.
7. Rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars by flicking your wrists before bending your elbows to lower the safety hooks securely onto the safety bars.
## Description
While training the [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) and [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) to a lesser degree than a [close grip bench press](Close%20grip%20bench%20press%201a05c6f170d8807c9f16f226db24074d.md), this exercise can develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) particularly well.

## Setting up
1. Place a pair of furniture sliders on the ground hip-width apart from each other.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground, and situate the bottom of your heels on top of the sliders with your knees fully bent.
    1. You can rest the back of your head on the ground and leave your arms on the ground by your sides or in whichever position you prefer.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heels down into the sliders, squeezing your glutes, and tightening your abs.
    1. After performing this glute bridge motion, you should now be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    2. Focus on moving your hips and avoid arching your lower back excessively.
    3. As a cue for engaging your glutes, you can think about trying to hold onto a hundred-dollar bill by tightly squeezing it between your glutes.
2. Without bending your hips, move your feet forward by progressively straightening your knees in a controlled manner until they are almost fully straightened.
    1. Continue keeping your glutes squeezed, abs tensed, and pressure concentrated through your heels throughout the exercise.
    2. All the motion should occur from your shins moving at your knee joints, while you are still able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders.
    3. At the end of this lowering phase, your buttocks should just barely be above the ground.
    4. You do not have to perform this movement with an extremely slow tempo, but you should avoid letting your feet abruptly slide forward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by driving your heels toward your buttocks to bend your knees and pull the sliders backward.
    1. You should finish with your knees close to being fully bent as the sliders are vertically under your knees.
    2. If you experience a notably uncomfortable cramping sensation in your hamstrings when your knees are fully bent, you can stop bending your knees just before reaching that point.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to lower your buttocks to the ground by bending at your hips.
## Description
While statically engaging your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), this exercise can train all your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Hamstrings%201b95c6f170d88055a462c40b686f381a.md), which are assisted by your [gracilis](../Muscles/Gracilis%201925c6f170d880938681fbbe8f075831.md), [sartorius](../Muscles/Sartorius%201925c6f170d8801c8493cac115de0546.md), and [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md).

## Setting up
1. Fully lower the Smith machine’s safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) and position the bar near the height of your hands when standing with your arms at your sides.
2. Determine whether your machine has angled sliding rails, which will affect the direction you will face during the exercise and on which side of the bar you should subsequently place the object to create your deficit.
    1. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you should face the side in which the bar will track slightly backward when lifting it up to help the row feel most natural. Compared to the top of the rails, this will result in the bottom of the rails being farther in front of where you will place the object for your deficit, and then stand during the exercise.
    2. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face.
3. Position a sturdy object that you will use to create your deficit under the middle of the bar and slightly closer to the side of the bar on which you will stand.
    1. Objects you can use include a thick bumper plate, a deadlift block, and an aerobic step rated to withstand the combined loads of your bodyweight and the machine’s weight. With the flat surface facing up, you can also use a large diameter (e.g., 45lb (20kg)) cast iron weight plate for a smaller deficit or stack multiple plates for a larger deficit.
    2. Ideally, the object should be tall enough that you are able to achieve as close to a horizontal torso position as your flexibility permits without the bar reaching the bottom of the machine during your row. A 45lb (20kg) bumper plate or aerobic step without risers should be sufficiently tall for most lifters to accomplish this objective.
    3. Whichever object you select should be stable when you are standing with the soles of your feet fully on it in a near hip-width stance. Some people may not be able to situate both feet fully on one plate and can alternatively situate two plates next to each other to enable full foot contact.
4. Add weight plates of your desired load to the bar, and stand upright on the elevated object in a near hip-width stance with the middle of the bar above the middle of your feet.
5. With your arms pointing straight down toward the bar, sit your hips mildly backward while slightly bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
6. With straight elbows, firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside shoulder width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position.
2. By extending (straightening) your hips and knees, stand upright with the bar, and rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion.
3. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips as far as your flexibility comfortably permits
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight, lower back flat, chest up, core braced, and the soles of your feet fully on the elevated object.
    2. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    3. The degree to which you can hinge at your hips and consequently angle your torso closer to horizontal will be affected by your hamstring flexibility. You have achieved your fully bent-over position once you can no longer comfortably sit your hips back while keeping your back flat and shins vertical. With a sufficiently tall object you selected for your deficit, the bar should not reach the bottom of the machine in this position.
4. Pull the bar up toward your upper abdomen by driving your elbows simultaneously backward and upward as you pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Keep your torso in a hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set. All the movement should occur from motion at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows while your lower body remains stationary.
    2. Continue keeping your core braced, lower back flat, and chest up.
    3. Allow your elbows naturally to flare out away from your sides in a manner that feels comfortable to you, which may result in your upper arms forming near a 45-degree angle with your torso toward the end of the lifting phase.
    4. You can aim to row the bar until it touches near your upper abdomen or is close to doing so, which will result in your elbows being behind your torso (or at least aligned with your torso) at the end of the lifting phase.
5. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. Continue maintaining the same degree of forward torso lean with your chest up and lower back flat, which should result in the bar not reaching the bottom of the machine.
    2. During the lowering phase, your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another as your elbows move downward and forward while straightening.
    3. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be in clear control of the entire descent.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set.
7. Following your last rep, thrust your hips forward to stand upright with the bar before rotating the safety hooks toward the safety bars, and mildly bending your hips and knees to rerack the bar onto the safety bars.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. On the side of your body you are about to train, pick up one dumbbell and hold it by your side with your elbow straightened.
    1. Continue holding the dumbbell by your side throughout the exercise.
2. Approach a step or a sturdy object that can function as a step. You should be by a surface (e.g., handrail, wall, power rack) where you can place one hand to assist with maintaining your balance.
    1. Based on the equipment at your disposal, a variety of objects can serve as your step. Make sure the object can support your weight, will not move once you are on it, and allows you to lower your heel through the full range of motion your ankle mobility permits.
    2. As an alternative to a staircase’s bottom step, you may select a power rack’s bottom beam if the beam is sufficiently tall.
    3. Additionally, a calf raise block, aerobic step, deadlift block, or thick bumper plate can each be positioned near a wall or power rack for stability. Depending on your bodyweight, anchoring an aerobic step with weight on top of it may be required to prevent the step from tipping.
3. Place your free hand onto the nearby surface for balance assistance, and maintain this hand contact throughout the set.
    1. If you are using a surface that you can grasp (like a power rack) rather than a wall, do not grip it tightly.
4. Step onto the step with the front halves of your feet on the step while the back halves of your feet are hanging off the step.
5. While keeping your foot on the same side as the dumbbell on the step, lift your other foot off the step by bending that knee.
    1. Keep that foot off the step throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. With the leg that is standing on the step, push through the ball of your foot to raise your heel upward while keeping that side’s knee straight and your trunk upright.
    1. Only use your free hand for balance assistance as you avoid pushing down in a manner that can help you lift yourself upward.
    2. Once you have lifted your heel as high upward as your ankle mobility permits, you have finished the lifting phase. There is no need to pause at the top.
2. In a controlled manner, allow your heel to descend toward the ground through the full range of motion your calf flexibility permits while continuing to keep your working leg’s knee straight.
    1. Strive to lower your heel as far as you can below the ball of your foot to stretch your calf and train it the most effectively.
    2. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in your calf at the bottom, you likely are not descending through your full range of motion.
    3. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid quickly dropping down and trying to bounce out of the bottom into the next rep.
    4. You can optionally pause in the bottom position for a brief period of time (e.g., 1-2 seconds).
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat this exercise with your other side.
    1. If you ever feel that your foot is starting to slide down the step, you can return your free leg’s foot to the step for a moment to help you scoot your working leg’s foot forward onto the step before resuming your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop both your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md) while simultaneously improving calf flexibility through loaded stretching.

## Setting up
1. Place a dumbbell on the ground next to the side of a flat exercise bench (or a sturdy object of similar height).
    1. If your dumbbell has flat sides, you can position the dumbbell with one end on the ground and its handle directed vertically, resulting in one end remaining off the ground.
2. Sit down on the ground with the side of one of your hips directly next to the dumbbell and your upper back in contact with the bench.
3. Position your feet out in front of you with your soles flat on the floor, hip-width apart, toes pointing forward, and knees bent by a little greater than 90 degrees.
    1. The optimal degree of knee bend should allow your feet to feel stable while being firmly planted on the ground throughout the set. It is normally appropriate to position your feet far enough back that your knees will be bent by approximately 90 degrees at the top of your hip thrust. From this placement, you can adjust specifically where you situate your feet based on your preference.
4. Move the dumbbell onto the crease of your hips in a controlled manner using both hands. Based on your preference, you can situate the weight centered along the crease of both hips, or you can position one flat end of the dumbbell on the uppermost thigh of what will be your working leg.
    1. If you position the dumbbell onto only one side, the handle should be angled diagonally upward and backward, and you can hold it in place with your closer hand while placing your other hand across the bench for additional stability during the set.
    2. If you position the dumbbell across both hips, the handle should be horizontal, and you can use both hands to keep the weight in contact with the front of your hips throughout the set.
    3. Neither set-up approach is inherently better than the other, so feel free to try both out and continue using whichever one feels best to you.
5. Tuck your chin mildly toward your chest, and maintain this neck position throughout the exercise.
6. While leaving one foot on the ground, lift the other foot off the ground by marching that side’s thigh up.
    1. You have the option of keeping your free leg’s knee bent or straight. Either position for the free leg is similarly viable, so you can go with whichever you prefer, but keeping the knee straight may make the exercise mildly more challenging compared to keeping it bent.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
2. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heel into the ground and squeezing your glute.
    1. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your thigh through your hip to your shoulder (on the side of your body with the foot contacting the ground).
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid arching your lower back excessively.
    3. Strive to keep your hip bones level on each side, rather than letting your free leg’s hip bone drop down or hike up.
    4. If you wish to do so, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment, which may assist with feeling your glute engage during this exercise.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your hip mobility comfortably permits without rounding or excessively arching your lower back.
    1. Some people can descend all the way down until they lightly contact the ground with their glutes, but you can prioritize lowering through the range in which you can achieve through hip motion rather than lower back motion.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise will predominantly develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) while also training your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your back and head on a flat bench, with your legs straight and feet together.
    1. As an alternative to a bench, you can lie down on the ground with something sturdy (like a couch or bed) behind you that you can grasp for stability. If you select this option, you can optionally place an exercise mat under where you will lie for comfort.
2. Reach behind your head and grasp the bottom of the bench’s pad with both hands.
    1. If you opted to lie down on the ground, you can alternatively reach behind you and grasp whatever sturdy object you are positioned against.
    2. Continue holding onto the bench (or alternative object) for stability throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Tighten your abdominal muscles to press your lower back down into the ground. Simultaneously lift your legs up off the ground until your thighs are approximately vertical while keeping your knees mostly straight.
    1. Strive to keep your knees as close to straight as your hamstring flexibility comfortably permits.
2. While keeping your legs directed straight up, lift your buttocks, lower back, and middle back off the floor.
    1. You should now be bearing your weight predominantly through your upper back.
3. In a controlled manner, allow your legs to arc forward and downward while keeping your buttocks and most of your back off the bench until your thighs are about to contact the bench.
    1. In contrast to the lifting phase of this exercise that you perform during steps 1 and 2, this lowering phase should be a continuous movement as you lower your legs back together. Correspondingly, your buttocks should only contact the bench when your legs are angled mostly forward rather than upward.
    2. At the bottom of this movement, your legs should be directed straight forward with your back contacting the bench.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should strive to control the descent to the best of your ability rather than just dropping down abruptly.
    4. As you descend further, controlling the movement will become progressively more challenging.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise will primarily train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md), with assistance from your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Position the Smith machine’s bar slightly below the height of your hands when standing with your arms at your sides.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the bar, and stand upright in a near hip-width stance with the middle of the bar just in front of your legs.
    1. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you can position yourself to face the side in which the bar will track slightly backward when lifting it up (which results in the bottom of the rails being farther in front of you than the top of the rails). Facing this way will help the shrug feel most natural.
    2. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the bar, sit your hips mildly backward while slightly bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
4. With straight elbows, firmly grasp the bar with a near shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. By extending (straightening) your hips and knees, stand upright with the bar, and rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion.
3. Slightly hinge at your hips by sitting your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your lower back flat or mildly arched rather than rounding it or excessively arching it.
    2. Quickly proceed to the next step as soon as you finish this step.
4. Forcefully thrust your hips forward while straightening your knees to generate momentum from your lower body. Simultaneously shrug your shoulders upward through your available range of motion to lift the bar upward while keeping your elbows straight.
    1. The hip drive motion, which is similar to the lockout of a deadlift, will bring your torso into a vertical position. Refrain from leaning back through excessive lower back arching, which can be easier to avoid if you think about squeezing your glutes.
    2. While you are intentionally using momentum to help your upper traps lift the weight, you should not be “cheating” to the extent that you feel out of control.
    3. Throughout the exercise, look straight ahead to keep your neck near a neutral position.
    4. As a cue, you can think about driving your shoulders up toward your earlobes.
5. Allow your shoulders to descend fully in a controlled manner to lower the bar while keeping your torso upright and legs stationary.
    1. Your muscles are noticeably stronger during the lowering phase of an exercise compared to the lifting phase, so “cheating” during the lifting phase allows your upper traps to experience greater loading during the more controlled lowering phase.
    2. At the bottom, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the machine’s weight can provide.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the weight abruptly yank you downward. If you are unable to control the lowering phase to any reasonable degree, you are likely using a weight that is excessively heavy relative to your current ability.
6. Alternate between steps 3-5 until you have completed your set and are ready to re-rack the bar.
    1. Following your last rep, rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars, and mildly bend your hips and knees to rerack the bar onto the safety bars.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on a bench with an upright torso while holding the dumbbells by your sides with straight elbows as your palms are facing in toward your sides.
    1. You can opt to sit down on a seated bench with your back resting against the back support, or you can sit on a flat bench without any back support.
    2. While you do not necessarily need to have an exaggerated “proud chest” posture with your shoulders fully pulled back, avoid sitting with your shoulders rolled forward into a slouched upper back position.
## Exercise technique
1. Raise your arms out and away from your sides in an arcing motion while keeping your elbows straight.
    1. Keep your elbows straight throughout the exercise.
    2. You should resemble making a snow angel with your arms as they move straight outward rather than forward.
2. As your arms approach being parallel to the ground, point your palms forward and continue sweeping your arms up overhead through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. While you raise your arms through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blades to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    2. If you have the mobility to do so comfortably, you can finish the lifting phase once your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling. However, if you start feeling shoulder discomfort in the fully overhead position, you can simply move through the greatest range of motion that is comfortable to you.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering the dumbbells toward your sides in a smooth arcing motion.
    1. As your arms become approximately parallel to the ground, turn your palms down, which will result in your palms facing in toward your sides once your arms are by your sides again.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the dumbbells swing down in an uncontrolled fashion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While still meaningfully training your [lateral](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md) and [front](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) delts, this variation biases your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md) to a greater degree than standard lateral raises.

## Setting up
1. Place a stability ball (which is also known as a Swiss ball or physio ball) on the ground, and optionally place an exercise mat or cushion behind it for comfort.
    1. Ideally, select a ball with a diameter exceeding your shoulder width.
2. With your knees hip width apart, kneel with the ball in front of you as your torso and thighs are fully upright.
    1. From this tall kneeling position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to your knees when viewed from the side.
3. Place your palms on the ball with straight elbows, while positioning the ball as far in front of you while keeping your torso fully upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Keep your glutes squeezed and your core braced throughout the set to help you maintain a rigid back position.
2. Slowly lean your torso and thighs forward as one unit as you let the ball roll forward and your arms angle forward. Keep your elbows straight and torso rigidly braced as you avoid letting your lower back arch throughout the set.
    1. Only roll the ball as far forward as you can while maintaining a flat lower back position and keeping your knees, hips, and shoulders fully aligned when viewed from the side.
    2. Keeping your lower back flat will become progressively more difficult as you roll out further, so you can determine your range of motion based on your current ability.
    3. If you are new to this exercise, a rather short range may be appropriate. If you have the strength to do so with proper form, you can finish rolling out when your head is almost contacting the ball.
    4. The forward movement of the arms is the same type of shoulder motion that would occur when lifting your arms straight forward and up overhead.
    5. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag or your ribs flare, as this can arch your lower back. Continuing to squeeze your glutes and tighten your abs will help you keep your lower back flat.
    6. Keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by driving your arms backward to roll the ball back toward the starting position while lifting your torso and thighs up together.
    1. Continue avoiding letting your hips bend or arching your lower back.
    2. You should still be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. At the end of this step, your torso and thighs should be fully upright.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While also dynamically training your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), this exercise can statically train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that situates the handles level with your lower chest once you are seated.
    1. This is an appropriate starting point for most people, but feel free to try out different settings to determine what personally feels best to your body.
    2. The seat height that is ideal for you as an individual should allow your shoulders to feel comfortable throughout the exercise while simultaneously allowing you to feel meaningful tension in your chest.
    3. If the seat is too low (placing the handles near shoulder level or above), some lifters may be more likely to feel shoulder discomfort from having to flare their elbows outward excessively.
    4. If the seat is excessively high (placing the handles near your abdomen), the exercise may feel awkward and be suboptimal for developing the chest.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit down on the machine’s seat with your back and the back of your hip bones snugly against the back pad.
    1. Depending on the specific machine model you are using and what feels most stable to you, you can place your feet flat on the floor or on a foot bar.
    2. You can optionally rest your head against the back pad if it is tall enough, or you can simply keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead.
4. With your palms facing down, elbows bent, and hands moderately outside shoulder width, firmly grasp the handles. Position your elbows directly behind the handles, resulting in your elbows being level with the handles when viewed from the side.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. Aligning your elbows directly behind (rather than being above or below) the handles will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare during this exercise, provided that you selected a proper seat height.
    3. If your machine has sufficiently long handles, you may be able to adjust your grip width with different hand placements. Placing your hands moderately outside shoulder width can work well for many people, but you can try out different grip widths to determine where you personally feel best.
5. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. While keeping your elbows level with your wrists when viewed from the side, press the handles forward until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows forward and inward in an arcing manner.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together, back snugly against the back pad, and feet stationary.
3. Reverse the movement by allowing the handles to move backward in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. At the end range, you can lightly tap the machine’s arms against the stoppers behind them. A gentle tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows and wrists aligned as they remain level with the handles when viewed from the side.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s weight swing your arms abruptly back in an uncontrolled fashion.
    4. If your machine allows you to train through the full range of motion that your mobility enables, it is normal to feel a painless stretching sensation in your chest and/or the front of your shoulders at the end range.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) with a focus on its middle and lower regions while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a sturdy object (such as a thick bumper plate or ideally an aerobic step) that you will use as a step onto the floor, somewhat in front of the Smith machine’s bar.
    1. You can use a range of different heights for your stepping surface, but selecting an object that is near four inches (10cm) high (which is a typical height of many aerobic steps without additional risers) can be an appropriate starting point.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you will face and put the step in front of the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends (which results in the bottom of the rails being farther in front of you than the top of the rails).
    3. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face, so it does not matter which side you place the step.
    4. Strive to place your step far enough in front of the bar that you can keep your torso fairly upright when performing your split squat with one foot on the step, which may take a bit of trial and error if you are new to this exercise.
    5. Due to the fixed bar path of the Smith machine, situating the step directly under the bar would require you to adopt a bent-over torso position during this exercise.
    6. When using a sufficiently wide object (such as an aerobic step) as a step, you can simply place the step so that it is centered with the Smith machine’s bar.
    7. If what you use as a step does not have a large enough surface area for you to stand on it in a hip-width stance with both of your soles fully in contact with the step, situate your step slightly toward the side on which you initially will place your foot on the step.
    8. The appropriate step placement will allow you to perform your split squat with your elevated foot fully in contact with the step while your feet are hip-width apart from each other.
2. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a few finger widths below the height of your collarbone.
    1. The ideal starting height should allow you to position the bar on your upper back and un-rack it in a stable position with the soles of your feet fully on the ground.
    2. If you later need to rise up onto the balls of your feet and lift your heels off the ground in order to unrack the bar, you initially set it excessively high.
3. Position the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) so that they are slightly below the height of the bar when your rear knee taps the ground at the end of the lowering phase of your split squat.
    1. To find this point for your body, you can perform a rep or two of the split squat with the unloaded bar as described in the “exercise technique” section, but you can initially put the safety stops a little below the top of your hip bones when standing upright as an approximation.
4. Add your desired weight to the bar and face the center of the bar with approximately a hip-width stance.
5. Grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
6. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees to then walk under the bar and situate it on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    2. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
    5. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a bar on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to tighten your upper back muscles, and unrack it by starting to stand up as you straighten your knees.
2. After the bar rests fully on your upper back rather than the safety bars, rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars with a slight wrist flick before standing fully upright with the bar.
3. Step up onto the step with the entirety of your sole in contact with the step while leaving your other foot on the ground.
    1. If you positioned your step closer toward one side of your body (due to using a step with a small surface area), you will step up with the foot aligned with the step, while you can use either side if your step is centered.
    2. The knee on the side of your elevated foot should be mildly bent once on the step.
4. Shift your bodyweight into your elevated foot before taking a fairly long step backward with your other foot and contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. To shift your bodyweight into your elevated foot, you can lean your torso mildly forward by hinging at your hip as you bend that side’s knee slightly more.
    2. Once you step back and resume transferring some of your weight into your rear leg, you can return to keeping your torso in an upright position.
    3. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to split squats.
    4. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    5. Keep the entire sole of your elevated foot firmly planted on the step and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    6. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
5. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until your rear leg’s kneecap is just barely above the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the step.
    2. While the forefoot of your rear leg will stay in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
6. Hold the split squat position for your target duration as you remain completely stationary with your rear knee hovering above the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your knees aligned with your feet, the sole of your front foot fully on the step, and your torso upright.
    2. Since this is a static exercise, you will track how many seconds you hold the split squat rather than reps.
7. While keeping both of your feet planted, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
8. Re-rack the bar by bending at your hips and knees as you rotate the safety hooks onto the safety bars and return the bar to resting on the safety bars.
9. After you have sufficiently rested, repeat the exercise while switching which leg is in the forward position on top of the step.
    1. Since your rear leg can be meaningfully engaged during a split squat hold, it is recommended to rest before performing your next set with your sides switching positions.
    2. If you wish, you can alternatively perform your sets continuously without reracking the bar and resting, but fatigue may interfere with your performance of the second set if you switch lead legs without any rest.
## Description
This exercise will primarily train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad muscles](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md).
