## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat’s back pad to a position that aligns your knees with the machine’s pivot point while sitting up against the back pad with your thighs resting on the seat.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to its furthest back position that allows you to begin each rep with the greatest knee bend you can achieve.
    1. Certain machines can be used for leg extensions or hamstring curls based on how the lever arm is positioned.
3. Adjust the shin pad to a position that places it slightly above the front of your ankles on the lowest aspect of your shins when seated with your legs behind the shin pad with your knees bent.
    1. Adjusting this setting exclusively moves the shin pad without moving the lever arm, in contrast to step 2, where the machine lever arm and shin pad move together.
4. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin and sit down on its seat with your lower shins behind the shin pad, knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point, and back resting against the back pad.
    1. With the appropriate positioning, it should be comfortable for you to have your knees bent.
    2. Your knees are aligned with the machine’s pivot point if you can draw a straight line through the center of both knees to the pivot point.
5. Adjust the thigh pad to press down snugly against your lower thighs.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Through a controlled kicking motion, progressively extend (straighten) both knees to lift the shin pad up until you have fully straightened your knees.
    1. While you do not lift the weight in an intentionally slow manner, avoid kicking up in an uncontrolled jerky motion.
    2. As your lower legs move through motion at your knees, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set as your thighs remain in contact with the seat.
3. Fully bend one knee to pull that side’s leg away from the shin pad while continuing to keep your other leg against the pad.
4. With the leg still in contact with the shin pad, allow your knee to bend in a controlled manner to lower the shin pad until you have returned to the starting position with your knee bent as much as the machine permits.
    1. There is no need to use an extremely slow lowering tempo, but you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting it abruptly swing your lower leg down.
    2. Keep your free leg’s knee bent as you avoid touching the shin pad with your free leg throughout the lowering phase.
5. Repeatedly perform steps 2-4 as you alternate each rep which leg you keep in contact with the shin pad during steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you wish to do so, you can alternatively complete one set where you perform the lowering phase of each rep exclusively with one side before resting, and then complete another set where you perform the lowering phase of every rep with your opposite side.
    2. During each rep, continue to move the shin pad up with both legs as you control it on the way down with only one leg.
## Description

    2. If you wish to do so, you can alternatively perform your sets continuously without reracking the bar and resting, but fatigue may interfere with the performance of the next set if you do not rest at all between them.

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Optionally place a full diameter weight plate (like a thick bumper plate or a 45lb (20kg) plate with a flat surface facing up) slightly in front of the pulley and just to one side of the pulley.
    1. While not required, standing on a mildly elevated object with your non-working leg can help provide clearance above the ground for your working leg’s foot.
    2. The appropriate positioning of the plate (or a viable alternative like an aerobic step or deadlift block) should allow your working leg’s foot to hang fully off it while your knees are about hip width apart and pointing straight forward. The plate should also be sufficiently far in front of the pulley that you can experience resistance from the cable in the starting position of each rep when your feet are level with each other. If you situate the plate excessively close to the pulley, you will lose tension from the cable at the start of each rep when your working leg’s knee is straight.
3. Securely attach an ankle cuff just above the ankle of the leg you will train. Position the cuff so that one of its attachment rings is directed straight forward.
4. While facing the cable station in a hip-width stance, stand in front of the pulley with your non-working leg’s foot on the plate and your working leg’s foot directly in front of the pulley.
    1. With the appropriate placement of the plate, your working leg’s foot should be slightly further in front of your other foot in this position.
5. Bend over and connect the cable to your cuff’s attachment ring before standing mostly upright with your non-working side’s knee slightly bent.
    1. It will be easiest to connect the cable when your working leg is close enough to the pulley that the cable does not provide resistance when connecting it.
6. With your torso mildly leaned forward at your hips, grasp part of the cable station (with your fingers away from the weight stack) with your hands.
    1. Continue holding part of the cable station from now onward for additional stability.
7. Take a small step backward with your working side’s foot until your feet are aligned with each other and you feel resistance from the cable.
    1. If you do not feel resistance from the cable in this position, you should move the plate you are using as a step mildly further back away from the pulley. Then resume setting up.
8. Straighten your non-working side’s knee to lift your other foot off the ground without letting the cable pull your working leg forward.
    1. In this starting position, your hip bones and knees should be symmetrically level with each other.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to your working side’s leg.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your toes upward and back toward your shin by moving at your ankle. Maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankle in the same position in which it would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heel up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankle in this position can increase your hamstring curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
2. Drive your heel toward your buttock by bending your knee while keeping your thigh fixed in a vertical position.
    1. Strive to bend your knee through your full comfortable range of motion, which should result in you bending your knee by at least 90 degrees.
    2. If you experience a notable cramping sensation in your hamstrings when your knee is fully bent, you can stop the lifting phase just before the point where your hamstrings may cramp.
    3. While your lower leg arcs backward and upward through knee motion, aim to keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set. This will involve keeping your hip bones level with each other and avoiding letting your knee swing forward or backward via hip motion.
3. Reverse the movement by allowing your knee to extend progressively in a controlled manner until it has fully straightened.
    1. As you let your lower leg arc downward and forward in line with the cable’s resistance, continue keeping the rest of your body stationary as your thighs remain symmetrically aligned.
    2. There is no need to use an extremely slow tempo, but you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the cable abruptly swing your lower leg down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Place an inflated stability ball (which is also known as a Swiss ball or physio ball) on the ground.
2. Sit down on the center of the ball with your torso upright, knees bent, and feet on the floor.
3. Walk your feet forward while leaning your torso backward and rolling your buttocks closer to the front of the ball until your back is resting on top of the ball. Simultaneously allow your back to arch naturally.
    1. Your back and the back of your hip bones should be supported by the ball.
    2. After walking forward, your knees should be bent by about 90 degrees with your feet flat on the floor.
4. Place the fingertips of each hand lightly in contact with the sides of the back of your head as your upper arms and elbows are directed out away from your sides.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
    2. If you wish to reduce the difficulty of this exercise, you can alternatively cross your arms across your chest.
## Exercise technique
1. Curl your spine as you pull the bottom of your ribs toward the tops of your hip bones in a controlled manner while tightening your abs and lifting your upper back off the ball.
    1. Once you feel that you can no longer curl your lower and middle back while keeping your hip bones and lower back against the ball, you have reached your end range. In this position, your shoulder blades should be above the ball.
    2. To train your abs dynamically, you should be intentionally rounding your back, since this motion is performed by contraction of your abs.
    3. You can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the middle of your chest, and you are trying to point that closer toward the middle point between your knees.
    4. Keep your feet planted on the ground and your lower body stationary throughout the set.
    5. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
2. Reverse the movement by uncurling your back in a controlled manner as you lower your upper back to the ball.
    1. After transitioning from a rounded position to a flat position, allow your lower back to arch around the ball.
    2. The imaginary laser beam shooting out from your chest should angle progressively backward as you let your ribs flare away from your hip bones.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should actively control it the entire time rather than dropping down in an abrupt fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md), which is assisted by your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md).

## Setting up
1. If you are using an adjustable incline bench, position it in the fully upright setting. Otherwise, proceed to the next step.
    1. You can interchangeably use an adjustable bench that is positioned fully upright or a seated bench that is permanently fixed in an upright position.
    2. Alternatively, you can use a bench that is permanently fixed in a flat position. This will preclude you from resting your back against the bench, but otherwise allow you to use the same technique that the exercise involves when using back support.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and hold them with your palms facing in toward your sides.
    1. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
3. Sit down on a seated bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your lower thighs without leaning back onto the back rest.
    1. To move the dumbbells into the proper position, you can situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up against the end of the bench, and you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
    2. When seated, your elbows should be tucked by your sides with your palms facing in toward each other.
4. March your thighs up one at a time as you lift the dumbbells up near your shoulders with your elbows bent. Simultaneously lean back to situate your back against the bench.
    1. After doing so, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder-width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. Hold the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip you will maintain throughout your set.
5. With your elbows and upper arms in front of your torso, direct your palms straight backward as your wrists are in front of your shoulders.
    1. Your forearms should be in a vertical position, and your wrists should be stacked over your elbows.
    2. In contrast to a standard dumbbell overhead press, your elbows should not be flared out away from your sides.
6. While looking straight ahead with your neck near a neutral position, keep your chest up in a “proud chest” posture, rather than letting your shoulders and upper back round forward into a hunched position.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. While simultaneously flaring your elbows out away from your sides and rotating your palms forward, press the dumbbells upward.
    1. At the top of the press, the bony bumps on the back of your elbows should be pointing out away from your sides (rather than forward), your palms should be facing forward, and your elbows should be straight with your arms fully overhead.
    2. Rather than turning the exercise into a segmented movement, strive to have the outward elbow flare and palm rotation fluidly occur at the same rate at which you are driving your elbows upward.
    3. Throughout your set, continue keeping your feet flat on the floor along with your buttocks and upper back in contact with the bench.
    4. Keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering the dumbbells while simultaneously moving your elbows in front of your torso and rotating your palms backward.
    1. Move your elbows forward and rotate your palms backward progressively throughout the lowering phase, rather than just performing these motions during the initial part of the descent and lowering the dumbbells straight down in front of your body. This should result in you starting to lower the dumbbells with your elbows predominantly pointing out to the sides and your elbows only being fully in front of your shoulders at the bottom of the rep.
    2. Fully return to the starting position by lowering the dumbbells as far as you can while keeping your wrists in a straight position stacked over your elbows as your forearms remain vertical.
    3. You do not have to lower the dumbbells with an extremely slow tempo, but you should avoid letting them drop down in an uncontrolled fashion.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the dumbbells down in the opposite way in which you initially set up.
    1. After the lowering phase of the last rep, direct your palms in toward each other, march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and lower the dumbbells onto your thighs before standing up with them.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Anchor a long looped elastic band of your desired tension level around the center of a pull-up bar.
    1. To anchor the band, initially drape it over the bar, loop one end through the middle of the other, and pull that end until it is taut.
    2. If the bar is out of reach when standing on the ground, initially position yourself on an aerobic step, sturdy box, or bumper plate to bring the bar within reach. Then set the band and grasp the bar during the next step. Position the step slightly behind the bar rather than directly underneath it, so you can keep your legs straight during the exercise without contacting the step.
    3. If your bar has rough knurling rather than a smooth surface, anchoring the band directly around the bar can increase the risk of the band tearing over time. Placing a fat grip attachment or hand towel around the bar before anchoring the band can help prevent the bar with knurling from tearing the band.
    4. Before using it, inspect the band to confirm there are no small tears, as a small tear can quickly become a full tear when stretching the band.
2. Stand under the bar, and pull the band down with both arms.
    1. Each side of the band should be flat without any twists.
3. March up one leg and step into the band with the middle of your foot snugly against the bottom end of the band’s loop before lowering your foot while straightening your leg. Alternatively, you can bend one knee and loop the band around your upper shin.
    1. Since the band’s tension increases as you stretch it, situating the band around your foot with a straight knee will provide greater assistance compared to if you situate the band around your upper shin with your knee bent.
    2. If your pull-up bar is not tall enough to keep your foot from contacting the ground at the bottom of the rep while keeping your leg straight, looping the band around your upper shin will be a better option. Otherwise, you can select whichever approach best suits your preference while providing the level of assistance you prefer.
    3. With either setup, the band should feel secure rather than feeling like it may slide around during the exercise.
4. Reach overhead and firmly grasp the pull-up bar with your palms facing forward (an overhand grip) and your hands well outside shoulder width.
    1. Positioning your hands about 50% further apart than your shoulder width is appropriate, but a wide grip can encompass a range of grip widths, and specifically, how wide you grasp the bar is up to your preference.
    2. What is considered a wide grip to you can also be influenced by the specific grip width you use for your standard pull-up. For instance, with a wide grip, place your index finger on the bar just outside where you would otherwise place your little finger when performing a standard pull-up.
    3. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    4. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palm (rather than at the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your skin in an uncomfortable way and increases the risk of tearing a callus.
5. Hang on the bar with your elbows straightened. If you are standing on a step with the band under your foot, step off the step and let both legs hang straight down toward the ground. If you have the band around your upper shin, lift your other foot off the ground by bending that knee and keeping both knees bent throughout the exercise.
    1. You can optionally situate your other leg (that was not initially contacting the band) within the band if you wish to do so.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to assume a “proud chest” that is angled slightly upward.
    1. Maintain this “proud chest” posture throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides while progressively bending your elbows.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows naturally will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows being bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion that their bodies enable.
    3. Rather than swinging your legs, statically keep them in a similar position throughout the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your elbows straightened and arms fully overhead.
    1. You do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, you can return one foot onto the ground or step, shift your weight into step/ground, march your other leg up and out of the band, and release the bar.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat’s back pad to a position that aligns your knees with the machine’s pivot point while sitting up against the back pad with your thighs resting on the seat.
2. Adjust the machine’s lever arm (that will align with your shins) to its furthest back position that allows you to begin each rep with the greatest knee bend you can achieve.
    1. Certain machines can be used for leg extensions or hamstring curls based on how the lever arm is positioned.
3. Adjust the shin pad to a position that places it slightly above the front of your ankles on the lowest aspect of your shins when seated with your legs behind the shin pad with your knees bent.
    1. Adjusting this setting exclusively moves the shin pad without moving the lever arm, in contrast to step 2, where the machine lever arm and shin pad move together.
4. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
5. Sit down on the seat with your lower shins behind the shin pad, knees aligned with the machine’s pivot point, and back resting against the back pad.
    1. With the appropriate positioning, it should be comfortable for you to have your knees bent.
    2. Your knees are aligned with the machine’s pivot point if you can draw a straight line through the center of both knees to the pivot point.
6. Adjust the thigh pad to press down snugly against your lower thighs.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Through a controlled kicking motion, progressively extend (straighten) both knees to lift the shin pad up until you have fully straightened your knees.
    1. While you do not lift the weight in an intentionally slow manner, avoid kicking up in an uncontrolled jerky motion.
    2. As your lower legs move through motion at your knees, you should keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set as your thighs remain in contact with the seat.
3. Fully bend one knee to pull that side’s leg away from the shin pad while continuing to keep your other leg against the pad.
4. With the leg still in contact with the shin pad, allow your knee to bend in a controlled manner to lower the shin pad until you have returned to the starting position with your knee bent as much as the machine permits.
    1. There is no need to use an extremely slow lowering tempo, but you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting it abruptly swing your lower leg down.
    2. Keep your free leg’s knee bent as you avoid touching the shin pad with your free leg throughout the lowering phase.
5. Repeatedly perform steps 2-4 as you alternate each rep which leg you keep in contact with the shin pad during steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
    1. If you wish to do so, you can alternatively complete one set where you perform the lowering phase of each rep exclusively with one side before resting, and then complete another set where you perform the lowering phase of every rep with your opposite side.
    2. During each rep, continue to move the shin pad up with both legs as you control it on the way down with only one leg.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all four of your [quad muscles](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md), including your [rectus femoris](../Muscles/Rectus%20Femoris%201925c6f170d880f080b7cda6f5f3f0ee.md), which may not be trained as effectively by most squat, leg press, and lunge variations.

## Setting up
1. Lie down on your back with your knees bent to about 90 degrees.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can lie down on an exercise mat.
2. With straight elbows, raise both arms straight up toward the ceiling as your elbows and wrists are vertically stacked above your shoulders.
    1. You can point your palms in toward each other.
3. While keeping your knees bent to about 90 degrees, march both legs up until your knees are vertically stacked above your hips.
    1. In this position, your thighs should be perpendicular to the ground, and your shins should be parallel to the ground.
4. Based on your preference, you can keep your head resting on the ground, or you can slightly tuck your chin toward your chest to lift your head just barely off the ground.
    1. Lifting your head slightly off the ground can mildly increase the difficulty and allow you to train your neck muscles statically, but doing so is optional. If you opt to lift your head just off the ground, keep it there throughout your set. Otherwise, continue resting your head on the ground during the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forceful slap.
2. Press your lower back lightly into the floor to flatten your lower back, and continue doing so throughout your set.
    1. This can prompt you to feel your abs contract further as they keep the bottom of your ribs pulled down toward your hip bones.
    2. It is the opposite of if you were to arch your lower back, which would flare the bottom of your ribs away from your hip bones.
    3. If you are relaxed while lying down, your lower back naturally has a mild arch, allowing you to slide a hand between the ground and your lower back. When you use your abs to flatten your lower back, there should be no space between your lower back and the ground, preventing you from sliding a hand between them.
    4. Before proceeding to the next step, you can optionally try sliding one hand between your lower back and the ground. Being unable to slide your hand under your lower back confirms that you have effectively flattened it. If you choose to do so, lift your arm to the starting position before beginning the next step.
3. Sweep arms backward and downward while simultaneously straightening your legs and lowering them toward the ground.
    1. As you lower your arms and legs, you will have to continue bracing your core to prevent your lower back from arching up off the ground.
    2. Strive to move your arms and legs at the same rate through the full range of motion that you can while keeping your lower back flat against the ground.
    3. With sufficient core control, you can finish with your arms and legs parallel to the ground as they are fully straightened. From this position, you can gently tap the ground with your hands and heels simultaneously. If your lower back starts arching before this point, shorten the range of motion to what you can perform while maintaining a flat lower back.
    4. All the movement should occur from your shoulders, hips, and knees as your spine remains motionless.
    5. Move slowly and deliberately throughout your set, focusing on high-quality technique at every degree of motion.
4. Reverse the movement by lifting your arms and legs up to return to the starting position.
    1. Since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the lowering phase, no motion should occur at your lower back as you continue bracing your core.
    2. While keeping your elbows straight, bend your knees as you march your thighs up to finish with your knees bent to approximately 90 degrees.
    3. At the top, both of your knees should be stacked vertically above your hips, and your arms should be vertically stacked above your shoulders.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) to maintain a rigid back position as you refine your ability to move through your hips and shoulders with a stable trunk.

To do so, first sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and simultaneously rocking the dumbbells mildly backward. Move your elbows forward and rotate your palms backward progressively throughout the lowering phase, rather than just performing these motions during the initial part of the descent and lowering the dumbbells straight down in front of your body. This should result in you starting to lower the dumbbells with your elbows predominantly pointing out to the sides and your elbows only being fully in front of your shoulders at the bottom of the rep.

    1. After the lowering phase of the last rep, lower the dumbbells to your sides as you straighten your elbows and swing your elbows back by your sides.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).
2a25c6f170d880fa81aefd1874c63d76:
## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and stand upright in a near hip-width stance. Hold the dumbbells by your sides with straight elbows as your palms are facing in toward your sides.
    1. While you do not necessarily need to have an exaggerated “proud chest” posture with your shoulders fully pulled back, avoid standing with your shoulders rolled forward into a slouched upper back position.
## Exercise technique
1. Raise your arms out and away from your sides in an arcing motion while keeping your elbows straight.
    1. Throughout the exercise, keep your elbows and legs straight while maintaining an upright torso.
    2. You should resemble making a snow angel with your arms as they move straight outward rather than forward.
2. As your arms approach being parallel to the ground, point your palms forward and continue sweeping your arms up overhead through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. While you raise your arms through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blades to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    2. If you have the mobility to do so comfortably, you can finish the lifting phase once your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling. However, if you start feeling shoulder discomfort in the fully overhead position, you can simply move through the greatest range of motion that is comfortable to you.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering the dumbbells toward your sides in a smooth arcing motion.
    1. As your arms become approximately parallel to the ground, turn your palms down, which will result in your palms facing in toward your sides once your arms are by your sides again.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the dumbbells swing down in an uncontrolled fashion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While still meaningfully training your [lateral](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md) and [front](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) delts, this variation biases your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md) to a greater degree than standard lateral raises.
2a35c6f170d8800c9b3de01d90acbc44:
## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, and stand centered between its handles in a near hip-width stance with your back facing the machine.
2. With straight elbows and your arms directed toward the handles, sit your buttocks back while bending your knees to hinge at your hips until your hands are level with the handles.
    1. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
3. Firmly grasp each handle with a neutral grip such that your palms are facing in toward each other.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. While keeping your lower back flat and chest up, drive through your legs to begin lifting the handles before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand fully upright.
3. Dip down slightly by bending your knees while keeping your chest up.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your lower back flat or mildly arched rather than rounding it or excessively arching it.
    2. Quickly proceed to the next step as soon as you finish dipping down.
4. Forcefully drive your feet into the ground as you rapidly straighten your knees to generate momentum from your lower body. Simultaneously shrug your shoulders upward through your available range of motion to lift the handles upward while keeping your elbows straight.
    1. While you are intentionally using momentum to help your upper traps lift the weight, you should not be “cheating” to the extent that you feel out of control.
    2. Throughout the exercise, look straight ahead to keep your neck near a neutral position.
    3. As a cue, you can think about driving your shoulders up toward your earlobes.
5. Allow your shoulders to descend fully in a controlled manner to lower the handles while keeping your torso upright and legs stationary.
    1. Your muscles are noticeably stronger during the lowering phase of an exercise compared to the lifting phase, so “cheating” during the lifting phase allows your upper traps to experience greater loading during the more controlled lowering phase.
    2. At the bottom, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the weight can provide.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the weight abruptly yank you downward. If you are unable to control the lowering phase to any reasonable degree, you are likely using weights that are excessively heavy relative to your current ability.
6. Alternate between steps 3-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have finished your last rep, sit your buttocks back while bending your knees to hinge at your hips and set the handles down.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).

## Setting up
1. Anchor a long looped elastic band of your desired tension level around the center of a pull-up bar with parallel handles that are near shoulder width apart.
    1. To anchor the band, initially drape it over the bar, loop one end through the middle of the other, and pull that end until it is taut.
    2. If the bar is out of reach when standing on the ground, initially position yourself on an aerobic step, sturdy box, or bumper plate to bring the bar within reach. Then set the band and grasp the bar during the next step. Position the step mildly behind the bar rather than directly underneath it, so that you have the option of keeping your legs straightened during the exercise without contacting the step.
    3. If your bar has rough knurling rather than a smooth surface, anchoring the band directly around the bar can increase the risk of the band tearing over time. Placing a fat grip attachment or hand towel around a bar before anchoring the band can help stop a bar with knurling from tearing a band.
    4. Before using it, inspect the band to confirm there are no small tears, as a small tear can quickly become a full tear when stretching the band.
2. Stand under the bar, and pull the band down with both arms.
    1. Each side of the band should be flat without any twists.
3. March up one leg and step into the band with the middle of your foot snugly against the bottom end of the band’s loop before lowering your foot while straightening your leg. Alternatively, you can bend one knee and loop the band around your upper shin.
    1. Since the band’s tension increases as you stretch it, situating the band around your foot with a straight knee will provide greater assistance compared to if you situate the band around your upper shin with your knee bent.
    2. If your pull-up bar is not tall enough to keep your foot from contacting the ground at the bottom of the rep while keeping your leg straight, looping the band around your upper shin will be a better option. Otherwise, you can select whichever approach best suits your preference while providing the level of assistance you prefer.
    3. With either setup, the band should feel secure rather than feeling like it may slide around during the exercise.
4. Reach overhead and firmly grasp the parallel handles with your palms facing each other (i.e., a neutral grip).
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
5. Hang on the bar with your elbows straightened. If you are standing on a step and have the band under your foot, step forward off the step and allow both legs to hang straight down toward the ground. If you have the band around your upper shin, lift your other foot off the ground by bending that knee and keeping both knees bent throughout the exercise.
    1. You can optionally situate your other leg (that was not initially contacting the band) within the band if you wish to do so.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to assume a “proud chest” that is angled slightly upward.
    1. Maintain this “proud chest” posture throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and back toward your sides as you progressively bend your elbows.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows will not actually drive downward. However, the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows being bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion that their bodies enable.
    3. Rather than swinging your legs, statically keep them in a similar position throughout the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your elbows straightened and arms fully overhead.
    1. You do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, you can return one foot onto the ground or step, shift your weight into step/ground, march your other leg up and out of the band, and release the bar.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the seat so that your upper arms can be parallel with the floor or a little lower while grasping the handles.
    1. Some people notice that their shoulders feel more comfortable when the seat is set to a height that allows their elbows to be slightly lower than their shoulders, compared to when their elbows are completely level with their shoulders. Consequently, if you find that your shoulders do not feel the best when performing this exercise with your elbows at shoulder height, you can try increasing the seat height to let you utilize a slightly lesser degree of elbow flare.
    2. If your machine lacks handles, you can adjust the seat to a height that allows you to rest your arms comfortably against the arm pads when your upper arms are reasonably close to being parallel to the ground. When using a machine without handles, you can naturally ignore the instructions about grasping the handles and otherwise use the same setup and exercise technique.
2. Select your weight with the loading pin, and sit down on the seat with your back against the back pad and your feet flat on the floor.
3. With your elbows bent by about 90 degrees, spread your arms backward into a “T-position” through your full range of motion.
    1. Note how far backward your shoulder mobility permits you to spread your arms apart comfortably, since this will indicate where you should adjust the lever arms.
4. Adjust the machine’s lever arms to a position that allows you to situate your arms just behind the arm pads when your upper arms are fully spread apart in the “T-position.”
    1. The ideal starting position of the lever arms should allow you to perform this exercise through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    2. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in your chest or the front of the shoulders after you assume the starting position, you likely can move the lever arms a bit further back.
    3. If you feel shoulder discomfort in the starting position with your upper arms fully spread apart, you likely set the lever arms excessively far back relative to your shoulder mobility.
    4. Some trial and error may be required to find what is personally the best setting for you.
5. Pull your shoulder blades back together to adopt a “proud chest” posture.
6. With your elbows bent by about 90 degrees, spread your arms backward into a “T-position” to rest your arms against the arm pads and grasp the handles.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows fully in toward each other in an arcing manner to pull the machine’s lever arms together.
    1. You can finish once your elbows are directly in front of your shoulders or once you lightly tap the lever arms against each other.
    2. While you do not have to keep your shoulder blades fully pulled back together as your elbows approach each other, avoid letting your shoulders round forward into a slouched posture.
    3. Maintain the same degree of elbow bend throughout the exercise.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your elbows to spread apart from each other and arc backward through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. You should finish in a “proud chest” posture with your upper arms fully spread apart from each other as they form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. While you do not have to perform this step extremely slowly, avoid letting the machine’s resistance abruptly swing your arms apart in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed the set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also meaningfully training your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).

## Setting up
1. If your machine allows you to do so, adjust the stoppers (that are positioned under the arms) to a height that allows you to press through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Ideally, position the stoppers as low as you can while being able to grip the handles comfortably with elbows stacked under your wrists in the starting position.
    2. Finding the optimal height may require some trial and error, but you can initially position the stoppers to the bottom setting before performing a couple of warm-up reps without any additional load on the machine. If you experience shoulder discomfort getting into the starting position or are unable to grasp the handles with vertical forearms, the stoppers are likely too low, and you should try raising them. Otherwise, the stopper height is appropriate, and you can proceed to add weight to the machine.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit down on the bench while snugly positioning the front of your ankles and the top of your feet under the foot/ankle pad.
    1. Your legs should feel securely locked in place and not permit any sliding.
4. Lie down with your back and head on the pad. Ideally align your lower chest with the handles if you can do so.
    1. Since you have to set up with your feet under the foot/ankle pad, you can be limited in terms of positioning your body in a manner that aligns your lower chest with the handles. This can result in not all body types being well-suited to use this type of machine. If the handles are situated horizontally behind your shoulders or meaningfully further forward than your chest (resulting in the handles being level with your abdomen) when lying down, this machine may not be the best tool for you.
5. Firmly grasp the handles with your bent elbows stacked directly under the handles, resulting in your forearms being in a vertical position.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. How wide a grip you can use, along with whether you can use an overhand or neutral grip, can be determined by the design of your machine’s handles.
    3. If you cannot comfortably grasp the handles and position your elbows directly under them, you may have to increase the height of the machine’s stoppers before resuming your setup. If you still find that the machine forces you into an uncomfortable position to grasp the handles, a different exercise may be more suitable for you.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. While keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists, press the handles upward until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together, back and buttocks snugly against the pad, and feet locked in place.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the handles in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. At the end range, you can lightly tap the machine’s arms to the stoppers under them. A gentle tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists and the handles as you allow your elbows to move outward and downward while bending.
    3. If your machine allows you to train through the full range of motion that your mobility enables, it is normal to feel a painless stretching sensation in your chest and/or the front of your shoulders at the end range. Some machines will limit the range of motion before reaching this point, even when set up ideally.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) with a focus on its [middle and lower regions](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md) while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a furniture slider on the ground.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground, and situate the bottom of one heel on top of the slider with your knees fully bent and feet hip-width apart.
    1. You can rest the back of your head on the ground and leave your arms on the ground by your sides or in whichever position you prefer.
3. On the side not in contact with the slider, lift your foot off the ground by marching that side’s thigh up with your knee bent.
    1. Statically keep this leg lifted off the ground throughout the set you perform with your other side.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the leg contacting the slider.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heel down into the slider, squeezing your glute, and tightening your abs.
    1. After performing this glute bridge motion, you should now be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side.
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid arching your lower back excessively.
    3. Throughout the set, keep your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down or hike up above your working leg’s hip bone.
2. Without bending your hip, move your foot forward by progressively straightening your knee in a controlled manner until it is almost fully straightened.
    1. Continue keeping your glute squeezed, abs tensed, and pressure concentrated through your heel throughout the exercise.
    2. All the motion should occur from your shin moving at your knee joint, while you are still able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder.
    3. At the end of this lowering phase, your buttocks should just barely be above the ground.
    4. You do not have to perform this movement with an extremely slow tempo, but you should avoid letting your foot abruptly slide forward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Reverse the movement by driving your heel toward your buttock to bend your knee and pull the slider backward.
    1. You should finish with your knee close to being fully bent as the slider is vertically under your knee.
    2. If you experience a notably uncomfortable cramping sensation in your hamstrings when your knee is fully bent, you can stop bending your knee just before reaching that point.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to lower your buttocks to the ground by bending at your hip before repeating the exercise with your other side.
## Description
While statically engaging your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), this exercise can train all your [hamstrings](../Muscles/Hamstrings%201b95c6f170d88055a462c40b686f381a.md), which are assisted by your [gracilis](../Muscles/Gracilis%201925c6f170d880938681fbbe8f075831.md), [sartorius](../Muscles/Sartorius%201925c6f170d8801c8493cac115de0546.md), and [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md).
2a55c6f170d88077895ddf5fadda700f:
## Setting up
1. On the side you wish to train, pick up a dumbbell and stand behind a seated bench that is permanently fixed to an upright setting or a standing preacher curl bench that has a vertical arm pad on one side.
    1. For this Scott curl, you specifically want to use a bench with a vertical pad in contrast to a Preacher curl, which uses a sloped arm pad.
    2. While they are not available in most gyms, some standing Preacher curl benches have a sloped arm pad on one side and a vertical arm pad on the other side. To use this bench, you should stand on the side of the sloped arm pad.
    3. More commonly available are fixed seated benches with back pads that are shorter than adjustable exercise benches set to a fully upright position. To perform this exercise, the top of the pad should be no higher than your armpit, which precludes adjustable benches positioned fully upright from being used except for very tall lifters.
    4. If the seated bench or standing Preacher curl bench is a little too tall for you, you can elevate yourself by positioning and then standing on a bumper plate, a stack of standard full-diameter weight plates, an aerobic step, or a deadlift block behind the bench.
2. While initially standing with enough space between you and the bench that you will be able to curl the dumbbell upward, direct your palm forward, resulting in an underhand grip.
    1. Maintain this underhand grip and avoid rotating your palm as you finish setting up and perform the exercise.
    2. Unless stated otherwise, the directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell.
3. Curl the dumbbell upward by fully bending your elbow while lifting it upward to point straight ahead.
    1. Your arm and dumbbell should now be fully above the arm pad, which will make it easier to get into the starting position.
    2. Keep your wrist straight when setting up and performing the exercise.
4. While keeping your elbow bent, step forward until your torso is very close to the pad before resting your upper arm and elbow on the pad.
    1. You can use your free hand to help guide your other arm into the starting position if you wish to do so.
    2. Your elbow should now be vertically situated under your shoulder.
5. Hold the bench pad with your free hand for additional stability. While keeping your torso upright, adjust your stance and degree of knee bend to whichever position situates the top of the bench just below your armpit and allows most of your upper arm to contact the pad.
    1. The ideal position should allow your upper arm to feel well-supported and your feet to feel balanced.
    2. If you initially find that the pad only contacts your elbow and the lower part of your triceps, widening your stance and bending your knees to dip down with an upright torso can lower your arm and facilitate greater support from the bench. Keeping the feet closer to hip width apart with straighter knees may alternatively be better for shorter lifters if the top of the bench is fairly close to armpit height when standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow and triceps in contact with the bench, lower the dumbbell in a slow and controlled manner until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. While your forearm arcs forward and downward through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary with your palm facing inward throughout your set.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the dumbbell down.
    3. After initially pointing back toward you in the starting position, your palm should be angled forward and upward at the bottom of the rep.
2. Reverse the movement by bending your elbow to curl the dumbbell upward and back toward you in an arcing motion until your elbow is fully bent with your forearm contacting your biceps.
    1. Continue keeping your elbow and triceps snugly against the arm pad.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other arm.
    1. Once you have finished your last rep, lift your elbow up above the bench through shoulder motion while keeping it bent, and step backward before lowering the dumbbell. Feel free to assist your working arm with your free hand.
    2. If you become too fatigued to finish a rep during your set, you can also use your free hand to assist with curling the dumbbell up. Recognize that an assisted rep should not be recorded as a full rep for tracking progress.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
2a55c6f170d880f6aa9ed2abe35b5215:
## Setting up
1. Pick up a dumbbell with one hand, carry it over to a flat bench, and position yourself near the base of the bench and directly to its side with your side that is holding the dumbbell farther away from the bench.
    1. If you have to carry the dumbbell a meaningful distance before reaching your bench and your grip is somewhat fatigued, you can place the dumbbell on the bench before picking it up with your opposite hand to start your set with the side that does not have a fatigued grip.
2. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips, reach out with your free arm to place its hand on the bench with a straight elbow, and place your knee (on the side not holding the dumbbell) onto the bench.
    1. In this position, your torso should now be reasonably close to being parallel to the ground, and your lower back should be flat rather than being meaningfully rounded.
    2. While setting up, keep your elbow straight on the side holding the dumbbell and allow that arm to hang down toward the ground with your shoulder blade naturally pulled forward toward the ground from the weight.
    3. Based on your comfort and preference, you can place the open palm of your free hand onto the bench, or you can make a fist and place your knuckles onto the bench.
    4. Your foot on the side of the dumbbell should remain firmly in contact with the floor and be sufficiently far behind the dumbbell that your leg does not restrict your row. If you initially do not feel well-balanced, you can try positioning this foot somewhat further out to the side to widen your base of support.
3. Direct your palm so that it is angled between facing backward and in toward the opposite side of your body.
    1. Throughout your set, maintain this grip, which is a hybrid between an overhand grip and a neutral grip.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Drive your elbow in an arcing motion backward, upward, and moderately out away from your side to row the dumbbell. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blade backward.
    1. Aim to flare your elbow about 45 degrees out away from your side as your elbow moves equal parts backward and out to the side. Zero degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbow purely backward and keeping it completely tucked by your side, while 90 degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbow straight out to the side, which would result in your upper arm and torso forming half of a “T-shape” at the top.
    2. When allowing your elbow to bend naturally, your forearm should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    3. At the top of the row, your elbow should be close to level (with respect to height above the ground) with your torso when viewed from the side or front.
    4. Keep your torso in a mostly fixed position with your chest facing a similar direction throughout this movement. A mild degree of torso rotation is not problematic, but avoid letting it become excessive and turning the exercise into a cheat row.
    5. While performing this arcing motion, the dumbbell should not move straight upward in a vertical path.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled arcing motion until your arm is directed down toward the ground with your elbow straightened.
    1. Allow the weight to pull your shoulder blade forward, which will stretch your upper back muscles and result in your working side’s shoulder being mildly closer to the ground than your other side’s shoulder at the bottom of the row.
    2. Move your elbow diagonally inward and forward at a near 45-degree angle while it descends to reverse the moderate elbow flare you just utilized during the lifting phase.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weight rapidly pull your arm down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on a flat exercise bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your upper thighs near your abdomen, with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Position yourself so that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
    2. If you are using dumbbells that you consider fairly heavy, reaching forward from a bent-over position to pick up both dumbbells simultaneously from a rack may be awkward and challenging. For an easier setup, you can pick up one dumbbell, carry it, place it on a flat bench (or sturdy box), and move the other dumbbell onto the bench before picking up both dumbbells from a mechanically advantaged position. Initially, pick up the dumbbell with a deadlift or squat motion where you lift it by extending your hips and knees while keeping your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright (rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so).
    3. To move heavy dumbbells efficiently into the proper position, you can initially situate the dumbbells on the front of your thighs while standing up. Then you can rest them on your thighs while sitting down.
2. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
    2. You should now be holding the dumbbells right by your chest with your forearms in a vertical position, and your wrists stacked over your elbows as the handles of the dumbbells are parallel to your upper arms.
    3. You should be holding the dumbbells on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set.
3. Pull your shoulder blades back together and keep them in this position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel your upper back muscles contract while doing so, which places you into a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
4. Flare your elbows moderately out to your sides such that your upper arms form approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    1. Based on your preference and what feels comfortable for your shoulders, you can decide specifically how much you flare your elbows out within this range.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. One at a time, lift your feet off the ground and straighten your knees with your legs close together.
    1. While your thighs are on the bench, your calves may or may not be resting on the bench as well, depending on your height and the length of your bench.
3. Press the dumbbells up by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner as you progressively straighten them until your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, keep your forearms in a vertical position throughout the press, as your wrists and dumbbells remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, keep your feet off the floor while keeping your buttocks, upper back, and head in contact with the bench.
    3. At the end of the lifting phase, the dumbbells should be situated vertically over your shoulders.
4. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner toward the sides of your chest through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Let your elbows moderately flare out to your sides as they descend and bend enough to keep your wrists stacked above them with vertical forearms. Lifters often find that at least a mild degree of elbow tuck makes this exercise feel most comfortable for the shoulders compared to fully flaring the elbows straight out to the sides.
    2. How far you can lower the dumbbells with vertical forearms will be affected by your individual shoulder mobility, but most people have the mobility to descend until their hands are at least level with their chest.
    3. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and the front of the shoulders at the bottom.
    4. There is no need to lower the dumbbells extremely slowly, but you should actively control the entire descent.
5. Alternate between steps 3-4 until you have completed your set.
6. Following the lowering phase of your last rep, bend your knees to return your feet to the ground.
7. Bring your upper arms in line with your sides to tuck your elbows and position the dumbbells closer to your thighs.
8. March your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs before standing up with them.
## Description
While not loading your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) as effectively as a barbell bench press, this exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also meaningfully training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground.
    1. The size of the weight plates you add to the bar will determine how high the bar lies above the ground, which consequently affects your range of motion. Adding a pair of full-diameter plates (like 45lb (20kg) plates or any bumper plates) will elevate the bar to the standard height (about 9in (23cm)) when deadlifting from the floor. If you only use smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a deficit deadlift with a greater range of motion that may exceed the range of motion in which some people wish to train if they lack the mobility to perform a deficit deadlift with appropriate technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize 45lb (20kg) plates, you can perform a [block pull](Sumo%20low%20block%20pull%202395c6f170d8800dbd1ac184188c0ee5.md) with the bar elevated to where it would be when deadlifting from the floor with full diameter plates.
2. Stand with the middle of your feet under the bar, and spread your legs apart into a wide stance that is clearly outside shoulder width with your toes moderately rotated out away from your sides.
    1. Provided that your feet are wider apart than your shoulders but closer together than the plates, you can use a range of stance widths for your sumo deadlift.
    2. The ideal stance width can meaningfully vary among different individuals based on someone’s body structure and hip mobility.
    3. Trying out different foot positions will normally be required to determine which stance specifically feels best to you.
    4. As a starting point, you can widen your feet as far apart as you feel comfortable and stable while being able to push your knees out approximately over your heels, resulting in close to vertical shins. You will push your knees out when descending to reach the bar, so subsequent aspects of the setup can help you gauge if you should adjust your stance.
    5. The ideal amount of toe flare also varies among different lifters, but you can start with your toes pointing about 30-45 degrees out to the side before adjusting from there based on what feels best to you. Zero degrees of toe flare would mean your toes are pointing straight forward, while 90 degrees would mean your toes are pointing directly out to your side.
3. Direct your arms straight down toward the bar with your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up).
    1. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and help engage your back muscles.
## Exercise technique
1. Sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips while bending your knees and pushing your knees out until your hands are level with the bar. Rather than rounding your back, keep your lower back flat and chest up in a “proud chest” posture.
    1. Strive to keep your shins vertical as your knees essentially do not track forward (although a very slight degree of forward knee tracking can be used if that feels best to you).
    2. The proper balance of bending at your hips versus your knees should allow your shoulders to be stacked vertically above the bar and your hips to be higher than your knees at the bottom.
    3. Try to push your knees far enough out to the sides that they are vertically stacked over your heels.
    4. Throughout this exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
2. With your elbows fully straightened and the bar directly in front of your shins, firmly grasp the bar with an approximately shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. As an alternative to the double overhand grip, you can naturally use a mixed grip (with one palm facing forward and the other facing backward) or lifting straps with the double overhand grip if you wish to do so.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide down your hand while holding it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
4. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. This can help you wedge your hips into an advantageous starting position through a maneuver known as pulling the slack out of the bar.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
    3. Keep your soles fully in contact with the ground throughout your set.
5. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” by extending (straightening) your hips and knees while pushing your knees out. Prioritize keeping your chest up, lower back flat, the bar close to your legs, and your core braced throughout the entire exercise.
    1. As your hips and chest rise at the same rate, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull. Avoid letting your torso incline further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
6. After the bar reaches near your knees, focus on thrusting your hips forward until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
7. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips and bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. Continue keeping your lower back flat, chest up, and the bar close to your legs while driving your knees out with vertical shins.
    2. You can initially focus on sitting your hips back while allowing your knees to bend naturally. After the bar has cleared your knees, you can further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
8. Once the weight is fully resting on the ground, release the bar and stand upright to reset between reps.
9. Alternate between steps 1-8 until you have completed your set.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is on the ground.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can meaningfully train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md),  [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md).
