## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the Roman chair’s pad to a level that positions the top of your hip bones somewhat above the top of the pads when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. This position will allow you to move freely about your hips in contrast to if the pad is contacting the top of your hip bones, which would restrict hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    2. If the top of the pad is positioned much lower than the top of the hip bones (rather than only somewhat lower), some individuals may feel knee discomfort, so a sweet spot can exist for pad placement.
    3. Some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position after initially completing step 2.
2. While placing your hands onto the handles for balance support, step onto the foot plate one leg at a time with the back of your heels in contact with the back of the foot plate, so that the entirety of your soles are in contact with the foot plate.
    1. Position your feet symmetrically in a stance that feels comfortable to you, which can involve pointing your toes somewhat outward or pointing them fairly straight forward.
    2. Situating your feet approximately hip width to shoulder apart from each other will result in a viable stance width, but how wide of a stance you can use will be influenced by the width of your Roman chair’s foot plate.
    3. Your knees should be straight after you have finished setting your feet on the foot plate.
3. Check to make sure that the pad is positioned as described by step 1 and readjust the pad height if it is not prior to repeating step 2.
4. With your elbows straightened, lift your arms up fully overhead to form a “Y-shape” with your torso and arms.
    1. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
    2. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can point your palms in toward each other or forward.
## Exercise technique
1. Squeeze your glutes to keep your torso up such that you can draw approximately a straight line from your legs through your hips and to your shoulders as opposed to having your torso bent over.
    1. Throughout your set, keep your lower back and neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    2. This is the starting position of the exercise, where your body should look like it does when normally standing upright with your arms raised except at an incline.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
3. Hinge at your hips through your available range of motion in a controlled manner.
    1. Rather than simply bending over by rounding your lower back, nearly all the motion should occur from your torso moving as one unit about your hips, like an analog clock’s hand rotating about its center point.
    2. Maintain a straight knee position, but you should avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads.
    3. While hinging at your hips and keeping your arms raised, you should feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings that progressively intensifies.
    4. Most people will be able to descend until their shoulders are lower than their hips, but how deeply you are able to hinge without meaningfully rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    5. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch, you have finished descending through your available hip range of motion.
4. Reverse the movement by lifting your torso up through your hips until you have returned to the starting position, where your torso is aligned with your legs.
    1. You can finish the lifting phase by fully squeezing your glutes, which helps cue the intended hip movement.
    2. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top, since the lifting phase should simply be a reversal of the hip hinge you just performed during the lowering phase.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the preacher bench’s seat to a height that allows you to rest your elbow and most of your triceps (on the back of your upper arm) on the sloped arm pad when sitting on the seat.
    1. The appropriate seat height should allow the exercise to feel stable and comfortable, and it will also typically result in the top of the pad being close to your armpits once you are seated.
    2. Some trial and error may be needed to find the ideal seat height.
2. Slide a fat grip attachment onto a dumbbell’s handle, and pick it up on the side you wish to train. Hold the dumbbell firmly with your palm facing in toward your side (resulting in a neutral grip that is also called a hammer grip).
    1. Maintain this neutral grip and avoid rotating your palm as you finish setting up and perform the exercise.
    2. Unless stated otherwise, the directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell.
3. Straddle the seat with enough space between you and the pad that you will be able to curl the dumbbell upward.
4. Curl the dumbbell upward by fully bending your elbow while lifting it upward to point straight ahead.
    1. Your arm and dumbbell should now be fully above the arm pad, which will make it easier to get into the starting position.
    2. Keep your wrist straight when setting up and performing the exercise.
5. While keeping your elbow bent, step forward until your torso is very close to the pad before sitting down on the seat and resting your triceps and elbow on the pad.
    1. You can use your free hand to help guide your other arm into the starting position if you wish to do so.
    2. Once you are in position, you can hold the arm pad with your free hand for additional stability throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow and triceps in contact with the arm pad, lower the dumbbell in a slow and controlled manner until you have fully straightened your elbow.
    1. Maintain a tight grip on the dumbbell throughout the entirety of this exercise.
    2. While your forearm arcs forward and downward through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary with your palm facing inward throughout your set.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the dumbbell down.
2. Reverse the movement by bending your elbow to curl the dumbbell upward and back toward you in an arcing motion until your elbow is fully bent.
    1. Continue keeping your elbow and triceps snugly against the arm pad.
    2. If your preacher bench allows you to curl the dumbbell past the point when your forearm is completely vertical, you can finish curling once your forearm is fully vertical (rather than once your elbow is fully bent), since the target muscles will not be resisted beyond this point.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other arm.
    1. Once you have finished your last rep with your elbow fully bent, stand upright to lift your arm off the pad, and step backward before lowering the dumbbell.
    2. If you become too fatigued to finish a rep during your set, you can use your free hand to assist with lifting it up and dismounting the preacher bench.
## Description
While dynamically training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md), this exercise can statically train your [forearm’s extrinsic finger flexors](../Muscles/Extrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d88050a550fbeff6041573.md) and your [hand’s intrinsic finger flexors](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md).

## Setting up
1. Anchor a long looped elastic band of your desired tension level around the center of a pull-up bar.
    1. To anchor the band, initially drape it over the bar, loop one end through the middle of the other, and pull that end until it is taut.
    2. If the bar is out of reach when standing on the ground, initially position yourself on an aerobic step, sturdy box, or bumper plate to bring the bar within reach. Then set the band and grasp the bar during the next step. Position the step slightly behind the bar rather than directly underneath it, so you can keep your legs straight during the exercise without contacting the step.
    3. If your bar has rough knurling rather than a smooth surface, anchoring the band directly around the bar can increase the risk of the band tearing over time. Initially placing a fat grip attachment or hand towel around a bar before anchoring the band can help stop a bar with knurling from tearing a band.
    4. Before using it, inspect the band to confirm there are no small tears, as a small tear can quickly become a full tear when stretching the band.
2. Stand under the bar, and pull the band down with both arms.
    1. Each side of the band should be flat without any twists.
3. March up one leg and step into the band with the middle of your foot snugly against the bottom end of the band’s loop before lowering your foot while straightening your leg. Alternatively, you can bend one knee and loop the band around your upper shin.
    1. Since the band’s tension increases as you stretch it, situating the band around your foot with a straight knee will provide greater assistance compared to if you situate the band around your upper shin with your knee bent.
    2. If your pull-up bar is not tall enough to keep your foot from contacting the ground at the bottom of the rep while keeping your leg straight, looping the band around your upper shin will be a better option. Otherwise, you can select whichever approach aligns with your preference while providing your desired level of assistance.
    3. With either setup, the band should feel secure rather than feeling like it may slide around during the exercise.
4. Reach up overhead and firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing backward (i.e., an underhand grip) about shoulder-width apart.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
5. Hang on the bar with your elbows straightened. If you are standing on a step and have the band under your foot, step forward off the step and allow both legs to hang straight down toward the ground. If you have the band around your upper shin, lift your other foot off the ground by bending that knee and keeping both knees bent throughout the exercise.
    1. You can optionally situate your other leg (that was not initially contacting the band) within the band if you wish to do so.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to assume a “proud chest” that is angled slightly upward.
    1. Maintain this “proud chest” posture throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and back toward your sides while progressively bending your elbows.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows naturally will not actually drive downward, but having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows being bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, individuals may have different ranges of motion.
    3. Rather than swinging your legs, statically keep them in a similar position throughout the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your elbows straightened and arms fully overhead.
    1. You do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, you can return one foot onto the ground or step, shift your weight into step/ground, march your other leg up and out of the band, and release the bar.

This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the preacher bench’s seat to a height that allows you to rest your elbows and most of your triceps (on the back of your upper arms) on the sloped arm pad when sitting on the seat.
    1. The appropriate seat height should allow the exercise to feel stable and comfortable, and it will also typically result in the top of the pad being close to your armpits once you are seated.
    2. Some trial and error may be needed to find the ideal seat height.
2. Slide a pair of fat grip attachments onto two dumbbells, and pick them up. Hold them firmly with your palms facing in toward each other (resulting in a neutral grip that is also called a hammer grip).
    1. Maintain this neutral grip and avoid rotating your palms as you finish setting up and perform the exercise.
3. Straddle the seat with enough space between you and the pad that you will be able to curl the dumbbells upward.
4. Curl the dumbbells upward by fully bending your elbows while lifting them upward to point straight ahead.
    1. Your arms and dumbbells should now be fully above the arm pad, which will make it easier to get into the starting position.
5. While keeping your elbows bent, step forward until your torso is very close to the pad before sitting down on the seat and resting your triceps and elbows on the pad.
    1. In the starting position and throughout the exercise, your wrists should be straight.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows and triceps in contact with the arm pad, lower the dumbbells in a slow and controlled manner until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. Maintain a tight grip on the dumbbells throughout the entirety of this exercise.
    2. While your forearms arc forward and downward through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary with your palms facing in toward each other throughout your set.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the dumbbells down.
2. Reverse the movement by bending your elbows to curl the dumbbells upward and back toward you in an arcing motion until your elbows are fully bent.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows and triceps snugly against the arm pad.
    2. If your preacher bench allows you to curl the dumbbells past the point when your forearms are completely vertical, you can finish curling once your forearms are fully vertical (rather than once your elbows are fully bent), since the target muscles will not be resisted beyond this point.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have finished your last rep with your elbows fully bent, stand upright to lift your arms off the pad, and step backward before lowering the dumbbells.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. Stand with the side of your shoulder (that you will not train during this set) facing the cable.
3. Squat down, and reach across your body to grasp the handle with your arm on the side opposite the cable.
4. After standing upright, use your free hand to grasp a stable part of the cable station.
    1. Throughout the exercise, continue using this arm to help stabilize yourself.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm holding the handle.
5. Take a step forward with your foot that is further away from the pulley. Allow the cable’s resistance to pull your arm across your body and in toward the pulley with your elbow straightened.
    1. You should feel tension from the cable and will likely feel a stretching sensation on the side of your shoulder.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow straight, sweep your arm in a smooth arcing motion diagonally upward and outward away from the pulley.
    1. After sweeping your arm as if you were drawing a sword, you should finish with your arm angled out to the side and mildly upward.
    2. In contrast to a typical lateral raise, your arm should initially arc forward in front of you as it moves across your body. This will result in the movement functioning like a hybrid between a lateral raise and a front raise, with it involving a greater proportion of lateral raise motion than front raise motion.
    3. While you raise your arm through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blade to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary. This includes keeping your chest and imaginary belt buckle directed straight ahead throughout your set rather than rotating either one to the side.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your arm in toward the pulley and across your body in a controlled arcing manner through your full range of motion.
    1. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm downward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), which are assisted by your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust each pulley from a dual cable station to its lowest height, and select your desired weight with the loading pin of each stack.
    1. A dual cable station that can situate the two pulleys no further apart than your wingspan is ideal to use for this variation.
    2. A dual cable station that has its pulleys rather far apart from each other (often with a long upper beam connecting each end of the station) is not as practical to use. With this type of equipment, the [single arm cross-body cable Y-raise](Single%20arm%20cross-body%20cable%20Y-raise%202aa5c6f170d88015886fdf8eb2580e76.md) may be preferable.
2. Securely attach an ankle cuff just above each wrist. Position each cuff so that one of its attachment rings is facing the same direction as your palm.
3. Stand just in front of one pulley while facing in the direction of its weight stack.
4. Squat down, and connect the cable to the cuff on the side that is further away from the opposite pulley.
    1. For instance, if the opposite pulley is on your left side, connect your right arm’s cuff to the cable in front of you.
5. Connect the opposite cable to your other cuff, and stand upright centered in between the pulleys.
    1. Your left arm’s cuff should now be connected to the cable on your left side, while your right arm’s cuff is connected to the cable on your right side.
6. Pivot your body to face the opposite direction while stepping over one cable and allowing the cables to cross over behind your back.
    1. With your back facing in the direction of the weight stacks, your left arm’s cuff should now be connected to the cable on your right side, while your right arm’s cuff is connected to the cable on your left side.
7. Take a step forward into a staggered stance with one foot further in front than the other, and your lead knee slightly bent.
    1. Your shoulders should be mildly in front of the pulleys rather than being directly between them, resulting in the cables pulling diagonally backward but mostly inward.
    2. In this staggered stance, you should feel stable and balanced.
8. Assume a “proud chest” posture rather than slumping your shoulders forward. Allow the cables to pull your arms in toward your sides with your elbows straight and palms facing the pulleys if they are not already in this position.
    1. Due to the diagonal line of pull from the cables, your wrists should be slightly behind your shoulders in the starting position.
## Exercise technique
1. In a smooth arcing motion, sweep your arms diagonally upward, outward, and mildly forward away from the pulleys.
    1. Finish with your wrists near shoulder height as your arms are angled outward and slightly forward.
    2. While you raise your arms through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blades to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary as you keep your elbows straight.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering your arms in toward your sides and allowing them to move mildly back toward the pulleys.
    1. Strive to finish with your wrists near your buttocks as your arms are directed down toward the ground.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cables abruptly yank your arms downward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), which are assisted by your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat to a distance away from the foot platform that allows you to leg press through a full range of motion while keeping your lower back flat and heels fully on the platform in the starting position.
    1. Finding the ideal setting for you as an individual typically takes some trial and error. The only way to know if the seat setting is appropriate is to sit down on the seat and situate your feet on the platform in the same position you will use for your set.
    2. If the seat is excessively close to the foot platform relative to your hip mobility, your lower back may have to round to place your feet on the platform while seated. Alternatively, you may not be able to place your heels firmly in contact with the platform if it is too close.
    3. You should ideally place the seat as close to the foot platform as you can without having to round your lower back or lift your heels off the platform. Placing the seat meaningfully farther back beyond this point may decrease how much muscle growth the exercise is likely to stimulate.
    4. As a general starting point, you can find the seat setting that allows your knees to be bent by about 90 degrees when your feet are on the platform. If you are able to avoid rounding your lower back or lifting your heels up with this setting, you can incrementally bring the seat closer until you find your optimal starting position.
2. Select your weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on the seat with your back firmly supported by the backrest.
    1. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Place your feet fully on the lower half of the platform, near shoulder width apart, with your toes pointing slightly outward.
    1. Many people find that setting up with a stance reasonably close to this allows them to leg press effectively. However, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when leg pressing through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different stances over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    3. While placing your feet lower on the platform may help bias your quads during this variation, make sure that your heels are still fully in contact with the platform rather than hanging off it.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
3. Drive your feet into the platform to push it away from you as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees when leg pressing, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the platform. Rather than pushing all through your heels or all through your toes, you should be pushing evenly throughout your feet.
    3. Continue keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the seat and your back snugly up against the backrest.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    5. Certain machine models will involve you pressing yourself away from a stationary foot platform rather than pressing the platform away from you. The technique remains the same regardless.
4. Reverse the movement by bending at your knees and hips in a controlled manner through your full range of motion to return to the starting position.
    1. Continue keeping your feet fully on the platform, buttocks on the seat, back against the back rest, and knees aligned over your feet.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively in control the entire time. A sign of an appropriately controlled movement is having the weights you selected lightly contact the rest of the weight stack at the end range. Having the weights lightly touch down will also confirm that you have moved through your full range of motion.
    3. With the appropriate seat position, you should be able to avoid rounding your lower back or lifting your heels off the platform at the end range of this motion. If you notice your lower back starts rounding at the end or heels start lifting up, you could finish your rep and mildly move the seat backward before resuming your set.
    4. You can optionally briefly pause in the bottom position.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles while also meaningfully training your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station with pulleys not meaningfully further apart than your wingspan, adjust each pulley to its lowest height.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you can position the arms so that their pulleys are moderately outside shoulder width apart. Specifically, you can aim for about the same distance between your elbows when your arms are raised straight out away from your sides, parallel to the ground.
    2. A dual cable station that has its pulleys situated well outside your wingspan is not appropriate for this particular variation.
2. Connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.
3. Squat down with one cable station by your side, and firmly grasp its handle with a straight elbow.
4. While keeping your elbow straight, stand upright with the handle, and walk over to grasp the handle from the other cable in the same manner.
    1. You can allow the resistance from the first cable you grasped to lift your arm out to the side before doing the same with the other cable during the next step.
5. Step to the side to center yourself between the cables, and direct your palms forward.
6. Bend your elbows while allowing them to swing mildly forward to curl the handles up to your shoulders.
    1. Use momentum from your lower body as needed in a cheat curl-like manner to help lift the handles into position.
7. With your wrist vertically stacked above your elbows, turn your palms in toward each other, and assume a “proud chest” posture with your chest up.
    1. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back along with your neck, like when you are normally standing upright.
8. Flare your elbows at least moderately out to your sides to a degree that feels comfortable for your shoulders.
    1. When 0 degrees of elbow flare means that your wrists are directly in front of your shoulders with your palms facing each other, and 90 degrees of elbow flare means that your wrists are fully out to your sides with your palms facing straight forward, using about 60-75 degrees of elbow flare is commonly appropriate. In this position, your elbows will point more out to the side than forward, but they will not be fully flared out.
    2. If your shoulders feel comfortable when pressing with a greater degree of elbow flare, you can certainly flare your elbows beyond that point, but some people find that utilizing a closer to moderate degree of elbow flare feels most comfortable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the handles upward by driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner until you are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. While your elbows progressively, your forearms should be in a vertical position throughout the press as your wrists and handles remain stacked over your elbows.
    2. Throughout your set, continue keeping your knees and hips straightened as you avoid using your legs to help lift the weights or leaning your torso back via lower back arching.
    3. Allow your shoulder blades to move naturally.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the handles in a controlled manner as you allow your elbows to move outward and downward while bending.
    1. Continue keeping your wrist stacked over your elbows to maintain a vertical forearm position.
    2. Strive to lower the handles as far as you comfortably can while keeping your forearms vertical, which should result in your elbows bending by greater than 90 degrees.
    3. There is no need to perform this lowering phase extremely slowly, but you should actively resist the cables rather than letting them abruptly yank your arms down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [lateral delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat to a distance away from the foot platform that allows you to leg press through a full range of motion while keeping your lower back flat and heels fully on the platform in the starting position.
    1. Finding the ideal setting for you as an individual typically takes some trial and error. The only way to know if the seat setting is appropriate is to sit down on the seat and situate your feet on the platform in the same position you will use for your set.
    2. If the seat is excessively close to the foot platform relative to your hip mobility, your lower back may have to round to place your feet on the platform while seated. Alternatively, you may not be able to place your heels firmly in contact with the platform if it is too close.
    3. You should ideally place the seat as close to the foot platform as you can without having to round your lower back or lift your heels off the platform. Placing the seat meaningfully farther back beyond this point may decrease how much muscle growth the exercise is likely to stimulate.
    4. As a general starting point, you can find the seat setting that allows your knees to be bent by about 90 degrees when your feet are on the platform. If you are able to avoid rounding your lower back or lifting your heels up with this setting, you can incrementally bring the seat closer until you find your optimal starting position.
2. Select your weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. Sit down on the seat with your back firmly supported by the backrest.
    1. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Place your feet fully on the upper half of the foot platform, mildly outside shoulder width apart, with your toes pointing mildly outward.
    1. Many people find that setting up with a stance reasonably close to this allows them to leg press effectively. However, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when leg pressing through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different stances over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    3. While placing your feet higher on the platform may help bias your glutes during this variation, make sure that your toes are still fully in contact with the platform rather than hanging above it.
## Exercise technique
1. For additional stability, firmly grasp the handles and continue holding them throughout your set.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
3. Drive your feet into the platform to push it away from you as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees when leg pressing, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. You can emphasize pushing through your heels while still keeping the entirety of your soles (including the middle of your feet and the balls of your feet) firmly in contact with the platform.
    3. Continue keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the seat and your back snugly up against the backrest.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    5. Certain machine models will involve you pressing yourself away from a stationary foot platform rather than pressing the platform away from you. The technique remains the same regardless.
4. Reverse the movement by bending at your knees and hips in a controlled manner through your full range of motion to return to the starting position.
    1. Continue keeping your feet fully on the platform, buttocks on the seat, back against the back rest, and knees aligned over your feet.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively in control the entire time. A sign of an appropriately controlled movement is having the weights you selected lightly contact the rest of the weight stack at the end range. Having the weights lightly touch down will also confirm that you have moved through your full range of motion.
    3. With the appropriate seat position, you should be able to avoid rounding your lower back or lifting your heels off the platform at the end range of this motion. If you notice your lower back starts rounding at the end or heels start lifting up, you could finish your rep and mildly move the seat backward before resuming your set.
    4. You can optionally briefly pause in the bottom position.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md) while also meaningfully training three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, position each pulley near hip height.
    1. This variation will feel the most natural when using a dual cable station that can situate the two pulleys no further apart than your wingspan.
    2. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you can position the arms straight forward, parallel to each other.
    3. With a dual cable station that has its pulleys rather far apart from each other (often with a long upper beam connecting each end of the station), it may be more practical to use the [single arm variation](Single%20arm%20Bayesian%20curl%201a15c6f170d88027bdddc238baa28936.md) of this exercise.
2. Connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.
3. While standing with the sides of your shoulders facing the two pulleys, firmly grasp one of the handles before side-stepping to then grasp the other handle.
4. Center yourself between the cables before walking forward with your palms facing forward and wrists straight. Allow the resistance from the cables to pull your arms backward with straight elbows.
    1. You can stop walking forward once you feel that your arms are angled about 45 degrees behind your torso, or once you have reached the end range to which your shoulder mobility comfortably permits your arms to pull backward.
    2. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders and/or biceps with your arms pulled backward, but you should not experience shoulder joint discomfort when you have appropriately walked forward.
5. While mildly bending your knees, adopt a staggered stance with one foot in front of the other as your feet are approximately hip width apart from each other.
    1. In this position, you should feel stable and balanced.
6. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to curl the handles forward and upward in an arcing manner. Keep your upper arms stationary as you avoid swinging them forward through shoulder motion.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully bent as your forearms contact your biceps.
    2. While you move your forearms through elbow joint motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set, which will result in your elbows remaining behind your torso.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing the handles to arc downward and back toward the pulleys as your elbows straighten.
    1. Finish the lowering phase with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cables abruptly yank the handles back in an uncontrolled manner.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Following your last rep, walk backward until the cables are no longer tensed before releasing the handles.
## Description
While also meaningfully developing your [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md) and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md), this exercise can effectively train [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md) from a notably lengthened position.

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, adjust each pulley’s height to be mildly above the top of your head, connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you can position the arms to a setting that places the pulleys about as far apart as your wingspan.
2. While standing to the side of one cable, grasp its handle, and then step over to grasp the handle from the other cable with your palms facing forward and your elbows slightly bent.
    1. Keep your elbows slightly bent throughout the exercise.
3. Center yourself between the pulleys, and take a step forward with one leg to adopt a staggered stance.
4. Lean your torso forward closer to horizontal by hinging at your front leg’s hip and bending your front leg’s knee while keeping your rear knee straight. Allow the cables to spread your arms apart while pulling them up and back through a range that your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. Strive to lean forward until the cables form approximately 90-degree angles with your torso when viewed from the side. This will result in your shoulders being in essentially the same position as if you positioned the pulleys to shoulder height and set up while standing fully upright.
    2. Avoid rounding your back as you lean forward through hip motion while keeping your back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. In this position, you should feel resistance from the cables with your arms fully spread apart. If you currently do not, you should take a step forward so that the cables can exert resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
5. Pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that you will maintain throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Sweep the handles in toward each other by arcing them diagonally forward and downward while keeping your elbows mildly bent.
    1. You should finish with your hands about to touch each other as your arms form approximately 90-degree angles with your torso when viewed from the side.
    2. The wide arcing motion should resemble hugging a thick barrel, as all the motion comes from your shoulders while you keep the rest of your body stationary throughout the set.
    3. Keep your chest up as you avoid hunching over with your shoulders slouched forward.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your hands to spread apart from each other in a controlled manner as they move diagonally backward and upward in line with the resistance from the cables.
    1. At the end, your arms should be fully spread apart through the full range your shoulder mobility comfortably permits, which normally produces a stretching sensation in the chest and shoulders.
    2. Aim to maintain the same 90-degree angles between the cables and your torso when viewed from the side, which should naturally occur when following the direction of resistance from the cables.
    3. Avoid bending your elbows any further and turning this exercise into a chest press.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also meaningfully training your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley near shoulder height or slightly higher, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Stand with the side of your body that you will not train during this set facing the cable station.
3. Reach across your body (with your hand further away from the pulley), and grasp the handle with your palm facing backward. To assist with getting into position, you can use your other hand to grasp the ball of the cable next to the pulley.
4. Take a step out to the side, and lunge backward into a half-kneeling position with your knee further away from the pulley resting on the ground.
    1. Keep your torso upright with the center of your chest and your imaginary belt buckle facing straight ahead in the same direction.
    2. Allow the cable’s resistance to keep your arm (that is holding the handle) pulled across your body.
    3. Your knee on the same side as the pulley should now be in front of you, while your other knee is under your torso.
5. While holding the handle with your working side’s hand, let go of the cable’s ball with your other hand. Brace that free hand against your lower thigh for additional stability.
    1. Continue bracing that hand against your thigh throughout the exercise to help avoid twisting your chest toward the pulley.
    2. All the subsequent instructions will refer to the arm whose hand is holding the cable.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout the set.
2. Drive your elbow diagonally outward and down toward your side while keeping your forearm aligned with the cable and palm facing backward.
    1. You should finish with your elbow bent by your side, as the handle is in front of your torso.
    2. Continue keeping the center of your chest and imaginary belt buckle pointing straight ahead throughout the set, as you avoid twisting your chest to either side.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing the cable to pull your elbow diagonally inward and upward across your body.
    1. While letting your elbow straighten, strive to move through your shoulder’s full range of motion with your arm fully across your body, angled toward the pulley.
    2. At the end of this step, it is common to feel a stretching sensation in your back muscles with your elbow in front of your breastbone or slightly further across your body.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the cable yank your arm across your body in an uncontrolled fashion.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side while facing the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop train your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and rear delt while also training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Lie down with your back on the ground, knees straight out in front of you, and your arms straight by your sides.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can lie down on an exercise mat.
2. Lift your arms slightly off the ground, pointing forward, and keep them pointing forward throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. As you tighten your abdominal muscles, curl your back to lift it off the ground while keeping the backs of your hip bones and legs on the ground.
    1. To train your abdominal muscles dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain flat (which could happen if you predominantly lift your torso through your hip flexors). With the appropriate focus on curling your back, you should feel meaningful tension in your abs rather than in your hip flexors on the front of your upper thighs.
    2. As a cue, you can think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the top of your hip bones, which is the action that contraction of your abdominal muscles can produce.
    3. You have reached the end of the lifting phase once you feel that you have fully curled your back and crunched the bottom of your ribs down toward the top of your hips.
    4. In contrast to a sit-up, your shoulders should remain clearly behind your hips at the top of this lift, since you should exclusively be moving through back motion without any hip motion.
    5. Based on what feels most comfortable to you, you can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest at the start of the lifting phase, or you can keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
2. Reverse the movement by uncurling your back in a controlled manner as you lower your back to the ground.
    1. When transitioning from having a rounded back to a straighter back, your ribs should flare away from your hip bones.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should avoid dropping onto the ground in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md), which is assisted by your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a pair of dumbbells on the floor wide enough apart that you can lie down between them and grasp their handles with your arms by your sides.
    1. You can optionally situate an exercise mat on the ground where you will lie for comfort.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground, your arms near your sides, and your palms under the dumbbells’ handles as they are facing up.
3. Bend your knees and situate the soles of your feet flat on the floor in a position where you feel comfortable and stable.
4. Firmly grasp the dumbbells and curl them up by bending your elbows until your forearms are vertical.
5. Direct your palms toward each other to use a neutral grip.
6. In a bench pressing motion, press the dumbbells upward until you have straightened your elbows with your arms directed up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a bench press rep), the dumbbells should be sitting on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists. Maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the dumbbells in a controlled arcing manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Based on what feels most natural and comfortable, you can keep your elbows tucked in, or you can allow your elbows to flare out to your sides slightly.
    2. Avoid letting your elbows drift back and down with the dumbbells through shoulder motion. When viewed from the side, the proper elbow position should result in your upper arms remaining in a vertical position.
    3. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
    4. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the dumbbells the entire way.
2. Based on your preference, finish lowering the dumbbells once they are just barely above the floor or once they gently tap the floor.
    1. You can optionally briefly pause in this bottom position if you wish to do so.
    2. If you decide to tap the dumbbells to the ground (which can help standardize your range of motion each rep), emphasize a very light contact as you avoid bouncing the dumbbells off the floor.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the dumbbells into the starting position.
    1. Continue keeping your upper arms in a vertical position as you avoid pushing your elbows forward (toward your chest) through shoulder motion.
    2. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the dumbbells are vertically above your shoulders.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, lower your elbows and triceps to the floor (like you would during a neutral grip dumbbell floor press) before returning the dumbbells to the floor by straightening your elbows (like during the lowering phase of a biceps curl).
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. If your machine permits you to adjust it, set the seat to the most reclined position that allows your back to be well-supported by the backrest when seated with your feet on the foot platform.
    1. Starting with the most reclined position (which tilts the seat down in a closer to horizontal position) generally works well for most people.
    2. Compared to using a closer to upright seat angle, using an appropriately reclined position will allow you to leg press through a longer range of motion without rounding your lower back.
    3. The most reclined setting on certain machine models may be excessively reclined to the extent that the backrest may no longer be able to stabilize your body when leg pressing. If this occurs, your buttocks may lift off the seat, and your torso may slide back along the backrest due to the backrest being angled too close to a horizontal position. However, most leg press machines will not have an excessively reclined seat setting available.
    4. To determine if the seat angle you initially selected is appropriate for you, you can perform a couple of reps with the technique described in the “exercise technique” section without adding any weight plates to the leg press. If you feel stable and well-supported by the backrest, the seat is not excessively reclined, and you have selected a viable seat angle.
    5. Note that not all machine models permit you to adjust the seat angle.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
    1. Note that the sled will provide resistance even without any additional weight plates. The weight of the sled will vary depending on the specific model, but it commonly weighs near 120lb (54kg).
3. Sit down with your buttocks fully on the seat and your whole back firmly supported by the backrest.
    1. Rather than being rounded in a slouched posture, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck in a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Place your feet fully on the lower half of the foot platform, near shoulder width apart, with your toes pointing slightly outward.
    1. Many people find that setting up with a stance reasonably close to this allows them to leg press effectively. However, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when leg pressing through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different stances over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    3. While placing your feet lower on the platform may help bias your quads during this variation, make sure that your heels are still fully in contact with the platform rather than hanging off it.
    4. In the starting position, your knees should be at least slightly bent to allow you to unlock the sled and begin your set. If your legs are too short to achieve this position with a leg press that has multiple safety stopper heights, you can ask a taller lifter to reposition the platform to a lower starting height that you can reach. If you are using a machine that does not permit a lower starting height of the sled, that particular machine may not be feasible for your body type.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your feet into the platform to push it away from you by straightening your knees.
    1. After doing so, the sled should no longer be resting on the machine’s safety stoppers.
    2. Your knees should now be straight or just slightly bent.
3. Unlock the safety handles with your hands to move the safety stoppers out of the sled’s way.
    1. The specific location of the safety handles and how to unlock them can vary among different machine models. However, the safety handles are often near where your hands will be when resting by your sides, and rotating the handles outward will commonly disengage the safety stoppers.
4. For additional stability, firmly grasp the fixed handles (not the movable safety handles) and continue holding them throughout your set.
5. Lower the sled toward you in a controlled manner by simultaneously bending at your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the platform.
    2. Continue keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the seat and your back snugly up against the backrest.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet. It can help to think about pushing your knees out if you notice them starting to drift inward.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively in control the entire time.
6. Continue lowering the sled through the full range of motion you can while keeping your buttocks firmly on the seat, lower back flat against the back rest, and heels fully on the platform.
    1. What constitutes a full range of motion will vary from person to person and will be influenced by your individual ankle and hip mobility.
    2. If you reached the end range to which your ankle mobility allows your knees to track over your toes, lowering the sled any further would cause your heels to start lifting off the platform.
    3. If you reached the end range to which your hips can bend, lowering the sled any further would cause your lower back to start rounding. This would be demonstrated by your buttocks starting to curl up off the seat.
    4. You can optionally briefly pause in the bottom position.
7. Drive your feet into the platform to push the sled away from you as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees when leg pressing, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. Rather than pushing all through your heels or all through your toes, you should be pushing evenly throughout your feet.
    3. Continue keeping your feet fully on the platform, buttocks on the seat, back against the back rest, and knees aligned over your feet.
8. Alternate between steps 5-7 until you have completed your set.
9. After your knees are straightened following the lifting phase of your last rep, lock the safety handles with your hands to return the safety stoppers to being fully under the sled.
10. Lower the sled onto the safety stoppers by bending your knees.

This exercise can effectively develop three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles while also meaningfully training your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

3. Sit down with your buttocks fully on the seat and your whole back firmly supported by the backrest.
    1. Rather than being rounded in a slouched posture, your back should be near a neutral position ,like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Place your feet fully on the upper half of the foot platform, mildly outside shoulder width apart, with your toes pointing mildly outward.
    1. Many people find that setting up with a stance reasonably close to this allows them to leg press effectively. However, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when leg pressing through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different stances over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    3. While placing your feet higher on the platform may help bias your glutes during this variation, make sure that your toes are still fully in contact with the platform rather than hanging above it.
    4. In the starting position, your knees should be at least slightly bent to allow you to unlock the sled and begin your set. If your legs are too short to achieve this position with a leg press that has multiple safety stopper heights, you can ask a taller lifter to reposition the platform to a lower starting height that you can reach. If you are using a machine that does not permit a lower starting height of the sled, that particular machine may not be feasible for your body type for this specific variation, but situating your feet lower on the platform potentially may allow you to still use the leg press.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your feet into the platform to push it away from you by straightening your knees.
    1. After doing so, the sled should no longer be resting on the machine’s safety stoppers.
    2. Your knees should now be straight or just slightly bent.
3. Unlock the safety handles with your hands to move the safety stoppers out of the sled’s way.
    1. The specific location of the safety handles and how to unlock them can vary among different machine models. However, the safety handles are often near where your hands will be when resting by your sides, and rotating the handles outward will commonly disengage the safety stoppers.
4. For additional stability, firmly grasp the fixed handles (not the movable safety handles) and continue holding them throughout your set.
5. Lower the sled toward you in a controlled manner by simultaneously bending at your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the platform.
    2. Continue keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the seat and your back snugly up against the backrest.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet. It can help to think about pushing your knees out if you notice them starting to drift inward.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively in control the entire time.
6. Continue lowering the sled through the full range of motion you can while keeping your buttocks firmly on the seat, lower back flat against the back rest, and heels fully on the platform.
    1. What constitutes a full range of motion will vary from person to person and will be influenced by your individual hip and ankle mobility.
    2. If you reached the end range to which your hips can bend, lowering the sled any further would cause your lower back to start rounding. This would be demonstrated by your buttocks starting to curl up off the seat, which can more easily occur when situating your feet high on the platform for this glute-biased variation.
    3. If you reached the end range to which your ankle mobility allows your knees to track over your toes (which is uncommon for this glute-biased variation), lowering the sled any further would cause your heels to start lifting off the platform.
    4. You can optionally briefly pause in the bottom position.
7. Drive your feet into the platform to push the sled away from you as you simultaneously extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees when leg pressing, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. Focus on especially pushing through your heels while still keeping the entirety of each sole fully in contact with the platform.
    3. Continue keeping your buttocks on the seat, back against the back rest, and knees aligned over your feet.
8. Alternate between steps 5-7 until you have completed your set.
9. After your knees are straightened following the lifting phase of your last rep, lock the safety handles with your hands to return the safety stoppers to being fully under the sled.
10. Lower the sled onto the safety stoppers by bending your knees.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md) while also meaningfully training three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.
2aa5c6f170d880c0bf4bfd09f8e10edc:
## Setting up
1. On the side of your body you are about to train, pick up one dumbbell and hold it by your side with your elbow straightened.
    1. Continue holding the dumbbell by your side throughout the exercise.
2. Approach a step or a sturdy object that can function as a step. You should be by a surface (e.g., handrail, wall, power rack) where you can place one hand to assist with maintaining your balance.
    1. Based on the equipment at your disposal, a variety of objects can serve as your step. Make sure the object can support your weight, will not move once you are on it, and allows you to lower your heel through the full range of motion your ankle mobility permits.
    2. As an alternative to a staircase’s bottom step, you may select a power rack’s bottom beam if the beam is sufficiently tall.
    3. Additionally, a calf raise block, aerobic step, deadlift block, or thick bumper plate can each be positioned near a wall or power rack for stability. Depending on your bodyweight, anchoring an aerobic step with weight on top of it may be required to prevent the step from tipping.
3. Place your free hand onto the nearby surface for balance assistance, and maintain this hand contact throughout the set.
    1. If you are using a surface that you can grasp (like a power rack) rather than a wall, do not grip it tightly.
4. Step onto the step with the balls of your feet on the step while the back halves of your feet are hanging off the step.
5. While keeping your foot on the same side as the dumbbell on the step, lift your other foot off the step by bending that knee.
    1. Keep that foot off the step throughout the exercise.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the leg in contact with the step.
6. Slightly bend your knee while allowing your heel to fully lower below the ball of your foot.
## Exercise technique
1. While simultaneously straightening your knee quickly, forcefully push through the ball of your foot to raise your heel upward as you keep the ball of your foot planted on the step.
    1. Once you have lifted your heel as high upward as your ankle mobility permits with your knee fully straightened and torso upright, you have finished the lifting phase. There is no need to pause at the top.
    2. As you use your calf to perform most of the work with some assistance from your quad, this quick movement should resemble a jump rope motion, but without the ball of your foot leaving the step.
    3. Only use your free hand for balance assistance as you avoid pushing down in a manner that can help you lift yourself upward.
2. In a controlled manner, allow your heel to descend toward the ground through the full range of motion your calf flexibility permits while slightly bending your knee.
    1. Strive to lower your heel as far as you can below the ball of your foot to stretch your calf and train it the most effectively.
    2. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in your calf at the bottom, you likely are not descending through your full range of motion.
    3. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid rapidly dropping down and trying to bounce out of the bottom into the next rep. Only the lifting phase should be quick.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat this exercise with your other side.
    1. If you ever feel that your foot is starting to slide down the step, you can return your free leg’s foot to the step for a moment to help you scoot your working leg’s foot forward onto the step before resuming your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop both your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md) while simultaneously improving calf flexibility through loaded stretching.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley near its lowest height before connecting a bar with a straight (or mostly straight) body to the cable and selecting your weight with the loading pin.
    1. The pulley should be set to a height that allows you to reach back and grasp the bar once you are lying on the bench. The appropriate pulley should simultaneously allow the cable to exert resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise. The lowest pulley height or the second-to-lowest pulley height typically satisfies these criteria.
    2. Any bar that enables you to perform this exercise with a near shoulder-width overhand grip can be similarly used, including a standard straight bar, a lat pulldown bar (with a long straight body and angled ends), and a multi-grip EZ bar.
2. Position a flat exercise bench slightly in front of the pulley.
    1. The bench should be close enough to the pulley that you can grasp the bar when setting up and then be able to direct your arms straight up toward the ceiling (in the starting position of each rep) without the cable contacting the bench or your head.
3. Lie down on your back on the bench, with your head resting on the end near the cable.
    1. Place your feet flat on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent.
4. Reach back behind your head with your elbows bent, and firmly grasp the bar with a near shoulder-width overhand grip.
    1. The overhand grip should result in your palms being angled backward in this position.
    2. If you cannot grasp the bar, you may have to mildly increase the pulley height before resuming your setup.
5. Pull the bar upward and forward by driving your elbows upward and forward until your upper arms are vertical. Simultaneously straighten your elbows so that your arms are directed straight up toward the ceiling.
    1. If the cable brushes up against the back of the bench or your head when your arms are fully vertical with your elbows stacked over your shoulders, you can keep your arms angled slightly backward. This will result in your elbows being slightly horizontally closer to the pulley than your shoulders.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the bar in a controlled arcing manner while keeping your elbows up.
    1. Based on what feels most natural and comfortable to you, you can allow your elbows to flare out to your sides to a degree, or you can keep your elbows tucked in.
    2. Avoid letting your elbows drift back and down with the bar through shoulder motion.
    3. Essentially all the motion should occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbows as the center of an analog clock, while your forearms are the hands that rotate about these center elbows during this exercise.
2. Finish lowering the bar just before it reaches your forehead or until you have bent your elbows as much as you can without letting your elbows drift backward.
    1. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way, especially when the bar approaches your head.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the bar into the starting position.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is vertically above you.
    2. Continue keeping your upper arms mostly stationary as you avoid pushing your elbows forward (toward your chest) through shoulder motion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, lower the bar behind your head toward the pulley while bending your elbows until you lose tension from the cable and can set the bar down.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by compound pressing exercises.
