## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a position that allows your knees to be bent by about 45 degrees when your feet are on the bottom of the foot plate.
    1. The appropriate seat position should permit you to bend your knees mildly each rep, which can involve situating the seat further forward than you would for a standard leg press calf raise.
    2. If you notice that you lose resistance from the machine at the bottom of your reps during the set, you should position the seat further back to experience tension throughout the full range of motion for this variation.
2. Sit down with your buttocks fully on the seat and your whole back firmly supported by the back rest.
    1. Your back should be flat rather than being rounded in a slouched posture, which may occur if you do not situate your hips far enough back against the back rest.
3. With a near hip width stance, place the balls of your feet onto the bottom of the foot plate with your heels hanging off the edge.
    1. Ensure that the balls of your feet are firmly on the foot plate to the extent that they will not slide down during the exercise.
4. While grasping the hand grips, press the platform away from you by straightening your knees until they are only mildly bent.
## Exercise technique
1. While simultaneously straightening your knees quickly, forcefully push through the balls of your feet to point your feet away from you (like when stepping on a car’s gas pedal) and press the platform away.
    1. Keep the balls of your feet firmly in contact with the foot plate throughout the exercise.
    2. Once you have pointed your feet as far as your ankle mobility permits with your knees fully straightened, you have finished the lifting phase. There is no need to pause at the top.
    3. As you use your calves to perform most of the work with some assistance from your quads, this quick movement should resemble a jump rope motion but without the ball of your foot leaving the platform.
    4. Aiming to fully straighten your knees does not mean hyperextending your knees, which is when the knees bend backward beyond a straight position. If you have the mobility to hyperextend your knees, there is no need to forcefully lock your knees into a hyperextended position, since straightening them is appropriate.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner, by allowing your feet to point back closer toward you through the full range of motion your calf flexibility permits while mildly bending your knees.
    1. While ensuring that they remain firmly on the foot plate, strive to bring the balls of your feet fully back toward your shins to stretch your calves and train them most effectively.
    2. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in your calves or ankles at the bottom, you likely are not descending through your full ankle range of motion.
    3. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid rapidly dropping down and trying to bounce out of the bottom into the next rep. Only the lifting phase should be quick.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to return the platform to its initial position by further bending your knees until the weights you selected are resting on the rest of the weight stack.
    1. If you have rather flexible calves and high ankle mobility, you may feel most stable when bringing the platform back if you do so when your ankles are near a neutral position (like near the mid-range of each rep) rather than when your feet are bent fully back toward you (like at the bottom of each rep).
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop both your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md) while simultaneously improving calf flexibility through loaded stretching.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to be above head height, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. So long as the pulley is set to a height that allows the cable to move diagonally downward during this exercise’s pulling phase, a range of pulley heights can be viably used for this variation. Feel free to try out different pulley heights to determine which one feels best to you.
2. Connect to the cable a rope attachment that is ideally a long rope attachment, or two standard rope attachments that are each fully pulled to one side of the attachment.
    1. Compared to using a single standard-length rope attachment, using a long rope attachment or two standard-length rope attachments (together replicating the length of a long rope attachment) can help you emphasize shoulder external rotation at the end of this exercise’s lifting phase. However, this exercise can still be effectively performed with a single standard-length rope attachment, so you do not need to use a long rope or a combination of two standard ropes.
    2. In addition to the attachments that are just longer versions of the standard rope attachments, long rope attachments functionally include the long strap attachments (that can be used for cable crunches) that have a pair of looped ends into which you can place your hands.
3. While facing the cable station, grasp each end of the rope with your index fingers and adjacent aspects of your hands contacting the flat surfaces of the attachment’s rubber stoppers. Wrap your thumbs over the rounded outer aspects of the stoppers.
    1. If you are using a long strap attachment with looped ends rather than ropes, you naturally will situate your hands within the loops and grasp the inner part of each loop.
4. With your elbows straightened and arms raised to be parallel with the cable, step backward until the machine’s weight plates separate and you feel tension from the cable.
    1. In this position, your palms should be directed down as your arms are outstretched in front of your torso while you are standing upright with your hands close to each other.
5. With your feet near hip width apart, slightly bend your knees, and adopt a staggered stance with one foot mildly in front of the other, or keep your feet symmetrical with each other.
    1. Utilize whichever stance helps you feel the most stable and balanced.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows diagonally backward and down toward shoulder height while flaring them out away from your sides. Simultaneously spread your hands apart as you pull the cable back toward your eyes.
    1. At the end of this motion, your elbows should be pointing straight out to your sides, and your upper arms should be approximately parallel with the ground as they form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. The end position should resemble a double biceps flexing pose with your hands pulled as far backward as your elbows, rather than your hands remaining in front of your elbows like they would during a row.
    3. Finish pulling with your shoulder blades fully pulled back together and your chest up in a “proud chest” posture.
    4. If you are using a long rope attachment or two ropes together, strive to finish with your hands vertically above your elbows with your elbows bent by about 90 degrees. With a single standard rope attachment, you will not be able to spread your hands as far apart and will finish the pull with a greater degree of elbow bend.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your hands and elbows to move diagonally forward toward the pulley as they come together.
    1. Allow your elbows to straighten and your shoulder blades to spread apart naturally as your arms move in line with the cable’s resistance.
    2. You should finish in the starting position with your elbows straightened and arms outstretched in front of you.
    3. You do not have to perform this step with an extremely slow tempo, but you should actively control it the entire time rather than letting the cable abruptly pull your arms forward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While also meaningfully training your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), this exercise can effectively develop your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md) and [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), along with the [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md) to a lesser degree.
2ab5c6f170d88019aa12c43015e4e22c:
## Setting up
1. Position a flat exercise bench centered underneath a Smith machine’s bar in a spot that will situate the bar over your chest when lying down on the bench.
    1. Specifically how you should set up can be influenced by whether your Smith machine has sliding rails that are purely vertical or angled. With either type, you want to set up in a manner that results in the bar being able to touch your lower chest at the bottom of the press.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, place the side of the bench where you will place your feet on the side in which the bar will track slightly forward as it descends. This will result in the top of the rails being horizontally closer to your head than the bottom of the rails when lying down on the bench. An angled Smith machine will allow you to use a bar path that most closely resembles that of a standard barbell bench press.
    3. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which side of the bar you place your feet.
2. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to a height that allows you to grasp it with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently.
    1. The ideal height allows you to unrack the bar while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together without requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    2. If the bar is situated too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart to lift the bar off the safety bars (on which the safety hooks that are attached to the bar rest). This can place you in a less stable position to start your set since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    3. If the bar is situated excessively low, you will have to grasp the bar initially with a greater degree of elbow bend, and unracking it will involve a greater than ideal pressing range of motion. This will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    4. If neither of the two closest bar heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    5. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best starting bar height for you.
3. After positioning the bar to the appropriate height, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section. Use these reps to determine the appropriate height of the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails under the bar) prior to re-racking the bar.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety stops to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could untuck your shoulder blades and flatten out your back to lose your arch. This will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety stops.
    2. Certain Smith machine models have fairly wide spaces between where you could position safety stops. This may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your bench press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. If this applies to your Smith machine, it is not ideal, and you have the option of using a spotter. However, the safety stops can still enhance safety if they are high enough to stop the bar from reaching your neck if you are pinned under a bar and try to scoot out.
    3. If you cannot press the bar fully up and lack a spotter or safety stops that are able to receive the bar when flattening your back, you may be able to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars above your chest if you are able to complete part of the press. If you happen to become pinned in this situation and are initially unable to reach the nearest safety bars above you, you can let the bar rest on your chest until you feel recovered enough to press the bar up high enough to re-rack the bar on the closest safety bars.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your chest is underneath the bar, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor approximately shoulder width apart.
    1. If your Smith machine has vertical slide rails, situate your lower chest under the bar.
    2. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, situate your upper chest under the bar to allow the bar to reach your lower chest at the bottom of the rep.
    3. With the fixed bar path from the Smith machine, it may be worthwhile to try scooting slightly forward or backward on the bench if the exercise feels a bit awkward with your initial positioning.
    4. Starting with your feet on the floor, as you would with a standard bench press, can help you set up optimally and feel more stable when unracking the weight compared to if you lifted your feet off the ground before unracking the bar.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning to bench press, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development. However, if you are specifically training to bench press as much weight as possible, you can optionally exaggerate your lower back arch, which may allow you to shorten the range of motion a bit and potentially lift heavier weights.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
2. Press the bar off the safety bars by straightening your elbows before rotating the safety hooks out away from the safety bars through a slight wrist flick motion.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. One at a time, lift your feet off the ground and straighten your knees with your legs close together while keeping the bar stationary above your shoulders.
    1. Keep your legs in this position until you finish your set.
    2. While your thighs are on the bench, your calves may or may not be resting on the bench as well, depending on your height and the length of your bench.
4. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner. Progressively bend your elbows and allow them to flare out moderately away from each other while descending until you can tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set.
    2. To touch your lower chest, you will have to keep your elbows tucked to a degree instead of being fully flared out, and the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar to your lower chest. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    3. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
5. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up until you have fully straightened your elbows. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. Continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together and your feet off the ground as your buttocks, upper back, and head remain firmly planted on the bench.
6. Alternate between steps 4 and 5 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
    1. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless for about one second.
7. Rotate the safety hooks toward the safety bars by flicking your wrists before bending your elbows to lower the safety hooks securely onto the safety bars.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).
2ab5c6f170d8801a9c0eef1917dc7993:
## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the machine’s shoulder pads to a level that initially allows you to stand under the pads with mildly bent knees, which will enable you to perform full range of motion calf raises.
    1. The appropriate shoulder pad height should make it easy for you to assume the starting position and also allow you to feel resistance from the machine both when your heels are fully lowered and fully raised.
    2. If the pads are too high, your knees may be straightened when initially standing under the pads, and you may lose tension from the machine when your heels are fully lowered.
    3. If the pads are too low, you may need to bend your knees excessively to stand under the pads, and you may be restricted from fully raising your heels.
2. Select your desired weight with the loading pin.
3. With your knees mildly bent, position the balls of your feet onto the foot plate with your heels hanging off the edge while your shoulders are snuggly resting under the shoulder pads.
4. Straighten your knees to stand fully upright and receive the weight from the machine.
    1. Throughout the set, keep the balls of your feet firmly planted on the step.
    2. Depending on their mobility, some people may be able to adopt a position of knee hyperextension, which is when the knees bend backward beyond a straight position. Being able to reach a mildly hyperextended knee position is normal for many individuals and is not inherently problematic. However, certain individuals may experience knee discomfort if they allow their knees to bend backward into hyperextension during this exercise, so keeping a straight knee position instead of a hyperextended knee position may be preferable.
## Exercise technique
1. Push through the balls of your feet to raise your heels fully upward while keeping your knees straight and your trunk upright.
    1. Once you have lifted your heels as high upward as your ankle mobility permits, you have finished the lifting phase.
2. Mildly bend one knee, and lift that side’s foot off the foot plate while keeping your other foot firmly planted on the foot plate.
3. In a controlled manner, allow your working side’s heel to descend toward the ground through the full range of motion your calf flexibility permits.
    1. Continue keeping your free leg’s foot not in contact with the foot plate while maintaining a straight knee position with your working leg.
    2. Strive to lower your heel as far as you can below the ball of your foot to stretch your calf and train it the most effectively.
    3. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in your calf at the bottom, you likely are not descending through your full range of motion.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid quickly dropping down and trying to bounce out of the bottom into the next rep.
4. Once you have fully lowered your working leg’s heel, return your free leg’s foot to the foot plate to have both feet symmetrically on the foot plate.
5. Repeatedly perform steps 1-4 as you alternate each rep which foot you keep in contact with the foot plate during steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After finishing your last rep, mildly bend your knees to lower the weight to its resting position (where it no longer provides any resistance to you) before stepping off the foot plate.
    2. If you wish to do so, you can alternatively complete one set where you perform the lowering phase of each rep exclusively with one side, rest, and then complete another set where you perform the lowering phase of every rep with your opposite side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop both your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md) while simultaneously improving calf flexibility through loaded stretching.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to near waist height, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. Securely attach an ankle cuff just above your wrist on the side you will train this set. Position the cuff so that one of its attachment rings is facing the same direction as your palm.
3. Stand with the side of your other shoulder (that you will not train during this set) facing the cable, and take a small step backward, so that the cable is slightly in front of you by your side.
4. Reach across your body and attach the cuff to the cable with your palm facing the pulley.
5. With your closer free hand, grasp part of the cable station for stability, and step out to the side away from the pulley until you have straightened that side’s elbow.
    1. Throughout the exercise, continue using this arm to help stabilize yourself.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm using the cuff.
6. Allow the cable’s resistance to pull your arm across your body and in toward the pulley with your elbow straightened.
    1. In this position, your hand should be close to being just in front of your opposite side’s thigh with your palm facing the pulley.
    2. You should feel tension from the cable and will likely feel a stretching sensation on the side of your shoulder.
    3. While predominantly pointing downward, your arm should be angled forward just enough to allow it to sweep across your body without your torso getting in the way. If your arm is outstretched forward beyond this point, take a small step forward to position the rest of your body closer to the handle.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow straight, sweep your arm out and away from the pulley until your arm is close to parallel with the ground.
    1. At the top of the raise, your palm should be facing down, and your arm should form half of a “T-shape” with your torso when viewed from the front or back.
    2. While you raise your arm through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blade to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your arm in toward the pulley and across your body in a controlled arcing manner through your full range of motion.
    1. You should finish with your elbow just in front of your torso.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm downward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md) and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), which are assisted by your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to be near the height of the top of your head, select your desired weight with the loading pin, and leave the cable without any attachment.
    1. The appropriate pulley height should allow you to move the cable at about a 45-degree angle during this exercise.
2. Stand sideways with the side of your body you will not train during this set closer to the pulley.
3. With the arm further away from the pulley, reach up across your body, and firmly grasp the ball-shaped stopper at the end of the cable. For additional stability, you can grasp part of the cable station with your free hand.
    1. Hold the stopper in the palm of your hand by wrapping your four smaller fingers around it and positioning your thumb on top of these fingers.
    2. All the subsequent directions will refer to the arm holding the cable.
4. Drive your elbow diagonally downward and across your body until it is level with your side when viewed from the side. Simultaneously let your elbow bend from the cable’s resistance, and keep your forearm aligned with the cable,
    1. When viewed facing the front of your body, you should be able to draw essentially a straight line from your elbow that passes your wrist and the cable to the pulley.
    2. To achieve this alignment, you should finish with your upper arm flared out reasonably close to 45 degrees from your side, resulting in your elbow being angled diagonally outward and downward. Zero degrees of elbow flare would mean your upper arm is pinned directly by your side, while 90 degrees of elbow flare would mean your upper arm is parallel to the ground.
    3. In this context, having your elbow level with your side means it is not in front of your torso or behind your torso when viewed from the side.
5. While maintaining the same arm position, take a small step backward so that the pulley is now slightly in front of you
    1. In this starting position, your elbow should be fully bent or very close to being fully bent.
## Exercise technique
1. Without moving your upper arm, drive your forearm diagonally outward and downward in an arcing manner by straightening your elbow.
    1. Finish with your elbow fully straightened.
    2. All the motion should occur from your forearm hinging at your elbow, without any shoulder motion. You can think of your elbow as the center of an analog clock, while your forearm is the hand that rotates about this stationary center elbow.
    3. Keeping your upper arm angled about 45 degrees out from your side without letting your elbow move forward or backward will indicate that you are successfully avoiding any shoulder motion.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your forearm to arc diagonally upward and in toward the pulley as you bend your elbow in a controlled manner.
    1. Continue keeping your upper arm stationary, and finish with your elbow fully bent.
    2. There is no need to perform this extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your hand toward the pulley in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all three heads of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including its large [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which may not be trained as well by compound pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell and hold it by your side with your elbow straightened.
    1. Continue holding the dumbbell by your side throughout the exercise.
2. Approach a step or a sturdy object that can function as a step. You should be by a surface (e.g., handrail, wall, power rack) where you can place one hand to assist with maintaining your balance.
    1. Based on the equipment at your disposal, a variety of objects can serve as your step. Make sure the object can support your weight, will not move once you are on it, and allows you to lower your heel through the full range of motion your ankle mobility permits.
    2. As an alternative to a staircase’s bottom step, you may select a power rack’s bottom beam if the beam is sufficiently tall.
    3. Additionally, a calf raise block, aerobic step, deadlift block, or thick bumper plate can each be positioned near a wall or power rack for stability. Depending on your bodyweight, anchoring an aerobic step with weight on top of it may be required to prevent the step from tipping.
3. Place your free hand onto the nearby surface for balance assistance, and maintain this hand contact throughout the set.
    1. If you are using a surface that you can grasp (like a power rack) rather than a wall, do not grip it tightly.
4. Step onto the step with the balls of your feet on the step while the back halves of your feet are hanging off the step.
## Exercise technique
1. Push through the balls of your feet to raise your heels upward while keeping your knees straight and your trunk upright.
    1. Only use your free hand for balance assistance as you avoid pushing down in a manner that can help you lift yourself upward.
    2. Once you have lifted your heels as high upward as your ankle mobility permits, you have finished the lifting phase.
2. Mildly bend one knee, and lift that side’s foot off the step while keeping your other foot firmly planted on the step.
3. In a controlled manner, allow your working side’s heel to descend toward the ground through the full range of motion your calf flexibility permits.
    1. Continue keeping your free leg’s foot not in contact with the step while maintaining a straight knee position with your working leg.
    2. Strive to lower your heel as far as you can below the ball of your foot to stretch your calf and train it the most effectively.
    3. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in your calf at the bottom, you likely are not descending through your full range of motion.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid quickly dropping down and trying to bounce out of the bottom into the next rep.
4. Once you have fully lowered your working leg’s heel, return your free leg’s foot to the step to have both feet symmetrically on the step.
5. Repeatedly perform steps 1-4 until you have completed your set. Each rep, alternate which foot you keep in contact with the step during steps 2 and 3.
    1. If you wish to do so, you can alternatively complete one set where you perform the lowering phase of each rep exclusively with one side, rest, and then complete another set where you perform the lowering phase of every rep with your opposite side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop both your [gastrocnemius](../Muscles/Gastrocnemius%201b95c6f170d880b59622dd4a8639aa2f.md) and [soleus](../Muscles/Soleus%201925c6f170d88052bbb6c59dc04f2e1a.md) while simultaneously improving calf flexibility through loaded stretching.

## Setting up
1. Connect to a cable, a rope attachment that is ideally a long rope attachment, or two standard rope attachments that are each fully pulled to one side of the attachment.
    1. Compared to using a single standard-length rope attachment, using a long rope attachment or two standard-length rope attachments (together replicating the length of a long rope attachment) can help you emphasize shoulder external rotation at the end of this exercise’s lifting phase. However, this exercise can still be effectively performed with a single standard-length rope attachment, so you do not need to use a long rope or a combination of two standard ropes.
    2. In addition to the attachments that are just longer versions of the standard rope attachments, long rope attachments functionally include the long strap attachments (that can be used for cable crunches) that have a pair of looped ends into which you can place your hands.
2. Select your weight with the loading pin, and adjust the cable station’s pulley to a height that allows you to just reach the rope when you are sitting on the ground.
    1. The appropriate pulley height should allow you to experience resistance from the cable when your arms are fully outstretched in the starting position. If you do not feel resistance from the cable in the starting position, a higher pulley height is warranted.
    2. For comfort, you optionally can situate an exercise mat on the ground near the cable where you will lie.
3. Sit down on the ground with an upright torso as you are facing the cable.
    1. You can bend your knees and position both feet flat on the floor, or you can place one foot against the cable column for additional stability.
4. Reach your arms toward the rope, and grasp each of its ends with your index fingers and adjacent aspects of your hands contacting the flat surfaces of the attachment’s rubber stoppers. Wrap your thumbs over the rounded outer aspects of the stoppers.
    1. If you are using a long strap attachment with looped ends rather than ropes, you naturally will situate your hands within the loops and grasp the inner part of each loop.
5. With your elbows straightened and arms aligned with the cable, lean backward to rest your back on the ground.
    1. Based on your preference, you can rest your head on the ground, or you can keep your head up, looking toward the pulley.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows down to the floor while flaring them out away from your sides. Simultaneously spread your hands apart while pulling the cable down toward your eyes.
    1. At the end of this motion, your elbows should be pointing straight out to your sides, allowing your upper arms to form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. Strive to pull your hands toward the floor horizontally behind your elbows (i.e., further away from the cable station). This should result in the end position resembling a double biceps flexing pose.
    3. Finish with your shoulder blades fully pulled back together and your chest up in a “proud chest” posture.
    4. If you are using a long rope attachment or two ropes together, aim to finish with your hands as far apart from each other as your elbows, which should be bent by about 90 degrees. With a single standard rope attachment, you will not be able to spread your hands as far apart and will finish the pull with a greater degree of elbow bend.
2. Pause in the bottom position with your arms on the ground for a brief period of time (e.g., about two seconds).
    1. During this pause, you should feel meaningful tension in the muscles on the back of your shoulders.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your hands and elbows to move diagonally up toward the pulley as they come together.
    1. Allow your elbows to straighten and your shoulder blades to spread apart naturally as your arms move in line with the cable’s resistance.
    2. You should finish in the starting position with your arms fully outstretched toward the pulley.
    3. You do not have to perform this step with an extremely slow tempo, but you should avoid letting the cable abruptly pull your arms upward in an uncontrolled fashion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While also meaningfully training your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), this exercise can effectively develop your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md) and [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), along with the [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Set the foot plate to a height that aligns the machine’s pivot point with your hips while standing on the center of the foot plate.
    1. The pivot point will be the center of the machine’s wheel, about which the lever arm rotates.
    2. Strive to align the pivot point specifically with the bony bump (greater trochanter) that you could feel on the side of your hip.
    3. Some machines do not allow you to adjust the foot plate.
2. Position the machine’s lever arm to point straight down.
    1. This will help you adjust the machine to your body proportions before moving the lever arm into the exercise’s starting position.
3. Adjust the machine’s roller pad to be slightly above knee height when standing on the foot plate.
4. Rotate the lever arm out to the side to arc the roller pad to a height that allows the machine to provide resistance when your leg is raised as far out to the side as your flexibility comfortably permits.
    1. How high up you should rotate the lever arm will be determined by your flexibility, and some trial and error may initially be required to find your ideal setting.
    2. The appropriate setting should allow you to stretch the muscles on the inside of your thigh when your leg is fully lifted.
    3. As a starting point, you can rotate the lever arm about 60 degrees beyond vertical out to the side of your body you will train during this set. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in the muscles within your inner thigh when your leg is fully lifted with this setting, you should rotate the lever arm closer to horizontal until you are able to train through the full range of motion your flexibility comfortably enables.
5. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin, and stand on the foot plate facing the weight stack
6. Align the leg that is on the same side as the roller pad with the machine’s pivot point. Stand with that leg just behind the path of the roller pad as your other leg is aligned with the path of the roller pad.
    1. This will result in you adopting a split stance with what will be your working leg behind what will be your resting stance leg.
7. While grasping the roller pad with your hand, pull the lever arm down into a vertical position.
8. Step forward with your rear leg and situate its lower inner thigh snugly against the outer aspect of the roller pad before moving your hand off the roller pad.
9. While standing upright with your legs together, grasp the handlebars by your sides with both hands for stability.
    1. In this starting position, your kneecaps, chest, and imaginary belt buckle should be directed straight ahead toward the center of the machine.
## Exercise technique
1. Allow the machine’s resistance to sweep your leg out to the side and upward in a controlled arcing manner. Let your leg lift as high upward as your flexibility comfortably permits.
    1. Continue keeping your kneecap, chest, and imaginary belt buckle pointing straight forward throughout your set.
    2. Keep the foot of your resting leg firmly planted on the ground.
    3. With the appropriate lever arm setting, you should feel a meaningful stretching sensation within the muscles on the inner aspect of your thigh when your leg is fully lifted.
    4. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine rapidly swing your leg up in an uncontrolled fashion.
2. Reverse the movement by driving your leg downward and inward in an arcing manner.
    1. You can finish this step by tapping the roller against the inner aspect of your resting stance leg.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. After your last rep, you can hold the roller pad down with your hand before lifting your leg off the roller pad and guiding the roller pad up to its starting setting with your hand.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train all your [hip adductor muscles](../Muscles/Hip%20Adductors%201b95c6f170d880018bacca7f9e66c637.md) in an isolated manner.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable bench at a moderate incline angle (near 45 degrees).
    1. Naturally, you can also use a bench permanently fixed to a moderate incline.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on the incline bench with your upper back resting on it and your feet flat on the floor.
    1. While you do not necessarily need to have an exaggerated “proud chest” posture with your shoulders fully pulled back, avoid sitting with your shoulders rolled forward into a slouched upper back position.
3. With your elbows straight and arms hanging down toward the ground, rotate your arms to direct your palms and the front of your biceps out to the sides.
    1. If you lack the mobility to point your palms fully out to the sides, simply rotate them as close to this position as you comfortably can.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to curl the dumbbells upward in an arcing manner while keeping the front of your biceps pointing out to the side.
    1. Since you will not rotate your arms throughout the exercise, the dumbbells should initially arc outward away from your sides before arcing in toward the sides of your shoulders after your forearms have lifted beyond the point where they are parallel to the floor.
    2. While your forearms move through elbow joint motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout your set.
    3. At the top of the curl, your elbows should be fully bent with your forearms touching your biceps and the backside of your hands close to pointing straight out to the side.
2. Without rotating your arms, reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner until your elbows have fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the dumbbells down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable’s pulley to its lowest setting, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. For comfort, you can optionally place an exercise mat on the ground where you will lie in front of the pulley.
2. With your chest facing down, lie down on the ground so that your shoulder (on the side of your body that you will train) is aligned with the pulley.
3. Position yourself where you can just barely reach the handle with the arm in front of the pulley.
    1. If you are situated any closer to the pulley, the cable will not provide resistance when your arm is fully outstretched in the starting position. Provided that the weight you selected is not too heavy to do so, you may be able to crawl back mildly away from the pulley after grasping the handle if you initially are too close to the pulley to experience tension from the cable with your elbow fully straightened.
    2. If you are situated any further away from the pulley, you will not be able to grasp the handle.
4. On the side of your body that you will train, bend your knee and position out to the side, such that your inner thigh is facing the ground.
5. On the side of your body that you will not train, prop your forearm onto the ground, and use this arm to brace against the ground throughout the exercise.
    1. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm that is aligned with the cable, since that is the side you will train.
6. Reach forward toward the pulley and firmly grasp the handle with your elbow straight.
    1. Based on your preference, you can angle your palm down toward the ground or in toward your other side.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbow back toward your side while progressively bending it to pull the handle toward you.
    1. Move your elbow through a path of motion that feels comfortable to you, which may involve keeping your elbow tucked closer to your side (and moving closer to the floor) or flaring it out further from your side (resulting in the handle staying slightly higher above the ground). Feel free to try out different degrees of elbow flare to determine what personally feels best to you.
    2. Pull through your full range of motion, which typically results in your upper arm ending directly by your side.
    3. The appropriate degree of elbow should result in your forearm remaining aligned with the cable throughout the set.
    4. While motion occurs at your working side’s shoulder girdle and elbow, the rest of your body should remain stationary as you continue bracing against the ground.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing the handle to move toward the pulley as you let your elbow move forward away from your side in a controlled manner.
    1. Allow your elbow to arc fully toward the pulley until it straightens to train through a full range of motion.
    2. There is no need to perform this step with an extremely slow tempo, but you should avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm forward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can train your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) especially well while also training your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a seated exercise bench centered between two pulleys from a dual cable station. Situate the bench so that your shoulders will be aligned with the pulleys (rather than being behind or in front of the pulleys) once you are sitting on it.
    1. As an alternative to a seated bench with a backrest or an adjustable bench positioned fully upright, you may use a flat bench and perform the exercise without any back support.
2. Adjust each pulley to be near the height of the top of your head when you are seated on the bench.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, position the ends of its arms further apart than your wingspan. The proper setting should allow you to feel tension from the cables when your arms are fully outstretched to your sides.
    2. Dual cable stations that have their two weight stacks facing each other (often with a pull-up in between them) normally lack adjustable arms. If the two pulleys are not situated further apart than your wingspan, this specific exercise may not be feasible for you to perform with that equipment. If that applies to your dual cable station, you can select an alternative cable curl variation from this database, such as the [low pulley dual cable biceps curl](../Alternative%20Name(s)/High%20pulley%20dual%20cable%20biceps%20curl%202795c6f170d880c994f8ca0b62506f0b.md).
3. Connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.
4. While standing with the sides of your shoulders facing the two pulleys, reach out to your side and firmly grasp one of the handles with a straight elbow.
5. While keeping your elbow straight, walk over to grasp the handle from the other cable in the same manner.
    1. Allow the resistance from the first cable you grasped to keep your arm raised out to the side before doing the same with the other cable during the next step.
6. Step to the side to center yourself between the cables, and sit down on the seated bench with an upright torso.
    1. Your elbows should be straightened, and your arms should be fully aligned with the cables, such that you can draw a straight line from each shoulder through your arm to the cable and then the pulley.
7. Rotate your palms to point up toward the ceiling if they are not already facing this way.
    1. Your wrists should be mostly straight and remain mostly straight throughout the exercise.
8. Pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to curl the handles in toward your ears. Keep your upper arms stationary as they remain directed toward the pulleys.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully bent as your forearms are contacting your biceps or are close to doing so. Depending on the length of your forearms, you may not be able to fully bend your elbows if your hands are about to contact your head.
    2. At the end of this movement, you should look like you are flexing for a double biceps pose.
    3. While you move your forearms through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to straighten to move the handles outward in a controlled manner.
    1. Finish with your elbows fully straightened, like they were in the starting position.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cables abruptly yank the handles outward in an uncontrolled manner.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
2ab5c6f170d88056b4b7ecef4d1ae9b4:
## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to be clearly lower than chest height, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. So long as the pulley is set to a height that allows the cable to move diagonally upward during this exercise’s lifting phase, a range of pulley heights can be viably used for this variation. Setting the pulley near hip height can be an appropriate starting point, but feel free to try out different pulley heights to determine what feels best to you.
2. Connect to the cable a rope attachment (that is ideally a long rope attachment), or two standard rope attachments that are each entirely pulled to one side of the attachment.
    1. Compared to using one standard length rope attachment, using a long rope attachment or two standard rope attachments (that together replicate the length of a long rope attachment) can help you emphasize shoulder external rotation at the end of this exercise’s lifting phase. However, this exercise can still be effectively performed with a single standard-length rope attachment, so you do not need to use a long rope or a combination of two standard ropes.
    2. In addition to the attachments that are just longer versions of the standard rope attachments, long rope attachments functionally include the long strap attachments (that can be used for cable crunches) that have a pair of looped ends into which you can place your hands.
3. While facing the cable station, grasp each end of the rope with your index fingers and adjacent aspects of your hands contacting the flat surfaces of the attachment’s rubber stoppers. Wrap your thumbs over the rounded outer aspects of the stoppers.
    1. If you are using a long strap attachment with looped ends rather than ropes, you naturally will situate your hands within the loops and grasp the inner part of each loop.
4. With your elbows straightened and arms raised to be parallel with the cable, step backward until the machine’s weight plates separate and you feel tension from the cable.
    1. In this position, your palms should be directed down as your arms are outstretched in front of your torso while you are standing upright with your hands close to each other.
5. With your feet hip-width apart, slightly bend your knees, and adopt a staggered stance with one foot slightly in front of the other, or keep your feet symmetrical.
    1. Utilize whichever stance helps you feel the most stable and balanced.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows diagonally backward and upward while flaring them out away from your sides. Simultaneously spread your hands apart as you pull the cable up toward your eyes.
    1. At the end of this motion, your elbows should be pointing straight out to your sides, and your upper arms should be approximately parallel with the ground as they form a “T-shape” with your torso.
    2. The end position should resemble a double biceps flexing pose with your hands pulled as far backward as your elbows, as opposed to your hands remaining in front of your elbows like they would during a row.
    3. Finish pulling with your shoulder blades fully pulled back together and your chest up in a “proud chest” posture.
    4. If you are using a long rope attachment or two ropes together, strive to finish with your hands vertically above your elbows with your elbows bent by about 90 degrees. With a single standard rope attachment, you will not be able to spread your hands as far apart and will finish the pull with a greater degree of elbow bend.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your hands and elbows to move diagonally forward and downward while coming closer together as your elbows straighten.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to spread apart naturally and move forward as your arms move in line with the cable’s resistance.
    2. You should finish in the starting position with your elbows straightened and arms angled forward and downward in front of you.
    3. You do not have to perform this lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, but you should actively control it the entire time rather than letting the cable abruptly pull your arms forward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While also meaningfully training your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), this exercise can effectively develop your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md) and [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), along with the [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to near hip height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Stand with the pulley by the side of your body you will train during this set, and firmly grasp the handle with that side’s hand.
3. With your palm directed forward, take a step out to the side away from the pulley until the weight stack separates and you feel resistance from the cable.
    1. Allow the cable’s resistance to lift your arm out to the side with a straight elbow, which should result in your arm being angled diagonally outward and downward.
    2. Situate your free arm wherever you prefer throughout the exercise, since all the instructions apply to the side on which you are holding the handle.
4. Take a step forward with your foot further away from the cable to adopt a staggered stance that allows you to feel stable and balanced.
5. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. In the starting position, your shoulders should be level as your chest is facing the same direction as your imaginary belt buckle, rather than being twisted toward the pulley.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbow to curl the handle in toward your shoulder while keeping your upper arm stationary.
    1. You should finish with your elbow fully bent as your forearm is contacting your biceps or very close to doing so.
    2. While you move your forearm through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set.
    3. Resist the urge to swing your elbow forward through shoulder motion, and keep your wrist mostly straight.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbow to straighten in a controlled manner as you let your forearm arc outward toward the pulley.
    1. Finish this step with your elbow fully straightened.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank the handle back in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a moderate incline near 45 degrees, and pick up a pair of dumbbells.
    1. Alternatively, you can use a fixed moderate incline bench for this exercise.
    2. Any bench angle that is greater than 30 degrees but less than 60 degrees can be considered a moderate incline.
2. Lie down with your chest contacting the head of the bench and your legs spread out as you position the balls of your feet on the ground.
    1. With the appropriate positioning, your feet should feel stable on the ground, and your torso should be well-supported by the bench.
    2. Shorter lifters may be able to assume this position with straight knees, but taller lifters may have to bend their knees in order to rest their chest comfortably on the head of the bench.
3. Allow your arms to hang down toward the ground with straight elbows as your palms are angled diagonally in toward each other and backward.
    1. Maintain this grip (which is a hybrid between an overhand grip and a neutral grip) throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Sweep your arms diagonally backward and outward away from each other in an arcing motion through the full range your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straightened and chest in contact with the bench throughout the exercise.
    2. Strive to sweep your arms equal parts backward and outward, which should result in your arms forming approximately 45-degree angles near the top of the exercise when viewed from behind.
    3. When moving through your full range of motion, your arms should finish at least slightly behind/above your torso.
    4. While you lift your arms through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blades to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering your arms diagonally forward and inward until they are pointing straight down toward the ground.
    1. You should finish with dumbbells vertically aligned under your shoulders.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the weights downward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also training your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and two [rotator cuff](../Muscles/Rotator%20Cuff%201b95c6f170d880b3b0d8eab69c3a7683.md) muscles to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to near shoulder height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. While standing with the side of your shoulder (on the side of your body you will train during this set) facing the pulley, reach out to your side and firmly grasp the handle with a straight elbow.
3. Take a step out to the side, away from the pulley, while allowing the resistance from the cable to keep your arm raised out to the side.
4. Perform a controlled lunging motion into a half-kneeling position by stepping back with one leg and resting its knee on the ground.
    1. Based on what feels most stable to you, you can decide which knee you situate on the ground.
    2. Keep your torso upright, shoulders level with each other, and your arm aligned with the cable, such that you can draw a straight line from your shoulder through your arm to the cable and then the pulley.
    3. In this position, your imaginary belt buckle should be facing about 90 degrees away from the cable station.
5. Rotate your palm to point up toward the ceiling with a straight wrist if it is not already facing this way.
    1. Situate your free hand wherever you like, such as against your front leg’s lower thigh for additional stability. Keep your free hand in your preferred position throughout the exercise.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbow to curl the handle in toward your ear. Keep your upper arm stationary as it remains directed toward the pulley.
    1. You should finish with your elbow fully bent as your forearm is contacting your biceps or is close to doing so. Depending on the length of your forearm, you may not be able to fully bend your elbow if your hand is about to contact your head.
    2. At the end of this movement, you should look like you are flexing for a biceps pose.
    3. While you move your forearm through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbow to straighten to move the handle outward in a controlled manner.
    1. Finish with your elbow fully straightened, like in the starting position.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank the handle outward in an uncontrolled manner.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side as you face the opposite direction.

## Setting up
1. Determine whether you will set up to bench press within a power rack, which could be modified to perform a variety of barbell lifts and would require you to position a mobile flat bench within the rack, or within a specific bench press station in which the bench is fused to the rack.
    1. Most power racks allow you to position J-hooks (on which the barbell rests before being unracked) and safety pins at incrementally different heights, respectively, to help you situate the bar close to your ideal starting position and to receive the bar safely if you fail a rep.
    2. Bench press stations may also have spotter arms (that function just like safety pins by receiving the bar if you fail a rep) and J-hooks that can be adjusted in height, but a variety of models lack spotter arms and have multiple pairs of fixed height J-hooks. While most people can find a J-hook height that allows them to bench press effectively, some people will notice that their ideal starting position of the bar cannot be achieved with the available J-hook heights, which can make it difficult to unrack the bar independently.
    3. If you have access to a power rack with safety pins and a bench press station without spotter arms, bench pressing within the power rack is recommended for its additional safety mechanism. The con of using a power rack is that it typically takes longer to prepare compared to a specific bench press station.
2. With a power rack, position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. With a bench press station, find which J-hook height places you closest to this position.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
3. After situating a bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks, use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of bench press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins/spotter arms prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
4. Load the bar with your intended weight, and position the safety pins/spotter arms to be slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your bench press.
    1. If you are not training with safety pins/spotter arms that can be positioned to an appropriate height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
5. Lie down with your back on the bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Based on what feels most stable, you can position the soles of your feet flat on the ground with your shins close to being vertical, or you can bend your knees beyond this point to dig the balls of your feet and toes into the ground with your heels off the ground.
    2. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
6. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for the bench press is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning to bench press, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
7. Tightly pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling. Maintain your lower back’s natural curvature rather than arching it any further.
    1. When lying down, your lower back normally exhibits a mild arch, so there is no need to try to flatten it fully. The objective is simply not to exaggerate this natural curvature, which results in you having a closer to flat back compared to if you fully arched your back actively.
    2. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground and squeeze your glutes. Simultaneosuly brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set to create full-body tension.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. Maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your lower chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set.
    2. When aiming to touch the bar to your lower chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    3. To touch your lower chest, you will have to keep your elbows tucked to a degree instead of being fully flared out, and the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar to your lower chest. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your lower chest.
    3. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
6. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
7. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also meaningfully training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and stand upright in a near hip width stance with your arms hanging down by your sides as your elbows are straight.
## Exercise technique
1. Turn your palms in toward your sides to adopt a neutral grip, which is also called a hammer grip.
2. Curl the dumbbells upward in an arcing manner by bending your elbows while keeping your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Keep your wrists straight, torso upright, and elbows by your sides, rather than swinging your elbows forward through shoulder motion.
    2. While your forearms move through elbow joint motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary
    3. At the top of the curl, your elbows should be fully bent with your forearms touching your biceps.
3. Rotate your palms back toward your shoulders to adopt an underhand grip.
4. Lower the dumbbells in a controlled manner by allowing your elbows to straighten progressively without rotating your palms.
    1. Since you will maintain an underhand grip during this lowering phase, your palms should be facing upward when your forearms are parallel to the ground before facing forward once you have fully straightened your elbows.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the dumbbells down.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.

Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively develop your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
