## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable bench at a low incline angle (e.g., near 30 degrees) and set a pair of dumbbells under the head of the bench.
    1. You can alternatively set your bench at a moderate incline (e.g., near 45 degrees) if your bench lacks a low incline setting, or if you personally prefer to use a mildly greater incline.
    2. The dumbbells may be easiest to grasp while lying on the bench if you initially place one end of each dumbbell on top of the bench’s horizontal base leg (which is where wheels may be located) and the other end of each dumbbell on the floor closer to where you will be on the bench.
2. Lie down with your chest contacting the head of the bench and your legs spread out as you position the balls of your feet on the ground.
3. Firmly grasp one dumbbell at a time, and angle your palms diagonally backward and in toward each other while your arms are hanging down with straight elbows.
    1. Rather than just rotating your palm as your elbow and upper arm remain still, rotate your whole arm through shoulder motion, resulting in the bony bump on the back of each elbow pointing diagonally outward and backward. This is the direction in which you will row.
    2. Throughout your set, maintain this grip, which is a hybrid between an overhand grip and a neutral grip.
    3. To be able to row through a full range of motion, the dumbbells should not be in contact with the ground or the base of the bench, which may be more challenging to avoid for individuals with longer arms. To create greater clearance between the dumbbells and the ground, you can scoot further up toward the head of the bench.
    4. If it is difficult for you to grasp the dumbbells, which may be more likely if you have shorter arms, you can initially place the dumbbells closer to the bench’s seat before setting up with your torso scooted further down on the bench to situate your hands closer to the floor. After grasping the dumbbells, you can then press your feet into the ground to scoot further up on the bench so that your head can hang off the bench rather than having your face pressed into the head of the bench.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows in an arcing motion backward, upward, and moderately out away from your sides to row the dumbbells. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Aim to flare your elbows about 45 degrees away from your sides as you move them equally backward and out to the side. Zero degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows purely backward and keeping them completely tucked by your sides, while 90 degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows straight out to the sides, which would result in your upper arms and torso forming a “T-shape” at the top.
    2. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being level with your torso or slightly behind your torso at the top.
    3. Keep your torso in contact with the bench throughout the set rather than arching your lower back to lift your chest up.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
    5. When allowing your elbows to bend naturally, your forearms should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    6. The dumbbells should move in an arcing motion rather than move straight up toward your shoulders.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled arcing motion until your arms are directed down toward the ground with straight elbows.
    1. Allow the weights to pull your shoulder blades apart to stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. Move your elbows diagonally inward and forward at a near 45-degree angle while they descend to reverse the moderate elbow flare you just utilized during the lifting phase.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weights pull your arms down rapidly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to place the dumbbells back onto the ground.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
    1. If your machine has an adjustable seat, you can also initially adjust the seat to whichever position feels most comfortable to you, but the seat position is unlikely to affect exercise.
    2. Note that the sled will provide resistance even without any additional weight plates. The weight of the sled will vary depending on the specific model, but it commonly weighs near 120lb (54kg).
2. Sit down with your buttocks fully on the seat and your whole back firmly supported by the back rest.
    1. Your back should be flat rather than being rounded in a slouched posture, which may occur if you do not situate your hips far enough back against the back rest.
    2. The machine’s safety stoppers (which can be moved with one or two safety handles depending upon the specific machine) should already be locked, and you will keep them locked throughout your set.
3. With a near hip width stance, place the balls of your feet onto the bottom of the foot plate with your heels hanging off the edge.
    1. Ensure that the balls of your feet are firmly on the foot plate to the extent that they will not slide down during the exercise.
4. While grasping the hand grips, press the platform away from you by straightening your knees until they are only mildly bent.
## Exercise technique
1. While simultaneously straightening your knees quickly, forcefully push through the balls of your feet to point your feet away from you (like when stepping on a car’s gas pedal) and press the platform away.
    1. Keep the balls of your feet firmly in contact with the foot plate throughout the exercise.
    2. Once you have pointed your feet as far as your ankle mobility permits with your knees fully straightened, you have finished the lifting phase. There is no need to pause at the top.
    3. As you use your calves to perform most of the work with some assistance from your quads, this quick movement should resemble a jump rope motion but without the ball of your foot leaving the platform.
    4. Aiming to fully straighten your knees does not mean hyperextending your knees, which is when the knees bend backward beyond a straight position. If you have the mobility to hyperextend your knees, there is no need to forcefully lock your knees into a hyperextended position, since straightening them is appropriate.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner, by allowing your feet to point back closer toward you through the full range of motion your calf flexibility permits while mildly bending your knees.
    1. While ensuring that they remain firmly on the foot plate, strive to bring the balls of your feet fully back toward your shins to stretch your calves and train them most effectively.
    2. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in your calves or ankles at the bottom, you likely are not descending through your full ankle range of motion.
    3. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid rapidly dropping down and trying to bounce out of the bottom into the next rep. Only the lifting phase should be quick.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to lower the platform back onto the safety stoppers by further bending your knees.
    1. If you have rather flexible calves and high ankle mobility, you may feel most stable when lowering the platform if you do so when your ankles are near a neutral position (like near the mid-range of each rep) rather than when your feet are bent fully back toward you (like at the bottom of each rep).

## Setting up
1. Situate a pair of dumbbells on an elevated surface (like an exercise bench) or the ground with their handles oriented vertically from one side of each dumbbell facing up.
2. Spread your fingers apart, and firmly grasp the top end of each dumbbell with your palms directed down.
3. In a near hip-width stance, stand upright with your arms by your sides and your elbows straight.
## Exercise technique
1. While forcefully squeezing the dumbbells, curl them upward in an arcing manner by bending your elbows. Strive to keep the dumbbells’ handles fairly aligned with your forearms, such that the handles and your forearms point in a similar direction throughout the curl.
    1. When your elbows are bent by about 90 degrees, and your forearms are in a horizontal position, the dumbbells’ handles should be mostly horizontal. This will require cocking your wrists back and pointing your palms forward rather than down toward the ground with straight wrists, which would situate the handles in a vertical position.
    2. When your elbows are fully bent at the top of the curl, the dumbbells’ handles should be angled upward like your forearms.
    3. Keep your upper arms fixed by your sides rather than allowing them to swing forward through shoulder motion.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner until you have straightened your elbows. Continue keeping the handles pointing in a similar direction as your forearms while you resist letting your wrists straighten.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the dumbbells down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While dynamically training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md), this exercise can statically train your hand's [intrinsic finger flexors](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md) and your forearm’s [wrist extensors](../Muscles/Wrist%20extensors%202c35c6f170d8804ab377fe1e53371f25.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the machine’s shoulder pads to a level that initially allows you to stand under the pads with mildly bent knees, which will enable you to perform full range of motion calf raises.
    1. The appropriate shoulder pad height should make it easy for you to assume the starting position and also allow you to feel resistance from the machine both when your heels are fully lowered and fully raised.
    2. If the pads are too high, your knees may be straightened when initially standing under the pads, and you may lose tension from the machine when your heels are fully lowered.
    3. If the pads are too low, you may need to bend your knees excessively to stand under the pads, and you may be restricted from fully raising your heels.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. With your knees mildly bent, position the balls of your feet onto the foot plate with your heels hanging off the edge while your shoulders are snuggly resting under the shoulder pads.
4. Straighten your knees to stand fully upright and receive the weight from the machine.
    1. Throughout the set, keep the balls of your feet firmly planted on the step.
    2. Depending on their mobility, some people may be able to adopt a position of knee hyperextension, which is when the knees bend backward beyond a straight position. Being able to reach a mildly hyperextended knee position is normal for many individuals and is not inherently problematic. However, certain individuals may experience knee discomfort if they allow their knees to bend backward into hyperextension during this exercise, so keeping a straight knee position instead of a hyperextended knee position may be preferable.
## Exercise technique
1. Push through the balls of your feet to raise your heels fully upward while keeping your knees straight and your trunk upright.
    1. Once you have lifted your heels as high upward as your ankle mobility permits, you have finished the lifting phase.
2. Mildly bend one knee, and lift that side’s foot off the foot plate while keeping your other foot firmly planted on the foot plate.
3. In a controlled manner, allow your working side’s heel to descend toward the ground through the full range of motion your calf flexibility permits.
    1. Continue keeping your free leg’s foot not in contact with the foot plate while maintaining a straight knee position with your working leg.
    2. Strive to lower your heel as far as you can below the ball of your foot to stretch your calf and train it the most effectively.
    3. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in your calf at the bottom, you likely are not descending through your full range of motion.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid quickly dropping down and trying to bounce out of the bottom into the next rep.
4. Once you have fully lowered your working leg’s heel, return your free leg’s foot to the foot plate to have both feet symmetrically on the foot plate.
5. Repeatedly perform steps 1-4 as you alternate each rep which foot you keep in contact with the foot plate during steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After finishing your last rep, mildly bend your knees to lower the weight to its resting position (where it no longer provides any resistance to you) before stepping off the foot plate.
    2. If you wish to do so, you can alternatively complete one set where you perform the lowering phase of each rep exclusively with one side, rest, and then complete another set where you perform the lowering phase of every rep with your opposite side.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to near knee height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
2. Stand with the pulley by the side of your body you will train during this set, squat down, and firmly grasp the handle with that side’s hand.
3. Stand upright, and take a step out to the side away from the pulley before taking a step backward.
    1. Allow the cable’s resistance to lift your arm out to the side with a straight elbow, which should result in your arm being angled diagonally outward and downward in addition to mildly forward.
4. Perform a controlled lunging motion into a half-kneeling position by stepping back with your leg closer to the cable and resting its knee on the ground.
5. Brace your free hand against your front knee for additional stability, and direct your other side’s palm forward.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. In the starting position, your shoulders should be level as your chest is facing the same direction as your imaginary belt buckle, rather than being twisted toward the pulley.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbow to curl the handle across your body toward your opposite shoulder while keeping your upper arm stationary.
    1. You should finish with your elbow fully bent as your forearm is contacting your biceps or very close to doing so.
    2. While you move your forearm through elbow motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set.
    3. Resist the urge to swing your elbow forward through shoulder motion, and keep your wrist mostly straight.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbow to straighten in a controlled manner as you let your forearm arc outward toward the pulley.
    1. Finish this step with your elbow fully straightened.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank the handle back in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. On the side you will train during this set, pick up a dumbbell and hold it with a straight arm as your palm is facing in toward your side.
2. Stand with the side of your opposite shoulder (on the side not holding the dumbbell) facing a sturdy surface onto which you can place one hand and lean.
    1. A variety of objects can be used, such as a cable station’s vertical beam, power rack, or wall.
3. Raise your free arm out to the side until it is close to parallel to the ground with a straight elbow, and place its palm against the surface.
4. While leaning into the surface, take a small step out to the side, and situate both feet together.
    1. Through the hand holding the surface, predominantly bear your weight through the base of your palm (i.e., heel of your hand).
    2. Allow your arm holding the dumbbell to rest against your side. The subsequent directions will apply specifically to this arm.
    3. Specifically how far out you position your feet and consequently lean to the side is up to your preference, but you should be stable and balanced in this position.
    4. While being tilted to the side, your torso and legs should be aligned, like when you are standing upright with your feet together.
## Exercise technique
1. Without bending your elbow, sweep your arm out and away from your side until it is parallel to the ground or a little above that point.
    1. While you raise your arm through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blade to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    2. At the top of the raise, your palm should be directed down toward the ground with a straight wrist.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your arm in toward your side in a controlled arcing manner until the dumbbell lightly contacts your side.
    1. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the weight abruptly yank your arm downward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. As the side of your shoulder (that you will not train during this set) is facing the cable station, stand in a staggered stance with one foot a little in front of the pulley and your other foot a little behind the pulley.
    1. If you step forward with your foot on the side that is closer to the pulley, the cable may be less likely to brush up against your leg during the exercise.
3. Lunge down, grasp the handle between your legs with your hand on the side opposite to the cable, and stand upright.
    1. Your working side’s arm should now be in a vertical position close to your body with your palm facing in toward the pulley and your elbow straight or slightly bent (depending on what feels most comfortable to you).

    1. In this starting position, you should feel stable with your hand firmly holding onto the cable station.
    2. Throughout the set, maintain this leaned body position, and continue supporting yourself with your one arm.

1. Sweep the handle out and away from your side until your upper arm is close to parallel with the ground.
    1. At the top of the raise, your working arm should form half of a “T-shape” with your torso when viewed from the front or back.
    2. While you raise your arm through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blade to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your arm in toward your side in a controlled arcing manner until your arm lightly contacts your torso.
    1. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm downward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. If your machine allows you to do so, adjust the stoppers (that are positioned under the arms) to a height that allows you to press through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. Ideally, position the stoppers as low as you can while being able to grip the handles comfortably with elbows stacked under your wrists in the starting position.
    2. Finding the optimal height may require some trial and error, but you can initially position the stoppers to the bottom setting before performing a couple of warm-up reps without any additional load on the machine. If you experience shoulder discomfort getting into the starting position or are unable to grasp the handles with vertical forearms, the stoppers are likely too low, and you should try raising them. Otherwise, the stopper height is appropriate, and you can proceed to add weight to the machine.
    3. Some machine models do not allow you to adjust the stoppers.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine after determining your appropriate stopper height.
3. Lie down with your back, buttocks, and head on the pad. Position yourself so that your lower-to-middle chest is aligned with the handles.
    1. Your elbows will naturally tuck closer to your sides as you position yourself further back on the pad (situating your shoulders horizontally further behind the handles).
    2. You can decide specifically where you lie down on the pad based on what feels comfortable to your shoulders throughout the exercise, while simultaneously allowing you to feel meaningful tension in your chest.
    3. If you experience shoulder discomfort when pressing with the handles near mid-chest, you can try positioning yourself with the handles by the lowest part of your chest to be able to press with a lower degree of elbow flare.
    4. You can initially keep your feet on the ground until you are ready to finish setting up.
4. With your palms facing forward and elbows bent, firmly grasp the horizontally directed handles. Position your elbows directly under the handles, resulting in your forearms being in a vertical position.
    1. Hold the handles on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists that allow for a comfortable and stable grip that you will maintain throughout your set. Squeezing the handles firmly can help promote this wrist position.
    2. If you cannot comfortably grasp the handles and position your elbows directly under them, you may have to increase the height of the machine’s stoppers before resuming your setup.
    3. Aligning your elbows directly under (rather than being in front or behind when viewed from the side) the handles will naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow flare during this exercise, provided that you positioned your body appropriately on the pad.
    4. If your machine has sufficiently long handles, you may be able to adjust your grip width with different hand placements. Placing your hands moderately outside shoulder width can work well for many people, but you can try out different grip widths to determine where you personally feel best while stacking your elbows under the handles.
5. Pull your shoulder blades back together to assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
    1. Maintain this posture throughout your set.
    2. Rather than excessively arching your lower back, maintain the natural curvature of your lower back like when you are normally standing upright.
    3. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades.
6. One at a time, lift your feet off the ground and straighten your knees with your legs close together.
    1. Keep your legs in this position until you finish your set.
    2. While your thighs are on the pad, your calves may or may not be resting on the pad as well, depending on your height and the length of your pad.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help your body function as a stable platform from which to press.
2. Press the handles upward until you have straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your elbows upward and inward in an arcing manner.
    2. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, your elbows should remain stacked under your wrists and the handles when viewed from the side.
    3. Throughout your set, continue keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together, back and buttocks snugly against the pad, and feet off the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the handles in a controlled manner toward the starting position.
    1. At the end range, you can lightly tap the machine’s arms against the stoppers under them. A gentle tap will confirm that you have moved through the full range of motion in a controlled manner.
    2. Continue keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists and the handles as you allow your elbows to move outward and downward while bending.
    3. If your machine allows you to train through the full range of motion that your mobility enables, it is normal to feel a painless stretching sensation in your chest and/or the front of your shoulders at the end range. Some machines will limit the range of motion before reaching this point, even when set up ideally.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also training your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable bench at a low incline angle (e.g., near 30 degrees), and pick up a dumbbell on the side you are about to train.
    1. As a different variation, which you can use if your bench does not have a low incline setting, you can alternatively select a moderate incline angle (e.g., near 45 degrees) and otherwise use the same technique for this exercise.
2. Sit down sideways on the bench with your arm holding the dumbbell further away from the elevated head of the bench.
3. Lie down with your side (not holding the dumbbell) on the bench in a manner that feels comfortable and stable to you.
    1. There is no single correct way specifically how to situate your body when lying on your side, since individuals with different body types will differ in terms of which exact positions are most comfortable.
    2. For instance, some people will prefer to situate both feet on the ground with fairly straight knees, while others may prefer to keep their feet off the ground with a more pronounced knee bend.
    3. Similarly, certain lifters may feel most comfortable using their free arm to support their head with their upper arm lying on the bench and elbow bent. Others may feel better wrapping the free arm around the bench and holding it for stability.
    4. Feel free to try out different body positions to determine what personally feels most comfortable and stable to you.
    5. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell.
4. With a straight elbow, position your arm moderately in front of your torso so that it can hang down toward the ground without being restricted by contacting the rest of your body.
    1. When setting up, you can begin with your arm directly by your torso (which would naturally prevent your arm from hanging down any lower) and move it somewhat forward beyond this position.
    2. With your arm hanging down across the midline of your body, you should feel a stretching sensation in your shoulder musculature.
    3. To train your lateral delt effectively, avoid positioning your arm meaningfully further forward than is needed (such as where your wrist would be straight forward in front of your chest), which would situate more so to emphasize your rear delt. Your wrist should be closer to your imaginary belt buckle than your chest.
## Exercise technique
1. Sweep your arm diagonally upward and backward until it is aligned with the side of your torso and your elbow is moderately above the height of your top shoulder.
    1. While you do not need to keep it locked, you should keep your elbow essentially straight throughout the exercise.
    2. Having your arm become aligned with the side of your torso means that your arm is no longer in front of your torso when viewed straight on from the lower side of the bench (where your feet are) due to the backward motion of this step
    3. At the top, your arm should be angled diagonally upward and out to the side. When viewed from the front of your body, you can aim to lift your arm upward until it is reasonably close to forming a 90-degree angle with your torso.
    4. As you raise your arm through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blade to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
2. While moving mildly backward, lower your arm behind your torso in a smooth arcing manner through your shoulder’s full comfortable range of motion.
    1. Strive to move your arm just far enough backward that the side of your body will not contact the dumbbell and physically restrict your range of motion.
    2. How far you can lower your arm will be affected by your shoulder mobility, but individuals with normal mobility can often finish with the dumbbell behind the higher buttock. When moving through your full range of motion, it is common to feel a stretching sensation in the muscles on the side of your shoulder.
    3. At the end of this step, the dumbbell should be closer to your buttocks than your imaginary belt buckle.
    4. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should actively control the entirety of this motion.
3. Reverse step 2’s movement by sweeping your arm upward and mildly forward until you have returned to the end position of step 1 with the dumbbell above you.
    1. Your arm should once again be angled upward and outward, as it is no longer behind your torso.
4. Reverse step 1’s movement by allowing your arm to sweep diagonally downward and forward in a controlled manner
    1. Move through your shoulder’s full range of motion while allowing your arm to point downward and forward with your wrist closer to your imaginary buckle than your chest.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. Each rep involves completing steps 1-4.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md) while also training your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md) , [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), and [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells, and sit down on a bench with your torso upright, feet flat on the floor, and arms hanging straight down.
    1. You can opt to sit down on a seated bench with your back resting against the back support, or you can sit on a flat bench without any back support.
## Exercise technique
1. While holding the dumbbells by your sides with straight elbows, turn your palms in toward your sides, resulting in a neutral grip that is also called a hammer grip.
2. Curl the dumbbells upward in an arcing manner by bending your elbows while keeping your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Keep your wrists straight and your elbows by your sides, rather than swinging your elbows forward through shoulder motion.
    2. While your forearms move through elbow joint motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    3. At the top of the curl, your elbows should be fully bent with your forearms touching your biceps.
3. Rotate your palms back toward your shoulders to adopt an underhand grip.
4. Lower the dumbbells in a controlled manner by allowing your elbows to straighten progressively without rotating your palms.
    1. Since you will maintain an underhand grip during this lowering phase, your palms should be facing upward when your forearms are parallel to the ground before facing forward once you have fully straightened your elbows.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the dumbbells down.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively develop your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to near waist height, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.
2. Stand with the side of your shoulder (that you will not train during this set) facing the cable, and take a small step backward, so that the cable is slightly in front of you by your side.
3. With your arm on the side opposite the cable, reach across your body to grasp the handle.
4. With your closer free hand, grasp part of the cable station for stability, and step out to the side away from the pulley until you have straightened that side’s elbow.
    1. Throughout the exercise, continue using this arm to help stabilize yourself.
    2. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm holding the handle.
5. Allow the cable’s resistance to pull your arm across your body and in toward the pulley with your elbow straightened.
    1. In this position, your hand should be close to being just in front of your opposite side’s thigh with your palm facing the pulley.
    2. You should feel tension from the cable and will likely feel a stretching sensation on the side of your shoulder.
    3. While predominantly pointing downward, your arm should be angled forward just enough to allow it to sweep across your body without your torso getting in the way. If your arm is outstretched forward beyond this point, take a small step forward to position the rest of your body closer to the handle.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow straight, sweep your arm out and away from the pulley until your arm is close to parallel with the ground.
    1. At the top of the raise, your palm should be facing down, and your arm should form half of a “T-shape” with your torso when viewed from the front or back.
    2. While you raise your arm through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blade to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your arm in toward the pulley and across your body in a controlled arcing manner through your full range of motion.
    1. You should finish with your elbow just in front of your torso.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm downward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md) and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), which are assisted by your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md).

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, adjust each pulley to be near shoulder-width apart and near head height.
2. Select your desired load with the two weight stacks, and leave the cables without any handle attachments.
3. While facing away from the base of the cable station, stand centered between the pulleys, slightly behind the pulleys.
4. Reach up with bent elbows, and firmly grasp the ball-shaped stoppers at the end of each cable.
    1. Hold the stoppers in the palms of your hands by wrapping your four long fingers around them and positioning your thumbs on top of these fingers.
5. Take a couple of steps forward, and adopt a staggered stance with one foot further in front than the other.
6. For balance, slightly bend your front knee and slightly lean your torso forward by hinging at your front leg’s hip.
7. If you did not already do so, hold your upper arms approximately parallel to the ground with your elbows bent to assume the starting position.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your forearms forward in an arcing manner by straightening your elbows. Keep your elbows up as your upper arms remain essentially stationary throughout the set.
    1. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. Strive to have all the movement occurring from your forearms hinging at your elbows without any shoulder motion.
    3. You can think of each elbow as the center of an analog clock, while your forearm is the hand that rotates about this stationary center elbow.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to bend in a controlled manner as your forearms arc back toward the pulleys.
    1. Let your elbows bend through the full range of motion provided by the cables until your forearms are aligned with them.
    2. There is no need to perform this extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the cables abruptly yank your hands toward the pulleys in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, step backward and bring the cable ends toward the pulleys until the cables lose tension and you can release them.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by compound pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. At a dual cable station, adjust each pulley to near waist height, select your desired load with the two weight stacks, and leave the cables without any handle attachments.
    1. A dual cable station that can situate the two pulleys no further apart than your wingspan is ideal to use for this variation.
    2. A dual cable station that has its pulleys rather far apart from each other (often with a long upper beam connecting each end of the station) is not as practical to use. With this type of equipment, the [single arm cable overhead triceps extension](Single%20arm%20cable%20overhead%20triceps%20extension%201a15c6f170d880bea7f6e5698ee2a6f7.md) may be preferable.
2. Stand centered between the pulleys facing toward the base of the cable station.
3. Firmly grasp the ball at the end of each cable with the hand that is closer to that cable.
4. Pivot your body 180 degrees while simultaneously bending your elbows and lifting them upward to cross the cables over each other.
    1. Finish with your hands close to each other behind your neck as your elbows are fully bent and raised to head height.
    2. The cable you are holding with your right hand should now be exerting a force angled to your left, while the cable you are holding with your left hand is exerting a force angled to your right.
5. Adopt a staggered stance by stepping forward with one foot, and slightly lean forward by hinging at your hips
    1. In this starting position, your upper arms should be angled out to your sides, upward, and somewhat forward as they are aligned with the cables exerting a force that is angled inward, downward, and somewhat backward.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your hands upward, outward, and mildly forward in an arcing motion by extending your elbows until they are fully straightened. Keep your elbows up as your upper arms remain essentially stationary throughout the set.
    1. While your upper arms remain aligned with the direction in which the cables are pulling, this movement should resemble drawing a pair of katana from their sheaths behind your back.
    2. During this exercise, nearly all the motion should occur from your forearms hinging at your elbows without any shoulder motion. You can think of each elbow as the center of an analog clock, while your forearm is the hand that rotates about this stationary center elbow.
2. Reverse the motion in a controlled manner by bending your elbows and allowing your hands to move downward, in toward each other, and back behind your neck.
    1. Allow your elbows to bend fully, which typically produces a stretching sensation in your triceps.
    2. There is no need to perform this extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the cables abruptly yank your hands toward the pulleys in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, perform the opposite of the pivoting maneuver you utilized while setting up to uncross the cables and face toward the base of the cable station.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all three heads of your [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including its large [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which may not be trained as well by compound pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. Adjust each pulley from a dual cable station to be near hand height when standing with your arms relaxed by your sides.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you can set the arms so that their ends are as close to shoulder width apart as you can.
    2. Dual cable stations that have their pulleys rather far apart from each other (often with a long upper beam connecting each end of the station) are not as practical to use for this variation compared to dual cable stations that have their pulleys closer together. If you use cables situated fairly far apart from each other, the cables will exert a force angled out to the sides to a notable degree, which will influence the technique compared to if the cables are chiefly pulling backward.
2. Position a seated exercise bench (or an adjustable bench positioned fully upright) centered in front of two pulleys.
    1. Place the bench far enough in front of the pulleys that the cables will be able to provide resistance to you when your arms are situated fully back behind you in the starting position.
3. Connect a D-handle attachment to each cable, and select your weight with the loading pin at each weight stack.
4. Stand in between the pulleys while facing toward the bench.
5. Grasp the two handles with your elbows straightened and palms facing forward.
6. While keeping your arms reasonably close to your torso, walk forward on one side of the bench until you can straddle the bench and sit down with your back snugly against the back pad.
    1. Keep your elbows bent with the handles close to you while walking forward against the cables’ resistance.
    2. Place your feet flat on the floor or against the foot bar if your seated bench has a foot bar.
7. Pull your shoulder blades back together with your chest up to assume a “proud chest” posture.
8. With straight elbows, allow the cables to pull your arms back behind your torso through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to curl the handles forward and upward in an arcing manner. Keep your upper arms stationary as you avoid swinging them forward through shoulder motion.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully bent as your forearms contact your biceps.
    2. While you move your forearms through elbow joint motion, the rest of your body should remain still throughout your set, which will result in your elbows remaining behind your torso.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing the handles to arc downward and back toward the pulleys as your elbows straighten.
    1. Finish this step with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cables abruptly yank the handles back in an uncontrolled manner.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, drive your elbows forward to bring your arms to your sides before standing up. Then step to one side of the bench, and walk backward until the cables are no longer tensed before releasing the handles.
## Description
While also meaningfully developing your [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md) and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md), this exercise can effectively train [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md) from a notably lengthened position.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a weight plate with each hand, and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance while holding the plates by your thighs with straight elbows as your palms face your thighs.
    1. Plates that have grip holes (cutouts that allow the rim of a plate to function as a handle) will be the easiest to hold.
    2. If you are using weight plates that lack grip holes but have a raised outer lip, you can hook the tips of your four long fingers under the lip while positioning your thumbs on the other side of the plate.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your earlobes through the full range of motion you can to lift the plates upward.
    1. You should not turn this shrug into an upright row, but it is not problematic if your elbows naturally bend a bit rather than remaining completely straight.
    2. Throughout the exercise, continue standing upright with straight legs, and look straight ahead to keep your neck near a neutral position.
3. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulders to descend fully in a controlled manner to lower the plates.
    1. At the bottom, your shoulders should ideally be positioned a little lower than where they are normally situated while standing at rest due to the downward stretch that the weights can provide.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the weights abruptly yank you downward.
4. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper traps](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md).

## Setting up
1. At a cable station, adjust the pulley to be near the height of your lower chest, connect a D-handle attachment to the cable, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. If you are using a machine (like the Freemotion dual cable cross) that has its pulleys connected to adjustable arms that can be swiveled forward or backward, you can position the arm of the cable you will not be using in a position where you can grasp it with your free hand for stability during the exercise.
2. Stand with the side of your body that you will train during this set facing the handle.
3. Using your closer hand, firmly grasp the handle with your elbow bent and forearm approximately parallel to the ground as it is pointing straight ahead.
    1. Based on your preference, you could hold the handle with your palm facing in toward you, down toward the ground, or angled diagonally in between these two directions. Feel free to try out different positions and utilize whichever feels best to you.
4. Pivot your body about 45 degrees away from the pulley, and use your free hand to grasp part of the cable station for additional stability if your cable station allows you to do so.
    1. Keep your chest and imaginary belt buckle pointing straight ahead in the same direction rather than letting the cable twist your body when turning.
    2. Not all cable stations will have a surface available against which to brace with your free hand.
    3. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the handle.
5. If you are not currently experiencing resistance from the cable, step forward until you do.
6. Adopt a staggered stance with one foot further in front than your other and your knees slightly bent. Your elbow should be flared out away from your side toward the pulley in line with where the cable’s resistance naturally pulls it.
    1. In this position, you should feel sufficiently stable and balanced, as your elbow is flared out away from your side toward the pulley
7. As you are standing with an upright torso, pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture that lifts your chest slightly up toward the ceiling.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Press the handle across your body by driving your elbow inward as it straightens.
    1. Press through the full range of motion across your body. This often results in the elbow finishing in front of the breastbone, and the hand finishing in front of the opposite shoulder.
    2. You should feel like you are squeezing your pec, particularly at the end of this step, with your arm fully across your body.
    3. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulder and elbow, strive to keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
    4. Continue keeping your chest and imaginary belt buckle pointing straight ahead in the same direction as you avoid twisting your body.
    5. Keep your elbow level with your straight wrist, which will align your forearm with the direction in which you are pressing
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing your elbow to move out toward the pulley while naturally bending.
    1. Allow the cable to pull your elbow fully out to the side as you avoid twisting your chest toward the pulley.
    2. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm outward in an uncontrolled fashion.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise will primarily develop your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), which is assisted by your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).

## Setting up
1. Connect a standard lat pulldown attachment with a straight bar shaft to a seated cable row machine, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. If your machine allows you to adjust the seat height, you can set it to a height that allows the cable to run approximately horizontally during this exercise rather than meaningfully angling upward or downward. A seat height that situates the pulley a little lower than your chest (once you are seated with an upright torso) is normally appropriate.
2. Sit down on the seat, and position your feet in contact with the machine’s foot plates as your knees are mildly bent.
    1. The appropriate degree of knee bend should allow you to feel stable and comfortable throughout the exercise while experiencing resistance throughout its full range of motion. If you lose resistance (from the weight you selected contacting the rest of the weight stack) at any point during your set, it can be preferable to adopt a lesser degree of knee bend to scoot yourself further back.
3. Fully reach your arms forward, and lean forward by rounding your back until you can grasp the bar firmly with a slightly outside shoulder-width overhand grip, resulting in your palms facing downward.
    1. If you initially cannot reach the bar, you can scoot forward closer toward the cable by bending your knees further.
    2. Rather than rounding just one part of your back, round your lower, middle, and upper back together through a range that feels comfortable to your back.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar back toward your torso by driving your elbows backward and pulling your shoulder blades together. Simultaneously straighten your back to assume an upright torso position.
    1. Allow your elbows naturally to flare out away from your sides in a manner that feels comfortable to you.
    2. At the end of this step, your lower back should exhibit the mild curvature it naturally has when you are standing upright, which should result in your shoulders being vertically aligned above your hips. Avoid excessively arching your lower back beyond this point, which can occur if you exaggerate leaning back.
    3. You should finish the row in a “proud chest” posture with your chest up and shoulder blades fully back. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together as if you were trying to pinch a pencil between them.
    4. Aim to drive your elbows fully backward, which should result in the bar being directly in front of your torso with your elbows slightly behind your torso at the end.
    5. Rather than performing the two motions in a segmented manner, strive to row the bar toward you in sync with the same rate at which you are straightening your back. This should result in the bar reaching just in front of your torso at the same moment in which your torso becomes fully upright.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by allowing the cable to pull your elbows forward as you simultaneously round your back through a comfortable range and let your shoulder blades spread apart.
    1. You should finish with your back comfortably rounded and arms fully outstretched in front of you with straight elbows. This position should resemble if you were seated and leaning forward to try to reach an object just barely within your reach.
    2. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation throughout your back in this position, but you should not experience lower back discomfort. If you begin feeling lower back discomfort at the end range, it may be appropriate to not round your back quite as much, since you should only move through what is your back’s comfortable range of motion.
    3. There is no need to perform this step with an extremely slow tempo, but you should certainly avoid letting the cable abruptly yank you forward. Using a fairly slow tempo can help reinforce the controlled technique desirable for this variation.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop most of your back musculature, including your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), and [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the seat so that the handles are level with your shoulders once you are seated with an upright torso.
2. Adjust the lever arms to position the handles as close together (on the side of the chest pad) as your machine enables.
3. Select your desired weight with the loading pin.
4. Sit down sideways on the seat with what will be your working side further away from the chest pad.
    1. Rest your feet on the floor with your knees bent.
5. With your arm further away from the chest pad, reach across your body to grasp the horizontal handle with your palm facing down. Simultaneously turn your chest toward the handle to help you reach it.
    1. To grasp the handle, you can initially stand up before sitting back down during the next step if that helps you reach it.
6. While holding the handle with a straight or slightly bent elbow, turn your chest until it is facing the same direction as your imaginary belt buckle.
    1. In this starting position, your working arm should be situated fully across your body, which should prompt you to feel a stretching sensation in the back of your shoulder.
    2. Position your free hand wherever you prefer throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Without bending your elbow, smoothly sweep your arm outward and across your body in a wide arcing motion.
    1. For the standard version of this exercise, you can finish once your arm is directed straight out to the side of your shoulder, resulting in your torso and arm forming half of a “T-shape.”
    2. While you move your arm through shoulder motion, keep the rest of your body stationary throughout your set.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your arm to sweep fluidly in toward the starting position through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility permits.
    1. Just like when you finished setting up, you should feel a stretching sensation in the back of your shoulder as your arm is fully across your body.
    2. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should actively resist the weight rather than letting it abruptly yank your arm inward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which is assisted by your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), along with your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Attach your desired load (e.g., weight plates or a kettlebell) to a pull-up/dip belt around your waist, and stand upright under a pull-up bar.
    1. The back of your belt should be securely resting on top of your buttocks, and the belt’s chain or strap (depending on the belt model) should be looped through the center hole of a weight plate or under the handle of a kettlebell. If you have a loading pin on your belt, you can alternatively loop the chain or strap through the loading pin after adding weight plates.
    2. It will be easiest if you carry the weight over to the pull-up bar and add the weight to your belt while you are under the bar, rather than adding the weight to your belt farther away from the bar before walking over to the bar.
    3. As an alternative to using a pull-up/dip belt, you can wear a weighted vest.
    4. While less stable and more awkward than using a belt or weighted vest, you also have the option of holding a dumbbell between your thighs or feet, but you will be limited in how much weight you can add when using a dumbbell.
2. Reach up overhead and firmly grasp the pull-up bar with your palms facing forward (i.e., an overhand grip) and your hands situated well outside shoulder width.
    1. Positioning your hands approximately 50% wider than shoulder width is appropriate; however, a wide grip encompasses a range of grip widths, and the specific width you grasp the bar is up to your preference.
    2. What you consider a wide grip may also be influenced by the grip width you use for your standard pull-up, which you can widen to individualize your grip. For instance, for a wide grip, place your index finger on the bar just outside where you would otherwise place your little finger when performing a standard pull-up.
    3. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    4. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
3. With your elbows straightened, lift your feet up off the ground by bending your knees to begin hanging on the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging on the bar with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to assume a “proud chest” that is angled slightly upward.
    1. Maintain this “proud chest” posture throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and toward your sides as you progressively bend your elbows.
    1. Since the bar is fixed, your elbows will not naturally drive downward; however, maintaining the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows being bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, individuals may have different ranges of motion.
    3. Rather than swinging your legs, statically keep them in a similar position throughout the rep.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your elbows straightened and arms fully overhead.
    1. You do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to return your feet to the ground before releasing the bar.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. If you are using a step, position it slightly in front of the pull-up bar. The step should be positioned so that you can readily reach the bar without the step interfering with your feet or your weight during the exercise.
    1. Objects that can be used as a step include a plyometric box, an aerobic step, a bumper plate, and a flat exercise bench.
    2. Ideally, the step will be tall enough that you can grasp the bar with your elbows fairly bent, which will minimize how high you have to hop.
2. Attach your desired load (e.g., weight plates or a kettlebell) to a pull-up/dip belt around your waist, and stand upright under a pull-up bar.
    1. The back of your belt should be securely resting on top of your buttocks, and the belt’s chain or strap (depending on the belt model) should be looped through the center hole of a weight plate or under the handle of a kettlebell. If you have a loading pin on your belt, you can alternatively loop the chain or strap through the loading pin after adding weight plates.
    2. It will be easiest if you carry the weight over to the pull-up bar and add the weight to your belt while you are very close to the bar, rather than adding the weight to your belt farther away from the bar before walking over to the bar.
    3. As an alternative to using a pull-up/dip belt, you can wear a weighted vest.
3. While standing under the pull-up bar on the step or ground, reach up and firmly grasp it with a slightly outside shoulder-width overhand grip, resulting in your palms facing forward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Hop up while pulling down on the bar to bring your chest toward the bar, keeping your elbows fully bent at your sides.
    1. You should now be in the top position of a pull-up.
    2. The degree to which you have to use your legs to hop up will naturally be affected by how high the bar is above your chest at the end of the setup. With a sufficiently tall step, you may be able to step forward without hopping up.
    3. Since you can use meaningful assistance from your legs or start with your chest already close to the bar, this step should not feel particularly strenuous to your back and arm muscles. The objective is to make getting your chest up to the bar feel relatively easy, so that your muscles are fresh and ready to control the descent.
2. While keeping your chest by the bar for a moment, bend your knees as much as is required to avoid your feet contacting the step or ground during the lowering phase. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.

1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to its highest level, and select your desired weight with the loading pin.

    3. Throughout the exercise, avoid swinging your elbows backward or forward through shoulder motion.

    1. Strive to have your elbows as close to fully bent as you can by the time you have finished this movement to train your triceps through a full range of motion.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the machine’s seat to a height that allows you to rest your torso against the chest pad and enables you to row comfortably with your elbows tucked fairly close to your sides.
    1. The appropriate seat height often naturally allows you to finish the lifting phase with your elbows bent by about 90 degrees.

    3. If the seat is too high, you may notice that you have to pack your shoulder blades down to reach the handles with your arms directed further downward than forward. This could limit your range of motion and prompt the row to not feel as natural as it otherwise could.
2. If your machine has an adjustable chest pad, set it to a position that allows you to just grasp the handles when your arms are fully outstretched with straight elbows.
    1. Machines often lack an adjustable chest pad.
3. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, and sit down on the seat with your torso against the chest pad.
    1. Based on your preference, you can position your feet against the machine’s foot plates (if your machine model has foot plates), or you can place your feet flat on the floor.
    2. As an alternative to sitting on the seat, you optionally can adopt a staggered stance with one foot forward and the other backward as you lightly contact the seat with your buttocks while predominantly bearing weight through your feet.
    3. Set up in whichever position feels most stable and comfortable to you.
4. Reach forward and firmly grasp the handles. If your machine allows you to use different grips, grasp the handles at a spot where you can angle your palms in toward each other.
    1. Hold the handles with straight wrists and elbows.
    2. If the handles are situated far enough in front of you to make it difficult to grasp both of them simultaneously, it may be easier for you to grasp one handle at a time.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handles back toward you by driving your elbows backward while bending them. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Rather than meaningfully flaring them out away from your sides, keep your elbows tucked reasonably close to your sides to a degree that feels natural and comfortable to you. This should keep your forearms aligned with the direction in which you are rowing.
    2. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being slightly behind your torso or at least level with your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    3. Instead of moving straight backward in a fully horizontal direction, this machine type will normally have its handles move at an upward angle while you pull them backward.
    4. Keep your torso in contact with the chest pad throughout the set.
    5. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to move forward in a controlled manner as they progressively straighten until your arms are fully outstretched in front of you.
    1. Your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another, but you can exaggerate this motion by intentionally allowing the weight to pull them further apart than your resting position at the end, which will stretch your upper back muscles.
    2. While you do not have to perform this step extremely slowly, you should avoid letting the weight abruptly yank your arms forward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

1. After adding weight plates to the machine’s weight sleeve, straddle the machine by standing on the foot plates as you are facing toward the weights.
    1. This variation specifically uses a T-bar row machine without any chest support, and other exercises using chest-supported T-bar row machines are included in this database.

    3. The foot plates of most machines will require you to adopt a close to shoulder-width stance.
    4. Position your feet in a manner that places the machine’s handles just in front of you so that you do not have to reach far forward in order to grasp the handles initially.
2. With your arms pointing down toward the handles, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the handles. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track far forward. However, you can let your knees shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
3. Firmly grasp the outer handles with a wide grip, such that your hands are clearly outside shoulder width with palms angled backward.
    1. The appropriate grip width for this upper-back focused variation should naturally let your elbows flare prominently out away from your sides. At the top of your row, this should result in your upper arms being closer to forming a “T-shape” with your torso when viewed from behind, rather than being closer to being tucked by your sides (which can naturally occur with a closer grip).
    2. To find a viable wide grip based on your typical grip, you can place your index fingers on the handles where you would otherwise place your little fingers when performing your standard overhand grip T-bar row.
    3. The handles that permit a wide grip are completely horizontal (which points your palms straight backward) on some machines, but angled outward and backward on other machines (which points your palms backward and inward at an angle). Consequently, the specific grip you can use will vary based on your machine model.

    1. Continue bracing your core from now on.

    1. The objective is to use your hip and thigh muscles to lift the bar just high enough that you can experience resistance from the weight when your elbows are fully straight in the starting position of each rep.

1. Pull the bar upward and back toward your torso by driving your elbows simultaneously upward and backward. Simultaneously bend your elbows and pull your shoulder blades back together.
    1. Rather than trying to keep them tucked close to your sides, allow your elbows to flare out meaningfully away from your sides to a degree that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    2. Keep your torso in a fixed hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set while keeping your core braced and your lower back near a neutral position.

    2. While you do not have to lower the bar extremely slowly, you should avoid letting the bar drop abruptly in an uncontrolled fashion.

## Setting up
1. Approach a step or a sturdy object that can function as a step. You should be by a surface (e.g., handrail, wall, power rack) where you can place one hand to assist with maintaining your balance.
    1. Based on the equipment at your disposal, a variety of objects can serve as your step. Make sure the object can support your weight, will not move once you are on it, and allows you to lower your heel through the full range of motion your ankle mobility permits.
    2. As an alternative to a staircase’s bottom step, you may select a power rack’s bottom beam if the beam is sufficiently tall.
    3. Additionally, a calf raise block, aerobic step, deadlift block, or thick bumper plate can each be positioned near a wall or power rack for stability. Depending on your bodyweight, anchoring an aerobic step with weight on top of it may be required to prevent the step from tipping.
2. Place one free hand onto the nearby surface for balance assistance, and maintain this hand contact throughout the set.
    1. If you are using a surface that you can grasp (like a power rack) rather than a wall, do not grip it tightly.
    2. Keep your other hand wherever you prefer throughout your set.
3. Step onto the step with the balls of your feet on the step while the back halves of your feet are hanging off the step.
## Exercise technique
1. Push through the balls of your feet to raise your heels upward while keeping your knees straight and your trunk upright.
    1. Only use your free hand for balance assistance as you avoid pushing down in a manner that can help you lift yourself upward.
    2. Once you have lifted your heels as high upward as your ankle mobility permits, you have finished the lifting phase.
2. Mildly bend one knee, and lift that side’s foot off the step while keeping your other foot firmly planted on the step.
3. In a controlled manner, allow your working side’s heel to descend toward the ground through the full range of motion your calf flexibility permits.
    1. Continue keeping your free leg’s foot not in contact with the step while maintaining a straight knee position with your working leg.
    2. Strive to lower your heel as far as you can below the ball of your foot to stretch your calf and train it the most effectively.
    3. If you do not feel a stretching sensation in your calf at the bottom, you likely are not descending through your full range of motion.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid quickly dropping down and trying to bounce out of the bottom into the next rep.
4. Once you have fully lowered your working leg’s heel, return your free leg’s foot to the step to have both feet symmetrically on the step.
5. Repeatedly perform steps 1-4 until you have completed your set. Each rep, alternate which foot you keep in contact with the step during steps 2 and 3.
    1. If you wish to do so, you can alternatively complete one set where you perform the lowering phase of each rep exclusively with one side, rest, and then complete another set where you perform the lowering phase of every rep with your opposite side.
