## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a sled situated in an area where you have sufficient space for pulling it backward.
    1. With certain wheeled sleds, you may also be able to adjust your resistance level with a lever that changes its friction. For these sleds, increasing the friction will increase the intensity of the exercise, similar to adding weight plates.
    2. Note that the type of surface on which you will move the sled will affect how much resistance you experience during this exercise. When tracking progress, it is consequently best to compare sets performed on the same surface.
2. Attach a strap to the base of the sled before connecting a belt to the other end of the strap.
    1. With an appropriate strap, viable belt options include a sled drag belt (that is specifically designed for sled drags), a belt squat belt (that is designed for machine belt squats), or a dip/pull-up belt.
    2. A belt that has padding will naturally be the most comfortable for this exercise.
3. Stand centered behind the sled, step into the belt, and situate the belt around your waist.
    1. Rather than positioning the belt higher on your lower back, it is generally appropriate to have the belt resting on the back of your upper hip bones.
4. While using your hands to keep the belt in place, walk backward until the strap becomes taut with the belt snuggly around your waist.
5. Release your hands from the belt, and position your feet approximately hip-width apart with your toes pointing straight ahead.
6. With your torso upright, adopt a “proud chest” posture with your shoulder blades pulled mildly backward.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. While keeping your torso upright, bend your knees into a near half squat position or your preferred degree of knee bend.
    1. For stimulating increases in quad muscle size and developing strength through a longer range of motion, it is appropriate to reach at least a moderate degree (i.e., about 60 degrees) of knee bend during this exercise. However, you have the option of utilizing a milder degree of knee bend if you wish to do so.
3. Begin dragging the sled backward by straightening one leg’s knee while simultaneously bending your other leg’s knee to step backward with its foot.
    1. While using your legs to move the sled, the rest of your body should remain in essentially a static position during your set as the belt stays around your waist.
    2. Keep your back flat and chest up to maintain an upright torso position throughout the drag.
    3. Throughout the exercise, allow your arms to move naturally, like when you would normally walk backward.
4. At the moment you finish fully straightening your one knee, plant your other foot onto the ground.
    1. While straightening your knee, you should feel tension in that side’s quad.
    2. With the proper technique, you should first and foremost be using your quads to drag the sled.
5. Continue fluidly dragging the sled backward as you reciprocally straighten one leg’s knee while stepping backward with your other leg’s foot until you have reached your target distance or the end of your available space and have to switch to dragging it the opposite direction.
    1. Throughout the set, be aware of any individuals who may potentially enter the path in which you are pulling to avoid an unintended collision.
    2. If your sled has an attachment point on each side of the sled, you can connect the straps to the other side before dragging the sled in the opposite direction.
    3. If your sled only has an attachment point on one side, you will naturally have to rotate your sled 180 degrees before dragging it back in the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise will chiefly train your [quads](../Muscles/Quadriceps%20Femoris%201b95c6f170d88058a905d88715b5e628.md) while being easier from which to recover compared to most quad exercises.

## Setting up
1. Determine the object that will serve as the box onto which you will sit during this exercise. The object should be of a height that allows you to reach your desired squat depth, sufficiently stable that it will not slide, and sturdy enough to support your bodyweight.
    1. Provided that they satisfy the aforementioned criteria, a variety of objects can be effectively used.
    2. Viable objects include a squat box, plyometric box, aerobic step elevated on risers, flat exercise bench, stack of deadlift blocks, couch, and chair (that will not slide).
    3. While not ideal due to its lower stability, you can also stack bumper plates on top of each other to form a “box” of your desired height. If you opt to do so, make sure that the plates are completely centered on top of each other.
    4. As the height of your object decreases, the intensity of each rep will naturally increase in turn, so the weight that is appropriate for you will be influenced by the height of your object. For most goals, it is typically appropriate to select an object that is near the lowest height that allows you to complete your intended number of reps with high-quality technique. It is generally recommended to progress initially to an object of a low height that allows you to train through a full range of motion prior to progressing to a heavier weight.
2. Pick up a kettlebell or dumbbell and hold it right next to your chest with bent elbows, as your upper arms are slightly in front of your sides (i.e., in the goblet position).
    1. You can use either a kettlebell or a dumbbell, but some people find holding a kettlebell in the goblet position to feel more stable and comfortable, especially with a fairly heavy weight.
    2. Based on your preference and the load you use, you can transfer your kettlebell or dumbbell into the goblet position through a couple of different approaches.
    3. An effective approach is initially to pick up the weight by the handle through a deadlift motion and set it on an elevated surface (like a bench or plyometric box) with the handle facing up if you use a kettlebell or the handle directed vertically if using a dumbbell (as only one end of the dumbbell is on the surface). Then squat down until the weight is right in front of your chest, firmly grasp it in the goblet position, and squat up with the weight. If you use a kettlebell, grasp it by its horns (i.e., side handles). If you use a dumbbell, cup your hands around the top end of the weight with the base of your palms by the handle, and your fingers wrapped around the rest of that end of the weight.
    4. With a lighter kettlebell, you can tilt it onto its side with the weight base directed toward you, squat down to grasp its horns, stand upright with it, and curl it into the goblet position.
    5. With a lighter dumbbell, you can also pick it up with one hand and curl it up across your body to be in front of your chest. Then cup your free hand around the top end of the dumbbell with the base of its palm by the handle and fingers wrapped around the top end of the weight before repositioning your other hand to cup the other side of the weight in the same manner.
3. In a near hip-width stance with your toes pointing straight ahead, stand upright while holding the weight to your chest with the box behind you.
    1. The box should be close enough to you that you can sit on it.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your weight onto one foot (on the side you will train), and lift your other foot up off the ground by lifting that side’s leg up with a mostly straight knee.
    1. Keep your free leg’s foot off the ground throughout the set.
2. With the leg in contact with the ground, progressively bend at your knee and hip to sit back in a controlled manner.
    1. It can be helpful to initiate the descent by mildly sitting your buttocks back through a hip hinge motion that somewhat inclines your torso, as if you are closing a car door with your buttocks as your hands are carrying something.
    2. Keep the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your working leg’s foot firmly in contact with the ground throughout your set.
    3. Strive to have your knee track straight forward in line with your second and third toes (when counting your big toe as your first toe) as you descend, while not letting your knee cave inward.
    4. Throughout the set, continue keeping the weight close to your chest and your chest up rather than letting your chest collapse through excessive upper back rounding.
    5. To the best of your ability, keep the tops of your hip bones level with each other rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your free leg drop down.
    6. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    7. Through motion at your working leg’s hip, your torso should naturally transition to at least a mildly inclined position rather than remaining completely upright. While you should not intentionally round your lower back, it is common to experience a degree of rounding toward the bottom of the rep if you are using a low box.
    8. There is no need to descend with an extremely slow tempo, but you should avoid dropping down abruptly. If you are having a difficult time keeping your hip bones level or preventing your knee from caving inward, a slower descent may help improve your technique quality.
3. Continue to squat down until you can sit onto the box in a controlled manner, as you avoid plopping onto the box or rocking back onto the box.
    1. As you sit on the box, strive to maintain the same degree of forward lean that you had right before reaching the box. If your torso transitions to a more upright position after sitting on the box compared to at the end of your descent, you have rocked back onto the box.
    2. Try not to speed up your descent right before reaching the box, which can increase the likelihood that you plop onto the box.
4. Briefly pause on the box as your body remains visibly stationary for at least a moment.
5. Reverse the movement by progressively standing up as you drive through the ground while extending (straightening) your knee and hip until you are fully upright.
    1. Avoid rocking your torso forward to generate momentum before you start squatting upward.
    2. Like during the descent, continue keeping your working leg’s foot fully in contact with the ground as you keep your hip bones level and avoid letting your knee cave inward.
6. Alternate between steps 3-6 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
While statically training your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md) and [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), this exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a dumbbell on the ground.
    1. Optionally place an exercise mat on the ground near the dumbbell for comfort.
2. Lie down on your side with the side of your body that you are about to train facing up and the dumbbell in front of your torso.
    1. In this side-lying position, you can rest the bottom side of your head on the hand of your bottom arm for comfort by situating your upper arm out to the side with your elbow bent.
    2. Place your legs in whichever position feels most comfortable and stable to you, which people commonly find involves about 90 degrees of knee bend.
3. Grasp the dumbbell with your top arm as your elbow is bent by about 90 degrees and your palm is facing down.
    1. All the subsequent directions will apply to this top arm.
4. Position your upper arm and elbow on the front aspect of your torso’s side (which is facing up) while allowing the weight to rotate your forearm down toward the ground.
    1. Aligning your upper arm with the front aspect of your torso’s side rather than the middle of your side can increase the range of motion you can use for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow bent by about 90 degrees and pinned by your side, rotate your forearm upward through your shoulder’s full range of motion.
    1. How high up you can rotate your forearm will be affected by your shoulder mobility, but people with normal mobility should finish with the forearm angled upward and forward, as the wrist is clearly above shoulder height.
    2. Throughout the exercise, all the motion should occur from shoulder rotation as you avoid moving your elbow away from your side.
    3. When thinking about this technique, it can be helpful to view your forearm as a clock’s hand, while your elbow is the center about which rotation occurs.
    4. When performing this exercise appropriately, you should feel the muscles on the back of your shoulder working.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your forearm to rotate down toward in a controlled arcing motion.
    1. You should finish with your forearm contacting your torso while it is angled downward.
    2. There is no need to lower the weight extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting it swing your forearm down in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md) and [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), along with a portion of the [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a stability ball (which is also known as a Swiss ball or physio ball) on the ground.
    1. Ideally select a ball with a diameter exceeding your shoulder width.
2. Kneel with the ball in front of you as your elbows are bent by approximately 90 degrees.
3. Hinge at your hips to lean your torso forward, and position your bent elbows on top of the ball about shoulder width apart.
    1. Lean forward enough that you can stack your shoulders directly above your elbows.
    2. With a sufficiently large ball, your forearms can rest on the ball with your elbows, but you will chiefly be bearing weight through your elbows.
    3. The appropriate elbow placement should make sure that the ball does not roll once you press down into the ball through your elbows.
    4. Once on the ball, you optionally can clench each hand into a fist to promote full body tension.
## Exercise technique
1. Walk your legs back until your knees are fully straightened with the bottom of your toes dug into the ground.
    1. Position your feet approximately hip-width apart with your soles facing backward.
    2. You should be bearing your bodyweight into the ground through your feet and into the ball through your elbows.
2. Tighten your abs and squeeze your glutes to maintain a rigid back position while pushing your elbows into the ball and keeping your knees straight.
    1. Doing so keeps your hips held up (but not excessively hiked up) rather than letting them sag downward, which would result in an exaggerated arch of your lower back.
    2. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag down, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together. Thinking about pushing your elbows down into the ball can help keep your shoulder blades apart.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position like you would normally do when standing upright.
3. Drive your elbows forward to push the ball forward through the range in which you can keep your lower back flat.
    1. Keeping your lower back flat will become progressively more difficult as you roll out farther, so you can determine specifically how far you move based on your current ability. If you are new to this exercise, aiming to move the ball a couple of inches (or a few centimeters) forward can be appropriate. If you have a high level of core strength, you can move farther forward through a range that provides your desired intensity.
    2. While you push the ball forward through shoulder motion and allow your elbows to straighten naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    3. Particularly avoid letting your hips sag down or your ribs flare up, which will arch your lower back.
4. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by pulling the ball back toward the starting position. Drive your elbows backward until they are once again under your shoulders without moving your hips.
    1. Continue keeping your lower back in the same flat position you maintained while rolling out.
    2. After being closer to straight at the end of the last step, your elbows should naturally return to being bent by about 90 degrees by the end of this step.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to bend your knees and return to kneeling before standing up.
## Description
While also dynamically training your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), this exercise can statically train your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. After adding weight plates to the machine, adjust the seat or thigh pad height to a level that lets you position your thighs snugly against the thigh pad while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. Certain machine models have an adjustable seat, others have an adjustable thigh pad, and some have both an adjustable seat and an adjustable thigh pad.
2. While facing the thigh pads and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the handles with your palms facing in toward each other (i.e., a neutral grip).
    1. If your machine has rotating handles (rather than fixed parallel handles), you naturally can rotate your palms inward for this variation.
3. While holding the handles, sit down on the machine’s seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad. Slightly lean your torso backward at your hips.
    1. When seated, allow your elbows to straighten in a controlled manner and your arms to raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
    2. If you do not feel tension from the machine in this position (which may occur for individuals who are tall and have long arms), lowering the seat height may be necessary to achieve resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows down toward your sides while progressively bending them to pull the handles downward.
    1. Pull through your full range of motion until you can no longer drive your elbows closer to your torso, which often results in the handles finishing below the height of your ears and slightly above the tops of your shoulders.
    2. Maintain the same slight backward lean of your torso that you adopted while setting up, rather than progressively leaning further backward.
    3. Allow your elbows to move naturally in a manner that feels comfortable with the path of your machine’s handles. With a machine whose handles spread apart as you pull them down, it is typically most comfortable to let your elbows flare outward from your sides during the initial portion of the pull. With a machine that has handles that remain closer together throughout the rep, it is typically most comfortable to keep your elbows tucked closer to shoulder width apart rather than meaningfully flaring them outward.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten in a controlled manner.
    1. You should finish with your arms positioned fully overhead with straight elbows.
    2. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance swing your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can train your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) especially well while also effectively training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a pair of securely anchored gymnastic rings to be slightly outside shoulder width apart.
2. Set the rings to a height that allows your elbows to be aligned with the center of the rings or to whatever is your preferred starting height. Set up a step (like a plyometric box, aerobic step on risers, or a couple of bumper plates stacked on each other) slightly behind the rings so that you can grasp the rings with straight elbows once you are standing on it while mildly leaning your torso forward.
    1. The appropriate ring height should allow you to train dips through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits, while also allowing you to get into the proper starting position with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. The right ring height should also enable you to set your feet onto the ground or step while holding onto the rings if you fail a rep.
    3. While setting up the rings so that their centers are near elbow height is an appropriate starting point for many people, the ideal ring height can vary among different individuals. Someone’s shoulder mobility and preferred knee position during dips can affect where it is best to set the rings.
    4. While not required since you can jump up into the starting position, setting up a step is highly recommended if you are not already accustomed to performing ring dips, where you jump up from the ground. Correspondingly, the directions will describe the usage of the step.
3. Step up onto the step while facing the rings.
4. Firmly grasp the rings with your palms facing each other. Hold the rings directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the rings tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
5. Step forward off the step, and hold yourself up with straight elbows.
    1. Keep your knees as straight as you can without your feet restricting your range of motion from contacting the ground before you reach the bottom of your rep. Initially, you can maintain a slight knee bend and then adjust your knee position during your set if warranted.
6. Pull your shoulder blades back and down to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. You chiefly want to prevent your shoulders from rolling forward or shrugging up during this exercise.
    2. It is not required to keep your shoulder blades packed down further than they normally are at rest, but the intent to pack them down will prevent your torso from sagging down, which would place you into a shrugged shoulder position.
    3. Similarly, you do not necessarily need to have your shoulder blades fully back in the starting position, but pulling them back can make it easier to avoid tilting your shoulders forward, which is undesirable.
7. Rather than keeping your torso fully upright, mildly lean your torso forward and maintain this mild lean throughout your set.
    1. The appropriate degree of lean should result in your chest being slightly in front of your hips (when viewed from the side) while helping your shoulders feel comfortable throughout the set.
    2. Feel free to try out different degrees of torso lean over time to determine what personally feels best to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Throughout your set, avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up. If you notice that either motion starts occurring, strive to pull your shoulder blades further backward and/or downward.
    2. Your elbows should be predominantly pointing backward rather than out to your sides from excessive elbow flare. However, you do not have to keep your elbows completely tucked by your sides, and you can allow them to flare mildly outward if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    3. Rather than letting them swing, keep your legs stationary relative to your hips until you finish your set.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point in which their upper arms are at least parallel to the ground, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Once you have finished lowering to your end range, pause in that bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds).
    1. Continue to stay braced with your shoulder blades pulled back and down.
    2. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Reverse the movement by pushing through the rings to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your hands and elbows downward to lift your body upward.
6. Alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step back onto the step before releasing the rings.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) while being able to improve both your horizontal and vertical pressing strength.

## Setting up
1. After loading your desired weight onto the machine, adjust the thigh pad or seat to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against the thigh pad while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. Most machines have an adjustable thigh pad, but some models have an adjustable seat, while others let you adjust both.
2. While standing above the seat and facing the torso pad, firmly grasp the handles with a grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. Which grip (e.g., overhand, underhand, neutral) is most comfortable will be affected by the angle of your specific machine’s handles.
3. While holding the handles, sit down on the seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the thigh pad and your torso contacting the torso pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to straighten in a controlled manner and your arms to raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
    2. If you do not feel tension from the machine in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), you may need to lower the seat height to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your elbows down and back toward your sides while progressively bending them to pull the handles toward you.
    1. Simultaneosuly pull your shoulder blades down away and back together. At the end of the pull, you can think about squeezing them together as if you were trying to pinch a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    2. Keep your torso in the same position throughout your set rather than progressively leaning backward.
    3. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows finishing slightly behind your torso.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your elbows to move forward and upward while straightening in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally forward as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your elbows fully straightened and the handles fully returned to the starting position.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This row primarily trains your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), which are assisted by your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell on the side you are about to train, and stand over one end of a flat exercise bench.
    1. All the directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the dumbbell, since that is the side you will be training first.
    2. Throughout the exercise, you can situate your free arm wherever is comfortable to you.
2. Sit down on the bench while lifting the dumbbell onto your upper thigh near your abdomen.
    1. Ensure that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie down with your head on the end of the bench.
    2. Your palm should be facing inward with your upper arm by your side.
3. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbell back toward your chest with your elbow bent, lean back to lie down on the bench. Your head should be right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be on the ground in a stable position with your knees bent. Keep them in this position throughout the exercise.
4. In a bench pressing motion, press the dumbbell up until your elbow is straight and your arm is directed up toward the ceiling.
    1. In this starting position (that should look like the end of a single arm dumbbell bench press rep), the dumbbell should be sitting on top of the base of your palm (AKA heel of your hand) with a reasonably straight wrist. Maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
5. Rotate your arm to point your palm forward and the bony bump on the back of your elbow out to the side.
## Exercise technique
1. Without bending your elbow, lower your arm across your body in a wide arcing motion toward your opposite shoulder.
    1. Move through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits, which should prompt you to feel a stretching sensation in the back of your shoulder at the bottom.
    2. Let your shoulder blade move naturally throughout the exercise, but keep your back resting on the bench rather than twisting your torso to the side where you are lowering the dumbbell.
    3. There is no need to lower the weight extremely slowly, but you should actively control the descent rather than letting the weight pull your arm down rapidly.
2. Reverse the movement by fluidly sweeping your arm upward and outward until it is vertical or almost vertical.
    1. When your arm is fully vertical, the dumbbell will no longer provide any resistance to your rear delt, so you decide whether you finish with the dumbbell over your shoulder or the middle of your chest. Either approach can be similarly effective, so you can select whichever end position you prefer.
    2. Continue keeping your elbow straight.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which is assisted by your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), along with your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Place a dumbbell on the floor near one of the two longer sides of a flat exercise bench.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can place an exercise mat or cushion on the floor next to the dumbbell where you will kneel.
2. Kneel on the floor next to the dumbbell, and pick up the dumbbell with the arm you will train during this set.
3. On the side holding the dumbbell, place your forearm on the bench with your palm facing up, elbow straight, and wrist hanging just off the edge of the bench.
4. Rest your free forearm on the bench and grasp its edge with your hand for additional stability.
    1. All the subsequent directions will apply to the arm in which you are holding the weight.
5. Sit your hips back toward your heels by bending your knees and inclining your torso until your elbow is comfortably supported by the bench.
    1. Depending on how close you initially kneeled next to the bench, you may have to scoot your knees a bit back at this point to rest your elbow on the bench.
    2. The appropriate position should let you keep your shoulder relaxed due to the support the bench provides.
6. Let the force from the dumbbell bend your wrist to angle your palm forward.
    1. If the dumbbell touches the bench in this starting position, scoot your forearm forward until it no longer does.
7. Let the dumbbell roll down your fingers while maintaining your grip on the dumbbell.
    1. This downward motion will occur from movement at the joints formed by your knuckles and the finger bones closest to your knuckles.
    2. After it rolls down your fingers, the dumbbell should no longer be fully contacting the palm side of your knuckles, in contrast to when you typically maintain a firm grip on a dumbbell with a fist-like hand position.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift the dumbbell upward by simultaneously curling your wrist and fingers until your palm is facing toward you and your fingers are fully wrapped around the dumbbell’s handle.
    1. Throughout the set, keep your forearm and elbow supported on the bench as you lift the dumbbell through motion at your wrists and the joints your fingers form with your knuckles.
    2. You should feel tension in the muscles on the palm side of your forearm and finish with your knuckles higher than your wrist.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled manner as it rolls down your fingers while you angle your palm forward.
    1. When moving through your full range of motion, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the muscles on the palm side of your forearm at the bottom of the rep when your knuckles are below your wrist.
    2. Avoid letting the dumbbell roll excessively down your fingers to the extent that it could slip out of your hand. Your fingertips should remain wrapped around the handle.
    3. There is no need to lower the dumbbell extremely slowly, but you should actively control the weight rather than letting it pull your hand down abruptly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train the six [wrist flexor muscles](../Muscles/Wrist%20flexor%20muscles%202c85c6f170d880a49749f7d7a9f307c8.md) on the palm side of your forearm, along with the [hand muscles](../Muscles/Intrinsic%20Finger%20Flexors%201bb5c6f170d880648d61d9b5db235bf6.md) involved in gripping.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench at a low incline with an angle up to 30 degrees.
    1. If your bench can be adjusted to a moderate incline near 45 degrees but does not have a low incline setting, you can alternatively select the moderate incline barbell bench press from this database.
2. Place the bench centered within a power rack with the head of the bench in between the posts, where you will adjust the J-hooks.
    1. You should position the bench in a spot that allows your mouth to be directly under the barbell after setting up the rack and lying down on the bench.
3. Position the J-hooks to a height that initially allows you to grasp the bar with slightly bent elbows once you are set up on the incline bench, which will allow you to unrack the bar efficiently. Then place the bar on top of the appropriate J-hooks.
    1. After fully straightening your elbows to lift the bar off the J-hooks, the bar should ideally be close to 2in (5cm) above the top of the J-hooks while keeping your shoulder blades tucked back together.
    2. The proper height easily enables you to avoid bumping the J-hooks when unracking the bar while simultaneously not requiring much effort to lift the bar initially.
    3. If the J-hooks are too high, you may have to spread your shoulder blades apart in order for the bar to clear the J-hooks when unracking, which can place you in a less stable position to start your set, since it can be challenging to reposition your shoulder blades after unracking the bar.
    4. If the J-hooks are too low, the unrack will involve a greater-than-ideal pressing range of motion, which will require greater effort and generate more fatigue before your set begins.
    5. If neither of the two closest J-hook heights is ideal, it is generally better to use the height that is a little too low, since being able to start the set with optimal positioning is typically more advantageous than the alternative.
    6. Some trial and error is often needed to find the best J-hook height for you.
4. Use the unloaded bar to perform a couple of incline press reps with the form described under the “exercise technique” section to determine the appropriate height of the safety pins prior to re-racking the bar onto the J-hooks.
5. Position the safety pins slightly under the lowest point at which the bar descends by the end of the lowering phase of your incline press.
    1. If you happen to fail a rep without a spotter, you could flatten out your back to lose your arch, which will lower your chest and ideally allow the bar to rest on the safety pins.
    2. Certain power rack models have fairly wide spaces between safety pinholes that may result in the highest setting that does not restrict your incline press range of motion being too low to receive the bar after you flatten your back. It is not ideal if this applies to your rack, but the safety pins can still enhance safety if they are high enough to receive the bar if you dump it forward, in case you are completely pinned without anyone to assist you.
6. Load the bar with your intended weight, and lie down with your back and head on the incline bench. Position yourself so that your mouth is close to being directly underneath the barbell, and your knees are bent with your feet on the floor, approximately shoulder-width apart.
    1. Firmly situate the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    2. Based on what feels most stable, you can position your heels directly under your knees with vertical shins, or you can bend your knees a bit beyond this point to position your heels slightly behind your knees with slightly angled shins.
    3. Similarly, you can decide whether you point your toes moderately out to the sides or straight ahead based on your preference.
    4. If you are not training with safety pins that can be positioned to the ideal height, you can avoid adding a pair of collars to the end of the bar. This would allow you to dump the weight to one side and allow the weights to slide off the bar if you become pinned underneath the bar after failing a rep. The con of not using collars is that the plates can accidentally slide to one side when pressing if you happen to tilt the bar asymmetrically, but it can be an acceptable tradeoff to make sure that you can avoid being pinned if you fail a rep.
7. Firmly grasp the bar with your palms facing forward (resulting in an overhand grip) with your hands moderately outside shoulder width. Let the bar sit on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists.
    1. A moderate grip width for bench press variations is commonly considered to be around 1.5 times your shoulder width, with a bit of leeway both narrower and wider. Feel free to try out different hand widths over time to determine where you feel best.
    2. For stability, wrap your thumbs around the bar, resulting in the bar being fully enclosed by your hands. If you’re just learning this exercise, avoid positioning your thumbs on the same side of the bar as your other fingers (which is known as a thumbless grip, or a “suicide grip”).
    3. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid grasping the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar as hard as possible will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
    4. After grasping the bar in a manner that allows you to feel comfortable and stable, you will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
8. While allowing your lower back to arch naturally, assume a “proud chest” posture that puffs your chest slightly up toward the ceiling by tightly pulling your shoulder blades back together. Maintain this chest position throughout your set.
    1. As a cue for pulling your shoulder blades back, you can think about trying to squeeze a pencil between your shoulder blades. This should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting like at the end range of a rowing exercise.
    2. Focusing on adopting a “proud chest” position can naturally place your lower back into a mildly arched position, which is sufficient for optimizing muscle growth and general strength development.
## Exercise technique
1. Drive your feet into the ground, squeeze your glutes, and brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing in this manner throughout your set. This will help create full-body tension and allow your body to function as a stable platform from which to press.
    2. From this starting position, your feet should be firmly dug into the ground, while your buttocks, upper back, and head are firmly planted on the bench. You will maintain these five points of contact throughout your whole set to maximize your stability and performance.
2. Press the bar off the J-hooks by straightening your elbows, and move the bar forward away from the J-hooks until it is approximately above your shoulders, where you will hold it for a moment before starting to lower the bar.
    1. Focus on keeping your shoulder blades pulled back together to avoid losing your upper back tightness.
3. Lower the bar toward your middle chest in a controlled manner by progressively bending your elbows and allowing them to flare out moderately away from each other while descending until you are able to tap your lower chest lightly with the bar.
    1. While motion simultaneously occurs at your shoulders and elbows, strive to keep your elbows stacked underneath your mostly straight wrists as your forearms remain close to vertical throughout the set.
    2. When aiming to touch the bar to your middle chest, the bar will track slightly forward toward your abdomen rather than moving exclusively in a vertical line.
    3. To touch your middle chest, you will have to keep your elbows tucked to a degree instead of being fully flared out, and the appropriate balance between elbow tuck and elbow flare can naturally occur when keeping your elbows stacked under your wrists as you bring the bar to your middle chest. Near the bottom of the rep, the proper balance should result in your upper arms forming approximately 45-75-degree angles with your torso (when 0 degrees means your upper arms are completely tucked by your sides and 90 degrees means your upper arms form a “T-shape” with your torso).
    4. Make sure to control the entire lowering phase before gently contacting your chest with the bar, since you will not be bouncing the bar off your chest.
4. Once the bar contacts your chest, pause in that bottom position as you remain completely stationary for a brief period of time (e.g., approximately two seconds) while staying tight.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
5. Reverse the movement by pressing the bar up. It may help to focus on driving your elbows upward and inward.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened and the bar situated above your shoulders.
    2. The bar will arc slightly back toward your face as you press it, so that you finish the rep with the bar over your shoulders instead of your middle chest.
    3. Continue driving your feet into the ground while keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the bench, and your shoulder blades pulled back together.
6. Alternate between steps 3 and 5 until you have completed your set and are ready to rerack the bar.
7. After completing the lifting phase of your last rep, keep the bar motionless over your shoulders for about one second before moving the bar back until it contacts the back of both J-hooks.
8. Bend your elbows slightly to lower the bar onto the J-hooks to finish reracking the weight.
    1. Only begin lowering the bar after you have already contacted the back of the J-hooks.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) with a slight emphasis on the [upper pec](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md) while also training the [middle and lower pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20Sternocostal%20Head%201905c6f170d8807d8e58cc809442a60b.md), along with the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md).

## Setting up
1. Connect a lat pulldown bar to a seated cable row machine, and select your weight with the loading pin.
    1. While a lat pulldown bar is typically used, you can perform this exercise with any attachment you can comfortably hold throughout the set, so it is up to you which specific attachment you use.
    2. If your machine lets you adjust the seat, you can set it to a height that positions the pulley approximately level with your upper chest once you are seated with an upright torso. This height will keep your arms close to parallel to the ground during the exercise. The exercise can still be very effective with a different seat height, so it is not problematic if your machine does not enable this position.
2. Sit down on the seat and place your feet in contact with the foot plates, as your knees are bent enough to position the bar within your reach after leaning forward.
3. Lean forward at your hips and firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside shoulder-width overhand grip, resulting in your palms facing down.
4. Assume an upright torso position while pressing your feet into the foot plates to scoot your hips back until you are in a position where you feel stable and comfortable.
    1. People commonly find that a mildly bent knee position feels most comfortable.
## Exercise technique
1. Without bending your elbows or leaning your torso back, pull your shoulder blades backward and in toward each other as far as you can.
    1. As a cue, you can imagine pinching a pencil between your shoulder blades, which should prompt you to feel your upper back muscles contracting.
    2. In contrast to a row, the bar will only move a short distance during this variation, since you are isolating motion of your shoulder blades without moving your arms directly.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your shoulder blades to move forward and spread apart from each other as far as they can in a controlled manner.
    1. Avoid bending your elbows, leaning forward at your hips, or rounding your lower back.
    2. At the end of this motion, your shoulder girdles should resemble a slouched posture as they are pulled forward beyond their normal resting position, which often produces a stretching sensation in your upper back muscles.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise effectively trains your [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md) and all three regions of your [trapezius](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) in a more isolated manner than row variations do.

## Setting up
1. Position an adjustable exercise bench to an incline of about 30-45 degrees.
    1. A 30-degree incline can provide greater resistance to your delts in the starting position of each rep than a 45-degree incline, but the moderately higher incline is still completely viable for this exercise.
    2. As an alternative to an adjustable bench, you have the option of using a fixed moderate incline bench.
2. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and sit down on the incline bench with your feet flat on the ground.
    1. Keep your upper back in contact with the bench throughout the set. Based on your preference, you can rest your head on the bench or keep it slightly above it.
    2. While you do not necessarily need to have an exaggerated “proud chest” posture with your shoulders fully pulled back, avoid sitting with your shoulders rolled forward into a slouched upper back position.
3. With your palms angled in toward each other and slightly backward, direct your arms down toward the ground with straight or slightly bent elbows.
    1. Whether you keep your elbows straight or slightly bent is up to your preference, but you should statically maintain your preferred elbow position throughout the set.
    2. You can perform this step simultaneously with step 2.
## Exercise technique
1. In a smooth arcing motion, sweep your arms diagonally upward, outward, and mildly forward through a range of motion comfortable to your shoulders.
    1. Lifting until the hands are near ear height is often appropriate, but you can determine specifically how high up you finish based on your personal preference and what feels comfortable. The right range of motion for you should not prompt you to feel any shoulder discomfort in the top position.
    2. As you raise your arms through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blades to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in toward your sides in a controlled manner.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your arms pointing down toward the ground.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the weights downward.
    3. The dumbbells should predominantly arc downward and inward, while simultaneously tracking slightly backward to reverse the forward motion that occurred during step 1.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), which are assisted by your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md).

## Setting up
1. Follow the set-up instructions for the [dual kettlebell clean](Dual%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d88030b58fd481d9951983.md), and perform the lifting phase of the [dual kettlebell clean](Dual%20kettlebell%20clean%202cf5c6f170d88030b58fd481d9951983.md) described in steps 1-5 of its exercise technique instructions.
    1. After doing so, you should now be holding the kettlebell in the front rack position. This involves situating them in front of your shoulders with your elbows bent slightly in front of your ribcage, palms facing in toward each other, and the weights resting on your forearms, which are mostly vertically with your wrists slightly closer to the midline of your body than your elbows. The handle should also be diagonally contacting your palms, such that the sides of the handles by your thumbs are angled mildly higher than the sides of the handles by your little fingers.
    2. As an alternative to cleaning the kettlebells, you can curl them up into the same front rack position described above if you are using loads that are light enough to do so. With this technique, initially grasp the handles with your little fingers directly next to one of the horns (i.e., side handles) on each kettlebell to help the handles rest diagonally across your palms in the front rack position. Feel free to perform a cheat curl-like motion where you initially generate some momentum by swinging the weights mildly backward with straight elbows before swinging your elbows forward while curling them. This is a less technically complicated means of moving the kettlebells into the front rack, but it is not as efficient when using heavy weights for lifters who are proficient with cleaning kettlebells.
2. Assume a “proud posture” with your chest up, as you avoid letting the weights pull you into a hunched position with your upper back and shoulders excessively rounded.
    1. Maintain the natural curvature of your lower back and neck, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
3. Position your feet near shoulder-width apart from each other, and point your toes at least slightly out to your sides.
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside of shoulder width with their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position.
2. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest and elbows up.
    1. Throughout the set, avoid dropping your elbows or letting your chest cave down.
    2. As you descend, it is natural for your torso to lean forward mildly at your hips to maintain your balance, but maintain a mostly upright torso position with your back flat.
    3. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
    5. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
3. Continue to squat down through the full range of motion your mobility allows without rounding your back, lifting your heels off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, your heels lift off the ground, or your knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting too deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
4. Reverse the movement by driving through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips to stand upright.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees aligned with your feet as you squat up.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
6. Following your last rep, set the kettlebells down in the opposite manner to how you initially lifted them into the front rack position.
    1. If you initially cleaned the kettlebells, you can let the kettlebells fall forward as you swing your arms down while straightening your elbows and hinging at your hips to absorb the force of the lowering phase.
    2. If you initially curled the kettlebells up, you can similarly guide them down by letting your elbows straighten and swinging your elbows mildly back to help control the weights.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.

## Setting up
1. After determining whether you want to use the high or low handles of a trap bar, add weight plates of your desired load to the bar.
    1. The ideal handle height should let you train through the full hip hinge range of motion that your mobility comfortably permits. If you are new to this exercise, you start with the high handles and then switch to the lower handles if the high handles limit your range of motion.
    2. If the plates touch the ground at the bottom of your Romanian deadlift before you have achieved the end range to which your hamstrings can comfortably stretch when using the high handles, the low handles are likely preferable.
    3. Note that training this exercise over time can increase your hamstring flexibility, so it may be appropriate to switch to the low handles in the future, even if the high handles are ideal for you at first.
    4. The setup for this exercise is simply performing the lifting phase of a high handle or low handle trap bar deadlift.
2. In a near hip-width stance, stand within the middle of the trap bar.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the handles, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the handles. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track far forward. However, you can let your knees shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
4. With your elbows fully straightened, firmly grasp the center of the handles with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the handles closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the handles can slide down your hands while holding the bar, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
    3. Keep your elbows fully straightened throughout the exercise.
5. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
6. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. The initial submaximal pull allows you to check if you have grasped the handles correctly, which will be indicated by the handles not rotating forward or backward when applying the pre-tension.
    2. If you pick up a trap bar with your hands positioned slightly away from the middle of the handles, the trap bar can start rotating in a manner that makes it very difficult to hold and lift appropriately.
    3. Even for experienced lifters, it can be easy to grasp a trap bar’s handles without having their hands truly centered initially, so applying the pre-tension can make sure you are in your ideal starting position.
    4. If the bar starts rotating when you apply the pre-tension, re-center your grip, and apply the pre-tension again until the bar no longer rotates.
7. While keeping your lower back flat and chest up, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Strive to lower the bar in a straight line, rather than letting it drift forward, which may be more likely to occur if you think about “bending over” rather than “sitting back.”
    2. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the bar.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    5. Throughout the set, keep your feet fully planted on the ground and your neck near a neutral position, as when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move.
    1. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar until their hands are at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    3. If you have high hamstring flexibility and can hinge until the plates contact the ground, descend until you can tap the plates very lightly on the ground, but do not let the weight rest on the ground.
    4. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should clearly be in control of the entire descent.
3. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward to lift your torso upright into the starting position.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so keep your lower back flat, chest up, core braced, and feet fully on the ground.
    2. When you have finished lifting the bar, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back at the top through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips properly stacked under your shoulders, preventing excessive arching.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down onto the floor.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe between reps in the fully upright position, rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
    2. After finishing the last rep, set the bar down in the same manner in which you initially picked it up (i.e., bending your hips and knees while keeping your back flat).
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a pair of securely anchored gymnastic rings to be slightly outside shoulder width apart.
2. Set the rings to a height that allows your elbows to be aligned with the center of the rings or to whatever is your preferred starting height. Set up a step (like a plyometric box, aerobic step on risers, or a couple of bumper plates stacked on each other) slightly behind the rings so that you can grasp the rings with straight elbows once you are standing on it while mildly leaning your torso forward.
    1. The appropriate ring height should allow you to train dips through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits, while also allowing you to get into the proper starting position with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. The right ring height should also enable you to set your feet onto the ground or step while holding onto the rings if you fail a rep.
    3. While setting up the rings so that their centers are near elbow height is an appropriate starting point for many people, the ideal ring height can vary among different individuals. Someone’s shoulder mobility and preferred knee position during dips can affect where it is best to set the rings.
    4. While not required since you can jump up into the starting position, setting up a step is highly recommended if you are not already accustomed to performing ring dips, where you jump up from the ground. Correspondingly, the directions will describe the usage of the step.
3. While standing in front of the rings, add your desired load (in the form of weight plates or a kettlebell) to a dip/pull-up belt you have around your waist.
    1. The back of your belt should be securely resting on top of your buttocks. You can loop the belt’s chain or strap (depending on the belt model) through the center hole of a weight plate or under the handle of a kettlebell. If you have a loading pin for your belt, you would alternatively loop the chain or strap through the loading pin after adding weight plates to it.
    2. It will be easiest if you carry the weight over to the rings and add the weight to your belt while you are by them. Adding the weight to your belt farther away from the bar before walking over to the bar can be awkward.
    3. As an alternative to using a pull-up/dip belt, you can wear a weighted vest.
    4. While less stable and more awkward than using a belt or weighted vest, you also have the option of holding a dumbbell between your thighs or feet. This approach is suboptimal and will limit how much weight you can use.
4. Step up onto the step while facing the rings.
5. Firmly grasp the rings with your palms facing each other. Hold the rings directly under the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with mostly straight wrists.
    1. Squeezing the rings tightly can help you avoid letting your wrists excessively cock back.
6. Step forward off the step, hold yourself up with straight elbows, and position your legs against the weight (if you are using a dip belt).
    1. Keep your knees as straight as you can without your feet restricting your range of motion from contacting the ground before you reach the bottom of your rep. Initially, you can maintain a slight knee bend and then adjust your knee position during your set if warranted.
    2. Based on your preference, you can spread your legs just enough to position the weight between them, or you can position your legs together with the weight just in front of them. Which option is most comfortable will be influenced by how you set up your belt and the shape of your weight(s). With either option, positioning your thighs in a close to vertical position is typically the most practical. Contacting the weight with your legs can help you prevent the weight from excessively swinging during your set.
7. Pull your shoulder blades back and down to assume a “proud chest” posture.
    1. You chiefly want to prevent your shoulders from rolling forward or shrugging up during this exercise.
    2. It is not required to keep your shoulder blades packed down further than they normally are at rest, but the intent to pack them down will prevent your torso from sagging down, which would place you into a shrugged shoulder position.
    3. Similarly, you do not necessarily need to have your shoulder blades fully back in the starting position, but pulling them back can make it easier to avoid tilting your shoulders forward, which is undesirable.
8. Rather than keeping your torso fully upright, mildly lean your torso forward and maintain this mild lean throughout your set.
    1. The appropriate degree of lean should result in your chest being slightly in front of your hips (when viewed from the side) while helping your shoulders feel comfortable throughout the set.
    2. Feel free to try out different degrees of torso lean over time to determine what personally feels best to you.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Bend your elbows to lower your body in a controlled manner.
    1. Throughout your set, avoid letting your shoulders roll forward or shrug up. If you notice that either motion starts occurring, strive to pull your shoulder blades further backward and/or downward.
    2. Your elbows should be predominantly pointing backward rather than out to your sides from excessive elbow flare. However, you do not have to keep your elbows completely tucked by your sides, and you can allow them to flare mildly outward if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    3. Rather than letting them swing, keep your legs stationary relative to your hips until you finish your set. If you are using a dip belt, keeping your legs in contact with the weight can help you stabilize it. If the weight is between your legs, squeezing your thighs together can stop the weight from swinging.
3. Continue descending through the full range of motion that your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. It is common for people with healthy shoulders to reach the point at which their upper arms are at least parallel to the ground, but specifically how deeply you should descend will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. At your end range, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in the front of your shoulders, but you should not feel any shoulder discomfort or pain.
    3. If you feel joint discomfort or pain at the bottom, you most likely lowered yourself excessively far relative to your current mobility. Training dips over time may improve your mobility, but you should not force yourself into an aggravating range.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, using a slow and controlled tempo as you approach the bottom position is recommended.
4. Reverse the movement by pushing through the rings to lift yourself up until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. You can think about driving your hands and elbows downward to lift your body upward.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
    1. Once you have fully straightened your elbows after your last rep, step back onto the step before releasing the rings.
## Description
This exercise effectively trains your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md), [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md), and [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md) while improving both your horizontal and vertical pressing strength.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the seat so that the middle of the handles will be level with your mid-chest once you are seated.
    1. After initially adjusting the seat, you will naturally have to sit down to confirm whether the height is appropriate.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit with your back against the backrest, and spread your arms backward into a “T-position” through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. People with normal shoulder mobility are able to spread their arms back until their elbows are slightly behind their shoulders.
4. Adjust the pins above the handles to a position that lets you comfortably grasp the handles when your arms are fully spread apart in this “T-position.”
    1. After initially adjusting the handles, you can recheck to see if they are positioned appropriately for you.
    2. If the handles are excessively far back relative to your shoulder mobility, it may be difficult or uncomfortable to grasp them.
    3. If the handles are not sufficiently far back, the range of motion you can use for this exercise will be limited, and you will not be able to train your chest in a stretched position.
5. Pull your shoulder blades back together with a “proud chest” posture.
    1. Maintain this “proud chest” posture throughout your set.
6. Spread your arms apart into the “T-position” with a slight bend in your elbows before grasping the handles with your palms facing forward.
    1. It may be easiest to grasp the handles one at a time.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your arms together to move the handles toward each other until they are just about to touch or lightly make contact.
    1. You can think about sweeping your arms together in a wide arcing motion, as if you were hugging a thick barrel.
    2. All the motion should come from your shoulders, as you keep your elbows mildly bent throughout the set.
    3. As your hands approach each other, it is natural for your shoulder blades to move slightly forward, but you should avoid letting your shoulders round forward into a slouched posture.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your arms to spread apart in a controlled manner as they arc backward through the full range of motion that is comfortable for your shoulders.
    1. Finish in a “proud chest” posture with your chest up and shoulder blades pulled back.
    2. If you were initially able to adjust the handles to start as far back as your mobility permits, it is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your chest and/or the front of your shoulders with your arms fully spread apart
    3. While you do not have to perform this step extremely slowly, avoid letting the machine abruptly swing your arms apart in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed the set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop all regions of your [pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%201b95c6f170d880539f8ee236e09d4728.md) while also training your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [coracobrachialis](../Muscles/Coracobrachialis%201905c6f170d880f78a01c57799591868.md).
