## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, and adjust the height of the seat so that your upper arms can be parallel with the floor or a little lower while grasping the handles.
    1. After initially adjusting the seat height, spread your arms outward so that your hands are level with the handles.
    2. You may have to re-adjust the seat if your upper arms are not parallel with the floor or a little lower.
    3. Some people will find their shoulders feel more comfortable when the seat is set to a height that allows their hands to be a bit lower than their shoulders, compared to when their hands are completely level with their shoulders.
2. Adjust the pins above the handles to a position that allows you to grasp the handles with your hands as close as they can be to each other while your chest is facing the machine’s pad.
3. After sitting down with your chest against the pad, grasp the vertical handles with your palms facing in toward each other, and slightly bend your elbows.
    1. Maintain the slight bend in your elbows throughout the set.
## Exercise technique
1. Spread the handles apart and backward until your arms and torso form a “T-shape.”
2. Reverse the motion by bringing the handles forward and toward each other until they have returned to their starting position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which is assisted by your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), along with your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates to the machine to use your desired level of assistance, and ensure the machine’s knee pad or foot bar is down.
    1. In contrast to most machines, the difficulty of this exercise decreases as you add heavier loads to the assisted pull-up machine since the weight determines the extent to which the machine will support your bodyweight.
    2. Certain machine models have a knee pad, and others have a foot bar, but essentially the same exercise technique can be used with either type of machine.
2. Step up onto the machine’s elevated foot plates and reach overhead to grasp the handles that let you comfortably direct your palms backward (i.e., an underhand grip) with your hands near shoulder-width apart.
    1. Some machines have fully horizontal handles that let you use a pure underhand grip as your palms point straight backward. Others have handles that are angled diagonally outward and backward, which let you use a grip that is a hybrid between an underhand grip and a neutral grip, as your palms angle backward and inward. Either type of handles can be used for this variation.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
3. One leg at a time, kneel onto the machine’s knee pad (if your machine has a knee pad) or step onto the machine’s foot bar (if your machine has a foot bar) while continuing to grasp the handles firmly.
    1. If using a machine with a knee pad, keep your knees bent on the pad throughout your set. If using a machine with a foot bar, keep your knees straight while standing on the bar throughout your set.
    2. Certain machines with knee pads may not allow shorter individuals to pull through a full range of motion when kneeling on the pad, so you can switch to standing on the knee pad if the machine does not allow you to fully pull yourself up while kneeling.
4. Allow your body to descend in a controlled manner until your arms are fully overhead with straight elbows.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will put you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up by your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back puts you in a "proud chest" posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the handles by driving your elbows down and toward your sides as you progressively bend your elbows.
    1. Since the handles are fixed, your elbows won't actually drive downward; having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. If you are using a machine with a knee pad and notice it restricts your range of motion when kneeling on the pad, switch to standing on the pad before resuming your set to pull through your full range of motion.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Place one weighted end of a dumbbell on the ground with its handle directed vertically, resulting in one end remaining off the ground.
    1. Placing a dumbbell on the ground in this manner will make it easier to position onto your lap compared to if you placed both ends of the dumbbell on the ground. However, if the ends of your dumbbell are not flat (such as with a plate-loaded adjustable dumbbell), you will alternatively have to place both ends of the dumbbell on the ground with a horizontal handle.
2. Lie down with your back on the ground (or an exercise mat) and the side of one of your hips directly next to the dumbbell.
3. Roll onto your side toward the dumbbell, hold the dumbbell in contact with the front of your waist with both hands, and roll onto your back with the dumbbell situated in the crease of your hips.
    1. With a sufficiently light weight, you can simply pick up the dumbbell while seated, but the rolling technique is most efficient for transferring a heavier weight into position.
4. While using both hands to keep the dumbbell in the crease of your hips, bend your knees to at least 90 degrees to position the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can position your feet shoulder-width apart, but it is up to you whether you would like them closer together or farther apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can point your toes forward or slightly out to the sides.
    3. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is also up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
    4. In this position, you can rest the back of your head on the ground.
5. While leaving one foot on the ground, lift your other foot off the ground by straightening your knee.
    1. Keep one foot off the ground throughout the set you perform with your other side.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heel into the ground and squeezing your glute while continuing to hold the dumbbell in the crease of your hips.
    1. At the top, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side (on the side of your body with the foot contacting the ground). Your thigh and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glute.
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glute engage.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you can lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side by switching which foot you keep on the ground.
    1. To remove the dumbbell from your lap after your next set, roll over to your side as you did when setting it up, and then place it on the ground.
## Description
This exercise will chiefly train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), which may be assisted by your [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md) and [piriformis](../Muscles/Piriformis%201925c6f170d88068a670ce338a8215cf.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell in a spot where you have sufficient space to lie down on the ground.
    1. The diameter of the weight plates you select can influence how easily you can set up while also affecting the range of motion for this exercise.
    2. It will be easiest to assume the starting position with at least one pair of full diameter plates, such as typical 45lb (20kg) Olympic plates or bumper plates. With full diameter plates, certain individuals who are very thick may need to utilize one of the strategies discussed below to set up under the bar.
    3. If you exclusively load the bar with smaller diameter plates, you may have to modify the standard setup in order to position your hips under the bar. When only using smaller diameter plates, you can elevate the bar just enough to fit your hips under it by situating the plates on top of deadlift blocks, aerobic steps, or stacks of full diameter weight plates. Alternatively, you may have a partner place the bar on top of your hip bones and load it with weight plates after you have assumed the starting position. If neither of these approaches is practical to you, you lack bumper plates that allow you to elevate the bar fully with light loads, and you do not currently have the strength to use 135lb (or 60kg) for this exercise, you have the option of performing other glute bridge variations. For instance, you can select a [single leg dumbbell glute bridge](Single%20leg%20dumbbell%20glute%20bridge%202f45c6f170d8806cb6fdd5f6e6186759.md) or the standard [barbell glute bridge](Barbell%20glute%20bridge%201a35c6f170d880968781e5e96679c367.md).
2. Optionally, obtain a pad (or an object that can function as a pad) that you will place between the bar and your hips.
    1. Using a pad is not required but strongly recommended because it can be very uncomfortable to have a barbell directly resting on your hip bones with a meaningful load.
    2. You can wrap a hip thrust pad or a squat pad around the middle of the bar.
    3. Alternatively, you can place a thick foam or folded exercise mat on the crease of your hip during the next step and subsequently keep it there to cushion your hip bones. Be aware that foam pads not specifically designed for glute bridges or hip thrusts may be somewhat damaged from this exercise.
3. Sit down on the ground with an upright torso and your legs straight out in front of you under the bar.
    1. The middle of the bar should be aligned with the midline of your body.
4. Grasp the bar with your palms facing down and roll it toward the crease of your hips.
    1. So long as your hands are wider apart than your hips, you can adjust your grip width based on what feels stable and comfortable to you during this exercise.
    2. Continue holding the bar from this point onward.
5. Lie down with your back and head resting on the ground.
    1. Tuck your chin slightly toward your chest while resting the back of your head on the ground throughout the exercise.
6. Bend your knees until your shins are in an approximately vertical position with the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can position your feet shoulder-width apart, but it is up to you whether you would like them closer together or farther apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can point your toes forward or slightly out to the sides.
    3. The optimal degree of knee bend should allow your feet to feel stable while being firmly planted on the ground throughout the set. Bringing your heels toward your buttocks until they are vertically stacked under your knees is normally appropriate, but you can adjust how much you bend your knees if a different position feels more stable to you.
7. While leaving one foot on the ground, lift your other foot off the ground by straightening your knee.
    1. Keep one foot off the ground throughout the set you perform with your other side.
8. Confirm that the bar is directly above the crease of your hips and completely centered before initiating the set.
    1. Positioning the bar appropriately will help you avoid the excessive discomfort that may arise from positioning the bar too high (i.e., directly on your lower abdomen) or too low (i.e., directly on your groin).
    2. Some people may experience discomfort when the bar looks aligned with the crease of their hips if the bar is directly resting on the bony bumps on the front of their hip bones. If you notice that this occurs for you during your set, you can roll the bar slightly further down away from your abdomen to shift the pressure away from these bony bumps. When making any adjustments during a set, only do so in between reps when the weights are resting on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
2. Lift your hips up by driving your heel into the ground and squeezing your glute. Keep the bar balanced on the crease of your hips the entire set.
    1. At the top, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side (on the side of your body with the foot contacting the ground). Your thigh and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glute.
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glute engage.
    4. The purpose of holding the bar with your hands is to keep it stabilized on the crease of your hips. Avoid trying to lift the bar up or push it down with your hands.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you are able to lightly contact the ground with your buttocks or the plates.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should avoid simply letting gravity pull the bar down abruptly, as opposed to you using your glutes to control the descent actively.
    2. If you hear the plates crashing into the ground, you are not lowering the bar with sufficient control.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the plates on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps. The bar should come to a dead stop on the ground after each rep.
    2. After completing the lowering phase of your last rep, roll the bar forward before sitting up in the reversed manner to how you set up initially.
## Description
This exercise will chiefly train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), which may be assisted by your [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md) and [piriformis](../Muscles/Piriformis%201925c6f170d88068a670ce338a8215cf.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Use the machine’s loading pin to select your desired level of assistance, and ensure the machine’s knee pad or foot bar is down.
    1. In contrast to most machines, the difficulty of this exercise decreases as you select heavier loads on the assisted pull-up machine, since the weight determines how much the machine will support your bodyweight.
    2. Some machine models have a knee pad, and others have a foot bar, but the same exercise technique can be used with either type.
2. Step up onto the machine’s elevated foot plates and reach overhead to grasp the handles that let you comfortably direct your palms backward (i.e., an underhand grip) with your hands near shoulder-width apart.
    1. Some machines have fully horizontal handles that let you use a pure underhand grip as your palms point straight backward. Others have handles that are angled diagonally outward and backward, which let you use a grip that is a hybrid between an underhand grip and a neutral grip, as your palms angle backward and inward. Either type of handles can be used for this variation.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you position the bar closer to the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), it can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which can pull on your hand skin in an uncomfortable way and increase the risk of tearing a callus.
3. One leg at a time, kneel onto the machine’s knee pad (if your machine has a knee pad) or step onto the machine’s foot bar (if your machine has a foot bar) while continuing to grasp the handles firmly.
    1. If using a machine with a knee pad, keep your knees bent on the pad throughout your set. If using a machine with a foot bar, keep your knees straight while standing on the bar throughout your set.
    2. Certain machines with knee pads may not allow shorter individuals to pull through a full range of motion when kneeling on the pad, so you can switch to standing on the knee pad if the machine does not allow you to fully pull yourself up while kneeling.
4. Allow your body to descend in a controlled manner until your arms are fully overhead with straight elbows.
## Exercise technique
1. While hanging with straight elbows, simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. Doing so will put you in a more advantageous position to start your pull than if you kept your chest facing horizontally and allowed your shoulder blades to be shrugged up by your bodyweight.
    2. Arching your middle and upper back puts you in a "proud chest" posture, which you should maintain throughout your set.
2. Pull your chest up toward the handles by driving your elbows down and toward your sides as you progressively bend your elbows.
    1. Since the handles are fixed, your elbows won't actually drive downward; having the intention helps you pull yourself upward with an appropriate technique that effectively trains your back muscles.
    2. Strive to pull through your full available range of motion, which commonly results in the upper arms being close to the sides of the torso and the elbows bent enough that the forearms contact the biceps. However, different individuals may have different ranges of motion enabled by their bodies.
    3. If you are using a machine with a knee pad and notice it restricts your range of motion when kneeling on the pad, switch to standing on the pad before resuming your set to pull through your full range of motion.
3. Reverse the motion by lowering your body in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with your arms positioned overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than simply dropping down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the seat height to a comfortable position that will allow the lower aspect of your triceps to rest against the machine’s upper arm pads.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine, and sit down on its seat with an upright posture, your feet flat on the floor, and your back against the backrest.
3. After positioning your triceps against the machine’s upper arm pads, grasp the handles with an underhand grip that results in your palms facing forward.
## Exercise technique
1. Starting from a position where your elbows are straight, curl the handles upward by bending at your elbows while keeping your upper arms pinned against the machine’s arm pads (rather than allowing your upper arms to swing forward).
2. After your elbows have fully bent, reverse the motion by lowering the handles in a controlled manner until your elbows have straightened.
    1. Continue to keep your upper arms in contact with the arm pads.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to an axle bar (AKA thick bar) situated on the ground.
    1. Except for using a different bar, the setup and technique for an axle deadlift is the same as for a conventional deadlift.
    2. If you lack an axle bar, you can replicate the grip demands of an axle deadlift by connecting fat grip attachments to a standard barbell shoulder-width apart.
    3. The size of the weight plates you add to the bar will determine how high the bar lies above the ground, which consequently affects your range of motion. Adding a pair of full-diameter plates (like 45lb (20kg) plates or any bumper plates) will elevate the bar to the standard height (about 9in (23cm)) when deadlifting from the floor. If you only use smaller diameter plates, the exercise will function as a deficit deadlift with a greater range of motion that may exceed the range of motion in which some people wish to train if they lack the mobility to perform a [deficit deadlift](Deficit%20conventional%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d8809f90f5d4f2e2273493.md) with appropriate technique. If you do not have access to bumper plates and are using loads that are not heavy enough to utilize 45lb (20kg) plates, you can perform a [block pull](Conventional%20mid-shin%20block%20pull%201a35c6f170d880349a3beab3040acdc9.md) or [rack pull](Mid-shin%20rack%20pull%201a35c6f170d880fd8a71e340d039d10a.md) with the bar elevated to where it would be when deadlifting from the floor with full diameter plates.
2. While facing the center of the bar, stand in an approximately hip-width stance with the middle of your feet under the bar and your toes pointing straight ahead or slightly out to the sides.
    1. For most lifters, this situates the bar about one inch (2.5cm) away from the shins.
    2. While using a near hip-width stance places most people into a viable position, the precise stance width that is ideal for you as an individual may be influenced by your body structure and mobility, so you can feel free to modify your stance a bit based on where you feel strong and comfortable.
    3. You can similarly decide whether to point your toes straight ahead or slightly out to the side based on what feels best to you.
3. With your arms pointing straight down toward the bar and your shoulders packed down (opposite to if you shrugged your shoulders up), sit your hips backward while bending your knees until your hands are level with the bar. Keep your lower back flat and chest up rather than rounding your back.
    1. More motion should come from hinging at your hips than bending your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift mildly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something. After you have fully sat back and feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings, you can bend your knees further to reach the bar.
    3. Throughout this exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
    4. As a cue to pack your shoulders down, you can think about making yourself have long arms, which can place you into an efficient start position and help engage your back muscles.
4. With your elbows fully straightened, firmly grasp the bar with an approximately shoulder-width overhand grip such that your palms are facing backward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward to help you maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
2. Before lifting the bar, apply “pre-tension” to the bar as you develop tension throughout your whole body and start pressing the middle of your feet into the ground with enough force to hear the weight plates clink against the bar.
    1. Doing so can help you wedge your hips into your most advantageous starting position.
    2. When creating “pre-tension,” pressing through the ground should pull yourself further into position with your back locked into a stable position as the muscles running up the length of your back are fully tensed.
3. As you forcefully squeeze the bar, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar as you “push the floor away” while extending (straightening) your hips and knees. Prioritize keeping your chest up, lower back flat, the bar close to your legs, and your core braced throughout the entire exercise.
    1. As you move about your knees and hips, your torso should remain in a similar position when initiating the pull rather than inclining further toward horizontal, which could occur if your hips shoot up from not driving into the ground appropriately.
4. After the bar reaches near the middle of your shins, focus on thrusting your hips forward as you continue extending your hips and knees until you are standing fully upright with your chest up and shoulders back.
    1. Lock out the rep with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
    2. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
5. Reverse the movement by hinging at your hips while bending your knees to lower the bar until the plates have returned to resting on the ground.
    1. Just like when lifting the bar, keep your lower back flat and chest up as you descend while actively avoiding letting your lower back round or chest collapse.
    2. You can initially focus on sitting your buttocks back while keeping your shins vertical and allowing your knees to bend naturally until the bar has cleared your knees. Then you can allow your knees to track mildly forward as you further bend your knees and hips to finish lowering the bar.
6. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop on the ground for a moment (rather than simply tapping the ground and immediately deadlifting the bar up again) before continuing to alternate between steps 2-5 until you have completed your set.
    1. While you do not need to pause with the bar on the ground for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is on the ground rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before the next rep.
## Description
This exercise emphasizes grip training to a greater degree than other deadlift variations while still training the other muscles involved with deadlifting.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the machine’s thigh pad to a level that positions the tops of your hip bones somewhat above the top of the pad when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. This position will allow you to move freely about your hips in contrast to if the pad is contacting the top of your hip bones, which would restrict hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    2. If the top of the pad is positioned much lower than the top of the hip bones (rather than only somewhat lower), some individuals may feel knee discomfort, so a sweet spot can exist for pad placement.
    3. Some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position after initially completing step 3.
2. Select your weight with the machine’s loading pin.
3. While placing your hands onto the thigh pad or handles for balance support, step onto the foot plate and position your lower calves snugly against the lower leg pads with your heels on the back of the foot plate.
    1. Position your feet symmetrically in a stance that feels comfortable to you, which can involve pointing your toes somewhat outward or pointing them fairly straight forward.
    2. Situating your feet approximately hip width to shoulder apart from each other will result in a viable stance width, but how wide of a stance you can use will be influenced by the width of your machine’s foot plate.
    3. To set your lower calves against the pads, your heels may hang off the edge of the foot plate, but the rest of your soles should be firmly planted on the foot plate.
    4. Your knees should be straight after you have finished setting your feet on the foot plate.
4. With your knees straightened, snugly rest your thighs against the thigh pad, let your arms hang down, and confirm that the tops of your hip bones are now somewhat above the top of the pad.
    1. If the pad is not positioned appropriately, readjust before getting into this starting position again.
## Exercise technique
1. Hinge at your hips to lower your torso until you are low enough to grasp the bar firmly with your elbows straight, palms facing backward, and hands about shoulder-width apart.
    1. Keep your lower back flat or slightly arched, rather than rounding your lower back to reach the bar.
    2. Throughout the exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Maintain a straight knee position throughout your set, but avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads.
    4. Depending on your limb lengths and the height of your machine, you may have to round your upper back to reach the bar.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set.
3. While keeping your back in a rigid position, lift your torso up through your hips until you can fully squeeze your glutes with your torso aligned with your legs.
    1. Throughout your set, aim to have all the movement occur from hip motion.
    2. At the top, you should essentially be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side, like you could do when standing upright.
    3. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top, which can occur if you try to lift up as high as you physically can, rather than finishing once your glutes are fully squeezed and your torso is in alignment with your legs.
4. Reverse the movement to lower your torso by hinging at your hips through your full range of motion in a controlled manner without rounding your lower back.
    1. How deeply you are able to hinge without rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch, you have finished descending through your available hip range of motion.
    3. With sufficient flexibility, you may be able to lower the bar until the weight you selected lightly taps the rest of the weight stack, indicating you have moved the full range of motion in which the machine can provide resistance.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar back down and dismount the machine.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise dynamically trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Position a cable station’s pulley to its lowest height, select your weight with the loading pin, and connect a D-handle attachment to the cable.
2. With your feet near shoulder-width apart, stand with the side of one shoulder (on the same side of your body you intend to train) facing the cable station.
3. Squat down and grasp the handle firmly with the hand closer to the cable station as your palm faces in toward your side and your elbow is straight.
    1. Avoid rounding your lower back while setting up.
4. By extending (straightening) your hips and knees, stand upright with the handle while keeping your lower back flat, elbow straight, and arm aligned with the cable.
    1. If it helps you feel more stable, you can optionally maintain a slight bend in your knees rather than fully straightening them.
    2. You can situate your resting hand wherever you feel helps maintain your balance, such as raised out to the side or resting on your hip.
    3. All the subsequent directions will apply to the side in which you are holding the cable.
5. In the starting position, you should feel tension from the cable pulling your shoulder girdle down lower than your other side. If you do not feel tension when standing directly above the pulley, step out to the side away from the pulley until you do.
    1. While the cable’s resistance should pull your shoulder girdle down, avoid letting it bend your whole torso to the side through spinal motion.
    2. Aim to keep your chest up and back near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
## Exercise technique
1. Without bending your elbow, shrug your shoulder up toward your earlobe through the full range of motion you can to lift the handle upward.
    1. Keep your torso upright as you avoid letting the cable’s resistance bend your torso toward the pulley, as would otherwise occur during a side-bend exercise.
    2. Throughout the exercise, look straight ahead to keep your neck near a neutral position.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by letting the cable’s resistance pull your shoulder fully down.
    1. Move through your full range of motion, which may prompt you to feel a stretching sensation in the region of your upper trap (on the back of your neck and uppermost upper back) at the bottom.
    2. At the end of this motion, your working side’s shoulder should be positioned a little lower than your resting side’s shoulder due to the downward stretch that the cable can provide.
    3. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and the smaller [levator scapulae](../Muscles/Levator%20Scapulae%201955c6f170d880048119fd4b2c6c5737.md) situated deep to your upper trap.

## Setting up
1. Fully lower the Smith machine’s safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) and the machine’s bar before adding weight plates to the bar and making sure that the safety hooks are rotated out away from the safety bars (rather than being underneath the safety bars).
2. Stand close in front of the middle of the bar with approximately a hip-width stance.
    1. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, you can position yourself to face the side where the bar will track slightly backward when lifting it (which places the bottom of the rails farther in front of you than the top of the rails). With an angled Smith machine, stand with the middle of your feet under the bar to leave a bit of space between it and your legs. If you stand too close to the bar, your torso can restrict the bar path when lifting it, so you adjust where you stand if that occurs during the set.
    2. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face, and you can stand with the bar just in front of your legs.
3. Sit your hips back and bend your knees until you can firmly grasp the bar with a mildly outside shoulder-width grip as your elbows are straight and your palms point backward.
    1. A mildly outside shoulder-width grip works well for many lifters, but feel free to try out somewhat different grip widths to determine if any particular hand positions feel best to you as an individual.
4. While keeping your elbows straight, stand upright with the bar.
    1. You can optionally maintain a slight forward torso lean throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift the bar upward by driving your elbows upward and out to your sides through a range of motion that feels comfortable to your shoulders while bending your elbows.
    1. Your mobility will affect how high you are comfortably able to lift the bar, and there is no need to force your shoulders into a range that provokes any discomfort.
    2. While different individuals may be able to lift higher up and others not quite as high, people often can lift their upper arms until their elbows are near shoulder height for a comfortable and effective range of motion.
    3. While motion occurs at your shoulder girdles and elbows, keep the rest of your body stationary throughout the exercise.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your elbows to descend in toward your sides as you lower the bar in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with straight elbows.
    1. There is no need to lower the bar with an extremely slow tempo, but you should actively control the descent rather than letting the weight abruptly pull your arms down.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), which are assisted by your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md).

## Setting up
1. After loading your desired amount of weight onto the machine, stand centered between its handles in a near hip-width stance while facing away from the base of the machine.
    1. If your machine model lets you adjust the handle height, you can initially set the handles to the lowest setting. If you cannot grasp the handles during the next step without rounding your lower back, you can subsequently raise the handles to a height that lets you grasp them with a flat-back position.
2. While keeping your lower back flat, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can firmly grasp the handles with straight elbows as your palms face in toward each other.
    1. If your machine has multiple pairs of handles, it is generally recommended to grasp the lower handles to let you hinge through your full range of motion during the exercise.
3. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
4. Drive through your legs and thrust your hips forward to stand upright as you continue keeping your back flat and elbows straight.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Focus on “sitting back” rather than “bending over,” and your torso will naturally transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal.
    2. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit back without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    3. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    4. Throughout the set, keep your feet fully planted on the ground and your neck near a neutral position, as when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move.
    1. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically hinge until their hands are at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively bending your knees depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    3. If you have high hamstring flexibility and can hinge until the machine’s lever arms contact the stoppers underneath them, descend until you can tap the stoppers very lightly with the lever arms without resting in the bottom position.
    4. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should clearly be in control of the entire descent.
3. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward to lift your torso upright into the starting position.
    1. This should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so keep your lower back flat, chest up, core braced, and feet fully on the ground.
    2. At the end of the lifting phase, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back at the top through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips properly stacked under your shoulders, preventing excessive arching.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the handles down by sitting your hips back and bending your knees.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe between reps in the fully upright position, rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. You can select either a fixed-weight EZ bar or an adjustable plate-loaded EZ bar, which are functionally interchangeable for this exercise.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down or hinge at your hips with straight elbows.
    1. If the EZ bar is already positioned in an elevated rack at mid-thigh level or above, you naturally would not have to squat down or hinge at your hips before picking it up.
3. Grasp the bar with approximately a shoulder-width grip and a semi-underhand grip (AKA semi-neutral grip) such that your palms are directed at an angle that is facing forward and inward.
    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it before a shoulder-width semi-underhand grip is accessible on the bar.
4. While keeping your elbows straight, stand fully upright while gripping the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set, which will help you maintain a rigid trunk position while you use hip motion instead of lower back motion to help drive the bar up.
2. While keeping your elbows straight, sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and your torso to incline slightly forward.
    1. Keep your lower back near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright, rather than meaningfully rounding your lower back while doing so.
3. As you simultaneously drive your hips forcefully forward to generate momentum from your lower body, curl the bar upward in an arcing manner by bending at your elbows while allowing your elbows to swing a bit forward.
    1. The hip drive motion, which is similar to the lockout of a deadlift, will bring your torso into a vertical position with your knees straightened.
    2. Continue keeping your lower back near a neutral position instead of arching back excessively.
    3. While you are intentionally using momentum to help your biceps and other arm muscles lift the weight, you should not be “cheating” to the extent that you feel out of control.
4. After your elbows have fully bent, lower the bar in a controlled manner, allowing your elbows to straighten and return to your sides until you return to the starting position with straight elbows and the bar just in front of your thighs.
    1. Keep your torso upright and hips stationary as your biceps and other arm muscles control the descent without assistance from the rest of your body.
    2. Your muscles are noticeably stronger during the lowering phase of an exercise compared to the lifting phase, so “cheating” during the lifting phase allows your biceps to experience greater loading during the more controlled lowering phase.
    3. If you are unable to control the lowering phase to any reasonable degree, you are likely using a weight that is excessively heavy relative to your current ability.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust a cable station’s pulley to near shoulder height, select your desired weight with the loading pin, and remove any handle attachment if it is connected to the cable.
2. Stand with the side of what will be working your shoulder facing the cable.
3. With your closer hand, firmly grasp the ball at the end of the cable, or the end of the cable directly with your little finger and the adjacent side of your hand contacting the ball. You can use your free hand to assist with setting your working side’s grip.
    1. Use whichever hand placement feels most comfortable and stable to you, but if you decide to grasp the cable directly, be aware to avoid pinching any fingers when returning the cable to its initial position after finishing your set.
    2. All the subsequent directions refer to the arm in which you are holding the cable. Keep your free arm in your preferred comfortable position throughout the exercise.
4. With your palm facing forward, walk out to the side away from the cable until you feel tension from the cable with your arm raised out away from your side in alignment with the cable.
    1. Your wrist should be straight as the cable is contacting the little finger-side of your hand. Keep your wrist straight throughout the exercise.
5. Set your feet about hip-width apart while standing upright with a mostly straight elbow (which can be slightly bent or fully straight based on what feels most comfortable to you).
    1. While you do not necessarily need to have an exaggerated “proud chest” posture with your shoulders fully pulled back, avoid standing with your shoulders rolled forward into a slouched upper back position.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbow mostly straight, sweep your arm upward and inward in an arcing manner to pull your biceps toward your ear.
    1. Strive to finish with your arm fully overhead or as close to fully overhead as your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    2. While you raise your arm through shoulder motion and let your shoulder blade move naturally, keep the rest of your body stationary.
2. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering your arm toward the pulley until your elbow is close to shoulder height.
    1. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the cable abruptly yank your arm downward.
    2. At the end of this step, your arm should be outstretched close to parallel to the ground.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
While still meaningfully training your [lateral](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md) and [front](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) delts, this variation biases your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md) to a greater degree than standard lateral raises.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a weight plate in each hand with your middle, ring, and little fingers in their holes, gripping the sides of the plates opposite to your thumbs and index fingers, which should be flat against the outer sides of the plates.
    1. Inserting three fingers into the holes is commonly performed and an appropriate grip with which to start, but some people with thick fingers may feel most comfortable when only inserting their middle and ring fingers.
2. Stand upright in a near hip-width stance, and hold the plates just in front of your legs with slightly bent elbows and your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. While you do not necessarily need to have an exaggerated “proud chest” posture with your shoulders fully pulled back, avoid standing with your shoulders rolled forward into a slouched upper back position.
## Exercise technique
1. Sweep your arms out and away from your sides in an arcing motion while keeping your elbows slightly bent.
    1. Throughout the exercise, keep your legs straight and torso upright as you avoid bending your elbows any further than the slight bend you exhibited in the starting position.
    2. You should resemble making a snow angel with your arms as they move outward rather than forward.
2. As your arms approach being parallel to the ground, angle your palms forward and continue sweeping your arms up overhead through the full range of motion your shoulder mobility comfortably permits.
    1. While you raise your arms through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blades to move naturally, the rest of your body should remain stationary.
    2. If you have the mobility to do so comfortably, you can finish the lifting phase once your arms are fully overhead with your biceps by your ears. However, if you start feeling shoulder discomfort in the fully elevated position, you can simply move through the greatest range of motion that is comfortable to you.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering the plates in a smooth arcing motion until they have returned to being just in front of your legs.
    1. As your arms reach close to parallel to the ground, rotate your palms down, which will result in your palms facing in toward each other in the bottom position.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the plates swing down in an uncontrolled fashion.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While still meaningfully training your [lateral](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md) and [front](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) delts, this variation biases your [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md) and [serratus anterior](../Muscles/Serratus%20Anterior%201955c6f170d880a8b8b9e712f2ec58e0.md) to a greater degree than standard lateral raises.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of dumbbells and sit down on a flat exercise bench on a flat exercise bench while lifting the dumbbells onto your upper thighs near your abdomen, with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Position yourself so that there is enough room on the bench behind you so that you can lie your head down onto the end of the bench.
2. While marching your thighs up to help lift the dumbbells back toward your chest with your elbows bent, lean back to lie down with your back and the back of your head in contact with the bench as your head is right by the end of the bench.
    1. Once you are lying down, your feet should be flat on the ground, approximately shoulder width apart from each other, in a stable position stacked under your bent knees.
3. Tuck your chin toward your chest to lift your head off the bench. Simultaneosuly perform a slight crunching motion to lift the uppermost part of your upper back just off the bench without rolling your shoulders forward into a slouched position.
    1. Maintain this position throughout your set.
4. Point your palms backward to assume an underhand grip.
## Exercise technique
1. Straighten your elbows in a controlled manner and let the weights pull your arms down toward the ground through a range of motion comfortable to your shoulders.
    1. If your shoulders feel comfortable doing so, you can finish letting your arms descend once the dumbbells are barely above the ground.
    2. To prevent the dumbbells from contacting the bench, you may have to spread your arms slightly out away from your sides.
    3. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your biceps and the front of your shoulders in the bottom position, but you should not experience any shoulder discomfort when moving into the position appropriate for you.
2. Curl the dumbbells upward by fully bending your elbows without moving your upper arms.
    1. While your forearms move through elbow joint motion, the rest of your body should remain stationary as you avoid swinging your elbows upward through shoulder motion.
    2. Once you have fully bent your elbows at the top of the curl, your palms should be facing back toward you, since you should maintain an underhand grip with straight wrists throughout the set.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbells in a controlled manner until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. Continue keeping your upper arms still as all the motion occurs from your forearms hinging about your elbows like the hand of an analog clock rotating about its center.
    2. To prevent your elbows from drifting down, you will have to perform a static front raise effort, since the force from the dumbbells will pull your upper arms down through the shoulder if you do not resist this force.
4. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. Following your last full rep, you can repeat step 2 to curl the dumbbells again before turning your palms inward to face each other and lifting your elbows up to be tucked by your sides. Then march your thighs up toward the dumbbells, and rock forward to sit up with the dumbbells on your upper thighs as you would following a set of dumbbell bench pressing.
    2. If your mobility and arm length allow you to do so comfortably, you can alternatively set the dumbbells on the ground while lying down on the bench after resting your head and upper back fully on the bench and letting your arms drift downward. In contrast to the first approach described, setting the dumbbells down onto the ground is not recommended for everyone because it requires a greater degree of shoulder mobility than some people have. However, the first technique described requires you to curl the dumbbells up, which may not be feasible if you reach true muscular failure during the set.
## Description
Like other curl variations, this exercise can effectively train your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Horizontally adjust the machine’s footplate to a setting that will allow you to position part of your buttocks just off the front edge of the pad when you set up with your feet on the footplate.
    1. The appropriate position should allow your thighs to rest comfortably on the pad.
    2. If the footplate is positioned excessively far from the pad, you will have to sit closer toward the middle of the pad rather than just off the front edge.
    3. If the footplate is positioned excessively close to the pad, the back of your upper thighs will not be in contact with the pad.
    4. Since a sweet spot exists, some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position.
2. If your machine allows you to adjust the height of the footplate, select a height that allows you to feel comfortable and secure with slightly bent knees once you are in the starting position.
    1. As a starting point, you can select a height that positions the lower pair of leg rollers level with the pad and the upper pair of leg rollers higher than the pad.
    2. Not all machines permit you to adjust the footplate height.
3. Position the weight you intend to use in a spot that you can comfortably reach after you set your feet on the footplate.
    1. When using a weight plate or kettlebell, you can hang the weight on one of the machine’s handles.
    2. For the easiest setup, you can have a partner hand you the weight after you set your feet on the footplate during the next step. Besides a weight plate or kettlebell, a partner can hand you a medicine ball or dumbbell, which cannot be hung on the handles. This partner approach is ideal if you are using a heavy weight, since it can otherwise be awkward to get into the starting position with the weight independently.
    3. Some lifters will alternatively set the weight on the ground directly in front of the machine between its handles and fully lean backward to pick up the weight after setting their feet on the footplate. Not everyone has the mobility to set up in this manner, and it is most practical when using a large medicine ball, which makes it less difficult to pick up from the ground.
4. Climb up onto the machine, and hook your lower legs between the leg rollers with the top of your feet snugly pressed into the top roller as your soles are facing the footplate.
    1. Your feet should be securely anchored so that they will not slide during the exercise. The top rollers should be just above the lowest part of your shins by your ankles, while the bottom rollers should be just under your Achilles tendons (which attach to the top of your heels).
    2. Depending on the machine you are using, you can step up onto a middle beam or a step to help you get into position.
    3. While you are setting your feet, you can hold the base of the leg rollers for stability.
5. Pick up the weight, hold it with both hands close to your chest, and sit upright with your buttocks just hanging off the front edge of the pad.
    1. The precise way in which you will pick up and hold the weight will naturally vary based on the specific implement you selected and where you placed it initially. What matters is that you have a firm grip on the weight and are able to keep it in a stable position throughout your set.
    2. Your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright, looking straight ahead. Throughout your set, keep your neck in this position and the weight close to your chest.
## Exercise technique
1. Lean your torso back in a controlled manner until your torso is approximately parallel to the ground or slightly beyond this point.
    1. Allow your lower back to arch to a degree that feels comfortable to you.
    2. Specifically how much of an arch is comfortable will vary from person to person, but it is often appropriate to finish the lowering phase with your lower back arched to a similar degree as when you are normally standing upright. It is not inherently injurious to arch beyond this point, but meaningfully arching the lower back beyond this point can provoke lower back discomfort in some people.
    3. If you feel lower back discomfort at the bottom, you can strive to keep your lower back closer to a flat position with less of an arch, or you can reduce the range in which you lean back. Thinking about keeping your ribs tucked down to a greater degree as you avoid flaring them can help limit excessive arching.
2. Reverse the movement by curling your back to lift your torso up until your shoulders are vertically above your hips.
    1. To train your abs dynamically, your back should progressively round rather than remain in a flat position (which could occur if you predominantly lift your torso up through your hip flexor muscles).
    2. As a cue to emphasize your abs, think about driving the bottom of your ribs down toward the tops of your hip bones while tightening your abs.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
    1. After your last rep, set the weight down in the opposite way in which you initially picked it up before dismounting the machine.
    2. Like when setting up, you can grasp the base of the rollers for stability when getting off the machine.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) while also training your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
1. Select your weight with the machine’s loading pin(s), and adjust the thigh pad to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. Some machines will have a single weight stack that provides resistance to each cable, while others will have one weight stack for each cable.
    2. If you notice that your thighs do not snugly rest under the thigh pad when sitting down on the seat, you can readjust the pad before resuming your setup.
2. While facing the center of the machine and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the handles.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
3. While holding the handles, sit down on the machine’s seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to straighten and your arms to raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
4. Slightly lean your torso backward at your hips, and maintain this slight backward lean throughout your set.
    1. From this position, you should feel tension from the cables holding your arms overhead with straight elbows.
    2. If you notice that the cables remain slack when your elbows are fully straightened (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), you may have to lean a bit further back for the cables to provide resistance in the starting position. If that does not take the slack out of the cables, the machine may not be designed to provide resistance through the full range of motion for people with your stature, so you may have to perform a different pulldown variation on another machine if you wish to train through a full range of motion.
5. Let your palms face a direction that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    1. The dual handles allow you to use whichever grip you prefer, so you have the ability to point your palms forward for an overhand grip, inward for a neutral grip, backward for an underhand grip, or at an angle between two of those grips for a hybrid grip.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears. Simultaneously drive your elbows down toward your sides to pull the handles down toward the sides of your upper chest.
    1. Let your palms freely rotate in a manner that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    2. Bend your elbows to the extent that your forearms remain aligned with the cables, allowing you to draw straight lines from your elbows through your wrists to the cables.
    3. Maintain the slight backward lean of your torso you adopted while setting up, rather than leaning further backward.
    4. When pulling through your full range of motion, you should finish with your elbows close to the sides of your torso.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the handles in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Allow your palms to rotate if that feels natural to you.
    3. Finish with your arms overhead and your elbows fully straightened.
    4. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md) and [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Select your desired weight with the machine’s loading pin(s), and adjust the seat to a height that lets you rest your lower chest comfortably against the chest pad once you are seated.
    1. The proper seat height should let the exercise feel smooth and natural while ideally letting you experience resistance from the machine in the starting position with your elbows fully straightened.
    2. An excessively high seat can prevent the machine from providing tension in the starting position and restrict your range of motion.
    3. When using this machine for the first time, trying out different seat heights may be helpful to determine specifically which setting helps this exercise feel best to you based on your body proportions.
2. If your machine has a thigh pad, adjust it to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting down.
3. While facing the chest pad and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the handles with a grip that feels comfortable to you based on the design of your machine.
4. Sit down on the seat with your torso against the chest pad. Let your elbows straighten and your arms raise in line with the machine’s resistance.
    1. Set your feet on the foot bar or the floor, based on your preference and machine design.
    2. If you do not feel tension from the machine in this position with straight elbows, you may need to lower the seat height to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion.
## Exercise technique
1. While pulling your shoulder blades down and back, drive your elbows down and back to pull the handles toward you.
    1. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows finishing slightly behind your torso.
    2. Strive to keep your forearms aligned with the angle in which you are pulling, which should naturally promote the appropriate degree of elbow bend.
    3. Keep your torso upright against the chest pad throughout your set rather than leaning backward during the row.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil between them.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your elbows to move forward and upward while straightening in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move fully forward as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This row primarily trains your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), which are assisted by your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Select your weight with the loading pin, and sit down on the machine with your feet in contact with its foot plates.
    1. Allow your knees to bend to an angle that allows you to feel stable and comfortable, which can be a mild to moderately mild knee bend for many people.
    2. With greater knee bend, you will be able to sit closer toward the handles, so you can bend your knees further if you initially cannot reach them during the next step.
2. Lean forward at your hips until you are able to grasp the handles firmly with straight elbows.
    1. How you angle your palms (e.g., in toward each other or downward) when setting up is up to your preference and what feels comfortable to you with the machine you are using.
3. Lean your torso backward at your hips until you are sitting with an upright torso as your arms are aligned with the cables and your palms are angled in toward each other.

## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handles back toward you by driving your elbows backward while pulling your shoulder blades together into a “proud chest” posture.
    1. Let your elbows move through a path of motion that feels comfortable to you, whether that involves keeping them tucked fairly close to your sides or moderately flaring them out. Simulatnesouly let your palms rotate if that feels natural to you.
    2. Keep your forearms aligned with the machine’s arms connected to the handles, which naturally promotes the appropriate degree of elbow bend.
    3. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your knees, hips, and lower back should remain nearly stationary in a stable position throughout the set as you keep your torso upright.
    4. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows finishing slightly behind your torso.

2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to move forward in a controlled manner as they progressively straighten to move the handles forward.
    1. Finish with your arms fully outstretched in front of you.
    2. Like when rowing the handles toward you, let your palms rotate if doing so feels natural and comfortable to you.

Your shoulder blades will naturally move apart, but you can exaggerate this motion by intentionally allowing the weight to pull them further apart than your resting position at the end, without rounding your lower back. This will stretch your upper back muscles and may help you to train them more effectively.
