## Setting up
1. If your machine has an adjustable seat, set it to the most reclined position that allows your back to be well-supported by the backrest when seated with your feet on the foot platform.
    1. Starting with the most reclined position (which tilts the seat down in a closer to horizontal position) generally works well for most people.
    2. Compared to using a closer to upright seat angle, using an appropriately reclined position will allow you to leg press through a longer range of motion without rounding your lower back.
    3. The most reclined setting on certain machine models may be excessively reclined to the extent that the backrest may no longer be able to stabilize your body when leg pressing. If this occurs, your buttocks may lift off the seat, and your torso may slide back along the backrest due to the backrest being angled too close to a horizontal position. However, most leg press machines will not have an excessively reclined seat setting available.
    4. To determine if the seat angle you initially selected is appropriate for you, you can perform a couple of reps with the technique described in the “exercise technique” section without adding any weight plates to the leg press. If you feel stable and well-supported by the backrest, the seat is not excessively reclined, and you have selected a viable seat angle.
    5. Note that not all machines have an adjustable seat.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. Sit down with your buttocks fully on the seat and your whole back firmly supported by the backrest.
    1. Rather than being rounded in a slouched posture, your back should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright.
    2. Based on your preference, you can decide to rest your head against the back of the seat or keep it slightly in front of the seat. Regardless, keep your neck near a neutral position, like when you are normally looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Place your feet fully on the middle of the foot platform, near shoulder-width apart, with your toes pointing slightly outward.
    1. Many people find that setting up with a stance reasonably close to this allows them to leg press effectively. However, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Some people will feel that they can move their hips more freely with a wider stance, while others may prefer a closer stance. Similarly, certain lifters may feel better with their toes pointing straight up, while others may feel more comfortable with their toes pointing moderately further outward.
    3. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when leg pressing through your full range of motion. Trying out somewhat different stances over time can often help you find out which position is personally best for you.
    4. While recognizing that near the middle of the platform works well for many people, you can also adjust how high up on the platform you position your feet based on your preference. Wherever you select, your heels should be firmly on the platform along with the rest of your feet. Placing your feet higher up potentially may bias the gluteus maximus to a degree, while placing your feet lower down potentially may train the quads preferentially. Avoid positioning your feet toward either end of the platform if doing so feels awkward and/or limits your range of motion.
    5. In the starting position, your knees should be at least slightly bent to let you unlock the leg press and begin your set. If you have short legs, you potentially may have to situate your feet lower on the platform to reach the platform with slightly bent knees. If you are using a machine that does not permit a lower starting height of the sled, that particular machine may not be feasible for your body type.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. You will continue doing so throughout your set, which will help create full-body tension to amplify your stability and performance.
2. Drive your feet into the platform to push it away from you by straightening your knees.
    1. After doing so, the sled should no longer be resting on the machine’s safety stoppers.
    2. Your knees should now be straight or just slightly bent.
3. Unlock the safety handle with your hand to disengage the safety stopper.
    1. The specific location of the safety handle and how to unlock it can vary among different machine models. However, the safety handle is often near where one of your hands will be when resting by your side.
4. For additional stability, firmly grasp the fixed handles (not the movable safety handle) and continue holding them throughout your set.
5. Lower the foot platform toward you in a controlled manner by simultaneously bending at your knees and hips.
    1. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the platform.
    2. Continue keeping your buttocks firmly planted on the seat and your back snugly up against the backrest.
    3. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet. It can help to think about pushing your knees out if you notice them starting to drift inward.
    4. While you do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should be actively in control the entire time.
6. Continue bending your knees and hips through the full range of motion you can while keeping your buttocks firmly on the seat, lower back flat against the backrest, and heels fully on the platform.
    1. People can reach the point where their knees are bent by at least 90 degrees. However, what constitutes a full range of motion will vary from person to person and be influenced by your individual hip and ankle mobility, along with your foot placement.
    2. If you reached the end range to which your hips can bend, continuing any further would cause your lower back to start rounding. This would be demonstrated by your buttocks starting to curl up off the seat.
    3. If you reached the end range to which your ankle mobility allows your knees to track over your toes, continuing any further would cause your heels to start lifting off the platform.
7. Drive your feet into the platform to push it away from you as you extend (straighten) your knees and hips.
    1. Based on your preference, you can finish with your knees fully straightened or ever so slightly bent. It is not inherently dangerous to fully straighten your knees when leg pressing, but avoid forcibly snapping your knees into a locked-out position in an uncontrolled manner.
    2. Rather than pushing all through your heels or all through your toes, strive to push evenly throughout your feet.
    3. Continue keeping your feet fully on the platform, buttocks on the seat, back against the back rest, and knees aligned over your feet.
8. Alternate between steps 5-7 until you have completed your set.
9. After your knees are straightened following the lifting phase of your last rep, lock the safety handle with your hand to engage the safety stopper.
10. Bend your knees to return the weight fully onto the safety stopper.

## Setting up
1. Select your desired load with the machine’s loading pin, and set the knee pad to the side you will not train during this set if your machine has an adjustable knee pad.
    1. Some machines have a pair of fixed knee pads rather than a single adjustable knee pad.
    2. Your kneeling leg will be the non-working leg during this exercise.
2. With what will be your non-working leg, kneel on the knee pad with your thigh snugly against the thigh pad.
    1. Since you will keep this non-working leg in a kneeling position throughout your set, all the subsequent directions will apply to your working leg.
3. Position your working leg’s thigh snugly against the other thigh pad with the back of your lower leg contacting the front of the roller pad.
4. Lean forward at your hips until you can firmly grasp the handles in a comfortable position with your forearms resting on the forearm pads.
    1. In this starting position, your knee should be aligned with the machine’s pivot point (i.e., the center about which the machine’s lever arm rotates), which should naturally occur when your thigh contacts the thigh pad. Keeping your knee aligned with this pivot point will help the exercise feel smooth and natural.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched or rounded, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position with its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright. The forward torso lean should come from your hips rather than your back.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your toes and foot back up toward your shin by moving at your ankle. Maintain this ankle position throughout your set.
    1. You should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract while doing so.
    2. This places your ankle in the same position in which it would be at the bottom of a calf raise on a step. It is the opposite of the ankle motion you would perform when lifting your heel up off the ground during a calf raise.
    3. Holding your ankle in this position can increase your leg curl strength (as explained in detail under the “notes” section).
2. Without moving your thigh, drive your heel toward your buttock by bending your knee through the full range of motion you can perform.
    1. The degree to which you can bend your knee can be influenced by which specific machine you use, but you have reached your end range once you can no longer pull your heel closer toward your buttock.
    2. If you experience a notable cramping sensation in your hamstrings at the end range, you can optionally stop curling the weight up just before the point where your hamstrings may cramp.
    3. Throughout your set, continue holding the handles while keeping your forearms resting on the forearm pads.
    4. While your lower leg moves through motion at your working knee, the rest of your body stationary.
    5. Particularly avoid lifting your thigh off the pad or excessively arching your lower back.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering your heel in a controlled manner to straighten your knee and return to the starting position.
    1. While there is no need to use an extremely slow tempo for this movement, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire time, rather than letting the weight abruptly swing your lower leg down.
4. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell, hold it by your side with your palm facing inward, and stand facing a sturdy object reasonably near knee-height, such as a flat exercise bench.
    1. If you are tall, the head of an incline bench set to a low incline may be better for you to brace your hand against during this exercise, compared to a lower flat bench.
    2. Viable alternatives to a bench can include a plyometric box, sturdy chair, dumbbell rack, racked Smith machine bar, or a barbell on a rack’s J-cups.
    3. The appropriate object should let you achieve a position that feels stable and comfortable with a flat back once you brace against it.
    4. While using an object reasonably near knee height can let you set up effectively and is most common, some lifters may prefer to use a higher object closer to hip height, which can let you keep the non-working arm higher during the exercise. Using a taller object may also be sensible for people with mobility limitations who cannot comfortably support themselves on a shorter object without rounding their backs.
    5. For brevity, the instructions will refer to the use of a bench from this point on.
2. While standing with the head of the bench in front of your free arm, situate your feet near shoulder-width apart.
    1. When aligning your free arm with one end of the bench, you should have space in front of your arm holding the dumbbell, so you will not have to worry about the bench getting in the way of the dumbbell after you have assumed the starting position for this row.
    2. A near shoulder-width stance is an appropriate starting point, but feel free to widen your stance a bit if that feels more stable to you.
3. Based on your preference, you can adopt a staggered stance by taking a step backward with the foot on the same side as the dumbbell, or you can keep your feet symmetrical.
    1. Either stance can be effectively used for this exercise, so you can try out a set or two with each option and continue with the position where you feel most stable.
4. Lean your torso forward by sitting your hips back while allowing your knees to bend mildly until you can brace your free hand against the bench with a straight elbow.
    1. Keep your lower back flat, and let your arm (that is holding the dumbbell) hang down toward the ground with your arm angled in toward your opposite side (resulting in neutral grip).
    2. When standing appropriately close to the bench, your non-working side’s arm should ideally be angled downward to a greater degree than forward, so that you are not reaching excessively far forward.
    3. Keep your hand braced against the bench throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Drive your elbow backward and upward in an arcing motion to pull the dumbbell toward your hip. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blade backward, and keep your elbow tucked by your side rather than flaring it outward.
    1. When bending your elbow by the appropriate degree, your forearm should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    2. Row through your full range of motion, which should result in your elbow finishing slightly behind your torso or at least in alignment with your torso at the top of the rep.
    3. Strive to keep your lower body and torso in a fixed position with your chest facing a similar direction throughout this movement. A mild degree of torso rotation is not problematic, but avoid letting it become excessive and turning the exercise into a cheat row.
    4. While performing this arcing motion, the dumbbell should not move straight upward in a vertical path.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled arcing motion until your arm is directed down toward the ground with your elbow straightened.
    1. Allow the weight to pull your shoulder blade forward, which will stretch your upper back muscles and result in your working side’s shoulder being mildly closer to the ground than your other side’s shoulder at the bottom of the row.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weight rapidly pull your arm down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Place a kettlebell on the ground next to the side of a flat bench (or whichever stable object on which you will rest your upper back) with the handle parallel to the length of the bench.
    1. As an alternative to a flat bench or a specialized hip thrust bench, you can use a soft plyometric box or couch reasonably close to knee height.
2. Sit down on the ground with the kettlebell directly in front of your hips as your legs straddle the weight, and your upper back contacts the edge of the bench.
    1. Specifically placing the lower part of your shoulder blades against the edge of the bench often is ideal, but feel free to adjust your upper back positioning mildly from this point based on what feels most stable to you.
3. Use both hands to grasp the horns (side handles) of the kettlebell and lift it up onto the midline of your pelvis with the handle facing up.
    1. The base of the kettlebell should be resting on your pubic bones, which lie directly below your bladder and just above your genitals. If you situate the weight above or below your pubic bones, applying pressure to those areas can naturally be uncomfortable.
    2. Continue holding the horns of the kettlebell with your palms facing in toward each other throughout the exercise.
4. While keeping the kettlebell resting on your pelvis, place the soles of your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart, with your toes pointing forward and your knees bent by a little greater than 90 degrees.
    1. The optimal degree of knee bend should allow your feet to feel stable while being firmly planted on the ground throughout the set. It is normally appropriate to position your foot far enough back that your knee will be bent by approximately 90 degrees at the top of your hip thrust.
5. Tuck your chin mildly toward your chest, and maintain this neck position throughout the exercise.
6. While leaving one foot on the ground, lift your other foot off the ground by straightening your knee.
    1. Keep one foot off the ground throughout the set you perform with your other side.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set to help stabilize your lower back.
    2. From this starting position, your back should either be flat or exhibit its natural curvature, like when you are normally standing upright.
2. Lift your hips up by driving your heel into the ground and squeezing your glute while continuing to hold the kettlebell on your pubic bones.
    1. At the top, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side. Your thighs and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glute.
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glute engage.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner through the full range of motion your hip mobility comfortably permits without rounding or excessively arching your lower back.
    1. Some people can descend all the way down until they lightly contact the ground with their glutes, but you can prioritize lowering through the range in which you can achieve through hip motion rather than lower back motion.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
    1. When you are ready to set the weight down, rest both feet and your buttocks on the ground, and place the kettlebell onto the ground in front of your hips.

    3. The appropriate object should let you achieve a position that feels stable and comfortable with a flat back once you brace against it.
    4. While using an object reasonably near knee height can let you set up effectively and is most common, some lifters may prefer to use a higher object closer to hip height, which can let you keep the non-working arm higher during the exercise. Using a taller object may also be sensible for people with mobility limitations who cannot comfortably support themselves on a shorter object without rounding their backs.
    5. For brevity, the instructions will refer to the use of a bench from this point on.
2. While standing with the head of the bench in front of your free arm, situate your feet near shoulder-width apart.
    1. When aligning your free arm with one end of the bench, you should have space in front of your arm holding the kettlebell, so you will not have to worry about the bench getting in the way of the kettlebell after you have assumed the starting position for this row.
    2. A near shoulder-width stance is an appropriate starting point, but feel free to widen your stance a bit if that feels more stable to you.
3. Based on your preference, you can adopt a staggered stance by taking a step backward with the foot on the same side as the kettlebell, or you can keep your feet symmetrical.
    1. Either stance can be effectively used for this exercise, so you can try out a set or two with each option and continue with the position where you feel most stable.
4. Lean your torso forward by sitting your hips back while allowing your knees to bend mildly until you can brace your free hand against the bench with a straight elbow.
    1. Keep your lower back flat, and let your arm (that is holding the kettlebell) hang down toward the ground with your arm angled in toward your opposite side (resulting in neutral grip).
    2. When standing appropriately close to the bench, your non-working side’s arm should ideally be angled downward to a greater degree than forward, so that you are not reaching excessively far forward.
    3. Keep your hand braced against the bench throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Drive your elbow backward and upward in an arcing motion to pull the kettlebell toward your hip. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blade backward, and keep your elbow tucked by your side rather than flaring it outward.
    1. When bending your elbow by the appropriate degree, your forearm should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    2. Row through your full range of motion, which should result in your elbow finishing slightly behind your torso or at least in alignment with your torso at the top of the rep.
    3. Strive to keep your lower body and torso in a fixed position with your chest facing a similar direction throughout this movement. A mild degree of torso rotation is not problematic, but avoid letting it become excessive and turning the exercise into a cheat row.
    4. While performing this arcing motion, the kettlebell should not move straight upward in a vertical path.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the kettlebell in a controlled arcing motion until your arm is directed down toward the ground with your elbow straightened.
    1. Allow the weight to pull your shoulder blade forward, which will stretch your upper back muscles and result in your working side’s shoulder being mildly closer to the ground than your other side’s shoulder at the bottom of the row.
    2. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weight rapidly pull your arm down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively train much of the musculature constituting your middle and upper back, including your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md).

## Setting up
1. Adjust the Smith machine’s bar to near mid-chest height.
    1. The optimal starting height should let you position the bar on your upper back and unrack it without lifting your heels off the ground.
2. Position the safety stops (that are attached to the sliding rails) so that they are slightly below the lowest height at which the bar descends at the bottom of your squat.
    1. To find this point for your body, you can perform a couple of squat reps with the unloaded bar as described in the “exercise technique” section, but you can initially put the safety stops somewhat below the top of your hip bones when standing upright as an approximation.
3. Add your desired weight to the bar, and face the center of the bar with approximately a shoulder-width stance.
    1. If your Smith machine has angled sliding rails, position yourself to face the side where the bar will track slightly forward as it descends (so the bottom of the rails is farther in front of you than the top).
    2. If your Smith machine has purely vertical sliding rails, you can perform the same movement regardless of which direction you face.
4. Grasp each side of the bar with a somewhat wider than shoulder-width grip that feels comfortable to you.
    1. The proper grip width will vary from person to person, and what feels best to you will be influenced by your shoulder mobility.
    2. If you are not accustomed to exercises that have a bar on your back, you may have to try out different hand placements to find one that personally suits you well.
5. While holding onto the bar, shallowly bend at your hips and knees to then walk under the bar and situate the bar on your upper back in a position that feels comfortable and stable for you.
    1. Where precisely the bar feels most comfortable and stable will vary among different individuals, but the bar should feel like it is securely resting on the muscles of your upper back.
    2. If you feel like the bar is placing pressure on your neck, you most likely have the bar placed too high on your back.
    3. In particular, you should avoid placing the bar excessively high to the extent that the weight is pressing on any of the bony prominences at the base of your neck.
    4. If you feel like the bar may slide down your back after standing upright with it, you most likely have the bar placed too low on your back.
    5. While positioning the bar on your upper back, you may have to readjust where you are grasping the bar if your shoulders, elbows, or wrists feel uncomfortable with your initial placement.
    6. If you are not accustomed to having a bar on your back, you may not feel particularly comfortable doing so, especially when it is loaded with additional weight, but whichever position you use should not be painful.
6. Position the back of your heels slightly in front of the bar with your feet near shoulder width apart from each other as your toes are pointing somewhat out to the sides (rather than pointing straight ahead).
    1. In contrast to when you barbell back squat, placing your feet a bit in front of the bar when Smith machine back squatting can assist with comfortably achieving a deep squat.
    2. Your feet should not be so far in front of the bar that you feel that they may slide out in front of you when squatting.
    3. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    4. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    5. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside of shoulder width with their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull down on the bar to tighten your upper back muscles, and unrack it by starting to stand up as you straighten your knees.
2. After the bar rests fully on your upper back rather than the safety bars, rotate the safety hooks out away from the safety bars with a slight wrist flick before standing fully upright with the bar.
3. Your neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright. Keep your neck in this position throughout the exercise.
4. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward while leaving your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to help you maintain a rigid back position.
5. Initiate the descent by simultaneously breaking at your knees and hips. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your chest up and back flat.
    1. As you descend, it is natural for your torso to lean forward mildly at your hips, but avoid letting your lower back round or chest cave down from upper back rounding.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet, especially the deeper your squat.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
6. Continue to squat down through the available range of motion that your mobility enables without rounding your back, lifting your heels up off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, heels lift off the ground, or knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting excessively deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
7. Once you reach the bottom of your squat, pause in that position, remaining completely stationary for a brief period (e.g., about two seconds) while staying tight.
    1. Avoid rushing your pause to the best of your ability.
8. Reverse the movement by progressively standing up as you drive through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips until you have returned to a fully upright position.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees stacked over your feet as you squat up.
9. Alternate between steps 5-8 until you have completed your set.
    1. Whenever you feel like you could use a breath, you can breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position.
    2. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
10. After finishing the set, rerack the bar by bending at your hips and knees in a quarter squat-like manner as you rotate the safety hooks onto the safety bars and return the bar to resting on the safety bars.
## Description
While statically training your [spinal extensors](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.

Based on your preference, set up with a [full hand clean grip](Full%20hand%20clean%20grip%20front%20squat%201a25c6f170d880068daae293704193e0.md), [fingertip clean grip](Fingertip%20clean%20grip%20front%20squat%202165c6f170d880048694f9a5579ba6ab.md), [cross-arm grip](Cross-arm%20grip%20front%20squat%201a25c6f170d88038b559cf1d5dbd8366.md).
    1. With either type of clean grip, initially grasp the bar with your palms facing down and your hands slightly outside shoulderwidth. Keep as many fingers wrapped around the bar and the bar as close to the bases of your fingers as is comfortable to you during the subsequent steps when using a clean grip. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your wrists with a clean grip, but if it is painful, you can alternatively set up with the [cross-arm grip](Cross-arm%20grip%20front%20squat%201a25c6f170d88038b559cf1d5dbd8366.md).
    2. With a cross-arm grip, you will cross your forearms into an “X-shape” as your hands are on top of the bar with your palms facing down during the following steps. Based on what feels more stable to you, you can position your hands very close together, such that your thumbs are touching each other, or you can have your hands slightly wider apart, such that you have fingers contacting your front delts.
    3. Additional details and demo videos specific to setting up with each grip are included in the [full hand clean grip](Full%20hand%20clean%20grip%20front%20squat%201a25c6f170d880068daae293704193e0.md), [fingertip clean grip](Fingertip%20clean%20grip%20front%20squat%202165c6f170d880048694f9a5579ba6ab.md), and [cross-arm grip](Cross-arm%20grip%20front%20squat%201a25c6f170d88038b559cf1d5dbd8366.md) front squat pages, which display the barbell variations but with the same grip details that apply when using a Smith machine.
5. While simultaneously bending your elbows, shallowly bend at your knees and hips with an upright torso to walk under the bar and situate it on the front of your shoulders just in front of the base of your neck.
    1. The bar should be resting on your front delts (which are the muscles on the front of your shoulders that attach to the outer aspects of your collarbones) and the outer portions of your collarbones, which together form a shelf with the base of your neck to cradle the bar.

6. With the bar now on the front of your shoulders, lift your elbows up until your upper arms are parallel to the ground.

    2. The bony prominence on the back of each elbow should now be pointing straight forward.

## Setting up
You have the option of performing this exercise while standing on a step and keeping both knees straight or standing on the ground and mildly bending one knee to keep that side’s foot off the ground. You can use essentially the same technique to perform the exercise with either approach, but their setups differ. Correspondingly, each approach receives its own setup section, but they share the same exercise technique instructions.

### **Setting up on a step**

1. Position what you will use as you step (e.g., aerobic step, thick bumper plate, short plyometric box) or approach the bottom step of a staircase.
    1. If you are using a mobile step, you can position it next to something where you can place a hand for balance assistance while standing on the step if you wish to receive balance assistance. This may involve setting up next to a rack, wall, chair, or exercise bench positioned upright.
    2. A step height of a few inches (about 8-10cm) is sufficiently tall for most people performing this exercise, since it involves a low amplitude of motion. This means that an aerobic step without risers or a 45lb (20kg) bumper plate is normally sufficiently tall, but a taller step naturally can be used as well.
2. Stand directly to the side of the step, and place one foot fully onto the step while leaving your other foot on the ground. Situate your feet about hip-width apart, and point your toes straight ahead.
    1. Step up with the side of your body you wish to train during this set.
3. Optionally place one hand against a nearby surface for balance assistance. Otherwise, keep your hands in your preferred position throughout the exercise, such as resting on your hips or by your sides.
4. Drive through your elevated leg and straighten your knee to step up until your feet are level, keeping your one foot hanging off the step.
5. On the side hovering off the step, pull your toes and the ball of your foot up toward your shin through an ankle motion that brings your heel closer to the ground than the ball of your foot.
    1. This is the opposite of the ankle motion that occurs when lifting your heels up during a calf raise, and you should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract.
    2. The purpose of keeping your foot in this position is to make sure that your toes do not contact the ground during the exercise and restrict your range of motion. If your step is tall enough that your free foot would not touch the ground in any position during the exercise, you can ignore this step and let the ball of your foot hang down.

### **Setting up on the ground**

1. In a hip-width stance, stand next to something where you can place a hand for balance assistance if you wish to receive balance assistance.
2. Optionally place one hand against a nearby surface for balance assistance. Otherwise, keep your hands in your preferred position throughout the exercise, such as resting on your hips or by your sides.
3. Bend one knee enough to lift that side’s foot off the ground, and keep that knee bent with your foot off the ground throughout the exercise.
    1. You will be training your hip muscles on the side of your body on which you keep your foot on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your torso upright and your stance leg straight, lower your free foot toward the ground by letting your hip bone (on the side of your free foot) tilt down in a controlled manner.
    1. Descend until you feel that your hip bones are fully tilted, which may prompt you to feel a mild stretching sensation in the side of your hip (of the hip bone whose leg remains on the step).
    2. As a cue, you can imagine that you have a basin of water on top of your hip bones, and you are trying to pour as much of the water as you can out to one side.
    3. There is no need to perform this step with an extremely slow tempo, but you should be using your hip muscles to control the descent actively, rather than just letting your hip bone abruptly drop.
2. Reverse the movement by hiking your hip up to lift your free foot up and tilt your hip bones in the opposite direction.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and your legs straight as you exclusively move at your hip.
    2. Strive to finish with your free leg’s hip bone higher up than your stance leg’s hip bone.
    3. When imagining that you have a basin of water on top of your hip bones, you can think about leveling the basin before trying to spill the water toward the side of your stance leg.
    4. With the appropriate technique, you should feel tension in the muscles on the side of your stance leg’s hip as they contract.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat this exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the musculature on the side of your hip, including your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), and [tensor fascia latae](../Muscles/Tensor%20Fascia%20Latae%201925c6f170d8806fb83bf08142d940fc.md).

## Setting up
1. Optionally set up a pair of aerobic steps, thick bumper plates, or deadlift blocks near hip-width apart if you wish to extend this exercise’s range of motion beyond what you could achieve when standing on the ground.
    1. When standing on the ground, individuals who are sufficiently flexible may find that the kettlebell will contact the ground at the bottom of a rep before they reach their full range of motion. Standing on top of elevated objects (as you would during a deficit kettlebell deadlift) can alternatively permit a greater range of motion.
    2. Initially performing this exercise while standing on the ground will let you determine whether an elevated surface is required for you to train through your full range of motion.
    3. If your range of motion is not restricted when standing on the ground during this exercise, there is no purpose in standing on these objects to elevate your feet.
2. Pick up one kettlebell and stand upright with approximately a shoulder-width stance while holding the kettlebell just in front of your thighs with your elbows straight and your palms back toward you.
    1. At this point, you will naturally be standing on the elevated objects if you wish to use them, or you can stand on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move without rounding your back.
    1. Throughout the set, keep the soles of your feet fully planted and your arms in a vertical position, perpendicular to the ground.
    2. This step is essentially the same as the lowering phase of a Romanian deadlift without keeping the weight as close to your legs (since the arms angle slightly backward during a Romanian deadlift, rather than hanging straight down during this exercise).
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal. How close to horizontal you can incline your torso will be affected by your hamstring flexibility.
    5. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range.
2. In a controlled curling manner, allow your whole back to round slowly through your comfortable range of motion without moving your lower body.
    1. The degree to which you can round your back will be affected by your spinal mobility.
    2. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your back muscles in the bottom position, but you should not feel any discomfort at the end range. Only round your back as far as is comfortable.
    3. Rather than moving only one part of your back, strive to round your lower, middle, and upper back simultaneously. Due to the anatomy of the spine, most of the motion will occur at the lower half of your back, but moving the upper half of your back as well can help you train more of your back musculature.
    4. As a cue, you can think about bringing the bottom of your ribs toward the top of your hip bones.
    5. While keeping your lower body in the same position throughout each rep, you should continue feeling a stretching sensation in your hamstrings. During the descent, particularly avoid dropping your hips by bending your knees.
3. While maintaining the same hinged-hip position, uncoil your spine in a controlled manner as you transition from a rounded-back to a flat-back position.
    1. All the motion should come from your back muscles, extending (straightening) your spine without any movement at your hips or knees, which should prompt you to feel tension in the muscles running along your spine as you flare your ribs up and away from your hip bones.
    2. Based on your preference, you can finish this step once your back is straight or when your lower back is mildly arched, like it normally is when standing upright.
    3. Performing this lifting phase with a controlled tempo can help you isolate the intended spinal motion without inadvertently moving your hips or knees.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the kettlebell down as you lower your hips by bending your knees.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep intrinsic spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) that run along the length of your entire back.

## Setting up
1. Prepare the barbell with your desired load by adding weight plates to it or leaving the barbell unloaded, which is recommended if performing this exercise for the first time.
    1. The setup for this exercise is simply performing the lifting phase of a [conventional deadlift](Conventional%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880f7a755cd3780a63371.md).
    2. As an alternative to a standard barbell, in which you can load plates onto its sleeves, you can similarly use a fixed-weight barbell for this exercise.
2. Optionally set up a thick bumper plate, deadlift block, or aerobic step centered under the bar if you wish to extend this exercise’s range of motion beyond what you could achieve when standing on the ground.
    1. When standing on the ground, individuals who are sufficiently flexible may find that the weight can contact the ground at the bottom of a rep before they reach their full range of motion. Standing on top of elevated objects (as you would during a deficit deadlift) can alternatively permit a greater range of motion. Compared to loading the bar with large diameter plates, exclusively loading it with small diameter plates can also serve a similar function as standing on an elevated object.
    2. If your range of motion is not restricted when standing on the ground during this exercise, there is no purpose in standing on an object to elevate your feet.
3. In a near hip-width stance, stand with the middle of your feet centered under the bar.
    1. At this point, you will naturally be standing on the elevated object if you wish to use it, or you can stand on the ground.
4. Sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can grasp the bar with a near shoulder-width grip as your palms face backward (i.e., overhand grip) and your elbows are straight.
5. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move without rounding your back.
    1. Throughout the set, keep the soles of your feet fully planted and your arms in a vertical position, perpendicular to the ground.
    2. This step is essentially the same as the lowering phase of a Romanian deadlift without keeping the weight as close to your legs (since the arms angle slightly backward during a Romanian deadlift, rather than hanging straight down during this exercise).
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain in a vertical position throughout your set, but you should not keep your knees fully straightened. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward, without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. While you hinge at your hips, your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal. How close to horizontal you can incline your torso will be affected by your hamstring flexibility.
    5. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range.
2. In a controlled curling manner, allow your whole back to round slowly through your comfortable range of motion without moving your lower body.
    1. The degree to which you can round your back will be affected by your spinal mobility.
    2. It is normal to feel a stretching sensation in your back muscles in the bottom position, but you should not feel any discomfort at the end range. Only round your back as far as is comfortable.
    3. Rather than moving only one part of your back, strive to round your lower, middle, and upper back simultaneously. Due to the anatomy of the spine, most of the motion will occur at the lower half of your back, but moving the upper half of your back as well can help you train more of your back musculature.
    4. As a cue, you can think about bringing the bottom of your ribs toward the top of your hip bones.
    5. While keeping your lower body in the same position throughout each rep, you should continue feeling a stretching sensation in your hamstrings. During the descent, particularly avoid dropping your hips by bending your knees.
3. While maintaining the same hinged-hip position, uncoil your spine in a controlled manner as you transition from a rounded-back to a flat-back position.
    1. All the motion should come from your back muscles, extending (straightening) your spine without any movement at your hips or knees, which should prompt you to feel tension in the muscles running along your spine as you flare your ribs up and away from your hip bones.
    2. Based on your preference, you can finish this step once your back is straight or when your lower back is mildly arched, like it normally is when standing upright.
    3. Performing this lifting phase with a controlled tempo can help you isolate the intended spinal motion without inadvertently moving your hips or knees.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the weight down as you lower your hips by bending your knees.
## Description
This exercise can dynamically train the [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md) and [deep intrinsic spinal extensor muscles](../Muscles/Deep%20Intrinsic%20Thoracolumbar%20Extensors%201bb5c6f170d880f58501d5f27212caed.md) that run along the length of your entire back.

## Setting up
1. After placing the base of a kettlebell on the ground, sit down on the ground with the kettlebell directly in front of your hips with your legs straddling the weight.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can place an exercise mat on the ground where you will lie.
2. Use both hands to grasp the horns (side handles) of the kettlebell and lift it up onto the midline of your pelvis with the handle facing up.
    1. The base of the kettlebell should be resting on your pubic bones, which lie directly below your bladder and just above your genitals. If you situate the weight above or below your pubic bones, applying pressure to those areas can naturally be uncomfortable.
    2. Continue holding the horns of the kettlebell with your palms facing in toward each other throughout the exercise.
3. While keeping the kettlebell resting on your pelvis, lean your torso backward and bend your knees to at least 90 degrees to position the soles of your feet flat on the ground.
    1. You can position your feet shoulder-width apart, but it is up to you whether you would like them closer together or farther apart.
    2. Based on what feels comfortable to you, you can point your toes forward or slightly out to the sides.
    3. Specifically how much you wish to bend your knees (and correspondingly bring your heels toward your buttocks) is also up to your preference and which position feels comfortable to you.
    4. In this position, you can rest the back of your head on the ground.
4. While leaving one foot on the ground, lift your other foot off the ground by straightening your knee.
    1. Keep one foot off the ground throughout the set you perform with your other side.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift your hips up off the ground by driving your heel into the ground and squeezing your glute while continuing to hold the kettlebell on your pubic bones.
    1. At the top, you should be able to draw a straight line from your knee through your hip to your shoulder when viewed from the side (on the side of your body with the foot contacting the ground). Your thigh and torso should naturally become aligned when you fully contract your glute.
    2. Focus on moving your hip and avoid excessively arching your lower back. Rather than flaring up (which occurs from lower back arching), the bottom of your ribs should remain pointing down toward your hip bones.
    3. If you wish, you can hold the full glute squeeze at the top for a moment to help you feel your glute engage.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your hips in a controlled manner until you can lightly contact the ground with your buttocks.
    1. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the descent with your glutes rather than letting your hips drop abruptly.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side by switching which foot you keep on the ground.
    1. Once you are ready to set the weight down, you can march both knees up toward you and rock forward into an upright torso position while placing the base of the kettlebell onto the ground between your thighs.
## Description
This exercise will chiefly train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), which may be assisted by your [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md) and [piriformis](../Muscles/Piriformis%201925c6f170d88068a670ce338a8215cf.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Connect a lat pulldown bar to the cable, select your weight with the loading pin, and adjust the thigh pad to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
    1. While a standard lat pulldown bar attachment is most commonly used, you can perform this exercise with essentially any attachment that you can comfortably hold throughout the set, so it is up to you which specific attachment you use.
2. While facing the bar and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside shoulder-width overhand grip, such that your palms face forward.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
3. While holding the bar, sit down on the seat with an upright torso and the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the thigh pad.
    1. When sitting down, allow your elbows to straighten as your arms and shoulder blades are pulled upward in line with the machine’s resistance.
    2. In this starting position, you should feel tension from the cable. If you notice the cable remains slack (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), widening out your grip may be needed to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your elbows straight and your torso upright, fully pull your shoulders down away from your ears
    1. You can think about packing your armpits down into your pockets as a technique cue.
    2. While the range of motion for this exercise may vary among different individuals, this exercise involves a low amplitude of total movement.
2. Reverse the motion in a controlled manner by allowing the cable’s resistance to pull your shoulders upward into a fully shrugged position.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise will train your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [lower traps](../Muscles/Lower%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d88092b0bfc88e7ed9e50a.md), and [pec minor](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Minor%201905c6f170d88030b03dd3f99706ecb0.md).

## Setting up
1. Load an adjustable EZ bar with your desired weight, or approach a fixed-weight EZ bar.
    1. Either type of EZ bar can be used interchangeably for this exercise.
2. While facing the middle of the bar, squat down and firmly grasp it with your palms angled backward and in toward each other (resulting in a semi-overhand grip). Your hands should be about shoulder-width apart or mildly closer.
    1. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it before a shoulder-width or mildly closer semi-overhand grip is accessible on the bar.
    2. The proper hand placement should result in your wrists and elbows feeling comfortable during this exercise.
3. Stand upright with the bar, and carry it to a flat or seated bench that is situated directly behind you.
    1. If you use a seated bench, the backrest should be low enough that it will not be in the path of the bar and restrict your range of motion for this exercise.
    2. The tall backrest of an adjustable bench, positioned fully upright, may be more likely to limit your range than a fixed seated bench with a backrest that does not reach your head.
4. Move the bar up to your shoulders with your elbows fully bent underneath and slightly in front of the bar.
    1. If the load is light enough to do so, you can just curl the bar up.
    2. With a heavier load, you can perform a cheat curl, where you generate momentum with your hips to help you curl the bar up. Initially sit your buttocks back while allowing your knees to bend mildly and your torso to incline slightly forward. Then drive your hips forcefully forward while bending your elbows and mildly swinging them forward.
    3. The bar should now be in essentially the same position it would be for an overhead press.
    4. The bar should be sitting on top of the bases of your palms (AKA heels of your hands) with reasonably straight wrists. You will maintain this hand and wrist position throughout your set.
    5. While your wrists do not need to be completely straight, you should avoid holding the bar with your wrists cocked back into an excessively extended position that may contribute to an increased risk of experiencing wrist discomfort. Simply squeezing the bar hard will usually keep your wrists from cocking back excessively.
5. Sit down on the bench with an upright torso position.
6. Press the bar up overhead in a shoulder press motion until you have fully straightened your elbows.
    1. The bar should be vertically stacked above your shoulders and hips.
    2. Rather than being excessively arched, your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position, like when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
## Exercise technique
1. Bend your elbows to lower the bar behind your head in a controlled manner. Based on your preference and what feels most comfortable to your elbows, you can select one of two approaches with respect to your elbow position.
    1. Option 1: Keep your elbows completely up with your upper arms in a vertical position throughout the rep. This will result in the bar moving in an arcing manner exclusively from your forearms hinging at your elbows.
    2. Option 2: Mildly arc your elbows forward and down while bending your elbows to lower the bar. You can mildly tuck your chin toward your chest to create additional space for the bar. This option will result in the bar moving in a closer to vertical path from a combination of shoulder and elbow motion.
    3. Neither of the approaches is inherently superior to the other, so you can feel free to try out both ways and continue using the technique you prefer.
    4. With either option, predominantly keep your elbows tucked in. However, you can allow them to flare slightly out away from your sides if that feels natural and comfortable to you.
2. Continue lowering the bar until you have fully bent your elbows or can lightly tap the base of your neck or your upper back muscles with the bar.
    1. How far you can lower the bar may be limited by the flexibility of your long head of the triceps, particularly if you keep your elbows completely up. While some lifters have the flexibility to reach near their upper back with the bar, others will reach the limit to which they can comfortably bend their elbows before that point. Do not lower the bar beyond the range that your flexibility permits without discomfort.
    2. While you do not have to perform the lowering phase with an extremely slow tempo, you should be actively controlling the weight the entire way.
3. Reverse the movement by straightening your elbows to lift the bar into the starting position overhead.
    1. You should finish with your elbows fully straightened as the bar is vertically above your shoulders.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set.
    1. After you completed the lifting phase of your last rep, lower the bar in front of your head toward your shoulders like you would during an overhead press.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the [triceps](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88032be38d4f3e73c9e4c.md), including the [long head](../Muscles/Triceps%20Brachii%20Long%20Head%201905c6f170d880b1a0a7eda6c9b74382.md), which is not trained particularly well by pressing exercises.

## Setting up
1. Don a weight vest, and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance in a location that has sufficient space in front of you for lunging forward repeatedly.
    1. You can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides, on top of your hips, in front of your chest, etc.
    2. Keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
    3. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one foot on the ground, take a fairly long step straight forward with your other foot far enough ahead that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee when lunging down.
    1. Like when you step forward while walking, you can initially contact the ground with your front foot’s heel prior to lowering the entirety of your sole onto the ground in a fluid motion, which will likely occur naturally without having to think about it.
    2. When your front foot contacts the ground, you can allow your rear leg’s heel to start lifting up off the ground, which is also likely to occur naturally.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Strive to step forward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    6. If you are new to walking lunges, you may have to try out different step lengths to determine which step length places you in the appropriate position.
2. After contacting the ground with your front foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep your rear leg’s forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes) and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot’s sole in contact with the ground.
    2. Continue keeping your torso upright and your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step forward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step forward during your next rep.
3. Progressively extend (straighten) your knees to lift your body up until you can repeat step 1 to step forward with your rear leg past your stationary leg in the same manner that you initially performed with your other side.
    1. Strive to begin stepping forward as you are lunging up in a fluid manner, which will advance your body forward.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat step 2 with your other side now in the forward position, as you lunge down just like you previously did.
5. Continue repeating steps 1-4 as you progressively lunge forward with alternating legs until you have completed your set or have to turn around and continue lunging in the opposite direction.
## Description
This exercise primarily trains your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md), [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. If you are using a step, position what you will use as your step slightly in front of the pull-up bar. The step should be situated where you can readily reach the bar without the step getting in the way of your feet during the exercise.
    1. Objects that can be used as a step include a plyometric box, aerobic step, bumper plate, and flat exercise bench.
    2. Ideally the step will be tall enough that you can grasp the bar with your elbows fairly bent, which will minimize how high you have to hop.
2. While standing under the pull-up bar on the step or ground, reach up and firmly grasp it with your palms facing backward (i.e., an underhand grip), about shoulder-width apart.
    1. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    2. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Hop up while pulling down on the bar to bring your chest up toward the bar with your elbows fully bent by your sides.
    1. You should now be in the top position of a pull-up.
    2. The degree to which you have to use your legs to hop up will naturally be affected by how high the bar is above your chest at the end of the setup. With a sufficiently tall step, you may be able to just step forward off the step without having to hop up.
    3. Since you can use meaningful assistance from your legs or start with your chest already close to the bar, this step should not feel particularly strenuous to your back and arm muscles. The objective is to have getting your chest up to the bar feel fairly easy, so that your muscles will feel fresh and ready to control the descent.
2. While keeping your chest by the bar for a moment, bend your knees as much as is required to avoid your feet contacting the step or ground during the lowering phase. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. If you can do so without the step getting in your way, you can allow your thighs to hang straight down toward the ground.
3. In a controlled manner, lower your chest away from the bar by allowing your elbows to straighten while your torso moves away from them.
    1. Maintain a “proud chest” posture as you avoid letting your shoulders shrug up toward your ears from the force of your bodyweight.
    2. Finish with your elbows fully straightened as your arms are in an overhead position.
    3. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should use your back and arm muscles to control the entirety of the descent rather than letting your body quickly drop down.
    4. If you are not currently strong enough to perform a full pull-up, it can be beneficial to have the intent to try to pull your chest up to the bar by driving your arms down toward your side. Without the strength to lift yourself up, striving to do so can help you control the descent.
4. Return your feet to the step or ground to assume the same position you had when you finished setting up.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

    2. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
    3. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to backward lunges.
    2. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
2. After contacting the ground with your rear foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    7. If you initially took an excessively short step backward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step backward during your next rep.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step forward with your rear leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging backward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Don your weighted vest, and stand upright with your feet near shoulder-width apart, as your toes are pointing somewhat out to the sides rather than pointing straight ahead.
    1. While people may commonly find that setting up reasonably close to this stance allows them to squat effectively, the specific stance width and degree of toe flare that is ideal will vary among different individuals based on their hip structure and mobility.
    2. Ultimately, you want to position your feet in a manner that results in you feeling comfortable and stable when squatting, which typically requires trying out different stances over time and assessing how you feel with them.
    3. Some people may feel most comfortable squatting with their feet close to hip width apart as their toes are pointing straight ahead, while others will feel best with their feet outside of shoulder width with their toes rotated out to the sides at 45-degree angles.
2. Raise your arms out in front of you until they are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. You can alternatively keep your arms in a different position if you wish to do so, but keeping your arms outstretched throughout the set provides a counterbalance that often allows people to reach a greater squat depth and not have to lean as far forward to maintain balance.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout your set.
2. Initiate the descent by starting to sit your buttocks back. Progressively bend at your knees and hips to squat down in a controlled manner while keeping your knees aligned with your feet.
    1. Let your torso naturally lean forward at your hips to maintain your balance, but keep your back flat and chest up, as you avoid rounding your lower back or letting your chest cave down through upper back rounding.
    2. Keep the entire sole of each foot (including the heel, outer aspect of the midfoot, and inner aspect of the midfoot) firmly planted on the ground as your weight is evenly distributed throughout your feet (rather than being all on your heels or toes) during your set.
    3. As you bend your knees, it is normal for them to track forward over your feet (especially the deeper your squat) to help you maintain your balance.
    4. Strive to keep each knee aligned with the second toe (the toe next to your big toe) or the third toe of that side’s foot as you avoid letting your knees cave inward relative to your feet.
3. Continue to squat down through the available range of motion that your mobility enables without rounding your back, lifting your heels up off the ground, or letting your knees cave inward.
    1. People can often descend at least until their thighs are fairly close to being parallel to the ground, but what constitutes a full range of motion for a squat will vary among different individuals.
    2. If your back starts rounding, heels lift off the ground, or knees cave inward at the bottom of your squat, you may be squatting excessively deep relative to your current level of mobility and body control.
4. Reverse the movement by progressively standing up as you drive through the ground while extending (straightening) your knees and hips until you have returned to a fully upright position.
    1. Continue keeping your chest up, back flat, feet fully on the ground, and knees stacked over your feet as you squat up.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.

This exercise primarily trains your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) muscles.
