## Setting up
1. Connect a straight bar attachment or a V-bar row handle (AKA double D-handle) to the machine.
    1. If you prefer to use an overhand grip (with your palms facing backward), select a straight bar attachment, whether that be a standard lat pulldown bar with a long straight body and angled ends, or a straight bar closer to shoulder-width in length.
    2. If you prefer to use a neutral grip (with your palms facing each other), select a V-bar row handle.
    3. Neither attachment type is inherently better than the other, so feel free to try out both to determine which one personally feels better to you when performing this exercise.
2. Without any weight plates added to the machine, stand on the platform with the bar between your feet.
    1. Prior to getting into the starting position for your set, you need to adjust the machine so that its safety horn (on which the weight trolley initially rests) no longer restricts downward motion of the weight trolley. This adjustment requires the use of one hand, so you cannot perform it when your working weight is loaded onto the machine, in contrast to when you are belt squatting, where you can hold the machine’s handles rather than the bar you connect.
3. Squat down to grasp the bar with one hand, and stand upright with it before using your other hand to pull the handles back toward you to disengage the safety horn.
    1. It is unusual to grasp the center of a straight bar attachment with one hand or only one part of a V-bar row handle, but you will not be lifting meaningful resistance without any plates added to the machine, so the awkward grip is not problematic.
    2. If you prefer, you have the option of disengaging the safety horn while wearing a belt connected to the machine prior to swapping a bar for the belt.
    3. With the safety horn no longer resting under the weight trolley, the machine is now set for you to be able to hinge through your full range of motion.
4. Squat down and set the bar onto the platform before adding weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
5. Step up onto the platform with the cable centered between the middle of your feet. Position your feet approximately hip-width apart.
6. While keeping your back flat, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can firmly grasp the bar with straight elbows.
    1. Regardless of whether you use an overhand or neutral grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles for the most stable grip.
7. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
8. Without rounding your back, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    2. Without thinking about “bending over,” your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the bar when focusing on “sitting back.”
    3. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    4. Throughout the set, keep your feet fully planted on the platform and your neck near a neutral position, as when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move without rounding your back or excessively bending your knees.
    1. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    2. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your back or excessively bending your knees depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    3. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should clearly be in control of the entire descent.
3. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward to lift your torso upright into the starting position.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    2. When you have finished lifting the bar, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back at the top through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips properly stacked under your shoulders, preventing excessive arching.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down onto the platform.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe between reps in the fully upright position, rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
    2. After finishing the last rep, set the bar down in the same manner in which you initially picked it up, which includes keeping your lower back flat.

While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Don a weight vest, and stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance with the back of your legs against the edge of the sturdy elevated object you will use to elevate your foot.
    1. If available, a padded cylindrical object positioned near knee height will normally be most comfortable and is recommended.
    2. A Smith machine bar with a squat/hip thrust pad on it, a barbell on top of the J-cups of a power rack, the leg pad of a lying hamstring curl machine, and a split squat roller stand are all high-quality cylindrical options that you can position to knee height.
    3. Alternatively, you can use an object like a flat exercise bench, couch, or plyometric box with a somewhat compliant surface, but objects with a flat surface tend not to be as comfortable for this exercise.
2. While keeping your feet approximately hip-width apart, step forward with one foot until its heel is just in front of your other foot’s big toe before doing the same with your opposite foot.
    1. This results in your front foot now being about two “foot lengths” in front of where you started when your calves were touching the object you will use to elevate your rear foot.
    2. While this strategy can consistently situate most people in a viable starting position for the exercise, a range of foot placements can be effectively used, including having your front foot two and a half “foot lengths” in front of where you started (which may be even more comfortable for some people).
    3. You can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides, on top of your hips, in front of your chest, etc.
    4. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Shift your bodyweight into your front foot before placing the top surface (on the side of your shoe laces) of your rear foot on top of the elevated surface with that side’s knee bent.
    1. To help shift your bodyweight into your front foot, you can lean your torso mildly forward by hinging at your hip as you slightly bend that side’s knee.
    2. Once you have situated your rear foot into the elevated position, you can return to keeping your torso in a fairly upright position, which should involve you maintaining the natural curvature of your lower back, like when you are normally standing upright (rather than excessively arching beyond that position).
    3. Strive to move your rear foot backward in a straight line to keep your feet approximately hip-width apart, rather than bringing your rear foot closer toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    4. Keep the entire sole of your front foot firmly planted on the ground and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    5. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    6. If you are using a cylindrical object to elevate your foot, you can contact the surface with the front of your ankle along with your foot, but only your foot will contact the elevated surface if it is flat, like a bench.
2. From your split stance position, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep most of your weight shifted onto your front foot while you are primarily using your rear foot to assist with balance.
    2. Continue keeping your torso fairly upright and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    3. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    4. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    5. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    6. If you initially positioned your front foot excessively far in front of your elevated object, you may reach the end of your available hip range of motion before your rear knee reaches the ground.
    7. If you initially positioned your front foot too close to the elevated object, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    8. In either case of suboptimal foot placement, you do not need to force your rear knee to tap the ground, and you can adjust how far in front your front foot is situated after finishing your rep.
3. While keeping your front foot firmly planted on the ground and your rear foot in its elevated position, reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees to lift your body up until you have returned to an upright position in your split stance.
    1. You can finish the ascent with a slight bend in your front knee rather than fully locking it out.
    2. Like during the descent, keep your torso fairly upright and knees aligned with your feet while having most of your weight shifted onto the front foot.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until you have finished your set and are ready to repeat the exercise by switching which leg is in the forward position and which leg is in the elevated position.

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates to an open trap bar with the low handles up and sufficient space behind the open part of the trap bar for lunging backward.
    1. Load weight plates with diameters that will permit you to lunge until one knee lightly contacts the ground without the weight plates reaching the ground during your reps.
    2. Whether the diameter of the weight plates can affect this exercise’s range of motion for you will be affected by your body proportions, but full diameter plates (like 45lb (or 20kg) plates and bumper plates) can commonly restrict lunge depth.
    3. Loading the bar exclusively with plates that do not weigh more than 25lb (or 10kg) and avoiding bumper plates is generally appropriate to be able to lunge through your full range of motion when holding the low handles of a trap bar, but this may differ for you as an individual.
2. While facing the close part of the trap bar, stand within the middle of the bar in a hip-width stance with your toes pointing straight ahead.
3. Without rounding your back, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can firmly grasp the center of the parallel handles with your palms facing in toward each other.
    1. Avoid grasping the handles too close to the front or back of the bar.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the handles with the handles pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.

    1. The initial submaximal pull allows you to check if you have grasped the handles correctly, which will be indicated by the handles not rotating forward or backward when applying the pre-tension.
    2. If you pick up a trap bar with your hands positioned slightly away from the middle of the handles, the trap bar can start rotating in a manner that makes it very difficult to hold and lift appropriately.
    3. If the bar starts rotating when you apply the pre-tension, re-center your grip, and apply the pre-tension again until the bar no longer rotates.
6. While keeping your lower back flat and chest up, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.

1. While keeping the entire sole of one foot firmly planted on the ground, step backward with the other leg before contacting the ground with your forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes).
    1. Step far enough backward that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee, which may initially require trying out different step lengths if you are new to backward lunges.
    2. Strive to step backward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    3. Keep the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
2. After contacting the ground with your rear foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Continue keeping the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot in contact with the ground.
    2. Keep your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. As you keep your back flat, let your torso lean slightly forward to a degree that feels natural and comfortable to you.
    5. While the forefoot of your rear leg will be in contact with the ground, the rest of the foot’s sole will be off the ground as it is directed backward.
    6. Strive to perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.

If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step backward during your next rep.

    1. Continue keeping your knees aligned with your feet and your hip bones level.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging backward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down in a deadlift motion by bending your hips and knees while keeping your back flat.

1. If you are using a step, position what you will use as your step slightly in front of the pull-up bar. The step should be situated where you can readily reach the bar without the step getting in the way of your feet during the exercise.

    2. Ideally the step will be tall enough that you can grasp the bar with your elbows fairly bent, which will minimize how high you have to hop.
2. While standing under the pull-up bar on the step or ground, reach up and firmly grasp the parallel handles with your palms facing in toward each other (i.e., a neutral grip)
    1. If your bar has multiple pairs of parallel handles, select the pair that positions your hands close to shoulder-width apart.
    2. For the most stable grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. If you situate the bar closer toward the middle of your palms (rather than the bases of your fingers), the bar can slide up your hand while hanging on it, which pulls on your hand skin in an uncomfortable manner that increases the risk of tearing a callus.
## Exercise technique
1. Hop up while pulling down on the bar to bring your chest up toward the bar with your elbows fully bent by your sides.
    1. You should now be in the top position of a pull-up.
    2. The degree to which you have to use your legs to hop up will naturally be affected by how high the bar is above your chest at the end of the setup. With a sufficiently tall step, you may be able to just step forward off the step without having to hop up.
    3. Since you can use meaningful assistance from your legs or start with your chest already close to the bar, this step should not feel particularly strenuous to your back and arm muscles. The objective is to have getting your chest up to the bar feel fairly easy, so that your muscles will feel fresh and ready to control the descent.
2. While keeping your chest by the bar for a moment, bend your knees as much as is required to avoid your feet contacting the step or ground during the lowering phase. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blades down and mildly arch your middle and upper back to angle your chest slightly upward.
    1. If you can do so without the step getting in your way, you can allow your thighs to hang straight down toward the ground.
3. In a controlled manner, lower your chest away from the bar by allowing your elbows to straighten while your torso moves away from them.
    1. Maintain a “proud chest” posture as you avoid letting your shoulders shrug up toward your ears from the force of your bodyweight.
    2. Finish with your elbows fully straightened as your arms are in an overhead position.
    3. There is no need to lower yourself extremely slowly, but you should use your back and arm muscles to control the entirety of the descent rather than letting your body quickly drop down.
    4. If you are not currently strong enough to perform a full pull-up, it can be beneficial to have the intent to try to pull your chest up to the bar by driving your arms down toward your side. Without the strength to lift yourself up, striving to do so can help you control the descent.
4. Return your feet to the step or ground to assume the same position you had when you finished setting up.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
You have the option of wearing a weighted vest (which is the ideal option if available to you) or positioning a weight plate on the front of your torso to provide resistance for this exercise. The technique is the same when using either type of equipment, but some setup details differ based on which option you select, which is why usage of each equipment option receives its own setup section.

### **Setting up with a vest**

1. Position a barbell in the J-cups of a rack set approximately to the height of your hips while standing, or alternatively position a Smith machine’s bar to the same height.
    1. This exercise can be performed with the same technique whether you use a barbell and rack or a Smith machine.
    2. If you use a rack, situate the barbell snugly in contact with the back corner of the J-cups since the middle portion of certain J-cups can be wide enough to allow the barbell to roll forward or backward, which is undesirable for this exercise.
2. Don your weighted vest, and sit on the ground with your shoulders under and slightly behind the bar, as your legs are straight out in front of you.
    1. The back of your heels should be on the ground, while the soles of your feet are off the ground and facing forward.
3. Slightly lean your torso backward, and firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside of shoulder-width overhand grip, resulting in your palms facing forward.
4. While holding the bar, drive your heels into the ground and squeeze your glutes to bridge your hips up and recline your torso until you can draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.

### **Setting up with a weight plate**

1. Position a barbell in the J-cups of a rack set approximately to the height of your hips while standing, or alternatively position a Smith machine’s bar to the same height.
    1. This exercise can be performed with the same technique whether you use a barbell and rack or a Smith machine.
    2. If you use a rack, situate the barbell snugly in contact with the back corner of the J-cups since the middle portion of certain J-cups can be wide enough to allow the barbell to roll forward or backward, which is undesirable for this exercise.
2. Place your weight plate slightly in front of the bar and on one side of the bar, so that you can sit down under the bar and reach the plate.
3. Sit on the ground with your shoulders under and slightly behind the bar, as your legs are straight out in front of you.
    1. The back of your heels should be on the ground, while the soles of your feet are off the ground and facing forward.
4. Place the weight plate against the front of your torso, with the bottom of the plate situated close to the crease of your hips.
    1. If you have a training partner, you can alternatively have your partner position the weight plate on your torso after you complete step 6.
5. Slightly lean your torso backward, and firmly grasp the bar with a slightly outside of shoulder-width overhand grip, resulting in your palms facing forward.
6. While holding the bar, drive your heels into the ground and squeeze your glutes to bridge your hips up and recline your torso until you can draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your chest toward the bar by driving your elbows simultaneously downward and backward while progressively bending them and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. Allow your elbows naturally to flare out away from your sides in a manner that feels comfortable to you.
    2. Pull through your full range of motion while aiming for your chest to reach the bar.
    3. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your torso and lower body should remain nearly stationary in the bridged position that is akin to holding a [reverse plank](Reverse%20plank%201a45c6f170d880faa555d3e604efa65f.md). This should result in you being able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side throughout the set.
2. Reverse the movement by letting your chest move down away from the bar in a controlled manner as your elbows progressively straighten and your shoulder blades naturally spread apart.
    1. Fully return to the starting position with your arms outstretched up in front of you.
    2. Continue keeping your knees, hips, and shoulders aligned as you avoid letting your hips sag.
    3. While you do not have to lower yourself extremely slowly, you should actively resist the descent rather than abruptly dropping in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This row can effectively develop your [lats](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres majores](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), which are assisted by your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Determine what you will use as your weight that can securely rest on your middle and upper back while performing your plank.
    1. Wearing a weighted vest is an excellent option if you have one due to its stability and ease of setting up, but most people lack a weighted vest.
    2. If someone can assist you, a partner can also place a weight plate or stack of weight plates on your back once you have assumed the plank position. With this approach, a rubber-coated plate is best since it is less likely to slide than a purely iron plate. If you are in a gym without a designated training partner, many lifters would be open to lending a hand if you just politely ask them to do so. Communicate to the other person that you would like him/her to lift the plate off your back after finishing your last rep, in addition to placing it on your middle back to begin the set.
    3. As a substitute for a weighted vest, you can add weighted objects to a sufficiently sturdy backpack. If you do so, you would want to try to have the weight as evenly distributed as possible to reduce the likelihood of it sliding around or shifting to rest on your lower back, which may be difficult to avoid with weight plates in many backpacks. Chains may be more likely to fill up a backpack evenly, and textbooks can also be viable when using lighter loads. When present, securely fastening chest straps and hip straps on a backpack can increase its stability.
    4. If you decide to use a vest or a loaded backpack to carry your weight, put it on yourself now. If you decide to use a weight plate, make sure your partner is standing nearby with your desired weight and understands what to do before proceeding to the next step.
2. Position yourself with your hands, knees, and toes on the ground as your elbows are straight and your knees are bent.
3. Prop your forearms onto the ground with your upper arms directed straight down such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    1. Based on your preference, you can make a fist with each hand and direct your palms in toward each other, or you can place your palms flat on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. Straighten one knee to move your foot behind you, and position the bottom of its toes onto the ground before doing the same with your other leg.
    1. In this position, your feet should be approximately hip-width apart, with your heels facing backward.
    2. Keep your neck near a neutral position, as you would normally do when standing upright, which should direct your gaze to the ground slightly out in front of you.
2. Tighten your abdominal muscles and squeeze your glutes to maintain a flat back position while keeping your knees straight and elbows bent.
    1. Doing so keeps your hips up (but not excessively hiked) rather than letting them sag, which would result in an exaggerated arch in your lower back.
    2. In this position, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your torso.
    3. Do not allow your chest to sag, which would result in your shoulder blades being pinched back together.
    4. Keep your neck near a neutral position, like you would normally do when standing upright.
3. If you are using a weight plate for your resistance, have your partner now position it symmetrically on your middle and upper back, but you will naturally ignore this step if you are using a vest or backpack.
4. Statically hold your plank position for your target duration until you have completed your set.
    1. Continue keeping your abs tensed, glutes squeezed, and lower back flat throughout the set.
    2. If you are using a weight plate, direct your partner to remove the weight after finishing your last rep.
## Description
This exercise can statically train your core muscles, including your [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) and your  [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md), as they function to maintain a rigid trunk position.

## Setting up
1. Strap an ankle weight to each of your ankles, and lie down on your back with straight legs as your feet are approximately hip width apart.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can lie down on an exercise mat.
2. Place the fingertips of each hand lightly in contact with the sides of the back of your head as your upper arms and elbows are directed out away from your sides.
    1. Since you are not interlocking your fingers along the middle of the back of your head, you should not have to lift your head up off the ground to situate your hands in the appropriate position.
    2. Keeping your hands and arms in this position can help you avoid inadvertently pulling down on your head during the exercise, which would otherwise be easier to do if you interlocked your fingers and directed your upper arms up toward the ceiling.
    3. Maintain this arm position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Tighten your abs to flatten your lower back and press it lightly into the ground. Keep your lower back flattened against the ground throughout all subsequent steps.
    1. In contrast to if your abs were relaxed and your lower back exhibited its natural arch, you should not be able to slide a hand under your lower back.
2. March your left leg up and back toward your chest while bending its knee.
    1. How far you can march this leg back will be affected by your hip mobility.
    2. So long as you follow the same movement pattern described here, you can choose whether you begin with your left or right leg marched, but mentioning the sides as an example can help with technique clarity.
3. With a straight knee, lift your right leg slightly off the ground or higher up for a lower intensity.
    1. As you lift this leg higher up, the difficulty of the exercise will decrease, so you can determine specifically how high you lift it based on your current ability.
    2. If you notice that you cannot keep your lower back flat with your leg slightly off the ground, you can try lifting it up to a height that allows you to avoid aching your lower back.
4. Tuck your chin slightly toward your chest to lift your head just above the ground.
5. In a crunch-like motion, mildly curl your upper back to lift your shoulder blades slightly up off the ground.
    1. While they are presented as distinct steps for instructional clarity, you can perform the actions from steps 1-5 simultaneously with each other once you understand the proper positioning that each step achieves.
6. March your right leg up and back toward your chest while bending its knee as you lower your left leg while straightening its knee. Simultaneously rotate your chest to the right to bring your left elbow toward your right knee.
    1. Strive to move your legs reciprocally at the same speed in sync with your torso rotation. This should result in you finishing lowering your left leg at the same time you have finished marching your right leg and turning your chest to the right.
    2. Move through the range of motion permitted by your spine and hip mobility. You have reached your end range once you feel that you can no longer rotate your chest to the right while marching your right leg back. This may involve achieving contact between the knee and elbow for some people, but touching your elbow to your knee is not the focus of this exercise.
    3. Your elbows should only move because you are twisting your torso, and your arms are attached to your torso through your shoulders. Keep your arms mostly relaxed to avoid moving your arms by themselves through shoulder motion.
    4. Finish lowering your left leg once it is slightly above the ground or has reached the starting height you initially opted to use for your right leg.
    5. You can imagine that a laser beam is shooting out from the center of your chest as you rotate that laser beam out to the right. If your chest and the laser beam do not turn toward the right, you are not appropriately rotating your torso.
    6. Avoid letting your lower back arch up as you continue keeping it flattened against the ground by tightening your abs.
7. Fluidly reverse the movement by performing the opposite motion with each leg and rotating your chest the other way.
    1. This will involve lowering your right leg, marching your left leg up, and turning your chest to the left based on the directionality of the last step.
8. Alternate between steps 6 and 7 until you have completed your set and are ready to rest your feet on the ground.
## Description
This exercise can develop your [obliques](../Muscles/Abdominal%20Obliques%201b95c6f170d880f5bdc1c2ca4cd25d5f.md) and [rectus abdominis](../Muscles/Rectus%20Abdominis%201955c6f170d880ffa74fdc1ed9f102dd.md) while additionally training your [hip flexors](../Muscles/Primary%20Hip%20Flexors%202845c6f170d8808187a5fdcaf3da8985.md).

## Setting up
To be able to hinge through your full range of motion, the machine’s safety arm (on which its lever arm rests) will have to be disengaged prior to starting your set. Some machines are designed to have the safety arm automatically disengage after lifting the lever arm up, while others require you to pull the handle back with your hand to disengage it. Steps 2-4 of the setup describe how to adjust a machine that involves manually disengaging the safety arm. If your machine has the automatic disengagement feature, you can add weight plates to the machine during step 1 and skip steps 2-4 of the setup.

1. Connect a straight bar attachment or a V-bar row handle (AKA double D-handle) to the machine.
    1. If you prefer to use an overhand grip (with your palms facing backward), select a straight bar attachment, whether that be a standard lat pulldown bar with a long straight body and angled ends, or a straight bar closer to shoulder-width in length.
    2. If you prefer to use a neutral grip (with your palms facing each other), select a V-bar row handle.
    3. Neither attachment type is inherently better than the other, so feel free to try out both to determine which one personally feels better to you when performing this exercise.
    4. Different machine models vary in their design, since some machines have a lever arm with a single attachment point, while others have a lever arm with multiple attachment points.
    5. When using a lever arm with multiple attachment points, the machine will provide less resistance when using a point near the base of the lever arm compared to the free end of the lever arm. Consequently, the specific lever attachment point can affect the difficulty of each rep, in addition to how much weight you add to the machine via plates. Consistently connecting the bar to the attachment point furthest from the base of the machine will minimize how many plates you have to add to the machine to provide your intended level of resistance.
2. Without any weight plates added to the machine, stand on the platform with the bar between your feet.
3. Squat down to grasp the bar with one hand, and stand upright with it before using your other hand to pull the handles back toward you to disengage the safety horn.
    1. It is unusual to grasp the center of a straight bar attachment with one hand or only one part of a V-bar row handle, but you will not be lifting meaningful resistance without any plates added to the machine, so the awkward grip is not problematic.
    2. If you prefer, you have the option of disengaging the safety horn while wearing a belt connected to the machine prior to swapping a bar for the belt.
4. Squat down and set the bar onto the platform before adding weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
5. Step up onto the platform with the bar’s attachment point centered between the middle of your feet. Position your feet approximately hip-width apart.
6. While keeping your back flat, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can firmly grasp the bar with straight elbows.
    1. Regardless of whether you use an overhand or neutral grip, wrap your fingers around the bar with the bar pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles for the most stable grip.
7. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point on to maintain a rigid back position while using your lower body muscles to lift the weight.
8. Without rounding your back, drive through your legs to begin lifting the bar before thrusting your hips forward and squeezing your glutes to stand upright with the bar.
    1. Continue keeping your elbows straight throughout the exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    2. Without thinking about “bending over,” your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the bar when focusing on “sitting back.”
    3. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    4. Throughout the set, keep your feet fully planted on the platform and your neck near a neutral position, as when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
2. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move without rounding your back or excessively bending your knees.
    1. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    2. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your back or excessively bending your knees depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    3. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should clearly be in control of the entire descent.
3. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward to lift your torso upright into the starting position.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    2. When you have finished lifting the bar, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back at the top through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips properly stacked under your shoulders, preventing excessive arching.
4. Alternate between steps 1-3 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down onto the platform.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe between reps in the fully upright position, rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before initiating the descent for the next rep.
    2. After finishing the last rep, set the bar down in the same manner in which you initially picked it up, which includes keeping your lower back flat.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. After loading your desired amount of weight onto the machine, stand centered between its handles in a near hip-width stance while facing away from the base of the machine.
    1. If your machine model lets you adjust the handle height, you can initially set the handles to the lowest setting. If you cannot grasp the handles during the next step without rounding your lower back, you can subsequently raise the handles to a height that lets you grasp them with a flat-back position.
2. While keeping your lower back flat and chest up, sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can firmly grasp the handles with straight elbows as your palms face in toward each other.
    1. If your machine has multiple pairs of handles, it is generally recommended to grasp the lower handles to let you train through a longer range of motion if you can reach those handles without rounding your lower back.
    2. More motion should come from hinging at your hips than bending your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift somewhat forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    3. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks as you sit back while your hands are carrying something. After you have fully sat back and feel a stretching sensation in your hamstrings, you can bend your knees further to reach the handles.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed, or simply sucking your belly button in.
    2. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Drive through your legs to begin lifting the handles as you “push the floor away” before thrusting your hips forward to stand fully upright. Prioritize keeping your chest up, lower back flat, and your core braced throughout the entire exercise.
    1. You should chiefly be using your lower body muscles to lift the handles through hip and knee motion while keeping your back in a rigid position.
    2. Avoid letting your hips shoot up and/rounding your back to start the rep, which could occur if you do not sufficiently drive your feet through the ground.
    3. Once upright, you should be able to draw a straight line from your legs through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side.
    4. Finish with your glutes squeezed as you avoid leaning your torso back through excessive lower back arching, which can occur if you do not focus on squeezing your glutes.
3. Reverse the movement by sitting your hips back and bending your knees to lower the handles to the starting position.
    1. This should simply be a reversal of the lifting phase, so keep your lower back flat, chest up, core braced, and feet fully on the ground.
    2. Avoid trying to squat straight down with an upright torso and excessive forward knee travel. Particularly to begin the descent, emphasize sitting back while letting your knees naturally bend, and your torso transitions closer to horizontal.
4. Allow the weight to come to a dead stop at the bottom for a moment, rather than trying to bounce the machine’s lever arms off the stopper underneath them.
    1. While you do not need to pause in the bottom position for more than a second between reps, there should not be any momentum transferred between reps.
    2. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while the weight is resting on the stoppers rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, resume bracing your core before the next rep.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md) and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), along with your [quads](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md) and [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Don a weight vest, and stand upright with approximately a hip-width stance in a location that has sufficient space in front of you for lunging forward.
    1. You can position your hands wherever you prefer, such as resting by your sides, on top of your hips, in front of your chest, etc.
    2. You will keep your arms in your preferred position throughout your set.
    3. Positioning yourself into a hip-width stance rather than a narrower stance can help you maintain your balance during this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping one foot on the ground, take a fairly long step straight forward with your other foot far enough ahead that you will be able to contact the ground with your rear knee when lunging down.
    1. Like when you step forward while walking, you can initially contact the ground with your front foot’s heel prior to lowering the entirety of your sole onto the ground in a fluid motion, which will likely occur naturally without having to think about it.
    2. When your front foot contacts the ground, you can allow your rear leg’s heel to start lifting up off the ground, which is also likely to occur naturally.
    3. Keep your torso in an upright position and the top of your hip bones level with each other to the best of your ability, rather than letting the hip bone on the side of your back leg drop down.
    4. As a cue for keeping your hip bones level, you can imagine that you have a basin of water filled to the brim on top of your hip bones, and you are trying not to spill any water by tipping it to either side.
    5. Strive to step forward in a straight line rather than stepping closer in toward the midline of your body, which would position your feet horizontally closer together and narrow your base of support.
    6. If you are new to forward lunges, you may have to try out different step lengths to determine which step length places you in the appropriate position.
2. After contacting the ground with your front foot, allow your knees to bend as you lower your body in a controlled manner until you are able to tap the ground gently with the kneecap of your rear leg.
    1. Keep your rear leg’s forefoot (ball of your foot and bottom of your toes) and the entirety (heel, inside of forefoot, and outside of forefoot) of your front foot’s sole in contact with the ground.
    2. Continue keeping your torso upright and your knees aligned with your feet rather than letting either knee cave inward relative to that side’s foot (when viewed from the front or the back).
    3. As a cue for the appropriately controlled descent, you can imagine that a weight scale is underneath your rear knee, and gently tapping it will not cause the scale to read more than about two pounds (one kilogram).
    4. At the end of the lowering phase, your front leg’s thigh should be close to parallel to the ground.
    5. You should perform steps 1 and 2 as a smooth and continuous movement.
    6. If you initially took an excessively short step forward, you may not be able to tap the ground with your rear knee unless you also lift the heel of your front foot up off the ground.
    7. If you find that you have to lift your front heel up to tap the ground, simply descend as much as you can without lifting up your front heel, and take a longer step forward during your next rep.
3. Reverse the movement by progressively extending (straightening) your knees as you step backward with your front leg to lift your body up until you have returned to the starting position with your feet symmetrically hip-width apart and your torso fully upright.
    1. Like during the descent, keep your torso upright and knees aligned with your feet while doing so.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 while lunging forward with your opposite side.
5. Alternate between steps 1-4 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise will primarily train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and three of your four [quad muscles](../Muscles/Monoarticular%20Quadriceps%20Femoris%201be5c6f170d880119155c2e8184c0d0d.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates of your desired load to a barbell situated on the ground.
    1. To set up for this row, you can perform the lifting phase of a [conventional deadlift](Conventional%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880f7a755cd3780a63371.md) with a rather wide grip, followed by the lowering phase of a [Romanian deadlift](Barbell%20Romanian%20deadlift%201a35c6f170d880bebc64f4dce0d5f5f1.md).
2. In a near hip-width stance, stand with the middle of your feet under the middle of the bar.
3. Sit your hips backward while bending your knees until you can firmly grasp the bar with a well outside shoulder-width overhand grip. Keep your lower back flat and chest up throughout the exercise.
    1. It is generally appropriate to use a grip width that is approximately the distance between your elbows when your arms are raised straight out to your sides, parallel to the ground. The right grip for you should make flaring your elbows out from your sides during the row feel natural and comfortable.
    2. More motion should come from your hips than your knees as you descend, and your knees should not track particularly far forward, but you can allow your knees to shift slightly forward rather than maintaining completely vertical shins.
    3. Throughout the exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, as when you are looking straight ahead while standing upright.
4. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue keeping your core braced from this point on.
5. Stand upright with the bar by driving through your legs and thrusting your hips forward.
6. While allowing your knees to bend mildly and keeping your back flat, sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and incline your torso as close to horizontal as your flexibility permits.
    1. To avoid rounding your lower back, you should think about sitting back rather than bending over.
    2. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    3. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain mostly vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    4. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically lower the bar at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your lower back or excessively pushing your knees forward depends on your flexibility.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the bar up toward your chest by driving your elbows upward and pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. Keep your torso fixed in a hinged position as you maintain the same angle of bend in your hips and knees throughout your set while keeping your core braced and your lower back flat.
    2. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your lower body should remain essentially stationary.
    3. While you do not need to touch your chest with the bar, you should finish with the bar close to reaching it, in contrast to a typical row, where you pull the bar lower down toward your abdomen.
    4. When viewed from behind, your upper arms and torso form close to a “T-shape” at the top of the row with flared elbows, in contrast to a standard row with a narrower grip that finishes with the elbows tucked closer to the sides.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering the bar in a controlled manner. Let your elbows move downward and your shoulder blades move apart from each other until you have returned to the starting position with straight elbows.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar down onto the floor by bending your knees further.
## Description
This row effectively develops your [rear delts](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md) while also training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md), and three [rotator cuff](../Muscles/Rotator%20Cuff%201b95c6f170d880b3b0d8eab69c3a7683.md) muscles.

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright in a near hip-width stance while holding the kettlebells at your sides with your palms facing in toward your thighs.
2. Slightly bend your elbows and slightly lean forward at your hips.
    1. While you do not need to have an exaggerated “proud chest” posture with your shoulders fully pulled back, avoid standing with your shoulders rolled forward into a slouched upper back position.
## Exercise technique
1. Sweep your arms out and away from your sides until they are approximately parallel to the ground.
    1. While you raise your arms through shoulder motion and allow your shoulder blades to move naturally, keep the rest of your body stationary as you maintain a slight elbow bend and slight forward lean throughout your set.
    2. Let the handles rotate in your hands to keep the base of each kettlebell facing the ground.
    3. At the top of the raise, your palms should be directed down toward the ground with mostly straight wrists.
2. Reverse the movement by lowering your arms in toward your sides in a controlled arcing manner until the kettlebells are directly next to your legs.
    1. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the weights abruptly yank your arms downward.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md) and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md) while also training your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) and [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md).

## Setting up
1. Pick up a pair of kettlebells and stand upright in a near hip-width stance while holding the kettlebells at your sides.
2. While letting your knees naturally bend and keeping your back flat, sit your buttocks back to hinge at your hips and incline your torso as close to horizontal as your flexibility permits.
    1. As a cue for hinging at your hips, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something. Focusing on “sitting back” rather than “bending over” can help you avoid rounding your lower back
    2. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain mostly vertical, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriate degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
3. As your arms hang down toward the ground with the kettlebells vertically under your shoulders, point your palms in toward each other if they are not already facing this direction.
## Exercise technique
1. While letting your elbows bend slightly, sweep your arms out and away from your sides in a wide, arcing motion until your elbows are near shoulder height.
    1. Statically maintain your hinged torso position throughout the set as you avoid moving your lower body or lower back.
    2. The appropriately slight degree of elbow bend can naturally occur if you do not actively try to keep them fully locked. If you feel like you need to bend your elbows to a greater degree to lift the kettlebells up in a row-like motion, you likely selected a weight that is excessively heavy for this variation.
    3. As you move your arms outward and upward, avoid pulling them back toward your hips.
    4. Let the handles rotate in your hands to keep the base of each kettlebell facing the ground.
    5. At the top of the raise, your palms should be directed down toward the ground with mostly straight wrists.
2. In a controlled arcing manner, reverse the motion by moving your arms downward and in toward each other until they are hanging down toward the ground.
    1. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting the weights abruptly swing your arms downward. The weights should not bang against each other in the bottom position.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the kettlebells down.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), which is assisted by your [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md) and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), along with your rotator cuff’s [infraspinatus](../Muscles/Infraspinatus%201905c6f170d88026aebcf3953e2e440f.md), [teres minor](../Muscles/Teres%20Minor%201905c6f170d88098824dc8136557c410.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. While placing one hand on each of a kettlebell’s horns (i.e, the side handles) with your palms facing in toward each other, pick up the kettlebell and stand upright in a near hip-width stance. Hold the kettlebell in front of your thighs with straight elbows.
    1. It may be awkward to use this grip to pick up a kettlebell directly from the floor (especially if you are using a heavier weight), so you have the option of initially deadlifting the kettlebell with a double overhand grip from the top handle and setting it on an elevated surface like a bench before grasping its horns with your palms facing in.
    2. Due to the shape of the kettlebell, it is not feasible to have the top handle pointing straight upward (like it would when the bottom base of the kettlebell is resting on the ground) while your elbows are straight, so you will have to angle the kettlebell’s base toward you.
    3. To hold the kettlebell in front of your thighs with straight elbows, you will need to move your upper arms slightly in front of your torso.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core throughout the set.
2. While keeping your elbows straight, sweep your arms forward and upward in an arcing manner to lift the kettlebell to approximately shoulder height.
    1. Allow your shoulder blades to move naturally rather than trying to keep them in any particular position.
    2. All the movement should occur from shoulder motion while you keep your legs and torso stationary throughout the exercise.
    3. At the top, your arms should be outstretched straight in front of you, parallel to the ground.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the kettlebell in a controlled manner until it is directly in front of your legs.
    1. You should finish in the starting position with your arms pointing down toward the ground.
    2. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, avoid letting gravity abruptly swing the weight downward.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md) while also training your [upper pec major](../Muscles/Pectoralis%20Major%20(Clavicular%20Head%201905c6f170d880ef9b6bd48adbf440bd.md), [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md).

## Setting up
1. With your palms facing back toward you (i.e., an overhand grip), firmly grasp the handle of one kettlebell with both hands and stand upright in approximately a hip-width stance. Hold the kettlebell just in front of you with straight elbows.
    1. Pick up the kettlebell with a deadlift motion, where you lift it by extending (straightening) your hips and knees while keeping your back flat.
    2. For the most stable grip, firmly wrap your fingers around the handle with the handle pressed into where the bases of your fingers meet the palm side of your knuckles.
    3. Your neck should be near a neutral position, as when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead. Maintain this neck position throughout your set.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. For additional stability, you can initially take a deep “belly breath” (AKA diaphragmatic breath) that expands the front and sides of your abdominals outward. Avoid taking a “chest breath” that predominantly lifts your chest upward and leaves your abdominals relaxed or simply sucking your belly button inward.
    2. Bracing your core will help you maintain a rigid torso position as you subsequently move about your hips rather than your back.
2. While allowing your knees to bend mildly, sit your buttocks backward to hinge at your hips in a controlled manner as you keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    1. Most of the motion should come from your hips, and your shins should remain vertical throughout your set, but do not keep your knees fully straight. You do not need to focus on bending your knees, since the appropriately mild degree of knee bend can naturally occur when you sit your buttocks backward without intentionally keeping your knees locked.
    2. Without thinking about “bending over,” your torso will transition to an angle that is closer to horizontal as you lower the kettlebell when focusing on “sitting back.”
    3. As a cue, you can think about closing a car door with your buttocks while your hands are carrying something.
    4. Keep the kettlebell just in front of your legs and your feet fully planted on the ground throughout the set.
3. Continue hinging at your hips through the full range of motion in which you can comfortably move without rounding your back or excessively bending your knees.
    1. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch and can no longer sit back any farther, you have reached your personal end range. Descending past this point would require you to begin rounding your back or bending your knees in a squat-like manner.
    2. Lifters with normal flexibility can typically hinge until their hands are at least below their knees, but how deeply you can hinge without rounding your back or excessively bending your knees depends on your hamstring flexibility.
    3. If you have the flexibility to hinge until the kettlebell contacts the ground, descend until you can tap the weight very lightly on the ground, but do not let the weight rest on the ground.
    4. While you do not need to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, you should clearly be in control of the entire descent.
4. Reverse the movement by thrusting your hips forward to lift your torso upright into the starting position.
    1. The lifting phase should simply be a reversal of what you just performed, so keep your lower back flat, chest up, and core braced.
    2. When you have finished lifting the kettlebell, you should be able to draw a straight line from your shoulders through your hips to the middle of your feet when viewed from the side.
    3. Avoid leaning back at the top through excessive lower back arching that would pull your shoulders a little behind your hips. Squeezing your glutes at the end of the lifting phase can help you finish with your hips properly stacked under your shoulders, preventing excessive arching.
5. Alternate between steps 2-4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the kettlebell down.
    1. You will be able to brace most effectively when you breathe in between reps while in the fully upright position rather than during a rep. After taking a breath, make sure to resume bracing your core prior to initiating the descent for the next rep.
    2. After finishing the last rep, set the kettlebell down in a deadlift motion by bending your hips and knees while keeping your back flat.
## Description
While statically training your [erector spinae](../Muscles/Thoracolumbar%20Erector%20Spinae%201bb5c6f170d880a7a719e8f6d05d00a8.md), this exercise can effectively develop your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md), and [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md).

## Setting up
1. Select your desired load at each weight stack with the machine’s loading pins, and adjust the seat to a height that lets you rest your chest comfortably against the chest pad once you are seated.
    1. It is generally appropriate to situate the seat where your upper chest can be positioned slightly above the top of the chest pad, while your middle and lower chest contact the pad once you are seated.
    2. The proper seat height should let the exercise feel smooth and natural, so if you think your arm path feels somewhat awkward during the set, it is recommended to adjust the seat height. When using this machine for the first time, trying out different seat heights may be helpful to determine specifically which setting helps the row feel best to you based on your body proportions.
2. Adjust the thigh pad to a height that lets you position your thighs snugly against it while sitting with your feet flat on the floor.
3. While facing the chest pad and standing above the seat, firmly grasp the handles with an underhand grip that points your palms facing backward.
4. Sit down on the seat with the lower portion of your thighs snugly pressed against the machine’s thigh pad. Simultaneously let your elbows straighten as your arms raise overhead in line with the machine’s resistance.
    1. If you do not feel tension from the machine in this position (which may occur for certain individuals who are quite tall and have long arms), you may need to lower the height of the seat and thigh pad to experience resistance throughout the full range of motion for this exercise.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull your shoulder blades down away from your ears. Simultaneously drive your elbows down and back in an arcing manner to pull the handles toward you.
    1. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows finishing slightly behind your torso.
    2. When focusing on driving your elbows down and back, they should naturally bend to the appropriate degree.
    3. Keep your torso upright against the chest pad throughout your set rather than leaning backward during the pull.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your elbows to lift upward and away from your torso as they progressively straighten to raise the handles in a controlled manner.
    1. Let your shoulder blades move naturally as they elevate with your arms.
    2. Finish with your elbows fully straightened.
    3. There is no need to perform this step extremely slowly, but you should avoid letting the machine’s resistance yank your arms up in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), and [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md) while also meaningfully training your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).

## Setting up
1. Face the middle of an EZ bar loaded with your desired weight, whether that be a fixed-weight EZ bar or an adjustable plate-loaded EZ bar
2. With a slightly outside shoulder-width overhand grip, firmly grasp the bar at a point where the grips angle downward as they move out to the sides of the bar.
    1. This angled grip should result in your hands being mildly tilted toward the thumb-side of your forearms.
    2. With the zig-zag-like shape of the EZ bar, you may have to rotate it before this grip is accessible on the bar.
    3. A slightly outside shoulder-width grip works well for many lifters, but feel free to try out somewhat different grip widths to determine if any particular hand positions feel best to you as an individual.
3. Stand upright with the bar, and hold it just in front of your legs with straight elbows.
## Exercise technique
1. Lift the bar upward by driving your elbows upward and out to your sides through a range of motion that feels comfortable to your shoulders while bending your elbows.
    1. Your mobility will affect how high you are comfortably able to lift the bar, and there is no need to force your shoulders into a range that provokes any discomfort.
    2. While different individuals may be able to lift higher up and others not quite as high, people often can lift their upper arms until their elbows are near shoulder height for a comfortable and effective range of motion.
    3. The bar should remain close to your torso throughout the exercise as it moves vertically.
2. Reverse the motion by allowing your elbows to descend in toward your sides as you lower the bar in a controlled manner until you have returned to the starting position with straight elbows.
    1. There is no need to lower the bar with an extremely slow tempo, but you should actively control the descent rather than letting the weight abruptly pull your arms down.
    2. At the end of the lowering phase, the bar should be situated in front of your thighs.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop your [lateral delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Lateral%20Head%201905c6f170d8804b9b6ef12253eec774.md), [upper trap](../Muscles/Upper%20Trapezius%201925c6f170d880009e2cf04b5b29b467.md), and [supraspinatus](../Muscles/Supraspinatus%201905c6f170d880efb440c1614caf1c97.md), which are assisted by your [front delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Anterior%20Head%201905c6f170d8805da59fc8f9dc0a59e4.md).

## Setting up
1. Add weight plates to the machine and adjust the seat to a height that allows your chest to rest comfortably against the chest pad.
    1. It is generally appropriate to situate the seat where your upper chest can be positioned slightly above the top of the chest pad, while your middle and lower chest contact the pad once you are seated.
    2. The proper seat height should let the exercise feel smooth and natural, so if you think your arm path feels somewhat awkward during the row, it is recommended to adjust the seat height. When using this machine for the first time, trying out different seat heights may be helpful to determine specifically which setting helps the row feel best to you based on your body proportions and the machine model you are using.
    3. To row through your full range of motion, ideally place the chest pad far enough back that you have to push your shoulder blades forward and apart to grasp the handles with your elbows fully straight.
2. If your machine has an adjustable chest pad, set it to a position that lets you grasp the handles with straight elbows only when your shoulders are fully rounded forward.
    1. Setting the chest further forward (toward the base of the machine) than this point can limit the row’s range of motion.
3. Sit down with your chest resting snugly against the chest pad and your feet resting on the foot bar or the floor.
4. Reach fully forward and firmly grasp the handles with straight elbows and your palms angled upward.
    1. It may be easiest to grasp the handles one at a time.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handles back toward the sides of your torso by driving your elbows backward while simultaneously pulling your shoulder blades together.
    1. Move your elbows through a path that feels comfortable to you, which will typically involve keeping them tucked fairly close to your sides with this machine rather than notably flaring your elbows away from your sides.
    2. Keep your chest in contact with the chest pad throughout the set.
    3. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows being slightly behind your torso at the end of the lifting phase.
    4. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to move forward in a controlled manner, progressively straightening until they are outstretched in front of you.
    1. Your shoulder blades will naturally move apart from one another, but you can exaggerate this motion by intentionally allowing the weight to pull them further apart than your resting position at the end. This will stretch your upper back muscles and may help you train them more effectively.
    2. While you do not have to perform this step extremely slowly, you should avoid letting the weight abruptly yank your arms forward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.
## Description
This row primarily trains your [lat](../Muscles/Latissimus%20Dorsi%201905c6f170d880109e73f99ab91d4d47.md), [teres major](../Muscles/Teres%20Major%201905c6f170d880dbba32f6bd22e3abe6.md), [rear delt](../Muscles/Deltoid%20Posterior%20Head%201905c6f170d880a29e5ec26f4d257c01.md), [traps](../Muscles/Trapezius%201b95c6f170d880bebf89c759b592e81f.md), and [rhomboids](../Muscles/Rhomboids%201b95c6f170d880c8a84de94f5232a509.md), which are assisted by your [biceps](../Muscles/Biceps%20Brachii%201b95c6f170d88027b895ed4c0bb40b68.md), [brachialis](../Muscles/Brachialis%2018f5c6f170d880c181eed18b5b379fe9.md), and [brachioradialis](../Muscles/Brachioradialis%201905c6f170d8808f8207e301c4acd3b3.md).
