## Setting up
1. Select your weight with the loading pin(s), and sit down facing the dual cable row machine with a D-handle connected to each cable.
    1. Some machines will have a single weight stack that provides resistance to each cable, while others will have one weight stack for each cable.
2. Position your feet in contact with the machine’s foot plates.
    1. Allow your knees to bend to an angle that allows you to feel stable and comfortable, which can be a mild to moderately mild knee bend for many people.
    2. With greater knee bend, you will be able to sit closer toward the cables, so you can bend your knees further if you initially cannot reach the handles when leaning forward by bending at your hips.
3. Lean forward at your hips until you are able to grasp the handles firmly with straight elbows.
4. Lean your torso backward at your hips until you are sitting with an upright torso as your arms are aligned with the cables and your palms are angled in toward each other.
    1. When seated upright with straight elbows, you should feel tension from the cables, so if the cables are still slack, you can scoot yourself backward by extending your knees until you feel the resistance.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handles back toward the sides of your torso by driving your elbows backward while pulling your shoulder blades together into a “proud chest” posture.
    1. Keep your elbows tucked close to your sides, rather than flaring them out away from your sides.
    2. Keep your forearms aligned with the cables, which naturally promotes the appropriate degree of elbow bend. This will let you draw a straight line from your elbows through your wrists to the cables’ pulleys.
    3. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your knees, hips, and lower back should remain nearly stationary in a stable position throughout the set as you keep your torso upright.
    4. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows finishing slightly behind your torso.
    5. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to move forward in a controlled manner as they progressively straighten to move the handles forward.
    1. Finish with your arms fully outstretched in front of you.
    2. ## Setting up
1. Select your weight with the loading pin(s), and sit down facing the dual cable row machine with a D-handle connected to each cable.
    1. Some machines will have a single weight stack that provides resistance to each cable, while others will have one weight stack for each cable.
2. Position your feet in contact with the machine’s foot plates.
    1. Allow your knees to bend to an angle that allows you to feel stable and comfortable, which can be a mild to moderately mild knee bend for many people.
    2. With greater knee bend, you will be able to sit closer toward the cables, so you can bend your knees further if you initially cannot reach the handles when leaning forward by bending at your hips.
3. Lean forward at your hips until you are able to grasp the handles firmly with straight elbows.
4. Lean your torso backward at your hips until you are sitting with an upright torso as your arms are aligned with the cables and your palms are angled down.
    1. When seated upright with straight elbows, you should feel tension from the cables, so if the cables are still slack, you can scoot yourself backward by extending your knees until you feel the resistance.
## Exercise technique
1. Pull the handles back toward you by driving your elbows backward and out away from your sides while pulling your shoulder blades together into a “proud chest” posture.
    1. Aim to flare your elbows about 45 degrees away from your sides as you move them equally backward and out to the side. Zero degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows purely backward and keeping them completely tucked by your sides, while 90 degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbows straight out to the sides, which would result in your upper arms and torso forming a “T-shape” at the top.
    2. Keep your forearms aligned with the cables, which naturally promotes the appropriate degree of elbow bend. This will let you draw a straight line from your elbows through your wrists to the cables’ pulleys.
    3. Movement should occur at your shoulders, shoulder blades, and elbows, but your knees, hips, and lower back should remain nearly stationary in a stable position throughout the set as you keep your torso upright.
    4. Pull through your full range of motion, which will typically result in your elbows finishing slightly behind your torso.
    5. As a cue for training your upper back muscles, you can think about squeezing your shoulder blades together at the end of the pull as if you were trying to pinch a pencil with your shoulder blades.
2. Reverse the movement by allowing your elbows to move forward in a controlled manner as they progressively straighten to move the handles forward.
    1. Finish with your arms fully outstretched in front of you.
    2. Your shoulder blades will naturally move apart, but you can exaggerate this motion by intentionally allowing the weight to pull them further apart than your resting position at the end, without rounding your lower back. This will stretch your upper back muscles and may help you to train them more effectively.
    3. While you do not have to perform this step extremely slowly, you should avoid letting the weight abruptly yank your arms forward in an uncontrolled fashion.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set.

## Setting up
1. Adjust the height of the machine’s thigh pad to a level that positions the tops of your hip bones somewhat above the top of the pad when you set up with your feet on the foot plate.
    1. This position will allow you to move freely about your hips in contrast to if the pad is contacting the top of your hip bones, which would restrict hip motion and prompt you to perform the exercise via spinal motion.
    2. If the top of the pad is positioned much lower than the top of the hip bones (rather than only somewhat lower), some individuals may feel knee discomfort, so a sweet spot can exist for pad placement.
    3. Some trial and error may be needed to find your ideal pad position after initially completing step 3.
2. Add weight plates of your desired load to the machine.
3. While placing your hands onto the thigh pad or handles for balance support, step onto the foot plate and position your lower calves snugly against the lower leg pads with your heels on the back of the foot plate.
    1. Position your feet symmetrically in a stance that feels comfortable to you, which can involve pointing your toes somewhat outward or pointing them fairly straight forward.
    2. Situating your feet approximately hip width to shoulder apart from each other will result in a viable stance width, but how wide of a stance you can use will be influenced by the width of your machine’s foot plate.
    3. To set your lower calves against the pads, your heels may hang off the edge of the foot plate, but the rest of your soles should be firmly planted on the foot plate.
    4. Your knees should be straight after you have finished setting your feet on the foot plate.
4. With your knees straightened, snugly rest your thighs against the thigh pad, let your arms hang down, and confirm that the tops of your hip bones are now somewhat above the top of the pad.
    1. If the pad is not positioned appropriately, readjust before getting into this starting position again.
## Exercise technique
1. Hinge at your hips to lower your torso until you are low enough to grasp the bar firmly with your elbows straight, palms facing backward, and hands about shoulder-width apart.
    1. Keep your lower back flat or slightly arched, rather than rounding your lower back to reach the bar.
    2. Throughout the exercise, keep your neck near a neutral position, like you have when you are normally standing upright and looking straight ahead.
    3. Maintain a straight knee position throughout your set, but avoid intentionally locking your knees out by squeezing your quads.
    4. Depending on your limb lengths and the height of your machine, you may have to round your upper back to reach the bar.
2. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set.
3. While keeping your back in a rigid position, lift your torso up through your hips until you can fully squeeze your glutes with your torso aligned with your legs.
    1. Throughout your set, aim to have all the movement occur from hip motion.
    2. At the top, you should essentially be able to draw a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders when viewed from the side, like you could do when standing upright.
    3. Avoid arching your lower back excessively at the top, which can occur if you try to lift up as high as you physically can, rather than finishing once your glutes are fully squeezed and your torso is in alignment with your legs.
4. Reverse the movement to lower your torso by hinging at your hips through your full range of motion in a controlled manner without rounding your lower back.
    1. How deeply you are able to hinge without rounding your lower back will be dependent on your hamstring flexibility.
    2. Once you have achieved what feels like the end range to which your hamstrings can safely stretch, you have finished descending through your available hip range of motion.
    3. With sufficient flexibility, you may be able to lower the bar until the weight you selected lightly taps the rest of the weight stack, indicating you have moved the full range of motion in which the machine can provide resistance.
5. Alternate between steps 3 and 4 until you have completed your set and are ready to set the bar back down and dismount the machine.

## Setting up
You have the option of performing this exercise while standing on a step and keeping both knees straight or standing on the ground and mildly bending one knee to keep that side’s foot off the ground. You can use essentially the same technique to perform the exercise with either approach, but their setups differ. Correspondingly, each approach receives its own setup section, but they share the same exercise technique instructions.

### **Setting up on a step**

1. Position what you will use as you step (e.g., aerobic step, thick bumper plate, short plyometric box) or approach the bottom step of a staircase.
    1. If you are using a mobile step, you can position it next to something where you can place a hand for balance assistance while standing on the step if you wish to receive balance assistance. This may involve setting up next to a rack, wall, chair, or exercise bench positioned upright.
    2. A step height of a few inches (about 8-10cm) is sufficiently tall for most people performing this exercise, since it involves a low amplitude of motion. This means that an aerobic step without risers or a 45lb (20kg) bumper plate is normally sufficiently tall, but a taller step naturally can be used as well.
2. Pick up a dumbbell, kettlebell, or weight plate and hold it by the side of your body that you will not train during this set. Alternatively, strap an ankle weight around the ankle on the side of your body that you will not train during this set.
    1. When using a dumbbell, kettlebell, or weight plate, you will hold it with your arm straight by your side throughout the exercise.
3. Stand directly to the side of the step, and place your foot (that is opposite to the weight) fully onto the step while leaving your other foot on the ground. Situate your feet about hip-width apart, and point your toes straight ahead.
4. Optionally place your free hand against a nearby surface for balance assistance. Otherwise, keep your free hand in your preferred position throughout the exercise, such as resting on your hip or by your side.
5. Drive through your elevated leg and straighten your knee to step up until your feet are level, keeping your one foot hanging off the step.
6. On the side hovering off the step, pull your toes and the ball of your foot up toward your shin through an ankle motion that brings your heel closer to the ground than the ball of your foot.
    1. This is the opposite of the ankle motion that occurs when lifting your heels up during a calf raise, and you should feel the muscles on the front of your shin contract.
    2. The purpose of keeping your foot in this position is to make sure that your toes do not contact the ground during the exercise and restrict your range of motion. If your step is tall enough that your free foot would not touch the ground in any position during the exercise, you can ignore this step and let the ball of your foot hang down.

### **Setting up on the ground**

1. Pick up a dumbbell, kettlebell, or weight plate and hold it by the side of your body that you will not train during this set. Alternatively, strap an ankle weight around the ankle on the side of your body that you will not train during this set.
    1. When using a dumbbell, kettlebell, or weight plate, you will hold it with your arm straight by your side throughout the exercise.
2. In a hip-width stance, stand next to something where you can place a hand for balance assistance if you wish to receive balance assistance.
3. Optionally place your free hand against a nearby surface for balance assistance. Otherwise, keep your free hand in your preferred position throughout the exercise, such as resting on your hip or by your side.
4. Bend one knee enough to lift that side’s foot off the ground, and keep that knee bent with your foot off the ground throughout the exercise.
    1. You will be training your hip muscles on the side of your body on which you keep your foot on the ground.
## Exercise technique
1. While keeping your torso upright and your stance leg straight, lower your free foot toward the ground by letting your hip bone (on the side of your free foot) tilt down in a controlled manner.
    1. Descend until you feel that your hip bones are fully tilted, which may prompt you to feel a mild stretching sensation in the side of your hip (of the hip bone whose leg remains on the step).
    2. As a cue, you can imagine that you have a basin of water on top of your hip bones, and you are trying to pour as much of the water as you can out to one side.
    3. There is no need to perform this step with an extremely slow tempo, but you should be using your hip muscles to control the descent actively, rather than just letting your hip bone abruptly drop.
2. Reverse the movement by hiking your hip up to lift your free foot up and tilt your hip bones in the opposite direction.
    1. Continue keeping your torso upright and your legs straight as you exclusively move at your hip.
    2. Strive to finish with your free leg’s hip bone higher up than your stance leg’s hip bone.
    3. When imagining that you have a basin of water on top of your hip bones, you can think about leveling the basin before trying to spill the water toward the side of your stance leg.
    4. With the appropriate technique, you should feel tension in the muscles on the side of your stance leg’s hip as they contract.
3. Alternate between steps 1 and 2 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat this exercise with your other side.
## Description
This exercise can effectively develop the musculature on the side of your hip, including your [gluteus medius](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Medius%201925c6f170d880f38e56e316eab6e33b.md), [gluteus minimus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Minimus%201925c6f170d880468a1ac852b36eeaf8.md), and [tensor fascia latae](../Muscles/Tensor%20Fascia%20Latae%201925c6f170d8806fb83bf08142d940fc.md).

## Setting up
You have the option of performing this exercise with an ankle weight or a dumbbell. You can use the same exercise technique with either form of resistance, but the setup details can differ depending on which type of weight you select. Correspondingly, each approach receives its own setup section, but they share the same exercise technique instructions.

### **Setting up with an ankle weight**

1. Strap an ankle weight around the ankle on the side of your body that you will train during this set.
2. Position yourself on your palms, knees, and toes, with your elbows straight and your knees bent by about 90 degrees.
    1. In this “on all fours” position, your upper arms and thighs should be directed straight down such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    2. Your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position with the natural curvature you have when normally standing upright, rather than being rounded or excessively arched.
    3. For comfort, you optionally can set up on an exercise mat.

### **Setting up with a dumbbell**

1. Set a dumbbell on the ground, and kneel next to it with the side of your body that you will train during this set closer to the dumbbell.
    1. For comfort, you optionally can set up on an exercise mat.
2. Place the dumbbell on the back of your knee crease with its handle resting between your upper calves and lower hamstrings.
    1. Keep the dumbbell in this position throughout the exercise.
    2. When you set up appropriately and use the correct technique for this exercise, the dumbbell should remain snugly in place.
3. Position yourself on your palms, knees, and toes, with your elbows straight and your knees bent by about 90 degrees.
    1. In this “on all fours” position, your upper arms and thighs should be directed straight down such that they are approximately perpendicular to the ground.
    2. Your lower back and neck should be near a neutral position with the natural curvature you have when normally standing upright, rather than being rounded or excessively arched.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing throughout your set.
2. While keeping one knee on the ground, drive your working side’s knee backward and upward in an arcing manner while keeping it bent by about 90 degrees. Move through your hip’s full range of motion until you can squeeze your glute at the top.
    1. Strive to maintain the natural curvature of your lower back as you avoid excessively arching or twisting it. Excessive lower back arching can occur if you try to kick your leg up as high as you possibly can, rather than finishing the movement once you have reached the end of your hip’s range of motion.
    2. Being able to squeeze your glute fully is a sign that you have reached an appropriate end range. You can optionally pause in this top position briefly and hold the full glute squeeze for a moment if you wish to do so.
    3. How high up you can lift your leg through hip motion will be affected by your individual hip mobility, but people can commonly reach the point at which the thigh is approximately parallel to the ground.
    4. While motion occurs at your hip, the rest of your body should remain stationary throughout the exercise.
3. Reverse the movement in a controlled manner by lowering your leg to the starting position, where your thighs are aligned with each other.
    1. There is no need to lower your leg with an extremely slow tempo, but you should actively control the descent, rather than letting your leg abruptly swing down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

This exercise will chiefly train your [gluteus maximus](../Muscles/Gluteus%20Maximus%201bb5c6f170d8805380e7c611cd051f9f.md), which may be assisted by your [piriformis,](../Muscles/Piriformis%201925c6f170d88068a670ce338a8215cf.md) [adductor magnus](../Muscles/Adductor%20Magnus%201b95c6f170d880518436f037bd6a822d.md), and [hamstrings](../Muscles/Biarticular%20Hamstrings%201bd5c6f170d8802cacc4e4bbc2a290cb.md) to a lesser degree.

## Setting up
1. Pick up one kettlebell, hold it by your side, and stand facing a sturdy object reasonably near knee-height, such as a flat exercise bench.
    1. If you are tall, the head of an incline bench set to a low incline may be better for you to brace your hand against during this exercise, compared to a lower flat bench.
    2. Viable alternatives to a bench can include a plyometric box, sturdy chair, kettlebell rack, racked Smith machine bar, or a barbell on a rack’s J-cups.
    3. The appropriate object should let you achieve a position that feels stable and comfortable with a flat back once you brace against it.
    4. While using an object reasonably near knee height can let you set up effectively and is most common, some lifters may prefer to use a higher object closer to hip height, which can let you keep the non-working arm higher during the exercise. Using a taller object may also be sensible for people with mobility limitations who cannot comfortably support themselves on a shorter object without rounding their backs.
    5. For brevity, the instructions will refer to the use of a bench from this point on.
2. While standing with the head of the bench in front of your free arm, situate your feet near shoulder-width apart.
    1. When aligning your free arm with one end of the bench, you should have space in front of your arm holding the kettlebell, so you will not have to worry about the bench getting in the way of the kettlebell after you have assumed the starting position for this row.
    2. A near shoulder-width stance is an appropriate starting point, but feel free to widen your stance a bit if that feels more stable to you.
3. Based on your preference, you can adopt a staggered stance by taking a step backward with the foot on the same side as the kettlebell, or you can keep your feet symmetrical.
    1. Either stance can be effectively used for this exercise, so you can try out a set or two with each option and continue with the position where you feel most stable.
4. Lean your torso forward by sitting your hips back while allowing your knees to bend mildly until you can brace your free hand against the bench with a straight elbow.
    1. Keep your lower back flat, and let your arm (that is holding the kettlebell) hang down toward the ground.
    2. When standing appropriately close to the bench, your non-working side’s arm should ideally be angled downward to a greater degree than forward, so that you are not reaching excessively far forward.
    3. Keep your hand braced against the bench throughout the exercise.
    4. All the subsequent directions apply to the arm holding the kettlebell.
5. Angle your palm diagonally backward and in toward the opposite side of your body.
    1. Rather than just rotating your palm as your elbow and upper arm remain still, rotate your whole arm through shoulder motion, resulting in the bony bump on the back of your elbow pointing diagonally outward and backward. This is the direction in which you will row.
    2. Throughout your set, maintain this grip, which is a hybrid between an overhand grip and a neutral grip.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Drive your elbow in an arcing motion backward, upward, and moderately out away from your side to row the kettlebell. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blade backward.
    1. Aim to flare your elbow about 45 degrees out away from your side as your elbow moves equal parts backward and out to the side. Zero degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbow purely backward and keeping it completely tucked by your side, while 90 degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbow straight out to the side, which would result in your upper arm and torso forming half of a “T-shape” at the top.
    2. When bending your elbow by the appropriate degree, your forearm should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    3. Row through your full range of motion, which should result in your elbow finishing slightly behind your torso or at least in alignment with your torso at the top of the rep.
    4. Strive to keep your lower body and torso in a fixed position with your chest facing a similar direction throughout this movement. A mild degree of torso rotation is not problematic, but avoid letting it become excessive and turning the exercise into a cheat row.
    5. While performing this arcing motion, the kettlebell should not move straight upward in a vertical path, which could occur if you bend your elbow excessively.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the kettlebell in a controlled arcing motion until your arm is directed down toward the ground with your elbow straightened.
    1. Allow the weight to pull your shoulder blade forward, which will stretch your upper back muscles and result in your working side’s shoulder being mildly closer to the ground than your other side’s shoulder at the bottom of the row.
    2. Move your elbow diagonally inward and forward at a near 45-degree angle while it descends to reverse the moderate elbow flare you just utilized during the lifting phase.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weight rapidly pull your arm down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.

## Setting up
1. Pick up one dumbbell, hold it by your side, and stand facing a sturdy object reasonably near knee-height, such as a flat exercise bench.
    1. If you are tall, the head of an incline bench set to a low incline may be better for you to brace your hand against during this exercise, compared to a lower flat bench.
    2. Viable alternatives to a bench can include a plyometric box, sturdy chair, dumbbell rack, racked Smith machine bar, or a barbell on a rack’s J-cups.
    3. The appropriate object should let you achieve a position that feels stable and comfortable with a flat back once you brace against it.
    4. While using an object reasonably near knee height can let you set up effectively and is most common, some lifters may prefer to use a higher object closer to hip height, which can let you keep the non-working arm higher during the exercise. Using a taller object may also be sensible for people with mobility limitations who cannot comfortably support themselves on a shorter object without rounding their backs.
    5. For brevity, the instructions will refer to the use of a bench from this point on.
2. While standing with the head of the bench in front of your free arm, situate your feet near shoulder-width apart.
    1. When aligning your free arm with one end of the bench, you should have space in front of your arm holding the dumbbell, so you will not have to worry about the bench getting in the way of the dumbbell after you have assumed the starting position for this row.
    2. A near shoulder-width stance is an appropriate starting point, but feel free to widen your stance a bit if that feels more stable to you.
3. Based on your preference, you can adopt a staggered stance by taking a step backward with the foot on the same side as the dumbbell, or you can keep your feet symmetrical.
    1. Either stance can be effectively used for this exercise, so you can try out a set or two with each option and continue with the position where you feel most stable.
4. Lean your torso forward by sitting your hips back while allowing your knees to bend mildly until you can brace your free hand against the bench with a straight elbow.
    1. Keep your lower back flat, and let your arm (that is holding the dumbbell) hang down toward the ground.
    2. When standing appropriately close to the bench, your non-working side’s arm should ideally be angled downward to a greater degree than forward, so that you are not reaching excessively far forward.
    3. Keep your hand braced against the bench throughout the exercise.
    4. All the subsequent directions apply to the arm holding the dumbbell.
5. Angle your palm diagonally backward and in toward the opposite side of your body.
    1. Rather than just rotating your palm as your elbow and upper arm remain still, rotate your whole arm through shoulder motion, resulting in the bony bump on the back of your elbow pointing diagonally outward and backward. This is the direction in which you will row.
    2. Throughout your set, maintain this grip, which is a hybrid between an overhand grip and a neutral grip.
## Exercise technique
1. Brace your core by tensing the front and sides of your abdominals outward, like you would if you were bracing for someone to strike your stomach with a punch or forcible slap.
    1. Continue bracing your core from this point onward.
2. Drive your elbow in an arcing motion backward, upward, and moderately out away from your side to row the dumbbell. Simultaneously pull your shoulder blade backward.
    1. Aim to flare your elbow about 45 degrees out away from your side as your elbow moves equal parts backward and out to the side. Zero degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbow purely backward and keeping it completely tucked by your side, while 90 degrees of flare would mean arcing your elbow straight out to the side, which would result in your upper arm and torso forming half of a “T-shape” at the top.
    2. When bending your elbow by the appropriate degree, your forearm should remain fairly close to being perpendicular to the ground throughout the row.
    3. Row through your full range of motion, which should result in your elbow finishing slightly behind your torso or at least in alignment with your torso at the top of the rep.
    4. Strive to keep your lower body and torso in a fixed position with your chest facing a similar direction throughout this movement. A mild degree of torso rotation is not problematic, but avoid letting it become excessive and turning the exercise into a cheat row.
    5. While performing this arcing motion, the dumbbell should not move straight upward in a vertical path, which could occur if you bend your elbow excessively.
3. Reverse the movement by lowering the dumbbell in a controlled arcing motion until your arm is directed down toward the ground with your elbow straightened.
    1. Allow the weight to pull your shoulder blade forward, which will stretch your upper back muscles and result in your working side’s shoulder being mildly closer to the ground than your other side’s shoulder at the bottom of the row.
    2. Move your elbow diagonally inward and forward at a near 45-degree angle while it descends to reverse the moderate elbow flare you just utilized during the lifting phase.
    3. You do not have to perform an extremely slow lowering phase, but you should actively control the entire descent rather than letting the weight rapidly pull your arm down.
4. Alternate between steps 2 and 3 until you have completed your set and are ready to repeat the exercise with your other side.
